units.la: DVAE sunt potissimùm causæ, Magnifici Domini, quæme-cur has meas in Augustinum commentationes vobis dedicarem, impulerunt : vestrorum erga me beneficiorum recordatio, atque vtilissimum ipsius libri argumentum. Nam quum anteactæ vitæ meæ rationem ineo, & mecum, sicuti par est, expendo, qua via Domino Patri misericordiarum placuerit me primùm ex illis horrendis idololatriæ tenebris ad salutarem Euangelij sui lucem traducere, plurimùm me vobis, ac quantùm neq; parentibus quidem ipsis debere ingenuè profiteor. Quanquam enim parentum in liberos beneficium est omnino ingens, & quantum à liberis nunquam satis pro dignitatē vel agnosci, vel rependi posse◡ fatendum est: longè tamen nos plura ijs debere◡, per quos veram pietatem didicimus, nemo sana mentis, opinor, negabit: per hos enim Christiani, per illos nihil amplius quàm homines sumus. Maxime vero, si quanta sit in Papismo (cui tanquam pecudes mancipati serviuimus) errorum lerna, cogitabimus, tanto nos beatiores, qui semel e tanto naufragio emersimus, feliciores(que)◡ iudicemus necesse est, eoque◡ pluris eos faciamus, per quos a Domino sumus tantum beneficium consequuti. Itaque◡ quum anno temporis vltimi M.D.LIX. Iurisconsul. ille◡ doctissimus, & Senator plane sanctissimus Anna Burgius, cui per quadriennium operam in Iure civili Aurelia dederam, effet propter puram Euangelij doctrinam Lutetia crematus, eo ipso igne◡ ad huius, quam tantum leuiter degustaram, doctrinae cognitionem assequendam acrius sum inflammatus, adeo vt me◡ totum in eorum, qui & verè & sincere illam profitebantur, scholam & disciplinam tradere◡ postea cogitarim. Nec enim temerè vel leuibus argumentis eam à tanto viro, quem toties vniversa Gallia docentem esset admirata, defendi posse statuebam. Sic factum est, vt anno sequenti, qui fuit M.D.LX. in hanc vestram Academiam, non tanquam nostra Galliæ vicinam ( erant enim & aliæ) sed tanquam ad limpidissimū cœlestis illius doctrinæ fontem, summa animi alacritate meipsum conferrem. Eò vero quū venissem, quales, quantosque viros, præceptores habuerim, non dico. Satis enim in omnium hominum ore versantur eorum partim iam defunctorum, partim adhuc viuentium laudes. Hoc tamen libere, & citra piorum omnium inuidiam dixero, mihi tot mundi lumina, & præstantissimos, celeberrimosque in omni artium genere viros tunc illuxisse, vt vna hæc ciuitas totius humanæ literaturæ ditissimum quoddam emporium videretur. Imprimis autem in ea, quam maximè tunc quærebam, Euangelicæ doctrinæ scientia, in-signem illum Dei seruum & pastorem vestrum Ioannem Caluinum ita sum admiratus, & ita me tunc Dominus per illius tum conciones tum etiam prælectiones suauitate quadam ipsius doctrinæ pellexit, vt abdicato prorsus Iuris ciuilis studio, quod ad eum diem sequutus eram, totum me sacræ Theologiæ devouerem. Me[?] vero, quemadmodum & plerosque alios, tunc quoque plurimum rapiebat, & afficiebat ipsa vita morumque ciuitatis huius publica sanctitas, quæ tanquam splendor quidam in omni hominum ordine effulgebat, adeo ut in ea ciuitate, in qua tam iusta rerum omnium administratio regna-ret, esse & degere nunquam non postea de-siderarim. Sed id neque valetudo mea tunc fieri passa est: neque importuna eorum pre-ces, qui verbi Dei ministros efflagitabant, quietem mihi concesserunt. Itaque ex Pasto-rum huius vrbis consilio, ad suscipiendum di-uinum ministerium in patriam sum remis-sus, vbi quum tuta quietaque speraremus o-mnia, ecce summa rerum perturbatio, atque inexpectata Ecclesiarum ruina accidit, & re-centes isti furores Gallici, qui hodie nemini non auditi sunt, pios plerosque, quibus peper-cit gladius, in exilium expulerunt. Sed in hac ipsa communi patria calamitate & fuga mea, nouum quoque a vobis in me beneficium ac-cessit. Praeterquam enim quod hic, quae ve-stra est in Christianos omnes humanitas, benigne sum exceptus: sum etiam Ecclesia suffragijs in Pastorum collegium cooptatus, ciuitatem hanc patria ipsa longe humania-rem expertus. Et certe haec mea conditio eo mihi iucundior est, addo etiam magis salu-taris, quod eos doctores & collegas habeam, quorum domesticis exemplis, & excellenti eruditione, magna tum pietatis, tum do-ctrina[?] Trinæ[?] fidei incrementa in me⁓ fieri quotidie⁓ possunt. Atque utinam tantum mihi roboris & animi largiatur Dominus, vt corum exemplum imitatus, in hoc sacrosanćto munere⁓ ad ipsius gloriam, atque⁓ huius ædificationem Ecclesiæ verser, eam diligentiam afferam, vt neque Ecclesiam ipsam mihi tantum onus ( cui me sane prorsus imparè sentio) demandasse: neque meipsum illud in me⁓ recepisse pæniteat. Quum igitur tot & tanta vestra in me⁓ beneficia extent, quis memorem & gratum esse me debere⁓ non fatebitur? Sed altera quoque huius libri vobis nuncupandi ratio, & priore⁓ quidem non minus iusta accedit, quod ex huius libri argumento, quanta Deus in vos ipsos beneficia contulerit, & quot quantisque⁓ malis vos eripuerit, dum & Papismo, & variis erroribus liberat, animadvertetis. Quanquam enim ea est divina & Euangelicæ veritatis vis, vt hominibus ad eam attendentibus, omnes errorum nebulas, & turpissima hæresĕon mendacia luce sua discutiat, singulare tamen, & quodammodo peculiare videri potest hoc Dei erga vos munus, quod mira felicitate⁓ & celeritate illud infelix lolium, quod bono verbi Dei feminini Satan admiscere⁓ solet, penitus ex vestra ciuitate[?] extirpastis. Magna quidem Pastorum vestrorum, in primis autem magni illius Caluini vigilantia id factum esse, nemo quantumuis inuidus diffiteri potest: sed tamen in eo non parua certè laus vestra est, quod sanis Pastorum vestrorum consiliis paruistis, neque aduersariorum iudicia veriti, neque potentissimorum regum inuidiam & minas pertimescentes. Itaque in ea, quam nobis Dominus verbo suo patefecit, veritatē purissima constanter & intrepidè permansi-stis. Neque non tamen in vestra hac ciuitate Satā sua flabella, & pessimorum errorum dis-seminatores habuit, sed summo Dei benefi-cio nunquā isti quicquam inter vos obtinere & efficere potuerunt. Vicit enim veritas, & statim extincta sunt ea veneni semina, quæ pater ille mendacij serere inter vos conaba-tur. Quod sigillatim etiam commemorare me non pigebit. Nam cùm anno Domini M.D. XXXV. salutarē illud Euangelij lumen tota ciuitas vestra diuino potius miraculo, quàm humana vlla industria lubenter am-plexa esset, quàm variè vos teterrimus ille humani generis hostis per suos emissarios sit aggressus, satis constat. Neque vero de iis tantùm loquor, qui vos à iam recepta cælesti doctrina, callido quodam artificio & blandis verborum verborum lenociniis abducere tentarunt, quales astuti & ab ipso Romano Antichristo redempti homines P. Caroli, & Iacob. Sadoletus extiterunt. Non eos etiam solum intelligo, qui aperta vi & nefaria seditione Evangelium ipsum, cui introducendo gnauiter operam nauasse prius videbantur, procul abigere atque adeo prorsus profligare postea voluerunt. Eos potius hic commemoro, qui ipsius Christiana religionis retinenda, fovenda, illustrandaq; falso quidem, sed tamen plausibili praetextu foedissimarum haeresion sordes in eam, quam iam purissimam susceperatis, fidei doctrinam inuehere moliebantur, à quibus omnibus vos mira felicitate, incredibilique bonitate sua Dominus liberauit. Nec enim potestis non meminisse, aut unquam vos posterique vestri obliuisci possunt, quemadmodum post receptum purum illud Dei verbum (quo certe tempore desiistis. Post tenebras sperare lucem, sed lucem illam caelestem & optatissimam vidistis) anno Domini M. D. XXXVI[?] per Anabaptistas genus hominum obstinatissimum, & primum fere in omnibus reformatis Ecclesiis bono semini adnascens lolium, Satanas vos oppugnarit. Verum hi post disputationem de eorum doctrina publice habitam erroris damnati, pulsíque urbe nunquam postea in hac ciuitate nidulari, aut vestram Ecclesiam tentare sunt ausi. Successit deinde annus Domini M. D. XLI. quo demum iustam aliquam Ecclesiasticae disciplinae formam delineastis, quae aliquot post annis perfectior atque auctior facta, magno tandem omnium huius ciuitatis ordinum con-sensu comprobata est. Hoc eodem anno per Sebastianum illum Castellionem fictae pieta-tis hominem Satan vos fidemque vestram impellere, & leui primum, ut videbatur, ictu, sed periculosissimo quatere voluit: quo tamen malo & occulto veneno ciuitas vestra anno XLV, homine ipso tanquam spuma expulso purgata est. Secutus est annus M.D.L. (nec enim diutius Satan quiescere potuit) quo e mediis ciuibus ipsis extitit Gruetus quidam portentosae impietatis monstrum, utpote qui Samosatenissimum cum Manicheismo in eandem erroris farraginem conflauerat, qui, nisi maturè Dominus occurrisset, eo fauore, quo apud suos populares com-mendabatur, plurimos labefactare potuit. Sed ipso authore a vobis iusta eaque capitali poena sublato, illa quoque periit impietas. Quid igitur? Saepe toties depulsus Satan tamen alia vos est aggressus via. Anno siquidem siquidem M. D. LI. Hieronymum Bolsecum è cellis & pædore Monachorum excitavit, qui verissimam de Sanctorum Prædestinatione doctrinam, id est, certissimum salutis nostræ fundamentum evertere, & aperto Pelagianismo commutare conaretur. Sed erroris convictus urbe primum à vobis, deinde tota etiam vicina ditione extrusus est. Atque hic uti reliquo vitæ tempore incertis sedibus vagatur, ita certam animo religionem nullam tenet. Jam vero toties deiectus veritatis hostis præcipuum è suis ducibus & antesignanis tandem produxit. Anno enim M. D. LIII. ad vos horrendum illud & ex omni errorum colluvie conflatum monstrum Servetus venit: vel, ut ego potius sentio, Dominus ad justam nominis sui (quod impurus ille toties & ore & scriptis blasphemaverat) ultionem Servetum ad vos dignum de ipso supplicium sumpturos adduxit, cuius vel solo halitu Satan nocentissimum erroris venenum (per quod Domino nostro Jesu Christo sua veraque Deitas adimitur, id est, fidei nostræ basis convellitur) ita quibusdam afflavit, ut ne gravi quidem istius supplicio illi territi postea silerent, aut saniores essent. Nam anno M. D. LVIII. extiterunt Serveti discipuli impudentissimi, totius generis humani pestes, qui Tritheitarum errorem cum Samosatenismo & Arianismo. i. monstra monstris cumularunt. Hi autem fuerunt Valentinus Gentilis, Georgius Blandrata & Paulus Alciatus nebulones & impostores maximi. Inter quos Valentinus deprehen-sus & blasphemia sua conuictus hic palino-diam cecinit, errorémque ciurauit, sed tan-dem cum insania sua sociis non magis vrbis huius aërem, quàm noxij serpentes suauem balsami odoré ferre potuit. Itaque hi omnes se vestra vrbe clàm proripuerunt, atque etiā Valentinus ipse contra iusiurandum à sepu-blicè datum, quò venena sua liberè exspue-rent, quæ hic inter vos omnino & supprimi & perire oportere cernebant. Ergo cùm vos tot tantisque hæreseòn malis magna sua mi-sericordia tàm facile Dominus liberarit, vt ne exigua quidem earum semina nunc ex-tent, quantas vos Deo Optimo Maximo pro tanto ipsius beneficio gratias agere : quanta diligentia in posterum cauere oportet, ne qua Christiana doctrina labes inter vos oriā-tur & sobolescat? Quanquam vero hæc cura ad nos Pastores vestros maximè pertinere videtur, vestrum tamen est eadem animi constantia, qua prius, pergere : & vestram illam authoritatem artibus Satanæ hæretico-rúmque rumque conatibus fortiter opponere: hominum aduersariorum iudicia non reformidare, imo ne totius quidem mundi vim aut minas timere. In Deum ipsum potius, Viri fortissimi intuemini, & ipsum sperate, quem iam toties protectorem vestrum experti estis, contra omnium hostium vestrorum furores & conspirationes defensorem futurum. Quin potius illam ipsam sanctam morum regulam & disciplinam, ne quadam, ut fit, humana natura ad peius ruentis conditione & animorum remissione labascat, illam ipsam inquam, Viri Christiani, perficite & in quamoptimo statu collocate, ne tacita forte consuetudine mali paulatim mores obrepant, & ad publica nequitiam audacia nō tantum inter vos inuehatur, sed etiā crescat. Verum enim illud est, Proclive hominis ingenium ad libidinem, & qui primis tatæ[?] ruinæ initiis mature non occurrunt, quodammodo ad maiores lapsus & errores viam sternere & concedere videntur. Hoc ne fiat, vestrum est nobiscum prospicere: nec hominum sanctam illam vitæ institutionem graue & durum iugum appellantium querimonias audire: Hoc vestra atque etiam paterna virtute dignum est. Hoc Deo gratum. Hoc animis vestris salutare. Hoc vestræ civitatis incolumitati (quam totam ex uno Deo pendere agnoscitis) omnino & utile & necessarium est. Ad quod ego quāto maximo possum animi affectu vos adhortor, Deumque ipsum per unigenitum Filium suum ut vobis eam mentem semper tribuat, ardentissimis precibus obsecro. Caeterum hic Augustini libellus, quaeq; [?]sunt a nobis addita, a quot quantisque erroribus sit vobis cauendum demonstrant. Continent enim omnes penè haereses, quae a condito mundo, certè a passio pro salute generis humani Domino nostro Iesu Christo usque ad constitutum tum Papismum, tum etiam Mahumetismum (quae utraque est Apostasia a fide Christi universalis) in Ecclesia Dei natae sunt & grassatae. Alias enim, quae haereses vocantur, quaeq; post illa tempora dicuntur extitisse, tum quod partim haereses non fuerunt: tum etiam quod si quae fuerint, earum tantum, quas hic commemorauimus, interpolationes & renouationes quaedam esse apparent, omisimus, quia crambe praesertim tam virulenta, vel semel apposita nedum repetita, mors est. Accertè qui post stabilitum Papismum pro haereticis magna veritatis Euangelicae ignoratione traducti sunt, quales qui VVicleuenses, Hussitae, Picardi, Begardi, Lollardi, VValdenses, Albicenses, Pauperes de Lugduno dicuntur, hi,imprimis autem VValdenses,quorum celebres & religiosæ vigent Ecclesiæ, rectè de Christianæ fidei articulis senserunt: & pro veris Christianis sunt habendi. Sed quia à Papismi,id est,vniuersalis & fœdæ illius Apostasiæ doctrina discesserat[?], ab apostatis ipsis, id est Papistis, vt hæretici damnabantur: à nobis autem & Christiani & Dei Martyres sunt nominandi:nedum vt eos inter hæreticos recensemus. Quæ vero dogmata ab Anabaptistis, Syluanistis, Serue-tanis, Nea-rianis & aliis fœdè regeruntur,illa sunt rancida tantum veterum hæreseon repotia, quæ iam millies refutata legimus. Quamobrem in constituto iam Antichristi regno substitimus à mundo condito ad annum, qui à Christo non nato, sed passo numerandus erit, 675, progressi,quo iam tempore aperte in Dei Ecclesia, vt numen,sedebat Filius ille perditionis,quem appellat Paulus.Ioannis autem Funccij chronologiam maximè in hoc opere secuti sumus.Hæc autem anno à nato Christo & temporis vltimi M.D.LXXVI. scribebamus cum Geneuæ Cal.Ianuarii, Syndici sine Cō-sules creati essent M.Rosetus,Iac.Blondetus, Cl.Domonouanus, & Steph.Mailletus: Vrbi autem esset Præfectus Amadeus Castelnonanus: Profesfores autem publici, & magnæ quidem mūdi lumina, hi essent : Theologiæ, Theod. Beza, parens in Domino & præceptor meus : Iuris ciuilis, Franciscus Hotomanus : Linguæ Hebraicæ, Cornelius Bertramus : Linguæ Græcæ, Franciscus Portus : Philosophiæ, Matthæus Beroaldus. Atque hic tunc erat vestra tum ciuitatis, tum schole status, quem vobis saluum & incolumemDominus Deus perpetuó conseruet, & veritatis suæ pura luce semper foueat, & locupletet.
units.tr: There are two main reasons, Magnificent Lords, that have prompted me to dedicate these commentaries of mine on Augustine to you: the memory of your kindnesses to me, and the very useful subject of the book itself. For when I review the course of my former life, and weigh it with myself as is right, by what road the Lord, the Father of mercies, was pleased first to lead me out of those dreadful shadows of idolatry into the saving light of his Gospel, I openly confess that I owe more to you than to my own parents. Parents, it is true, confer enormous benefits on their children, and it must be admitted that children can never sufficiently acknowledge or repay them as they deserve. Yet no sane person, I think, will deny that we owe far more to those through whom we have learned true godliness: through them we are Christians, whereas through our parents we are no more than men. And if we consider how great a whirlpool of errors Popery is (to which we were enslaved like cattle), we must judge ourselves the more blessed, and more fortunate, for having come up out of so great a shipwreck, and we must therefore value all the more those through whom we obtained so great a benefit from the Lord. So when, in the last year, 1559, that most learned jurist and truly most holy senator Anne du Bourg, under whom I had studied civil law for four years at Orléans, was burned at Paris for the pure doctrine of the Gospel, by that very fire I was inflamed more eagerly to gain knowledge of that teaching, of which I had only lightly tasted, so that I afterwards resolved to devote myself wholly to the school and discipline of those who professed it truly and sincerely. For I did not think that it could be defended, by a light or trivial argument, against so great a man, whom all France had so often admired as a teacher. So it came about that in the following year, 1560, I betook myself with the greatest eagerness of mind to this your Academy, not as to a neighbour of our France (there were other such), but as to the most limpid fountain of that heavenly doctrine. When I had come there, I will not say what sort of men, and how great, were my teachers. The praises of some of them, now dead, and of others still living, are sufficiently on everyone's lips. I will say this freely, and without offence to all the godly, that so many lights of the world, and most eminent and celebrated men in every kind of art, shone upon me then, that this one city alone seemed to be a very rich emporium of all human learning. Above all, in that knowledge of the Gospel doctrine which I was then especially seeking, I so admired that distinguished servant of God and your minister, John Calvin, and the Lord so drew me on by the sweetness of that doctrine through his sermons and also his lectures, that, having utterly abandoned the study of civil law which I had followed up to that day, I devoted myself entirely to sacred theology. Then too, as with most others, I was greatly carried away and affected by the life and manners of this city and by the public holiness that shone like a certain splendour in every rank of men, so that I have never ceased to wish, since, to live and dwell in a city where so just an order of all things prevailed. But my health did not allow this then, nor did the importunate entreaties of those who demanded ministers of God's Word leave me in peace. So, on the advice of the Pastors of this city, I was sent back to my homeland to take up the divine ministry, where, while we hoped all would be safe and quiet, behold, a sudden upheaval of affairs and an unexpected ruin of the Churches came, and those recent French frenzies, of which everyone has heard today, drove most of the godly, whom the sword had spared, into exile. But in this very public calamity of our country and in my own flight, a new benefit from you also came to me. For besides the fact that here I was kindly received, owing to that humanity which is yours towards all Christians, I was also, by the votes of the Church, co-opted into the college of Pastors, and I have found this city far more humane than my own homeland. And truly this my condition is the more pleasing to me, and I would add also more salutary, because I have as teachers and colleagues those men by whose domestic examples and excellent learning great increases of piety and of doctrine of the Trinitarian faith can daily come to me. And would that the Lord might grant me such strength and courage that, imitating their example, I may be occupied in this most sacred office to his glory and the building up of this Church, and bring such diligence to it that neither the Church shall repent of having committed to me so great a burden (to which I feel myself truly unequal), nor I of having undertaken it. Since, then, your benefits to me are so many and so great, who will not admit that I ought to be mindful and grateful? But there is also a second reason for dedicating this book to you, and not less just than the first: from the subject of this book you will observe how great the benefits God has conferred upon you, and how many and how great evils he has delivered you from, while he frees you both from Popery and from various errors. For although the power of divine and Evangelical truth is such that, to those who attend to it, it dispels with its own light all the clouds of error and the most shameful lies of heresies, nevertheless this gift of God to you may seem singular, and in a certain way peculiar: that with wonderful good fortune and speed you have utterly uprooted from your city that unhappy darnel which Satan is wont to sow among the good seed of God's Word. No one, however envious, can deny that this was done through the great vigilance of your Pastors, and especially of that great Calvin; yet in this too your praise is certainly not small, that you obeyed the sound counsels of your Pastors, neither fearing the judgments of adversaries, nor dreading the hatred and threats of the most powerful kings. Thus you have constantly and fearlessly persisted in that most pure truth which the Lord has revealed to us in his Word. Nor, however, has Satan lacked in this your city his fans and disseminators of the worst errors, but by the highest benefit of God these men were never able to gain or accomplish anything among you. For truth conquered, and immediately those seeds of poison which that father of lies was trying to sow among you were extinguished. I will not hesitate to recall these in detail. For when in the year of the Lord 1535 your whole city gladly embraced that saving light of the Gospel, more by a divine miracle than by any human effort, it is well known in how many ways that most foul enemy of the human race attacked you through his emissaries. Nor do I speak only of those who tried, by a cunning device and the smooth flatteries of words, to draw you away from the heavenly doctrine already received, such as the crafty men, redeemed by the Roman Antichrist himself, Peter Caroli and Jacopo Sadoleto. I do not mean only those who, by open force and wicked sedition, wished afterwards to drive away and utterly overthrow the Gospel itself, to whose introduction they had previously seemed to labour diligently. I rather mention here those who, under the false yet plausible pretext of retaining, cherishing and illustrating the Christian religion itself, laboured to import into that doctrine of faith, which you had now received in its purity, the filth of the most foul heresies. From all these the Lord has freed you by his wonderful good fortune and incredible goodness. For you cannot fail to remember, nor can you and your descendants ever forget, how, after the pure Word of God had been received (at which time you ceased to hope for light after darkness, but saw that heavenly and most desired light), in the year of the Lord 1536 Satan attacked you through the Anabaptists, a most obstinate race of men, a darnel springing up among the good seed in almost all the reformed Churches. But these, after a public disputation on their doctrine, were condemned as heretics, and driven from the city, and never afterwards dared to nestle in this city or to tempt your Church. Then came the year of the Lord 1541, in which at last you drew up a definite form of ecclesiastical discipline, which, made more perfect and enlarged some years later, was finally approved by the great consent of all the orders of this city. In this same year Satan, through that Sebastian Castellio, a man of feigned piety, tried to drive you and your faith, and to shake it with a light blow at first, as it seemed, but a most dangerous one; yet by this evil and hidden poison your city was cleansed in the year 1545, the man himself being cast out like scum. The year 1550 followed (for Satan could not rest any longer), in which from the midst of the citizens themselves arose a certain Gruet, a monster of portentous impiety, since he had blended the Samosatene doctrine with Manichaeism into the same mixture of error; and had not the Lord come to the rescue early, he could have made many fall, by the favour with which he was commended among his fellow citizens. But when the author himself was removed by you with a just and capital punishment, that impiety too perished. What then? Satan, though so often repulsed, attacked you again by another road. For in the year 1551 he stirred up Jerome Bolsec from the cells and filth of the monks, who tried to overturn the most true doctrine of the predestination of the saints, that is, the most certain foundation of our salvation, and to exchange it for open Pelagianism. But convicted of error, he was first expelled from the city by you, and then from the whole neighbouring territory. And as he has wandered in uncertain abodes for the rest of his life, so he holds no fixed religion in his mind. But now the enemy of truth, so often cast down, at last brought forward his chief leader and standard-bearer. For in the year 1553 that dreadful monster, forged from every heap of errors, Servetus, came to you; or rather, as I myself think, the Lord, for the just vengeance of his own name, which that impure man had so often blasphemed both by mouth and by writings, brought Servetus to you to receive the punishment he deserved. By the mere breath of this man Satan so breathed the most harmful poison of error upon certain persons (through which the essential Deity of our Lord Jesus Christ is taken away, that is, the foundation of our faith is overturned) that, although they were terrified by his grievous punishment, they afterwards neither kept silent nor became wiser. For in the year 1558 there arose the most shameless disciples of Servetus, pests of the whole human race, who heaped monsters upon monsters, combining the error of the Tritheites with Samosatenism and Arianism. These were Valentine Gentile, Giorgio Biandrata, and Paolo Alciati, the greatest scoundrels and impostors. Among them Valentine, caught and convicted of his blasphemy, sang a palinode here and recanted his error, but at last, with his madness, he could no more bring a sweet fragrance of balsam to the air of your city than harmful serpents could. So all of them secretly fled from your city, and even Valentine himself, contrary to the oath given publicly, so that they might freely spew out their poisons, which they saw must be wholly suppressed and destroyed here among you. Therefore, since the Lord by his great mercy has so easily freed you from so many and so great evils of heresies, that not even small seeds of them now remain, with what great gratitude ought you to thank God Most Good and Most Great for so great a benefit, and with what great diligence must you take care in future that no blemish of Christian doctrine arise and grow among you? Although this care seems chiefly to pertain to us your Pastors, it is nevertheless your duty to continue with the same constancy of mind as before, and to oppose bravely to the arts of Satan and the heretical attempts that authority of yours; not to dread the judgments of adversaries, nor to fear the power or threats of the whole world. Rather, most brave men, look to God himself, and hope in him, whom you have already so often experienced as your protector, and who will be your defender against all the fury and conspiracies of your enemies. Nay, more, perfect that holy rule of morals and discipline itself, lest through a certain human condition, as usually happens, which tends towards the worse, and through relaxation of minds, it totter; that very thing, I say, Christian men, perfect and set in the best possible state, lest through some silent custom evil manners creep in gradually, and public wickedness be introduced among you with boldness, and grow. For that is true: the nature of man is prone to lust, and those who do not promptly meet the first beginnings of ruin seem in some way to pave the way and yield to greater falls and errors. That this may not happen is your duty, to watch over it together with us; and not to listen to the complaints of those who call that holy institution of life a heavy and hard yoke. This befits your virtue and even your fatherly virtue. This is pleasing to God. This is salutary for your souls. This is altogether useful and necessary for the safety of your city, which you acknowledge to depend wholly on the one God. To this I exhort you with the greatest emotion of mind that I can, and I beseech with most ardent prayers that God himself, through his only-begotten Son, may always grant you that mind. Moreover, this little book of Augustine, together with what we have added, shows from how many and how great errors you must be on your guard. For it contains almost all the heresies that have arisen and spread in the Church of God, from the foundation of the world, certainly from the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ for the salvation of mankind, down to the established Papacy and also to Mahometanism (both of which are a universal apostasy from the faith of Christ). For the other things, which are called heresies, and which are said to have arisen after those times, I have omitted, partly because they were not heresies, and partly because, if there were any, they appear to be only certain interpolations and renewals of those which we have mentioned here; especially since such a virulent dish, even once set before us, let alone repeated, is death. Certainly those who after the establishment of Popery were branded as heretics through great ignorance of the Evangelical truth, such as those called Wycliffites, Hussites, Picards, Beghards, Lollards, Waldenses, Albigensians, and the Poor Men of Lyons: these, and especially the Waldenses, whose famous and pious Churches flourish, rightly thought about the articles of the Christian faith, and must be regarded as true Christians. But because they had departed from the doctrine of Popery, that is, of that universal and foul apostasy, they were condemned as heretics by the apostates themselves, that is, the Papists; while by us they must be named both Christians and Martyrs of God, far from being counted among heretics. As for the dogmas which are poured out by the Anabaptists, Sylvanists, Servetians, Nearians and others, these are only the rancid leftovers of ancient heresies, which we read have already been refuted a thousand times. Therefore, having advanced to the year 675, to be counted from the Passion of Christ and not from his birth, from the creation of the world, we have settled in the already established kingdom of Antichrist, in which at this time that son of perdition, whom Paul calls by that name, openly sat in the Church of God as if he were God. In this work we have followed especially the chronology of John Funck. These things we were writing in the year since the birth of Christ 1576, the last of the times, when at Geneva on the first of January the Syndics or Consuls were created: M. Rosset, Jacques Blondet, Claude Domonoveau, and Étienne Mallet; and Amadeus Chastelnon was the Prefect of the city. The public professors, and indeed great lights of the world, were these: for theology, Theodore Beza, my father in the Lord and my teacher; for civil law, François Hotman; for Hebrew, Cornelius Bertram; for Greek, François Porto; for philosophy, Matthew Beroalde. And such was then the state of your city and of your school; may the Lord God preserve it safe and sound for ever, and always cherish and enrich it with the pure light of his truth.

units.tr: To D. Lambert Daneau, Theologian.

units.la: Impia facta colit cupido mens impia voto: Dicta viris veluti sunt, pia grata pijs. Ergo Danæe audes impuras tangere sectas, Cum doctor puri sis pius eloquij? Scilicet, vt medici miscent medicamina virus, Φάρμακον & faciunt, quod sit ἀλεξίκακον. Impia diuini condis sic nectare verbi, Impius vt doleat, gaudeat hisque pius. Hoc opus est artis sacræ: quod temperat, actis Impia, iam profint, vt pia scripta pijs.
units.tr: The impious mind, with a wicked wish, cultivates impious deeds; words that are fitting for men are pleasing to the pious. Why then do you dare, Daneau, to touch impure sects, since you are a teacher and a pious speaker of pure doctrine? Clearly, just as physicians mix poisons into medicines and make a remedy that drives off harm, so you mingle the impious with the nectar of the divine word, so that the impious may grieve and the pious rejoice at it. This is the work of sacred art: that, by tempering the impious matter in your acts, your writings may now benefit the pious.

units.la: CAPUT I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: In omni doctrinæ & artium genere fuisse hæreses.
units.tr: That there have been heresies in every kind of teaching and art.

units.la: ANTEQVAM ad ipsius argumen-ti longè quidem uberrimi & uti-lissimi explicationem aggredior, quædam mihi videntur pręfanda, ex quibus tum utilitas huius ope-ris intelligetur: tum variis quęstionibus, quę in harum rerum tractatione fieri solent, respon-debitur, ne quid sit, in quo tanquam in aqua, huius operis studiosus lector hæreat. Ac primùm quidem illud certo certius est, nullum unquam artium doctrinæque genus fuisse, in quo hæreses aliquę tandem non extiterint, siue Philosophiam siue Christianam religionem spectemus. Quot enim inter ipsos Philosophos sectæ fuerunt, & in eadem secta quot diuortia & familię exortæ, tot proculdubio hæreses diuersæque sententiæ, aliæ ab aliis etiam de eadem re dissentientes, sunt dicendæ. Hoc autem Clemens Alexandr. Stromat. libr. i. verissimè docet his verbis: Cùm una sit veritas, ait, falsum innumerabilia habet diuerticula, quemadmodum Bacchæ, quę Penthei membra diuellebāt, sic Philosophiæ tam barbarę quàm Græcę, hæreses. Vnaquæque enim id quod sortita est tanquam tota iactat veritatem, & certè nulla tam absurda fuit unquam sententia, quę non, ut ait Quintilianus, suum authorem defensoremque habuerit. Ac de Philosophia quidem fidem nobis faciunt & Epiphanius & Celsus is, de quo in proœmio huius libri postea meminit Augustus & Diogenes Laertius: & Plutarch. in lib. quinque, de placitis Philosophorum, qui omnes diuersas Philosophorum sectas & sententias nobis descripserunt. In doctrina vero fidei idem euenisse testatur & verbum ipsum diuinum: & Epiphanius grauis scriptor, qui hæreseon, tum earum quę ab initio mundi & ante Christum incarnatū extiterunt: tum earum, quæ postea natæ sunt, luculenter meminit. Hoc autem malū tum ex natiua & propria hominis ipsius malitia, & cęcitate, quę utraque nobis iam propter peccatum inest, accidit: tum Satanę astu & suggestione, qui veritatem odit, factum est.
units.tr: Before I approach the explanation of my subject, which is very rich and very useful, some things seem to me to need saying first. From them the usefulness of this work will be understood, and answers will be given to the various questions that usually arise in treating these matters, so that the diligent reader of this work has nothing to stick on, as in shallow water. First of all, this is most certainly true: there has never been any kind of art or teaching in which heresies have not in the end arisen, whether we look at philosophy or at the Christian religion. For as many sects as there have been among the philosophers themselves, and as many divisions and schools as have arisen within the same sect, so many heresies and differing opinions must undoubtedly be spoken of, some dissenting from others even about the same matter. Clement of Alexandria teaches this most truly in the first book of his Stromata, in these words: "Since truth is one," he says, "falsehood has countless byways, just as the Bacchae who tore apart the limbs of Pentheus. So too are there heresies of philosophy, both barbarian and Greek. For each one boasts of what it has obtained as if it were the whole truth." And certainly no opinion was ever so absurd that it did not, as Quintilian says, have its author and its defender. Concerning philosophy, Epiphanius, Celsus (of whom Augustine makes mention later in the preface to this book), and Diogenes Laertius give us assurance, and Plutarch in his five books on the opinions of the philosophers, who have described for us all the diverse sects and opinions of the philosophers. In the teaching of the faith, the divine Word itself testifies that the same thing has happened, and Epiphanius, a weighty writer, clearly records the heresies both those that arose from the beginning of the world and before Christ was incarnate, and those that arose afterwards. This evil has come about partly from the natural and proper malice of man himself and his blindness, both of which now dwell in us because of sin, and partly by the cunning and suggestion of Satan, who hates the truth.

units.la: CAP. II. Utrum utile sit hæreses nosse, eisque commemorare, & de utilitate ex hæreticis capienda.
units.tr: CHAPTER II. Whether it is useful to know heresies and to make mention of them, and on the benefit to be drawn from heretics.

units.la: Sequens quæstio est; Utrum operæpretium sit hæreses, & eas imprimis, quæ in recta fide sanaq; doctrina, quæ Christiana est, euenerunt; nosse & legere, & tractare. Primum ne quid labis & contagionis inde trahamus. Sępe enim nescio quomodo sensim influit, & incautis obrepit quidam gustus earum opinionum, quas tractamus, ut arrideant & a nobis postea defendantur. Deinde vt Clemens Strom.lib.5. ex Æschylo docet, Ne in iis labores temere, quæ nihil iuuant.
units.tr: The next question is whether it is worth while to know, read and handle heresies, especially those which have arisen within the right faith and sound Christian doctrine. First, so that we do not catch any stain or contagion from them. For often, I know not how, a certain taste for those opinions which we handle creeps in gradually and steals upon the unwary, so that they begin to please us and afterwards we end up defending them. Second, as Clement teaches in the fifth book of the Stromata, quoting Aeschylus: Do not labour rashly over those things that help nothing.

units.la: Quid autem prodest hæreses nosse, quæ sunt religionis Christianæ carcinemata & pestes? Postremo, ex huiusmodi recitatione magnum infirmis, ne dicam, Paganis hominibus & Euangelium iam odio profequetibus[?] offendiculum præbetur, quasi in fide Christiana nihil sit certi & constituti, quod sequi possimus. Quod recte præuidit Nicephorus Callistus, cum varias Eutychianorum hæreses enumeraret libro 14. cap.48. Respondeo vero tribus maximè de causis vtilissimum esse, hæreses, quæ in doctrina fidei emerserunt, & cognosci & explicari. Primum, vt refutentur, atque vt tanquam scopuli quidam à nobis & ab aliis euitetur. Cum enim hæresis sit velut saxum periculosum, ad quod alij naufragium fecerunt, de eo admoniti alij sibi melius prudentiusque cauebut. Nec enim, vt ait Theodoretus lib. 1. Hæreticar. fabul. eo animo audire vanos istos errores, qui teterrimum odorem emittunt, debemus, vt eos libeter audiamus, aut vt amplectamur: sed vt reliquos doceamus, quæ sit recta & publica via, quam Prophetæ & Apostoli triuerunt: nobisque tutissimam aduersus omnes Satanæ insidias reliquerunt. Itaque vt medici, quemadmodum tradit Epiphanius, De venenis & deleteriis libros scribunt, non vt iis vti doceant homines, sed vt potius ab iis nobis caueamus: sic hære-ses describuntur, vt euitentur: non autem vt suscipiantur. Nam etsi est necesse vt sint hære-ses, non est tamē suauc[?], vt ait Bernar. epist. 189. itaque sunt cauendæ. Secunda ratio & vtilitas est, quòd ex iis ipsis recitatis sana doctrina melius diligentiúsq; examinatur, & magis pèsicularè: adeò vt quæ festinanter antea percurreba-mus, incipiamus attentè iam legere & singula ponderare. Nam, vt verè ait Euagr. lib. 1. cap. 9. per eos, qui Ecclesiam discerpserūt, recta fidei dogmata emerserunt: quod ipsum etiam in Arianis ostendit Nicephorus lib. 13. cap. 1. Itaque Paulus 1. Corinth. 11. v. 19, Oportet hæreses esse, vt qui probati sunt, manifestentur. Tertia denique huius lectionis & cognitionis vtilitas in eo est, quòd ea ratione & cum scelera-tissimorum istorum dogmatū abominatio retegitur, tanto magis inuisi redduntur, tum ij, qui genuerunt: tum etiam ij, qui stolidè illis crediderunt. Sic enim hæc tractatio legenda est, vt vera doctrina erroribus istis ineptissimis semper opponatur. Itaque apud Eusebium libro 7. histor. ca. 7. Dionys. Corinthiorum Episcopus rectissimè, Ego, ait, tractatus hæreticorum legō, & traditiones eorum perscrutor, etiamsi videor ad horam illorum verbis pollui. Sed multum mihi confert hoc ipsum, quòd ex ipsorum verbis arguere eos possum. Et concilio Carthaginensi 4. cap. 16. decretum est, vt Episcopi hæreticorum libros legerent, quanquam iidem à Paganorum poetarum scriptis iubētur abstinere. Idem Viennensi concilio constitutū anno salutis 1311. Vera est enim illa Plutarchi, quanquam scriptoris profani, sententia, Nos ex ipsis inimicis nostris etiam maximam vtilitatem capere posse. Rationes autem illæ, quæ contra afferuntur,ex eo facilè omnes dissoluuntur,quòd à Deo spiritus fidei & discretionis petendus nobis est,vt & ipsius soli verbo inhæreamus,& quæ illi repugnant,sententiæ à nobis nulla hominum authoritate victis repudientur.
units.tr: But what good is it to know heresies, which are the cancers and plagues of the Christian religion? Lastly, by such a recital a great stumbling-block is put before the weak, not to say before pagans who already hate the Gospel, as if there were nothing certain and settled in the Christian faith that we could follow. Nicephorus Callistus foresaw this rightly when he listed the various heresies of the Eutychians in book 14, chapter 48. I answer, however, that it is most useful for heresies which have arisen against the doctrine of faith to be known and explained, for three main reasons. First, so that they may be refuted, and so that, like certain rocks, they may be avoided by us and by others. For since heresy is like a dangerous reef on which others have been shipwrecked, others, warned about it, take better and more prudent care of themselves. For, as Theodoret says in the first book of the Fables of the Heretics, we ought not to listen to those empty errors, which give off a most foul odour, with the intention of gladly hearing them or embracing them, but in order to teach the rest which is the right and public way that the Prophets and Apostles trod, and which they left us as the safest defence against all the snares of Satan. Thus, as Epiphanius relates, physicians write books on poisons and deadly substances, not to teach men to use them, but rather so that we may beware of them; so heresies are described so that they may be avoided, not so that they may be embraced. For although it is necessary that there be heresies, it is not pleasant, as Bernard says in letter 189, and therefore they are to be guarded against. The second reason and use is that, by the very recital of these heresies, sound doctrine is examined more diligently and more clearly, so that what we used to run through hastily we begin to read attentively and to weigh each point. For, as Evagrius truly says in book 1, chapter 9, the right dogmas of faith have emerged through those who tore the Church apart; Nicephorus shows this also in the case of the Arians, book 13, chapter 1. Thus Paul says in 1 Corinthians 11:19, "There must be heresies, that those who are approved may be made manifest." Third and finally, the usefulness of this reading and knowledge is that in this way the abhorrence of these most wicked doctrines is laid bare, and they are rendered all the more hateful, both to those who begot them and to those who foolishly believed them. For this subject must be read in such a way that true doctrine is always set against these most absurd errors. Thus Dionysius, bishop of the Corinthians, quoted by Eusebius in book 7 of the Histories, chapter 7, rightly says: "I read the writings of the heretics and examine their traditions, even though I seem for a while to be polluted by their words. But this very thing helps me greatly, that I can refute them from their own words." And the Council of Carthage, the fourth, chapter 16, decreed that bishops should read the books of heretics, although the same council orders them to abstain from the writings of pagan poets. The Council of Vienne decreed the same in the year of salvation 1311. True is that saying of Plutarch, though he was a secular writer: that we can gain the greatest benefit even from our enemies themselves. The arguments which are brought against this are easily overturned by the fact that we must ask God for the Spirit of faith and discernment, so that we may cling to his Word alone, and that whatever is opposed to it should be rejected by us, having been overcome by no human authority.

units.la: CAP. III. Quid sit hæresis, & hæreticus, & de quorundam aliorum vocabulorum definitione.
units.tr: CHAPTER III. What heresy and a heretic are, and the definition of certain other terms.

units.la: HÆresis vox Græca est (Αἵρεσιν enim illi appellant) qua tamen vsus est M. Tullius in proœmio Paradoxorum. Hæresis autem quid sit, est omnino, vt ait Augustinus, difficile definire. Nos tamen tentabimus, Christo duce. Ac primùm in vniuersum hæresis est, quæ à quoque electa est animi sententia, & opinio, siue à nobis ipsis illa sit inuenta, siue ab alio accepta. Quæ significatio primùm & in bonam & in malam partem sumebatur, Act. 24. versu 14. & Clemens Strom. lib. 8. Vnde apud philosophos αἵρεσις animi, est electio animi de re aliqua persequenda vel fugienda, quam prægressa est deliberatio. Vsus tamen postea, maximè apud Christianos, effecit, vt in malam tantùm partem acciperetur, nimirum pro animi peruersa sententia, quam obstinatè & pertinaciter tuetur aliquis, ex qua dissidia, contentiones & rixæ oriuntur. Paulus enim sic hac voce vtitur, Galat. 5. versu 20. Tandem ad solas quæstiones, quæ de fide Christiana fiùt, & in quibus erratur, referri & restringi coepit propter locū Pauli,qui est 1.Cor.ii[?].v.19.Oportet inter vos hęreses esse.& Tit.3.versu 10.Hæreticum homine post unam & alteram admonitionem deuita. Quo iam significato toto hoc opere sumitur a nobis,& hic definitur.
units.tr: "Heresy" is a Greek word (for they call it αἵρεσις), though Marcus Tullius also used it in the preface to his Paradoxes. What heresy is, as Augustine says, is altogether difficult to define. Nevertheless, with Christ as our guide, we shall try. First, in general, a heresy is an opinion or belief that someone has chosen, whether he himself devised it or received it from another. This meaning was at first used both in a good and in a bad sense (Acts 24. verse 14; and Clement, Stromata, book 8). Hence among the philosophers, αἵρεσις of the mind is the choice of the mind to pursue or avoid some matter, which has been preceded by deliberation. Later usage, however, especially among Christians, brought it about that the word was taken only in a bad sense, namely for a perverse opinion of the mind, which someone defends obstinately and stubbornly, and from which dissensions, quarrels and brawls arise. Paul uses the word in this way (Galatians 5. verse 20). At last it began to be referred and restricted solely to questions concerning the Christian faith in which people go wrong, on account of the passages of Paul: "There must be heresies among you" (1 Cor. 11. verse 19), and "Avoid a heretical man after one or two warnings" (Titus 3. verse 10). It is in this sense, now, that the word is taken throughout this work, and it is defined here.

units.la: Hæresis igitur est electio peruersæ falsæque de eo,quod ad animarum salutem credi exDei verbo debet, sententiæ, quam pertinaciter defendimus,siue illa a nobis noua reperta: siue ia ab alio inuenta sit, & vetus, vti ex Tertulliano, libro De præscript.aduersus hæretic.facile colligi potest.Est igitur error genus hæreseos.Neque enim hæresis est ea sententia, in qua minimè reipsa erratur, etsi errari a nobis homines dicunt:sed est ea tantum,in qua reuera erratur, & a veritate discedit.Erroris autem tria sunt genera, vt docet Augustinus in libris De doctrina Christiana: & lib. De vtilitate cred.c.4.
units.tr: A heresy, then, is the choice of a perverse and false opinion about what must be believed from God's Word for the salvation of souls, which we defend stubbornly, whether that opinion has been newly devised by us or has been discovered by another and is old, as can easily be gathered from Tertullian, in his book On Prescription against Heretics. Error, therefore, is the genus of heresy. For that opinion is not a heresy in which men are scarcely wrong in fact, even if they say that we are wrong; rather, a heresy is only that opinion in which one is truly wrong and departs from the truth. There are three kinds of error, as Augustine teaches in his books On Christian Doctrine, and in On the Profit of Believing, chapter 4.

units.la: Primum genus,in quo id quod est falsum putatur verum,præter mentem eius a quo tamen nos illud sumere dicimus, vt si quis putet idola esse ex mente Scripturæ veros deos,quia dij sæ-pe appellatur.Secundum genus,quuum id quod falsum est,putatur verum, & id creditur quod reipsa sensit is, a quo sumimus: veluti si putes, legens & euoluens libros Lucretij, De natura rerum, animā constare ex atomis,quod & scripsit & sensit Lucretius,error est. Tertium genus est,quum ex alieno scripto aliquid veri creditur,quod tamen ille, cuius scriptum profers, non sensit, aut putauit: veluti si quis existimet Epicurum, quia continentiam laudat, possuisse summum bonum in virtute. Hæresis autem hic definita est error,ex primo erroris genere,quū nimirum quis verum putat,quod falsum est,& praeter eius mentem, à quo suae sententiae con-firmatione petit. Est igitur haeresis adulterina sacrae Scripturae interpretatio. Itaq; rectè Hic-ronymus in epistola Pauli ad Galat.cap.5. Qui-cunque,ait,aliter Scripturam sacram intelligit, quàm sensus Spiritus sancti flagitat,à quo con-scripta est, licet de Ecclesia non recesserit, tamen haereticus appellari potest,maximè si eam falsam sententiam defendit. Quare haeresis est omnis constituta defensáque contra veritatem verbi Dei scripto comprehensi sententia. Sed à verbo Dei dupliciter receditur, nimirum vel materiae,vel formae ratione. Ac ratione materiae variis modis. Quum enim verbum Dei & caelestè sacra Scriptura comprehensum,quaedam tradat tanquam generales & communes Christianae doctrinae ἐννοίας [?] & ἀφορισμὺς [?], qui fidei articuli dicuntur: Quaedam autem,tanquam parti-culares rerum gestarum narrationes & historias, certè quicunque vel in illis generalibus sententiis errat: vel in his particularibus, idque obsti-natè,potest haereticus dici,quaquam hic quàm illic minus periculosè erratur. Nullus enim est levis in iis, qui Christianae fidei articuli vocan-tur,error. In particulari autem rerum gestarum narratione,quę à Scriptura traditur,si fallimur, potest saepe levis esse error,quem tamen si per-tinaciter & obstinatè postea defendimus, gra-vis & periculosus tandem evadit. Denique hoc sit conclusum,neque ullum extra doctrinam,& res à Scriptura sacra traditas, errorem solere à Christianis hominibus hæresin appellari: Neque etiam in sacra Scriptura tractanda omnem errorem hæresin debere dici. Nam circa particularem aliquam Scripturæ historiam, leuis nostra hallucinatio, quales circa chronologiæ, vel topographiæ rationem, vel in nominum & personarum distinctione, multi errores etiam peritissimis sæpe obrepunt, & accidunt, qui neque solent, neque debent odioso illo & infami hæreseos nomine notari, & appellari: sed tantum voce erroris mitiore. Diuersæ autem diuersorum interpretationes & sententiæ, de eodem loco sacræ Scripturæ, quæ ab analogia fidei non recedunt, non sunt hæreses: sed sunt explicationes tantum tolerandæ, & sæpe etiam, quia lumen obscuris Scripturæ locis afferunt, laudandæ. Ex quo fit vt iam etiam proprium & vsitatum hæreseos significationem restringamus, dicamusque quum tam odiose hæresis nomen a nobis damnatur, vt hic & vulgò solet, quum hæretici malè olent, & audiût [?], hæresin pro ea solùm perversa falsaque animi sententia sumi, per quam aliquid contra ipsam fidei Christianæ doctrinam, & contra vniuersales illos articulos & creditur & defenditur. In his autem articulis tripliciter peccari potest. Nam vel in Omnibꝰ fidei nostræ articulis erratur, Aliquibus, & quidem pluribus, Vno tantum. Nusquam vero, quemadmodum diximus, leuiter in fidei articulis hallucinamur. Ratione vero formæ duobus etiam modis a nobis errari potest. Quum enim aliquid in facra Scriptura contineri dupliciter dicatur, vel expresse, & ijs ipsis verbis, quibus à nobis pronuntiatur: vel ex mente Scripturæ,& ex analogia fidei, ut vox hæc Trinitas: si ab eo, quod Scriptura sacra tradit vel ipsissimis verbis, vel ex analogia fidei, in doctrina, & substantia fidei recedatur, hæresis est huiusmodi sensus & error, maximè si defendatur obstinatè. Inde est illud Hilarij,libro 8. De Trinitate, De intelligentia enim hæresis, non de scriptura, & sensus, non sermo, sit crimen.Hierony.in Galat.1.Non putemus in verbis Scripturarum esse euangelium, sed in sensu: Non in superficie, sed in medulla: Non in sermonum foliis,sed in radice rationis.
units.tr: The first kind is when what is false is thought true, contrary to the mind of the one from whom we say we take it: for example, if someone thinks that idols are the true gods according to the meaning of Scripture, because gods are often so called. The second kind is when what is false is thought true, and one believes what the man from whom we take it actually held: for example, if you, reading and turning over the books of Lucretius, On the Nature of Things, think that the soul consists of atoms, which Lucretius both wrote and thought, that is an error. The third kind is when something true is believed from another's writing, which yet the author whose writing you cite did not think or hold: for example, if someone supposes that Epicurus, because he praises self-control, held that the highest good lies in virtue. Heresy, however, is here defined as an error of the first kind, namely when someone thinks that something false is true, and against the mind of the one from whom he seeks confirmation of his opinion. Heresy is therefore an adulterated interpretation of Holy Scripture. Hence Jerome rightly says, in his commentary on Paul's Epistle to the Galatians, chapter 5: "Whoever understands Holy Scripture otherwise than the sense of the Holy Spirit by whom it was written requires, although he has not departed from the Church, may yet be called a heretic, especially if he defends that false opinion." Therefore heresy is any opinion held and defended against the truth of the Word of God comprehended in writing. But one departs from the Word of God in two ways, namely with respect either to matter or to form. And with respect to matter, in various ways. For since the Word of God, contained in the heavenly Holy Scripture, sets forth some things as general and common notions [ἐννοίας] and definitions [ἀφορισμούς] of Christian doctrine, which are called the articles of faith, while other things are narratives and histories of particular events, certainly whoever errs either in those general statements, or in these particular ones, and does so obstinately, may be called a heretic, although one goes wrong less dangerously in the latter than in the former. For there is no slight error in those things which are called the articles of the Christian faith. In the particular narration of events that Scripture hands down, however, if we are mistaken, the error can often be slight; yet if we afterwards defend it stubbornly and obstinately, it eventually becomes grave and dangerous. Finally, let this be concluded: that no error outside the doctrine and the matters handed down by Holy Scripture is usually called a heresy by Christians, nor should every error in handling Holy Scripture be called a heresy. For concerning some particular historical account in Scripture, our slight mistakes, such as those about the order of chronology or geography, or in the distinction of names and persons, often steal in even upon the most skilled, and these are not usually, nor should they be, marked and named with that odious and infamous name of heresy, but only with the milder word "error." Moreover, different interpretations and opinions of different men concerning the same passage of Holy Scripture, which do not depart from the analogy of faith, are not heresies; they are explanations to be tolerated, and often even to be praised, because they shed light on obscure passages of Scripture. From this it follows that we should now restrict the proper and common meaning of heresy, and say that when the name of heresy is condemned by us so odiously, as it commonly is, when heretics stink and are spoken of ill, heresy is taken only for that perverse and false opinion of the mind by which something is both believed and defended against the very doctrine of the Christian faith and against those universal articles. Now in these articles one may err in three ways: either one errs in all the articles of our faith, or in some, and indeed in several, or in only one. But one never, as we have said, slightly goes astray in the articles of faith. With respect to form, too, we can err in two ways. For since something is said to be contained in Holy Scripture in two ways, either expressly and in the very words by which we pronounce it, or from the meaning of Scripture and from the analogy of faith, as the word "Trinity" is, then if one departs in doctrine and in the substance of faith from what Scripture hands down, either in the very words or by the analogy of faith, such a sense and error is a heresy, especially if it is obstinately defended. Hence that saying of Hilary, in book 8 On the Trinity: "For it is the understanding that makes a heresy, not the Scripture; it is the meaning, not the words, that incurs the charge." And Jerome, on Galatians 1: "Let us not suppose that the gospel lies in the words of the Scriptures, but in their sense; not on the surface, but in the marrow; not in the leaves of the words, but in the root of the reason."

units.la: Tunc Scriptura utilis est audiétibus, cum absque Christo non dicitur,cùm absquePatre nō profertur, cùm sine Spiritu non eam insinuat qui eam prædicat. Utrum autem ex verbis inordinatè pronuntiatis incurratur hæresis, disputant operosè ex Hieronymo Scholast. in libro 4. Sentent. P. Lombardi, distin.13.cap. Ne autem. quod omnino futile est, si modò ipse sensus verus conseruetur. Pertinaciam autem requirit hæresis, non leuem tantum & momentaneam opinionem, quæ statim in nobis labascat, pereat, & mutetur, quia propositum animi requirit hæresis. Unde fit autem analogia fidei (sic enim Paulus loquitur, Rom.12.versu 6.) sumenda, in ijs quæ præscriptis verbis à Scriptura sacra non traduntur, videndus & legendus est sedulò Pater Irenæus libro 2.cap. 46, & 47.lib.4. cap.63. Erit autem, ut breuiter dicam, si ex iis quæ analoga fidei Christianæ dicimus, nihil cōcludi possit & effici, quod verbo scripto adversetur,& repugnet. Anfel.itaque rectè in lib. De Concord. Grat. & Lib. arbitrij. Sic itaque, ait, sacra Scriptura omnis veritatis, quam ratio colligit, autoritatem continet, cùm illa aut aperte affirmat, aut nullatenus negat. Quod enim aperta ratione colligitur, & illi ex nulla Scriptura parte contradicitur, quoniam ipsa, sicut nulli adversatur veritati: ita nulli favet falsitati, hoc ipso quia non negat, quod ratione dicitur, eius autoritate suscipitur.
units.tr: Scripture is useful to its hearers only when it is not expounded without Christ, when it is not set forth without the Father, and when he who preaches it does not present it without the Spirit. Whether a heresy is incurred by words spoken in disorder, the Schoolmen debate at length, following Jerome, in book 4 of Peter Lombard's Sentences, distinction 13, chapter "Ne autem." This is altogether trivial, provided only that the true sense is preserved. Heresy, however, requires obstinacy, not a slight and momentary opinion which at once wavers in us, perishes and is changed, because heresy implies a settled purpose of the mind. Next, the analogy of faith (for so Paul speaks, Romans 12. verse 6) is to be taken, in those matters which are not handed down by Scripture in set words; and Father Irenaeus, book 2, chapters 46 and 47, and book 4, chapter 63, is to be carefully read and studied. It will be sufficient, to put it briefly, if nothing can be concluded or drawn from what we call the analogy of faith that opposes or contradicts the written Word. Anselm therefore rightly says in his book On the Harmony of Grace and Free Will: "Thus Holy Scripture contains the authority of every truth that reason gathers, since it either affirms it openly or nowhere denies it. For what is gathered by clear reason, and is contradicted by no part of Scripture, is itself received on the authority of Scripture, since, just as it opposes no truth, so it favours no falsehood, and for this very reason, that it does not deny what is said by reason, it is accepted on Scripture's authority."

units.la: Ab hæresi dictus est hęreticus. Est autem hęreticus, qualem hic quidem cogitamus & appellamus, non omnis qui deserto, quod prius fuerat, id postea sibi eligit, quod antea non erat, ut tamen definire videtur Tertullianus, libro 1. ad-versus Marcionem (qui enim abiecta idololatria, quam prius sequuti erant, postea fidem veram amplectuntur, essent hæretici dicendi) sed is est hæreticus, qui iam suscepto Baptismi sacramento, hæresin quam definiuimus, ample-xus est, id est, cōtrariam vel verbis ipsis, vel mentis sacræ Scripturæ in iis præsertim, quæ ad summam, & substantiam doctrinæ Christianæ per-tinent, fideique nostræ articulis comprehendū-tur, sententiam sequitur, & eam obstinatè tuc-tur & defendit. Addimus autem, suscepto Ba-ptismi sacrameto, quia qui contraria fidei dog-mata sequitur, nec unquam in Ecclesiam coe-tumque Dei receptus est, infidelis potius quàm hæreticus est appellandus: fidei enim Christia-næ se prius obligarit quis necesse est, id est, sa-cramentum Christianismi susceperit, quàm hęreticus dici possit. Augustinus autem libro De vtilitate credendi, cap. i. aliter definit, & eum vult esse hæreticum, qui temporalis commodi, & maxime gloriæ principatúsque sui gratia novas ac falsas opiniones circa doctrinam fidei vel gignit, vel sequitur. Quæ definitio finem etiam, quem sibi proponit hæreticus, complectitur. In summa hæreticus est, qui hærefin, id est, falsam de aliquo fidei capite sententiam sequitur, quam obstinatè defendit, siue ipsa fidei & articuli verba oppugnet: siue ipsius veram mentem, δόγμα, & analogiam. Differt autem ab hæretico is qui ab August. libro De vtilitate credend. cap. i. dicitur hæreticis credens.
units.tr: A heretic is so called from heresy. The heretic we are here concerned with and name is not everyone who, having abandoned what he once held, then chooses for himself something he did not hold before. Tertullian seems to define it that way in book 1 against Marcion, but on that definition those who give up the idolatry they once followed and then embrace the true faith would have to be called heretics. The heretic is rather one who, having already received the sacrament of baptism, embraces the heresy we have defined, that is, follows and stubbornly defends an opinion contrary to the sacred Scripture, either in its words or in its meaning, especially in those matters that belong to the sum and substance of Christian doctrine and are contained in the articles of our faith. I add "having already received the sacrament of baptism" because someone who follows doctrines contrary to the faith, but has never been received into the Church and the assembly of God, should be called an unbeliever rather than a heretic. A person must first bind himself to the Christian faith, that is, receive the sacrament of Christianity, before he can be called a heretic. Augustine, in the first chapter of his book On the Profit of Believing, defines it differently, holding that the heretic is one who either begets or follows new and false opinions about the doctrine of faith for the sake of temporal advantage, and above all for the sake of glory and his own supremacy. This definition also takes in the aim that the heretic sets before himself. In short, a heretic is one who follows a heresy, that is, a false opinion about some article of faith, and defends it stubbornly, whether it assails the very words of the faith and its articles, or their true meaning, dogma, and analogy. He differs from the one whom Augustine, in the first chapter of On the Profit of Believing, calls "one who believes heretics."

units.la: Hæreticis credens est, qui imaginatione quadam veritatis & pietatis ab iis illusus assentitur eorum errori, non animi quidem obstinatione, sed quadam cordis simplicitate & facilitate, siue leuitate temeritateque credendi. Itaque de suo errore admonitus, neque contendit, neque pugnat, sed vel resipiscit, vel cedere paratus est.
units.tr: One who believes heretics is a person who, deceived by some false image of truth and piety, gives assent to their error. He does this not from obstinacy of mind but from a certain simplicity and credulity of heart, or from lightness and rashness in believing. Therefore, when he is admonished about his error, he neither argues nor fights, but either comes to his senses or is ready to give way.

units.la: Saluiā. Mafsil. Episcopus lib. 5. de Pro uid. Dei, Errant quidam, ait, sed bono animo; non odio, sed affectu Dei, honorare se Deum, atque amare credentes. Impij sunt, sed hoc putant veram esse pietatem.
units.tr: Salvian, bishop of Marseilles, book 5 On the Providence of God: "Some err," he says, "but with a good intention. Not from hatred, but out of love for God, they believe that they honour and love God. They are impious, but they think this is true piety."

units.la: Schismaticus differt ab vtroque, vti schisma ab hæresi. Etsi enim ferè ex schismate postea fit hæresis, vt docet Augustinus contra Donatistas: est tamen schisma crimen hæresi leuius, vt Tertullianus in libro De præscript. hæreticorū ait. Est igitur Schisma in honesta ceremonia, siue iam recepto ab Ecclesia ritu & decoro perui-cax &. cax & temeraria alicuius discessio.Itaque schis-ma de ceremoniarum, & rituum Ecclesiae ob-servatione nascitur:hęresis de doctrina. Et schisma est non cuiuslibet ritus iam observati & recepti[?] prętermissio,& oppugnatio:sed eius tantum,qui & probabiliter,&,velut decorũ quoddam,iam receptus est in Ecclesia,& nullam doctrinę vel morum labem inducit & affert.Nam qui ritus labefactionem vel fidei, vel morum sanctitatis afferunt, & superstitionem inducut, non modo prętermitti debent:sed sunt fortiter a nobis oppugnandi,quales sunt infinitae in Papatu ineptae ceremoniae. Manichaei aliter schisma definiebant, sed ad suę blasphemię patrocinium,& male, quemadmodum docet Augustinus libro 20.contra Faustum cap.3.Schismaticus igitur est is , qui retenta fidei vera doctrina,eaque tota , sine probabili tamen & meliori ratione honestos illos & decoros Ecclesiae ritus nõ sequitur, quasi sit ille vnus tota ipsa Ecclesia sapientior, aduersus quem afferri certe debet quod ait Paulus, 1. Cor.7. v.26:14. versu 40:11.v.16.
units.tr: The schismatic differs from both, as schism differs from heresy. For although schism often later becomes heresy, as Augustine teaches against the Donatists, schism is nonetheless a lesser crime than heresy, as Tertullian says in his book On the Prescription of Heretics. A schism is therefore a stubborn and rash departure from some honest ceremony, or from a rite and decorum already received in the Church. So schism arises from the observance of ceremonies and rites of the Church, while heresy arises from doctrine. Schism is also the neglect and attack not of any rite whatever that has already been observed and received, but only of one that is probably good, and has been received in the Church as a kind of ornament, and that brings no stain or harm to doctrine or morals. For those rites which undermine either the faith or the holiness of morals, and introduce superstition, must not only be neglected but must be vigorously attacked by us, such as the countless foolish ceremonies in the Papacy. The Manichaeans defined schism differently, but to defend their blasphemy, and wrongly, as Augustine teaches in book 20 against Faustus, chapter 3. The schismatic, then, is one who, while keeping the true doctrine of the faith entire, does not follow those honest and decorous rites of the Church, without any probable and better reason, as though he alone were wiser than the whole Church. Against such a person must certainly be brought what Paul says in 1 Cor. 7. v. 26; 14. v. 40; 11. v. 16.

units.la: Paganus,siue Gentilis,& a schismatico,& ab hęretico distat.Est autem is Gentilis, qui nullo sacrorum librorum vinculo & religione tenetur, neque se vllo modo aut sacramento Ecclesiae, fideique Christi obstrinxit,vt definit Augustinus lib.11.contra Faustum,cap.2.Sacras enim Scripturas Paganus non recipit, quia nullam Christo fidem dedit. Vnde ex Tris-megisti,Pla-tonis, Sibyllae testimoniis potius, quàm ex sacra Scriptura est reiiciedus, vt est in libro contra Jud. & Paganos. Sic Arnobius, sic Lactantius contra Paganos disputarunt. Hęreticus autem sacras Scripturas admittit, & nos ad eas prouocat, etsi sepe eas ex parte truncat, nec omnes ἐνδιαθήκου γραφῆς[?] libros recipit, sed tantum quosdam ex iis, quod fecerunt Marcionitæ, & Manichæi. Eatenus autem diuinæ Scripturæ credunt Pagani, quatenus humanæ rationi co-sentanea videri potest. Augustinus De utilitate credendi, capite 14. Alia vero fidei dogmata ingenij humani φαντασμάτων[?] repugnantia spernunt & irridént.
units.tr: The pagan, or Gentile, differs from both the schismatic and the heretic. The Gentile is one who is bound by no bond or reverence of the sacred books, and who has in no way bound himself to the sacrament of the Church or to the faith of Christ, as Augustine defines in book 11 against Faustus, chapter 2. The pagan does not receive the sacred Scriptures, because he has given no faith to Christ. Hence he must be refuted from the testimonies of Trismegistus, Plato, and the Sibyl, rather than from sacred Scripture, as is done in the book against Jews and pagans. Thus Arnobius and Lactantius argued against the pagans. The heretic, however, admits the sacred Scriptures and appeals to them against us, although he often mutilates them in part, and does not receive all the books of the "endiathēkos graphē" [ἐνδιαθήκου γραφῆς], but only some of them, as the Marcionites and Manichaeans did. Pagans believe the divine Scriptures only so far as they seem consonant with human reason. Augustine, On the Profit of Believing, chapter 14. But they scorn and mock the other doctrines of faith as repugnant to the imaginations [φαντασμάτων] of the human mind.

units.la: Judęus religione est, quicunque veteris tantum Testamenti scripta recipit, & ex eo ceremonias adhuc retinet. Novum enim omnino damnant & reiiciunt Judęi. Itaque etsi Messiam aliquem promissum esse Patribus suis agnoscunt, & fatentur: exhibitum tamen negant: imprimis autem Jesum Christum Dominum nostrum, qui ex virgine Maria natus est, execrantur & oderunt, neque pro Propheta Dei agnoscunt, nedum pro vero mundi apud Deum mediatore, & redemptore, tam sunt in Deū ipsum blasphemi[?]. Hi peiores in ea parte sunt hęreticis & Paganis. Sunt autem quidam secundum carnem tantum Judæi, qui tamen religione vere Christiani sunt.
units.tr: A Jew by religion is anyone who receives only the writings of the Old Testament and from it still retains the ceremonies. For the Jews utterly condemn and reject the New. Thus, although they acknowledge and confess that some Messiah was promised to their fathers, they deny that he has been revealed. Above all they curse and hate Jesus Christ our Lord, who was born of the Virgin Mary, and they do not acknowledge him as a prophet of God, much less as the true mediator and redeemer of the world before God; so blasphemous are they against God himself. In this respect they are worse than heretics and pagans. There are, however, some who are Jews only according to the flesh, yet who are truly Christians in religion.

units.la: Papista est, qui Papæ Romani doctrinam, in iis dogmatis & rebus, in quibus a vera fide ille recessit, ut veram & salutarem amplectitur, & defendit. Vel, ut verius dicam, Papistæ sunt qui Christianum nomen profitetes, & Baptismum retinetes, purum putum Dei verbum tanquam solam & veram Christianæ fidei regulam non admittunt, sed humanas traditiones, cásque maximè, quæ à Romana Ecclesia præscriptæ sunt, pares Euangelio faciunt, & cum eo coniungūt, quas, vt fidei fundamentum, laudant, & retinent.Papistæ igitur minus longè, quàm Iudæi, & Pagani à Christo absunt, quia Baptismum Christi adhuc habent, tamen sunt illius hostes domestici.
units.tr: A Papist is one who embraces and defends the doctrine of the Roman Pope as true and saving, in those dogmas and matters in which that man has departed from the true faith. Or, to put it more truly, Papists are those who, professing the Christian name and retaining baptism, do not admit the pure Word of God as the sole and true rule of the Christian faith, but make human traditions, and above all those prescribed by the Roman Church, equal to the Gospel and join them with it, praising them and retaining them as the foundation of faith. Papists, therefore, are far less distant from Christ than Jews and pagans, because they still have the baptism of Christ; yet they are his domestic enemies.

units.la: Mahumetanus est, qui doctrinâ Mahumetis pro vera religione amplectitur: siue, qui etsi Christum venisse agnoscit, eum tamen neque pro vero & solo mediatore habet, neque eius Baptismo intingitur. Et hæc fere sunt tot & tam varia superstitionū & blasphemiarum vo-cabula.
units.tr: A Muslim is one who embraces the teaching of Muhammad as the true religion, or one who, although he acknowledges that Christ has come, does not hold him to be the true and only mediator, nor is he baptised into his name. And these are about all the many and varied names of superstitions and blasphemies.

units.la: CAP. IIII. Quibus rebus hæresis & hæreticus fere comparentur.
units.tr: CHAPTER IIII. By what things heresy and the heretic are commonly described.

units.la: Bseruari[?] autem multa possunt, quibus tū hæreses, tum etiā hæretici cōparan-tur, ex quibus huius mali vis, magnitudo, siue etiā natura commodè cognoscetur. Nos igitur quædam tum ex Dei verbo, tum ex Patribus ipsis, veluti Irenæo, Tertulliano, Epiphanio, Augustino, HistoriaEcclesiastica, & aliis scriptoribus breuiter collegimus. Ac primùm hæresis Helena Græcorum nominatur, quòd dissensiones pariat pro re turpi.Dicitur Pellex Ecclesiæ, quia non est vera sponsa Christi. Deinde varijs animalium generibus cōfertur, quorum naturam & vitium quodam modo repræsentat. Dicitur enim hæresis Cha-mæleon, quia ad nutum principum se fingit: Vipera, quia matrem Ecclesiam occidit: Scorpio, quia cauda & insidiose ferit: Draco squamosus, quia facile non cedit: Aspidis semen, quia venenosa est: Serpens implicatus, quia in sese varias contradictiones habet, & vix deprehendi poterit: Cantharus volitas, quia facile spargitur: Mus araneus, & venenosus, quia clam latet, & nocet cuniculis actis: Fera & Κυνόλλον[?], quia res est tetra & immanis, quæ animas devorat: Σκο-λόπενδρα[?], i. eruca, quia specie tenuis, est tamē no centissima: Sepia, quia iacit atramentū, quo o-mnia inficit, & turbat: Perdix, quia alienis ovis, i. Ecclesiæ, incubat: Simia, quia Christianorum gestus & orationem imitatur: Taurus, quia su-perba quædam res est: Vulpes, quia subdola res est, & astutum figmentum. Comparatur etiam hæresis zizanijs, quia bonum semen enecat: Pa-leæ, quia latet sæpe in Ecclesia cum bono gra-no: Gramini lethali, quòd facile non dignosci-tur: Monti, quia superbit. Torrenti, sive aquæ, quia res est inanis. Dicitur etiam ab effec-tu hæ-resis, Lepra, quia totum hominem inficit & maculat: Venenum, quia morte animis affert. Nau-fragium, quia est amissio salutis: Salum & tem-pestas maris, quia turbat Ecclesiam: Euripus quidā, quia est instabilis. Et hæc fere sunt quib' similes esse dicuntur & hæreses & hæretici, quò res odiosa magis, uti est, nobis quoq; appareat[?].
units.tr: Many things may be noted by which both heresies and heretics are characterised, and from which the force, the magnitude and also the nature of this evil can be readily known. We have therefore briefly gathered some points, both from the Word of God and from the Fathers themselves, such as Irenaeus, Tertullian, Epiphanius, Augustine, the Ecclesiastical History, and other writers. And first, heresy is called Helena by the Greeks, because it produces dissensions in place of a shameful thing. It is called the harlot of the Church, because it is not the true bride of Christ. Next, it is compared to various kinds of animals, which in some way represent its nature and its vice. For heresy is called a chameleon, because it shapes itself at the nod of princes; a viper, because it kills its mother, the Church; a scorpion, because it strikes with its tail and by stealth; a scaly dragon, because it does not readily yield; the seed of an asp, because it is venomous; an entangled serpent, because it contains within itself various contradictions and can hardly be grasped; a flying beetle, because it is easily scattered; a shrew-mouse, and a poisonous one, because it lies hidden secretly and harms by gnawing underground; a wild beast and a mad dog [κυνόλυσσα], because it is a foul and savage thing that devours souls; a scolopendra [σκολόπενδρα], that is, a caterpillar, because although slight in appearance it is most harmful; a cuttlefish, because it throws out ink, by which it stains and disturbs everything; a partridge, because it sits upon another's eggs, that is, those of the Church; an ape, because it imitates the gestures and prayers of Christians; a bull, because it is a certain proud thing; a fox, because it is a crafty thing and a cunning fabrication. Heresy is also compared to tares, because it kills the good seed; to chaff, because it often lies hidden in the Church along with the good grain; to deadly darnel, because it is not easily recognised; to a mountain, because it is proud; to a torrent or a body of water, because it is an empty thing. It is also named from the effect of heresy: leprosy, because it infects and stains the whole man; poison, because it brings death to souls; a shipwreck, because it is the loss of salvation; the sea and a storm at sea, because it disturbs the Church; a certain Euripus, because it is unstable. And these are nearly the things to which both heresies and heretics are said to be similar, so that the hateful thing may appear to us also, as it is, the more plainly.

units.la: CAP. V. Hæresin quæ vitia comitari soleant.
units.tr: CHAPTER V. The vices that usually accompany heresy.

units.la: ÆC autem vitia solent hæreticos comitari; pertinacia, ficta retractatio & dissimulatio; morum & disciplinæ ἀ-ταξία. Ac pertinacia quidem animi, quia illa est quodammodo ipsius hæreseos pars vel potius mater. Et certè vera est hæc Galeni sententia, ὥσπερ ἀεὶ διασπηθέντων κακὸν ἔχειν ἡ περὶ τὰς αἱρέσεως φιλονικίας, ἡ [?] ἐν τοῖς μάλιστα, ἢ [?] διαπονηρευομένη ἐκ ταύτης ἐστὶν ἀπόστασις. Itaque vix illæ sordes abstergūtur, si semel aliquem commacularint, vt exemplo Bardesanis docet Eusebius libro 4. ca. 29. Semel igitur inuecta & suscepta hæresis vix reprimitur postea, vel extinguitur, quò diligentius nobis ab ijs cauendum intelligamus.
