Nam, vt ait Tertullianus, Hæreses mortem æternam, & maioris ignis ardorem inferentes, malunt quidam mirari, quòd hoc possint, quàm deuitare, ne possint. Ficta verò retractatio & dissimulatio res est hæreticis omnibus vsitatissima, & familiaris, vt his verbis docet Clemens Stromat.lib.7. Nonnunquam autem, ait, quumconuincuntur, sua negant dogmata, apertè confiteri erubescentes; quæ se seorsim sic docere gloriantur. Sic enim in omnibus hæresibus videre licet, perseqvendo ipsorum dogmatum nequitias, &c. Ἀ-ταξία verò morû, & omnis disciplinæ contemptus, est etiam hæresèon perpetua comes. Qui enim doctrinam Dei spernit, idem facilè & disciplinam. Hoc verum esse probat Tertullianus his verbis in libro De præscript. aduersus hæreticos. Simplicitatem, ait, volunt esse post rationem disciplinæ, cuius curam apud nos lenocinium vocant. Pacem quoque passim cum omnibus miscent. Ante sunt perfecti catechumeni, quam edocti. Quis fidelis, quis catechumenus, incertum est. Hodie alius episcopus, cras alius: hodie diaconus, qui cras lector: hodie presbyter, qui cras laicus. Ipsæ mulieres hæreticæ, quam procaces, quæ audent docere, contendere, exorcismos agere, curationes repromittere, forsitan & tingere. Cæterum nec suis precibus reuerentiam nouerunt. Notata sunt etiam hæreticorum commercia cum magis, cum circulatoribus, cum astrologis, cum philosophis curiositati scilicet deditis. Doctrina index disciplinæ est. Negant Deum timendum. Itaque libera sunt illis omnia & soluta. Ubi metus in Deum, ibi gratuitas honesta. Item Theodoret. lib.i.hæret.fabul. Quæ autem, ait, ab iis lege lata instituta, & reipsa præstita est impudicitia, vitæque obscoenitas, ne qui in scena quidem educti sunt, vel dicere, vel alios narrantes audire sustinuerint. Hoc a communi præceptore Simone Mago omnes didicerunt, cuius sunt discipuli. Sed & Bernard. Sermo.66. in Cant. Cantic. summos quoque esse hypocritas his verbis ostendit: Non sufficit hæreticos esse, nisi & hypocritæ sint. Hi sunt qui veniunt in vestimentis ouium. Quinam isti prædones? Hi oues sunt habitu, astu vulpes, actu & crudelitate lupi. Neque enim est apud eos virtutes colere, sed vitia colorare quodam quasi virtutum minio. [?Ἀπωλείαν] autem,& mortem æte nā hęreses afferūt,2. Pet. ɜ[?]. v.12. Denique apostasiam tandem vniuersalem[?]
units.tr: These vices usually accompany heretics: obstinacy, feigned retraction and dissimulation, and disorder [ἀ-ταξία] in morals and discipline. Obstinacy of mind comes first, because it is in a way part of heresy itself, or rather its mother. And this saying of Galen is surely true: just as those who are always scattered suffer harm from their contentiousness about heresies, and the apostasy that comes from it grows worse in the most important matters [ὥσπερ ἀεὶ διασπηθέντων κακὸν ἔχειν ἡ περὶ τὰς αἱρέσεως φιλονικίας, ἡ [?] ἐν τοῖς μάλιστα, ἢ [?] διαπονηρευομένη ἐκ ταύτης ἐστὶν ἀπόστασις]. So those stains can scarcely be wiped away once they have soiled someone, as Eusebius shows by the example of Bardesanes, book 4, chapter 29. Once a heresy has been brought in and embraced, then, it is hardly ever restrained or extinguished afterwards, and so we should understand all the more carefully that we must be on our guard against such people. For, as Tertullian says, some would rather marvel that heresies, which bring eternal death and the burning of a greater fire, can do this, than take care to avoid being able to. Feigned retraction and dissimulation, however, is a thing most common and familiar to all heretics, as Clement teaches in these words, Stromata book 7: "Sometimes, when they are refuted, they deny their own doctrines, blushing to confess openly what they boast of teaching in private. For in every heresy one may see this, if one pursues the wickedness of their doctrines," and so on. And disorder [ἀ-ταξία] in conduct, and contempt for all discipline, is also the constant companion of heresies. For whoever despises the teaching of God easily despises discipline as well. Tertullian proves this is true in these words from his book On the Prescription of Heretics: "They want simplicity to come after reason and discipline, whose care among us they call flattery. They also mix peace with everyone everywhere. Their catechumens are made perfect before they are taught. No one knows who is a believer and who a catechumen. Today one is a bishop, tomorrow another; today a deacon, tomorrow a reader; today an elder, tomorrow a layman. Even the heretical women are so bold: they dare to teach, to dispute, to perform exorcisms, to promise cures, and perhaps even to baptize. Yet they show no reverence even for their own prayers." Heretics' dealings with magicians, charlatans, astrologers and philosophers, men given over to mere curiosity, have also been noted. Doctrine is the index of discipline. They deny that God is to be feared; therefore everything is free and loose for them. Where there is no fear of God, there is licence in place of honest liberty. Likewise Theodoret, book 1 of Heretical Fables: "The immodesty and obscenity of life that they have established by law and actually practised are such that even men brought up on the stage could not bring themselves to speak of them, or to listen to others recounting them." All of them learned this from their common teacher, Simon Magus, whose disciples they are. Bernard too, in Sermon 66 on the Song of Songs, shows that they are also supreme hypocrites in these words: "It is not enough for heretics to be heretics unless they are also hypocrites. These are they who come in sheep's clothing. What kind of robbers are these? They are sheep in appearance, foxes in cunning, and wolves in deed and cruelty. For among them it is not a matter of cultivating virtues, but of coloring vices with a kind of rouge of virtue." Moreover, heresies bring destruction [ἀπωλείαν] and eternal death, 2 Peter 2:12.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: Hæreseôn quæ primæ & præcipuæ causæ:quæ secundariæ,& accessoriæ.
units.tr: Of the primary and principal causes of heresies, and of the secondary and accessory ones.

units.la: OC ipsum est quod quærebat tam so-licitè Augustinus, nimirū quid faciat, vt homines sint hęretici. Quod ab illo prętermissum, nos sic breuiter expli-camus. Etsi futuras hęreses pronūtiauit ipse Christus, Matth.24.vti Spiritus sanctus per Paulum,1.Corinth.11.versu 19: & 1.Timoth.4.1. tamen quędam huius mali nascendi & spargendi caussę nobis sunt considerandę, ne tanti veneni & ruinę in Deum culpa transferatur, quę tota penes homines ipsos residet. Ergo hęreseon duplex imprimis causa est, efficiens, & finis. Nam forma est ipse error: materia vero is articulus & caput fidei, in quo peccatur. At efficiens quidem omnium hęreseon causa est etiam duplex. Prima & remotior, Dei scilicet iustissima voluntas, qui sic verbi sui contemptum vlciscitur, & suos probat. Secunda & propinquior, hominum ipsorum naturalis tum rebellio, tum cęcitas: quibus incentiua quędam accedunt ex naturali hominum corruptione accensa & enata:(1.Timoth.2.versu 9:2.Timoth.3.vers.2:Tit.1.versu 16.) Ambitio. Auaritia, Cotetionis studium, Mala conscientia. scili-cet,
units.tr: This is precisely what Augustine sought so diligently, namely, what makes men heretics. Since he passed it over, we explain it briefly as follows. Although Christ himself foretold future heresies (Matt. 24), and the Holy Spirit did so through Paul (1 Cor. 11:19; 1 Tim. 4:1), nevertheless some causes of the origin and spread of this evil must be considered, lest the blame for so great a poison and ruin be transferred to God, when it rests wholly with men themselves. Therefore there is first a twofold cause of heresies, the efficient and the final. For the form is error itself; the matter is that article and head of faith in which the error is committed. The efficient cause of all heresies is also twofold. The first and more remote is the most just will of God, who thus avenges contempt of his Word and tests his own people. The second and nearer is the natural rebellion and blindness of men themselves, to which certain incentives are added, kindled and born from the natural corruption of man (1 Tim. 2:9; 2 Tim. 3:2; Titus 1:16): ambition, avarice, the desire for contention, and an evil conscience.

units.la: Est enim Superbia mater hæreseon[?], Augustinus contra epistolam Manichæorum fundam. cap.6. Bernard. Sermo.65. in Cant. Omnibus vna intentio hæreticis semper fuit, captare gloriam de singularitate scientiæ.
units.tr: For pride is the mother of heresies, as Augustine says in his work against the letter of the Manichaeans, chapter 6; Bernard, Sermon 65 on the Song of Songs: heretics have always had one aim, to catch glory from the singularity of their knowledge.

units.la: Quum igitur hæc vitia vel omnia, vel singula, rebellionem & cæcitatem nostram accenderint, & impulerint, tunc varios errores, variasque in Deum blasphemias humana insolentia non tantum parturit, sed etiam excludit. Aliæ quoque sunt eiusdem mali causæ, velut secundariæ & iis subseruientes, & succenturiantes, quæ enumerantur a Paulo, Ephes. 4. versu 14. veluti Desultoria quædam animi leuitas, quam Κυβεία[?] vocat: Πανουργία[?], id est, malitia, qualis est in iis qui lucrum ex iis rebus captant, quas debebant venerari. Denique & hoc ipsum, quod idem Paulus 1. Thessal. 2. v. 3. 4. 5. ait, huc quoque referri potest. Sunt autem tria, Impostura, vel Tecta, Dolo dicitur. Manifesta, Malignitas. Assentandi studium, Auaritia & quæstus, quæ proculdubio magnas semper hæreses in Dei Ecclesia pepererunt.
units.tr: Therefore, when these vices, either all or singly, have kindled and driven on our rebellion and blindness, then human arrogance not only gives birth to various errors and various blasphemies against God, but also shuts them in. There are other causes of the same evil, secondary ones which serve and support these, and are listed by Paul (Eph. 4:14): such as a restless levity of mind, which he calls kubeia (cheating at dice), and panourgia, that is, malice, such as is found in those who seek gain from the very things they ought to revere. Finally, what Paul says in 1 Thess. 2:3-5 may also be referred here. There are three kinds: imposture, or concealment, which is called deceit; open malice; the desire to please, avarice and profit, which without doubt have always brought forth great heresies in the Church of God.

units.la: Nam propter personas, quas magni faciunt, quidam in hæreses incidunt, vt ait Tertullianus. Contra quos recte excipit idem ipse, Traditor Christi de discipulis fuit, nec etiamsi martyr aut Episcopus lapsus sit a regula fidei, ideo hæreses reses veritatem obtinebunt. Deniq; aliæ & primæ hæreses aliarum & sequentium profemina-trices,& matres sæpe esse deprehenduntur, adeo vt quædam fundamentales hæreses, ex quibus aliæ sunt propagatæ, dici possint, quas septem ex Egesippo enumerat Nicephorus lib.3. cap.7: 4. cap. 2. Augustinus autem eas quinque tantum esse vult, in lib. De quinque hæresibus. Philippus vero Melanchthon lib. 3. Chronic. quatuor,nempe Cerinthianam,quę FiliumDei negat Deum.Ebionianam,quæ ceremonias legales statuit necessarias ad salutem,Marcionitiam, quæ Deum facit causam mali. Et Carpocratianam,quę communionem vxorum,& bonorum inducit. Quibus omnibus hoc fuit dogma commune, vt dicerent homines per propria opera iustos esse. Nos autem in nostra hæreticorum arbore, alias omnium hęreseon fundamentales hæreses constituimus,& iustius, vt nobis quidem videtur: de quo tamē sit aliorum iudicium.Et hæc quidem de causa efficiente hęreseon.Finis vero hęreseos est,qui&sophisticę, inquit Clemens libro 1.Stromat.Nam vti sophisticę officium est,contentio:finis vero victoria: ita etiam hęreseos. Duplex tamen à nobis constitui potest,1. Piorum probatio,1. Cor.11.v.19: 2.Impiorū iusta punitio,qui veritati Dei placide obedire & acquiescere noluerunt,2.Thessa. 2. versu 11. De quo vide Augustinum libro De quinque hęresibus,cap.final.Lactant.lib.4.cap.30.Hilar.lib.1.De Trinitat. Facile autem hæreses recipiuntur, quia mellis specie & pietatis veritatisque prætextu nobis obtrudutur, id est, pos poculi, in quo est haeresis eamque propinat, oblinit Satan, ut ait Lucretius fieri, cum absynthia tetra medentes dant aegrotis. Atque de causis haereseon hactenus.
units.tr: For some fall into heresies on account of the persons whom they hold in high esteem, as Tertullian says. Against such people the same author rightly objects: "Christ's betrayer was one of the disciples; nor, even if a martyr or bishop has fallen away from the rule of faith, will heresies therefore obtain the truth." Finally, the first heresies are often found to be the parents and mothers of other and later heresies, so that certain fundamental heresies, from which others have been propagated, may be called such. Nicephorus (book 3, chapter 7; book 4, chapter 2) lists seven of these from Epiphanius. Augustine, however, wants there to be only five, in his book On Five Heresies. Philip Melanchthon, in book 3 of his Chronicle, names four: the Cerinthian, which denies that the Son is God; the Ebionite, which holds that legal ceremonies are necessary for salvation; the Marcionite, which makes God the cause of evil; and the Carpocratian, which introduces community of wives and goods. The common doctrine of all of these was that men are made righteous by their own works. We, however, in our tree of heretics, have set up other fundamental heresies as the roots of all others, and more justly, as it seems to us; yet let others judge this. And so much for the efficient cause of heresies. The end of heresy is, as Clement says in book 1 of the Stromata, sophistic: for just as the office of sophistry is contention, its goal victory, so too with heresy. Yet we may set up a twofold end: (1) the testing of the godly (1 Cor. 11:19); (2) the just punishment of the ungodly, who were unwilling to obey and calmly assent to the truth of God (2 Thess. 2:11). On this see Augustine's book On Five Heresies, the final chapter; Lactantius, book 4, chapter 30; Hilary, book 1 On the Trinity. Heresies are readily received because they are offered to us under the appearance of honey and the pretext of piety and truth; that is, Satan smears the rim of the cup with honey, as Lucretius says is done when physicians give sick people bitter wormwood. And so far concerning the causes of heresies.

units.la: CAP. VII. Haereticorum quae praecipua esse soleant fundamenta; eorumque breuis refutatio & euersio.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII. The foundations on which heretics are usually based, and a brief refutation and overthrow of them.

units.la: Undamenta[?] vero haereseon, quibus eorum rationes vel omnes vel praecipuae innituntur, tria enumerat & recenset Paulus Coloss.2.vers.8. Nimirum: Philosophiam vanam, Humanas traditiones & [illegible, ~9 letters], Ceremonias legales siue Iudaica elementa.
units.tr: The foundations of heresies, on which their arguments rest either entirely or chiefly, Paul enumerates and recounts in Colossians 2:8, three in number: vain philosophy, human traditions, and [illegible, about nine letters], and legal ceremonies or Jewish elements.

units.la: Quibus quarta addi potest, falsa nimirum Scripturę Sacrae interpretatio. Ac quod ad Philosophiam attinet, longe verissima est illa Tertulliani sententia, Patriarchę hereticorum, Philosophi: & in lib. De Præscription. sic ait, Inde Æones (i.ex Philosophis) & formę nescio quę & Trinitas hominis apud Valentinum: Platonicus fuerat. Inde Marcionitis Deus melior de tranquillitate, a Stoicis venerat. Et uti anima interire dicatur, ab Epicureis obseruatur. Et ut carnis restitutio negetur, de una omnium Philosophorum schola sumitur. Et ubi materia cum Deo ęquatur, Zenonis disciplina est. Et ubi aliquid de igneo Deo allegatur, Heraclitus interuenit. uenit. Eædem materiæ apud hæreticos & Philosophos volutantur:iidem tractatus implicantur. Quid vero Athenis cum Hierosolymis? Quid Academiæ & Ecclesiæ? Viderint, qui Stoicum,& Platonicum,& Dialecticum Christianis præferunt. Hactenus Tertullianus. Quod autem ad humanas traditiones, negant hæretici Apostolos omnia sciisse:vel etiam omnia, quæ sciuerint, omnibus tradidisse. Respondet vero eodem libro Tertullian. In utroque, ait, Christum ipsum reprehendunt, qui aut minus instructos, aut parum simplices & synceros Apostolos miserit. Enthousiasmos etiam suos, & suorum authorum miracula prædicant hæretici, itemque de suorum doctorum authoritate multa adiiciunt in erroris commendationem. Quasi & hoc fore prædictum non fit, respondet Tertullianus: venturósque esse falsos doctores, qui magnas virtutes ederent ad fallaciam munien-dam, Matth. 24. Quod etiam ad Legis Ceremonias spectat, eas revocant in usum hæretici, quasi plenum earum corpus & veritas non fuerit in Christo, contra Paulum Coloss. 2. vers. 17. Denique quod ad Scripturas, eas quoque corrumpunt. Nam, ut ait Tertullianus, & post Tertullian. Augustin. contra Adimant. cap. 14. neque eas integras admittunt: neque quas admittunt, illæ sunt ab iis incorruptæ relictæ. Nam illis addunt, vel detrahunt. Neque mirum videri debet, quod Scripturis utuntur, quia & diabolus ipse Scripturarum testimonio detorto usus est aduersus Christum, Matth. 4. Cæterum ad illud quod habent semper in ore, Quærite & inuenietis, Respondet Tertullian. Vnum & certum quiddam constitutum esse à Christo, quod credendum est. Habemus enim Mosen & Prophetas, ad quos remittimur, & Scripturas, Ioann.5. Vnius porrò & certi instituti, infinita inquisitio non est. Itaque in haereticos competit potius illud Pauli, Semper discentes, & nunquam ad cognitionem veritatis perucnientes[?]. id quod est omnino miserrimum. Semper enim fatigan-tur, nec habent, ubi tandem conquiescant. Vnde nec illud à se postulari sibi volunt, Quomodo. Quod & Tertullian. & Chrysostom. annotarunt. Ex superioribus igitur intelligi potest, quę sint haereticorum fundamenta & quomodo aduersus eos præscribi possit. Quæ autem ad diligentiorem eorum refutationem pertinent, dixi-mus copiosè in libello nostro, qui est, De Elenchis haereticor. qui iam editus est.
units.tr: To these a fourth may be added, namely a false interpretation of Holy Scripture. As far as philosophy is concerned, that saying of Tertullian is by far the truest, the patriarch of heretics being a philosopher; he says in his book On Prescription against Heretics: "Hence the Aeons (that is, from the philosophers), and I know not what forms, and the Trinity of man among Valentinus: he had been a Platonist. Hence Marcion's better God of tranquillity had come from the Stoics. And that the soul perishes is maintained by the Epicureans. And that the restoration of the flesh is denied is taken from the one school of all the philosophers. And where matter is equated with God, that is the doctrine of Zeno. And where something is alleged about a fiery God, Heraclitus turns up. The same subject-matter is tossed about among heretics and philosophers; the same discussions are entangled. But what has Athens to do with Jerusalem? What has the Academy to do with the Church? Let those look to it who put the Stoic, the Platonic and the dialectical above Christians." Thus far Tertullian. As for human traditions, the heretics deny that the Apostles knew everything, or even that they handed on to all everything that they did know. Tertullian answers in the same book: "In either case, he says, they accuse Christ himself, who sent Apostles either less instructed or not sufficiently simple and sincere." The heretics also proclaim their own enthusiasms and the miracles of their authors, and they add much about the authority of their teachers in commendation of their error. As if this had not been foretold, Tertullian replies: that false teachers would come, who would perform great powers to fortify their deception, Matthew 24. As for the ceremonies of the Law, the heretics revive them in use, as if the full body and truth of them were not in Christ, against Paul, Colossians 2:17. Finally, as for the Scriptures, they corrupt these too. For, as Tertullian says, and after him Augustine against Adimantus, chapter 14, they admit them neither whole, nor, of those they admit, are they left by them uncorrupted; for they add to them or take away from them. Nor should it seem strange that they use the Scriptures, since the devil himself also used a distorted testimony of Scripture against Christ, Matthew 4. Moreover, as to that saying which they always have on their lips, "Seek and you will find," Tertullian replies: that one fixed and certain thing has been established by Christ, which must be believed. For we have Moses and the Prophets, to whom we are sent back, and the Scriptures, John 5. But of one fixed and certain teaching there is no endless inquiry. Therefore the words of Paul apply rather to the heretics: "always learning and never coming to the knowledge of the truth" (2 Timothy 3:7), which is altogether most wretched. For they are always wearied and have nowhere at last to rest. Hence they do not wish that "How?" be demanded of themselves either. This Tertullian and Chrysostom also noted. From the foregoing, therefore, it can be understood what the foundations of the heretics are and how one may prescribe against them. What pertains to their more careful refutation we have set out at length in our little book, which is entitled On the Refutations of Heretics, and which has already been published.

units.la: CAP. VIII. De haereticis puniendis.
units.tr: Chapter 8. On the punishment of heretics.

units.la: [?]etus & utilis quæstio est, Utrū à magistratu puniendi sint haeretici, qui in errore perstat. Negarunt enim omnino eos esse à magistratu civili puniendos Donatistæ. Augustin. ipse aliquando in libro contra Epistol. Manich. fundam. cap. 1. & 2. sic scripsit, Homines haereticos potius emendandos esse, quam puniendos. Illi, ait, in eos saeviant, qui nesciunt, quanto labore verum inveniatur, & quàm difficilè caveantur errores. Itaque que idem contra Adimant.cap.13.Fraus & malitia, inquit, hæreticorum vel dolenda est, tanquam hominum:vel cavenda[?], tanquam hæreticorum:vel irridenda, tanquam imperitorum & superborum. Et certè in ea sententia primùm fuisse August. ut castigandos à Magistratu hære-[?]ticos negaret, non diffitetur ipse.Sed hanc sententiam postea sapientior factus idem retractauit.Aperté enim postea censuit,scripsitque esse eos puniendos, uti apparet ex ipsius epist.48.50. 204.Tract.ii.in Joan.cap.3.Tertullianus autem contra Gnosticos, jampridem id senserat. Ad officium hæreticos,ait, compelli, non inlici dignum est. Duritia vincenda est, non suadenda. Idem defenditur,statuitúrque 23. quæst. 4. cap. Nimium, & seqq. Idem censet Bernard. epist. 195, non tam fugandum nimirum quàm ligandum hæreticum obstinatum, qui iam cōuictus, neque quiescit, neque resipiscit. & epist. 240. Idem Serm. 66.in Canticum Cantic.Fides suadenda est, non imponenda. Quanquam melius proculdubio coercerentur gladio, illius videlicet qui non sine causa gladium portat, quàm in suum errorem multos traiicere permittantur. Ut Mahumetani censendi aut appellandi non sint, qui hæreticos coercendos, puniendós-que à civili Magistratu esse sentiunt, modò quinam sint verè hæretici, prius intelligatur & definitum sit. Nam & in vita Constant. Magni lib.3. Eufeb. edictum tam pij Imperatoris De hæreticis puniendis commemorat, ne noua quædam sententia & tantùm nostra esse videatur: & vetus Christiána que Ecclesia contra Sa-
units.tr: It is a difficult and useful question whether heretics who persist in error are to be punished by the magistrate. The Donatists, at any rate, altogether denied that such people are to be punished by the civil magistrate. Augustine himself once wrote this in his book against the Epistle of the Manichaeans, chapters 1 and 2: "Heretics are to be corrected rather than punished. Let them rage against those who do not know how much labour it takes to find the truth and how hard it is to avoid error." And in his work against Adimantus, chapter 13, he says: "The fraud and malice of heretics must be lamented as of men, guarded against as of heretics, and laughed at as of the unskilled and the proud." Augustine does not deny that at first he held the view that heretics should not be chastised by the magistrate. But later, having become wiser, he retracted this opinion himself. For afterwards he openly judged and wrote that they are to be punished, as appears from his letters 48, 50 and 204, and from Tractate 2 on John, chapter 3. Tertullian, indeed, against the Gnostics had already long before held this view: "It is fitting that heretics be compelled to duty, not enticed. Hardness is to be overcome, not persuaded." The same is defended and laid down in Causa 23, question 4, the chapter "Nimium" and those following. Bernard holds the same view in letter 195: a stubborn heretic, who, though convicted, neither rests nor repents, should be bound rather than driven away; and in letter 240 and Sermon 66 on the Song of Songs: "Faith is to be urged, not imposed." Yet undoubtedly they would be better restrained by the sword (of him, surely, who does not bear the sword in vain) than be permitted to draw many into their error. Those who hold that heretics should be restrained and punished by the civil magistrate are not to be counted or called Mahometans, provided first it is understood and settled who are truly heretics. For Eusebius, in the life of Constantine the Great, book 3, also records the edict of that most pious emperor concerning the punishment of heretics, so that this opinion may not seem some new notion and only ours. And the ancient Christian Church, against the heretic Samosatenus, implored the help and aid of the emperor Hadrian, although he was a heathen.

units.la: mofatenum hæreticum opem & auxilium A-driani Imperatoris, quanuis ethnici, implora-uit. Denique placuit etiam addere ipsa Melan-chthonis Theologi inter Germanos summi & facile principis de ea re verba, quæ extant in ipsius ad Bullingerum epistola inferta Caluini epiftol. his verbis, Legi etiam, ait, qua de Serueti blasphemijs respondiffis, & pietatem & iudicia ve-ftra probo. Iudico etiam Senatum Geneuensem recte fecisse, quod hominem pertinacem, & non omissurum blasphemias sustulit. Ac miratus sum esse, qui seue-ritatem illam improbent. Hæc doctor ille eximius Philippus, de quo argumento extat præter D. Caluini responsum, liber eruditissimus D. Be-zæ, ad quem lectores remitto. Neque nos insulsę quæstiones Iacobi Simnacę Pacensis Episcopi in Enchirid. inscripto, Iudicium violatæ religionis, mouere debent. Sunt enim rationes quæstionesque ineptissimæ. Interea tamen distinguendum est. Neque enim omnes hæreses pari pœna sunt dignæ: neque etiam semper hæretici omnes capitali supplicio sunt afficiendi, etiam qui dogmatizarunt, vt vocant. Præterea, vt ait Augustinus, interest, quàm facile quis corrigatur: vel quàta[?] pertinacia suum errorem defendat. Itaque hoc totum, quia facti est, relinquendum est cognitioni & iudicio prudentis Magistratus, vt qua pœna dignus sit deprehensus, damnatúsq; erroris quilibet hæreticus, capitisne supplicio, an exilio, an ictu fustiu[?], an tantum multa, definiat. Quod idem Augusti. lib. 3. contra Crefconium cap. 50. ait, Nullis bonis in Catholica hoc placet, si vsq; ad mortem in
units.tr: Finally, I have decided to add the very words on this matter of Philip Melanchthon, the outstanding teacher and by far the chief of the Germans as theologian, which stand in his letter to Bullinger, inserted in Calvin's letters. He writes: "I have read also what you replied concerning the blasphemies of Servetus, and I approve both your piety and your judgements. I also judge that the Senate of Geneva acted rightly in removing a stubborn man who would not stop blasphemy. And I am surprised that there are those who disapprove of that severity." Thus that eminent teacher Philip. On this subject there is, besides Calvin's reply, a most learned book by Beza, to which I refer the readers. Nor should the foolish questions of James Simnacus, bishop of Pace, in his manual entitled "The Judgement of Violated Religion," disturb us. For his reasons and questions are most inept. Meanwhile, however, a distinction must be made. Not all heresies deserve the same penalty, and not all heretics, even those who (as they say) have propagated their doctrine, are always to be subjected to capital punishment. Moreover, as Augustine says, it matters how easily someone is corrected, or how stubbornly he defends his error. Therefore this whole matter, since it is a matter of fact, is to be left to the knowledge and judgement of the prudent magistrate, so that he may determine what penalty the apprehended and convicted heretic deserves: whether death, exile, a flogging, or only a fine. Augustine says the same in book 3 against Cresconius, chapter 50: "It has pleased no good men in the Catholic Church that anyone, even a heretic, be raged against unto death; it has been said more gently than is right. For some heretics may be punished, according to the gravity of their error, even with death, not merely with a fine."

units.la: Lib. 3. contra Crefconium cap. 50. [sic: "si vsq;" printed on the line below] in quenquam, licet hęreticum, sæuiatur: lenius dictum est, quàm oporteat. Possunt enim quidam hęretici pro erroris grauitate etiam morte, non autem tantum multa, puniri. Qui autem veteres patrum errores amplectuntur, vti Papistæ, & iam Mahumetani, eorum honestus error, ait Quintilianus, videtur esse, ut puniendi non censeantur. Contrà tamen, & melius quidem, meo iudicio, Augustin. qui insulsam esse huiusmodi excusationem & ineptam scribit. Perinde enim faciunt, atque si auitum homicidium imitari vellent, & Petri abnegationem, quia vetus est. Quanquam humana quadam commiseratione, & quòd ipsa vetustas erroris malitiam, id est, malam errantis conscientiam, apud homines excusare quodammodo videtur, non puniuntur tam grauiter, quàm puniuntur hęretici, qui de nouo Ecclesiam turbant & emergunt. Atque factum olim esse, ut vetus idololatria non esset impunita, docemur exemplo matris Asæ regis Iudę, quę propterea deposita est de gradu, quanquam pœna capitali non est punita, 1. Regum 15. versu 13. Et hæc quidem nos breuius attingimus, quia extant erudita aliorum, & doctissimorum quidem virorum, de hac quæstione scripta, ad quæ lectores remittimus.
units.tr: Those who embrace the old errors of the fathers, as the Papists do, and now the Mahometans, have, as Quintilian says, an honourable error, so that they are not thought to deserve punishment. On the contrary, and indeed better in my judgement, Augustine wrote that such an excuse is foolish and absurd. For they act just as if they wished to imitate an ancestor's murder, or Peter's denial, because it is old. Yet by a certain human compassion, and because antiquity itself seems in some way to excuse before men the wickedness of error, that is, the bad conscience of the one who errs, they are not punished as severely as heretics are punished, who newly disturb and rise up against the Church. And that old idolatry was once not left unpunished we are taught by the example of Asa's mother, queen of Judah, who was for that reason deposed from her rank, though she was not punished with capital punishment: 1 Kings 15, verse 13. These matters we touch on more briefly, because learned writings of others, and indeed most learned men, exist on this question, to which we refer the readers.

units.la: CAP. IX. De varia diuisione hæresēon[?].
units.tr: CHAPTER IX. On the various division of heresies.

units.la: IAm vero propius ad institutum & opus suscceptum accedamus. Quod ut fiat, varia hæresēon[?], quæ fieri potest, diuisio à nobis proponenda est.Diui-duntur igitur hæreses Authore, ut Simoniani, Basilidiani, vel ab Tempore. (Manichæi[?], &c. Materia.
units.tr: Now let us come closer to our plan and the work we have undertaken. To do this, a division of heresies as varied as possible must be set out by us. Heresies are divided, therefore, by their author, as the Simonians and Basilidians, or by time, or by matter (Manichaeans, etc.).

units.la: Ab authore diuersis nominibus hæreses appellantur: ut in primo Indice nostro demonstratur. A tempore autem sic distinguntur hæreses, ut dicatur Ante Christum. (resis[?]. aliæ fuisse Sub Christo, ut Capernaitarum hæPost Christum passum. In quibus ipsis aliæ sunt aliis priores.
units.tr: Heresies are named after their authors by various names, as is shown in our first Index. Heresies are distinguished by time in such a way that some have existed before Christ, some under Christ, and some after Christ suffered. Among these, some are earlier than others (for example, the heresy of the Capernaites).

units.la: Ac quidem vera est hæc Tertulliani sententia, Vera doctrina, ait, hæreses præcessit. In omnibus enim veritas imaginem & corruptionem antecedit. Itaque id est dominicum & verum, quod prius traditum est. Hactenus ille.Ex media enim Ecclesia extiterunt hæreses velut illius morbi quidam. Nam uti è nucleo mitis oliuæ oleaster asper & sylvestris oritur:ita ex sana & suavi Christi doctrina nascitur acerba hæresis, quæ uti fungus è terra statim existit, quemadmodum ait Irenæus lib .i. cap. 33. Quo au-tem primum tempore post Christum passum extiterint hæreses, quærit Clemens lib.7. Stromat. cuius tamen sententiae non assentior. Omnino enim tardius, quam oportet, hærefcon exortum ille constituit, nempe demum sub Adriano imperatore, nisi fortasse de iis hæresi-bus, quæ cœtus & scholam & successionem habuerunt, quis dictum Clementis accipiat. Sunt autem hæc ipsius Clementis verba: Nam Domini, quæ fuit, ait, in aduentu doctrina cum coepisset sub Augusto, medio tempore Tiberij consummatur. Apostolorum autem eius doctrina vsque ad Pauli ministerium Neronis tempore consummatur. Inferius autem circa tempora Adriani imperatoris fuerunt, qui hæreses excogitarunt, & peruenerunt vsque ad ætatem Antonini natu maioris, vt Basilides, etiamsi Glauciam sibi ascribit magistrum, qui fuit Petri familiaris, &c. At recte Theodor.lib. 1. Hæret. fabul. cap. 1. ait, Non expectauit Satan, vt Apostolorum prædicatio confirmaretur, quod & parabola zizaniorum, & historia illius temporis verbo diuino comprehensa aperte verum esse docet. Hoc autem ipsum in 2. Indice nostro ostendimus.
units.tr: Indeed, this saying of Tertullian is true: "True doctrine," he says, "came before heresies. For in all things the truth precedes the image and the corruption. Therefore that which was handed down first is the Lord's and the true one." Thus far he. For heresies arose from the midst of the Church, as certain sores of that disease. For just as a wild and rough olive-tree grows from the kernel of a mild olive, so from the sound and sweet doctrine of Christ a bitter heresy is born, which, like a mushroom, springs up at once out of the earth, as Irenaeus says in book 1, chapter 33. But at what time first after Christ suffered heresies arose, Clement asks in book 7 of the Stromata, though I do not agree with his opinion. For he places the rise of heresies too late, namely only under the emperor Hadrian, unless perhaps Clement's saying is taken of those heresies which had a congregation, a school and a succession. These are Clement's own words: "For the teaching of the Lord, when it began in his coming, was under Augustus, and was completed in the middle of the reign of Tiberius. But the teaching of the apostles was completed in the time of Nero, up to the ministry of Paul. Later, however, around the times of the emperor Hadrian, there were those who devised heresies, and they reached as far as the age of Antoninus the Elder, such as Basilides, although he ascribes to himself as teacher Glaucias, who was a companion of Peter, etc." But Theodoret, in book 1 of the Heretical Fables, chapter 1, rightly says: "Satan did not wait for the preaching of the apostles to be confirmed," which both the parable of the tares and the history of that time, comprehended in the divine Word, clearly teach to be true. We have shown this very point in our second Index.

units.la: Ex materia denique sic distinguntur hære-fes[?], vt in tertio indice nostro explicuimus, quamquam nō ignoro in epistola Quodvultdei, & in ipsa Augusт.præfatione, ad hæc octo capita hæreses omnes reuocari, vt ad Fidé, Trinitatem, Baptismum, Poenitentiā, Hominem Christum, Deum Christum, Resurrectionem, Nouum & Vetus testamentum referantur: sed nostra ratio fortasse commodior aptiorque censebitur. Vera autem mihi videtur hæc sententia, Primos extitisse eos haereticos, qui se Christos esse di-cerent, id quod fore Dominus ipse noster Iesus Christus praemonuerat, Matt.24. qualis ille Simon Magus. Nam qui Deum Creatorem negarunt, postea extiterunt. Itaq; Tertullianus sic scribit: Nullam inuenimus institutionem inter tot diuersitates peruersitatum, quae de Deo creatore vniuersorum cōtrouersiam mouerit. Nemo alterum Deum ausus est suspicari: facilius de Filio, quam de Patre hęsitabatur, donec Marcion, &c. Plausibilior enim & minus odio-sa erat in obtrudendo nouo hominum mediatore sententia, quam in Deo creatore de gradu deijciendo. Itaque priores de Filio, quam de Patre fuerunt haereses, quanquam qui Filium negarunt, illi certe neque verum Patrem agno-uerunt, quemadmodum Simon ille Magus. Sed vt hunc locum atque haec nostra Prolegomena tandem concludamus, libuit illud Augustini pro coronide adijcere, quod est lib.2. Contra Ad-versar. Legis & Prophetar. cap.12. Post hunc, (ait, de Simone Mago agens) fuerunt nonnulli discipuli eius in eadem impietate, posteriores prioribus succedentes. Quorum in successione quartus extitit Basilides, qui primus apertius ausus est dicere, Deum, quem gens Iudaea coluit, nō fuisse verum Deum. Post istos fuit quidam etiam Carpocrates, qui negauit istum visibilem mundum a summo Deo creatum, sed a quibusdam virtutibus daemoniorum: negans etiam Legem, quae per Mosen data est, Deum dedisse. Cerdon postea surrexit, qui primus inuenisse dicitur duos deos, vnum bonum, alterum malum, longè antequam hęresis Mani-chęorum[?] emersisset, quorū in hoc furioso deliramento error est notior. Huius Cerdonis discipulus Marcion fuit. Hęc Augustinus, quæ cum superiori Tertull. sententia plane consentiunt. Crescente enim Ecclesia creuerunt, annitente Satana, hęreses, & tetriores obstinatio-resque[?] ortæ sunt, etiam post Synodos, & fidem Christianam publicè receptam: plures autem maioriqúe numero succreuerunt, & bono diuini verbi semini adnatę sunt, vt ait Isidorus lib. 6. Etymolog. cap.16. cùm feruore persecutionum durante, in vnum colligi Episcopi, synodique conuenire non potuerunt. Est enim frequens legitimarum synodorum cõuentus agri dominici pastinatio. Sed iam Augustinū ipsum prefari aliquid in futuri sui operis commendationem gestientem audiamus.
units.tr: Finally, heresies are distinguished by matter, as we have explained in our third Index, although I am not unaware that in the letter of Quodvultdeus, and in Augustine's own preface, all heresies are referred back to these eight heads: the Faith, the Trinity, Baptism, Repentance, the Man Christ, the God Christ, the Resurrection, and the New and Old Testament. But our method will perhaps be judged more convenient and suitable. This view seems true to me: that the first heretics were those who said that they themselves were Christs, which the Lord our Jesus Christ had himself foretold, Matt. 24, such as that Simon Magus. For those who denied God the Creator arose later. Therefore Tertullian writes thus: "Among so many varieties of perversity we find no institution which raised a controversy about God the Creator of all things. No one has dared to suspect another God. It was easier to doubt about the Son than about the Father, until Marcion, etc." For the opinion that brings in a new mediator of men was more plausible and less hateful than the opinion that casts the Creator God down from his place. Therefore the heresies concerning the Son came before those concerning the Father; yet those who denied the Son certainly did not acknowledge the true Father either, as Simon Magus did not. But, to conclude this passage and these our Prolegomena, it has pleased me to add by way of crown that saying of Augustine, from book 2 of Against the Adversary of the Law and the Prophets, chapter 12, where, speaking of Simon Magus, he says: "After him there were some disciples of his in the same impiety, the later ones succeeding the earlier. In their succession the fourth was Basilides, who was the first to dare to say more openly that the God whom the Jewish nation worshipped was not the true God. After them there was also one Carpocrates, who denied that this visible world was created by the supreme God, but by certain powers of demons; also denying that the Law given through Moses was given by God. Afterwards arose Cerdo, who is said to have been the first to invent two gods, one good and the other evil, long before the heresy of the Manichaeans emerged, whose error is better known in this mad delusion. Marcion was the disciple of this Cerdo." Thus Augustine, which clearly agrees with the earlier saying of Tertullian. For as the Church grew, heresies grew too, with Satan working hard, and more foul and stubborn obstinacies arose, even after the synods and the Christian faith had been publicly received; and many more, and in greater number, grew up and were sown among the good seed of the divine Word, as Isidore says in book 6 of the Etymologies, chapter 16, when, because the fury of persecutions lasted, the bishops could not be gathered together and synods could not assemble in one place. For the frequent assembling of lawful synods is a tilling of the Lord's field. But now let us hear Augustine himself, eager to say something by way of commendation of his future work.

units.la: DIVI AVRELII Augustini in librum De hæresi-bus ad Quodvultdeum; PRÆFATIO.
units.tr: THE PREFACE of St. Aurelius Augustine to the book On Heresies, addressed to Quodvultdeus.

units.la: QVOD petis sapissimè [?] atque instantissimè, sanctè fili Quodvultdeus{1}, ut de hæresibus aliquid scribam dignum lectione cupientium dogmata devitare contraria fidei Christianæ, & Christiani nominis obumbratione fallentia: scias me olim longè antequam peteres, facere cogitasse atque fuisse facturum, nisi diligenter considerans quale quantumque id esset, ultra meas vires esse sentirem. Sed quoniam fateor nullum mihi ut te instituisse poscendo, in ipsa tamen molesta instantia tua etiam tuum nomen attendi, & dixi, Aggrediar & faciam quod vult Deus. Hoc enim Deum velle confido, sine ad huius operis terminum misericordi fauore perduxe-rit, ut per ministerium lingua meæ tanta huius rei difficultas aut ostendatur tantummodo, aut ipso etiam plenius adiuvante tollatur: quorum duorum quod priore loco posui, jamdiu est quod animo voluo ac revoluo, & quadam meditatione contineor. Quod autem postea dixi, non me accepisse confiteor: & utrum dum hoc ago, ut efficiam, dum peto, dum quaero, dum pulso, sim fortasse accepturus, ignoro: scio me tamen nec petiturum, nec quaesiturum, nec pulsaturum quan-tum sat est, nisi & hunc affectum munere diuinae inspirationis accepero. In hoc igitur opere, quod, te vehementer vrgete, in Dei voluntate suscepi, cernis me vtid peragam, non tam crebrescentibus ad me tuis petitionibus esse cogendum, quàm pijs[?] ad Deum non solum tui, verùm & aliorum fratrum, quos tibi in hanc rem fideles socios potueris inuenire, orationibus adiuuandum. quod vt fiat, has ipsas primas huius laboris mei parteis, vbi est & ista præloquutio, curaui tua charitati, in auxilio Domini, accelerare mittendas, vt propter illa quae restant, noueritis quantum pro me orare debeatis, quicunque nosse potueritis, à me iam fuisse susceptum hoc tam grande negotium, quod à me desideratis impleri. Petis ergo, quod tuae indicant literae, quas ad me dedisti, cum primum à me petere ista coepisti, vt exponam breuiter, perstrikte, atque summatim, ex quo Christiana religio promissa hereditatis nomen accepit: quae haereses fuerint², sint: quos errores intulerint, inferat, quid aduersus catholicam Ecclesiâ senserint, sentiât-de fide, de Trinitate, de Baptismo, de Poenitentia, de homine Christo, de deo Christo, de Resurrectione, de Nouo & Veteri testamento. Istas autem inquisitiones tuas in immensum procedere cum videres, putasti cuiusdam generalitatis adhibendum esse compendium, atque dixisti, Et omnia omnino, quibus à veritate dissentiunt. Deinde addidisti, quae etiam Baptismum habeant, quaeve non habeat: & post quas baptizet, nec tamen rebaptizet, Ecclesia: qualiter suscipiat venientes & quid singulis, lege, authoritate atque ratione respondeat. Haec omnia cum queris vt exponantur à me, miror luculentum ingenium tuum, tot, tantarūmque rerum & sitire veri-tatem, & fastidium iam timendo poscere breuita-tem. Sed vidisti etiam ipse, quod possem hoc loco tuae huius epistolae cogitare: quasi vigilanter occurristi cogitationi meae, dicens, Nec me tanta beatitudo tua credat ineptia, ut non inspiciam quantis & quàm-ingentib. voluminibus opus sit, ut possint ista dissolui. verum hoc ego fieri non expeto: id enim multiplici-ter factum esse non dubito, & tanquam consilium subiiciens, quomodo possit & seruari breuitas & veritas pandi, adiungis ea verba, quae paulo ante iam posui, & dicis, Sed breuiter, perstricte, atque summatim, & opiniones rogo cuiuslibet haeresis poni: & quid contra teneat Ecclesia Catholica, quantum instructionis sa-tis est, subdi. Ecce iterum mittis in longum, non quia dici ista breuiter siue non valeant, siue non debeant: sed quia tam multa sunt, ut quamlibet breuiter dicenda, multas literas flagitent: tu autem ut, velut quodam, inquis, ex omnibus concepto commonitorio, si quis aliquam obiectionem aut conuictionem vbe-rius, plenius, ac planius nosse voluerit, ad opulenta & magnifica volumina transmittatur, quibus a diuer-sis, & praecipuis, inquis, a veneratione tua in hoc ipso constat esse elaboratum. Qua cum dicis, vnum quasi commonitorium de his omnibus te desiderare significa-cas. Audi ergo unde commouearis, quid petas. Opi-niones omnium philosophorum, qui sectas varias con-diderunt, usque ad tempora sua (neque enim plus poterat) sex non paruis voluminibus quidam Celsus absoluit. Nec redarguit aliquem, sed tantum quid sentirent aperuit, ea breuitate sermonis, ut tantum adhiberet eloquii, quantum rei nec laudanda nec vituperanda, nec affirmanda, aut defendenda, sed a-periendá, aperiendæ, indicandæq; sufficeret, cum firme centum Philosophos nominasset: quorum non omnes instituerunt hæreses proprias: quoniam nec illos tacendos putauit, qui suos magistros sine ulla differentione sequuti sunt.
units.tr: You ask me very often and very urgently, holy son Quodvultdeus{1}, that I write something worth reading on heresies, so that those who want to avoid doctrines opposed to the Christian faith, and doctrines that deceive under the cover of the Christian name, may know them. You should know that I had thought of doing this long before you asked, and would have done it, had I not considered carefully how great and how difficult the task is and judged it beyond my powers. But since I admit that I have no claim on you for having asked, I did pay heed, in your troublesome insistence, to your name as well, and I said: I will undertake it and do what God wills. For I trust that this is God's will: that he, in his merciful favour, will bring this work to its end, so that through the ministry of my tongue the great difficulty of this matter is either only shown, or, with his help, is removed altogether. Of these two, the first is what I have long turned over in my mind, and I am occupied with it in some meditation. As for what I said afterwards, I confess that I have not received it; and whether, while I do this, while I ask, seek and knock, I may perhaps receive it, I do not know. Yet I know that I would not ask, seek or knock as much as is enough, unless I also received this desire as a gift of divine inspiration. In this work, then, which I have undertaken by God's will at your strong urging, you see that I shall carry it through not so much because your requests to me keep growing and force me, as because I need the prayers of God, not only of yourself but of the other brothers whom you may find as faithful partners in this matter. So that this may happen, I have taken care to send to your charity, with the Lord's help, these first parts of my labour, where this preface also is, so that, for what remains, you may know how much you should pray for me, and whoever may come to know that I have already taken up this great undertaking which you ask me to complete. So you ask, as your letter to me shows, which you sent when you first began to ask me for these things, that I set out briefly, concisely and in summary, from the time when the Christian religion received the name of the promised inheritance: what heresies there have been and are; what errors they have brought in and bring in; what they have thought against the Catholic Church; what they think about the faith, the Trinity, baptism, repentance, the man Christ, the God Christ, the resurrection, and the New and Old Testament. Seeing that these inquiries of yours would run on without limit, you thought that a summary of some general kind should be used, and you said: and all those things in which they differ from the truth at all. Then you added: which of them also have baptism, and which do not; and whom the Church baptises but does not rebaptise; how she receives those who come to her, and what she answers to each, by law, authority and reason. When you ask that all these things be set out by me, I marvel at your brilliant mind, which both thirsts for the truth about so many and such great matters, and, fearing weariness, asks for brevity. But you yourself also saw what I might think at this point in your letter; you anticipated my thought as if on guard, saying: Let not your great goodness think me so foolish as not to see how many and how large volumes would be needed for these things to be resolved. But I do not desire this to be done that way: I do not doubt that it has been done in many volumes, and, as a suggestion, showing how brevity and truth may both be preserved in the exposition, you add the words I have already quoted, and say: But briefly, concisely and in summary, and I ask that the opinions of each heresy be set out, and what the Catholic Church holds against them, as much instruction as is enough is to be added. See, you again send me into a long undertaking, not because these things cannot or should not be said briefly, but because there are so many that, however briefly they are stated, they call for many letters. You, however, say that, as if from a single memorandum drawn up from all of them, if anyone wishes to know any objection or refutation more fully, more completely and more clearly, he should be referred to the rich and magnificent volumes, by various and outstanding authors, which, you say, were composed with your reverence's approval. When you say this, you make clear that you want a single memorandum on all these things. Hear, then, what has moved you, and what you ask for. The opinions of all the philosophers who founded various sects, down to their own times (for he could not do more), a certain Celsus completed in six not small volumes. He did not refute anyone, but only set out what each thought, in a manner of speech so brief that he used only as much language as sufficed to point out, indicate and show the matter, which was neither to be praised nor blamed, nor affirmed or defended, when he had named one hundred philosophers. Not all of these founded heresies of their own; he thought, however, that those too should not be passed over who followed their masters without any difference.

units.la: Noster vero Epiphanius Cyprius Epifc. abhinc non longe humanis rebus exemptus, de octo-ginta hæresibus loquens sex libros etiam conscripsit, historica narratione commemorans omnia, nulla disputatione aduersus falsitatem pro veritate decertans.
units.tr: Our Epiphanius of Cyprus, bishop, who was taken from human affairs not long ago, speaking of eighty heresies, also wrote six books, recalling everything by historical narrative, and contending for the truth against falsehood with no disputation at all.

units.la: Breues sane sunt libelli, & si in vnum libellum redigantur, nec ipse erit nostris vel aliorum quibusdam libris longitudine comparandus. Huius breui-tatem si fuero in commemorandis hæresibus imitatus, quid a me breuius postulare vel expectare debeas, non habebis: Sed non ibi huius mei laboris summa consistit, quod & tibi, vel me demonstrate vel etiam te praecurrente, poterit apparere, cum hoc fecero. Videbis enim in eo quod supradictus Episcopus fecit, quantum desit operi quod ipse vis fieri, quanto magis quod ego? Tu nanque quamuis breuiter, perstri-ctè atque summatim, tamen vis etiam respondere commemoratis hæresibus, quod ille non fecit.
units.tr: Certainly these little books are brief, and if they were gathered into one little book, not even that would be comparable in length to some of our books or those of others. If I shall have imitated their brevity in recounting the heresies, you will not have what more brief thing you should demand or expect from me. But the chief point of my labour does not lie there; this may become clear to you, either as I show it or as you anticipate it, once I have done this. For you will see in what that bishop did how much is lacking to the work which you want done, and how much more so to what I do. For you, though you ask for brevity, concision and summary, still want to answer the heresies recounted, which he did not do.

units.la: Ego vero hoc magis volo facere, si & Deus velit, vnde possit omnis hæresis & qua nota est, & qua ignota, vitari, & vnde rectè possit quacunque innotuerit, indicari. Non enim omnis error hæresis est, quamuis omnis hæresis, qua in vitio ponitur, nisi errore aliquo, hæresis esse non possit. Quid ergo faciat hæreticum, regulari quadam definitione comprehendi, sicut ego existimo, aut omnino non potest, aut difficillimè potest: quod in processu huius operis declarabitur, si Deus rexerit, atque, id quod intendo, perduxerit disputationem meam. Quid autem prosit ipsa inquisitio, etiamsi non potuerimus comprehendere quo-modo sit definiendus haereticus, suo loco videndum atque dicendum est: nam si hoc comprehendi potue-rit, quis non videat utilitas quanta sit? Erunt ergo prima partes operis huius de haeresibus, qua post Christi adventum atque ascensum aduersus doctri-nam ipsius extiterunt, & utcunque nobis innotescere potuerunt: in posterioribus autem partibus, quid faciat haereticum, disputabitur. Cum ergo Dominus ascenderit in caelum, hi haeretici exorti sunt.
units.tr: I, however, prefer to do this, if God wills: by which every heresy, both known and unknown, may be avoided, and by which whatever has become known may rightly be pointed out. For not every error is a heresy, although every heresy, which is counted as a vice, cannot be a heresy without some error. What makes a man a heretic cannot, as I think, be comprehended by any regular definition, or else only with the greatest difficulty; this will be made clear in the course of this work, if God guides it and brings my discussion to the end I intend. But what use the inquiry itself is, even if we cannot grasp how a heretic is to be defined, must be seen and said in its own place; for if this could be grasped, who would not see how great the usefulness would be? So the first parts of this work will be about the heresies which arose against his teaching after the coming and ascension of Christ, and which have in some way become known to us; in the later parts it will be discussed what makes a man a heretic. Therefore, when the Lord ascended into heaven, these heretics arose.

units.la: 1 Quodvultdeus.) Quodvultdeus, vox composita est, & ex illius seculi moribus affectata, veluti Adeodatus, ut in ipso nomine aliquid augustum homines Christiani prae se ferrent. Fuit autem hic Quodvultdeus Carthaginensis Ecclesiae diaconus Augustino familiaris, qui etiam in eadem fuit Diaconus, antequam Episcopus Hipponensis crearetur. Alius fuit Quodvultdeus de quo Augustinus lib. 3. Contra literas Petiliani cap. 32. Alius item is, de quo facta est mentio in concilio Carthag. qui propter contumaciam ab eodem concilio damnatus est, & Episcopus Centurienfis dicitur, de quo est in cap. 1. Extra, de foro competenti.
units.tr: 1 Quodvultdeus.) Quodvultdeus is a compound word, and, being affected by the customs of that age, like Adeodatus, so that Christian men might display something august in the very name. This Quodvultdeus was a deacon of the Church of Carthage, familiar to Augustine, who had also been a deacon in the same church before Augustine was made bishop of Hippo. There was another Quodvultdeus, of whom Augustine speaks in book 3, Against the Letters of Petilian, chapter 32. There is also another, mentioned in the council of Carthage, who was condemned by that same council for obstinacy, and is called bishop of Centuriae; he is referred to in chapter 1 of Extra, De foro competenti.

units.la: Scriptus autem est hic liber postrema Augustini aetate, ut ipse ait in 2. epi. ad Quodvultdeum, cum libros omnes suos iam retractaret & recognosceret. Itaque non videtur propter occupationes, quod erat pollicitus, implesse. Nam huius operis pars illa postrema deest, in qua quid esset haeresis, quid schisma tradebat Augustinus, itemque quid faciat homines haereticos, reticos, siue illa iniuria temporis amissa est, siue non addita omnino. Nos vero in Prolegomenis, ut potuimus, suppleuimus.
units.tr: This book was written in Augustine's last years, as he himself says in his second letter to Quodvultdeus, when he was revising and reviewing all his books. So he does not seem to have fulfilled, because of his other duties, what he had promised. For that final part of the work is missing, the part in which Augustine set out what heresy is, what schism is, and likewise what should be done with heretics. Whether that part was lost through the damage of time or was never added at all, I cannot say. In the Prolegomena, however, I have supplied it as well as I could.

units.la: 2 Quæ hæreses fuerint, sint..) Hæc sunt ipsius Quodvultdei verba, quæ in prima ipsius ad Augustinum epistola extant. itaque, etsi videri potuit esse glossema, non est tamen.
units.tr: 2 What heresies there have been, or are... These are Quodvultdeus's own words, found in his first letter to Augustine. So although it might seem to be a gloss, it is not one.

units.la: 3 Breues sane sunt libelli.) Hic locus ostendit vel non habuisse tunc in manibus Augustinum, magnum illud Epiphanij volumen, quod ille Panarium inscripsit, in quo prolixe hæreses omnes, de quibus agit, refutare conatus est: vel nondum illud opus Epiphanij ex Græco in Latinum sermonem conuersum fuisse, sed tantum illa paratitla & capita hæresecōn nota, & Latina lingua donata, quæ cuiusque libri tomo & sectioni præfigi solent. Neque vero ex hoc Augustini loco quisquam existimet Panarium esse nothum & supposititum Epiphanij opus. Est enim γνήσιον [?] & germanum. Sed ad rem ipsam & hæresecōn enumerationem, siue catalogum accedamus, Dominum precati, ut ab omnibus istis venenis semper liberemur: sacro autem & puro ipsius verbo tanquam firmissimæ salutis & fidei nostræ ancoræ semper constantérque adhæreamus. Amen.
units.tr: 3 Indeed the little books are brief. This passage shows either that Augustine did not yet have before him that great volume of Epiphanius, which he called the Panarion, in which Epiphanius tried at length to refute all the heresies he deals with, or that Epiphanius's work had not yet been translated from Greek into Latin, and that Augustine knew only those preliminary summaries and lists of heresies, given in Latin, which are usually prefixed to each book and section of it. Nor should anyone conclude from this passage of Augustine that the Panarion is a spurious and fabricated work of Epiphanius. It is genuine [γνήσιον] and authentic. But let us come to the matter itself and to the enumeration, or catalogue, of heresies. Let us pray to the Lord that we may always be delivered from all these poisons, and that we may always and steadfastly cling to his sacred and pure Word as the most firm anchor of our salvation and faith. Amen.

units.la: Haereses ab orbe condito ad Christum Dominum nostrum passum.
units.tr: Heresies from the creation of the world to Christ our Lord's passion.

units.la: Ex Epiphanio, & aliis, per L. Danaeum.
units.tr: From Epiphanius and others, by L. Danaeus.

units.la: VAE ante Christi adventum fuerunt haereses, eae enumerantur, & recensentur numero viginti, quae caeterarum omnium sunt prima velut origo, & stirps. Sed ex iis viginti tamen sunt primae quaedam & praecipuae, & tanquam reliquarum fontes quatuor, nimirum Barbarismus, Scythismus, Hellenismus, Samaritanismus, vel Samaritismus, qui & Pseudoiudaismus. Id quod colligi posse putat Epiphanius ex hoc Pauli loco, qui est Colos. 3. versu 11. <bl>ὅπου οὐκ ἔνι Ἕλλην καὶ Ἰουδαῖος, περιτομὴ καὶ ἀκροβυστία, βάρβαρος, Σκύθης, &c.</bl> Barbarismus appellatur, quod tunc temporis homines nullum communem inter se ducem, cui parerent, haberent: nec communem inter se concordiam, vel viuendi morem sequerentur: sed quisque sibi ipse dux esset, & pro animi sui libito ageret. Hoc tam agreste & ferum vitae genus ipsius humanitatis summa labes & corruptela fuit, & verissima eius societatis, quae inter homines esse debet, labefactatio, & haeresis. Docet enim ipse naturae sensus hominem esse <bl>ζῷον πολιτικόν</bl>, id est, animal gregabile, & sociabile. Quod tamen in tam barbara vitae ratione esse non potest, ubi nemo se ad alium adiungit,nec cum eo commune quicquam habet. Qui igitur primi efferantes naturam ipsam humanam, & delentes eum instinctum, qui mutuo nos inter nos conciliat,ita vixerunt, aut viuere docuerunt, primam inter homines hæresin,primúmque errorem introduxerút, contra naturam ipsam humanam peccantes. Hæc hæresis & pestis generis humani ex Epiphanij sententia durat ab orbis creatione,& ab hominibus propagatis vsque ad tempora, Noe patriarchæ,per decem generationes,& ætates.
units.tr: There were heresies before the coming of Christ. They are listed and counted, twenty in all, and they are the first origin and stock of all the others. Yet among these twenty some are first and chief, and serve as the four fountains of the rest: Barbarism, Scythism, Hellenism, and Samaritanism, or Samaritism, which is also called Pseudo-Judaism. Epiphanius thinks this can be gathered from Paul's words in Colossians 3:11: <bl>[ὅπου οὐκ ἔνι Ἕλλην καὶ Ἰουδαῖος, περιτομὴ καὶ ἀκροβυστία, βάρβαρος, Σκύθης, &c.]</bl> "where there is neither Greek nor Jew, circumcision nor uncircumcision, barbarian, Scythian, etc." Barbarism is so called because at that time men had no common leader whom they obeyed, no common agreement among themselves, and no shared way of living. Each was his own leader and acted as his own inclination pleased. This wild and savage way of life was the greatest blow to humanity itself and the most complete overthrow of that fellowship which ought to exist among men, and so it was a heresy. For nature itself teaches that man is <bl>[zōon politikon]</bl> "a political animal," that is, a creature that gathers in flocks and is sociable. Yet this cannot be so under such a barbarous way of life, where no one joins himself to another and has nothing in common with anyone. Therefore those first men who debased human nature, extinguished that instinct which binds us to one another, and lived thus, or taught others to live thus, introduced the first heresy and the first error among men, sinning against human nature itself. According to Epiphanius' view, this heresy and plague of the human race lasted from the creation of the world, and from the spreading of men, until the time of Noah the patriarch, through ten generations and ages.

units.la: Scythismus fuit aliud viuendi genus,quod etsi agreste quiddam & sœuum haberet in moribus, communem tamen inter quosdam vitæ societatem seruabat,& vnum magistratum vel principem inter se agnoscebant plures,cui subiiciebantur. Hoc vitæ genus à Scythis feris gentibus (quas à Phaleg & Ragau posteris Noe propagatas esse volunt) videtur denominatu,quorum mores & vitæ ratio quanquam communi quodam imperio regitur, sæuitiæ tamen & crudelitatis plena à veteribus existimata est.Et certe habent huiusmodi mores magnos quosdam humanitatis,à qua homo appellatur,nequos,estque verissima eius mansuetudinis, quæ in homine debet inesse,pestis,labes,& hæresis. Hanc autem vitæ rationem à quibusdam hominibus ambitiosè affectatâ,& retentam fuisse,itémque traditam,putat Epiphanius,veluti à Nemroth, Genesis 10. quæ durauerit à temporibus primi diluuij,quod sub Noa contigit, vsque ad turris Babylonicæ ædificationem, & ab eo ipso tempore vsque ad ætatem Tharræ, à quo Thraces appellatos fuisse scribit idé. Fuit autem Tharra pater Abrahami, Gen.ii.
units.tr: Scythism was another way of living. Although it had something wild and cruel in its customs, it kept a common social life among certain people, and several men acknowledged one magistrate or prince among themselves, to whom they were subject. This way of life seems to have taken its name from the Scythian savage nations, whom they hold to have sprung from Phaleg and Ragau, the descendants of Noah. Their customs and way of life, although governed by a certain common rule, were regarded by the ancients as full of savagery and cruelty. Indeed such customs have some great features of humanity, from which man is named, and yet they are the most complete destruction, blemish, and heresy of that gentleness which ought to be in man. Epiphanius thinks that this way of life was ambitiously practised and maintained by certain men, and handed down, as if from Nimrod (Genesis 10). It lasted from the time of the first flood, which happened under Noah, until the building of the Tower of Babel, and from that very time until the age of Terah, from whom, the same author writes, the Thracians were named. Terah was the father of Abraham (Genesis 11).

units.la: Hellenismus, siue Gręcismus, est tertia haeresis. Haec iam non in vitę feritate, & humanitatis violatione fuit: sed in ipsius verae pietatis (quae a Deo Adamo, & ab Adamo Noæ, a Noa autem filiis & posteris per manus tradita fuerat) labe-factatione. Nam Hellenismus dicitur idolorum cultus, & ea superstitio, quam quisque pro commodo & usu vel priuato vel publico inueniebat, & sequebatur, praeter iam receptam & traditam a Deo religionem. Primum enim verus Deus colebatur, isque solus, & sine ullo idolo, vel imagine. Postea imagines erigi coeperunt, & fieri, nec quidem Dei ipsius imagines, sed regum, & honoratorum tantum virorum, qui interierant. Atque eae etiam imagines, primum picturae tantum erat: vt scribit Epiphanius: po-stea vero etiam statuae esse coeperunt, quae lapide & luto, tum deinde auro & argento viuam hominum defunctorum effigiem repraesentabant, & eadem postea sunt cultae. In quam artem & nequitiam potissimum incubuerunt Babylonij, Aegyptij, Phryges: totius autem istius idololatriae primi inuentores fuerunt Hellenes, id est, Graeci. Vnde ea idololatria & superstitio Hellenismus est appellata. Hellenes autem dicti sunt a quodam Hellene, vt quidam volunt: alij ab Elaea.i.oliua, quae Athenis erat. Cuius gentis princeps natio & prima origo fuerunt Ionesi[?]; horum autem sator & primus autor fuit Iauan. Haec haeresis coepit sub initio vitae Tharrae patris Abrahami, vt ait Epiphanius. Durauit autem non tantum usque ad Iudaismum, id est, Legem datam: sed usque ad Christum, & Euágelij prædicationem, quæab Apostolis inter gentes & idololatras facta est.
units.tr: Hellenism, or Grecism, is the third heresy. It did not consist in the savagery of life or the violation of humanity, but in the corruption of true piety itself, which had been handed down by God to Adam, by Adam to Noah, and by Noah to his sons and descendants. Hellenism is the worship of idols and that superstition which each man found and followed for his own convenience, whether private or public, alongside the religion already received and handed down from God. At first the true God was worshipped, and he alone, without any idol or image. Afterwards images began to be set up and made, not images of God himself, but only of kings and honoured men who had died. At first these images were only paintings, as Epiphanius writes; later statues began to be made, which represented the living likeness of the dead in stone and clay, and then in gold and silver, and these were afterwards worshipped. The Babylonians, Egyptians, and Phrygians devoted themselves most of all to this art and wickedness, but the first inventors of all this idolatry were the Hellenes, that is, the Greeks. Hence this idolatry and superstition was called Hellenism. The Hellenes were named, some say, after a certain Hellen; others, after Elaea, that is, the olive tree, which was at Athens. The leading nation of this people, and their first origin, were the Ionians, and their father and first author was Javan. This heresy began in the early life of Terah, Abraham's father, as Epiphanius says. It lasted not only until Judaism, that is, until the giving of the Law, but until Christ and the preaching of the Gospel, which the Apostles carried out among the Gentiles and idolaters.

units.la: Hellenismus autem hic quatuor sectas, uti hydra quædam, i. quatuor præcipua capita produxit, quemadmodum vult Epiphanius, nempe Pythagoreos, sive Peripateticos(Peripateticos enim à Pythagoricis Aristoteles primus diuul-sit)Platonicos, Stoicos, & Epicureos. Hanc eadem totius philosophiæ Hellenicæ diuisionem sequutus est Clemens Alexandrinus lib. 1. Stro-mat. Alij tamen aliter distinguunt, ut Augustin. in libris De ciuitate Dei. Sed hos pacare inter se, aut de ijs latius disputare, non est hic nostri vel otij, vel instituti. Breuiter tantum ex Epi-phanio potius, quam ex Diogene Laertio exponam, quid illi senserint. Pythagorici à Pythago-ra Samio dicti, qui iidem & Peripatetici sunt, ut putat Epiphanius, docent unitatem & pro-uidentiam esse, neque sacrificandum diis. Ani-matis abstinent, & in vino temperantes suos es-se iubent. A lunæ autem orbe ad extimum usque cœlum docent omnia esse immortalia: inferiora autem omnia quæ sunt sub orbe lunæ, mortalia. Animas hominum è corporibus in corpora migrare, etiam in animalium & ferarum cadavera. Silentium per quinque annos præci-piunt discipulis suis, quam vocant κατηχημυθίαν[?], ut docet Aulus Gellius. Demum se Deum ap-pellauit Pythagoras.
units.tr: This Hellenism, like a kind of hydra, put forth four sects, that is, four chief heads, as Epiphanius holds: namely the Pythagoreans, or Peripatetics (for Aristotle first separated the Peripatetics from the Pythagoreans), the Platonists, the Stoics, and the Epicureans. Clement of Alexandria, in the first book of the Stromata, followed the same division of Greek philosophy. Others, however, distinguish differently, as Augustine does in his books On the City of God. But to reconcile these or to dispute about them at length is neither the time nor the purpose of our present work. I shall briefly set out, following Epiphanius rather than Diogenes Laertius, what these men held. The Pythagoreans, named after Pythagoras of Samos, who are also the Peripatetics, as Epiphanius thinks, teach that there is unity and providence, and that one must not sacrifice to the gods. They abstain from animal food, and they order their disciples to be temperate in wine. They teach that all things from the sphere of the moon up to the outermost heaven are immortal, but all things below the sphere of the moon are mortal. They hold that men's souls migrate from body to body, even into the carcasses of animals and wild beasts. For five years they impose silence on their disciples, which they call <bl>[katēchēmythian]</bl>, as Aulus Gellius reports. Lastly, Pythagoras called himself a god.

units.la: Platonici à Platone Atheniensi, qui fuit So-cratis discipulus & auditor, dicuntur. Ij Deum, materiam, & formam, id est, tria rerum omnium p incipia constituunt. Mundum autem ab Angelis & minoribus diis factū esse volunt, & mortalem: animas autem hominum esse ingenitas, immortales & diuinas. Animæ verò tres esse partes siue facultates, Ratiocinantem, Irascentem, Appetentem. Mulieres communes esse oportere docent, nec quenquam propriam vxorem habere in bene constituta republica debere.Retinet & ipsi animorum humanorum è corporibus etiam in ferarum corpora migrationem. Deos etiam multos ex vno extitisse affirmant.
units.tr: The Platonists are named after Plato of Athens, who was a disciple and hearer of Socrates. They set up three first principles of all things: God, matter, and form. They hold that the world was made by angels and lesser gods, and that it is mortal. They say that human souls are unbegotten, immortal, and divine. There are three parts or faculties of the soul: the reasoning, the irascible, and the appetitive. They teach that women ought to be held in common, and that in a well-ordered commonwealth no one should have a wife of his own. They also retain the migration of human souls from bodies into the bodies of wild beasts. They affirm too that many gods have come from one.

units.la: Stoici à Stoa porticu Atheniensi dicti, vbi Zeno Cittiæus eorum author docebat, omnia corporea esse dicunt.Mundum hunc sensibilem Deum esse contendunt. Quidam etiam hunc ipsum igne, tanquam materia, conflatum, & constare. Deum autem esse mentem, qui sit tanquam anima toti[?] huius vastitatis & vniuersitatis, quæ coelo & terra continetur, cuius corpus sit ipse mundus: lumina autem siue oculi sint sydera. Omnium autem carnem interituram esse, animas tamen è corporibus in corpora transfire.
units.tr: The Stoics are named after the Athenian porch, the Stoa, where Zeno of Citium, their founder, taught. They say that all things are corporeal. They maintain that this sensible world is God. Some hold that it is made up of fire as its matter and consists of it. God, they say, is the mind, which is like the soul of this whole vast universe contained by heaven and earth, whose body is the world itself; the lights or eyes of the world are the stars. They say that the flesh of all men will perish, but souls pass over from body to body.

units.la: Epicurei ab Epicuro Atheniensi philoso-pho nominati. Hi indiuidua corpora, quas atomos vocant, constituunt, quæ sint numero infinita & similaria, prima rerum omnium principia. Finem autem bonorum statuunt esse voluptatem corporis. Denique neque Deum, neque prouidentiam Dei esse concedunt. In libro De Epicureis & Stoicis, tom.9.operum Augustini, capite 4. sic distinguuntur Stoici ab Epicureis, quod horum, qui beatam vitam in corpore po-fuerunt, Epicuri tenent principatum. Horum autem qui eandem in anima hominis pofuerút[?], Stoici principes censentur.
units.tr: The Epicureans are named after Epicurus, the Athenian philosopher. They posit individual bodies, which they call atoms, infinite in number and alike, as the first principles of all things. They set the chief good in the pleasure of the body. In short, they grant that there is neither God nor the providence of God. In the book On the Epicureans and Stoics, in volume 9 of Augustine's works, chapter 4, the Stoics are distinguished from the Epicureans thus: the Epicureans, who placed the happy life in the body, hold the leadership of the one party, while the Stoics, who placed it in the soul of man, are considered the leaders of the other.

units.la: Samaritifmus, vel Samaritanifmus à Samaritanis dictus est: qui à Judaismo profectus quidè est,& ante Græcorum hæreses superius enumeratas viguit, post Hellenismum tamen jam in mundo receptum. Cœpit ante tempora Nabucadnezar régis Babyloniorum, post Israelitarum in Assyria captiuitatem. Sunt enim Samaritani Assyriorum coloni, qui in Judæam traducti, Deuteronomium Mosis suscipiunt, quod à captiuis Israelitis (Epiphanius dicit ab Esdra) ad eos missum fuerat. In cæteris sunt Judæis similes, præterquā quòd non abominantur Gentes, vti Judæi: Prophetas etiam, qui post Mosen fuerunt, reiiciunt. Negant carnis resurrectione, & quibusdam abstinent, à quibus nō solent Judæi. Inter Samaritanos autem sunt quatuor hæreses: Gortheni, Seuæi, Effeni, Dosithei. Gortheni festa celebrant, sed alio tempore quàm Seuęi. Consentiunt enim ipsi in tempore festorum cum Judæis. Seuæi à superioribus propter festa dissentiunt. Hi enim ira quadam veteri in Esdram, quòd ab ædificatione urbis Jerusalem ab eo prohibiti essent, quum primum illa post reditum captiuitatis Babylonicæ instau-raretur, tempora festorum mutarunt. Festum enim azymorum post naturale anni initium, quod est apud Judæos in mense Tifri (qui nostro Augusto respondet) agunt. In Autumno autem festum Pentecostes & Tabernaculorum celebrant. In quo à Iudæis discesserunt. Esseni ab utrisque diversi festa celebrant indiscrimi-natim cum iis in quos inciderint, & cum quibus versantur. Id quod faciunt Anabaptistę nostri temporis in Sacramentorum communicatione, siue cum Papistis, siue cum Euangelicis versentur.
units.tr: Samaritismus, or Samaritanismus, is so called from the Samaritans. It arose from Judaism and flourished before the Greek heresies listed above, though after Hellenism had already been received in the world. It began before the time of Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Babylonians, after the captivity of the Israelites in Assyria. The Samaritans are colonists of the Assyrians, who were brought into Judea and received the Deuteronomy of Moses, which had been sent to them by the captive Israelites (Epiphanius says by Ezra). In other respects they are like the Jews, except that they do not abhor the Gentiles as the Jews do. They also reject the prophets who came after Moses. They deny the resurrection of the flesh, and they abstain from certain things from which the Jews do not usually abstain. Among the Samaritans there are four heresies: the Gortheni, the Sevaei, the Esseni and the Dositheans. The Gortheni keep the feasts, but at a different time from the Sevaei, for they agree with the Jews about the timing of the feasts. The Sevaei differ from the others on account of the feasts. Out of some old anger against Ezra, because he had forbidden them to help build the city of Jerusalem when it was first restored after the return from the Babylonian captivity, they changed the times of the feasts. They keep the feast of unleavened bread after the natural beginning of the year, which among the Jews falls in the month Tishri (corresponding to our August). In autumn they celebrate Pentecost and Tabernacles. In this they departed from the Jews. The Essenes, differing from both, celebrate the feasts indiscriminately with those they happen upon and among whom they live. This is what our Anabaptists of the present time do in the communion of the sacraments, whether they associate with the Papists or with the Evangelicals.

units.la: Dofithei in rebus cæteris, ut Samaritani viuunt, Sabbato, Circuncisione, & aliis ceremoniis utentes. Pentateuchum Mosis probant. Superstitiosius autem, quàm cæteri Samaritani, animatis abstinent, & ieiunant assiduè. Virginitatem etiam quidam eorum obseruant: alii sunt abstinentes à quibusdam cibis, ut Monachi nostri temporis. Credunt etiam resurrectionem mortuorum, quod rarum est inter Samaritanos. Horum etiam Tertullianus meminit.
units.tr: The Dositheans live in other matters as the Samaritans do, keeping the Sabbath, circumcision and other ceremonies. They approve the Pentateuch of Moses. More superstitiously than the other Samaritans, they abstain from animate things and fast continually.
