Some of them observe virginity; others abstain from certain foods, like our monks of the present time. They also believe in the resurrection of the dead, which is rare among the Samaritans. Tertullian also mentions them.

units.la: Inter Iudæos verò ipsos, etiam ante Christum, fuerunt hęreses septem, Scribæ, Pharisæi, Sadducęi, Hemerobaptistę, Essęi, Nasachęi (sic enim apud Epiphanium legendum est, & themat is ignoratio fecit, ut apud eundem à scri bis varie hæc eadem vox scriberetur) & Herodiani. Omnium verò prima, & quæ cæterarum hæreseon caput merito censeri potest, post Dei Legem datam, fuit eorum, qui Deum ex animi sui libito & voluntate colere, non ex solo ipsius verbo docuerunt, Deuteronomij 12. versu 12. Sed institutum persequamur. Scribæ igitur, qui & Legis doctores dicti sunt, æmulatores traditionum, quas à senioribus acceperant, fuisse videntur. Mores etiam & ceremonias obseruant, quas non ex Lege habent, sed ipsi sibi imposueimposuerunt,tanquam iustitiæ adipifcendç[?] nouam meliorémque rationem,& Dei cultü sanctiorem,Matth.15.v.1.
units.tr: Among the Jews themselves, even before Christ, there were seven heresies: the Scribes, Pharisees, Sadducees, Hemerobaptists, Essaei, Nasachaei (for so it must be read in Epiphanius; ignorance of Hebrew caused the scribes to write this same word in various ways elsewhere) and Herodians. The first of all, and one that can rightly be regarded as the head of the other heresies after God's Law was given, was that of those who taught that God should be worshipped according to the whim and will of their own minds, and not from his word alone (Deuteronomy 12.12). But let us pursue our plan. The Scribes, who are also called teachers of the Law, seem to have been emulators of the traditions they had received from the elders. They also observe customs and ceremonies which they do not have from the Law, but which they imposed on themselves, as a new and better way of attaining righteousness and a holier worship of God (Matthew 15.1).

units.la: Pharisæi tanquam separati dicuntur. Alij vertunt, Interpretes. Hi exactissimè viuunt, & cæteris meliores pientiorẽsque[?] habentur. Denique exquisitam Iudaicæ legis formam profiteri censebantur[?], Actorum 22.versu.3. Fatentur autem, quemadmodum[?] & Scribæ, resurrectionem mortuorum, & esse Angelos, & Spiritum sanctum. Obseruant autem in vitæ ratione etiam plura, quàm ipsi Scribæ. Abstinent enim cibis quibusdam: virginitatem colunt: bis ieiunant in hebdomada. Sextarios, pocula & mensas suas purgant, & lauant. Et quemadmodum etiam Scribæ, decimas & primitias soluunt de suo. Assiduè precantur. Gestant in habitu signa quædam superstitiosa, veluti in vestis dalmaticæ, vel tunicæ limbo, fimbrias, quæ Phylacteria vocantur. Sunt autem phylacteria vittæ & fila purpurea, quæ in ora & laciniis vestis pendent, vt sint signa susceptæ ad tempus continentiæ. Hi horoscoporum, id est, natiuitatum inspectionem induxerunt, & fatum. Horum authoritas maxima esse cœpit sub Alexandra, regina Iudæorum, vt scribit Sabellicus.
units.tr: The Pharisees are said to be "separated"; others translate the name as "interpreters". They live most strictly and are considered better and more pious than others. In short, they were understood to profess the exact form of Jewish law (Acts 22.3). Like the Scribes, they confess the resurrection of the dead, and that there are angels and the Holy Spirit. In their way of life they observe even more than the Scribes themselves. They abstain from certain foods, cultivate virginity, and fast twice a week. They cleanse and wash their sextarii, cups and tables. And, like the Scribes, they pay tithes and firstfruits from their own goods. They pray continually. In their dress they wear certain superstitious signs, such as fringes on the dalmatic or the hem of the tunic, which are called phylacteries. Phylacteries are bands and purple threads that hang from the edges and hems of the garment, so that they are signs of a continence undertaken for a time. These men introduced the inspection of horoscopes, that is, of nativities, and fate. Their authority became greatest under Alexandra, queen of the Jews, as Sabellicus writes.

units.la: Sadducæi tanquam Iustitiarij vel iusti dicti sunt, vel à Sadoc summo sacerdote. Sunt tamen ex Samaritanorum genere. Mortuorum resurrectionem negant, neque Angelos, neque Spiritum admittunt. In cæteris autem cum Iudæorum doctrina consentiunt, Act.23.v.8:Mat.16.v.1:22.v.23.
units.tr: The Sadducees were called "justiciaries" or "the just", or were named after Sadoc the high priest. Yet they are of the stock of the Samaritans. They deny the resurrection of the dead, and admit neither angels nor spirit. In other matters, however, they agree with the doctrine of the Jews (Acts 23.8; Matthew 16.1; 22.23).

units.la: Hemcrobaptistæ[?]. Hi per omnia sunt Iudæi, hoc unum tamen dogma ratum & feorsim habent, neminem consequi posse vitam æternam, nisi quotidie lauetur.
units.tr: The Hemerobaptists. These are Jews in every respect, yet they hold this one dogma as settled and peculiar to themselves: that no one can attain eternal life unless he washes himself every day.

units.la: Eilæi[?] (quos Offenos vocat Epiphanius, tan-quam fortes, vel constantes) ex verisima interpretatione dicti sunt, quasi sectatores, vel ope-rarij, ab Assa, quòd salutem bonis hominum o-peribus acceptam ferant, non autem Dei gratiæ vel promissionibus. Quanquam alij ab Aza deducunt, quod est contemplari. Hi alijs etiam scripturis utuntur quàm Dei Legè: nullos au-tem ex Prophetis reijciunt & repudiant. Lon-gè Pharisæis excellentiores habentur, vt Euse-bius scribit, & contemplatiui dicti, & Θεωρητικοί[?]. Distribuerunt enim diem in tempora precum, laborum, cibi & potus, quos putant quidam non tantum Theologiæ, sed etiam Medicinæ scholas in sua solitudine & hortis habuisse. Certe rerum contemplationi vacabant. Itaque raro prodibant in publicum, omnino nostris ere-mitis simillimi. De quibus Iosephus libro 18. Antiquitatum cap.2. & lib.2. De bello Iudaico, cap.7. multa scribit. Plinius libr. 5. capite 17. eorum meminit. Apparet eos in extremam Iudeæ oram, ad lacum Asphaltitem, haud procul ab Hiericonte (vbi erant fragrates balsami horti-) se contulisse, & habitasse, vt remoti à conspectu hominum liberius philosopharentur. Hi denique cum Christo congressi non dicuntur.
units.tr: The Elaei (whom Epiphanius calls Offeni, as if "strong" or "steadfast") are named, according to the most likely interpretation, as followers or workers, from Assa, because they hold that salvation is obtained by the good works of men, not by God's grace or promises. Others, however, derive the name from Aza, which means to contemplate. These use writings other than God's Law, yet they reject and repudiate none of the prophets. They are considered far superior to the Pharisees, as Eusebius writes, and are called contemplative, and Theoretici [Θεωρητικοί]. For they divided the day into times for prayer, labour, and food and drink. Some think they had schools not only of theology but also of medicine in their solitude and gardens. Certainly they devoted themselves to the contemplation of things, and so they rarely came out in public, very much like our hermits. Josephus writes much about them in book 18 of the Antiquities, chapter 2, and in book 2 of the Jewish War, chapter 7. Pliny mentions them in book 5, chapter 17. It appears they withdrew to the furthest edge of Judea, to the Lake Asphaltites, not far from Jericho (where the fragrant balsam gardens were), and lived there, so that, remote from the sight of men, they could philosophize more freely. Finally, they are not said to have met Christ.

units.la: Nasachęi[?], qui & destructores vel mortificatores nominantur, omnem carnis esum damnant, vt Carthusiani monachi, & suis etiam prohibent.Animata vero ne attingunt quidem. Vsque ad Mo[?]em, & Iosue filium Naue sanctis Patribus qui in Pentateucho commemorantur, utuntur & ijs credunt, velut Abrahamo, Isaaco, Iacobo, atque etiam superioribus: denique ipsi Mosi, & Aharoni, & Iosuæ. Pentateuchon autem ipsum Mosis esse scriptum negant. Deniq; præ-ter illas Scripturas etiam alias se habere affirmant. Quod si quis potius Natsaraeos vocandos putet, Custodes appellabitur, à verbo Natsar, quod Græci dicunt Nazar.
units.tr: The Nasachaei, who are also called destroyers or mortifiers, condemn the eating of all flesh, like the Carthusian monks, and forbid it to their followers as well. They do not even touch animate things. They use and believe the holy fathers mentioned in the Pentateuch, up to Moses and Joshua the son of Nun: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and even those before them, and finally Moses himself, and Aaron, and Joshua. But they deny that the Pentateuch itself was written by Moses. Moreover, they affirm that they have other Scriptures besides these. But if anyone thinks they should rather be called Natsaraeans, they will be called "Guardians", from the Hebrew word natsar, which the Greeks render as nazar.

units.la: Herodiani, Iudæi erant per omnia. Herodem autem regem Antipatri Idumæi filium aiunt fuisse Christum illum Patribus antiquitus promissum. Nam eum Christi nomine & honore insigniunt. Hi sunt sæpe cum Christo congres-si, ut Pharisæi Matth.22.verf.16. Mar.3.verf. 6: 12.verf.13. Quorum authorem & principem fuisse Iudam quandam Gaulonitem volunt, Iosph.[?] lib.18.Antiquit.cap.2.
units.tr: The Herodians were Jews in every respect. They say that Herod, the son of Antipater the Idumaean, was that Christ promised to the fathers of old, for they honour him with Christ's name and dignity. They often met with Christ, like the Pharisees (Matthew 22.16; Mark 3.6; 12.13). They want their author and leader to have been a certain Judas of Gaulon (Josephus, Antiquities, book 18, chapter 2).

units.la: Non pigüit etiam attexere illa quæ de hæresibus Iudæorum Isidorus libro 8. Etymolo-giarum cap. 4. scribit.
units.tr: It is not tedious to add also what Isidore writes about the heresies of the Jews in book 8 of the Etymologies, chapter 4.

units.la: Vdæi confessores interpretantur. Multos enim ex iis sequitur confessio, quos antea perfidia possidebat. Hebrei tra-sitores dicuntur, quo nomine admonentur, ut de peioribus ad meliora transeant, & pristinos errores relinquant. Pharisæi & Sadducæi inter se contrarij sunt. Nam Pharisæi ex Hebræo in Latinum interpretantur diuisi, eò quòd traditionum & obseruationum suarum[?], quas illi [illegible, ~8 letters] vocant, iustitiam proferunt. Unde & diuisi vocantur à populo, quasi per iustitiam. Sadducæi interpretantur iusti. Vendicant enim sibi quod non sunt. Corporis resurrectionem negant, & animam interire cum corpore prædicant. Hi quinque tantum libros Legis recipiunt. Prophetarum vaticinia respuunt. Essæi (non autem, vt vulgo legitur, Efnæi) vel Effeni dicunt ipsum esse Christum, qui docuit illos omnem abstinentiam. Morbonei (fortasse Masbothei) dicunt ipsum esse Christum, qui docuit illos in omni re sabbatizare. Genistei dicti eò quòd de genere Abrahæ esse se glorientur. Nam cum in Babylonia venisset populus Dei plerique relinquentes uxores suas Babylonicis mulieribus adhæserunt: quidam autem Israelitis tantum coniugijs contenti, vel ex ijs geniti, dum reuersi essent de Babylonia, diuiserunt se ab omni populo, & assumpserunt sibi hoc nomen iactantiæ. Meristei appellati, eò quòd separant scripturas, non credentes omnibus Prophetis, dicentes alijs & alijs spiritibus illos prophetasse. Μέρος[?] enim Græcè, Latinè pars dicitur. Samaritæ dicti quòd Legem solùm custodiunt. Nam Prophetas non recipiunt. Hemerobaptistæ, eò quòd quotidie vestimenta sua & corpora lauent. Hactenus Isidorus.
units.tr: The Udaei are interpreted as "confessors", for many of them, who were once held by perfidy, are brought by confession to faith. The Hebrei are called "transgressors", by which name they are admonished to pass from worse things to better and to leave their former errors. The Pharisees and Sadducees are opposed to each other. For the Pharisees are interpreted from Hebrew into Latin as "divided", because they put forward the righteousness of their traditions and observances, which they call [illegible], and so they were called "divided" by the people, as if by righteousness. The Sadducees are interpreted as "just", for they claim for themselves what they are not. They deny the resurrection of the body and teach that the soul perishes with the body. They receive only the five books of the Law and reject the prophetic writings. The Essaei (not, as is commonly read, Efnaei) or Effeni say that Christ himself is the one who taught them all abstinence. The Morbonei (perhaps Masbothei) say that Christ himself is the one who taught them to keep the Sabbath in everything. The Genistei were so called because they boast of being of the stock of Abraham. When the people of God came to Babylon, many of them left their wives and clung to Babylonian women; but some, content only with marriages among Israelites, or born of such, when they returned from Babylon, separated themselves from the whole people and took this name for boasting. The Meristei were so called because they divide the Scriptures, not believing all the prophets, and saying that the prophets prophesied by different spirits. For μέρος [meros] in Greek is pars in Latin. The Samaritans were so called because they keep only the Law, for they do not receive the prophets. The Hemerobaptists, because they wash their clothes and bodies every day. So far Isidore.

units.la: Augustinus, siue quis alius author est eius libelli, qui aduersus quinque hæreses scriptus est. cap.1. enumerat has quinque tanquam omnium præcipuas & potisimas: nempe 1. Paganorum. Hi autem sunt, qui plures deos colunt, ait ille, & ita unum Deum admittunt, ut filium illi sine coniugio fuisse negent. 2 Iudæorum, qui Ie-sum negant esse Christum, & ita unum Deum colunt, ut Christum Filium Dei negent hominem fieri oportuisse ad homines saluandos. 3 Sabellianorum, qui tres personas negant esse in Trinitate. 4 Arianorum, qui Christū Deum esse negant. 5 Manichæorum, qui Christum negant esse hominem, & duo rerum principia constituunt.
units.tr: Augustine, or whoever is the author of that little book written against five heresies, in chapter 1 lists these five as the chief and most powerful of all: (1) of the pagans. These, he says, worship many gods, and admit one God in such a way that they deny he had a son without a wife. (2) Of the Jews, who deny that Jesus is the Christ, and worship one God in such a way that they deny that the Son of God had to become man to save men. (3) Of the Sabellians, who deny that there are three persons in the Trinity. (4) Of the Arians, who deny that Christ is God. (5) Of the Manichaeans, who deny that Christ is man, and posit two principles of things.

units.la: Tertullianus autem in lib. De præscriptionibus aduersus hæreticos, vult quatuor tantum fuisse Iudæorum ante Christum natum hæreses & sectas, Dositheos, Sadducæos, Pharisæos & Herodianos, de quibus etiam Euseb. lib. 4. cap. 22. Ergo Scribas, Essæos, Hemerobaptistas, & Nasachæos prætermittit. Alij etiam post Christum passum præter omnes superiores iam dictas, addunt has tres, quas à suis authoribus distinguunt. Theudæ Iudæi. Actor. 5. Hic Prophetam se dixit, qui verbo Iordanem scinderet & sisteret, ut olim. Vixit sub Cyrenio Proconsule & Præfecto Syriæ, Ioseph. lib. 20. Antiqu. cap. 1. Iudæ Galilæi, Actor. 5. Hic Gaulonites fuit & adiuncto sibi Sadduceo Pharisæo dixit omnes alios magistratus Iudæorum tollendos, unum autem Deum pro Domino & Rege habendum. Fuit ex oppido Gamala, Ioseph. 18. Antiqu. cap. 1. Denique addunt Simonis Galilæi, qui sub Coponio Syriæ Præside vixit. Docuit hic nulla esse tributa Romanis pendenda, Ioseph. lib. 2. Belli Iudaic.cap. 7. Sed hi tres videntur potius politici homines vel seditiosi fuisse, quàm in religione hæretici. Et de Iudæorum quidem hæreticis hactenus.
units.tr: Tertullian, in his book On the Prescriptions against Heretics, holds that there were only four Jewish heresies and sects before Christ's birth: the Dositheans, Sadducees, Pharisees and Herodians, about which also Eusebius, book 4, chapter 22. Therefore he passes over the Scribes, Essenes, Hemerobaptists and Nasaraeans. Others, after Christ's passion, add to all the above-mentioned these three, which they distinguish from their founders. (1) Theudas the Jew, Acts 5. He called himself a prophet, who by a word would split the Jordan and make it stand still, as of old. He lived under Cyrenius, proconsul and prefect of Syria, Josephus, Antiquities, book 20, chapter 1. (2) Judas of Galilee, Acts 5. He was a Gaulonite, and, with a Sadducee and a Pharisee joined to him, said that all other magistrates of the Jews should be removed, and that God alone should be held as Lord and King. He came from the town of Gamala, Josephus, Antiquities, book 18, chapter 1. (3) Finally, they add Simon of Galilee, who lived under Coponius, president of Syria. This man taught that no tribute should be paid to the Romans, Josephus, Jewish War, book 2, chapter 7. But these three seem to have been political men or seditious agitators rather than heretics in religion. And so far concerning the Jewish heretics.

units.la: Hæreseōn[?] divisio ab authore & nomine.
units.tr: The division of heresies by author and name.

units.la: H[?]anc partem persequitur hoc opere Augustinus. Diuersam enim diuersarum hæreseon appellationem explicat. Nam quę varietas atque etiam sæpe contrarietas ex materia inter hæreses reperiatur, cum antea dictum est, tum etiam postea in tertio indice nostro apparebit. Ergo hęreses varie denominantur. Id quod vel hic vnus Clementis Stromatei locus, qui est lib. 7. Stromat. ostendet. Ait enim, Ex hæresibus aliæ quidem appellantur ex nomine, vt Valetini, Marcionis, Basilidis. Aliæ à loco, vt Peratici. Aliæ ex gente, vt Phrygum hæresis. Aliæ ex operatione, vt Encratitarū. Aliæ ex propriis dogmatibus, vt Docitarum, & Hæmatitarum. Alię ex ijs quę honorarunt, vt Caianiftæ, & Ophiani. Aliæ ex ijs quę nefarie ausæ sunt, vt inter Simonianos, Eutychitæ. Quanquam vero variis nominibus hæretici sese tum alij ab aliis, tum à vera Ecclesia distinguunt, & ipsam orthodoxam & Catholicā Ecclesiam contumeliosis cognominibus appellat, tamen illi nomen cœtus orthodoxorum ipsum Ecclesię adimere non sunt ausi. Itaque sola Ecclesia vocatur. Unde Augustinus lib. De vtilitate credend.cap. 7. Una est Catholica Ecclesia, ait, cui hęreses alia diversa nomina imponunt, cùm ipsę singulę propriis vocabulis, quę negare nō audent, appellentur, & lib. Contra fundamétal. epistol. Manichęor.cap.4. Tenet, ait, me postre-mo ipsum Catholicę nomen, quod nō sine cau-sa inter tam multas hęreses sic ista Ecclesia sola obtinuit, ut cùm omnes hęretici sę Catholicos dicivelint, quęrenti tamen peregrino alicui, ubi ad Catholicam cōueniatur, nullus hęreticorum vel basilicam suam, vel domum audeat ostende-re. Est autem Catholica Ecclesia, quę Apostolorum doctrinę innititur, non hominum com-mentis, extra quam sunt omnes hęretici. Lactā-tius quoque his astipulatur lib. 4. Institut. Chri-stian. cap. ult. ubi etiam quę sit vera Ecclesia ostendit. Cùm enim, ait, Phryges aut Nouatiani, aut Valetiniani, aut Marcionitę, aut Anthropia-ni, seu quilibet alij nominantur, Christiani esse desierunt, qui Christi nomine amisso, humana & externa vocabula induxerunt. Sola igitur Catholica Ecclesia est, quę verum cultum retinet, &c. Sed ad Augustinum accedamus.
units.tr: Augustine pursues this part in this work, for he explains the diverse naming of diverse heresies. For the variety, and often the contrariety, that is found among the heresies in respect of their subject matter has been mentioned before, and will also appear later, in our third index. Heresies, then, are named in various ways. This is shown by this single passage from Clement of Alexandria, Stromateis, book 7. For he says: "Of heresies, some are named from a person, like the Valentinians, Marcionites and Basilideans; others from a place, like the Peratici; others from a nation, like the heresy of the Phrygians; others from an activity, like the Encratites; others from their own doctrines, like the Docetae and Haematitae; others from those whom they honoured, like the Caianists and Ophians; others from those who dared something wicked, like among the Simonians, the Eutychites." Although heretics distinguish themselves from one another, and from the true Church, by various names, and call the orthodox and Catholic Church itself by abusive nicknames, they have nevertheless not dared to take from the Church itself the name of the assembly of the orthodox. Thus the Church alone is called by that name. Whence Augustine, in the book On the Usefulness of Believing, chapter 7: "There is one Catholic Church," he says, "to which the heresies impose various other names, since each of them is called by its own name, which they do not dare to deny." And in the book Against the Fundamental Letter of the Manichaeans, chapter 4: "The very name of Catholic holds me, which this Church alone has obtained, not without reason, among so many heresies; so that, although all heretics want to be called Catholics, yet when some stranger asks where one meets with the Catholics, none of the heretics dares to show him his basilica or his house." The Catholic Church is that which rests on the teaching of the Apostles, not on the inventions of men, and outside it are all heretics. Lactantius also agrees with these men in book 4 of the Divine Institutes, last chapter, where he also shows which is the true Church. For, he says, when Phrygians, or Novatians, or Valentinians, or Marcionites, or Anthropians, or any others are named, they have ceased to be Christians, since, having lost the name of Christ, they have adopted human and outward names. Therefore the Catholic Church alone is the one that retains the true worship, etc. But let us come to Augustine.

units.la: CATALOGUS HÆRESEΩN, AC PRIMUM Haereses ex commentariis Eusebii & Epiphanii collecta, per D. Aurelium Augustinum Hipponensem Episcopum. CAPUT I.
units.tr: A Catalogue of Heresies, and first the heresies gathered from the commentaries of Eusebius and Epiphanius, by Augustine, Bishop of Hippo. Chapter I.

units.la: Simoniani unde dicti. Erroris autem capita sex praecipua hic enumerantur.
units.tr: Where the Simonians get their name. Six principal points of error are listed here.

units.la: Simoniani à Simone Mago,{1} qui baptizatus à Philippo Diacono (sicut in Actibus{2} Apostolorum legitur) pecunia voluit emere à sanctis A-postolis, ut etiam per impositionem-manus eius daretur Spiritus sanctus. Hic magicis fallaciis deceperat multos. Docebat autem detestandam turpitudinem indifferenter utendi fœmi-nis. Nec Deum fecisse mundum. Negabat etiam carnis resurrectionem. Et asserebat se esse Christum. Itemque Iouem se credi volebat. Mineruam vero meretricem quandam{4} Selenen, quam sibi sociam scelerum fecerat: imaginesque & suam & eiusdem meretricis discipulis suis praebebat adorandas, quas & Roma tanquam deorum simulacra auctoritate publica constituerat. In qua urbe beatus Apostololus Petrus eum vera omnipotentis Dei virtute ex-tinxit. Dixerat enim se in monte Sina Legem Moy-si in Patris persona dediße Iudæis. Tempore Tiberij in Filij persona putatiuè apparuiße: postea se in linguis igneis Spiritum sanctum super Apostolos venisse: Christum autem nec venisse, nec a Iudæis quicquam pertulisse.
units.tr: The Simonians are named after Simon Magus, who, having been baptized by the deacon Philip (as is read in the Acts of the Apostles), tried to buy from the holy Apostles the power to give the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands. He had deceived many by magical tricks. He taught that the shameful practice of using women indiscriminately was not to be condemned. He denied that God made the world. He also denied the resurrection of the flesh. He claimed to be Christ. He also wanted to be believed to be Jupiter, and Minerva, a certain prostitute named Selene, whom he had made his partner in crime. He offered images of himself and of this same prostitute to his disciples to be worshipped, and these were set up by public authority at Rome as images of gods. In that city the blessed Apostle Peter overthrew him by the true power of almighty God. For he had said that on Mount Sinai he had given the Law of Moses to the Jews in the person of the Father. In the time of Tiberius he had appeared in the person of the Son, in appearance only. Later he said that he had come to the Apostles as the Holy Spirit in tongues of fire. But Christ, he said, had neither come nor suffered anything from the Jews.

units.la: Simone Mago.) Hic Simon omnium quæ-sub Euangelio postea secutæ sunt hęresεon fons & parens fuit, quemadmodum Irenæ.lib.1.cap. 30.&Augustin.lib.2.contra aduersar.Leg.&Prophetar.cap.12. tradunt, non tantum primus inter Christianos hæreticus. Vnde illius hæresis, matrix & radix omnium appellatur, a qua omnis ψευδωνυμος Dei cognitio & adulterina initium sumit, quemadmodum idem scribit Irenæus lib.1. cap.20, & 30, & ex eo refert Eusebius lib.1.Histor.cap.13.tam fuit nimirum magus iste idoneum Satanæ instrumentum ad perdendum & fascinandum genus humanum. Augustinus tamen in Psal.54. Capernaitarum errorem, qui corpus Christi fructulatim & corporaliter in sacra Cœna edi, verbaque Christi de corpore suo manducando carnaliter, non spiritualiter accipi oportere censebat, primam hærefin facit, quam tamen nullius alterius erroris fontem constituit, vtpote qui nondum eas controuersias vidisset, quas hæc ætas nostra super sacra Domini Cœna mouet. Quod Augustinus dictum est in Cano. Prima quidem. Diftin.2.De Consecrat. Itaque eam hærefin prætermittit hic Augustinus, tanquam suo seculo infœcundam sterilem. Simonianorum autem caput & stirpem omnium ex totius Ecclesiæ receptæ sententia facit. Ac primum ab eo fonte amarissimo deducti & orti sunt septem alij riuuli, qui primùm in solam Iudææam irruperunt, magnumque illi ad suscipiendam Christi fidem impedimentum attulerunt. Hi autem à suis autoribus ita nominantur, Cicobiani, Dofitheani, Gorthcani, Masbothei, Adrianistæ, Eutychitæ, Canistæ ut refert Theodoret. lib.1. Hæretic. fabular. & Eusebius ex Hegesippo lib.4. Histor. Eccles. cap. qui etsi statim exaruerunt, ex iis alij surculi sunt enati, & ex illis septem Canistæ (qui à moribus turpissimis ita sunt appellati) fuerunt tetriores, quanquam Clemens Alexandr. lib.7. Stromat. putat fuisse Eutychitas, sed errorem subesse in codicibus impressis nemo qui aliorum de iisdem rebus scripta legerit, dubitabit. Fuit autem hic Simon Samaritanus, ex oppido Gython vel Gyttis, qui tempore Epiphanij erat adhuc vicus in Samaria, ut ipse scribit lib.1.& cum eo consentit Iustinus Martyr in priore Apologia: primum homo obscurus, sed qui propter magicas artes claruit, ut sunt homines vanarum & stupendarum rerum cupidi, adeo ut antequam Euangelium illis in regionibus prædicaretur, plurimum etiam in media ipsa urbe Samaria celebraretur: sed miraculis quæ à Philippo, postea verò à Petro fiebat, obstupefactus, maiora, quàm quæ ipse arte illa sanica præstare posset, effecta ab iis edi contemplatus & admiratus, accessit ad religionem & Baptisma Christianum, quod, quemadmodum ait Epiphan. nomine & titulo tenus am-plexus est: ceterum summus semper fuit hypo-crita. Eo tamen nocentior Christianae religioni fuit, quod & quaedam de ea didicisset, & nomen Christianum profitebatur. Coepit autem haec haeresis nō quidem sub ipso Christo, quod tamen sensisse videtur Epiphanius cum ait, ζ[?]μαγος γινεται τις Μάγου [illegible, ~18 letters] εἰς ἀρχὴν ἀπὸ Χριστοῦ ἢ εἰς τοῦ[?] ἁρπαγῆ[?]: sed post Christum & mortuum & in coelum receptum: sed nec proximo post morte Christi anno, quanquam tamen omnium, ut scribit Tertullianus, qui ex Euangelio haeretici esse voluerunt, primus fuit Simon Magus. Nec enim assentior Ioanni Funccio, qui omnia quae à primo capite Actorum Apostolicorum ad nonum usque continentur, anno à morte Chri-sti primo contigisse scribit. Sic igitur supputo. Anno post mortem Christi primo Stephanus protomartyr pro Christi nomine passus est: quo tempore propter persecutionem Hierosolymis excitatam dispersi sunt per Iudaeam & Samariam plures fratres & fideles, Actor.8. inter quos & Philippus unus e septem diaconis, qui cum aliquandiu Samariae praedicasset Euange-lium, missus est Petrus tandem cum Ioanne Sa-mariam. Quod non nisi secundo post Christū mortuum anno accidere potuit. Adhuc erat à partibus Ecclesiae Simon Magus, qui ne ipse statim haeresim illam suam vel fingere vel pro-pagare potuit. sed cum postea se propter mani-festam hypocrisin, suamque artem, quod esset magica, cotemni à pijs & Christianis perspice-ret, nec inter eos recipi posse videret, vt aliquo tamen honesto prætextu pro Christiano & π-πνευματικῷ[?] homine inter ignaros se venditaret, impia illa deliria commentus est. Nam nec cum nisi postquam Samaria excessisset, illa dissemi-nare ausum fuisse scribunt historici Ecclesiasti-ci: sed tunc maxime postquam Romam venit, ubi omnia illo seculo, ut etiam hoc nostro, licebant. Adeò ut non nisi sub initium imperij C. Caligulæ hanc hæresin cœpisse existimem, nec illis assentior qui Simonem Magum sub Tiberio Romam venisse sentiunt: totúmque illud quinquennium quod fuit a morte Christi ad finem imperij Tiberiani ab ea hæresi liberum cóstitit. Ergo sub Caligula cœpit hæc hæresis, circa annum a Christo passo sexto, cum etiam iam Euangelium propagaretur, quia inimicus ille diabolus zizania seminare una cum bono semine in agro Domini statim studuit, Matth.13. vers.24. Diffusa autem est latissimè non quidem ipso Simonianorum nomine, sed interpellato Menandrianorū, Saturnianorum & aliorum. Quotquot enim fuerunt postea hæretici, suas fæces ex hoc cœno hauserunt. Scribit tamen Gregorius Turonensis lib.10. cap. 24. etiam suo seculo & antea sub Martiano Imperatore Constātinopolitano in Gallia repullulasse, adeò nihil tam fœdum est, quod Satan regerere curiosis & veritati Dei non acquiescentibus hominibus non audeat. Perpetuam tamen ut aliæ multæ, successionem & continuam non habuit, tum quod autoritate Apostolorum repressa sit, tum etiam quòd propter absurdissima quæ habebat dogmata, contempta sit & a Christiana fide vel leuiter linitis hominibus irrisa. Quare vana est eorum narratio qui affirmant Petrum, cum hunc videret venena sua ubique spargetem, secutum esse in quascunque ille profectus esset terras, & tandem Romae publice cum eo pro religione Christiana miraculis certasse. Id quod in annum secundum imperij Claudij collocant, quemadmodum Platina. Hoc autem accidisse non potuit. Fuit enim usque ad concilium Hierosolymitanum in Syria Petrus, idest, usq; ad annum Claudij nonum: postea Babylone vixit, (sive illa Chaldaeorum, sive Aegyptiorum accipiatur) unde primam suam Epistolam scripsit. Denique ne in posteriore quidem sua Epistola quam morti iam proximus scripsit, 2.Pet.1. verf.14. Romae meminit. Romae tamen aliquandiu Simonem Magum vixisse, cum Iustino Tertullianus testatur in Apologet. cap.13. cui statua cum inscriptione hac, SIMONI SANCTO DEO, in campo Martio pop.R. dedicauit, ab isto impostore magicis portentis delusus & fascinatus. Nam eae artes sub Tiberio iam sene & Caligula Impp. Romae plurimum inualuerant. Tandem vero cum effecta vanissimae artis vellet ostentare, & per aerem volaret, decidit, & fracto crure statim miserrime periit, vulgi fabula factus, & ἀγύρτης[?] sive praestigiator deprehensus.
units.tr: Simon Magus. This Simon was the source and parent of all the heresies that later followed the Gospel, as Irenaeus (Book 1, chapter 30) and Augustine (Book 2 against the Adversaries of the Law and the Prophets, chapter 12) relate; he was not merely the first heretic among Christians. Hence his heresy is called the mother and root of all, from which every false-named (ψευδωνυμος) knowledge of God and every counterfeit doctrine takes its beginning, as Irenaeus writes in the same place (Book 1, chapters 20 and 30), and Eusebius reports this from him (Book 1 of the History, chapter 13). Certainly this magician was a fit instrument of Satan for destroying and bewitching the human race. Yet Augustine, in his commentary on Psalm 54, holds that the error of the Capernaites, who thought the body of Christ was eaten piecemeal and bodily in the holy Supper, and that Christ's words about eating his body must be taken carnally and not spiritually, is the first heresy. But he does not make it the source of any other error, since he had not yet seen those controversies which our age stirs up concerning the holy Supper of the Lord. This is what Augustine said in the canon Prima quidem, Distinction 2, De consecratione. So Augustine passes over that heresy here, as barren and unproductive for his age. But by the general judgment of the whole received Church, he makes Simon the head and stock of all the Simonians. From that most bitter fountain there sprang and were drawn off seven other little streams, which first burst into Judaea alone and put great obstacles in the way of receiving the faith of Christ. These were named after their authors: Cicobians, Dositheans, Gorthaeans, Masbotheans, Adrianists, Eutychians and Canists, as Theodoret reports (Book 1 of Heretical Fables), and Eusebius from Hegesippus (Book 4 of the Ecclesiastical History, chapter ...). Although these soon dried up, other shoots sprang from them, and of those seven the Canists (so called from their most shameful morals) were the foulest. Clement of Alexandria (Book 7 of the Stromata) thinks they were the Eutychians, but anyone who has read the writings of others on these matters will doubt this, since the error lies in the printed copies. Now this Simon was a Samaritan from the town of Gitto or Gittis, which in Epiphanius's time was still a village in Samaria, as he himself writes (Book 1); Justin Martyr in his first Apology agrees with him. At first he was an obscure man, but he became famous for his magic arts, as men eager for vain and astonishing things do. So much so that, before the Gospel was preached in those regions, he was widely celebrated even in the very city of Samaria. But when he was amazed by the miracles done by Philip, and later by Peter, and saw and admired works done by them that were greater than anything he could achieve by his magical art, he came to the religion and Christian baptism. As Epiphanius says, he embraced the name and title only, but he was always a great hypocrite. Yet he was more harmful to the Christian religion because he had learned some things about it and openly professed the Christian name. This heresy began not under Christ himself, though Epiphanius seems to have thought so when he says (ζ[?]μαγος γινεται τις Μάγου [illegible, ~18 letters] εἰς ἀρχὴν ἀπὸ Χριστοῦ ἢ εἰς τοῦ[?] ἁρπαγῆ[?]), but after Christ had died and been taken up into heaven. Nor did it begin in the year immediately after the death of Christ, although, as Tertullian writes, Simon Magus was the first of all who wished to be heretics from the Gospel. For I do not agree with John Funck, who writes that everything contained from the first chapter of the Acts of the Apostles to the ninth happened in the first year after the death of Christ. I reckon it thus. In the first year after the death of Christ, Stephen the first martyr suffered for the name of Christ. At that time, because of the persecution stirred up at Jerusalem, many brothers and believers were scattered through Judaea and Samaria (Acts 8), among them Philip, one of the seven deacons. After he had preached the Gospel for some time in Samaria, Peter at last was sent with John to Samaria. This could not have happened earlier than the second year after the death of Christ. Simon Magus was still on the side of the Church and could not yet either invent or spread his own heresy. But when he later perceived that he was despised by the godly and Christians because of his manifest hypocrisy and his art, which was magic, and saw that he could not be received among them, he devised those impious delusions so that he might, under some respectable pretext, pass himself off as a Christian and spiritual man among the ignorant. For the ecclesiastical historians write that he did not dare to spread those things until after he had left Samaria, and especially after he came to Rome, where at that time, as also in our own, everything was allowed. So I believe that this heresy began only at the beginning of the reign of Gaius Caligula. Nor do I agree with those who think that Simon Magus came to Rome under Tiberius. The whole five years from the death of Christ to the end of Tiberius's reign remained free from that heresy. So this heresy began under Caligula, about the sixth year after the passion of Christ, when the Gospel was already spreading, because that enemy the devil immediately strove to sow tares along with the good seed in the Lord's field (Matthew 13:24). It spread very widely, not indeed under the name of the Simonians, but under the names of the Menandrians, the Saturnians and others. For all the heretics who came afterwards drew their dregs from this mud. Gregory of Tours (Book 10, chapter 24) writes that in his own century, and earlier under the emperor Martian at Constantinople, it broke out again in Gaul. So nothing is so foul that Satan does not dare to bring it back upon curious men who do not acquiesce in the truth of God. Yet it did not have a continuous and lasting succession, as many others did, partly because it was suppressed by the authority of the Apostles, and partly because, on account of its absurd doctrines, it was despised and mocked by Christian faith and by men of even slight judgment. So the story of those who affirm that Peter, seeing that Simon was everywhere scattering his poisons, followed him to whatever lands he went, and at last contended with him publicly at Rome for the Christian religion by miracles, is empty. They place this in the second year of the reign of Claudius, as Platina does. But this could not have happened. For Peter was in Syria until the council at Jerusalem, that is, until the ninth year of Claudius. Afterwards he lived at Babylon (whether that is taken to mean the Babylon of the Chaldeans or of the Egyptians), from where he wrote his first Epistle. Finally, even in his second Epistle, which he wrote when he was already close to death (2 Peter 1:14), he makes no mention of Rome. Nevertheless, Tertullian bears witness with Justin (Apology, chapter 13) that Simon Magus lived at Rome for some time. There, by the Roman people, he had a statue dedicated to him in the Campus Martius with this inscription: To Simon the Holy God. He was deluded and bewitched in this by that impostor's magical marvels. For those arts flourished greatly at Rome under Tiberius, when he was already old, and under Caligula. At last, wishing to display the results of his most empty art and flying through the air, he fell, broke his leg, and at once died most wretchedly, becoming a story for the common people and being caught as a trickster (ἀγύρτης, that is, a charlatan).

units.la: Deceit autem vox aliqua, qualis, nominati sunt, quae infra cap.5. addita est, sed incuria scribarum videtur praetermissa.
units.tr: There is perhaps some word missing here, such as "they were named" (nominati sunt). It is added below in chapter 5, but it seems to have been left out through the carelessness of the scribes.

units.la: z Actibus.) Locus est Actor. cap.8. v.13. & 18.
units.tr: z Acts.) The passage is Acts 8:13 and 18.

units.la: 18. Ex eo autem quod sacra emere primus iste sub Euangelio tetauit, appellatū est crimen Si-moniæ illud, in quo spiritualis res, qualis sacra-menta, oratio, dignitas & munus aliquod ecclesiasticū, pro pretio terreno & temporali venditur vel emitur. Can. Qui pro pecunia. i.quęst.j. can. Altare. 1. quæst. iij. Quanquam Canonistæ ex Scholasticorum sententia distinguunt, vt emptores quidem rerum spiritualium dicatur Simoniaci: venditores autem Giezitæ à Giezi seruo Elisei Prophetę, 2.Reg.5.vt est apud P.Lombardum lib.4.dist.25. & ibi Durādus quęstio.3[?]. Vide Thomam 2.2*.quæst.100.
units.tr: 18. From the fact that this man was the first under the Gospel to attempt to buy sacred things, the crime called simony took its name. It is the sin in which a spiritual thing, such as the sacraments, prayer, dignity, or some ecclesiastical office, is sold or bought for an earthly and temporal price. See Can. *Qui pro pecunia*, i. quaest. j; Can. *Altare*, 1. quaest. iij. Yet the canonists, following the opinion of the Schoolmen, distinguish: those who buy spiritual things are called Simoniacs, but those who sell them are called Gehazites, after Gehazi, the servant of the prophet Elisha (2 Kings 5), as Peter Lombard has it in book 4, dist. 25, and there Durandus, question 3[?]. See Thomas, 2.2, question 100.

units.la: 3 Docebat autem.) Recenset Augustinus huius sectæ & hæreseos primæ capita quædam præcipua, nō omnia tamen, sed quæ ex Epiphanio in argumēto lib.1.tom.2.& Anacephalæosi collegit. Sunt autem hic sex capita imprimis enumerata: nos alias ex aliis authoribus hypotheses addemus, vt verè appareat eam omnium aliarum fontem fœdissimum fuisse. Omnes autem religionis Christianæ partes attigit Magus iste & subuertere connixus est iam in ipso exordio siue exoriente Euangelij luce. Nam Christiana pietas tradit aut Doctrinam de fide, quæ est de Deo, id est, Ipsa essentia Dei. Personis. Dono illo Dei incomprehensibili, quæ est salus hominum. Morum reformationem & sanctitatem.
units.tr: 3 He taught, moreover.) Augustine recounts certain principal heads of this sect and heresy, though not all of them, but those which he gathered from Epiphanius in the argument of book 1, tome 2, and in the Anacephalaeosis. Six heads are listed here first; we shall add other hypotheses from other authors, so that it may truly appear that this was the most foul fountain of all the others. This Magus attacked every part of the Christian religion and strove to subvert them, already at the very beginning, as the light of the Gospel was rising. For Christian piety teaches the doctrine of faith, which concerns God, that is, the very essence of God; the persons; that incomprehensible gift of God which is the salvation of men; and the reform and holiness of morals.

units.la: Has omnes partes labefactare statim per os impuri istius canis conatus est Satan, adeo ut in hac prima hæresi omnium femina præsemi-nata & præparata fuerint, ut hinc apparebit. Ista enim sunt quæ refert de Simonis dogma-tis hoc loco Augustinus: 1 Se verum deum es-se dixit. 2 Personas nullas reipsa subsistentes in diuina natura esse docuit. 3 Mundum ab Angelis,non a Deo creatum. 4 Christum non venisse,sed se imaginarie passum esse. 5 Car-nis resurrectionem ullam fore negauit. 6 Mo-rum turpitudinem omne, & promiscuum mu-lierum concubitu induxit. Quæ quot & quan-tarum postea hæresceon fundamenta& delinea-menta fuerint, iam examinemus. Postea ad a-lias eius hypotheses accedemus. Quod ad pri-mum caput,de eo Augustino cum Tertulliano, Irenæo, Theodoreto conuenit. Hoc autem di-uinam naturam & essentiam euertit, quæ nihil humanæ & creatæ naturæ simile habere doce-tur passim in Scriptura. Itaque verum Deum Patribus & Patriarchis ignotum fuisse docuit. Hæc una stirps postea multas & infelicissimas propagines habuit.Produxit enim Menandria-nos, Cerinthianos, Nicolaitas, Saturnianos, Basilidianos, qui omnes verù Deum Patribus & Prophetis ignotum fuisse impudentissime affirmarunt.Produxit postea Tertullianistas & Anthropomorphitas,qui diuinâ essentiam hu-manis membris efformarunt. Dedit denique Turcisimi siue Mahumetismi primordialia prin-cipia. Secundus error est,qui Patre,& Filiu, & Spiritum sanctum diuersa tantum esse eiusdem personæ nomina pro diuersa eius operatione docet. Ergo se unum & eundem esse inter Samaritanos Patrem: inter Judaeos Filium: inter gentes Spiritum sanctum. Hoc dogma postea Sabellianos genuit & propagauit, itemque infaustos istos surculos, nimirum Samosatenianos, Montanistas, Praxianos, Photinianos, Priscillianistas, praeterquam quod Judaeorum etiam errorem[?] qui Trinitatem negant, confirmauit tanquam a Christianis ipsis defensum & comprobatum. Tertius error est, Mundum ab Angelis conditum esse, non a Deo. Hic articulum fidei nostræ fundamentum, de Patre creatore euertit, seminauitque præter superiores hæreses etiam Marcionitas & Manichæos, & quia tatum[?] honoris Angelis defert, Angelicos hæreticos peperit, & Ἀγγελολατρείαν[?] induxit, quam damnauit iam sobolescentem suo seculo Paulus Col. 2. Quartus error, Christum non venisse in carnem, sed ipsum Simonem fuisse Christum, qui non vere, sed imaginarie passus sit. Hoc dogma infinitas hydras[?] postea peperit & hæreses teterrimas, quod iam suo seculo natum vidit, & ad uersus illud decertauit Joannes, 1. Joann. 4. v. 3. Proseminauit igitur Valentinianos, Cerdonianos, Marcionitas, Aphthardocitas, Docitas ipsos & Samosatenianos. Turcissimi denique magna fundamenta iecit. Hoc enim ipsum de Christo Turcæ sentiunt. Quintus error, negat carnis resurrectionem, quemadmodum etiam scribit Epiphanius. Hoc scholæ Simonianæ dogma præter iam enumeratas hæreses Basilidianorū, Valentinianorum, Carpocratianorum, etiam Apellitas, & Hierarchitas instruxit & informauit. Quanquam jam cōtrā disputasset copiosis-fimè Paulus 1.Cor.15. Deniq; negādę vitę æter-næ & futurę occasionem dedit. Unde Epicu-reismū, Atheismū, & Libertinismū procreauit. Sextus error, qui quia gratia & fide iustifica-mur, omnem ad vitia fenestrā patefacit, ut do-cet ex Simonianorum sententia Theodoretus, Basilidianos, Gnosticos, Manichæos, Aetia-nos, Eunomianos, & homines [?]ἐμπνευστικῆς turpis-simos, quos Petrus vocat, induxit in Eccle-siam Dei, adversus quos & Petrus ipse 2.Petri 2. & Judas in sua epistola, de qua ipsa peruersa gratiæ Dei interpretatione conqueritur Paulus Rom. 3. versu 8. & à scortatione abstinen-dum esse contra Simonis decreta jam soboles-censia monet concilium Apostolorum Actor. 15. versu 29. Hanc turpitudinem Mahumetani sunt amplexi. Ad has autem Simonianorū hy-potheses addunt alij alias. Irenæus hanc 7, Magię & incantationum, & exorcismorum diaboli-corum vsum, lib.1.cap.30. Theodoretus hanc 8, Idololatriam apud eos fuisse rem [?]ἀδιάφορον, & quam cum Euangelij professione sequi se posse & miscere contenderent contra præce-ptum Pauli 1.Corinth.8.& 10.versu 21. Epipha-nius has etiam adiicit, 9 Menstrua fœmina-rum ad sua sacra fœdissimè adhibuisse: quod & Gnostici & Manichæi sequuti sunt. 10 Nomina barbara Angelis indiderunt, quos à se per pleromata in Helena sua procreatos dixit Si-mon. Unde Æones & pleromata Valentinia-norum nata sunt, 11 Legem Mosis non esse Dei, sed infaustæ & sinistræ cuiusdam virtutis inuen-
units.tr: Satan immediately tried, through the mouth of this impure dog, to shake all these parts, so that in this first heresy the seeds of all the others were sown and prepared, as will appear from what follows. For these are the doctrines of Simon which Augustine sets out in this place: (1) He said that he was the true God. (2) He taught that no persons subsisting in reality exist in the divine nature. (3) That the world was created by Angels, not by God. (4) That Christ did not come in the flesh, but suffered only in appearance. (5) He denied that there would be any resurrection of the flesh. (6) He introduced complete moral depravity and indiscriminate intercourse with women. How many and how great foundations and outlines of later heresies these were, we shall now examine. Afterwards we shall come to his other hypotheses. As for the first head, Augustine agrees on this with Tertullian, Irenaeus and Theodoret. This head overturns the divine nature and essence, which Scripture everywhere teaches has nothing like human and created nature. Thus he taught that the true God was unknown to the Fathers and Patriarchs. This one stock afterwards bore many and most unhappy offshoots. For it produced the Menandrians, Cerinthians, Nicolaitans, Saturnians and Basilidians, who all most shamelessly affirmed that the true God was unknown to the Fathers and Prophets. It afterwards produced the Tertullianists and Anthropomorphites, who shaped the divine essence after human members. Finally it gave the first beginnings of Turkism, or Mahometanism. The second error is that the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are only different names of the same person, according to different operations. Thus he was one and the same person: among the Samaritans the Father, among the Jews the Son, among the nations the Holy Spirit. This dogma later begot and spread the Sabellians, and likewise those unlucky shoots, namely the Samosatenes, Montanists, Praxeans, Photinians and Priscillianists, besides confirming the error of the Jews, who deny the Trinity, as if it had been defended and approved by Christians themselves. The third error is that the world was founded by Angels, not by God. This overturns the foundation of our faith, the article concerning God the Father as creator, and it sowed, besides the earlier heresies, also the Marcionites and Manichaeans. And because it gives so much honour to Angels, it gave birth to Angelic heretics and introduced angel-worship [Ἀγγελολατρείαν], which Paul condemned in Colossians 2, already springing up in his own age. The fourth error: Christ did not come in the flesh, but Simon himself was Christ, and suffered not really but in appearance. This dogma afterwards gave birth to countless hydra-heads and most foul heresies; John, who saw it already born in his own age, contended against it, 1 John 4:3. It therefore produced the Valentinians, Cerdonians, Marcionites, Aphthartodocetes, the Docetae themselves and the Samosatenes. Finally it laid great foundations for the Turks, for the Turks hold this very view about Christ. The fifth error denies the resurrection of the flesh, as Epiphanius also writes. This dogma of the school of Simon, besides the heresies already listed, the Basilidians, Valentinians, Carpocratians, also furnished and equipped the Apellites and Hierarchites. Although Paul had already disputed this most fully against it, 1 Cor. 15. Finally it gave occasion for denying eternal and future life, whence it produced Epicureanism, Atheism and Libertinism. The sixth error, which, because we are justified by grace and faith, opens a window to all vices, as Theodoret teaches from the teaching of the Simonians, introduced into the Church of God the Basilidians, Gnostics, Manichaeans, Aetians, Eunomians, and those most foul men whom Peter calls [ἐμπνευστικῆς?] ... men; against them Peter himself in 2 Peter 2, and Jude in his epistle, complains of this perverse interpretation of God's grace; Paul also complains of it in Romans 3:8; and the council of the Apostles, Acts 15:29, already sprouting in the teeth of Simon's decrees, warns to abstain from fornication. The Mahometans have embraced this foulness. To these Simonian hypotheses others add still others. Irenaeus adds this seventh: the use of magic, incantations and diabolical exorcisms, book 1, chap. 30. Theodoret adds this eighth: that among them idolatry was a matter [ἀδιάφορον] of indifference, and that they claimed they could follow it and mix it with profession of the Gospel, against the precept of Paul, 1 Cor. 8 and 10:21. Epiphanius also adds these: (9) they used women's menstrual blood in their rites, which the Gnostics and Manichaeans also followed; (10) they gave barbarous names to the Angels, whom Simon said were produced by him through the pleromas in his Helena; whence the Aeons and pleromas of the Valentinians arose; (11) they held that the Law of Moses was not God's, but of some unlucky and sinister power, (12) that the Holy Spirit was Simon's Helena. The Priscillianists and Montanus imitated this. (13) The Holy Spirit is not the name of a thing or essence, but of an energy and operation; thus mind, voice and reason are from him alone. The Servetians drew this from the puddles of the Platonists. Plato, Epistle 3 to Dion. (14) The soul is not polluted by vices, but only the flesh; hence the Simonians did not condemn the wicked life of their disciples, nor did the Gnostic heretics. From this it already appears how many dregs have flowed and poured out from this one most vile mud. A great part of these errors was already known in the times of the Apostles. Therefore the Epistles of Peter 2, Jude, and Galatians 5 most sharply inveigh against the heresies which they call of destruction [ἀπωλείας] and against loose morals.

units.la: Note: a few words in the Greek are uncertain and marked [?]; the printed Greek letters should be checked against the scan. inuetum. 12 Spiritum sanctum esse Helenam Simonis. Hoc Priscillianistæ & Montanus sunt imitati. 13 Spiritum sanctum non esse nomen rei & essentiæ, sed energiæ & operationis. Itaque à se uno esse mentem, vocem, & rationem. Hoc Seruetiani & ex Platonicorum lacunis haustum est. Plato Epist.3.ad Dionem. 14 Animâ non pollui vitiis, sed tantum carnem, unde sceleratam discipulorum suorum vitam non damnarunt Simoniani, uti nec Gnostici hæretici. Ex quo iam apparet quot fæces ex hoc uno turpissimo cœno profluxerint & emanarint. Magna horum errorum pars iam temporibus Apostolorum innotuerat. Itaque aduersus hæreses quas appellant ἀπωλείας, & mores dissolutos acerrime inuehuntur 2. Petr. 2. Iud. epistolæ, Galat. 5.
units.tr: ... inuetum. (The text continues from the previous line; the Latin of the scan reads "inventum.") 12 The Holy Spirit is Helena of Simon. The Priscillianists and Montanus imitated this. 13 The Holy Spirit is not the name of a thing or essence, but of energy and operation. Thus mind, voice and reason are from him alone. The Servetians drew this from the puddles of the Platonists. Plato, Epistle 3 to Dion. 14 The soul is not polluted by vices, but only the flesh, whence the Simonians did not condemn the wicked life of their disciples, nor did the Gnostic heretics. From this it already appears how many dregs have flowed and poured out from this one most vile mud. A great part of these errors was already known in the times of the Apostles. Therefore the Epistle of 2 Peter 2 and Jude, and Galatians 5, most sharply inveigh against the heresies which they call of destruction [ἀπωλείας] and against loose morals.

units.la: 4 Selenen.) Alij Helenam vocant, vti Epiphanius & Irenæus & Theodoretus, quæ sit ea ipsa propter quam Troianum bellum susceptum est: & ouis illa perdita propter quam quærendam è cælo descendisset immutata Dei forma, ne ab Angelis qui cuique cælo præsunt, agnoscereatur. Ita os impudens sacro Christi dicto abutebatur, quod est Matth.15. & 18. versu 12. Consentit cum Augustino Eusebius lib.2. cap. 12. Histor. & quum locum ex Irenæo transcripserit, apparet apud Eusebium mendum esse, & pro Selenam, Helenam reponendum. Sed facile fuit ex Ἑλένη imperito scribæ facere Σελήνη, & postea σελήνην [?]. Fuit autem ista Tyrium scortum quod è telonio abs se abductum habuit in deliciis Simonis Magus, quam ut omnibus commendaret, vti suam Ægeriā Numa Pompilius, deam & Spiritum sanctum, & ἔννοιαν[?] diuinam appellabat, & esse affirmabat: ex qua Angelos procreari, adeò nihil est frontis in tam miseris hominibus, quos semel Satan inani gloriæ & lucri cupiditate etiam in media Ecclesia fascinauit.
units.tr: 4 Selene.) Others call her Helena, as Epiphanius, Irenaeus and Theodoret do; she is the very woman for whose sake the Trojan war was undertaken; and the lost sheep for whose seeking he had come down from heaven, his form changed so that he might not be recognised by the Angels who preside over each heaven. Thus the shameless man abused the sacred saying of Christ, which is in Matthew 15 and 18:12. Eusebius, book 2, chap. 12 of the History, agrees with Augustine; and since he has transcribed the passage from Irenaeus, it appears that there is an error in Eusebius, and Helena should be restored in place of Selene. But it was easy for an unskilled scribe to make Σελήνη [Selēnē] out of Ἑλένη [Helenē], and afterwards σελήνην [selēnēn]. This woman was a Tyrian prostitute whom Simon the Magus had taken away from the toll-house and kept among his delights. In order to commend her to everyone, as Numa Pompilius did his Egeria, he called her and declared her to be the divine goddess and Holy Spirit and thought [ἔννοιαν, ennoian]; from her, he said, the Angels were produced. So great is the impudence in such wretched men, whom Satan once bewitched by desire for empty glory and gain, even in the midst of the Church.

units.la: CAP. II. Menandriani cur sic dicti. Erroris autem caput vnum recitatum.
units.tr: Chapter II. Why the Menandrians are so called. One error of theirs is recited.

units.la: Menandriani à Menandro{1} etiam ipso mago, discipulo eius qui mundum asserebat{2} non à Deo, sed ab Angelis factum.
units.tr: The Menandrians, from Menander{1} also the magician himself, disciple of him who asserted that the world was made{2} not by God but by angels.

units.la: 1 Menandro.) Controuersa quæstio est inter Chronologos, vtri priores vixerint & innotuerint Menadriani isti an Nicolaitæ ij de quibus postea idem Augustinus. Multis enim videtur Nicolaitas præcessisse, qui proculdubio sub Ioanne Euangelista & ante illius exilium virus & venenum suum sparserint, Apocalyps.2. versu 6. circa annum imperij Domitiani, vt illi volunt, duodecimum. Sic Ioann. Funccius. Platina etiam antea fuisse scribit, nimirum sub V e-spasiano imperatore septimo eius cōsulatu, qui incidit in annum à Christo passo 45, & sub Clemente primo, Roman.Episcopo, quem volunt successisse Lino. At iidem collocant & reiiciut Menandrianos in annum imperij Domitiani 13. qui est annus à Christo passo sexagesimus fecundus, ut Menandriani sint posteriores Ni-colaitis septemdecim annis ex Platinæ senten-tia & supputatione. Sed hæc falsa est. Primùm enim doceri potest expungendum esse ex albo Pontificum Clementem, nec eum unquam fuisse Episcopum Romanum. Deinde melio-rum authorum, à quibus nec Platina, nec alij discedere debuerunt, calculo, hic Augustini ordo comprobatur, nempe Tertulliani in libro de præscriptio. Irenæi libro 1. cap.21. Eusebij lib.3, cap.26. Epiphan. lib.1. Tom.2. Thcodo-reti, qui præ Platina sunt classici authores, & minus ab illis temporibus remoti. Sunt ergo Menandriani Nicolaitis hæreticis tempore priores: itaque hic suo loco ab Augustino collocati. Dicti autem sunt à Menandro Menandriani vulgò: ab Egesippo autem Menandria-nistæ, ut scribit Eusebius libro 4. cap.22. Sunt enim utrique iidem, primarij illi quidem è Simoniana stirpe surculi, & ex primo & impu-rissimo Simonianorum fonte riui fœtidissimi, nec minus quàm priores horrendi & detestabiles. Fuit autem Menander Simonis Magi & conterraneus & contemporaneus, etsi ætate iunior. Nam, ut ait Epiphanius, aliquanto tempore cum eo vixit, tamen fuit primarius eius discipulus & ipse aperte magus, artesque magicas exercens, baptizatus tamen & baptizans, homo spurcissimus & impiissimus, cuius vitæ exitus quis fuerit nō est annotatum à scriptoribus: & hunc tamen suæ in Christum blasphemiæ pœnas sensisse credibile est. Fuit etiā primus Gnosticorum hæreticorum, qui postea innotuerunt,fons & author,ut scribit Iren. lib. 3.c.4.Romę vixit sub Tito imperatore,quo maximè tempore post mortem Simonis magistri sui cœpit inclarescerę. Eò enim se receperat propter varias afflictæ gentis suæ & Iudaicæ in ipso Iudæ solo calamitates. Fuit Samaritanus ex vico Chabrai,ut ait Theodoret. quem tamē Eusceb.appellat Capparetæā. Cœpit igitur hæc hæresis circa annum à Christo passo 40. quo regnauit Titus. Hæc Simonianorū hæresin,uti serpens serpente & nati viperæ matrem ipsam, absumpsit,ut suo nomine innotesceret,quæ tamen ipsa, ut ait Epiphanius, statim esse desiit, Nam à Saturniana & Basilidiana hæresi deleta est.
units.tr: 1 Menander.) There is a disputed question among the chronologers as to which came first and became better known: these Menandrians or those Nicolaitans of whom Augustine speaks later. Many think the Nicolaitans came earlier, who undoubtedly spread their virus and poison under the Evangelist John and before his exile, Rev. 2.6, in about the twelfth year of Domitian's reign, as they hold. So Johann Funck. Platina also writes that they were earlier, namely under the emperor Vespasian in his seventh consulship, which falls in the forty-fifth year after Christ's passion, and under Clement the First, Bishop of Rome, whom they hold succeeded Linus. But the same writers place and reject the Menandrians in the thirteenth year of Domitian's reign, which is the sixty-second year after Christ's passion, so that the Menandrians come seventeen years after the Nicolaitans, according to Platina's opinion and reckoning. But this is false. For first it can be shown that Clement must be struck from the list of Popes, and that he was never Bishop of Rome. Next, by the reckoning of the better authorities, from whom neither Platina nor the others ought to depart, Augustine's order is confirmed: that of Tertullian in his book De praescriptione, Irenaeus book 1 chapter 21, Eusebius book 3 chapter 26, Epiphanius book 1, volume 2, and Theodoret, who are classic authors before Platina and less remote from those times. So the Menandrians are earlier in time than the Nicolaitan heretics; thus Augustine rightly places them here in their own position. They were commonly called Menandrians after Menander, but by Hegesippus they are called Menandrianists, as Eusebius writes in book 4 chapter 22. Both names refer to the same people: the former indeed are a shoot from the Simonian stock and a stream most foul from the first and most impure fount of the Simonians, and no less horrible and detestable than the earlier heretics. Menander was a fellow countryman and contemporary of Simon the Magus, though younger in age. For, as Epiphanius says, he lived with him for some time, and was his chief disciple, and was himself openly a magician, practising magic arts; yet he was baptized and baptized others, a most filthy and impious man, whose end no writers have recorded; yet it is credible that he suffered punishment for his blasphemy against Christ. He was also the first source and author of the Gnostic heretics, who afterwards became known, as Irenaeus writes in book 3 chapter 4. He lived at Rome under the emperor Titus, and especially in the time after the death of Simon, his master, he began to become famous there, for he had withdrawn thither because of the various calamities of his afflicted nation and of the Jewish land itself. He was a Samaritan from the village of Chabrai, as Theodoret says, though Eusebius calls him a Capparetaean. This heresy therefore began about the fortieth year after Christ's passion, when Titus reigned. Like a serpent devouring a serpent, and like the viper's offspring devouring its mother, this man consumed the Simonian heresy, so that it might become known under his own name; yet that heresy itself, as Epiphanius says, immediately ceased to exist, for it was destroyed by the Saturnian and Basilidian heresies.

units.la: 2 Afferebat.)Partim cum Simonianis Menandrianos consensisse,partim etiam dissensisse testantur unà cum Augustino Tertullianus & Epiphanius. Eadem enim Menander dixit, ait Tertullian. quæ Simon ipse: quicquid se Simon esse dixerat, hæc se Menander esse dicebat,negas habere posse quenquam salutem,nisi in nomine suo baptizatus fuisset. Sed etiam in eo consentiebat cum Simone, Quod mundum non à Deo sed ab Angelis creatū dixerit:Quod Angelos ipsos ex illa ἐννοίᾳ[?] Simoniana à summa virtute procreatos affirmauit : Quod Magiam, concubitum mulierum promiscuum,omnémque merā turpitudinem lubēter amplexus est, tanquā gratiæ Dei & misericordiæ erga homines fructū:Quod deniq; bonos & sanctos mores, qui Lege Dei docentur & præscribuntur, per gratiæ Dei prædicationē, ut iam inutiles & vanū studiū, tolli & antiquari sensit. Sed vnum caput erroris ipsius tantùm persequutus est Augustinus, quòd in superiori haeresi sint alij enumerati. Theodoretus tamen, Irenæus & Euseb. lib.3.ca.26. alias eius hypotheses in quibus dissensit a pestilenti magistro, recessent, in quibus non fuit tamen impius discipulus praeceptore suo sanior aut melior. 1 Negauit summam virtutem, quæ hæc omnia fecisset & contineret & quam se esse Simon dicebat, cognosci posse. Id quod tamen contendebat Simon. 2 Dixit se, non autem Simonem ipsum, esse totius mundi seruatorem, non vnius tantùm Helenæ. Atque hinc intelligitur quàm maturè & neces-sario Dominus suos admonuisset, ne iis crederent qui se Christos esse dicturi erat, Matth.24. v.4.23. Hæc enim fuit prima hæreticorum homi-num post Euangelium prædicari cœptum, vox & coaxatio, vt se in vulgus commendarent, & opes sibi honorésque cumularent. 3 Homi-nes in ipsius nomine esse baptizandos. 4 Ba-ptizatorum in suo nomine, non autem in Chri-sti aut Simonis ipsius nomine, esse tantam dignitatem, vt ipsis Angelis potentiores essent, & immortales hìc manerent. Itaque carnis resurrectionem negabat. Id quod ex malè in-tellecto Pauli loco, qui est Ephes. 6. versu 12. & Rom 8. versu 38. & deprauata iam Baptismi & regenerationis natura ortum est. Ex eodem fonte orta haeresis Hymenaei, de qua Paulus 2. Timoth. 2. versu 18. & fuit sub Nerone circa annum a passo Christo 34. Ita bonus discipulus magna ambitione insatiabilique auaritia ad se
units.tr: 2 He asserted.) Tertullian and Epiphanius, together with Augustine, testify that the Menandrians partly agreed with the Simonians and partly dissented from them. For Menander said the same things as Simon himself, says Tertullian: whatever Simon had said he was, Menander said that he himself was, and he denied that anyone could have salvation unless he had been baptized in his name. But he also agreed with Simon in this: that he said the world was created not by God but by angels; that he affirmed the angels themselves were produced by the highest power from that Simonian [ἐννοίᾳ]; that he gladly embraced magic, promiscuous intercourse with women, and every kind of pure filth, as fruit of the grace and mercy of God towards men; and finally, that he taught that good and holy morals, which are taught and prescribed by the Law of God, were now useless and vain pursuits, and should be removed and abolished through the preaching of the grace of God. But Augustine pursued only one head of his error, because the others are listed in the preceding heresy. Theodoret, Irenaeus and Eusebius, book 3 chapter 26, however, record his other tenets, in which he dissented from his pestilent teacher; yet in these the impious disciple was no wiser or better than his master. 1 He denied that the supreme power which had made and contained all these things, and which Simon said he himself was, could be known; yet Simon contended for this. 2 He said that he himself, and not Simon, was the saviour of the whole world, not of Helen alone. From this one understands how early and how necessarily the Lord warned his people not to believe those who would come saying that they were the Christs, Matt. 24.4, 23. For this was the first voice and croaking of heretical men after the Gospel began to be preached, by which they commended themselves to the common people and heaped up wealth and honours for themselves. 3 That men must be baptized in his name. 4 That the dignity of those baptized in his own name, and not in the name of Christ or of Simon himself, was so great that they would be more powerful than the angels themselves and would remain here immortal. Therefore he denied the resurrection of the flesh. This arose from a badly understood passage of Paul, which is Eph. 6.12 and Rom. 8.38, and from the already corrupted nature of Baptism and regeneration. From the same source arose the heresy of Hymenaeus, concerning which Paul speaks in 2 Tim. 2.18; it was under Nero, about the thirty-fourth year after Christ's passion. Thus this good disciple, with great ambition and insatiable greed, drew to himself

units.la: honores eos rapuit, quos magistro viderat attributos, illiusque nomen prorsus obscurare conatus est.
units.tr: those honours which he had seen bestowed on his master, and tried entirely to obscure his name.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: Saturniniani cur dicti. Erroris autem capita duo praecipua.
units.tr: Why the Saturnians are so called. The two chief heads of their error.

units.la: Saturniniani a quodam Saturnino, qui turpitudinem Simonianam in Syria confirmasse perhibetur: qui etiam mundum solos Angelos septem praeter conscientiam Dei Patris fecisse dicebat.
units.tr: The Saturnians are named from a certain Saturninus, who is said to have confirmed the Simonian filthiness in Syria. He also said that the seven Angels alone made the world, without the knowledge of God the Father.

units.la: Dubitari non potest Saturninum & Basilidem eius socium tempore fuisse Nicolaitis haereticis, Cerinthianis & Ebionitis, posteriores, quanquam tamen hic priore loco recensentur. Sed non unus modo Augustinus, imo omnes tum veteres Ecclesiastici patres, tum historici Ecclesiasticarum rerum, hoc loco constituunt, ut seriem Simonianae haereseos prosequantur & facilius ostendant, quod a Simone primum orta, per hos continuata est & propagata. A Menandro enim, ut inquit Eusebius lib. 4. cap.7. iam coepit fieri biceps Simoniana hydra & haeresis & a se ipsa dividelli[?], quum ex eadem schola profecti Saturninus & Basilides, in diversas tamen sententias de iisdem rebus iuerint, & se ex eodem fonte in duo foedissima diuortia diduxerint. Quod monere fuit necesse, nequis hic ab Augustino scriptum temporum tenere immutatam, aut ignoranter perturbatam existimet. Saturninus autem ab Epiphanio & Theodoreto Saturnilus semper appellatur: à Tertulliano tamen, Eusebio, & Irenæo Saturninus, unde Saturniani, vel Saturniniani, non Saturniniliani dicti. Coepit innotescere temporibus Adriani imperatoris, cum eiusdem blasphemiæ socio Basilide, circa annum imperij Adriani x v. à Christo autem passo centesimum, cum Barco-chaba quidam Judæus, homo seditiosus, in Syria gravissime Christianos iam afflixisset, & dux suæ genti fuisset, atque incentiuum ad corripie-da contra Romanos arma. Unde totius Judaicæ gentis pene internecio accidit, certe inde contigit ea dissipatio & dispalatio per universas orbis regiones, in qua nunc miserrima versatur.
units.tr: There can be no doubt that Saturninus and his companion Basilides belonged to the same time as the Nicolaitan heretics, the Cerinthians and the Ebionites, though they are listed here before them. Not only Augustine but all the ancient fathers of the Church and the historians of ecclesiastical affairs place them at this point, in order to follow the sequence of the Simonian heresy and to show more easily that it began with Simon and was continued and spread through these men. For, as Eusebius says (book 4, chapter 7), the two-headed Simonian hydra, both heresy and schism, began to form with Menander, when Saturninus and Basilides, who came from the same school, went off in different opinions about the same matters, and divided themselves from the same source into two most foul separations. It was necessary to point this out, lest anyone think that Augustine has kept the order of the times unchanged, or disordered it through ignorance. Epiphanius and Theodoret always call Saturninus "Saturnilus," but Tertullian, Eusebius and Irenaeus call him Saturninus, whence the followers are called Saturnians or Saturninians, not Saturnilians. He began to become known in the time of the emperor Hadrian, together with his fellow-blasphemer Basilides, about the fifteenth year of Hadrian's reign, one hundred years after Christ's passion. At that time a certain Jew, Barcochba, a seditious man, had already grievously afflicted the Christians in Syria, and had become a leader of his people and an incitement to take up arms against the Romans. From this came nearly the complete destruction of the whole Jewish nation, and certainly from this came that dispersion and scattering through all the regions of the world, in which they now wretchedly live.

units.la: Fuit autem Antiochenus Saturninus, qui ita cum Basilide officia partitus est, ut ipse in Syria venenum suum efflaret, & eo Syros, homines leues, imbueret, Basilides autem illud in Ægypto spargeret, & vicinis regionibus, ubi jam superstitionum quædam fundamenta jaciebantur, quæ postea confirmata sunt. Durauit autem hæresis Saturninianorum & Basilidianorum aliquo tempore, & viguit donec novis Valentinianorum, qui subtiliores habiti sunt, deliriis & commentis exploderetur, ita nimirum sese mutuò confodientibus hæreticis justo Dei judicio, & extinguentibus. Quare Simonianorum pestis & hæresis prope sola sive suo ipsa nomine sive alieno & interpolato Menandrianorum & Saturninianorum prope per centum annos in orbe gravissime grassata est: postea vero aliis exorietibus sepulta.
units.tr: Saturninus was a native of Antioch, and he divided the work with Basilides in such a way that he himself breathed out his poison in Syria and infected with it the Syrians, a light-minded people, while Basilides scattered it in Egypt and the neighbouring regions, where certain foundations of superstition were already being laid, which were afterwards confirmed. The heresy of the Saturninians and Basilidians lasted for some time and flourished until it was thrown out by the new fancies and inventions of the Valentinians, who were considered more subtle; the heretics thus stabbed one another and destroyed one another by the just judgment of God. Hence the pest and heresy of the Simonians, either under its own name or under that of the Menandrians and Saturninians, a name borrowed and corrupted, raged most severely through the world for almost a hundred years; afterwards it was buried when other sects arose.

units.la: 2 Confirmasse.) Quae fuerint Saturniniani erroris capita, docent imprimis Epiphanius & Theodoretus, quę partim cum superioribus hęresibus consenserunt, partim dissenserunt. Ac quidem cum Simone Mago illa duo communia habuit, quae hic recefet Augustinus: 1 Vt suis discipulis turpiter viuere concederet, quia sola fide & cognitione, quae de ipso esset, salui fierent. 2 Mundum ab Angelis creatum, non a Deo: sed in eo a praeceptoribus dissensit, quod non ab omnibus Angelis, sed a septem tantum conditum affirmabat, idque praeter Dei Patris & summae illius Virtutis conscientiam & iussum, quasi praeter omnipotentis Dei voluntatem quicquam fieri posset. Itaque totum caput Geneseos primum euertebat. 3 Resurrectionem carnis nullam fieri, quod non fieret corpus salvum, sed scintilla tantum cuiusdam splendoris, qui in hominem deorsum lapsus esset, quum formaretur ab Angelis. Erat tamen hic articulus in primitiuae Ecclesiae catechesi, Hebr.6. & ab Apostolis, si quis alius, confirmatus. 4 Christum phantasmate non reipsa & apparuisse, & passum esse in cruce. Id quod Marcionitae potissimum retinuerunt. 5 Hominem non a Deo, sed ab Angelis creatum, qui dixerint inter se, Faciamus hominem ad imaginem nostram. Quum ij autem solum corpus formare potuissent, quod more vermis serpere tantum per terram posset, & propter virium imbecillitatem palpitare (id enim significat Scarizare, [?]σκαρίζειν quod apud Irenaeum libr. 1 .cap.22. retinuit in-terpres) terprçs) miserans summa Virtus in hoc opus tâ infirmũ immisit scintillam vitæ. Illa autem fuit splendor quidam luminis, quod de cœlo in rebus inferioribus resplenduit, & hominem in pedes erexit, valentemque effecit. Atque hoc figmentum ex Platonis in Timæo scriptis haustum est, & verissimam Mosis historiam euertit. 6 Alium Iudæorum Deum, alium Christi Patrem Christianorumque Deum esse. In quo Valentinianis & Marcionitis suppeditatum est delirij argumentum. 7 Natura homines esse malos. Duos.n.factos esse, vnum naturâ bonum: alterum naturâ & creatione malum. ex bono bonos: ex malo, malos ortos. Vt autem malis diabolus fauet: ita Christus bonis auxiliatum venit. Hoc ex commentitiis poetarum de Pandora & Epimetheo fabulis & narrationib. sumptum fuit. 8 Matrimonium ciûsque vinculum dixit esse doctrinâ diaboli contra Pauli sententiam, 1. Timoth. 4. verf. 3. Hebr. 13. versu 4. Hinc Encratitæ & Tatiani posterea. 9 Ab animatis abstinendum. Hinc Manichæi. 10 Quosdam è veteribus Prophetis, quorum scripta veteris Testamenti pars sunt, esse à Satana. Hinc Marcionitæ, Manichæi, & Legis atque Prophetarũ aduersarij. Ex iis autem intelligitur, quomodo paulatim & pedetentim creuit error, & vt Satan sibi gradus ad alias blasphemias fecerit. Occasio autem erroris fuit tum ambitio, tum etiâ crassissima rerum & articulorum in orthodoxa Ecclesia notissimorum & receptissimorum ignorantia. Tanti est nimirum veritatem à veteris interpretibus, & ex ipsa Scriptura didicisse, non ab impostoribus accepisse. Qualis vero huius Satanæ ministri & blasphemi hominis exitus fuerit, legisse me non memini: sua tamen pœna caruisse verisimile non est.
units.tr: 2 Confirmasse.) The chief heads of the Saturnian error are taught above all by Epiphanius and Theodoret, who partly agreed with the earlier heresies and partly differed from them. Indeed, they held in common with Simon Magus those two points which Augustine mentions here: (1) that they allowed their disciples to live shamefully, since they would be saved by faith alone and by the knowledge of him; (2) that the world was created by Angels, not by God; but in this they differed from their teachers, that they affirmed it was made not by all the Angels but by seven only, and that without the knowledge and command of God the Father and of that supreme Power, as though anything could happen apart from the will of almighty God. Thus they overturned the whole first chapter of Genesis. (3) That no resurrection of the flesh would take place, since the body would not be saved, but only a spark of a certain splendour, which had fallen down into man and was formed by the Angels. Yet this article was in the catechesis of the primitive Church (Heb. 6), and was confirmed by the Apostles as firmly as any. (4) That Christ appeared and suffered on the cross in appearance only, not in reality. This the Marcionites especially retained. (5) That man was created not by God but by Angels, who said to one another, "Let us make man in our image." Since they could form only a body, which could creep along the ground like a worm and, because of its feebleness, could only twitch (for this is what scarizare [σκαρίζειν] means, which the translator kept in Irenaeus, book 1, chapter 22), the most high Power, taking pity, put into this so weak a work a spark of life. This was a kind of splendour of light, which shone from heaven upon the lower things, and raised man to his feet and made him strong. This fiction was drawn from Plato's writings in the Timaeus, and it overturns the most true history of Moses. (6) That the God of the Jews is one, and the Father of Christ and the God of the Christians is another. In this the Valentinians and Marcionites found material for their nonsense. (7) That by nature men are evil. For they taught that two were made, one good by nature, the other evil by nature and by creation; good men arise from the good, and evil men from the evil. Just as the devil favours the evil, so Christ came to help the good. This was taken from the invented fables and stories of the poets about Pandora and Epimetheus. (8) That marriage and its bond are a doctrine of the devil, against the sentence of Paul, 1 Tim. 4:3, Heb. 13:4. Hence afterwards the Encratites and Tatian. (9) That one must abstain from living things. Hence the Manichaeans. (10) That certain of the old prophets, whose writings form part of the Old Testament, are from Satan. Hence the Marcionites, Manichaeans and enemies of the Law and the Prophets.
