From these points it can be understood how the error grew gradually and step by step, and how Satan made himself steps to other blasphemies. The occasion of the error was both ambition and the crassest ignorance of things and articles most well known and most accepted in the orthodox Church. So great a thing is it to have learned the truth from the old interpreters and from Scripture itself, and not to have received it from impostors. What the end of this minister of Satan and blasphemous man was, I do not remember having read; yet it is not likely that he escaped his punishment.

units.la: CAP. IIII. Basilidiani vnde dicti. Quid à Simonianis differant. Erroris autem capita recensentur.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV. Why the Basilidians are so called. How they differ from the Simonians. The heads of their error are listed.

units.la: Basilidiani à Basilide, qui hoc distabat à Simonianis, quòd recentos sexaginta quinque cælos esse dicebat, quo numero dierum annus includitur. Vnde etiam quasi sanctum nomen commendabat, Ἀβραξας [?]: cuius nominis litera secundum Græcam supputationem eundem numerum complent. Sunt enim septem α & ε, ρ & α, ξ & α, & σ, id est, vnum & duo, & centum & vnum, & sexaginta & vnum, & ducenta: quæ fiunt in summa trecenta sexaginta quinque. Mundum istum vel hominem non credunt à Deo factum, sed à trecentesimo sexagesimo quinto cælo. Amatoria carmina studiosè discunt. A Iudæis non credunt Christum crucifixum, sed Simonem Cyrenensem, qui angariatus sustulit crucem eius.
units.tr: The Basilidians are named after Basilides, who differed from the Simonians in this: he taught that there are three hundred and sixty-five heavens, a number that matches the days of the year. Hence he also commended as a holy name Abraxas [Ἀβραξας], whose letters, by the Greek reckoning, add up to the same number. For the letters are α and ε, ρ and α, ξ and α, and σ, that is, one and two, and one hundred and one, and sixty and one, and two hundred, which make three hundred and sixty-five in all. They do not believe that this world or man was made by God, but by the three hundred and sixty-fifth heaven. They eagerly study love songs. They do not believe that Christ was crucified by the Jews, but Simon of Cyrene, who was pressed into service and carried his cross.

units.la: Suprà demonstratum est contemporaneas fuisse has hæreses. Ex vna enim & eadem Menandri schola tanquam riuo profecti Saturninus & Basilides in duo se diuortia cœnosa diduxerunt. Quanquam autem incom-pertum sibi esse dicit Epiphanius vtcr[?] virus suum alium docuerit, vel Saturninus Basilidem, vel Basilides Saturninum: tamen cæteri scriptores Saturninum prius docere cœpisse narrant, & ab eo iam sua dogmata spargente, Basilidem ex professo dissensisse, quo ingeniosior videretur. Denique Augustinus libr.2. contra aduersf. Leg. cap. 12. scribit Basilidem ordine quartum fuisse à Simone Mago, vt Saturnino posteriorem fuisse oporteat. Fuit igitur praua quædam Saturnini æmulatione commotus Basilides ad venenum euomendum. Vixit sub Adriano imperatore, circa annum imperij eius xv, anno à Christo passo fere centesimo, sub Alexandro primo, pontifice Romano, vt scribit Platina.
units.tr: It has been shown above that these heresies were contemporaneous. For Saturninus and Basilides, having flowed out as from one and the same stream, the single school of Menander, split into two muddy channels. Although Epiphanius says it is uncertain to him whether Saturninus taught Basilides or Basilides taught Saturninus, other writers report that Saturninus began to teach first, and that once he was spreading his doctrines, Basilides openly dissented from him in order to seem the more ingenious. Augustine, in book 2 of his work Against the Adversary of the Law and the Prophets, chapter 12, writes that Basilides was fourth in order after Simon Magus, so that he must have come after Saturninus. Basilides, then, stirred by a certain perverse rivalry with Saturninus, set out to vomit forth his poison. He lived under the emperor Hadrian, about the fifteenth year of Hadrian's reign, nearly a hundred years after Christ's passion, under Alexander I, Roman pontiff, as Platina writes.

units.la: Fuit autem Ægyptius & Alexandrinus, in qua vrbe etiam docuit, & in tota Saitide νόμῳ, id est, Præfectura, vt interpretatur C. Plinius, νόμων δὲ Αἰγυπτιακῶν[?], inquit Epiphanius, [illegible, ~20 letters]. Est autem Saitidis præfecturæ, de qua etiam Plato in Timæo meminit, Alexandria metropolis. Scripsit autem in Evangelia, & quædam ex lib. ipsius 23. Exegeticῶν citat Clemens Alexandrinus lib.4. Hic fere primus post Nicolaitas nouis & peregrinis, siue inauditis vocibus sua illa putida deliria hominibus commendauit. In quo facem præstulit Valentinianis, qui postea eum in huiusmodi portentis imitati sunt. Itaque prophetas suos his nominibus appellabat, vt Theodoretus & Eu-seb.lib.4.cap.7. scribunt, nimirum quòd eos nominabat Barcoph.i. filium præcepti: & Barcabad vel Barcabod, (sic enim apud vtrunque historicum legendum est.) Primum autem Syriacam terminationem habet, secundum Hebræa. Barcabod autem, est filius gloriæ. Fortasse etiam ex Epiphanio in Nazarenis legi potest Barcaba,id est, vt ipse interpretatur, filius prostitutæ. De quo infra in hæresi Nazarenorum. Durauit aliquandiu hæc hæresis Basilidianorum, maxime in Ægypto, vti ea gens & natio fuit ab initio Euangelij Monachismis & superstitionibus addicta, atque etiam ad errores imbibendos facilis. Continuata enim est & sustentata[?] ab Isidoro Basilidis filio post patris mortem, de quo Isidoro fecit mentionem Theodoretus, & illius ipsius libros de Moribus, legit & commemorat Clemes Strom.libr.3. item lib. 6. cuius prophetam appellat Barchar, non autem Parchar, vt est in impressis. Propagata autem est postea, etsi aucta & interpolata, a Valentinianis. Quis Basilidis vitæ exitus fuerit, non est annotatum a scriptoribus. Fuit tamen nocentissimum & pestilentissimum Satanæ instrumentum.
units.tr: He was an Egyptian and an Alexandrian, and he taught in that city and throughout the whole Saitic nome, that is, prefecture, as C. Pliny translates it. Epiphanius says of the Egyptian nomes [illegible, about twenty letters]. Alexandria, the metropolis of the Saitic prefecture, which Plato also mentions in the Timaeus, is the city in question. He wrote on the Gospels, and Clement of Alexandria, in book 4, cites some passages from his twenty-three books of Exegetica. He was almost the first after the Nicolaitans to commend his foul fancies to people in new, foreign, or unheard-of words. In this he set the torch to the Valentinians, who later imitated him in such monstrosities. Thus he called his prophets by these names, as Theodoret and Eusebius (book 4, chapter 7) write: he called them Barcoph, that is, son of the precept, and Barcabad or Barcabod (for so it must be read in both historians). The first has a Syriac ending, the second a Hebrew one. Barcabod means son of glory. Perhaps Barcaba can also be read in Epiphanius under the Nazarenes, which, as he himself explains, means son of a harlot. On this see below, under the heresy of the Nazarenes. The Basilidian heresy lasted for some time, especially in Egypt, since that people and nation, from the beginning of the Gospel, were given to monasticism and superstitions and were also easily led into swallowing errors. For it was continued and sustained by Isidore, son of Basilides, after his father's death. Theodoret mentions this Isidore, and Clement reads and cites his books On Morals in book 3 of the Stromata; also in book 6, where Clement calls Isidore's prophet Barchar, not Parchar as in the printed editions. Afterwards the heresy was spread, though enlarged and corrupted, by the Valentinians. What the end of Basilides' life was has not been recorded by writers. Still, he was a most harmful and most pestilent instrument of Satan.

units.la: 2 [?](Simonianis.) Gestit animus pro Simo-nianis reponere Saturninianis. Primum quod Simonianorum nomen statim extinctum est, pro quo Menadi ianorum & Saturninianorum appellationes inualuerant. Deinde quod Basilidiani ipsi inter Simonianos proculdubio recensentur, sed non inter Saturninianos. Præterea quod cæteri scriptores ecclesiastici ita vtrasque hæreses istas referunt, vt primum Saturnini docuisse demonstrent: post autem Basilidem, qui studio a collega & condiscipulo dissentiendi nouam propriamque hæresin condidit, vt scribit Eufcb.lib.4. cap.6. & 22. Itaque Irenæus lib.1. cap.23. sic narrationis seriem connectit, vt post Saturninum statim subiiciat hæc verba, Basilides autem, vt altius aliquid & verisimilius inuenisse videretur, in immensum extendit sententiam doctrinæ suæ. Theodoretus enim scribit Basilidem contempsisse dogmata Saturnini commilitonis, vt viles & puerilès fabulas: ipsum autem alia commentum, vt quemadmodum ait Epiphanius, τὰ ... ἀξιῶ ἂν φαντα- σιάζειν [illegible, ~9 letters]. Itaque cum Basilidis studium fuerit, non à Simone, sed à Saturnino discedendi, lego A Saturninianis: quia tamen veteris codicis fide & auxilio destituor, immutare quicquam nolui sum ausus.
units.tr: 2 [?](Simonians.) My mind is eager to put Saturninians in place of Simonians. First, because the name of the Simonians was soon extinguished, and in its place the names of the Menandrians and Saturninians had prevailed. Second, because the Basilidians are undoubtedly counted among the Simonians, but not among the Saturninians. Moreover, the other ecclesiastical writers report these two heresies in such a way as to show that Saturninus taught first, and that afterwards Basilides, who from a desire to dissent from his colleague and fellow-pupil founded a new heresy of his own, as Eusebius writes in book 4, chapters 6 and 22. Thus Irenaeus, in book 1, chapter 23, links the sequence of his narrative so that right after Saturninus he adds these words: "Basilides, however, so as to seem to have found something loftier and more plausible, extended the teaching of his doctrine immensely." For Theodoret writes that Basilides despised the dogmas of Saturninus, his fellow soldier, as cheap and childish fables, but that he himself devised another, which, as Epiphanius says, [τὰ ... ἀξιῶ ἂν φανταζιάζειν, illegible]. Therefore, since Basilides' aim was to depart not from Simon but from Saturninus, I read "from the Saturninians". Yet since I lack the support and authority of an old manuscript, I have not dared to change anything.

units.la: Variæ fuerunt Basilidianorum hypotheses, e quibus quatuor tantum collegit Augustinus, quas primo loco recensebo, & quarum hæc Basilidis propria maxime fuit, quod ausus est apertissime negare cum Deum quem gens Iudæorum coleret, fuisse verum Deum. Augustin.lib.4. Contra aduersa.
units.tr: The hypotheses of the Basilidians were various. Augustine gathered only four of them, which I shall list first. Of these, the one most peculiar to Basilides was that he dared openly to deny that the God whom the Jewish nation worshipped was the true God. Augustine, book 4, Against the Adversary of the Law and the Prophets.

units.la: I Virtutem quandam esse summam & summum Deum ingenitum, & notum tamen, quem etsi, vt ait Irenæus, in sua essentia innominabilem esse docent, tamen Abraxas, Græcè autem Ἀβραξας vocant sacro, vt ipsi aiunt, nomine. Hunc solum volunt increatum: reliqua autem esse creata, at mentem quidem illam primogeniam, quam νοῦν[?] nominant. Vnde apud Theodoretum male Abraxax legitur: peius etiam apud Epiphanium alicubi Ἀβραξαξ. Ratio nominis huius Ἀβραξας fuit, quod numerum 365, quot diebus conflat annus solaris, per literarum significatione colligere ex certo quodam vocabulo vellet, vt docet hoc loco Augustinus. Unde uti Abram non temere Abraham dictus est: sic iste suum Deum magico quodam matæologias mysterio contendit vocari Abraxas voce Græca: non Hebraica, nec Syriaca, contrà quàm tamen quidam existimant. Ex hoc iam procreatam esse illam primogenitam mentem quam verbo ab Anaxagora sumpto νοῦν appellabat. Unde mentem creatam νοῦν esse dicebat. Ex quo fit ut locus apud Tertullian. in lib. De Præscrip. sit plane corrigendus. sic enim legitur, Hic esse dicit (de Basilide loquens) summum Deum nomine ‹Abraxan›, quo mentem creatam, quam Græce νοῦν appellat. Falsa enim est hæc sententia, quia ut mentem hanc creatam ab increata illa & summa Virtute, reipsa distinguebat & essentia siue ὑπόστασις: ita etiam nomine. id quod docet Epiphan. his verbis, ὧν ἐν τῷ ἀγεννήτῳ, ὁ μόνος δὲ πάντων πατὴρ [?] νοῦς. Itaque sic apud Tertullianum restituendum locum puto, quanquam nihil annotat B. Rhenanus. Hic esse dicit summum Deum nomine ‹Abraxas› (sic enim lego, non Abraxan) ex quo mentem creatam, quam Græce νοῦν appellat. Admonuit tamen me Hieremias Bastingius Frisius adolescens honestissimus, videri posse cum qui ex Abraxas progenitus esset nō vocatum esse νοῦν à Basilide Græca voce, sed potius Hebræa נין Nin, quæ filium significat. Id quod diiudicandum aliis relinquo. facile enim fuit ex Nin Hebræo facere νοῦν Græcum ab hominibus Hebraicæ linguæ ignaris. Cæterum ex hac mente procreatum λόγον, id est, Verbum: ex Verbo, Providentiam: ex hac, Sapientiam: ex qua ipsa Angeli nati sint, quorum ultimus fuit Iudaeorum Deus, quem & turbulentum & ambitiosum fuisse fingit, quique suae genti reliquas omnes subiicere tentasset. Ex hoc delirio plane Valentinianorum & Marcionitanum fæces hau-stæ sunt. Itaque Clemens cum Basilidianis istos fere ubique coniungit. Haec de Abraxas.
units.tr: I. That there is a certain supreme Virtue and supreme God, unbegotten and yet known, whom, although they teach that in his essence he is unnameable (as Irenaeus says), they nonetheless call by the sacred name, as they themselves say, Abraxas [Ἀβραξας] in Greek. This alone they want to be uncreated; all the rest they hold to be created, but that first-born mind which they call [νοῦς]. Hence in Theodoret the name is wrongly read as Abraxax, and worse still, in one place in Epiphanius, as Abraxaxas. The reason for the name Abraxas was that he wished to draw the number 365, the days of the solar year, from the letters' meanings in a certain word, as Augustine teaches here. Just as Abram was not without reason called Abraham, so he, by a certain magical mystery of letter-numbers, contended that his God should be called Abraxas in Greek, not in Hebrew or Syriac, contrary to what some think. From this, he taught, that first-begotten mind was produced, which he called by the word νοῦς, taken from Anaxagoras. Hence he said that the created mind is νοῦς. From this it follows that the passage in Tertullian's De Praescriptione must be plainly corrected. For it is read thus: He says that the supreme God is named ‹Abraxan›, by whom the created mind, which he calls in Greek νοῦς. For this statement is false, since Basilides distinguished this created mind from that uncreated and supreme Virtue in fact and in essence or ὑπόστασις, and so also in name, as Epiphanius teaches in these words: [ὧν ἐν τῷ ἀγεννήτῳ, ὁ μόνος δὲ πάντων πατὴρ νοῦς, illegible in part]. Therefore I think the passage in Tertullian should be restored thus, although B. Rhenanus notes nothing on it: He says that the supreme God is named ‹Abraxas› (for so I read it, not Abraxan) from whom the created mind, which he calls in Greek νοῦν. However, Jeremias Bastingius of Friesland, a most honourable young man, reminded me that it may be that the one begotten from Abraxas was not called νοῦς by Basilides in Greek, but rather by the Hebrew נין Nin, which means son. I leave it to others to decide this. For it was easy for people ignorant of Hebrew to turn the Hebrew Nin into the Greek νοῦς. Moreover, from this mind was produced the Logos, that is, the Word; from the Word, Providence; from this, Wisdom; and from Wisdom the Angels were born, the last of whom was the God of the Jews, whom he imagined to have been turbulent and ambitious, and who tried to subject all the other nations to his own people. From this delirium the dregs of the Valentinians and Marcionites were plainly drawn. Thus Clement almost everywhere couples these men with the Basilidians. So much on Abraxas.

units.la: 1 Error: Esse trecentos sexaginta quinque coelos distinctos, & alios ex aliis defluentes, quia totidem diebus constet solaris annus, & tot membra habeant singulorum hominum corpora. Cuique coelo suum Angelum praefici, ex Angelis autem ipsis alios aliis esse priores. Irenaeus libr.2.cap.66.à trecentesimo vero & 65 coelo hominem formatum fuisse. Id quod qua-dantenus ex Peripateticorum doctrina sumptum est libr.8.de Physicor. audit. & Ἀγγελολα-[?]τρείαν[?] plane confirmat. 3 Morum turpitudinem, φίλτρα[?] & amatoria pocula, magiam & incantationes probauit. Clemes Strom.lib.3. 4 Christum ficte, non vere passum, sed pro eo Simonem Cyrenensem, de quo Matth. 27. versu 32. Hoc etiam ex Magicis phantasmatis & illusionibus, quibus impius Basilides addictus fuit, in religionem Christianam translatum est, quasi fuerit Christus Dei filius quidam magus. Id quod ethnici obiecerunt, ut scribit August. lib.1.de Cons. Evangel. Christum autem non à Deo qui mundum creauit, missum, sed ab Abraxas, ut Iudaeorum Deo omnia turbanti & ad se rapienti resisteret. Christum autem nouo & inusitato antea nomine Goala & Goalna ( à themate Hebraico [illegible, ~3 letters] vel [illegible, ~3 letters] quod redimere significat) appellauit. i. Redemptor, vel Redemptor noster: non autem Iesum, quomodo ab Angelo vocatus est, Matth. 1. versu 21. Sic Irenæus libro 1. cap. 3. Saluatorem esse Caula, & postea Caulana. Qui certè locus apud eum est depravatissimus: sed tamen facilè sanari posse videtur. Reposuit quidem N. Galasius vir doctissimus ex Epiphanio de Nicolaitis Caulaucau, Græcè [?]. Putat autem Epiphan. vocem esse sumptam ex Isa. 28. versu 10. sed frustrà. In veteri Irenæi exemplari veteris & veræ lectionis vestigia apparent quæ retenta esse oportuit, non immutata. Nó.n. Caulaucauch vel Caulaucau illic: sed Caula pro Goala, & Caulana pro Goalana Syriaca terminatione legitur. Quod autem pro 1 & 3 Hebræis literis pronuntiarint & Græci & Latini au, & pro g, dixerint c, in diphthongo, mirum illi non videbitur, qui quàm idiomata diuersa diuersè pronuntient, obseruarit. Est autem Goala Redemptio vel Redeptor Syris hominibus. Vtitur hac voce Iob 19. versu 25. Isa. 63. vers. 16. Atque hęc est mea de reponendo Irenæi loco coiectura. 5 Error, Carnis resurrectionem negant. 6 Martyria pro nomine Christi non esse toleranda, quia cùm pius patitur & affligitur, non Dei voluntate affligitur. Hinc fidei abnegationes introductæ, & turpissimæ à Deo defectiones. 7 Prophetias non à Deo esse, sed tantùm ab Angelis. 8 Imagines habere Christianis licere, & idolothytis vesci, tanquam rebus mere [?], etiam non spe-stata[?] stata alterius infirmi conscientia. 9 Non omnia peccata dimitti à Deo, sed tantùm inuoluntariè commissa. 10 Fidem esse naturalem, quemadmodum & electionem nostram, pro cuiusque opere, & merito: non autem esse Dei donum. 11 Secreta hæc, & fidei mysteria celanda esse, vel paucis omnino reuelanda. Irenæus libr.1.cap.23. Ita paulatim creuit error, & abyssus abyssum inuexit, vt iam ab illis nullum dogma fidei intactum sit relictum, tam nimirum profundè in barathrum delabimur & mergimur, vbi semel nos in illud volentes demi-simus[?].
units.tr: This is the error: that there are three hundred and sixty-five distinct heavens, some flowing down from others, because a solar year consists of that many days, and the bodies of individual men have that many members. A separate angel is set over each heaven, and among the angels themselves some are prior to others. Irenaeus, book 2, chapter 66: man was formed from the three hundred and sixty-fifth heaven. This is taken, in some measure, from the teaching of the Peripatetics, in book 8 of the Physics lectures, and it plainly confirms angel-worship [ἀγγελολατρείαν]. (2) He approved of wicked conduct, love potions [φίλτρα] and philtres, magic and incantations. Clement, Stromata book 3. (3) Christ did not really suffer but only seemingly, and Simon of Cyrene suffered in his place, of whom Matthew 27:32 speaks. This too was carried over into the Christian religion from the magical phantasms and illusions to which the impious Basilides was devoted, as if Christ were some sort of magician, the Son of God. The heathen objected to this, as Augustine writes in book 1 of the Harmony of the Gospels. Christ was sent not by the God who created the world but by Abraxas, to resist the God of the Jews, who throws everything into confusion and drags everything to himself. (4) He called Christ by the new and hitherto unusual names Goala and Goalna (from the Hebrew theme [illegible, about three letters] or [illegible, about three letters], which means to redeem), that is, Redeemer or our Redeemer, and not Jesus, as he was called by the angel, Matthew 1:21. So Irenaeus, book 1, chapter 3, says that the Saviour is Caula, and afterwards Caulana. That passage in him is certainly very corrupt, yet it seems it can easily be restored. The very learned N. Galasius indeed proposed Caulaucau, from Epiphanius on the Nicolaitans, in Greek [?]. Epiphanius thinks the word was taken from Isaiah 28:10, but wrongly. In the old copy of Irenaeus traces of the old and true reading appear, which ought to have been kept and not changed. For there is no Caulaucauch or Caulaucau there, but Caula is read for Goala, and Caulana for Goalana, with the Syriac ending. As for the fact that both Greeks and Latins pronounced the Hebrew letters 1 and 3 as au, and wrote c for g in the diphthong, this will not seem strange to anyone who has observed how different languages pronounce the same things differently. Goala means redemption or redeemer to the Syrian people. He uses this word in Job 19:25 and Isaiah 63:16. This is my conjecture about how Irenaeus's passage should be restored. (5) The error that they deny the resurrection of the flesh. (6) Martyrdoms for the name of Christ should not be endured, because when the godly man suffers and is afflicted, he is not afflicted by the will of God. Hence denials of the faith were introduced, and the most shameful apostasies from God. (7) Prophecies are not from God, but only from angels. (8) Christians may keep images and eat food offered to idols, as things that are merely indifferent, even without regard to the conscience of another weak person. (9) God does not forgive all sins, but only those committed involuntarily. (10) Faith is natural, just as our election is, according to each person's work and merit, and not a gift of God. (11) These secrets and mysteries of the faith must be hidden, or revealed only to a very few. Irenaeus, book 1, chapter 23. Thus the error grew little by little, and abyss called up abyss, so that by now no doctrine of the faith has been left untouched by them. So deeply, surely, do we slide and sink into the pit, once we have willingly let ourselves down into it.

units.la: CAP. V. Nicolaitæ unde dicti.Erroris autem capita quatuor explicantur.
units.tr: CHAPTER V. Whence the Nicolaitans got their name. Four heads of this error are explained.

units.la: Nicolaitæ à Nicolao {1}nominati sunt, vno, vt perhibetur, ex illis septem, quos Apostoli diaconos ordinauerant. Ille cùm de zelo pulcherrimæ coniugis culparetur, veluti purgandi sui causa permisisse fertur, ut ea, qui vellet, uteretur. Quod eius factum in sectam {2}tur-pissimam versum est, in qua placet usus indifferens fœminarum. Hi nec ab iis quæ idolis immolantur, cibos suos separant: & alios ritus gentilium superstitionum non auersantur. Narrant etiam quosdam fabulosa de mundo, nescio quæ barbara principum nomina miscentes disputationibus suis, quibus terrent auditores, quæ prudentibus risum potius faciunt, quàm timorem. Intelliguntur autem etiam isti non Deo tribuere &[?] creaturam, sed quibusdam pote-statibus, quas mirabili vel fingunt, vanitate, vel credunt.
units.tr: The Nicolaitans are named after Nicolaus, supposedly one of those seven whom the Apostles had ordained as deacons. When he was accused of jealousy over his very beautiful wife, he is said to have allowed, as a way of clearing himself, anyone who wished to make use of her. That deed was turned into a most shameful sect, in which the indiscriminate use of women is approved. These people do not keep their food separate from things sacrificed to idols, and they do not shun other rites of pagan superstitions. They also tell stories about the world, mixing into their discussions certain barbarous names of principalities, which they use to frighten their hearers, though to sensible people such things cause laughter rather than fear. It seems that these men too do not ascribe creation to God, but to certain powers, which they either invent with wondrous vanity or believe in.

units.la: Theodoretus lib.3. hanc hæresin commemorat post alias multas. Quidam tamen prætermittunt, sive quòd tam fœda & turpia huius dogmata essent, ut quemadmodum loquitur Tertullianus, pudor sit dicere: sive quòd magna ex parte in Gnosticis & Valentinianis (utrique enim a Nicolaitis profecti sunt, sed in primis Gnostici, ut ait Epiphanius) explicetur. Irenæus tamen, Tertullianus, Eusebius & Epiphanius retinent. Et dubitari non potest hanc aliquando fuisse, cum illius aperte meminerit sacra Scriptura Apocalyp. 2. verf. 6. & 15. Collocat tamen eam post Cerinthum & Ebionitas Irenæus. Eusebius autem libr. 4. cap. 29. eodem tempore quo Cerinthianam, docet exortam esse. Tertullianus, Augustinus & Epiphanius ante Cerinthianos constituunt. Quæ postrema ratio temporis & series mihi videtur esse verior, etsi non longo interuallo inter se hæ discrepant. Platina sub Cleto Romano Episcopo qui ante Clementem vixit, reponit. Nicolaus autem quem huius sectæ principem faciunt, fuit, quemadmodum Epiphan. scribit, Antiochenus: virus autem suum maximè sparsisse traditur circa initium imperii Domitiani, annum autem a Christo passo 52. ante D. Ioannis Apostoli & Euangelistæ in Patmo insula exilium. Volunt autem hunc ipsum fuisse unum ex septem illis Diaconis qui ab Apostolis consensu Ecclesiæ primi electi fuerant, Actor. 6. Quæ fuerit autem huius tam horrendæ sectæ occasio, attingit breuiter hic Augustinus, latius autem persequitur Clemens Alexandrinus, qui etiam Stromateus dicitur, libr.3. Stromat. quod suspicione zelotypiæ, qua apud Ecclesiam propter egregiam vxoris suæ formam laborabat, purgatum se vellet. Itaque eam omnibus profituit[?]. Quod in consuetudinem siue imitationem a quibusdam postea in Ecclesia vsurpatum est. Dicit Augustinus, Quod in sectam versum est. Quæ Augustini verba admonent me vt locum apud Isidorum libr.8.cap.5. meo quidè iudicio, depravatum emendem. Nam qui error est in Isidoro, postea irrepsit atque retectus est in Ca-no. Quidam autem.24. quæst.3. Sic igitur apud Isidiorum legitur, propter pulchritudinem relinquens vxorem dixit, vt qui vellet, ea vteretur, & versa est in stuprum talis consuetudo. Reponendum est ex hoc Augustini loco, ex quo haud dubiè transcriptus est, Et versa est in sectam hæc consuetudo. Nec enim est stuprum turpis cum coniuge aliena coitus, sed adulterium. Stuprum enim vel in viduam, vel in virginem tantùm committitur, vt omnes loquuntur & sentiunt qui Latinè sciunt. Aliam verò huius tam furiosæ impietatis & turpitudinis causam affert Epiphanius lib.1.tom.2. quæ mihi longè videtur probabilior, Nimirum quòd cùm Nicolaus iste ad quorundam continentium & virginum imitationem ἐγκρατείας[?] & perpetuò a coniuge sua abstinere contra Pauli præceptum 1.Corinth.7.verf.1. promisisset, impatiēs coitus iterum ad vxore redijt, & propter intermissam consuetudinem intemperantius ea, quæ formo sissima censebatur, vsus est. Cùm se inconstantiæ & intemperantiss. libidinis vitio apud Ecclesiam prægrauari sentiret, [illegible, ~10 letters] vt ait Epiphanius, Hoc primùm dixit, omnino necessarium esse vxores habere & cum ijs cohabitare, adeò vt, quemadmodum scribit Epiphanius, dixerit, [illegible, ~20 letters]. Deinde longius progressus (nam abyssus abyssum trahit) in absurdissima & obscœnissima quæque lapsus est, tanti est Dei præceptum, & Apostoli admonitionem semel contempsisse. Durauit pauco tempore hæc hæresis ipso Nicolaitarum nomine. statim enim extinsta est, vt ait Eusebius lib. 4. cap. 29. postea tamen interpolata à Gnosticis & Valentinianis reuixit. In Asia minore maximè grassatum esse hoc tam pestilens venenum, apparet ex Apocalypsi. Retulit tamen Bohemus quidam quum hæc chartis illinerem, etiam aliquas tam miseræ sectæ reliquias in Bohemia superesse, quæ etiamnum hodie ieiunij Iudaici formam certa anni tempestate obseruant. Postea verò turpissimè & promiscuè mi-scentur.
units.tr: Theodoret, book 3, records this heresy among many others. Some, however, pass it over, either because its doctrines were so foul and shameful that, as Tertullian puts it, it is a shame even to speak of them, or because they are for the most part explained under the Gnostics and Valentinians (for both of these came from the Nicolaitans, but chiefly the Gnostics, as Epiphanius says). Yet Irenaeus, Tertullian, Eusebius and Epiphanius retain it. Nor can it be doubted that it once existed, since Holy Scripture clearly mentions it, Revelation 2:6 and 15. Irenaeus, however, places it after Cerinthus and the Ebionites. Eusebius, book 4, chapter 29, teaches that it arose at the same time as the Cerinthians. Tertullian, Augustine and Epiphanius put it before the Cerinthians. This latter order of time and sequence seems to me the more accurate, although these accounts do not differ greatly from one another. Platina places it under Cletus, the Roman bishop, who lived before Clement. Nicolaus, whom they make the leader of this sect, was, as Epiphanius writes, a man of Antioch. It is handed down that he spread his poison especially around the beginning of the reign of Domitian, in the fifty-second year after the Passion of Christ, before the exile of the Apostle and Evangelist John on the island of Patmos. They hold that this same Nicolaus was one of those seven deacons who were chosen by the Apostles with the consent of the Church, Acts 6. What the occasion of this most horrible sect was, Augustine touches on briefly here, but Clement of Alexandria, also called Stromateus, pursues it more fully, in book 3 of the Stromata: out of suspicion of jealousy, from which he suffered in the Church on account of his wife's outstanding beauty, he wished to clear himself. So he offered her to everyone. Later some in the Church made this a custom or an imitation. Augustine says, "which was turned into a sect." These words of Augustine remind me that I should emend a passage in Isidore, book 8, chapter 5, which in my judgement has been corrupted. For the error which is in Isidore later crept into the Canon Law and was there exposed: "Certain people, however, 24, question 3." So in Isidore it is read thus: "leaving his wife on account of her beauty, he said that whoever wished might use her, and such a custom turned into fornication (stuprum)." It should be restored from this passage of Augustine, from which it was undoubtedly copied: "and this custom turned into a sect." For intercourse with another man's wife is not stuprum but adultery. Stuprum is committed only with a widow or a virgin, as all who know Latin speak and understand. Epiphanius, book 1, volume 2, gives another cause of this so mad impiety and shamefulness, which seems to me far more probable: namely, that when this Nicolaus, in imitation of certain continent men and virgins, had promised ἐγκρατεία [self-control] and to abstain constantly from his wife, contrary to the precept of Paul, 1 Corinthians 7:1, he, being unable to bear the lack of intercourse, returned to his wife, and because of the interrupted habit he made use of her, who was reckoned most beautiful, more intemperately. When he felt himself weighed down in the Church by the vice of inconstancy and of most intemperate lust, [illegible], as Epiphanius says. He first said that it was altogether necessary to have wives and to live with them, so that, as Epiphanius writes, he said [illegible]. Then, progressing further (for the abyss draws abyss), he fell into every most absurd and obscene thing; so great is the harm of having once despised God's precept and the Apostle's admonition. This heresy lasted only a short time under the very name of the Nicolaitans, for it was soon extinguished, as Eusebius says, book 4, chapter 29; afterwards, however, it was revived, having been interpolated by the Gnostics and Valentinians. That this most pestilent poison raged especially in Asia Minor appears from the Apocalypse. Yet a certain Bohemian, when I was setting these things down on paper, related that some remnants of this most wretched sect still survive in Bohemia, which even today observe the form of a Jewish fast at a fixed season of the year. Afterwards, however, they mix together most shamefully and indiscriminately.

units.la: Quàm foetida & immunda fuerit hæc hæresis tum in dogmate, tum multò magis in ipsa praxi & vitæ genere, docet Scriptura, quæ nominatim [?] detestatur Apocal. 2. vers. 6. Docent etiam Tertullianus & Epiphanius. Tertullianus enim ne illa quidem commemoranda esse censet, tam erant obscoena. nimirum quando illi etiam turpitudines, complexus, & ipsas permixtiones execrabiles suos discipulos docerent. Qui locus est in lib. De præscript. quia tamen valde depravatus est, describendum existimavi, ut qua potui conie-ctura restituerem. Sic igitur in impressis, Sunt & cætera obscœna. Omnes enim refert quosdam turpitudinis natos, & complexus, & permixtiones execrabiles, obscœnásque coniun-ctas, & quædam ex ipsis adhuc turpiora. At vero locum ita legendum & emendandum puto. Sunt & cætera obscœna. Homines enim refert quosdam turpitudinis natos, & complexus, & permixtiones execrabiles, obscœnásque coniunctiones, & quædam ex ipsis adhuc turpiora. Quæ verba jam planum & facilem sensum habent: illa vero superiora & recepta vel nullum vel omnino barbarum. Epiphanius autem scribit eos, cum tam turpia & nefanda perpetra-rent in promiscuo illo suo cum omnibus mulieribus coitu respondere solitos fuisse, τῆς γυναικοκοινωνίας συλλήψεως ὑπὸ τῶν σωμάτων, διὰ [?] (ait Epiphanius) ψυχῆς καὶ κατα[?]. Et certè Gnosticorum & Manichæorum, quæ fuerunt fœdissimæ in ipso vitæ genere & mysteriorum suorum actione hæreses, fuit fons & origo Nicolaitarum error & doctrina. Refert autem hic Augustinus quatuor erroris eorum hypotheses. 1 Vxores docent esse communes, & promiscuum more pecudum fœminarum vsum in Ecclesiam Dei inducunt: nec tantum, vt putat Isidorus, coniugia permutanda censent. Ex Platonicorum dogmatis ortus hic error
units.tr: How foul and unclean this heresy was, both in its doctrine and much more in its very practice and manner of life, Scripture teaches, which expressly condemns it, Revelation 2:6. Tertullian and Epiphanius also teach this. For Tertullian thinks that even those things should not be recorded, so obscene were they, since they taught their disciples detestable acts of lust, embraces and mixings. This passage is in the book On Prescription against Heretics; because, however, it is badly corrupted, I thought it should be written out, so that I might restore it by whatever conjecture I could. Thus it stands in the printed editions: "There are also other obscene things. For he relates that all of them are born of shameful acts, and embraces, and detestable mixings, obscene unions, and some things still more shameful than these." But I think the passage should be read and emended thus: "There are also other obscene things. For he relates that men are born of shameful acts, and embraces, and detestable mixings, obscene unions, and some things still more shameful than these." These words now have a plain and easy sense; but the earlier, received reading is either senseless or altogether barbarous. Epiphanius writes that when they committed such shameful and unspeakable acts in their promiscuous intercourse with all women, they used to answer: τῆς γυναικοκοινωνίας συλλήψεως ὑπὸ τῶν σωμάτων, διὰ [?] (ait Epiphanius) ψυχῆς καὶ κατα[?] [of the conception of the community of women by the bodies, through [?] (says Epiphanius) soul and [?]]. And certainly the error and doctrine of the Nicolaitans was the fountain and origin of the Gnostic and Manichaean heresies, which were the most foul in the whole manner of life and in the practice of their mysteries. Here Augustine sets out four hypotheses of this error. (1) They teach that wives are to be held in common, and they introduce into the Church of God a promiscuous use of women, like beasts; nor do they, as Isidore thinks, merely hold that marriages should be exchanged.

units.la: b.iij. videri potest,quemadmodum etiam scribit Clemens Stromat.lib.3. quem refutat Ariftot.libro 2.Πολιτικῶν, & Mahumetanis postea ad polygamiam probandam & sequendam profuit. 2 Idolothyta edi posse à Christianis nulla contraria protestatione aut idololatriae detestatione facta, id est, citra auersatione idoli.Id quod tamen negat Scriptura,Apocal.2.ver.20:1.Ioan. 5.verf.21.
units.tr: b.iij. This error can seem to have arisen from the doctrine of the Platonists, as Clement also writes, Stromateis book 3, whom Aristotle refutes in Politics, book 2; and it later served the Muslims to defend and follow polygamy. (2) That meat offered to idols may be eaten by Christians, with no contrary protest and no detestation of idolatry, that is, without aversion from the idol. Scripture denies this, Revelation 2:20; 1 John 5:21.

units.la: De qua quaestione interrogatus Paulus respondit,etsi idolum per fe nihil est, neque quae idolis immolata sunt, dijs sunt proprie dicata (nullus enim est praeter vnum illum verum Deus) tamen quia & infirmiorum fratrum co-scientiae ratio habenda est: & non possumus mensae Domini & mensae idolorum fiue daemoniorum esse participes, idcirco idolothytis, id est immolatitijs fiue carnibus fiue aliijs rebus,vt loquitur Augustinus contra Adimant. cap.14. est abstinendum: id est, ijs quae immolata sunt idolis, & ex eorum sacris ad vescendum in eorum epulo reseruata porrigebantur.
units.tr: Asked about this question, Paul replied: although an idol is nothing in itself, and things sacrificed to idols are not properly dedicated to gods (for there is no god except the one true God), yet because we must also have regard to the conscience of weaker brethren, and we cannot be partakers of the table of the Lord and the table of idols or demons, therefore we must abstain from idol-meats, that is, from things sacrificed to idols, whether flesh or other things, as Augustine puts it against Adimantus, chapter 14; that is, from those things which were offered to idols and, reserved from their sacred rites, were set before people to eat at their feasts.

units.la: Quod ab ethnicis hominibus ad sacrificiorum Dei (quae Eucharistica dicebantur in Lege) [illegible, ~9 letters] fiebat. Vide Paulum 1.Corinth.8.vel f. 9,& 10: cap.10.verf.20.21.
units.tr: This was done by heathen men to the sacrifices of God (which were called eucharistic in the Law) [illegible]. See Paul, 1 Corinthians 8, or 9 and 10; chapter 10, verses 20 and 21.

units.la: Nec enim tales cibi sunt ex rerum vere mediarum & ἀδιαφόρων genere, nedum vero licitarum, quemadmodum docebant Nicolaitae. Nec obstat quod Christiani ijs rebus bona conscientia vescebantur, quae Iulianus apostata in macello dijs suis & idolis lustrali aqua consecrauerat. Nam vt scribit Theodoretus libro 3.capite 15. impius ille vt aliquos Christianis laqueos indueret, & eos i-dola dola venerari persuaderet, vel cogeret, iussit Antiochiæ fontes omnes,& omnia edulia quales panes,carnes,olera,lustrari &diis consecrari, vt vel idolothytis vesci Christianos vel fame perire cogeret. Itaque ex iis cibis edebant & salua quidem conscientia Christiani,etsi tamen vt ait Theodoretus,lugentes & gementes,quia ista consecratio vniuersalis ciborum omnium longè differt ab εἰδωλοθύτῳ[?], & re idolis proprio specialique sacrificio dicata & oblata. Quæ di-ftinctio notanda est propter Papifticos ritus & confratrias,quibus interesse Christianis hominibus non licet, vti nec pane miffatico indif-ferenter vti. Vsus est quidem Dauid pane sancto & propositionum,qui Deo,non idolis, fa-cer erat: sed vrgente demum necessitate,& inter eos quibus nullum ex eo esu præbebat of-fendiculum,Matth.12.v.3: 1.Samuel 21. 3 Er-ror Nicolaitarum fuit, Mundum hunc ortum ex concupiscentia & coitu tenebrarū cum lu-mine,ex quo nati Dæmones,& Angeli,& post-ea fœdissimo genere copulæ,homines ipsi. Vn-de femen e virili membro emissum,& mestrua mulierum pro rebus sanctissimis habebant.
units.tr: Nor are such foods of the class of things truly indifferent [ἀδιαφόρων] and neutral, much less lawful, as the Nicolaitans taught. Nor does it count against this that Christians ate, with a good conscience, those things which the apostate Julian had purified with lustral water in the meat market and consecrated to his gods and idols. For as Theodoret writes in book 3, chapter 15, that impious man, in order to lay snares for Christians and to persuade or compel them to worship idols, ordered that all the fountains at Antioch and all foodstuffs, such as breads, meats and vegetables, be purified and consecrated to the gods, so that he might force Christians either to eat idol-meats or to die of hunger. Thus Christians ate those foods, and indeed with a clear conscience, although, as Theodoret says, lamenting and groaning, because this universal consecration of all foods differs far from the idol-offering [εἰδωλοθύτῳ?], that is, the special sacrifice proper to idols and offered to them. This distinction is to be noted on account of the Papist rites and confraternities, in which Christians may not take part, nor use Mass-bread indiscriminately. David indeed used the holy bread of the Presence, which was holy to God, not to idols; but only under pressing necessity, and among those to whom that eating gave no offence (Matthew 12:3; 1 Samuel 21:3). The error of the Nicolaitans was that this world arose from the lust and union of darkness with light, from which were born demons and angels, and afterwards men themselves by the most foul kind of union. Hence they regarded the semen emitted from the male member, and the menstrual fluids of women, as most holy things.

units.la: 4 Angelos,non Deum condidisse hæc inferiora atque iis dominari. Hos autem diuerso modo & gradu diftribuût,vt intelligant ij qui nobis Angelorum Hierarchiam describunt, vnde suæ matæologias initia hauserint. Atq; eosdem peregrinis nominibus atque barbaris primi appellarunt.Barbelo enim esse qui octauo coe-lo præsit ex Peripateticorum decretis. Est au-tem Barbelo filius veteris vel vetustatis, cuius mater sit Ialdaboth. Est autem Ialdaboth, ma-ter Patrum, vel genita à Patribus. Eandem Sa-baoth appellant. Est autem exercitus. De Cau-laucaux (quod vocabulum addit Epiphanius) quid sentiendum existimem, dixi superius. Hæc secta superioribus magis portentosa, & exitia-lis fuit.
units.tr: (4) That angels, not God, made these lower things and rule over them. They distribute angels in different ways and degrees, as those who describe for us the hierarchy of angels understand, and from whom they drew the beginnings of their own "mataeologies." And the first of them gave these same beings foreign and barbarous names. For Barbelo, they say, is the one who presides over the eighth heaven, according to the decrees of the Peripatetics. Barbelo is the son of the old one, or of antiquity, whose mother is Ialdabaoth. Ialdabaoth is the mother of the Fathers, or born from the Fathers. They also call her Sabaoth, which means army. What I think should be held about Cau-laucau (a word Epiphanius adds) I have said above. This sect was more monstrous than the earlier ones, and more pernicious.

units.la: 3 Creaturam.) Dixit Augustinus Creatu-ram pro rebus creatis. Paulus κτίσιν[?] Græce appellat, Roman.i.vers.20. Ergo tribuunt Angelis creaturam, id est, tribuunt Angelis rerum creationem, & res ipsas creatas Nicolaitæ, non Deo. Id quod apertissimè repugnat Scripturæ, Genes.i.
units.tr: (3) Creature.) Augustine used "creatura" for created things. Paul calls it creation [κτίσιν] in Greek, Romans 1:20. Therefore the Nicolaitans ascribe the creature to the angels; that is, they ascribe to angels the creation of things, and the created things themselves, not to God. This most plainly contradicts Scripture, Genesis 1.

units.la: CAP. VI. Gnostici unde dicti. Erroris capita quatuor.
units.tr: CAP. VI. Why the Gnostics are so called. Four heads of error.

units.la: Nostici{1} propter excellentiam scientiæ sic se appellatos esse, vel appellari debuisse gloriantur, cum sint superioribus omnibus vaniores, atq; turpiores. Denique cum ab aliis atque aliis per diuersas terrarum partes aliter atque aliter nuncupetur, nonnulli eos etiā Borboritas vocant, quasi cœnosos, propter nimiam turpitudinem, quam in suis mysteriis exercere dicuntur. Aliqui eos à Nicolaitis exortos putant, alij à Carpocrate, de quo post loquemur. Tradunt{2} autem dogmata fabulosissimis plena figmetis. Etiam ipsi Principum vel Angelorum nominibus terribilibus infirmas animas capiunt: & de Deo, rerumq; natura fabulosa, & à sanitate veritatis aliena multa contexunt. Animarum substantiā Dei dicunt esse naturā, earūnque aliarum quoque aduentum in hæc corpora cum aliis aereis animalibus dicunt fieri, per quas peccata in corporibus committuntur. Nam illas animas, quæ ex Dei procedunt substantia, reuerti ad Deum immaculatas. Dicuntur quoque bonum Deum & malum Deum in suis habere dogmatibus.
units.tr: The Gnostics{1} boast that they are so called, or ought to be called, on account of the excellence of their knowledge, though they are more empty and more base than all the others. Since they are named differently by different people in different parts of the world, some call them Borborites, as if "muddy," on account of the great filthiness they are said to practise in their mysteries. Some think they arose from the Nicolaitans, others from Carpocrates, of whom we shall speak later. They hand down doctrines full of most fabulous fictions. They also catch weak souls with the terrible names of princes or angels, and they weave together many fabulous things about God and the nature of things, alien to the health of truth. They say that the substance of souls is the nature of God, and that other souls also come into these bodies together with other airy animals, and through them sins are committed in bodies. For those souls which proceed from the substance of God return to God undefiled. They are also said to hold in their doctrines a good God and an evil God.

units.la: 1 Gnostici ) Quàm varia sit de tempore huius hæreseos hominum & authorum Ecclesiasticorum sententia, ex eorum scriptis appareret. Quidam enim illam omnino prætermittunt, si nomen ipsum Gnosticorum quæratur, quemadmodū in lib. De fabulis Hæreticorum Theodoret. quanquam idem Borboritarū meminit, & Tertullianus in lib. De Præscript. Platina etiam in vitis Paparum. Alij confundunt vt Eusebius. Alij vero distinguūt, vti Augustinus, & Epiphanius ipse, cuius ordinem sequitur hoc loco & libro. Isidorus etiam meminit, & alij plures. Cuius tantę varietatis causa vt intelligatur, & vt ab aliis hi separentur, sunt nobis qui proprio specialíque nomine Gnostici vocantur, à Carpoc.atianis & Nicolaitis, cum quibus tamen in dogmate conueniunt, secernendi. Videntur enim ij demum & foli ita appellati, qui repudiato vtrorumque maiorum & authorum suorum vili, & iam odioso nomine, splendido se & nouo Gnosticos superbè nominarūt, non ab vllo homine mortali sumpta appellatione, ne de hominibus gloriari viderentur: sed ab ipsa eximia, excellenti, & singulari cognitionis suæ de Dei arcanis intelligentia & comprehensione, quam sibi falsò tribuebant. Gnosticos enim se dixerunt ἀπὸ τῆς γνώσεως[?], tanquam πνευ-ματικούς[?], & qui in Dei mysteria altius quàm caeteri superioresque omnes penetrassent. Γνῶσις autem praestantem Dei cognitionem, & fidem, & veritatis, operumque Dei revelationem atque agnitionem saepe apud Paulum significat, quemadmodum Coloss.2.verf.3: 1.Corinth.12. versu 8.Gnostici igitur quatenus suo se nomine iactant & à Carpocratianis & Nicolaitis (ex quibus tamen duobus cœnosis fontibus tetrarum orti sunt) distinguuntur, & aliam sectam constituunt. maximè cœperunt sub Aniceto Roman.episcopo,anno à Christo passo 129. sub initium imperij M.Aurelij Antonini Philosophi & L.Veri Impp.Roman. & annis postea tribus Cataphryges alij haeretici. ita ex abysso a-byssus.Gnostici quidem etiam in Asia noti fuerunt, sed potissimum, & vt mihi quidem videtur, primùm Romae, cùm Marcellina, quae huius sectae erat, vt scribit Irenaeus lib.1. cap.24. & Carpocratianorum & Nicolaitarum appellatio nem iam Ecclesiae exosam dimiserat, Romam ex Asia venisset, & sua illa tabe multos infecissent: quod factum est sub Aniceto Romano Episcopo, vti dixi, circa annum à Christo passo 130. vel 132. ex quo merito verè concludi potest eos Carpocratianis aetate posteriores esse. Nec tamen perperam hoc ordine collocantur post Nicolaitas, quia ex Epiphanij sententia putat Augustinus à Nicolao potius, quàm à Carpocrate hos serpentes esse progenitos. Sic enim ille, postquam de Nicolao haeresiarcha egit, subijcit, Ναασσηνοὶ[?] οἱ γνωστικοὶ διαφόρως ἀπὸ τῶν φυμετὰ[?] ἀπηλπισμένου[?] ἀνθρώπου ὥσπερ ἀπὸ πηγῆς καρπόν[?]. In quo tamen ipso varia est autorum sententia. Irenæus enim hos potius esse putat infœlicem Carpocratianorum fœtum. Id quod etiam in lib.De anima,sentit Tertullianus. Quanquam idem in Scorpiaco contra Gnosticos, stirpem unde aului sint & propagati tâ noxij rami non explicat. Irenæus lib.3. cap.4. à Menandro Simonis discipulo fatos fuisse tanquam Medeos serpentes scribit. Utcunque, seges sunt infœlicium illorum zizaniorum, quæ in agro & Ecclesia Domini seminavit Satan, ut mysterium iniquitatis operaretur, ac tandem perageret, quod effecit. Duravit autem Gnosticorum hæresis multis seculis, tum in Asia, tum maxime in Ægypto: ex qua Valentinianorum primum, post Manichæorum, deinde Priscillianistarum lernæ[?] & hæreses disseminatæ sunt, & natæ, adeo ut in Hispania etiam post annum Domini 386. non tantum instaurata fuerit, sed late pullulaverit, ut Sigebertus scribit. Guillelmus autem Postellus fæx mundi nostro seculo renovavit. Fuerunt autem omnium mortalium in dogmate fœdissimi, & Nicolaitis turpibus magistris, longè tamen ipsi turpiores. Unde variis se nominibus & sæpe de industria mutatis insinuarunt & texerunt, ne execrabili Gnosticorum nomine noti, statim ab Ecclesia explode-rentur. Nec ulla fuit unquam hæresis, quæ tot tamque diversis appellationibus se interpolarit, & celaverit: aut quæ se in plures sectas & particulas citius dissecuerit. Nam qui hic ab Augustino Gnostici dicuntur, ab aliis Barbeliotæ à Barbelo quem colebant, sunt nominati. Alibi Borboritæ, à cœno, voce ex Petri Apostoli Epistola sumpta. Est enim βορβόρῳ[?] sordes & cœnum, 2.Petr.2 v.22. In Ægypto, vt ait Epiphanius, Stratotici & Phibionitæ. Alibi Secundiani, So-cratitæ, Zachæi, Leuitici, Coddiani. Vt autem etiam addit Theodoretus, Naasini. Et Clemens lib.3.Stromat.Epiphanij: ita se nunquam tuto latere posse exiftimarunt. Denique quemadmodum scribit Eusebius libr.4.cap.7. Nullum vnquam fuit hominum genus, nomen Christianum profitentium, vnde plura & maiora infidelibus & gentibus offendicula præberentur, quàm ab istis. Docuerunt enim eos qui suæ mysagogiæ participes esse vellent, turpissima quæque operari & perpetrare quod alias vim diaboli effugere non possent, nisi sua cuique potestati debita soluerentur. Vnde tandem in vniuersum Christianum nomen magnum hominum odium conflatum est, & in Deum blasphemia excitata, tam fuit Satan in hoc malo excudendo nimirum & potens & astutus. His omnino contrarij fuerunt qui Gnosimachi à Damasceno vocantur, qui omne cognitionis studium in Christianis hominibus damnant, etiam Sacrarum literarum.
units.tr: 1 Gnostics) How varied the opinion of men and ecclesiastical authors about the time of this heresy is, appears from their writings. Some pass it over altogether when the name of the Gnostics is sought, as Theodoret does in his book On the Fables of the Heretics, although the same Theodoret mentions the Borborites, as do Tertullian in the book On Prescription and Platina in the Lives of the Popes. Others confuse them, as Eusebius does. Others distinguish them, as Augustine does, and Epiphanius himself, whose order I follow here and in the book. Isidore also mentions them, and many others. So that the cause of such great variety may be understood, and so that these may be separated from others, there are those who are called Gnostics by their own proper and special name, to be distinguished from the Carpocratians and Nicolaitans, with whom they nevertheless agree in doctrine. For they seem to be the only ones so called, who, having rejected the base and now hateful name of their two forebears and authors, proudly called themselves Gnostics by a splendid and new name. This name was taken from no mortal man, lest they seem to glory in men, but from the excellent, distinguished and singular understanding and comprehension of God's secrets, which they falsely attributed to themselves. For they called themselves Gnostics from γνῶσις [gnōsis, knowledge], as if they were "spiritual" [πνευματικοί] and had penetrated into the mysteries of God more deeply than all the others and their superiors. Now γνῶσις often signifies in Paul the excellent knowledge of God, and faith, and the revelation and acknowledgment of the truth and of God's works, as in Col. 2.3 and 1 Cor. 12.8. So the Gnostics, insofar as they boast of their name and are distinguished from the Carpocratians and Nicolaitans (from which two foul fountains they nevertheless sprang), constitute another sect. They first began especially under Anicetus, bishop of Rome, in the year 129 after the passion of Christ, at the beginning of the reign of M. Aurelius Antoninus the philosopher and L. Verus, Roman emperors, and three years later the Cataphrygians, other heretics. Thus abyss follows abyss. The Gnostics were indeed known also in Asia, but chiefly, and as it seems to me, first at Rome, when Marcellina, who belonged to this sect, as Irenaeus writes in book 1, chapter 24, had come from Asia to Rome. She had already dismissed the name of the Carpocratians and Nicolaitans, now hateful to the Church, and had infected many with her plague. This happened under Anicetus, Roman bishop, as I said, about the year 130 or 132 after the passion of Christ. From this it can rightly be concluded that they are later in age than the Carpocratians. Nor is it wrongly placed in this order after the Nicolaitans, because according to the opinion of Epiphanius, Augustine thinks these serpents were born from Nicolaus rather than from Carpocrates. For after treating of Nicolaus the heresiarch, he adds: "The Gnostics, the Naassenes, differently from the ... desperate man, as from a spring, fruit ..." On this very point, however, the opinions of the authors vary. Irenaeus thinks they are rather the unhappy offspring of the Carpocratians, and Tertullian also holds this in his book On the Soul, though in the Scorpiace against the Gnostics he does not explain the stock from which such noxious branches sprang and were propagated. Irenaeus, in book 3, chapter 4, writes that they were born from Menander, a disciple of Simon, like Median serpents. However that may be, they are the seed of those unhappy tares which Satan sowed in the field and Church of the Lord, so that he might work out and finally accomplish the mystery of iniquity, which he did accomplish. The heresy of the Gnostics endured for many centuries, both in Asia and above all in Egypt. From it the Valentinians first, then the Manichaeans, then the Priscillianists, like the Hydra's heads, were spread abroad and born, so that in Spain, even after the year of the Lord 386, it was not only renewed but spread widely, as Sigebert writes. Guillaume Postel, the dregs of the world, renewed it in our century. They were indeed the most foul of all mortals in doctrine, and although the Nicolaitans were their base masters, they were far more base themselves. Hence they insinuated and concealed themselves under various names, often changed on purpose, lest, known by the execrable name of Gnostics, they should at once be cast out by the Church. Nor was there ever any heresy which disguised and hid itself under so many and such diverse appellations, or which split itself more quickly into several sects and fragments. For those who are here called Gnostics by Augustine are called by others Barbeliotes, from Barbelo whom they worshipped. Elsewhere they are called Borborites, from the mud (cœnum), a word taken from the Second Epistle of the Apostle Peter, for βόρβορος means filth and mud (2 Pet. 2.22). In Egypt, as Epiphanius says, they are Stratiotici and Phibionites. Elsewhere they are Secundians, Socratites, Zachaeans, Leviticals, Coddians. As Theodoret also adds, Naassenes. And Clement, in book 3 of the Stromata, and Epiphanius: thus they never thought they could lie hidden safely. Finally, as Eusebius writes in book 4, chapter 7: there has never been any kind of men professing the Christian name by whom more and greater stumbling-blocks were offered to unbelievers and Gentiles than by these. For they taught those who wished to share in their mystic rites to do and perpetrate all the most shameful things, since otherwise they could not escape the power of the devil, unless each one paid what was owed to his own power. Whence at last the Christian name in general was kindled with great hatred among men, and blasphemy against God was stirred up, so powerful and cunning was Satan in forging this evil. Entirely opposed to these were those whom Damascene calls Gnosimachi, who condemn all pursuit of knowledge in Christian men, even of the Sacred Letters.

units.la: 2 ) Tradunt autem. ) Videtur Tertullianus in lib.De præscriptionib.Ophitis tribuere, quæ alij Gnosticis.Idem autem aliud Gnosticis,id est, id tantum concedit vt proprium hæreseos eorum caput, quod martyria vel morte pro Christi nomine & gloria tolerandam negarent, Tertullianus in Scorpiaco. Id quod tamen Basilidianorum esse proprium docuimus. Alij pene omnes iis tantum morum turpitudinem illam quidem insignem & relatu indignâ vendicant, adeo ut quod de Carpocratianis commemorat Clemens lib.3. Stromat. de Gnosticis proprie intelligendu putent. Sunt autem hæc Clemen-tis verba, Hos dicunt,ait,& aliquos alios simi-lium malorum æmulatores, ad cœnas conue-nientes (neque enim dixerim Agapen eorum congressionem) viros simul & mulieres, post-quam satietate venerem excitate exsatiati sunt, lumine amoto quod eorum fornicatoriam hac iustitiam pudore afficiat, auersa lucerna coire quomodo velint, & cum quibus velint. Me-ditatos autem in eiusmodi Agapæ communio-nem interdiu iam, a quibus velint mulieribus exigere Carpocrateæ (diuinæ enim nefas est di-cere) legis obedientia. Hactenus Clemens. Eu-sebius autem addit eos promiscue & inceftuo-se cum matribus & sororibus coiisse, & vetitis cibis, qualia sunt menstrua mulierum, atque e-tiam nefandis maxime in suis mysteriis vsos esse. Inde vero ortæ & aspersæ in veros Chri-stianos hæ calumniæ, quod Christiani humana carne vescerentur, quod incestuosos & promi-scuos coitus haberent, quod extinctis lucernis fœda quæque peragerent, pro quibus abster-gendis & Iustinus Martyr vtramque apologiam scripsit, & Tertullianus eruditissimum illum A-pologeticum librum. Astutè id quidem Satan, qui quum Christianorum doctrinam per se in odium hominum adducere non posset, mores & vitam eorum criminari atque calumniari, quia diabolus est, salsorum Christianorū prætextu cœpit. Capita verò & hypothecs huius hæreseos enumerantur multæ. Quatuor hic ab Augustino. 1 Dogmata ineptissima ʻde mundi cæterarumque rerum creatione, quæ hic non recenset Augustinus: Theodoretus tamen in Barbeliotis, & Irenæus lib.1.ca.33.&34. habent, quorum hæc pene summa est. Ex summo & primario Æone, complures alios Æones extitisse, inferiores tamen summo: ex iis præstantiorem esse Ialdabaoth, qui quum in superiora eniti vellet, depressum grauitate adhæren tis materiæ aquæ non potuisse ad superna devenire. Itaque in medio loco subsistentem extendisse ex sua illa aqua cœlum, & hæc omnia quæ cernimus. Triplicem filium summi Æonis constituut. Vnum qui fit lumen illud Bythi incorruptibile. Alterum Ennœan [illegible, ~6 letters], qui ex illo Bythi lumine incorruptibili secudum hominem natus fit, & homo fit ab omni interitu alienus, & in virginali spiritu seruetur. Hunc Barbeloth vocant, i.filium vetustatis. Tertium filium productum ex primo illo homine, &Spiritu sancto, quem vocant fœminā. Hunc filium Christum nominant &Prunicum. Ex Chao autem, Aquis, Tenebris, & Abysso miras propagationes & [illegible, ~6 letters] faciunt, adeo vt quod plane & perspicuè de rerum & mundi huius creatione narrat Moses, absurdissimis verborum inuolucris tegat. Platonicorum & Pythagoreorum deliria & commenta sequuti. Prunicon putat Epiphanius Græcā vocem esse, & scribit [illegible, ~6 letters]-, quæ veloxsignificat. Alij vero Syriacam, quæ Redemptorem significat, פרוקא[?] Paruka. Dempto enim Camets fit Pruca & Prucon.ad-diderunt Græci syllabam ni, unde Πεψϋκόν[?] effecerunt. Alij aliunde deriuant. Hebraicis enim nominibus non autē Græcis, figmenta sua eos obscurasse testatur Theodoretus. {2}Animas in hominibus fidelibus duas constituunt, unam sanctam ex Dei substantia, quam Christus minuens Patris imperium, eo ignorante fit solus habiturus. Alteram esse adventitiam, quæ ex Dei insufflatione insit homini, uti cæteris animalibus, quam solam Pater fit habiturus. Ita Irenæus sub finem cap.34. libri 1. Hinc Manichæorum delirium de duabus animabus, quę in homine sunt hodiè permissæ, ut aiunt. Vide Augustin. libro De duabus anim.cap.12. Ex quo jam apparet, quàm sit hic locus apud Augustinium depravatus, ubi pro earūmque legendum est aliarum quoque, vel aliarūmque, ut duplex anima ex Gnosticorum mente constituatur. Alias totus hic locus est valde obscurus. Verba autem, per quas peccata in corporibus committun-tur, adiectitia videri non debent. Putant enim illi eas animas, quæ in hominibus peccant, esse nobis cum brutis communes. Itaque rursum eas in alia corpora etiam animalium brutorum Pythagorica μετεμψύχωσις[?] migrare & mitti. Nec id mirum, quando Thnatopsychitæ hæretici, de quibus Ioannes Damascenus, docent hominum animas pecudum animis similes esse, & eas una cum corporibus interire. Quod longè pejus & grauius fuit. Sanctas autem animas quæ insunt in hominibus, docêt Gnostici non peccare,nec iterum in alia corpora mitti. Sed quasi iam non satis esset erroris in ipsa Gnosticorū hæresi,addidit librarius in transcribendo errorem,ut in ipso errore intelligendo pene ipsi eraremus. Huius autem erroris fundamentum & causam sumpserunt Gnostici,ut scribit Hieronymus in Galat.1. vers.15. quòd cùm alij sint electi à Deo: alij reprobati antequam aliquid boni fecerint aut mali:hoc iuste à Deo fieri non posset, nisi esset pereuntium, & saluandorū diversa natura: in unis spiritualis,in aliis carnalis[?]. 3 Angelos ex summo Patre & Æone procreatos, quibus nomina barbara imponunt. Septem autem genitos cocubitu humano. Hoc à superioribus hæresibus sumptū est. 4 Duplicem Deum primi illi salsissimè induxerunt, unum bonum:alterum malum. Hinc Manichæi fæces suas apertissimè depropserunt. 5 Christum distinguunt, ut aliam personam, à Iesu. Descendisse enim Christum in Iesum iam natum,& grādem,& pene triginta annorum,quo primum tepore cœpit miracula edere. Demum autem post resurrectione unitū esse Christum Iesu. Irenæus. Hinc Nestorianismi & Eutychianismi vetustissima & venenosissima femina,quę postea excitauit, & robustius germinare fecit Satan. 6 Christum post resurrectionem per octodecim menses hic in mundo versatum citra manifestissimam Scripturę fidem. Act.1.v.3. Irenæus. 7 Martyria negarūt pro nomine Dei subeunda Christianis. Tertullianus. 8 Imagines Christi depictas coluerunt, & in summa veneratione,ut gentes,suorū deorum picturas habuehabuerunt. Quod ipsum hæresin esse docet Ire-næus, quia nondum in Dei Ecclesia erat idolo-latria uti nunc est. Habetur enim nunc istud valde inter Papistas religiosum: inter rectè sentientes Patres, ethnicum.
units.tr: 2) They report, however.) Tertullian in his book De praescriptionibus seems to attribute to the Ophites what others attribute to the Gnostics. He also makes a different point about the Gnostics in the Scorpiace, namely that the one feature he grants as the distinctive mark of their heresy is that they denied that one must endure martyrdom or death for the name and glory of Christ. Yet we have shown that this was peculiar to the Basilidians. Almost all the others claim for the Gnostics only that notorious and unspeakable depravity of morals, so much so that they think Clement, in book 3 of the Stromata, is to be understood as speaking properly of the Gnostics when he mentions the Carpocratians. Clement's words are these: "They say, he writes, and some others who imitate such evils, that they gather for feasts (I would not call their gathering an agape), men and women together. When they have been stirred to lust and satisfied with it, they put out the light, which they say shames their fornicating justice, and, with the lamp turned away, they mate as they wish and with whom they wish. They have devised a communal agape of this kind, in which by day they demand from whichever women they wish, in the name of Carpocratian obedience to the law (for it would be impious to say 'divine'), what they want." So far Clement. Eusebius adds that they had intercourse promiscuously and incestuously with mothers and sisters, that they ate forbidden foods such as women's menstrual blood, and that they used the most abominable practices in their mysteries. From this, however, these slanders arose and were spread against the true Christians: that Christians ate human flesh, that they had incestuous and promiscuous intercourse, and that in the dark they committed every filthy act. To wipe these charges away Justin Martyr wrote both of his Apologies, and Tertullian wrote his most learned book, the Apologeticus. Satan was clever indeed: since he could not by itself bring the teaching of Christians into hatred among men, he began, as the devil he is, to slander and accuse their morals and way of life under the pretext of the depraved Christians. The heads and foundations of this heresy are listed in many forms. Four are given here by Augustine. 1 Most absurd dogmas about the creation of the world and of other things, which Augustine does not recount here; Theodoret, however, in his account of the Barbeliotes, and Irenaeus in book 1, chapters 33 and 34, give them, and their substance is nearly this. From the highest and first Aeon many other Aeons came forth, all inferior to the highest. Among them Ialdabaoth was the most excellent, who, wishing to strive upward, was weighed down by the heaviness of the matter that clung to him and could not reach the heights. Therefore, standing in the middle place, he stretched out from that water of his the heaven and all the things we see. They posit a threefold son of the highest Aeon. One is that incorruptible light of Bythos. The second is Ennoea [illegible], who was born according to the human pattern from that incorruptible light of Bythos, and becomes a man free from all corruption, and is preserved in a virginal spirit. They call him Barbeloth, that is, son of antiquity. The third son was produced from that first man and the Holy Spirit, whom they call the female. They name this son Christ and Prunicus. From Chaos, Waters, Darkness and the Abyss they make wondrous generations and [illegible], so that what Moses narrates plainly and clearly about the creation of this world is hidden under the most absurd wrappings of words, following the dreams and inventions of the Platonists and Pythagoreans. Epiphanius thinks Prunicus is a Greek word and writes [illegible], which means swift. Others derive it from the Syriac, which means Redeemer, פרוקא [Paruka]. For by dropping the qamets it becomes Pruka and Prukon. The Greeks added the syllable ni, whence they made Πεψϋκόν [Pepsykon]. Others derive it from elsewhere. Theodoret testifies that by Hebrew names, and not Greek ones, they obscured their fictions. {2} They posit two souls in faithful men: one holy, from the substance of God, which Christ, diminishing the Father's rule, will alone possess when the Father is unaware of it; the other is an adventitious soul, which is in man by God's breathing, as in other animals, and which the Father alone will possess. Thus Irenaeus near the end of chapter 34 of book 1. Hence came the Manichaean raving about two souls which, as they say, are today present in man. See Augustine, De duabus animabus, chapter 12. From this it is now clear how corrupted this passage in Augustine is, where instead of earumque one should read est aliarum quoque, or aliarumque, so that a double soul is set up according to the mind of the Gnostics. Otherwise this whole passage is very obscure. The words autem, through which sins are committed in bodies, ought not to be regarded as an addition. For they think that those souls which sin in men are common to us and the brute beasts. Therefore they again have them migrate and be sent into other bodies, even those of brute animals, by Pythagorean metempsychosis [μετεμψύχωσις]. Nor is this surprising, since the heretical Thnetopsychites, of whom John Damascene writes, teach that the souls of men are like the souls of beasts and perish together with their bodies. That was far worse and more grievous. The Gnostics, however, teach that the holy souls which are in men do not sin, nor are they again sent into other bodies. But as if there were not enough error already in the Gnostic heresy itself, the copyist, in transcribing, added an error, so that in understanding the error itself we almost became part of it. The Gnostics took the foundation and cause of this error, as Jerome writes on Galatians 1:15, from the fact that since some are chosen by God and others rejected before they have done any good or evil, this could not justly be done by God unless there were a different nature of those who perish and of those who are saved: in some spiritual, in others carnal. 3 Angels produced from the highest Father and Aeon, to whom they give barbarous names. Seven, however, were born from human intercourse. This was taken over from the earlier heresies. 4 The first of them most foolishly introduced a double God, one good and the other evil. Hence the Manichaeans most openly brought forth their dregs. 5 They distinguish Christ as a person other than Jesus. For Christ, they say, descended upon Jesus when he was already born and grown, and nearly thirty years old, at the time when he first began to perform miracles, and only after the resurrection was Christ united with Jesus. Irenaeus. Hence came the very ancient and most poisonous seed of Nestorianism and Eutychianism, which Satan later stirred up and made to sprout more vigorously. 6 That Christ after the resurrection dwelt in this world for eighteen months, contrary to the plainest faith of Scripture, Acts 1:3. Irenaeus. 7 They denied that Christians must undergo martyrdom for the name of God. Tertullian. 8 They worshipped painted images of Christ and held them in highest reverence, as the Gentiles did with pictures of their gods. Irenaeus teaches that this itself is heresy, because idolatry, as it now is, did not yet exist in the Church of God. For this is now regarded as very religious among the Papists, but among the Fathers who thought rightly it is regarded as heathen.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: Carpocratiani unde appellati. Erroris autem capita sex referuntur.
units.tr: The Carpocratians, and why they are so called. Six heads of their error are reported.

units.la: Carpocratiani sunt à {1} Carpocrate, qui docebat {2} omnem turpem operationem, omnemque adminuentionem peccati: nec aliter euadi atque transiri principatus & potestates, quibus hæc placent, ut possit ad cælum superius peruenirí. Hic etiam Iesum hominem tantummodo, & de utroque sexu natum putasse perhibetur, sed accepisse talem animam, quæ sciret ea quæ superna essent, atque nuntiaret. Resurrectionem corporis cum Lege abjciebat. Negabat mundum à Deo factum, sed nescio à quibus virtutibus Secta ipsius fuisse traditur. Socia quædam Marcellina {3}, quæ colebat imagines Iesu, & Pauli, & Homeri, & Pythagoræ, adorando, incensumque ponendo.
units.tr: The Carpocratians are so named from Carpocrates, who taught that every shameful action and every diminishing of sin is permitted, and that the rulers and powers who delight in such things cannot be escaped or passed through otherwise, so that one may reach the higher heaven. He is also said to have held that Jesus was a mere man, born of both sexes, but that he received a soul of such a kind that it knew the things above and proclaimed them. He rejected the resurrection of the body together with the Law. He denied that the world was made by God, but it is handed down that his sect was founded by I know not what powers. A certain companion, Marcellina, worshipped images of Jesus, Paul, Homer and Pythagoras, adoring them and setting incense before them.

units.la: 1 A Carpocrate.) Carpocratiani hæretici, propter morum dissolutionem, etiam præter superiores hæreticos, omnes Ecclesiæ carcinomata & verrucæ habiti sunt. Ex nulla enim secta tantum odij in Christianos conflatum est, quantum ex ista.Itaque de ijs ita scribit Epipha-nius lib.2.Tom.1, Εἰ δ᾽ ἐν τῇ Σατυρᾷ [?] παρεισάγει [?] ἀφυέστατοι [?] καὶ ἀκάνθαλον [?] εἰς ἀθεότητα [?] τῆς Θεοῦ Ἐκκλησίας. Ex ijs enim maximum in no-men Christianum emanauit probrum propter turpes & nefandos mores, quemadmodum scribit Clemens lib.3.Stromat. Id enim fore prae-dixerat Petrus, nimirum vt per exitiales haere-ses via veritatis blasphemaretur, 2.Pet.2.versu 2. Post Gnosticos collocat Augustinus, sequutus Epiphanium, vt Augustinum ipsum sequutus est Isidorus, quia vitae turpitudine, & dogmatum vanitate inter se similimi fuerunt. Ophitis autem & aliis hos postponit Tertullianus, praeponit vero Theodoretus: tam est incerta de ijsdem rebus scriptorum Ecclesiasticorum sententia. Carpocrate autem siue Carpocra-tes,a quo sunt appellati,vixit sub initio imperij Antonini Pij,circa annum a Christo passo 109, quanquam Theodoretus sub Adriano potius eum floruisse scribit, sed potuit notus esse sub utroque. Eusebius libro 4.cap.8. ait eum fuisse contemporaneum & aequalem Saturnino. Fuit autem Ægyptius Carpocrates, genere Alexan-drinus, vbi patre Ægyptio, & matre Alexandra Cephalenia natus est, Platonicae disciplinae, & omnis encyclopaediae scientissimus: diuinae vero theologiae ignorantissimus, in qua etiam Plato nica schola filium Epiphanem erudiuit, vt scribit Clemens Alexandrinus. Inde vero haereseos fons, quod Platonis dicta & ampullas, Euangelicae veritati magno fastu praeponeret. Grassata autem est Carpocratianorum pestis non in Ægypto tatum, sed & in Asia, & Romæ nomine Gnosticorum. Retenta tamen est aliquandiu, & sustentata ipsa suo nomine & appellatione post Carpocratem ab Epiphane filio Carpocratis, ut scribit Theodoretus, qui doctus inter Platonicos habitus est, & librum edidit, quem inscripsit [illegible, ~4 letters], & hunc citat Epiphanius: item alium [illegible, ~4 letters], id est, De iustitia. Iustitiam autem definit esse κοινωνίαν Θεοῦ μετ' ἀνθρώπων. Quæ definitio plane obscura est, ut docet Clemens lib.3.Stromat. Hic vixit, iusto Dei iudicio sublatus, tantum 17.annis, & in insula Cephalenia, unde propter matrem oriundus erat, pro Deo cultus est, imprimis Samiæ, quæ fuit urbs Cephaleniæ. Epiphani successit in eadem secta Prodicus quidam, ut est apud Theodoretum. Hic vero numero superiorum errorum non contentus, excudit & ipse novam hæresim Adamitarum, qui præter Carpocratianica dogmata, hoc suæ hæresi addiderunt, Deum non esse orandum, quia novit qui bonis digni sint, qui vero non sint. Clemens lib.7.Strom.
units.tr: 1 From Carpocrates.) The Carpocratian heretics, on account of their dissolute morals, were regarded, even beyond the other heretics, as the cancers and warts of the Church. For no sect has kindled so much hatred against the Christians as this one. Epiphanius, book 2, volume 1, writes about them thus: "If they introduce into the Satyra [?] ... the most ignorant ... and a thorn into the atheism of the Church of God" [Εἰ δ᾽ ἐν τῇ Σατυρᾷ παρεισάγει ἀφυέστατοι καὶ ἀκάνθαλον εἰς ἀθεότητα τῆς Θεοῦ Ἐκκλησίας]. For from them the greatest reproach to the Christian name came forth, on account of their foul and unspeakable morals, as Clement writes in book 3 of the Stromata. For Peter had foretold that this would happen, namely that through pernicious heresies the way of truth would be blasphemed (2 Pet. 2.2). Augustine places them after the Gnostics, following Epiphanius, and Isidore followed Augustine, because they were very similar to one another in the baseness of their lives and the vanity of their doctrines. Tertullian places them after the Ophites and others, but Theodoret places them before them; so uncertain is the judgement of the ecclesiastical writers on these same matters. Carpocrates, or Carpocras, from whom they take their name, lived under the beginning of the reign of Antoninus Pius, around the year 109 after Christ's passion, although Theodoret writes that he flourished rather under Hadrian; but he could have been known under both. Eusebius, book 4, chapter 8, says that he was a contemporary of Saturninus and of the same age. Carpocrates was an Egyptian by birth, a native of Alexandria, where he was born to an Egyptian father and a mother from Cephalonia, a man most learned in Platonic learning and in all the encyclopaedia of knowledge, but most ignorant of divine theology, in which also the Platonic school trained his son Epiphanes, as Clement of Alexandria writes. The source of the heresy lay in this, that he preferred the sayings and empty show of Plato, with great arrogance, to the Gospel truth. The plague of the Carpocratians spread not only in Egypt but also in Asia and at Rome, under the name of Gnostics. It was nevertheless retained for some time and maintained by its own name and designation after Carpocrates by his son Epiphanes, as Theodoret writes; Epiphanes, who was regarded as learned among the Platonists, published a book which he entitled [illegible, ~4 letters], and Epiphanius cites it; likewise another, [illegible, ~4 letters], that is, On Justice. He defines justice as a fellowship of God with men [κοινωνίαν Θεοῦ μετ' ἀνθρώπων]. This definition is plainly obscure, as Clement shows in book 3 of the Stromata. He lived only 17 years, and was taken away by the just judgement of God; and in the island of Cephalonia, from which his mother's family came, he was worshipped as a god, especially at Samos, which was a city of Cephalonia. Prodicus, a certain man, succeeded Epiphanes in the same sect, as is found in Theodoret. But he, not content with the number of the earlier errors, himself hammered out a new heresy, that of the Adamites, who, besides the Carpocratian dogmas, added to their heresy this: that God is not to be prayed to, because he knows who are worthy of good things and who are not. Clement, book 7 of the Stromata.

units.la: Quæ fuerint huius sectæ hypotheses, tum ex hoc Augustini loco, tum ex eiusdem lib.2.contra aduersar.Legis,cap.12. tum etiam ex Irenæo lib.1.cap.24. Tertulliano, Epiphanio, & Theodoreto facile potest intelligi. Primum enim eius hæresεos authorem omnes constituunt, quæ duos deos, diuersæ penitus dissimilisque naturæ finxit.
