Ex qua aliæ innumerabiles natæ sunt, imprimis autem Manichæi, quorum in hoc error notior fuit. Ergo prima hæc eorum hypothesis fuit, quòd omnem morum turpitudinem suos discipulos docerēt. Lege enim Dei quæ bona opera docet & exigit, contemnebant, quia sola fide & gratia Dei salui [?]simus. Itaque posse nostrum quemque libere cuilibet uitio indulgere. Præter fidē enim omnia bona vel mala opera rerum indifferentium numero & pretio censenda, quia non natura, sed tantum hominum opinione iustum & iniustum, bonum & malum constaret & distingueretur. Itaque rerum delectum sustulerunt. Imo vero nec aliter nos posse potestatum malarum, quibus hic subiicimur, iura & iram euitare, nisi peccemus & turpiter uiuamus. Eo enim modo illæ a nobis placantur, fiuntque nobis, ut illi quidem sentiunt, propitiæ. Quo dogmate quid deterius aut unquam foedius Satan mundo adhuc propinarat? Itaque & communes uxores esse oportere dixerunt, & Magiam exercuerunt, & [illegible, ~12 letters] .i. familiares habuerunt, ut ait Epiphanius. Nos hic agentes esse sub imperio malarum potestatum & angelorum (hi autem sunt diaboli) quibus non nisi superatis, in supremum & extimum cælum peruenire possumus. Superari autem, si male & dissolute uiuamus. Ita honesto[?] prætextu turpissimos mores induxerunt. Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum pure hominem fuisse & posse quemque eo & miraculis potentiorem & uitæ sanctitate puriorem uiuere, non modo esse parem, si plus, quam ille, mundo renuntiare uelit. Quare & seipsos & præceptorem suum Carpocratem Christo meliores esse impudentissime affirmant & mentiuntur. Dei enim uirtutc assidente tantùm & communicata fuisse Christum & potentem factis, & sanctùm moribus. Quae haeresis postea Samosatenū genuit, & futurae Arianorum haereseos fundamenta nō centissima collocabat, & eius praesertim, quae hodie sentit non aliter Deum esse in homine Christo quam in Paulo & Petro. Itaque hanc de Christo fuisse Carpocratianorum sententiā docet Epiphanius his verbis, Εἶναι δ' αὐτὸν ὅμοιον[?] τοῖς ἀνθρώποις, βίῳ δὲ [illegible, ~10 letters] σωφροσύνῃ τε καὶ ἀρετῇ καὶ βίῳ δικαιοσύνης.
units.tr: What the foundations of this sect were may easily be understood both from this passage of Augustine, from the same author's book 2 against the adversaries of the Law, chapter 12, from Irenaeus, book 1, chapter 24, and from Tertullian, Epiphanius and Theodoret. For all agree that the author of this heresy was the first, who imagined two gods of entirely different and dissimilar nature. From this many other innumerable sects were born, above all the Manichaeans, whose error in this respect was better known. Their first foundation, therefore, was that they taught their disciples every turpitude of morals. For they despised the Law of God, which teaches and requires good works, because we are saved by faith alone and the grace of God. Hence each of us may freely indulge in any vice whatever. For apart from faith, all good or bad works are to be counted among things indifferent, in number and worth, since justice and injustice, good and evil, were established and distinguished not by nature but only by the opinion of men. Hence they abolished the choice of things. Indeed, they said that we could not otherwise escape the power and wrath of the evil powers to which we are here subjected, unless we sin and live shamefully. For in that way those powers are appeased by us and become, as they indeed think, propitious to us. What more wicked or more foul doctrine had Satan ever yet served up to the world? And so they said that wives ought to be held in common, and they practised magic, and kept [illegible, ~12 letters], that is, familiars, as Epiphanius says. They taught that we, living here, are under the dominion of evil powers and angels (and these are the devils), and that we cannot reach the highest and outermost heaven unless these have been overcome. But they are overcome if we live badly and dissolutely. So under a specious pretext they introduced the most shameful morals. They held that our Lord Jesus Christ was purely a man, and that anyone could live both more powerful than he in miracles and purer in holiness of life, and not merely equal to him, if he wished to renounce the world more than he did. Wherefore they most shamelessly affirm and lie that both themselves and their teacher Carpocrates are better than Christ. For Christ, they said, was only empowered by the sharing of God's virtue dwelling with him, and was made powerful in deeds and holy in morals. This heresy later gave birth to Samosatenus, and laid, not very firmly, the foundations of the future heresy of the Arians, and especially of that which today holds that God is in the man Christ no otherwise than in Paul and Peter. Hence Epiphanius teaches that this was the opinion of the Carpocratians about Christ, in these words: "He was like other men, but in his life [illegible, ~10 letters] in sobriety and virtue and a life of righteousness."

units.la: 4 Christum ad modum caeterorum hominum ex Iosephi patris & Mariae matris femine natum, cuius sola anima in caelū ascenderit, & ibi est, non etiam corpus, quia illius anima robustior & valentior corpore fuit.
units.tr: 4 That Christ, like other men, was born of the seed of Joseph his father and Mary his mother, whose soul alone ascended into heaven and is there, but not his body, because his soul was stronger and more powerful than the body.

units.la: 5 Carnis resurrectionem negat futuram, Με-τεμψύχωσιν[?] tamen animarum in alia corpora retinet, & probat ex Pythagoreorum & Platonicorum dogmatis, dissimillima tamen ab illis ratione. Nam Plato ad criminum in hac vita perpetratorum iustam ultionem fieri putat, ut animae ex improborum corporibus migrates, post mortem in belluarum corpora, vel hominum seniorum mittantur ad prius scelus eluendum. Carpocrates autem contrà sentit, idcirco post vitam hanc mitti in alia corpora animas hominum, quòd non se satis voluptatibus expleverint & conspurcarint. Unde quae animae temperantius hic vixerint, sæpius in corpora detrudi.
units.tr: 5 They deny that the resurrection of the flesh will take place, yet they retain the transmigration of souls into other bodies, and prove it from the dogmas of the Pythagoreans and Platonists, though with a reasoning very unlike theirs. For Plato thought that just vengeance is taken for crimes committed in this life, so that souls, migrating from the bodies of the wicked, are after death sent into the bodies of beasts or of lower men, to wash away their earlier wickedness. Carpocrates, on the contrary, thinks that the souls of men are sent after this life into other bodies because they have not sated and defiled themselves enough with pleasures. Hence those souls which have lived more temperately here are more often thrust down into bodies.

units.la: 6 Mundum hunc negat à Deo factum, sed ab inferioribus angelis, inter quos praecipuus fit diabolus. Hi sunt nimirum Platonicae philosophiae fructus, & contemptae simplicis & cælestis veritatis, quæ in libris sacris tradita est, iusta sane ultio & supplicium, per quod in reprobum sensum homines à Deo inducuntur, ut qui ethnicæ isti sapientiæ tantopere sunt addicti, tantùmque tribuunt, discat tandem aliquando sibi displicere: & tamen impudenter illi Christum suarum nugarum autorem profitebatur, quasi eas discipulis suis clã[?] tradidisset. Unde nec ipsi hæc tam fœda mysteria quibusuis patefacienda esse dicebant, sed discipulos suos in auricula dextra subula & stigmate aliquo notabant, ut scribunt Irenæus & Epiphanius.
units.tr: 6 He denies that this world was made by God, but says it was made by inferior angels, among whom the chief is the devil. These are indeed the fruits of Platonic philosophy, and of the contempt of the simple and heavenly truth which is delivered in the holy books; a just vengeance and punishment, by which men are led by God into a reprobate mind, so that those who are so devoted to this heathen wisdom, and attribute so much to it, may at last learn to be displeasing to themselves. Yet he shamelessly professed that Christ was the author of his trifles, as if he had secretly handed them down to his disciples. Hence they themselves also said that these so foul mysteries were not to be revealed to just anyone, but marked their disciples on the right ear with an awl and some brand, as Irenaeus and Epiphanius write.

units.la: De Marcellina ista prius diximus in Gnosticis, de qua etiam meminit in hæresi Epiphanius & Eusebius lib.5.cap.16. Cum ea fornicatus & consuetudinem habuisse traditur Carpocrates.
units.tr: We have said these things about Marcellina before, under the Gnostics; Epiphanius also mentions her in his account of the heresy, and Eusebius, book 5, chapter 16. It is handed down that Carpocrates committed fornication with her and had intercourse with her.

units.la: CAP. VIII. Cerinthiani, unde dicti, & erroris eorum capita quinque.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII. The Cerinthians, whence they are named, and their five heads of error.

units.la: Erinthiani à Cerintho, ydemque Merinthiani à Merintho, Mundum {*}ab Angelis factum esse dicentes, & carne circuncidi oportere, atque alia huiusmodi Legis præcepta seruari. Iesum hominem tantummodo fuisse, nec surrexisse, sed resurrecturum affirmantes. Mille quoque annos post resurrectionem in terreno regno Christi secundum carnales ventris & libidinis voluptates futuros fabulantur: unde etiam Chiliastæ{3} sunt appellati.
units.tr: The Erinthians are named from Cerinthus, and the Merinthians from Merinthus. They say that the world was made by angels, that the flesh must be circumcised, and that other precepts of this kind of the Law must be kept. They affirm that Jesus was only a man, and that he did not rise but will rise. They also fable that a thousand years after the resurrection Christ will reign in an earthly kingdom, with carnal pleasures of belly and lust; whence they were also called Chiliasts.

units.la: Cur Cerinthiani Carpocra-tianis subiiciantur, quæstio est, quum ætate prio res fuisse videantur. Nam qui postremos ortos fuisse putant, falluntur: quanquam tamen Tertullianus & Epiphanius in ea sunt sententia vt à Carpocratianis profectos & deductos Cerinthianos velint. Epiphanium autem sequutus est Augustinus, & Augustinum Isidorus lib.8.Etymolog.capite 5. Ratio fortasse hæc fuit, quod in dogmate simillimi, & pene iidé apparent vtriq; Cerinthiani & Carpocratiani, vt ait Tertullian. Quę certé ratio nihil efficit. Vixerunt enim eodem tempore Cerinthus & Ebion, & tamen inter se dissenserunt, nec eadem dogmata semper sunt amplexi, qui ijsdem temporibus vixerunt, vti in Cerintho & Ebione apparet, quemadmodum scribit Eusebius lib.3.cap.28. Quod autem ad Epiphanium attinet, à seipso refutatur. Idem enim ille, qui Cerinthum post Carpocrate collocat, scribit diserté Cerinthum iam ætate Petri & Pauli vixisse, & iis sæpe restitisse, esséque vnû ex iis quos pseudoapostolos vocat Paulus, & qui Antiochiæ propter circuncisionem Gentium turbas mouerunt, vt est Act.15. Carpocrates autem multis post annis extitit, vt ne coæui quidé illi fuisse iam videri posint. Quid igitur? Errorem Epiphanij & indiligetem hoc loco suppu-tationem sequutus est Augustinus. Nos vero ex Irenæo, Dionysio Alexandrino, Caio, Polycarpo, qui illis temporibus proximi fuerunt, itémque Eusebio libro 3.cap.23. & 24. sic obseruaui-mus. Theodoretum enim omittimus, quia de Cerinthianis nihil à nostra sententia diuersum scripsit. Cerinthum temporibus Ioannis Euan- geliftæ vixisse, & iam tum suum illud virus & hærefin sparsisse, & passim vt blasphemum innotuisse apparet ex narratione Polycarpi, quæ refertur ab Irenæo libro 3.cap.3. & Eufeb.libro 4.cap. 14. libro 7.cap.23. nimirum quòd in balneum, lauandi causa, ingressurus Ioannes, postquam illic esse Cerinthum audiuit, abiit, locum execratus, & adiecit se vereri ne balneum ipsum concideret, in quo tantus hostis veritatis lauisset. Præterea videtur Ioannes quibusdam locis errorem Cerinthi perstringere, vti 1. Ioann. 2. v. 19. 22. & cap. 4. versu 3. Refertur autem huius ætas ad imperium Domitiani, & videtur maxime circa annum à Christo passo 62, hærefin suā euulgasse. Sparsit autem eam in Asia præsertim, id est, Asia minore & Syria, orsus ab Antiochiæ vrbe, vt vult Epiphanius, qui de eo ita scribit, Ἐψἕετο δ' ἐξ ὁ Κηρινθος ἐν τῇ Ἀσίᾳ διατρίβων, κάκεῖσε τῆς ἐν ὑμνογραφίας τῆς ἀρχῆς παρθενικῆς· Latissime autem postea peruagata est, & disseminata, adeo vt suos fautores habuerit, sed etiam interpolatores. Fuit autem Cerinthus natione Iudæus, vti Epiphanius scripsit, & circumcisus. Itaque omnes Christianos circumcidendos contendebat. In Ægypto philosophia eum didicisse quidam tradunt, sed vt postea apparuit, infeliciter. Vtrunque ambitiosum hominem, & prorsus corporis voluptatibus deditum fuisse demonstrant ipsius errores. Merinthiani etiam dicti sunt, ait ex Epiphanio Augustinus, siue quòd hic ipse Cerinthus se dissimulato nomine Merinthum appellarit: siue quòd Merinthus quidā fuerit eius & collega & discipulus. Utrum enim ex iis sit verius, ignorat Epiphanius ipse. Εἶπ᾽ ἂν ait, ὁ αὐτὸς Κήρινθος, Μένανδρος πάλιν ἐκαλεῖτο, οὐ πάντως οὗ τούτου ἴσχυσεν[?]. Εἶτα ἄλλος τις ἦν Μένανδρος ὄνο-μα, συνήθης τούτῳ, Θεῷ ἐγνώσθη[?]. Raro tamen Merinthianorum nomine citantur. Nomen etiam ipsum Cerinthianorū statim concidit, sed Carpocratiani, & Samosateniani hanc ipsam blasphemiam nouis nominibus restituerunt, & sustentarunt. Ex quo fit ut multis in Asia seculis pessimę grassata sit.
units.tr: Why the Cerinthians are placed under the Carpocratians is a question, since they seem to be older in time. For those who think they arose later are mistaken. Yet Tertullian and Epiphanius hold the view that the Cerinthians were derived and descended from the Carpocratians. Augustine followed Epiphanius, and Isidore, in book 8 of the Etymologies, chapter 5, followed Augustine. Perhaps the reason was that the Cerinthians and Carpocratians appear very similar, and almost the same in doctrine, as Tertullian says. Yet this reason proves nothing. For Cerinthus and Ebion lived at the same time, and nevertheless disagreed with each other, and those who lived at the same times did not always embrace the same doctrines, as appears in Cerinthus and Ebion, as Eusebius writes in book 3, chapter 28. As for Epiphanius, he is refuted by himself. For the same man who places Cerinthus after Carpocrates writes plainly that Cerinthus lived already in the time of Peter and Paul, and often opposed them, and was one of those whom Paul calls false apostles, who stirred up disturbances at Antioch over the circumcision of the Gentiles, as is in Acts 15. But Carpocrates appeared many years later, so that they cannot even seem to have been contemporaries. What then? Augustine followed the error of Epiphanius and his careless reckoning of time in this place. We, however, have observed the matter thus from Irenaeus, Dionysius of Alexandria, Gaius, Polycarp, who were nearest to those times, and likewise from Eusebius, book 3, chapters 23 and 24. For we pass over Theodoret, because he wrote nothing about the Cerinthians different from our view. It appears from the account of Polycarp, which Irenaeus reports in book 3, chapter 3, and Eusebius in book 4, chapter 14, and book 7, chapter 23, that Cerinthus lived in the time of the Apostle John and had already spread his poison and heresy, and was known everywhere as a blasphemer. Namely, when John was about to enter a bath to wash, and heard that Cerinthus was inside, he left, cursing the place, and added that he feared the bath itself might collapse, since so great an enemy of the truth had washed in it. Moreover, John seems in some passages to attack the error of Cerinthus, as in 1 John 2:19, 22, and chapter 4, verse 3. His time is referred to the reign of Domitian, and he seems to have published his heresy most of all around the year 62 after Christ's passion. He spread it especially in Asia, that is, Asia Minor and Syria, beginning from the city of Antioch, as Epiphanius holds, who writes of him thus: Cerinthus, while living in Asia, began there with the first of the virginal hymnody [Ἐψέετο δ' ἐξ ὁ Κηρινθος ἐν τῇ Ἀσίᾳ διατρίβων, κάκεῖσε τῆς ἐν ὑμνογραφίας τῆς ἀρχῆς παρθενικῆς]. But afterwards it spread and was disseminated very widely, so that he had his supporters but also his distorters. Cerinthus was a Jew by nation, as Epiphanius wrote, and he was circumcised. Therefore he insisted that all Christians must be circumcised. Some report that he learned philosophy in Egypt, but, as later appeared, to his misfortune. His errors demonstrate that he was an ambitious man, wholly given over to the pleasures of the body. Augustine says, on Epiphanius's authority, that they were also called Merinthians, either because Cerinthus himself, under a disguised name, called himself Merinthus, or because a certain Merinthus was his colleague and disciple. Epiphanius himself does not know which of these is more true. He says: The same Cerinthus was again called Menander, not altogether ... Then there was another named Menander, a companion of his, known to God [Εἶπ᾽ ἂν ... ὁ αὐτὸς Κήρινθος, Μένανδρος πάλιν ἐκαλεῖτο, οὐ πάντως οὗ τούτου ἴσχυσεν. Εἶτα ἄλλος τις ἦν Μένανδρος ὄνομα, συνήθης τούτῳ, Θεῷ ἐγνώσθη]. Yet the name Merinthians is rarely cited. The very name of the Cerinthians soon fell away, but the Carpocratians and Samosatenes revived and sustained this same blasphemy under new names. From this it came about that it flourished in Asia for many centuries in its most wicked form.

units.la: 2 Praeter morum turpitudinem (quae a Carpocratianis addita fuit) idem est error Carpocratianorum, & Cerinthianorum. Huius autem hic quinque capita siue hypotheses recenset Augustinus. 1 Mundum hunc non a Deo summo, vero & primo factum esse, sed ab inferiore quadam virtute, quae etiam verum Deum ignorarit. Iren. lib. i. c. 25. 3 Iesum non esse natum ex virgine, sed ad modum caeterorum hominum, ex Iosephi & Mariae coitu & femine. Itaque merum esse hominem, non Deum. Contra quam blasphemiam scripsit Ioannes Euangelium suum, in cuius primo capite Christi diuinitas certissime asseritur & demonstratur. Ex virgine enim hominem nasci nō posse: & maiori quodam virtutum profectu Iesum caeteris hominibus praestitisse. Itaque Iesum a Christo tanquam duas personas diuidunt, in quo est delirium Nestorianorum iam antiquissimum. Affirmant enim Christum descendisse in Iesum specie columbae quum a Ioanne baptizaretur, & Iesum quidem passum, & resurrexiffc : Christum vero non item, quia è Iesu euolâ-rit. quo quid magis portentosum? 3 Christum non resurrexisse, sed Iesum tantum, quem etiam solum & passum esse & mortuum contendunt.
units.tr: 2 Apart from the foulness of morals (which was added by the Carpocratians), the error of the Carpocratians and the Cerinthians is the same. Augustine lists five heads, or hypotheses, of this error. 1. That this world was not made by the highest, true and first God, but by some inferior power, which did not even know the true God. Irenaeus, book 1, chapter 25. 2. That Jesus was not born of a virgin, but like other men, from the intercourse and seed of Joseph and Mary; and so he is a mere man, not God. Against this blasphemy John wrote his Gospel, in whose first chapter Christ's divinity is most certainly asserted and demonstrated. For a man cannot be born of a virgin, and by a greater advance in virtues Jesus excelled other men. Thus they divide Jesus and Christ into two persons, and in this lies the delirium of the Nestorians, already very ancient. For they affirm that Christ descended upon Jesus in the form of a dove when he was baptized by John, and that Jesus indeed suffered and rose, but Christ did not, because he flew away from Jesus. What could be more monstrous than this? 3. That Christ did not rise, but only Jesus, whom they also contend alone suffered and died.

units.la: 4 Circuncisionem carnis & cæteras legis Mosaicæ ceremonias esse Christianis hominibus ad salutem necessarias. Itaque etiam hodie in Dei ecclesia omnino usum habere oportere, contra quam sententiam sæpe Paulus disputauit.
units.tr: 4. That circumcision of the flesh and the other ceremonies of the Mosaic law are necessary to salvation for Christian men. Therefore they hold that these must be fully practised even today in the Church of God, a view against which Paul often disputed.

units.la: 5 Vitam æternam fieri in hac terra, & in vrbe Hierosolymorum. Esse autem eam omnium carnis voluptatum fruitione & usum, quæ per mille tantum annos sit duratura. Cuius suæ sententiæ fundametum ponunt, quod mille annorum in Apocal.20.verf.2.facta sit mentio, ex quo factum est ut eum librum quidam Patres repudiarent, quemadmodū Eusebius lib.7.cap.25. scribit. Origenistæ hunc errorem postea sunt secuti, & Mahumetani auidè illud de vita æterna voluptuosa amplexi. Sed si post mille annos finitur hæc vita, non est æterna.
units.tr: 5. That eternal life will be on this earth and in the city of Jerusalem. It will consist in the enjoyment and use of all carnal pleasures, and will last only a thousand years. They lay as the foundation of this opinion that mention is made of a thousand years in Apocalypse 20:2, from which it came about that some Fathers rejected that book, as Eusebius writes in book 7, chapter 25. The Origenists afterwards followed this error, and the Mahometans eagerly embraced the idea of a voluptuous eternal life. But if this life ends after a thousand years, it is not eternal.

units.la: Chiliastæ sunt Millenarij, ut est in cano. Quidam.24.quæst.3. Primus igitur huius erroris fons est à Cerinthianis:auctus postea est & defensus à quodam Nepote, qui fuit Ægyptiorum Episcopus, & vixit sub Galeno Imperatore Romano, anno post Christum passum 231. cuius meminit Eusebius lib.7. cap.23.24. Ex quibus apparet Cerinthianica dogmata fuisse diutisimè latisimèque propagata.
units.tr: Chiliasts are Millenarians, as in the canon Quidam, 24 q. 3. The first source of this error is therefore the Cerinthians. It was later increased and defended by a certain Nepos, who was bishop of the Egyptians and lived under the Roman emperor Gallienus, in the year 231 after Christ's passion; Eusebius mentions him in book 7, chapters 23 and 24. From these facts it appears that the Cerinthian doctrines were spread very long and very widely.

units.la: CAP. IX. Nazaraeorum error.
units.tr: The error of the Nazaraeans.

units.la: Nazarai{1} cum Dei filium confiteantur esse Christum, omnia tamen veteris Legis obseruant, quæ Christiani per Apostolicam traditionem non obseruare carnaliter, sed spiritualiter intelligere didicerunt.
units.tr: The Nazaraei, although they confess that the Son of God is Christ, nevertheless keep all the observances of the old Law, which Christians have learned through apostolic tradition not to observe carnally but to understand spiritually.

units.la: 1 Nazarei.) Hæc hæreticorum secta à pluribus prætermittitur, quàm obseruetur. Neque enim de ea quicquam Irenæus, Tertullian. Eusebius. Commemorant tamen Epiphanius, Augustinus, Theodoretus lib.2. & Isidorus. Sed primum de voce ipsa Nazarei quæstio est. Nã quos hic Augustinus Nazaraeos vocat, Epiphanius Græce Ναζωραῖος appellauit & dixit. Dif-ferunt autem hæc tria vocabula inter se & origine siue themate, & significatione: & sono siue pronuntiatione, Ναζωραῖοι, Ναζιραῖοι, & Ναζαρ-αῖοι. Ναζωραῖοι vel Ναζωρηνοί (utrunque enim di-citur) est nomen gentile deductum ab urbe Nazareth, quæ fuit in Galilæa gentium. Habet autem originem ab Hebræa voce נצר Netser quæ florem significat vel Germen, à qua ipsa urbis Nazareth appellatio videtur deducta, quòd in loco floribus & arboribus confito, sita esset. Bernard. ex Cantic. 1. Delectatur floribus Christus qui in Nazareth & concipi voluit, & nutriri. in lib. de Diligen. Dei. Ναζωραῖος autem est vox sectæ. Eum enim significat qui Deo co-fecratus & separatus erat ad certum tempus eoque modo, quem Deus ipse praescripserat Numer.6. Sic Samson erat Ναζιραῖος[?]. Deriuatur ab Hebraeo vocabulo נזיר[?] Nazir, quod segregare notat. Haec duo facile apud Græcos & Hebræos vel sono ipso vocis distinguuntur, nedum scriptura: apud Latinos vero non item. Verterunt enim Latini scriptores utrunque vocabulum Nazaræi, uti Tertullianus libro 4. adversus Marcion. & hic Augustinus adeo ut nomen gentis cum voce sedam significante apud Latinos confundatur. Nos autem totius huius ob-scuritatis tollendæ gratia viros doctissimos secuti sic dicamus, ut Ναζωραῖος qui a Nazareth appellantur, Nazarenos: Ναζωραῖοι qui sunt ἡγιασμένοι[?] & sancti Deo, Nazaræos nominemus. Tertium autem vocabulum Ναζωραῖοι[?] vel Ναζαραῖοι[?] (Tf, enim Hebræorum Græci per suum ζ pronuntiant) unde sumptum sit supra ex Epiphanio expositum, cum ageremus de Hæresibus Iudæorum. Nazaræi igitur, de quibus hic agit Augustinus, sunt ij quos melius Nazarenos appellandos diximus, & ipse Augustinus libro 19. Contra Faust. cap.4. Symmachianos vocatos fuisse scribit, ne quid perturbationis in hac disputatione inducatur. Sed Tertullianum in loquendo sequitur hic Augustin. Nazareni autem dicti sunt ab vrbe Nazareth, quæ iam non est, sed tempore Christi erat vrbs Galilæ, sed culo autem Epiphanij vicus tantum. Unde & Christus ipse Ναζωραῖος, id est, Nazarenus vocatus est. Tertullian. libro 4. Aduerf. Marcion. Nazarenus vocari habebat secundum prophetiam Christus creatoris. Unde & ipso nomine nos hos Iudæi Nazarenos appellant per eum. Nam & fumus de quibus scriptum est, Nazaræi exalbati sunt super niuem, qui scilicet retro lurida- ti delinquentiæ maculis, & nigrati ignorantiæ tenebris. Christo autem appellatio Nazaræi competitura erat ex infantiæ latebris, in quas apud Nazareth descendit vitando Archelaum filium Herodis. Hactenus ille. Christus igitur Nazaræus vel potius Nazarenus, id est, Naζωραῖος fuit, Actor. 2. versu 22:3. versu 6.Ioann. 19.versu 19. Matth.2. versu 23.A Christo autem Nazareno Christiani primum Nazareni dicti, vt apparet ex Actor.24. versu 5. & ex superiore Tertulliani loco, itemque Epiphanio. Nam primum omnium μαθηταί, postea Ναζωραῖοι, demum Antiochiæ Χριστιανοί sunt appeliati, qui Euangelicam fidem & doctrinam profitebantur. Hoc Nazaræorum nomen in probro fuit, non honori inter infideles, vti appellatio Galilæorum postea temporibus Iuliani apostatæ imperatoris, Ioann. 1. versu 47. & Sarmentariorum & Exorcistarum, quibus nominibus igno-miniosè vocabantur ab ethnicis Christiani. Inter fideles autem laudi ducebatur, primis illis Christianismi temporibus. Ex quo factum est, vt hæretici, de quibus nunc agitur, fallaciosa ostentatione se Nazaræos appellarent, licet a vera Christi doctrina desciuissent. Quanquam vero ignorare se fatetur Epiphanius, quo potisimum tempore extiterint, vtrum ante Cerinthianos, vel postea: tamen alibi idem scribit tunc primum innotuisse atque apparuisse, cum Christiani diuinitus admoniti omnes Hierosolymis se subduxerunt, & in urbem Pel-lam receperunt metu & præsensione quadà proximè futuræ Hierosolymorum ruinæ. Id quod incidit in postrema imperij Neronis tempora circa annum à Christo passo 37: ubi initium huius hæreseos à nobis collocabitur. Nam & ipse scribit post prædicatum in Ægypto Euangelium statim hæc zizania ibidem emersisse & enata esse, ut inter primas hæreses merito sit censenda. Augustinus scribit ex eo natam hæresin, quòd quæ Apostoli concesserant ad tempus inter Iudæos observari, illa vellent semper esse retinenda inter omnes Christianos, etiam eos qui è gentibus converterebantur. Quod enim quidam hos à Nicolaitis edoctos & professos putant, non est verisimile, quanquam fieri potuit ut utraque hæresis, quæ Legis ceremonias tuebatur & observabat, se mutuo conseruarit & confirmarit. Hi ipsi, ut tradit Epiphanius, postea Iessæi à Iesse patre Dauidis & Christi secundum carnem progenitore dicti sunt. Maximè verò propter persecutiones, quæ tunc undique Christianis hominibus à Iudæis inferebantur, natus & probatus videtur hic error, ut Christi Euangelium cum usu & observatione ceremoniarum Legis misceretur, contra disputationes tamen Pauli Apostoli, quem etiam unum Nazareni isti potissimum repudiarunt atque improbarunt. Sic enim furor Iudæorum euitabatur, dum eorum ceremoniis & errori de necessario ad salutem ceremoniarum cultu homines assentiebantur. Sic hi ipsi Nazaræi Christianis Euangelium profitentibus annumerari videbantur, quia Iesum filium Mariæ fatebantur & agnoscebant esse Dei filium & Christum illum siue Mefsiam pro missum Patribus. De quo fuerunt variæ Apostolorum ipsorum contra Iudæos disputationes, quæ etiamnum hodie nobis cum illis restat, ut Act.18.verf.28:13. verf.32. Plausibilis sane ratio humanæ carni, per quam & periculum effugere, & Deum sequi sibi prudenter videbatur.
units.tr: 1 Nazarei.) This sect of heretics is mentioned by more writers than actually follow it. Irenaeus, Tertullian and Eusebius say nothing about them at all. Epiphanius, Augustine, Theodoret (book 2) and Isidore do mention them. But first there is a question about the word Nazarei itself. For those whom Augustine here calls Nazaraei, Epiphanius called in Greek Nazōraios [Ναζωραῖος]. These three words differ from one another in origin or stem, in meaning, and in sound or pronunciation: Nazōraioi [Ναζωραῖοι], Nazirajoi [Ναζιραῖοι], and Nazarajoi [Ναζαραῖοι]. Nazōraioi, or Nazōrēnoi (both forms are used), is a gentile name derived from the town of Nazareth, which was in Galilee of the Gentiles. It has its origin in the Hebrew word netser [נצר], meaning flower or shoot, from which the name of the town Nazareth seems to be derived, because it lay in a place planted with flowers and trees. Bernard, from the Song of Songs 1, and in the book On Loving God: Christ, who wished to be conceived and brought up in Nazareth, delights in flowers. But Nazōraios is the name of a sect. For it means one who was consecrated and set apart to God for a fixed time, in the manner which God himself prescribed in Numbers 6. Thus Samson was a Nazirite [Ναζιραῖος]. It is derived from the Hebrew word nazir [נזיר], which means to separate. These two words are easily distinguished by Greeks and Hebrews, even by the sound, not to mention the spelling. Among Latins, however, they are not distinguished. For Latin writers have rendered both words as Nazaraei, as Tertullian does in book 4 against Marcion, and as Augustine does here, so that the name of the people is confused among Latins with a word meaning a sect. But to remove all this obscurity, we, following very learned men, will speak thus: those who are called from Nazareth, Nazōraios, we shall call Nazarenes; those who are consecrated and holy to God we shall call Nazaraei. The third word, Nazōraioi or Nazaraioi (for the Greeks pronounce the Hebrew letter with their zeta), from which it was taken, was explained above from Epiphanius when we treated of the heresies of the Jews. The Nazaraei, then, of whom Augustine speaks here, are those whom we said should more properly be called Nazarenes. Augustine himself, in book 19 Against Faustus, chapter 4, writes that they were called Symmachians, so that no confusion may be introduced into this discussion. Here, however, Augustine follows Tertullian in his usage. Tertullian says: "The Nazarenes were so named from the town of Nazareth, which no longer exists, but at the time of Christ was a town of Galilee, and in Epiphanius' day was only a village. From this, Christ himself was called Nazōraios, that is, Nazarene." Tertullian, book 4 Against Marcion: "Christ was to be called a Nazarene, according to the prophecy of the Creator. From this very name the Jews call us Nazarenes through him. For those are the 'Nazarites' of whom it is written, 'they were made whiter than snow,' that is, those who were formerly stained with the spots of sin and blackened with the darkness of ignorance. The title Nazarene was to belong to Christ from his hidden infancy, when he went down to Nazareth to escape Archelaus, son of Herod." Thus far Tertullian. Christ, then, was a Nazaraean, or rather a Nazarene, that is Nazōraios: Acts 2:22; 3:6; John 19:19; Matthew 2:23. From Christ the Nazarene, Christians were first called Nazarenes, as appears from Acts 24:5 and from the passage of Tertullian quoted above, and likewise from Epiphanius. For first of all they were called disciples (mathētai), afterwards Nazarenes, and finally at Antioch Christians, those who professed the Gospel faith and doctrine. This name Nazarene was a reproach, not an honour, among unbelievers, as the name Galileans was later under the emperor Julian the Apostate (John 1:47), and as the names "Sarmentarii" and "Exorcists," by which Christians were disgracefully called by the heathen. Among the faithful, however, it was counted an honour in the earliest times of Christianity. Hence it came about that the heretics of whom we now speak, with a false display, called themselves Nazaraei, although they had fallen away from the true doctrine of Christ. Although Epiphanius confesses that he does not know at what time they arose, whether before or after the Cerinthians, yet elsewhere the same writer says that they first became known and appeared when the Christians, divinely warned, all withdrew from Jerusalem and retired to the city of Pella, out of fear and a certain foreboding of the imminent ruin of Jerusalem. This happened near the end of Nero's reign, about the year 37 after the passion of Christ, and there we shall place the beginning of this heresy. For Epiphanius also writes that, immediately after the Gospel was preached in Egypt, these tares sprang up and grew there, so that they rightly deserve to be counted among the first heresies. Augustine writes that the heresy arose because what the apostles had allowed for a time among the Jews, these men wished to be kept for ever among all Christians, including those converted from the Gentiles. As for the claim of some that these men were taught and professed by the Nicolaitans, this is not probable, although it may be that each of these two heresies, which defended and observed the ceremonies of the Law, strengthened and confirmed the other. These same men, as Epiphanius reports, were later called Iessaeans, from Jesse, father of David and Christ's forefather according to the flesh. But this error seems to have arisen and gained approval chiefly because of the persecutions which were then inflicted everywhere on Christians by the Jews: the aim was to mix the Gospel of Christ with the practice and observance of the ceremonies of the Law, in spite of the arguments of the apostle Paul, whom these Nazarenes in particular rejected and condemned. In this way the fury of the Jews was avoided, while men assented to their ceremonies and to the error that the worship of the ceremonies was necessary for salvation. So these Nazaraei were thought to be numbered among those who professed the Gospel, because they confessed that Jesus, son of Mary, was the Son of God and the Christ, that is the Messiah, promised to the Fathers. Concerning this the apostles themselves had various disputes with the Jews, which still remain with us today against them (Acts 18:28; 13:32). Indeed it seemed a plausible reason for human flesh, by which one might both prudently escape danger and follow God.

units.la: Itaque breui tempore latissime propagata est, etiam per omnes Orientis synagogas, sed imprimis ut ait Epiphanius, circa Pellam urbem, ubi primum orta est, & Beræam Syriam, Decapo-lin,Basanitida regionem eam, quæ Cocabe dicebatur. Durauit vero usque ad Epiphanij ætatem & postea. Nam illius meminit Hieronym. in epist. ad August.&Augustin.ipse lib.1.contra Cresco.Circumcisionem,ait,habent Iudæorum, & baptisma Christi:& lib.19. contra Fauft.cap. 18. Qui ad nostra usque tempora, ait, jam quidem in exigua, sed adhuc tamen vel in ipsa paucitate perdurant. Denique intantum excreuit hæc familia, & laudata est a Philone, ut eam cæteris sectis præferat. Habuerunt enim sua mo-nasteria eaque plura, & in Ægypto & in Cyrenaica regione illi vicina ad Tritonidis paludem, quæ olim dicebatur, sita, temporibus autem Christianorum Mariæ palus. Iudæi autem ipsi hos postea sunt odio prosecuti, adeo ut,quem-admodum tradit Epiphan. bis quotidie contra eos precarentur, eosque præ ceteris diserte nominarent, quibus gravissima quæque imprecantur: nisi fortasse Epiphanius ipse fallitur. Na-zarenos enim adhuc hodie Iudæi appellant veros Christianos, quos in publicis suis precibus execrantur.
units.tr: And so in a short time it spread very widely, even through all the synagogues of the East. But especially, as Epiphanius says, it spread around the city of Pella, where it first arose, and into Beroea, Syria, Decapolis, and the region of Basanitis, which was called Cocabe. It lasted indeed until Epiphanius' own time and afterwards. For Jerome mentions it in his letter to Augustine, and Augustine himself in book 1 Against Cresconius: "They have circumcision of the Jews and the baptism of Christ." And in book 19 Against Faustus, chapter 18: "They persist even to our own times, now indeed in small numbers, yet still persisting even in their paucity." In the end this sect grew so much, and was so praised by Philo, that he ranked it above the other sects. For they had their own monasteries, and these were many, both in Egypt and in the neighbouring region of Cyrenaica, near the marsh of Tritonis, as it was formerly called, but in Christian times the marsh of Mary. The Jews themselves afterwards pursued them with such hatred that, as Epiphanius reports, they prayed twice daily against them and openly named them above all others in their curses, unless perhaps Epiphanius himself is mistaken. For even today the Jews call true Christians Nazarenes, and they curse them in their public prayers.

units.la: Omnia tamen. ) Vnum tantum erroris caput recenset Augustin. Epiphanius plura, e quibus quaedam ad alias etiam haereses videntur pertinere. Nos praecipuas hypothecs collegimus, quae sunt huiusmodi, & numero quinque.
units.tr: Yet all of them. Augustine recounts only one main head of this error, whereas Epiphanius lists more, some of which seem to belong also to other heresies. We have gathered the chief tenets, which are of this kind and number five.

units.la: Legis Mosaicae ceremonias vti ad salutem necessarias obseruandas esse docent. In hoc igitur vno sunt a Iudaeis dissimillimi, quod Iesum Mariae filium, Christum esse credunt: ad cetera pene gemelli. Quanquam in eo ipso manifestissima contradictio est, quod Christum iam venisse & passum esse concedunt, ceremonias tamen, quae sunt venturi & nondum exhibiti signa, retinendas docent, contra Paulum in tota epistola ad Galatas.
units.tr: They teach that the ceremonies of the Mosaic law must be observed as necessary to salvation. In this one point, then, they differ most from the Jews, in that they believe Jesus, the son of Mary, to be Christ; in almost everything else they are very nearly twins of the Jews. Yet in this very point there is a most obvious contradiction, for they concede that Christ has already come and suffered, and yet they teach that the ceremonies, which are signs of what was to come and not yet fulfilled, must still be retained. This is contrary to Paul throughout the epistle to the Galatians.

units.la: Multa de Nouria vel Ouria (utrunque enim apud Epiphanium legitur, & quidem recte) fabulantur, quam fuisse vxorem Noae Patriarchae volunt, & interpretantur Ignem vel Estam, Graeci vero Πυρρὰν, Latini autem homines Vestam, quae publico foco & igni sacro praesit. Epiphanius tamen v-xorem Noae vocat Βαρσῶνον[?]. At Berosus & Aretiam & Vestam, qui locus cum hoc optime conſentit. נוּרָא[?] Noura enim vel Oura apud Chaldaeos ignem denotat, id quod ex Daniele apparet cap.3. v.17. vti apud Hebraeos Esch. Vnde Esta, & ex Esta, Vesta Latinis, quae eadem est quae Pyrrha Graecis. Hanc dicunt saepe arcam Noae incendisse, & propterea arcam saepius refectam fuisse. Sed etiam eam potestates illas supranaturales, quae Angeli dicuntur, prius quidem ignotas ; hominibus manifeftasse. Cuius filius dicatur [?]בר קובא Barkubba, id est, filius prostitutæ & meretricis, vt ait Epiphanius. Ita illi in meras nugas sacram Scripturam transformant, dum [?]ἰδίαν ἐπίλυσιν in Prophetarum & Verbi diuini interpretatione sequuntur & afferunt. Simile quiddam habent Saturniniani. 3 Error.
units.tr: They tell many fables about Nouria or Ouria (for both forms are read in Epiphanius, and rightly so), whom they claim was the wife of the patriarch Noah. They interpret her as Fire or Hestia; the Greeks call her Pyrrha, and the Latins Vesta, who presides over the public hearth and the sacred fire. Epiphanius, however, calls Noah's wife Barsōnō[?]. But Berosus calls her Aretia and Vesta, and this agrees very well with the present view. For Noura or Oura among the Chaldeans signifies fire, as appears from Daniel 3:17, just as esch [אש] does among the Hebrews. Hence Esta, and from Esta the Latin Vesta, which is the same as Pyrrha for the Greeks. They say she often set fire to Noah's ark, and that for this reason the ark was often repaired. But they also say that she revealed those supernatural powers which are called angels, previously unknown to humans. Her son is said to be Barkubba, that is, the son of a prostitute and harlot, as Epiphanius says. In this way they turn Holy Scripture into mere trifles, while in their interpretation of the Prophets and of the divine Word they follow and put forward their own private explanation. The Saturninians have something similar. (3) Error.

units.la: Plura Euangelia, & alia habent quàm vera. Habent enim Euangelium perfectionis quod vocant, carmine scriptum, & Euangelium Euæ.
units.tr: They have more Gospels than the true ones. For they have a Gospel of Perfection, as they call it, written in verse, and a Gospel of Eve.

units.la: 4 Visiones, [?]ἐνθουσιασμὸς, priuatas reuelationes atque falsa miracula iactant, quemadmodum olim Mirabiliarij, & nunc Anabaptistæ, vt sua deliria confirment. Ab his enim Anabaptistarum [?]ἐνθουσιασμοὶ videntur petiti. 5 Esse eiusdem substantiæ animam quæ in hominibus, brutis animantibus, & plantis ipsis insit, quem errorem postea Manichæi sunt amplexi. Ita error latius propagatus est.
units.tr: (4) Visions [ἐνθουσιασμός], enthusiasm: they boast of private revelations and false miracles, as the Mirabilarii once did and the Anabaptists do now, to confirm their delusions. For the enthusiasms of the Anabaptists seem to have been taken from these. (5) That the soul which is in humans, in brute animals and even in plants is of one and the same substance. The Manichaeans later embraced this error, and so it spread more widely.

units.la: CAPVT X. Ebionitorum error duplex. Ebionitis autem accensentur Sampsei, & Elcefei vel Elcefaitæ: & quid hi postremi ab Ebionitis differant.
units.tr: CAPUT X. The Ebionite error is twofold. The Sampsaeans and the Elcesaites, or Elcesaites, are counted among the Ebionites, and the difference between these latter and the Ebionites is explained.

units.la: Bionei{1} Christum etiam tantummodò {2}hominem dicunt. Mandata carnalia Legis obseruant, Circuncisionem scilicet carnis, & catera, à quorum oneribus per Nouum Testamentum liberati sumus. Huic hæresi Epiphanius Sampseos, & Elcesios ita copulat, vt sub
units.tr: The Ebionites also say that Christ was only a man. They observe the carnal precepts of the Law, namely circumcision of the flesh and the rest, from whose burdens we have been freed by the New Testament. Epiphanius couples the Sampsaeans and Elcesaites with this heresy in such a way that he places them under the same number, as though it were one heresy, yet indicating that there is some difference.

units.la: eodem numero, tanquam vna fit harefis, ponat, aliquid tamen interesse significans. Quanuis & in consequentibus loquatur de illis, ponens eos sub numero suo. Eusebius vero Elcesaitarum sectam commemorans, fidem in persecutione dicit negandam docuisse, & in corde feruandam.
units.tr: Although in what follows he also speaks of them, placing them under their own number. Eusebius, however, in recounting the sect of the Elcesaites, says that they taught that faith should be denied during persecution, while being kept in the heart.

units.la: 1 Ebionei.) Neque hoc loco seruata est ratio temporis, fiue à Tertulliano, fiue ab Augu-stino, fiue potius ab Epi-phanio, quem sequitur χ̄ πο[illegible, ~3 letters] Augustinus. Nam ipse se refutat Epi-phanius, qui cum post Cerithianos & Nicolai-tas collocet Ebioneos siue Ebionitas (vtrunque enim ab authoribus dicitur) eos tamen dicit cœpisse & innotuisse iam ex ipso Hierosolymitanæ vrbis excidio, quod incidit in secundum annum Vespasiani imperatoris, anno à Christo passo 40, quod tempus præcesisit hæresin Nicolaitarum. Longè turpius falli videtur Eusebius, qui lib.5. cap.8. dicit cùm legisset Ebion versione Bibliorum Hebræorum ab Aquila Pontico factam in eum errorem incidisse, vt sentiret Christum merum hominem esse, & ex viri coitu, non autem ex virgine Maria natum, quia locum Isa. 7. ita conuersum ab Aquila legisset, Ecce iuuencula concipiet, non autem, Ecce virgo, &c. Sed magna certè hallucinatio & magnus calculi error est. Vixit enim sub Adriano imperatore Aquila ille Ponticus. Iam autem pene desierat esse Ebionitarum secta, & mortuus est sub Domitia-no Ebion. Verius est illud quod idem Eusebius lib.6.cap.17. scribit Symmachum Hebræorum Bibliorum interpretem videri fuisse Ebionitā, quia omnes veteris Testamenti locos in sua translatione corrupit, qui divinam Christi naturam, & illius ex Virgine nativitatem demonstrant. Isidorus autem libro 8. cap. 5. etymologiæ, omnium longissimè a vera temporis supputatione recesit, qui Ebionitas post Motanos & Novatianos collocat, deceptus plusquam 200 annis in temporis ratione ineunda. Et cùm videatur vbique autor ille Augustinum secutus, non improbabiliter credi potest illa Ebionitarum sedes transpolita, quales μεταθέσεις[?] sæpissime scribarum negligentia in bonis authoribus describendis accidunt, & omnia pertur-bant. Ergo censerem apud Isidorum Ebionitas post Nazaræos poncendos, quando eo ipso de Ebionitis loco apud eundem Isidor. alia quoque sunt menda, sive impressus, sive manuscriptus codex consulatur, quæ suis locis erunt annotanda. Ebionei igitur sive Ebionitæ ab Ebione dicti sunt. Ebion autem ab Hebræo אביון[?] Æbion, quæ vox pauperem & afflictum significat, deducitur. Ex quo fit vt Eusebius hanc sectam non de nomine autoris cuiusquam appellatam existimet, sed de ratione professionis & vitæ, quòd hi hæretici instar medicantium qui dicuntur, Monachorum, & Cynicorum Philosophorum, perpetuam paupertatem & inopiam sequerentur & vouerent. Alij & ij quidem probati scriptores aliud sentiunt, Ebioneos, ab Ebione quodam qui hoc nomen habuerit sic nominatos, quanquam Ebion ab Hebreis etymologiam eam habet quam diximus, & egenum designat. Fuit autem Ebion, vt scribit Epiphanius, [illegible, ~20 letters] Σαμαρείτης [?] ἢ ἵγει τὸ βαπτ[?] ἰουδαίων [?] ὁ τὸ ὄνομα, Ὀσσαίων δὲ καὶ Ναζωραίων τὴν γνῶσιν, Κηρινθιανῶν τὸ εἶδος, Καρποκρατιανῶν τὴν ἀκολουθίαν, καὶ Χειρινθιανῶν [?] τὴν παραγγελίαν. Natione erat Samaritanus, sed quod nomen hoc odiosum esse intelligeret, & periculi propter suæ gentis seditiones plenum. Iudæum se nominare & af-firmare maluit. Vixit autem sub Domitiano, & cùm adhuc in terris ageret D. Ioannes Euange-lista qui propter hunc & Cerinthum Christum Deum & λόγον Dei æternum esse demonstra-uit. Virus suum sparsit Ebion ante Nicolaitas, ut docet Irenæus libr. 1. cap. 23. circa annum à Christo passo 44: quanquam Ebionem fuisse Cerinthi discipulum, scribit Tertullian. sed nō satis perpensa temporum ratione, & authorum varietate. Platina sub Clemente primo Romano Episcopo floruisse putat. Theodoret. lib. 2. eodem quo Corinthum tempore Ebionitas collocat. Cœpit autem hæc hæresis primum, ut ait Epiphanius, circa Pellam, urbem Syriæ in vico Cochaba, quæ latius postea propagata est, & Basanitida regionem, deinde vicinam Nabataeam & Arabiam celerrime peruasit, ex qua in Asiam minorem traductus est infœlix iste surculus, qui suo pestifero succo infecit, corruptque multos. Denique Romam ipsam peruenit & tentauit. Perstitit autem in Armenia diutius, ut ait Epiphanius, de Archont. Sed huius sectæ homines statim se in varias partes & diuortia alij ab alijs secuerunt, ut a seipso dis-sidet tandem mendaciū. Retenta tamen est diutis-sime, sed interpolato & mutato priore nomine Sampseorum autem & Elcesaitarum assumpto, ut docet cum Epiphanio hoc loco Augustinus. Pauperes autem Ebionei appellabantur, & quidem contumeliosè. quòd sensu & cognitione verè & salutaris doctrinæ turpissimè destituerentur, ut ait Eusebius, qui se tamen altius in arcana Dei penetrasse ostentabant. Sed ipsi aliam nominis huius & professæ paupertatis rationem afferebant. Nempe, quòd temporibus Apostolorum illi, qui primi huius suæ sectæ authores & principes fuerant, omnia sua in pauperes benignissimè erogassent, cuius maiorum suorum charitatis exemplum imitari & retinere se profitebantur. Sed quid charitas sine vera fide, id est, ramus à sua radice avulsus potest? Hac tamen operum bonorum commendatio-ne, professione & larva, pessimi nebulones isti imposuerunt multis infirmis & externa tantum facta admirantibus. Quo fuci & hypocriseos genere adhuc hodie multi, quemadmodum Monachi, homines decipiunt & fascinant demen-tissimè.
units.tr: 1 Ebionites.) Here the order of time has not been kept, whether by Tertullian, by Augustine, or rather by Epiphanius, whom Augustine follows [a word here is illegible]. For Epiphanius himself refutes himself: although he places the Ebionites or Ebionaeans after the Cerinthians and Nicolaitans (for both names are derived from their founders), he says that they began and became known already from the destruction of the city of Jerusalem, which fell in the second year of the emperor Vespasian, in the fortieth year after Christ's passion, a time that preceded the heresy of the Nicolaitans. Eusebius seems to have been far more shamefully mistaken, for in book 5, chapter 8, he says that when Ebion had read the Hebrew Bible in the version made by Aquila of Pontus, he fell into the error of thinking that Christ was a mere man, born of the union of a man and not of the virgin Mary, because he had read Isaiah 7 as Aquila translated it: "Behold, a young woman shall conceive," not "Behold, a virgin," etc. But this is certainly a great delusion and a great miscalculation. For that Aquila of Pontus lived under the emperor Hadrian, and by then the sect of the Ebionites had almost ceased to exist, while Ebion died under Domitian. What Eusebius writes in book 6, chapter 17, is more accurate: that Symmachus, the translator of the Hebrew Bible, seems to have been an Ebionite, because he corrupted in his translation all the passages of the Old Testament that demonstrate Christ's divine nature and his birth from a virgin. Isidore, in book 8, chapter 5 of the Etymologies, departs furthest of all from the true reckoning of time, for he places the Ebionites after the Montanists and Novatians, being deceived by more than two hundred years in his calculation of dates. And since that author appears everywhere to follow Augustine, it can not improbably be believed that the place of the Ebionites has been displaced, as transpositions very often occur through the carelessness of scribes when copying good authors, and throw everything into confusion. Therefore I would think that in Isidore the Ebionites should be placed after the Nazarenes, especially since in the same passage on the Ebionites in Isidore there are other faults, whether one consults the printed or the manuscript copy, which will be noted in their places. The Ebionei, or Ebionites, are therefore so called from Ebion. Ebion, moreover, is derived from the Hebrew אביון, Ebion, a word that means poor and afflicted. From this it comes that Eusebius thinks this sect was named not after the name of any author, but from the manner of their profession and life: that these heretics, like those called healers, the monks, and the Cynic philosophers, pursued and vowed perpetual poverty and want. Others, and these are approved writers, think differently: that the Ebionaeans were so named from a certain Ebion who bore this name, although Ebion has, from the Hebrews, the etymology we have mentioned and signifies a needy man. Ebion, moreover, as Epiphanius writes, [a passage here is illegible] was a Samaritan by nation, but he perceived that this name was hateful and full of danger, because of the seditions of his people; he preferred to call himself and affirm that he was a Jew. He lived under Domitian, while the apostle John the Evangelist was still living on earth, who, on account of him and Cerinthus, demonstrated that Christ is God and the eternal Word of God. Ebion spread his poison before the Nicolaitans, as Irenaeus teaches in book 1, chapter 23, around the year forty-four after Christ's passion, although Tertullian writes that Ebion was a disciple of Cerinthus, but without sufficient weighing of the chronology and the variety of authors. Platina thinks he flourished under Clement, the first bishop of Rome. Theodoret places the Ebionites in the same period as Corinthus. This heresy first began, as Epiphanius says, around Pella, a city of Syria, in the village of Cochaba, and afterwards spread more widely, and very quickly occupied the region of Basanitis, then the neighbouring Nabataea and Arabia, from which this unhappy shoot was carried into Asia Minor, infecting it with its pestilent sap and corrupting many. At last it even reached Rome itself and made an attempt there. It persisted longer in Armenia, as Epiphanius says in his book On the Archons. But the members of this sect immediately split into various parts and divisions, some separating from others, so that, as the saying goes, a lie is in the end at odds with itself. Yet the name was retained for a very long time, though altered and changed, the earlier name being replaced by that of Sampsaeans and Elcesaites, as Augustine, following Epiphanius here, teaches. The Ebionites were called Poor, and indeed as an insult, because they were most shamefully lacking in the understanding and knowledge of true and saving doctrine, as Eusebius says, although they boasted that they had penetrated more deeply into the secrets of God. But they themselves gave another reason for this name and their professed poverty: namely, that in the time of the apostles those who were the first authors and leaders of their sect had most generously distributed all their goods to the poor, and they professed that they imitated and kept this example of charity of their ancestors. But what can charity without true faith be, that is, a branch torn from its root? Yet by this commendation of good works, this profession and mask, those most wicked scoundrels deceived many weak people who admired only outward acts. By this kind of pretence and hypocrisy, even today many, like the monks, deceive and bewitch men most madly.

units.la: 2 Tantummodo hominem,) Duo tantùm Ebionei erroris capita refert Augustinus, verùntamen Epiphanius pene infinita. His autem duobus quædam addidimus. Ergo primus error est, Christum merum hominem fuisse, ex Iosephi & Mariæ coitu natum: qui propter virtutum profectum & progressus, quos maiores fecerat, iustus præ cæteris fuerit. Hic locus admonet ut Isidorum emendem, qui pro Profectu[?]in,habet in impressis Prophetiam. Et omnino optimè restitutus erat locus in cano. Quidã[?].24. quæst.3. Ex hoc capite alij haeretici qui secuti sunt, suas blasphemias & faeces impudentissimas haufe-runt. Christum etiam primum quidem in coelo conditum fuisse, quidam ex iis ipsis affirmarunt, qui postea Adami personam assumpserit, deinde eam deposuerit, & demum ex Iosepho & Maria postremis seculis natus sit. Haec sunt nimirum humani ingenij, vbi à veritate Dei se-mel recesit, inepta deliria. 2 Ceremonias Legis Mosaicae tanquam necessarias ad salutem observant & retinent, ad excludendum, vt recte annotat Tertul. Euangelium (quanquâ se Christianos dicunt, & Euangelio credere profitentur) & ad vindicandum Iudaismum. Ergo Semijudaei ab Isidoro dicuntur. & ita in dict.can. Quidam. restituendum est, & pro ijs verbis, Hi enim Iudaei, ex manuscripto legendum est, Hi Semijudaei sunt. Itaque circumciduntur, & sabbata custodiunt, & quotidie lauant, more Iudaeorum. Nec alia fuit ceremoniarum cum Euangelio miscendarum ratio, quam habuerint, nisi vt grauissimas illas persecutiones à Iudaeis excitatas euitarent, quemadmodum satis ex illo Pauli loco colligi potest, qui est in epistola ad Galat.5.verf.11. 3 Carnis vsum damnant. Docent enim animalium esu abstinendum tanquam re nefaria quòd illa sint immunda, quia è coitu nascuntur. Hanc pestem ex Pythagoreorum lacunis prodiisse, sed tamen futu-ram praedixit Spiritus sanctus, 1. Timoth.4.v.3.
units.tr: 2 Only a man,) Augustine records only two heads of the Ebionite error, although Epiphanius records almost an infinite number. To these two we have added some others. The first error, then, is that Christ was merely a man, born of the union of Joseph and Mary, who, because of the advance and progress of his virtues, which had grown greater, was more righteous than others. This passage reminds me that I must correct Isidore, who in the printed editions has "Prophetiam" where it should be "Profectum," and the passage in the canon "Quidam" (C. 24, q. 3) is altogether best restored in this way. From this head other heretics who followed drew their blasphemies and most shameless filth. Some of those same people affirmed that Christ was first created in heaven, then assumed the person of Adam, afterwards laid it aside, and at last was born of Joseph and Mary in the final ages. These are no doubt the foolish delusions of the human mind, once it has departed from the truth of God. 2 They keep and retain the ceremonies of the Mosaic Law as necessary for salvation, so as to exclude, as Tertullian rightly notes, the Gospel (although they call themselves Christians and profess to believe the Gospel), and to vindicate Judaism. Therefore they are called Semi-Jews by Isidore, and in the said canon "Quidam" this must be restored, and instead of the words "Hi enim Iudaei," it must be read from the manuscript, "Hi Semijudaei sunt." Accordingly they are circumcised, keep the sabbaths, and wash daily, in the manner of the Jews. Nor was there any other reason for mixing ceremonies with the Gospel than that they might avoid the very grievous persecutions stirred up by the Jews, as can be gathered sufficiently from that passage of Paul in the Epistle to the Galatians 5:11. 3 They condemn the use of flesh. For they teach that one must abstain from the eating of animals as a wicked thing, because those animals are unclean, since they are born of coition. The Holy Spirit foretold that this plague would come forth from the cesspools of the Pythagoreans, yet that it would still come in the future, 1 Timothy 4:3.

units.la: 4 Solum Euangelium, quod est secundum Matthaeum, quia Hebraice scriptum est, reti-nent & probant:reliquas noui Testamenti partes& Scripturas repudiant, imprimis autem omnes Pauli epistolas, quòd contra vsum ceremoniarum accuratissimè disputauit. Atqui& Euangelium secundum Ioannem, & Acta Apostolorum, suo seculo Hebraicè scripta commemorat Epiphanius, & à quodam Iosepho Iudæorum patriarcha in Tiberiade vrbe,tempore Constantini Magni, reperta Christianisque liberaliter fuisse communicata. 5 Prophetias vanis & inanibus allegoriis corrumpunt, dum nodum in scirpo quærunt,& res faciles curiosis speculationibus obscurant, & peruertut.
units.tr: 4 They retain and approve only the Gospel according to Matthew, because it was written in Hebrew, and they reject the remaining parts and Scriptures of the New Testament, above all the epistles of Paul, because he argued very carefully against the use of the ceremonies. Yet Epiphanius records that the Gospel according to John and the Acts of the Apostles were also written in Hebrew in his own age, and that they were found in the city of Tiberias by a certain Joseph, a patriarch of the Jews, in the time of Constantine the Great, and were generously communicated to the Christians. 5 They corrupt the prophecies with vain and empty allegories, while they seek a knot in a rush, and they obscure and pervert plain matters with curious speculations.

units.la: Sic nimirum spiritu vertiginis aguntur,& in reprobū sensum tandem traduntur, qui magni animi fastu vt supra Christum sapiant, simplici Dei veritate non sunt contenti,sed ab ea scientes prudentesque desciscunt.
units.tr: Thus, no doubt, they are driven by a spirit of giddiness and at last are handed over to a reprobate mind; in the pride of a great spirit they wish to be wiser than Christ, are not content with the simple truth of God, but knowingly and wisely turn away from it.

units.la: {3} Eusebius.) De his agit Eusebius lib.6.hi-stor.ecclesiast.cap.28.& nos infrà.
units.tr: {3} Eusebius.) Eusebius treats of these men in book 6 of his Ecclesiastical History, chapter 28, and we shall return to them below.

units.la: CAP. XI. Valentiniani à quo appellati. Erroris autem capita sex recensentur.
units.tr: CHAP. XI. The Valentinians, named after their founder. Six heads of this error are listed.

units.la: Valentiniani[?] à Valentino{1}, qui de natura rerum multa fabulosa confinxit. Triginta{2} Αἰῶνας, id est secula, afferens extitisse, quorum principium esse Profundum & Silentium, quorum Profundum etiam Patrem appellat. Ex quibus duobus velut ex coniugio processisse perhibet Intellectum & Veritatem, & protulisse in honorem patris Æonas octo. De Intellectu autem & Veritate procedisse Verbum & Vitam, & protulisse Æonas decem. Porrò de Verbo & Vita procedisse Hominem & Ecclesiam, & protulisse Æonas duodecim. Itaque octo & decem & duodecim fieri triginta Æonas habentes, vt diximus, primum principium de Profundo & Silentio. Christum autem à Patre missum, id est, à Profundo, spirituale vel cœleste corpus secum attulisse, nihilque assumpsisse de virgine Maria, sed per illam tanquam per rimam, aut per fistulam sine vlla de illa assumpta carne transiisse. De tricesimo sæculo dicit Diabolum genitum, & à Diabolo alios natos qui fecerint hunc mundum. Et ideo malitiam non arbitrio tribuit, sed naturæ mundi, id est, generi diabolico. Carnis resur-rectionem negat, animam tantum & spiritum affirmat per Christum saluari.
units.tr: The Valentinians are named after Valentinus, who invented many fabulous things about the nature of things. He asserted that thirty Aeons, that is, ages, had come into being, the beginning of which was the Deep and Silence, and he calls the Deep also the Father. From these two, as if from a marriage, he says Intellect and Truth proceeded, and they brought forth eight Aeons in honour of the Father. From Intellect and Truth proceeded Word and Life, and they brought forth ten Aeons. Further, from Word and Life proceeded Man and Church, and they brought forth twelve Aeons. Thus eight, ten and twelve make thirty Aeons, as we have said, with the first principle in the Deep and Silence. Christ, sent by the Father, that is, by the Deep, brought with him a spiritual or heavenly body, and he took nothing from the Virgin Mary, but passed through her as through a channel or a pipe, without taking on any flesh from her. He says that the thirtieth age produced the Devil, and that other beings were born from the Devil who made this world. For this reason he attributes wickedness not to the will but to the nature of the world, that is, to the devilish kind. He denies the resurrection of the flesh and affirms that only the soul and spirit are saved through Christ.

units.la: 1 [?]A Valentino.) Ex ijs hæresibus quæ superius expositæ sunt, tanquam initijs longius progressus est Satan, & quod molicbatur, tandem obtinuit & effecit, vt miris modis vniuersum salutis nostræ fundamentum, quod in duplici Christi natura consistit, inuoluceret. Antea quidem dubiam & absurdam per superiora deliria persuaserat esse humanam Christi naturā & natiuitatem, nunc etiam diuinam eiusdem natiuitatem & naturam per hos impurisimos, & longè omnium anteriorum teterrimos hæreticos Valentinianos labefactat & euertit. Quanquam enim prorsus non negarunt diuinā Christi naturam, & ex Patre natiuitatem: ita tamē fabulis[?], figmetis, & nugis intricarunt, vt plane ridiculam efficerent, & prorsus satius fuerit Chri shum[?] Dei Filium ex Deo Patre omnino non na-sci, quàm eo modo iisque gyrationibus na-sci. Sed in eo primum peccatum est, quòd rem dictu ineffabilem, cogitationi, angustæq; comprehensioni impossibilem, nempe divinâ Christi de Deo Patre generationem, vani homines, & terreni non modò se animo completi posse crediderunt, sed etiam verbis explicare, tam est vanum curiosorum hominũ ingenium. Unde nihil nisi meras nugas & fabulas nobis propinarunt. Fuit autem hæc hæresis eò cæteris & superioribus omnibus pestilentior, quòd maiori quadam ratione, & subtiliori investigatione niti videbatur, haberetque multa cum scriptis poetarum & genealogiis deorum, quæ ab ethnicis laudabantur, consentientia, tanquam illi veritatem tantùm fabulis suis obscurassent, quàm unus hic impostor Valentinus perspicuè vidisse atque commodè attigisse videretur. Itaque quum tam multa cum ethnicorum & gentilium opinionibus de diis suis cōvenientia haberet, hæc hæresis facilè placuit, & propterea statim recepta est, & propagata latissimè, id quod vel ex eo apparet, quòd uno momento plures eandem amplexi sunt, & hi ipsi Gnostici ab excellentia cognitionis pene soli postea sunt appellati, & ut nomen ab eo sibi parerent alij, quædam in eius secta & dogmate immutarunt, sed retentis tamen semper illius de AEonum propagatione fundamentis & nugamentis tanquam quæ maximè omnibus tunc grata & plausibilia cernerentur. Itaq; omnium hæreseon quæ deinceps explicabuntur, infelicissima stirps Valentinus videri potest. vnde Αἱρεσιάρχῳ[?] cum Epiphanius appellat, & Valentinianorum vti præcipuorum Christianæ Ecclesiæ vulnerum meminit Lactantius libro 4. Institut. Imò verò omnium nocentissimorum venenorum, quibus vera Euangelij doctrina de Christo mediatore nostro Deo & homine credendo,aspersa est, radix,& toxicorum, quæ Ariani, Samosateniani, Nestoriani,& alij spar-serunt, lethale fuit armamentarium. Denique Mahumetismi fons spurcissimus, & maxi-mus. Cæterum Valentinus hic,à quo Valentiniana hæresis cognominata est,natione AEgyptius, nomo autem Pharbæbites fuit, vt scribit Epiphanius. Sic enim apud eum legendum est, non autem vt nunc corruptè Φρεζωνίτης[?]. Fuit enim Pharbæbites AEgypti nomos & præfectura, vt Plinius lib.5. cap.9. scribit, ab oppido Pharbæbito dicta, quod fuit oppidum maritimum ad Pelusium Nili ostium situm, vt ait idem cap.10. Alexandriæ vicinum, & Bubasti, vnde ortus est Valentinus hic, humani generis pernicies & pestis. Alexandriæ autem studuit, vbi literis Græcis institutus, Platonicus & Pythagoricus potius euasit quàm Christianus. Platonis enim sectatorem vocat & Tertullianus & Isidorus: Philastrius autem Pythagoricum. Aristotelicis etiam præceptis addictum fuisse, & dialecticę sophisticę tradunt. Iam tum verò Christianos philosophiæ ethnicæ, & imprimis Platonicæ plus æquo deditos fuisse, & in AEgypto maxime, apparet ex authorum illius tèporis scriptis, veluti Clemente Alexandrino, & & aliis, uti Philone Iudæo, quæ etiam retenta illic diutissimè floruit, usque ad Plotinum magnum illum Platonicum philosophum, & Abnebonem sacerdotem AEgyptium. Vixit autem Valentinus sub Antonino Pio imperatore, ut docet Eusebius lib.4. cap.11, & post Cerinthum & Ebionitas innotuisse scribit Epiphanius sub Higino pontifice Romano, circa annum a passo Christo 110. post Telesphorum mortuum, ad quem tamen eum refert Platina, sed graviores authores ad Higinum. Vixisse autem scribit usque ad Anicetum, id est annum a passo Christo 126, Irenæus libro 3. cap.4. qui idem lib.1.cap.5. sentit a Gnosticis, id est, Car-crate[?] productam esse hanc inauspicatam propaginem, nec sane immerito. Illius enim & aliorum erroribus imbutus est Valentinus, sed postea huiusmodi venena acuit ipse, & nocentiora fecit. Ex prioribus enim omnibus hoc monstrum conflatum est, sed superiores hæreses quòd rudiores viderentur, ipse admissis ethnicorum poetarum fabulis & linimentis, expoliuit & commendauit, quòd quæ ipse traderet a Matthia Apostolo Domini & discipulo relicta, impudentissimè mentitus est. Quædam vero ipse scribit, veluti epistolas & homilias, quarum particulas quasdam recitat Clemens Strom. lib.2. & 4. & 6. vbi ipsius præcipuum fundamentum commemorat, quod ex eius scriptis apparet fuisse huiusmodi. Multa sunt, inquit, quæ scripta sunt in libris publicis (id est, Clemente ipso authore, Iudaicis & philosophicis) & inueniuntur scripta in Dei Ecclesia. Unde eorum fabulas cum vera theologia, & fa-cra prophanis miscere iam sibi libere permisit. Ex quo ipso admonemur quàm sit periculo-sum diu multumq; huiusmodi literis inhaerere, à quibus tamen Christiani hodie abduci vix ta-men possunt. Versipellem autem Valentinum appellat Tertullianus, & artificem struendi & destruendi. Romae etiam vixit aliquandiu, vbi haec haeresis diffusa est, & inde Galliās suo veneno afflauit, adeo vt Rhodanusias mulieres illo corruptas fuisse scribat Irenaeus. Maximè tamen in AEgypto, vbi primum nata est, viguit. Postea Antiochiæ etiã tempore Tertulliani, vbi eam profitebatur Axionicus quidam. Occasio haereseos ex Tertull. Sperauerat episcopatum Valetinus, quia ingenio poterat, & eloquio. Sed alium ex martyrij praerogatiua loci potitu, indignatus de Ecclesiae authenticae regula abrupit, vt solet animi pro prioratu exciti, & veritatem expugnat. Statim autem in varias se sectas hic error diduxit & dispescuit, vt ad minus decem ex vnius & eiusdem praeceptoris schola profecti dissimillimi discipuli commemoretur ab Iren. & Epiphan. συγχρόνοι πάντες[?] & Gnostici nominati. Perstitit autem haec haeresis tum suo vero, tum etiã mutato nomine in multa secula. Nam quae sequutae sunt, eas tantum exaedificarunt blasphemiarum moles, quarum femina longo antea tempore haec iecerat. Successores autem & collegium magnum habuit, in quo praecipui hi recensentur, Secundus, Ptolemaeus, Marcus, Colarbasus, Heracleon, Cerdon, omnes infelices ex infelici arbore rami, de quibus postea.
units.tr: 1 [?]From Valentinus.) Satan, having advanced further along the path of the heresies set out above, as though from their beginnings, at last achieved what he had been attempting, and by these means in marvellous ways he has entangled the whole foundation of our salvation, which rests on the twofold nature of Christ. Previously, through the earlier delusions, he had persuaded people that the human nature and birth of Christ were doubtful and absurd; now, through these most impure heretics, the Valentinians, who are by far the most foul of all those before them, he also undermines and overthrows the divine nature and birth of the same Christ. For although they did not altogether deny the divine nature of Christ and his birth from the Father, they so entangled it in fables, fictions and trifles that they made it utterly ridiculous, and it would have been far better for the Son of God not to be born of God the Father at all than to be born in that manner and with those contortions. But the first sin lies in this, that vain and earthly men have believed not only that they could grasp in their minds, but even explain in words, the matter that is unspeakable, beyond thought and beyond narrow comprehension, namely the divine generation of Christ from God the Father. So vain is the mind of curious men. Hence they have served us nothing but mere trifles and fables. This heresy was more pestilent than all the others and those before it, because it seemed to rest on a certain greater reasoning and a subtler investigation, and it had much in common with the writings of the poets and the genealogies of the gods, which the pagans praised, as though those men had only obscured the truth with their fables, which this single impostor, Valentinus, seemed to have clearly seen and aptly touched upon. And so, since it had so much in agreement with the opinions of the pagans and Gentiles about their gods, this heresy easily pleased, and for that reason it was at once received and spread very widely. This is evident from the fact that in a single moment many embraced it, and these very Gnostics were afterwards called, almost alone, by the excellence of their knowledge. And others, in order to win a name for themselves from him, changed some things in his sect and doctrine, but always retained the foundations and trifles of his teaching about the propagation of the Aeons, as being those which then seemed most pleasing and acceptable to everyone. Therefore, of all the heresies that will be explained hereafter, Valentinus may be regarded as the most unhappy stock. Hence Epiphanius calls him a heresiarch [Αἱρεσιάρχῳ], and Lactantius, in book 4 of the Institutes, mentions the Valentinians as chief wounds of the Christian Church. Indeed, he was the root of the most harmful of poisons, with which the true doctrine of the Gospel concerning Christ our Mediator, God and man, was sprinkled by the Arians, Samosatenes, Nestorians and others who scattered the deadly poisons, and he was the deadly arsenal of those poisons. Finally, he was the most foul and greatest fountain of Mahometanism. Moreover, this Valentinus, from whom the Valentinian heresy takes its name, was an Egyptian by nation, and, as Epiphanius writes, a native of Pharbaethus. For that is how it must be read in him, and not as the corrupt form now found, Phrezonites [Φρεζωνίτης]. For Pharbaethus was a nome and prefecture of Egypt, named after the town of Pharbaethus, as Pliny writes in book 5, chapter 9. This was a maritime town situated near Pelusium, at the mouth of the Nile, as the same author says in chapter 10, near Alexandria, and near Bubastis, from which this Valentinus, the ruin and plague of the human race, sprang. He studied at Alexandria, where, trained in Greek literature, he became a Platonist and Pythagorean rather than a Christian. Tertullian and Isidore call him a follower of Plato, and Philastrius calls him a Pythagorean. They also report that he was devoted to Aristotelian precepts and to sophistic dialectic. Indeed, that the Christians of that time were too much addicted to pagan philosophy, and above all to Platonic philosophy, appears especially in Egypt from the writings of the authors of that age, such as Clement of Alexandria and others, and Philo the Jew, which also flourished there for a very long time, down to the great Platonic philosopher Plotinus and the Egyptian priest Abnebo. Valentinus lived under the emperor Antoninus Pius, as Eusebius teaches in book 4, chapter 11. Epiphanius writes that he became known after Cerinthus and the Ebionites, under the Roman bishop Hyginus, about the year 110 after the passion of Christ, after the death of Telesphorus, to whom Platina refers him, but the more weighty authors refer him to Hyginus. Irenaeus, in book 3, chapter 4, writes that he lived until Anicetus, that is, to the year 126 after the passion of Christ. The same Irenaeus, in book 1, chapter 5, holds that this ill-omened offshoot was produced by the Gnostics, that is, by Carpocrates, and not without good reason. For Valentinus was steeped in the errors of Carpocrates and others, but afterwards he himself sharpened these poisons and made them more harmful. For this monster was compounded from all the earlier ones, but because the earlier heresies seemed cruder, he himself, admitting the fables and ointments of the pagan poets, polished and commended them. He shamelessly lied that what he taught had been left to him by Matthias the Apostle and disciple of the Lord. He did write certain things himself, such as letters and homilies, some fragments of which Clement recites in books 2, 4 and 6 of the Stromata, where he records Valentinus's chief foundation, which appears from his writings to have been of this kind: "There are many things," he says, "which are written in public books" (that is, Jewish and philosophical books, as Clement himself says), "and which are found written in the Church of God." Hence he has now freely allowed himself to mix their fables with true theology, and profane things with sacred. From this very fact we are warned how dangerous it is to cling long and much to writings of this kind, from which Christians today, however, can hardly be drawn away. Tertullian calls Valentinus a shape-shifter, and a craftsman in building up and tearing down. He also lived for some time at Rome, where this heresy was spread, and from there he breathed his poison upon the Gauls, so that Irenaeus writes that women of the Rhone region were corrupted by it. Yet it flourished most in Egypt, where it was first born. Afterwards it was also at Antioch, in the time of Tertullian, where a certain Axionicus professed it. The occasion of the heresy, from Tertullian: Valentinus had hoped to become bishop, because he had ability and eloquence. But when another obtained the place by the privilege of martyrdom, he was indignant and broke away from the rule of the authentic Church, as men usually do when their spirit is stirred up for the sake of precedence, and he assailed the truth. This error then at once divided and dispersed itself into various sects, so that at least ten very dissimilar disciples are recorded by Irenaeus and Epiphanius as having come forth from the school of one and the same teacher, all called contemporaries [συγχρόνοι πάντες] and Gnostics. This heresy persisted for many centuries, both under its true name and under a changed one. For those that followed were only built up as a mass of blasphemies, the seeds of which this heresy had cast long before. It had many successors and a great company, among whom the following are chiefly reckoned: Secundus, Ptolemy, Marcus, Colarbasus, Heracleon and Cerdo, all unhappy branches of an unhappy tree, of whom more will be said later.

units.la: 2 Triginta ÆOnas.) Breuius huius erroris hypothesis perstringam, quod & Epiphanius, & Theodoretus, & Tertullianus, & ante hos omnes Irenæus abundè, imò verò ad nauseam vsque referunt. Sex autè capita hîc habentur. Clemens autem Alexandrinus vbique Basilidem & Valentinum in dogmate coniungit.
units.tr: 2 Thirty Aeons.) I will set out the outline of this error briefly, since Epiphanius, Theodoret, Tertullian, and before them all Irenaeus, report it at length, indeed almost to the point of nausea. Six heads are listed here. Clement of Alexandria, however, everywhere couples Basilides and Valentinus in doctrine.

units.la: 1 Continet fabulosam de triginta ÆOnum tanquam deorum generatione narrationem, vbi nascentes & nubentes, & generantes sunt, AEones, inquit Tertullianus. Illæ autè nugæ de Hesiodi Θεογονία potius quàm Antiphani in Theologiam sacrosanctam ab isto nebulone traductæ sunt, & nominibus Pythagoricorum numerorum dyadis & octoadis venditatæ. Sic igitur Hesiodus, & longè quidem, quàm Valentinus, melius, vt ait Iren. lib. 2. cap. 19.
units.tr: 1 It contains a fabulous account of the generation of thirty Aeons as if they were gods, who are born, marry and beget. "Aeons," says Tertullian. Those trifles were taken from Hesiod's Theogony rather than from Antiphanes and transferred into sacred theology by that scoundrel, and were peddled under the names of the Pythagorean numbers, the dyad and the ogdoad. So Hesiod, and far better than Valentinus, as Irenaeus says in book 2, chapter 19.

units.la: Ἐ[?]χάος δ' Ἐρέβος τε, μέλαινα τε Νὺξ ἐγένοντο. Νυκτὸς δ' αὖ Αἰθήρ τε καὶ Ἡμέρη ἐξεγένοντο, ὧς τίκτε κυοφορηθεῖσα Ἐρέβει φιλότητι μιγεῖσα,&c.
