units.tr: [Ἐκ Χάεος δ' Ἐρέβός τε, μέλαινά τε Νὺξ ἐγένοντο. Νυκτὸς δ' αὖ Αἰθήρ τε καὶ Ἡμέρη ἐξεγένοντο, τὼς τίκτε κυοφορηθεῖσα Ἐρέβει φιλότητι μιγεῖσα] Hesiod: "From Chaos came Erebus and black Night. And from Night in turn came Aether and Day, whom she bore, having conceived and mingled in love with Erebus," etc.

units.la: Ergo Valentinus [?]πλήρωμα quodam ex triginta AEonibus fecit, in quo prima octoas, ex qua cæteri AEones nati sunt, fuit per quatuor [?]ζυγίας siue copulationes, coiens mas AEon cum fœmina.
units.tr: Therefore Valentinus made a pleroma [πλήρωμα] of thirty Aeons, in which the first ogdoad, from which the other Aeons were born, came about through four syzygies [ζυγίας], or couplings, the male Aeon uniting with a female.

units.la: Primum coniugium & syzygia, siue dyas,
units.tr: The first marriage and syzygy, or dyad,

units.la: Profundi & Siges siue Bythi siue Silentij. Octoas prima Valentinianorum, & præcipua. Ex quibus nati Mens & Veritas Νοῦς Ἀλήθεια Ex quibus inter se coeuntibus fit 2. coniugium, siue secunda syzygia & dyas. ex qua Æones octo producti sunt. Ex his ipsis nascuntur Verbum & Vita λόγος ζωή Hi quoq; Æones duo coeuntes faciunt 3. coiugium, siue tertiam syzygiam siue dyadē. ex qua Æones decem nati sunt. Ex his denique gignuntur Homo & Ecclesia ἄνθρωπος Ἐκκλησία Hi quoque coniuncti connubio, faciunt quartā syzygiam siue dyadem. ex qua copula nati sunt Æones duodecim.
units.tr: of Profundity and Silence, that is, Bythus or Sige. This is the first and chief ogdoad of the Valentinians. From them are born Mind and Truth [Νοῦς, Ἀλήθεια]. From these two uniting comes the second marriage, or second syzygy and dyad, from which eight Aeons were produced. From these in turn are born Word and Life [λόγος, ζωή]. These two Aeons, uniting, make a third marriage, or third syzygy or dyad, from which ten Aeons were born. Finally from these are begotten Man and Church [ἄνθρωπος, Ἐκκλησία]. These also, joined in wedlock, make a fourth syzygy or dyad, from whose union twelve Aeons were born.

units.la: Iam vero ex 8.10.& 12.simul collectis fiunt triginta. Vnde apparet fuisse triginta Æones, qui, vt ait Tertullianus, crimina sunt, non numina.
units.tr: Now if the eight, the ten and the twelve are added together, they make thirty. From this it is clear that there were thirty Aeons, who, as Tertullian says, are crimes, not deities.

units.la: Tricesimus autem AEon vt abortiuus quidam errantis Sapientiæ fœtus fuit, vt ait Hieronymus,à quo cælum,& terra & mare cōdita sunt.
units.tr: The thirtieth Aeon, however, was a kind of abortive offspring of an erring Wisdom, as Jerome says, and from her heaven, earth and sea were made.

units.la: Quum enim Bythum, siue Profundum patrem suum videre gestiret, propterea in superiora ascendere voluisse, sed quum patris videndi non esset capax, terrore perculsus pene dissolutus est, & ex eo pauore haec omnia eaduca quibus hic mundus constat concepit & edidit. Nam ex eius pauore, inquit Tertullianus, tenebræ factæ sunt: ex timore & ignorantia spiritus nequitiæ & malignitatis, id est, diaboli: ex tristitia & la-chrymis humida fontium, & fluminū materia, & maris: ex risu eiusdem lucem extitisse. Christum autem a Bytho siue Profundo (quem & Propatrem appellant) ad huius tricesimi AEonis, & eorum quæ produxit auxilium missum, qui, vt Pādora eiusdem Hesiodi, sit ex omnium AEonum flosculis delibatus & compactus, quem Christum etiam σωτῆρα[?] vocant. Habere enim cum a Sapientia quod est spiritale: a Creatore quod est animale: ab œconomia corpus. ita nimirum unam & eadem Christi personam miserè divellunt & dissipant. Cuique autem AEoni affixam esse suam fœminam, quam Crucem vocant. Extra pleroma denique Chacmot .i. sapientiam (sic enim legendum est ab Hebrea voce חכמה[?] non autem vt vulgo apud Latinos aut Græcos scriptores Achamoth) constituunt, quæ luce percepta statim ad Christum accurrerit. Adducunt ad sui delirij confirmationem eos Scripturæ locos vbi vox Plenitu-do sæculi, & numerus duodecim legitur, quibus tamen apertissime & insulsissime abutun-tur. Sed quid hæc omnia aliud sunt, quàm, vt loquitur Spiritus sanctus, profunditates Satanæ, Apocal.2.versu 24. & ægrorum somnia, quæ tamen Menno quidam nostro seculo infelicissi-me renouauit, de quo dogmate vide D.Calui-ni epistolas. 2 Christum negant verum cor-pus humanum habuisse, sed cælcste & spirituale & per Mariam ὡς δὶα πωλῶος .i.fistulam tantùm percolatum pertransisse. Itaque primi Marcio-nitis ers andi occasionem præbuerunt. 3 Dia-bolum de tricefimoAEone procreatum dicunt non primùm à Deo Angelum factum. 4 Mun-dum ab Angelis malis eo quem diximus mo-do,& metu tricesimi AEonis creatum. 5 Ma-litiam inesse rebus à prima earum origine & creatione natiuam.Itaque Deum autorem ma-li faciunt. Quod dogma quum Manichæi im-prudentius cauere voluissent,in alium errorem & ipsi siue scopulum impegerunt,atque sic illis euenit quod vulgò dicitur,
units.tr: For when she longed to see her father Bythus, the Profound, she wished to rise to higher things; but since she was not able to grasp the sight of her father, she was struck with terror and almost dissolved, and from that fear she conceived and brought forth all those fleeting things of which this world consists. For from her fear, says Tertullian, darkness came to be; from fear and ignorance the spirit of wickedness and malice, that is, the devil; from sadness and tears the moist matter of springs, rivers and the sea; from her laughter, light came forth. Christ, however, was sent from Bythus or the Profound (whom they also call Propater) to help this thirtieth Aeon and the things she had produced. He was, like the Pandora of that same Hesiod, gathered and compacted from the flowers of all the Aeons, and they also call this Christ Saviour [σωτῆρα]. For they say he had from Sophia what is spiritual, from the Creator what is animal, and from the economy a body. In this way they wretchedly tear apart and scatter the one and the same person of Christ. Moreover, they assign to each Aeon its own female, whom they call Cross. Finally, outside the pleroma they posit Chacmoth, that is, Wisdom (for so it must be read from the Hebrew word חכמה [chokmah], not Achamoth as is commonly written by Latin or Greek writers), who, once she perceived the light, at once ran to Christ. To confirm their delirium they adduce those passages of Scripture where the phrase "fullness of the age" and the number twelve occur, which yet they abuse most plainly and foolishly. But what are all these things other than, as the Holy Spirit speaks, "the depths of Satan" (Apoc. 2, verse 24), and the dreams of sick men? Yet a certain Menno in our century unhappily revived them; on this doctrine see Doctor Calvin's letters. 2 They deny that Christ had a true human body, but say he was celestial and spiritual and passed through Mary as through a pipe [ὡς διὰ σωλῆνος], merely as water is filtered through a tube. Thus they gave the Marcionites their first occasion. 3 They say the devil was produced from the thirtieth Aeon, and was not first made an angel by God. 4 The world was created by evil angels in the manner we have described, and out of the fear of the thirtieth Aeon. 5 Malice is inherent in things, born from their first origin and creation. Thus they make God the author of evil. When the Manichaeans wanted to avoid this doctrine more carefully, they themselves ran into another error, and so it happened to them as is commonly said:

units.la: Incidit in Scyllà, cupiens vitare Charybdim.
units.tr: He falls into Scylla, wishing to avoid Charybdis.

units.la: 6 Carnis resurrectionem Valentiniani ne-gant.Solas enim animas, non autem corpora à Christo redemptas esse. 7 Fidem hominib. inesse à natura, sibi autem excellentius ex co-pia excellentis feminis quo constarent. Itaque & salutem sibi ex eadem natura esse,alijs autem etsi non omnibus,accidere merito operū.Hinc Pelagianismi semina & initia, postea repetita, & illa quæ optimè extincta putabantur, vti in-cendium rursum excitata sunt.Triplex enim ho-minum genus faciunt, vt ait Epiphanius, πνευματικῶν, ψυχικῶν, σαρκικῶν. Pneumaticos, quales ipsi sint, & fidem habere excellentismam, & à na-tura,& sine vllis operibus fieri saluos, quos ex Seth esse volūt:vnde Sethiani hæretici. ψυχικὸς habere etiam ipsos à natura fidem, sed exiguam, quòd è peiori sint semine, operibus autem salu-uari. Hos ex Abel genitos, vnde Abelitae. σαρ-κικοὺς[?] & Carnales nullo modo ad salutem peruenire posse. Hos ex Cain natos affirmant, vnde Cainiani haeretici. Vnde illud Tertull. Apud Valentinianos, Trinitas hominum. Inde 8 error est, cognitione sola contenti sunt, bona verò opera spernunt, vt inutilia, & multo risu excipiunt. Itaque quodlibet sceleris genus intrepidè perpetrant. Ἄνυτον[?] enim putant [illegible, ~40 letters] inquit Epiphanius. 9 Idolothytis vescuntur, etiam perfectissimi horum, quae in honore idolorum mactantur, & festa gentilium celebrant, vt inquit Theodoretus. Denique Prophetas veteris Testamenti explodunt. Tres enim Prophetarum spiritus constituunt, à Bytho, ab Vnigenito, à Patre, omnes inter se dissimiles. Ita omni erroris vitio & genere miseri illi & impostores homines sunt fascinati. Aduersus hos Iustinus, Irenaeus, Proculus, Miltiades, & Tertullianus scripserunt.
units.tr: 6 The Valentinians deny the resurrection of the flesh, for they say that only souls, not bodies, were redeemed by Christ. 7 They hold that faith is inborn in men by nature, but that in their own case it is more excellent, from the abundance of excellent seed from which they were constituted. Thus they also hold that salvation comes to them from that same nature, but to others, though not to all, through the merit of works. Hence the seeds and beginnings of Pelagianism, later revived, and those things which were thought to be thoroughly extinguished were kindled again like a fire. For they make a threefold race of men, as Epiphanius says: pneumatic, psychic, carnal [πνευματικῶν, ψυχικῶν, σαρκικῶν]. The pneumatics, such as they themselves are, have the most excellent faith, and by nature, without any works, are made safe; these they want to be descended from Seth, whence the heretical Sethians. The psychics also have faith by nature, but a small one, because they come from a worse seed, and are saved by works; these they say were born of Abel, whence the Abelites. Carnal men [σαρκικούς] can by no means attain salvation; these they affirm were born of Cain, whence the heretical Cainites. Hence that saying of Tertullian: "Among the Valentinians, a Trinity of men." From this comes 8 their error: they are content with knowledge alone, but scorn good works as useless and greet them with great laughter. Thus they fearlessly commit every kind of crime. For they think [illegible], as Epiphanius says. 9 Even the most perfect of them eat meat sacrificed to idols, and celebrate the festivals of the Gentiles, as Theodoret says. Finally, they reject the Prophets of the Old Testament. For they posit three spirits of the Prophets, from Bythus, from the Only-begotten, and from the Father, all unlike one another. Thus those wretched and deceiving men are bewitched by every fault and kind of error. Against these Justin, Irenaeus, Proculus, Miltiades and Tertullian wrote.

units.la: CAP. XII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XII.

units.la: Secundiani quid à Valentinianis differant.
units.tr: How the Secundians differ from the Valentinians.

units.la: {1}Ecundiani[?] hoc à Valentinianis distare dicuntur, quòd addunt{2} opera turpitudinis.
units.tr: The Secundians are said to differ from the Valentinians in this, that they add works of filthiness.

units.la: {1} Secundiani.) Quemiadmodum Dominus noster Iesus Christus habuit suos Apostolos, per quos salutarem doctrinam annuntiari mundo voluit, ita etiam Satan suos emissarios & errones, per quos zizania in agro Domini, quae est Ecclesia, seminauit. Inter eos autem præcipuus quidem fuit Valentinus, de quo iam diximus, & post eum illi, qui ab eo, tanquam ex fœtida fornace, incendiarii prodierunt. Fuerunt autem ii plures, & latissime sparsi, & in varias sectas & familias divisi, qui superiores Valentini errores diutissime retinuerunt. Nam, ut scribit Tertullianus, fuit frequentissimum Valentinianorum collegium, quia plurimum ex apostatis veritatis & ad fabulas facile est, & disciplina nō terretur. Deduxit igitur & Heracleon inde tramites quosdam, & Secundus, & magus Marcus. Multum circa imagines Legis Theotimus operatus est. Ita nusquam iam Valentinus, & tamen ubique Valentiniani, qui per ipsum Valentinum. Solus etiam, inquit idem Tertullianus, ad hodiernū Antiochiæ Axionicus memoriam Valentini integra custodia regularum eius consolatur. Addunt autem alij alios quoque discipulos Valentini præter commemoratos, veluti Theodoretus, Cossianum, Ptole-mæum, Theodotiu, Colarbasium: Epiphanius autem, Epiphane & Isidorum, qui duo postremi ad Carpocratianam hæresin proprie dictam potius pertinent. Cur autem tam facile una & eadem doctrina in tam contrarias se diffundere-ret opiniones & minutula, ratio est, non ea modo, quod nunquam sibi constat mendacium (una enim veritatis via, infinita vero mendacij diuerticula)sed etiam hæc,quam affert Tertullianus,nimirum,quòd si qui in ea secta noui aliquid astruerent,reuelationem statim appellabant præsumptionem: & charisma,ingenium: nec varietatem,sed diuersitatem (sic enim apud Tertullianum lego pro Nec vnitatem.) Hi autem omnes,vt scribit Epiphanius,fuerunt [illegible, ~8 letters], adeo vt interuallum temporis inter tot nouas compertas sectas obseruari magnum nō possit. Quæque autem sequentium Valentinianarum hæreseon pene cum suo authore interiit, eiusque appellatio intercidit, origo tamen ipsa & blasphema Valentini dogmata manserunt, vt nobis de cuiusque duratione & successione magnopere laborandum non fit. Regiones autem orbis eas peruaserunt & corruperunt, in quibus doctores ipsi vixere & docuere: uniuersum autem terrarum orbem ipsa Valentiniana hæresis quàm longo tempore vexauit. Secundiani à Secundo dicti sunt. Hic autem primarius Valetini discipulus & schol[?] fuc cessor in Ægypto fuisse perhibetur, quanquam alij Ptolemæum malunt, alij Heracleonem. Ut autem magistro ingeniosior videretur, quædam in accepta à Valentino doctrina immutauit, quædam, vt scribit Epiphanius, magis peregrinis & exoticis, sed sonantioribus vocabulis obscurauit: quædam etiam addidit, quia nullum est abyssi & erroris imum, nullúsque finis. Secundi etiam meminit Irenæus, vt primi & præcipui Valentini discipuli, lib.1.cap.5.
units.tr: {1} Secundians.) Just as our Lord Jesus Christ had his Apostles, through whom he willed the saving doctrine to be announced to the world, so Satan also has his emissaries and wanderers, through whom he has sown tares in the Lord's field, which is the Church. Among these, the chief was Valentinus, of whom we have already spoken, and after him those who came forth from him, like incendiaries from a foul furnace. These were many and widely scattered, and divided into various sects and families, and they retained the earlier errors of Valentinus for a very long time. For, as Tertullian writes, the Valentinian college was very large, since most of it was made up of apostates from the truth, and it is easy for such people to turn to fables, and discipline does not frighten them. Heracleon and Secundus, and the magician Marcus, therefore drew certain paths out of it. Theotimus worked much on the images of the Law. Thus Valentinus himself is nowhere now, and yet Valentinians are everywhere, who are so called after Valentinus. Tertullian says that Axionicus alone at Antioch, even to this day, comforts the memory of Valentinus by keeping his rules intact. Other writers add other disciples of Valentinus besides those mentioned, such as Theodotus, Cossianus, Ptolemy, Theodotion, and Colarbasus; Epiphanius adds Epiphanes and Isidore, the last two of whom belong more properly to the Carpocratian heresy. Why one and the same doctrine spread so easily into such contrary opinions and trifling details is explained not only by the fact that lying never keeps to one line (for there is one road of truth, but endless byways of falsehood), but also by what Tertullian adds: namely, that if anyone in that sect put forward something new, they at once called the novelty "presumption," and the gift "talent," and what was new "diversity" rather than "variety" (for so I read in Tertullian, instead of "nor unity"). All these, as Epiphanius writes, were [illegible, about eight letters], so that no great interval of time can be observed between so many new sects. And although the later Valentinian heresies almost perished together with their author, and his name has died out, yet the origin itself and the blasphemous doctrines of Valentinus have remained, so that we need not labor greatly over the duration and succession of each. These heresies have pervaded and corrupted the regions in which their teachers themselves lived and taught, and the Valentinian heresy has troubled the whole world for a long time. The Secundians are named from Secundus. He is said to have been the first disciple of Valentinus and his successor in Egypt, although others prefer Ptolemy and others Heracleon. But in order to seem more gifted than his master, he altered some things in the doctrine received from Valentinus; some, as Epiphanius writes, he obscured with more foreign and exotic, yet more sonorous, words; and some he even added, since there is no bottom or limit to the abyss of error. Irenaeus also mentions Secundus, as the first and chief disciple of Valentinus, in book 1, chapter 5.

units.la: {2} Addunt opera.) Vnum hoc Secundianorum dogma ex Epiphanio in argumento lib.1.
units.tr: {2} They add works.) Epiphanius, in the argument of book 1, relates this one dogma of the Secundians,

units.la: Tom.2. refert Augustinus, quòd præter superiores blasphemias vitæ turpitudinem sectatoribus suis indulgebant. Cuius dogmatis ratio ex ipsius Valentini lacunis & dictis sumpta est, qui se suòsque non operibus, sed sola cognitione salvos esse affirmauit. Itaque siue bene, siue male agerent perinde esse. Tertullianus scribit Valentinianorum successores & hæreses tatum sibi permittere, quantū lupæ & meretrices foeminæ quibus formâ quotidie supparare solene est. Itaq; & vita turpissimos, & in dogmate inconstantissimos fuisse certum est. Nos autem ex aliis alias quoque Secundianorum hypotheses & errores collegimus. 2. Error, per quem pigmenta deliriis Valentini addùt, est, Quòd primariam illam octoadem Valentini diuidunt in dextrum & siniistrû latus, nimirum vt quatuor dextro lateri, alia vero quatuor siniistro tribuantur, Pythagoreos imitati, qui omnia rerum genera eodem modo partiuntur in dextra & sinistra, vt scribit Plutarch. lib.1. De placit. Philos. cap.3. Sed & ad illos octo præcipuos Æonas Valentini ipsi addùt Lucem & Tenebras. Præterea & quem desertorem Æonem constituit Valentinus, nempe tricesimum, Secundus dicit fuisse alium, & nullum ex illis triginta, vt ait Tertullianus. Deinde illos Æonas diuinæ mentis affectus tantùm & ideas Valentinus esse docuit. Secundiani vero contendunt esse veras essentias, & per se subsistentes. Denique nomina ipsa Æonum Valentini, ipsi primi immutarunt, & à communi captu remotiora fecerunt, vt, quemadmodum scribit Epiphanius, supra Valentinum sapere viderentur: ita bonis discipulis male cum suo præceptore Valentino conueniet. 3 Error, negant Christum vere incar-natum, & hominem factum esse.
units.tr: Augustine, in volume 2, reports that, besides the earlier blasphemies, they indulged their followers in a life of baseness. The reason for this dogma was drawn from Valentinus' own lacunae and sayings, for he affirmed that he and his people were saved not by works but by knowledge alone. Therefore it made no difference whether they acted well or badly. Tertullian writes that the successors of the Valentinians and their heresies allowed themselves as much as wolves and harlots, whose beauty it is customary to make up daily. So it is certain that they were both most vile in life and most inconstant in doctrine. We, however, have gathered from other sources other hypotheses and errors of the Secundians as well. 2. The error by which they add embellishments to the fancies of Valentinus is this: they divide that primary Ogdoad of Valentinus into a right and a left side, so that four aeons are assigned to the right side and the other four to the left, imitating the Pythagoreans, who divide all kinds of things in the same way into right and left, as Plutarch writes in book 1 of the Placita of the Philosophers, chapter 3. But to those eight principal aeons they also add Light and Darkness. Moreover, the deserter aeon whom Valentinus set up, namely the thirtieth, Secundus says was another, and none of those thirty, as Tertullian says. Next, Valentinus taught that those aeons were only affections and ideas of the divine mind, whereas the Secundians contend that they are true essences subsisting in themselves. Finally, the Secundians themselves changed the very names of the aeons of Valentinus and made them more remote from common understanding, so that, as Epiphanius writes, they might seem to be wiser than Valentinus. Thus they agree badly with their master Valentinus, even though they are good disciples. 3. The error that they deny that Christ was truly incarnate and made man.

units.la: CAP. XIII. Ptolemiani quid à Valentinianis differant.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIII. How the Ptolemaeans differ from the Valentinians.

units.la: Tolemæus{1} quoque discipulus Valentini, hæresin nouam condere cupiens, quatuor{2} Æonas, & alios quatuor afferre maluit.
units.tr: Ptolemy too, a disciple of Valentinus, wishing to found a new heresy, preferred to introduce four Aeons and four others.

units.la: 1 Ptolemæus.) Fere hæc hæresis prætermittitur, uti à Clemente, Theodoreto, Eusebio, & Isidoro, quia cum superiori consentit. Tertullianus Ptolemæum & Secundum coniunxit. Alii tamen, uti hic Augustinus & Epiphanius, seorsim separant. Ptolemæum tamen in schola successis-se Secundo tradit apertè Epiphanius. alij cum ex Marci, cuius hæresis sequenti capite explicabitur, præstigiis extitisse malunt. Certè fuerunt hi omnes fermè contemporanei, quemadmodum antea diximus. Viuebat tamen adhuc Irenæi ætate (qui tamen Valentino ipso posterior fuit) hic Ptolemæus & in Occidentis partibus notior videtur fuisse, uti Secundus in Oriente. Id quod ex ipso lib.i.proœmio aduersus Valentinum facilè colligetur. Vsus autem est ad sua dogmata propaganda Ptolemæus Flora quadā fœmina ad quam longa epistola scripsit suam sententiam, & quam sororem suam appellat. Nec ea est tamen, à qua Floriani hæretici nomi-nantur, de quibus postea. Magno autem in pre-tio hunc fuisse vel ex eo apparet, quòd totius Valentinianorum scholæ flos & corculum, vt ait Irenæus, diceretur. Vt autem ex ipsius scriptis intelligimus, nec ingenio, nec eloquio caruit. Ergo ab hoc Ptolemiani vel Ptolemæi (vtrunque enim reperitur) hæretici sunt appellati.
units.tr: 1 Ptolemy.) This heresy is for the most part passed over, as by Clement, Theodoret, Eusebius and Isidore, because it agrees with the earlier one. Tertullian joined Ptolemy and Secundus together. Others, such as Augustine and Epiphanius here, treat them separately. Epiphanius, however, plainly states that Ptolemy succeeded Secundus in the school. Others prefer to say that he arose from the tricks of Marcus, whose heresy will be explained in the following chapter. Certainly all of these were nearly contemporaries, as we said before. Yet Ptolemy was still alive in the time of Irenaeus, who was later than Valentinus himself, and he seems to have been better known in the parts of the West, as Secundus was in the East. This may be readily gathered from the preface to book 1 of Irenaeus against Valentinus. Ptolemy used a certain woman named Flora to spread his doctrines, to whom he wrote a long letter setting out his opinion, and whom he calls his sister. She is not, however, the one from whom the Florinian heretics take their name, of whom we will speak later. That he was held in high esteem is clear from the fact that, as Irenaeus says, he was called the flower and heart of the whole school of the Valentinians. And, as we learn from his own writings, he lacked neither talent nor eloquence. Therefore the heretics were called Ptolemaeans or Ptolemaeans (for both forms are found) after him.

units.la: Quatuor αἰῶνας[?].) Quanquam vtiliter ignoratur, quæ fuerint harum hæresèon dogma-ta, & in quo diuersa, quia tamen illius rei explicatio ad hunc locum alias obscurum illustran-dum pertinet, breuiter exponam, vel propterea maximè, quòd in eo Irenæus, à quo Epipha-nius sua sumpsit, videtur à Tertulliano aperte dissentire. Fuit autem Tertulliano antiquior Irenæus, & à Valentinianorum seculo minus aberat. Iren. igitur lib. 1. cap. 6. docet hunc Ptole-mæum, cuius scripta tunc in manibus hominum versabantur, octonarium quidem AEonum numerum tanquam fontem aliorum omnium re-tinuisse: sed alios, alitérque quàm Valentinum constituisse & appellasse. Valentinus enim Bytho vnâ tantùm coniugem dedit, eámque Sigen nominauit. At Ptolemæus Bytho duas vxores liberaliter gratificatus est, & donauit, ne parcè coire videretur, quarum vnam quidem Ἔννοιαν, cogitationem: alteram verò Θέλησιν[?], vt loquitur Irenæus: vt autem Epiphanius Θέλημα. i. Voluntatem vocauit. Ex vtraque illa coniuge Bythus propagines emisit, vt essent earum rerum, quæ sunt apud se inuisibiles & inconspicuæ, visibiles imagines. Ἐννοίας quidem inconspicuæ ima-go conspicua est Νοῦς, id est, Mens. Θελήσεως autem visibilis typus est Ἀλήθεια, id est, Veritas. Itaque & nominibus & modo ipso procreandi Æonas diuersus fuit a præceptore Valentino Ptolemæus. Sed iam in eo differunt Tertullia-nus & Irenæus, quòd Irenæus dicat Ptolemæum facere hos Æonas Bythi, id est, summi Dei Βυθοῦ tantum quasdam & Δυνάμεις, id est, affectus tantum & qualitates siue potestates. Tertullianus contrà scribit eum distinxisse Æonas in per-fonales substantias, & cesuisse esse res per se subsistentes, non tantum Dei affectus. Itaque uti Plato ideas suas ἰδέας esse dixit, sic iste Æonas suos, si Tertullianum sequimur. Ego tamen po-tius Irenæo assentior, quem etiam Epiphanius sequitur: & in eo Ptolemæus a Secundo condi-scipulo suo dissentire voluit, præceptorisque Valentini sententiam tueri, quam Secundus op-pugnarat.
units.tr: Four Aeons [αἰῶνας?].) Although the particular doctrines of these heresies and the points on which they differ are not well known, I will briefly set them out, since the explanation of this matter helps to clarify a passage that is otherwise obscure here. I do this especially because on this point Irenaeus, from whom Epiphanius took his account, seems to differ openly from Tertullian. Irenaeus was older than Tertullian and was less distant from the age of the Valentinians. Irenaeus, then, in book 1, chapter 6, teaches that this Ptolemy, whose writings were then in people's hands, retained the number of eight Aeons as the source of all the others, but set them up and named them differently from Valentinus. For Valentinus gave Bythus only one consort, whom he called Sige. But Ptolemy generously gave Bythus two wives, so that he would not seem to couple sparingly. One of them he called Thought [Ἔννοιαν], the other Will [Θέλησιν], as Irenaeus puts it; Epiphanius calls her Will [Θέλημα]. From these two consorts Bythus put forth offspring, so that there would be visible images of those things which are invisible and unseen in themselves. The visible image of the unseen Thought is Mind [Νοῦς], and the visible figure of Will is Truth [Ἀλήθεια]. Thus Ptolemy differed from his teacher Valentinus both in the names of the Aeons and in the very manner of their generation. But Tertullian and Irenaeus differ further here: Irenaeus says that Ptolemy made these Aeons merely certain powers [Δυνάμεις] and affections or qualities or capacities of Bythus, that is, of the supreme God. Tertullian, on the contrary, writes that he distinguished the Aeons into personal substances, and held them to be things subsisting in themselves, and not merely affections of God. So, just as Plato called his ideas [ἰδέας], so this man's Aeons would be, if we follow Tertullian. I, however, rather agree with Irenaeus, whom Epiphanius also follows. In this matter Ptolemy wished to dissent from his fellow disciple Secundus, and to defend the opinion of his teacher Valentinus, which Secundus had attacked.

units.la: 2 Error. Legem veteris Testa-menti non totam à Deo esse dixit, sed partim à Deo, partim à Mose ipso: partim ex quibusdam seniorum traditionibus constare.
units.tr: 2 Error. He said that the Law of the Old Testament was not wholly from God, but partly from God and partly from Moses himself, and partly consisted of certain traditions of the elders.

units.la: 3 Deum u-num & eundem, cùm aliquid emittit Patrem uo-cari: cùm vera dicit, Veritatem: cùm se manife-stat, Hominem, vt Sabellianorum errorem spar-sisse, etsi obscurè, cū Simone videri debeat Pto-lemæus. Ita Irenæus lib.i.cap.6.
units.tr: 3 He taught that God is one and the same, but when he sends forth something he is called Father, when he speaks true things, Truth, and when he manifests himself, Man. So Ptolemy seems, though obscurely, to have spread the error of the Sabellians, and to be aligned with Simon. So Irenaeus, book 1, chapter 6.

units.la: CAP. XIIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIV.

units.la: Marcus à quo Marcitæ hæretici. Erroris autem capita quatuor enumerata.
units.tr: Marcus, from whom the Marcite heretics take their name. Four heads of his error are enumerated.

units.la: Marcus etiam nescio quis hæresin condidit, negas resurrectionem carnis: & Christum non vere, sed putatiuè passum asseuerans. Duo quoque opinatus est ex aduersò sibi esse principia. Quiddam tale etiam ipse de Æo-nibus, sicut Valentinus, affirmans.
units.tr: Marcus, I know not who, also founded a heresy. He denies the resurrection of the flesh, and asserts that Christ suffered not truly but only in appearance. He also supposed that there were two opposing principles, and he affirmed something similar about the Aeons, as Valentinus did.

units.la: 1 Marcus etiam.) Et hic quoque ex eadem Valentinianæ viperæ aluo procreatus est. Fuit enim condiscipulus Colarbasij, de quo postea, in eadem Valentini schola, eiusdémque doctrinæ blasphemæ & auditor & sectator. Itaque cum Colarbasio coniungit Tertullianus. In quo illud ab Irenæo patre verissimè de Valentinianorum hæresi dictum esse apparet. Nemo, ait, inter eos perfectus est, qui non magna mendacia velut fructus suæ disciplinæ produxerit, libro 1. cap.15. Hic igitur nouam sectam ambitiose parturiens tandem edidit, in quo maiorum suorum, & ipsius adeo Valentini improbitatem, impietatémque superauit, in tantum quidem, vt hic plures sibi lucrifaceret & decipe-ret, captósque [?] potentius retineret, quia & miraculis, & prophetiis, quę magicis artibus faciebat, doctrinam suam confirmare & commendare videbatur. Fuit enim summus magus, quemadmodum aduers. Valentinian. scribit Tertullianus, & Irenæus quoque lib. 1. cap. 9. Assiduè namque incantationibus & præstigiis vtebatur, ad infirmos & mulierculas imprimis deludendas & stupefaciendas propter imbecillitatem sexus, speciosò nimirum prætextu religionis summæque pietatis. Id quod fore prædixerat Paulus 2. Timoth. 6. verf. 6. Maxime vero diuites & opulentas matronas affectabatur, quarum & animum suis erroribus: & corpora suis stupris misere fœdeque corrumpebat. Denique [illegible, ~6 letters] & amatoria pocula [illegible, ~7 letters] illis bibenda porrigebat, vt quid ex tam nefando impostore sani[?] bonive sperandum fuerit, iam tum homines ex ipsius moribus intelligere potuerint. Habuit tamen non paucos discipulos tum ex viris, tum etiam ex mulieribus Christianis quas dementauit. Atque tam late serpsit hoc infelix lolium & pestiferum gramen, vt Ægyptum, Asiam, & Galliam, adeoque Lugdunum ipsum vrbem celeberrimam & Rhodanenses mulieres tabe sua infecerit, quemadmodum ex Irenæo facile colligi poterit. Vnde Antichristi præcursor hic fere primus appellatus est. Dæmonem [illegible, ~8 letters] id est, familiarem habuit, Irenæus libr.1. cap. 9. Idolorum defensor aut certe non improbator fuit. Anaxilai quoque philosophi Pythagorici æmulator, quia Pythagoreorum nugas de numeris, imprimis autem mysterium septenarij muneri cum sua astrologia miscens, sapientissimè & sublimissimè de Deo, ciusque natura, & emissionibus philosophari censebatur. Nam obscurissimè, & quibusdam verborum tanquam mysteriorum inuolucris utens, loquebatur de Deo, vt stuperent audientes homines potius, quàm intelligerent. Hebræq; quo-que linguæ fuit peritus, itaque vocabulis Hebræis & Græcis hominibus exoticis deliria sua tegebat, ex quo etiam illud facilè intelligi poterit eum cum Pythagorica Platonicàque Philosophia, Rabbinorum Hebræorum commenta, ad Christianæ doctrinæ veritatem simplicitatémque obruedam confudisse. Id quod post-ea imitatus est Mahumetes. Quanquam, ut Ter-tullianus scribit, ex Græcorum alphabeto dogmatum suorum fundamenta & mysteria sumpsit, quò se suámque sectam, etiam ethnicis Philosophis & hominibus probaret. Referunt au-tem huius hæreseos initia in annum Antonini Pij imperatoris nonum, qui fuit annus à Chri-sto passo c x v. ut iam recte collocari appareat post Secundianos. Huius Marci discipuli Μαρκῶσι[?] ab Epiphanio: à Latinis autem Marcitæ dicti sunt. Hi verò se Perfectos vocabant, lon-géque Paulo ipso & Petro Domini nostri Ie-su Christi Apostolis, præstantiores esse iactant. Ut autem latissimè vagata est, plurimúmque nocuit hæc hæresis: ita diutissimè, sed interpo-lato nomine, fuit retenta & sustentata. Pullula-uit enim maximè, ut scribit Theodoretus, & Colarbasios, Ascodrutas, Archonticos, Ophi-tas & alios hæreticos, tanquam vipera nocen-tissima fœtus crudelissimos profudit: qui o-mnes in Dei Ecclesiam pessimè, tanquam in matrem, suis erroribus sunt grassati.
units.tr: 1 Marcus also.) He too was born from the same womb of the Valentinian viper. For he was a fellow pupil of Colarbasus, of whom more later, in the same school of Valentinus, and a hearer and follower of that man's blasphemous teaching. Accordingly Tertullian links him with Colarbasus. In this, what Irenaeus, the father, said very truly about the heresy of the Valentinians is evident: "There is no one among them who is perfect who does not produce great lies as the fruit of his discipline" (Book 1, ch. 15). So this man, ambitiously giving birth to a new sect, at last brought it forth, and in it surpassed the wickedness and impiety of his predecessors and of Valentinus himself. He did so to such a degree that he gained more followers for himself, deceived them, and held those captured more powerfully. For he seemed to confirm and commend his teaching by the miracles and prophecies which he performed by magic arts. He was, as Tertullian writes in his work against the Valentinians, and Irenaeus also (Book 1, ch. 9), a supreme magician. For he constantly used incantations and tricks, chiefly to beguile and stupefy the weak and little women on account of the frailty of their sex, under the specious pretext of religion and supreme piety. This Paul had foretold (2 Timothy 3:6). He especially sought out rich and wealthy matrons, whose minds he wretchedly corrupted with his errors and whose bodies he foully corrupted with his debaucheries. Finally he offered them [...] and love potions to drink, so that already at that time men could understand from his morals what could be expected from so impious an impostor, whether for good or ill. Nevertheless he had not a few disciples, both men and Christian women whom he drove out of their minds. And this unhappy tare and pestilent weed spread so widely that it infected with its poison Egypt, Asia, and Gaul, and even the very famous city of Lyons and the women of the Rhone, as may easily be gathered from Irenaeus. Hence this man was called almost the first forerunner of Antichrist. He had a demon, that is, a familiar spirit (Irenaeus, Book 1, ch. 9). He was a defender of idols, or at least not a disapprover of them. He was also an imitator of the Pythagorean philosopher Anaxilaus, since he mixed the Pythagorean trifles about numbers, and especially the mystery of the number seven, with his own astrology, and was thought to philosophize most wisely and sublimely about God, his nature, and his emanations. For he spoke of God most obscurely, using certain veils of words as if they were mysteries, so that his hearers were astonished rather than understood. He was also skilled in the Hebrew language, and so he covered his nonsense with Hebrew and Greek words, foreign to ordinary men. From this it can also easily be understood that he confused the Pythagorean and Platonic philosophy and the fictions of the Hebrew rabbis, in order to overwhelm the truth and simplicity of Christian doctrine. Mahomet later imitated this. Yet, as Tertullian writes, he took the foundations and mysteries of his doctrines from the Greek alphabet, so that he might commend himself and his sect even to the pagan philosophers and people. They date the beginnings of this heresy to the ninth year of the emperor Antoninus Pius, which was the year 115 after Christ's passion, so that it now appears rightly placed after the Secundians. The disciples of this Marcus are called Μαρκῶσι [Marcosians] by Epiphanius, but by the Latins they are called Marcites. They called themselves "the Perfect," and boasted that they were far superior to Paul himself and to Peter, the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ. But as this heresy spread very widely and did very great harm, so it was held and sustained for a very long time, though under a changed name. For it sprouted especially, as Theodoret writes, and like a most harmful viper it poured forth most cruel offspring: Colarbasians, Ascodrutae, Archontics, Ophites, and other heretics, all of whom raged against the Church of God with their errors, as if against a mother.

units.la: 2 Resurrectionem carnis.) Quatuor erroris eorum hypotheses recenset hîc Augustinus. A-lij autem, veluti toto libr.i.Irenæus, plures. Sed Epiphanij argumentum tom.3.lib.1. secutus est Augustinus. Ergo hæ fuerunt Marci hypothe-ses. 1 Carnis resurrectionem negauit futuram. 2 Christum item negat & verè humanam carnem assumpsisse & passum esse, de quo adhuc puero narrat fabulam, quæ vt est salsissima, sic indigna relatu. 3 Duo rerum principia sibi contraria constituit, Sigen & λόγῳ[?].i. Silentium & Sermonem. Inde Marcionitæ & Manichæi orti. 4 Æones quidem, sed eorum quaternationem, tanquam omnium aliorum parentem ex sententia & vestigiis Valentini retinet. Quaternitatem enim pro verissima personarum diuinarum Trinitate, quam Christiani confitentur, impudentissimè supposuit, atque eas ipsas personas separatas fingit, Nempe Sigen, Logo, & præterea alios duos Æones innominatos, & tamen pares duobus illis, quos suis nominibus appellat. 5 Literis, syllabis, & characteribus singulos homines, & singula singulorum hominum membra subiici & gubernari dixit, atque adeo hæc vniuersa, vt cùm omnia ad vnam eandémque literam redierint, sint omnia instauranda, & futurus sit rerum omnium finis. Hoc ex præceptis & nugis Magiæ cui addictissimus fuit, affirmauit. Itaque in iis literis plenam perfectámque veritatis cognitionem inesse, sine quibus illa nullo modo percipi possit. Quod ex Iudaicarum & Cabalistarum quæ iam tunc erant superstitionum atque fabularum fontibus haustum esse dubitari non potest. Omne enim secis genus ad veritatem Euangelij obruendam, miscuit impostor iste, & omne Satanicum inventum ad Christum oppri-mendum aduocauit. Græcorum autem quàm Hebræorum literas & alphabetu sequi maluit, tum quòd plures sunt Græcorum literæ (nam etiam ipse earum numero non fuit contentus, sed ad xxiiii literas Græcorum sex alias addidit, ut essent numero xxx, ad quem numerum AEonas omnes reuocauit) tum etiam quòd hac ratione acceptior & gratior Græcis hominibus & Ethnicis esset futurus. Sic itaque eas divisit, ut A & Ω, regerent atque haberent caput hominis: B & Ψ, collum: Γ & X, humeros: Δ & Φ, pectus: E & T, septum transversum: Z & T, dorsum: H & Σ, ventrem: Θ & P, femora: I & Π, genua: K & O, tibias: Λ & Ξ, talos: M & N, pedes. Nomen autem [illegible, ~6 letters] uti augustius cæteris præferebat. Mutas autem novem quæ vocantur à Grammaticis, literas retulit ad Deū Patrem quem Silentium appellauit, tanquam illius proprias. Semiuocales octo ad λόγον & ζωὴν[?]. Vocales septem ad Hominem & Ecclesiam. Et hæc sunt vani hominis deliria, quæ ipsa etiamnum hodie regerere nobis, & ex inferis revocare quosdam non pudet. 6 Baptismum domini nostri, etiam ipsi, quemadmodum & Simoniani, corrumpunt & prorsus immutant. Baptizat enim in nomine ignoti Patris & Veritatis matris omnium, & eius qui descendit in Iesum. Baptismi Valentiniani meminit Hieronym. in epistolam ad Ephes.Sed etiam initiandas mulieres ad thalamum deducunt, & ibi mystagogiam suam adhibitis nefandis quibusdam gesticulationibus peragunt, quod spirituale coniugium vocant.Eufeb.lib.4.cap.ii. 7 Sacrosanctam Domini Coenam polluunt. Nam Marcitae profitentur verbis & incantationibus vinum, quod est in calice, & in coena Domini fe mutare in sanguinem, & gratiam Dei in eum ipsum calicem deducere, vt ex eo omnes vel gustare cupiant. Annotare libet Epiphanium voce μετουσίας[?] ante Ioan. Damascen. vsum esse. Est autè Transubstantiatio, quam vt prorsus ineptam haereticis obiicit Epiphanius.
units.tr: The resurrection of the flesh. 2) Augustine here lists four of their hypotheses of error. Others, such as Irenaeus throughout his first book, list more. But Augustine followed the account of Epiphanius in the third volume, first book. So these were Marcus's hypotheses. (1) He denied that the resurrection of the flesh would take place. (2) He likewise denies that Christ assumed true human flesh and suffered, and he tells a fable about Christ as a child, which is as silly as it is unworthy of repeating. (3) He set up two contrary principles of things, Sigē and Logos [Σιγή, λόγος], that is, Silence and Word. From this the Marcionites and Manichaeans arose. (4) He keeps the aeons, but following the opinion and footsteps of Valentinus, he keeps their quaternity as the parent of all the others. For he shamelessly put this quaternity in place of the most true Trinity of the divine persons, which Christians confess, and he imagines these very persons as separate: namely Sigē, Logos, and besides them two other unnamed aeons, equal to those two whom he calls by their own names. (5) He said that individual men, and the individual members of individual men, are placed under and governed by letters, syllables and characters, and that therefore all these things, when everything has returned to one and the same letter, will have to be restored, and there will be an end of all things. He affirmed this from the precepts and trifles of magic, to which he was most devoted. Thus he held that the full and perfect knowledge of truth lies in those letters, without which it cannot be grasped in any way. That he drew this from the sources of Jewish and Cabalistic superstitions and fables, which already then existed, cannot be doubted. For this impostor mixed every kind of sect together to overthrow the truth of the Gospel, and summoned every satanic invention to oppress Christ. He preferred to follow the letters and alphabet of the Greeks rather than those of the Hebrews, partly because the Greek letters are more numerous (for he was not content even with their number, but added six other letters to the twenty-four Greek letters, so that there were thirty, and to this number he reduced all the aeons), and partly because in this way he would be more acceptable and pleasing to Greeks and Gentiles. So he divided them thus: A and Ω govern and hold the head of man; B and Ψ the neck; Γ and X the shoulders; Δ and Φ the chest; E and Θ the diaphragm; Z and Τ the back; H and Σ the belly; Θ and P the thighs; I and Π the knees; K and O the shins; Λ and Ξ the ankles; M and N the feet. But the name [illegible, about six letters], being more august, he put before the others. He assigned the nine mute letters, as they are called by the grammarians, to God the Father, whom he called Silence, as being his own. The eight semivowels he assigned to Logos and Zoē [ζωή]. The seven vowels he assigned to Man and the Church. And these are the empty delusions of a foolish man, which even today some are not ashamed to bring back to us and recall from the dead. 6) They also corrupt and utterly change the baptism of our Lord, just as the Simonians do. For they baptize in the name of the unknown Father, of Truth the mother of all, and of him who descended into Jesus. Jerome, in his commentary on the Epistle to the Ephesians, mentions the baptism of the Valentinians. But they also lead women to the bridal chamber to be initiated, and there they carry out their mystagogy with certain unspeakable gestures, which they call spiritual marriage. Eusebius, book 4, chapter 11. 7) They defile the most holy Supper of the Lord. For the Marcites profess that by words and incantations the wine that is in the cup is changed into blood in the Lord's Supper, and that they draw the grace of God down into that very cup, so that all desire to taste of it. It is worth noting that Epiphanius used the word metousia [μετουσία] before John of Damascus. This is transubstantiation, which Epiphanius objects to the heretics as utterly absurd.

units.la: CAP. XV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XV.

units.la: Colarbafij,& eorum dogma.
units.tr: The Colarbasians and their doctrine.

units.la: C[?]olarbafus secutus est istos non multum aliter sentiens. Vitam omnium hominum & generationem in septem syderibus con-sistere affirmans.
units.tr: Colarbasus followed these men, thinking not much differently. He affirmed that the life of all men and their generation depend on the seven stars.

units.la: 1 Colarbafus.) Colarbas & Colarbafus appellatur huius sectę author, cuius meminit Ire-næus lib.1.cap.9. & Tertull. & uterque cū Marco coniungit. Epiphanius tamen scribit eos nō solum ex Valentinianorum, sed etiam superiorum haereticorum schola profectos & fatos, ex qua tanquam ex hydra plura capita nata sunt. Theodoretus quoque libro i. horum meminit. fuit haec haeresis eodem tempore, quo superior. Cùm autem pauca omnino de Colarbafo tradita sint, quis fuerit & vbi docuerit, obscurum hominem fuisse & statim sectam hanc concidi-disse verisimile est. In catalogo tamen retenta est, vt quàm varie à Satana vexata sit Ecclesia, & oppugnata doctrina Christi, intelligeretur.
units.tr: 1 Colarbasus.) Colarbas, also called Colarbasus, is the name given to the author of this sect, whom Irenaeus mentions in book 1, chapter 9, and Tertullian too, and both join him with Marcus. Epiphanius, however, writes that they came forth from the school of the Valentinians and also of the earlier heretics, from which, as from a hydra, many heads have sprung. Theodoret also mentions them in book 1. This heresy arose at the same time as the previous one. Since very little at all has been handed down about Colarbasus, who he was and where he taught, it is likely that he was an obscure man and that this sect soon collapsed. It has nevertheless been kept in the catalogue so that it may be understood how variously the Church has been harassed by Satan and the teaching of Christ assailed.

units.la: 2 Vitam omnium.)Unum dogma eorum recenset Augustinus, quòd astris imprimis autem septem planetis vitam actionésque hominum & eventa rerum tribuerent. Quod commetum ex nimio astrologiæ iudiciariæ studio profectum est, quem errorem secuti sunt postea Priscillianistæ. 2 Error. Deum unum & eūdem in persona una & ὑπόστασις[?] diuersis nominibus appellari, & diuersas personas ceseri, Patrem cum cogitat: Veritatem cum patefactus est, & Hominem in his terris. Itaque Deum ipsum appellat hominem & naturarum confusionem inducit. 3 Christum ex xxx, AEonibus tanquam flosculum compactum & decerptum esse tanquam Hesiodi Pandoram, unde appellari ἀλ-κυτὸν[?], quòd πᾶν πληρωμα νοσικὸς[?]. 4 Iesum à Christo tanquam duas separatásque personas diuellit. Hinc Nestoriani.
units.tr: 2 Vitam omnium.) Augustine lists one doctrine of theirs: that they ascribed to the stars, and above all to the seven planets, the life and actions of men and the events of things. This error, committed through an excessive devotion to judicial astrology, was later followed by the Priscillianists. 2 Error: that God is one and the same, called by diverse names in one person and one hypostasis, and that he is given diverse persons: he is called Father when he is thought of, Truth when he is revealed, and Man when he is on this earth. Thus they call God himself man and introduce a confusion of natures. 3 That Christ was put together out of thirty aeons, like a little flower gathered and plucked, like Hesiod's Pandora, whence he is called Alkyton [ἀλκυτὸν], because all the fullness [πᾶν πληρωμα] ... 4 They tear Jesus apart from Christ as two separate persons. Hence the Nestorians.

units.la: CAP. XVI.
units.tr: CHAP. XVI.

units.la: Heracleonitæ unde dicti. Quorum erroris tres hypotheses hic traduntur.
units.tr: The Heracleonites, whence they were named. Three of their errors are set out here.

units.la: Eracleonitæ ab Heracleone{1} discipulo su-periorum. Duo asserunt{2} principia, unum ex altero, & ex his duobus alia plurima. Feruntur autem suos moriẽtes novo modo quasi redimere, id est, per oleum, balsamum, & aquā, & innocationes, quas Hebraicis verbis dicunt super capita eorum. Heracleon, non autem Heraclion (sic enim legendum est) Valentiniani dogmatis defensor fuit, qui differt & secta & tempore à quodam alio haeretico nomine Theo-co, qui Heracleota à patria Heraclea, quae urbs est Thraciae, nominatus est, & Arianam haeresin amplectebatur: itemque ab Hieracla vel Heracla à quo Heraclitae haeretici postea dicti sunt. Hic autem Heracleon ab Epiphanio constituitur Colarbasio & Marco aetate posterior, atque tanquam eorum noxius & nefarius surculus. Contrà vero à Tertulliano, qui superiori illi aetati propinquior erat, scriptum est cum ante Marcum fuisse suumque venenum sparsisse. Quod si Irenaeo credimus, cuius apud me auctoritas in istarum rerum narratione praeponderat, coaevus contemporaneúsque Ptolemaeo haeretico, de quo antea, dicetur fuisse Heracleon. Nam illum aequalem iis temporibus scribit Irenaeus lib.2.cap.4. adeo ut huius haeresios initium constituendum videatur in annum à passo Christo Huius autem magna fuit, ut scribit Clemens libr.4. Stromat. in Valentinianorum schola auctoritas, & facile nomen suum illi imposuit, cuius discipulos ob celebritatem famae ad se traduxerat. Haec haeresis proprio nomine non stetit diuturna: sed novis aliorum succedentium in eadem schola dogmatibus obscurata, & ambitione Marcitarum & Colarbasiorum deleta, in uno tantum capite postea retenta est, quod fuit de ungendis in peccatorum remissionem morientibus Christianis. Id quod adhuc hodie in Papatu fit. Videtur in AEgypto Heracleon vixisse. Nam Hebraica lingua vsus est siue Syria-ca, vt alij haeretici, qui ibidem floruerunt: & in Occidentalibus Ecclesijs vix nota fuit haec pestis & lues, nisi ex solo Graecorum catalogo. Huius meminit Theodoretus libr.1. De fabul.Haereticor.sed breuissime.
units.tr: The Heracleonites took their name from Heracleon, a disciple of the Superiors (the Valentinians). They assert two principles, one derived from the other, and from these two many more. They are said to redeem their dying in a new manner, that is, with oil, balsam and water, and with invocations which they call in Hebrew words over the heads of the dying. Heracleon, not Heraclion (for so the name must be read), was a defender of the doctrine of Valentinus. He differs both in sect and in time from another heretic named Theocus, who was called the Heracleota from his homeland Heraclea, a city of Thrace, and who embraced the Arian heresy. He also differs from Hieracles or Heracla, from whom the heretics later called Heracliteans took their name. Epiphanius places this Heracleon later in time than Colarbasus and Marcus, and as a noxious and wicked offshoot of theirs. Tertullian, who was nearer to that earlier age, however, writes that he came before Marcus and spread his poison. But if we believe Irenaeus, whose authority in the telling of these matters weighs most with me, Heracleon was a contemporary of the heretic Ptolemy, of whom I spoke earlier. For Irenaeus writes that Heracleon was of the same age as those men (Book 2, chapter 4), so that the beginning of this heresy seems to be placed in the year after the passion of Christ. Its authority in the school of the Valentinians was great, as Clement writes (Stromata, Book 4), and it was easy for him to give his own name to it, since he had drawn its disciples to himself by the fame of his reputation. This heresy did not last long under its own name. Overshadowed by the new doctrines of others who succeeded in the same school, and destroyed by the ambition of the Marcites and Colarbasians, it was afterwards retained in one point only, namely the anointing of Christians at death for the remission of sins. This is still done today in the Papacy. Heracleon seems to have lived in Egypt, for he used the Hebrew or Syriac language, as did the other heretics who flourished there. In the Western churches this plague and pest was scarcely known, except from the Greek catalogue alone. Theodoret mentions him in Book 1 of his De fabulis haereticorum, but very briefly.

units.la: 2 Duo afferunt.)Ex malo coruo Valentino malum Heracleon ouum. Primus huius sectae error est, Quod duo rerum omnium principia constituit, e quibus tamen ipsis vnum altero tempore sit prius. Bython igitur dicit esse primum illum & praecipuum Deum, ex quo nata sit Sige, id est, Silentium. Ex Bytho & Sige reliqui omnes Aeones variis coitionibus nati, qui sunt caeterarum rerum creatarum principia. Hoc partim ex Platone & Pythagora sumptum est: partim ex Valentino, & Manichaeorum delirij de duobus principiis semen fuit.
units.tr: They assert two.) From the bad crow Valentinus, Heracleon hatched a bad egg. The first error of this sect is that it posits two principles of all things, of which one is nevertheless prior to the other in time. Bython, therefore, they say is the first and chief God, from whom Sige, that is Silence, was born. From Bython and Sige all the other Aeons were born through various couplings, and these are the principles of the other created things. This was partly taken from Plato and Pythagoras, and partly from Valentinus, and it was the seed of the mad doctrine of the Manichaeans about two principles.

units.la: 2 Octoadem illam Aeonum primariam a Pto-lemaeo excogitatam probauit Heracleon, & eius diuisionem in dextros sinistrosque[?] Aeonas tanquam bonos & malos, siue, vt postea Manichaei locuti sunt, in gentem Lucis & Tenebrarum retinuit & docuit, tam nimirum placuit humanae vanitati ineptissimum illud, si vllum aliud Valentini commentum, de Aeonibus, id est, de Chimaeris.
units.tr: 2 Heracleon approved the primary set of eight Aeons devised by Ptolemy, and he kept and taught its division into right and left Aeons, as good and evil, or, as the Manichaeans later put it, into the race of Light and the race of Darkness. Of course human vanity was pleased by this most absurd invention, more than by any other fiction of Valentinus concerning the Aeons, that is, concerning chimaeras.

units.la: 3 Error.Hominem triplici natura & essentia constare, Corpore, Anima, & quodam tertio. Id quod Didymum Alexandrinum episcopum postea fefellit, qui locum Pauli 1. Thessal. 5. male intellexit, corrupitque.
units.tr: 3 Error.) Man consists of a threefold nature and essence: body, soul, and a certain third thing. This later deceived Didymus, bishop of Alexandria, who misunderstood and corrupted the passage of Paul in 1 Thessalonians 5.

units.la: 4 Duplicem Dei confessionem finxerunt, vt approbarent eos, tanquam nullius sceleris reos, qui periculi mortisque metu veram religionem abnegant. Vnam enim esse quæ vita & fide fit, & sit satis: alteram quæ voce quam homini Christiano necessariam non putant. Clemens lib.4.Stromat. 4 Morientes ut a morte æterna redimantur, unguunt oleo, aqua, & balsamo, impiissime illo Iacobi loco abusi; qui est Iacobi 5.verf. 14, Inde etiam orta est illa unctionis extremæ non tantum superstitiosa, sed etiam blasphema institutio, quæ in Papatu ob-scruatur[?]. Ita quod in ea re habet Romana Ecclesia, ab hæreticis, non autem ab Apostolis accepit, ut alia multa. Quanquam non diffiteor etiam post Apostolorum ætatem, unctionem in baptismo & clinicis ægrotantibus a Patribus adhibitam fuisse. Sed id quam recte & legitime fieret, quæritur; quicquid Sozom.lib. 6.cap.29. scribat, & Manichæi Christianis obiecerunt quod defunctorum umbras ritu & more paganorum vino & dapibus placarent, ut refert Augustinus libro 20.contra Faust. capite 4. Heracleonis[?] autem ratio hæc fuit, quod ita unctí[?] Christiani æreas & invisibiles potestates effu-giant. 5 Denique superstitiosas Deo invocationes peregrinis exoticisque vocabulis faciunt, maxime ad dæmones fugandos & arcendos viles, quod etiam hodie Papistæ retinent. Illa autem vocabula sunt hæc, quæ Epiphanius commemorat lib.1.tom.2. Mesia, Vphara, Matsda, Melchona, Noffom, Idag, Ecpharon, Tscnoua[?], Iesu, Nazareni, id est, ut quidem conijcere potui (sunt enim hæc omnia partim Hebraea, partim Syriaca verba) Vnctus & Radix, Turris; Rex,Spiritus,Sciens,discooperiens,præcipiens, Iesus Nazarenus: quæ quanquam nihil nisi verum de Christo enuntient, quia tamen sine fide & verbo Dei fiunt, merito & magicæ incantationes à patribus appellantur: & non preces, sed ut peccata grauissima esse censentur, & damnari debent.
units.tr: 4 They devised a double confession of God, so that they might approve those who deny the true religion out of fear of danger and death, as men guilty of no crime. For they hold that there is one confession which is made by life and faith and is sufficient, and another made with the voice, which they do not think necessary for a Christian man (Clement, Stromata, Book 4). 4 Dying persons, that they may be redeemed from eternal death, they anoint with oil, water and balsam, most impiously abusing that passage of James, chapter 5, verse 14. From this there also arose that institution of extreme unction, not only superstitious but also blasphemous, which is observed in the Papacy. Thus whatever the Roman Church has in this matter, it received from the heretics and not from the Apostles, as it has much else. Yet I do not deny that even after the age of the Apostles the Fathers used anointing in baptism and for sick people confined to bed. But how rightly and lawfully this was done is a question; whatever Sozomen writes (Book 6, chapter 29), and the Manichaeans objected to the Christians that they appeased the shades of the dead with wine and feasts, in the manner and custom of the pagans, as Augustine reports (Against Faustus, Book 20, chapter 4). The reasoning of Heracleon, however, was this: that Christians so anointed escape the bronze and invisible powers. 5 Finally, they make superstitious invocations of God with foreign and exotic words, chiefly for banishing and warding off demons, which the Papists still retain today. These words are the following, which Epiphanius recalls (Book 1, vol. 2): Mesia, Vphara, Matsda, Melchona, Noffom, Idag, Ecpharon, Tscnoua, Iesu, Nazareni. That is, as far as I could conjecture (for all of these words are partly Hebrew and partly Syriac): Anointed and Root, Tower; King, Spirit, Knowing, uncovering, commanding, Jesus the Nazarene. Although these words express nothing but truth about Christ, because they are nevertheless used without faith and without the Word of God, they are rightly called magical incantations by the Fathers, and they are judged not to be prayers but very grievous sins, and they ought to be condemned.

units.la: CAP. XVII.
units.tr: CAP. XVII.

units.la: Ophitæ unde dicti, & eorum erroris caput duplex hic comprehensum.
units.tr: The Ophites, whence they are named, and the twofold head of their error comprehended here.

units.la: Ophita à colubro nominati{1} sunt. Coluber enim Græce ὄφις dicitur. Hunc autem colubrum, qui decepit Adam & Euam Christum arbitrantur. Sed habent etiam verum colubrum, quem nutriunt, & venerantur, qui & incantante sacerdote egreditur de spelunca, & ascendit super altare innixum spelunca, & oblationes eorum lambit, & inuoluens se circa eas regreditur ad speluncam, & ita confringunt oblationes in Eucharistiam, quasi à serpente Christo sanctificatas. Tradunt huius serpentis cultum à Nicolaitis siue Gnosticis ad ipsos deductum.
units.tr: The Ophites are named from the serpent. For the serpent is called ὄφις in Greek. They think that this serpent, which deceived Adam and Eve, was Christ. But they also keep a real serpent, which they nurse and worship. When the priest chants incantations, it comes out of a cave, climbs up onto an altar, resting against the cave, licks their offerings, and, coiling itself around them, goes back into the cave. And so they break the offerings into the Eucharist, as if they had been sanctified by Christ in the form of a serpent. They relate that the worship of this serpent was brought to them from the Nicolaitans or Gnostics.

units.la: I Nominati.) Varijs nominibus ab eodem fonte deductis hi nominantur, nimirum Ophitæ, Ophei, & Ophiomorphi, vti à Theodoreto lib.1. ne nos nominum diuersitas fallat, & diuersos esse existimemus, qui sunt ijdem. Hos cum Sethianis quidam coniungunt: alij cum Nicolaitis, vti Tertullianus. Ante Valentinia-nos collocat Isidorus, sed Augustinus Epipha-nium secutus est,qui Heracleonitis subiicit.Irenaeus libro i. cap. 34. demum post Gnosticos & Valentinianos exortos esse scribit, a quibus tan quam è coenoso fonte impurissimus riuus fluxerunt. Ergo circa annum a Domino passo 132. a nobis constituentur longe post Nicolaitarum hærefin,a qua tamen,vt scribit Epiphanius,dogmatis & erroris occasionem acceperunt. Maxime in AEgypto,vt aliæ multæ,viguit,ex cuius regionis & gentis idololatria & moribus initiu videtur sumpsisse. AEgyptij enim Ibes,Croco-dilos,& huiusmodi ferarum genera pro diis habuerunt, atque etiam tunc colebant,vt docent M.Tull.Cicero,Plutarchus,Iuuenalis Satyr.14. & alij:quorum exemplum hi secuti Draconem serpentémque venerati sunt alio quidem,quàm AEgyptij,prætextu,sed tamen serpentem,id est, immanem & homini funestissimam beluam. Sæpe vero Satan magnas præstigias fecit hominibus non tantum fidelibus, sed etiam infidelibus per serpentem, quod in Adamo primo parente nostro manifestissimum est. & de ea re scribit author prophanus in Pseudoalexandro. Durauit autem vsque ad tempora Iustiniani primi Constantinopolitani imperatoris hęc hęrefis,& postea quoque,quàquam est fœdissima.De iis enim meminit l.xj.C.de Episcop.audientia.& l.Arrii ni.C.de Hæretic.
units.tr: I Named. These men are called by various names derived from the same source: namely Ophites, Opheans, and Ophiomorphites, as Theodoret says in book 1. Lest the variety of names deceive us into thinking they are different groups when they are the same. Some join them with the Sethians, others with the Nicolaitans, as Tertullian does. Isidore places them before the Valentinians, but Augustine, following Epiphanius, places them after the Heracleonites. Irenaeus, in book 1, chapter 34, writes that they arose only after the Gnostics and Valentinians, from whom the most impure stream flowed, as if from a muddy spring. So they arose around the year 132 after the Lord's passion, long after the heresy of the Nicolaitans, from which, however, as Epiphanius writes, they took the occasion for their doctrine and error. It flourished especially in Egypt, as did many other sects, and seems to have derived its beginnings from the idolatry and customs of that land and people. For the Egyptians regarded ibises, crocodiles, and kinds of such beasts as gods, and worshipped them even then, as Marcus Tullius Cicero, Plutarch, Juvenal (Satire 14), and others teach. The Ophites followed their example in venerating the dragon and the serpent, though under a different pretext from the Egyptians, yet still a serpent, that is, a monstrous beast most deadly to man. Satan has often worked great deceptions on men, not only on believers but also on unbelievers, through the serpent, which is most evident in Adam, our first parent. A profane author also writes about this matter in the Pseudo-Alexander. This heresy lasted until the times of Justinian the First, emperor of Constantinople, and afterwards too, though it is most foul. Indeed, the law at C. de Episcopali audientia 11 mentions these people, and the law of Arius at C. de Haereticis.

units.la: Hunc autem colubrum)Multiplex fuit huius hæreticorum familiæ error, & tam late fœdeque sparsus, vt Tertullianus hanc erroris scenam appellauerit. Duo illius capita recefet hoc loco Augustin. alij autem & alia & plura.
units.tr: Hunc autem colubrum (But this serpent). The error of this family of heretics was manifold, and spread so widely and foully that Tertullian called this stage of their error a scene. Augustine here touches on two heads of it, but others and many more exist.

units.la: 1 Colunt & adorant serpentem, per quem Eua primum decepta est, tanquam is fuerit Christus. Sapientiæ enim datorem siue in homine autorem fuisse contendunt. Itaque diuinam illi non tantum vim & potentiam tribuunt: sed etiam naturam & essentiam. Dicunt enim eum natum esse ex summo Deo qui Ialdaboth vocatur,& materia quadam. Itaque ὀφιόμορφον potius quàm ὄφιν id appellant, quod venerantur. Magnam autem esse vim huius formæ ex eo docet, quod & intestina nostra in aluo in spiras serpentum more conuoluta habeamus: & Moses serpentem exaltauit in deserto, cuius aspectu isti ab aliis serpentibus sanarentur, Ioann.3. & Numer.21. Vnde Christum ipsum serpentis forma subiisse in vterum Mariæ volunt, quæ omnia magnos errores continent. Incantationibus autem serpentem aliquam Domini Cœnam celebraturi euocant, quam Augustinus in spelunca esse scribit. Irenæus & Epiphanius in cista gestari & ab illis circumferri narrant, quibus potius credo. Ex quo apparet Ophitas turpissimam πολυ-θείαν [?] nempe Dei & Serpentis inducere.
units.tr: 1 They worship and adore the serpent by which Eve was first deceived, as if it were Christ. For they maintain that he was the giver of wisdom, or the author of wisdom in man. Therefore they attribute to him not only divine power and might but also divine nature and essence. For they say that he was born of the highest God, who is called Ialdabaoth, and of a certain matter. Hence they call the thing they worship ophiomorphon [ὀφιόμορφον], rather than ophin [ὄφιν]. Moreover, they teach that this form has great power, because we have our intestines coiled in the belly in the manner of serpents' coils; and because Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert, by whose sight the people were healed from the other serpents (John 3 and Numbers 21). Hence they hold that Christ himself took on the form of a serpent in the womb of Mary. All these things contain great errors. By incantations they summon a serpent to celebrate the Lord's Supper, which Augustine writes was in a cave. Irenaeus and Epiphanius relate that it was carried in a chest and paraded about by them; I rather believe these. From this it is evident that the Ophites introduce a most shameful polytheism [πολυθείαν], namely of God and the Serpent.

units.la: 2 Error. Panem Cœnæ Domini & Eucharistiæ non prius sanctificatum esse putant quàm serpens ille euocatus lambat & attingat eum siue degustet. Itaque hoc iis euenit, quod damnat Paulus 1.Corinth.10.verf.21. vt mensæ Domini & mensæ Dæmoniorum fieri velint participes.
units.tr: 2 Error. They think the bread of the Lord's Supper and the Eucharist is not sanctified until that serpent, once summoned, licks it, touches it, or tastes it. So it happens to them what Paul condemns in 1 Corinthians 10:21, that they wish to become partakers of the table of the Lord and the table of demons.

units.la: 3 Christum verè hominem factum esse negat, id quod illis cum superioribus hæreticis commune est.
units.tr: 3 They deny that Christ was truly made man, which they hold in common with the earlier heretics.

units.la: 4 Carnis etiam resurrectionem irridént, vt scribit Tertullianus.
units.tr: 4 They also mock the resurrection of the flesh, as Tertullian writes.

units.la: CAP. XVIII.
units.tr: CAP. XVIII.

units.la: Caini unde dicti, erroris autem eorum capita tria.
units.tr: Why the Cainites are so called, and the three heads of their error.

units.la: C[?]Aini propterea sic appellati, quoniam Cain honorant, dicentes eum fortissima esse virtutis: simul & Iudam traditorem, diuinum aliquid putant esse, & scelus eius beneficium deputant, afferentes eum præscisse, quantum esset generi humano Christi passio profu-tura, & occidendum Iudais propterea tradidisse. Illos etiam, qui schisma facientes in primo populo Dei, terra dehiscente perierunt, Core, Dathan, & Abiron, & Sodomitas colere perhibentur. Blasphemant Legem, & Deum Legis authorem: Carnisque resurrectionem negant.
units.tr: The Cainites are so called because they honour Cain, saying that he was endowed with the greatest courage. At the same time they hold that Judas the traitor was something divine, and they count his crime a benefit, claiming that he foresaw how much the passion of Christ would profit the human race, and that for this reason he handed Christ over to be killed by the Jews. They are also said to honour Korah, Dathan and Abiram, who caused a schism among the first people of God and perished when the earth opened, and the Sodomites. They blaspheme the Law and the God who gave the Law, and they deny the resurrection of the flesh.

units.la: 1 Sic appellati,) De voce ipsa, qua hæc hæ-resis nominatur, dubia est analogia. Alij enim Cainos vocant, vt Theodoretus lib .i. alij Cai-nianos: alij Cainæos, vt Tertullianus: alij Caia-nos, vti Epiphanius his verbis, Καϊανοί τινες ὀνομαζόμενοι[?], ἀπὸ τῆς Καϊν [illegible, ~10 letters] τῆς αἱρέσεως, & Epiphanium sequi gaudens Augustinus, quę nominis formatio & nomenclatura minimę omnium mihi probatur. Et facile ex voce Καϊνιανοί vel Καϊνοί in Καιανοί lapsus & error in Epiphanio primum à scribis & librarijs admissus est, qui postea ab Augustino retentus fuit, A voce autem Cain nullæ Grammaticorum regulæ ferunt vt Caianos deriuemus & dicamus, sed potius Cainos, vel Cainianos. Et hæc quidē de huius hæreseos appellatione, quam hic in Augustino correximus, nevulgarem descriptionem à nobis mutatam esse vel miretur vel improbet quisquam. Alij enim sunt ab istis & di-uersi Caiani hæretici, qui idem, vt scribit Ioan-nes Damascenus Aphtartodocitæ dicti sunt, nostris posteriores, & à Caiano Alexandrino, & Iuliano Halicarnasseo profecti, de quibus vide in Proclianitis. Dicti sunt autem Caini non ab authore sectæ, sed ab argumento erroris, quem sunt sequuti, quia Cainum illum, de quo est Genes.4. tanquam primum & principem bonorum omnium, quæ homines sentiunt, authorem co-lunt, & postea alios, in quos Dei iudicia tanquam in reprobos homines aperte in Sacra scriptura legimus, qualis est Esau. Malach.1.Hebr.12.vers. 16. quales Core, Dathan, & Abiron, Numer.16. versu 26, qualis denique impius ille Iudas Iscariotes, quem Caini vti salutis humanæ dispen-satorem colunt, de quo tamen aperte pronun-tiat ipsa veritas, Væ illi homini, per quem Filius hominis proditur. Bonum erat homini illi, si natus non fuisset, Matth.29.vers.24. ita miseri isti homines spiritu vertiginis abrepti, & in reprobam mentem traditi, se Deo bonisque & sanctis omnibus contrarios & repugnantes im-pudenter profitentur. Ortam autem & propa-gatam esse hanc hærefin tanquam infelicem sur-culum & stolonem ex infausta Nicolaitarum stir-pe scribit Tertul.Epiph.ex Gnosticis & Carpo crate. Iren. autem lib.i.c.35. ex Satanica Valentinianorum schola,cui magis tanquam diligentissimo earum rerum perfcrutatori & scriptori aflentior. Itaque eodem pene tempore enatam fuisse puto, quo superior Christianæ doctrinæ labes, nempe Ophitarum hæresis. Durarunt ad tempus aliquod, & sese doctorum suorum fama & celebritate fuftentarunt, quorum scripta ad Epiphanij vsque ætatem peruenerunt, quemadmodum ipse refert, inter quæ fuit liber ab iis dictus Ἀναβατικὸν[?] Παύλου. Illic mendaciffime exponere fe fingunt, quæ Paulus in tertium cœlum raptus viderit, ex quibus suarum nugarum & præftigiarū fundamenta quærunt. At illa nec à Paulo, qui vidit, enarrata sunt, & dicit ipse,nefas esse homini illa loqui & efferre, 2.Corinth.12. versu 4. In plures autem sectas hæc postea diuulsa est & diducta, e quibus alij Antitactæ Ἀντιτακτικοί[?] i. Deo ipsi repugnantes dicti sunt, quia quanto maximo possunt animi conatu Dei præceptis aduersantur, veluti quia dixit Deus, Non mœchaberis, Non furaberis: ipsi contrà quantum possunt & mœchantur, & furantur,vt sic,quemadmodum aiunt,fe aduersus illum Deum,qui zizania & mala in mudum immisit, vleifcantur. Ita peruerso plane animi iudicio, & nullo conscientiæ sensu præcipites in omne mali genus non modo feruntur, sed sponte prudentesque ruunt. Atque hæc Antitactarum discipulorum caterua Cainorum præceptorum furores mire auxit, de quibus: Antitactis & Theodoretus libro i. & Clemens lib.3. Strom. agit. Alij ab iisdem Cainis prosesti dicti sunt Peratæ à Peratico Euphratensi,& Ademe Carystio, qui præter Cainorum errores dixerunt Christum fuisse Tricorporem, propter tres diuersas mundi partes,quibus constat, ut aiunt,Christi corpus: & duplicem esse mundum,unum ingenitum:alterum genitum,quem vocant specialem, & huiusmodi quasdam ineptissimas fabulas fingunt, & rerum ortum ex Agennefia,quam vocant,de quibus vide Theodoretum lib.i. Hæreticar.fabular. Alij aliis nominibus, ut Monoimi, qui à Monoimo Arabe ita sunt appellati, videntur ex eodem cœno errores suos, quos Arithmeticorum numeris confirmare conantur,hausisse.Ex quo fit mihi verisimile, ut etiā scribit Epiphanius in hæresi Sethianorum, primum in Ægypto ortum esse hoc malum, & in vicinas gentes deinde effusum, adeo ut in Orietem ipsum penetrarit, sed tamen Asiam potius quàm Europam corruperit. Interpolata autem nouis sectatorum nominibus, Cainorum hæresis proprium nomë amisit. His contrarij sunt Abelitæ, vel Abeloitæ , de quibus infrá.
units.tr: 1 So called.) The name by which this heresy is called is an uncertain formation. Some call them Cainites, as Theodoret does in book 1; others Cainianites; others Cainaeans, as Tertullian does; others Caianites, as Epiphanius does in these words, "Some who are called Kaianoi, from Kain ... of the heresy" [Καϊανοί τινες ὀνομαζόμενοι, ἀπὸ τῆς Καϊν ... τῆς αἱρέσεως]. Augustine, who gladly follows Epiphanius, uses this form, but of all the forms of the name it is the one I least approve. A slip from Kaïnianoi or Kaïnoi into Kaianoi was easily made, and the error was first admitted into Epiphanius by scribes and copyists and was later retained by Augustine. But from the word Cain no rule of grammar leads us to derive Caianites; we should rather say Cainites or Cainianites. Let no one be surprised or object that I have changed the ordinary spelling of this heresy's name, which I have corrected here in Augustine. There are other Caianites, who are different from these heretics, and who, as John of Damascus writes, were also called Aphthartodocetae. They are later than our heretics and came from Caianus of Alexandria and Julian of Halicarnassus; on them see under the Proclianites. The Cainites were named not after the founder of the sect but after the subject of the error they followed, because they worship that Cain of whom we read in Genesis 4 as the first and chief author of all the good things men think, and afterwards others in whom we read in Holy Scripture that God's judgements were openly executed on reprobate men, such as Esau (Malachi 1; Hebrews 12:16), and Korah, Dathan and Abiram (Numbers 16:26). Lastly they worship that impious Judas Iscariot as a dispenser of human salvation, although the truth itself pronounces plainly on him: "Woe to that man by whom the Son of man is betrayed; it would have been good for that man if he had not been born" (Matthew 26:24). These wretched men, carried off by a spirit of giddiness and given over to a reprobate mind, shamelessly profess themselves opposed and hostile to God and to all that is good and holy. Tertullian writes that this heresy arose and spread as an unhappy shoot and offshoot from the ill-omened stock of the Nicolaitans; Epiphanius derives it from the Gnostics and Carpocrates; Irenaeus, in book 1 chapter 35, derives it from the satanic school of the Valentinians, and I incline more to him, as the most diligent investigator and writer of these matters. I therefore think it arose at about the same time as the earlier blemish on Christian doctrine, namely the heresy of the Ophites. They lasted for some time and maintained themselves by the fame and reputation of their teachers, whose writings survived down to Epiphanius' own time, as he himself reports. Among these was a book which they called the Ascent of Paul [Ἀναβατικὸν Παύλου]. In it they pretend to describe most falsely what Paul saw when he was caught up into the third heaven, and from this they seek the foundations of their trifles and deceits. But those things were never recounted by Paul, who saw them, and he himself says that it is not lawful for a man to utter or relate them (2 Corinthians 12:4). Later this sect was split and divided into several sects, of which some were called Antitactae [Ἀντιτακτικοί], that is, opposed to God himself, because with the utmost effort of their minds they set themselves against the precepts of God. For instance, God said, "You shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal." They on the contrary commit adultery and steal as far as they can, so that, as they say, they may take revenge on that God who sowed tares and evils in the world. Thus, with a plainly perverse judgement and no sense of conscience, they are not only carried headlong into every kind of evil but rush into it willingly and knowingly. This band of Antitactae disciples greatly increased the frenzies of the precepts of Cain, of whom Theodoret in book 1 and Clement in book 3 of the Stromata treat in discussing the Antitactae. Others, called Perates after Peratices of Euphrates and Ademus of Carystus, also derived from the Cainites, besides the errors of the Cainites said that Christ was threefold in body, because of the three different parts of the world of which, they say, the body of Christ consists; and that there are two worlds, one unbegotten and one begotten, which they call special. They invent other most absurd fables of this kind and derive the origin of things from what they call Agennesia; on these see Theodoret, book 1 of the Fabulae haereticorum. Others, under other names, such as the Monoimi, who were so called from Monoimus the Arab, seem to have drawn their errors, which they try to confirm with the numbers of the arithmeticians, from the same mire. Hence it is probable to me, as Epiphanius also writes under the heresy of the Sethians, that this evil first arose in Egypt and then spread into the neighbouring nations, so far that it even penetrated to the East, though it corrupted Asia rather than Europe. The heresy of the Cainites, however, having been overlaid with the new names of its followers, lost its own name. The Abelites, or Abeloites, of whom below, are opposed to these.

units.la: I Dicentes enim.)
