Siqua unquam hominum phrenesis pietatis studium labefactauit & restinxit, maxime Cainorum delirium id potuit & effecit,quando in eo toti fuerunt Satanæ spiritu plane impulsi, ut omnes eos damnaret qui à Scriptura honestum testimonium habent: eos autem probarent, qui ab illa reiiciuntur & damnantur. Itaque ex eorum sunt numero, quos Spiritus sanctus tanquam Deo obnitentes & prorsus resistentes execratur, Psal.61. versu 4. Tres autem eorum hypotheses commemorat hoc loco Augustinus, fuerunt tamen plures. Prima est blasphemia, Quod Cain & omnes reprobos laudant, colunt, & admirantur, veluti Esau, Core, Abiron, Sodomitas, & Iudam ipsum Domini nostri Iesu Christi proditorem, quasi fuerint salutis humanae autores. Cain, inquit Tertullianus, magnificant, quasi ex quadam potenti virtute conceptum. Nam Abel ex inferiori virtute procreatum volunt. Iudam proditorori defendunt, admirabilem illum & magnu messe [?] dicentes propter utilitates, quas humano generi contulisse iactatur. Animadvertens enim, inquiunt, Iudas, quia potestates mundi nolebant Christum pati, ut salus humano generi per illius mortem pararetur, saluti consulens generis hominum, Christum tradidit, id quod perspicue cum illo Act. Apostolicorum loco pugnat, qui est cap.4.verf.28. Unde periculosa est illa Gregorii Magni sententia, qui de peccato Adami loquens sic ait, O felix culpa, quae talem ac tantum meruit habere redemptorem. Cerinthiani antea Iudam adorauerant, & post hos Marcionitae, ut scribit Irenaeus libro 1. cap.29. Ex hac sententia doctrina de electione & praedestinatione non modo labefactari, sed etiam irrideri coepit, & impietati atque improbitati summa laus tribui. Videtur autem hic error ortus ex doctrina de Providentia Dei perperam intellecta, quod non distinguebatur apte in uno & eodem facto Dei & hominis opus. 2 Error. Legem a Mose traditam damnant, & Deum illius authorem velut zizaniorum in mundo seminatorem oderunt & detestantur, tanquam Rhodij solem. Quod Marcionitis postea ansam erroris & incessendi Dei veteris Testamenti audaciam praebuit. 3 Carnis resurrectione fore negant. 4 Mundi creatorem vocant ὕλην[?], id est, Vuluam, quem & ignotum deum esse dicunt, & inuidum Caino, Esau, & Iudae. Itaque pro blasphemia in eum spuunt. 5 Angelos & eos quidem malos invocant & colunt, vt ait Epiphanius, quibus singulas singulis tribuunt suas libidines, & scelera, tanquam eorum authoribus, & quibus, quum illa perpetrant, se placere & gratificari docent, vt narrat Theodoretus. 6 Denique contendunt nos non voluntate & sponte nostra, sed natura malos vel bonos esse, quae fuit vetus superiorum haereticorum corniculatio & insania.
units.tr: I Saying.) If ever any human madness has weakened and extinguished zeal for godliness, the madness of the Cainites was surely able to do so, since they were wholly given over to it, driven entirely by the spirit of Satan, so that they condemn all whom Scripture gives an honourable testimony and approve those whom Scripture rejects and condemns. They are therefore among those whom the Holy Spirit execrates as resisting God and wholly opposed to him (Psalm 61:4). Augustine mentions three of their theses in this place, but there were more. The first is blasphemy: they praise, worship and admire Cain and all the reprobate, such as Esau, Korah, Abiram, the Sodomites, and Judas himself, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ, as if they had been authors of human salvation. Tertullian says, "They magnify Cain as if he were conceived from some powerful virtue; for they hold that Abel was produced from an inferior virtue. They defend Judas the traitor, calling him admirable and great, on account of the benefits he is boasted to have brought to the human race. For, they say, Judas, seeing that the powers of the world did not want Christ to suffer, and that salvation for the human race would be prepared by his death, handed Christ over, consulting for the salvation of mankind." This plainly contradicts the passage of the Acts of the Apostles, chapter 4, verse 28. Hence the saying of Gregory the Great is dangerous, who, speaking of the sin of Adam, says, "O happy fault, which deserved to have so great a Redeemer!" The Cerinthians had previously worshipped Judas, and after them the Marcionites, as Irenaeus writes in book 1, chapter 29. From this opinion the doctrine of election and predestination began not only to be weakened but even to be mocked, and the highest praise was given to impiety and wickedness. This error seems to have arisen from a perversely understood doctrine of the providence of God, because a work of God and a work of man were not properly distinguished in one and the same deed. 2 Error. They condemn the Law given through Moses, and they hate and detest God as its author, as a sower of tares in the world, like the Rhodians with the sun. This later gave the Marcionites an occasion of error and the audacity to attack the God of the Old Testament. 3 They deny the resurrection of the flesh. 4 They call the Creator of the world hyle [ὕλην], that is, the womb, whom they also say is an unknown God, and envious of Cain, Esau and Judas. Therefore they spit at him in blasphemy. 5 They invoke and worship angels, and indeed evil ones, as Epiphanius says; to each of them they assign their own lusts and crimes, as though they were their authors, and they teach that when they commit these they please and gratify them, as Theodoret relates. 6 Finally they maintain that we are evil or good not by our own will and choice but by nature. This was the old folly and madness of the earlier heretics.

units.la: CAP. XIX. Sethiani unde dicti, quorum erroris tria capita recensentur.
units.tr: CAP. XIX. The Sethians, whence they are named, and three heads of their error are set out.

units.la: Ethiani nomen{1} acceperunt a filio Adae, qui vocatus est Seth. Eum{2} quippe honorant, sed fabulosa & haeretica vanitate. Dicunt enim eum de superna matre natum, quam perhibent convenisse cum superno patre. Unde diuinum semen aliud nasceretur, tanquam filiorum Dei. Hi quoque multa de principatibus & potestatibus vanissima fabulantur. Quidam eos dicunt Sem filium Noe Christum putare.
units.tr: The Sethians took their name from the son of Adam who was called Seth. They honour him, indeed, but with a fabulous and heretical vanity. For they say that he was born of a heavenly mother, whom they claim had come together with the heavenly father, so that another divine seed should be born, as children of God. They also tell many very vain tales about principalities and powers. Some say that they think Shem, the son of Noah, is Christ.

units.la: 1 Nomen acceperunt.) Et hic quoque ab aliis authoribus dissentit Tertullianus: quos enim omnes alij Sethianos vocant, ille Sethoitas appellat, nisi fortasse in impressis sit error, quod mihi videtur verisimilius, & pro Sethoitæ apud Tertullianum, Sethitæ legendum esse maximus. Atque hi cum Ophitis, de quibus antea, coniunguntur à Theodoreto lib. 1. quasi eiusdem dogmatis fuerint, quos tamen diversa ab illis sensisse fatis ex hypothesibus apparebit. Ante Carpocratem constituit Tertullianus. Isidorus autem post Archonticos & Adamianos, adeo ut tota de horum origine & tempore disputatio & definitio incerta sit. Dicam igitur quod sentio. Mihi videntur Sethiani eodem quo Caini & Abeliani tempore exorti, quum ex eodem erroris fonte scaturierint. Fuerunt enim hi omnes infelicissimæ Valentinianorum stirpis & radicis surculi, qui quanuis dissimiles, pari tamen ratione impulsi à veritate deflexerunt. Quum enim quærerent causam salutis hominum, nec eam in Euangelio, sed ex ingenij sui commento invenstigaret, aliis Cain placuit, aliis Abel, aliis Seth. Quæ tanta opinionum varietas inter eos accidit, quod alij aliorum sententiæ, in qua tam multa absurda dici videbat, non poterant assentiri. Itaque unius hæresis exortus & improbatio, alterius inducendæ & excogitandæ causa fuit, ut non loge diverso tempore omnes hæ natæ videantur. Viguit autem hæc secta in Ægypto maximè, quæ tamen non diuturna perstitit, sed concidit statim. Scribit enim Epiphanius sua iam ætate nulla illius vestigia vsquam extitisse. Itaque non late vagata est, ut ex supe-rioribus haeresibus multae, sed pene in ipsis cu-nis extincta conticuit & periit.
units.tr: 1 They took their name.) Here too Tertullian differs from other authors. Those whom all others call Sethians, he calls Sethoites, unless perhaps the printed text has an error, which seems more likely to me, and the maximal reading should be Sethites for Tertullian's Sethoites. These are joined by Theodoret in book 1 with the Ophites, discussed above, as though they held the same doctrine; yet it will appear from their hypotheses that they thought differently from those. Tertullian places them before Carpocrates. Isidore, however, places them after the Archontics and the Adamians, so that the whole discussion and determination of their origin and date remains uncertain. I shall therefore say what I think. It seems to me that the Sethians arose at the same time as the Cainites and Abelites, since they all sprang from the same source of error. For all of these were shoots of the most unhappy stock and root of the Valentinians, who, although unlike one another, were yet driven from the truth by the same reasoning. For when they sought the cause of human salvation, and did not look for it in the Gospel but in the invention of their own wit, some preferred Cain, some Abel, and some Seth. This great variety of opinions arose among them because each could not assent to the opinions of the others, in which so many absurdities seemed to be asserted. Thus the emergence and rejection of one heresy was the occasion for introducing and devising another, so that all of these appear to have arisen at not very different times. This sect flourished chiefly in Egypt, yet it did not last long but collapsed at once. For Epiphanius writes that in his own time no trace of it anywhere remained. So it did not spread widely, as many of the earlier heresies did, but was nearly extinguished and perished in its very cradle.

units.la: 2 Eum quippe.) Quum Valentinianorum sententia de causa salutis generis humani quidā nō probarent, tentata est ab eorum discipulis, qui postea sequuti sunt, illius opinionis emendatio & correctio quaedam. Iam enim Aeones velut vetus quaedam fabula, obsoleuerant, & illa incepta & intricata natiuitas diuina Christi a Valentino conficta, explosa fuerat: errores tamen de Mediatore nostro apud Deum, de causa vitiositatis hominum, & peccati originalis fonte manserant, quos auxerunt homines, dum falsas sententias & explicationes extra Dei verbum quaerunt. Hæ vero sunt præcipuæ Sethianorum erroris hypotheses. 1 Seth natum esse volunt ex superiore quadam virtute, quam appellant Matrem, quæ cum summo omnium Deo & Patre coiens Sethum tanquam electorum omnium, & bonorum virorum parentem procreavit, non e terra, ut primi Valentiniani docebāt, quemadmodum Irenæus scribit lib.i.cap.15. sed ex Dei ipsius substantia, & ad veram illius imaginem. Creatum autem esse Sethum, propterea quod Abel qui futurus erat stirps bonorum hominum, invidia & suggestione Angelorum quorundam a Caino interemptus fuerat. In di-luuio vero (quod etiam ulciscendæ Abelis ne-cis gratia ab illa matre & summa virtute inductum esse contendunt) astu eorum angelorum, qui Cainum crearant, immissum fuisse aliquod semen Caini in arcam Noe: & inde tot homines improbos postea fatos dicunt. Scthi autem vxorem appellant Ἀ'ζ[?]ἰαν, ex qua bonos omnes ille scuerit, quam potius Ἀ'ζοῦζαν[?] nominatam scribit Epiphanius. 2 Error, Christum,qui è virgine Maria natus est, non alium fuisse quàm Sethum. 3 Carnis resurrectionem negant, quod dogma impijsimum omnibus Valentinianis commune fuit ex Simonianorum schola sumptum. 4 Angelos cum mulieribus coiisse ad homines gignendos,& primùm duos homines ex ijs natos,vnū è terra:alterum è femine cœlesti,qui masculofœminina esset, & velut Androgynus, & ad Dei imaginem solus formatus. Deus autem, vt aiunt, duplicem illam naturam simul coniunctam in se habet, maris scilicet & fœminæ. Hoc caput ex falsa cap.6. Genef.inter pretatione natum est, cuius vestigia etiā in scriptis veterum, adeoque Lactantij institutionibus adhuc manet, & in libris Rabbinorum,qui putant Adamum ita creatum à Deo,vt mas fœminæ in eodem indiuiduo & [illegible, ~5 letters] sibi latere adhærerent.
units.tr: 2 For indeed.) Since some did not approve of the Valentinian opinion about the cause of the salvation of the human race, an emendation and certain correction of that opinion was attempted by their disciples who followed later. For the Aeons had by now grown obsolete like an old fable, and that intricate and tangled divine birth of Christ, invented by Valentinus, had been rejected. Yet errors about our Mediator before God, about the cause of human corruption, and about the source of original sin had remained, and men increased them while they sought false opinions and explanations outside the Word of God. These are the principal hypotheses of the Sethian error. (1) They maintain that Seth was born of a certain higher power, which they call the Mother, who, coming together with the supreme God and Father, produced Seth as the parent of all the elect and good men. He was not produced from the earth, as the first Valentinians taught, as Irenaeus writes in book 1, chapter 15, but from the very substance of God and in his true image. Seth was created, they say, because Abel, who was to be the stock of good men, had been slain by Cain at the envy and suggestion of certain angels. In the flood (which they also claim was brought about by that Mother and the supreme power, to avenge the death of Abel) some seed of Cain was secretly placed in Noah's ark through the cunning of those angels who had created Cain; and from this, they say, so many wicked men afterwards came. The Sethians call the wife [Azoia, Ἀζωΐα] from whom that man begot all the good; Epiphanius writes that she was rather named [Azouza, Ἀζοῦζα]. (2) The error that Christ, who was born of the Virgin Mary, was none other than Seth. (3) They deny the resurrection of the flesh, a most impious doctrine common to all the Valentinians, taken from the school of the Simonians. (4) That angels had intercourse with women to beget men, and that first two men were born of them, one from the earth and the other from a heavenly seed, who was male and female, and, as it were, an androgyne, formed alone in the image of God. God, they say, has within himself that double nature joined together, namely of male and female. This head arose from a false interpretation of Gen. 6, and traces of it remain even in the writings of the ancients, and indeed in the Institutes of Lactantius, and in the books of the rabbis, who think that Adam was so created by God that male and female adhered to each other in one individual [illegible, ~5 letters].

units.la: CAP. XX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XX.

units.la: Archontici cur dicti. Erroris autem eorum caput hic triplex.
units.tr: Why the Archontici are so called. Their error here is threefold.

units.la: Archontici à principibus appellati, Vniuer-sitatem, quàm Deus condidit, operae[?]esse principum dicunt. Operantur etiam quandam turpitudinem. Resurrectionem carnis negant.
units.tr: The Archontici, named after the rulers, say that the universe which God created is the work of rulers. They also practise a certain filthiness. They deny the resurrection of the flesh.

units.la: A principibus appellati.)Non videtur hoc loco temporis obseruata ratio. Nam si Epiphanio credimus, coeperat iam Constantius Constantini magni filius imperare Constantinopoli, quum coepit hæc hæresis. Primus autem Constantij imperatoris annus incidit in annū a passo Christo 308. Hic tamē Archontici ante Marcionitas (qui iam extremo Antonini Pij imperatoris tempore coeperant esse) collocantur, id est, ante annum a Christo passo 128. vt quantum inter vtrosque temporis interuallum intercedat, facile colligi possit. Ratio vero huius ordinis, quem etiam Epiphanius ipse seruat, videtur esse, quòd Archontici vltimi Valentinianorum fuerint, quorum sectam, & successiones quum Epiphanius continua serie persequeretur, hos cum superioribus, quanquam tempore distent inter se, coniunxit propter dogmatum similitudinem, & scholæ successionem. Fuit enim hæc hæresis vltima Valentinianorum fæx, & postremus partus. Ex quo apparet Valentinianos, si tempus ortus & interitus eorum spectemus, pene per annos ducentos in Ecclesiam Dei grassatos esse. Sed iis cessantibus, alij non minus crudeles & damnosi suborti sunt. Dicuntur autem hi Archontici, ὑπὸ τῶν ἀρχόντων[?], vel ἀρχῶν[?].i. Potestatibus, quas statuebant velut se-cundarios quosdam deos, & Angelorum etiam ipsorum patres. Isidorus appellat Archontia-cos, nescio quàm recte, quemadmodum nec illud ab eodem satis accurate scriptum est, cos Ἀρχοντας[?], quos colebant Archontici, & a quibus mundum conditum affirmabant, esse Archage-los los. Imò verò longè ipsis Archangelis superiores & diuiniores faciunt isti suos Ἀ[?]ρχόντας, quos etiam volùt esse ipsorum & Angelorum & Archangelorum patres ex matre Photenia. Quanquam tamen non diffiteor vanas illas de Angelis & variis eorū ordinibus speculationes, quæ inter scholasticos locum habent, ab istis initiis, & nugis & hæreticorū cœnosis erroribus hauflas fuisse. Cœpit igitur hæc pestis tetrum suum odorem spargere sub Constantio, vt ait Epiphanius, Constantini magni filio, cuius autor fuit Petrus quidam Anachoreta & monachus Palæstinus, qui in pago Carbaricha tribus milliaribus ab urbe Hebron remoto agebat, & magnā pietatis & sanctitatis inter homines opinionem sibi vindicarat. Sed in illa solitudine, vanis istis & perniciosis de Angelorum, & cœlestium potestatum natura & operibus, disputationibus se dedidit, turgens carnis suæ sensu, & in ea quæ non viderat, se ingerens, tam boni nimirum & felices ex isto solitario & melancholico vitæ genere fructus apparent. Hunc suum errorem sparsit idem postea latius per quendam Armenium monachum nomine Eutactum, qui in patriam Sethalem rediens hoc lethale virus per totam vicinam regionem effudit. Itaque quemadmodum scribit Epiph. Armenia minor primum, deinde autem maior etiam Armenia hoc veneno imbuta est vnà cum Palæstina. Nec illud cuomere tam cito hæ prouinciæ postea potuerunt. Itaque propagatum est hoc malum, & duravit aliquandiu in illis locis, in quibus etiam in plures sectas se diffecuit & diuisit. Ex Archōticis enim orti sunt hi haeretici, quos Ascodru-ptas vel Ascothryptas (utroque enim nomine dici possunt. Hierony. etiam in Prologo lib.2. ad Galat. Ascodrobos corrupte vocauit.) Graece Ἀσκοδρύπται vel Ἀσκοθρύπται [?] vocât: propterea quod omnia vasa Sacramentis administrandis destinata frangerent & furiose comminuerent. Hi enim uti & Archontici Sacramentorum usum in Ecclesia mire detestabantur, & damnabant, de quibus Ascodruptis agit Theodoretus lib.1. De Archonticis autem pauci scribunt. Nam eos & Tertullianus & Irenaeus nosse non potuit, quorum seculo isti haeretici nondum nati erant. Variae tamen & horrendae fuerunt Archonticorum hypotheses.
units.tr: Named after the rulers. The order of time observed here does not seem right. For if we believe Epiphanius, Constantius, the son of Constantine the Great, had already begun to reign at Constantinople when this heresy began. The first year of the emperor Constantius, however, fell in the year 308 after the passion of Christ. Yet here the Archontici are placed before the Marcionites (who had already arisen at the very end of the reign of the emperor Antoninus Pius), that is, before the year 128 after the passion of Christ, so that the interval of time between the two can easily be worked out. The reason for this order, which Epiphanius himself also keeps, seems to be that the Archontici were the last of the Valentinians. Epiphanius, pursuing the sect and its successions in an unbroken series, joined them to the earlier groups, although they were separated from them in time, on account of the similarity of their doctrines and their succession within one school. For this heresy was the last dregs and the final offspring of the Valentinians. From this it is clear that the Valentinians, if we consider the time of their rise and their ruin, raged in the Church of God for nearly two hundred years. When they ceased, others no less cruel and harmful arose. These Archontici are so called from ὑπὸ τῶν ἀρχόντων or ἀρχῶν, that is, from the Powers, whom they set up as secondary gods, and as the fathers of the angels themselves. Isidore calls them Archontiani, not, I think, correctly, and it is not quite accurately written by the same author that the Ἄρχοντες whom the Archontici worshipped, and by whom they affirmed the world was made, are the Archangels. Indeed these men make their Ἄρχοντες far superior and more divine than the Archangels themselves, and they wish them to be the fathers of the angels and archangels alike, born of the mother Photenia. Yet I do not deny that those vain speculations about the angels and their various orders, which have a place among the schoolmen, were drawn from these beginnings, and from the trifles and foul errors of heretics. This plague, then, began to spread its foul stench under Constantius, as Epiphanius says, the son of Constantine the Great. Its author was a certain Peter, an anchorite and Palestinian monk, who lived in the district of Carbaricha, three miles from the city of Hebron, and had won for himself a great reputation for piety and holiness among men. But in that solitude he gave himself over to vain and pernicious disputations about the nature and works of the angels and heavenly powers, puffed up by the sense of his own flesh and intruding into things he had never seen. Such were the good and happy fruits that appeared from this solitary and melancholy manner of life. This error he afterwards spread more widely through a certain Armenian monk named Eutactus, who, returning to his homeland of Sethale, poured this deadly poison over the whole neighbouring region. Thus, as Epiphanius writes, Lesser Armenia was first infected with this poison, and then Greater Armenia too, together with Palestine. Nor could these provinces afterwards be cleansed of it so quickly. So the evil spread and lasted for some time in those places, where it also split and divided into several sects. For from the Archontici arose those heretics whom they call Ascodrupitae or Ascothryptae (for they can be named by either name; Jerome in the preface to his second book on Galatians also called them, corruptly, Ascodrobi), in Greek Ἀσκοδρύπται or Ἀσκοθρύπται, because they broke and furiously smashed all the vessels destined for administering the sacraments. For these men, like the Archontici, wonderfully detested and condemned the use of the sacraments in the Church. Theodoret treats of the Ascodrupitae in his first book. But few write about the Archontici. Neither Tertullian nor Irenaeus could know them, since in their age these heretics had not yet been born. Nevertheless, the doctrines of the Archontici were many and horrible.

units.la: 2 Opera esse principum.) Erroris capita tria recenset Augustinus ex Epiphanio. 1 Mundum hunc a quibusdam caelestibus potestatibus conditum esse, non a Deo. Hoc ex Valentinianorum fermento, & Aeonum commento fuit. Cuique autem caelo (septem autem tantum caelos constituunt) praefectu esse Angelum unum, & illi, tanquam glebae, addictum a quo recedere non possit. Angelos autem ab illis Potestatibus ex Photenia matre i.luce, tanquam a pluribus adulteris cū uno scorto coeuntibus progenatos. Istud ex Aristotelicis scriptis sumptum est, praefectas esse caelis quasdam intelligentias, quod commentum etiam Hieronym. alicubi probavit, & retinuit: authoritate tamen Scripturae confirmari non potest. Plane autem in Archöticis erronea est illa de generatione Angelorum sententia, & haec eorundem, Animas hominum esse cibum & alimentum illarum potestatem spiritualium. 2 Turpitudinem morum, & imprimis stuprorum, cum suo dogmate coniungunt, quia bona opera prorsus esse spernenda, tanquam inutilia, homini Christiano docent. Itaque Epiphanius appellat eorum vitam [illegible, ~8 letters]. i. spurcitiei plenam. 3 Carnis resurrectionem negant, quanquam Heracleonitas imitati, mortuorum suorum capitibus oleum & aquam cum quorundam verborum demurmuratione infundunt, vt eos à peccatis expiant. Inde Purgatorij & Extremae vnctionis Papisticae error coepit. 4 Sacramenta à Domino nostro Iesu Christo instituta & nobis relicta tollunt, & ex Ecclesia prorsus eiiciunt, quod indignum putent vt res spiritualis vllius terreni elementi similitudine repraesentetur, & res caelestis per corporalia & sensibilia significetur, aut peragatur. Itaque hi vere sunt Sacramentarij. 5 Vetus Testamentum in multis calumniatur, non tollunt tamen omnino, sed apocryphos libros habent, è quibus hi sunt praecipui, Maior & Minor Concordantia, item [illegible, ~8 letters] [illegible, ~7 letters] Isaiae Prophetae ex cap.10. Ex iis fundamentis sua deliria confirmant. 6 Salvos fieri homines, quanquam turpissime & flagitiosissime viuant, modo prae se ferant Dei cognitionem. Fidem enim tanquam mortuam quandam arborem somniant (quae bona opera non producat, sed sit in nuda dogmatum cognitione & mataeologia, non autem in charitate & praestatione) quam Iacobus cap.2. difertissime damnat & Christus ipse Luc. 11. versu 28. 7 Diabolum esse filium Dei Sabaoth, siue Dei Iudæorum, non autè Dei Christianorum. 8 Diabolum ipsum ex Eua generasse Cain & Abel, quorum vterque est reprobatus à Deo, & miser. Hæ sunt Valentinianorum scholæ & doctrinæ infelicissimæ propagines, & postremæ sordes, nisi quis Florianos addat, de quibus postea. Itaque ad Marcionitas, & eorum parentem veniamus.
units.tr: The works are those of rulers. Augustine, following Epiphanius, lists three heads of their error. (1) They hold that this world was made by certain heavenly powers, not by God. This came from the leaven of the Valentinians and the invention of the Aeons. Each heaven (they posit only seven heavens) has an angel set over it, bound to it as to a clod of earth, from which he cannot withdraw. These angels they say were born of those Powers and the mother Photenia, that is, Light, as if from several adulterers who had intercourse with one harlot. This was taken from the writings of the Aristotelians, that certain intelligences preside over the heavens. Jerome also approved of this invention somewhere and kept it, but it cannot be confirmed by the authority of Scripture. Indeed, in the Archontici this opinion about the generation of the angels is erroneous, as is their view that the souls of men are the food and nourishment of those spiritual powers. (2) They join to their doctrine the filthiness of their morals and especially fornication, since they teach the Christian man that good works are to be utterly despised as useless. So Epiphanius calls their life … that is, full of filth. (3) They deny the resurrection of the flesh, though, imitating the Heracleonites, they pour oil and water on the heads of their dead, with a mumbling of certain words, to cleanse them from sins. From this arose the error of the Papistical Purgatory and Extreme Unction. (4) They abolish the sacraments instituted by our Lord Jesus Christ and left to us, and cast them utterly out of the Church, because they think it unworthy that a spiritual thing should be represented by the likeness of some earthly element, and that a heavenly thing should be signified or performed through bodily and sensible things. Therefore these men are truly Sacramentarians. (5) They slander the Old Testament in many respects, yet they do not reject it altogether; they have apocryphal books, among which the chief are the Major and Minor Concordance, likewise … of the prophet Isaiah, chapter 10. On these foundations they confirm their delusions. (6) Men are saved, however foully and shamefully they live, provided they show a knowledge of God. For they dream of faith as a dead kind of tree, which produces no good works, but lies in bare knowledge of doctrines and empty talk, not in love and practice, which James in chapter 2 most plainly condemns, and Christ himself in Luke 11, verse 28. (7) The devil is the son of the God of Sabaoth, or the God of the Jews, not of the God of Christians. (8) The devil himself begot Cain and Abel from Eve, both of whom were rejected by God and were wretched. These are the most unhappy offshoots and final filth of the Valentinian school and doctrines, unless one adds the Florinians, of whom later. So let us come to the Marcionites and their parent.

units.la: CAP. XXI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXI.

units.la: Cerdoniani vnde dicti. Erroris autem eorum capita quatuor recitata.
units.tr: The Cerdonians, whence so called. Four heads of their error are recited.

units.la: C[?]erdoniani à Cerdone{1} nominati, qui duo {2}principia sibi aduersantia dogmatizant, Deúmque Legis ac Prophetarum non esse patrem Christi, nec bonum Deum esse, sed {3}iustum: Patrem vero Christi bonum: Christúmque ipsum neque natum ex fœmina, neque habuisse carnem, sed nec vere mortuum, vel quicquam passum, sed simulasse passionem. Quidam vero in duobus suis principijs duos deos ita eum dixisse perhibent, vt vnus eorum esset bonus: alter autem malus. Resurrectionem mortuorum negant. Spernunt etiam Testamentum vetus.
units.tr: The Cerdonians are named after Cerdo, who teach two opposing principles, and deny that the God of the Law and the Prophets is the Father of Christ or a good God, but hold him to be just. The Father of Christ, they say, is good. Christ himself, they claim, was neither born of a woman nor had real flesh, and he did not truly die or suffer anything, but only feigned the passion. Some report that in his two principles he spoke of two gods, one good and the other evil. They deny the resurrection of the dead. They also despise the Old Testament.

units.la: Quod in bellis homines faciunt, idem in oppugnanda Christi veritate Satan molitus est, & tandem perfecit, vt pluribus in locis variisque stratagematis insi-dias dias strueret, ne, si aliquæ ex iis detectæ effent, & cederent male, omnino victus superatúsque maneret. Itaque eodem penè tempore Valentinum & Cerdonem ex eadem infelicissima Simonianorum schola produxit, qui diuersam prorsus viam ingressi, fidei tamen Christianæ doctrinam euerterent. Quia enim Euangelica doctrina vnum & eundem Christum mediatorem nostrum, & Deum verum, & hominem verum fuisse tradit (alioqui enim pax nobis apud Deum constare non potest) vtrunque hoc fidei nostræ fundamentum diruendum suscepit. Erant enim iam putidiores & notiores primi illi Simonis Magi errores, quàm vt quisquam vel leuiter fide Christiana imbutus iis assentiretur. Itaque alios peperit Satan ex iis quidem ipsis cœnosis fontibus haustos, sed tamen nouis coloribus nouáque forma interpolatos, vt quid nouum & prorsus adhuc inauditum Ecclesiæ proponi videretur, eóque ipso commendaretur. Ita vero inter Valentinum & Cerdonem munera illa sæuissima partitus est Satan, vt Valentinus quidem intricatissimis fabulis & percensionibus Æonum & genealogiarum ineptissimis diuinam Christi natiuitatem de Deo Patre prorsus inuolueret, & incredibilem redderet. Cerdo vero & post eum Marcio humanam Christi de Maria virgine natiuitatē aperte negaret, & ementitā esse cōtenderet. Quibus sententiis & erroribus semel receptis, vtrunq; fidei nostræ fulcimentū & fundamētum plane conuellitur & ruit. Vide Theodoretum Dialog.2. qui dicitur Inconfusus. Præclarè enim August[?]. lib.13. cótra Fauft.c.8. Sic.n.ait, Quidam deum credendo Christum, & hominem negando errauerunt: & rursus quidam hominem putando, & Deum negando, aut contempserunt, aut in homine spem suam posuerunt. De Valentinianis vero & eorum secta, siue longa schola successione ad hunc vsque locum diximus. Ergo de Cerdone, Marcione, & Marcionitis tractatus ab Augustino, qui Epiphanij vestigia [illegible, ~5 letters] sequutus est, nūc instituitur. Ex quo facilè intelligitur hic non haberi rationem temporis in recensendis haeresibus: sed potius dogmatis, & continuationis schola. Fuit enim nefarij istius erroris de tollenda & perneganda humana Christi natura primus author Cerdo, quamquam de eo quiddam Simon antea dixerat, sed nullis penè rationibus erat vsus, vt non tam ab illo defendi, quàm tantum proponi hic error videretur. Cerdo vero ille, à quo postea tam pestilentem halitum Marcionitae biberunt & traxerunt, acerrimè tutatus est, & in eo propagando, se mirum impostorem praestitit. Vixit autem Cerdo ante Marcionem, vt scribit Irenaeus lib.3. cap.4. sub Higino primo, Romano pontifice, & Antonino Pio Imperatore, cuius haeresis innotuit eodem tempore, quo Valentiniani, circa annum à Christo passo 110. Et Syria profectus est Romam, vbi, quemadmodum etiam alij haeretici & antea fecerant, & postea quoque continuatum est, venenum suum spargit. Fertur autem mortuus esse demum anno temporis vltimi, i. à Christo passo 148, adeo vt totos 38. annos hic impostor bellum aduersus Christum gesserit. Sæpe tamen fictam erroris pœ-nitentiam simulauit, sæpe exomologesin in Ec-clesia fecit, idque Romæ, tamen immani ambi-tione abreptus latenter ibidem loci hæresin suam docebat, vbi tandem à coetu fidelium est excommunicatus. Propter magnitudinem enim vrbis Romæ & ciuium libertatem, in eo potis-simum loco tantæ pestes latere poterant, quan-quam deprehensæ non tolerabantur, sed iam in vrbe Septicolli agebat Satan mysterium illud iniquitatis, quod demum absoluit. Quidam Cer-donianos constituunt recentiores, quasi anno tantum à Christo passo 147. cœperint & exorti fuerint post Blastum & Florianos hæreticos, atque etiam post Tatianos, qui vt primum sub Commodo Imperatore nati sunt. Sic Theodo-retus lib.1. Irenæus tamen lib.1.cap.28. Epipha-nius, Eusebius lib.4.cap.10. Histor. sub Higino collocant. Nec moror ordinem quem secutus est Isidorus, qui recenset eos post Angelicos & Adamitas & Apostolicos hæreticos, quia mul-ta [?]in eo autore corrupta & peruersa videntur. Quod ad Tertullianum attinet, qui ponit post Marcionem & Colarbasium, rationem diximus. Ille enim omnes Valentinianos continua serie persequi maluit, quam institutum ordinem ab-rumpere. Ergo à Simonianis ortus est Cerdo-nis error, vt omnes tradunt. Alius enim est hic Credo, quàm ille qui vixit sub Traiano & Ale-xandrinæ Ecclesiæ fuit Episcopus, de quo Eu-seb.lib.3.cap.21. Clemens non meminit Cerdo-nis, quanquam Marcionitarum hæresin sæpe refutauit.
units.tr: As men do in war, so Satan, in attacking the truth of Christ, schemed and at last achieved this: he laid snares in many places with varied stratagems, so that if some of them were detected and went badly, he would not be utterly defeated and overcome. Thus at about the same time he produced Valentinus and Cerdo from the same most unhappy school of Simon, and they, taking a quite different path, nevertheless overturned the doctrine of the Christian faith. For the Gospel teaches that one and the same Christ is our Mediator, true God and true man (otherwise peace with God cannot stand for us), and so they undertook to destroy both foundations of our faith. For those first errors of Simon Magus were by now too foul and too well known for anyone imbued even slightly with the Christian faith to assent to them. So Satan brought forth other errors, drawn indeed from those same filthy springs, but dressed in new colours and a new form, so that something new and entirely unheard of might seem to be put before the Church, and so be recommended by that very fact. Satan so divided those most savage services between Valentinus and Cerdo that Valentinus, with most intricate fables, the enumerations of the Aeons and the most absurd genealogies, entirely entangled the divine nativity of Christ from God the Father and made it incredible. Cerdo, however, and after him Marcion, openly denied the human nativity of Christ from the Virgin Mary and contended that it was made up. Once these opinions and errors were received, both props and foundations of our faith are plainly overthrown and collapse. See Theodoret, Dialogue 2, which is called "Inconfusus". For Augustine has excellently said in book 13 against Faustus, chapter 8: "Some erred by believing Christ to be God and denying him to be man, and again some, thinking him man and denying him God, either despised him or placed their hope in a man." We have already spoken of the Valentinians and their sect, with its long succession of teachers, up to this point. Now, therefore, the treatment of Cerdo, Marcion and the Marcionites, which Augustine undertook following the footsteps of Epiphanius, is begun. From this it is easily understood that here no account is taken of chronology in listing the heresies, but rather of doctrine and the continuity of the school. Cerdo was the first author of that wicked error of removing and utterly denying the human nature of Christ, although Simon had said something about it earlier, but he had used almost no arguments, so that this error seemed to be put forward here rather than defended by him. That Cerdo, however, from whom the Marcionites afterwards drew in and breathed so pestilent a vapour, defended it most fiercely, and in spreading it he showed himself a remarkable impostor. Cerdo lived before Marcion, as Irenaeus writes in book 3, chapter 4, under Hyginus, the first Roman bishop, and under the emperor Antoninus Pius. His heresy became known at the same time as that of the Valentinians, about the year 110 after Christ's passion. He set out from Syria for Rome, where, as other heretics had also done before and this has continued since, he spread his poison. He is said to have died at last in the final year of his life, that is, in the year 148 after Christ's passion, so that this impostor waged war against Christ for a full 38 years. Yet he often feigned a repentance of his error, and often made public confession in the Church, and that at Rome; still, carried off by immense ambition, he secretly taught his heresy in the same place, until at last he was excommunicated by the assembly of the faithful. For because of the greatness of the city of Rome and the freedom of its citizens, such pests could lie hidden most easily in that very place; yet when they were detected they were not tolerated, but already Satan was working in the city of the seven hills that mystery of iniquity which he finally completed. Some more recent writers set up the Cerdonians as if they had begun only in the year 147 after Christ's passion and arose after the heretics Blastus and the Florians, and even after the Tatians, who were first born under the emperor Commodus. So Theodoret, book 1. Irenaeus, however, book 1, chapter 28, and Epiphanius, and Eusebius, Church History book 4, chapter 10, place them under Hyginus. Nor do I dwell on the order which Isidore followed, who lists them after the Angelic, Adamite and Apostolic heretics, because many things in that author seem corrupt and perverse. As for Tertullian, who places them after Marcion and Colarbasus, I have already given the reason: he preferred to pursue all the Valentinians in an unbroken series rather than break off the order he had adopted. Therefore, as all writers report, the error of Cerdo arose from the Simonians. For this Cerdo is different from that Cerdo who lived under Trajan and was bishop of the Church of Alexandria, of whom Eusebius writes in book 3, chapter 21. Clement does not mention Cerdo, although he often refuted the heresy of the Marcionites.

units.la: 2 Qui duo principia ) Locus hic ex Epipha. tom.3.lib.1.sumptus est. Continet quatuor Cerdoniani veneni capita. 1 Duos esse deos & principia sibi mutuo pugnantia & contraria. Unum enim esse superiorem Deum, qui bonus & misericors & clemens sit, & pater Domini nostri Iesu Christi, quanquam ante Evangelium fuit, ait ille, ignotus. Alterum Deum esse saevum punientem mala, & rigidum, & quem vocat hic Augustinus iustum: (sed illam Dei iustitiam opponebat Misericordiae, tanquam res inter se pugnantes) Itaque iubet, ait Cerdo, hic alter Deus oculum pro oculo, & dentem pro dente eruere: ille autem prior praecipit ut inimicos diligamus. Hunc quem vocat saevum & iustum, saepe etiam malum appellavit, quem dixit esse Mundi creatorem, & iampride Iudaeis notum Deu. Hic error iugulatur Hebr.1. verf.1. Roman.1. verf.1.Galat.4.verf.4. 2 Legem Dei per Moysen datam & Prophetas veteris Testamenti, qui fuerunt illius interpretes, repudiat tanquam illius saevi Dei ministros, & Deo Evangelii contrarios. Attamen ab iis Christus ipse testimonium accipit, Ioan.5. verf.39. 3 Christum ex Maria virgine natum negat, vel hominem factum & vere passum, sed tantum simulate & ficte. Denique summum impostorem facit Christum impium & blasphemus Cerdo, & totum salutis nostrae fundamentum subruit. 4 Carnis resurrectionem negat, quod nobis tanquam rancida Simonianorum repotia apponit.
units.tr: 2 Who teach two principles) This passage is taken from Epiphanius, vol. 3, book 1. It sets out four heads of the Cerdonian poison. (1) That there are two gods and principles mutually opposed and contrary. For there is one superior God, who is good, merciful and kind, and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, although, he says, he was unknown before the Gospel. The other God is cruel, punishing evils, and stern, whom Augustine here calls just (but Cerdo set that justice of God against mercy, as things at odds with each other). Therefore, says Cerdo, this other God commands an eye to be torn out for an eye and a tooth for a tooth; but the former commands us to love our enemies. This God, whom he calls cruel and just, he often also called evil, and he said that he was the creator of the world, and long known to the Jews. This error is refuted at Heb. 1 v. 1, Rom. 1 v. 1, Gal. 4 v. 4. (2) He rejects the law of God given through Moses and the Prophets of the Old Testament, who were its interpreters, as ministers of that cruel God and opposed to the God of the Gospel. Yet Christ himself receives testimony from them, John 5 v. 39. (3) He denies that Christ was born of the Virgin Mary, or that he was made man and truly suffered, but says it was only pretended and feigned. Finally, impious and blasphemous Cerdo makes Christ the greatest impostor, and undermines the whole foundation of our salvation. (4) He denies the resurrection of the flesh, which he sets before us like the stale leftovers of the Simonian banquets.

units.la: 3 Sed iustum. ) Sic legendum, non autem ut est in margine impressi codicis, Nec iustum. Iustitiam enim Misericordiæ tanquam contrariam opponebat, & negabat Deum, qui aliquas de scelerib[?]us hominum pœnas sumeret, esse misericordem, quasi non benè inter has pulcherrimas virtutes, Iustitiam dico & Misericordiam conveniat. Denique vocem hanc, Iustum, retinendam esse docet locus Eusebij, qui est lib. 4.Histor.Eccles.cap.ii. vbi sit hæc inter iustum & misericordem Deum [illegible, ~5 letters], & unde hic Augustini locus procul dubio sumptus est. Confirmatur etiam authoritate Theodoreti, in libr. Epitome Divinorum Decretor.cap. Quod idé sit bonus & iustus.
units.tr: 3 But just.) It should be read thus, not as in the margin of the printed codex, "Nor just." For he set justice against mercy as contrary, and denied that God, who exacts some punishment for men's wickedness, is merciful, as if justice and mercy, those most beautiful virtues, did not agree well together. Lastly, that this word "just" should be retained is taught by a passage of Eusebius, Church History book 4, chapter 11, where this distinction between the just and the merciful God occurs [illegible], and from which this passage of Augustine was undoubtedly taken. It is also confirmed by the authority of Theodoret, in the Epitome of the Divine Decrees, chapter "That the same God is both good and just."

units.la: CAP. XXII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXII.

units.la: Marcionitæ unde dicti. Unum autem erroris eorum caput describitur.
units.tr: Whence the Marcionites are named. A chief point of their error is described.

units.la: Arcion quoque{1} à quo Marcionitæ sunt, qui Cerdonis secutus est, dogmata de duobus principiis: quanvis Epiphanius eum tria dicat asseruisse principia, bonum, iustum, prauum. Sed Eusebius{2} Synerum quendam, non Marcionem, trium principiorum atque naturarum scribit autorem.
units.tr: Arcion too, from whom the Marcionites take their name, followed Cerdo and held the doctrine of two principles, although Epiphanius says he asserted three principles: good, just, and evil. But Eusebius writes that a certain Syneros, not Marcion, was the author of the doctrine of three principles and natures.

units.la: I A quo Marcionitæ.) Marcionitæ an Marcionistæ dici debeant, quæri potest, & utroque modo tum à Græcis tum à Latinis scriptoribus appellantur: melius tamen & analogiæ aliorum nominatorum convenientius Marcionitæ nominantur, quemadmodum a Tertulliano pas-sim. Fuit autem haec haeresis nocentissima Cerdoniani feminis seges, qua tetriorem & Ecclesiae Dei pestilentiorem antea non produxerat Satan: sed paulatim creuit ipsius Satanae improbitas, & ut ita dicam, ingenium: quod fidem nostram tentando, & subinde novos errores significando videtur in dies euasisse subtilior & acutior Satan, adeo ut iam maioribus viribus & robustiori fraude se suaque venena seminaret & tueretur. Itaque Marcion hic, a quo dicti sunt Marcionitae, & serpens & lupus Ecclesiae, & primogenitus Diaboli appellatus est, etiam a Polycarpo ipso Ioannis Euangelistae discipulo, ut refert Irenaeus lib. 3. cap. 3. Euseb. libr. 4. cap. [?]13. Vulgo autem in contemptum totius sectae idem Marcion Ponticus & nauta & nauclerus appellabatur, quemadmodum ab Irenaeo lib. 1. cap. 29. Tertulliano, Iustino, Clemente & Euseb. lib. 4. cap. 11. [?]II. Fuit igitur hic Marcion Cerdonis discipulus, quem Romae vidit, & cum eo familiariter conversatus; illius furores auxit, natione Ponticus, ortus Synope civitate, quae ad Potum Euxinum sive Hellespontum sita est in Paphlagonia, sicuti Xenophon in Hellenicis scribit, & veteres Milesiorum colonia erat; sed Scytha tetrior, Massageta inhumanior, Istro fallacior, ut ait Tertullianus lib. 1. Aduersus eum, in Europam migravit haec belua Marcion. Ac episcopo patre viro probo natus erat; fuitque in adolescentia sanctitatis ostentator, adeo ut, quemadmodum scribit Epiphanius, virginitatem Monachi habitu profiteretur. Fuit enim [illegible, ~3 letters] Tam boni nihilrum & suaues fructus ex hoc vitæ genere & vo-to castitatis nascuntur, nempe gratuissimæ hæ-reses. Christianam igitur primum pietatem & orthodoxā fidem professus est & amplexus, vi-nens unā cum patre suo Marcio, quod ex ipsius epistola apparere scribit in lib. De carne Christi, Tertullian. Sed cum virginem stuprasset, à patre excommunicatus est, qui postea cum, quan-quam animi resipiscentiam fingentem admitte-re in Ecclesiam noluit, quòd subdolum filij sui ingenium norat pater & episcopus. Quamobrē Marcion Romam venit, ubi se veniam facilius ab Ecclesia impetraturum sperabat, quam tamen non obtinuit. Nam Romæ Episcopus eam tyrannidem, quam nunc in alios episcopos exercet, nondum usurpauerat, ut episcoporum episcopum se diceret, sed episcopatus sui finibus se modeste continebat. Respondit igitur Marcioni se [illegible, ~24 letters] si-ne iussu proprij patris & episcopi, ut scribit Epi-phanius, eum absoluere non posse ab excommu-nicatione, quæ ab alio facta esset, quod veterum synodorum decretis consentaneum est, & diu quoque fuit visitatum, quemadmodum Ruffin. libro i. Histor. cap. 6, refert, ut ab uno episcopo excommunicatus ab alio non absolueretur. Sed hanc impetrandæ veniæ desperatione percussus Marcion se Cerdoni adiunxit, quòd seueriorem in se Ecclesiæ disciplinam experiretur, & esse conquereretur. Venit autem Romam quem-admodum lib. i. Aduersus eum scribit Tertullian sub Antonino Pio, circa annum à Christo passo 115, sub Higino, ut ait Platina; Tertullian sub Eleuthero. Coepit autem post Cerdonem innote- scere illius haeresis sub M. Antonino Philoso- pho imperatore, & Aniceto pontifice Roma- no, circa annum a passo Christo 133. quanquam Clemens lib.7.Stromat.vult adhuc eo ipso tem- pore vixisse,& fuisse Romae Valentinum haere- ticum, quem iam senem Marcion iuuenis vide- rit. Occasio erradi fuit, quod circa quaestionem De origine mali & peccati langueret, vt excu- saret suum scelus.Itaque ex eo quod dictum est Matth.7.verf.17.Omnis arbor bona bonos fru- ctus facit, mala vero malos: errorem Cerdonis amplexus est & defendit. Stoicae tamen disci- plinae fuisse a prima statim aetate studiosum, & illi nimium addictum volunt,unde Isidorus vo- cat eum Stoicum philosophum, quanquam Christianum se, non Ethnicum philosophum profitebatur. Inde illud Tertullian. Marcioni- tis Deus melior de tranquillitate a Stoicis ve- nerat. Scribit tamen Clemens libr.7. Stromat. Marcionem iactare solitum se sua commenta non ab se, sed ab ipsis Apostolorum discipu- lis habuisse, iis nempe qui Matthiae, de quo est Actor.1. auditores fuerant, quae iactatia est sal- sissima. Itaque Romae ab Ecclesia excommu- nicatus iterum est, & reddita sunt illi cc hs. quae apud eam depositae erant. Tamen poeniten- tiam agere & errorem abiurare paratus hac con- ditione veniam impetrauerat, vt quos corru- perat Ecclesiae restituisset, sed morte praeuentus praestare non potuit. Alij vero Synerum quen- dam potius huius erroris, quem Marcion secu- tus est, autorem faciunt, de quo postea. Caete- rum rūm[?] latissime vagata est hæc hæresis,& ut ait E-piphanius,Romam ipsam,Italiam,AEgyptum, Thebaida,Arabiam, Palæstinam, Cyprum, de-nique Persidem remotissimam gentem perua-sit hoc venenum. Diutissimè etiam hoc malum in Ecclesia grassatum est, adeò ut ad nostra vsque tempora durauerit. Quanquam verò Im-perator.Christianorum legibus seuerissimè sta-tim coerceretur,tamen etiam Constantini Ma-gni temporibus erupit,utin eius vita libr.3.scri-bit Euseb. & tempore Arcadij imperatoris, vi-vente Theodoreto Cyri[?] episcopo, qui se huius sectæ homines vidisse ait, libro 5.Histor.cap.31. & lib.Fabul.hæretic. commemorat responsum-senis cuiusdam Marcionitæ qui mane sputo, non autem aqua manus suas abluebat, ne re-bus creatoris uteretur. Denique Epiphanius scribit suo seculo adhuc quosdam Marcionitas Romæ natos fuisse. Multas hæreses uti vipera viperas, sic hæc hæresis peperit, & successorcs[?] scholæ plurimos audacissimòsque homines habuit, inter quos hi fuere primi & præcipui, Lucianus quidam, Potitus, Blastus, Synerus, Prepo,Pithon,Hermogenes,Afer,Apelles & alij.Denique interpolata tandem est hæc hæresis nouo nomine Adversariorum Legis & Prophetarum,quod genus hominum suo seculo inimi-cum habuit Augustinus. Martyres etiam se habere iactant,ut scribit Euseb.libr.5.cap.16.inter quos recesset[?] Methodorum Smyrnæ crematum libr.4.cap.16. sed falsò.Nam causa facit marty-res, quemadmodum Cyprianus ait, non autem pœna. Multi autem tum Græci tum Latini patres adversus Marcionitas scripserunt, neque orthodoxi solùm, sed etiam ex aliis haereticis quidam, velut è Tatianis Rhodon quidam, & Bar-desanes. Prudentius poeta Latinus praeter Tertullianum adversus eos edidit quaedā carmina, ut ex eo satis appareat etiam illa aetate, quae fuit aetas Ambrosij Mediolanensis episcopi, Romae viguisse adhuc Marcionitas.
units.tr: I. From whom the Marcionites. It may be asked whether they should be called Marcionites or Marcionists. Both forms are used by Greek and Latin writers alike, but "Marcionites" is better and better matches the names of other sects, as Tertullian uses it throughout. This heresy was a most harmful offspring of the seed of Cerdo, and Satan had never before brought forth a more foul or more destructive one for the Church of God. But the wickedness and, so to speak, the cunning of Satan himself grew gradually. By testing our faith and from time to time showing new errors, Satan seems to have become daily more subtle and sharp, so that now with greater strength and more robust deceit he sows and defends his poisons. Thus Marcion, from whom the Marcionites are named, was called both serpent and wolf of the Church and firstborn of the devil, even by Polycarp himself, the disciple of the evangelist John, as Irenaeus reports (Irenaeus, bk. 3, ch. 3; Eusebius, bk. 4, ch. [?]13). Commonly, however, to bring the whole sect into contempt, this same Marcion of Pontus was called a sailor and a shipmaster, as Irenaeus (bk. 1, ch. 29), Tertullian, Justin, Clement, and Eusebius (bk. 4, ch. [?]11) record. This Marcion was a disciple of Cerdo, whom he saw at Rome and with whom he associated closely, and he increased Cerdo's madness. He was a native of Pontus, born in the city of Sinope, which lies on the Euxine Sea or Hellespont in Paphlagonia, as Xenophon writes in the Hellenica; it was an old colony of the Milesians. Tertullian says (bk. 1, Against Him) that he was a Scythian more foul, a Massagete more savage, and a Danube-dweller more deceitful, and this beast Marcion migrated to Europe. He was born to a father who was a bishop and an upright man. In his youth he made a show of holiness, so much so that, as Epiphanius writes, he professed virginity in the dress of a monk. For from this kind of life and vow of chastity there arise (as the saying goes) some fine and sweet fruits, namely the most pernicious heresies. He therefore first professed and embraced Christian piety and orthodox faith, living together with his father, as Tertullian writes in his book On the Flesh of Christ, where he says this appears from Marcion's own letter. But when he had debauched a virgin, he was excommunicated by his father, and afterwards, when he feigned a change of heart, the father, who knew the crafty character of his son, as bishop refused to admit him to the Church. Therefore Marcion came to Rome, where he hoped to obtain pardon from the Church more easily, but he did not obtain it. For at Rome the bishop had not yet claimed that tyranny which he now exercises over other bishops, of calling himself the bishop of bishops; he kept himself modestly within the bounds of his own see. He therefore replied to Marcion that he could not absolve him, without the command of his own father and bishop, from an excommunication pronounced by another, as Epiphanius writes. This accords with the decrees of the ancient synods, and it was long the custom, as Rufinus reports (bk. 1 of his History, ch. 6), that one excommunicated by one bishop should not be absolved by another. But Marcion, struck by despair of obtaining pardon, attached himself to Cerdo, because he wished to experience and complain of the harsher discipline of the Church. Tertullian (bk. 1, Against Him) writes that Marcion came to Rome under Antoninus Pius, about the year 115 after the passion of Christ, under Hyginus, as Platina says, and under Eleutherius, according to Tertullian. Moreover, after Cerdo, his heresy began to become known under the emperor Marcus Antoninus the Philosopher and the Roman bishop Anicetus, about the year 133 after the passion of Christ, although Clement (bk. 7 of the Stromateis) wishes that Valentinus the heretic was still living at that very time and was at Rome, and that Marcion, as a young man, saw him when he was already old. The occasion of his error was that he was troubled by the question of the origin of evil and sin, so that he might excuse his own wickedness. Accordingly, from what is said in Matthew 7:17, "Every good tree bears good fruit, but a bad tree bears bad fruit," he embraced and defended the error of Cerdo. Yet they say he was zealous from the very beginning of his youth for the Stoic discipline and was devoted to it excessively, whence Isidore calls him a Stoic philosopher, although he professed himself a Christian and not a pagan philosopher. Hence Tertullian's words: "The better God of the Marcionites came from the Stoics' tranquillity." Clement, however, writes in bk. 7 of the Stromateis that Marcion used to boast that he had received his inventions not from himself but from the disciples of the apostles themselves, namely from those who had been hearers of Matthias, of whom we read in Acts 1. That boast is most false. So Marcion, excommunicated by the Church at Rome, was again cut off, and the 200 sesterces that he had deposited with it were returned to him. Nevertheless, he was ready to do penance and abjure his error, on condition that he would restore to the Church those whom he had corrupted, and he had obtained pardon on that basis, but, forestalled by death, he could not fulfil it. Others, however, make a certain Syneros rather than Marcion the author of this error, which Marcion followed; of him later. Otherwise this heresy spread very widely, and, as Epiphanius says, this poison persuaded Rome itself, Italy, Egypt, the Thebaid, Arabia, Palestine, Cyprus, and finally Persia, the most remote nation. This evil also raged in the Church for a very long time, so that it lasted down to our own times. Although the emperors at once punished the Christians of this sect most severely by their laws, nevertheless it broke out again even in the times of Constantine the Great, as Eusebius writes in his Life of Constantine (bk. 3). And in the time of the emperor Arcadius, when Theodoret, bishop of Cyrus, was still alive, who says he saw people of this sect, it is recorded in bk. 5 of his History (ch. 31) and in his Fabulae haereticorum, that an old Marcionite who washed his hands in spittle in the morning, not in water, so that he would not use the things of the Creator. Finally, Epiphanius writes that in his own age some Marcionites were still born at Rome. Just as a viper brings forth vipers, so this heresy brought forth many successors, and the school had many very bold men, among whom these were the first and chief: a certain Lucian, Potitus, Blastus, Syneros, Prepo, Pithon, Hermogenes, Afer, Apelles, and others. Finally, this heresy was at last furnished with a new name, "Adversaries of the Law and the Prophets," a class of men whom Augustine had as enemies in his own age. They also boast that they have martyrs, as Eusebius writes (bk. 5, ch. 16), among whom Methodius of Smyrna, burned, is mentioned (bk. 4, ch. 16); but this is false. For, as Cyprian says, the cause makes the martyr, not the punishment. Many Fathers, both Greek and Latin, wrote against the Marcionites, not only orthodox writers but also some from other heretics, such as Rhodon from the Tatians, and Bardesanes. The Latin poet Prudentius, besides Tertullian, published some poems against them, so that it sufficiently appears from this that even in that age, which was the age of Ambrose, bishop of Milan, the Marcionites were still flourishing at Rome.

units.la: Dubitare videtur Augustinus utrum Marcion duos an tres deos & principia prima constituerit. Nec caret ea dubitatio ratione. Epiphanius enim, quem vnum maxime sequitur Augustinus, & qui videtur haec diligentissime scrutatus, tres deos eum constituisse scribit, Summum, quem bonum & invisibilem[?] esse dicebat: Imum, quem visibilem factum esse dicebat, & malum appellabat: Medium, quem quoque esse dicebat Diabolum. Theodoretus autem lib. 1. De fabul. Haereticor. ait eum finxisse non tres tantum, sed quatuor deos. Tribus enim superioribus addidit Materiam, & pro Diabolo Serpentem substituit. Theodoretus quem ait a Marcione pro Deo cultum esse. Itaque Hermogenianae haeresios parens & primus autor est Marcion. Verior tamen est eorum sententia, qui duos tantum deos ab eo inductos scribunt. Vnum Creatorem huius mundi, quem non tantum iustum vocauit, quemadmodum Cerdon, sed etiam saevum, crudelem, & malum. Itaque vbique vocatur Marcion a Clemente & imprimis libr. 3. & 4. Stromat. ingratus in autorem suum, & totius naturae parentem. Alterum autem Deum dicebat esse Patrem Domini nostri Iesu Christi, & eum bo-num, clementem, & misericordem appellabat. Atque vtrosque hos deos magna inter se distantia separatos. Hæc Irenæus lib.2.cap.1.lib.4 cap.57. Tertullianus passim. Euscb.lib.9.Histo-riæ, & Isidorus. Hinc autem Manichæorum de-liria & semina sumpta fuisse videntur, & tota illa distinctio inter gentem Lucis & Tenebra-rum, quæ à Manichæis inducta est. Hic est pri-mus Marcionis error, qui ex veteris & noui Testamenti discrimine non intellecto, & aliquot locis Scripturæ perperam explicatis natus est.
units.tr: Augustine seems uncertain whether Marcion posited two gods and first principles or three. And this doubt is not without reason. For Epiphanius, whom Augustine especially follows, and who seems to have examined these things most diligently, writes that Marcion posited three gods: the highest, whom he said was good and invisible; the lowest, whom he said was made visible and whom he called evil; and the middle one, whom he also said was the devil. Theodoret, however, in bk. 1 of his Fabulae haereticorum, says that he invented not three but four gods, for he added Matter to the three above, and substituted the Serpent for the devil. Theodoret says that Marcion had Matter worshipped as a god. Thus Marcion is the parent and first author of the Hermogenian heresy. The opinion of those is more correct, however, who write that he introduced only two gods: one, the Creator of this world, whom he not only called just, as Cerdo did, but also cruel, savage, and evil. Hence Marcion is everywhere called by Clement, and above all in bks. 3 and 4 of the Stromateis, ungrateful towards his own author and the parent of all nature. The other God, he said, was the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, and he called him good, merciful, and compassionate. And he held these two gods to be separated from one another by a great distance. These things are recorded by Irenaeus (bk. 2, ch. 1; bk. 4, ch. 57), by Tertullian throughout, by Eusebius (bk. 9 of the History), and by Isidore. From this source the ravings and seeds of the Manichaeans seem to have been drawn, and that whole distinction between the race of Light and the race of Darkness, which was introduced by the Manichaeans. This is the first error of Marcion, which arose from a failure to grasp the distinction between the Old and New Testaments, and from some passages of Scripture wrongly explained.

units.la: 2 Error, non leuior: Christum Dominum nostrum non esse Filium Dei Creatoris, imò nec hominem verè fuisse, sed fictum & phantasticum corpus habuisse & gestasse, quod è cœlo non ex virginis Mariæ substantia sumpserit. Vt nec eum verè pro nobis esse passum, sed tantùm δοκήσει[?] & phantasmate quodam siue illusione. Et certè veteres quidam, quemadmodū Hilarius lib.19.de Trinit. dum nimium Christi humanam naturam à nostra separare conantur, huius Marcionitarum hærereos semina aut potius propagines in suis scriptis retinuerunt. Basilius lib.5.Contra Eunom. vocat corpus Christi ἀψυχώμυον[?], quòd fuerit à Spiritu S. creatum, non quòd Marcionitarum exoleto iam errori faueret. Marcion denique totam illam de Christi passione & morte historiam, tragicam tantùm fabulam fuisse contendebat, per quam præstigijs quibusdam Christus illuserit spe-ctatorum, imò verò discipulorum suorum oculis. Væ autem istius hominis furori, qui cùm diabolis ipsis testibus revincatur, Marc. 1. verf. 24. tamen & a Manichaeis antea, & nunc a quibusdam Anabaptistis defenditur. Itaque genea-logiam Christi a Matthaeo & Luca descriptam delebat ex Euangeliis, quod etiam postea fecit Faustus Manichęus, vt scribit Augustin. libr. 2. 3. & 7. Contra Faust. Hæc ipsa ex Simonianis fabulis hausta sunt. 3 Creationem mundi fabulosis figmentis inuoluit. Primum quidè mundum hunc totum esse vult opus indignum bono Deo, propter summam ἀπ[?]αξίαν quę in eo apparet. Nec distinguit insanus Marcion a Deo ne an a peccato hominis hæc labes mundo iam facto & pulcherrimo quidem infusa fit. Deinde cœlum ait esse ex materiæ (quam coæternam Deo constituit, vt Hermogeniani) suprema & purissima parte conditum: ex fæce eiusdem materiæ Tartarum siue infernum factū: ex mediis seu reliquis eius partibus mundi huius elementa & res cæteras productas. Hos furores Her-mogenes postea retinuit & auxit. 4 Legem Dei per Mosen promulgatam, itemque Pro-phetas veteris Testamenti omnes repudiat & re-jicit. Denique totum vetus Testamentum damnat. In quo varias ἀντιθέσεις, quemadmodum scribit Tertullian. afferebat, quas ipse collegit: & in hoc uno maxime laborauit ille venenatis scriptis & sibilis[?], vt Legem contrariam Euangelio χ̄ῡ πάντα[?] demonstraret. Itaque hoc proprium & principale opus Marcionis fuisse ait Tertullianus. 5 Carnis resurrectionem fore negauit, quòd animam solùm fore saluam credidit, non etiam corpus hominis. Atque hoc illi cum superioribus hæreticis & Simonianis com-mune fuit. 6 Per Iesu Christi Domini nostri descensum ad inferos animas Sodomitarum, Esau, Caini & aliorum reproborum & damnato-rum hominum è morte æterna ereptas, & in cœlum traductas. Id quod & Cainorum errorem confirmauit, & Limborum Papisticorū funda-menta iecit. 7 Nuptias dānauit, & ad suæ sec-tæ commendationem suos virginitatem & ca-stitatem profiteri voluit. Itaque etiam concor-dantes inter se coiuges separauit, & induxit sua-sitque fieri diuortia inter bene constituta matri-monia cōtra verbum Dei. Sed & carnium esum, imprimis autem animalium, prohibuisse Mar-cionem scribit Irenæus lib.1.cap.30. 8 Baptis-mum repetendum esse docuit, si quis post pri-mum acceptum lapsus est, nec id semel tantum, sed ter, & sæpius. & quoties quis peccaret. Ana-baptistarum familiam hæc opinio seminauit.
units.tr: 2 A no less serious error: that Christ our Lord is not the Son of God the Creator, and was not truly man either, but had and bore a fictitious and phantasmal body, which he took from heaven and not from the substance of the Virgin Mary. Likewise, he did not truly suffer for us, but only in appearance [δοκήσει] and by a kind of phantasm or illusion. Certainly some of the ancients, such as Hilary in book 19 of On the Trinity, while they try too hard to separate Christ's human nature from ours, have retained in their writings the seeds, or rather the offshoots, of this Marcionite heresy. Basil in book 5 Against Eunomius calls the body of Christ inanimate [ἀψυχώματον], because it was created by the Holy Spirit, not because he favoured the Marcionite error, which had by then died out. Marcion further contended that the whole history of Christ's passion and death was only a tragic fable, by which Christ had mocked the eyes of the spectators, or rather of his own disciples, with certain tricks. Woe to the madness of this man, who is refuted even by the devils as witnesses (Mark 1, verse 24), and yet was defended earlier by the Manichaeans and now by some Anabaptists. Accordingly he deleted from the Gospels the genealogy of Christ as written by Matthew and Luke, which Faustus the Manichaean later also did, as Augustine writes in books 2, 3 and 7 Against Faustus. These very things were drawn from the fables of the Simonians. 3 He wrapped the creation of the world in fabulous fictions. First, he holds that this whole world is a work unworthy of the good God, on account of the great unworthiness [ἀπαξία] that appears in it. And the mad Marcion does not distinguish whether this stain was poured into the world, already made and very beautiful, by God or by the sin of man. Then he says that the heavens were formed from the highest and purest part of matter (which he, like the Hermogenians, held to be coeternal with God); from the dregs of the same matter was made Tartarus, or hell; and from the middle or remaining parts of it were produced the elements and other things of this world. Hermogenes later retained and increased these frenzies. 4 He rejects and repudiates the law of God promulgated through Moses, and likewise all the Prophets of the Old Testament. Indeed he condemns the whole Old Testament. In this he brought forward various antitheses, as Tertullian writes, which he himself collected; and in this one matter above all he laboured with his poisonous writings and hisses, to demonstrate that the Law is contrary to the Gospel. Accordingly Tertullian says that this was Marcion's own and chief work. 5 He denied that there would be a resurrection of the flesh, since he believed that only the soul would be saved, not the body of man. And this was common to him with the earlier heretics and the Simonians. 6 Through the descent of our Lord Jesus Christ into hell, the souls of the Sodomites, Esau, Cain and other reprobate and condemned men were snatched from eternal death and transferred into heaven. This both confirmed the error of the Cainites and laid the foundations of the Papists' limbo. 7 He condemned marriage, and wished his followers to profess virginity and chastity in commendation of his sect. Accordingly he also separated spouses who agreed with each other, and induced and persuaded divorces between well-established marriages, contrary to the word of God. But Irenaeus, in book 1, chapter 30, writes that Marcion also forbade the eating of meat, and especially of animals. 8 He taught that baptism must be repeated if anyone fell after receiving it the first time, and not only once but three times, and as often as anyone sins. This opinion sowed the family of the Anabaptists.

units.la: 9 Pro mortuis Catechumenis quosdā substi-tuunt, quos illorum nomine baptizât, vt illi iam mortui salui fiant. Pauli loco abutentes qui est 1.Corinth.15.verf.29. Inde pro defunctis oratio, & animabus eorum intecesio inualuit. Quin e-tiam praeter veteris Ecclesiae morem praesenti-bus Catachumenis & baptizant, & sacramenta administrant. 10 Docent mulieres posse ba-ptizare, quod ipsum hodie Papistae ab iis acce-ptum retinent, & pro sana doctrina ample-ctun-tur: Can.Adiicimus.10.quæst.1. & can. Mulier. De consecrat.Distinct. 4. Atqui vetus Ecclesia pro haeresi semper id habuit, & rectè quidem & consentienter verbo Dei, 1.Timoth.2:1. Corin.
units.tr: 9 They substitute certain persons for the dead catechumens, whom they baptize in their name, so that those already dead may be saved. They abuse the words of Paul, 1 Corinthians 15, verse 29. From this came the custom of praying for the dead and interceding for their souls. Moreover, contrary to the custom of the ancient Church, they even baptize and administer the sacraments in the presence of catechumens. 10 They teach that women may baptize; the Papists themselves have retained this today, received from these heretics, and they praise it as sound doctrine: Can. Adiicimus, dist. 10, qu. 1, and Can. Mulier, De consecr., dist. 4. Yet the ancient Church always held this to be heresy, and rightly and in agreement with the word of God (1 Timothy 2; 1 Corinthians 14). And it was forbidden by the Council of Carthage that women should do this. Accordingly, Epiphanius, in book 3 of Against Heresies, especially against the Collyridians, writes that not even the Virgin Mary, the mother of Christ, was permitted to baptize.

units.la: 14.& est prohibitum concilio Carthaginensi, ne id mulieres faciant. Itaque ne virgini quidem Mariæ matri Christi baptizare licuisse scribit Epiphanius lib.3.Aduers. Hæres. maxime contra Collyridian.
units.tr: 14. 11 He defended the transmigration of human souls into other bodies, and metempsychosis [μετενσωμάτωσις]. This came from the dreams of the Platonists and Pythagoreans. Hence that opinion of some Schoolmen, "the soul which is separated from one body can perfect another," is without doubt false. For this reasoning confirms rebirth [παλιγγενεσία] and attacks the resurrection.

units.la: 11 Error.Animarum humana-rum in alia corpora reuolutionem & μετενσωμα-τῶν[?] defendit. Quod ex Platonicorum & Pythagoreorum somniis profectum est. Unde procul dubio falsa est illa quorundam Scholasticorum sententia, Potest anima quæ separatur a corpo-re uno, perficere aliud. Confirmat enim hæc ra-tio παλιγγενεσίαν[?], & oppugnat resurrectionem.
units.tr: 12. Finally, he condemned wars altogether, as the work of an evil god, and he thinks it is not lawful for a Christian magistrate to wage war for any cause, nor for a godly man to handle and bear arms. The Anabaptists have retained this. These are almost the poisonous weapons of this man, and the pestilential breath of this serpent against the orthodox faith.

units.la: 12 . Bella denique omnino damnauit tanquam mali dei opus, nec ea putat licere magistratui Christiano gerere vlla ex causa: nec homini pio tractare & gestare arma. Quod Anabaptistæ re-tinuerunt. Atque hæc ferè sunt venenata homi-nis tela, & flatus huius serpentis pestilentes ad-versus orthodoxam fidem.
units.tr: 12 . Finally, he condemned wars altogether, as the work of an evil god, and he thinks it is not lawful for a Christian magistrate to wage war for any cause, nor for a godly man to handle and bear arms. The Anabaptists have retained this. These are almost the poisonous weapons of this man, and the pestilential breath of this serpent against the orthodox faith.

units.la: {3} Sed Eusebius.) Locus Eusebij est libr. 3. Histor.ecclesiast. cap.13. Et facit Theodoretus hunc Synerum discipulum Marcionis libr.1. de Fabul.Hæreticor.
units.tr: {3} But Eusebius. The passage of Eusebius is in book 3 of his Ecclesiastical History, chapter 13. And Theodoret makes this Syneros a disciple of Marcion, in book 1 of On the Heretical Fables.

units.la: CAP. XXIII. Apellitæ cur dicti. Erroris autem eorum capita tria recensentur.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIII. Why the Apellites are so called. Three heads of their error are listed.

units.la: Pellitæ sunt, quorum Apelles est princeps, qui{1} duos quidem introducit deos, unum bonum, alterum malum, non tamen in duobus diversis, aut inter se adversis esse esse principiis: sed unum esse principium, Deum scili-cet bonum, & ab illo factum esse alterum, qui cum malignus esset, inventus est in sua mundum malignitate fecisse. Hunc Apellem dicunt quidam etiam de Christo tam falsa sensisse, ut diceret eum non quidem carnem duxisse de coelo, sed ex elementis mundi accepisse, qua [?] mundo reddidit, cum sine carne resurgens in coelum ascendit.
units.tr: The Apellites are named after Apelles, their leader, who indeed introduces two gods, one good and one evil, but holds that they are not two different and mutually opposed principles. He holds that there is one principle, namely God the good, and that the other was made by him, and that this other, being malicious, made the world in its own malice. Some say that Apelles also taught such false things about Christ, namely that he did not indeed take flesh from heaven, but received it from the elements of the world, and that when he rose without flesh and ascended into heaven, he gave back to the world what he had received from it.

units.la: Quàm varie statim diffe-renta fuerit Marcionitarum hæresis docet Irenæus, & post eum Euseb. lib. 5. Histor. ecclesiast. cap. 13. Nam quemadmodum Tertullianus ait, Idem licuit Marcionitis quod Marcioni, de arbitrio suo fidem innovare. Quò fit ut inter hæreticos schismata nascatur, nec tamè schismata videantur, quia cùm sint, nō apparent esse schismata, propterea quòd licet cuique animi sui sententiam tueri, & liberè profiteri exemplo præceptorum. Inter primos verò & notissimos Marcionis discipulos hi recensentur, Potitus, Blastus, Synerus, Basilicus, & Lucianus quidam, à quo Lucianistæ hæretici dicti sunt, non ij quidem qui Arriani fuerunt, & his longè sunt tempore posteriores, quorum autor Lucianus tempore Constantini Magni vixit, ut ait Epiphanius: sed hi sunt Lucianistæ qui Marcionitarum errores amplexi, nuptias damna-runt tanquam mali Dei opus & præceptum, & Deo Euangelij contrarias, de quo Tertullianus & Epiphanius. Luciano igitur in schola successit Apelles, ætate iunior, & ipse tamen auditor Marcionis, qui propriam & à se denominatam hæresin condidit, quos alij Apellitas vocant, vt hic Augustinus & Isidorus: alij Apelleianos, vt Epiphanius, alij Apellicanos vel Apellicianos, vt Tertullianus in libr. De carne Christi. Fuit hic Apelles non pictor ille memoratus, qui ante tempora manifestati in carne Christi vixit, fuitque natione Græcus: non etiam is qui vt vir sanctus à Sozomeno libr.6.cap.28.commendatur, fuitque anachoreta: sed hic Apelles fuit natione Syrus, Marcionis discipulus, qui propter scortationes ab oculis Marcionis magistri Alexandriam Roma fecesit. Primùm enim cum Philumena quadam, quam Prophetissam vocabat: post autem cum alia passim scortatus est, quanquam præceptor Marcion doceret suos vovere cotinentiam. Florere verò coepit postquam à magistri dogmate declinasset in alium errorem, & in Ægyptum venisset, ubi, quemadmodum & in Asia, maximè propagata est hæc hæresis. Hic enim adulter & scortator impurus magnam vitæ sanctimoniam iactabat, eóque nomine apud multos [illegible, ~7 letters] commendabatur.
units.tr: How greatly the heresy of the Marcionites differed from the start is shown by Irenaeus, and after him by Eusebius, book 5 of the Ecclesiastical History, chapter 13. As Tertullian says, the Marcionites had the same liberty as Marcion, to renew the faith at their own pleasure. Hence schisms arise among the heretics, yet they do not appear as schisms, because although they are schisms, they do not look like schisms: each man is free to defend the opinion of his own mind and to profess it openly, on the model of his teachers. Among the first and best-known disciples of Marcion are counted Potitus, Blastus, Synerus, Basilicus, and a certain Lucian, from whom the heretics called Lucianists took their name. These are not the Lucianists who were Arians, who came much later; the author of that sect, Lucian, lived in the time of Constantine the Great, as Epiphanius says. The Lucianists of whom we speak embraced the errors of the Marcionites and condemned marriage as the work and command of an evil god, contrary to the Gospel of God; Tertullian and Epiphanius write of them. So after Lucian, Apelles succeeded him in the school. He was younger than Lucian, yet he too was a hearer of Marcion. He founded a heresy of his own, named after himself, which some call Apellites, as Augustine and Isidore do here, others Apelleians, as Epiphanius does, and others Apellicans or Apellicians, as Tertullian does in his book On the Flesh of Christ. This Apelles was not that famous painter, who lived before the time of the manifestation of Christ in the flesh, and who was a Greek by nation. Nor was he that man commended as a holy man by Sozomen, book 6, chapter 28, who was an anchorite. This Apelles was a Syrian by nation, a disciple of Marcion, who left Rome and Alexandria because of his fornications, which offended the eyes of his master Marcion. First he fornicated with a certain Philumena, whom he called a prophetess; afterwards he indulged in fornication with others, although his teacher Marcion taught his followers to vow continence. He began to flourish when he had turned away from his master's doctrine to another error and had come into Egypt, where this heresy, as also in Asia, spread most widely. For this adulterer and impure fornicator boasted of great holiness of life, and was for that reason commended by many [illegible, about 7 letters].

units.la: Romæ autem fuit sub Eleuthero Pontifice Romano & Commodo Imperatore, adeò vt huius hæresis cœpisse demum videatur anno post Christum passum 150. & tempore Tertulliani adhuc viuebant qui Apellem Romæ viderant, & post Tatianum hæreticum vixit, cùm Pantænus Alexandriæ doceret. Scripsit quædam veluti librum quem Philumenæ scorti sui φανερώ-σεις & revelationes appellavit, item alium quem inscripsit, Syllogismi, vt tradit Tertullian. Philumenam tamen quidam ad sequentem hæresin referunt. Non videtur diu perstitisse hoc virus. Noua enim nouorum ex eadem Marcionis schola haereticorum successione nomen Apel-litarum extinctum est. Fuerunt tamen perniciosissimae, & plenae blasphemiae illius hypo-theses.
