units.tr: He was at Rome under Eleutherus, the Roman bishop, and under the emperor Commodus, so that this heresy seems to have begun only about 150 years after the passion of Christ. In Tertullian's time there were still living those who had seen Apelles at Rome. He lived after the heretic Tatian, while Pantaenus was teaching at Alexandria. He wrote certain works, such as a book which he called, after his fornicating companion Philumena, Revelations [φανερώσεις], and another which he entitled Syllogisms, as Tertullian reports. Some, however, refer Philumena to the following heresy. This poison does not seem to have lasted long. For the name of the Apellites was extinguished when new heretics arose from the same school of Marcion in succession. Yet those hypotheses were most pernicious and full of blasphemy.

units.la: 2 Qui duos.) Varia sunt erroris Apelleiani capita, hic tria enumerantur. 1 Unum esse Deum [?] & summum, vt ait Epiphanius, qui sit aliorum deorum principium, & velut informator siue essentiator, quemadmodum postea loquuti sunt impiissimi Seruetani. Itaq; a praeceptore discesisse ille, quod Marcion deos duos & aequales constituebat: hic vero vnum tantum, quia natura singularitatem amat principiorum. Ab hoc autem summo Deo esse & alium secundum qui sit quidem ipse lucidus, inclytus, gloriosus & [illegible, ~6 letters], id est, igneus (quia nimirum Mosi in rubo ardenti Deus apparuerat) & is fecundus est Deus Israel, creator mundi, qui quia postea malus extitit, condidit mundum malis plenum. Haec deorum propago ex Platonicorum & Valetinianorum sordibus est. Manichaei etiam ex his lacunis suos foetores hauserunt postea. 2 Christum corpus quidem habuisse ex mundi substantia, vt ait Theodoretus, id est, ex 4. elementis & syderea quadam materia compactum, quam quum e caelo veniret, excerpsit. Hinc Seruetanum delirium, & Manichaeanum, eum tamen non esse hominem, nec carnem humanam induisse, quod illa plena est ignominiae & dedecoris. Itaque quod Christus homo videtur fuisse, phātasmate tātum quodam talem visum esse, non quòd reipsa homo esset» vel passus,vel crucifixus, vel resurgens. 3 E-undem Christum quum in cælum ascenderet, corpus illud quod ex elementis, non ex Maria virgine assumpserat, depositisse, & quanque e-ius partem in sua principia rediisse, aeream ad aerem: cœlestem ad sydera: igneam ad ignem. Vnde solum Christi spiritum in cælo esse, non etiam eius corpus. 4 Legem Dei & Prophetas reiicit, imprimis autem Mosem damnat, adversus quem multa scripsit, tanquam falsi conuicturus eum. 5 Resurrectionem carnis fore negauit, id quod & Simoniani & Marcionitæ sumpserunt à Sadduceis, quemadmodū Ter-tullianus, & rectè quidem, sentit. Et hæ sunt tetterrimi hominis adversus Deum blasphemiæ, adversus quas etiam Theodotion Tatianus scripsit, quemadmodum Platina scribit.
units.tr: 2 Who introduce two.) The errors of the Apellean heresy are many, and here three heads are enumerated. (1) There is one God, supreme, as Epiphanius says, who is the source of other gods, and as it were their shaper or essence-giver, just as the most impious Servetians later spoke. So he departed from his teacher: Marcion posited two gods, equal to each other, whereas he posited only one, since nature loves the singleness of principles. From this supreme God there proceeds another, subordinate, who is himself bright, renowned, glorious and [illegible, about 6 letters], that is, fiery (because God had appeared to Moses in the burning bush). This second God is the God of Israel, the creator of the world, who afterwards became evil and built a world full of evils. This line of gods comes from the filth of the Platonists and Valentinians. The Manichaeans later also drew their stinking dregs from these same sinks. (2) Christ had a body indeed from the substance of the world, as Theodoret says, that is, compacted of the four elements and of a certain starry matter, which he gathered up when he came from heaven. Hence the Servetian and Manichaean delirium, that he was not a man, nor did he put on human flesh, because that is full of shame and disgrace. Therefore, although Christ seemed to be a man, he appeared so only by a certain phantasm, and was not really a man, nor did he really suffer, nor was crucified, nor rise again. (3) The same Christ, when he ascended into heaven, laid aside that body which he had taken from the elements and not from the Virgin Mary, and each part of it returned to its own principles: the airy part to the air, the heavenly part to the stars, the fiery part to fire. Hence only the spirit of Christ is in heaven, not also his body. (4) He rejects the law of God and the Prophets, and above all condemns Moses, against whom he wrote much, as if he were going to convict him of being a false prophet. (5) He denied that there would be a resurrection of the flesh, a view which the Simonians and Marcionites took over from the Sadducees, as Tertullian rightly judges. These are the most foul blasphemies of this wretched man against God, against which Theodotion and Tatian also wrote, as Platina writes.

units.la: CAP. XXIIII. Seueriani cur sic appellati. Erroris autem eorum capita quatuor explicata.
units.tr: CHAPTER 24. Why the Severians are so called. Four heads of their error are explained.

units.la: Eueriani à Seuero{1} exorti, vinum{2} non bibunt, eo quòd fabulosa vanitate de Satana & terra germinasse asserunt vitem. Etiam ipsi non sanam doctrinam suam, quibus volunt, inflant[?] principum nominibus: Carnis resurrectionem cum veteri Testamento respuentes. Hic præterea Philumenam quandam puellam di-cebat inspiratam diuinitus ad prænuntianda futura,ad quam somnia atque astus animi sui referens, diuinationibus seu praesagijs eius secretim erat soli- tus praemoneri, eodem phantasmate eidem Philume- na pueri habitu se demonstrante, qui puer apparens Christum se aliquando, aliquando esse afferebat Pau- lum, a quo phantasmate scisciitans ea soleret respon- dere quae se audientibus diceret. Nonnulla quoque illam miracula operari solitam, inter quae illud prae- cipuum, quod in angustissimi oris ampullam vitream panem grandem immitteret, eumque extremis digi- tulis leuare soleret illaesum, eoque solo quasi diuini- tus sibi cibo dato fuisset contenta.
units.tr: The Severians, who arose from Severus, do not drink wine, because in their fabulous vanity they assert that the vine sprang from Satan and the earth. They also puff up their unsound doctrine with the names of princes, and they reject the resurrection of the flesh together with the Old Testament. Moreover, Severus used to say that a certain girl, Philumena, had been inspired by God to foretell the future. He would refer his dreams and the movements of his mind to her, and he was accustomed to be secretly instructed in advance by her divinations or predictions, since the same phantom appeared to Philumena in the form of a boy. This boy, appearing, sometimes declared that he was Christ and sometimes that he was Paul. From this phantom Severus would inquire, and she would answer what she said to her hearers. She was also said to work many miracles, of which the chief was this: she would put a large loaf of bread into a glass flask with a very narrow mouth, and would lift it out unharmed with her fingertips. She was content with that alone as food, as though it had been given to her by God.

units.la: I Seuero.) Superiori capite dictum est Marcionitarum haeresin tanquam truncum in varios statim ramos pullulasse,& eos quidem in felices & inauspicatos, e quibus etiam haec haeresis vnus est. Dicti vero sunt hi Seueriani, quemadmodum etiam Isidorus vocat, non Seueritae, vt duae haereses quae & diuerso tempore natae sunt,& de diuerso dogmate distinguerētur. Nā Seueriani videntur exorti circa annum a Chri- sto passo 156.extremo tempore Episcopatus E- leutheri Romani Pontificis,& sub Commodo imperatore. Seueritae autem qui & ipsi a quodā Seuero dicti sunt, sub Anastasio imperatore Constantinopolitano, post consilium Chalce- donense.Fuerunt autem & alij haeretici nomi- ne Seueriani praeter hos, nec procul tamen ab his nostris remoti,sed qui Tatiani,non proprie Marcionitae erant, & qui Legem & Prophetas admittebant, quos hi nostri Seueriani repu- diant & reijciunt, de quibus Tatianis Seuerianis agit & Eusebius lib.4.Hist.cap.28. & Theodoret.libr.1.Haeret.fabular.qui quum sint à nostris diuersi, quidam tamen eos imperitè confundunt. Fuit igitur Seuerus is de quo nunc agimus, Apellis in schola Marcionitarum successor, vel etiam, vt scribit Epiphanius, illi συγγενὴς[?], cuius tamen haeresis aliquanto posterius innotuit, maximè in Orientali Syria, quum iam Apelles in eadem Syria Meridionali & in Aegypto instituisset suam: sed Apellis aemulatione impulsus Seuerus, errorem & ipse suum cudere voluit. In postrema igitur tempora Eleutheri Rom. Episcopi incidit, adeò vt nec Irenaeo nota fuerit haec pestis, nec iis patribus & Ecclesiasticis scriptoribus, qui ante Commodi imperium mortui sunt. Quò magis miror quid Platinae venerit in mentem vt Seuerianos sub Pio primo Rom. Episcopo collocaret, qui annis plus quàm 27, Eleutherum antecessit. Fuisse autem sub Eleuthero vel ex eo maximè apparet, quòd idem Platina scribit, eum voluisse, ne quis vllā[?] cibi genus propter superstitionem respueret, quos fert humana consuetudo, quia iam tum sobolescebant & inualescebant istae de vino, & carnibus reiiciendis haereses. Non videtur tamen haec diutius ipso suo nomine durasse, quia agmine aliarum haereseon eodem tempore nascentium ingruente suffocata est, & velut in cunis extincta.
units.tr: 1 Severus.) In the previous chapter it was said that the heresy of the Marcionites, like a trunk, at once sprouted into various branches, some fortunate and some ill-omened, and this heresy is one of them. These are called Severians, as Isidore also calls them, not Severites, so that the two heresies, which arose at different times and differ in doctrine, may be distinguished. For the Severians seem to have arisen around the year 156 after Christ's passion, in the last period of the episcopate of Eleutherius, Bishop of Rome, and under the emperor Commodus. The Severites, who were also named after a certain Severus, arose under the emperor Anastasius of Constantinople, after the Council of Chalcedon. There were also other heretics called Severians besides these, not far removed from our Severians, but they were followers of Tatian rather than strictly Marcionites, and they admitted the Law and the Prophets, which our Severians reject and cast off. Concerning these Tatianist Severians, Eusebius also treats in book 4 of his History, chapter 28, and Theodoret in book 1 of his Heretical Fables. Since these are different from ours, some ignorantly confuse them. The Severus with whom we are now concerned was therefore a successor of Apelles in the school of the Marcionites. Or, as Epiphanius writes, he was a kinsman [συγγενής] of Apelles, although his heresy became known a little later, especially in eastern Syria, when Apelles had already established his own in the same southern part of Syria and in Egypt. But Severus, moved by rivalry with Apelles, wished to forge his own error too. He therefore fell into the last times of Eleutherius, Bishop of Rome, so that this plague was known neither to Irenaeus nor to those Fathers and ecclesiastical writers who died before the reign of Commodus. I wonder all the more what came into Platina's mind, that he placed the Severians under Pius I, Bishop of Rome, who preceded Eleutherius by more than 27 years. That they existed under Eleutherius is shown most of all by the fact that the same Platina writes that Severus wished that no kind of food be rejected out of superstition, such as human custom bears, because already at that time these heresies about wine and the rejection of meat were growing and gaining strength. Yet this sect does not seem to have lasted long under its own name, since it was smothered by the onrush of other heresies arising at the same time, and was extinguished, as it were, in its cradle.

units.la: Haec iam haeresis docet quò Satan spectarit, quum de mundi creatione fabulas spargeret, nempe vt animis hominum scrupulum iniiceret, ne liberè Dei creaturis uris cum gratiarum actione uterentur, sed iis abstinerent velut fœdis, spurcis, & diabolicis operibus. Quod iam in Saturnianorum haereti-corum dogmate apparuit, & adhuc magis in Encratitarum & Manichaeorum erroribus vi-debitur. Recitantur autem hoc loco quatuor huius haeresis hypotheses. 1 Vino abstinent tanquam spurca creatura. Vinum enim ex diaboli in serpentis forma cum terra coeuntis femine productum putat, & vitem enatam. Nam eam tortuosam esse docent. Acinum autem, qui est in botro, similem veneno serpentis, imo vi-num ipsum uti venenum homini esse noxium. Botrum denique qui niger est, similem esse dra-coni inuoluto. Hae sunt fabulosae de mudi creatione narrationis consecutiones & fructus. At qui Dominus noster Iesus Christus vinum bi-bit, & vinum pro signo in sacrosancta Coena instituit. Addidit tamen Platina Seucrianos e-tiam damnasse carnis esum, quod unde sum-pserit, non video, nisi ex eo fortasse quod Mar-cionem, quem sectabatur, scribit Irenaeus lib.1. cap.30. carne animalium vesci suos prohibuis-se. 2 Error, Vetus Testamentum & Prophe-tas reiiciunt Severiani, ipsi autem apocryphos quosdã libros habent, quibus utuntur. 3 Car-nis resurrectionem, quemadmodum superio-res negant; & proinde vitam aeternam. Nam, ut ait Augustinus lib.16. contra Faust. cap.29. Mortuum Christum & Pagani credunt: resurrexisse autem Christum, propria est fides Christiano-rum. 4 Mundi creationem certis quibusdam potestatibus & Angelis tribuit Severus, quos barbaris & magicis nominibus ad terrendos simplices vocat, & his praestigiis doctrinæ suæ virus celat. 5 Mulieres tanquam diaboli & infelicis potestatis opus detestatur, & auersatur, præclarissimum Dei opus calumnians, quod ad ipsius Dei imaginem conditum esse docet ipsa Scriptura, Genef.i. Hinc confirmatum errorem de impuritate nuptiarum fuisse nemo sanus ignorat. 6 Magia & præstigiis utitur ex Philumenæ suæ præcepto & exemplo, quâ verum est dæmonem familiarem habuisse, quæ, quod fieri vix posse videtur, efficeret, illudens oculis hominum. Ergo quod ait Christus fieri non posse ut camelus per foramen acus ingrediatur, Matth.19, iste præstigiator quid simile se præstare, sed ministerio diaboli ostentauit. Quæ autem de Philumena scorto ab isto Seuero adamata scribit Augustinus hoc loco, alij ad superiorem hæreticum nempe Apellem referunt, quemadmodum diximus, quanquam fortasse uterque suam Philumenam, & suum scortum habuit.
units.tr: This heresy now shows what Satan aimed at when he spread fables about the creation of the world: namely, to put a scruple into men's minds, so that they would not freely use God's creatures with thanksgiving, but would abstain from them as foul, filthy, and devilish works. This had already appeared in the doctrine of the Saturnian heretics, and it will be seen even more in the errors of the Encratites and Manichaeans. Four hypotheses of this heresy are set out in this place. (1) They abstain from wine as an unclean creature. For they think that wine was produced from the seed of the devil mingling with the earth in the form of a serpent, and that the vine sprang up from it. For they teach that the vine is twisted, that the grape in the cluster is like the poison of a serpent, and that wine itself is harmful to man like poison. Finally, the black cluster is like a coiled dragon. These are the consequences and fruits of that fabulous narrative about the creation of the world. But our Lord Jesus Christ drank wine, and instituted wine as a sign in the most holy Lord's Supper. Platina added that the Severians also condemned the eating of flesh; I do not see where he got this, unless perhaps from the fact that Irenaeus writes, in book 1, chapter 30, that Marcion, whom they followed, forbade his followers to eat the flesh of animals. (2) The Severians reject the Old Testament and the Prophets, but they have certain apocryphal books which they use. (3) Like the earlier heretics, they deny the resurrection of the flesh, and consequently eternal life. For, as Augustine says in book 16 against Faustus, chapter 29: "Even the pagans believe that Christ died; that Christ rose again is the peculiar faith of Christians." (4) Severus attributes the creation of the world to certain powers and angels, whom he calls by barbarous and magical names to terrify simple people, and by these tricks he conceals the poison of his teaching. (5) He detests and shuns women as the work of the devil and of an unhappy power, slandering the most excellent work of God, although Scripture itself, Gen. 1, teaches that they were made in the image of God. Hence no sane person is unaware that the error about the impurity of marriage was confirmed by this. (6) He uses magic and tricks, following the precept and example of his Philumena, who truly had a familiar demon, and who did what seems hardly possible, deceiving the eyes of men. Therefore, when Christ says that it is impossible for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle (Matt. 19), this trickster showed that he could do something similar, but by the ministry of the devil. But the things Augustine here writes about Philumena, a harlot beloved by this Severus, others refer to the earlier heretic, Apelles, as we have said, although perhaps each of them had his own Philumena and his own harlot.

units.la: CAP. XXV. Taciani,qui & Encratitæ,unde dicti. Erroris autem eorum hypothecses quatuor describuntur.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXV. The Tatians, who are also called Encratites, and why they are so named. Four hypotheses of their error are set out.

units.la: Taciani{1} à Tacio quodam instituti sunt, qui & Encratitæ{2} appellati. Nuptias damnant{3} atque omnino pares eas formicationibus aliisque corruptionibus faciunt, nec recipiunt in suorum numerum coniugio utentem, sive marem, sive fœminam. Non vescuntur carnibus, eàsque omnes abominantur. Prolationes quasdam fabulosas sæculorum etiam ipsi sapiunt. Salutis primi hominis contradicunt. Epiphanius Tacianos & Encratitas ita discernit, ut Encratitas Taciani schismaticos dicant.
units.tr: The Tacianists were founded by a certain Tatian, and they were also called Encratites. They condemn marriage and make it wholly equal to fornication and other corruptions. They do not admit into their number anyone who is married, whether male or female. They do not eat meat and abominate all of it. They also themselves favour certain fabulous genealogies of the ages. They contradict the salvation of the first man. Epiphanius distinguishes the Tacianists and the Encratites in such a way that they call the Encratites schismatic Tacianists.

units.la: 1 (A Tacio.) Suspicor mendum esse in impressis, & pro Tacio reponendum Taciano. Nam constanter omnes authores Tacianum vocant, non Tacium, veluti Irenæus, Tertullianus, Clemens Strom. lib. 3. Epiphanius ipse, quem in hoc toto opere sequitur χ̄ [illegible, ~6 letters] Augustinus, & ita Isidorus quoque suo seculo legebat apud Augustinum, cuius hoc scriptum in epitomen redegit libro 8. Etymolog. nisi fortasse idem & Tacius & Tacianus ἐγκρατικῶς vulgò diceretur. Fuit autem hæc hæresis fœcundissima. Aquarios enim, Encratitas, Valesios, & Apostolicos peperit, sed tamen quæ nihil aliud est ipsa, nisi infelicissima multarum aliarum farrago & colluvies, &, ut scribit Irenæus libro 1. cap. 36. connexio quæ partim ex Valentinianorum errore, partim ex Marcionitarum dogmate (fuit enim contemporaneus Marcioni Tacianus ) partim etiam ex Simonianorum deliriis velut hydra ex pluribus capitibus conflata est: id quod cum Tertulliano docet Theodoretus libro 1. Videntur autem Taciani exorti post Marcionitas, quorum fuerunt discipuli, & sub Sotere Episcopo Romano, & M. Antonino Philosopho circa annum à passo Christo 142. quanquam Epiphanius scribit eum Seuero de quo diximus,
units.tr: 1 (From Tacius.) I suspect there is an error in the printed text, and that Tacianus should be put in place of Tacius. For all the authors consistently call him Tacianus, not Tacius: Irenaeus, Tertullian, Clement in the third book of the Stromata, Epiphanius himself (whom the whole of this work follows), χ̄ [illegible, about six letters] Augustine. Isidore too read it so in Augustine in his own age, and he abridged this writing of Augustine in book 8 of the Etymologies, unless perhaps the same man was commonly called both Tacius and Tacianus ἐγκρατικῶς. This heresy was, however, extremely fruitful. For it gave birth to the Aquarians, the Encratites, the Valesians and the Apostolics. Yet it is itself nothing other than the most unhappy hodgepodge and jumble of many other heresies, and, as Irenaeus writes in book 1, chapter 36, a combination which was formed like a hydra with many heads, partly from the error of the Valentinians, partly from the doctrine of the Marcionites (for Tatian was a contemporary of Marcion), and partly also from the delusions of the Simonians. Theodoret, in book 1, teaches this together with Tertullian. The Tacianists seem to have arisen after the Marcionites, whose disciples they were, under Soter, Bishop of Rome, and under the philosopher Marcus Antoninus, about the year 142 after the suffering of Christ. Although Epiphanius writes that he succeeded Severus, of whom we have spoken,

units.la: { } Ἐγκρατικῶς: as printed, with a small accent over the first syllable. successisse, in quo fallitur. Venit quidem sub Antonino Pio Romā Tacianus è Syria, quemadmodum Epiphanius tradit, sed illic in Christiana Ecclesia & orthodoxa fide perstitit toto Iustini Martyris tempore, qui Taciani præceptor erat, & Samaritanus natione, sed tamen summus philosophus, & verè pius & Christianus. Ergo mortuo Iustino, cuius metu & reuerentia tenebatur (quemadmodum impostor Ochinus P. Martyris pudore in sana Ecclesiæ doctrina retentus est aliquandiu) mortuo, inquam, Iustino, vt ipse sibi nomen aliquod compararet, nouam sectam instituit Tacianus. Fuit enim φιλόξενος[?], vt etiam Eufeb. lib.4. Hist. scribit. Atque hic Tacianus alius fuit ab eo qui Alexandriæ Episcopus sub imperio Iuliani Apostatæ vixit, de quo Ruffinus libro 2. Historiæ. & alius etiam ab eo qui fuit Phryx, & sub eodem imperatore martyr pro nomine Christi, quemadmodum refert Sozomen. lib.5. cap.11. Fuit e-nim hic noster Tacianus natione Syrus, è Me-sopotamia, quod cum Clemente lib.3. Strom. tradit Epiphan. lib.1. Tom.3. in ethnicorum philosophia apprimè doctus, rhetor magnus, qui aliquot suæ eruditionis monimenta reliquit, eáque plura, sed imprimis librum contra Gentiles in quo Iustinum laudauit: librum De perfectione secundum Seruatorem, cuius meminit Clemens, & Harmoniam Euangeliorum, quam appellauit διὰ τεσσάρων[?]: cuius meminerunt omnes, & quæ diu vsum habuit in Ecclesia, sed quum pro Euangeliis substituerctur, & in eo o-pere genealogiam Christi, quia nuptias danabat, abscidisset, à Theodoreto reiecta est hæc Harmonia, & damnata, quemadmodum scribit ipse lib.1.Hæretic.fabul. Cœpit autem hæc hæ-resis Romæ, sed statim in Asiam delata est, & Antiochiam Syriæ, Mesopotamiam, Pisidiam, Pamphyliam, & vniuersam pene minorem Asiam. i. Græcos curiosos homines, & nouis doctrinis iam assuetos, persuasit, quos corrupit, tam grata & plausibilis propter fucatæ continentiæ opinionem nimirum visa est. Denique infelicis-sime & saeuissime in Phrygiam, & Galatiâ graf-fata est, vbi tandem pessimum fructum & sobolem viperinam, nimirum Montanistarum lucem & hæresin peperit. Habuit Tacianus Seuerum quendam scholæ suæ successorem, non eum quidem de quo iam diximus: sed alium, à quo Seueriani Taciani dicti sunt, vt Theodoretus vocat. Propagatus vero hic error est latis-sime & citissime, quia venena facillime serpunt. Durauit autem diutissime. Nam in Phrygia Encratitarum conuentus publici erant, maximè Ancyræ, quæ fuit metropolis, & ad tempora vsque Iuliani imperatoris durarunt, qui Bufirin episcopum Encratitarum interfecit, vt scribit Sozom.lib.5.cap.11. Scribit tamen Epiphan.sua ætate iam eorum [illegible, ~9 letters] esse desiuisse: sed interpolata tantum fuit hæresis, non sublata. Nam Montanistæ & Manichæi huius feminis diabolici seges & propago fuit, & hodie etiam in Papatu multa Tacianorum dogmata retinen-tur & confirmantur.
units.tr: {Ἐγκρατικῶς: as printed, with a small accent over the first syllable.} in which he is mistaken. Tatian indeed came to Rome from Syria under Antoninus Pius, as Epiphanius reports, but there he remained in the Christian Church and the orthodox faith throughout the time of Justin Martyr, who was Tatian's teacher. Justin was a Samaritan by nation, yet a supreme philosopher, and truly pious and Christian. Therefore, when Justin had died, by whose fear and reverence Tatian was restrained (just as the impostor Ochino, restrained for a while by respect for Peter Martyr, kept to the sound doctrine of the Church), when Justin, I say, had died, Tatian founded a new sect in order to win for himself some name. For he was fond of strangers [φιλόξενος?], as Eusebius also writes in book 4 of the History. This Tatian was different from the one who lived as Bishop of Alexandria under the reign of Julian the Apostate, of whom Rufinus speaks in book 2 of the History, and different also from the one who was a Phrygian, and under the same emperor died a martyr for the name of Christ, as Sozomen relates in book 5, chapter 11. For our Tatian was by nation a Syrian, from Mesopotamia, as Clement reports in book 3 of the Stromata, and Epiphanius in book 1, volume 3. He was thoroughly learned in the philosophy of the Gentiles, a great rhetorician, who left several monuments of his learning, and more besides, but chiefly a book against the Gentiles in which he praised Justin; a book On Perfection according to the Saviour, which Clement mentions; and a Harmony of the Gospels, which he called dia tessaron [διὰ τεσσάρων]. All mention this, and it was long in use in the Church. But when it was substituted for the Gospels, and in that work he had cut out the genealogy of Christ, because he condemned marriage, this Harmony was rejected by Theodoret and condemned, as he himself writes in book 1 of his Heretical Fables. This heresy began at Rome, but was at once carried into Asia, and it persuaded Antioch in Syria, Mesopotamia, Pisidia, Pamphylia and almost all of Asia Minor, that is, the curious Greeks, already accustomed to new doctrines, whom it corrupted; so attractive and plausible did it seem, no doubt because of the reputation of a counterfeit continence. Finally, it raged most unhappily and most savagely in Phrygia and Galatia, where at last it brought forth its worst fruit and viperine offspring, namely the light and heresy of the Montanists. Tatian had a certain Severus as successor to his school, not the one of whom we have already spoken, but another, from whom the Severians were called Tatianists, as Theodoret calls them. This error spread very widely and very quickly, because poisons creep most easily. It lasted for a very long time. For in Phrygia the assemblies of the Encratites were public, especially at Ancyra, which was the metropolis, and they lasted down to the time of the emperor Julian, who put to death Bufirinus, bishop of the Encratites, as Sozomen writes in book 5, chapter 11. Epiphanius nevertheless writes that in his own age they had already ceased to exist, but the heresy was only altered, not abolished. For it became the seed and offspring of the devilish Montanists and Manichees, and even today in the Papacy many Tatianist doctrines are retained and confirmed.

units.la: Encratitæ dicti sunt à professione, quòd cœlibatum, & à vino atque esu carnium abstinentiam profiterentur. unde ὑπὸ τῆς ἐγκρατείας vocantur Ἐγκρατῖται, ad licentiam vitiorum nomine conficto. Sic semper Satan homines delusit, ut potius externa quædam opera, quàm doctrinam sanâ in pietate & religione sectarentur & probarent. Hos igitur Encratitas vult Epiphanius lib.2. Tom.1. esse schisma & ὑπόστασιμα [?]. i. defractum à Tacianorum stirpe furculum. Eusebius tamen lib.4. cap.27. & 28. Tacianum horum parentem & authorem fuisse scribit. Hi usi sunt apocryphis libris præter cætera dogmata, & Thomæ & Andreæ Apostolorum scriptis confictis. Hoc veneni genus suo tempore plurimùm in Phrygia, quæ κεκαυ-μένη dicebatur, fuisse & pullulasse scribit Epiphanius. Taciani verò non tantùm Encratitæ dicti sunt, sed etiam tertio quodã nomine, quemadmodum Theodoretus narrat, quò maior pudor à Christianis hominibus tanto errori incuteretur, sed peruicit Satan, ut nihilo minus ad tempus regnaret et obtineret, sic Domino Deo verbi sui contemptum vlciscente, & socordiam hominum excitate. Nominati sunt igitur etiam hi ipsi ὑδροπαραστάται [?] Hydroparastatæ. i. Aquæ adhibitores & repræsentatores, quòd in Eucharistia pro vino, quòd tamen diserte Dominus esse voluit alterum Cœnæ sacræ signum, aquam ipsi substituerent. Vinum enim ex Christianorum Ecclesia & usu prætextu cuiusdam sanctioris abstinentiæ, & maioris sobrietatis prorsus expulerant Taciani, quòd vulgus hominum vino ad ebrietatem abutitur. Hi sunt quos infrà Aquarios Augustinus appellat.
units.tr: The Encratites were so called from their profession, because they professed celibacy and abstinence from wine and the eating of flesh. Hence they are called Encratites [Ἐγκρατῖται] under the pretext of self-control [ὑπὸ τῆς ἐγκρατείας], with a name invented to cover licence in vice. Thus Satan has always deceived men, so that they pursue and prize certain external works rather than doctrine grounded in sound piety and religion. Epiphanius, in book 2, volume 1, therefore wishes these Encratites to be a schism and a branch [ὑποστασιμα?], that is, a shoot broken off from the stock of the Tacianists. Yet Eusebius, in book 4, chapters 27 and 28, writes that Tatian was their parent and author. Besides their other doctrines, they used apocryphal books, and the writings of Thomas and Andrew, which were fabricated. Epiphanius writes that this kind of poison was very prevalent and sprouted up in his time, especially in Phrygia, which was called "burnt" [κεκαυμένη]. The Tacianists were called not only Encratites, but also by a third name, as Theodoret relates, so that greater shame might be struck into Christian men by so great an error. But Satan was persistent, so that nonetheless he reigned and held on for a time, the Lord God thus avenging the contempt of his Word and rousing the carelessness of men. These men were therefore also named Hydroparastatae [ὑδροπαραστάται], that is, bringers-in and representers of water, because they substituted water for wine in the Eucharist, although the Lord clearly wished the other sign of the Lord's Supper to be wine. For the Tacianists had altogether expelled wine from the Church's use under the pretext of a holier abstinence and greater sobriety, because the common people abuse wine to drunkenness. These are the men whom Augustine calls Aquarians below.

units.la: 3 Nuptias damnant.) Etsi paucas Taciani erroris hypothcses refert hic Augustinus, fuerunt tamen multæ, quas nos è variis authoribus collegimus. Prima & eorū maximè propria, ꝗ Adamum primum hominem dānatum, nec ex lapsu suo saluti restitutum putant & docet.Qui leuis error in speciem videri potest, sed Nouatianæ hæreseos, quæ lapsis spem veniæ denegat, prima fundamenta & semina iacit. Deinde ex eo homines omnes damnatos esse, nulla spe salutis relicta concludit, exceptis modò Tacia-nis, qui suis operibus & continentiæ fidunt, atque ita vis mortis Christi aboletur, & Ecclesia Dei morti æternæ addicitur. Denique Patres aliud omnino de Adamo sentiunt, nempe eum Dei gratia saluum esse: idque colligunt tum ex Genes.3.versu 15. tum ex 1.Corinth.15.versu 45. quæ & solida sunt argumenta & viderunt ipsi, qua ratione merito caput hoc erroris Taciani damnatum est. Itaque Tacianos refutat Irenæus lib.3.cap.39. 2 Valentinianorum somnia & deliria de Æonibus & eorum progenie reuocat & ampleƈtuntur, per quæ diuina Christi natiuitas non tantum obscuratur, sed verius tollitur & irridetur.
units.tr: 3 Nuptias damnant.) Although Augustine here reports only a few of the errors of the Tacianists, there were many, which we have gathered from various authors. The first, and that most peculiar to them, is that they hold and teach that Adam, the first man, was condemned and was not restored to salvation after his fall. This error may seem slight at first sight, but it lays the first foundations and seeds of the heresy of the Novatians, who deny hope of pardon to the lapsed. Next, from this they conclude that all men are condemned, with no hope of salvation left, except only the Tacianists, who trust in their own works and continence; and so the force of Christ's death is abolished, and the Church of God is given over to eternal death. Finally, the Fathers think quite otherwise about Adam, namely that he was saved by the grace of God; and they gather this both from Genesis 3:15 and from 1 Corinthians 15:45. These are solid arguments, and they themselves saw by what reasoning this chief error of the Tacianists was rightly condemned. Accordingly Irenaeus refutes the Tacianists in book 3, chapter 39. Those who revive and embrace the dreams and delusions of the Valentinians about the Aeons and their progeny, by which the divine nativity of Christ is not only obscured, but more truly destroyed and mocked.

units.la: 3 Carnium, imprimis autem animalium, esum tanquam rem foedam prohibent, quam esse diaboli opus sentiunt, & vinum quoque damnant, quo non concedūt suis discipulis vti, ac ne in Cœnæ quidem Dominicæ administratione contra Christi institutum, Matthæi 26. versu 26. Itaque quemadmodum diximus aquam meram pro vino in Cœna Domini adhibent. Qui sane error ctiam tempore Cypriani adhuc viguit, & contra quem ipse scripsit, ut apparet ex ipsius epistolis. ψεωφαγία[?] iampridem a Pythagoricis, sed insul-se damnata est, quasi verae humanitati & aequitati contraria, ut docet Plutarch.in libro de ea re scripto, & P. Ouidius Naso libro 15. Meta-morphof.-sed Saturniani primum, Marcionitae deinde errorem hunc ab inferis revocarunt, & in Ecclesiam inducere tentarunt, quem Taciani sunt sequuti. Vinum autem quod prohibent, habent cum Apellitis haereticis commune. At de carnium esu, Dei verbum docet quid & Lege veteri & novo Testamento sit constitutum, Genef.9.verf.13.Acto.10. verf.13. Vide Augustin. libr.1.De ciuit.Dei,cap.20.21.contra Adimant. Manich. cap.14. & 15. & contra Faustum lib. 6. cap.6.7.8.De vino quid sentiendum sit, & ut eo uti liceat homini Christiano vide 1. Timoth.5. verf. 23. Hos errores iampridem praeuiderat praedixeratque Dei Spiritus, ut est 1. Timoth. 3.& damnarat, sed ad Pauli praecepta non attendrunt homines, commentis suis plus tribuentes, quam Dei verbo. Hoc caput haereseos Tacianae renouarunt Manichei omnino.& Papistę ex parte. 4 Nuptias tanquam Diaboli opus damnant, & appellant fornicationem. Itaque nec admittunt Deum creasse marem & foeminam, ut tamen est Genesis 1. & 2. nec genealogiam Christi ab Euangelistis descriptam retinent, ne a coniugibus proauis natum Christum concedere cogantur.Euscb.lib.4.cap.28. Denique generationem liberorum opus & foetum diabolicum vocant, quos refutat Clemens Stromat. mat.lib.3.Pelagiani hunc errore interpolarunt, ut docet Augustinus libro 2.contra Pelag. cap. 33.34.35. Sed Syricius Papa Rom. aperte reuocauit, & suos Papistas docuit hunc ipsum errorem. Itaque quod Taciani faciut, etiam foedum caelibatum iusto cōiugio prætulit, & plane cōntrā id sensit quod est Hebr.13. versu 4. Dictum Syricij extat in Can. Proposuisti. dist.82. Cœli-batum autem prætulisse nuptiis Tacianos scribit Theodoretus, & hanc sententiam inter errores & blasphemiæ capita recenset. 5 Mo-nogamiam tantum, quanquam inuiti, permittunt, id est, ut quis semel uxorem ducat, qua mortua ducere alia omnino non concedunt. Quum quis enim aliam ducit priore defuncta, & illi & Clemens vocant Polygamiam, sed Clemens concessam esse homini Christiano defendit libro 3. Stromat. illi Taciani negant. Hoc caput & semen Montanos postea peperit, qui hoc dogma salsissimum sequuti sunt, & postremam aetate defendit Tertullianus. 6 Negant Christum ex femine Dauidis natum, ergo negat verum fuisse Messiam, & eum qui Patribus promissus fuit, Psal.132. dum nuptias reiicere pergunt obstina-te. 7 Legem Mosis danat Tacianus, quod in ea coniugiorum benedictiones & proles promittuntur. Non enim esse eam Dei Euangelij, sed alterius asserunt, quod ex Marcionitis sumptum est: sed in tot blasphemias inciderunt, dum doctrinam suam de pollutione coniugiorum ambitiose tueri contendunt. Atque sic abyssus abyssum inter eos attraxit. Hæ vero sunt Tacia-norum hypothescs ineptæ & blasphemæ.
units.tr: 3 Meat, and especially the flesh of animals, they forbid as something foul, which they judge to be a work of the devil. They also condemn wine, and do not allow their disciples to use it, not even in the administration of the Lord's Supper, contrary to Christ's institution, Matt. 26:26. Accordingly, as we have said, they use plain water in place of wine in the Lord's Supper. This error still flourished in the time of Cyprian, and he wrote against it, as is clear from his letters. Psychophagy [ψυχοφαγία] was long ago condemned by the Pythagoreans, but foolishly, as if it were contrary to true humanity and fairness, as Plutarch teaches in his book written on this subject, and P. Ovid Naso in book 15 of the Metamorphoses. But the Saturnians first, and then the Marcionites, recalled this error from the dead and tried to introduce it into the Church, and the Tatianists followed it. Moreover, the prohibition of wine they hold in common with the heretics called Apellites. But concerning the eating of meat, the Word of God teaches what has been ordained both in the Old Law and in the New Testament: Gen. 9:3; Acts 10:13. See Augustine, On the City of God, book 1, chapters 20 and 21; against Adimantus the Manichaean, chapters 14 and 15; and against Faustus, book 6, chapters 6, 7 and 8. As to what must be thought about wine, and that a Christian man may lawfully use it, see 1 Tim. 5:23. The Spirit of God had already foreseen and foretold these errors, as in 1 Tim. 3, and had condemned them; but men have not heeded the precepts of Paul, attributing more to their own inventions than to the Word of God. The Manichaeans altogether, and the Papists in part, have revived this heresy of the Tatianists. 4 They condemn marriage as a work of the devil, and call it fornication. Accordingly they do not admit that God created male and female, as Genesis 1 and 2 nevertheless say, nor do they keep the genealogy of Christ described by the Evangelists, lest they be forced to concede that Christ was born of married ancestors. See Eusebius, book 4, chapter 28. Finally, they call the begetting of children a work and a diabolical product; Clement in the Stromata, book 3, refutes them. The Pelagians corrupted the Church with this same error, as Augustine teaches in book 2 against the Pelagians, chapters 33, 34 and 35. But Siricius, the Pope of Rome, openly recalled it and taught his Papists this very error. Accordingly, like the Tatianists, he preferred foul celibacy to lawful wedlock, and plainly thought contrary to what is written in Heb. 13:4. The saying of Siricius is found in Can. Proposuisti, dist. 82. Theodoret writes that the Tatianists preferred celibacy to marriage, and he reckons this opinion among their errors and chief blasphemies. 5 They permit only monogamy, though unwillingly, that is, that a man may take a wife once, and once she is dead they do not at all allow him to take another. For when a man marries another after the first has died, both they and Clement call it polygamy; but Clement defends that it was permitted to a Christian man, in book 3 of the Stromata, whereas the Tatianists deny it. This doctrine the Montanists afterwards brought forth as its seed; they followed this most unsavoury dogma, and in our own age Tertullian defended it. 6 They deny that Christ was born of the seed of David, and therefore deny that he was the true Messiah, and the one promised to the Fathers, Ps. 132, while they persist obstinately in rejecting marriage. 7 Tatian condemns the Law of Moses, because in it the blessings of marriage and offspring are promised. For they assert that it is not the Law of God's Gospel, but of another, a notion taken from the Marcionites; yet they fell into so many blasphemies while they ambitiously strive to defend their doctrine of the defilement of marriage. And so one abyss has drawn another abyss after it among them. These, indeed, are the foolish and blasphemous hypotheses of the Tatianists.

units.la: CAP. XXVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVI.

units.la: Cataphryges unde dicti. Quis eorum author. Errores autem tres eorundem recensentur.
units.tr: Where the Cataphrygians got their name. Who their author was. Three of their errors are listed.

units.la: Ataphryges{1} sunt, quorum authores fuerunt Montanus{2} tanquam paracletus, & duae prophetissae ipsius, Prisca, & Maxi-milla. His nomen provincia Phrygia dedit, quia ibi extiterunt, ibique vixerunt, & etiam-nunc in eiusdem partibus populos habent. {3}Adventum Spiritus sancti a Domino promissum in sepotius, quam in Apostolis eius fuisse afferunt. {4}Secundas nuptias pro fornicationibus habent, & ideo dicunt eas permisisse Apostolum Paulum, quia ex parte sciebat, & ex parte prophetabat. Nondum enim venerat quod perfectum est. Hoc autem perfectum in Montanum & in eius prophetissas venisse delirant. Sacramenta perhibentur funesta habere. Nam de infantis anniculi sanguine, quem de toto eius corpore minutis punctionum vulneribus extorquent, quasi Eucharistiam suam conficere perhibentur, miscentes eum farina, panemque inde facientes: qui puer si mortuus fuerit, habetur apud eos pro martyre: sin autem vixerit, pro magno sacerdote.
units.tr: The Cataphrygians (Cataphryges) were founded by Montanus, who called himself the Paraclete, and by his two prophetesses, Prisca and Maximilla. They took their name from the province of Phrygia, because they arose there, lived there, and still have followers in those parts. They maintain that the coming of the Holy Spirit promised by the Lord was fulfilled in themselves rather than in his apostles. They regard second marriages as fornication, and they claim that the Apostle Paul allowed them only because he knew in part and prophesied in part, for "that which is perfect" had not yet come. They insanely believe that this perfection came in Montanus and his prophetesses. They are said to have deadly sacraments. For they draw the blood of a one-year-old infant from its whole body through tiny pricks, and mix it with flour, as if to make their own Eucharist, and from this they make bread. If the child dies, they count him a martyr; if he lives, they count him a great priest.

units.la: {1} (Cataphryges.) Variis nominibus appellata fuit hæc vna & eadem hæresis, vt Epiphanius docet. Dicti sunt enim Cataphryges, Montanistæ, Tascodrongitæ, Spirituales, Pepuziani, & Quintilliani. Primum quidem Montanistæ, quoniam huius veneni, quod tota hæc secta bibit, propipropinator & author fuit Montanus, vti Eusch. libro 5. Histor. Ecclesiast. Theodoret. lib. 3. Haeret. fabul. & Isidorus lib. 8. Etymolog. vna cum Augustino tradunt, quanquam ipsum Montanum ex Tacianis fontibus & dogmate sua deriuasse. itaque illius errorem ex Encratitis profectum putant, quod non est vero absimile. Fuerunt enim hae haereses duae σύγχρονοι[?], quemadmodum Epiphanius scribit. Itaque Tertullianus ait hos Tacianis successisse. Montanos autem haereticos Isidorus distinguit a Montanistis, quos a montibus dictos scribit, in quos tempore afflictionis recesserant, & ad communem totius Ecclesiae coetum reduci agresti illo suo vitae genere delectati postea non potuerunt, quorum nullum dogma fuisse tradit, sed tantum schisma. Ac Cataphryges nomine compositi dicti sunt Montanistae, voce a Graecis accepta κατὰ Φρύγας[?], vti ex eadem Montanistarum secta quidam Procliani dicti, vocantur a Tertullian. Cata Procli, alij Æschiniani, cata Æschinem, id autem Graece dicitur κατὰ Πεπούζιλον[?] & κατὰ Αἰσχίνην[?]. Regio vero vnde primum hic erroris fons scaturijt indicatur. Fuit enim Phrygia, quae est regio minoris Asiae, supra Troadem, Lycaoniae, Pisidiaeque contermina, quemadmodum docet Plinius lib. 5. cap. 32. quae regiones nunc omnes vno Anatoliae nomine vocantur a Turcis, a quibus possidentur, maximeque gens Ottomanica ex ijs regionibus orta creditur. Duplex autem Phrygia statuitur, Maior, cuius etiam Galatia pars est: & Minor, quae est inferior & magis meridiana. Montanus autem non tantum Phryx vel Phrygius fuisse commemoratur, sed etiam natione Galata. Grassata vero est haec haeresis in utraque Phrygia, atque adeo Ancyra, quae fuit totius Phrygiae metropolis, & Montanistarum nomen amittens, quia Montanus propter infoelicem vitae exitum odiosus esse coeperat, aliud accepit a regione deductum Phrygum. Nam annotat in Encratitis Epiphan. Phrygiae partem quandam κεκαυμένην[?] fuisse dictam, quae tota haeresibus erat labefactata, Encratitis autem & Montanistis imprimis. Sed & Hieronymus in Proœmio libr. 2. ad Galatas mirum in modum totam Galatarum gentem haeresibus deformatam etiam suo seculo fuisse scribit. Ac certe ex D. Pauli epistolis apparet eam regionem, cum fidem Christianam primum suscepisset, statim ab ea deflexisse, & errores grauissimos secutam esse, ut mirum videri non possit, si postea corruptelae omnis fons & velut scaturigo quaedam fuerit, adeoque tandem Turcismi, & ipsius Turcarum gentis & sobolis matrix iusto Dei iudicio. Iidem autem haeretici Tascodrogitae nominati sunt, quod, ut ait Epiphanius inter orandum digitum manus, qui dicitur index, in nares rectū immitterent, tanquam palum quendam, ut in precibus suis seueriores attentioresque viderentur. Τάσσος[?] enim est, ut ait Epiphan. πάτταλος[?]: & ἔγγυος[?] est μυκτὴρ[?] ex ea-rum regionum idiomate. Vide infra Pattalorin chitae, quos ex Phrygia natos esse scribit Hiero-nym. Nominantur spirituales saepe a Tertullia-no, qui ipsi ita se vocari gaudebant, quod Spiri-tus S. maxima dona & χαρίσματα[?] habere se pro-fitebantur fitebatur:à se vero difsidetes orthodoxos vocabant ψυχικοί[?] & Animales. De aliorū nominum ratione, postea dicetur. Quando vero primum coeperit innotescere hæc hæresis, varia est auctorum sententia. Platina sub Sotere Romano Episcopo:alij sub Eleuthero, quæ verior est sententia, & circa annum à Christo passo 145. quam quam diutius & sub Zepherino Pontifice, Proclum qui primarius fuit auditor Montani adhuc vixisse scribit Eusebius lib.2. cap.25. Dura-uit vero diutissime in Galatia & Phrygia præsertim, vt annotat Sozomen.lib.2.cap.32. vbi populariter[?] receptam fuisse docet: alibi autem repudiatam, quia se Martyrum quorundam ostentatione apud populos commendabat. Quan-quam autem Theodoretus Cyri Episcopus scribit suo seculo nullos pene amplius Montanistas extitisse, tamen hoc loco testatur Augustinus author non temerarius nec levis, se vivo superfuisse adhuc hanc hæresin, id est, postquam esse coepit perstitisse annos paulo minus 250. De-nique etiam sub Leone Isaurico Imperatore adhuc permansit, nimirum plus quam 555. à sua nativitate annos, vt apparet ex Chronologiæ ratione. Latissime etiam propagata est,quando Asiam pene totam infecit sua tabe, Ciliciam, Paphlagoniam, Orientem, Aegyptum,& Constantinopolin etiam ipsam, adeò vt inter nocentissimas fidei Christianæ pestes à Constantino Magno fuerit edicto diserte comprehensa & præscripta.Denique Tertullian. in lib.Aduersf. Praxeam, scribit Romanum ipsum Episcopum eam approbasse, & literis ad alias Ecclesias imprimis Phrygios Episcopos datis commendaf-fe. Cur autem tam facile reciperetur, non tan-tum humani ingenij leuitas causa fuit, sed etiam lis & dissensio de die Cœnæ siue Paschatis celebrandi, quæ tunc magna erat, cum alij se Joan-nis doctrinam in eo sequi jactarent, nempe Asiani: alij vero Petri & aliorum Apostolorum exemplum, scilicet homines occidentales. Deinde utebantur eo Pauli dicto Montanistæ, ut se sapientiores ipsis Apostolis ostenderent, quod est 1.Corinth.13. ubi de se aliisque fidelibus loquens Paulus ait, Ex parte tantum cognoscimus. Denique suis sectatoribus & dogmatis noui propagatoribus & concionatoribus salaria quædam præbebat Montanus siue à se, siue ex suorum opibus, quod alij nulli hæretici antea fecerant, fuitque magna illex discipulorum, Eu-seb.lib.5. Histor. cap.16, & 17. Statim tamen in varias sectas & partes lacerata est hæc hæresis, & ipso Montanistarum primo nomine vix pau-co tempore perstitit. Primus autem in schola Mōtani successor fuit Theodotius: postea Pro-clus: deinde alij, qui tamen omnes magno fastu animi & ambitione impulsi, proprias & à se de-nominatas hæreses condiderunt, ita mendacium sibi constare non potest, & ut hydra, plura venenata capita parit.
units.tr: (Cataphrygians.) This one and the same heresy was called by various names, as Epiphanius teaches. They were called Cataphrygians, Montanists, Tascodrogitae, Spirituals, Pepuzians, and Quintillians. They were called Montanists first, because Montanus was the one who first poured out, and the author of, the poison which this whole sect drank, as Eusebius (Church History, book 5), Theodoret (Heretical Fables, book 3), and Isidore (Etymologies, book 8) relate, together with Augustine. Yet Montanus himself is said to have drawn his doctrine from the sources of the Tatianists. Hence some think his error came from the Encratites, which is not unlikely. For these two heresies were contemporaneous, as Epiphanius writes. So Tertullian says that these men succeeded the Tatianists. Isidore, however, distinguishes the Montanist heretics from the Montanists, whom he says were so called from the mountains, to which they had withdrawn in a time of persecution, and who, delighted with their rustic way of life, afterwards could not be brought back to the common assembly of the whole Church. He reports that they had no doctrine, only a schism. The Cataphrygians, a name compounded from the Greek preposition κατὰ ("after") and Phrygians, were called Montanists. Likewise, some of the same sect were called Proclians by Tertullian, from Proclus (cata Procli); others Aeschinians, from Aeschines (cata Aeschinen). In Greek these are called κατὰ Πεπούζιλον and κατὰ Αἰσχίνην (after Pepuzilon and after Aeschines). The region where this source of error first welled up is also named. Phrygia is a region of Asia Minor, above the Troad, bordering on Lycaonia and Pisidia, as Pliny teaches (book 5, chapter 32). All these regions are now called by the single name Anatolia by the Turks, who hold them, and the Ottoman people is believed to have sprung chiefly from these regions. Phrygia is divided into two parts: Greater Phrygia, of which Galatia is also a part, and Lesser Phrygia, which is lower and more southern. Montanus is recorded not only as a Phrygian, but also as being of Galatian birth. This heresy spread through both Phrygias, and especially through Ancyra, which was the metropolis of all Phrygia. Losing the name Montanists, because Montanus had become odious on account of his unhappy end, the sect took another name, derived from the region, Phrygians. Epiphanius notes among the Encratites that a certain part of Phrygia was called "burnt" (κεκαυμένην), because it was wholly shaken by heresies, especially by the Encratites and Montanists. Jerome too, in the preface to his second book on Galatians, writes that the whole Galatian people was wonderfully deformed by heresies even in his own age. Indeed, it is clear from the epistles of St. Paul that this region, as soon as it had first received the Christian faith, immediately turned aside from it and followed most grievous errors. So it is no wonder if it later became a fountain and, as it were, a spring of all corruption, and at last, by the just judgment of God, the mother of Turkism itself and of the Turkish nation and stock. These same heretics were called Tascodrogitae, because, as Epiphanius says, while praying they would thrust the finger of the hand which is called the index finger straight into their nostrils, like a kind of peg, so that they might seem more severe and more attentive in their prayers. For τάσσος (tassos), as Epiphanius says, means a peg (πάτταλος), and ἔγγυος (enguos) is the nostril (μυκτήρ), in the idiom of those regions. See below on the Pattalorynchitae, whom Jerome writes were born in Phrygia. They are often called Spirituals by Tertullian, who was glad to be called this, since they professed that they had the greatest gifts and graces (χαρίσματα) of the Holy Spirit; but they called the orthodox, who distrusted them, psychics (ψυχικοί), that is, Animals. The reason for the other names will be given later. As to when this heresy first became known, opinions of authors differ. Platina places it under the Roman bishop Soter; others under Eleutherius, which is the truer view, and around the year 145 after Christ's passion. Yet Eusebius (book 2, chapter 25) writes that Proclus, who was the chief disciple of Montanus, was still living even under the bishop Zephyrinus. It lasted for a very long time, especially in Galatia and Phrygia, as Sozomen notes (book 2, chapter 32), where he says it was popularly received, but rejected elsewhere, because it commended itself to peoples by displaying certain martyrs. Although Theodoret, bishop of Cyrus, writes that in his age there were almost no Montanists left, yet Augustine, an author who is neither rash nor shallow, testifies that in this place this heresy still survived in his lifetime, that is, that it had persisted for a little less than 250 years since it began. Finally, it still continued under the emperor Leo the Isaurian, namely for more than 555 years from its origin, as appears from the reckoning of chronology. It also spread very widely, when it infected almost all of Asia with its poison, and Cilicia, Paphlagonia, the East, Egypt, and even Constantinople itself, so that among the most harmful plagues of the Christian faith it was expressly included and condemned in an edict of Constantine the Great. Lastly, Tertullian, in his book against Praxeas, writes that the Roman bishop himself approved it and commended it by letters sent to other churches, especially to the Phrygian bishops. The reason it was so readily received was not only the lightness of the human mind, but also the dispute and disagreement about the day on which the Lord's Supper or Passover should be celebrated, which was then great. Some boasted that they followed the teaching of John in this matter, namely the Asians; others the example of Peter and the other apostles, namely the men of the West. Then the Montanists used that saying of Paul to show that they were wiser than the apostles themselves, namely 1 Corinthians 13, where Paul, speaking of himself and other faithful people, says: "We know only in part." Finally, Montanus gave certain salaries to his followers, to the spreaders of his new doctrine and to its preachers, whether from his own resources or from those of his followers. No heretic before him had done this, and it was a great lure for disciples (Eusebius, book 5, chapters 16 and 17). Yet this heresy was soon torn into various sects and factions, and the very name of Montanists hardly lasted a short time. The first successor of Montanus in his school was Theodotus; after him Proclus; then others. All of these, driven by great pride of spirit and ambition, founded their own heresies, named after themselves. Thus a lie cannot remain consistent with itself, and like the hydra it produces many poisonous heads.

units.la: Montanus ambitiosus & jam Encratitarum fermeto fœtido corruptus suam & ipse sectam priuatim habere voluit. Fuit autem ex vico Ardaban, alij ex Pepuza, uterque locus in superiore Phrygia, vicinus Marcipni[?] natali solo: & qui, ut maiorem fucum faceret, ad Simonis Magi imitationem secum habuit scortum, non vnum tantùm, vt ille: sed duo, Priscam & Maximillam, quas à propriis maritis abductas secum circunduxit. Zeli autem & pietatis praetextu illae Montanum impostorem relictis propriis viris sequebantur, sed fuco & stibio facie medicata, & ad perditissimarum meretricum exemplum cultae & vestitae, quemadmodum & Apollonius qui eas vidit, & Hieronym. postea in epist. Pauli ad Titum scripserūt. Harū autem deliria Montanus Spiritus sancti reuelationes & oracula vocabat, ex quibus quemadmodum Numa ex sua Ægeria, sic agyrtes ille dogmata sua compingebat & cudebat. Quare inter eos habebātur scriptae istarum insanarum & lymphatarum foeminarum somniationes, & sanctissimè diligentissimèque ab iisdem asseruabantur. Continebant enim etiam quasdam de rebus & bellis futuris prophetias siue praedictiones, quae omnino falsae sunt postea deprehensae, & passim irrisae. Scripsit autem quaedam Montanus ipse. Nam ex eius libris nonnulla refert Epiphanius. Tandem iusto Dei iudicio, cùm iam nimium multos istae fascinassent, & suo veneno corrupissent, se ipsas cum Montano diaboli instinctu, à quo prorsus agebantur, laqueo suspenderūt & stran gulārunt: sic miserrimè vitam omnes isti canes finierunt, Eusebius lib. 5. cap. 16.
units.tr: Montanus, ambitious and already corrupted by the foul leaven of the Encratites, wished to have his own sect privately. He came from the village of Ardaban, or, according to others, from Pepuza, both places in Upper Phrygia, near Marsipnum, his native soil. In order to make a greater show, he imitated Simon Magus, and kept with him not one harlot, as Simon did, but two, Prisca and Maximilla, whom he led about with him after taking them from their own husbands. Under the pretext of zeal and piety, these women left their husbands and followed the impostor Montanus. Their faces were painted with paint and antimony, and they were dressed and adorned after the manner of the most abandoned prostitutes, as both Apollonius, who saw them, and Jerome afterwards in his commentary on Paul's epistle to Titus, wrote. Montanus called the ravings of these women revelations and oracles of the Holy Spirit. Just as Numa did with his Egeria, so that charlatan built and hammered out his doctrines from them. Therefore the writings of these insane and frenzied women, their dreams, were held among them in high esteem, and were preserved by them with the greatest care and diligence. They also contained certain prophecies or predictions of future wars and events, which were afterwards found to be entirely false and were everywhere laughed at. Montanus himself also wrote some things; Epiphanius reports some passages from his books. At last, by the just judgment of God, since these women had already bewitched too many and corrupted them with their poison, they hanged and strangled themselves, driven on by the devil, who was entirely in control of them, together with Montanus. So all these dogs ended their wretched lives (Eusebius, book 5, chapter 16).

units.la: 3 Aduentum spiritus sancti.
units.tr: 3 The coming of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Hae passim Cataphrygarum hypotheses apud authores reperiuntur. 1 Se spiritum esse & illum quidem sanctum affirmauit, qui iampridem Ecclesiae & Apostolis promissus erat, quem ex parte tan-tum & ea quidem exigua & tenui illi in die Pentecostes accepissent: ipse autem Montanus haberet, ut ipsius discipuli contendebant, una cum Prisca & Maximilla sine mensura. Basil. libro 2. contra Eunomium scribit Montanum primum omnium haereticorum atrociter blas-phemasse in Spiritum sanctum. 2 Secunda coniugia damnavit, in quo discessit ab Encratitis praeceptoribus. Quod ipsum Augustinus libro 32. cap.17. contra Faustum confirmat. Unicum autem non reiecit, sed si quis uxore priore amissa quaereret aliam, eum ut impium eiiciebat Montanus ex Ecclesia. Propterea vero maxime se spirituales esse & censeri volebant. alios autem omnes, qui secundas nuptias non damnant, ψυχικοὺς[?] & carnales appellabat. Fuisse autem adulterii maxime ofores Phryges scribit Socrat. lib.4. cap.28. 3 Incestuosos concubitus & contra ius divinum sive gentium initos non improbavit, imo concessit Montanus.
units.tr: These are the Cataphrygians' main claims, as they are found scattered through the authors. (1) Montanus declared that he himself was the Spirit, and indeed the Holy Spirit, who had long been promised to the Church and to the Apostles, and whom they had received only in part, and that in a small and slight measure, on the day of Pentecost. Montanus himself, as his own disciples maintained, together with Prisca and Maximilla, possessed the Spirit without measure. Basil, in book 2 against Eunomius, writes that Montanus was the first of all heretics to blaspheme the Holy Spirit outrageously. (2) He condemned second marriages, and in this he departed from his teachers, the Encratites. Augustine confirms this very point in book 32, chapter 17, against Faustus. Yet he did not reject a single marriage: if anyone sought another wife after losing the first, Montanus cast him out of the Church as ungodly. The reason why they especially wished to be and to be called spiritual was this. All others who did not condemn second marriages he called psychical [ψυχικούς] and carnal. Socrates, in book 4, chapter 28, writes that the Phrygians were above all committers of adultery. (3) Incestuous unions, and those entered into contrary to divine or natural law, Montanus did not disapprove; indeed he allowed them.

units.la: 4 Enthusiasmis & Revelationibus sive ecstasi animi, si qua incidit, tantum tribuunt Montanistæ, ut iis credant, & ea deliria potius sequantur, quàm Dei verbum scriptum. Hoc Anabaptistæ retinuerunt, sed maxime refutat Epiph. tanquam non tantum ineptum, sed pessimum fidei fundamentum. 5 Confundunt personas in Trinitate, ut Simoniani fecerant, adeo ut Noetus, a quo Sabelliani orti sunt, Montani discipulus fuisse tradatur a Theodoreto, & ex ipsius lacunis & coeno suum errorem de Patre Deo passo hausisse. 6 Eucharistiæ & Sacrosanctæ Domini nostri Iesu Christi cœnæ panem, qui est alterum Cœnæ symbolum, cum sanguine humano miscent, & pinsunt, ut hic scribit Augustin. & ante eum Epiphan. fortasse quod iam ille error obrepserat & spargebatur, panem in ipsum corpus Christi transsubstantiari & transmutari in Cœna Domini, & idcirco in pane sanguinem inesse: tot tantasque absur-ditates unus ille error nimirum peperit. Quæda[?] fabulosa de statu corporum affirmant & nugantur, quæ pij & fideles homines sunt recepturi. Definiunt enim quanta lucis mensura nostra illa corpora solem ipsum superabunt, alia nimirum, ut illi volunt, 100. alia pluribus: alia paucioribus luminis gradibus, loco Pauli abutētes qui est 1. Corinth. 15. verf. 41. & Daniel. cap. 12. ita cū errore curiositas, animiq; vanitas semper est cōiuncta. Ipsi vero Cataphryges, ut est apud Theodoret. conquerebantur, quod multa falsò de se-se calumniose spargerentur, quæ tamen non admitterent: sed in iis quæ recitaui, constans est omnium scriptorum narratio & sententia: nihil enim illis affingo.
units.tr: (4) The Montanists give so much weight to enthusiasms and revelations, or ecstasies of the mind, whenever any occur, that they believe them and follow these delusions rather than the written Word of God. The Anabaptists retained this view, but Epiphanius refutes it especially, as not merely foolish but a most pernicious foundation for faith. (5) They confuse the persons in the Trinity, as the Simonians had done, so that Noetus, from whom the Sabellians arose, is said by Theodoret to have been a disciple of Montanus, and to have drawn his error concerning God the Father suffering from Montanus' own pools and mire. (6) They mix human blood into the bread of the Eucharist and of the most holy Supper of our Lord Jesus Christ, which is the other symbol of the Supper, and they grind it up, as Augustine writes here, and Epiphanius before him. Perhaps this was because that error had already crept in and was spreading: that the bread is changed and transmuted into the very body of Christ in the Lord's Supper, and that therefore blood is present in the bread. That one error, of course, gave birth to so many and such great absurdities. They also make up and babble fabulous things about the state of the bodies that pious and faithful people are going to receive. For they define how great a measure of light our bodies will surpass the sun itself: some, as they wish, by 100 degrees, others by more, others by fewer degrees of light. In doing so they misuse a passage of Paul, 1 Corinthians 15:41, and Daniel 12. So curiosity and vanity of mind always go together with error. The Cataphrygians themselves, as Theodoret records, complained that many false and slanderous things were spread about them which they did not admit. But in those things I have recited, the account and judgement of all the writers agree; for I invent nothing about them.

units.la: 4 Fuisse afferunt.) In impressis additum erat, Redditum: apud Isidorum autem est, Traditum, quod utrumque aut saltem alterum eorum irreptitium est, & ex glossemate in textum ascitum. Si enim illud Redditum, apud Augustinum legeretur, ab Isidoro procul dubio retineretur. Denique longè melius fluit sententia, & elegantior est oratio, quam deturbata illa voce restituimus, etsi vetustiore codice vel manuscripto destituti.
units.tr: They affirm that they had been.) In the printed editions this was given as "Redditum" (rendered back); in Isidore, however, it is "Traditum" (handed down). Either one of these, or at least one of them, has crept in unnoticed and was taken into the text from a marginal gloss. For if the word "Redditum" were read in Augustine, Isidore would undoubtedly have kept it. In short, the sense flows far better and the wording is more elegant with the word we have restored in place of that corrupted reading, although we lack an older codex or manuscript to confirm it.

units.la: CAP. XXVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVII.

units.la: Pepuziani & Quintilliani unde dicti. Erroris autem capita tria referuntur.
units.tr: The Pepuzians and Quintillians, and why they were so called. Three heads of this error are recounted.

units.la: Pepuziani à loco{1} quodam nominati sunt, quam ciuitatem desertam dicit Epiphanius. Hanc{2} autem isti diuinu aliquid esse arbitrantes, Hierusalem vocant: tantum dantes mulieribus principatum, vt sacerdotio quoque apud eos honorentur. Dicunt enim Quintillæ & Priscillæ in eadem ciuitate Pepuza, Christum specie fœminæ reuelatum. Vnde ab hac Quintilliani etiam nuncupantur. Faciunt & ipsi de sanguine infantis quod Cataphryges facere supra dixi mus. Nam & ab eis perhibentur exorti. Denique alij hanc Pepuzam non esse ciuitatem, sed villam dicunt fuisse Montani, & prophetissarum eius Priscæ & Maximillæ, & quia ibi vixerunt, ideo locum meruisse appellari Hierusalem.
units.tr: The Pepuzians were named from a certain place, which Epiphanius says was a deserted city. These men, thinking it something divine, call it Jerusalem, and they give such authority to women that they are honoured among them even with the priesthood. For they say that Christ appeared in the same city, Pepuza, in the form of a woman, to Quintilla and Priscilla. Hence they are also called Quintillians after her. They also do with the blood of an infant what I said above the Cataphrygians do; for they are said to have sprung from them too. Finally, others say that Pepuza was not a city but a village belonging to Montanus, and to his prophetesses Prisca and Maximilla, and that because they lived there, the place deserved to be called Jerusalem.

units.la: {1} Pepuziani à loco.) Dicti sunt etiam Montanistæ Pepuziani à Pepuza: & Quintilliani à Quintilla, quæ Priscæ & Maximillæ scortis aggregatur tanquam socia, & eorundem erroru prophetissa. Fuit autem Pepuza, quemadmodum scribit Epiphan.oppidum quod inter Galatiam & Cappadociam Asiæ regiones situm erat.ab Hieronym. autem & Euseb[?] .lib.5.cap.18. Tynnium appellatum, cuius ætate, non iam vrbs erat, sed pagus tantùm. Fortasse fuit illud ipsum oppidum quod à Plinio lib.6.cap.2. Triu[?] nominominatur,& in illis ipsis regionibus ab eo col-locatur, quod propter istas haereses à Deo suis-se desolatum verisimile est. Alius autem est vi-cus Pazo in Phrygia,vbi sunt fontes Sangarij flu-minis,quàm Pepuza.De quo vide Socrat.lib. 4. cap.28. Ergo Montanistarum haeresis illic, id est,in Phrygia, Galatia, Cappadocia, & vicinis locis plurimum & latissimè grassata est. Pepu-zianos autem, quos alij Pepuzitas vocant, cum Montanistis coniungit Theodoret.libr. 2. tan-quam prorsus eosdem: hîc autem separat cum Epiphan. Augustin, omnino verò praetermisit Isidorus. Equidem censuerim istos riuum qui-dem fuisse superioris haeresis, qui & innotue-rint postea: & suum quoddam atque peculiare dogma habuerint, quemadmodum ex hoc lo-co apparet, vtpote qui natalitia perditi homi-nis Montani caeteris impensius coluerint. Hi e-nim non tātum Montanū ipsum, sed etiam Pe-puzam,siue quia nativitatis illius hic locus erat, siue incolatus domicilium, sunt venerati. Sic enim insani homines faciunt &idololatrę.Nam locis ipsis terrenis sanctitatem alligant, si quos indigenas honorant. Exorti sunt autem Pepu-ziani eodem tempore, quo Cataphryges,& va-riis nominibus ijdem haeretici sunt appellati,vt de istorum ortu, successione, & propagatione, nihil sit nobis amplius necesse dicere.
units.tr: {1} The Pepuzians were named from a place. The Montanists were also called Pepuzians after Pepuza, and Quintillians after Quintilla, who was joined to Prisca and Maximilla as their companion and prophetess of the same errors. Pepuza, as Epiphanius writes, was a town situated between Galatia and Cappadocia, regions of Asia; Jerome and Eusebius (book 5, chapter 18) call it Tynnium, and in their time it was no longer a city but only a village. Perhaps it was that same town which Pliny (book 6, chapter 2) names Trium Nominum, and places in those same regions; it is likely that God laid it waste on account of these heresies. But Pazo, a different village in Phrygia, where the springs of the river Sangarius are, is other than Pepuza; on it see Socrates, book 4, chapter 28. So the heresy of the Montanists was there, that is, in Phrygia, Galatia, Cappadocia and the neighbouring places, and spread most widely and far. Theodoret, book 2, joins the Pepuzians, whom others call Pepuzites, with the Montanists as though they were altogether the same; here Epiphanius separates them. Augustine, and Isidore altogether passes them over. For my part I would judge that they were indeed a stream of the earlier heresy, which became known later, and had a certain distinctive dogma of their own, as appears from this place, since they honoured the birthday of the lost man Montanus more eagerly than others did. For they venerated not only Montanus himself but also Pepuza, either because this place was the place of his birth or the home of his residence. Indeed, mad men do this, and idolaters too; for they attach holiness to earthly places themselves, if they honour certain natives. The Pepuzians arose at the same time as the Cataphrygians, and under various names these same heretics were called; so, concerning their origin, succession and spread, there is no need for us to say anything more.

units.la: 2 Hanc autem. ) En quò mentis humanae vanitas tandem delabitur. Montanum, Christo relicto, sequuntur: ita Montani crepundia, natale solum,& patriam, id est, pestis generis humani productricem atque altricem terram venerantur, quam odisse debuerant. Haec tanta est humani ingenij a puritate verbi Dei discedentis caecitas. Fuerunt autem hæ Pepuzianorum hypotheses. 1 Pepuzam, qui locus est in superiore Phrygia, esse cœlestem illam Hierusalem & civitatem, de qua Prophetæ vaticinati sunt, & de qua est in epist. ad Heb.12.v.22. & Apoc.21. v. 2. & ad quam sit nobis omnibus aspi-randum, cum tamen illa Dei vivi civitas, non in terris ullis, sed in cœlo ipso sit nobis reposita, Coloss. 3. Quamobrem vitam æternam illi in hac terra necessario constituunt. 2 Mulieres ad ministerium ecclesiasticum, contra verbi Dei præceptum, 1.Timoth.2.verf.12. & 1.Cor. 14.admittunt, ut sint & Presbyteræ, & Episcopæ, id est, doceant, atque sacramenta Domini nostri Iesu Christi administrent. Hoc granum ex Marcionitarum infelici segete collectum est.
units.tr: 2 Hanc autem. Behold where the vanity of the human mind finally falls! Christ having been abandoned, they follow Montanus; thus they venerate the toys of Montanus, his native soil and fatherland, that is, the earth which produced and nourished the plague of the human race, which they ought to have hated. Such is the great blindness of the human mind, which departs from the purity of the Word of God. Now these were the hypotheses of the Pepuzians. First, that Pepuza, a place in upper Phrygia, is that heavenly Jerusalem and city of which the prophets prophesied, and of which there is mention in the Epistle to the Hebrews 12:22 and Revelation 21:2, and towards which all of us ought to aspire; although that city of the living God is laid up for us not in any lands but in heaven itself, Colossians 3. Wherefore they necessarily place eternal life for that city in this earth. Second, they admit women to ecclesiastical ministry, against the precept of the Word of God, 1 Timothy 2:12 and 1 Corinthians 14, so that they may be both presbyters and bishops, that is, teach and administer the sacraments of our Lord Jesus Christ. This seed was gathered from the unhappy harvest of the Marcionites.

units.la: 3 Fœdè & spurcè panem in sacra Cœna Domini sanguine humano pinsunt, ut horrendum potius sacrilegium, quam plenum consolationis sacramentum esse videatur sanctissima Domini Cœna.
units.tr: 3 They foully and filthily knead the bread of the Lord's Supper with human blood, so that the most holy Lord's Supper seems rather a horrible sacrilege than a sacrament full of comfort.

units.la: 4 Euam quæ fuit prima mulier, summè laudant, quòd ederit de vetita arbore, tanquam ea ratione facta sit nostræ salutis causa, sitque hoc Euæ magnum erga nos beneficium, & non potius summum flagitium, ut docet Paulus, 1.Timoth.2.verf.14.
units.tr: 4 They praise Eve, who was the first woman, very highly, because she ate of the forbidden tree, as though by that means she was made the cause of our salvation, and this was a great benefit of Eve towards us, and not rather the greatest shame, as Paul teaches, 1 Timothy 2:14.

units.la: 5 Christum suarum blasphemiarum authorem esse dicunt. Itaque eum sibi ipsi contrarium faciunt, quod vel animo cogitare nefas est. Volunt enim ea quæ ipsi docent, reuelasse per Quintillam lymphaticam & abreptitiam mulierem. Sed & in eo quoque ipso præter Scripturæ fundametum sentiunt, Christum mulieris forma tunc vel unquam apparuisse, muliebremque sexum propterea supra marem extollunt, cùm nusquam tamen legamus Deum vel Angelos ipsos, quamquam mulieres & virginem ipsam B. Mariam alloquerentur, mulieris specie hominibus apparuisse: sed semper virili forma. 6. Quædam eos de Paschate celebrando statuisse scribit Sozomen.lib.7.cap.18. in quibus à reliquis Ecclesiis dissenserunt: sed hoc in parte erroris non constituo, cùm in eo ipso multæ Ecclesiæ nimia quadam contentione & superstitione ipsæ errauerint.Hæc de Pepuzianis.
units.tr: 5 They say that Christ is the author of their blasphemies. Thus they make him contrary to himself, which it is wicked even to think in the mind. For they wish that the things which they teach were revealed through Quintilla, a frenzied and deranged woman. But in this very point too, beyond the foundation of Scripture, they hold that Christ appeared then or ever in the form of a woman, and therefore they exalt the female sex above the male; yet we never read that God or the angels themselves, though they spoke to women and to the Blessed Virgin Mary herself, appeared to men in the form of a woman, but always in a male form. 6. Sozomen (book 7, chapter 18) writes that they decided on certain matters concerning the celebration of Easter, in which they differed from the other Churches; but I do not count this as part of their error, since in that very matter many Churches themselves erred through a certain excessive contention and superstition. These things concern the Pepuzians.

units.la: CAP. XXVIII. Artotyritæ cur sic dicti. Erroris caput unum.
units.tr: CAP. XXVIII. Why the Artotyritae are so called. One error.

units.la: Artotyritæ sunt{1} quibus oblatio{2} hoc no-men dedit. Offerunt{3} enim panem & ca-seum, dicentes à primis hominibus oblatio-nes de fructibus terræ & ovium fuisse celebratas. Hos Pepuzianis iungit Epiphanius.
units.tr: The Artotyritae are those whom the offering gave their name. For they offer bread and cheese, saying that offerings of the fruits of the earth and of sheep were celebrated by the first men. Epiphanius joins these to the Pepuzians.

units.la: {1} Artotyritæ sunt.) Hi sunt iidem cum Pepu-zianis Epiphanio, quos tamen hoc loco seperat Augustinus. certè Montanistarum fuisse propaginem certum est, & verisimile etiam eos fuisse schismaticos Pepuzianorum, à quibus propter suam illam casei oblationem recesse-runt, cùm in reliquo dogmate plane inter se consentirent.Dicti sunt autem Artotyritæ,Græce Ἀρτοτυρῖται, ἀπὸ τῆς Ἄρτ[?].i. Pane, & τυρ[?].i. caseo.
units.tr: {1} Artotyritae sunt.) These are the same as the Pepuzians of Epiphanius, though Augustine here separates them. It is certain that they were an offshoot of the Montanists, and it is also likely that they were a schismatic branch of the Pepuzians, from whom they withdrew because of this practice of offering cheese, although they agreed with them entirely in the rest of their doctrine. They were called Artotyritae, in Greek Ἀρτοτυρῖται, from ἄρτος [artos], bread, and τυρός [tyros], cheese.

units.la: Quo vero tempore ista lues primum extiterit, & quandiu grassata fit, quibus item successori-bus defensa, dici non potest, quia pauci omnino huius hæreseos meminerunt, & statim collapsam, propter manifestam Cœnæ corruptelam, & discipulorum paucitatem crediderim. Huius tamen meminit Isidor. & retenta est in cano. Quidam. 24. quæst. 3. Horum meminit Hieronym. lib.2.in Galat.in Prœemio.
units.tr: When this plague first arose, how long it spread, and how far it was maintained by their successors, cannot be said, because hardly anyone mentions this heresy. I suspect it collapsed quickly, on account of the obvious corruption of the Lord's Supper and the small number of its disciples. Isidore does mention it, and it is retained in the canon Quidam, 24 q. 3. Jerome mentions them in the preface of his second book on Galatians.

units.la: 2 Oblatio hoc. ) In impressis, Oblatio eorum hoc,inepte. Vox enim eorum, non modo redundat, sed procul dubio monachicū glossema fuit, quod ex Isidoro facile potest intelligi. Ait enim, Artotyritæ ab oblatione vocati, reiecto pronomine relatiuo, eorum. Itaque expunximus. Est autem locus hic Augustini apud Isidorum ex vetustis, quos habuit, codicibus emendatior, quàm in nostris & impressis, quos manibus hodie terimus.
units.tr: 2 Oblatio hoc.) In the printed editions it reads Oblatio eorum hoc, which is foolish. The word eorum is not only superfluous but was undoubtedly a monkish gloss, as can easily be seen from Isidore. For he says Artotyritae ab oblatione vocati, with the relative pronoun eorum dropped. So we have struck it out. This passage of Augustine as it appears in Isidore is more accurate than in our printed texts, which we handle today, being drawn from the old manuscripts he had.

units.la: 3 Offerunt enim, Quanquam non fuit vnus Artotyritarum error, quia cum Pepuzianis in reliquis dogmatibus consentiebant, tamen quia hoc vnum fuit eorum proprium facinus & speciale caput hæreseos, quod caseum & panem offerebant, illud solum commemorauit Augustinus.
