Oblationem autem istam interpretor in Eucharistia fieri solitam ab illis. Itaque addidisse tertium hoc signum, nempe caseum, ad duo quæ Christus instituerat, nempe ad panem & vinum: vel substituisse loco vini caseum, quod Deo gratior videretur casei oblatio, quàm vini. Cascus enim est fructus ouium, quo sacrificii genere Deus primùm esset valde delectatus, Genes. 4. Nam addita fuisse paulatim quaedam signa in Eucharistia, id est, alia substituta pro iis quae Dominus noster Jesus Christus dedit, apparet ex Can. Didicimus. & can. Cum omne. de Consecrat. distinct. 2. vbi quibusdam in locis hac adiunctum, scribit Julius, ad panem & vinum: alibi molam vino intinctam solitam porrigi docet idem. Denique in Papatu tertium signum manifeste in Coena Domini additur & retinetur, nimirum aqua, quae miscetur cum vino. Quis autem miretur tot iam erroribus corruptis Montanistis accidisse, ut de Coenae Dominicae signis, qualia esse oporteret, disputaret, qui legit apud Scholasticos libr. 4. Sentent. dist. ij. & sequent. curiosas & anxias nugas & animi vexationes de pane & vino, cur conueniens materia Eucharistiae esse possint? Non diffiteor autem hanc Artotyritarum sententiam, de pane & caseo offerendis, etiam intelligi posse extra Eucharistiam, quasi hoc genere sacrificii veteribus & legalibus sacrificiis, quae multi haeretici veluti Nicolaitae retinebant, & adhuc vsurpabant. Nec dubium est quin huiusmodi dogmata & blasphemiae fundamenta erroris Manichaeorum, qui postea sunt secuti, iecerint, sumptaeque fuerint ex Paganorum deliriis. Dixit enim Theophrastus nullam victimam Deo gratam esse, quia sanguinem effundere esset crudele, & a Dei natura prorsus alienum. Itaque οὐσίαν[?] appellatam esse docuit, non οὐ τῆς θυσίας[?], quod est mactare: sed ἀλλὰ τῇ θυμά-[?] μάτος[?] .i.suffitu , quod gratisimum Deo sacrificium sit herbarum incensarum & naturalium odorum vapor & suffitus:non autem iugulatæ pecudes & mactatæ.Id quod sensit quoque Pythagoras.Sed errat vterque. Nec enim propter rem ipsam,quæ offerebatur, Deo grata sacrificia fuerunt: sed propter fidem , id est , propter præceptum Dei & finem offerentis.Is autem erat attestatio futuri Christi, Augustin. libr. 20. Contra Faust. cap. 23. Sed ita reposita est nobis per hæreticos omnis Paganorum hominum insania:& omnium errorum crambe, quæ nos enecat,&,vt est in veteri prouerbio, mors est.
units.tr: 3 Offerunt enim, Although the error of the Artotyritae was not the only one, since they agreed with the Pepuzians in the rest of their doctrines, Augustine mentioned only this one, because it was their own peculiar offence and the distinctive head of their heresy: that they offered cheese and bread. I interpret this offering as the one customarily made by them in the Eucharist. So they added this third sign, namely cheese, to the two that Christ had instituted, namely bread and wine; or they substituted cheese for wine, since a cheese offering seemed more pleasing to God than wine. For cheese is the fruit of sheep, and by this kind of sacrifice God was first greatly delighted, Genesis 4. That other signs were gradually added to the Eucharist, that is, other things substituted for those which our Lord Jesus Christ gave, appears from the canons Didicimus and Cum omne, De consecratione, dist. 2, where Julius writes that in some places this was added to bread and wine, and the same author teaches that elsewhere a cake dipped in wine was customarily offered. Finally, in the Papacy a third sign, namely water mixed with the wine, is clearly added and retained in the Lord's Supper. Who would be surprised that the Montanists, already corrupted by so many errors, should dispute about the signs of the Lord's Supper, what they ought to be, when one reads among the Scholastics, in the fourth book of the Sentences, distinction 2 and those following, their curious and anxious trifles and torments of mind about bread and wine: why they might be a suitable matter for the Eucharist? I do not deny, however, that this opinion of the Artotyritae, about offering bread and cheese, can also be understood apart from the Eucharist, as a kind of sacrifice like the old and legal sacrifices, which many heretics, such as the Nicolaitans, retained and still practised. Nor is there doubt that doctrines of this sort and the foundations of blasphemy were laid by the Manichaeans, who followed later, and were taken from the ravings of the pagans. For Theophrastus said that no victim is pleasing to God, because shedding blood is cruel and wholly alien to the nature of God. So he taught that the sacrifice was so called not from θυσία [thysia], which means slaughter, but from θυμίαμα [thymiama], that is, incense, since the most pleasing sacrifice to God is the vapour and smoke of burnt herbs and natural odours, not slaughtered and butchered animals. Pythagoras also held this view. But both are mistaken. For sacrifices were not pleasing to God because of the thing offered, but because of faith, that is, because of God's command and the purpose of the one offering. And this was a testimony to the Christ who was to come, Augustine, book 20 Against Faustus, chapter 23. But thus has all the madness of the pagans been handed down to us through the heretics, and the whole cabbage of errors that kills us, and, as the old proverb says, is death.

units.la: CAP. XXIX.
units.tr: CAP. XXIX.

units.la: Teffareskædecatitæ cur sic nominati. Eorum autem hypothesis vna recensetur.
units.tr: The Tessareskaidekatitae: why they are so named. One of their hypotheses is recounted here.

units.la: Effareskædecatitæ{1} hinc appellati sunt, quod non nisi quartadecima{2} luna, mense Martio Pæscha celebrant, quilibet e septè occurrat dies: & si dies Dominicus occurrerit, ipso die ieiunant & vigilant.
units.tr: They are called Tesseradecatitae because they celebrate Easter in March only on the fourteenth day of the moon, and whichever of the seven days that falls on, and if it falls on the Lord's day, they fast and keep vigil on that very day.

units.la: {1} Teffareskædecatitæ.) Græca vox est, quàm Latini Theologi Quartidecimanos vertunt. Ac quo tempore grauis illa de die Paschatis celebrandi controuersia primùm in Ecclesia coeperit, anxia quæstio est, & authores alij ab aliis dissentiunt. Isidorus demum post Heluidianos hæreticos collocat, quasi post 300. à Christo passo annos extiterit. Alij ex superiori tempore repetunt, & huius quæstionis & hærefcos authores constituunt ante Irenęi Lugdunensis epi-scopi, & Tertulliani tempora. Sic Eufeb.sentit lib.1.Histor. cap. 25. cùm tamen in eorum scri-ptis nulla huius rei vestigia reperiantur, præter-quàm quod Tertullianus in libr. De præscript. aduersus hæret.ante sua tempora Blastum quê-dam extitisse tradit hominem hæreticum, qui Pascha secundum Legem Mosis docere custodiendum. Alij ex Cataphrygibus & Quintillia-nis ortos putant, vt Epiphanius. Alij ex Nico-laitis. Alij ex Nouatianis, ita est origo eorum incerta. Cuius sententiæ hæc fortasse ratio videri potest, quòd, vt scribit Socrat.lib.4. cap. 28.& lib.5.cap.21,& 22.à Sabbatio quodam Nouatiano mota hæc quæstio fuerit, & in eorum synodis deinde varie & animose agitata, quà li-beram tamen esse definierunt. qui & ipsi inter Nouatianos Sabbatiani dicti sunt, vt scribit Sozomen.lib.7.cap.29. Sed cùm hæc certamina in Valentis Imperatoris tempus inciderint, quo iam exorti erant Quartidecimani, male censetur huius erroris initium eo demum tempore coepisse. Verior igitur, subductis aliorum omnium argumentis, mihi videtur esse hæc sententia, sub Victore qui fuit Romanus Episcopus post Eleutherum, & sub Seuero Romano imperatore de Paschate nata esse in Ecclesia dissidia, nimirum anno post Christum passum 165. non quòd antea diuersa & dissimilis Ecclesiarum consuetudo non fuisset, quemadmodum docet Socrat.lib.5.cap.22.sed quòd ea res & diucrsitas nondum in contentionem & certamen erupisset, & quæque suum morem, & a maioribus acceptum, sine animi scrupulo & superstitione sequens, aliam erroris & schismatis non damnabat. Sed postquam ambitiosius quidam se suumque institutum aliarum Ecclesiarū consuetudini præferre voluerunt, nec secuti Pauli moderationem & consilium, Roman.14.in rebus ἀδιαφορίας[?] libertatem aliis concesserunt, inde tandem acerrima certamina & luctuosa de re primum quidem leui concitata sunt, sed quæ manifestum errorem postea pepererit, tanti nimirum est, in omnibus rebus etiam levissimis Ecclesias inter se consentire, quemadmodum docet Paulus 1.Corinth.1.& 11.Quod ut melius intelligatur, rem totam paulo altius repetam. Hoc fuit in more primis Ecclesiis, & quæ tempora Apostolorum sequutæ sunt, positum, ut quanquam sæpius in anno, imo vero quoque mense Christiani συνάξεις[?] agerent, & Eucharistiam siue Cœnam Domini sumerent, semel tamen tantum in anno Pascha Domini celebrarent, a quo nemo Christianus qui modo per ætatem posset, neque esset catechumenus aut suspensus a communione Sacramentorum, eo die posset abstinere. Huius rei testimonia extant in Can. Nos. & Cano.sequ. De consecrat.Distinct. 4. adeo ut Carthaginensi concilio 4.& 5.constitutum fuerit, ut die natalis Domini quo mense Pascha sequens celebrandum esset, plebi denuntiaretur. Extant etiam huius rei præcepta in cōciliorum volumine, & Can.Paschæ solennitas. & Can.fe-quent.De consecrat.Distinct.4.Fuit autem pri-mum
units.tr: {1} Tessareskaidekatitae [Τεσσαρεσκαιδεκατῖται]: this is a Greek word, which the Latin theologians render as Quartodecimans. When this grave controversy about the day of keeping Easter first arose in the Church is a difficult question, and the authors disagree with one another. Isidore places it late, after the heretics Helvidius, as though it arose only about 300 years after Christ's passion. Others trace it back to an earlier time and assign the origin of this question and this heresy to the period before Irenaeus, bishop of Lyons, and Tertullian. Eusebius holds this view in book 1 of his History, chapter 25, although no trace of the matter is found in their writings, except that Tertullian, in his book On Prescription against Heretics, reports that before his own time there was a heretical man named Blastus, who taught that Easter should be kept according to the Law of Moses. Others think they sprang from the Cataphrygians and the Quintillians, as Epiphanius does. Others derive them from the Nicolaitans, and others from the Novatians; so their origin is uncertain. The reason for this opinion may perhaps be this: as Socrates writes in book 4, chapter 28, and book 5, chapters 21 and 22, the question was raised by a certain Sabbatius, a Novatian, and was then debated in their synods in various and heated ways, yet they decided it was a matter of freedom. These men too were called Sabbatians among the Novatians, as Sozomen writes in book 7, chapter 29. But since these contests fell in the time of the emperor Valens, when the Quartodecimans had already arisen, it is wrongly judged that the beginning of this error came only then. The truer view, therefore, after weighing the arguments of all others, seems to me to be this: under Victor, who was Roman bishop after Eleutherus, and under the Roman emperor Severus, disagreements about Easter arose in the Church, in the year 165 after Christ's passion. This was not because the custom of the Churches had not been different and dissimilar before, as Socrates teaches in book 5, chapter 22, but because this difference had not yet broken out into dispute and strife, and each church, following its own custom received from its elders without scruple of conscience or superstition, did not condemn the other as error or schism. But after some men, with too much ambition, wished to put their own practice above the custom of other Churches, and did not follow Paul's moderation and counsel in Romans 14, who granted liberty to others in matters of indifference [ἀδιαφορία], then at last most bitter and sorrowful contests arose over a matter at first slight, which afterwards produced manifest error. So much is it important that the Churches agree with one another even in all the smallest things, as Paul teaches in 1 Corinthians 1 and 11. That this may be better understood, I shall go back a little further into the whole matter. In the first churches, and in the times that followed the Apostles, it was the custom that, although Christians held their assemblies [συνάξεις] more often in the year, indeed even every month, and received the Eucharist or the Lord's Supper, they celebrated the Lord's Easter only once a year, and no Christian who was of an age to do so, and was not a catechumen or suspended from communion in the sacraments, could abstain from it on that day. Evidence of this is found in the canons Nos and the following canons, De consecratione, distinction 4. So much so that the Council of Carthage, in its fourth and fifth canons, ordered that the day of the Lord's birth, and in which month the following Easter was to be celebrated, should be announced to the people. Precepts on this matter also exist in the volume of councils, in the canon Paschae solennitas and the following canon, De consecratione, distinction 4. Now at first the observance of this day was free, so that whether it fell on the fourteenth day of the first month of the moon or on another day, the Churches did not dissent from one another on that account nor diminished their agreement. But when each wished to defend the custom of its own Church, reasons were devised for why Easter should be said to be kept on this day rather than that, and better so. Victor, the Roman bishop, with great rashness and ambition, condemned the Eastern bishops, who did not follow the Roman Church's custom in this, and excommunicated them as schismatics. For this he was severely rebuked both by the Eastern bishops themselves and by Irenaeus, bishop of Lyons, as Eusebius writes. From this, disputes arose, and books were written on both sides, especially by Anatolius, as Eusebius says in the same book 7, chapter 32, and Socrates in book 5, chapter 22. For the Easterners appealed to the authority of the Apostle John, from whose custom they contended that Easter must be kept on the fourteenth day of the moon; the Westerners followed the different custom of the Apostle Peter. But both were wrong. For although Paul teaches that our Passover, who is Christ, has been sacrificed (1 Corinthians 5:7), he does not recall us to that ceremonial observance of the Law; and the Apostles themselves, gathered together, among whom John then was, with one consent judged that the old ceremonies were to be abolished as a heavy yoke by no means necessary (Acts 15). Therefore this was a fabricated argument, whenever each church tried to derive its custom from the Apostles. How great the dissension among the Churches was over this matter and day appears from this: some held that Easter must be kept precisely on the fourteenth day of that moon which is born first in the year's first month, Nisan, corresponding to our March, that is, at the full moon of the first moon of the year. Others said the day of Easter should be measured not by the course of the moon but rather of the sun, as the Pepuzians did, so that Easter would not be celebrated more than once a year, which was held to be wicked. And so, on the same day of March on which Christ once suffered, they kept Easter, that is, when the sun held the twelfth degree of Aries after the vernal equinox, a day they always observed whether it fell at the full moon or not. Others, however, from what they called the Acts of Pilate, fell on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, that is, 23 March; others on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of the same month, that is, 18 March; others indeed contended for the thirteenth, that is, the 20th day. So great, no doubt, was the contention over a slight matter, and so great the division of minds. Those who obstinately and stubbornly held to the fourteenth moon were plainly Judaizing. Yet they flourished for a very long time and spread most widely. For they were scattered through Asia, Caria and Lydia, and especially through Phrygia and Galatia, where they were the seed and receptacle, or nest, of all heresies. Sozomen, book 7, chapter 29. Socrates writes that this schism turned out badly for its first authors, so that they killed themselves, carried away by the spirit of Satan (Socrates, book 7, chapter 5). But first an attempt was made at concord, lest the Church of God be divided for so trivial a cause. Accordingly, seven synods, which, as Eusebius writes in book 5, chapter 23 of his History, had therefore met in different places and at different times, at last brought it about that the Church should coalesce into one opinion and that all should celebrate Easter on one and the same day. But this wound of the Church broke out again. And first indeed under Constantine the Great; but this discord was calmed lightly and easily by the Synod of Nicaea, which condemned the Quartodecimans, as is found in Rufinus, book 1 of his History, chapter 6; Theodoret, book 1, chapter 10; Sozomen, book 1, chapter 16. Then again under Theodosius the Younger, when Nestorius, the heretic, who was then bishop of Constantinople, persecuted and assailed them most savagely (Socrates, book 7, chapter 29). At last this heresy, having spread most wretchedly through the Church for so many years, that is, more than 200, was utterly weakened and fell silent. Nevertheless the Audaeans later revived this error.

units.la: Ecclesiarū: text in this line is printed as in the body; no footnote on this page. mum libera huius diei obseruatio, ut siue quartadecima luna prima mensis, siue alia die fieret, propterea a sese non dissentirent Ecclesiae, neque consensionem imminuerent. Sed quum quisque suę Ecclesię morem tueri vellet, inuentę sunt rationes, cur hoc potius quā illo die & melius Pascha fieri diceretur. Primus autem Victor episcopus Romanus magna temeritate & animi ambitione Orientales Episcopos, qui Romanae Ecclesiae morem in eo non sequebantur, damnauit, & excommunicauit tanquam schis-maticos. Qua de re & ab iis ipsis Episcopis Orientalibus, & ab Irenaeo, ut scribit Euseb. Lugdunensi Episcopo graviter reprehensus est. Inde lites natae, & libri utrinque scripti, imprimis ab Anatolio, ut ait Eusebius idem libr.7.cap.32. & Socrat.lib.5.cap.22. Nam Orientales Ioannis Apostoli proferebant authoritatem, ex cuius consuetudine 14. luna Pascha celebrandum esse contendebant. Occidentales autem Apostoli Petri diuersum morem. Sed falso utrique. Quanquam enim Paulus Pascha nostrum, qui est Christus, immolatum esse tradit,1. Corinth. 5. versu 7, non revocat tamen nos ad ceremonialem illam Legis observationem, & Apostoli ipsi collecti, inter quos tunc erat Ioannes, uno consensu veteres ceremonias tollendas esse censuerunt tanquam grave iugum minime necessarium, Actor. 15. Quare fuit haec commentitia ratio, dum quisque Ecclesiae suę morem ab Apostolis deriuare conatur. Quanta vero Ecclesiarum inter se de ea re & die dissensio fuerit, apparet ex eo, quòd alij 14. tantùm die eius lunæ,quæ nascitur primo anni mese,qui est Ni-san,& nostro Martio respondet, agendum Pascha præcisè censebant,id est,in plenilunio primæ anni lunæ. Alij non ex lunæ,sed solis potius cursu metiendam Pafchatis diem dixerunt, veluti Pepuziani, ne sæpius quàm semel in anno Pascha celebraretur, id quod nefas habebatur. Itaque simili, qua Christus olim passus erat,die mense Martio faciebant Pascha.i.sole duodecimum Arietis gradum tenente post Æquinoctium vernum, quâ diem semper obseruabant, siue ea fuisset in plenilunio,siue non.Alij tamen ex Actis Pilati, quæ vocabant, incidere in viii. Kalend.April.i.23.Martij mensis: alij in xv. Kalend. eiusdem mensis. i. 18. Martij: alij vero in xiii,id est 20.diem contendebant: tanta nimirum fuit de re leui contentio, tantumque animorum diuortium. Qui vero quartadecimam lunam mordicus & obstinatè retinebant, plane Iudaizabant. Viguerunt tamen diutissimè, & sunt latissimè propagati. Nam per Asiam, Cariam, Lydiam sparsi sunt, imprimis autem per Phrygiam, & Galatiam, vbi omnium hæreseôn semen & receptaculum, siue nidus fuit. Sozomen.lib.7.capite 29.Quod schisma male primis authoribus suis cessisse scribit Socrates, adeò vt seipsos interfecerint Satanæ spiritu abrepti. Socrat.lib.7.cap.5. Sed concordia primum tentata est, ne diuideretur ob tam nullam causam Ecclesia Dei. Quamobrem septè synodis,quæ, vt scribit Eusebius libro 5. cap.23. Histor. propterea diuersis locis & temporibus conuenerant, tandem effectum, vt in unam sententiam Ecclesia coalcsceret, & vno eodemque die omnis Pascha celebraret. Sed recruduit hoc Ecclesiae vulnus. Ac primum quidem sub Constantino Magno: verum leuiter & facile placata est haec discordia Nicaena Synodo, quae Quartide-cimanos damnauit, vt est apud Ruff.lib.i.Hist. cap.6. Theodor. libro i.cap.10. Sozom.libro i. cap.16. Deinde vero sub Theodosio Iuniore, nimirum Nestorio haeretico, qui tum Episcopus Constantinopolitanus erat, illos saeuissime persequente & impugnante. Socrat.libro 7.cap. 29. Demum prorsus labefactata conticuit haec haeresis, postquam esset per tot annos in Ecclesia miserrime grassata, id est, plus quam 200. Audæani tamen hunc errorem postea renouarunt.
units.tr: ...mum: the observance of this day was at first free, so that whether it fell on the fourteenth day of the first month of the moon or on another day, the Churches did not on that account differ from one another or weaken their agreement. But when each wished to defend the custom of its own Church, reasons were found for why Easter should be said to be kept on this day rather than that, and better so. Victor, the Roman bishop, however, with great rashness and ambition, condemned the Eastern bishops, who did not follow the Roman Church's custom in this, and excommunicated them as schismatics. For this he was severely rebuked both by those Eastern bishops themselves and by Irenaeus, bishop of Lyons, as Eusebius writes. From this, lawsuits arose, and books were written on both sides, especially by Anatolius, as Eusebius says in the same book 7, chapter 32, and Socrates in book 5, chapter 22. For the Easterners appealed to the authority of the Apostle John, from whose custom they contended that Easter must be kept on the fourteenth day of the moon; the Westerners followed the different custom of the Apostle Peter. But both were wrong. For although Paul teaches that our Passover, who is Christ, has been sacrificed (1 Corinthians 5:7), he does not recall us to that ceremonial observance of the Law; and the Apostles themselves, gathered together, among whom John then was, with one consent judged that the old ceremonies were to be abolished as a heavy yoke by no means necessary (Acts 15). Therefore this was a fabricated argument, whenever each church tried to derive its custom from the Apostles. How great the dissension among the Churches was over this matter and day appears from this: some held that Easter must be kept precisely on the fourteenth day of that moon which is born first in the year's first month, Nisan, corresponding to our March, that is, at the full moon of the first moon of the year. Others said the day of Easter should be measured not by the course of the moon but rather of the sun, as the Pepuzians did, so that Easter would not be celebrated more than once a year, which was held to be wicked. And so, on the same day of March on which Christ once suffered, they kept Easter, that is, when the sun held the twelfth degree of Aries after the vernal equinox, a day they always observed whether it fell at the full moon or not. Others, however, from what they called the Acts of Pilate, fell on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, that is, 23 March; others on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of the same month, that is, 18 March; others indeed contended for the thirteenth, that is, the 20th day. So great, no doubt, was the contention over a slight matter, and so great the division of minds. Those who obstinately and stubbornly held to the fourteenth moon were plainly Judaizing. Yet they flourished for a very long time and spread most widely. For they were scattered through Asia, Caria and Lydia, and especially through Phrygia and Galatia, where they were the seed and receptacle, or nest, of all heresies. Sozomen, book 7, chapter 29. Socrates writes that this schism turned out badly for its first authors, so that they killed themselves, carried away by the spirit of Satan (Socrates, book 7, chapter 5). But first an attempt was made at concord, lest the Church of God be divided for so trivial a cause. Accordingly, seven synods, which, as Eusebius writes in book 5, chapter 23 of his History, had therefore met in different places and at different times, at last brought it about that the Church should coalesce into one opinion and that all should celebrate Easter on one and the same day. But this wound of the Church broke out again. And first indeed under Constantine the Great; but this discord was calmed lightly and easily by the Synod of Nicaea, which condemned the Quartodecimans, as is found in Rufinus, book 1 of his History, chapter 6; Theodoret, book 1, chapter 10; Sozomen, book 1, chapter 16. Then again under Theodosius the Younger, when Nestorius, the heretic, who was then bishop of Constantinople, persecuted and assailed them most savagely (Socrates, book 7, chapter 29). At last this heresy, having spread most wretchedly through the Church for so many years, that is, more than 200, was utterly weakened and fell silent. Nevertheless the Audaeans later revived this error.

units.la: 2 Nisi quartadecima.)Prima quidem horum haereticorum hypothesis fuit, Pascha nonnisi 14. luna celebrandum esse ad morem Iudæorum. Itaque in quamcunque hebdomadæ diem inciderit illa luna, ieiunabant, & vigilias agebant, siue ea dies Dominica fuisset, siue alia. Qua in re dupliciter peccari Patres Ecclesiastici censebant. Primum propter imitationem Iudæorum, à quorum iugo & cæremoniis Christi beneficio liberati sumus. Et hoc quidem recte. Secundum, propterea quod die Dominica, & imprimis Paschae, ieiunare nefas omnino veteres existimabant, vt apparet ex Conciliorum decretis, & est non tantum in Can.Scire debet, distinct. 76. sed etiam apud Eusebium lib.5.Histor.cap.23. Hoc vero ridiculum fuit, ne dicam superstitiosum. Quemadmodum & illud, quod tam anxie Paschatis festum in Ecclesia Christiana commemorari & celebrari debere voluerunt, quum non Pascha, sed Coena Domini fit nobis nec quidem semel tantum in anno, sed quoties coetus commoditas id patitur, celebranda. 2 Poenitentiam hominibus post Baptismum lapsis denegant. Id quod ex Nouatianorum fæce sumptum est, seu potius a Nouatianis ex Quartidecimanorum errore. Socrat. lib.5. cap. 22. Sic de-lirant, ut ait Augustinus lib.2. contra Faust. qui sinam doctrinam non sustinentes, ad fabulas convertuntur.
units.tr: 2 Unless on the fourteenth. The first tenet of these heretics was that Easter must be kept only on the fourteenth day of the moon, after the custom of the Jews. So whatever day of the week that moon fell on, they fasted and kept vigils, whether it was the Lord's Day or another day. In this the Fathers of the Church held that there were two faults. The first was imitation of the Jews, from whose yoke and ceremonies we have been freed by the benefit of Christ. In this they were right. The second was that the ancients thought it utterly wrong to fast on the Lord's Day, and above all on Easter, as appears from the decrees of the councils. This is found not only in the canon Scire debet, distinction 76, but also in Eusebius, Histories, book 5, chapter 23. Yet this was ridiculous, not to say superstitious. So too was their anxious wish that the feast of Easter be commemorated and celebrated in the Christian Church, when for us it is not Easter but the Lord's Supper that is to be celebrated, and not only once a year but as often as the opportunity of the congregation allows. 2 They deny repentance to people who have fallen after baptism. This was taken from the dregs of the Novatians, or rather the Novatians took it from the error of the Quartadecimans. Socrates, book 5, chapter 22. They rave in this way, as Augustine says in book 2 against Faustus, since they cannot bear sound teaching and turn to fables.

units.la: CAP. XXX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXX.

units.la: Alogiani cur dicti. Erroris autem eorum capita duo recensentur.
units.tr: Why the Alogians are so called. Two heads of their error are listed.

units.la: A[?]logiani proterea sic{1}vocantur, tanquam sine verbo (λόγος enim Graece verbum dicitur) quia Deum Verbum recipere noluerunt, Ioannis Euangelium respuentes, cuius nec Apocalypsin accipiunt. Has videlicet Scripturas negant esse ipsius.
units.tr: The Alogians are so called as if they were "without the Word" (for λόγος is the Greek word for word), because they refused to accept God the Word, rejecting the Gospel of John, and they do not accept the Apocalypse either. Namely, they deny that these Scriptures are his.

units.la: 1 Sic vocantur.) Immanior vero & tetrior superiore fuit hæc pestis & hæresis, de qua nunc sumus dicturi: quam qui sequuntur, Alogi, Alogij, Alogiani, & Artemonitæ vocantur. His enim tot nominibus una illa secta dicta est. Ἀλόγοι[?] quidem & Ἀλόγια[?] ab Epiphanio & alijs: quas voces Latini Alogos & Alogianos verterunt, vti hoc loco Augustinus. Ifidorus vero Alo-gios, quod λόγον Θεοῦ, qui est Christus, negarent esse & Deum, & Dei Filium. Itaque quod λό-γον significationem & vocabulum, quo Ioannes Euangelista tamen vtitur, repudiarent, Alogij sunt appellati. Sed etiam Berilliani a Berillo Boftrenfi, vel vt alij volunt, Boffeenfi Episcopo (est autem episcopatus Arabiae) qui λόγον Θεοῦ Christum no prius fuisse dicunt, quam ex Maria nasceretur, vt & Eufeb. lib. 3. c. 27. & Niceph. libro 5. cap. 22. tradunt. & antea Artemonitae ab Artemone primo huius erroris parente, homine profano & blasphemo, qui de Ebionis hæretici cæno & latrina suum illud pestiferum lac & dogma bibit, quod in Ecclesiam effudit. Alij ex Aristotelicorum schola profectos volunt, vti Funccius libr. 6. commentar. Illud autem semel sparsum latissime propagatum est. Ergo hæc eadem ab authore Artemonis hæresis appellatur. Videtur tamen Tertullianus in libro De præscriptionibus aduerf. hæret. primum huius veneni inuentorem facere Theodotiu quendam Byzantinum, sed quemadmodum docet Alexander Alexandriae Episcopus, qui primus Arianis se opposuit, & refert Theodoret. lib. 1. Hiftor. cap. 4. altius est arcessendum huius mali caput, nempe ab Ebione. Ebioni tamen non tribuitur, sed Artemoni, quia falsarum rationum pigmentis & coloribus acceptum ab illo malum sic exornauit, vt author, non hæres aut successor huius dogmatis videretur. Theodotius autem ille Byzantinus tantum illius propagator, diligentissimus quidem & defensor acerrimus fuit, Artemonísque primarius discipulus, quemadmodum ex Eufcb.Hiftor.lib.5. cap.28. facilè colligi poterit. Uixit autem Artemo vel Artemas (nam utroque nomine vocatur) & suum illud nocentissimum virus ex Ebionis libris recoctum euomuit, extremo tempore pontificatus Victoris episcopi Romani, sub imperatore Seuero circa annum à Christo passo 167. Quis autem fuerit Artemo iste, & unde primùm prodierit, & quem vitæ exitum habuerit, apud probatos scriptores, quibus fidem habere velim, non inuenio, tantùm à Victore episcopo Romano excommunicatum fuisse tradunt. Nec certè tam nefarij hominis vita aut memoria nisi ad vituperationem cognoscenda est. Hic igitur error aliquandiu post Artemonē à Theodotio ipsius discipulo defensus est: sed tandem variis doctorum Episcoporum dispu-tationibus confutatus conticescebat, donec pe-nè 60. post annis à Paulo Samosateno reuoca-tus, & postea ab Ario interpolatus, iterum vi-xit funestum certè quidem humano generi ma-lum, & pessimum, si quod aliud, Satanæ vene-num, & quo sanam Euangelij doctrinam maxime labefactauit: & summas in Ecclesia dis-cordias implacabilesque immisit. Latissimè i-gitur vagata est hæc hæresis, & omnes orbis Christiani regiones infecit. Diutissimè præter-ea retenta est, quando ne nunc quidem periit, sed à variis per singulas hominum ætates repeti-ta & interpolata viget adhuc, & grassatur. Præ-cipuum enim salutis nostræ fundamétum euer-tit, quod est, Dominum nostrum Iesum Chri-stum, stum, nostrum apud Deum mediatorem, & in quem speramus, esse verum Deum, vti verus quoque homo est. Neque enim Ἰησοῦς [?] & Seruator noster esse potest Christus, nisi Deus, atque adeo verus, & per se, non autem emendicatus & factitius, fuerit.
units.tr: 1 (They are so called.) This plague and heresy, of which we are now going to speak, was fiercer and more loathsome than the one before. Those who follow it are called Alogi, Alogii, Alogians, and Artemonites. That one sect has been given all these names. Epiphanius and others call them Ἀλόγοι [Alogoi] and Ἀλόγια [Alogia], which the Latins have rendered as Alogos and Alogianos, as Augustine does here. Isidore calls them Alogios, because they deny that the Word of God [λόγον Θεοῦ] is God and the Son of God, namely Christ. So they were called Alogi because they rejected the meaning and the word λόγος, which the Evangelist John nevertheless uses. There were also the Berillians, named after Beryl, bishop of Bostra, or as others prefer, of Bosra (which is a bishopric in Arabia). They said that Christ, the Word of God, did not exist before he was born of Mary, as Eusebius (book 3, chapter 27) and Nicephorus (book 5, chapter 22) report. Earlier they were called Artemonites, after Artemon, the first parent of this error, a profane and blasphemous man, who drank that pestilent milk and doctrine from the filth and sewer of the heretic Ebion and poured it out into the Church. Others think they came from the school of the Aristotelians, as Funccius does in book 6 of his Commentaries. But once this was sown, it spread very widely, so this same heresy is also named after the author of it, Artemon. Tertullian, in his book On Prescription against Heretics, seems to make a certain Theodotus of Byzantium the first inventor of this poison. But as Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, who was the first to oppose the Arians, teaches, and as Theodoret reports (book 1 of the History, chapter 4), the root of this evil must be traced further back, namely to Ebion. Yet it is not ascribed to Ebion but to Artemon, because he decked out the evil he had received from Ebion with the paint and colours of false arguments, so that he appeared as the author of this doctrine rather than its heir or successor. That Theodotus of Byzantium was only its propagator, though a most diligent and fierce defender, and Artemon's chief disciple, as can easily be gathered from Eusebius, History, book 5, chapter 28. Now Artemon (or Artemas, for he is called by either name) lived and vomited forth that most harmful poison, recooked from the books of Ebion, at the end of the pontificate of Victor, bishop of Rome, under the emperor Severus, about the year 167 after Christ's passion. But who this Artemon was, and where he first appeared, and what end he came to, I cannot find in approved writers whom I would wish to trust; they report only that he was excommunicated by Victor, bishop of Rome. Nor indeed is the life or memory of so wicked a man worth knowing, except for reproach. This error, then, was defended for some time after Artemon by Theodotus, his own disciple. But at last it was refuted by various disputations of learned bishops and fell silent, until nearly sixty years later it was revived by Paul of Samosata, and afterwards corrupted by Arius, and it lived again, certainly a deadly evil for the human race, and the worst poison of Satan, if there ever was one, by which it greatly undermined the sound doctrine of the Gospel and brought great and implacable discords into the Church. This heresy therefore wandered very widely and infected all the regions of the Christian world. Moreover, it has held on for a very long time, since it has not perished even now, but is repeated and corrupted in various ages of men and still flourishes and rages. For it overturns the chief foundation of our salvation, which is that our Lord Jesus Christ, our mediator with God, in whom we hope, is true God as he is also true man. For Jesus [Ἰησοῦς] and our Saviour cannot be Christ unless he is God, and therefore true and God in himself, not a beggar's borrowed and made-up god.

units.la: In impressis, Domini Verbum: in margine Deum Verbum, & omnino rectius. Primum, quia melius mentem Artemonis exprimit, qui non negabat aliquod omnino esse Dei verbum, quum Deus esset locus: sed negabat λόγον & Verbum quod appellat Ioannes in Euangelio cap. I. esse Θεὸν, id est, Deum. Sic enim loquitur Ioan. versu 1. καὶ Θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος, erátq; Sermo ille Deus. nō dicit autem tantùm καὶ Θεοῦ ἦν ὁ λόγος, erátq; Sermo ille Dei, quod postremum Artemon facilè admitteret. Deinde, quia sic legitur apud Isidor. Deum Verbum negant, qui sua ex Augustino manifestè descripsit, vt ambigi non possit, quo modo illo seculo hic Augustini locus legeretur. Ergo primum huius hæreseos caput fuit, Christum merum esse hominem, non esse Deum, non Dei Filium, non λόγον. Nam vocem ipsam λόγου, qua Christi deitas castissimè, vt veteres sentiunt, à Ioanne describitur, expungunt, totúmque adeò Ioannis Euangelium, quod non recipiunt. Hoc fuit & Samosatcniani & Ariani erroris semen, & postea Mahumetani, nunc etiam Seruetani: in quem etiam scopulum antea & Ebion, & Cerinthus infeliciter impegerant, sed eorum tristi naufragio non est factus Artemon prudentior. Christum igitur ex virgine Maria tantum natum,& hominem esse:no etiam ex Deo, quia non sit Deus:& quod Christus caeteris hominibus & Prophetis ipsis excellentior extitis-set,id factum esse, non natura,sed eadem gratia quae nobis a Deo confertur,quae maiori mensura in Christum collata est. Theodoret.lib.2. hae retic.fabul. Λόγον [?] autem imprimis repudiabat, quod ab aliis Euangelistis Christus non dicere-tur λόγος. Sed Deum demonstrari ab ijs & probari negare, quantumuis impius sit Artemon, non potest, quum eum hominum corda nosse, & secretas animi cogitationes,quum eum miracula non aliena,sed sua propriaq; virtute edidisse,quum Emmanuelem illum verum fuisse alij Euangelistae ubique doceant,Matth.1. v. 23, 22. vers.18,7.vers.22.Marc.1.vers.24.Luc.1. vers.32. Praeterea ne profani quidem ipsi tam fuerunt in Christum blasphemi quam Artemon. Nam quemadmodum in libro De praepar. Euange-lica scribit Eusebius. Numenius quidam Platoni-cus philosophus admirabatur assentiebatur-que Ioanni Christum Dei Filium vocati & λόγον & Deum,quod & recte & vere dici fatebatur,ne-dum ut id negent homines qui se Christum amplecti venditant. Christum quidem etiam hominem agnoscimus,qui ex Maria virgine natus sit ut putat Epiphanius, die quinta Ianuarij mensis, & qui triginta post annis eadem die baptizatus est.Alij alio die censent. 2 Caput erroris fuit, Quod Ioannis Euangelium & Apocalypsin hi quoque reijcerent. Nam utrumque a Cerintho scriptum esse non a Ioanne conten-dcbant. De Apocalypsi fuit aliqua in Ecclesia controuercontrouersia à quo scripta fuerit, quanquam nulli Patres orthodoxi eam haeretici hominis esse volunt. De Euangelio nemo dubitauit vnquam, aut controuersiam mouit. Praeterea Cerinthus ipse Christi deitatem negauit, vt Euangelium illud scripsisse dici non possit. Denique si Ioannis epistolas admittunt, quas non repudiabant, ex iisdem reuincentur. Nam 1. Epist. cap.i.versu i. idem de Christo, quod in Euangelio confirmatur, eum & verum Deum & verum hominē fuisse. Sed quid istis beluis facias, quae furore animi abreptae & se & alios miserè perdunt?
units.tr: In the printed editions it reads "the Word of the Lord," but in the margin "God the Word," and altogether that is more correct. First, because it better expresses the mind of Artemon, who did not deny that there was some word of God at all, since God had spoken; but he denied that the λόγος, the Word which John calls in the Gospel, chapter 1, is θεός, that is, God. For John says in verse 1: καὶ Θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος [kai Theos ēn ho logos], "and the Word was God." He does not say only καὶ Θεοῦ ἦν ὁ λόγος [kai Theou ēn ho logos], "and the Word was of God," which Artemon could easily have admitted. Second, because Isidore reads it thus: "they deny God the Word," and he plainly described his words from Augustine, so that there can be no doubt how this passage of Augustine was read in that age. So the first head of this heresy was that Christ is a mere man, not God, not the Son of God, not the λόγος. For they strike out the very word λόγος, by which the deity of Christ is most chastely described by John, as the ancients understand it, and so they reject the whole Gospel of John. This was the seed of the error of the Samosatenes and the Arians, and afterwards of the Mahometans, and now also of the Servetians. Ebion and Cerinthus had previously struck unhappily on this same rock, but Artemon was not made wiser by their sad shipwreck. Therefore they hold that Christ was born only of the virgin Mary and is only a man, not also of God, because he is not God; and that Christ surpassed other men and the prophets themselves in excellence, and that this came about not by nature but by the same grace that is conferred on us by God, which was poured into Christ in a greater measure. (Theodoret, book 2, Heretical Fables.) But Artemon rejected the λόγος above all, because Christ was not called λόγος by the other evangelists. Yet no matter how impious Artemon is, he cannot deny that God is shown and proved by them, since God knows the hearts of men and their secret thoughts, since he worked miracles not by another's but by his own proper power, and since the other evangelists everywhere teach that he was that true Emmanuel (Matthew 1:23; 22; verse 18; 7; verse 22; Mark 1:24; Luke 1:32). Moreover, even the profane were not so blasphemous against Christ as Artemon. For, as Eusebius writes in his book On the Preparation for the Gospel, Numenius, a certain Platonic philosopher, admired John and agreed with him that Christ is called the Son of God, both λόγος and God, and he confessed that this is rightly and truly said; much less should men who boast that they embrace Christ deny it. We acknowledge Christ also as man, who was born of the virgin Mary on the fifth day of January, as Epiphanius thinks, and who was baptized on the same day thirty years later. Others think on another day. 2 The second head of the error was that these men also rejected the Gospel of John and the Apocalypse. For they contended that both had been written by Cerinthus and not by John. There was some controversy in the Church about who wrote the Apocalypse, although no orthodox Fathers wished it to be the work of a heretic. No one ever doubted or raised controversy about the Gospel. Moreover, Cerinthus himself denied the deity of Christ, so that the Gospel could not be said to have been written by him. Finally, if they admit the Epistles of John, which they did not reject, they are refuted by those same epistles. For in 1 John 1:1 the same thing is confirmed about Christ as in the Gospel, that he was both true God and true man. But what can one do with such beasts, who, carried away by the fury of their minds, ruin both themselves and others miserably?

units.la: CAP. XXXI.
units.tr: CAP. XXXI.

units.la: Adamiani cur sic nominati. Erroris autem tria capita commemorantur.
units.tr: Why the Adamians are so named. Three heads of this error are recounted.

units.la: ADamiani ex Adam{1} dicti, cuius imitantur{2} in paradiso nuditatem, quae fuit ante peccatum. Unde & nuptias auersantur, quia nec prius quam peccasset Adam, nec prius quam dimissus esset de paradiso cognouit uxorem. Credut ergo quod nuptia futura non fuissent, si nemo peccasset. Nudi itaque mares fœmi-næq; conueniunt, nudi lectiones audiunt, nudi orant, nudi celebrant Sacramenta. Et ex hoc paradisum-suam[?] arbitrantur Ecclesiam.•
units.tr: The Adamians are so called from Adam, whose nakedness in paradise, which existed before sin, they imitate. Hence they also shun marriage, because Adam did not know his wife before he sinned, nor before he was sent out of paradise. They therefore believe that marriages would not have taken place had no one sinned. So men and women meet naked, hear the lessons naked, pray naked, and celebrate the sacraments naked. And from this they regard their Church as paradise.

units.la: {I} Adamiani.) Non videtur in hac haeresi collocanda diligenter ab Augustino obseruata ratio tēporis, sed nec ab Epiph. quem August. sequi gaudet. Quare potius Isidoru sequor, qui hos cum Cainianis & Sethianis coniungit. Eodem enim pene tempore videntur hi omnes exorti, & ex stirpe Carpocratianorum vel femine sunt infelicissimus prouetus & seges. Unde post Gnosticos erat reponendi. Nam Gnostici & Adamiani sunt ex eodem Valentinianorum turbido fonte diuortia duo, & riui diuersi. Dicuntur autem ijdem hi Prodiciani, quod à Prodico profecti sint, quemadmodum Theodoretus lib.i: Hæret.fabul.tradit. Dicuntur ab aliis Adamitæ non Adamiani, quaquam alij separant, quasi Adamitæ non sint hæretici, sed monachorum genus inter veteres Christianos receptum. Adamiani vero sint hæretici, quos vetus Ecclesia damnauit. Adamiani vero dicti sunt ab Adamo primo illo homine, cuius nuditatem & vitæ genus, & puritatem illi se imitari putant, sed falso. Videtur tamen Epiphanius in argumento libro 2. Tom.i. sentire ab authore suo sic nominatos, qui Adam vocaretur. Ἀδαμιανοί, ait, ἀπό τινος Ἀδὰμ ζῶντος καλούμενοι[?]. Huius sectæ pauci scriptores meminerunt, quia, ut ait Epiphanius, fuit minuta hæresis, & statim ex Ecclesia Dei non tantùm explosa, sed etiam in orbe terrarum extincta. Ac ne nunc quidem nomen eius extaret, nisi Monachi quidam qui se falsò pietatis & vitæ austeritatis prætextu commendarunt, horum hæreticorum impudentes prorsus mores retinuissent, & inter sanctissima ordinis & regulæ suæ præcepta posuissent, quales ij qui etiam nunc hodie Adamitæ dicuntur, viguntque plurimùm in Italia: & alij quidam qui Theodosij iunioris seculo vixerunt, de quibus scribit Euagr.lib.i.Historor.cap.2i.[?] Viuunt enim nudi non necessitate quidem adacti, vel inopia vestimentorum, sed ex voti professione. Quo conuersationis genere nihil certe dici vel cogitari potest foedius & turpius: sed foedis hominibus Monachis perplacent foedi mores. In quo sunt primis & sanctioribus Monachis dissimillimi, qui, quanquam soli, tamen nunquam se nudos videre sustinuerunt, quod refert variis in locis Historia Ecclesiastica, Socrat. libro 4. cap.23. Sozom. libro 1. cap.14. Fuerunt autem Adamiani haeretici, quemadmodum scribit Epiphanius, ex μοναζόντων[?] & ἐγκρατευομένων[?], id est, Monachorum genere, ne qui eorum nuditatem probarunt & secuti sunt, putent se haereticis illis esse propter monachalem vitæ rationem meliores. Quanquam autem & Prodici & Carpocratis soboles appellantur: verius tamen Cynicorum illorum, qui ab inverecundia & impudentia dicti sunt, propago fuisse videntur, quos ubique ex sacra Scriptura damnat August. imprimis autem in libris De ciuit. Dei.
units.tr: {I} Adamians.) The order of time, which Augustine observed carefully, does not seem to place this heresy here, nor does Epiphanius, whom Augustine is pleased to follow. Therefore I prefer to follow Isidore, who joins these with the Cainites and Sethians. For all of them seem to have arisen at about the same time, and they are the most unhappy offshoot and crop from the stock, or seed, of the Carpocratians. Hence they should be placed after the Gnostics. For the Gnostics and the Adamians are two streams flowing from the same muddy spring of the Valentinians, and are different rivulets. These same people are also called Prodicians, because they came from Prodicus, as Theodoret relates in book 1 of his Heretical Fables. Others call them Adamites rather than Adamians, although others distinguish the two, as if the Adamites were not heretics but a kind of monks received among the ancient Christians. But the Adamians are heretics, whom the ancient Church condemned. The Adamians are named from Adam, that first man, whose nakedness, way of life and purity they think they imitate, but falsely. Yet Epiphanius, in the argument of book 2, vol. 1, seems to hold that they were named after their founder, who was called Adam. "Adamians," he says, "are called from a certain living Adam" [Ἀδαμιανοί, ἀπό τινος Ἀδὰμ ζῶντος καλούμενοι]. Few writers mention this sect because, as Epiphanius says, it was a small heresy, and it was not only at once cast out of the Church of God but also extinguished throughout the world. Its name would not even survive now, unless certain monks, who falsely commend themselves under a pretence of piety and austerity of life, had retained the utterly shameless morals of these heretics and placed them among the most holy precepts of their order and rule. Such are those who are even today called Adamites and flourish greatly in Italy, and certain others who lived in the age of Theodosius the Younger, of whom Evagrius writes in book 1 of his Histories, chapter 21. For they live naked, not indeed compelled by necessity or lack of clothing, but from a profession of vow. Certainly nothing can be said or imagined as more foul and shameful as a way of life; but foul morals please foul men, the monks. In this they are most unlike the first and holier monks, who, although alone, never endured to see themselves naked, as Church history reports in various places: Socrates, book 4, chapter 23; Sozomen, book 1, chapter 14. The Adamians were heretics, as Epiphanius writes, from the class of monastics and ascetics [μοναζόντων, ἐγκρατευομένων], that is, of the monastic kind. Some of these approved their nakedness and followed it, thinking themselves better than those heretics because of their monastic way of life. Although they are also called offspring of Prodicus and Carpocrates, they seem more truly to have been a progeny of those Cynics, who were named for their shamelessness and impudence, and whom Augustine condemns everywhere from Holy Scripture, especially in the books On the City of God.

units.la: 2 Cuius imitantur.)Hæ fere sunt horum hominum & haereticorum hypotheses. 1 Oportere Christianos homines versari in publico, in coetu Ecclesiæ, in precibus, nudos, sive mares sint sive fœminæ, ad imitationem Adami, ad cuius statum & puritatem renouauit nos Christus. Si enim iam nos vllius membri nostri pudet, nos secundum carnem & externum hominem, qui in nobis periisse debet, viuere: nō secundum internum. Denique quum vestimenta sint peccati testimonia, & taquam corporis nostri vin-cula, exuenda esse iis qui Christi beneficium sentiunt. Haec phalerata hominum oratio refu-tatur illo Pauli loco qui est 1.Corinth.12. versu 23. & plane in reprobum sensum traditi viden-tur, quos ne suae quidem & manifestae foedita-tis pudeat. Sunt igitur ἀναίσχυντοι [?]. i. impudentes. Atque tamen hi sunt alij ab illis haereticis, qui nudis pedibus incedunt, de quibus infra. Hi au-tem Persarum Gymnosophistas imitati viden-tur, qui totam vitam nudi transfigunt, & dicun-tur σκύμνοι [?], vt ait Clemens lib.3.Strom. 2 Nu-ptias damnant, vt Satanae consilium & opus, con-tra illud quod est, Hebr.13.versu 4. 3 Mulie-res tamen communes habent, & habendas esse contendunt. Itaque extinctis in suo coetu lucer-nis promiscue coeunt, quemadmodum ex Cle-mente Strom. notat Theodoretus. 4 Deum a nobis precandum & orandum esse negant, quia scit ipse per se quibus egeamens. Clemens hoc de illis tradit, lib.7. Strom. At dicit Chri-stus, Petite & accipietis, Matth.6. & iubet Psal. 50. ut Deum invocemus in afflictione. 5 Coe-tus suos dicunt esse illum paradisum qui a Deo beatis sit promissus: adeo ut ex eorum senten-tia sit in his terris vita aeterna & felix quaeren-da nobis, quam tamen in altero demum seculo iubentur fideles exspectare, 1.Corinth.13.ver.12. Matth.25. Decepti sunt homines insulsi, quod factas Ecclesiae promissiones, hic impleri exi-stimaret. In quo eode scopulo multi naufragiu fecerunt, ut Pepuziani, Basilidiani, postea Serue-tani. Sed etiam Nepotiani, qui a Nepote quodam Ægyptiacæ vrbis Episcopo dicti sunt, idé senserunt, quemadmodum Theodoretus scri- bit lib.3. hæreticar.fabul. & Platina in vita Sixti Rom. Episcopi. Atque hæ tot ex vna illa Ada- mianorum cauerna exhalant pestes.
units.tr: 2 Whom they imitate.) These are nearly the assumptions of these men and heretics. (1) That Christians ought to live in public, in the assembly of the Church, and in prayers, naked, whether men or women, in imitation of Adam, to whose state and purity Christ restored us. For if we are now ashamed of any member of ours, we live according to the flesh and the outward man, which ought to perish in us, not according to the inward man. Finally, since garments are testimonies of sin and, as it were, chains of our body, those who perceive Christ's benefit ought to strip them off. This ornate speech of men is refuted by that passage of Paul, 1 Corinthians 12:23, and they seem plainly delivered over to a reprobate mind who are not even ashamed of their own manifest foulness. They are therefore shameless [ἀναίσχυντοι], that is, impudent. And yet these are different from those heretics who walk barefoot, about whom below. These seem to imitate the Gymnosophists of the Persians, who spend their whole life naked and are called "skymni" [σκύμνοι], as Clement says in book 3 of the Stromata. (2) They condemn marriage as the counsel and work of Satan, against that which is honourable, Hebrews 13:4. (3) Yet they hold wives in common, and contend that they ought to be held in common. Thus, when the lamps have been extinguished in their assembly, they come together promiscuously, as Theodoret notes from Clement's Stromata. (4) They deny that God must be prayed to and besought by us, because he himself knows by himself what we lack. Clement reports this of them, book 7 of the Stromata. But Christ says, "Ask and you shall receive," Matthew 6, and Psalm 50 bids us call upon God in affliction. (5) They say that their assemblies are that paradise which is promised by God to the blessed, so that in their opinion eternal and happy life is to be sought by us on this earth, which the faithful are nevertheless bidden to await only in the age to come, 1 Corinthians 13:12, Matthew 25. Foolish men have been deceived, thinking that the promises made to the Church are fulfilled here. Many have suffered shipwreck on this same rock: the Pepuzians, the Basilidians, and later the Servetians. But also the Nepotians, who were named after a certain Nepos, bishop of an Egyptian city, held the same view, as Theodoret writes in book 3 of his Heretical Fables, and Platina in the life of Sixtus, bishop of Rome. So many pests breathe out from that one cave of the Adamians.

units.la: CAP. XXXII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXII.

units.la: Elcefei cur sic appellati. Erroris autem eorum caput vnum hoc loco commemoratum.
units.tr: Why the Elcesaites were so called. Their chief error is mentioned here.

units.la: Lcefeos & Sampseos hic tanquam ordi- ne suo commemorat Epiphanius, quos di- cit a quodā pseudoprophetā esse deceptos, qui vocatur Elci, ex cuius genere duas mulieres tanquam deas ab eis perhibet adoratas. Cetera Ebioneis tenere similia.
units.tr: Epiphanius mentions the Lcesaeans and Sampsaeans here, as if in their proper order. He says they were deceived by a certain false prophet called Elci, from whose family he says two women were worshipped by them as goddesses. In other respects they hold views similar to the Ebionites.

units.la: 1 Elcefeos & Sampseos.) Variis nominibus & hi quoque dicti sunt Elcefei, vel Elcefaitæ, ab Elcefai quodā homine impostore, qui Chri- stianam fidem & nomen ementitus est, quum vtrunque oppugnarit apertissimè. Sic igitur & hoc etiam loco legendum puto, Elcefai, non autem Elci, vt vulgò in impressis: sed facilis fuit scribarum lapsus, qui nomen hoc abbreuiatu- ris descriptum, Elci, imperitè legerunt, & po- stea transmiserunt. Etiā in Epiphanio Ηλξα cor rupte, meo quidem iudicio, legitur. Melius au- tem & emendatius apud Eusebium, & Theo- doretum lib.2.hæret.sabul. sed quia prætermis- sa est ab Isidoro hæc hæresis, non videmus quomodo veteres apud Augustinum olim legerint. Fuit autem Elcesai primus huius erroris author, unde dicti sunt Elcesaitae, quanquam cum ex Ebionitarum, Nazareorum, &c, quod peius est, Essenorum coeno impurissimo hauserit, adeo ut Elcesaitas annumeret Ebionitis Epiphanius, sed propriam sectam & erroris genus separatu constituunt Epiphanius & Theodoretus. Varie autem sparsa Elcesai haeretici dogmata collegit, acerrimeque pro iis propugnauit primus Alcibiades quidam ex Apamaea Coelesyriae urbe profectus. Vocati sunt etiam Sampsaei, Graece Σαμψαῖοι[?], ut ait Epiphanius, quasi illi lacertarum generi similes, quas ἀλλαχῆς[?] Graeci i. stelliones appellant, genus animalis variis notis maculatum & mutabile: sic isti fuerunt ex pluribus haereticis conflati, & in moribus ποικιλόμορφοι[?] & versipelles, quum fidem Christianam abnegare non reformidarent. Utrum illa vox Sampse fuerit Arabica, sive Aegyptiaca, ambi-gitur, tamen in iis maxime regionibus valuit & obtinuit haec haeresis, quaquam & Syriaca vox fuisse videri potest argument. c.4. v.23. Esdrae.
units.tr: 1 Elcesaeans and Sampsaeans.) These people were also called by various names: Elcesaeans, or Elcesaites, after Elcesai, a certain impostor who falsely assumed the Christian faith and name, while he openly attacked both. So I think that in this passage too we should read Elcesai, not Elci as in the printed editions. It was an easy slip for the copyists, who misread Elci, written in abbreviated form for this name, and then passed the error on. In Epiphanius too the name is corruptly read, in my judgement, as Ηλξα. It is read better and more correctly in Eusebius and in Theodoret, Book 2 of the Heretical Fables. But since this heresy was passed over by Isidore, we cannot see how the older writers read it in Augustine. Elcesai was the first author of this error, and so they were called Elcesaites, although he drew from the most impure filth of the Ebionites, Nazarenes and others, and, what is worse, of the Essenes, so much so that Epiphanius counts the Elcesaites among the Ebionites. Epiphanius and Theodoret, however, set them up as a separate sect and a distinct kind of error. Elcesai gathered together the scattered doctrines of heretics in various ways, and Alcibiades, a man from Apamea, a city of Coele-Syria, was the first to come forward and defend them most fiercely. They were also called Sampsaeans, in Greek Σαμψαῖοι, as Epiphanius says, as if they were like that kind of lizard which the Greeks call ἀλλαχῆς, that is, stellions, an animal marked with various spots and changeable in colour. So these men were compounded out of several heretics, and in their conduct they were many-shaped [ποικιλόμορφοι] and turncoats, since they did not shrink from denying the Christian faith. It is uncertain whether the word Sampse was Arabic or Egyptian. Yet this heresy flourished and held sway above all in those regions, though the word may also seem to be Syriac; see Esdrae c.4 v.23.

units.la: Ipsi vero se Prognosticos & Prophetas appel-lant, quia quibusdam incantationibus & astro-logicis etiam obseruationibus confisi profiten-tur se futura posse praedicere. Coepit autem hoc malum in Ecclesia Dei grassari, Origene iam fere, aduersus quod ille scriptis suis pugnauit, sub Anthero Rom. episcopo, & Gordiano imperatore, circa annum a passo Christo 210. quam quam Ioan. Funccius in annum 218. reiicit, sed nos nostram sententiam ex Eusebio libro 6. Histor.cap.38.apertissimè cōfirmare possumus.
units.tr: They, however, call themselves Prognostics and Prophets, because they rely on certain incantations and astrological observations, and profess that they can foretell the future. This evil began to spread in the Church of God, already almost in Origen's time, against which he fought in his writings, under Anterus, bishop of Rome, and the emperor Gordian, about the year 210 after the suffering of Christ. John Funccius places it in the year 218, but we can confirm our view very clearly from Eusebius, Book 6 of the History, chapter 38.

units.la: Durauit autem ad tempora vsque Epiphanij (vixit sub Theodosio iuniore Epiphan.) in Arabia maximè, quæ vergit ad mare mortuum, item in Moabitide & Iturææ Syriæ prouinciis.
units.tr: It lasted, however, down to the times of Epiphanius (he lived under Theodosius the Younger), chiefly in Arabia, which borders on the Dead Sea, and likewise in the provinces of Moabitis and Iturea in Syria.

units.la: Orta est in Peræa, non autem in Petræa Arabiæ regione. Peræa verò est Iudæ pars, quæ Arabiæ & Ægypto proxima asperis dispersa est montibus, & à cæteris Iudæis Iordane amne discreta, quemadmodum Plinius docet libro 5. Natural.Histor.cap.14. sed ibi primum nata,latissimè postea propagata est, & à Rhetorianis hæreticis, qui subsecuti sunt, interpolata & repetita. de quibus infrà.
units.tr: It arose in Peraea, not in Petraea, a region of Arabia. Peraea is a part of Judea, lying near Arabia and Egypt, scattered over rough mountains, and separated from the other Jews by the river Jordan, as Pliny teaches in Book 5 of the Natural History, chapter 14. But it first arose there and was afterwards spread very widely, and was corrupted and renewed by the Rhetorian heretics who followed, of whom more below.

units.la: 2 Duas mulieres.) Multa fuerunt horum phantasticorum dogmata peruersa. Consenserunt enim cum Ebionitis, quorum furorem etiam auxerunt suis additamentis. Ergo primum eorum erroris caput hoc fuit: Duos fuisse Christos, vnum infernum qui ex Maria virgine natus sit, & merè sit creatura: alterum supernum qui non sit cum illo inferno coalescens in vnam personam, etsi in eo ipso primo suo dogmate varius fuit hic doctor, tam est anceps mendacium. 2 Spiritum sanctum partim eundem cum Christo facit, eum tamen ab eo distinguit, quòd Christus in singula diffusus dicatur Spiritus: partim sororem Christi esse contendit, quæ nomine masculino appelletur, Theodoret.lib.2.Hæret. adeò puerili-ter de tantis mysteriis nugantur. Atqui Lex Dei vetat ne fœmina vel ipsum solum viri vestimentum induat, nedum vt se in illius speciem transformet, Deuter. 22.
units.tr: 2 Two women.) Many of these fantastical men's doctrines were perverse. For they agreed with the Ebionites, whose madness they even increased by their own additions. So the first head of their error was this: that there were two Christs, one lower, who was born of the Virgin Mary and was purely a creature, and another higher, who was not joined with that lower one into one person. Yet in this very first doctrine this teacher was inconsistent, so doubtful is his lie. He makes the Holy Spirit partly the same as Christ, yet distinguishes him from him, in that Christ is said to be the Spirit diffused into each individual; partly he contends that the Spirit is the sister of Christ, and is called by a masculine name. Theodoret, Book 2 of the Heresies. They trifle so childishly about such great mysteries. And yet the law of God forbids a woman to wear a man's garment, or even to use his clothing alone, let alone to transform herself into his likeness; Deut. 22.

units.la: 3 Deinde de utriusque longitudine & latitu-dine & locali diffusione blasphemè sentiunt.
units.tr: 3 Next they hold blasphemous opinions about the length and breadth of each of them, and about their spatial extension.

units.la: 4 Astrologia iudiciaria, Magia & variis incantationibus utuntur, per quas futura se praenun-tiare affirmant; quanquam manifestissimè de-prehendantur mentiri.
units.tr: 4 They use judicial astrology, magic and various incantations, by which they affirm that they foretell the future, although they are most plainly shown to be lying.

units.la: 5 Aquam tanquam Deum adorant. Epiphan. itemque duas quasdam foeminas sanctè vt deas colunt; quarum vnius nomen fuit Marthus: alterius Marthana, quarum pedum puluerem & saliuae screatum seruant & colunt, vti Papistae reliquias suorum sanctorum, per quae se morbis multis mederi dicunt. Fuerunt autem Elcesai cognatae, vt quidam volunt: vt alij vero, scorta.
units.tr: 5 They worship water as God. Epiphanius also says they reverently worship two women as goddesses, one of whom was named Marthus, the other Marthana. They keep and venerate the dust of their feet and the spittle they have spat out, just as the Papists do the relics of their saints, by which they say they cure many diseases. Some hold that these women were kinswomen of Elcesai, while others say they were prostitutes.

units.la: 6 Negant peccare eos qui persecutionis tempore fidem Christianam negant vel eiurant. Aduersus quem errorem accuratè disputauit Origines eumque confutauit, quemadmodum etiam à Christo damnatur, Matth.10. vers.33. & à Paulo Rom. 10. vers.10. Dixit autem & sensit hoc Elcesai propter persecutiones acerbissimas à Iul. Ma-ximino Imperatore Romano excitatas, in quas incidit, & quarum terrore perculsus hoc suum dogma finxit, vt sibi in abnegatione Christi faceret delicias, & impunitatem concederet.
units.tr: 6 They deny that those who deny or abjure the Christian faith in a time of persecution sin. Origen argued carefully against this error and refuted it, as it is also condemned by Christ, Matt. 10:33, and by Paul, Rom. 10:10. Elcesai said and held this because of the most bitter persecutions stirred up by the Roman emperor Julius Maximinus, in which he was caught up, and, struck with terror at them, he invented this doctrine so that he might make himself comfortable in denying Christ and grant himself impunity.

units.la: 7 Librum quendam Apocryphum à se conscriptum tantopere commendant, vt ex eius vel sola lectione omnium peccatorum remissionem à nobis obtineri contendat, non tantùm fidem & doctrinam percipi. Haec autem insanorum istorum deliria fuerunt.
units.tr: 7 They commend so highly a certain apocryphal book written by themselves that they contend we can obtain forgiveness of all sins from the mere reading of it, not merely to receive faith and doctrine. These were the delusions of those madmen.

units.la: CAP. XXXIII. Theodotiani cur sic appellati. Erroris autem eorum caput vnum,& causa haereseos explicata.
units.tr: CAP. XXXIII. Why the Theodotians were so called. Their one chief error is set out, and the cause of the heresy explained.

units.la: Theodotiani a Theodotione{1} quodam instituti hominem tantummodo{2} Christum asseuerant. Quod dicitur quidem Theodotion propterea docuisse, quia in persecutione lapsus, isto modo se casus sui deuitare putabat opprobrium, si non Deum negasset, sed hominem videretur.
units.tr: The Theodotians were founded by a certain Theodotion, and they affirm that Christ was only a man. It is said that Theodotion taught this because, having fallen away in the persecution, he thought that in this way he would avoid the disgrace of his lapse, provided that he seemed to have denied not God but only a man.

units.la: Hanc haeresin praetermisit Isidorus. Epiphanius tamen, Theodoretus & ijs antiquior Eusebius habet libro 5. Histor. cap. 28. Qui fuit huius haereseos parens & autor ab aliis Theodotus, vti a Tertulliano, appellatur, non autem Theodotion. Et Epiphanius ipse Θεόδοτον[?] nominat. Unde hoc quoque loco ex omnium scriptorum consensu reponerem, a Theodoto: delerem autem Theodotione. Nam hi ipsi ab aliis dicti sunt etiam Theodotij. Fuit autem & tempore & haeresi, & natione alius hic Theodotus de quo nunc Augustinus agit, a Theodotione; quem inter haereticos recensent scriptores Ecclesiastici. Theodotion enim quamquam Christum purum ψιλὸν[?] merum tantummodo hominem dixit, vti hic noster: Taciani tamen haeresin potius, quam Artemonis amplexus fuisse scribitur (nam Taciani fuit discipulus) qui Ephesius natione fuit, & cum Aquila vixit, Bibliorum Hebraeorum malignus interpres,quanquam tamen peritus linguæ Hebraicæ, sed demum ad Iudaifinum defecit, de quo Eufcb. lib.3. cap.8. & cuius versionis meminit in Exaplo sæpissime Origenes. Hic autem Theodotus fuit Byzantinus & Thrax natione, arte Coriarius vel κυνεύς, vt ait Epiphanius, Græcorum tamen literaturæ non imperitus, Artemonis primarius discipulus, acer ingenio, & ætate posterior Theodotione, prior tamen illo Theodoto, qui quaquam & ipse suam hærefin condidit, quæ Melchisedechianorū appellatur, fuit tamen hoc nostro posterior & iunior, quemadmodum in lib. De præscription. hæretic. scribit Tertullian. Vixit autem hic noster Theodot. qui, quod obstinatius Artemone ipso Christi diuinitatem oppugnaret, primus illius hæreseos autor fuisse scribitur ab Eufcb. lib.5. cap.28. vixit, inquam, sub Victore Romanorum Episcopo, & Seuero Imperatore, circa annum à Christo passo 170. quo primum cœpit innotescere, quanquam Platina cum Samosateno tanquam contemporaneum & coæqualem manifesto errore coniungit. Cum autem sub Seuero fuisset grauis Ecclesiæ persecutio, fidem Christianam abnegauit Theodotus. Propterea pudore suffusus patria Byzantio relicta Romam venit, vbi pro proditore Christi & Dei abnegatore agnitus, vt crimen tegeret negauit se Deum idcirco abnegasse, quia Christum eiurasset, sed tantum hominem, propterea quod Christus esset tantummodo homo. Hæc Epiphanius narrat. A Victore igitur damnatus & statim excomunicatus est, sed non resipuit, imo suum errorem latius sparsit. Itaque ad multos manauit error, & scholam & discipulos habuit, eosque plures, inter quos hi fuerunt praecipui, Theodotus mensarius, Hermophilus, Apollo-nides, qui tamen statim se in varias sectas & diuortia ex eodem orti fonte secuerunt, & inter se dogmate diuersi fuerunt, ita nimirum est incertum omne mendacium, & a seipso dissen-tiens. Theodoret.lib.2.Haeretic.fabular. Nicephor.lib.4. cap.21. Durauit autem haec haeresis diutissime non ipso quidem Theodotianorum nomine, quando ne temporibus quidem Epiphanij hac appellatione amplius nota fuit, sed interpolato & renouato a Paulo Samosateno & Ario postea pessimo dogmate. Eusebius tamen lib.6.cap.33. scribit Beryllum quendam similia prorsus huic Theodoto & sensisse & docuisse, qui Theodoto posterior fuit. Narratur vero quaedam historiola de Natali quodam qui cum pretio a Theodotianis inductus esset vt se pro eorum Episcopo gereret, idque acceptaf-set, ab Angelo noctu castigatus & flagellatus a Deo, errorem suum publice in orthodoxorum coetu confessus est, & eiurauit.
units.tr: Isidore passes over this heresy. Epiphanius, Theodoret, and the earlier Eusebius, however, deal with it in Book 5 of the History, chapter 28. The father and author of this heresy is called Theodotus by others, as by Tertullian, and not Theodotion. Epiphanius himself calls him Θεόδοτος [Theodotus]. So here, with the agreement of all the writers, I would read "from Theodotus" and delete "Theodotion", since these men were themselves called by others Theodotians. There was, however, another Theodotus, of whom Augustine now speaks, different from Theodotion both in time and in heresy and in nation; the ecclesiastical writers count Theodotion among the heretics. For although Theodotion said that Christ was a mere man [ψιλὸν], just as our man does, he is written to have embraced the heresy of Tatian rather than that of Artemon, for he was a disciple of Tatian. He was an Ephesian by birth and lived with Aquila, the malicious translator of the Hebrew Scriptures, though he was skilled in the Hebrew language; in the end he fell away to Judaism. See Eusebius, Book 3, chapter 8, and Origen, who very often mentions his version in the Hexapla. This Theodotus, however, was a Byzantine and a Thracian by nation, a tanner or hunter [κυνεύς], as Epiphanius says, yet not unlearned in Greek literature. He was the chief disciple of Artemon, sharp in intellect, and later in time than Theodotion but earlier than that other Theodotus who also founded his own heresy, called that of the Melchizedekians. Yet he was later and younger than this one, as Tertullian writes in his book On the Prescription of Heretics. This Theodotus lived, as is written by Eusebius in Book 5, chapter 28, under Victor, bishop of the Romans, and under the emperor Severus, about the year 170 after Christ's passion. He was written to be the first author of this heresy, because he attacked Christ's divinity more stubbornly than Artemon himself. He first became known about that time, although Platina wrongly and manifestly joins him with Samosatenus as a contemporary and equal. When a severe persecution of the Church arose under Severus, Theodotus denied the Christian faith. Overcome with shame, he left his native Byzantium and came to Rome, where he was recognised as a traitor to Christ and a denier of God. To cover his crime, he denied that he had therefore abjured God because he had renounced Christ, but said that he had only renounced a man, because Christ was only a man. Epiphanius relates this. Condemned by Victor, he was at once excommunicated, but he did not repent; rather, he spread his error more widely. So the error spread to many, and he had a school and many disciples, among whom these were the most prominent: Theodotus the money-changer, Hermophilus, and Apollonides. Yet they at once split into various sects and divisions, arising from the same source, and they differed among themselves in doctrine. So indeed every lie is unstable and at odds with itself. See Theodoret, Book 2 of the Heretical Fables, and Nicephorus, Book 4, chapter 21. This heresy lasted a very long time, not indeed under the name of the Theodotians, since that name was no longer well known even in Epiphanius's time, but in a corrupted and renewed form, through Paul of Samosata and later through the most pernicious doctrine of Arius. Eusebius, however, in Book 6, chapter 33, writes that a certain Beryl held and taught things altogether similar to those of this Theodotus, and he was later than Theodotus. There is also a little story told about a certain Natalis, who was induced by the Theodotians, for a sum of money, to act as their bishop. After accepting this, he was rebuked and scourged by God through an angel at night, and then publicly confessed his error in the assembly of the orthodox and renounced it.

units.la: Reperio tantum huius haereseos capita tria, quia cum Artemone coniungitur. Christum negauit esse Deum, sed contendit eum tatummodo hominem fuisse, quia dixit Christus ipse, Ioan.8. verf.40. Nunc autem studetis me interficere hominem qui veritatem locutus sum vobis, quam audiui a Deo. Error, Christum ex viri femine conceptum. Hoc enim eos sensisse, scribit Epiphanius, quanquam Tertullian. tradit ipsum Theo-dotum fassum esse Christum ex virgine Maria per Spiritum sanctum natum: sed discipulorum fortasse hic error fuit, qui ab Epiphanio ascribitur praeceptori, & certè consequens omnino est ad superiorem. {3} Libros Euangelicos mutauit & mutilauit, pro animi arbitrio, hos probans, illos improbans per quos refutabatur. Haec fere sunt superioris haereseos, & pessimae pestis tanquam larvae capita nefanda & praecipua.
units.tr: I find only three heads of this heresy, since it is joined with Artemon. They deny that Christ is God but maintain that he was only a man, because Christ himself said, John 8.40: "But now you seek to kill me, a man who has told you the truth, which I heard from God." Their error is that Christ was conceived from the seed of a man. Epiphanius writes that they held this, although Tertullian relates that Theodotus himself confessed that Christ was born of the Virgin Mary through the Holy Spirit. But this error was perhaps that of his disciples, which Epiphanius ascribes to the teacher; certainly it is wholly consistent with the former. They changed and mutilated the Gospel books at their own pleasure, approving some and rejecting others, by which they were refuted. These are almost the wicked and chief heads of the former heresy, a monstrous plague, like a bogey.

units.la: CAP. XXXIIII. Melchisedechiani quid senserint.
units.tr: CAP. XXXIIII. What the Melchisedechians held.

units.la: Elchisedechiani {1} Melchisedech sacerdotem Dei excelsi non hominem {2} fuisse, sed virtutem Dei esse arbitrantur.
units.tr: The Melchisedechians {1} hold that Melchisedech, priest of the most high God, was not a man {2} but the power of God.

units.la: 1 Melchisedechiani.) Mirum est nihil tam sancte à Dei Spiritu dictum esse quo non Satan abusus sit ad errores eosque grauissimos confingendos & tuendos. Nihil ad Christi dignitatem & sacerdotium illud singulare commendandum aptius dici potuit, quam quod Apostolus ad Hebraeos cap.7. ex Psalm.110. de Melchisedech affert. Hoc ipsum ita postea pervertit Satan, ut inde pestem corruptelamque fidei nostrae maximam excuderet, & haeresin hanc inuecheret, quae Melchisedechianorum appellata est à materia, circa quam deliri homines isti & insani errant, non autem ab illius authore. Fuit enim, ut Tertullianus & Theodoret. lib.2. Haeretic. fabulae tradunt, huius erroris primus au-thor & parens Theodotus quidem argentarius Theodoti superioris & coriarij, de quo iam di-ximus, discipulus & sectator: qui tamen nec cum suo praeceptore, nec cum Apollonide & Her-mippo condiscipulis, in doctrina consensit, ita mendacij via est multiplex & tortuosa. Nec etiam fuerunt inter se concordes Artemonicae haere-ticos haeredes, vt ait Eusebius lib.5. cap.28. Ergo magna ambitione ductus, hęrefin, & ipse suam, id est, proprium errorem habere voluit, quo fe inter alios haereticos iactaret. Vixisse autem vi-detur Theodotus iste sub Zepherino Pontifice Romano, & Seuero Imperatore, circa annum à Christo passo 174, quia proximè Theodotianis haereticis successit, quorum errorem à se auctum & multiplicatum in aliis capitibus secutus est vir audax & impius. Fuit enim haec haeresis tanquam avulsus ab illa mala stirpe ramus, quanquam Epiphanius dubitasse de prima origine & radice huius mali videtur. Quandiu perstite-rit non annotant scriptores, & statim concidif-se fit mihi verisimile, quia partim orthodoxorum disputationibus iugulata est: partim robu-stiore Samosatenianorum & Arianorum, qui horum fuerunt successores, fraude & nomine notiore oppressa & sepulta. Quas etiam in regiones orbis & Ecclesiae grassata fit, non est diligenter obseruatum, Romae tamen nota fuit, & in Graecia, vbi leui disputationis ictu deiecta periit. Ifidorus hunc locum transcripsit. Primum igitur huius erroris caput hoc fuit, Quòd Melchisedechum, de quo Gcnef.14. fit mentio, non putant fuisse hominem, sed Dei virtutem Christo ipso & Dei filio potentiorem, augustiorem, & feliciorem, ad cuius imaginem & typum Christus ipse fuerit à Deo factus. Tertulliani vero hæc verba sunt de hoc capite. Nam illum Melchisedech ait præcipuæ gratiæ coelestem esse virtutem, eò quòd agat Christus pro hominibus, deprecator & advocatus ipsorum factus: Melchisedech vero pro coelestibus Angelis atque virtutibus. Huius erroris occasio videri potest sumpta ex ea comparatione, quæ fit in epistola ad Hebr. cap.7. sed si rectè percipitur, nihil quicquam ex eo loco tale colligi potest. Christus enim superior, non autem inferior Melchisedecho esse ostenditur. & quæ sit vis huius comparationis inter Christū & Melchisedechum, vide Theodoret. Dialog.2. qui dicitur Inconfusus. Deinde ut Melchisedechi genealogia non recensetur, cur inde colligetur non fuisse hominem, quando nec Eliæ Prophetæ, nec Danielis, nec aliorum multorum pater nec mater, nec prosapia commemoratur, qui tamen omnes veri homines fuerunt? Sed hunc Melchisedechum fuisse Sem filium Noæ, qui adhuc ætate Abrahami superstes vixerit, atq; Rex & Sacerdos Dei summi fuerit, plerique fere omnes existimant. Præterea Epiphanius, sed quo authore non addit, patrem Melchisedechi appellat Heraclan, matrem vero Astaroth.
