Propter hunc locum à Melchisedechianis corruptum, & alterum qui est in cap.6. à Nouatianis depravatum, epistola ad Hebræos à multis uti Apocrypha, & non satis confirmata, reiecta est: quæ tamen verè Apostolica est & Divina. 2 Error. Christum mere hominem esse contendunt, uti Theodotiani, & ita Paulo Samosateno error hic per manus traditus est, & jampridem à Satana excogitatus. Sic ex malo ovo malus corvus enatus, & cum aliquius mali femina semel iacta fuint, con-firmantur paulatim, nec meliora tempore fiunt, sed peiora, & tandem evadunt periculosissima, ut principiis etiam levibus statim obviam sit nobis eundum.
units.tr: 1 Melchisedechians.) It is remarkable that nothing so sacred was said by the Spirit of God that Satan has not abused to devise and defend the gravest errors. Nothing could have been said more fittingly to commend Christ's dignity and that unique priesthood than what the Apostle brings from Psalm 110 about Melchisedech in Hebrews chapter 7. Satan later so perverted this very passage that from it he forged the greatest plague and corruption of our faith and introduced this heresy, which was named after the Melchisedechians from the subject about which these mad and insane men err, not from its author. For, as Tertullian and Theodoret in the second book of the Heretical Fables relate, the first author and parent of this error was Theodotus the money-changer, the disciple and follower of the earlier Theodotus the leather-worker, of whom we have already spoken. Yet he did not agree in doctrine even with his own teacher, nor with his fellow-students Apollonides and Hermippus; so multiple and winding is the road of falsehood. Nor were the heirs of the heretic Artemon in agreement among themselves, as Eusebius says in the fifth book, chapter 28. Driven, then, by great ambition, this man wished to have a heresy of his own, that is, a peculiar error, by which he might make himself conspicuous among the other heretics. Now this Theodotus seems to have lived under Zephyrinus, Bishop of Rome, and the emperor Severus, about the year 174 after the passion of Christ, since he immediately succeeded the Theodotian heretics, whose error he, a bold and impious man, followed, increased and multiplied in other points. For this heresy was like a branch torn from that wicked stock, although Epiphanius seems to have doubted about the first origin and root of this evil. The writers do not record how long it lasted, and I think it likely that it quickly collapsed, partly because it was slaughtered by the disputations of the orthodox, partly because it was overwhelmed and buried by the deceit and the better-known name of the more robust Samosatenians and Arians, who were its successors. In which regions of the world and of the Church it spread has not been carefully observed; it was, however, known at Rome and in Greece, where, struck by a light blow of disputation, it perished. Isidore transcribed this passage. The first head of this error, then, was this: they do not think that Melchisedech, of whom mention is made in Genesis 14, was a man, but the power of God, mightier, more august and more fortunate than Christ himself, the Son of God, after whose image and type Christ himself had been made by God. Tertullian's own words on this point are these: for he says that Melchisedech is the heavenly power of a pre-eminent grace, because Christ acts for men, having been made their intercessor and advocate, whereas Melchisedech acts for the heavenly angels and powers. The occasion of this error may seem to have been taken from the comparison made in the epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 7; but if it is rightly understood, nothing of that kind can be gathered from that passage. For Christ is shown to be superior to Melchisedech, not inferior. For the force of this comparison between Christ and Melchisedech, see Theodoret, Dialogue 2, which is called Inconfusus. Next, since Melchisedech's genealogy is not recounted, why should it be inferred from this that he was not a man, when neither the father nor the mother nor the lineage of the prophet Elijah, or of Daniel, or of many others, is recorded, though all of them were true men? But most people almost universally think that this Melchisedech was Shem, the son of Noah, who lived on still in the time of Abraham and was king and priest of the most high God. Besides, Epiphanius, though he does not add on what authority, calls Melchisedech's father Heraclas and his mother Astarte. Because of this passage, corrupted by the Melchisedechians, and another in chapter 6, perverted by the Novatians, the epistle to the Hebrews has been rejected by many as apocryphal and insufficiently attested; yet it is truly apostolic and divine. 2 Error. They contend that Christ was a mere man, as the Theodotians did; and so this error was handed down through Paul of Samosata and was devised long ago by Satan. Thus, as a bad crow hatches from a bad egg, and as the seeds of some evil are once sown, they are gradually confirmed, and do not become better with time but worse, and at last turn out most dangerous; so we must meet even the slightest beginnings at once.

units.la: CAP. XXXV. Bardesanistæ cur sic dicti. Erroris autem eorum capita duo recensentur.
units.tr: CHAP. XXXV. Why the Bardesanists are so called. Two of their errors are listed.

units.la: Bardesanistæ{1} à quodam Bardesane, qui in doctrina Christi prius perhibetur extitisse insignis, quamuis postea per omnia in Valentini hæresin{2} lapsus sit, addens de suo, ut fato ascriberet conversationes hominum.
units.tr: The Bardesanists{1} are so called from one Bardesanes, who is reported to have been a distinguished figure in the teaching of Christ at first, although he later fell completely into the heresy of Valentinus, adding things of his own, so as to ascribe the conduct of men to fate.

units.la: 1 Bardesanista.) Neque temporis, neque dogmatis ratione videtur suo loco recenseri hæc hæresis, sed prorsus alieno. Nam quod ad tempus, extitit circa annum à Christo passio 144.sub Sostero Pontifice Romano. & M. Antonino & L. Vero Impp. sed sub Vero fuisse potius annotatur, quia ille notior fuit Orientalibus populis, inter quos viguit & receptus est hic error, & ad quos bellorum que Romanis cum Parthis administrādorum gratia profectus est, denique inter eos vixit. L. Verus Imperator, quemadmo-dum tradit Dion in eius vita. M. Antoninus, qui eodem tempore regnauit, ignotior iisdem populis fuit, quia non vltra Ephesum in eā orbis par-tem progressus est, sed bella Germanica, & Marcomannica in Septentrione gesiit. Vnde error est apud Theodoretum lib.1. Hæretica, fabul-orum[?] in hæresi Bardesanistarum Seuerus pro Verus legitur. Fuit autem Bardesanes Syrus è Me-sopotamia regione oriundus & Edessa urbe, quæ propter religionem celebris fuit, quāquam eam alij Comagenæ attribuunt, alij vero Arabiæ, vt Plinius lib.5. cap.24. Christianam religionē pri-mum profitebatur, in qua sic excelluit, vt ad-uersus Marcionitas etiam scriberet, atque illius libri probarentur ab Ecclesia. Erat enim & Sy-riacè, id est, Hebraicè, & Græce doctus. Sed e-tiam aduersum eum errorem scripsit, in quem tamen incidit ipse postea, nimirum eorum qui omnia quæ hic fiunt, Fato Stoico regi & eueni-re dicunt. Id quod tradit Eusebius libro 4. cap. 29. quos ipsius contra Fatum libros legisse se testa-tur Theodoret. Postquam autem Verus Impe-ratorin Orientem venit, & Babylonem vsque progressus Magos & Mathematicos secum ex illis locis abduxit, quorum apud eum magna e-rat autoritas, & frequentes de Astrorum in-fluentiis & potestate disputationes, euocatus ab Imperatore propter doctrinam insignem Bar-desanes, Abidam quendam summum Fati pro-pugnatorem, vt scribit Epiphan. audiuit, cuius argumentis quanquam salsissimis cedens, mutauit sententiam, & Fatum probauit, & ad alia paulatim deliria delapsus omnia in religione confudit. Denique Christianae fidei naufragium fecit, tanti est nimirum ab aula principum hu-iusmodi & familiari cum Ethnicis colloquio abstinere. Viguit autem in Syria & Oriente maximè Bardesanis error, qui vix in Occidentalibus Ecclesiis notus fuit, nisi quod eum postea Priscillianistae, quorum haereseos Bardesanes parens & autor fuisse videtur, in Hispaniam usque propagarunt, sed multis post seculis Successorem haereseos & ex se procreatum habuit Ar-monium filium, virum in Graecis eruditum, quique propterea Athenas usque ex Oriente remotissimo venerat, sed nondum paterni[?] veneni labe correptus & infectus. Pauci autem de hac secta scripserunt veteres scriptores & pro-bati. Nostro enim seculo aequales non morör[?]. Tres fuerunt Bardesanisticae[?] haereseos hypotheses. Valenti-ni blasphemias de Aeonum productione, per quam diuina Christi natiuitas irridetur, & sub-fannatorum calumniis exponitur, renouauit[?] sepultas. Hominum malos bonosque mo-res, actus, & totam vitae humanae rationem fato tribuit & subiecit, a quo nos regi contendebat. Fatum autem vocant eam causarum inferiorum cum superioribus connexionem, quae necessitatem imponat rebus omnibus inevitabilem, adeo ut ne Deus quidem ipsa ab ea Lege & iugo liberetur. Quò fit ut iam non sit libera Dei ipsius voluntas. Deinde fit, ut in hominib. vitae sanctitas non sit Dei donum, sed syderum, & stellarum influentia: vitæ autem improbitas nō sit vitium & peccatum in homine ipsius voluntate admissum, sed necessitas cogens eum vi i-stius connexionis causarum, ut etiam peccet invitus.
units.tr: 1 Bardesanista.) This heresy seems to be listed here neither in its proper place by time nor by its doctrine, but quite out of place. As to time, in the year 144 after Christ, under Soter, Roman bishop, and the emperors M. Antoninus and L. Verus, it appeared; but it is noted as having arisen under Verus rather than under the others, because he was better known to the peoples of the East, among whom this error flourished and was received, and to whom he went for the conduct of the wars that the Romans waged against the Parthians, and among whom he finally lived. The emperor L. Verus, as Dio relates in his life, and M. Antoninus, who reigned at the same time, were less known to those peoples, because he did not advance beyond Ephesus into that part of the world, but waged the German and Marcomannic wars in the north. Hence there is an error in Theodoret's book of heresies, where in the section on the Bardesanists "Severus" is read for "Verus". Bardesanes was a Syrian, born in the region of Mesopotamia and the city of Edessa, which was famous for its religion, although others assign it to Commagene and others to Arabia, as Pliny does in book 5, chapter 24. At first he professed the Christian religion, and he excelled in it so much that he even wrote against the Marcionites, and his books were approved by the Church. For he was learned both in Syriac, that is Hebrew, and in Greek. But he also wrote against that error into which he himself later fell, namely that of those who say that everything that happens here is ruled and brought about by Stoic fate. Eusebius relates this in book 4, chapter 29; Theodoret testifies that he himself read Bardesanes' books against Fate. Later, when the emperor Verus came to the East and advanced as far as Babylon, he led away with him from those places Magi and mathematicians, who had great authority with him, and frequent disputes about the influences and power of the stars. Bardesanes, summoned by the emperor because of his notable learning, heard Abidas, a certain chief champion of Fate, as Epiphanius writes; yielding to his arguments, however feeble, he changed his view, approved Fate, and gradually slipped into other follies, confusing everything in religion. At last he suffered shipwreck of the Christian faith, so much does it matter to keep away from the courts of princes and from familiar conversation with the heathen of this kind. The error of Bardesanes flourished chiefly in Syria and the East, and was scarcely known in the Western Churches, except that the Priscillianists, of whose heresy Bardesanes seems to have been the parent and author, later spread it even as far as Spain. But after many centuries he had a successor and offspring of his heresy, his son Harmonius, a man learned in Greek, who for that reason had come from the furthest East even to Athens, but was not yet stained and infected by the taint of his father's poison. Few ancient and approved writers have written about this sect. For our own age, I do not delay over its contemporaries. The heresy of the Bardesanists had three underpinnings. It revived the blasphemies of Valentinus about the production of the aeons, by which the divine birth of Christ is mocked and exposed to the slanders of scoffers, which had been buried. It assigned and subjected the good and bad morals, actions and the whole manner of human life to fate, by which it contended that we are ruled. Now they call fate that connection of lower causes with higher ones which imposes on all things an inevitable necessity, so that not even God himself is freed from that law and yoke. Hence it follows that the will of God himself is no longer free. Then it follows that holiness of life in men is not a gift of God but of the stars and the influence of the constellations; and wickedness of life is not a fault and sin committed in man by his own will, but a necessity compelling him by the force of that connection of causes, so that he sins even against his will.

units.la: Denique tollitur gratuita Dei electio, si salus nostra damnatioque ex astris & eorum potentia & influentia dependet. Hic fuit Stoicorum philosophorum error grauissimus, qui a quibusdam haereticis primum in Ecclesiam invectus & retetus[?] est, veluti a Colarbasiis, postea a Bardesane fortiter defensus, & a Priscillia-nistis turpius confirmatus, probatusque reui-xit. Ethnici etiam ipsi tam dirum errorem irri-serunt apertissime. Unde est illud Iuvenalis,
units.tr: Finally, God's free election is removed, if our salvation and damnation depend on the stars and their power and influence. This was the gravest error of the Stoic philosophers, which was first brought into the Church by certain heretics, such as the Colarbasians, and was refuted; afterwards it was vigorously defended by Bardesanes, and shamefully confirmed and approved by the Priscillianists. The heathen themselves also openly mocked so dreadful an error. Hence there is that line of Juvenal:

units.la: Fata regūt homines:fatum est in partibus illis Quas sinus abscondit.
units.tr: Fate rules men; there is fate in those parts which the bay conceals.

units.la: Itaque alii in contrariam sententiam lapsi dixerunt, omnia fieri for-tuito. Nos autem Dei verbo edocti dicimus docemusque omnia Dei liberrima,nō autem coacta aut constricta voluntate fieri, per quam agit, operatur & implet omnia in omnibus, ut ait Paulus Ephes. i.[?] verf.23. & 3.verf.20. 3 Carnis resurrectionem negarunt, quod illis fuit cū superioribus haereticis commune. Sic Epipha-nius. Sequuntur aliæ hæreses.
units.tr: Therefore others, falling into the opposite opinion, said that everything happens by chance. But we, taught by the Word of God, say and teach that all things are done by God's most free will, not by a compelled or constrained will, through which he acts, works and fulfils all things in all, as Paul says, Ephes. i. vers. 23, and iii. vers. 20. Denying the resurrection of the flesh was common to them with the earlier heretics. So Epiphanius. Other heresies follow.

units.la: CAP. XXXVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXVI.

units.la: Noetiani unde dicti. Erroris autem eorum caput unum descriptum.
units.tr: Whence the Noetians got their name. A single head of their error is described.

units.la: Oetiani{1} a quodam Noeto, qui dicebat Christum eundem{*} ipsum esse Patrem, & Spiritum sanctum.
units.tr: The Noetians, named from a certain Noetus, who taught that Christ is the same as the Father and the Holy Spirit.

units.la: I Noetiani a quodam.) Neque haec haeresis uno [?] loco videtur recenseri. Nam cum Bardesa-nistarum errore nihil habet comune, nisi quod est haeresis & auersio a vera fide. Potius ad Simonianos pertinet, ex quorum sacce & coeno sua venena sumpserunt Noetiani, qui in capite de personis diuinis eadem cum illis senserunt, longo tamen postea tempore post Simonianorum nomen extinctum, atque ex Ecclesia Dei explosum, extiterunt, nec se Simonianos dici voluerunt.
units.tr: 1 The Noetians from a certain man.) This heresy does not seem to be recorded in any one place. It has nothing in common with the error of the Bardesanists, except that it is a heresy and a turning away from the true faith. It belongs rather to the Simonians, from whose sack and mire the Noetians drew their poisons. In their teaching about the divine persons they held the same views as the Simonians, but they arose a long time after the name of the Simonians had died out and been cast out of the Church of God, and they did not want to be called Simonians.

units.la: Sed non est spectandum, quo nomine, sed quo dogmate & errore grassati sint & veritatem oppugnarint, vt ad suum fontem & originem reuocari quaeuis haereticorum secta possit. Ergo ad Simonianos hos refero, quemadmodum & omnes alios qui idem cum illis de personarum diuinarum confusione & abnegatione docuerunt.
units.tr: But we must look not to the name but to the doctrine and error by which they ran riot and assailed the truth, so that any sect of heretics may be traced back to its source and origin. So I refer these men to the Simonians, as I do all others who taught the same as they did about the confusion and denial of the divine persons.

units.la: Dicti sunt tamen hi suo & peculiari nomine Noetiani a Noeto. Fuit autem Noetus Asianus. Nam Smyrnae natus est, quae fuit Ioniae ciuitas in ora maris Asiatici, sita ad amnem Meletem, quemadmodum Plinius scribit libr.5.cap.29. & ea ipsa de qua post Ephesum facta est mentio, Apocal. 2. verf. 8. cuius fuit Episcopus tempore Ioann. Euangelistae, insignis ille & celebris Polycarpus. Epiphanius tamen modo Ephesinum, modo Smyrnaeum Noetum appellat. Iampridem vero Smyrnaea Ecclesia Iudaeorum errore corrupta fuerat, vt scribit illic Dei Spiritus. A Iudęis autem perfo-narum diuinarum distinctio non modò irridetur, sed plane tollitur, è quorum fermento & lacunis pestiferum illud suum dogma Noetum hausisse & inuexisse credibile est. Fuit autem Montani discipulus, vt Theodoretus scribit lib. 3. Hæret. fabul. & confirmatur illa sententia ex eo quòd Tertullian. annotat Praxeanorum hæresin, quæ eadem est atque hæc, vnà cum doctrina de nouo Spiritu natam, propagatámque fuisse, in lib. Aduerf. Praxeam. Certissima verò iræ Dei in hanc hæresin testimonia statim exstiterunt. Nam & Noetus ipse insepultus proiectus est, vt Epiphanius tradit: & Smyrna ipsius patria octo post hanc hæresin sparsam annis terræ motu concussa est & deiecta, quemadmodum scribunt historici. Innotuit autem hic error circa annum à passo Christo 140. sub Sotero Roman. Episcopo & M. Antonino & L. Vero Roman. Impp. annis pene 84. ante quàm à Sabellio recoqueretur. Cùm primùm exoriri coepit, ad Senatu Ecclesiasticum vocatus Noetus abiurauit errorem, postea tamen ambitione nominis sibi comparàdi adductus, iterum renouauit & sparsit, & decem omnino discipulos primùm habuit, inter quos praecipui fuerunt Cleomenes, vt ait Epiphanius, & Callixtus quidam, vt Theodoret. scribit. Nomen ipsum Noetianorum non diu perstitit, sed, vt ait Theodoret. lib. 3. Haeretica. fabula. cap. De Nepote hæretico, statim concidit, quòd eodem tempore plures extiterunt, qui hoc idem venenum tanquam suum & proprium euomuerint, quanquā tamen scholæ successionem quandam recenset Theodor. Callixtum enim Noeti dogma post illius mortem defendisse vult. Vulgò quidem Sabellio tribuitur hic error, certum est tamen longè ante Sabellium etiam natum Ecclesiam damnasse hanc hæresin: sed illius intermortuæ instaurator & propugnator fuit Sabellius. Unde quæsitum est quis fuerit primus huius erroris renouandi ( nam à Iudæis primùm Euangelium oppugnantibus, post autem à Simone Mago procul dubio natum esse, supra docuimus) author. Theodoretus lib. 3. Hæret. fabul. facit Epigonium quendam: Tertullian. libr. De præscriptionib. aduersus Hæreticos, Praxeam, qui ipsius seculo viuebat. Post hos omnes, inquit, etiam Praxeas quidam hæresin introduxit, quâ Victorinus corroborare curauit. Hic Deu Patrem omnipotentem Iesum Christum esse dixit, hunc crucifixum, passumque contendit, mortuum prætereå, seipsum sibi sedere ad dextram suam, cum profana & sacrilega temeritate proponit. Unde hi quoque Praxeani dicti sunt: & Patripassiani, quia Patrem Deum passum esse dixerunt. Sed quum distet Noeti ætas à Praxea & Tertulliano, annis tantùm circiter 25. nihil mirum videri debet, si quo tempore hoc malum in Minore Asia per Satanâ à Noeto disseminabatur: eodem aut paulo post in Africa per Praxeam spargebatur. Sed Noeti nomen Orientalibus Ecclesiis notius fuit: Praxeæ verò Africanis & Occidentalibus: Sabellij autem postea omnibus Ecclesiis & nationibus, quia eas grauissimè vexauit. Durauit autè diutissimè interpolata aut repetita à Sabellianis.
units.tr: Yet these men were called Noetians by their own particular name, after Noetus. Noetus was an Asian. He was born at Smyrna, a city of Ionia on the shore of the Asian sea, situated by the river Meles, as Pliny writes in book 5, chapter 29. This is the same city mentioned after Ephesus in Revelation 2:8, whose bishop in the time of the Evangelist John was the famous and renowned Polycarp. Epiphanius, however, sometimes calls Noetus the Ephesian and sometimes the Smyrnaean. Long before, the church at Smyrna had been corrupted by the error of the Jews, as the Spirit of God writes there. Among the Jews the distinction of the divine persons is not only mocked but altogether removed, and it is credible that Noetus drew this pestilent dogma of his from their leaven and pools and brought it in. He was a disciple of Montanus, as Theodoret writes in book 3 of the Haereticarum fabularum, and this opinion is confirmed by the fact that Tertullian notes that the heresy of the Praxeans, which is the same as this, arose together with the doctrine of the new Spirit and spread, in his book Against Praxeas. Clear evidences of God's wrath against this heresy appeared at once. Noetus himself was thrown out unburied, as Epiphanius reports, and Smyrna, his homeland, eight years after this heresy spread, was shaken and overthrown by an earthquake, as historians write. This error became known about the year 140 after the suffering of Christ, under Soter, bishop of Rome, and the emperors Marcus Antoninus and Lucius Verus, nearly eighty-four years before it was revived by Sabellius. When it first began to arise, Noetus was summoned before the ecclesiastical senate and renounced his error. Afterwards, however, moved by ambition to win a name for himself, he again revived and spread it, and he had at first ten disciples in all, among whom the chief were Cleomenes, as Epiphanius says, and a certain Callixtus, as Theodoret writes. The name of the Noetians did not last long but, as Theodoret says in book 3 of the Haereticarum fabularum, chapter "On the heretic Nepos," soon fell away, because at the same time several arose who spat out this same poison as their own and peculiar doctrine. Yet Theodoret does recount a certain succession of the school, for he holds that Callixtus defended the doctrine of Noetus after his death. This error is commonly attributed to Sabellius, but it is certain that long before Sabellius the Church had already condemned this heresy as well. Sabellius, however, was the restorer and champion of this long-dead error. Hence the question has arisen who was the first author of reviving this error (for we have shown above that it was born first among the Jews, who attacked the Gospel, and afterwards, without doubt, from Simon Magus). Theodoret in book 3 of the Haereticarum fabularum names a certain Epigonius. Tertullian, in his book On Prescription against Heretics, names Praxeas, who lived in his own age. "After all these," he says, "a certain Praxeas also introduced a heresy, which Victorinus took pains to strengthen. This man put forward, with profane and sacrilegious rashness, that the almighty God the Father is Jesus Christ, that he was crucified and suffered, and, moreover, that he died, and that he himself sat at his own right hand." Hence these too were called Praxeans and Patripassians, because they said that God the Father suffered. But since the time of Noetus is separated from that of Praxeas and Tertullian by only about twenty-five years, it ought not to seem strange if, at the time when this evil was spreading in Asia Minor through Satan's work from Noetus, at the same time or a little later it was being spread in Africa through Praxeas. Yet the name of Noetus was better known to the Eastern churches, that of Praxeas to the African and Western churches, and that of Sabellius later to all churches and nations, because he troubled them most grievously. The heresy lasted longest in forms corrupted or repeated by the Sabellians.

units.la: 2 Eundem ipsum.) Duo fuerunt erroris Noetiani capita. 1 Eandem esse personam diuinam, quæ sit Pater, Filius, & Spiritus sanctus. Itaque hunc ipsum esse visibilem, & inuisibilem: mortalem, & immortalem: patibilem, & impatibilem. In cælis impatibilem: in terris patibilem: in cælis Deum, in terris hominem ex Maria virgine. Denique, ut scribit Isidorus, Trinitatem non personis, sed officiorum tantùm nominibus accipiunt. Nam in cælis Patrem appellari: in terris Filium: in viribus creaturarum, Spiritum volunt Noetiani. Unde idem de Patre, & Filio, & Spiritu sancto dicunt impiissimè, quod poetæ ethnici de sua Diana, quam in cælo Lunam: in syluis Dianam: in inferis Hecaten & Proserpinam vocant. Ex quo est illud Virgil. libr. 4. Æneid. -tria virginis ora Dianæ. His omnino dissimiles fuerunt Theodotiani, de quibus diximus, quia hi Filium omnino esse Deum negant. Noetiani verò Filium omnino idem quod Pater est etiam ὁμοούσιον. Etsi verò una est & eadem numero Patris, & Filij, & Spiritus sancti essentia siue natura: est tamen triplex ὑπόστασις [?], & cuiusque persona reipsa, non tantùm animi quadam imaginatione, distincta ab alia. Unde non est Pater notionale tantùm ens, sed reale, & distinctum à Filio. Id quod vel in uno Christi baptismo apparuit, ubi Pater de cælis loquitur: Filius in Jordane à Joanne baptizatur: Spiritus sanctus in columbæ formam descendit, Matth. 3. vers. 16. 2 Error Noeti, in eo est, quòd se Mosem esse dixit: fratrem autem suum Aaronem, ut suas blasphemias pulchro nomine commendaret.Ex quo enim fermento Pharisaico & Iudaico imbutum & corruptum fuisse facile colligi potest. Et haec de tam olida peste dicta sint.
units.tr: 2 The very same.) There were two heads of the Noetian error. 1. That the same divine person, who is the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, is the one who is visible and invisible, mortal and immortal, capable of suffering and incapable of suffering: impassible in heaven, passible on earth; God in heaven, man on earth, born of the Virgin Mary. In short, as Isidore writes, the Noetians take the Trinity not as persons but only as names of offices: they want the one called Father in heaven, Son on earth, and Spirit in the powers of creatures. Hence they impiously say the same of Father, Son and Holy Spirit as the heathen poets say of their Diana, whom they call the Moon in heaven, Diana in the woods, and Hecate and Proserpina in the underworld. From this comes that line of Virgil in book 4 of the Aeneid: "the three faces of the virgin Diana." The Theodotians, whom we have mentioned, were entirely unlike these, because they deny that the Son is God at all, whereas the Noetians hold that the Son is altogether the same as the Father, even homoousios [ὁμοούσιον]. Yet although the essence or nature of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit is one and the same in number, it has three hypostases [ὑπόστασις], and each person is distinct from the other in reality, not merely by some imagining of the mind. Hence the Father is not merely a notional being but a real one, and distinct from the Son. This appeared even in the one baptism of Christ, where the Father speaks from heaven, the Son is baptized by John in the Jordan, and the Holy Spirit descends in the form of a dove (Matt. 3:16). 2. The error of Noetus lies in this, that he said he was Moses, and called his brother Aaron, so that he might commend his blasphemies under a fine name. From what Pharisaic and Jewish leaven he was steeped and corrupted can easily be gathered. Let this be said about so foul a pestilence.

units.la: CAP. XXXVII.
units.tr: CAP. XXXVII.

units.la: Valesiorum haereticorum erroris caput duplex.
units.tr: The double error of the Valesian heretics.

units.la: Alesii{1} & seipsos castrant,{2} & hospites suos, hoc modo existimātes Deo se debere seruire. Alia quoq; haeretica docere dicun-tur, & turpia, sed qua illa sint,nec ipse commemorauit Epiphanius, nec uspiam potui reperire.
units.tr: They castrate both themselves and their guests, thinking in this way that they must serve God. They are also said to teach other heretical and shameful doctrines, but what these are, neither Epiphanius himself has recorded, nor have I been able to find anywhere.

units.la: {1} Valesii.) Valesios à Valente quodam didtos esse scribit Epiphanius, qui fuerit Arabs, ex Bacascamis oppido, quod ipse Bacathon appellat, Plinius autem libr. 6. Natur. hist. capite 28. Bacascamos; & in ea Arabiae regione situm est, quod vltra Iordanem & mare mortuum ad Petraeam Arabiam pertinet, quam Philadelphicam Epiphanius nominari scribit. Idem cū Epiphanio sentit Damascenus. Quando autem & unde haec haeresis extiterit, quaestio est, quae facile propter obliteratam iampridem huius sectae memoriam definiri non potest. Certum est autem ex hypothesibus istos haereticos coniugia damnasse, & liberorum procreationem tanquam diaboli opus esse auersatos, cuius erroris parentem facit Carpocratem, & Taciānū Clemens Alexandrinus libr. 3. Stromat.adeo ut infelicis illius Carpocratianæ vel Encratitæ stirpis[?] videatur hic error esse velut surculus quidam. Alij tamen à Gnosticis deducere tanquam à vero fonte malunt. Vtcunque malæ fermentis pessima seges hæc fuit, quæ Satanæ astu, & castitatis speciosæ prætextu turpissima homicidia perpetrauit, dum isti se & discipulos & plures hospites exsecant: & grauissimum errorem induxit, dum à Deo ipso instituta coniugia reiiciunt & damnant: cum quibus etiam consentiunt Paterniani, de quibus postea. Itaque ad Tacianos sive Encratitas tanquam ad propriam radicem istos refero. Extitisse vero & primum innotuisse videntur post Origenem, cuius secu-lo variæ per vniuersam Arabiam hæreses ortæ sunt, quemadmodum ex historiis apparet, & cuius etiam exemplo Valesij suam fortasse sententiam & errorem confirmarunt. Nam ille quum adhuc adolescens esset, ad summæ castitatis comprobationem exsecuit sese & castrauit, ut scribit Eusebius libro 6. Histor. cap. 8. quum dicta Christi, Matth. 19. versu 12. perperam intellexisset, quod Origenis factum hi fortasse sequuti, in omnibus Christianis idem habere locum voluerunt. Unde nisi me fallit coniectura, huius hæresis ortus sub Anthero Romano episcopo, & Juliano Philippo imperatore collocadus est, circa annum à Christo passo 216. Quanquam in primo concilio Niceno damnati sunt Christiani, qui se libidinis impatientia castrarent, adeo ut iam huius hæreseos tenuia quædam femina à Satana iacta fuisse facile credam. Neque vero late peruagata est, neque a pluribus, quòd in-signem maribus iniuriam faceret, defensa. Neminit quidem Euagr. libro quarto capite 2. Abasgorum gentis ad Euphratem sitæ, quæ, vt plurimùm se hospitésque suos maioris pretij à mercatoribus consequendi causa castrabat: sed ea fuit gens tota, non hæresis: præterea adhuc ethnica, non autem Christiana, quales Valesij videri voluerunt.
units.tr: {1} The Valesians. Epiphanius writes that the Valesians were named after a certain Valens, an Arab from the town of Bacascamis, which he himself calls Bacathon; Pliny in book 6 of the Natural History, chapter 28, calls it Bacascamos. It lies in that region of Arabia which extends beyond the Jordan and the Dead Sea towards Petraean Arabia, which Epiphanius says is called Philadelphian. Damascene agrees with Epiphanius. When and whence this heresy arose is a question which cannot easily be settled, since the memory of this sect has long since been obliterated. It is certain, however, from their principles that these heretics condemned marriage and shrank from the procreation of children as the work of the devil. Clement of Alexandria, in book 3 of the Stromata, makes Carpocrates the parent of this error, and Tatian too, so that this error seems to be a sort of offshoot of that unhappy Carpocratian or Encratite stock. Others, however, prefer to derive it from the Gnostics as from its true source. Whatever its origin, this was a most wicked crop sprung from evil leaven, which by Satan's cunning and under the pretext of a splendid chastity committed the most shameful murders, while these men castrated both themselves, their disciples and many guests. It also introduced a most grievous error, in that they reject and condemn marriages instituted by God himself; the Paternians, of whom I shall speak later, agree with them. Accordingly I refer these men to the Tatianists or Encratites as to their proper root. They seem indeed to have come into existence and first to have become known after Origen, in whose age various heresies arose throughout all Arabia, as appears from the histories; and by Origen's example the Valesians perhaps confirmed their opinion and error. For when he was still a young man, to prove his supreme chastity, he cut off and castrated himself, as Eusebius writes in book 6 of the Church History, chapter 8, having misunderstood the words of Christ in Matthew 19:12; these men perhaps followed Origen's deed and wished it to hold for all Christians. Hence, unless my conjecture deceives me, the origin of this heresy should be placed under Anterus, bishop of Rome, and Julian, or Philip, the emperor, about the year 216 after Christ's passion. Yet at the first Council of Nicaea, Christians who castrated themselves from impatience of lust were condemned, so that I readily believe some small seed of this heresy had already been sown by Satan. Nor did it spread widely, nor was it defended by many, since it did a great wrong to males. Euagrius does indeed mention, in book 4, chapter 2, the Abasgi, a people living by the Euphrates, who for the most part castrated themselves and their guests in order to obtain a higher price from merchants; but that was a whole people, not a heresy; moreover they were still heathen, not Christian, as the Valesians wished to appear.

units.la: Et ipsos castrant.) Hæ videntur fuisse hu-ius sectæ hypothecs. Neminem in regnu cælorum peruenire posse, nisi qui se eunuchum fecerit, & reipsa castrauerit, id est, virilia exse-cuerit, quia hoc genus eunuchorum laudat maximè Christus, qui se pro regno Dei castrant, Matth.19.versu12. & Apocalypf. 14.versu 4. Itaque hi & se & discipulos suos & hospites ex-secant, priuantque virilibus etiam inuitos. At neque eo pertinet dictum Christi, neque fit quis idcirco ad regnum cæli aptior, quia ea cor-poris parte caret, si lasciuiis, concupiscentiis, & desideriis intus vritur. Et illa castitas voluntaria, de qua Christus, est Dei ipsius donum, non artificis cuiusquam, aut Armenij exfectoris opus, quemadmodum multis verbis Clemens lib.3.Stromat. explicat, & Theodoret. in libro Epitome decret. Diuinor. cap. De castitate. & Epiphanius hoc loco. Hæc igitur fuit prima Valesiorum hypothecs, quæ certè in ipsam naturam hominum iniuriosa fuit, & sensus repro-bi certisimum indicium. Coniugia & co-gressus maritorum cum vxoribus docent esse detestabiles, & damnandos. Et hæc fuerunt immensarum laudum, quae postea Monachico coelibatui sunt tributae, fundamenta ex his erroribus sumpta: & daemoniacae doctrinae, quam appellat Paulus 1. Timoth. 4. verf. 4. verisima femina & messes. 3[?] Multa turpia & inhonesta fieri concedunt. Quod omnino cofequi necesse est. Nam qui coniugium, quod a Deo institutum est, damnat, is omnem incontinentiam, & fornicationem toleret & permittat necesse est.
units.tr: And they castrate themselves. These seem to have been the premises of this sect. That no one can attain to the kingdom of heaven unless he has made himself a eunuch and actually castrated himself, that is, cut off his genitals, because Christ especially praises this kind of eunuch, who castrate themselves for the kingdom of God (Matthew 19:12; Revelation 14:4). So these men cut off both themselves, their disciples and their guests, and deprive even unwilling men of their genitals. But the saying of Christ does not refer to this, nor is anyone the more fit for the kingdom of heaven because he lacks that part of the body, if he burns inwardly with wantonness, lusts and desires. That voluntary chastity of which Christ speaks is God's own gift, not the work of any craftsman or Armenian eunuch-maker, as Clement explains at length in book 3 of the Stromata, and Theodoret in the Epitome of the Divine Decrees, chapter "On chastity", and Epiphanius in this place. This, then, was the first premise of the Valesians, which is certainly an insult to human nature itself and a most certain sign of a reprobate mind. They teach that marriages and the intercourse of husbands with their wives are detestable and to be condemned. From these errors were drawn the foundations of the immense praises that were afterwards bestowed on monastic celibacy, and of the demonic doctrine which Paul calls so in 1 Timothy 4:1. They allow many shameful and dishonourable things to happen, which must necessarily follow. For whoever condemns marriage, which was instituted by God, must necessarily tolerate and permit all incontinence and fornication.

units.la: Id quod videmus accidisse in Papatu, vbi Presbyteris legitima coniugia non licent, foedissima autem stupra conceduntur: ita nimirum vlciscitur Dominus verbi fui contemptum, & stultas, vel potius blasphemas hominum in ipsius sapientem ordinationem voces, vti in his exemplis perspicue videmus.
units.tr: We see this has happened under the Papacy, where marriage is not allowed to the elders, while the foulest fornications are permitted. In this way, no doubt, the Lord avenges the contempt of his Word and the foolish, or rather blasphemous, utterances of men against his wise ordinance, as we plainly see in these examples.

units.la: CAP. XXXVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXVIII.

units.la: Cathari cur sic dicti, unde profecti. Erroris autem eorum caput duplex enumeratum.
units.tr: Why the Cathari were so called, and where they came from. The twofold head of their error is set out.

units.la: Cathari[?] qui seipsos isto nomine, quasi propter mundiciem, superbissime atque odiosissime nominant: Secundas nuptias non admittunt, poenitentiam denegant, Nouatum sectantes haereticum. Unde etiam Nouatiani appellantur.
units.tr: Cathari[?] who, with the most arrogant and hateful pride, call themselves by this name as if for their purity. They do not admit second marriages, they deny repentance, and they follow the heretic Novatus. For this reason they are also called Novatians.

units.la: 1 Cathari qui seipsos. Vna haec & eadem haeresis varia nomina sortita est. Ipsa autem ab autore Nouato, Nouatianorum dicta est, quae est Catharorum fons & mater. Cathari vero dedu stus ex ea riuulus: vti ex Carpocratianis prose-sti sunt, quemadmodu superius diximus, Gnostici. Quanquam enim vulgo Catharos & Nouatianos eosdem omnino faciunt, & tunc [illegible, ~3 letters]-[illegible, ~2 letters] dicantur, quatenus a reliquo Christianorum hominum coetu se tanquam sanctiores separat: tunc autem Nouatiani, quatenus a suo denominantur parente: statui tamen potest aliqua inter utrosque differentia, vti in hypothesibus videbimus. Appellantur autem etiam hi ipsi a Græcis Meletiani, de cuius nominis & erroris secta postea dicemus. Ergo primum Nouatiani dicti sunt.
units.tr: 1 Cathari who call themselves. This one and the same heresy has taken on various names. It was called Novatian after its author Novatus, and it is the fountain and mother of the Cathari. The Cathari are a stream derived from it, just as the Gnostics descended from the Carpocratians, as we said above. Although in common usage the Cathari and the Novatians are made altogether the same, and [illegible] are so called, inasmuch as they set themselves apart from the rest of the Christian assembly as holier, while the Novatians are so called inasmuch as they take their name from their parent. Still, some difference can be established between the two, as we shall see in the hypotheses. These same people are also called Meletians by the Greeks, concerning which name and sect of error we shall speak later. So first they were called Novatians.

units.la: Extitit autem & innotuit Nouatus hæreticus tempore Cornelij episcopi Romani, Cypriani Carthaginensis episcopi, & Decij imperatoris, circa annum a Christo passo 220. Catharorum autem appellatio postea iis addita fuit sub Stephano Romano pontifice, & Gallo atque Volusiano Impp. circiter annum post Christum passum 253. quanquam hæ voces confunduntur, quemadmodum apparet ex Catalo-go & Indicatione hæresεon, in historia Ecclesiastica, Theodoreto lib.3. Hæreticarum fabul. Eusebij historia, & concilij Niceni artic.9. quæ refert Ruff. lib.1. hist.c.6. separantur tamē ab Isidoro lib.8. & aliis, qui Catharos Nouatianorum fruticationem appellant.
units.tr: Novatus the heretic emerged and became known in the time of Cornelius, bishop of Rome, Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, and the emperor Decius, around the year 220 after the passion of Christ. The name Cathari was added to them later, under Stephen, pope of Rome, and the emperors Gallus and Volusianus, about the year 253 after the passion of Christ. These terms are confused, as appears from the Catalogue and Indication of heresies, from Theodoret book 3 of the Ecclesiastical History (Heretical Fables), from Eusebius's history, and from the ninth article of the Council of Nicaea, which Rufinus reports in book 1, chapter 6 of his history. Nevertheless, Isidore in book 8 and others distinguish them, calling the Cathari an offshoot of the Novatians.

units.la: Fuit autem Nouatus, non autem Nouatianus huius sectæ primus author, quanquam eadem ætate uterque vixit, sed in utroque distinguendo falluntur multi. Nouatus enim fuit Afer natione, & virus suum in Africa primum post persecutionem Decia-nam sparsit, aduersus quem Cyprianus libro ¶ Epist.5.& libr.4.cap.2. edidit multa.sed tantum nominis celebritate valuit, ut etiam à Cornelio episcopo Romano Ecclesiæ presbyter creare-tur. Sed hic ad episcopatum aspirans, dolore repulsæ, nouum hoc & certè perniciosissimum dogma in Ecclesiæ exitium cudit. de cuius ho-minis vafro & malitioso ingenio, vide Eusebiũ lib.6.cap.43. Nouatianus autem fuit Romanus, & Nouati discipulus, qui præceptoris lethiferum venenum latissimè propagauit, & furtim à tri-bus Episcopis, imprimisque ab ipso Nouato creatus est in Italia Episcopus, ut Theodoret. scribit(ubi Nouatianum pro Nouato legi opor-tuit, ut apparet ex Cypriano) quemadmodum ab eodem Nouato in Africa Nicostratus factio-nis & suarum partium Episcopus factus est, ne authoritate episcopali ipsius pars & secta de-stitueretur, quemadmodum etiam tradit Platina in vita Cornelij Romani episcopi. Cathari vero idcirco dicti sunt, quòd se reliquis vita mori-busque puriores esse iactarent. Christianos au-tem {καθαροὺς} esse oportet. {Τὸ δὲ καθαρεύειν} vocabu-lo sæpe vtitur agens de Dei Ecclesia Paulus, Ephef.5. versu 26. Tit.2. versu 14. Itaque honesto & speciosò illo Purificatorum & Sanctorum nomine & fuco turpissima tum in doctrina tum in vita scelera tegebant. Qui autem proprie & Græcè scientibus Cathari dicuntur, à barbaris & imperitis scriptoribus Gazari postea sunt ap-pellati. Sic enim in constitutione quadam Fri-derici secundi imperatoris, quæ ex conciliis sumpta est, vocantur, uti eodem sæculo Diabo-lus Zabulus, siue id ignoratione linguæ Græcæ factum est, siue propter vitium blæsę hominum illius ætatis linguæ. Sed etiam Catheræi nominantur eadem græcanitatis imperitia, quemadmodum in decretali constitutione Gregorij ix. libr. 5. Decretal. tit. De hæreticis. Eosdem alij Patrinos, alij Patharinos vocarunt, vt apparet ex concilio Lateranensi, quod fuit sub Alexandro tertio, & est in 2. Tomo cociliorum. Quum autem hæc Catharorum hęresis esset omnibus, & merito quidem, odiosa: posterior ætas ad prægrauandam bonam sacrosancti Euangelij causam, homines verè Euangelicos infami Catharorum nomine calumniata est, quos eosdem etiam Valdenses, Pauperes de Lugduno, Arnaldistas, ab Arnaldo quodam, qui sub Imperatoribus Germanis vixit, vt Sigonius scripsit in Historia Regni Italici lib. xi. & Bernard. epist. 195. idem sentit. Denique eosdem Toflepinos vocauit. Citissimè verò propagata est Nouatianorum hæresis. Nam cum orthodoxis in multis confessionis & veræ fidei articulis, imprimis autem de Trinitate consensit. Itaque ab Arianis & Macedonianis persequutionem passi sunt Nouatiani, vt scribit Socrat. libro secundo capite 38. quemadmodum & ipsi vicissim inita cum orthodoxis amicitia, Arianos exegerunt, si quando potuerunt. Ac parum abfuit quin cum orthodoxis coadunarentur (confessionem enim ab iis fecerant, & seorsim suas ecclesias & basilicas habebant) sed vt ait Sozomen. libro quarto cap. 9. & 21. liuor quorundam obstitit, imò potius Dei prouidentia, ne in veræ sinum Ecclesiæ recepti suo dogmate sani[?] doctrinam misere labefactarent. Præterea quod in disciplina & ceremoniis in multis ab orthodoxis dissentirent. Per universum autem Christianum orbem latissime diffusi sunt Novatiani, nec ulla pene fuit mundi regio & plaga, quæ non hoc veneno, quod merita hominum stabilit, inficeretur. Constantinopoli præsertim suos greges, & eos quidem numerosos, item & episcopos continua diuturnaque successione habuerunt, item & Ephesi, quæ duæ fuerunt Orientalis imperii civitates præcipuæ. Sed & Cyzici, & aliis in oppidis. Socrat. libro 5. cap.10.
units.tr: Novatus, however, not Novatian, was the first author of this sect, although both lived in the same age; but many are mistaken in distinguishing the two. Novatus was an African by birth, and he first spread his poison in Africa after the Decian persecution. Cyprian published much against him in his letter (Epist. 5) and in book 4, chapter 2. Yet he was so influential by the fame of his name that Cornelius, bishop of Rome, appointed him a presbyter of the Church. But he, aspiring to the episcopate, and embittered by his rejection, forged this new and certainly most pernicious dogma to the ruin of the Church. For this man's crafty and malicious character, see Eusebius, book 6, chapter 43. Novatian, however, was a Roman and a disciple of Novatus, who very widely spread the deadly poison of his teacher. He was secretly made bishop in Italy by three bishops, and above all by Novatus himself, as Theodoret writes (where "Novatian" must be read for "Novatus", as appears from Cyprian). In the same way, Nicostratus was made bishop of the faction and of their party in Africa by Novatus, so that the party and sect would not lack episcopal authority, as Platina also relates in the life of Cornelius, bishop of Rome. The Cathari were so called because they boasted of being purer than the rest in life and conduct. Indeed, Christians ought to be [καθαροὺς] "pure". Paul often uses the verb [καθαρεύειν] "to be pure" when speaking of God's Church, Eph. 5.26 and Titus 2.14. So under that honest and specious name of Purified and Holy they covered the most shameful crimes, both in doctrine and in life. Those who are properly and in Greek called Cathari were later called Gazari by barbarous and unskilled writers. Thus in a certain constitution of the emperor Frederick II, taken from the councils, they are so named, just as in the same century Diabolus was called Zabulus. This happened either through ignorance of the Greek language or because of the corrupt speech of men of that age. But they are also called Catheraei through the same lack of Greek learning, as in the decretal constitution of Gregory IX, book 5 of the Decretals, title On Heretics. Others called them Patrini, others Patharini, as appears from the Lateran Council held under Alexander III, which is in the second volume of the councils. Since this heresy of the Cathari was hateful to all, and rightly so, later ages slandered truly evangelical men with the infamous name of Cathari, in order to burden the good cause of the holy Gospel. These same men were also called Waldensians, Poor Men of Lyons, and Arnaldists, from a certain Arnold who lived under the German emperors, as Sigonius wrote in his History of the Kingdom of Italy, book 11, and Bernard agrees in letter 195. Finally, they called the same people Toflepini. The heresy of the Novatians spread very quickly, for they agreed with the orthodox in many articles of the confession and the true faith, especially on the Trinity. Therefore the Novatians suffered persecution from the Arians and Macedonians, as Socrates writes in book 2, chapter 38. In turn, having entered into friendship with the orthodox, they drove out the Arians whenever they could. And it came close to their being united with the orthodox (for they had made a confession with them, although they had their own churches and basilicas apart). But, as Sozomen says in book 4, chapters 9 and 21, the envy of some stood in the way, or rather the providence of God, so that they, received into the bosom of the true Church, would not miserably weaken sound doctrine by their dogma. Moreover, they differed from the orthodox in many matters of discipline and ceremonies. The Novatians spread very widely throughout the whole Christian world, and there was almost no region or quarter of the world that was not infected with this poison, which the merits of men establish. Especially at Constantinople they had their flocks, and those numerous, and also bishops in continuous and lasting succession; likewise at Ephesus, which were the two chief cities of the Eastern empire. They were also at Cyzicus and in other towns (Socrates, book 5, chapter 10).

units.la: Romæ tamen tam libere convenire nunquam sunt ausi, sed nec potuerunt, quod Occidentalis Ecclesia purior adhuc in eo doctrinæ capite & in vitanda cum hæreticis societate erat. Itaque statim eiecti Roma, alio demigrarunt. Idem Socrat. libr. 7. cap. 11. Non fuerunt tamen ipsi inter se concordes Novatiani, sed sectas quasdam constituerunt, quales erat Quartidecimani. Durauit autem hæc hæresis diutissime, adeo ut sub Arcadio imperatore etiam continuatione quaedam floruerint. i. post annos 148. à suo exordio. Tandem variis Joannis Chrysostomi Constantinopoli, Cyrilli episcopi Alexandriæ, & Innocentii I. Romæ disputationibus & concionibus exagitati & refutati, delituerunt. Denique prorsus ipso Novatianorum nomine (nam & Romana Synodo damnati fuerant) esse desierunt.
units.tr: At Rome, however, they never dared to meet so openly, nor could they, because the Western Church was still purer in that point of doctrine and in avoiding fellowship with heretics. So they were immediately expelled from Rome and moved elsewhere (Socrates, book 7, chapter 11). The Novatians, however, were not in agreement among themselves, but formed certain sects, such as the Quartodecimans. This heresy lasted a very long time, so that under the emperor Arcadius some of them still flourished in a continuous line, that is, 148 years after their beginning. At last, harassed and refuted by the various disputations and sermons of John Chrysostom at Constantinople, Cyril bishop of Alexandria, and Innocent I at Rome, they went into hiding. Finally they ceased entirely under the name of Novatians, for they had also been condemned by a Roman synod.

units.la: Recepta tamen est hæc hæresis, & repetita, interpolato nomine à Pelagianis: deinde à Papistis retenta: quia omnes hi meritu operum nostrorum defendunt.
units.tr: Yet this heresy was received, and revived under a changed name by the Pelagians. Then the Papists retained it, because all of them defend justification by the merit of our works.

units.la: 2 Secundas nuptias.) Variæ fuerunt Noua-tianorum hypotheses. Ac prima hæc, De meritis operum suorum gloriantur, Isidor. Hæc enim una ratio vel maxime fanaticos istos impulit ut se Catharos appellarent. Hoc venenum nocentissimum est, & facile in omnium hominum pectora gliscit, qui se su q; stulta quadam φιλαυτίᾳ admirantur. Ex quo factum ut statim hoc dogma plausibiliter exceptum, & alte fuerit impressum, quod infinitas alias propagines non minus inauspicatas & infelices effudit.
units.tr: 2 Second marriages.) The hypotheses of the Novatians were various. The first is this: they glory in the merits of their own works, as Isidore says. For this one reason above all drove these fanatics to call themselves Cathari. This poison is most harmful, and it easily takes root in the breasts of all men who admire themselves with a certain foolish self-love. Hence it came about that this dogma, once plausibly received, was deeply imprinted, and it poured forth countless other offshoots, no less ill-omened and unhappy.

units.la: 2 Pœnitentiam denegat hominibus qui post baptismum susceptum in abnegationem fidei lapsi sunt infirmitate quadam & vi perfequutionis. Dicit enim Nouatus, μὴ τὸ λουτρὸν μηκέτι [?] ἐλεεῖσθαι πεπτωκότας [?], ut ait Epiphanius. Ad cuius suæ sententiæ confirmationem abusus est loco Scripturæ qui est Hebr.6. qui tantum pertinet ad peccatum contra Spiritum sanctum, non autem ad hæc peccatorum genera. At Christus exemplo Petri docet lapsis pœnitentiam peccatorumque remissionem non adimi: quæ si prorsus iis esset denegada, frustra dixisset idem, Quæcunque solueritis in terra, erunt soluta & in cælo, Matth.18. versu 18. Cathari duriores suo præceptore, omnibus in vniuersum lapsis veniam denegarunt. 3 Admonitiones priuatas publicasque hac ratione tollunt. 4 Secundas nuptias damnant, quas post Baptismum perinde atque adulterium ipsum detestantur. Epiphan. Cuius rei rationem referunt, cp[?] Paulus Episcopum iubet vnius tantum vxoris virum esse, 1.Timoth.3. quasi vnius vxoris virum esse fit secunda coniugia ex honestarum legum praeceptis contracta damnare. Est autem ei vxori cum qua ex Dei verbo diuortium facere non potes, viuæ aliam superinducere. Id quod illo seculo frequens & visitatum fiebat magno sacri coniugij contemptu.Hoc venenosum dogma a Montanistis hauserunt Cathari, & ad doctoris sui errores adiecerunt.
units.tr: 2 They deny repentance to those who, after receiving baptism, have fallen away into denial of the faith through a certain weakness and the violence of persecution. For Novatus says that those who have fallen after the bath [μὴ τὸ λουτρὸν μηκέτι ἐλεεῖσθαι πεπτωκότας] cannot be pitied any longer, as Epiphanius says. To confirm this opinion he misused a passage of Scripture, Heb. 6, which pertains only to the sin against the Holy Spirit and not to these kinds of sins. But Christ, by the example of Peter, teaches that repentance and the remission of sins are not taken away from the fallen. If these were wholly denied them, he would have spoken in vain: "Whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven" (Matt. 18.18). The Cathari, harsher than their teacher, denied pardon altogether to all who had fallen. 3 By this reasoning they abolish both private and public admonitions. 4 They condemn second marriages, which after baptism they detest just as they detest adultery itself (Epiphanius). They give as the reason for this that Paul bids a bishop be the husband of one wife only (1 Tim. 3). As if being the husband of one wife meant condemning second marriages contracted under the precepts of honest laws! But a man cannot take another wife while the wife with whom, by the word of God, he cannot divorce, is still alive. This was frequent and common in that age, to the great contempt of holy marriage. The Cathari drew this poisonous dogma from the Montanists and added it to the errors of their teacher.

units.la: 5 Rebaptizant iam baptizatos si post Baptismum labantur & publice peccent.Id quod fuit illis cum Marcionitis commune, & postea Donatistarum infa-niae fundamentum. Hoc enim Catharorum er-roris caput maxime sunt amplexi Donatistæ, adeo vt Epiphanius eos cum Nouatianis eosdem faciat. Addit Theodoretus libro 3. hæret. fabul. eos quoque in eo ab orthodoxis diuersos fuisse, quod in baptizando chrisma ex more iam tum in Ecclesiis recepto non adhiberent. Et certè ex Fabiani episcopi Romani actis & vita discimus magnum iam fuisse chrismatis in baptismis vsum, quando ille ipse præcepit quotannis confici, vetuit autem comburi, & est in Can. Literis. De consecrat. dist.3. Idem appareret ex Tertulliani scriptis. Sed quo Scripturæ fundamento Patres chrisma in baptizando, quaeso,sanxerunt?
units.tr: 5 They rebaptize those already baptized if after baptism they fall and sin publicly. This was common to them with the Marcionites, and later became the foundation of the Donatists' madness. For the Donatists embraced this chief error of the Cathari most of all, so much so that Epiphanius makes them the same as the Novatians. Theodoret adds, in book 3 of his Heretical Fables, that they also differed from the orthodox in this: that in baptizing they did not use the chrism, which by then had already been received in the Churches by custom. And certainly from the acts and life of Fabian, bishop of Rome, we learn that the use of chrism in baptisms was already great, since he ordered it to be made every year, and forbade it to be burned; and this is in the canon Literis, De consecratione, distinctio 3. The same appears from the writings of Tertullian. But on what foundation of Scripture, I ask, did the Fathers sanction chrism in baptizing?

units.la: CAP. XXXIX. Angelicorum hæresis quid docuerit.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXIX. What the heresy of the Angelici taught.

units.la: N[?]gelici in Angelorum cultu inclinati, quos Epiphanius iam omnino defecisse testatur.
units.tr: Angelici, inclined to the worship of angels, which Epiphanius testifies had altogether died out.

units.la: 1. Angelici.) Dicuntur Ἀ[?]γγελικοὶ Graecè, in cuius vocis etymo perquirendo cur laboret Epiphanius, non video. Ἀ[?]πὸ τῶν ἀγγέλων denominantur, quorum se cultores exhibet: non autem ab Ingilino, quem Mesopotamiae vicum esse scribit, sed nec ab Ingaenonum populorum appellatione. Haec autem haeresis quum statim extincta fuerit cū ipso Angelicorū nomine, pau ca de ea scribi possunt. Nec enim huius meminit Theodoretus, nec Eusebius, nec tota historia Ecclesiastica: quanquam Simonianorum, Caianorum, Archonticorum, à quibus hic error primùm excogitatus est, faciūt mentionem. Ac fieri potest, vt interpolato tantùm nomine Angelici, Simonianorum haeresin renouarint, in hoc praesertim capite quod est de Angelorum cultu. Seleucianorum etiam postea meminit Augustus. qui in hunc ipsum errorem videtur incidisse, vel certè parem: quanquam tamen nec Archonticos, nec Seleucianos legimus Angelos adorasse, aut vnquam coluisse, sed tantùm deorū potestate & operibus multa praeter mentem Scripturae blatterasse. Angelicos tamen commemorat in catalogo haereseon Isidorus, & Can. Quidam autem.24.quaest.3. Ex quo Isidori loco colligi facile mihi videtur posse, quo demum tempore haec haeresis extiterit. Collocat enim post Melchisedechiana, vt circa annū à Christo passo 180. exorti fuerint: sed eodem pené momentó evanuerint, atque (quemadmodum Epiphanius scribit) perierint. Quanquam autem non est latissimè propagatum hoc virus, tenacissimè tamen in hominum animis semel sparsum inhęsit[?], adeò ut Papistæ etiamnum hodie hunc errorem retineant, & colant Angelos.
units.tr: 1. Angelici.) In Greek they are called Ἀγγελικοί [Angelikoi]. I do not see why Epiphanius labours over the etymology of this word. They are named from ἀπὸ τῶν ἀγγέλων [apo tōn angelōn], from the angels, whose worshippers they profess to be. The name does not come from Ingilinus, which he writes is a village in Mesopotamia, nor from the name of the Ingaevones people. Since this heresy was extinguished at once, together with the very name Angelici, few things can be written about it. Neither Theodoret, nor Eusebius, nor the whole Ecclesiastical History mentions it, although they do mention the Simonians, the Caianites and the Archontics, from whom this error was first devised. It may be that, merely by changing the name to Angelici, they revived the heresy of the Simonians, especially in the matter of the worship of angels that this chapter concerns. Augustine also later mentions the Seleucians, who seem to have fallen into this same error, or a similar one. Yet we do not read that the Archontics or the Seleucians ever worshipped or honoured angels; they only babbled much, beyond the mind of Scripture, about the powers and works of the gods. Isidore, however, does list the Angelici in his catalogue of heresies, as does Can. Quidam autem, 24, q. 3. From Isidore's passage it seems easy to gather when this heresy arose. For he places it after the Melchisedechians, so that it arose about the year 180 after Christ's passion; but it vanished almost at the same moment and (as Epiphanius writes) perished. Although this poison was not widely spread, it nevertheless clung very tenaciously once sown in men's minds, so much so that the Papists even today retain this error and worship angels.

units.la: Esse vero antiquissimum, & iam inde ab Apostolorum, & Apostolicorum virorum ætate repetitum, ex eo apparet, quòd Paulus in epist. ad Coloss.2. vers.18. Θρησκείας Ἀγγέλων. i. cultus Angelorum iam meminit, quem damnat & reiicit.
units.tr: That it is very ancient, and was already revived in the time of the Apostles and Apostolic men, appears from the fact that Paul, in Colossians 2:18, already mentions the worship of angels (θρησκείας Ἀγγέλων [thrēskeias angelōn]), which he condemns and rejects.

units.la: Quæ sententia ex Platonicæ sectæ, & philosophiæ fontibus hausta, primùm à Simonianis in Ecclesiam invecta est, sed ab Apostolis explosa, demum horum Angelicorum industria recruduit, ut ad Simonem Magum tanquam ad proprium authorem & parentem revocari debeat. Hanc autem hæresin maximè in Pisidia & Phrygia viguisse scribit Theodoret. Cyri episcopus, adeò ut Laodicena synodo (est autem illa Laodicea metropolis Phrygiæ) sit vetitum, ne Christiani precarentur Angelos.
units.tr: This opinion, drawn from the springs of the Platonic sect and philosophy, was first brought into the Church by the Simonians, and was rejected by the Apostles. At last, through the efforts of these Angelici, it revived, so that it ought to be traced back to Simon Magus as its proper author and parent. Theodoret, bishop of Cyrus, writes that this heresy especially flourished in Pisidia and Phrygia, so much so that the Synod of Laodicea (Laodicea being a metropolis of Phrygia) forbade Christians to pray to angels.

units.la: 2 Angelorum cultu.) Hoc fuit istorum hominum delirium, quòd Angelos colerent. In quo primùm non distinguitur, utrum bonos æquè ac malos, an bonos tantùm adorandos censuerint. Quòd si malos, certè eos coluisse diabolos verum erit, atque ita fuerint turpissimè superstitiosi, & furiosissimè dementati. Sin autem bonos tantùm Angelos & cælestes colendos esse docuerint, refutantur apertissimis sacræ Scripturæ locis, velut Coloss.2. versu18. Apocal.19. versu10,22. v.8. Deuter.17. v.3. Deinde Patrum ipsorum orthodoxorum authoritate, quemadmodum Theodoreti patris in Epito-me Decretorum diuinorum cap.de Angelis, & Augustini infinitis pene locis, imprimis lib.10. de Ciuit.Dei. cap.7. Lactantij lib.2.& Arnobij lib.3. Intelligunt, ait, se communiter honorari cum suo rege. Quanquam autem statim ab ipsa pene Apostolorum aetate coeperunt homines multa de Angelis curiose philosophari, & definire, adeo ut Clemens lib.6.Strom. dicat ex iis septem fuisse primogenitos quorum maxima sit potentia, & Tertull.in lib.De orat. Dominica, pios appellet Angelorum candidatos,colendos tamen venerandosque propterea non censebat, quod hi fanatici homines & hæretici apertissi-me salsissimeque voluere. Meminit Chrysost.in Coloss. 2. homil.7. quorundam hæreticorum, qui nos Deo, non per Christum, sed per Ange-los reconciliatos dicerent, qui ab istis Angelicis videntur profecti: aut potius ab Arianis, quo-rum hæc sententia & verba sunt, quemadmodum extant apud Augustin. in Actis contra Maximinum Arianum, Est officium Angeli, ut animam restituat ante conspectum Domini, non tamen anima potest Angelum videre, & exhibere: Angelus autem animas nostras spiri-tales videre & penetrare potest. Quam senten-tiam nunc Papistae retinent, & tuentur. Sed de hac hæresi satis.
units.tr: 2. The worship of angels.) The madness of these men was that they worshipped angels. Here it is first not made clear whether they thought that good and evil angels alike, or only good ones, were to be adored. If evil ones, then it will certainly be true that they worshipped devils, and so they were most shamefully superstitious and most furiously demented. But if they taught that only good and heavenly angels were to be worshipped, they are refuted by the plainest passages of Holy Scripture, such as Colossians 2:18; Revelation 19:10, 22:8; Deuteronomy 17:3. They are also refuted by the authority of the orthodox Fathers themselves, as of Theodoret the Father in his Epitome of the Divine Decrees, chapter on angels, and of Augustine in almost countless places, especially book 10 of De Civitate Dei, chapter 7; Lactantius book 2 and Arnobius book 3. "They understand," he says, "that they are honoured in common with their king." Although almost from the very age of the Apostles men began to philosophise curiously and to define many things about angels, so that Clement in Stromata book 6 says that among them seven were firstborn, whose power is greatest, and Tertullian, in his book On the Lord's Prayer, calls them pious candidates of the angels, he did not think they were therefore to be worshipped and venerated, because these fanatical and most openly and most absurdly heretical men wished it. Chrysostom, in his seventh homily on Colossians 2, mentions certain heretics who said that we are reconciled to God not through Christ but through angels; these seem to have come from the Angelici, or rather from the Arians, whose opinion and words are these, as they stand in Augustine in the Acts against Maximinus the Arian: "It is the office of the angel to restore the soul before the sight of the Lord; yet the soul cannot see and present the angel, whereas the angel can see and penetrate our spiritual souls." This opinion the Papists now retain and defend. But enough about this heresy.

units.la: CAP. XL.
units.tr: CAP. XL.

units.la: Apostolici haeretici, quorum erroris hic duo capita recensentur.
units.tr: The Apostolic heretics, whose error is set out here under two heads.

units.la: [?]Postolici{1} qui se ipso nomine arrogantissime vocauerunt, eo quod in suam communionem non reciperent vtentes coniugibus, & res proprias possidentes, quales habet catholica Ecclesia & Monachos, & clericos plurimos. Sed ideo isti haeretici sunt, quoniam se ab Ecclesia separantes, nullam spem putant eos habere, qui vtuntur iis rebus, quibus ipsi carent. Encratitis isti similes sunt. Nam & Apotactita appellantur. Sed alia nescio quae propria haeretica docere perhibentur.
units.tr: The Apostolics, who most arrogantly called themselves by that name, because they did not receive into their communion those who use wives and hold private property, as the catholic Church does, and monks, and very many clergy. But these are heretics, because by separating themselves from the Church they think that those who use the things they themselves lack have no hope. They are similar to the Encratites, for they are also called Apotactites. But they are said to teach some other peculiar heresies, I know not what.

units.la: Apostolici. Ἀπὸ τῶν Ἀποστόλων dictos esse Apostolicos, quorum vitam & sanctitatem imitari videntur velle, nemo dubitare potest qui vel primis labris Graecam linguam degustarit. Appellantur autem iidem Apotactitae a Latinis: a Graecis autem auctoribus Ἀποτακτικοί, quasi qui huic mundo prorsus renuntiarent. Fuerunt autem procul dubio stirpis Encratitarum siue Tatianorum infelix propago & amara fruticatio, quae suas & ipsa radices egit, multosque postea palmites produxit inauspicatos. Quotquot enim sunt coelibum Monachorum in Papatu genera, tot sunt huius haeresis adhuc surculi, & propagines astu Satanae interpolatae, & transplantatae mutatis nominibus. Haec enim haeresis vniuersi Monachismi, imprimis autem fratrum, qui dicuntur Mendicantium, fundamentum est. hi præcipuè hæc tria tanquam omnino necessaria vouent, nempe Paupertatem, Continetiam, id est, Ἀκτημοσύνην[?], vt nihil proprium possideat, Cœlibatum & Obedientiam, vt docet Thomas Aquinas in 2.2*. Nec mirum est Monachos ex hæreseòn colluuie sua vota & regulas confarcinasse, quando grauis author & orthodoxus Theodoretus Cyri Episcopus lib.1. cap.9. Historiæ scribit eos quædam ex Iudæorum, & Samaritanorum deliriis ad se transtulisse, quæ etiam hodie religiosè, ne dicam superstitiosè, obseruat. Imprimis autem Apostolicorum hæreticorum fascino hac nostra ætate & velut extrema mundi senecta, illecti videntur Iesuitæ Monachi, quos ad viuum nobis hodie referunt & repræsentant. Quod si Isidoro credimus, secuti sunt hi Angelicos hæreticos. Si verò coniecturis verioribus locus est, longè priores iis extiterunt, proximè post Encratitas, iam visitatis in Ecclesia & receptis illis monachalis habitus, victus, & continentiæ differentiis & ceremoniis, ut si a nobis hæc hæresis circa annum à Christo passo 145. collocetur, non multum abErrare videamur. Nec mirum est eosdem tam breui tempore totiens nouis nominibus se vocasse Tacianos, Encratitas, Apostolicos, quia cùm statim priorum error deprehensus & ab Ecclesia damnatus esset, interpolandus & fucandus erat, quùm iterum Ecclesiæ propinaretur. Itaque nomina mutabant homines astuti & Diabolici, vti nomine priori abdicato, aliud nouum & plausibilius introducerent, & quasi priori appellatione obliterata nullum errorem iam damnatum ipsi sequi,vel reponere videren-tur. Tenebras enim ea ratione melius simpli-cioribus hominum mentibus offundebant. Coe-pit autem haec haeresis in ea Pisidiae parte, quae ad Homonadum gentem & Pamphyliam per-tinet (Sic enim apud Epiphanium ex Plinio le-gere malo, οἱ ἀπὸ τῆς Πισιδίας ὁμοναδῶν[?], non autem ut vulgo est in impressis (μόνον[?]) quae latius propagata Pamphyliam, Ciliciam & Phrygiam i-psam infecit. Denique vniuersum terrarum orbem, ut in Papatu videmus. Ita vero paulatim hoc venenum invaluit, & una cum aetate accreuit, ut Gangrensi synodo (est autem Gangra Paphlagoniae civitas) circa Nicenæ synodi tempora reprobari damnarique oportuerit, sed tamen propterea non fuit extinctum. Nam & a Monachis cellulariis retentum est, & falso nomine hodie à fratribus Medicantibus omnino recoctum apponitur & laudatur. Apostolicos suo seculo vocatos esse scribit Bernard. in Cant. cantic. sermo. 66. haereticos qui erant Donatistis similes, & nullam Ecclesiam Apostolicam agnoscebant ubi non esset vita Apostolica.
units.tr: Apostolici. That the Apostolics were named from the Apostles [Ἀπὸ τῶν Ἀποστόλων], whose life and holiness they seem to wish to imitate, no one who has tasted even the first lips of the Greek language can doubt. Latin writers call the same people Apotactites, but Greek authors call them Ἀποτακτικοί [Apotaktikoi], as though they utterly renounced this world. Without doubt they were an unhappy offshoot and a bitter growth from the stock of the Encratites, or Tatianists, which also struck its own roots and afterwards put forth many ill-omened shoots. For as many kinds of celibate monks as there are in Papacy, so many twigs and cuttings of this heresy still survive, grafted in by the craft of Satan and transplanted under changed names. This heresy is indeed the foundation of all monasticism, and especially of the brothers who are called Mendicants. These chiefly vow three things as wholly necessary: poverty, continence (that is, ἀκτημοσύνη [aktemosyne], so that one possesses nothing of his own), celibacy, and obedience, as Thomas Aquinas teaches in 2.2. Nor is it strange that the monks have patched together their vows and rules from the filth of heresies, since the weighty author and orthodox Theodoret, bishop of Cyrus, writes in book 1, chapter 9 of his History that they took over some things from the delusions of the Jews and Samaritans, which they still observe today with religious zeal, not to say superstition. Above all, in our own age, and as it were in the old age of the world, the Jesuit monks seem to have been enticed by the spell of the Apostolic heretics, and they present them to us today to the life. If we believe Isidore, these followed the Angelici heretics. But if there is room for more probable conjecture, they arose far earlier, soon after the Encratites, when the distinctions of monastic dress, diet, continence and ceremonies had already been introduced and accepted in the Church. So if we place this heresy about the year 145 after Christ's passion, we shall not seem to be far wrong. Nor is it surprising that the same people called themselves so often in so short a time by new names: Tatianists, Encratites, Apostolics. Once the error of their predecessors had been detected and condemned by the Church, it had to be disguised and painted over before it was offered to the Church again. So cunning and diabolical men changed their names, so that, with the former name abandoned, they might introduce another new and more plausible one, and, as if the old designation had been erased, they might seem to be following or restoring no error already condemned. For in this way they poured darkness more effectively over the minds of simpler people. This heresy began in that part of Pisidia which belongs to the people of Homonada and to Pamphylia (I prefer to read thus in Epiphanius, following Pliny, οἱ ἀπὸ τῆς Πισιδίας ὁμοναδῶν [hoi apo tes Pisidias Homonadon], rather than as is commonly found in the printed editions, μόνον [monon]). It spread more widely and infected Pamphylia, Cilicia and Phrygia itself, and finally the whole orb of the earth, as we see in Papacy. And this poison gained such strength gradually, and grew with age, that it had to be rejected and condemned by the Synod of Gangra (Gangra is a city of Paphlagonia) around the time of the Synod of Nicaea. Yet it was not thereby extinguished. For it was retained by the cellular monks, and today it is again brewed up under a false name, set forth and praised by the Mendicant brothers. Bernard, in his sermon 66 on the Song of Songs, writes that in his century there were heretics called Apostolics, similar to the Donatists, who acknowledged no apostolic Church where there was not an apostolic life.

units.la: Haec fuerunt istius erroris capita. Primum coniugia & coniuges damnant, adeo ut nunquam æternæ vitæ fieri participes posse putent. Id quod ab Encratitis hauserunt. At hanc esse diabolicam doctrinam docet Paulus, 1 Timoth.4.vers.3.Hebr.13.vers.4.& Epiphanius ipse, [illegible, ~30 letters], id est, non modo caelibes, sed etiam coniuges. & idem, [illegible, ~30 letters]. Allegant autem pro fe primum dictum quod aiunt esse Christi ex falso Euangelio quod vocant Secundum Ægyptios, vbi sic legi volunt, Veni ad dissoluendum opera foeminæ. Sed Clemens Stromat. libro 3. qui prolixè aduersus primos huius erroris autores disputauit, non modò librum nihili & apocryphum esse docet: sed etiam vocem foeminæ pro intemperantia & praua cupiditate sumi ipsis illis interpretibus ostendit. Deinde afferunt exemplum Gymnosophistarum qui inter Persas laudati sunt, quòd abstinerent coniugio. Sed frustra & perperam adfidem[?]dem Christianam stabiliendam profanorum hominum exempla nobis obiiciuntur. Est autem coniugium sacrosancta Dei institutio, vt docet his verbis Christus, Quod Deus coniunxit, homo non separet, Matth.19.verf.6. Denique si coniugia damnanda sunt, ergo & homines omnes, & liberorum procreatio, quia sunt fructus coniugij, in quo tamen ipso foeminæ salutem esse, demonstrat Paulus 1.Timoth.2. versu 15. 2 Error, Apostolos omnes coelibes fuisse & perpetuò vixisse contendunt. Falsum etiam istud est, quemadmodum Paulus ipse docet 1.Corinth.9. verf.5, & arguit textus Euangelij, Matth.8.verf. 14. Praeterea testimonio Clementis Alexandrini, Strom.lib.3. reuincuntur, qui de Apostolorum coniugio disputat, cuius sententia etiam repetita est ab Eusebio libro 3. Histor.cap.30. 3 Damnat eos qui aliquid proprium possident, quasi exsortes, & alienos prorsus à regno coelorum. Ipsi vero vt loquitur Epiphan. Ἀκτημοσύνῃ[?] inducebant, per quam nihil erat proprium cuiufquam. Hoc contrarium verbo Dei dogma & Iesuitæ & Anabaptistæ maximè sunt amplexi. Nituntur autem loco qui est in Act.Apost. cap.4. versu 32. vbi dicuntur omnia fuisse non tantum inter Apostolos, sed etiam inter omnes Christianos communia: sed sequitur explicatio, nimirum, ne quis inter eos egeret. Ergo propter summam charitatem, quæ inter eos ferue-bat, erant eorum bona χρήσει [?] μὲν κοινά, κτήσει δὲ ἴδια. i. usu quidem communia, ut loquitur Tullius, non tamen mancipio. Quare tam absurdam sententiam pulcherrimè refutant Clemens lib.3. Stromat. & hoc loco Epiphan. 4 Libris quibusdam Apocryphis pro Euangelicis utuntur, quibus suum errorem confirmant, qualia sunt Acta Thomæ & Andreæ quæ vocant, & Euangelium secundum Ægyptios inauditum. 5 Lapsos post Baptismum Christianos nunquam postea, sed ne pœnitentes quidem in Ecclesiam recipiunt. Epiphanius. quod illis est cum Nouatianis commune, vel quod venenum Nouatiani ab istis porrectum acceperunt & lubenter ebiberunt. Ita citò pullulant & perniciosè crescunt, quæ primùm infœliciter sparsa & seminata sunt.
units.tr: These were the heads of this error. First, they condemn marriage and married people, so much so that they think such people can never become partakers of eternal life. They drew this from the Encratites. But Paul teaches that this is a devilish doctrine, 1 Timothy 4:3; Hebrews 13:4; and Epiphanius himself [illegible, ~30 letters], that is, not only celibates but also married people; and again [illegible, ~30 letters]. They allege for themselves, first, a saying which they say is Christ's, taken from the false gospel that they call According to the Egyptians, where they want it read thus: "I came to destroy the works of the woman." But Clement, in book 3 of the Stromata, who disputed at length against the first authors of this error, not only teaches that the book is worthless and apocryphal, but also shows that the word "woman" is taken for intemperance and wicked desire by those very interpreters. Next they cite the example of the Gymnosophists, who were praised among the Persians because they abstained from marriage. But it is in vain and wrongly that examples of profane men are thrown at us to establish the Christian faith. Marriage, however, is a most sacred institution of God, as Christ teaches in these words: "What God has joined together, let not man put asunder," Matthew 19:6. Finally, if marriages are to be condemned, then so are all men and the procreation of children, since children are the fruit of marriage, in which very thing Paul shows that the salvation of the woman lies, 1 Timothy 2:15. 2. They contend that all the Apostles were celibate and lived unmarried for ever. This too is false, as Paul himself teaches, 1 Corinthians 9:5, and the text of the Gospel refutes it, Matthew 8:14.
