Moreover, they are refuted by the testimony of Clement of Alexandria, Stromata book 3, who discusses the marriage of the Apostles, and whose opinion Eusebius also repeats in book 3 of his History, chapter 30. 3. They condemn those who possess anything as their own, as if they were wholly cut off from the kingdom of heaven and strangers to it. But they, as Epiphanius puts it, introduced ἀκτημοσύνη [aktēmosynē], by which nothing was anyone's own. Jesuits and Anabaptists have most eagerly embraced this doctrine, which is contrary to the Word of God. They rely on the passage in Acts 4:32, where it is said that all things were held in common not only among the Apostles but among all Christians. But the explanation that follows, namely, "so that no one among them was in need," shows otherwise. Therefore, on account of the great love that burned among them, their goods were κοινά [koina] in use, but ἴδια [idia] in ownership, that is, in use held in common, as Tully puts it, but not in ownership. Wherefore Clement, in book 3 of the Stromata, and Epiphanius in this passage, refute so absurd an opinion most admirably. 4. They use certain Apocryphal books as if they were Gospels, to confirm their error, such as the so-called Acts of Thomas and of Andrew, and the Gospel According to the Egyptians, which is unheard of. 5. They never receive back into the Church Christians who have fallen after baptism, not even when they repent. Epiphanius. In this they agree with the Novatians, or else they received the poison of Novatian from these people and drank it gladly. Thus those things which were first sown and scattered unhappily shoot up quickly and grow to ruin.

units.la: CAP. XLI.
units.tr: CAP. XLI.

units.la: Sabellius quis fuerit. Sabellianos autem vix aut parum admodum à Nouatianis differre, qui & ipsi Patripassiani, & Praxiani & Hermogeniani dicuntur.
units.tr: Who Sabellius was. The Sabellians differ little, or hardly at all, from the Novatians, and they are also called Patripassians, Praxeans and Hermogenians.

units.la: Abelliani[?]{1} ab illo Noeto, quem supra memorauimus, defluxisse dicuntur. Nam & discipulum eius quidam perhibent fuisse Sabellium. Sed qua causa duas hæreses Epiphanius computet, nescio, cum fieri potuisse videamus, vt fuerit Sabellius iste famosior, & ideo ex illo celebrius hoc hæresis nomen acceperit. Noetiani enim difficillime ab aliquo sciuntur: Sabelliani autem sunt in ore multorum. Nam & Praxianos a Praxea quidam vocant, & Hermogeniani{2} vocari ab Hermogene potuerunt, qui Praxeas & Hermogenes eadem sentientes in Africa fuisse dicuntur. Nec tamen ista plures sectæ sunt, sed vnius sectæ plura nomina ex iis hominibus, qui in ea maxime innotuerunt, si-cut Donatistæ idem Parmenianistæ: sicut Pelagiani, idem Celestiani. Vnde ergo sit fa-ctum, vt Noetianos & Sabellianos, non vnius hæresis duo nomina, sed tanquam duas hæreses supradictus Episcopus poneret, liquido inuenire non po-tui, quia si quid inter se differunt, tam obscure dixit studio breuitatis, vt non intelligam[?]us. Loco quidem, isto, quo, & non tam longe a Noetianis, Sabellianos commemorans, Sabelliani, inquit, similia Noeto dogmatizantes, præter hoc quod dicunt Patrem non esse passum, quomodo de Sabellianis intelligi potest, cum sic innotuerint dicere Patrem passum, vt Patripassiani, quam Sabelliani crebrius nuncupentur? Aut si forte in eo quod ait, Præter hoc quod dicunt Patrem esse passum, Noetianos hoc dicere intelligi voluit, quis eos in hac ambiguitate discernat? Vel quomodo possunt intelligi eorum Patrem passum fuisse non dicere, cum dicant{3} eundem ipsum esse Patrem & Filium, & Spiritum sanctum? autem Brixianus Episcopus in prolixo libro, quem De Haeresibus condidit, & cxxxviii. haereses arbitratus est computandas, Sabellianos continuo post Noetianos ponens. Sabellius, inquit, discipulus eius, qui similitudinem sui doctoris itidem secutus est: unde & Sabelliani postea sunt appellati, qui & Patripassiani, & Praxeiani a Praxea, & Hermogeniani ab Hermogene, qui fuerunt in Africa, qui & ista sentientes abiecti sunt ab Ecclesia catholica. Certe iste eosdem postea Sabellianos dixit appellatos, qui ea, quae Noetus, sentiebant. Et alia nomina eiusdem sectae commemorauit, & tamen Noetianos & Sabellianos sub duobus numeris tanquam duas haereses posuit: qua causa, ipse viderit.
units.tr: The Sabellians are said to have sprung from that Noetus whom I mentioned above, for some say that Sabellius was his disciple. But I cannot see why Epiphanius counts these as two heresies, since it is plain that Sabellius may have been the more famous of the two, and so the heresy received its name from him more widely. The Noetians are scarcely known to anyone, whereas the Sabellians are on everybody's lips. Some call the Praxeans after Praxeas, and the Hermogenians could be named after Hermogenes, who are said to have held the same views as Praxeas and Hermogenes in Africa. Yet these are not several sects, but one sect with several names taken from the men who were most prominent in it, just as the Donatists and the Parmenianists are the same, and the Pelagians and the Celestians are the same. How it came about that the bishop mentioned above set down the Noetians and the Sabellians not as two names for one heresy but as two heresies, I have been unable to discover clearly. If they differ at all, he expressed this so obscurely, in the interest of brevity, that I cannot understand him. In the passage where he mentions the Sabellians, not far from the Noetians, he says: "The Sabellians, teaching things similar to Noetus, except that they deny the Father suffered." How can this be understood of the Sabellians, when they are better known for saying that the Father suffered, so much so that they are more often called Patripassians than Sabellians? Or if by the words "except that they say the Father suffered" he meant that the Noetians said this, who could sort out such ambiguity? Or how can it be understood that they did not say the Father suffered, when they affirm that the same one is Father, Son and Holy Spirit? Moreover, the bishop of Brescia, in the long book he wrote On Heresies, and which counts a hundred and thirty-eight heresies, placed the Sabellians immediately after the Noetians. Sabellius, he says, was a disciple of Noetus, who followed the example of his teacher in the same way; hence the Sabellians were afterwards called also Patripassians, Praxeans after Praxeas, and Hermogenians after Hermogenes, who were in Africa, and who, holding these views, were cast out by the catholic Church. Certainly this writer said that those who held the views of Noetus were afterwards called Sabellians. He also recorded other names of the same sect, and yet he set down the Noetians and the Sabellians under two numbers as two heresies. Let him see to the reason for that.

units.la: I Sabelliani.) Sabelliani a Sabellio dicti sunt, qui iidem antea Noetiani vocabantur, deinde Monarchici, quia Deum tanquam Monarcham mundi inducerent unum, non autem tres personas, qui postea Photinianos pepererunt, ut est in Indicat. Haeref. in Histor. Eccles. Quemadmodum enim Montanus erroris Noetianorum & Sabellianorum fons & primus auctor esse creditur, ut tradit Socrat. lib.1. Histor. cap.23. sic Sabelliani parentes Photinianorum appellantur. Qua vero ratione Noetiani a Sabellianis distinguantur: etsi scrupulose quaerit hoc loco Augustinus, frustra tamen mihi videtur disputari, cum nihil aliud Sabelliani plane fuerint, quam Noetiani nouo nomine donati, qui iidem a Prudent. poeta in Hamart. vocatur Vnionitae, sed Sabellianorum nomen inualuit, Noetianorum autem statim extinctum est, siue quòd huius dogmatis & fcholæ difcipuli Sabel-lianos fe dici maluerint,feu cp Sabellius doctior acutiórq; in hoc errore defendendo vifus huic fectæ nomen dedit. Quod enim fcribit Epiph. Noetianos non dixiffe Patrem paffum effe,fatis vel ex eo refutatur, quòd Noetiani Patripaffia-ni dicti funt, vt Theodoret. fcribit: & quod o-mnino neceffe fit ei, qui in Trinitate perfonas tollit, & vnam tantum conftituit, illud fateri, Patrem ipfum paffum effe,cumFilius paffus eft. Nifi fortaffe vt Marcellus Galata ftatueret Pa-trem fefe extendiffe, & hanc eius extenfionem paffam effe,quæ Filius dicebatur: Spiritum au-tem fanctum effe extefionem extenfionis prio-ris. Vide Theodoret.lib.2.Hereticfabular.Sed ftatim nouo nomine ornata & venditata fuit Noctianorum hærefis priore repudiato. Fuit autem Sabellius Afer,& ex ea Africæ regione & prouincia quę Lybia proprie dicta eft,in qua Pentapolis fiue Cyrenaica regio quę eadem eft, comprehendebatur , vnde fæpe Sabellius co-gnominatur Lybicus à fcriptoribus Ecclefia-fticis. Natus autem eft Sabellianifmus, vt Eu-febdocet,lib.7.Hiftor.cap.7. Ptolemaide, quæ ciuitas eft Cyrenaicæ fiue Pentapoleos, olim à prifcis Barce dicta , quemadmodum Plinius fcribit lib.5.cap.5. ex quo ipfo oppido verifimi-le eft ortum Sabellium. Ecclefia vero excom-municauit Sabellium, vt tradit hic ex Philaftro Auguftinus, cuius quis vitæ exitus fuerit, à ne-mine, quod fciam, obferuatur. Hominem ta-men iftum dirum,&errorem hunc ipfum meri-to maledictum atque etiam anathema pronuntiamus, qui tam insignem in Deum iniuriam & blasphemiam contineat. Coepit autem Sabel-liani nomen innotescere sub Sixto Romano Pon-tifice, durante adhuc Deciana vel potius iam Valeriana persecutione, quemadmodum Platina vult & circa annū à Christo passo 224. quan-quam quidam existimant temporibus Cypriani iam quodammodo errorem hunc degustatum & delibatum fuisse: sed de Montanistis potius intelligenda sunt, quę Cyprian. in Sabellianos iaculari videtur. Propagatus autem est hic error latissime, adeo ut ex Africa statim Mesopotamiam inuaserit, denique Romam ipsam. Perstitit autem diutissime, in Oriente & Asia maximè, quando plures Episcopos etiam aetate Constantini Magni Sabellianos & Sabelliani-zantes fuisse annotat perspicue Socrates lib.1. Histor.cap.24.
units.tr: 1 Sabellians.) The Sabellians were so called from Sabellius, and they were formerly called Noetians. Then they were called Monarchians, because they taught that God is one monarch of the world and not three persons. Afterwards they gave birth to the Photinians, as is set out in the Index of Heresies and in the Ecclesiastical History. For as Montanus is believed to be the source and first author of the error of the Noetians and Sabellians, as Socrates relates (Hist. bk. 1, ch. 23), so the Sabellians are called the parents of the Photinians. As to the reason why the Noetians are distinguished from the Sabellians, although Augustine inquires into this scrupulously at this point, it seems to me that the question is pursued in vain, since the Sabellians were plainly nothing other than the Noetians given a new name. The same people are called "Unionites" by the poet Prudentius in the Hamartigenia. But the name Sabellian prevailed, while the name Noetian was at once extinguished, either because the disciples of this doctrine and school preferred to be called Sabellians, or because Sabellius, seen as the more learned and shrewder in defending this error, gave his name to the sect. What Epiphanius writes, that the Noetians did not say the Father suffered, is sufficiently refuted by the fact that the Noetians were called Patripassians, as Theodoret writes. And it must necessarily be admitted by anyone who removes the persons in the Trinity and posits only one, that the Father himself suffered, since the Son suffered. Unless perhaps, like Marcellus of Galatia, one holds that the Father extended himself, and that this extension, which was called the Son, suffered, and that the Holy Spirit is the extension of the first extension. See Theodoret, Heretical Fables, bk. 2. But the heresy of the Noetians, having its earlier name repudiated, was at once adorned with a new name and put on sale. Sabellius was an African, from that region of Africa and province which is properly called Libya, in which Pentapolis, or the Cyrenaic region, which is the same, was included. For this reason Sabellius is often given the surname "Libyan" by the ecclesiastical writers. Sabellianism arose, as Eusebius teaches (Hist. bk. 7, ch. 7), at Ptolemais, a city of Cyrenaica or the Pentapolis, once called Barce by the ancients, as Pliny writes (bk. 5, ch. 5). It is therefore likely that Sabellius came from that very town. The Church excommunicated Sabellius, as Augustine here relates from Philastrius. What the end of his life was, no one has observed, so far as I know. Yet we rightly pronounce that man accursed, and this very error too, and even anathema, since it contains such a notable injury and blasphemy against God. The name of the Sabellians began to become known under Sixtus, the Roman bishop, while the Decian persecution was still going on, or rather already the Valerian, as Platina maintains, and about the year 224 after the suffering of Christ. Some, however, think that this error had already in some measure been tasted and touched upon in the time of Cyprian, but the things Cyprian seems to aim at against the Sabellians are better understood as directed at the Montanists. This error spread very widely, so much so that it at once invaded Mesopotamia from Africa, and finally Rome itself. It persisted for a very long time, especially in the East and in Asia, when Socrates clearly notes that many bishops, even in the age of Constantine the Great, were Sabellians or Sabellianisers (Hist. bk. 1, ch. 24).

units.la: 2 Hermogeniani.) Cur Hermogenianos etiam vocari putet Augustinus, vel alius quispiam, eos qui Sabelliani dicuntur, non video. Fuit enim Hermogenes Afer quidem, ut scribit Tertullianus, & pictor, sed & dogmate & aetate a Sabellianis prorsus dissimilis & diuersus. Ac dogmate quidem, quod in ea secta fuit duplex, nullo fuit modo cum Sabellianis consentiens. Quod materiam ex qua mundus hic conditus est, Deo coaeterna esse statueret, id quod a Stoicis acceperat. 2 Quod duos deos esse hac ratione doceret, vnum bonum: alterum malum, qui Physico nomine ab eo ὕλη. i. Materia vocabatur. Hoc autem sumpserat a Marcionitis. Hujus errores grauissimos Tertull. praeclarissima disputatione confutauit, ubi de Sabellianis nec ψῷ[?] quidem. Ætate vero prior fuit Hermogenes Sabellianis annis penè 58. ut non fuerit dicendum hos illis in nomen successisse, sed potius Sabellianos Hermogenianis, quorum hæresin statim concidisse testantur autores Ecclesiastici, & penè ipso natiuitatis momento, adeò ut raro de iis mentionem faciant, si unum Tertullian.excipias. Obiter tamen commemoratur veluti à Theodoreto lib.1. Hæret. fabul. Eusebio lib.4.cap.24.& Isidoro': cuius etiam defensor fuit Nigidius quidam, de quo in lib.de præscript.adu erf.hæretic. Tertullian.
units.tr: 2 Hermogenians.) I do not see why Augustine, or anyone else, should think that those who are called Sabellians are also to be called Hermogenians. Hermogenes was indeed an African, as Tertullian writes, and a painter, but in doctrine and in date he was entirely unlike and different from the Sabellians. In doctrine, indeed, which in his sect was twofold, he in no way agreed with the Sabellians. First, he held that the matter from which this world was made was coeternal with God, which he had taken from the Stoics. Second, by this reasoning he taught that there are two gods, one good and the other evil, the latter called by its physical name "matter" [ὕλη]. He had taken this from the Marcionites. Tertullian refuted these very serious errors of his in a most excellent disputation, in which he does not even mention the Sabellians. In date Hermogenes was older than the Sabellians by almost fifty-eight years, so that it should not be said that these succeeded to his name, but rather that the Sabellians gave their name to the Hermogenians. Ecclesiastical writers testify that his heresy collapsed at once, almost at the very moment of its birth, so that they rarely make mention of it, if you except Tertullian alone. It is, however, mentioned in passing by Theodoret (Heretical Fables, bk. 1), Eusebius (bk. 4, ch. 24) and Isidore. Nigidius, a certain man, was also a defender of it, concerning whom Tertullian speaks in his book On Prescription against Heretics.

units.la: Una fuit Sabelliano-rum hypothesis, sed multarum blasphemiarum instar. Personas enim in Trinitate non tantum confundunt, sed omnino tollunt. Itaque Patrem, Filium & Spiritum sanctum unam & eandem esse ἑνωσιν[?] volunt, quæ variis nominibus, prout necessitas & usus exigit, appellata est, ut unum & idem solis corpus, lux, splendor, & calor pro diuersis effectis nominatur. Confirmat autem suam sententiam, quia Deuter.6. dictum est, Audi Israel, Dominus Deus tuus, Deus unus est. quod certè perperam intellectum Iudæos ipsos, à quibus prima huius hæreseos fundamenta iacta sunt, in eundem errorem induxit, atque etiamnum hodie retinet. Clamant enim πολυθεῖαν[?], i. deorum multitudinem à Christianis Ethnicorum more renouari, si tres in una & eadem diuina essentia personæ reipsa distinctæ & subsistentes ponantur. Responsio vero facilis est. Nos unam quidem & eandem etiam numero, non tantùm genere & speciè ὁμοούσιον, id est, essentiam diuinam docere, constituere & defendere: in ea verò essentia tres ὑποστάσεις id est, personas & subsistentias agnoscere, vt veteres verterunt. Itaque neque deos numero multos facimus, cùm non separemus diuinam illam naturam: neque personas tollimus, quia quenque, id est Patrem, Filium, & Spiritum sanctum in diuina essentia propriam personam habere demonstrauimus. Vt autem hæc commodissimè docerentur, voces ὑπόστασις & ὁμοούσιος sunt à Patribus receptæ, vt ait Socrat. lib. 3. cap. 7. Ruffin. libr. 1. cap. 29. ac ὑπόστασις quidem vocabulũ aduersus Arianos: ὁμοούσιος autem aduersus Sabellianos: vt omnis in disputando ambiguitas tolleretur.
units.tr: The Sabellian hypothesis was one, but it amounted to many blasphemies. For they not only confuse the persons in the Trinity, but altogether abolish them. Thus they hold that the Father, Son and Holy Spirit are one and the same unity [ἕνωσις], which, as need and usage demand, is named by various names, just as one and the same body of the sun is called light, brightness and heat according to its different effects. They confirm their opinion by the words of Deuteronomy 6: "Hear, O Israel, the Lord thy God is one God." This was certainly misunderstood by the Jews themselves, from whom the first foundations of this heresy were laid, and it led them into the same error, which they still hold today. For they cry out that a multitude of gods [πολυθεΐα], that is, polytheism, is being revived by Christians in the manner of the heathen, if three persons, really distinct and subsisting, are posited in one and the same divine essence. The reply, however, is easy. We teach, constitute and defend that there is one and the same God, one in number and not only in kind and species, that is, one divine essence [ὁμοούσιον]. In that essence we acknowledge three hypostases [ὑποστάσεις], that is, persons and subsistences, as the ancients translated the words. Thus we do not make the gods many in number, since we do not separate that divine nature, nor do we abolish the persons, since we have shown that each, that is, the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, has his own person in the divine essence. So that these things might be taught most conveniently, the words hypostasis [ὑπόστασις] and homoousios [ὁμοούσιος] were received by the Fathers, as Socrates says (bk. 3, ch. 7) and Rufinus (bk. 1, ch. 29). The word hypostasis was used against the Arians, and homoousios against the Sabellians, so that all ambiguity in disputing might be removed.

units.la: CAP. XLII. Origeniani vnde dicti. Erroris autem eorum caput vnum recensetur.
units.tr: CAP. XLII. Why the Origenians are so called. One chief error of theirs is recorded.

units.la: Rigeniani¹ à quodam Origene dicti sunt, non ab illo, qui fere omnibus notus est, sed ab alio nescio quo, de quo vel sectatoribus eius Epiphanius loquens, Origeniani, inquit, sunt cuiusdam Origenis discipuli, turpis autem sunt operationis. Ipsi sunt nefanda facientes, sua corpora corruptioni tradentes.
units.tr: The Origenians were so called from a certain Origen, not from the one who is known to almost everyone, but from some other man, I know not who. Epiphanius, speaking of his followers, says: "The Origenians are disciples of a certain Origen, and their practice is shameful. They are the ones who do unspeakable things, handing their bodies over to corruption."

units.la: 2. Origeniani.) Pauca sunt omnino quæ de hac hæresi dici queant, cùm præter vnum Epiphanium nemo fide dignorum scriptorum scripserit. pferit,atque is ipfe breuifsimé. Authorem non nominat fiue Origenes, fiue Origenius dictus fit, ex propagine tamen Gnofticorum, & imprimis Epiphanis, qui fuit Carpocratis filius, errore profectum effe hoc malum putat. Cuius aliquot veftigia etiam ipfius Epiphanij feculo in aliquot Palæftinæ ciuitatibus manferat.Poft-ea vero prorfus deleta funt & extincta.Coepiffe vero videntur ifti paulò poft Gnofticos. Habi-tu certè & profefsione monasticę vitæ fefe plurimum commendarunt, quæ fuit turpifsimarū actionum, & in his & in alijs obfcurifsimum velum. Vnde non eft vero abfimile hunc Origenem fuiffe fenem illum qui in Ægypto Antonij Magni difcipulus vixit, & Monachifmum profeffus eft, de quo Sozom. lib.7. cap.30. Nec modò viri & mares, fed etiam fœminæ hoc virus amplexæ funt,& diffeminarunt. Origeniani enim ifti fœminas sibi comites & adiunctas ha-buerunt, quas εἰσάκτυς[?] appellabant, cum quibus perpetrabant turpifsima quæque, quem morem quanquam fœdifsimum. tamen Epifcopi & Presbyteri quidam Ioannis Chryfoftomi tē-pore retinere ftudebant,interim caftitatem vo-ventes:nunquam tamen eum in vfu effe, cùm fit iftud concubinarum genus certifsima coniugij peftis,concefsit Chryfoftomus. Hodie vero pafsim regnat inter clericos in Papatu. Origeniani vero videntur hi nominati, ut à fequentibus hæreticis diftinguerentur, qui ab Origene Adamătio,Origeniftæ,melius quàm Origenia-ni dicti funt.
units.tr: 2. Origeniani.) Very little at all can be said about this heresy, since apart from Epiphanius no trustworthy writer has written about it, and he does so very briefly. He does not name the author, whether he was called Origenes or Origenius. He does, however, think this evil arose from error and came from an offshoot of the Gnostics, and especially of Epiphanes, who was the son of Carpocrates. Some traces of it remained in a few cities of Palestine even in Epiphanius's own time. Afterwards it was utterly destroyed and extinguished. These people seem to have begun a little after the Gnostics. Certainly they commended themselves greatly by the dress and profession of the monastic life, which was a most obscure veil for the most shameful actions, both in these and in others. Hence it is not at all unlikely that this Origen was that old man who lived in Egypt as a disciple of Anthony the Great and professed monasticism, of whom Sozomen writes in book 7, chapter 30. Not only men but also women embraced this poison and spread it. For these Origenians kept women as companions and attendants, whom they called "sisactae" [εἰσάκτους], and with them they committed every kind of most shameful act. Although this custom was most foul, certain bishops and presbyters in the time of John Chrysostom tried to keep it, while vowing chastity; yet Chrysostom granted that it was never practised, since this sort of concubinage is a most certain pest of marriage. Today, however, it reigns everywhere among the clergy in Papacy. These people seem to have been named Origenians so that they might be distinguished from the heretics who followed them, who were called Origenists, more properly than Origenians, after Origen Adamantius.

units.la: Tria recenfentur erroris huius hæresèos capita. 1 Nuptias & con-iugia damnant, quemadmodum plerique alij hæretici. 2 Semen humanum si quando co-eunt (coeunt autem cum suis meretricibus, & inductitiis mulieribus sæpissimè & impudentissimè) in terram deijciunt & spargunt, vt Onan ille propterea maledictus à Deo, de quo est Ge[?]nef.38.ver.8.9.quòd humanum conceptum detestantur. Hoc idem postea fecerunt Manichæi, vt scribit Auguft.cōtra Secundinum cap.[?]21. Sed illud ipsum postquam in terram cecidit, occant & conculcant, ne ab immundis spiritibus rapiatur & fiat prægnans. Exosum enim Deo dicunt & impurum appellant omne semen humanum, fortasse propter peccatum originale, in quo erant toto cœlo. Nam proles & soboles est Dei benedictio in coniugio, vti disputat contra Julian. Donatistam luculenter Augustinus. 3 Error. Quosdam Veteris & Noui testamenti libros reiiciunt, ex quibus eorum error turpitu-do sceleratissima redarguitur. Peccant enim isti in vniuersum genus humanum, quod extingue-re conantur, cum semen hominis abolent, & perdunt: tam magnum est nimirum semel à Satana fascinatum esse,
units.tr: Three heads of this heresy are recorded. (1) They condemn marriages and wedlock, as many other heretics do. (2) When they do come together (and they come together with their prostitutes and with introduced women, very often and most shamelessly), they cast and scatter the human seed on the ground, like that Onan who was cursed by God, of whom we read in Gen. 38. vers. 8, 9, because they detest human conception. The Manichaeans later did the same, as Augustine writes against Secundinus, chapter 21. But they trample and tread underfoot that very seed after it has fallen to the ground, lest it be snatched away by unclean spirits and make a woman pregnant. For they say that every human seed is hateful to God and call it impure, perhaps on account of original sin, in which they were utterly at odds. For offspring is God's blessing in marriage, as Augustine argues admirably against Julian the Pelagian. (3) Error. They reject some books of the Old and New Testaments, by which their error and most wicked shamefulness is refuted. For these men sin against the whole human race, which they try to extinguish when they destroy and waste the seed of man. So great, surely, is the harm of having once been bewitched by Satan.

units.la: CAP. XLIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XLIII.

units.la: Origenistę & Adamantij cur sic dicti. Erroris autem eorum capita sex describuntur.
units.tr: Why they are called Origenists and Adamantians. The six heads of their error are set out.

units.la: Lios autem Origenianos subiyciens conti-nuo, Origeniani, inquit, alij, qui & Adamantij,{1} tractatoris illius sectatores, qui & mortuorum{2} resurrectionem negat: Christum autem & Spiritum sanctum creaturam dicunt: Paradisum autem & coelos & alia non credunt esse secundum literam, sed in allegoria. Haec quidem de Origene Epiphanius refert. Sed defensores eius dicunt Origenem Patrem & Filium & Spiritum sanctum unius eiusdemque substantiae docuisse, neque resurrectionem repulisse mortuorum. Sed qui eius plura legerunt, contradicunt. Sunt & alia huius Origenis dogmata, quæ Catholica Ecclesia omnino nō recepit, in quibus nec ipsum falso arguit, nec potest ab eius defensoribus excusari, maximè de purgatione, & libe-ratione, ac rursus post longum tempus ad eandem malam revolutione rationalis universæ creaturæ. Quis e-nim catholicus Christianus vel doctus vel indoctus non vehementer exhorreat eam, quam dicit malorum purgationem, id est, etiam eos qui hanc vitam in flagitijs & facinoribus & sacrilegijs atque impietatibus quamlibet maximis finierunt, ipsum etiam postremo diabolum, atque angelos eius, quamuis post lon-gissima tempora purgatos atque liberatos regno Dei lucique restitui? Et rursus post longissima tempora omnes, qui liberati sunt, ad hæc mala denuo relabi & reuerti, & has vices alternantes beatitudinum & miseriarum rationalis creaturæ semper fuisse, sempérque fore? De qua vanissima impietate aduersus Philosophos, à quibus ista didicit Origenes, in libris de Civitate Dei {3} diligentissimè disputaui. Dicit praterea ipse Origenes, quod Filius Dei sanctis coparatus, veri-tas sit: Patri collatus mendacium: & quantum distat
units.tr: Going on to the other Origenists, he says: Other Origenists, who are also called Adamantians, are followers of that teacher. They deny the resurrection of the dead, they say that Christ and the Holy Spirit are creatures, and they do not believe that Paradise, the heavens and other things are to be taken literally but allegorically. Epiphanius reports these things about Origen. His defenders, however, say that Origen taught that the Father, Son and Holy Spirit are of one and the same substance, and that he did not reject the resurrection of the dead. But those who have read more of him contradict this. There are also other dogmas of Origen, which the Catholic Church has not received at all. In these he is not wrongly accused, and his defenders cannot excuse him, especially concerning purgation and liberation, and the return after a long time of the whole rational creation to the same evil. For what Catholic Christian, learned or unlearned, does not vehemently shudder at what he calls the purging of evils? He means that even those who have ended this life in crimes, wickednesses, sacrileges and impieties of any magnitude, and even the devil himself at last and his angels, after very long times of purging and liberation, are restored to the kingdom of God and its light. And again, after very long times, all who have been liberated relapse into these evils and return to them, and these alternating changes of blessedness and misery have always been and always will be for the rational creature. I have disputed very thoroughly against this most empty impiety, in the books On the City of God, against the philosophers from whom Origen learned these things. Origen himself further says that the Son of God, compared with the saints, is truth; compared with the Father, falsehood; and as far as

units.la: Apostoli Christo, tantum Filius Patre. Unde nec o-randus est Filius cum Patre, quia non est author in-dulgendarum petitionum, sed supplicator.
units.tr: the apostles are from Christ, so far is the Son from the Father. Hence the Son is not to be prayed to together with the Father, because he is not the author of granting petitions but a suppliant.

units.la: 1 Qui & Adamantij.) Origenes Adamantius, tum propter summam in fide Christi constantiam, tum etiam propter assiduum & indefcffum fcriptionis & disputationis laborem dictus est. Unde & Suidas eundem propter multos libros, quos scripsit, συνταχτικὸν [?] vocatum ef-fe scribit, quasi dicas Compositorem. Ab hoc igitur appellati sunt hi hæretici & Origeniftæ & Adamantij, vel etiam Adamantiani, quemadmodum a falsi dogmatis capite, quod primus & præcipuè Origenes induxit, Chiliastæ, vel Latinè Millenarij, quòd regnum Dei post re-furrectionem futurum & promissum intra mille annos finiendum esse contenderent, abusi loco Apocalypf.qui est cap.20.versu 2. Dicti sunt etiam Nepotiani à Nepote quodam Ægyptio Episcopo, qui eundem errorem postea tutatus est acerrimè & in vanis illis Origenis allegoriis sibi nimium placuit, cuius error innotuit sub Gallieno Imperatore Romano. & Xysto Episcopo, circa annum à Christo passo 231. Cœpit autem hæc hæresis maximè post Cyprianum iam mortuum, & post Origenem etiam ipsum defunctum, quod sub Gallo Imperatore accidisse scribit Eufeb.libro 7.cap.1. Unde demum Gallieno imperante, & Valeriano ipsius patre iam à Sapore Persarum rege capto, Xysto verò Román. Pontifice initium habuit circa annum à Christo passo 227. Latissimè verò sparsa est & citisimè propagata, tum propter celebre nomen Origenis, tum etiam propter curiosum hominum ingenium, qui iam mysticis allegoriis & scriptis istius autoris mirum in modum delectabantur. Admiscuit enim & aspersit Origenes varia ethnicorum philosophorum dogmata Christianorum & Apostolicorum pręcepto-rum simplicitati, ut ait Euagr.libro 4.capite 38. quæ illius ætatis homines tanquam flores in Origene admirabantur, & laudabant: res tamen ipsa postea certissimas Christianæ doctrinę pe-stes & corruptelas esse docuit, adeo ut verisi-ma absurdissimæ Manichæorum hæresços fundamenta etiam iecisse dici possit: quanquam a-lij eum à Manichæis suas fæces hausisse malunt, ut Constantinopolitana Synodus, id quod per temporum rationem defendi non potest, quum Manichæanus error demum 20. annis postjam vegetam, vagantem & receptam Origenistarum pestem exortus sit, nimirum sub Aureliano imperatore, anno à Christo passo 247. Ex Ægypto igitur, & imprimis ex Monachorum & Asce-tarum (quibus plurimùm primùm illius doctri-na grata fuit) cellis tanquam carceribus fœti-dus ille Origeniani erroris halitus & vapor exhalavit, qui tamen ipsi postea summe Origeniaenæ doctrinæ fuerunt infensi, ut docent Socrates libro 6. cap.7. & Sozomen.libro 8. capite 11, & 12. quum Anthropomorphitarum sententiam, contrariam Origeni, verum de Deo invisibili sentienti, ut docet Paulus 1. Timoth.6.verf.16. hęresin illi probassent, stolidis nimirum de Deo visibili cogitationibus stolidi homines Monachi delectati. Ergo Origenem, quem primum ut viscera fuerant amplexi Monachi, postea ut blasphemum & abominabilem, quia recte de Dei natura inuisibili scripserat, cane peius & angue oderunt, in quo Theophili Alexandrini episcopi odio, astu & factione maxime confirmati sunt, id quod ostendit Socrates lib.7. cap. 45.& libr.6.cap.7.& 9. Peruasit igitur hic error uniuersam Ægyptū, Syriam, Asiam, sed & Constantinopolim imprimis labefecit, adeo ut in monasterio quod Noua Laura prope Constantinopolim situm erat pene extingui non potuerit etiam post multa secula, sed à Theodoreto Ascetæ Cæsareæ Cappadociæ Episcopo defensus & retentus est, ut ait Euagr. libro 4.cap.38. Doctissimos etiā homines & suo seculo claros scriptores corrupit, quando Eusebium Pamphili, Basilium, Ioannem Chrysostomum, & Hieronymum ipsum illius fautores fuisse, ex apologia Ruffini apparet. Diutissimè permansit, & plus quam per 334. annos tanquam continua successione & propagatione sustentatus est, quando etiam sub imperatore Mauricio, & Gregorio Magno pontifice Romano adhuc extabant Origenistæ, quemadmodum ipse in Iob lib.34.& Cassiodorus in Psalm.9. testantur. Nec tamen suis aduersariis caruit, quando Epiphanius, & Theophilus, & Methodius, & Proclus episcopi, grauiter Origenis errores oppugnarunt: quin etiam duabus Synodis sunt damnati. Ac prima quidem Alexandrina, anno 200. etiā statim post Origenis mortem: posteriori verò Constantinopolitana, quæ quinta generalis Synodus dicta est;& a Iustiniano primo imperatore Constantinopolitano dicitur collecta, quemadmodum Socrat.libro 6.cap.9. scribit, & post eum Euagrius. Fuit autem hic Origenes Leonidis martyris filius, Ammonij monachi discipulus, vt Eusebius tradit, qui cum maxime laudat,libr.6. cap.18.19.20. Ægyptius, & Alexandrinus, & in omni literarum genere exercitatus, & ethnicae philosophiae, imprimis autem Platonicae peritissimus, e cuius assidua tractatione, aut coeno potius suas illas erroris sordes videtur sumpsisse. Nam vt Valentiniani, ita hic nugis Platonicis,&vanis eius sectae speculationibus addictus, coepit vbique in sacram Scripturam nouos sensus & ἀλληγορίας[?], plausibiliter quidem curiosis hominibus, sed maxime ipsi rerum veritati & sano Scripturae intellectui contrarias inducere, vt haec haeresis Valentinianae tantum fruticatio & propago fuisse mihi videri solcat. Quae res sanum prius hominis iudicium ita peruertit, vt etiam in seipsum esset sæuus. Incidens enim in locum Matth. 19. de eunuchis, seipsum castrauit:in quo ipso non est allegoria vsus:vel, vt mauult Epiphanius, φαρμακωτικοῖς[?] medicamentis virilia sibi stupefecit, ne semen emittere propter frigiditatem ascitam possent. Coepit autem ἀλληγορεῖν[?] non statim, sed quum iam Exaplo illi suo & collatione variae Bibliorum versionis manum admonuisset, quod opus in Ambrosij comitis cuiusdam Palatini fauore aggressus est, vt docet Socrates libr.3.cap.7. quae Ambrosium ex Sabellianorum, vt ait Epiphanius, & verius quidem, vt autem vult Eusebius libr.6. cap.16. Valentinianorum errore ad orthodoxos traduxit. De variis rebus scripsit. Nec enim Theologica tantum illius opera, sed etiam physica quaedam extitisse tradit Epiphanius, adeoque tanti habitus est etiam a prophanis, vt a Mammæa Alexandri imperatoris Romani matre euocatus sit & benigne exceptus, & sub ea Alexandrū ipsum Christianæ fidei initiarit. Vnde postea Alexander in suo larario Christum habuisse scribitur. Multos errores, qui suo seculo nati erant, imprimis autem in Arabia, suis disputationibus Origenes iugulauit & extinxit. Demum anno ę-tatis 70[?] sub Gallo imperatore, quum sub Commodo natus esset, vita functus est, sui seculi lumen habitus, & Christianæ Ecclesiæ doctor eximius, quanquam tamen huius hæreseos grauissimæ conditor, & parens fuit, ne quis ingenij sui viribus confidat.
units.tr: 1 Also called Adamantians.) Origen was called Adamantius both for his great steadfastness in the faith of Christ and for his constant and tireless labour in writing and disputing. Hence Suidas also writes that, on account of the many books he wrote, he was called syntaktikon [συνταχτικὸν], as if you should say Compiler. These heretics were therefore called Origenists and Adamantians, or Adamantianists, from him. They were also called Chiliasts, or in Latin Millenarians, from the head of a false dogma, which Origen first and chiefly introduced: they contended that the kingdom of God would come after the resurrection and was to be completed within a thousand years, misusing a passage of the Apocalypse, chapter 20, verse 2. They were also called Nepotians, from a certain Egyptian bishop, Nepos, who afterwards defended the same error most fiercely and took too much pleasure in those empty allegories of Origen. This error became known under the Roman emperor Gallienus and Bishop Xystus, around the year 231 after Christ's passion. The heresy began chiefly after Cyprian was already dead, and after Origen himself had died, which Eusebius writes happened under the emperor Gallus, book 7, chapter 1. Hence, under Gallienus, while his father Valerian was already captured by Sapor, king of the Persians, but under Xystus the Roman pontiff, it began around the year 227 after Christ's passion. It spread most widely and propagated most quickly, both because of the famous name of Origen and because of the curious nature of men, who already delighted wonderfully in the mystical allegories and writings of that author. For Origen mixed and sprinkled various dogmas of the pagan philosophers into the simplicity of Christian and apostolic teaching, as Evagrius says in book 4, chapter 38. The men of that age admired and praised these as flowers in Origen. Yet the thing itself was later shown to be the most certain pest and corruption of Christian doctrine, so that it can be said he even laid the very foundations of the most absurd heresy of the Manichaeans. Others, however, prefer to say that he drew his dregs from the Manichaeans, as the Synod of Constantinople does; but this cannot be defended by the reckoning of times, since the Manichaean error arose only twenty years after the Origenist pest had become vigorous, widespread and accepted, namely under the emperor Aurelian, in the year 247 after Christ's passion. Out of Egypt, therefore, and especially from the cells of the monks and ascetics (to whom his teaching was at first most welcome), like prisons, that foul breath and vapour of Origenist error exhaled. Yet these same men later became most hostile to Origenist doctrine, as Socrates teaches in book 6, chapter 7, and Sozomen in book 8, chapters 11 and 12. They had approved the opinion of the Anthropomorphites, which is contrary to Origen and holds the true view of the invisible God, as Paul teaches in 1 Timothy 6:16; the foolish monks delighted in foolish thoughts about a visible God. Therefore they hated Origen, whom the monks had first embraced as their very vitals, more than a dog or a snake, calling him blasphemous and abominable, because he had written rightly about the invisible nature of God. They were especially confirmed in this hatred by the cunning and faction of Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, as Socrates shows in book 7, chapter 45, and book 6, chapters 7 and 9. This error therefore pervaded all Egypt, Syria and Asia, and especially undermined Constantinople, so that in the monastery called the New Laura, near Constantinople, it could not be extinguished even after many centuries, but was defended and retained by Theodoret, bishop of the ascetics at Caesarea in Cappadocia, as Evagrius says in book 4, chapter 38. It also corrupted very learned men and writers famous in their own age: Rufinus's apology shows that Eusebius of Pamphilus, Basil, John Chrysostom and Jerome himself were its supporters. It lasted a very long time, sustained for more than 334 years as if by continuous succession and propagation. Even under the emperor Maurice and Gregory the Great as Roman pontiff, Origenists still existed, as Gregory himself attests in Job, book 34, and Cassiodorus on Psalm 9. Nor did it lack opponents: Epiphanius, Theophilus, Methodius and Proclus, bishops, vigorously attacked Origen's errors, and it was condemned by two synods. The first was the Alexandrian synod, in the year 400, immediately after Origen's death; the second was the Constantinopolitan synod, which is called the fifth general synod, and is said to have been convened by Justinian, the first emperor at Constantinople, as Socrates writes in book 6, chapter 9, and Evagrius after him. This Origen was the son of the martyr Leonides and a pupil of the monk Ammonius, as Eusebius relates, whom he greatly praises in book 6, chapters 18, 19 and 20. He was an Egyptian and an Alexandrian, trained in every kind of literature, and very expert in pagan philosophy, especially Platonic. From his constant handling of it, or rather of its mud, he seems to have taken up those filthy errors. For, like the Valentinians, he was addicted to Platonic trifles and the empty speculations of that sect, and began everywhere to introduce new senses and allegories [ἀλληγορίας] into Sacred Scripture. These were plausible to curious men, but most contrary to the truth of things and to the sound understanding of Scripture, so that this heresy seems to me to have been merely a shoot and offshoot of the Valentinian heresy. This thing so perverted his earlier sound judgment that he became cruel even to himself. For, falling upon the passage in Matthew 19 about eunuchs, he castrated himself, and in that matter he did not use allegory. Or, as Epiphanius prefers, he deadened his male organs with medicines [φαρμακωτικοῖς], so that because of the frigidity he had brought on, they could not emit semen. He began to allegorize not at once, but after he had already applied to his work his Hexapla and the comparison of the various versions of the Bibles. He undertook this work with the favour of a certain Ambrose, a count of the palace, as Socrates teaches in book 3, chapter 7. Ambrose, as Epiphanius says (and more truly, as Eusebius wishes, book 6, chapter 16), he led from the error of the Sabellians, or of the Valentinians, to the orthodox. He wrote on various subjects: Epiphanius reports that not only his theological works but also certain physical works existed. He was so esteemed even by pagans that Mammaea, mother of the Roman emperor Alexander, summoned him, received him kindly, and under her he instructed Alexander himself in the Christian faith. Hence it is written that Alexander afterwards kept Christ in his household shrine. By his disputations Origen cut short and extinguished many errors which had arisen in his own age, especially in Arabia. At last he died in the seventieth year of his life, under the emperor Gallus, though he had been born under Commodus. He was regarded as the light of his age and an outstanding teacher of the Christian Church; yet he was the founder and parent of this most grievous heresy, so that no one should trust in the strength of his own wit.

units.la: 2 Mortuorum resurrectionem. Hæc fere potiora & notiora Origenistarum hæreseos capita fuerunt, partim ab ipsis conficta, partim ex ethnicorum scriptis deprompta, & sacro Dei verbo admixta, quemadmodum Constantinopolitana Synodus apertissimè pronuntiauit. Euagr.lib.4.cap.38. Nec Christum, nec Spiritum sanctum Patrem videre posse. Quæ enim differentia est hominum ad Angelos, quos illi non vident, eandem esse statuit Filij & Spiritus sancti ad Patrem, quem videre non possunt. Vnde pessimus Arianorum & Anomiorum error postea fluxit, vt rectè obseruat Epiphanius.
units.tr: 2 The resurrection of the dead. These were pretty much the principal and best-known heads of the Origenist heresy, partly invented by the Origenists themselves, partly drawn from the writings of the heathen and mixed into the sacred word of God, as the Synod of Constantinople most plainly declared. Evagrius, book 4, chapter 38. That neither Christ nor the Holy Spirit can see the Father. For he held that the relation of the Son and the Holy Spirit to the Father, whom they cannot see, is the same as the relation of men to the angels, whom men do not see. From this the most wicked error of the Arians and Anomoeans afterwards flowed, as Epiphanius rightly observes.

units.la: 2[?] Filium esse quidem eiusdem cum Patre essentiæ, ab eo tamen creatum, adeo vt ex Origenis genis sententia fit tantum gratia, non autem natura Deus. Quod ipsum Arianorum venenum postea seuit. Itaque quanquam Filium ὁμοούσιον Patri primus vocauit Origenes, quemadmodu & Athanasius docet, & Socrates lib. 3. cap. 7. i-temque Mariam θεοτόκον: tamen animas nostras unum esse cum Dei Filio, eiusdemq; substantiæ docuit, ut tradit Theodoretus Dialogo 2. qui dicitur Inconfusus. 3 Spiritum sanctum creaturam esse dixit, non de Dei Patris, & Filii substantia, ut etiam annotat Hieronym. ad Aui-tum. quem errorem sub Conrado Imperatore renouauit Abailardus quidam, ut Bernard. scri-bit epist. 190. 4 Animas hominum non tunc a Deo creari, quum in corpora nostra infundū-tur: sed iam pridem antea in cælo vixisse, ubi etiam peccauerint, & pro peccati admissi genere in terram hanc, & in corpora nostra tanquã in carcerem a Deo supplicii causa mitti & detrudi. Unde corpus nostrum σῶμα tanquam vinculum appellatur: & anima ψυχὴ tanquam refrigeratus quidam cælestis halitus, propter corporis huius nostri, quod est frigidum, contagione & contactum. Hic error ex Platonicorum deliriis emanauit, & Pelagianos postea in disputatione De anima, & de peccato originali decepit quemadmodum docet Augustinus aduersus Vincent. Victor. 5 Mundum hunc propter supplicia animarum factum esse, ut esset locus in quo culpæ in cælo ab iis admissæ, grauęs pœ-nas luerent. Isidor. 6 Carnis resurrectionem negat, etsi non aperte, tamen ex consequutione, quia & vitam æternam, & animas nostras in ea perpetuo futuras non concedit: sed ἐμψυχώσιν [?], si-ue μεταγγισμὸν [?] tantum, id est, animarum revolu-tionem, more Pythagoreorum docet & indu-cit. De quo capite incidit grauis Ruffino Aqui-leiensi episcopo cum Hieronymo presbytero Bethleemensi contentio, uti etiā de principiis re-rum ab Origene constitutis. Sed hic quoque error fuit Origenis in argumento & doctrina de Resurrectione carnis, quod corpora post resurrectionem tam subtilia & tenuia fore contendit, quām est spiritus. Itaque ex istius sententia corpora esse desinent & carnem & ossa ha-bere. Quem errorem refutat Hieronymus in epi-stol. ad Pamachium contra Ioan. Hierosolymi-tanum, & in alia eiusdem Hieronymus ad Pamachium & Oceanum. 7 Poenas reproborum hominum, sed & diabolorum ipsorum fore nega-t aeternas, sed mille annorum spatio finiendas: itaque postea cos esse saluandos, uti & Christi regnum post resurrectionem iisdem finibus concludit, & electos postea vicissim damnados putat: male explicans locum Apocalyp. 20. verf. 2. Hanc rerum & mundi vicissitudinem nō tantum a Platonicis didicerat ex Timaeo: sed etiam ab Aristotelicis, ex libr. De caelo & mundo. Papias vero Hierapolitanus primus huius grauissimi erroris author fuit, qui vitam aeternam voluptatibus corporeis definiuit, quem postea sequuti sunt Mahumetani. 8 Ἀλληγορίαις [?] pertuo in Scripturae interpretatione, adeo ut nihil firmum certumque relinquat, nec paradisum illum a Deo creatum, nec hominem, nec Euam a Deo creatos, nec aquas, nec alia quę toto Genefeos libro tradit Mofcs. Vnde aduersus huiusmodi allegoriftas, & sacrae Scripturae corruptores scripsit libr. 12. De Genesi ad literam Augustinus. Denique infinitum effet, quanta fit vbique huius authoris impuritas colligere, quae Bernardus perstrinxit tum Homilia de Dicto Origen. tum Sermo. 54. in Cantat. Cant. quem tamen tanquam oculos suos quidam diligunt: quum & de peccato Originis, & de Purgatorio pessime senserit, magnaque errorum qui post-ea sunt consecuti, femina sparserit: tanti est ad sobrietatem sapere, neque vanis animi fui commentis more [illegible, ~8 letters] indulgere, quod fecit Origenes.
units.tr: 2[?] That the Son is indeed of the same essence as the Father, yet created by him, so that according to the opinion of Origen, God is God only by grace and not by nature. This very poison the Arians afterwards spread with fury. Thus, although Origen was the first to call the Son homoousios with the Father, as Athanasius also teaches, and Socrates in book 3, chapter 7, and (he called) Mary theotokos, nevertheless he taught that our souls are one with the Son of God and of the same substance, as Theodoret relates in the second Dialogue, which is called Inconfusus. 3 He said that the Holy Spirit is a creature, not of the substance of God the Father and the Son, as Jerome also notes in his letter to Avitus, which error a certain Abailard renewed under the Emperor Conrad, as Bernard writes in letter 190. 4 That the souls of men are not created by God at the time when they are infused into our bodies, but had already lived long before in heaven, where they also sinned, and, according to the kind of sin committed, are sent and thrust down by God into this earth and into our bodies, as into a prison, for the sake of punishment. Hence our body is called soma as a chain, and the soul psyche as a certain heavenly breath grown cold, because of the contagion and contact of this our body, which is cold. This error flowed from the dotage of the Platonists, and afterwards deceived the Pelagians in the dispute concerning the soul and original sin, as Augustine teaches against Victorinus. 5 That this world was made on account of the punishments of souls, so that there might be a place in which the faults committed by them in heaven might pay heavy penalties. Isidore. 6 He denies the resurrection of the flesh, if not openly, yet by consequence, because he does not grant eternal life, nor that our souls will remain in it forever; but he teaches and introduces only enpsychosis [?] or metangismos [?], that is, a revolution of souls, after the manner of the Pythagoreans. Over this point a serious dispute arose between Rufinus, bishop of Aquileia, and Jerome, presbyter of Bethlehem, as also concerning the principles of things laid down by Origen. But this was also an error of Origen's in his argument and doctrine on the resurrection of the flesh, for he maintained that after the resurrection bodies will be as subtle and thin as spirit is. Accordingly, on his view, bodies will cease to have flesh and bones. Jerome refutes this error in his letter to Pammachius against John of Jerusalem, and in another letter of Jerome to Pammachius and Oceanus. 7 He denies that the punishments of the reprobate, and even of the devils themselves, will be eternal, but will be ended within the space of a thousand years; and so afterwards they will be saved, just as he also limits the kingdom of Christ after the resurrection by the same bounds, and thinks the elect will in turn afterwards be damned, badly explaining Revelation 20:2. He had learned this alternation of things and of the world not only from the Platonists, from the Timaeus, but also from the Aristotelians, from the book On the Heavens and the World. Papias of Hierapolis, however, was the first author of this most serious error, who defined eternal life in terms of bodily pleasures; the Muslims afterwards followed him. 8 Allegories [?] pervade his interpretation of Scripture, so that nothing firm and certain is left: he does not accept that paradise was created by God, nor man, nor Eve created by God, nor the waters, nor the other things that Moses relates throughout the whole book of Genesis. Hence Augustine wrote book 12 of On Genesis according to the Letter against allegorists of this kind and corruptors of sacred Scripture. Finally, it would be endless to gather how great the impurity of this author is everywhere, which Bernard lashed both in his homily on the saying of Origen and in sermon 54 on the Song of Songs, though some people love him as their own eyes, although he thought very badly both about the sin of origin and about Purgatory, and sowed many seeds of the errors which afterwards followed. So much it is to be sober-minded, and not to indulge in the vain inventions of one's own mind in the manner that Origen did.

units.la: 3 In libris de Ciuitate Dei.) Vide librum 20. De ciuitate, cap. 7. & 9. item libr. 21. cap. 23. item etiam eiusdem operis libr. 22. & Tertullianum in libr. De anima. & saepe Basilium in Homiliis.
units.tr: 3 In the books On the City of God. See book 20, De civitate, chapters 7 and 9; likewise book 21, chapter 23; likewise book 22 of the same work; and Tertullian in the book On the Soul, and often Basil in the homilies.

units.la: CAP. XLIIII.
units.tr: CAP. XLIIII.

units.la: Pauliani, vel Samosateniani cur sic dicti. Erroris autem eorum capita duo declarantur.
units.tr: Why the Paulians, or Samosatenians, are so called. Two heads of their error are set out.

units.la: Auliani{1} à Paulo Samosateno, Christum{2} non semper fuisse dicunt, sed eius initium, ex quo de Maria natus est, asseuerant, nec eum aliquid amplius, quàm hominem putant. Ista haeresis aliquando cuiusdam Artemonis fuit: sed quum defecisset, instaurata est à Paulo: & postea sic a Photino confirmata, vt Photiniani quàm Pauliani celebrius nuncupentur. Istos sane Paulia-nos baptizandos esse in Ecclesia catholica Niceno concilio constitutum est. Vnde credendum est, eos regulam baptismatis non tenere, quam secum multi haeretici quum de catholica discederent, abstulerunt, eámque custodiunt.
units.tr: The Paulians are so named from Paul of Samosata. They say that Christ did not always exist, but assert that his beginning was when he was born of Mary, and they think he was nothing more than a man. This heresy once belonged to a certain Artemon, but when it had died out it was revived by Paul, and afterwards it was so strengthened by Photinus that the followers are more commonly called Photinians than Paulians. It has been decreed at the Council of Nicaea that these Paulians are to be baptized in the catholic Church. Hence it must be believed that they do not keep the rule of baptism, which many heretics carried away with them when they departed from the catholic Church, and which they still preserve.

units.la: I Pauliani.) Post Nouatum, Sabellium, & Origenem extitit Paulus, qui ab vrbe patria Samosata Σαμοσατεὺς dictus est, id est, Samosatensis, quanquam alij malunt dicere Samosatenus, & ita vulgò appellatur. Fuit autem Samosata metropolis Commagenes regionis, sita prope Euphratem amnem, qua parte & latere Syriam & Mesopotamiam spectat, vt tradunt Epiphanius, & Plinius libr. 5. cap. 24. in qua vrbe est stagnum cuius limus flagrans olidis rebus adhaeret, & eas adurit, vt idem Plinius ait, libro 2. cap. 104. cui tamen nunquam fuit tam noxia labes, quàm Paulus iste ciuis & alumnus ipsius. Nam fuit teterrima religionis Christianae pestis. Ab hoc autem Paulo Samosateno dicti sunt qui errorem ipsius amplectuntur, Pauliani, Paulistae, Paulia-nistae, itemque Samosateniani & Samosatæi, ab Epiphanio Σαμοσατηνοί: postea vero Photiniani, Luciani, & Marcelliani, tot nimirum fuerunt huius erroris & scholae successores, & propugnatores. A foeditate vero & impietate dogmatis ab Epiphanio cognominantur Θεοκτόνοι[?], & ἀπαρχνιτοθεοί[?], quòd praecipuum salutis nostrae caput, & fundamentum, quòd est de diuina Christi natura, conuellere tentarunt. Vnde poftea Mahumetifmi certissima semina proflu-xerunt, & in animis hominum inhæserunt. Fuit autem hæc hæresis Artemonis vel Artemæ infelix propago, quanquam & ante hunc etiam quosdam alios idem quod Paulum Samosate-num sensisse, Christum nimirum ante incarnationem non extitisse,nec Deum esse,scribit Eu-seb.lib.3.Histor.cap.27. quem errorem iam per sexaginta annos per Artemonis mortem extinctum,ab inferis reuocauit Samosatenus, propagauit Photinus,excepit Marcellus,pene sibi continua serie succedentes,saltem ex eadem Satanæ officina profecti.Coepit autem hæc hæresis nomine Samosatenianorum innotescere sub Gallieno imperatore, & Xysto Romano Pontifice, circa annum à Christo passo 232, quæ diutissime, sed interpolato & mutato postea nomine permansit, quando Ariani ipsi fuerunt huius radicis amarissimæ tantum surculi quidam, vel riuuli male illi quidem & fœdè olentes. Latissime vero disseminata est,quando Arianismus,& Mahumetismus, qui sunt inde orti, sese postea in vniuersum terrarum orbem diffuderunt, & omnia contaminarunt. Diutissimè quoque perstitit, quando etiam nunc durat plus quam 1343.annis,postquam primùm nata est. Ex ea vero primùm occasione Samosatenus sese & alios decepit,quòd, vt scribit Theodor.libro 2.Hæretic. fabul. Zenobiam Arabiæ,Syriæ, & Phœnicię reginam potentissimam , & Iudæorum erroribus de Christo sanentem sibi concilia-re & demereri, id est, principibus & aulæ ser-uire vellet homo ambitiosus & sastuosus,sed iā
units.tr: I Paulians.) After Novatus, Sabellius and Origen came Paul, who was called Samosateus [Σαμοσατεὺς] from his native city Samosata, that is, the Samosatene, though others prefer to say Samosatenus, and this is the common name. Samosata was the metropolis of the region of Commagene, lying near the river Euphrates, on the side where it faces Syria and Mesopotamia, as Epiphanius and Pliny (book 5, chapter 24) report. In this city there is a pool whose mud clings to foul things and burns them, as the same Pliny says (book 2, chapter 104). Yet that pool never brought so harmful a blight as this Paul, a citizen and nursling of that city. For he was the most foul plague of the Christian religion. From this Paul of Samosata those who embrace his error are called Paulians, Paulists, Paulianists, and likewise Samosatenians and Samosateans, in Epiphanius Samosatenoi [Σαμοσατηνοί]. Later they were called Photinians, Lucianists and Marcellians, since this error and school had so many successors and champions. Epiphanius also names them Theoktonoi [Θεοκτόνοι], and aparchnitotheoi [ἀπαρχνιτοθεοί], because of the foulness and impiety of their doctrine, since they tried to overthrow the chief head and foundation of our salvation, namely the doctrine of the divine nature of Christ. Hence afterwards the most certain seeds of Mahumetism sprouted forth and took root in men's minds. This heresy was an unhappy offshoot of Artemon or Artemas, although, as Eusebius writes (book 3 of the History, chapter 27), some others before him also held what Paul of Samosata held, namely that Christ did not exist before the incarnation and was not God. This error had been extinguished for about sixty years by the death of Artemon, but Samosatenus called it back from the dead, Photinus spread it, and Marcellus took it up, these men succeeding one another in an almost unbroken line, all coming at least from the same workshop of Satan. This heresy began to become known under the name of Samosatenians under the emperor Gallienus and the Roman bishop Xystus, about the year 232 after Christ's passion. It lasted a very long time, though afterwards under an altered and corrupted name, when the Arians themselves were only certain small shoots or streamlets of this very bitter root, bad and foul-smelling indeed. It was spread most widely when Arianism and Mahumetism, which sprang from it, afterwards poured out over the whole world and polluted everything. It has also persisted most lastingly, for it still endures more than 1343 years after it was first born. Now, Samosatenus first deceived himself and others from this beginning, because, as Theodorus writes (book 2 of the Heretical Fables), an ambitious and haughty man wished to win over and gain favour with Zenobia, the most powerful queen of Arabia, Syria and Phoenicia, who was favouring the errors of the Jews about Christ, that is, to serve the princes and the court. But although he was already bishop of the Antiochene church, he secretly said that he thought about Christ what the Jews and Zenobia, the ruler of the region, thought.

units.la: O.iij. tamen Antiochenæ ecclesiæ Episcopus, clàm idem se de Christo sentire dixit, quod Iudæi & Zenobia ipsa regionis princeps. De quo à vicinis Episcopis sæpius admonitus, quum tamen errorem suum spargeret, & saltu creparet, denique luxu & ostentatione diffluceret, adeò vt pro Dauidicis de suis laudibus compositos psalmos in Ecclesia publice cani sineret, vt ait Eusebius libr. 7. cap. 30. de sede episcopali per Synodum Antiochenam deiectus est. Cui decreto quum parere nollet, & in presbyterio siue Ecclesiæ domo adhuc maneret, interpellatus ab Episcopis imperator Aurelianus, eum expulit, & Ecclesiæ pacem restituit. Nec enim in publicæ pacis tranquillitate tuenda, Imperatoris, quanquam ethnici, auxilium implorare boni illi & Christiani viri & subditi dubitarunt, quod nobis potest prodesse ad exemplum, vt in Chronicis suis annotat D. Philippus Melanchthon.
units.tr: O.iij. Although he was often admonished about this by the neighbouring bishops, yet he went on spreading his error and, as it were, bursting with pride, and at last he dissolved in luxury and display, so much so that he allowed psalms composed in David's manner in praise of himself to be sung publicly in the Church, as Eusebius says (book 7, chapter 30). He was deposed from his episcopal see by the Synod of Antioch. When he would not obey this decree but still remained in the presbytery, or house of the Church, the emperor Aurelian, who was called upon by the bishops, expelled him and restored peace to the Church. Nor did those good Christian men and subjects hesitate to seek the help of an emperor, even though a heathen, in maintaining the tranquillity of public peace, which can be of use to us as an example, as D. Philip Melanchthon notes in his Chronicles.

units.la: Theodoret. dial. 2. Inconfuf. sic scribit, Simon, Valentinus, Marcion negauerunt humanitatem Christi. Artemon, Samosatenus, Theodorus negarunt eiusdem diuinitatem. Arius & Eunomius creatam eius diuinitatem dixerunt. Apollinaris corpus quidem Christum habuisse, & illud quidem animatum concedit, animam tamen humanam, & rationis participem illi denegat. Vnde apparet ex quo fonte scaturiit hic tam teter & foetidus riuus. Fuerunt autem huius hæresis hypotheses istæ. i Christum esse ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον, id est, merum hominem, gratia tamen diuina insigniter ornatum. Tunc autem demum esse coepisse, etsi antiqua de eo vaticinia praecesserant, quum in utero Mariae virginis conceptus est. Isidorus & Eufeb.lib.7. cap.30. Itaque μὴ Χριστὸν Θεῷ ξυνπάσαντον[?] docuit, ut loquitur Epiphanius: quanquam aperte dicat ipse Christus aliud, Ego sum, ait, in Patre, & Pater in me: & Ioannes, In principio erat Verbum, & Verbum erat apud Deum, Ioan.i.v.1,14.v.10. 2 Error, In Christo non aliter quàm in aliis Prophetis habitasse verbum Dei vel Deum: itaque nō fuisse illi σωματικῶς & ἐνθεοφορικῶς[?] vnitum, sed tantum gratia & efficacia assidentem. Hoc de Samosateno tradit Indicat. haeref. in historia Ecclesiast. quem infelicissimum errorem revocat hodie ij, qui vnionem hypostaticam in Christo definiunt esse effusionem omnium diuinae naturae proprietatum in humanam. 3 Christū dicit esse λόγον Θεοῦ, sed ἐνφορικὸν[?] & ἀνυπόστατον[?], non autem διαθητικὸν[?], ut loquuntur Theologi. Epiphanius autem, Atqui μία θεότης[?], ait, κατὰ Patris & Filij, & Spiritus, ἐν ἀξίωμα. οὐ γὰρ ἐστιν τὸ γεννητὸν, οὐδὲ ταὐτὸν, ἀλλ' ὁμοούσιος, ἡ τῶν ὀνομάτων διαφορὰ, ἡ κατὰ Υἱὸν τῇ πατρί[?].
units.tr: Theodoret, in the second dialogue, Against Confusion, writes thus: Simon, Valentinus and Marcion denied the humanity of Christ. Artemon, Samosatenus and Theodotus denied his divinity. Arius and Eunomius said that his divinity was created. Apollinaris concedes that Christ had a body, and that it was animated, but denies him a human soul that participates in reason. From this it appears from what source this so foul and stinking stream welled up. The hypotheses of this heresy were these. (1) Christ is a mere man [ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον], that is, merely a man, though notably adorned with divine grace; he is said to have begun to be only when he was conceived in the womb of the virgin Mary, even though ancient prophecies about him had gone before. Isidore and Eusebius (book 7, chapter 30) so teach, so that Christ is not co-eternal with God, as Epiphanius puts it, although Christ himself plainly says otherwise: "I am in the Father, and the Father is in me"; and John: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God" (John 1:1, 14; 10:30). (2) The error that the Word of God, or God, dwelt in Christ no otherwise than in the other prophets; so he was not united to him bodily [σωματικῶς] and in a God-bearing manner [ἐνθεοφορικῶς], but only attended him by grace and efficacy. The Indicator of heresies in the Ecclesiastical History reports this of Samosatenus, and it is this most unhappy error that those who define the hypostatic union in Christ as the outpouring of all the properties of the divine nature into the human nature revive today. (3) They say Christ is the Word of God, but inherent [ἐνφορικὸν] and without subsistence [ἀνυπόστατον], not distinct [διαθητικὸν], as the theologians speak. Epiphanius, however, says: "Yet there is one divinity of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, in one dignity; for the begotten is not the same, nor is he another, but consubstantial; the difference of names is according to the Son and the Father." The one divinity [μία θεότης] ...

units.la: 4 Baptisma corruperunt, neque substatiam formamque eius veram retinuerunt, quum non baptizarent in nomine Christi. Itaque concilio Niceno iubentur baptizari, quia prior eorum baptismus, non fuit baptismus. Quod decretū commemorat Ruff. lib. 1. Histor. cap. 6. & est Canon Synodi 21. Atque hi fuerunt amarissimi ambitionis & fastus Samosateni fructus, qui ab Ecclesia tamen multos abduxerunt.
units.tr: (4) They corrupted baptism, and did not keep its true substance and form, since they did not baptize in the name of Christ. Therefore by the Council of Nicaea they are ordered to be baptized, because their former baptism was not baptism. This decree is recorded by Rufinus (book 1 of the History, chapter 6), and it is canon 21 of the Synod. These were the very bitter fruits of the ambition and pride of Samosatenus, who nevertheless drew many away from the Church.

units.la: CAP. XLV.
units.tr: CAP. XLV.

units.la: Photiniani quem errorem sequuti sint.
units.tr: Which error the Photinians followed.

units.la: Hotinus1 ab Epiphanio non continuo post Paulum, sine cum Paulo, sed aliis interpositis ponitur: nō tacetur sane similia credidisse, secundum aliquid tamen adversatus ei dicitur: sed quid sit ipsum aliquid, omnino nō dicitur. Philaster autem continuatim ponit ambos sub singulis & proprijs numeris, quasi haereses duas, quum dicat Photinum in omnibus Pauli sequutum fuisse doctrinam.
units.tr: Hotinus (Photinus) is placed by Epiphanius not directly after Paul of Samosata, nor together with him, but with others interposed. It is indeed not passed over that he believed similar things, and he is said to have opposed him in some respect; but what that respect was is not stated at all. Philaster, however, places both in succession under separate numbers of their own, as though they were two heresies, although he says that Photinus followed Paul's teaching in all things.

units.la: 1 Photinus. ) Non tam est hoc loco temporis, quàm dogmatis observata ratio, quando inter Samosatenum & Photinum intercesserc me dij varij haeretici, ab ijs plane dissimiles: idque docet Epiphanius. Sed quia tetrum Samosateni errorem Photinus renouauit, propterea hunc illi subiecit Augustinus. Hieronym. in Galat.1. coniungit Photinianos cum Ebionitis: sed dogmatis ratio, etsi cum Ebionitis habuit aliquid commune, plura tamen cum Samosatenianis retinuit. Haec autem haeresis à Photino Photiniana, à Marcello Marcelliana, & à Lucio episcopo, Luciana quoq; dicta est. Fuit autem tempore prior Marcellus & Photini praeceptor, Ancyrae, quae fuit Galatiae metropolis, vt ait Plin. libro 5. capite 32. episcopus. Vnde Ancyranus appellatur, non Anticyranus, vt ignoranter à quibusdam appellatur. Fuit enim Anticyra Phocidis vrbs in Graecia, longisimo terrarum
units.tr: 1 Photinus.) Here the observed order is one of doctrine rather than of time. Between Samosatenus and Photinus, as Epiphanius teaches, several other heretics came in, clearly unlike them. But because Photinus revived the foul error of Samosatenus, Augustine placed him directly after Samosatenus. Jerome, in his commentary on Galatians 1, links the Photinians with the Ebionites. Yet the doctrine, though it had something in common with the Ebionites, kept more points from the Samosatenians. This heresy was called Photinian after Photinus, Marcellian after Marcellus, and also Lucianist after Bishop Lucius. Marcellus was earlier in time than Photinus and was his teacher. He was bishop of Ancyra, the metropolis of Galatia, as Pliny says in book 5, chapter 32, and so is called Ancyranus, not Anticyranus, as some ignorantly call him. Anticyra was a city of Phocis in Greece, a very long way from Galatian Ancyra.

units.la: 1 Photinus. ) Non tam est hoc loco temporis... rarum interuallo ab Ancyra Galatiana dissita. Marcellus autem vixit sub Constantino Magno, qui quum Asterio Ariano respondere vellet, more stultorum, qui dum vitat vitia, in contraria currunt, incidit in Samosatenismum. Itaque primum Hierosolymitana, deinde Constantinopolitana Synodo damnatus, iussusque librum suum comburere, non paruit: unde episcopatu abdicatus est, in quem tamen postea Sardicensi concilio, quòd se suumque scriptum nunquam intellectu suisse diceret, restitutus est, quemadmodum tradunt Socrates lib.1.cap.36. & Sozomen. lib.2. capite 33. Fuerunt autem hæ illius hypotheses erroneæ. 1 Trinitatem esse deitatis vti cerae cuiusdam liquefactae extensionem, quæ etiam pro visu & œconomia contraheretur postea in vnum. Itaque ex Patre extefo[?] Filium, ex Filio extenso Spiritum sanctum productum esse. Theodoretus. 2 Christum esse merum hominem, quem Asterius Dei tantum virtutem esse dixerat. Extant quædam Marcelli epistolæ apud Epiphanium, & fidei confessio, quæ non admodum videtur reprehendi posse. Sed more hæreticorum egit, qui venena sua clam inter suos spargebant: publice vero, ne conuicti tenerentur, non proferebant. Marcello successit Photinus ipsius discipulus, acerbior Marcello, & obstinatior. Hic ex minore Galatia ortus, vt ait Socrates libro 2.capite 18. primum Ancyranæ Ecclesiæ presbyter fuit: post autem Sirmij, non autem Smyrnæ episcopus. In quo grauissime lapsus & hallucinatus est Isidorus, qui eu[?] Gallogræciæ[?] Smyrnæ episcopu facit.Fuit
units.tr: 1 Photinus.) Here the observed order is one of doctrine rather than of time... Marcellus lived under Constantine the Great. Wishing to answer Asterius the Arian, he did what fools do: in avoiding one vice he ran into its opposite, and fell into Samosatenianism. He was therefore condemned first by the Synod of Jerusalem and then by the Synod of Constantinople, and ordered to burn his book. He did not obey, and so he was deprived of his bishopric. Yet at the Council of Sardica he was restored to it, on the ground that he said he had never understood himself or his own writing, as Socrates reports in book 1, chapter 36, and Sozomen in book 2, chapter 33. His erroneous opinions were these. (1) The Trinity is an extension of the Godhead like a stretched piece of melted wax, which contracts again into one when it comes to view and to the economy of salvation. Thus the Son was produced from the extended Father, and the Holy Spirit from the extended Son (Theodoret). (2) Christ is a mere man, whom Asterius had said was only the power of God. Some letters of Marcellus survive in Epiphanius, along with a confession of faith which does not seem very open to blame. But he acted in the manner of heretics, who scattered their poisons secretly among their own people and did not put them forward in public, lest they be convicted and held to account. Marcellus was succeeded by his own disciple Photinus, who was harsher and more obstinate than Marcellus. He came from Lesser Galatia, as Socrates says in book 2, chapter 18, and was first an elder of the Ancyran church. Afterwards he was bishop of Sirmium, not of Smyrna. Isidore badly erred and was misled here, for he makes him bishop of Smyrna in Gallo-Greece.

units.la: autem Sirmium oppidum Pannoniæ, Illyrico conterminæ, ad Saum amnem in Europa, vt ait Plinius lib.3. cap.25. Smyrna verò Ioniæ vel potius Æoliæ ciuitas ad mare sita, in minori Asia, vt idem Plinius docet libr.5. cap.29. Cœpit hæc hæresis ísto Photinianorum nomine innotescere, etiam ante Nicenam Synodum, quando in ea istorum mentio facta est, vt apparet ex Ruffini historia: sed tamen quia nondum inualuerat, collocatur prima illius origo sub Constantio imperatore, & Liberio episcopo Romano, circa annum à passo Christo 323. cuius scintillæ Sirmij primum accensæ in Asiam, & reliquas orbis regiones magna incendia postea pepererunt. Itaque latissime statim sparsus est hic error, cuius immani fœtore offensi Patres orthodoxi Sirmium conuenerunt, ibíque cum communibus sententiis damnarunt, Photino ipso audito, & à Basilio Ancyræ episcopo erroris conuicto, vt tradit Socrates libro 2. capite 29,&30. tamen ad imperatorem prouocauit, apud quem neque causam suam approbare, neque obtinere potuit. Itaque Sardicensi Synodo iterum damnatus, & ab Arianis ipsis explosus est, & vt blasphemus reiectus, quemadmodum scribit Sozomen. libro 4. capite 6. tam teter nimirum & grauis habitus est vel solus istius erroris cdor, vt ne ab hæreticis quidem ipsis sustineri posset. Certè in constitutione Iustiniani lib.1.Codicis inter capitales fidei Christianæ hostes Photiniani enumerantur. Et quum sub Theodosio maiore variis hæresibus suas synaxes habere concessum esset, vt scribit Socrates crates libro 5. cap.2. idem tamen priuilegium Photinianis, Manichæis, & Eunomianis, tanquā intolerandis blasphematoribus denegatum est. Perstitit tamen hæc tam immanis blasphemia aliquādiu: quandoquidem Lucius quidam eam retinuisse & defendisse dicitur. Unde Luciani Photinianis coniungi solent tanquam eorum successores & discipuli. Fuit autem Lucius non tam Arianus, quàm Samosatenianus, ab Arianis tamen in locum Georgij orthodoxi, quem pepulerant, Alexandriæ episcopus constitutus, ut scribit Socrates lib.3. cap.4. qui mortuo Athanasio illo sui seculi lumine, tam atrociter in Ecclesiam ipsam cui præerat sæuiit, & ita Monachos exagitauit, ut primum toti populo invisus euaserit, ut ait Ruffin. lib.2. Histor. capite 3.& 6.& ex Ruff.Socr.lib.4.c.24. Deinde quū in eadē sæuitia pergeret, lapidibus pene obrutus demum Alexandria expulsus & eiectus summo totius Ecclesiæ gaudio, ut historiæ suæ libro 4. capite 15.20.& 37. narrat Theodoretus, Samosata translatus est, vel potius ipse profectus, illic errorem suum consimilem veteribus Samosa-teni repotiis propagauit. Quæ omnia sub Valente Imperatore Ariano, & Syricio Romano Episcopo contigerunt, circa annum à Christo passo 343. quemadmodum Ruffinus tradit, ut plus quàm 200. annos infœlicissimè & liber-rimè hæc hæresis vagata fit, quando ne nunc quidem post mille annos sopita est, sed à quibusdam reuocata turbat in Ecclesia Dei multos. Suo tamen seculo prorsus extinctam fuisse scribit Theodoret, libro 2.Hæretic.fabular.sed [?] astu Satanæ nostris temporibus à Nearianis in-terpolata & excitata est,uti diximus.
units.tr: Sirmium was a town of Pannonia, bordering on Illyricum, on the river Sava in Europe, as Pliny says in book 3, chapter 25. Smyrna, however, is a city of Ionia, or rather of Aeolis, on the sea in Asia Minor, as the same Pliny teaches in book 5, chapter 29. This heresy began to become known under the name of the Photinians even before the Nicene Synod, when mention of them was made there, as appears from the history of Rufinus. But since it had not yet taken hold, its origin is placed under the emperor Constantius and the Roman bishop Liberius, about the year 323 after the passion of Christ. Its sparks, first kindled at Sirmium, afterwards spread into Asia and the other regions of the world, and produced great fires. So this error was at once spread very widely. The orthodox Fathers, offended by its monstrous stench, met at Sirmium and condemned it there together with the common opinions. Photinus himself was heard, and was convicted of error by Basil, bishop of Ancyra, as Socrates reports in book 2, chapters 29 and 30. Nevertheless he appealed to the emperor, before whom he could neither defend his cause nor prevail. He was therefore condemned again at the Synod of Sardica, and was rejected even by the Arians themselves, who cast him off as a blasphemer, as Sozomen writes in book 4, chapter 6. Certainly the stench of this error alone was so foul and grave that even the heretics could not endure it. In the constitution of Justinian in book 1 of the Code, the Photinians are listed among the chief enemies of the Christian faith. And when, under Theodosius the Great, various heresies were permitted to hold their assemblies, as Socrates writes in book 5, chapter 2, the same privilege was denied to the Photinians, Manichaeans and Eunomians, as intolerable blasphemers. Yet this monstrous blasphemy persisted for some time, since a certain Lucius is said to have kept it and defended it. Hence the Lucianists are usually joined to the Photinians as their successors and disciples. Lucius was less an Arian than a Samosatenian. Nevertheless the Arians made him bishop of Alexandria in place of the orthodox Georgius, whom they had driven out, as Socrates writes in book 3, chapter 4. After the death of Athanasius, that light of his age, Lucius raged so savagely against the church he governed, and harassed the monks so much, that he first became hateful to the whole people, as Rufinus says in book 2 of his History, chapters 3 and 6, and from Rufinus, Socrates in book 4, chapter 24. Then, as he continued in the same fury, he was almost stoned to death, and was at last driven out of Alexandria and thrown out, to the great joy of the whole church. Theodoret narrates this in book 4 of his history, chapters 15, 20 and 37. He was carried off to Samosata, or rather went there himself, and there he spread his error, very like the old Samosatene fancies. All these things happened under the Arian emperor Valens and the Roman bishop Siricius, about the year 343 after the passion of Christ, as Rufinus relates. This heresy then wandered for more than 200 years, most unhappily and most freely, and even now, after a thousand years, it has not been put to sleep. Some have revived it and it still troubles many in the church of God. Theodoret writes that in his own age it was utterly extinct, in book 2 of his Heretical Fables. But by the cunning of Satan, in our own times it has been reinserted and stirred up again by the Nearians, as we have said.
