units.la: 2 Similia credidisse.) Photinianos alij Hebionitarum, uti Isidorus: alij Sabellianorum, uti Sozomen. lib.4. cap.6. propaginem faciunt. Verius sentiunt qui Artemonicæ radicis & stirpis amaræ surculum inauspicatū esse volunt, quando paria fuerunt erroris utriusque capita. Fuerunt autem hæc. 1 Christum nudum & merum esse hominem. Socrates libro 7. capite 32. non etiam Deum. 2 Christum tunc demum [?]ἀρχὴν initium habere coepisse, cùm ex Maria conceptus est. Theodor. libro 5. Histor. cap.11. Sozomen. lib.4. cap.6. Alij vero ut hanc tam manifestam Charybdin & errorem euitarent, inciderunt in Scyllam, & alium pepererunt. Docuerunt enim duos esse Christos, unum ante sæcula & æternum: alterum in tempore qui in mundum venit. Idem Theodoret. tam varia sunt nimirum, ubi semel à recta via discessum est, erroris diverticula. Et hæc quidem de Photinianis.
units.tr: 2 Similar beliefs.) Some make the Photinians an offshoot of the Ebionites, as Isidore does; others of the Sabellians, as Sozomen does in book 4, chapter 6. Those are closer to the truth who hold that this unlucky shoot came from the root and bitter stock of Artemon, since the main points of the two errors were the same. These were: (1) that Christ is merely and only a man, not also God (Socrates, book 7, chapter 32); (2) that Christ began to have a beginning [ἀρχήν] only when he was conceived of Mary (Theodoret, book 5 of his History, chapter 11; Sozomen, book 4, chapter 6). Others, wishing to avoid this so manifest Charybdis and error, fell into Scylla and produced another. For they taught that there are two Christs: one before the ages and eternal, and the other who came into the world in time (Theodoret again). So varied, indeed, are the byways of error once one has strayed from the straight road. And this is enough about the Photinians.

units.la: CAP. XLVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XLVI.

units.la: Manichæi cur sic dicti. Erroris autem eorum quanvis infinita pene sint capita, tamen octo tantùm velut præcipua recensentur hoc loco.
units.tr: Why the Manichaeans were so called. Although their errors are almost endless in number, eight only are listed here as the principal ones.

units.la: Anichaei1 a quodam Persa extiterunt, qui vocabatur Manes: quanvis & ipsum cum eius insana doctrina coepisset nomen prædicari. Nam antehac Urbicus vocabatur.
units.tr: The Manichaeans arose from a certain Persian called Manes, although his name became known through his mad teaching only after it had begun. Before this he was called Urbicus.

units.la: Sed in Gracia discipuli eius vitantes nomen infamiæ, (quasi doctiores, & eo ipso mendaciores) geminata n, litera Mannichæum quasi manna fundentem, pro Manichæo, id est infamo, appellauerunt. Ipse duo prin- cipia inter se diuersa, atque aduersa, eademq; æterna & coæterna, hoc est, semper fuisse composuit: duasque naturas atq; substantias boni scilicet & mali, sequutus alios antiquos hæreticos opinatus est: quarum inter se pugnam & commixtionem, & boni à malo purga- tionem: & boni, quod purgari non poterat, cum malo in æternum damnationem, secundum sua dogmata asseuerás multa fabulatur, quæ cuncta intexere huic operi nimis longum est. Ex his autem suis fabulis vanis & impiis cogitur dicere, animas bonas (quas cœlesent ab animarum malarum natura scilicet contrariæ commixtione liberandas) eius, cuius est Deus, esse natura. Proinde mundum à natura boni, hoc est, à natura Dei factum confitentur quidem, sed de commixtione boni & mali, quæ facta est, quando inter se utraque natura pugnauit. Ipsam vero boni à malo purgationem ac liberationem non solum per totum mundum & de omnibus eius elementis virtutem Dei facere dicunt: verum etiam Electos suos per alimenta quæ sumunt, & eis quippe alimentis, sicuti vniuerso mundo, Dei substantiam perhibent esse commixtam, quam purgari putat in Electis suis eo genere vitæ, quo viuunt Electi Manichæorum, velut sanctius & excellentius auditoribus suis. Nam his duabus professionibus Electorum & Auditorum ecclesiam suam constare voluerunt. In cæteris autem hominibus, etiam in ipsis auditoribus suis hanc partem bonæ diuinæque substantia, quæ mixta & colligata in escis & potibus detinetur, maximeque in eis, qui generant filios. arctius & inquinatius colligari putant. Quicquid vero undique purgatur luminis per quasdam naues (quas esse lunam & solem volunt) regno Dei tanquam propriis sedibus reddi. Quas itidem naues de substantia Dei pura perhibent fabricatas, lucemque istam corpoream animantium mortalium oculis adiacentem, non solum in his nauibus (ubi eam purissimam credunt) verum etiam in aliis quibusque lucidis rebus (ubi secundum istos tenetur admixta) Dei dicunt esse naturam. Quinque enim elementa quae genuerunt principes proprios, genti tribuunt tenebrarum, eaque elementa his nominibus nuncupant, Fumum, Tenebras, Ignem, Aquam, Ventum. In fumo nata animalia bipedia, unde homines ducere originem censent. In tenebris serpentia: in igne quadrupedia: in aquis natatilia: in vento volatilia. His quinque elementis malis debellandis alia quinque elementa, de regno & substantia Dei missa esse, & in illa pugna fuisse permixta fumo aera, tenebris lucem: igni malo, ignem bonum: aquam malam, aquam bonam: vento malo, ventum bonum. Naues autem illas .i. duo coeli luminaria ita distinguunt, ut lunam dicant factam ex bona aqua: solem vero ex igne bono. Esse autem in eis nauibus sanctas virtutes, quae se in masculos transfigurant, ut illiciant feminas gentis aduersas, & per hanc illecebram commota eorum concupiscentia fugiat de illis lumen, quod membris suis permixtum tenebant, & purgandum fusce-perant[?] ab Angelis lucis, purgatumque illis nauibus imponatur ad regna propria reportandum. Qua occasione vel potius execrabilis superstitionis quadam necessitate cogutur[?] Electi eorum velut Eucharistiam conspersam cum femine humano sumere, ut etiam inde, sicut de aliis cibis quos accipiunt, substantia illa divina purgetur, sed hoc se facere negant, & alios nescio quos suo nomine Manichaeorum facere affirmat. Detecti sunt tamen in Ecclesia, sicut scis, apud Car-thaginem iam te ibi Diacono constituto, quando instante Vrso tribuno, qui tunc domui regiae praefuit, aliqui adducti sunt, ubi puella illa nomine Margarita istam nefariam turpitudinem prodidit, quae cum esset annorum nondum duodecim, propter hoc scelestum mysterium se dicebat esse violatam. Tunc Eu-sebiam quandam Manichaeam quasi sanctimonialem idipsum propter hoc ipsum passam vix compulit fiteri, cum primum illa se asseruisset integram atque ab obstetrice inspici postulasset: quae inspecta, & quid esset inventa, totum illud turpissimum scelus ubi ad excipiendum & commiscendum concumbentium semen farina subsernitur, quod Margarita indicant[?] absens non audierat, similiter indicavit: & recenti tempore nonnulli eorum reperti & ad Ecclesiam-ducti, sicut gesta episcopalia quae nobis misisti, ostendunt: hoc non sacramentum, sed execramentum sub diligenti interrogatione confessi sunt, quorum unus nomine Viator eos qui ista faciunt proprie Cathari-stas, id est, mundatores vel purgatores vocari dicens, cum alias eiusdem Manichaeae sectae partes in Ma-carios, & specialiter Manichaeos distribui perhi-beret, omnes tamen has tres formas ab uno autore propagatas, & omnes generaliter Manichaeos esse negare non potuit. Certe illi libri Manichaei sunt o-mnibus sine dubitatione communes, in quibus libris illa portenta ad illiciendos, & per concupiscentiam dissoluendos utriusque sexus principes tenebrarum, ut liberata fugiat ab eis, quae captiuata tenebatur in eis diuina substantia, de masculorum in feminas, & feminarum in masculos transfiguratione conscripta sunt. Unde ista eorum, quamlibet negent ad se pertinere, turpitudo defluxit. Diuinas enim virtutes quas tum possunt imitari se putant, ut purgent Dei sui partem: quam profecto sicut in omnibus corporibus coelestibus & terrestribus, atque in omnium rerum seminibus, ita & in hominis femine teneri existimat inquinatam. Ac per hoc sequitur eos, ut sic ea & de femine humano, quemadmodum de aliis feminibus, quae in alimentis sumunt, debeant manducando purgare. Unde etiam Catharistae appellantur, quasi purgatores, tanta eam purgantes diligentia, ut se nec ab hac tam horrenda cibi turpitudine abstineant, nec vescantur tamen carnibus tanquam de mortuis vel occisis fugerit diuina substantia, tantumque ac tale inde remanserit, quod iam dignum non sit in electorum ventre purgari, nec ova saltem sumunt, quasi & ipsa cum franguntur, expirent, nec oporteat ullis mortuis corporibus vesci, & hoc solum viuat ex carne, quod in farina, ne moriatur, excipitur.
units.tr: In Greece, however, his disciples, wishing to avoid the name of infamy (as if they were more learned and therefore more deceitful), wrote the letter n twice and called them Mannichaeans, as if "manna-pouring," in place of Manichaeans, that is, the infamous. He himself taught that there are two principles, mutually different and opposed, and also eternal and coeternal, that is, that they have always existed. Following other ancient heretics, he held that there are two natures and substances, namely of good and of evil. He invents many fables, asserting according to his dogmas the conflict between these two, their mixing, and the purging of the good from the evil, and the good that could not be purged being condemned to eternity together with the evil. It would be too long to weave all of these into this work. From these vain and impious fables he is forced to say that the good souls (which, they hold, must be freed from the mixture with the contrary nature of evil souls) are of the nature of him whose God is. Accordingly they confess that the world was made from the nature of the good, that is, from the nature of God, but out of a mixture of good and evil, which came about when the two natures fought against each other. They say that the purging and liberation of the good from the evil is effected not only throughout the whole world and from all its elements by the power of God, but also in their Elect through the foods they take. They maintain that the substance of God is mixed in those foods just as in the whole world, and that it is purged in their Elect by the way of life the Elect of the Manichaeans lead, as being holier and more excellent than their hearers. For they wished their Church to consist of these two classes, the Elect and the Hearers. In other men, even in their own hearers, they think this part of the divine substance, which is held mixed and bound up in food and drink, is bound more tightly and defiled, and especially in those who beget children. Whatever light is purged from all sides they hold to be returned to the kingdom of God as to its proper seat, by certain ships (which they say are the moon and the sun). These ships, they also say, were fashioned from the pure substance of God. They affirm that this bodily light which is present to the eyes of mortal creatures is of the nature of God, not only in these ships (where they believe it is most pure) but also in all other luminous things (where, according to them, it is held mixed). For they assign the five elements, which their principles produced, to the race of darkness, and they name them by these names: Smoke, Darkness, Fire, Water, Wind. In smoke, they think, were born two-footed animals, from which they believe men derive their origin; in darkness, serpents; in fire, quadrupeds; in waters, swimming creatures; in wind, flying creatures. To subdue these five evil elements, they say, five other elements were sent from the kingdom and substance of God, and in that struggle air was mixed with smoke, light with darkness, good fire with evil fire, good water with evil water, good wind with evil wind. They distinguish those ships, that is, the two luminaries of heaven, so that they say the moon was made from good water and the sun from good fire. In these ships, they say, are holy powers which transform themselves into males in order to entice the hostile females of that race, and, by this allurement, when their lust has been stirred, the light that was mixed with their members and held captive, and that had been taken up to be purged by the Angels of Light, escapes from them and is placed in those ships to be carried back to its proper kingdom. On this occasion, or rather by a certain necessity of this execrable superstition, their Elect are compelled to take what they call the Eucharist, mixed with human semen, so that the divine substance may be purged in it, as in the other foods they receive. They deny that they do this, and affirm that some others, I know not who, do it in the name of the Manichaeans. Yet they were detected in the Church, as you know, at Carthage, when you were already appointed deacon there. When Ursus, the tribune who then presided over the royal household, pressed the matter, some were brought in, and a girl named Margarita revealed that foul wickedness. Although she was not yet twelve years old, she said she had been violated by this wicked rite. Then they hardly compelled a certain Manichaean woman, Eusebia, who passed for a holy woman, to confess that she had suffered the same thing, once she had declared herself intact and asked to be examined by a midwife. When she was examined and found to be what she was, she likewise disclosed that whole most shameful crime, in which flour is sprinkled to receive and mix the semen of those who lie together. Margarita had indicated this, though she was absent and had not heard it. Recently, too, some of them were found and brought to the Church, as the episcopal records you sent us show, and under careful questioning they confessed this to be not a sacrament but an abomination. One of them, named Viator, said that those who do these things are properly called Cathari, that is, cleansers or purgers. He also said that other parts of the same Manichaean sect are divided into Macarii and, especially, Manichaeans; yet he could not deny that all three forms were propagated from one author and that all are generally Manichaeans. Certainly the books of the Manichaeans are common to all without doubt, and in those books those monstrous things are written: how the princes of darkness of either sex transform themselves, males into females and females into males, in order to entice and, through lust, to dissolve, so that the divine substance held captive among them may escape and be freed. From these books their foulness flowed, although they deny it belongs to them. For they think they must imitate the divine powers, so that they may purge the part of their God, which they believe is held polluted in all heavenly and earthly bodies, and in the seeds of all things, and likewise in human semen. It follows that they must purge it by eating, as they do with other seeds that they take in food. Hence they are also called Cathari, as if purgers, purging it with such diligence that they do not abstain from this so horrible filthiness of food. Nor do they eat flesh, as if the divine substance had fled from dead or slaughtered bodies, and as if so much and such a portion had remained in them that it is no longer fit to be purged in the bellies of the Elect. They do not even take eggs, as if these too, when broken, expire, nor do they think it right to eat any dead bodies. The only thing they live on from flesh is what is taken up in the flour, lest it die.

units.la: Sed nec alimonia lactis utuntur, quanuis de corpore animantis viuentis mulgeatur siue fugatur: non quia putant diuina substantia nihil ibi esse permixtum, sed quia ipsi sibi error non constat. Nam & vinum non bibunt, dicentes fil esse principum tenebrarum cum vescantur uvis. Nec musti aliquid vel recentissimi sorbent.
units.tr: Nor do they use the nourishment of milk, although it is drawn or milked from the body of a living animal, not because they think the divine substance is not mixed in it, but because their own error is inconsistent. For they do not drink wine either, saying that it is the gall of the princes of darkness, even though they eat grapes. Nor do they sip any new wine or must.

units.la: Animas auditorum suorum in electos revolui arbitrantur, aut feliciore compendio in eas electorum suorum, ut iam inde purgatae in nulla corpora revertantur. Ceteras autem animas & in pecora redire putant, & in omnia quae radicibus fixa sunt, atque aluntur in terra. Herbas enim atque arbores sic pu-tant tant vivere, ut vitam, qua illis inest, & sentire cre-dant, & dolere, cum laduntur, nec aliquid inde sine cruciatu eorum quenquam posse vellere, aut carpere. Propter quod agrum spinis purgare nefas habent. Unde agriculturam, qua omnium artium est innocentissima, tanquam plurium homicidorum rea dementes accusant: suisque auditoribus ideo hac arbitrantur ignosci, quia praebent inde alimenta electis suis, ut divina illa substantia in eorum ventre purgata impetret eis veniam, quorum traditur oblatione purganda. Itaque ipsi Electi nec in agris operantes, nec poma carpentes, nec saltem folia ulla vellentes, expectant hæc[?] afferri usibus suis ab auditoribus suis, viventes de tot ac tantis secundum suam vanitatem homicidiis alienis: monent etiam eosdem auditores suos, ut si vescuntur carnibus, animalia nō occidant, ne offendant principes tenebrarum in cœlestibus colligatos, à quibus omnem carnem dicunt originem ducere. Et si utuntur coniugibus, conceptum tamen generationémque devitant, ne divina substantia, qua in eos per alimenta ingreditur, vinculis carneis ligatur in prole. Sic quippe in omnem carnem, id est, per esas & potus, venire animas credunt. Unde nuptias sine dubitatione condemnant, & , quantum in ipsis est, prohibent: quando generare prohibent, propter quod coniugia copulanda sunt. Adam & Euam ex parentibus principibus sumi afferunt natos, cum pater eorum nomine Saclas sociorum suorum fœtus omnium devorasset, & quicquid inde commixtum divina substantia ceperat, cum vxore concumbens in carne prolis, tanquam tenacissimo vinculo, colligasset. Christum autem fuisse affirmant (quem dicit nostra Scriptura) Serpentem, a quo illuminatos eos asserunt, ut cognitionis oculos aperirent, & bonum malumque dignoscerent, eumque Christum novissimis temporibus venisse ad animas, non ad corpora, libe-randas: nec fuisse in carne vera, sed simulatam speciem carnis ludificandis humanis sensibus praebuisse, ubi non solum mortem, verum etiam resurrectionem similiter mentiretur. Deum qui Legem per Moysen de-dit, & in Hebraïs Prophetis loquutus est, non esse verum Deum: sed unum ex principibus tenebrarum: Ipsiusque novi Testamenti scripturas, tanquam in-falsatas, ita legunt, ut quod voluerint inde accipiant, quod nolint, reiciant, eisque tanquam non totum, verum habentibus, nonnullas apocryphas anteponat. Promissionem Domini Jesu Christi, de paracleto Spiritu sancto, in suo haeresiarcha Manichæo dicunt esse completam: unde se in suis literis Jesu Christi A-postolum dicit, eo quod Jesus Christus se missurum esse promiserit, atque in illo miserit Spiritum sanctu. Propterquod etiam ipse Manichæus duodecim discipulos habuit ad instar Apostolici numeri, quem numerum Manichæi hodieque custodiunt. Nam ex Electis suis homines duodecim, quos appellant magi-stros, & tertium decimum principem ipsorum: Episcopos autem septuaginta duos, qui ordinantur a magistris: & presbyteros, qui ordinantur ab Episcopis: habent etiam Episcopi Diaconos. Iam cateri tantummodo Electi vocantur, sed mittuntur etiam ipsi, qui videntur idonei ad hunc errorem, vel ubi est, su-stentandum & augendum, vel, ubi non est, etiam se-minandum. Baptismum in aqua nihil cuiquam per-hibent salutis afferre, nec quenquam eorum, quos decipiunt, baptizandum putant. Orationes faciunt ad solem per diem, quaquaversum circumit: ad lu-nam nám per noctem, si apparet: si autem non apparet, ad Aquilonarem partem, qua Sol, cum occiderit ad Orientem reuertitur: stant orantes. Peccatorum originem non libero arbitrio voluntatis, sed substantiae tribuunt gentis aduersae, quam dogmatizantes esse hominibus mixtam omnem carnem non Dei, sed malae mentis perhibent esse opificium, quam a contrario principio Deo coæternam esse aiunt. Carnalem concupiscentiam, qua caro concupiscit aduersus spiritum, non ex vitiata in primo homine natura nobis inesse infirmitatem, sed substantiam volunt esse contrariam, sic nobis adhærentem, vt quando liberamur atque purgamur, separetur a nobis, & in sua natura etiam ipsa immortaliter viuat: eosque duas animas vel duas mentes, vnam bonam, alteram malam, in vno homine inter se habere conflictum, quando caro concupiscit aduersus spiritum, & spiritus aduersus carnem. Nec in nobis sanatum hoc vitium, sicut nos dicimus, vnquam futurum: sed a nobis seiunctam atque seclusam substantiam istam malam, & finito isto seculo post conflagrationem mundi, in globo quodam, tanquam in carcere sempiterno esse victurum, cui globo affirmant accessurum semper, & adhaesurum, quasi coopertorium atque tectorium ex animabus, naturae quidem bonis, sed tamen quæ non potuerunt a natura mala contagione purgari.
units.tr: They think that the souls of their hearers pass into their Elect, or, by a more favourable shortcut, into the souls of their own Elect, so that once purified there they return to no bodies. The other souls, they hold, pass into cattle and into everything that is fixed by its roots and nourished in the earth. For they think that herbs and trees live in the same way, and they believe that the life within them is felt, and that they suffer pain when they are hurt, and that no one can pluck or pick anything from them without their torment. For this reason they hold it wicked to clear a field of thorns. Hence they accuse agriculture, the most harmless of all the arts, as if it were guilty of many murders, and madly so. They think their hearers are pardoned for this only because they supply food from it to their Elect, so that the divine substance, once purified in the belly of the Elect, may obtain pardon for those whose offering is said to be the means of its purification. Thus the Elect themselves, neither working in the fields nor picking fruit, nor even pulling up any leaves, wait for these things to be brought to them for their use by their hearers. They live, by their own vanity, on the many great murders committed by others. They also warn the same hearers that, if they eat meat, they must not kill the animals, lest they offend the princes of darkness bound in the heavens, from whom they say all flesh takes its origin. And if they use wives, they nevertheless avoid conception and childbirth, lest the divine substance, which enters them through food, be bound by carnal chains in offspring. For they believe that souls come into every flesh in this way, that is, through food and drink. Hence they condemn marriage without hesitation and, as far as in them lies, forbid it; when they forbid begetting children, they forbid the very thing for which marriages are contracted. They assert that Adam and Eve were born from the princes, the parents, since their father, named Saclas, had devoured the offspring of all his fellows, and whatever divine substance had been mixed in and taken from them, he had bound fast, as with the tightest chain, in the flesh of his offspring when he lay with his wife. They affirm that Christ (whom our Scripture speaks of) was the Serpent, by whom they say those people were enlightened, so that they might open the eyes of knowledge and distinguish good from evil. They say that this Christ came in the last times to free souls, not bodies; that he had no true flesh, but only offered a feigned appearance of flesh to deceive human senses; and that in the same way he falsely presented not only death but also resurrection. They say that God, who gave the Law through Moses and spoke through the Hebrew prophets, is not the true God but one of the princes of darkness. As for the Scriptures of the New Testament itself, they read them as if they were falsified, taking from them whatever they wish and rejecting whatever they do not like; and they prefer certain apocryphal books, as if the others were not whole or true. They say that the promise of the Lord Jesus Christ concerning the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, was fulfilled in their founder Manichaeus. Hence he calls himself an apostle of Jesus Christ in his writings, because Jesus Christ promised that he would send the Holy Spirit and, in him, sent the Spirit. For this reason Manichaeus himself also had twelve disciples, after the pattern of the apostolic number, and the Manichaeans keep this number to this day. For from among their Elect there are twelve men, whom they call teachers, and a thirteenth, their chief; and seventy-two bishops, who are ordained by the teachers; and presbyters, who are ordained by the bishops. The bishops also have deacons. The rest are called only Elect; but those who seem fit for this error are sent out, either to sustain and increase it where it exists, or to sow it where it does not. They hold that baptism in water brings no salvation to anyone, and they think none of those whom they deceive should be baptized. They make prayers to the sun by day, as it travels round in every direction, and to the moon by night, if it is visible; if it is not visible, they pray towards the northern quarter, whence the sun, after it has set, returns to the east. They pray standing. They attribute the origin of sins not to the free choice of the will but to the substance of the hostile nation, which, as they teach, is mixed into men; and they say that all flesh is the work not of God but of an evil mind, which they declare to be co-eternal with God from an opposite principle. Carnal concupiscence, by which the flesh lusts against the spirit, they say does not arise in us from the infirmity of nature corrupted in the first man; they claim it is a contrary substance, clinging to us in such a way that when we are freed and cleansed it is separated from us and lives on immortally in its own nature. They say that in one man there are two souls or two minds, one good and the other evil, which have conflict between them, when the flesh lusts against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh. They say this evil will never be healed in us, as we say it will, but that this evil substance, separated and shut off from us, will live on after this age, after the conflagration of the world, in a certain globe, as in an everlasting prison; and they affirm that this globe will always be growing and adhering to itself, like a covering and roof made of souls, which are indeed good by nature but could not be cleansed of the contagion of the evil nature.

units.la: Si qua fæx, si quæ farrago, si quis teter vnquam errorum odor exhalauit, is est, qui ab impurissimo Manetis ore efflatus Manichæorum blasphemias euomit & continet. Qui quanquam error est ipse per se pessimus & obscurissimus, peior tamen & difficilior alterius erroris accumulatione factus est, dum scriptores inter se de eo dissentiunt, vel posteriores non satis attente attendunt ad ea quae fuerant a prioribus & minus ab aetate Ma-netis remotis autoribus tradita. Nos igitur rem totam quam possumus & breuissime & verissi-me perscribemus. Quod eo diligentius & accu-ratius mihi faciundum videtur, quod haec Ma-nichaeorum haeresis maximus & praecipuus Ma-humetismi qui postea secutus est, & fons & origo merito censeri debet, siue dogmatum vesaniam, siue modum nascedi & rationem spectes. Ac quidem quod ad dogmata spectat, postea docebuntur: quod autem ad nascendi modum, in eo Mahumetismus & Manichaeismus conueniunt, quod uterque primum abs Saracenis & Arabibus profectus est. Nam de Mahumete dubitari non potest, quem Arabem & Sarace-num fuisse fatentur omnes. Manichaeismum autem, id est, eum errorem, quem Manes Persa postea fortissime defendit, primus inuexit Scy-thianus quidam nomine, mercator Saracenus, quemadmodum Epiphanius & Socrat. lib.1. cap. 22. scribunt, qui ut suam blasphemiam aliqua ratione commendaret, Hierosolymam venit, tan-quam ibi ex Dei ipsius ore ea accepisset. Quod ipsum postea, ut suum Alcoranum melius hominibus propinaret, fecit Mahumetus. Scythia-nus autem domus suae ruina oppressus miserè periit. Discipulum autem & successiorem doc-trinae suae habuit quendam nomine Buddam, cognomine Terebinthum, qui & ipse a Satana in solitudinem abreptus stragulatus est. Buddae successit Manes, qui, quòd hunc occultum adhuc errorem in lucem produxit, & libros quatuor à Scythiano scriptos, sed à Budda clàm habitos & custoditos tanquam suos euulgauit, primus huius hæresios parens & author credi- turus est, quam tamen tanquam per manus ab homine Saraceno Manes iste mastigia insanus & præstigiator acceperat. A quo qui secuti sunt hæretici, Manichæi dicti sunt. Hi autem ipsi etiam Acouanitæ sunt appellati, & Agonistæ. Acouanitæ, ut Epiphanius scribit, à quodam Acouana Manetis discipulo, qui in Mesopotamia hunc errorem latissimè diffudit, & acerrimè propugnauit. Agonistæ autem, quòd se contra gentem Tenebrarum, & illius principem Diabolum perpetuò pugnare sua vita suisque præceptis & doctrina dicerent. Cœpit autem hæc hæresis Manichæorum nomine innotescere sub Aureliano Imperatore, & Felice Romano Epi- scopo, ut Euseb. tradit, circa annum à Christo passo 247. Id quod etiam docet Platina, & Epiphan. quanquam sub Probo vixisse Manetem, idem scribit August. lib.13. contra Faust.cap.4. Latissimè vero citissimèq; propagata est. Nam ex Arabia statim in Mesopotamiam & Persidem delata est. Ex Perside in Syriam rediit, & in Ægyptum, Africa, & postea in Hispaniā, Galliam, mari traiecto, penetrauit. In Asia etiam, Paphla- gonia & reliquis orbis partibus multos infecit. Habuit enim Manes tres præcipuos discipulos, Aldam, quem ad hoc venenum spargendum in Syriā dimisit, vt ait Theodor. lib.1. Hæret. fabul. Thomam, quem ad Indos tanquam apostolum suum ire præcepit: & Herman, quem ad Ægy-ptios; quanquâ præter hos alios duodecim præ-cipuos, sibique perpetuò comites ad imitatio-nem D. N. Iesu Christi, habuit tanquam apo-stolos. quem numerum in Electis suis eligendis etiamnum postea Manichæi retinuerunt, qui essent duodecim summi doctrinæ suæ antisti-tes, & ad quos LXXII. Episcopi, quos per totum orbem dispersos habebant, se suaque dubia re-ferebant. Itaque Romam ipsam occupauit hæc hæresis, unde tamen expulsa est à Leone Pontifice Romano circa annum à Christo pas-so 414. In Arabia tamen, Persidæ & Ægypto maximè viguit potuitque, unde postea Mahu-metismus tanquam ex serpentis viperæque ouo enatus & exclusus. Diutissimè etiam subsistit. Nam & Anastasij Imperatoris temporibus ad-huc in Persidę, Mesopotamia, & Syria grassaba-tur apertè: & Gregorij Magni pontificatu in Si-cilia, id est, annos post Manetem mortuum plus quàm 340. ut apparet ex Gregorij epist. 6. lib. 4. & P. Diaconi lib. 15. Historiar. ubi Indaginam [?] eorum episcopum commemorat. Fuit autem Docetarum hæreticorum postremus Manes, quemadmodum eorum primus author & prin-ceps Simon Magus, ut ait Theodoret. Dialog. 1. Polymorphos. In varias etiam sectas diuisam fuisse hanc infœlicem familiam docet hoc loco Augustinus, cum inter eos alij se tantum & sim-pliciter Manichæos appellarent: alij autem Ca-thariftas: tertij denique Macarij à fortis felici-tate dicerentur. Cæterum Manes (quem fere Manichæum alibi vocat Augustinus, ut Suidas etiam) de quo nunc agimus, fuit natione Persa, conditione primum seruus, qui manumissus dominam cui prius seruiebat, in coniugem accepit, à qua ditatus in hanc phrenesin magna ambitione excaecatus extumuit. Id quod idem Mahumeto accidit. Manes autem Persica vox est, non autem Graeca vel Latina, ut falso argutantur qui à Graeca & Hebraea voce deducunt, Μανιχαῖον vel Μανιχαῖος, quasi qui Manna vel insaniam fundat, ut hic tradit Augustin. & lib.19. contra Faust.cap.22. Epiphanius tamen à Chaldaica deriuatam putat, quae significat vas. Chaldaei enim siue Babylonij מנה[?] Manah vocant κάνως[?]. Dictus autem est hic idem Cubricus, ut Socrates & Epiphan. testantur, & est barbara vox, non autem Urbicus, ut hic Augustinus scribit, & post eum pari errore alij, quae est Latina nomenclatura: non etiam Scythianus, ut Theodoret. falso voluit. Hic vero postquam multos in fide labefactassset (quanquam eum unquam Christianam religionem didicisse negat Augustin. in lib. de Actis contra Felicia. cap.8.) adeoque suis incantationibus regis Persarum filium necasset, viuus ab eo excoriatus est, ficq;. insignis illa humani generis pestis tandem periit. De Manichaeorum autem moribus siquis plura didicisse volet, legat Augustinum, qui & ipse aliquādo Manichaeus fuit, sed postea ab eo errore magno Dei beneficio liberatus est, lib.2. de Manichaei morib. cap.16. & lib.De fide contra Manich. cap.40. & 41. Scripsit etiam quaedam Manes ipse, quando lib.2. Thesauri citat Augustin. in lib. De fide Trinitat. cap.5. nec is unus fuit ex illis quatuor Scythiani libris. Nam septimum eiusdem operis notat August.cap.14.
units.tr: If there was ever any dregs, any hodgepodge, any foul stench of errors, it is the one that breathed out from the most filthy mouth of Manes and pours forth and contains the blasphemies of the Manichaeans. Although this error is in itself the most wicked and obscure, it has become worse and harder to grasp through the piling up of another error, since writers disagree among themselves about it, or later writers do not pay close enough attention to what was handed down by earlier authors who lived nearer to the age of Manes. I will therefore set out the whole matter as fully and briefly as I can. This seems to me to need doing with more care and precision, because this Manichaean heresy must rightly be regarded as the greatest and chief source and origin of the Mahometism that followed later, whether you look at the madness of its doctrines or at its manner of arising and its method. As for the doctrines, they will be taught later. As for the manner of arising, Mahometism and Manichaeism agree in this, that each first came forth from the Saracens and Arabs. For there can be no doubt about Mahomet, whom all admit was an Arab and Saracen. Manichaeism, that is, the error which Manes the Persian later defended most vigorously, was first introduced by a certain Scythian by name, a Saracen merchant, as Epiphanius and Socrates write (Socr. bk. 1, ch. 22). In order to recommend his blasphemy by some pretext, he came to Jerusalem, as if he had received these things there from the very mouth of God. Mahomet later did the same thing, so that he might serve his Alcoran more pleasingly to men. The Scythian, however, was crushed by the collapse of his own house and perished wretchedly. He had as disciple and successor in his teaching a certain man named Buddas, surnamed Terebinthus, who was himself carried off into the wilderness by Satan and was torn to pieces. Buddas was succeeded by Manes, who, because he brought this still hidden error into the light, and published as his own the four books written by the Scythian but kept and guarded in secret by Buddas, is to be believed the first parent and author of this heresy. Yet this Manes, a mad and deceitful juggler, had received it, as it were by hand, from the Saracen man. Those heretics who followed him were called Manichaeans. They were also called Acouanites and Agonists. They were called Acouanites, as Epiphanius writes, from a certain Acouanes, a disciple of Manes, who spread this error very widely in Mesopotamia and defended it most fiercely. They were called Agonists because they said that by their life, their precepts and their teaching they were always fighting against the kingdom of Darkness and its prince, the Devil. This Manichaean heresy began to become known under the Emperor Aurelian and the Roman bishop Felix, as Eusebius reports, about the year 247 after Christ's passion. Platina also teaches this, and Epiphanius, although Augustine writes (bk. 13 against Faustus, ch. 4) that Manes lived under Probus. It spread very widely and very quickly. For it was carried at once from Arabia into Mesopotamia and Persia. From Persia it passed into Syria, and into Egypt, Africa, and afterwards, crossing the sea, into Spain and Gaul. It also infected many in Asia, Paphlagonia and the other parts of the world. Manes had three chief disciples: Aldas, whom he sent into Syria to scatter this poison, as Theodore says (bk. 1 of the Heretical Fables); Thomas, whom he ordered to go to the Indians as his apostle; and Hermas, whom he sent to the Egyptians. Besides these, however, he had twelve other principal companions, who were always with him, as apostles, in imitation of our Lord Jesus Christ. The Manichaeans have kept this number even to the present in choosing their Elect, namely twelve chief bishops of their teaching, to whom seventy-two bishops, whom they had scattered throughout the whole world, referred themselves and their doubtful questions. This heresy indeed occupied Rome itself, but it was driven out from there by Pope Leo of Rome about the year 414 after Christ's passion. Nevertheless it flourished and held most power in Arabia, Persia and Egypt, from where Mahometism afterwards hatched and emerged, like a viper born from the egg of a serpent. It also persisted for a very long time. For even in the time of the Emperor Anastasius it was still openly raging in Persia, Mesopotamia and Syria; and in the papacy of Gregory the Great it was found in Sicily, that is, more than 340 years after Manes' death, as appears from Gregory's sixth letter, book 4, and from Paul the Deacon, book 15 of the Histories, where he mentions their bishop Indaginas. Manes was the last of the Docetic heretics, just as their first author and chief was Simon Magus, as Theodoret says (Dialogue 1, Polymorphus). That this unhappy family was also divided into various sects is taught by Augustine in this place, since among them some called themselves simply Manichaeans, others Cathari, and yet others, finally, Macarians from their supposed happy fortune. Moreover, Manes (whom Augustine elsewhere mostly calls Manichaeus, as does Suidas also), the man with whom we are now concerned, was by nation a Persian, at first a slave by condition. Having been freed, he took in marriage his former mistress whom he had served, and, enriched by her, he was blinded by great ambition and swelled up into this frenzy. The same thing happened to Mahomet. Manes is a Persian word, not Greek or Latin, as those argue falsely who derive it from the Greek and Hebrew words Μανιχαῖον or Μανιχαῖος, as if it meant one who pours out manna or madness, as Augustine says here and in book 19 against Faustus, ch. 22. Epiphanius, however, thinks it is derived from the Chaldee, which means a vessel. For the Chaldeans or Babylonians call [מנה] manah [κάνως] kanos. This same man is also called Cubricus, as Socrates and Epiphanius testify, and this is a foreign word, not Urbicus, as Augustine writes here, and after him others with the same error, which is a Latin name. Nor was he Scythianus, as Theodoret wrongly wished. Now after he had caused many to waver in the faith (although Augustine denies that he ever learned the Christian religion, in his book on the Acts against Felix, ch. 8), and by his incantations had killed the son of the King of the Persians, he was flayed alive by him, and thus that famous plague of the human race at last perished. If anyone wishes to learn more about the morals of the Manichaeans, let him read Augustine, who was himself once a Manichaean but was afterwards freed from that great error by the great benefit of God (book 2 On the Morals of the Manichaeans, ch. 16; and On Faith against the Manichaeans, chs. 40 and 41). Manes himself also wrote some things; when Augustine cites the second book of his Treasure in his book On the Faith of the Trinity, ch. 5. Nor was this one of those four books of the Scythian. For Augustine notes it as the seventh of the same work, ch. 14.

units.la: 2 Iste duo principia.) Nulla fuit unquam Acherontis cauerna, unde tot repente pestes prodierint, quàm ex infernalibus unius Manetis faucibus. Una enim hæc hæresis omnium pe-nè superiorum sordes collegit. Unde factu est ut ab aliis attribuatur Montanistis, ut à Socrat. lib.7. cap.32. ab aliis autem Sabellianis: ab aliis denique Marcionitis & Valentinianis, à quibus proculdubio profecti sunt. Theodor.Dial.3.Incofusus & Index hæref.infinitæ verò sunt erroris eorum hypothecses, quando uniuersam religionem suffulerunt, corruperunt, susque deque habuerunt. Ergo capita istius hæreseos sic breuiter colligo ex omnibus.
units.tr: 2 These two principles.) There was never any cave of Acheron from which so many plagues suddenly came forth as from the infernal jaws of Manes alone. For this one heresy has gathered together almost all the filth of the earlier ones. Hence it happens that some attribute it to the Montanists, as Socrates says (bk. 7, ch. 32), others to the Sabellians, and others finally to the Marcionites and Valentinians, from whom it undoubtedly arose. Theodoret (Dialogue 3, Incofusus) and the Index of Heresies speak of their endless hypotheses, since they have overturned, corrupted and disregarded the whole of religion. So I gather together the heads of this heresy briefly from all of them.

units.la: 1 Caput. Duo esse diuersa rerum principia æterna, sibi mutuo contraria, quorum unum bonum sit, & autor boni alterum malum, qui est mali & gentis tenebrarum princeps: illum Deum vocant, hunc autem Diabolum, & Hylen. Hoc caput est. Vetus verò fuit & perantiqua huius erroris origo, quia vetus est quæstio, vt docet Eusebi lib.5.ca.27. Unde sit malum: & ex Pythagoreorum συστοιχείων, & Marcionitarum lacunis haustus est, qui Marcionitæ ex lib.1. Platonis de legib. hūc errorem didicerunt. Animam, ait Plato, quæ hæc omnia administrat, vtrum unam, an plures constituemus? Plures ergo pro vobis respondebo: non minus vtique quàm duas esse eas posuerimus, nempe eam, quæ est benefica: & eam quæ potest efficere contraria. Clemens Stromat. libro 5.
units.tr: 1 Point. There are two diverse and eternal principles of things, mutually opposed, one of which is good and the author of good, and the other evil and the prince of evil and of the race of darkness. They call the former God and the latter the Devil, and also Hyle (matter). This is the point. The origin of this error is old and very ancient, because the question is old, as Eusebius teaches in book 5, chapter 27: whence comes evil? It was drawn from the Pythagoreans' συστοιχείων [systoicheia, pairs of opposites] and from the gaps of the Marcionites, who learned this error from the first book of Plato's Laws. "Plato says: 'Shall we posit one soul, or several, as the soul that administers all these things?' I will answer for you that there are several; at least we must posit no fewer than two, namely the one that is beneficent and the one that can produce the contrary." Clement, Stromata, book 5.

units.la: 3 Dei boni substantiam fruitatim in omnes creatucreaturas fusam esse, & inhærere. Vnde Dei membra in lapidibus, frugtibus, & aliis creaturis, etiam stercoribus & virili semine vincta & ligata detineri docent, quæ sint ab iis vinculis soluenda, & liberanda primùm per Christi aduentum, deinde per esum qui fit à Manichæorum Electis, per quorum ventres tanquam per igneos canales illæ Dei particulæ secernantur & separentur à reliqua creaturæ, cui insunt, fæce. Quod quo modo fiat, hîc copiosè explicat August. & lib.2. Contra Faust. cap.5. Vnde fit, vt carnibus, ouis, & laćte etiam abstineat. id quod ex Pythagoreorum nugis & Encratitarum furore & hæresi sumptum est. Atqui Papistæ dum in suis ieiuniis ex Gregorij decreto quod est in cano. Denique, Distinćt.4. refugiunt damnántque esum eorum omnium, quæ sementinam, vt ipsi loquuntur, trahunt originem carnis, manifestè in Manichæorum errorem incidunt. Iubent enim carne, laćte, caseo & ouis abstinere. Hoc ipsum damnat Paulus 1. Corinth. 9. vers. 7. 1. Timoth. 4. vers. 3. & Dominus ipse Genef. 9. vers. 4. 5. Actor. 10. vers. 13. Sed etiam vini vsum execrantur, quasi sit illud fel & sordes principum tenebrarum. August. libr. 16. contra Faust. cap. 31. Hoc Mahumetani de Manete sumpse-runt. 3 Gentem tenebrarum cum gente lucis pugnasse & aliquando conflixisse volunt, Deo ipso bono aggrediente tenebras. In qua collućtatione ipsius Dei partes captiuæ effectæ sint, pro quarum redemptione & liberatione Deus ipse iam laboret. Hanc autem pugnam à quodam primo homine initam fuisse, ex quo fit Christus natus. Augustin.lib.2. contra Fauft. cap.3.& Theodoret. 4 Deum Legis nō esse verum Deum. itaque vetus Testamentum re-pudiant, & nouum partim mutilant & truncat: partim vero reiiciunt, qualia illa sunt, quæ de genealogia Christi loquuntur. Idem antea Mar-cion. Idem postea Mahumetus. 5 Christum Deum esse negant, sed etiam negant vere hominem fuisse: itaque ficte & imaginarie tantum passum, crucifixum, mortuum, sed esse Patrem ipsum gentis tenebrarum, id est, Diabolum, qui tunc passus sit & crucifixus. Vide quanta sit insania furoris apud Augustin. libr. De fide Trinit. cap. 28. & 32. Denique illusione quadam oculorum videri Christū resurrexisse. Augustin. idem in libr. contra epist. funda.cap.7.8. & lib.5. contra Fauft. 6 Christum fuisse illum serpe-tem qui Euam & Adamum deceperit. Ophita-rum error est. 7 Christi corpus in stellis li-gatum & affixum esse, vti poeticus Prometheus Caucaso, imprimis autem lucido illi globo Solis infusum: Et hæc dicitur esse illius ascensio in cœlum. 8 Christum animas tantum sua mor-te redemisse, non autem corpora nostra. itaque non perfecte σωτὴρ est. 9 Resurrectionem carnis fore negant, pro qua corporum μετεμψυχώσεων [?], & animarum ἀσωμάτων [?] subστituunt, per quam humanæ animæ in alia corpora migrabunt, eorum nempe quos quisque in hac vita amauit, vel etiam occidit, vti qui muscam vel murem occiderit, in muscam vel murem mu-tabitur. Atque, vt ijdem aiunt, contrariam sortē sortietur illi, quam hic quisque nostrum habuit, Diues enim in pauperem, pauper in diuitem re-nascetur. Epiphanius. 10 Se esse Paracletum illum à Christo promissum dixit Manes. Montanisticum est. 11 De mundi creatione ineptissima quædam nugatur, nempe Adamum & Euam à quodam conditos, qui Sacla vocetur, id est, opifex. סכלו[?] Schacla enim Chaldæi & Per s[?] vocant opificem & structorem. Solem & Lunam esse naves inversas: fuit hoc Anaxagoricum delirium. Lapides esse offa principum lucis. Poeticum hoc quoque figmentum est. De lunæ quoque defectibus & incrementis, insulsa prorsus fabulantur. 12 Solem & Lunam adorant tanquam deos: itémque alia idola, ut se ethnicis commendent & insinuent, non respuunt. Augustinus contra Adimant. cap.13. Hinc etiam nati alij hæretici, quos Heliotropitas vocat Damascenus, quòd heliotropium, & alias herbas, quæ ad solem folia convertunt, cernui adorarent. 13 Atlatem fingunt qui humeris cælum sustineat, quem & Laturarium vocant, & Splendi-potentem, qui per singulos 30.annos latus de-fessum in aliud mutet, ut ille poetarum Enceladus, qui Ætnam montem gestat. Augustin. lib.15. contra Faustum cap.5. Epiphan. Hoc plane fabulosum est. 14 Iurant sæpissimè, nulloque metis scrupulo, per creaturas Manichæi, ut etiam Mahumetani. Augustin. libr.19. contra Faust. cap.22. 15 Cuique nostrum duas animas, duásque mentes separatas tribuunt, & in-esse[?] ipsa putant, quarum una cum altera pugnet, & assiduè confligat. Augustin. lib.6. contra Faust. cap.8. Theodoret. 16 Anima arboris & hominis esse eiusdem essentiae, quia vtraque Dei pars sit & substantia. Augustt. contra Adimant. cap.22. contra Faust.lib.3.cap.6. 17 Coniugia & foetus damnant, tanquam miseros & horribiles subsantiae Dei carceres, & vincula. Itaq; nec coeundum nec vxores ducendas esse, vt proles suscipiatur, sed voluptatis & libidinis tantum explendae gratia: quam vt proritaret Deus mutasse quasdam sui partes in foeminas, quas masculis obiecit: & alias in masculos, vt foeminas prouocaret, vnde nascatur coeundi appetitus. Augustt. contra Faust.lib.19.cap.26:15.cap.7. Ad Secund.cap.21. Hoc etiam dogma postea Mahumetanum factum est. 18 Peccatum esse subsantiam, & κακὸν per se viuentem & subsistentem, quia a parentibus in filios transfunditur, & quia mali principij opus est: non autem tantum qualitatem quandam affectionemque, vel μετοχῆς metis a ratione auersae, quae subsantiae superuenerit. 19 Voluntatem male agendi, quod vocant Liberum arbitrium, nobis a natura ipsa insitam, non ex rebellione nostra accersitam, vel ex inobedientia natam: quanqua homines propria voluntate peccant. 20 Eleemosynā pauperi dandam negant, ac ne Christiano quidem, & fratri supplici, quia sit sustentatio materiae, & mali dei patrocinium, & fauor. Augustt. contra Adimant.cap.17. & Theodor. 21 Baptisimum nobis prodesse conferendumque cuiquam negant. Itaque illius contemptum induxerunt. Denique infinita sunt, quae misera illa hominum colluuies in Deum debacchatur, & euomit, quae singula colligere non possumus, neque etiam opecoperæpretium duximus, quia hæc etiā ipsa nausea piissimis hominibus movebunt. Sed tot tantasque blasphemias tum ambitio, tum ignorantia veritatis produxit.
units.tr: 3 The substance of the good God is poured out in pieces into all created things and clings to them. Hence they teach that the members of God are bound and held fast in stones, fruits and other creatures, even in dung and male seed, and that these bonds must be loosed and the members freed, first by the coming of Christ, then by the eating that is done by the Manichaean Elect, through whose bellies those particles of God are separated and set apart from the rest of the creature in which they lie, as through fiery channels, leaving the dregs behind. How this happens Augustine explains at length in book 2 Against Faustus, chapter 5. Hence they abstain from meat, eggs and milk too, a practice taken from the Pythagoreans' trifles and the frenzy and heresy of the Encratites. Yet the Papists, in their fasts under Gregory's decree which is in the canon, Dist. 4, shun and condemn the eating of all those things which, as they themselves say, draw their origin from the seed of flesh, and so they manifestly fall into the error of the Manichaeans. For they order abstinence from flesh, milk, cheese and eggs. Paul condemns this very thing in 1 Corinthians 9:7, 1 Timothy 4:3, and the Lord himself in Genesis 9:4–5, Acts 10:13. But they also loathe the use of wine, as if it were the gall and dregs of the princes of darkness (Augustine, book 16 Against Faustus, chapter 31). The Mahometans took this from Manes. 3 They claim that the race of darkness fought and at some point clashed with the race of light, God himself, the good one, attacking the darkness. In this struggle the parts of God himself were taken captive, and God now labours for their redemption and liberation. They say this battle was begun by a certain first man, from whom Christ was born (Augustine, book 2 Against Faustus, chapter 3, and Theodoret). 4 The God of the Law is not the true God; therefore they reject the Old Testament and partly mutilate and truncate the New, and partly reject it, such as those passages which speak of the genealogy of Christ. Marcion held this before, and Mahomet afterwards. 5 They deny that Christ is God, and also deny that he was truly a man; therefore they say he suffered, was crucified and died only in a feigned and imaginary way, but that the Father himself of the race of darkness, that is the Devil, suffered and was crucified then. See how great is the madness of this frenzy in Augustine, On the Faith of the Trinity, chapters 28 and 32. Finally, by a certain illusion of the eyes, Christ seems to have risen (Augustine, the same, in the book Against the Fundamental Letter, chapters 7–8, and book 5 Against Faustus). 6 That Christ was that serpent which deceived Eve and Adam: this is the error of the Ophites. 7 That the body of Christ is bound and fixed in the stars, as the poetic Prometheus was to the Caucasus, and especially that it is poured into that shining globe of the sun; and this, they say, is his ascension into heaven. 8 That Christ redeemed only souls by his death, not our bodies; therefore he is not perfectly Saviour (σωτήρ). 9 They deny that there will be a resurrection of the flesh, and in its place they substitute transmigrations of bodies [metempsychoseis] and incorporeal souls [asōmatōn], through which human souls will pass into other bodies, namely those of persons whom each one loved in this life, or even killed, so that one who has killed a fly or a mouse will be changed into a fly or a mouse. And, as the same men say, each will receive the opposite lot to that which he had here: the rich man will be reborn as a poor man, and the poor man as a rich man (Epiphanius). 10 Manes said that he was that Paraclete promised by Christ. This is Montanist. 11 They babble certain most absurd things about the creation of the world, namely that Adam and Eve were made by a certain being called Sacla, that is, the craftsman. For the Chaldeans and the Persians call the craftsman and builder Schacla (סכלו). They say the sun and moon are inverted boats; this was the delirium of Anaxagoras. They say the stones are the bones of the princes of light. This too is a poetic fiction. They also talk utter nonsense about the waning and waxing of the moon. 12 They worship the sun and moon as gods, and likewise other idols, and they do not reject them, so as to commend and insinuate themselves to the heathen (Augustine, Against Adimantus, chapter 13). From this also arose other heretics, whom Damascene calls Heliotropites, because they worshipped with bowed heads the heliotrope and other herbs which turn their leaves to the sun. 13 They invent an Atlas who bears the heavens on his shoulders, whom they also call Laturarius and Splendipotens, who every thirty years shifts his tired side to the other, like the poets' Enceladus who carries Mount Etna. (Augustine, book 15 Against Faustus, chapter 5; Epiphanius.) This is plainly fabulous. 14 They swear very often, and without any scruple, by creatures, as do the Manichaeans and also the Mahometans (Augustine, book 19 Against Faustus, chapter 22). 15 They attribute to each of us two separate souls and two minds, and think they are within us, one of which fights with the other and clashes with it constantly (Augustine, book 6 Against Faustus, chapter 8; Theodoret). 16 The soul of a tree and the soul of a man are of the same essence, because each is a part and substance of God (Augustine, Against Adimantus, chapter 22; Against Faustus, book 3, chapter 6). 17 They condemn marriages and offspring as wretched and horrible prisons and chains of the substance of God. Therefore one should neither copulate nor take wives in order to beget children, but only for the sake of satisfying pleasure and lust. God, to stir this up, is said to have changed some of his parts into women, whom he set before the men, and others into men, to provoke the women, whence the appetite for intercourse arises (Augustine, Against Faustus, book 19, chapters 26 and 15, chapter 7; Ad Secundinum, chapter 21). This doctrine too was afterwards made Mahometan. 18 Sin is a substance, and an evil [κακόν] living and subsisting in itself, because it is transmitted from parents to children, and because it is the work of an evil principle; not merely a certain quality or affection, or a participation [μετοχή] in what is turned away from reason, which has come upon a substance. 19 The will to act wickedly, which they call free will, is implanted in us by nature itself and is not derived from our rebellion or born of disobedience, although men sin by their own will. 20 They deny that alms should be given to a poor man, nor even to a Christian and a brother in need, because it is the sustaining of matter, a patronage and favour of the evil god (Augustine, Against Adimantus, chapter 17; Theodoret). 21 They deny that baptism profits us or should be conferred on anyone, and so they have introduced contempt for it. In short, there are endless things which that wretched sewer of men rages and vomits against God, which we cannot collect one by one, nor have we thought it worth the trouble, since even this nausea would move the most pious men. But so many and such great blasphemies have been produced both by ambition and by ignorance of the truth.

units.la: CAP. XLVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER 47.

units.la: Hierachitæ cur sic dicti. Erroris autem eorum capita tria recensentur.
units.tr: Why they are called Hierachitae. Three heads of their error are set out.

units.la: Ierachitæ, quorum author Hieracha nuncupatur, resurrectionem carnis{*} negant: monachos tantum & monachas, & coniugia non habentes in communionem recipiunt: ad regnum cælorum non pertinere parvulos dicunt, quia non sunt illis ulla merita certaminis, quo vitia{3} superentur.
units.tr: The Hierachitae, whose author is called Hierax, deny the resurrection of the flesh. They admit into their communion only monks and nuns, and those who have no marriage. They say that little children do not belong to the kingdom of heaven, because they have no merits of struggle by which vices might be overcome.

units.la: 1 Hierachitæ.) Non est hoc loco observata temporis ratio, sive Augustinum, sive Epiphanium, à quo ille sua sumpsit, spectes. Assen-tior enim iis qui hanc hæresin, Allegoristarum qui ab Origene orti sunt, propaginem esse censent, in quorum numero est Epiphanius.Di-cuntur autem hi non tantum Hierachitæ, sed etiam Heraclitæ, quemadmodum ab Isidoro, sive is scribarum error fuit, sive quòd duo præ-cipui fuerunt huius sectæ patroni & columnæ. Hierachitæ quidem ab Hieracha, vel Hierace, ut alij malunt, qui Ægyptius fuit, patria Leon-topolites. Est autem Leontopolis celebre Ægypti oppidum, à quo nomos Leontopolites appellatur, ut scribit Plinius libr.5. cap.9,& 10: Hunc autem sub Severo imperatore quidam collocant, in quo meo quidem iudicio fallitur, quemadmodum postea etiam apparebit. & Hieracem[?] hunc cum eo confundunt, qui laudatur ab Eusebio libr.7.Hist.cap.21. neque fuit hæreticus. Heraclitæ autem ab Heracla, non illo quidem qui commemoratur ab Eusebio libro 6.hist.capite 20. qui fuit & Ægyptius, & omnis Græcorum literaturæ peritissimus: sed ab hoc, qui Monachus fuit, & hoc teterrimo errore iam infectus: quanquam hunc etiam ipsum in Græca & Ægyptiaca lingua eruditissimum floruisse testatur Epiphanius. Fluxit igitur hæc hæresis ex Origenistarum schola: & post monachismū non modo exortum, sed etiam in pretio jam[?] habitum, adeo ut huius initia post Origenem, & Paulum Eremita, a quo primum monachatus, & sub Xysto quidem primo Rom.pontifice cœpit, collocentur. Innotuit igitur sub Gallieno imperatore, & Dionysio Romano pontifice, circa annum a passo Christo 254. fuitque laudū cœlibatus, monachatus, abstinentiæ immensa-rum, id est, Encratitarum, sive Montaniftarum erroris infelix fruticatio. Inter Monachos enim primum recepta est, qui, quam vocant, co-jugij & ciborum continentiam vouerant. Man-fisse autem diutissime, etsi non ipso Hierachitarum nomine, vel ex eo apparet, quod quædam huius erroris capita etiamnum hodie inter Monachos vigent, & defenduntur. Latissime denique tanquam teter quidam odor diffusa est; quando omnes Monachorum, non tantum Ægyptiorum, gyptiorum, sed Europæorum & Afianorū cel-las hic fœtor occupauit & peruasit.
units.tr: 1 Hierachitae.) The order of time is not observed here, whether you look to Augustine or to Epiphanius, from whom Augustine took his account. For I agree with those who think this heresy is an offshoot of the Allegorists who arose from Origen, and Epiphanius is among them. These people are called not only Hierachitae but also Heraclitae, as Isidore calls them, whether this was a scribal error or because two chief patrons and pillars of this sect existed. The Hierachitae take their name from Hierax, or Hierace, as others prefer, who was an Egyptian from Leontopolis. Leontopolis is a famous town of Egypt, from which the Leontopolite nome takes its name, as Pliny writes in book 5, chapters 9 and 10. Some place this man under the emperor Severus, and in my judgment they are mistaken in this, as will appear later. They also confuse him with that Hierax who is praised by Eusebius in book 7 of the History, chapter 21, but he was not a heretic. The Heraclitae take their name from Heraclas, not that Heraclas mentioned by Eusebius in book 6 of the History, chapter 20, who was also an Egyptian and thoroughly versed in all Greek literature, but from the one who was a monk and was already infected with this foul error. Yet Epiphanius testifies that this man too flourished as a most learned scholar in the Greek and Egyptian language. This heresy therefore flowed from the school of the Origenists. After monasticism had not only arisen but had already come into esteem, its beginnings are placed after Origen and Paul the Hermit, from whom monasticism first came, and it began under Xystus the first, bishop of Rome. It became known under the emperor Gallienus and Dionysius, bishop of Rome, about the year 254 after the passion of Christ. It was an unhappy offshoot of the error of the praise of celibacy, monasticism, and immense abstinence, that is, of the Encratites or Montanists. For among the monks there was first received what they call the vow of continence from marriage and from certain foods. That it lasted a very long time, even if not under the name Hierachitae, appears from this, that some heads of this error still flourish today among the monks and are defended. Finally, it has spread widely like some foul odour, since this stench has taken hold of and pervaded the cells of all monks, not only of the Egyptians but of the Europeans and Asians.

units.la: 2 Resurrectionem carnis.) Multæ fuerunt huius erroris & sectæ hypotheses. 1 Resurrectionem carnis negant. 2 Nuptias & coniugia adeo damnant, vt coniuges negent vitæ æternæ vnquam participes esse posse. Itaque cœlibes, & viduas tantum in suæ Ecclesiæ societatem & communionem admittunt contra manifestissimum Dei verbum, 1. Timoth. 4. Hebr. 13. versu 4. sed hi nimirum sunt Tatianorum, & Manichæorum, & in summa, humanæ ἐγκρατείας & ταπεινοφροσύνης fructus. 3 Paruulos & infantes fidelium negant ad regnum cælorum pertinere, quia nihil dum lucta sua aduersus peccatum, vel bonis operibus suis merari potuerunt. Itaque Operistarum errorem iam nō tantum sparsum aut seminatum, sed etiam receptum intelligimus. 4 Spiritum sanctum dictu esse Melchisedech, de quo meminit Moses Gen. 14. Epiph. 5 Paradisum in quo constitutus est Adamus, negant fuisse locum aliquem in his terris visibilem & terrenum, sed in eo interpretando contra Scripturæ fidem, more Origenis ἀλληγορεῖν, & verum Scripturę sensum pervertunt. Papistæ addiderunt eos iam contendisse Vnctionem extremam non esse sacramentum à Deo institutum, in quo recte sentiunt, etsi à Papistis damnantur, sed perperam & insulsé. Hierachitas istos Manichæis attribuit alicubi Augustinus, non autem, vt quidam faciunt, Origeniistis. Alius etiam fuit Hieracha qui post Niceanum concilium primum vixit, qui dixit personas in Trinitate esse vti diuisionem luminis in plures lucernas, & ita separat hypostases. Contra quem Hilarius lib. 6. operis de Trinit. agit. Mouebatur autem propter dictu patrum in Niceno concilio, lumen de lumine. sed quam vim ea comparatio habeat docet Hilarius. Nō enim posita est similitudo in diuisione: sed in eo quod Filius est de Patre sine diminutione & detrimento ipsius substantiae Patris, vti lumen de lumine procedit. Theodoret. ita explicat quoque lib.de Diuin. dogmat.
units.tr: 2 The resurrection of the flesh.) There were many hypotheses of this error and sect. (1) They deny the resurrection of the flesh. (2) They so condemn marriage and wedlock that they deny that married people can ever share in eternal life. Therefore they admit into the fellowship and communion of their Church only the unmarried and widows, against the most manifest word of God, 1 Timothy 4 and Hebrews 13:4. But these men are of course the followers of Tatian and the Manichaeans, and in sum the fruit of human [ἐγκρατείας] self-restraint and [ταπεινοφροσύνης] self-abasement. (3) They deny that the little children and infants of the faithful belong to the kingdom of heaven, because they have not yet been able to earn anything by their own struggle against sin or by good works. Hence we understand that the error of the Operists is not merely scattered or sown but already received. (4) They say that the Holy Spirit is Melchizedek, of whom Moses speaks in Genesis 14. Epiphanius. (5) They deny that Paradise, in which Adam was placed, was any visible and earthly place in this world, but in interpreting it, against the faith of Scripture, they follow Origen in [ἀλληγορεῖν] allegorizing, and pervert the true sense of Scripture. The Papists have added that these men have already contended that extreme unction is not a sacrament instituted by God. In this they judge rightly, although they are condemned by the Papists, but they judge it wrongly and foolishly. Augustine somewhere attributes these Hierachitae to the Manichaeans, not, as some do, to the Origenists. There was also another Hierax, who lived after the first Council of Nicaea, who said that the persons in the Trinity are like the division of one light into several lamps, and so separated the hypostases. Hilary, in book 6 of his work On the Trinity, argues against him. He was moved by the saying of the fathers at the Council of Nicaea, "light from light." But Hilary shows what force that comparison has. For the likeness was not set in division, but in the fact that the Son proceeds from the Father, as light from light, without diminution or loss of the Father's own substance. Theodoret also explains it in this way in his book On the Divine Dogmas.

units.la: 3 In vulgatis codicibus Separantur. Nihil hoc loco ab Isidoro Augustini ab breuiatore iuuamur. Ex coniectura tamen restituimus, Superentur.
units.tr: 3 In the printed codices it reads "Separantur." Here we get no help from Isidore or from Augustine's abridger. Nevertheless we restore it by conjecture as "Superentur."

units.la: CAP. XLVIII. Melitiani cur sic appellati. Erroris autem eorum caput vnum hic explicatur.
units.tr: CHAPTER XLVIII. Why the Meletians are so called. The main point of their error is explained here.

units.la: {1}Melitiani à Melitio nuncupati, nolentes {2}orare cum conuersis, id est, eis qui in persequutione ceciderunt, vel schisma fecerunt. Nunc autem dicuntur Arianis esse coniuncti.
units.tr: The Meletians were named after Meletius, refusing to pray with the converted, that is, with those who had fallen away in persecution or made a schism. But now they are said to be joined with the Arians.

units.la: 1 Meletianos quàm Melitianos appellare maluerim. Vocant enim eos Graeci Μελιτιανούς. Dicti sunt autem à Meletio, qui vt docet Socrat. libro 1. Histor. cap. 6. fuit Ægyptius, & in Thebaide regione vnius ciuitatis episcopus. Hic persequutionis illius saeuae, quae à DiocletiaDiocletiano facta est, tempore, à Culciano Thebaidis prouinciæ præside, quemadmodum Epiphanius scribit, in carcerem propter nomen Christi coniectus, constanter non perstitit, sed idolis sacrificauit. Inde de gradu à Petro Alexandriæ episcopo, & Thebaidis totiúsque illius tractus archiepiscopo deiectus, ut se ulcis-ceretur, eò vesaniæ propter impatientiā & ambitionem tandem prouectus est, ut ne laicos quidem, qui semel à fide defecissent, & postea resipiscerent, in ecclesiam recipiendos esse contenderet, si ipse propter lapsum episcopatu priuaretur. Sed alia est episcopi, alia vnius alicuius in grege Domini priuati ratio. Id quod Marcellini Romani episcopi eo quoque tempore idolis sacrificantis exemplum apprimè docet.
units.tr: I would prefer to call them Meletians rather than Melitians. The Greeks call them Μελιτιανούς [Melitianous]. They were named after Meletius, who, as Socrates teaches in book 1 of his History, chapter 6, was an Egyptian and bishop of one city in the region of Thebaid. In the time of that savage persecution which was carried out under Diocletian, he was thrown into prison for the name of Christ by Culcianus, governor of the province of Thebaid, as Epiphanius writes, and he did not stand firm but sacrificed to idols. Thereafter he was deposed from his rank by Peter, bishop of Alexandria and archbishop of Thebaid and of the whole of that region. Wishing to avenge himself, and carried by impatience and ambition to such a degree of madness, he at last contended that not even laymen who had once fallen away from the faith, and afterwards repented, were to be received into the Church, unless he himself, the bishop, were deprived of his office for his lapse. But the case of a bishop is one thing, and the case of someone who is a private member of the Lord's flock is another. The example of Marcellinus, bishop of Rome, who at that same time sacrificed to idols, teaches this very clearly.

units.la: Et quia vanis hominum ingeniis vana commentaperplacent, sequuti sunt Meletianum errore multi, qui schisma & secessionem à Petro & orthodoxa Ecclesia fecerunt, sibíque priuatim alios episcopos, & ad cœtum suum colligendum locos elegerút. Fuit autem hoc schisma potius, quàm hæresis, quia primùm in doctrina fidei cum orthodoxis plane consentiebat Meletius, eiúsque sequaces, adeò ut is dicatur esse, qui latentem, & virus suum concoquentem Arium primus subolfecerit & deprehenderit: Arianis tamen hæreticis postea sese Meletiani adiunxerunt, adeò ut grauiter & pene soli diuinum illū Athanasium in Tyria Synodo conarentur opprimere, & qui eum præcipuè homicidij accusauit Arsenius, erat Meletianus. Hi plane simi-les sunt Nouatianis, à quibus (erant enim frequentes in Africa) profecti sunt, sed tempore posteriores. Coepit igitur hoc schisma, quod hęresis postea fuit, sub Constantino imperatore, & Syluestro Romano episcopo, circa annum à Christo passo 286. Latissime sparsum est, & à Monachis statim praetextu seuerioris cuiusdam in ἀφνήσ[?] disciplinæ & zeli in Deum maioris probatum, ut Epiphanius scribit, adeo ut omnes pene hominis Christiani regiones labefecerit, & Constantinopolin etiam ipsam plurimum, ut tradit Socrates libr.4.cap.28. Diutissime etiam durauit, quando scribit Theodoretus libr.4.hęretic. fabular. suo adhuc seculo venenum hoc in Ægypto praesertim grassatum fuisse, multosque corrupisse. Vsi sunt ad sui erroris confirmationem Hebr. cap. 6. quod falsa interpretatione penitus enerterunt.
units.tr: And because vain fancies please vain human minds, many were led astray by the error of Meletius, and they made a schism and secession from Peter and from the orthodox Church, and chose for themselves separate bishops and places in which to gather their assembly. This was a schism rather than a heresy, because at first Meletius and his followers agreed fully with the orthodox in the doctrine of faith, so much so that he is said to have been the first to smell out and detect Arius, who was lurking and digesting his poison. Yet the Meletians afterwards joined themselves to the heretical Arians, so much so that they tried severely, and almost alone, to crush that divine Athanasius at the Synod of Tyre; and Arsenius, who chiefly accused him of murder, was a Meletian. These are plainly similar to the Novatians, from whom they had arisen (for the Novatians were numerous in Africa), but they came later in time. This schism, which afterwards became a heresy, therefore began under the emperor Constantine and Silvester, bishop of Rome, about the year 286 after Christ's passion. It spread very widely, and was approved by the monks at once under the pretext of a stricter discipline and greater zeal for God, as Epiphanius writes, so that it shook almost all regions of the Christian world, and very greatly Constantinople itself, as Socrates reports in book 4, chapter 28. It also endured for a very long time, since Theodoret writes in book 4 of his Heretical Fables that in his own age this poison was still spreading, especially in Egypt, and had corrupted many. They used Hebrews chapter 6 to confirm their error, which they utterly distorted by a false interpretation.

units.la: Hæc sunt fere erroris initius capita. 1 Nolunt cū iis qui semel Christi fidem abnegantes lapsi sunt, quanquam postea pœnituerint, & sérió resipuerint, convenire & communicare, vel in Sacramentis, vel in ipsa solius verbi Dei auditione, aut precatione. At cui Dominus dat pœnitentiam, is proculdubio ad Dei Ecclesiæ pertinet, est Dei Filius, neque à piorum coetu arceri potest: præterquam quod illud etiam est tritum, Nemo desperet me lioralapsis[?]. Videntur igitur à Nouatianis hi dissensisse, quòd Nouatiani resipiscetiam in lapsis esse vnquam posse negarent: hi verò nollent, quanquam in iis ineset, eos in Ecclesiæ coetum recipi. Quod dissidium inter eos & orthodoxos tam pertinaciter durauit, ut quanquam in reliquis fidei Christianae dogmatis fere conuenirent, tamen simul precari, etiam in mediis ipsis metallorum, quibus erant addicti, poenis recusarent, quemadmodum Epiphanius scribit.
units.tr: These are almost the chief points of the beginning of their error. (1) They refuse to meet or communicate with those who, having once denied Christ's faith, have fallen, even though they afterwards repented and seriously returned to repentance, either in the sacraments, or in the mere hearing of God's Word, or in prayer. But the one to whom the Lord gives repentance certainly belongs to God's Church, is a son of God, and cannot be shut out from the company of the godly; besides which that common saying is also well known: let no one despair, for I am a better ... [?]. It seems therefore that these men differed from the Novatians in that the Novatians denied that repentance could ever be possible for the lapsed, whereas these men would not receive them into the assembly of the Church, although repentance was in them. This disagreement between them and the orthodox lasted so stubbornly that, although they agreed with the orthodox on almost the remaining articles of the Christian faith, they nevertheless refused even to pray together with them, even among the very punishments of the mines to which they were condemned, as Epiphanius writes.

units.la: 2 Sanctimoniam quandam in repetitis lotionibus constituebant, more Iudaeorum, aliisque ceremoniis, vel à se recenter inuentis, vel ad Legalium imitationem confictis. Itaque hymnos canentes saltitabant, & tintinnabula varia vni cuidam funi alligata ad Deum placandum, & deprecandum simul pulsabant. Theodoret. lib. 4. haeretic. fabul. Id quod retinuerunt Papistae, tam est nimirum infelicis lolij & veneni ferax tenaxque humanum ingenium. Ac de Meletianis hactenus, quorum etiam ad Damasc. meminit Hieronymus.
units.tr: (2) They established a certain holiness in repeated washings, after the manner of the Jews, and in other ceremonies, either newly invented by themselves or devised in imitation of the legal ones. Thus, singing hymns, they danced, and beat together various little bells fastened to a certain cord, in order to appease and at the same time to entreat God. Theodoret, book 4 of Heretical Fables. This is what the Papists have retained, so truly is the human mind fertile and tenacious of this unhappy tare and poison. And so much for the Meletians, whom Jerome also mentions in his letter to Damasus.

units.la: CAP. XLIX. Ariani cur sic dicti. Erroris autem eorum capita quatuor enumerantur.
units.tr: CHAPTER XLIX. Why the Arians are so called. Four heads of their error are enumerated.

units.la: Ariani ab Ario{1} in eo sunt, notissimi errore, quo {2}Patrem, & Filium, & Spiritum sanctum nolunt esse vnius & eiusdem naturae, atque substantiae: aut vt expressius dicatur, essentia, quae οὐσία[?] Graece appellatur: sed esse Filium creaturam: Spiritum vero sanctum creaturae creaturam, hoc est, ab ipso Filio creatum volunt. In eo autem, quod Christum sine anima solam carnem suscepisse arbitrantur, minus noti sunt. Nec aduersus eos ab aliquo inueni de hac re aliquando fuisse certatum. Sed hoc verum esse & Epiphanius non tacuit, & ego ex eorum quibusdam scriptis & colloquutionibus certissime comperi. Rebaptizari quoque ab his catholicos nouimus, vtrum non catholicos, nescio.
units.tr: The Arians, named after Arius, are most notorious for the error by which they refuse to hold that the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are of one and the same nature and substance, or, to say it more precisely, essence, which is called ousia in Greek. They maintain instead that the Son is a creature, and the Holy Spirit a creature of the Son, that is, created by the Son himself. Their view that Christ took only flesh, without a soul, is less widely known. I have never found that anyone has at any time contended against them on this point. Epiphanius did not fail to record that this is true, and I have most certainly established it from some of their writings and conversations. We also know that they rebaptize Catholics; whether they rebaptize non-Catholics, I do not know.

units.la: 1 )Hæreticorum vti philosophorum, alij minuti dici videntur posse: alij vero maiores & insani horrendarum blasphemiarum authores. Inter quos Arius certe quidem est habendus. Etsi enim Paulo Samosateno, & Manete Persa fuit ætate posterior: dogmate tamen & erroris veneno fuit vtroque longe pestilentior, periculosiorque. Itaque magnum vniuersalis illius apostasiæ, quæ postea sequuta est, & non tantum Antichristianici, sed etiam Mahumetici regni, quod nunc exædificatum est, fundamentum videtur esse Arianismus, quo nec tetrior hæresis, nec diuturnior, nec etiam plausibilior reperta vnquam a quoquam fuit. Vnde Antichristi principium ab Hilario Arius nominatur. Accessit autem ad hoc malum aliud, nempe Græcorum hominum vanitas, & Christianorum in curiosis disputationibus tuendis nugacitas, potius quam in vera pietate, aut morum emendatione diligentia, seriumque studium. Quæ duæ res Arij furorem non solum gratanter exceperunt, sed etiam in Ecclesia comedarunt, & mirabiliter auxerunt, adeo vt nulla sit hæresis, de qua sæpius in historia Ecclesiastica mentio facta sit, queque plus aut diutius Ecclesiam Dei turbauerit. Fluxit autem tanquam fœtidissimus & turbidissimus quidam riuus, ex tetra Samosatenianorum schola & fonte. Cœpit enim sub Constantino Magno imperatore, & Syluestro Romano episcopo, anno à Christo passo 290. recreata iam publica pace Ecclesia, & Satana tantam populo Christiano quieté inuidente. Nam quos armis & igni amplius op-pugnare non poterat, sectis, hæresibus & corru-ptelis aggredi, atque adeo infense vexare nisus est, quod effecit. Dicti sunt hi vniuersi quidem Ariani, & Exoucontij, quòd Christum ἐξ [?] ὄντων[?] extitisse, conditumque fuisse contenderent: etsi postea qui hanc hærefin professi sunt, Chri-stum non ex nihilo creatum docuerunt, vt scribit Augustinus libro 3.contra Maximin. cap.14. singuli verò ab eius authoris nomine, qui in ea secta aliquid innouauit, velut Eunomiani, Eudoxiani, Actiani, Eufebiani, & Pytheciani. Plu-res autem feruntur esse primi huius tam letha-lis erroris authores & progenitores. Alij enim, quemadmodum Nicephorus libr.8.cap.4. Alexandrum Beucalem Alexandrinum, huius veneni primum seminatorem: alij, vt Zonaras, Origenem potius, qui Filium Dei vnigenitum conditum fuisse scribit, constituunt. Certior tamen est de Ario fides & historia, quem primùm in Dei Filium Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum hoc virus & blasphemiam euomuisse omnes fatentur, & imprimis Ruffinus contendit lib.1.Histor.cap.1. Vnde Χειρόμαχος[?] in Sardicensi Synodo contumeliosè vocatus est. Et in Aquileiensi concilio contra Palladium Arianum solius Arij tanquam huius monstri parentis epistola lecta est & recitata. Ortæ autem huius hæ-reseos plura statim fuerunt diuortia. In ipsis e-nim pene incunabulis tres sectas hominum
