units.tr: 1) Among heretics, as among philosophers, some may be called minor, while others are greater and are authors of dreadful blasphemies, insane as they are. Arius must certainly be counted among the greater. For although he was later in time than Paul of Samosata and Mani the Persian, he was far more pestilential and dangerous than either in doctrine and in the poison of error. Hence Arianism appears to be the foundation of that universal apostasy which followed later, and of the kingdom of Antichrist and also of Mahomet, which has now been built up. No heresy more foul, more long-lasting, or more plausible has ever been devised by anyone. For this reason Arius is called by Hilary the beginning of Antichrist. To this evil another was added: the vanity of the Greeks and the triviality of Christians who busied themselves with curious disputations, rather than with true piety, the amendment of morals, and serious and diligent study. These two things not only welcomed the madness of Arius gladly, but also fed upon it in the Church and wonderfully increased it, so that there is no heresy that has been mentioned more often in ecclesiastical history, or that has disturbed the Church of God more or for longer. It flowed out like a most foul and turbid stream from the wretched school and fountain of the Samosatenes. For it began under the emperor Constantine the Great and Silvester, bishop of Rome, in the year 290 after Christ's passion, when the Church had been restored to public peace and Satan envied the Christian people such quiet. For those whom he could no longer assail with arms and fire, he attempted to attack with sects, heresies and corruptions, and so to harass them bitterly, which he achieved. All these were called Arians and Exoucontians, because they contended that Christ had come into being and been made out of things that were not. Yet later those who professed this heresy taught that Christ was not created out of nothing, as Augustine writes in book 3 against Maximinus, chapter 14. Individual groups were named after the author who introduced something new in that sect: Eunomians, Eudoxians, Actians, Eusebians and Pytheconians. Several are said to be the first authors and progenitors of this deadly error. Nicephorus (book 8, chapter 4) names Alexander Beucalus of Alexandria as the first sower of this poison; Zonaras, however, prefers Origen, who wrote that the only-begotten Son of God was made. Yet the faith and history concerning Arius are more certain: everyone confesses that he first spewed out this venom and blasphemy against the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, and Rufinus especially maintains this (book 1 of the History, chapter 1). Hence at the Synod of Sardica he was insultingly called Cheiromachus. And at the council of Aquileia, against Palladius the Arian, the letter of Arius alone was read and recited, as that of the parent of this monster. Many divisions of this heresy arose at once. For almost in its very cradle it gave birth to three sects of men who disagreed among themselves about the deity of Christ: those of Arius himself, the Aetians or Eunomians (who were the same), and the Macedonians, as Rufinus (book 1 of the History, chapter 25) and Socrates (book 5, chapter 10) relate.

units.la: [The top line of the Greek on this page ("ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων") is blurred and only partly legible; those words are marked [?].] inter se diuerse de Christi deitate sententium peperit, Arianorum ipsorum, Aetianorum, siue Eunomianorum (qui fuerunt ijdem) & Macedonianorum, quemadmodum tradit Ruffin.lib. i.histor. cap.25. & Socrat. libro quinto cap.10. Sub Theodosio vero maiore duae quoque aliae illis tribus etiam accesserunt, Dorotheanorum, & Marianorum, vt iam haec hydra quinque pestifera capita gestaret. Marianos defendit & amplexus est Theoctistus quidam Antiochenus, ἀχυροπώλης. Est autem ἀχυρώδες[?] crustuli friabilis genus, quod ille publicè populo diuendebat. Vnde iidem Mariani postea Psathyriani quoque sunt ignominiose nominati, vt ait Socrates libro 5.cap.23. quanquam apud Theodoretum lib.4.haeret. fabul. Tapsyrianos pro Psathyrianos corrupte legitur. & apud Epiphanium perperam Psathyropolitanus, tanquam a loco deducta voce, quae mercaturae & artificij genus significat. Adiunxerunt se quoque iis duae adhuc sectae Pythecianorum, & Dulianorū, de quibus in Eunomianis agemus, vt iam deformia septe eiusdem beluae capita fuisse appareat. Tempore vero ipsius Arij tres quoque constituunt huius erroris praecipuos propugnatores, & propagatores, Arium ipsum presbyterum: Euzoium diaconum: & Achillam lectorem, omnes Alexandrinae Ecclesiae inseruientes: ita Hieronym. aduersus Luciferian. Alios autem adiungunt Arij & fautores & socios, qui ab illius dogmate ne latum quidem unguem discesserunt, Ursatium Singidonensem superioris Mysiae episcopum: Valentem Murfarum superioris Pannoniae episcopum, homines ad humanam generis perniciem natos,Acatianum à Cæsarea,Asterium, Eusebium Nicomedensem episcopum, qui Constantinnm Magnum & Constantium baptizauerat,propterea̛que in aula imperatoris gratiosus erat. Theogonium Nicenum episcopum,& alios penè infinitos, inter quos etiam omnium Historicorum consensu,Liberius Romanus Episcopus recensetur, ne quis Romana Ecclesiam errare posse neget.è quibus tamen ipsis quidam occultè, quidam autem apertè Arium defenderunt, ut mirum appareat in ea re Satanæ opus. Persequuti sunt autem Ariani or-thodoxos longè tetrius & durius quàm ulli unquam Pagani fecerant, ut scribit Socrates libro 5.cap.13.& Sozomen.libr.6.cap.37.Theodoret. libr.2.histor. cap.8. Latissimè verò propagata hæc hæresis, etiam perstitit diutissimè, ut scribit Socrates libro 6.cap.8.quando nec nunc quidem tetræ & amarę ipsius radices exscindi extirparíque è mundo potuerūt. Mahumetani enim sunt huius infelicis stirpis stolones,& nunc quoque plus quàm 1500.post primum ipsius ortum annos,inter Christianus(proh blasphemia) nomine Serucetanorum,Dauidicorum,Syluanista-rum,Blandratarum, Nearianorum repullulat. Floruit autem plus quàm 8o. annos publicè in Ecclesia recepta,uti apparet ex epist.Constatin. cōcilij ad Damasum, & nisi Deus per paucos quosdā orthodoxos episcopos,veluti per Athanasiū,magna sua misericordia hoc venenū repressisset,fidē Christiana,& verā de Christi deitate doctrinam prorsus sublaturum & abolitu-rum erat.Ergo inter Græcos durauit etiam sub Zenone imperatore Constantinopolitano, vt scribit Prosper ( nam sub Constantio, Valente, Theodosio, Valentiniano, & proximis alijs regibus etiam floruit, suaque templa publice concessa habuit) & postea sub Anastasio. Inter Latinos autem etiam fuit. Nam & Liberius episcopus Romanus illi errori fauit, & Auxentius,& alij pene innumerabiles, etiam Valentiniani mater. Longobardi anno Domini 700. hoc veneno infecti fuerunt. Ostgothi & VVest gothi etiam hanc hæresin sequuti sunt: sed & Vandali quoque, quam in Africa studiose propagarunt. Honoricus enim eorum rex Orthodoxos qui Carthagine erant, damnauit, collecta ex suis Synodo, cui Cyritta Arianus præfuit. In Gallia denique & Hispania,ne quid intactu relinqueret,viguit. Scribit enim Gregorius Turonensis Chilpericum Francorum regem edictis suis Arianis aperte fauisse, lib.5.cap.44. & lib.9.cap.15.& idem de Hispanis tradit Paulus Diaconus. Fuit autem Arius natione Libs, presbyter in Beucale ecclesia siue dioecesi, quæ intra Alexandrinæ ciuitatis mœnia comprehendebatur,qui siue subtili Alexandri episcopi argutiola commotus,vt Eusebius lib.2.de vita Constantini tradit,siue animi sui vanitate & ambitione impulsus, hunc certe pessimum errorem excudit, quo notior esset. Et quum primum clam eum Arius insusurraret, industria Meletij episcopi,de quo iam diximus, detectus est, & in lucem productus.Demum ad consilium Nicenum vocatus, ibíque damnatus, aliquandiu iussu Constantini imperatoris exulauit.Sed pœ nitentiæ simulatione,& technis Eusebij Nico-medensis aulici Episcopi perditissimi, ab eode restitutus & revocatus, quum in Constantino-politanâ Ecclesiam invito & renitente Alexâ-dro illius sedis episcopo, admittendus esset ex iussu imperatoris, pœna illi grauissima divini-tus inflicta est.Alvum enim exoneraturus,in publicas latrinas secesit,in quas viscera miscrè fœ deque ipse sua, tanquam alter Iudas, in tormi-nibus deiecit.Sozo. libro 2.cap. 30. Ex quo lo-cus ille inauspicatus habitus est,præterquam ab Arianis: & Divini numinis ira & plaga in tam horrendæ blasphemiæ autorem manifestissima apparuit. Propter quam tamen minimè re-sipuerunt homines, & ab illo errore nefario de stiterunt. Nam etiam tempore Caroli Magni extiterunt, sed ab authore Felicio Feliciani di-sti,idem cum Arianis sentientes.
units.tr: Within the very cradle of this heresy, the followers of Arius divided into three sects that held different views about the deity of Christ: the Arians themselves, the Aetians or Eunomians (who were the same people), and the Macedonians, as Rufinus (Hist. 1.25) and Socrates (5.10) report. Under Theodosius the Great two more sects were added to these three, the Dorotheans and the Marians, so that this hydra now bore five pestilent heads. Theoctistus of Antioch, a straw-dealer [ἀχυροπώλης], defended and embraced the Marians. The word for the chaff-like [ἀχυρώδες] is a kind of brittle biscuit, which he sold publicly to the people. For this reason the Marians were also shamefully called Psathyrians, as Socrates says (5.23), although Theodoret (Haer. fab. 4) wrongly reads "Tapsyrians" for "Psathyrians", and Epiphanius wrongly reads "Psathyropolitan", as if the word were derived from a place, when it names a trade and kind of merchandise. Two further sects also joined them, the Pythecians and the Dulians, of whom we shall speak among the Eunomians; so the seven misshapen heads of this same beast now appear. In the time of Arius himself, three men were the chief champions and propagators of this error: Arius the presbyter, Euzoius the deacon, and Achillas the reader, all serving the Church of Alexandria, as Jerome says against the Luciferians. Others too joined Arius as supporters and companions, who did not depart a hair's breadth from his doctrine: Ursacius, bishop of Singidunum in Upper Moesia; Valens, bishop of Mursa in Upper Pannonia, men born for the ruin of the human race; Acacius of Caesarea; Asterius; Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia, who had baptized Constantine the Great and Constantius, and for that reason was in favour at the emperor's court; Theognis, bishop of Nicaea; and almost countless others. Among them, by the agreement of all the historians, is counted Liberius, bishop of Rome, lest anyone deny that the Roman Church can err. Yet of these men some defended Arius secretly and some openly, so that it appears a marvellous work of Satan in this matter. The Arians persecuted the orthodox far more cruelly and harshly than any pagans ever had, as Socrates (5.13), Sozomen (6.37) and Theodoret (Hist. 2.8) write. This heresy spread most widely and endured for the longest time, as Socrates writes (6.8), so that not even now have its foul and bitter roots been plucked out and uprooted from the world. For the Mahumetans are the shoots of this unhappy stock; and even now, more than 1500 years after its first rise, it sprouts again among Christians (alas, what blasphemy!) under the names of Servetians, Davidists, Sylvanists, Blandrata's followers and Nearians. It flourished publicly and was received in the Church for more than eighty years, as appears from the letter of the Council of Constantinople to Damasus; and unless God, by his great mercy, had repressed this poison through a few orthodox bishops, such as Athanasius, it would utterly have taken away and abolished the Christian faith and the true doctrine of Christ's deity. Accordingly, among the Greeks it lasted also under the emperor Zeno at Constantinople, as Prosper writes (for it also flourished under Constantius, Valens, Theodosius, Valentinian and other rulers who followed, and had its churches publicly granted), and afterwards under Anastasius. Among the Latins too it was present: for Liberius, bishop of Rome, favoured that error, as did Auxentius and almost countless others, including the mother of Valentinian. The Lombards were infected with this poison in the year of the Lord 700. The Ostrogoths and Visigoths also followed this heresy; so did the Vandals, whom they zealously propagated in Africa. For their king Honoric condemned the orthodox at Carthage, having gathered a synod of his own men, over which the Arian Cyrila presided. Finally it flourished in Gaul and Spain, so that it might leave nothing untouched. For Gregory of Tours writes that Chilperic, king of the Franks, openly favoured the Arians in his edicts (5.44 and 9.15), and Paul the Deacon reports the same of the Spaniards. Arius was a Libyan by nation, a presbyter in the church or parish of Baucalis, which lay within the walls of the city of Alexandria. Whether he was stirred by the subtle wrangling of Bishop Alexander, as Eusebius reports (2 On the Life of Constantine), or was driven by the vanity and ambition of his own mind, he certainly devised this most wicked error so that he might become better known. As soon as Arius first began to whisper it secretly, he was detected through the diligence of Bishop Meletius, of whom we have already spoken, and brought into the light. At length he was summoned to the Council of Nicaea, where he was condemned, and for some time he was exiled by the command of the emperor Constantine. But by a pretence of repentance and by the tricks of Eusebius of Nicomedia, a most depraved courtier bishop, he was restored and recalled by the same emperor. When he was about to be admitted, by the emperor's order, into the church of Constantinople against the will and protest of Alexander, bishop of that see, a most grievous punishment was divinely inflicted upon him. For when he was about to relieve his bowels, he withdrew to the public latrines, and there, like another Judas, he poured out his entrails and his very self in the most wretched torments (Sozomen 2.30). From that time that place was regarded as ill-omened, except by the Arians; and the anger and stroke of the divine majesty appeared most manifestly against the author of so horrible a blasphemy. Yet men did not come to their senses on account of this, nor did they desist from that wicked error. For even in the time of Charlemagne it arose again, but it was called Felicianism after its author Felix, who held the same views as the Arians.

units.la: Quæ fuerint Arianorum hypotheses, videtur hoc loco complexus Augustinus. Christū neq; esse Deum, neque æternum,sed creaturam, excellentem quidem, & cæteris dignitate præstantiore. Itaque eum γενητὸν [?] τὸν Θεοῦ appellari, non autem adoptiuū tantum quemadmodū nos dici solemus,vt tradit Theodoretus Dialogo 2.Inconfus. Christū dici Deum non origine quidem,& naturâ, sed operatione tantum & gratiâ.Patrem autem Filio tanquam instrumento vsum esse ad cæteras res creandas. Unde Duliani hæretici nati, qui Filium Patris seruum esse dixerunt, quemadmodum ex eo quòd Ariani negât Christum natura Deum, orti sunt Bonosiani hæretici, de quibus post Innocentium primum, epist.20. & 21. & post Gregoriū in Epistola ad Quirinum, & can. Hi qui, De cõsecrat.distinct.4.Isidorus: qui Christum esse quidem FiliumDei, sed adoptiuum tátum cõtendűt, nec ante secula genitũ. ex ista enim lue innumerabiles hæreses extiterűt. Ergo Ariani volunt Christum esse ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων[?], ante omnes quidé creaturas, sed tamen creatum & conditũ fuisse. Unde aiunt fuisse tépus quum nondum ille esset, & existeret. Inde est vexata illa Arij sententia, Ἦν ὅταν ἐκ ἦν[?], i.erat quando non erat, & toties Synodis explosa, toties tamen ab Arianis reposita. Adduxerunt autem ad sui erroris confirmationem locum Prouerbiorum cap.8.versu 22. & Colossi.1.versu 15. quos Athanasius erudite explicat, & dissoluit. Perperam enim ille Prouerb. locus ex Hebraeo traductus est, Creauit,pro Possedit,habuit.Atq; sic Christus ipse Ioannis 17.versu 5.interpretatur.quanquam in huius gryphi & nodi solutione laboret & sese fatiget Epiphanius. Multis consiliis damnatus est hic error,sed multis etiam defensus. Nam & Ariminensi, quam hæreticam appellat Augustl.lib.3.contra Maxim.cap.14.& Hierosolymitana synodo,& aliis aliquot particularibus confirmatus est. Tandè iugulatus coquieuerat,donec à Mahumeto interpolatus,& reuocatus postea sub Carolo Magno à Felicio,nunc etiam ab impiis & profanis Nearianis in Transsyluania perfidissimè mundo propinatur. Quia vero in Eusebij, Ruffini, Socratis, & Theodoreti Eccle-
units.tr: Augustine seems here to have summed up the hypotheses of the Arians. Christ, they say, is neither God nor eternal, but a creature, excellent indeed and superior in dignity to the rest. Therefore he is called a begotten thing of God [γενητὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ], not merely adopted as we are usually said to be, as Theodoret teaches in his Dialogue 2 (Inconfusus). Christ is called God not by origin or nature but by operation and grace only. The Father, moreover, used the Son as an instrument in creating the other things. Hence the Dulianist heretics arose, who said that the Son is the servant of the Father. In the same way, from the Arian denial that Christ is God by nature, the Bonosian heretics arose, concerning whom see Innocent I, epistles 20 and 21, Gregory in his letter to Quirinus, the canon "Hi qui" (De consecratione, distinctio 4), and Isidore. They contend that Christ is indeed the Son of God, but only adopted, and not begotten before the ages. From this plague innumerable heresies have arisen. The Arians, then, want Christ to be "out of nothing" [ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων], created before all creatures, yet still made and created. Hence they say that there was a time when he was not yet and did not exist. From this comes that notorious saying of Arius, there was when he was not [ἦν ὅτε οὐκ ἦν], which has been repeatedly condemned by synods and yet repeatedly revived by the Arians. To confirm their error they cited Proverbs 8:22 and Colossians 1:15, which Athanasius explains and resolves learnedly. For that passage in Proverbs was wrongly translated from the Hebrew: "he created" for "he possessed, had". And Christ himself thus interprets it in John 17:5, although Epiphanius labours and wearies himself in trying to loosen this knot. This error has been condemned by many councils, but also defended by many: it was confirmed by the Council of Rimini, which Augustine calls a heretical council (Against Maximinus, book 3, ch. 14), by the Jerusalem synod, and by several other local councils. At last it lay strangled and quiet until, corrupted by Muhammad, it was recalled, and later under Charles the Great revived by Felix, and now too it is most treacherously poured out to the world by the impious and profane Nearians in Transylvania. But since all the things done concerning the succession, growth, condemnation and spread of this heresy are described fully in the ecclesiastical histories of Eusebius, Rufinus, Socrates and Theodoret, I refrain from listing them here.

units.la: Ecclesiastica historia perscribuntur omnia copiose, quae ad huius haereseos successionem, incrementa, damnationem & propagationem gesta sunt, iis recensendis supersedeo. 2 Error, Christum corpus tantum assumpsisse, non etiam animam humanam. Divinitatem enim in eo illas quae sunt animae propriae actiones & partes percegisse[?]. Theodor. Dial. 2. & lib. 4. Haeretic. fabul. Epiphanius quoque. Quod Arianismi caput alios quoque nempe Apollinaristas haereticos postea peperit. 3 Spiritum sanctum esse creaturam creaturae, id est, Filij, quem creaturam appellant. 4 Rebaptizant saepius etiam orthodoxos & ab orthodoxis baptizatos, quod vim salutis operi operato alligent. Formam quidem baptismatis a Christo constitutam non muta-vit Arius: sed ἀλογίαν[?] peruertit. Nec enim ita Deo laudes cecinit, quemadmodum in ortho-doxorum Ecclesiis fiebat, quia Hymnos suos sic concludebant Ariani, Gloria Patri per Filium in Spiritu sancto, pro eo quod in quolibet piorum coetu ex vera Triadis fide & confessione dicebatur, Gloria Patri & Filio, & Spiritui sancto. Inde institutus est trisagius ille, qui canebatur in Ecclesia, hymnus, pro quo tot postea contentiones sunt ortae, sed tamen orthodoxus & utilis Ecclesiae. Baptismum autem administran-tes, non totum hominem immergunt vel intingunt, sed tantum superiores eius partes usque ad umbilicum, inferiores enim hominis partes baptismo iudicant indignas. Itaque ut ne aqua in caput effusa in eas deflueret, fasciis paruulos vel homines baptizandos ab umbilico ad imos usque pedes involuebant. Quem baptizandi ri-tum retinuerūt imprimis Eunomiani, post Eu-nomij in Pamphylia exilium, quo ab Imperatore Constantino multatus est. Nam hos etiā formam Baptismi postea mutasse, scribit Socrat. lib.5.cap.24.de quibus conqueritur Chrysosto. Homil.1.in Galat. Atque hæc sunt pauca quidē numero, sed veneno & fœtore maxima erroris Arianorum capita, quæ Satan in magnam ipsius Christi contumeliam, & fidei Christianæ subuersionem & perniciosissima toti humano generi profudit. Siquis alias Arianorum hypotheses requirat, legat eorum sermonem qui extat apud Augustum Tom.6.
units.tr: 2 The error that Christ assumed only a body, not also a human soul; for they hold that the divinity in him performed the actions and functions proper to the soul (Theodoret, Dialogue 2, and book 4 of the Compendium of Heretical Fables; also Epiphanius). This head of Arianism later gave birth to others, namely the Apollinarist heretics. 3 The Holy Spirit is a creature of a creature, that is, of the Son, whom they call a creature. 4 They rebaptize repeatedly, even orthodox believers and those already baptized by the orthodox, because they bind the power of salvation to the work done (ex opere operato). Arius did not change the form of baptism instituted by Christ, but he perverted its sense [ἀλογίαν]. Nor did they sing praises to God as was done in the churches of the orthodox, for the Arians concluded their hymns thus: Glory to the Father through the Son in the Holy Spirit, whereas in every assembly of the pious it was said, from the true faith and confession of the Trinity, Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit. From this arose that trisagion hymn sung in the Church, over which many disputes later arose, yet it is orthodox and useful to the Church. In administering baptism, they do not immerse or dip the whole man, but only his upper parts as far as the navel, for they judge the lower parts of the body unworthy of baptism. So, lest the water poured on the head should run down to those parts, they wrapped infants or adults to be baptized in swaddling bands from the navel to the very feet. This rite of baptism was retained above all by the Eunomians, after the exile of Eunomius in Pamphylia, to which he was condemned by the Emperor Constantine. For Socrates writes (book 5, ch. 24) that these later also changed the form of baptism, and Chrysostom complains of them (Homily 1 on Galatians). These, then, are few in number but the greatest heads of Arian error, full of poison and stench, which Satan poured out for the great insult of Christ himself, the subversion of the Christian faith, and the most pernicious ruin of the whole human race. If anyone seeks other hypotheses of the Arians, let him read their sermon which is extant in Augustine, volume 6.

units.la: CAP. L. Audiani qui fuerint, & quod eorum dogma.
units.tr: CHAP. L. Who the Audians were, and what their doctrine was.

units.la: AUdianos quos appellant, (& Epiphanius schismaticos non hæreticos vult videri) alij vocant Anthropomorphitas, quoniam Deum sibi fingunt cogitatione carnali in similitudinem imaginis corruptibilis hominis: quod rusticitati eorum tribuit Epiphanius, parcens eis, ne dicantur hæretici. Eos autem separasse se dicit à [?]communione nostra culpando Episcopos di-uites [?], & Pascha cum Iudæis celebrando, quamuis sint qui eos in Ægypto Ecclesia Catholica communicare asseuerent. De Photinianis autem, quos [?]isto loco Epiphanius commemorat, iam superius sa-tis locutus sum.
units.tr: The Audians, as they are called (Epiphanius wishes them to be seen as schismatics rather than heretics), are called Anthropomorphites by others, because in their carnal thinking they imagine God in the likeness of a corruptible human image. Epiphanius puts this down to their rusticity and spares them the name of heretics. He says that they separated themselves from our communion, blaming the wealthy bishops and celebrating Easter with the Jews, although some assert that in Egypt they communicated with the Catholic Church. As for the Photinians, whom Epiphanius mentions at this point, I have already spoken of them sufficiently above.

units.la: In omnibus vulgò impressis atque adeò in ipso Augustini indice perperam legitur Vadiani pro Audiani, facta nimirum literarum transpositione. Neque enim qui sint Vadiani haeretici fando unquam auditum est: & quae de Vadianis scribit hic Augusti. ex Epiphanio transcripta sunt, ex indice nimirum lib.3. tom.1. ubi hi vocantur Αὐδιανοί, non autem Καδιανοί[?] vel βαδιανοί. Itaque locum hunc restituimus ex coniectura quidem, sed cui doctos omnes putamus assensuros. Hi vero & Au-diani & Audæi vocitantur, ab authore, vt appareret ex l. Ariani, & De haeret. & Manichaeis: quemadmodum ex dogmate postea dicti sunt à Graecis Anthropomorphitae, à Lactantio vero Anthropiani lib.4.cap.30. Ac Audianorum nomē prius innotuit sub Valentiniano primo Imperatore & Damaso Episcopo Ro. circa annum à Chri-sto passo 338. vt annotant chronographi, quanquam eorum parens Audæus homo lingua & natione Syrus, quemadmodum Theodor.lib.4. Histor. cap.10. tradit, ex Mesopotamia prose-ctus sub extrema Arij haeretici tempora vixisse & floruisse ab Epiphanio scribitur. Anthropomorphitae autem (qui sunt iidem cum superio-ribus) hoc nomine primùm ad huius erroris maiorem notationem & detestationem vulgò dicti videntur, sublata Audianorum appellatione, demum sub Arcadio Imperatore, & Anasta-sio Romano Episcopo circa annum à Christo passo 370. Fuit sanè haec haeresis non tantùm Manichaeismi propago & fruticatio, vt est Tri-part. histor. lib.1. cap.11. sed etiam Monachicæ stupiditatis fœtus. Quæ, vt aiunt, ex iis regioni-bus primùm prodiit, in quibus Manichæi con-ferti regnabant, nimirum ex Mesopotamia & Syria Euphratensi. Nam sæpe Manichæis obii-cit Augustinus, eos nihil ne de Deo quidem cogitare nisi terrenum posse. Duæ verò res potis-simùm Audæum istum hominem professione monachū ad nouum hunc errorem patiendum impulerunt. Prima quidem, nimia iam Episco-porum Christianorum in ipsum gregem Domini insolentia, & in viuendi more & genere superbia, luxus, otium, pompa, opes, & lautitiæ, quibus vir ille, & merito quidem, vt Epiphan. scribit, offensus sæpe eos coràm acerbè increpauit. Quamobrem illis inuisus & conuitiis im-petebatur, & vt austerior Prælatorúmque Ecclesiæ calumniator, accusabatur: tandem pugnis etiam ab iis cæsus & vi ex eius Ecclesiæ, cui præerant tales Episcopi, cœtu eiectus nouum sibi cœtum colligere coactus est. Nec verò nimius ille Episcoporum fastus, nimiæq; diuitiæ hunc soluit, qui duræ illi & monasticæ vitæ assuetus erat, offendit: sed postea quoque Mahumetem ipsum tam superbas suo seculo Episcoporum (qui se Christianos appellabant) aulas cernen-tem ita à fide Christiana auertit, vt de noua re-ligione, in qua pastores simpliciori vitæ gene-re vterentur, cogitarit, quemadmodum illius temporis historici scribunt. Quid igitur si Ro-manæ curiæ splendorem, si Cardinalitium luxum, qualis hodie est, vidisset? Altera verò Audiano-rum erroris inducendi causa fuit Monachalis stupor & ignorantia, qui in solitudine & procul à cultura ingenij semoti, solúmque vitam agrestem viuentes, nihil nisi corporeum, terrenum, crassum & sensibile, ac ne de Deo quidem imaginari meditarique apud se poterant. Vnde in cellis, & lustris monachorum statim hic error obtinuit, diúque perstitit. Quare rusticitati & ἀξιώσεως [?] potius, quàm ἀγνοίας [?] & ingenij peruersitati tribuitur ab Epiphanio: sed & ambitionis & αὐθαδείας [?] plané fructus fuit, quae in hoc hominum genere summa esse solet. Θρασυς γὰρ ἀμαθία. Ergo Audaeus hanc haeresin condidit, cuius tamen suae temeritatis, & in Deum blasphemiae poenas luit. Nam à Constantio (sic enim potius quàm à Constantino lego) in exilium actus in Gothia consenuit, quam etiam suo veneno infecit. Citissimè verò propagata est haec haeresis inter nouarum rerum cupidos & iam assuctos sectis homines Asianos & Orientales. Adeò ut è Mesopotamia profecta Syriam Damascenâ, Antiochenâ, Ægyptum, Asiam ipsam, imprimis autem monasteria, quae in Scenitide Ægypti nomo plurima erant, inuaderet, Episcopos haberet & Presbyteros ad imitationem orthodoxae Ecclesiae, atque etiam successores, veluti Vranium & Syluanum, ut tradit Epiphan. Denique regiones & vrbes totas occuparet, velut Chalcidem, quae ad Belum sita est, celebre, ut ait Plinius lib. 5. cap. 23, Coeles Syriae oppidum. Sed nec Italia, nec Gallia huius pestis immunis fuit. Imprimis autem Theophilus Alexandrinus Episcopus, ut Dioscurum Hermo-politanum Episcopum, rectè de spirituali Dei natura sentientem, quem oderat, opprimeret, hanc hæresin quiescetem & mitescentem renouauit, quâ postea defendit & propugnauit cum Ægyptiacis suis monachis, ut docet Sozomen. lib.8. cap.11. & 12. Diutissime vero non tantum inter monachos sed alios etiam mansit, quando in Italia sub Berengario Imperatore, qui Ludouico Pio Caroli filio successit, adhuc florebat. Denique inducendarum in Christianorum templa imaginum, post deinde cultus earum instituendi primum fundametum hinc videtur esse ortum. Nam postquam Deus ipse ad hominis similitudinem corporeus fingi coepit, tales imagines honestæ quoque & piæ habitæ sunt, tanquam per eas Dei ipsius forma repræsentaretur. Post Dei imaginem, Martyrum quoque & Apostolorum imagines induci coeptæ sunt & coli. Quem errorem uni maxime Monachi fouerunt & disseminarunt, ut apparet ex actis Nicenæ Synodi secundæ, ubi pro imaginibus & earum cultu acerrima mouerunt illi certamina.
units.tr: In all the printed editions, and even in Augustine's own index, the name is wrongly given as Vadiani instead of Audiani, through a transposition of letters, clearly. No one has ever heard of heretics called Vadiani, and what Augustine writes here about the Vadiani has been copied from Epiphanius. It is taken, that is, from the index of book 3, volume 1, where they are called Αὐδιανοί [Audianoi], not Καδιανοί or βαδιανοί. So we have restored this reading by conjecture, though we think all scholars will agree with it. They are called both Audiani and Audaei, by the author, as appears from the chapter on the Arians and the chapter on the heresies and the Manichaeans. In the same way, from their doctrine, the Greeks later called them Anthropomorphitae, and Lactantius called them Anthropiani (book 4, chapter 30). The name Audiani first became known under the emperor Valentinian I and Pope Damasus of Rome, around the year 338 after the suffering of Christ, as the chroniclers note. Their founder, Audaeus, was a man of Syrian language and nation; as Theodoret relates (Ecclesiastical History, book 4, chapter 10), he came from Mesopotamia, and Epiphanius writes that he lived and flourished in the last days of the heretic Arius. The Anthropomorphites (who are the same as those above) seem first to have been commonly so called under this name, to mark and denounce the error more strongly, after the name of Audians was dropped, finally under the emperor Arcadius and Pope Anastasius of Rome, around the year 370 after the suffering of Christ. This heresy was certainly not only an offshoot and growth of Manichaeism, as the Tripartite History says (book 1, chapter 11), but also the offspring of monkish stupidity. As they say, it first came forth from those regions where the Manichaeans reigned in great numbers, namely Mesopotamia and Euphratensian Syria. For Augustine often charged the Manichaeans with being unable to think even of God except as something earthly. Two things especially drove this Audaeus, a monk by profession, to adopt this new error. The first was the excessive arrogance of the Christian bishops toward the very flock of the Lord, and their pride in their way and manner of living: luxury, idleness, pomp, wealth, and fine living. Offended by these, and rightly so, as Epiphanius writes, he often rebuked them sharply to their faces. For this reason he was hated by them and attacked with insults, and was accused of being a severe and slanderous critic of the church's prelates. At last he was even beaten with fists by them and forcibly expelled from the congregation over which such bishops presided, and so he was compelled to gather a new congregation for himself. Yet it was not that excessive pride and wealth of the bishops which resolved him, nor was it that which offended him, since he was accustomed to a hard monastic life. Later, too, Muhammad himself, seeing the bishops of his age (who called themselves Christians) living in such proud courts, turned away so far from the Christian faith that he thought of a new religion in which ministers would live a simpler kind of life, as the historians of that time write. What, then, would he have thought if he had seen the splendour of the Roman court and the cardinals' luxury as it is today? The second cause of inducing the Audian error was monkish dullness and ignorance. Living in solitude and remote from the cultivation of the mind, living only a rustic life, they could imagine and ponder nothing in their own minds except what was bodily, earthly, gross and sensible, not even God. So this error at once took hold in the cells and dens of monks, and persisted for a long time. Therefore Epiphanius attributes it to rusticity and to a presumption of claims [ἀξιώσεως], rather than to ignorance and perversity of mind. But it was also clearly the fruit of ambition and self-will [αὐθαδείας], which is usually supreme in this class of men. For "boldness is ignorance" [Θρασυς γὰρ ἀμαθία]. So Audaeus founded this heresy, yet he paid the penalty for his rashness and his blasphemy against God. For he was driven into exile by Constantius (for so I read, rather than Constantine) and grew old in Gothia, which he also infected with his poison. This heresy spread very quickly among men of Asia and the East who were eager for novelties and already accustomed to sects. So much so that, setting out from Mesopotamia, it invaded Syria, Damascene and Antiochene, Egypt, Asia itself, and above all the monasteries, which were very numerous in the Scenitic nome of Egypt. It also had bishops and elders in imitation of the orthodox Church, and even successors, such as Uranius and Silvanus, as Epiphanius reports. Finally it occupied whole regions and cities, as Chalcis, which lies near Belus and is famous, as Pliny says (book 5, chapter 23), a town of Coele-Syria. But neither Italy nor Gaul was free of this plague. Above all Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, wishing to crush Dioscorus, bishop of Hermopolis, who thought rightly about the spiritual nature of God and whom he hated, revived this heresy, which had been lying dormant and growing mild, and afterwards he defended and promoted it with his Egyptian monks, as Sozomen teaches (book 8, chapters 11 and 12). It remained for a very long time, not only among monks but among others too, since it was still flourishing in Italy under the emperor Berengar, who succeeded Louis the Pious, son of Charlemagne. Finally, the first foundation of introducing images into Christian churches, and afterwards of instituting their worship, seems to have arisen from this source. For once God himself began to be imagined as bodily, in the likeness of man, such images were also held to be honourable and pious, as if the very form of God were represented through them. After the image of God, images of the martyrs and the apostles also began to be introduced and worshipped. This error the monks chiefly fostered and spread, as appears from the acts of the Second Council of Nicaea, where those monks raised the fiercest contests over images and their worship.

units.la: 2 Hæc sunt Audianorum, & postea Anthropomorphitarum hæreseos capita. 1 Deum esse corporeum humanæque formæ similem. Itaque & brachia, & pedes, & aures, & cætera huiusmodi membra nostris similia habere, cum & loqui dicatur, & audire, & progredi. Denique cum homines ad Dei imaginem esse conditi, diserte ab ipsa Scriptura pronuntientur. Theodoret. Isidor. Epiphan. Inde Ἀνθρωπομορφῖται[?] nominati, quòd Deum (qui mere spiritualis est, natura & essentia simplicissima, nullisque membris aut partibus constans, ut est Ioan.4.verf.24.) humanam corporis formam induat. Quod enim ad has Scripturae phrases, Deus videt, audit, &c. per [ἀνθρωποπαθείαν?] sunt accipiendae: quemadmodum etiam docet Ioan. Damascen. lib.1. Orthod.fidei,cap.12. Et quod de homine ad imaginem Dei creato afferunt, eorum inscitiam prodit, cum ea Dei imago in animo non in corpore vel membris quibus illud compositum est & distinctum: non in viribus ipsius: non in baptismate & charactere, quae nos accipere quidam volunt: in animo, inquam, hominis perspicue posita sit, qui quoad essentiam spiritualis est, invisibilis, intelligens: quoad qualitates autem & facultates primaeuas (quas ante peccatum velut dotes a Deo habuit) erat intellectu perspicax & cognoscens vere, certo, lucide & facile quae hominem intelligere oportuit: corde vero & voluntate recta, bona, & nihil mali per se appetens. Deleta vero est per peccatum in nobis magnam partem haec Dei imago: non tamen prorsus sublata. Per Christum autem D.nostrum renovatur in electis Dei. Huius ergo erroris de quo agimus, evitandi damnandique gratia, severe ad Hieron. & Epiphanij usque tempora in Ecclesia sanctitum [?] erat, ne in templis Christianorum ullae vel Dei vel Martyrum, ac ne ipsius quidem crucifixi Christi imagines erigerentur vel essent: & cum in Syriam proficiscens Epiphanius velum in quo pictus erat Christus, reperisset, propriis manibus illud discerpsit & discidit, ut ipse scribit, & ex ipsius epistola Hieronymus. Huic errori maxime fuerunt Origenistae contrarij, quo factum est ut Origenis scriptis maxime delectaretur Chry-sostomus, cuius aetate haec haeresis plurimum pul-lulabat. 2 Error, Tenebras, Ignem & Aquam esse aeterna & ingenita rerum principia ex Mani-chaeorum faece sumptum est, & Empedoclis deli-rium sapit. 3 Propter hominum vitia coetu or-thodoxae Ecclesiae deserunt. Quod Donatistarum erroris fuit postea seminarium. Quanqua enim Episcoporum, inter quos sana tamen manebat adhuc Christi Evangeliique doctrina, vitia, lu-xus, & fastus damnandi erant: & foenora Chri-stianorum, & concubinatus coelibum detestan-dus (propter quae crimina primum & merito invectus est in sui seculi ecclesias Audæus) coe-tus tamen ipse piorum, ubi retinebatur adhuc orthodoxa veritas, non fuit scindendus. 4 Si-ne publica poenitentia Christianos iam recep-tos grauissime peccantes in Ecclesiam tamen admittunt & ad sacramenta recipiunt. Quod non tantum contra veterem Ecclesiae discipli-nam fiebat, sed ipsa Domini Dei dona sanctis-sima & sacratissima profanat. Atque ex his ap-paret ut abyssus abyssum impellat, & qui pri-mum leuiter peccare videbantur, dum charita-tis Christianę normam non sequuntur, grauiter & in pluribus quidem impegerint, fideique naufragium fecerint.
units.tr: 2 These are the heads of the doctrine of the Audians, and afterwards of the Anthropomorphites. (1) God is corporeal and similar to human form. Therefore they hold that he has arms, feet, ears and other members like ours, since he is said to speak, to hear and to walk. Finally, since men are said by Scripture itself to have been created in the image of God, they say so plainly. (Theodoret, Isidore, Epiphanius.) They are named Anthropomorphites because they clothe God, who is purely spiritual, of the simplest nature and essence, and consisting of no members or parts (as in John 4:24), in the form of a human body. As for these phrases of Scripture, "God sees", "hears", and so on, they are to be understood by way of anthropopatheia [ἀνθρωποπάθειαν], as John of Damascus also teaches (On the Orthodox Faith, book 1, chapter 12). And what they bring forward about man created in the image of God betrays their ignorance, since that image of God is clearly placed in the mind, not in the body or its members by which it is composed and distinguished, not in its powers, not in baptism and the character, which some wish us to receive. It is placed, I say, in the mind of man, which in its essence is spiritual, invisible and intelligent. As for its primal qualities and faculties (which he had from God before sin, as if they were gifts), he was keen in understanding and truly, surely, clearly and easily knowing whatever man ought to understand. In heart and will he was upright and good, and by himself desired nothing evil. But this image of God in us was largely destroyed by sin, though not wholly taken away. It is renewed through Christ our Lord in the elect of God. Therefore, to avoid and condemn this error we are discussing, the Church until the time of Jerome and Epiphanius was strict in holding that no images of God or the martyrs, nor even of Christ crucified, should be set up or exist in Christian churches. When Epiphanius, travelling into Syria, found a veil on which Christ was painted, he tore and rent it with his own hands, as he himself writes, and Jerome from Epiphanius's letter. The Origenists were the chief opponents of this error, which is why Chrysostom was especially delighted with the writings of Origen, in whose time this heresy was flourishing greatly. (2) The error that darkness, fire and water are the eternal and unbegotten principles of things is taken from the dregs of the Manichaeans, and smacks of the madness of Empedocles. (3) On account of the vices of men they desert the assembly of the orthodox Church. This was afterwards the seedbed of the error of the Donatists. For although the vices, luxury and pride of bishops, among whom the sound doctrine of Christ and the Gospel still remained, were to be condemned, and the usury of Christians and the concubinage of the unmarried were to be detested (for which crimes Audaeus first and rightly attacked the churches of his age), yet the assembly of the godly itself, where orthodox truth was still kept, was not to be rent asunder. (4) They admit into the Church, and receive to the sacraments, Christians already received who have sinned most gravely, without public repentance. This was done not only against the ancient discipline of the Church, but also profanes the most holy and sacred gifts of the Lord God himself. From these things it appears that one abyss calls another, and that those who at first seemed to sin lightly, while they do not follow the rule of Christian charity, have stumbled grievously in many respects and have suffered shipwreck of the faith.

units.la: CAP. LI. Semiariani qui fuerint.
units.tr: CAP. LI. Who the Semiarians were.

units.la: {1}Emiarianos. Epiphanius dicit, qui similis {2}essentia dicunt Patrem, & Filium, tanquam non plenos Arianos, (quasi Ariani nec similem velint) cum hoc Euno-miani dicere celebrentur.
units.tr: {1}Emiarians. Epiphanius says these are the ones who say that the Father and the Son are of like essence, as though they were not full Arians (as if the Arians did not even want a like essence), although the Eunomians are commonly said to hold this view.

units.la: I Semiarianos.) Ariani ab Epiphanio Ἀρειο-μανῖται dicuntur: hi vero, quos Semiarianos vocat Augustinus, ille Ἡμαρτίας[?], non sunt Macedoniani, sed qui alio quoque nomine Acatiani, ab authore suo nimirum Acatio Caesareae Palestinae Episcopo monoculo & coclite, qui ut verum animi lumen amiserat ita corporis quoque alterum oculum, unde μονοφθαλμὸς[?]-nominatur. Ab hoc igitur Acatio, qui Eusebio Pamphili in episcopatu successit, Acatiani, Semiariani dicti sunt. De quo Tripart.histor.libro 4. & Socrat. libro 2. cap.45. & libro 4. cap. 22. & tota historia Ecclesiastica. Vt autem quae fuerit haec haeresis & unde emerserit intelligatur, res tota est altius ab ipso fonte arcessenda, qui est Arius. Ariani ab Ario, quemadmodum supra docuimus, appellantur, qui secantur & dividuntur[?] authoribus suis. vel ab dogmate. Ab authore quidem nominantur alij Ariani, Eudoxiani, Eunomiani, Actiani, Pytheciani vel Cyrtiani.
units.tr: I. The Semiarians. Epiphanius calls the Arians Areiomanites [Ἀρειομανῖται]. Those whom Augustine calls Semiarians, and whom Epiphanius calls by another name [Ἡμιαρειανοί?], are not the Macedonians. They are also called Acatians, after their author Acacius, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, a one-eyed man, who had lost the light of his mind as well as one eye of his body, and so is called monophthalmos [μονοφθαλμός]. From this Acacius, who succeeded Eusebius Pamphili in the bishopric, the Acatians were called Semiarians. On this see the Tripartite History, book 4; Socrates, book 2, chapter 45, and book 4, chapter 22; and the whole Ecclesiastical History. But to understand what this heresy was and where it came from, the whole matter must be traced back to its source, which is Arius. The Arians are named after Arius, as we showed above, and they are distinguished and divided either by their authors or by their doctrine. By author, some are called Arians, Eudoxians, Eunomians, Actians, Pytheciani or Cyrtiani.

units.la: Tot enim & tam varias huius unius hæreseos tradunt autores ecclesiastici.
units.tr: For ecclesiastical writers hand down so many and such varied names for this one heresy.

units.la: A dogmate vero item multipliciter. Alij enim affirmant & docent Christum esse Patri 1. ὁμοι-ον, ἰδιον; idq; vel κατὰ φύσιν & οὐσίαν, i.e. similis essentiæ Patri. Acatiani priores q. & Semiani dicuntur. κατὰ θέλησιν, i.e. similem voluntate tantum, nō autem essentia, qui eum etiam ἐνέργειαν postea dixerunt. Hi sunt Acatiani posteriores, & ἐπιδοξοι. 2. ἀνόμοιον, essentia. & voluntate. Aetiani, Eunomiani, Anomij. 3. ἴσον, seruum Patris. Eudoxiani, Duliani.
units.tr: Likewise, by doctrine, in many ways. Some affirm and teach that Christ is to the Father: (1) similar [ὅμοιον] and of his own kind [ἴδιον], and this either according to nature and substance, that is, of like essence with the Father [ὁμοιούσιον]. The earlier Acatians are also called Semiarians. Or according to will [κατὰ θέλησιν], that is, like only in will and not in essence; these later also called him similar in activity [ἐνέργειαν]. These are the later Acatians, and the "epidoxoi". (2) Unlike [ἀνόμοιον] in essence and in will: Aetians, Eunomians, Anomoeans. (3) Equal [ἴσον] and the Son of the Father: Eudoxians, Dulians.

units.la: Ex eodem igitur Satanico fonte apparet, quot enata sint hæræscôn diuortia, & fidei scopuli positi. Sed de Acatianis, quos & primos dixi- mus & Semiarianos, videamus. Hæc hæresis proximè secuta est & soboleuit post Arianum furorem sparsum, atque etiam damnatum Nicena synodo. Dixerat quidem Arius Filium nō esse ἀναρχον, καὶ ἀΐδιον, sed creaturam, & Patre posteriorem. Itaque diuersas in Trinitate substantias & ὑποστάσεις, non tantum ὑπόστασις[?] & personas constituebat Aduersus quem Patres Nicææ collecti aperte ex Dei verbo definierunt, consentiente etiam veterum orthodoxorum & sententia & phrasi, Filium esse Patri ὁμοούσιον &, ut postea per crafin pronuntiatum est, ὁμοούσιον, ad tollendas & euitandas Acatianorum technas, qui vna tantùm diphthongo οι adiecta ex ὁμοού-σιον, ὁμοιούσιον fecerant, ne diuersa sentire à Nicena synodo perciperentur, dum Homoufion ore proferrent. Socrat. lib.i. cap.8: 4.cap.ii: 3. cap.7. Esse autem ὁμοούσιον τῷ πατρὶ[?] Filium Patri sic docebant, & interprctabantur orthodoxi patres, vt & Deus verus & æternus, & Patri con-essentialis[?] esse Filius perspicuè intelligeretur. Hæc ipsa vox postea variis synodis orthodoxorum & recepta & probata est, imprimis OE-cumenicis conciliiis:sed iis quoque synodis quæ Nicenæ proximæ fuerunt, qualis Alexandrina, quæ ab Athanafio & Eusebio collecta est: & Sardicenfi, quæ ab Imperatore. Aduersus Arianos vocem οὐσίας introduxerunt Patres, quemadmodum ad iugulandum Sabellianorum errorem, vocem ὑποστάσεως, Socrat. lib.3.cap.7. Quæ cum effent scitè & pie & doctè constituta, exiterunt non tantùm curiosi, sed etiam audaces & impij homines, qui primùm hac ὁμοούσιε vocem nusquam in Scriptura legi cotenderent. Atqui, vt respondent Patres, & rectè, perinde est, cum res ipsa quæ hac voce denotatur, diserte extet. Deinde obiecerunt, fi ὁμοούσιον recipiatur, aperte plures Deos constitui. Hæ fuerunt præcipuæ hostium rationes, vt scribit Socrat. lib.i. cap.23.& 2.cap.40. Atque vt postremæ respondeatur, maximè vnus tantùm Deus esse docetur, cùm tres illæ hypostases, non solùm ὁμοιού-σιοι, sed quod longè plus est, ὁμοίους esse demonstrantur, iuxta illud Christi, Ego & Pater vnum fumus, Ioan.10.verf.30. Sed tamen impudenter ab istis & pluribus quidem eorum synodis vox ὁμοούσιον & ὁμοιούσιον damnata est, vti Philippenfi, Antiochena, Seleuciana, Nicea, quę à Nicæ vrbe Thraciæ dicta est, & à Valente & Vrfatio im-purissimis canibus & Episcopis sub Conftan-tio congregata. Ariminenfis quidem synodus vocem ὁμοούσιον omnino & de industria & caute, ne quid turbarum contra Constantij edictum moueret, prætermisit, Homoufianos tamen damnauit. Sic igitur vox hæc exagitata est, adeo quidè vt in Christum, & in Filium ὁμοούσιον Patri credere propositum fit à Græcis hominibus quibusdam Latinis Episcopis linguæ Græcæ ignaris, velut quædam duo sibi plane contraria & repugnantia, Ruffin. lib.1.cap.23. Sed tamen quia Nicenæ synodi plurimum, & iure quidem, semper valuit autoritas, Acatius hic, à quo Aca-tiani (alius enim est Acatius Eutychianus, qui & ipse quoque damnatus est, & de quo cano, Acatius.1.& 2.24.quæst.ii[?] fit mentio) falsò qui-dem conciliandarum Ecclesiarum prætextu vo-luit in Seleuciana synodo quæ sub Constantio Imperatore conuenit, pro ὁμοούσιον Chriftu, sub-stitui, dicíque ὁμοιούσιον. Nam eum ἑτερούσιον ap-pellare durius videbatur, quàm vt recipi ab or-thodoxis & Niccnam fidem sequentibus pos-set, præterquàm quòd etiam Constantij edicto ad placandas, vt ille voluit, tantas episcoporum rixas, stricte vetitum erat, ne Christus vel ἑτεροούσιος vel ὁμοιούσιος diceretur. Ergo tolerabilis vi-debatur Acatij sententia, sed cum sub eo fuco & melle venenum maximum lateret, obstiterũt patres, neque ὁμοούσιον tantùm Patri Christum esse negarunt, quòd ὁμοιούσιοι dicantur plura eiusdem speciei indiuidua, vti Ioannes homo est Petro homini ὁμοούσιος, Bucephalus equus est, Pyroei equo ὁμοιούσιος, in quibus tamen plures numero sunt essentiæ & humanitates, & equinæ essentiæ: at ὁμοούσιος dicitur Filius Patri in diuinis, quòd eiusdem omnino & numero vnius sit cum Patre essentiæ, quanquam Sozomen. aliam harum vocum interpretationem affert, libro 3. cap.18. Ac primùm quidem Acatiani Filiū Patri ὁμοιούσιον κατ᾽ οὐσίαν [?] & ἀνόμοιον dixerunt: sed cùm ab aliis Arianis, imprimis autem Valente & Vrsatio exagitarentur, quòd tam multa concederet orthodoxis, & ipsi quoque Constantio Imperatori, qui non obscurè fauebat Arianis, gratificari vellent, mutarunt sententiam: & Filium Patri κατὰ θέλησιν [?] duntaxat, i.e. secundum voluntatem similem, non autem secundum essentiam dixerunt. Quod ipsum postea mutantes in deterius, Filium Patri ἀνόμοιον esse docuerunt. Atque hi sunt posteriores Acatiani ἑτεροούσιοι [?] à primis nominati, qui ὁμοιούσιον etiam expunxerunt, vt tradunt Socrat. lib. 2. cap. 43. & Sozomen. libro 3. cap. 15. Epiphan. ex quo manifestissima vocis huius ὁμοιούσιος labes & fraus intelligitur, Sozomen. lib. 4. cap. 29. Dixit quidem Ancyrana synodus, vt Epiphan. refert, [illegible, ~14 letters] sed propter relationem personarum, nō autem ob diuersitatem essentiarū, aut quòd Patrem in diuinis Filij essentiatorem faciat. Cœpit autem hæc hæresis sub Constantio Imperatore & Liberio Romæ Pontifice, anno à Christo passo 330. Adiutores habuit Vrsatium, & Valentem Episcopos. Successores Basiliū Ancyranum & Gregorium Laodicenum Episcopum, Gymnasium, Syluanum. Sed nouis ex eodem Arianismi fonte subnascentibus hęresibus & peioribus quidē, huius nomen obrutū periit. Statim vero propagata est, & nomine Nicenae synodi commendata. Id factum fraude Vrsatij, qui Ariminensem confessionem oblatam principi subdole confirmauit, conuocata raptim synodo Niceam non Bithyniae, sed Thraciae urbem. Vnde suum symbolum vafre postea Nicenum appellarunt, cum Niceum potius nominandum esset. Sozomen. lib4. cap.19. Plures enim fuerunt Niceae ciuitates, è quibus vna est in Thracia, quemadmodum docet Suidas.
units.tr: From the same satanic fountain, then, it is clear how many divisions of heresies have sprung up, and how many rocks of faith have been set in the way. But let us look at the Acatians, whom we have named first and called Semiarians. This heresy followed closely upon and sprouted after the Arian fury had spread and had been condemned by the Synod of Nicaea. Arius had indeed said that the Son is not unbegotten and eternal but a creature, and later than the Father. Thus he set up different substances and hypostases in the Trinity, and not merely hypostases but persons. Against him the Fathers gathered at Nicaea defined plainly from the word of God, with the agreement also of the opinion and phrasing of the ancient orthodox, that the Son is homoousion [ὁμοούσιον] with the Father. This was afterwards proclaimed aloud, to remove and avoid the tricks of the Acatians, who by adding a single diphthong, oi, to homoousion made it homoiousion [ὁμοιούσιον], so that they might not be seen to think differently from the Nicene synod while they pronounced homoousion with their mouths. Socrates, book 1, chapter 8; book 4, chapter 11; book 3, chapter 7. The Fathers, as orthodox teachers, taught and explained that the Son is homoousion with the Father in such a way that it is clearly understood that he is the true and eternal God and consubstantial with the Father. This very word was afterwards received and approved by various synods of the orthodox, above all the Ecumenical councils, but also by those synods that came next after Nicaea, such as the Alexandrian, gathered by Athanasius and Eusebius, and the Sardican, convened by the emperor. Against the Arians the Fathers introduced the word ousia [οὐσία], just as they introduced the word hypostasis [ὑπόστασις] to slay the error of the Sabellians; Socrates, book 3, chapter 7. Although these terms were established wisely, piously and learnedly, there arose not only curious but also bold and impious men, who first contended that this word homoousion is nowhere read in Scripture. Yet, as the Fathers rightly reply, it makes no difference, since the thing signified by this word is plainly present. Next they objected that if homoousion were accepted, several gods would clearly be posited. These were the chief arguments of the enemies, as Socrates writes, book 1, chapter 23, and book 2, chapter 40. To answer the last objection: the one God is taught most of all, since those three hypostases are shown not only to be homoiousioi but, far more, to be one, according to Christ's saying, "I and the Father are one," John 10:30. Nevertheless, this word homoousion and homoiousion was shamelessly condemned by these men and by many of their synods, such as those of Philippi, Antioch, Seleucia, and Nice (named after the city Nice in Thrace), and the one gathered under Constantius by Valens and Ursacius, most impure dogs and bishops. The synod of Rimini indeed deliberately and cautiously passed over the word homoousion altogether, lest it stir up any disturbance against the edict of Constantius, yet it condemned the Homoousians. So this word was harassed, to such an extent that some Latin bishops, ignorant of the Greek language, were led by certain Greek men to believe that to believe in Christ as homoousion with the Father meant believing two things plainly contrary and repugnant to each other; Rufinus, book 1, chapter 23. Still, since the authority of the Nicene synod has always prevailed very much, and rightly, this Acacius, from whom the Acatians take their name (for there is another Acacius, Eutychianus, who was also condemned, and who is mentioned in Gratian's Decretum, Acacius 1 and 2, c. 24, q. 2), wished, under the pretext of reconciling the churches, falsely, to substitute homoiousion for homoousion for Christ in the Synod of Seleucia, which was convened under the emperor Constantius. For to call him heterousion [ἑτερούσιον] seemed too harsh to be accepted by the orthodox who follow the Nicene faith; moreover, by the edict of Constantius, meant to calm such great quarrels among bishops, as he wished, it had been strictly forbidden to call Christ either heterousios or homoiousios. So Acacius' opinion seemed tolerable, but since the greatest poison lay hidden under that honey and sweet coating, the Fathers resisted, and they denied that Christ is homoousion with the Father merely because homoiousioi are said to be several individuals of the same species, as John is a man homoousios with Peter the man, and Bucephalus is a horse homoiousios with the horse of Pyrrhus; in these there are several essences and humanities in number, and equine essences. But the Son is called homoousion with the Father in divine matters, because he is of altogether the same essence, one in number, with the Father, although Sozomen gives another explanation of these terms, book 3, chapter 18. At first indeed the Acatians said that the Son is homoiousion with the Father according to substance, and unlike; but when they were harassed by other Arians, especially Valens and Ursacius, because they conceded so much to the orthodox, and because they wished also to please the emperor Constantius, who openly favoured the Arians, they changed their view, and said that the Son is like the Father according to will only, and not according to essence. Afterwards, changing this for the worse, they taught that the Son is unlike the Father. These are the later Acatians, called heterousioi by the earlier ones, who also expunged homoiousion, as Socrates reports, book 2, chapter 43, and Sozomen, book 3, chapter 15. Epiphanius, from whom the very clear defect and fraud of this word homoiousios is understood; Sozomen, book 4, chapter 29. The Synod of Ancyra indeed spoke, as Epiphanius reports, [illegible, about 14 letters], but on account of the relation of the persons, not on account of a difference of essences, or as if it made the Father the source of the Son's essence in divine matters. This heresy began under the emperor Constantius and Liberius, bishop of Rome, in the year 330 after the passion of Christ. It had as helpers the bishops Ursacius and Valens. Its successors were Basil of Ancyra and Gregory, bishop of Laodicea, Gymnasius and Silvanus. But with new heresies springing up from the same fountain of Arianism, and worse ones too, the name of this sect was buried and perished. Yet it was soon spread abroad and commended under the name of the Nicene synod. This was done by the trickery of Ursacius, who cunningly secured the confirmation, by the prince, of the Rimini confession, which had been presented to him; a synod was hastily convened at Nice, a city not of Bithynia but of Thrace. From this they afterwards cunningly named their creed Nicene, though it ought rather to have been called Nicene in the other spelling. Sozomen, book 4, chapter 19. For there were several cities named Nice, one of which is in Thrace, as Suidas teaches.

units.la: 2 Similis essentia.) Hæ fuerunt hypotheses.
units.tr: Similar in essence.) These were the hypotheses.

units.la: 1 Christum esse Dei Patris creaturam, non tamen ex eo natum ad morem cæterorum qui filij nascuntur & procreantur ex patribus, quia in gignendo hoc Filio nullum laborem Deus Pater sensit, quem tamen alij patres & matres in liberis suis procreandis ferunt. Impium certe dogma, & plenum blasphemiæ, & fabularis historiæ, & illi simile quod de Minerua ex Iouis cerebro nata dicitur à poetis. 2 Christum non esse αὐτογεννητὸς[?] Deum, sed θελήσει[?] tantum, & ἐνεργίᾳ[?], id est, voluntate & operatione, non autem essentia. At nihil vel voluntatem vel operationem Dei habet, nisi fit hoc ipsum Deus. Præterea Christus ait, Qui me videt, videt & Patrem, Ioann.14. versu 9. Quod de nullo alio vel homine, vel Angelo dici potest. 3 Spiritum sanctum Filij creaturam esse, non esse autē Deum. Hæc est Macedonianorum stirps, quæ postea pullulat.
units.tr: (1) That Christ is a creature of God the Father, yet not born from him in the manner of other children, who are begotten and born of their fathers, because God the Father felt no labour in begetting this Son, whereas other fathers and mothers do bear labour in procreating their children. This is certainly an impious doctrine, full of blasphemy and of the kind of fable that the poets tell about Minerva being born from Jupiter's brain. (2) That Christ is not God by nature [αὐτογεννητὸς] but only by will [θελήσει] and by operation [ἐνεργίᾳ], that is, by will and operation, and not by essence. But nothing has the will or operation of God unless that very thing is God. Besides, Christ says, "He who sees me sees the Father also" (John 14.9), which can be said of no other, whether man or angel. (3) That the Holy Spirit is a creature of the Son, and not God. This is the stock of the Macedonians, which sprouted afterwards.

units.la: CAP. LII.
units.tr: CHAP. LII.

units.la: Macedoniani cur sic dicti. Erroris autem eorum caput unum recensetur.
units.tr: Why the Macedonians are so called. One head of their error is set out.

units.la: Macedoniani sunt a Macedonio Constantinopolitana Ecclesia Episcopo, quos & πνευματομάχους[?] Graeci dicunt, eo quod de Spiritu sancto litigent. Nam de Patre & Filio recte sentiunt, quod unius sint, eiusdemque substantiae vel essentiae: sed de Spiritu sancto hoc negant credere, creaturam eum esse dicentes. Hos potius quidam Semiarianos vocant, quod in hac quæstione ex parte cum illis sint, ex parte nobiscum. Quanuis à nonnullis perhibeantur, non Deum, sed deitatem Patris & Filij dicere Spiritum sanctum, & nullam propriam habere substantiam.
units.tr: The Macedonians are so called from Macedonius, bishop of the Church of Constantinople. The Greeks also call them pneumatomachoi [πνευματομάχους?], because they quarrel about the Holy Spirit. They think rightly about the Father and the Son, that they are one and of the same substance or essence; but about the Holy Spirit they refuse to believe this, saying that he is a creature. Some call these people semi-Arians rather, because on this question they are partly with the Arians and partly with us. Although some report that they do not say the Holy Spirit is God, but the deity of the Father and the Son, and that he has no substance of his own.

units.la: Infelicis Arianorum stirpis infelix surculus Macedoniani, qui & sibi ipsis parum consentientes, & ab autore suo Ario diuersi, monstrum potius quàm hæresis fuisse videntur, vt ait Epiphanius, quòd partim ex Arianis, partim ex orthodoxis conflati fuerint. Dicti sunt autem varijs nominibus. Ac primum Macedoniani à Macedonio. Fuit autem Macedonius primùm artis plumariæ, deinde presbyter in Ecclesia Constantinopolitana, de-mum[?] factione Arianorum, qui omnia sub Cóstantio poterant, eiusdem Ecclesiæ creatus e-piscopus. Fuit autem alius Macedonius etiam Constantinopolitanus episcopus, sed posterior isto nostro, & vir pius sub Leone seniore impe-ratore, anno a Christo passo 484. qui Gangris exulauit propter orthodoxam fidem. Hic igi-tur, de quo nunc agimus, malis artibus eū gra-dum consequutus insolentissimè se gesit. Trux enim & sæuus in omnes qui ab eius confessio-ne dissentiebant, fuit, in quos magnas persequu-tiones excitauit, etiam immissis militibus, qui illos impune trucidarent, propter quas & suis & aliis etiam inuisus, maximeque propter com-motam ab eo in Paphlagonia seditionem, ab i-pso imperatore crudelis iudicatus, tandem de-positus, & in exilium actus est, vbi circa locum, qui Pylæ dicuntur (nec tamen eæ Pylæ quæ a Plinio libro 6. in Troglodytis collocantur) con-senuit, iustas suæ blasphemiæ luens pœnas. Socrates libr. 2. cap. 38. 4. cap. 20. Sozom. lib. 4. cap. 26. De quo eodem[?] traditur a Theodoreto libr. 2. hist. cap. 5. curasse vt Paulus, quem episco-patu Constantinopol. perfide deiecerat, & pri-mauerat, Cucuzi, vbi exulabat, strangulaaretur[?]. Vnde Suidas improbum & impium Macedonium vocat. Nam & manes siue ossa Constantini Magni effodit, vt in alium locum transfer-ret. Sozomen. lib. 4. cap. 21. Qua re maximè offensus est populus Constantinopolitanus. Appellati quoque sunt Marathonij a Marathonio presbytero, quem primum huius sectæ authorem, etiam ante Macedonium fuisse volunt. Socrat. libr. 2. cap. 45. item & Πνευματομάχοι[?] a dogmate[?], quòd aduersus Spiritus sancti deitatem pugnarent, quo nomine sunt notissimi, & ab E-piphanio vocantur. Denique quidam sentiunt eosdem sub Valentiniano Tropicos, à tropis, quibus essent nimium addicti, praeter veram Scripturæ mentem, nominatos. Coepit autem hæc hæresis non sub Felice Romano episcopo, vt Platina scribit, sed sub Iulio primo, & Constantio imperatore Constantini filio, circa annum à Christo passo 312. ex Arianæ fæcis cœno hausta. Socrat. lib.1.cap.8. Habuit autem summos sui erroris propugnatores, & Eleusium Cyzicenum episcopum, & Eustathium, Socrat. lib.2. cap.38, & 45. Successores etiam multos post ipsius damnationem, & presbyteros multos: paucos autem omnino episcopos habuit, propter varias difficultates. Vexata enim est & à Valente imperatore, qui quum eos mere Arianos esse putaret, agnouit sentire in quibusdam cum Homousianis, & orthodoxis: & postea à Nestorio quoque episcopo, & haeretico. Fuerunt autem Macedoniani in fidei suę confessione retinenda inconstantissimi. Quum enim primum cū Semiarianis & Acatianis consensissent, postea se Homousianis adiunxerunt. Socrat. libro 2. cap. 45. Deinde quum quidā ex iis Constantinopoli essent, imperatori Constantio gratiosi, se ab illis diuulserunt. Sed quū separatim à Valente & Arianis affligerentur, ad Homousianorum partes iterum redierunt. Socrates libro 4. cap.11. & libr.7.cap.3. Denique quum sub Gratiano imperatore libera esset cuiusuis erroris professio, iterum se ab Homousianis distraxerunt.Socrat.libr.5.cap.4.Sozomen. libro 7.cap. 7.tam nimirum varium est hominum hæretico-rum ingenium. Latissimè vero propagata est, in Hellesponto præsertim retenta propter Synodum Lampsacenam, qua confirmata est hæc hæ-refis. Est autem Lampsacus in sinu Hellesponti sita. Socrat.libr.4.cap.4. sed & in Phrygia Paca-tiana viguit. Durauit autem diutissimè etiā sub Arcadio imperatore Synadæ, quæ est urbs Phrygiæ, etiam postquam Synodo illa œcumenica, quæ secunda fuit, & Constantinopoli à Theodosio Magno collecta, gravissimus istius sectæ error damnatus est. Socrates libro 7.cap.3. & 31. cui Synodo Macedonius adversam valetudinem causatus adesse noluit: quum vocatus tamen à Synodo fuisset. Sozomen.libro 2. cap.39. Deni-que tempore Bernardi Clareuallens.abbatis re-novata est à quodam Abailardo theologo, ut i-pse scribit epist.190.
units.tr: The unhappy shoot of the unhappy Arian stock, the Macedonians, who, agreeing poorly even with themselves and differing from their author Arius, seem to have been a monster rather than a heresy, as Epiphanius says, because they were cobbled together partly from Arians and partly from the orthodox. They have been called by various names. First, the Macedonians, from Macedonius. Macedonius was first a featherworker, then a presbyter in the Church of Constantinople, and at last, through the faction of the Arians, who held all power under Constantius, was made bishop of the same Church. There was another Macedonius, also bishop of Constantinople, but later than our man, and a pious man under the elder emperor Leo, in the year 484 after Christ's passion, who went into exile at Gangra for the orthodox faith. This Macedonius, of whom we are now speaking, reached that rank by wicked arts and behaved most arrogantly. He was fierce and savage towards all who dissented from his confession, and he stirred up great persecutions against them, even sending in soldiers to slaughter them with impunity. For these things he was hated both by his own people and by others, and especially because of the sedition he stirred up in Paphlagonia. He was judged cruel by the emperor himself, finally deposed and sent into exile, where he wore out his life near the place called Pylae (not those Pylae which Pliny in book 6 places among the Troglodytes), paying the just penalty for his blasphemy. See Socrates, book 2, chapter 38; book 4, chapter 20; Sozomen, book 4, chapter 26. It is related of him by Theodoret, book 2 of the History, chapter 5, that he arranged for Paul, whom he had treacherously thrown out of the see of Constantinople and had first banished, to be strangled at Cucusus, where Paul was living in exile. Hence Suidas calls Macedonius a wicked and impious man. For he also dug up the remains or bones of Constantine the Great, to move them to another place (Sozomen, book 4, chapter 21), which especially offended the people of Constantinople. They were also called Marathonians, from the presbyter Marathonius, whom some think was the first author of this sect, even before Macedonius (Socrates, book 2, chapter 45). They were also called Pneumatomachoi [Πνευματομάχοι] from their doctrine, because they fought against the deity of the Holy Spirit; by this name they are very well known, and Epiphanius calls them so. Finally, some think that the same people under Valentinian were named Tropici, from the tropes to which they were too much addicted, beyond the true mind of Scripture. This heresy began, not under Felix, Roman bishop, as Platina writes, but under Julius I and the emperor Constantius, son of Constantine, around the year 312 after Christ's passion, drawn from the dregs of Arianism (Socrates, book 1, chapter 8). It had as its chief defenders of its error Eleusius, bishop of Cyzicus, and Eustathius (Socrates, book 2, chapters 38 and 45). It had many successors after its condemnation, and many elders, but altogether few bishops, because of various difficulties. It was harassed by the emperor Valens, who, thinking them plainly Arians, found that in some points they agreed with the Homoousians and the orthodox; and afterwards by Nestorius, also a bishop and a heretic. The Macedonians were most inconstant in holding to their confession of faith. For when at first they had agreed with the Semi-Arians and the Acacians, they afterwards joined themselves to the Homoousians (Socrates, book 2, chapter 45). Then, when some of them were at Constantinople and in favour with the emperor Constantius, they separated from those people. But when, cut off from Valens and the Arians, they were afflicted, they returned again to the side of the Homoousians (Socrates, book 4, chapter 11, and book 7, chapter 3). Finally, when under the emperor Gratian the profession of any error whatever was free, they again drew away from the Homoousians (Socrates, book 5, chapter 4; Sozomen, book 7, chapter 7). So indeed varied is the character of heretics. The sect spread most widely, and was held especially in the Hellespont, on account of the Synod of Lampsacus, by which this heresy was confirmed. Lampsacus lies on the bay of the Hellespont (Socrates, book 4, chapter 4). But it also flourished in Pacatian Phrygia. It also lasted for a very long time at Synada, a city of Phrygia, under the emperor Arcadius, even after that ecumenical synod, the second, gathered at Constantinople by Theodosius the Great, had condemned the most serious error of this sect (Socrates, book 7, chapters 3 and 31). Macedonius, pleading ill health, refused to attend that synod, although he had been summoned by it (Sozomen, book 2, chapter 39). Finally, in the time of Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, it was revived by a certain theologian, Abelard, as he himself writes in letter 190.

units.la: 2 Creaturam eum esse.) Mirum est quòd quū[?] ante Macedonium plures Spiritum sanctū crea-turam esse dixerint, hic tamen error Macedo-nio tanquam primo tribuatur authori. Cuius rei hæc fortasse ratio est, quòd eum & robustius defenderit, quanquam non à se primùm inven-tum: & hunc solum ex Arianorum deliriis præsertim retinuerit. Ergo hæc sunt Macedoniani-ci erroris capita, quæ ex Theodoreto lib.4. hæretic. fabulár. collegimus. 1 Filium Dei nō esse Patri ὁμοούσιον, sed ὁμοιούσιον. Sic enim leni unius litere interpositione non leuem tamen errorem regebat. Itaque Acatianis assentiens, Filium nō eiusdem cum Patre essentiæ, sed similis tantùm asseuerabat: sed latebat error, nisi deprehensus esset.Haec Theodoret. Quanquam Ruff.libr. in cap.25. scribit in articulo de Filij & Patris dei-tate, Macedonium idem nobiscum sensisse, id est,cum orthodoxis.Id autem falsum esse vel ex eo solo apparet, quod tunc tantum cum Homoufianis conciliati dicuntur Macedoniani, quum amplexi sunt orthodoxam de Patre & Filio ὁμοούσιον fidem. Alias enim ab iis dissentie-bant. Quod ipsum non diffitentur. Causam tamen suae innouationis afferunt Heteroufiano-rum, & Homoufianorum rixas & disputationes, vt refert Socrat. libro 3.cap. 10.
units.tr: 2 That he is a creature. It is remarkable that although many before Macedonius said the Holy Spirit is a creature, this error is nevertheless attributed to Macedonius as its first author. The reason for this is perhaps that he defended it more vigorously, although it was not first invented by him, and that he alone kept it especially from the ravings of the Arians. Therefore these are the heads of the Macedonian error, which we have gathered from Theodoret, book 4 of the Heretical Fables. 1. That the Son of God is not homoousios [ὁμοούσιον] with the Father, but homoiousios [ὁμοιούσιον]. For by the slight insertion of a single letter he maintained an error that was not slight. So, agreeing with the Acacians, he asserted that the Son is not of the same essence as the Father, but only like him. The error lay hidden, however, until it was detected. Thus Theodoret. Although Rufinus, in his book on chapter 25, writes that on the article about the deity of the Father and the Son, Macedonius thought the same as we do, that is, as the orthodox, this is false, and it appears so from this alone: the Macedonians are said to have been reconciled with the Homoousians only when they embraced the orthodox faith of the homoousion concerning the Father and the Son. For otherwise they dissented from them. They do not deny this. They attribute the cause of their innovation, however, to the quarrels and disputes between the Homoiousians and the Homoousians, as Socrates reports, book 3, chapter 10.

units.la: 2 Error.
units.tr: 2 Error.

units.la: Spiritum sanctum Deum esse negant, sed Dei tantum ministrum faciunt, qui etiam creatura sit, nec quidem aeterna. Itaque vim esse dicit a Deo conditam, quae essentiae diuisione in singulis rebus creatis insit, adeo vt singulae creatu-rae essentiae Spiritus sancti partem intra se ha-beant. Id quod Serucetus postea retinuit. Hic tam pestilens error & noxius etiam Lampsacena Synodo confirmatus est, vt scribit Socrates libro 4.cap.4. quia quod cap.4. Amos versu 13. scriptum extat, Ecce Deus creans spiritum, perperam interpretantur. Nam hoc loco vox πνεῦμα Graecis, & רוח[?] Ruach Hebraeis ventum, & aerem emotum significat, non autem Spiritum sanctum. Praeterea afferunt pro se quod Synodus Nicena nihil de Spiritus sancti ὁμοουσίᾳ cum Patre definiuit. Respondeo vero id antea cla-rissime Synodo Alexandrina constitutum suis-se, vt est in historia Ecclesiastica. Nec praeci-pue de eo contendebat Arius: sed tantum de Filio, de quo definitio Synodi idcirco necessaria fuit. Denique scribit Gregorius Magnus libro 9.epist.6. etiam suo seculo quosdam de Spiritu sancto tam inepte sensisse, ut eum crederent esse paruum quendam hominem montanum. Sic ex uno praecipitio in aliud trahit homines Satan hostis vaferrimus.
units.tr: They deny that the Holy Spirit is God, and make him only a minister of God, who is also a creature, and not even eternal. Thus he says the Spirit is a power created by God, which by division of essence inheres in each created thing, so that each creature has within itself a part of the essence of the Holy Spirit. Serveto later retained this same view. This pestilent and harmful error was also confirmed at the Synod of Lampsacus, as Socrates writes in book 4, chapter 4. They wrongly interpret Amos 4:13, where it is written, "Behold, he who creates the spirit": for in this place the Greek word πνεῦμα and the Hebrew רוח [Ruach] mean wind and air set in motion, not the Holy Spirit. Moreover, they allege in their favour that the Nicene Synod defined nothing about the consubstantiality [ὁμοουσία] of the Spirit with the Father. I reply that this had been most clearly settled earlier by the Synod of Alexandria, as is recorded in the Ecclesiastical History. Nor did Arius contend chiefly about this; his dispute was about the Son, and it was for that reason that the definition of the Synod was necessary. Finally, Gregory the Great writes in book 9, epistle 6, that even in his own age some thought so foolishly of the Holy Spirit that they believed him to be a small man living on a mountain. Thus the most crafty enemy, Satan, drags men from one precipice into another.

units.la: CAP. LIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER LIII.

units.la: Aeriani cur sic dicti. Erroris autem eorum capita recensentur quatuor.
units.tr: Why the Aerians are so called. Four heads of their error are listed.

units.la: Aeriani ab Ἀερίου[?] quodam sunt nominati, qui quum esset presbyter, docuisse fertur {2}quod Episcopus non posset ordinare, & in Arianorum haeresin lapsus, propria quoque dogmata addidisse nonnulla dicens, Orare vel offerre pro mortuis oblationem non oportere, nec statuta solenniter celebranda esse ieiunia: sed quum quisque voluerit, ieiunandum, ne videatur esse sub Lege. Dicebat etiam presbyterum ab Episcopo nulla differentia debere discerni. Quidam perhibent, istos, sicut Encratitas, vel Apotactitas non admittere ad communionem suam, nisi continentes, & eos qui seculo ita renuntiauerint, ut propria nulla possideant. {4}Ab esu tamen carnium non eos abstinere dicit Epiphanius. Philaster vero & hanc eis tribuit abstinentiam.
units.tr: The Aerians are so named from a certain Aerius [Ἀερίου?]. When he was an elder, he is said to have taught that a bishop could not ordain. Having fallen into the heresy of the Arians, he also added some doctrines of his own, saying that one should not pray for the dead or offer oblations for them, that fasts should not be observed by solemn statute, but that each person should fast when he wishes, lest he seem to be under the Law. He also said that an elder should not be distinguished from a bishop by any difference. Some report that these people, like the Encratites or Apotactites, did not admit to their communion anyone except the continent and those who had so renounced the world that they possessed no property. Epiphanius says, however, that they did not abstain from eating meat. Philaster, indeed, attributes this abstinence to them as well.

units.la: {1} Aeriani ab Aerio.) Aerius à quo deductum est Aerianorum nomen ( sunt enim alij Aeriani,alij vero Aetiani & dogmate,& paren-te) fuit primum Monachus cum Euftathio,qui Sebastiæ (quæ in Pontica Cappadocia sita est: nisi fortasse illa sit Sebastia Armeniæ, in qua natus est Atticus Constantinopolitanus episcopus, & de qua Socrates libro 6. cap. 20.) postea Episcopus creatus est, & Arianum dogma sequutus: quanquam cum orthodoxis & Nicæna Synodo primum sentiret, quemadmodum cum Epiphanio scribit Sozomen.lib.4.cap.29.
