Ergo ab Eustathio episcopo statim presbyter factus Aerius Ptochodocheio, id est, domui alendis excipiendisque pauperibus destinatæ (quam nos Galli, Dei domum, vel Hospitalium, quasi extraneorum hospitium vocamus) præficitur, cuius quum libera administrationem habere non posset propter Eustathij episcopi, qui totā pecuniarum Ecclesiasticarum οἰκονομίαν[?] & tractationem sibi vsurpabat, auaritiam, primum dissensiones & rixæ ortæ sunt: deinde contentiones grauissimæ: demum aperta odia & diuortia, & quæstiones natæ, de presbyterorum & episcoporum iure, & iurisdictionis vtriusque muneris finibus. Quæ ex malis illis initiis profectæ, primum offendicula pepererunt, postea vero schisma, denique hæresin effecerunt. Sed quæstio-nis est, vtrum Aeriani pro hæreticis sint habendi, an potius Eustathius ipse, & Eustathiani, qui videntur magna Antichristi tyrannidis fundamenta illo suo dogmate iecisse. Epiphanius quidem, Augustinus hic, & Augustini abbreuiator Isidorus, Aerianos hæreticorum albo, in eo quòd presbyteri & episcopi parem dignitatem constituerunt, ascripsere: sed quam recte ipsi viderint. Nam neque Theodoretus in haeretic. fab. 4. libris, nec tota historia Ecclesiastica Aerianorum tanquam haereticorum meminit, etsi ante Socratem, Sozomenum, Euagrium vixit Aerius, nempe sub Valentiniano primo imperatore. & Damaso Episcopo Romano, circa annum a Christo passo 340. & temporibus Epiphanij, ut ipse scribit: quae tamen eadem Eustathianos contemporaneos saepe commemorat inter haereticos, adeo ut a paucis Aerij sententia damnata videri posset. Ac certe si quis ea excipiat, quae cum Arianis de Christi deitate sensisse fingitur potius, quam probatur Aerius, nihil erit, quod iuste in illius dogmate meritoque reprehendas. Sed insolentes iam Episcopi, & imperitando magis quam pascendo gregi assuefacti, contra Petri praeceptum, 1. Petr. 5. vers. 3. tam liberas adversus suam superbiam, insolentiam, & tyrannidem voces ferre non poterant, & ita tum agebant quod Rom. Antichristus crudelius postea imitatus & exequutus est, ut haberent pro haereticis quicunque adversus eorum vitia, vel ordinis ipsorum peccata mutire auderent: quanquam illorum fastus & arrogantia iam Audeanis occasionem recedendi ab Ecclesia praebuisset. Itaque quum Aerianis nihil aliud impingere possent, affinxerunt eos cum Arianis sensisse, coiugia damnare. esu carnium omnino abstinere. Sed illud prius in Eustathianos, non autem in Aerianos dictum verum est. Agrestes homines etiam fuisse Aerianos, & in sylvis potius quam cum hominibus vitam transegisse. egisse,nimirum quia ab Episcopis vbique cœtu Ecclesiastico arcebatur, quòd in eorum mores improbos inueherentur[?]. Ergo hęc hominum se ęta & hæresis(si tamen hæresis est) circa annum 340. primùm innotuit. Dicti sunt autem nō tantum Aeriani, sed etiam Syllabici, quasi verba & syllabas studiosè captarent, sed vafrè, & contentiosè. Serpsit autem dogma ad plures, quemadmodum etiam Epiphanius annotauit. Imprimis in Ponto & Cappadocia viguerunt Aeriani: inde longius profecti, ad alias quoque Ecclesias peruenerunt. Citissimè vero suppressi sunt, quòd communi omnium episcoporum consensu oppugnabantur, qui tantam episcopalis suæ dignitatis maiestatem tolli aut imminui molestè patiebantur. Nam sunt constituti episcopi, non tantùm propter Nicænæ Synodi decreta de metropolitanis &Patriarchis,sed etiam propter ἀξιώματι[?], & vetustum morem iampridem in Ecclesia vsurpatum, presbyteris, imò verò presbyterio ipso toto tum gradu, tum etiam τάξει & ordine superiores,vt illi tanquam imperarent. Quæ fuit causa dissidij inter Chrysostomum & presbyteros.
units.tr: {1} The Aerians from Aerius.) Aerius, from whom the name of the Aerians is derived (for there are other Aerians, and others called Aetians, both in doctrine and in origin), was first a monk together with Eustathius. He was later made bishop of Sebaste, which lies in Pontic Cappadocia (unless perhaps it is that Sebaste of Armenia where Atticus, bishop of Constantinople, was born, and of which Socrates speaks in book 6, chapter 20). He followed the Arian doctrine, although at first he agreed with the orthodox and with the Nicene Synod, as Sozomen writes, following Epiphanius, book 4, chapter 29. So Aerius, made an elder at once by Bishop Eustathius, was placed in charge of the Ptochodocheium, that is, the house set aside for feeding and receiving the poor (which we in Gaul call the House of God, or hospital, as a lodging for strangers). Since he could not have free administration of it, because Bishop Eustathius, who claimed for himself the whole management and economy of the Church's money, was greedy, first disagreements and quarrels arose, then very serious contentions, and at last open hatreds and separations. Questions also arose about the rights of elders and bishops, and about the limits of each office's jurisdiction. These, springing from those evil beginnings, first produced stumbling-blocks, afterwards a schism, and finally a heresy. But it is a question whether the Aerians should be counted as heretics, or rather Eustathius himself and the Eustathians, who seem to have laid by that doctrine of theirs the great foundations of the tyranny of Antichrist. Epiphanius indeed, Augustine here, and Isidore, Augustine's abbreviator, enrolled the Aerians on the list of heretics because they held that elders and bishops have equal dignity. But how rightly they judged this, let them see. For neither Theodoret in his Heretical Fables, book 4, nor the whole Ecclesiastical History mentions the Aerians as heretics, although Aerius lived before Socrates, Sozomen and Evagrius, namely under the emperor Valentinian I and Damasus, Bishop of Rome, about the year 340 after the passion of Christ, and in the times of Epiphanius, as he himself writes. Yet these same writers often mention the contemporary Eustathians among the heretics, so that the opinion of Aerius could seem to have been condemned by few. And certainly, if one excludes those views which Aerius is pretended, rather than proved, to have held with the Arians about the deity of Christ, there will be nothing in his doctrine that you can justly and rightly censure. But the bishops, already insolent and more accustomed to lord it over the flock than to feed it, contrary to the command of Peter (1 Pet. 5:3), could not bear such free words against their pride, insolence and tyranny. So they acted in the way that the Roman Antichrist later imitated and carried out more cruelly, namely, they regarded as heretics all who dared to murmur against their faults or the sins of their order. Although the pride and arrogance of those men had already given the Audeans an occasion to withdraw from the Church, so when they could allege nothing else against the Aerians, they pinned on them the charge that they agreed with the Arians in condemning marriage and abstaining altogether from eating meat. But that charge was true of the Eustathians, not of the Aerians. The Aerians are also said to have been rustic people who spent their life in the woods rather than among men, namely because they were everywhere excluded from ecclesiastical assembly by the bishops, who attacked their wicked customs. So this sect, and the heresy (if indeed it is a heresy), first became known about the year 340. They were called not only Aerians but also Syllabici, as if they eagerly caught at words and syllables, but cunningly and contentiously. The doctrine spread to many people, as Epiphanius also observed. The Aerians flourished especially in Pontus and Cappadocia, and from there, spreading further, they reached other churches too. But they were suppressed very quickly, because they were opposed by the common consent of all the bishops, who were grieved that the majesty of their episcopal dignity should be removed or diminished. For bishops were established not only by the decrees of the Nicene Synod concerning metropolitans and patriarchs, but also on account of their rank and the ancient custom long since used in the Church, so that they should be superior to the elders, indeed to the whole eldership, both in grade and in order and arrangement, as if they were to command them. This was the cause of the dispute between Chrysostom and the elders.

units.la: 2 Quòd episcopus. Hæc ferè sunt erroris qui ab Episcopis tribuitur Aerianis, capita.
units.tr: 2 That the bishop. These are more or less the heads of the error which the bishops attribute to the Aerians.

units.la: 1 Presbyterum ab Episcopo ordine & gradu (τάξει & ἀξιώματι, dixit Aerius) non differre: sed qui presbyter est, episcopum dici,quatenus in vno aliquo actu, in quo ab presbyterio electus est,præest coetui,quia in Ecclesia nihil consusè fieri geríve debet. Ex quo fit vt per vices præsidentes presbyteri, sint omnes Episcopi. Quæ sententia cur damnari debeat, non video. Primum enim eosdem presbyteros & episcopos esse agnoscit sacra Scriptura, nec eos distinguit, aut hos illis præfert, sed in commune vocat omnes eos ἡγουμένους[?]. Heb.13.v.7. Act.20.v.17. & 12. Nam presbyterum esse nihil aliud est, ait Petrus, quàm ἐπισκοπὴν[?].1.Petr.5.vers.1, & 3:1.Timoth.3. Unde & Hieronymus ad Tit. cap.1. & in epistola ad Euagr. scribit id non iure diuino, sed tantum hominum consuetudine & metu schismatis factum, ut e pluribus presbyteris unus crearetur Episcopus. De quo ipso anxiè Canonistæ disputant in cano. Legimus, distinct. 90. & cano. Olim presbyter, distinct. 93. Sed & scho lastici quoque veluti Durandus in libr. 4. Sententiarum distinct. 24. quæst. 5. vbi sacerdotali, quam ait cum episcopali eandem esse, nullam dignitatem maiorem à Christo esse institutam docet. Epiphanius ipse hæref.68.de Meletianis ita scribit. ἡ γὰρ Ἀλεξανδρείᾳ δύο ἐπισκόπους εἶχεν, ὡς αἱ ἄλλαι πόλεις[?]. adeo vt hoc discrimen & hæc prælatio vnius in Alexandrina ciuitate primùm nata fuisse videatur, ex qua vrbe etiam Monastica vita & variæ Ecclesiæ pestes ortæ sunt. Et quas hoc loco rationes affert Epiphanius contra Aerianos eæ sunt prorsus inanes. Denique Irenæus Pium & Higinum episcopos Romanos vocat presbyteros, & Eusb.lib.5.cap.26. Quanta verò huius episcopalis dignitatis & prostasiæ incommoda percepta fuerint, quia præter Dei verbum in Ecclesiam inducta est, rerum euentus docuit, & declarauit postea Synodus Carpetoratensis sub Leone. Epiphanius ipse tandem coactus con-cedit [?]cedit haric distinctione inter episcopos & pref-byteros tempore & seculo Apostolorum nondum fuisse, quasi vero in regenda Ecclesia postea rinofque ipsi iis sapientiores fimus.
units.tr: 1 That an elder does not differ from a bishop in order and rank (Aerius said τάξει and ἀξιώματι), but he who is an elder is called a bishop insofar as, in some one act for which he was chosen by the eldership, he presides over the assembly, since nothing in the Church ought to be done in confusion. From this it follows that elders presiding in turn are all bishops. I do not see why this opinion ought to be condemned. For first, holy Scripture acknowledges that elders and bishops are the same, and it does not distinguish them or set one above the other, but calls all of them rulers [ἡγουμένους] in common (Heb. 13:7; Acts 20:17, and 12). For to be an elder is nothing other, says Peter, than to be an overseer [ἐπισκοπήν] (1 Pet. 5:1, 3; 1 Tim. 3). Hence Jerome also, on Titus chapter 1 and in his letter to Evagrius, writes that it was done not by divine right but only by human custom and fear of schism, that one bishop should be created from among many elders. The canonists dispute anxiously about this very point in the canons: "We read," dist. 90, and the canon "Olim presbyter," dist. 93. But the schoolmen too, such as Durandus in book 4 of the Sentences, dist. 24, question 5, where he teaches that the priestly office, which he says is the same as the episcopal, was instituted by Christ with no greater dignity. Epiphanius himself, in heresy 68, on the Meletians, writes thus: "For Alexandria had two bishops, as the other cities did." So this distinction, and this preeminence of one bishop in the city of Alexandria, seems to have first arisen there, from which city monastic life and various plagues of the Church also came. And the reasons Epiphanius brings forward here against the Aerians are altogether empty. Finally, Irenaeus calls the Roman bishops Pius and Hyginus elders, and Eusebius (book 5, chapter 26) says so too. How great the inconveniences of this episcopal dignity and preeminence were, since it was introduced beyond the word of God, the outcome of events has shown, and the later Synod of Carpentras under Leo declared it. Epiphanius himself, finally compelled, concedes that this distinction between bishops and elders did not exist in the time and age of the Apostles. As if, indeed, we were wiser than they in governing the Church later on!

units.la: 2 Preces pro defunctis non esse fundendas & faciendas', quia huiusmodi nostris suffragiis nequeant iuvari. Hoc cur Christiani non admittant, non video, quando Papistae ipsi genus hominis su-perstitiosissimum, etiam de ea re diuersas Patrũ Ecclesiasticorum sententias annotarint, vt est in Can. Quibus peccata. & Can. In praesenti. Can. Tempus, 13. quaest. 2. & Epiphanius hoc loco negat aperte verbo Dei fundari & niti huiusmodi pro mortuis conceptas preces, sed tantum more & traditione quadam maiorum. At quicquid sine fide fit, peccatum est, Rom. 14. versu 23.
units.tr: 2 Prayers for the dead should not be poured out and made, because they cannot be helped by our suffrages. I do not see why Christians should not admit this, when the Papists themselves, a most superstitious race, have noted the diverse opinions of the Church Fathers on this very matter, as in the canons "Quibus peccata," "In praesenti," and "Tempus," 13 q. 2. And Epiphanius here plainly denies that prayers conceived in this way for the dead are founded on and rest upon the word of God, but only on a certain custom and tradition of forefathers. But whatever is done without faith is sin (Rom. 14:23).

units.la: 3 Certis statutisque annuatim diebus & solemnibus ieiunia non praefigenda & alliganda, quale erat ieiunium quadragesimale, & septimanae quae Pascha praecederet. Esse enim hoc totum ieiuniorum anniuersariorum genus Christianis hominibus & fugiendum, & superstitiosum, & in usum veteres de ieiunio septimi mensis, ceremonias reuocare. Quod verum certe quidem est. Ieiuniorum igitur vsum non damnant Aeriani (in quo ipso sane damnandi essent) sed illam tantum de certis diebus anniuersariis obseruationem, quae superstitionem dierum a Paulo damnatam non tantum sapit, sed retinet, Rom. 14. Hoc caput cur improbari potuerit, nulla ratio est, siquam ex Dei verbo quaerimus, unde peti debet.
units.tr: 3 Fixed and appointed fasts on certain yearly days and solemn occasions, not to be prescribed and bound, such as the Lenten fast and the week that precedes Easter. For all this kind of yearly fasting is to be shunned by Christians as superstitious, and it recalls the old ceremonies about the fast of the seventh month. This is certainly true. The Aerians, then, do not condemn the practice of fasting (in which very thing they would deserve condemnation), but only that observance of fixed yearly days, which not only smacks of the superstition of days condemned by Paul but actually retains it (Rom. 14). There is no reason why this chapter could have been disapproved, if we seek it from the word of God, where it ought to be sought.

units.la: 4 Nullum inter Christianos esse restare ve Pascha quod sit peragendum & celcbrandum. Quam suam sententiam authoritate Pauli confirmant,1. Corinth.5.7.Ait enim Paulus, Pascha nostrum immolatum est, Christus. Ergo non restat sacrificandum. Quod si obseruetur Pascha iterum,& ad legales ceremonias reuoluimur, & Christum in carne aduenisse negemus necesse est, simúsque,vt ait Ioannes,Antichristi. Quare nec hæc ipsa Aerianorum sententia damnari debuit, quia vera est,& manifestissime inter Coenā Domini &Pascha distinguendum esse docet. Quæ de inducta carnium abstinentia,& coniugiis ab iisdem improbatis,de Arianorum approbatione,episcopi addunt,reponuntque inter Aerianæ hæreseos hypotheses, si vera sunt, certe errarunt Ariani:sin minus (& mihi quidem ex hac ipsa Augustini oratione & titubatione,qui totum hoc dubium esse scribit, prorsus in eos calumniæ causa commentitia & confi&ta videntur)ex hæreticorum numero Aerianos eximemus: & inter schismaticos potius habebimus, si bene constitutū Ecclesiæ ordine temerè perturbare sunt conati.Quod tamen ab iis factum fuisse hactenus non apparet. Quare hos inter hæreticos minimè notauimus.
units.tr: 4 Among Christians there is no Passover remaining to be carried out and celebrated. The Aerians confirm this view by the authority of Paul, 1 Cor. 5:7. For Paul says: "Our Passover, Christ, has been sacrificed." Therefore nothing remains to be sacrificed. But if the Passover is observed again, and we return to the legal ceremonies, and we must deny that Christ has come in the flesh, and so, as John says, we are Antichrists. Wherefore this very opinion of the Aerians ought not to have been condemned, since it is true, and it clearly teaches that the Lord's Supper and the Passover are to be distinguished. As for what the bishops add about the introduced abstinence from meats and the marriages disapproved by the same men, and the approval of the Aerians, and what they place among the hypotheses of the Aerian heresy: if these things are true, then the Arians certainly erred; but if not (and to me, from this very discourse and hesitation of Augustine, who writes that the whole matter is doubtful, they seem entirely invented and fabricated against them for the sake of calumny), we will exclude the Aerians from the number of heretics, and we will rather count them among the schismatics, if they have attempted to disturb rashly the well-established order of the Church. Yet it does not appear so far that this has been done by them. Wherefore we have not marked these men among the heretics at all.

units.la: 3 Non potest ordinari.) Alibi Ordinare,alibi Ordinari.vtrunque constare potest.
units.tr: Non potest ordinari.) Elsewhere "Ordinare," elsewhere "Ordinari"; either reading can stand.

units.la: CAP. LIIII.
units.tr: CHAP. LIIII.

units.la: Aetiani & Eunomiani, cur sic dicti. Erroris autem eorum capita duo referuntur.
units.tr: The Aetians and Eunomians: why they were so called. Two heads of their error are reported.

units.la: Etiani ab Aetio {1} fuerunt vocati: idemque Eunomiani ab {2} Eunomio Aetij discipulo, quo nomine magis innotuerunt. Eunomius quippe in Dialectica praevalens, acutius & celebrius defendit hanc haeresin. Dissimilem per omnia Patri afferens Filium, & Filio Spiritum sanctum. Fertur etiam usque adeo fuisse bonis moribus inimicus, ut asseveraret, quod nihil cuiquam obesset quorumlibet perpetratio, ac perseverantia peccatorum, si huius, quae ab illo docebatur, fidei particeps esset.
units.tr: The Etians were called after Aetius, and the same people were called Eunomians after Eunomius, a disciple of Aetius, a name by which they became better known. Eunomius, being outstanding in dialectic, defended this heresy more sharply and more famously. He asserted that the Son is in every respect unlike the Father, and the Holy Spirit unlike the Son. He is also said to have been so hostile to good morals that he maintained that the commission and persistence of any sins whatever did no harm to anyone who shared in the faith he taught.

units.la: Haec una & eadem dogma-te quidem secta & haeresis, variis tamen nomi-nibus propter successores est appellata. Dicti sunt enim hi qui Christum Filium Dei Patri Deo non tantum ἑτερούσιον, sed κατὰ πάντα ἀνόμοιον esse docuerunt, Anomij, Anomoei, & Anomiani, quae tres voces idem significant. Sozom.libr. 3.cap.10. Ab authoribus autem & propugnatoribus suis iidem nominantur Aetiani, Eunomiani, Eudoxiani, Theophroniani, atq; etiam postquam imperatoris Theodosij Magni edicto ur-bibus omnibus in deserta & solitudines expul-si, ut scribit Sozomen.libr.6.cap.26. in cavernis & privatis aedibus clàm conueniebant Troglo-dytæ, id quod tradit Theodor.libr.4. hæret.fab.
units.tr: This one sect and heresy, one and the same in doctrine, was called by various names because of its successors. Those who taught that Christ the Son of God is not only of a different substance (heterousion [ἑτερούσιον]) from God the Father but in all respects unlike him (kata panta anomoion [κατὰ πάντα ἀνόμοιον]) were called Anomians, Anomoeans and Anomeans; these three names mean the same thing. Sozomen, book 3, chapter 10. But from their authors and champions they were also called Aetians, Eunomians, Eudoxians and Theophronians. Even after the edict of the emperor Theodosius the Great had expelled them from all the cities into deserts and solitudes, they gathered secretly in caves and private houses, and so were called Troglodytes, as Theodoret reports in book 4 of his Heretical Fables. Sozomen, book 6, chapter 26.

units.la: Denique Gothici, quòd Gothorū magna pars hunc errorem propter Ulphillam ipsorum Episcopum sequuta est. Sozomen. libr. 6. cap. 37. His igitur tot nominibus ad impiissimam eorum blasphemiam describendam & detestandam, haec haeresis vocata est, ut ait Socrates libr. 2. cap. 35. Sozomen. libr. 6. cap. 26. Fuit autem infelicis Arianorum fontis amarissimus & turbidissimus riuus, qui foetido eorum coeno maiores etiam sordes adiecit. Nam Arianorum immanes iam furores ipsa tamen auxit & locupletauit, quemadmodum libr. 2. histor. cap. 24. scribit Theodoret. Unde Aetius Ario successisse dicitur à Ruffino libr. 1. cap. 25. non tantum quòd eo mortuo impietate ipsius defendit, sed quòd eam propagauit, & tetriorem reddidit. Haec enim est successio haereticorum, nimirum erroris accepti amplificatio. Quo vero tempore primum coeperit, anceps & dubia est authorum sententia, quando nec in Aetij nomine, neque quot Aetij Ariani fuerint inter se consentiunt. Nam in eo aperte Suidas in voce Αἴτιος[?] ab Indicatio haeref. quae est in histor. Eccles. dissentit. Ergo alij sub Constantino hanc haeresin exortam & natam volunt, alij sub Constantio Constantini filio, & Felice Rom. episcopo, ut & Socrat. libr. 4. cap. 11. & Platina. Verior tamen mihi videtur eorum sententia, qui natam sub eodem quidem Constantio primum fuisse tradunt, Constante fratre iam mortuo, & ipso Constantio propterea audaciore, & ad alendas Arianorum haereses propensiore, sed sub Liberio Rom. episcopo, circa annum à Christo passo 325. non sub Felice. lice. Certè posterior fuit quàm Ariana, magisque displicuit. Unde & Constantinopoli statim atque emergere cœpit, Synodus congregata est, quæ eam damnauit, ut scribit Theodoret. libro 2. histor. cap. 28. Nec quum reliquæ hæreses templa sua habere permitterentur, hæc tamen sua retinere concessa est, ut Socrat. libr. 5. cap. 2. scribit. Sed & Seleucianam etiam Synodum propter hunc ipsum errorem præcipuè à Constantio conuocatam scribit quidem Sozomen. libro 3. cap. 19. quanquam nondum vulgò Aetij nomen auditum in Ecclesia erat, ut parum rationem temporis obseruasse videri eo loco posset Sozomen. quando ex Acatianis Aetianos istos o[?] os, idem ipse alibi tradit, nempe libr. 4. cap. {y}. qui in Seleuciana Synodo primùm extiterunt, seque prodiderunt. Latè verò sparsum est hoc venenum, quia multi iam propter varias hæreses, imprimis autem Arianismum, quem Satan inter Christianos valde plausibilem effecerat, vel à vera fide defecerant, vel in ea nutabant, ut levi impulsu facilè de vera confessione deiicerentur. Itaque etiam qui hanc hæresin sectabantur Constantinopolitani Episcopi creasunt, quemadmodum Eudoxius: & nisi Eunomius præter consilium Eudoxij & sociorum intempestiuè se suáque prodidisset, vniuersum pene terrarum orbem erat infectura. Sed à Constantio ipso etiam Arianis æquo exilio multata est, tantúsque istius blasphemiæ horror inuasit, ut Aetius ipsius author non tantùm hæreticus: sed apertè & passim etiam ἄθεος dicerētur: hæcq; ratione impulsus Imperator edicto vel ὁμοούσιον
units.tr: Lastly, the Goths, because a great part of the Gothic people followed this error on account of Ulfilas, their bishop (Sozomen, book 6, chapter 37). To describe and detest their most impious blasphemy, this heresy was called by so many names, as Socrates says (book 2, chapter 35; see also Sozomen, book 6, chapter 26). It was the most bitter and muddy stream from the unhappy fountain of the Arians, and it added greater filth to their foul mud. For it increased and enriched the already monstrous furies of the Arians, as Theodoret writes (Histories, book 2, chapter 24). Whence Rufinus (book 1, chapter 25) says that Aetius succeeded Arius, not only because after Arius's death he defended his impiety, but because he spread it and made it more hideous. For this is how heresies succeed one another: the error received is amplified. But at what time it first began, the authors' opinions are uncertain and doubtful, since they do not agree about the name of Aetius or about how many Aetiuses there were among the Arians. In this matter Suidas, under the word Aetius, plainly disagrees with the Indicatio haereseon in the Ecclesiastical History. Some therefore hold that this heresy arose and was born under Constantine, others under Constantius, Constantine's son, and Felix, bishop of Rome, as Socrates (book 4, chapter 11) and Platina also say. Yet the view of those seems more true to me who report that it first arose under the same Constantius, after his brother Constans had died, and that Constantius was therefore bolder and more inclined to nourish the Arian heresies; but that it arose under Liberius, bishop of Rome, about the year 325 after the passion of Christ, not under Felix. Certainly it was later than the Arian heresy and was more displeasing. Hence also at Constantinople, as soon as it began to emerge, a synod was gathered which condemned it, as Theodoret writes (Histories, book 2, chapter 28). And although other heresies were allowed to have their own churches, this one was not granted the right to keep its own, as Socrates writes (book 5, chapter 2). Sozomen also writes (book 3, chapter 19) that the Synod of Seleucia was convened by Constantius chiefly because of this same error, though the name of Aetius was not yet commonly heard in the Church. So Sozomen seems to have paid little attention to chronology in that place, since he himself says elsewhere (book 4, chapter {y}) that these Aetians arose from the Acacians and first revealed themselves at the Synod of Seleucia. This poison spread widely because many had already fallen away from the true faith, or wavered in it, on account of various heresies, above all Arianism, which Satan had made very plausible among Christians, so that with a light push they were easily cast down from the true confession. Thus even those who followed this heresy set up bishops of Constantinople, such as Eudoxius; and unless Eunomius, against the plan of Eudoxius and his associates, had untimely revealed himself and his party, it would have infected almost the whole world. But Constantius punished even the Arians with exile, and such horror of this blasphemy seized him that Aetius, its author, was called not only a heretic but openly and everywhere even an atheist [ἄθεος]. Moved by this, the emperor by edict strictly forbade that either homoousion [ὁμοούσιον]

units.la: {y} ... vel ἐπιτρόπῳ[?] in docendo nominari & usurpari seuerisimè vetuerit. Theodoret.libr.2. Hist.cap. 27. Unde longius progredi prohibita, & ipso Aetianorum nomine damnata, nouis tamen & interpolatis Eunomaniorum, & Eudoxianorū appellationibus retenta, & velut crambe recocta reposita est, tam est in se simulando Satan astutus artifex. Asia igitur quæ minor est, imprimis item à Tauro monte ad Hellespontum, Cappadocia, Paphlagonia, & Cilicia, unà cum Constantinopolitano tractu hac peste grauissimè laborauit, Sozomen.lib.6.cap.27. quæ Basilij Magni, & Gregorij Nazianzeni eruditissimis disputationibus, tanquam salubribus medicamentis, non tam sanata prorsus est, quàm ad tempus repressa. Hic autem Aetius tanti mali seminator patre Georgio milite natus est Antiochiæ, unde Syrus dictus non Cilix, vt Epiphanius tamen putat, sed eum refutat Sozom. lib.6. cap.26. alius ab Alexandrino & Ægyptio, quem refert Suidas etiam Arianam hærefin amplexum esse. Propter summam autem paupertatem hic noster primum χρυσοχοΐαν[?], vt omnes tradunt, exercuit, deinde Paulino Antiocheno Episcopo defuncto, spem adipiscendi aliquando Episcopatus magna animi ambitione & ingenij confidentia concipiens se Leontio Paulini successori adiunxit, à quo Diaconus Ecclesiæ factus, non autem à Georgio Alexandrino Episcopo (in quo hallucinatur Epiphanius, vt ex Suida facile intelligi potest. Nam duos Aetios confundit Epiphanius) inepta quædam & blasphema contra Christum Dei filium euomere[?] cœpit, Socrat.lib.2.cap.37. Sozomen.lib.4.cap. 12. sed à Flauiano & Diodoro monachis deprehensus & refutatus, tandem à Leontio gradu Ecclesiastico deiectus est, & vrbe pulsus. Hinc vero iratior & commotior Anazarbum (quae est vrbs superioris Tracheae Ciliciae, vt scribit Plinius) concessit, vbi nugator iste & praestigiator Sophisticis dialecticorum, & Aristotelis praesertim Elenchis, non autem Euangelicis scriptis operam dedit, itemque Geometricis studiis, vt cum Epiphanio Socrat.lib.2.cap.35.& Indicat.haeref. tradunt, tandemque sibi visus ad argutandum instructior, iterum prodiit, & nouum hoc suum certe insanum, & plane blasphemum in Christum Dominum nostrum aeternum Deum, aeterni Patris filium dogma cudit. Quod cum summe impium & adhuc nulli alij errori iam noto simile vel conferendum omnes iudicarent, ἄθεος[?] dictus est. Tandem cum magis magisque inualesceret, in exilium pulsus est Ae-tius, etiam à Constantio Imperatore, & in vastas & montosas Phrygiae solitudines relegatus ibi fredebat[?], atque consenescebat: sed in odium Christianorum à Iuliano Imperatore & apostata reuocatus mire suo illo veneno Ecclesiam afflixit, Theodoret.lib.2.Histor.cap.27.Sozom. lib.5.cap.5. Nam etiam schedium pro suo errore tuendo publicauit, quod descripsit Epiphan. & refutauit.
units.tr: {y} ... or [ἐπιτρόπῳ] be named or used in teaching (Theodoret, Histories, book 2, chapter 27). Hence the name was forbidden to go further, and the very name of the Aetians was condemned. Yet it was kept under new and altered names of the Eunomians and Eudoxians, and, like cabbage reheated, was served again. So crafty is Satan, the artist of disguise. Asia Minor, especially the region from the Taurus mountain to the Hellespont, along with Cappadocia, Paphlagonia and Cilicia, together with the district of Constantinople, suffered most severely from this plague (Sozomen, book 6, chapter 27). It was not so much cured as held back for a time by the most learned disputations of Basil the Great and Gregory Nazianzen, as by healthful medicines. Now this Aetius, the sower of so great an evil, was born at Antioch, the son of the soldier George, and was therefore called a Syrian, not a Cilician, as Epiphanius nevertheless thinks; but Sozomen refutes this (book 6, chapter 26). Another Aetius, from Alexandria and Egypt, whom Suidas also mentions, is said to have embraced the Arian heresy. Because of his extreme poverty, our man first practised goldsmithing, as all report. Then, when Paulinus, bishop of Antioch, died, he conceived the hope of one day obtaining the episcopate, with great ambition and self-confidence, and attached himself to Leontius, Paulinus's successor. Made a deacon of the Church by Leontius, not by George, bishop of Alexandria (here Epiphanius is mistaken, as can easily be understood from Suidas, for Epiphanius confuses two Aetiuses), he began to spew forth silly and blasphemous things against Christ, the Son of God (Socrates, book 2, chapter 37; Sozomen, book 4, chapter 12). But he was detected and refuted by the monks Flavian and Diodorus, and at last was deprived of his ecclesiastical rank by Leontius and driven from the city. Then, more angry and agitated, he withdrew to Anazarbus (a city of Upper Tracheia in Cilicia, as Pliny writes), where this trifler and juggler devoted himself to the sophistries of the dialecticians, especially Aristotle's Elenchi, and not to the Gospel writings; he also applied himself to geometry. So Epiphanius, Socrates (book 2, chapter 35) and the Indicatio haereseon report. At length, seeming to himself better equipped for disputing, he came forth again and coined this new dogma of his, certainly mad and altogether blasphemous against Christ our Lord, the eternal God, the eternal Son of the Father. Since everyone judged it most impious and not comparable to any other error hitherto known, he was called an atheist [ἄθεος]. At last, as it gained more and more strength, Aetius was driven into exile, even by the Emperor Constantius, and was relegated to the vast and mountainous wilds of Phrygia, where he lived in misery and grew old. But Julian the Emperor and apostate recalled him, out of hatred of the Christians, and he afflicted the Church with his peculiar poison (Theodoret, Histories, book 2, chapter 27; Sozomen, book 5, chapter 5). For he also published a pamphlet in defence of his error, which Epiphanius described and refuted.

units.la: Hic Aetio successit, qui nomen superioris sectae mutauit, virus tamen & dogma retinuit. Itaque ab hoc Eunomiani dicti sunt, qui videntur primùm hac appellatione noti sub Constantio Imperatore atque Liberio Episcopo Roman. anno à Christo passo 331. Fuit autem Eunomius è Dacora urbe, quae sita est in agro Argaeno à monte Argaeo nominato, qui extra Cappadociam est ad Euphratem prope Mazacam siue Caesaream, vt scribit Plinius lib.6. cap.3. Hic primum Aetij scriba & amanuensis, vt Suidas narrat, postea haeresiarcha, demum Cyzici episcopus opera Eudoxij factus est, Aetio praeceptori absenti gnauiter operam nauans, qui propter hunc animi errorem & fidei corruptelam à se late sparsam, propagatamque Leprosus dictus est. Post hunc in schola successit, nomenq; habuit Theophronius quidam Cappadox, deinde Eutychius. A quibus Eunomiani in duo iam diuortia ex eodē fonte se diduxerunt. Eorum enim alij Theophroniani, alij vero Eunomeutychiani nominari coepe-runt, Sozomen. lib.6.cap.17.& 26. Demum in exilium actus à Constantio Eunomius in Pamphyliae solitudine miseram & infœlicem vitam & animam iustas suae blasphemiae poenas pendens traxit, sub Valente mortuus. Hic Aetianorum etiam furores auxit, quibus tamen nihil addi videbatur posse, fuitque πολυγραφώτατος [?], vt Epiphanius tradit. Eudoxius vero ex Germanicia Syriae ciuitate fuit.
units.tr: Aetius was succeeded by one who changed the name of the earlier sect but kept its poison and doctrine. Hence those who were called Eunomians, who first appear under this name in the time of the Emperor Constantius and Liberius, bishop of Rome, about the year 331 after the passion of Christ. Eunomius was from the city of Dacora, which lies in the Argaean district, named after Mount Argaeus, outside Cappadocia, near the Euphrates, close to Mazaca or Caesarea, as Pliny writes (book 6, chapter 3). He was first Aetius's secretary and amanuensis, as Suidas relates; afterwards he became the founder of a heresy, and at last was made bishop of Cyzicus through the efforts of Eudoxius, zealously serving his absent teacher Aetius. For this corruption of mind and faith, which he spread widely, he was called a leper. After him, a certain Theophronius of Cappadocia succeeded in the school, and then Eutychius. Under them the Eunomians, from the same source, split into two parties: some began to be called Theophronians, others Eunomeutychians (Sozomen, book 6, chapters 17 and 26). Finally, Eunomius was driven into exile by Constantius and, living in the solitude of Pamphylia, dragged out a wretched and unhappy life, paying the just penalty for his blasphemy in his soul. He died under Valens. He increased the furies of the Aetians, though nothing seemed able to be added to them, and he was extremely prolific as a writer, as Epiphanius reports. Eudoxius, however, was from Germanicia, a city of Syria.

units.la: 3 Dissimilem per omnia). Variae fuerunt superiorum haereticorum hypotheses, quae ex variis scriptoribus à nobis collectae recensebuntur. 1 Deum à nobis plenè perfecteque comprehendi posse, qualis quantusque in se est, contendunt. Atqui Paulus 1.Tim.6. verf.16. aliud docet, eum nempe lucem inaccessam habitare. Nec cuiquam nisi sibi ipsi & soli comprehensibilem Deum esse, satis tritum est dogma in Christianorum scholis, Theodoret. & Ioan.Damascen.lib.1.De Orthodo.fide.cap.13. in Græco. 2 Filium Dei esse Patri Deo in omnibus dissimilem. Nam esse volunt creatura Patris ab eo ex superueniente voluntate procreatam. Itaque nec essentia, nec potestate, nec voluntate parem, ac ne similem quidem esse Patri Deo. In quo longè peius de Christi deitate isti sentiunt, quàm qui eum tantum Patri ὑπερ-οὐσίου [?] i.diuersæ essentiæ dixerunt: in reliquis enim attributis Heterousij hæretici tamen similem esse concedunt. Præcipuum autem Aetij argumentum totum in argutiola quadam positum erat, vt & Augustin. lib.5. de Trinit.cap.20. & Lombard. lib.1.distinct.6.cap.1. referunt, & ante vtrunque Basilius & Epipha.hac nempe, quòd cum ἀγέννητον [?] sit γεννητῷ ὁμοίον: Pater autem sit ἀγέννητος, id est, ingenitus: Filius vero γεννητὸς .i. genitus, Filium Patri dissimilem esse oporteat. Ad quod pene vnicum Aetij argumentum breui quidem, sed tamen verissima solutione respondet Basilius, Ἀγέννητος [?] ... τῆς ὑπάρξεως [?], id est, Genitum & ingenitu non diuersam essentiam, sed diuersum tantùm existentiæ modum significant. Rem vero exemplo doceo ex Augustino & Damasceno. Adam enim ἀγέννητος [?] dici potest, quia primus homo est à nullo patre genitus: Seth autem γεννητὸς, quia est ex Adamo: nō tamen est propterea diuersa Sethi & Adami natura & essentia. Imo vterque verus homo, eiusdemque naturae, Genef.5.v.3.quan-quam diverso modo ea natura in Adamo extitit, diverso vero in Setho, qui ab eo genitus fuit. Hoc Aetij argumentum regerunt nobis millies Servetani, Syluanistae & Neariani nostri temporis. 3 Spiritum sanctum a Filio creatum fabricatumque esse contendunt Aetiani. Itaque negant esse αὐτοσύστατον. i. propriae naturae & essentiae vi esse & vivere, sed esse Filij, & ut ipse loquebatur Μονογενὲς ὑπόστασιν tantum. Basil.libro 2.contra Eunomi.& lib.3. Theodoret.& Epiphan. 4 Rebaptizant etiam ab orthodoxis baptizatos. Quod non fuit Aetij, sed Eunomij iam exulis commentum & dogma, quod Eunomiani postea secuti sunt atque retinuerunt. Sozomen.lib.6.cap.26.& Epiphan. 5 Baptismum a Domino nostro Iesu Christo institutum non tantum corrumpunt, sed mutat. Primum enim superiores tantum hominis partes baptizandas putant, inferiores autem putant indignas tanto sacramento. Itaque baptizandos fascijs infra umbilicum involuunt, ne ulterius aqua fluat. Baptizant autem alia quam Christus docuit, forma, nempe sic, εἰς ὄνομα Θεοῦ κτισμένου[?], ἢ πνεύματος ἁγιαστικοῦ ἢ υἱοῦ κτισμένου ἢ οὗ κτισθέντος. Quare Spiritum sanctum nec sanctum vocant, nec Deum esse credunt. His verbis imprimis Theophronianos, Eunomianos baptizasse scribunt, in quibus quot sunt syllabae, tot sunt blasphemiae comprehensae. 6 Christum corpus tantum, non etiam animam assumpsisse humanam. Theodor. Dialog.2. Inconfusus. 7 Honestam vitam a vera fide .i. res inter se inseparabiles diuellunt, & fructum ab arbore distrahunt, & omnibus vitiis non tantum impunitatem, sed etiā licentiam concedunt, abusi loco Ioan.17.v.3. Hæc est vita æterna, &c. Hoc fuit antiquum Seuerianorum hæreticorum dogma. Quanquam enim opera bona quæ Dei Spiritu impulsi facimus, non sunt salutis nostræ causæ, sunt tamen fidei nostræ effectus: quæ sine illis vera esse non potest, vel viua: Iacob.2.[?] Itaque à fide separari nō possunt. Hæc sunt fœtidi oris Aetianorum & Eunomianorum vomitiones & venena.
units.tr: 3 Dissimilem per omnia). The earlier heretics held various views, which I shall list as I have gathered them from different writers. (1) They maintain that God can be fully and perfectly comprehended by us, in what kind of being and how great he is in himself. Yet Paul teaches otherwise in 1 Tim. 6:16, that God dwells in unapproachable light. The dogma is quite commonplace in the schools of the Christians that God is comprehensible to no one but himself alone (Theodoret and John of Damascus, De orthodoxa fide, bk. 1, ch. 13, in Greek). (2) They teach that the Son of God is in all respects unlike God the Father. For they want the Son to be a creature, produced by the Father from him by a subsequent will. So he is equal to the Father neither in essence, nor in power, nor in will, nor even similar to him. On this point these men think far worse of the deity of Christ than those who said only that he was of a different essence [ὑπερούσιος, that is, of different essence]. For the Heterousians, though heretics, concede that he is like the Father in the other attributes. Aetius's chief argument rested entirely on a certain subtle quibble, as Augustine (De Trinitate, bk. 5, ch. 20) and Lombard (bk. 1, dist. 6, ch. 1) report, and before them Basil and Epiphanius. It runs thus: since the unbegotten [ἀγέννητον] is unlike the begotten [γεννητῷ], and the Father is unbegotten [ἀγέννητος], that is, ingenerate, while the Son is begotten [γεννητὸς], the Son must be unlike the Father. Basil answers this almost unique argument of Aetius briefly but very truly: the terms "begotten" and "unbegotten" signify not a different essence but only a different mode of existence [ὑπάρξεως]. I shall illustrate the matter with an example from Augustine and Damascene. Adam can be called unbegotten, because he is the first man, begotten of no father; Seth, however, is begotten, because he comes from Adam. Yet for that reason the nature and essence of Seth and Adam are not different. Indeed both are true men and of the same nature (Gen. 5:3), although that nature existed in Adam in one way and in Seth in another, since he was begotten by Adam. Our own Servetians, Sylvanists and Arians of this time throw this argument of Aetius back at us a thousand times. (3) The Aetians contend that the Holy Spirit was created and made by the Son. Therefore they deny that he is autosystaton [αὐτοσύστατον], that is, that he exists and lives by the power of his own nature and essence, and they say he is the Son's, and, as Eunomius himself put it, only an only-begotten hypostasis [Μονογενὲς ὑπόστασιν]. (Basil, bk. 2 against Eunomius; bk. 3 of Theodoret; Epiphanius.) (4) They also rebaptize those who have been baptized by the orthodox. This was not a doctrine of Aetius but an invention and dogma of Eunomius, already in exile, which the Eunomians afterwards followed and kept. (Sozomen, bk. 6, ch. 26; Epiphanius.) (5) They not only corrupt but change the baptism instituted by our Lord Jesus Christ. For first, they think only the upper parts of the human body should be baptized, and consider the lower parts unworthy of so great a sacrament; so they wrap the infants to be baptized in swaddling bands below the navel, lest the water flow further. Moreover, they baptize with a form other than the one Christ taught, namely in the name of "the created God," or "the sanctifying spirit," or "the created or uncreated Son." Hence they neither call the Holy Spirit holy nor believe him to be God. Writers record that the Theophronians and Eunomians baptized especially with these words, in which there are as many blasphemies as there are syllables. (6) They hold that Christ assumed only a body, not also a human soul (Theodoret, Dialogue 2, Inconfusus). (7) They tear apart what cannot be separated, the honest life and the true faith, and they pull the fruit away from the tree; they grant not merely impunity but licence for every vice, abusing the passage John 17:3, "This is eternal life," etc. This was the ancient dogma of the Severian heretics. For although the good works we do, impelled by the Spirit of God, are not the cause of our salvation, they are nonetheless the effects of our faith, without which faith cannot be true or living (James 2). Therefore they cannot be separated from faith. These are the vomitings and poisons of the foul mouths of the Aetians and Eunomians.

units.la: CAP. LV.
units.tr: CAP. LV.

units.la: Apollinaristæ à quo primum dicti. Erroris autem capita duo recensentur.
units.tr: The Apollinarists, from whom they were first named. Two heads of this error are set out.

units.la: Apollinaristas{1} Apollinaris instituit, qui de anima Christi à Catholica dissenserunt, dicentes, sicut Ariani, Deū Christum carnem{2} sine anima suscepisse. In quæstione Euangelicis testimoniis victi, mentem (qua rationalis est anima hominis) non fuisse in anima Christi: sed pro hac ipsum Verbum in ea fuisse dixerunt. De ipsa vero eius carne sic à recta fide dissensisse perhibentur, ut dicerent carnem illam & Verbum unius eiusdemque substantiæ, contentiosissime asseuerantes Verbum carnem factum esse, hoc est, Verbi aliquid in carnem fuisse conuersum atque mutatum: non autem carnem de Maria carne susceptam.
units.tr: Apollinaris instituted the Apollinarists, who dissented from the Catholic Church concerning the soul of Christ, saying, like the Arians, that God the Son took on flesh without a soul. Pressed by the Gospel testimonies in this question, they said that the mind (which is the rational soul of man) was not in the soul of Christ, but that the Word itself was in it in its place. Concerning his flesh itself they are said to have departed from the right faith in this way: they said that this flesh and the Word were of one and the same substance, insisting most vehemently that the Word was made flesh, that is, that something of the Word was converted and changed into flesh; but that the flesh was not taken from the flesh of Mary.

units.la: 1 Apollinaris & Apollinarius dicitur. Apollinarij autem fuerunt multi. Ac quidem ante huius hæresfeos tempora quidam vir pius Hierapoleos Phrygiæ ciuitatis Episcopus, qui contra Marcionitas scripsit, vt Eufeb. tradit. lib.5.cap.16. Theodoret. lib.3. Hæreticar. fabul. Alius post hunc nostrum qui tempore Iustiniani fecundi vixit, & in Alexandriæ episcopatu claruit, de quo Euagr. lib.5. cap.16. Alius huius nostri hæresiarchæ seculo vir insignis & Laodicenus Episcopus, qui æqualis Basilio Magno, & Gregorio Nazianzeno, (est autem Nazianze portus Cappadociæ) fortiter pro fide Nicena scriptis suis depugnauit, quemadmodum & Suidas & Philoftorgius meminerunt. Hic autem noster à quo denominata est Apollinariftarum secta, duplex fuit, pater, & filius. Pater Alexandrinus natione & patria, qui docendi gratia in Syriam profectus, Beryti primum, post Laodiceæ (quæ est ad Libanum, & Laodicea libera dicitur à Plinio lib.5. cap.20.) Grammaticam professus est. Vbi inito coniugio filium sibi cognominem sustulit, qui Rhetoricam artem ætatis accessione felicissimè docuit. Vterque autem ad Ecclesiasticum ordinem Laodiceæ vocatus est, & pater quidem Presbyter: filius autem Lector creatus primùm orthodoxam & Nicenam fidem tenuit, vt apparet ex Socrat.lib.2.cap.46. & Sozomen.lib.5. cap.18. Postea cùm Episcopatus, quem affectabat, spe decidisset, à recta veráque Christi doctrina desciuit, vt ait Theodoret. lib.5. Hiftor. cap.4. vt falsa appareat Platinæ sententia, qui hunc nostrum Laodicenum Episcopum vocat, quemadmodum & eorum quædam hallucina-tio est, qui eundem Syrum appellari existimant, quòd fuerit patria Laodicenus, cùm Ægyptius fuerit, vide Indicat. Hærcf.[?] Accessit alia quo-que causa irritandi hominis, quod cùm nimium familiariter conuersaretur cum Epiphanio so-phista homine profano (nec enim Libanium, sed Epiphanium habet & Suidas & Socrat. lib. 2. capite 46. & Libanius Antiochiæ vixit, non autem Laodiceæ) à Georgio Episcopo Laodi-ceno sæpe admonitus, tandem est excomunica-tus. Sed ex ea nimia familiaritate nihil sani didicit. Itaque & rebellis Ecclesiæ factus, & animo turgens, ingeniique confidentia temerarius blasphemum hoc dogma protulit, ex quo innumerabiles postea pestes extiterunt, Monothelitarum, Agnoetarum, & imprimis Eutychianorum. Fuit tamè eruditus & linguæ Græcæ scientissimus, qui ad Homeri & Platonis & Euripidis imitationem multa ex sacris Scriptu-ris sumpto argumento carmine, & prorsa oratione scripsit, ne propter edictum Iuliani Imperatoris honestarum artium studia inter Christianos frigescerent: sed tamen illa scripta Ecclesia repudiauit, quòd cœleste Dei verbum sacrosanctum esse voluerit: neque Poetico more, in quo fabularis historia est: neque Rhetorico, in quo lenocinium potius orationis quàm vis veritatis & Spiritus Dei apparet, tractari legique censuerit operæpretium, Sozomen. lib. 5. cap.18. Alia quoque commentatus est, veluti Summam & Epitomen, De Fide,de Incarnatione, quæ in tribus dialogis Polymorphi fæ-pe citat Theodor. in quibus ipsis varium se & inconstantem (qualia sunt hæreticorum omnium ingenia) prodit, cum quæ ædificat destruat. Vnde Dialogo 2. vocat Theodoret. eius scripta fabulas & præstigias, quemadmodum & Socrat. lib.2.cap.46. Vnde vero nata sit hæc, de qua agimus, facta, dubitare videtur Epiph. Itaque ex nullius autoris nomine eam appellat, sed [illegible, ~8 letters] vocat qui hanc profitentur, quòd humanam naturam in Christo diuellunt, vnámque eius partem tantum tribuunt Christo. At omnium authorum consensu Apollinaristæ nominantur. Ergo & Dimoiritæ siue Duplares, & Apollinaristæ dicuntur. Cœpit autem hæc hæresis post Nicenam synodum (etsi tempore Athanasij nota iam fuerunt eius initia. Nam de ea scribit ad Epictetum Corinthiorum Episcopum, quod etiam refert Epiphan.) circa Valentis Imperatoris, & Damasi Roman. Episcopi, non autem Innocentij, vt Platina sentit, tempore, anno a Christo passo 350. Socrat.lib.2.ca.20. Quo primum tempore Talmud a Iudæis scribi cœptum esse historici Ecclesiastici tradunt. In Cilicia verò primum inualuit & recepta est Apollinaristarum hæresis, vnde se per totam diffudit Asiam, imprimis autem Antiochiam labefecit, Sozomen.lib.6.cap.27. Latissimè certè propagata est propter opinionem de Apollinaristarum illius authorum sanctimonia, qui propter exactam vitæ rationem hominibus penè admirabiles erant, vt Epiphanius scribit, nè nos fucus iste sanctitatis externus hodie deci-piat. piat. Deinde in affluefactis iam & imbutis multa rerum curiositate Syrorum Christianorum (propter iam enatas diversas haereses) ingeniis, facilem sibi aditum invenit. Tamen & a Damaso Romae synodo collecta: & Constantinopoli a congregatis Episcopis statim damnata est. Peruicerunt tamen animi peruicacia & contu-macia Apollinaristae, & se suumque errorem sustentarunt diutissime. Perstitit enim hic error continua quadam Episcoporum successione usque ad Leonis Imperatoris tempora. Nam ut scribit Theodoretus libro 5. Historiarum capite 38. sub Martiano in Alexandria maxime vigebat, & sub imperio Leonis in Antiochia seditionem Apollinaristae moverunt, quemadmodum traditur in collecta Theodori Lectoris, id est, post annum, postquam nata est haec haeresis plusquam 150. In duas tamen partes statim se discidit. Dicti sunt enim alij Apollinaristae simpliciter, qui Christum incarnatum dixerunt. Apollinaristae Marcionitici, qui Christum corpus suum de coelo sumpsisse, & in coelis ipsis [?]ὑπόστασιν ὁμοούσιον habuisse contenderunt.
units.tr: 1 He is called both Apollinaris and Apollinarius. There were many Apollinarii. Before the time of this heresy there was indeed a godly man, Bishop of Hierapolis, a city of Phrygia, who wrote against the Marcionites, as Eusebius relates, book 5, chapter 16; and Theodoret, book 3 of the Heretical Fables. Another, after our man, who lived in the time of Justinian the Second and was prominent in the see of Alexandria, concerning whom Evagrius, book 5, chapter 16. Another, a man of distinction in the age of our heresiarch, and Bishop of Laodicea, who was equal to Basil the Great and Gregory Nazianzen (Nazianzus is a town of Cappadocia), fought bravely with his writings for the Nicene faith, as both Suidas and Philostorgius record. Now this man of ours, from whom the sect of the Apollinarists takes its name, was twofold: father and son. The father was an Alexandrian by birth and origin; he went to Syria to teach, and first at Berytus, afterwards at Laodicea (which lies at Libanus, and is called Laodicea Libera by Pliny, book 5, chapter 20), he taught grammar. There, having married, he had a son of the same name, who taught rhetoric most successfully when he came of age. Both were called to the ecclesiastical order at Laodicea: the father as presbyter, but the son was appointed reader. At first he held the orthodox and Nicene faith, as appears from Socrates, book 2, chapter 46, and Sozomen, book 5, chapter 18. Afterwards, when he had lost hope of the episcopate he coveted, he fell away from the right and true doctrine of Christ, as Theodoret says, Church History, book 5, chapter 4. Thus the view of Platina is shown to be false, who calls our man the Bishop of Laodicea; and some are mistaken in thinking he was called the Syrian because he was a native of Laodicea, though he was an Egyptian; see the Index of Heresies. There was also another cause for provoking the man: because he associated too familiarly with the sophist Epiphanius, a profane man (for Suidas and Socrates, book 2, chapter 46, give the name Epiphanius, not Libanius; and Libanius lived at Antioch, not at Laodicea), and was often admonished by George, Bishop of Laodicea, he was at last excommunicated. But from that over-familiar association he learned nothing sound. Therefore, having become a rebel against the Church, and puffed up in mind, rash through confidence in his own wit, he put forward this blasphemous doctrine, from which afterwards countless plagues arose: the Monothelites, the Agnoetae, and above all the Eutychians. He was nevertheless learned and most skilled in the Greek language, and in imitation of Homer, Plato and Euripides he wrote much, taking his material from the sacred Scriptures, in verse and in prose, lest the study of the liberal arts should grow cold among Christians because of the edict of the Emperor Julian. Yet the Church rejected those writings, because he had wished the heavenly word of God to be treated as sacrosanct, and did not judge it worthwhile to handle it in the poetic manner, in which there is fabulous history, nor in the rhetorical, in which the embellishment of speech rather than the power of truth and the Spirit of God appears, Sozomen, book 5, chapter 18. He also wrote other commentaries, such as a Summary and Epitome, On the Faith, On the Incarnation, which Theodoret often cites from the three dialogues of Polymorphus, in which he reveals himself as varied and inconstant (such are the minds of all heretics), since he tears down what he builds up. Hence in the second dialogue Theodoret calls his writings fables and sorceries, as Socrates also does, book 2, chapter 46. Whence this doctrine with which we are dealing actually arose, Epiphanius seems uncertain. So he names it after no author, but calls those who profess it by the term that they divide the human nature in Christ and attribute only one part of it to Christ. Yet by the consensus of all authors they are called Apollinarists. Therefore they are called both Dimoerites or Duplares, and Apollinarists. This heresy began after the Nicene Synod (although its beginnings were known already in the time of Athanasius; for he writes about it to Epictetus, Bishop of Corinth, which Epiphanius also reports), in the time of the Emperor Valens and of Damasus, Bishop of Rome, not in that of Innocent, as Platina thinks, in the year 350 after Christ's passion, Socrates, book 2, chapter 20. It was at that very time, the church historians report, that the Jews began to write the Talmud. It first took hold and was received in Cilicia, whence it spread through the whole of Asia, and above all it shook Antioch, Sozomen, book 6, chapter 27. It was spread most widely because of the reputation for holiness of the authors of the Apollinarist doctrine, who, on account of their exact manner of life, were almost admired by men, as Epiphanius writes, lest this external mask of sanctity deceive us today as well. Then, among the Syrian Christians, whose minds were already accustomed and steeped in a great curiosity about things (because of the various heresies that had already sprung up), it found easy access. Nevertheless it was condemned at once by Damasus in a synod gathered at Rome, and by bishops assembled at Constantinople. Yet the Apollinarists persisted in their obstinacy and stubbornness, and maintained their error for a very long time. For this error persisted through an unbroken succession of bishops down to the times of the Emperor Leo. For, as Theodoret writes in book 5 of his Histories, chapter 38, under Marcian it was especially flourishing in Alexandria, and under the rule of Leo the Apollinarists stirred up a sedition in Antioch, as is related in the collection of Theodore the Lector, that is, about 150 years after this heresy arose. It split at once into two parts. For some were called simply Apollinarists, who said that Christ was incarnate. The Marcionite Apollinarists contended that Christ took his body from heaven, and that in heaven itself he had a hypostasis of the same substance.

units.la: Fuisse enim Christum in coelo ipso hominem antequam e Maria nasceretur. Socrat. libro 6. cap.27. ibique corpus habuisse divinae naturae aequale & omnino simile & ὁμοούσιον. Itaq; ex Maria nihil sumpsisse, sed [?]διὰ σάρκα καὶ φύσει corpus gestasse, quod nostris non esset par. Habuit igitur haec secta hos successores celeberrimos, Polemium, qui Verbum carni mixtum & confubstantia-tum dixit: Vitalianum qui vixit Antiochiae: &
units.tr: For Christ was a man in heaven itself before he was born of Mary, Socrates, book 6, chapter 27; and there he had a body equal to the divine nature, altogether like it and of the same substance. Therefore he took nothing from Mary, but bore a body through (?) and by nature, which would not be equal to ours. This sect therefore had these most celebrated successors: Polemius, who said that the Word was mixed with flesh and consubstantial with it; Vitalianus, who lived at Antioch; and

units.la: Theodorum Mopsuestiae Episcopum.
units.tr: Theodore, Bishop of Mopsuestia.

units.la: Grauissimam fuisse hanc haeresin ex Gregorio Nazianzeno testatur refertque Sozomenus, quae infinitas orthodoxae fidei labes peperit. Ex Arianis autem sumpta est, a quibus paululum deflexit. Illi enim Christum corpus omnino sine anima sumpsisse docuerunt: hi vero Christi corpus ἄψυχον fuisse nunquam contenderunt. Nā cō̄senserunt Christum assumpsisse σάρκα ἐμψυχωμένην quidem, sed anima rationali destitutam. Fuisse enim volunt in Christo animam quidem ψυχικὸν καὶ ἄλογον tantum, non autem λογικὴν, non eam animae partem, quae in homine νοῦς & ἡγεμονικὸν appellatur. In hoc igitur fuerunt ab Arianis dissimiles, vt Theodor. Dialog. 2. Inconfusus, docet, & Hesych. in Leuitic. cap. 14. In quo fallitur Isidorus, qui scribit Apollinaristas sensisse Christum assumpsisse dūtaxat corpus sine anima. Nec enim id illi docuerunt, sed potius Ariani. Pro mente autem & anima humana deitatem in Christo substituerunt Apollinaristae, ex qua & corpore constaret Christus, faceretque eadem illa diuina natura in Christo, quae ratio in nobis consulit & operatur. Vnde opposita est Apollinaristis haec confessio, ἐκ ἀψύχου, ἐκ ψυχῆς ἀνθρωπίνης, ἐκ ἀνθρώπου σάρκα ἔχειν σωτῆρα, vt docet Epiphan. Cur autem id statuerent ratio est, ne si similem nobis anima habere diceretur Christus, eum peccare potuisse concedendum esset. Deinde, quòd vt homines cum brutis animalibus corpore conueniunt, anima vero differunt: sic Christus cum reliquis hominibus carne quidem conuenit, anima vero ab iis differt, quia in eo λόγος[?] & diuina ipsa natura est animae vice: non autem, vt in nobis, est in illo νοῦς & διάνοια. Haec sane ratio ineptissima est. Primum quia vna est numero in quoque homine anima, non plures, quae facultatibus tantum distinguitur in corpore & differt, propter quas θρεπτικὴ[?], αἰσθητικὴ, λογικὴ nominatur: non sunt autem hae diuersarum & plurium essentiarum & separatarum appellationes, adeo vt in homine θρεπτικὴ[?] sine λογικῇ animae facultate & parte esse non posset. Esset enim copositum quid, corporeum, & partibile anima hominis. Deinde docet Christus ipse se habuisse eam animam, quam νοῦν & ἡγεμονικὸν appellant philosophi, quaeque vere est immortalis. Nam in morte ad Deum, qui eam condidit, redit. Hoc igitur probant verba Christi, cum ait, Luc.23. verf.46. Pater, in manus tuas depono spiritum meum. Denique, vt docet Augustinus. Contra Feli-cia. cap.13. Christus non est perfecte mediator noster, si animam nostram non assumpsit, quae & ipsa peccato, vti caro, pessime vulnerata est. Itaque sananda. Atque hoc est primum Apollinaristarum haereseos caput. 2 Quidam exil-lis[?] cum Sabellianis consentiunt, & in Trinitate personas tollunt vel confundunt, Theodoret.
units.tr: Theodoret testifies, and Sozomen reports, that this heresy was very grave, and that it brought forth countless ruins of the orthodox faith. It was, however, taken from the Arians, though it departed from them a little. For the Arians taught that Christ assumed a body wholly without soul [ἄψυχον], whereas these men never maintained that Christ's body was without soul. They agreed that Christ assumed flesh animated [ἐμψυχωμένην], but destitute of a rational soul. For they hold that in Christ there was only a soul that is sensitive and irrational [ψυχικὸν καὶ ἄλογον], and not the rational soul [λογικὴν], that part of the soul which in man is called mind [νοῦς] and the governing faculty [ἡγεμονικὸν]. In this they differed from the Arians, as Theodoret teaches in his Dialogue 2, Inconfusus, and Hesychius on Leviticus, chapter 14. Isidore is mistaken when he writes that the Apollinarists held that Christ assumed only a body without a soul. They did not teach this; the Arians did. The Apollinarists, however, put the deity in Christ in place of the human mind and soul, so that Christ consisted of a body and that divine nature, which in us deliberates and acts as reason does. Hence this confession was set against the Apollinarists: that Christ has flesh that is not without soul, but with a human soul, and from a human being, as Epiphanius teaches. The reason why they held this view was that, if Christ were said to have a soul like ours, it would have to be conceded that he could sin. Further, just as men agree with brute animals in body but differ in soul, so Christ agrees with other men in flesh but differs from them in soul, because in him the Word and the divine nature itself take the place of the soul, and not, as in us, does he have mind and understanding. This argument is indeed most foolish. First, because each man has one soul in number, not several; it is distinguished only by its faculties, which differ in the body, and for these it is called nutritive, sensitive and rational. These are not names of different and several separate essences, so that the nutritive faculty could not exist in a man without the rational faculty and part of the soul. For the soul of man would then be something composite, corporeal and divisible. Second, Christ himself teaches that he had that soul which philosophers call mind [νοῦς] and governing faculty [ἡγεμονικὸν], and which is truly immortal, for at death it returns to God who created it. This is what the words of Christ prove, when he says, Luke 23:46: "Father, into your hands I commit my spirit." Finally, as Augustine teaches, Against Felix, chapter 13: Christ is not a perfect mediator for us if he did not assume our soul, which, like the flesh, was grievously wounded by sin. It therefore needs healing. And this is the first chief point of the Apollinarist heresy. 2 Some of them agree with the Sabellians and either remove or confound the persons in the Trinity, Theodoret says.

units.la: 3 Diuersas essentias & dissimiles in Trinita-te constituunt. Tres enim, eosque diuersos potentiae gradus in Personis diuinis constituunt, cum dicunt, Magnus, Maior, Maximus. Spiritum enim sanctum Magnum appellant: Filium Maiorem: Patrem autem Maximum. Quae differentia & inaequalitas locum habere non potest,si trium personarum una sit essentia. Quare qui sic docent, tres diuersas in diuinis ὑποστάσεις[?] & impares fingunt & constituunt, Theodoret.lib. 4.Haeret.fabul.& lib.5. Histor.cap.3.
units.tr: 3 They posit three essences in the Trinity, which are diverse and unequal. For they set up three different degrees of power in the divine Persons, when they say: Great, Greater, Greatest. They call the Holy Spirit Great, the Son Greater, and the Father Greatest. Such a difference and inequality cannot hold if the three persons are one essence. Therefore those who teach in this way imagine and set up three diverse and unequal hypostases in the divine nature, Theodoret, Book 4 of the Heretical Fables, and Book 5 of the History, chapter 3.

units.la: 4 Λόγῳ[?] cum carne commixtum confusumque esse, & in eam mutatum, quia nō tantum vnionem, sed vnitatē deitatis & carnis defendebant, vt Theodoretus docet. Suidas de illis agens ait, μίαν φύσιν λόγῳ[?] ἢ σαρκὸς ὡς ἀτελὴς[?] εἰς τὸ ἓν[?]. Itaque Polemius Apollinaris discipulus dixit Λόγον[?] consubstantialem cum carne fuisse. Hinc postea infelicissima Eutychianorum soboles propagata.
units.tr: 4 They taught that the Word was mixed and confused with flesh and changed into it, because they defended not merely a union but a unity of deity and flesh, as Theodoret teaches. Suidas, speaking of them, says: one nature of the Word and of the flesh, as incomplete, into one [μίαν φύσιν λόγῳ ἢ σαρκὸς ὡς ἀτελὴς εἰς τὸ ἓν]. Thus Polemius, a disciple of Apollinaris, said that the Word was consubstantial with flesh. From this the most unhappy brood of the Eutychians was afterwards propagated.

units.la: 5 Christum non sumpsisse carnem ex Maria, sed eam e coelo secum detulisse, vt eandem postea per ascensionem in coelum intulit & euexit.
units.tr: 5 They held that Christ did not take flesh from Mary, but brought it with him from heaven, and afterwards carried it up and bore it into heaven by his ascension.

units.la: 6 Christum propriam humanamque voluntatem non habere aut habuisse, quemadmodum nos homines habemus: sed eam tantum, quae a diuinitate creatur, & diuina est. Hoc certe tollit duplicem illam naturam qua constat saluator noster Christus. Hinc Monothelitae genus hominum religioni Christianae infestissimum prognatum.
units.tr: 6 They held that Christ does not have, or did not have, a proper and human will, as we men have, but only that which is created by the divinity and is divine. This certainly removes that twofold nature of which our Saviour Christ consists. From this the race of Monothelites, most hostile to the Christian religion, was born.

units.la: 7 Animas ab animabus propagari & generari vti corpora a corporibus. Itaque partibilem diffolubilemque hominis animam facit, vnde & mortalem, quod est consequens.
units.tr: 7 They held that souls are propagated and generated from souls, as bodies are from bodies. Thus they make the soul of man divisible and dissoluble, whence it is also mortal, as a consequence.

units.la: 8 Post resurrectionem vltima inter pios Sabbatha, circuncisionem, Iudaicorum ciborum discrimen, caeterasque legales ceremonias locum habituras: imo etiam futurum templum inter nos. Qui error ex Apocal. cap. 21. & 22. perperam explicato natus est, vbi spiritalia rerum terrenarum & inter Iudaeos no-tisimarum tissimarum similitudine proponuntur. Atque hi sunt malæ arboris mali pestiferíque fructus, & Arianorum τέκνα [?] , vt est in veteri proverbio.
units.tr: 8 They held that after the resurrection the Sabbaths, circumcision, the distinction of Jewish foods and the other legal ceremonies would have a place again, and even that a temple would be in our midst in the future. This error arose from a wrong explanation of Revelation chapters 21 and 22, where spiritual things are set forth under the likeness of earthly things, and of those best known among the Jews. These are the bad fruits of the bad and pestilent tree, and children of the Arians [τέκνα], as the old proverb has it.

units.la: CAP. LVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER 56.

units.la: Antidicomarianitæ cur sic dicti. Erroris eorum caput vnum commemoratur.
units.tr: Why the Antidicomarianites are so called. One of their errors is recorded.

units.la: {1}Antidicomarianitæ appellati sunt, qui Mariæ virginitati vsqueadeo contradicunt, vt affirmentur [?] eam post Christum natum viro suo fuisse commixtam.
units.tr: {1} The Antidicomarianites are so named because they oppose the virginity of Mary to such a degree that they maintain she had marital relations with her husband after Christ was born.

units.la: I Antidicomarianitæ.) A dogmate non autem ab authore denominata est hæc hæresis. Dicuntur enim Ἀντιδικομαριανῖται quòd sint ἀν-τιδικοι Μαρίας, id est, Mariæ aduersarij, cuius virginitatem, quantum possunt, oppugnant. Appellantur etiam Antimaritæ & Heluidiani, ab Heluidio homine, vt ait Hieronymus in scripto aduersus eum edito, rusticano & vix literis imbuto, sed Auxentij Ariani Episcopi discipulo. Vnde fit, vt Arianorum sobolem hos quidam existiment. Alij Apollinaristarum [illegible, ~5 letters] & superfœturam obscœniffimam esse malunt, velut Epiphanius, quandoquidem huius sectæ error primum ab Apollinario patre, post autem ab ipsius auditoribus conceptus est, quem ante Heluidium vixisse nemo dubitat. Cœpisse vero videtur suo separatóque ab Apollinaristis nomine & cœtu hæc hæresis sub Theodosio Magno Imperatore & Syricio Roman. Episcopo, anno a Christo passo 355. In Arabia vero primum innotuit & propagata est, unde in Galliam & Italiam traiecit: sed statim tum ab Epiphanio Cypri Episcopo in Oriente: tum ab Ambrosio in epist. 79. tum etiam Hieronymo Stridonesi, presbytero Romano in Occidente, repressa conticuit. Neque enim ullos magni nominis insigniisque doctrinæ viros defensores & patronos habuisse videtur, nisi fortasse Bonosum episcopum, de quo idem Ambros. eadem epistola 79. meminit. Præterea jam tum adeo invaluerant virginitatis laudes, & B.Mariæ matris Domini nostri Iesu Christi veneratio, ut facile compesci quæcunque adversus Mariam blaterarent homines, potuerint. Quemadmodum vero ex huius erroris refutatione confirmatur articuli fidei nostræ & veræ, Natus de Maria virgine, sententia, eripiturque Iudæis occasio elevandæ in eo Evangelij certitudinis, quæ in dubium vocari videtur, si Maria post partum Domini nostri Iesu Christi, à Iosepho cognita dicatur: sic ex huius virginitatis præpostera & immodica certè defensione & commendatione auctæ sunt colendæ adorandæque Mariæ, & coniugij vitu-perandi cœlibatusque extollendi in immensum occasiones, adeo ut Syricius ipse sub cuius pontificatu hæc disceptatio agitata est, apertissimè pronuntiarit, sed tamen impiissimè, coniugium esse Deo exosum, & qui coniuges sunt in carne vivere, nec Deo jam placere posse, cuius sententia extat in Decreto. dist. 82. Denique eò tandem ventum est, ut soli cœlibes beati, felices, regno cælorum digni vel participes censeretur, cotra manifestā Spiritus Dei voce,Hebr.13.v.4: 1.Tim.4.v.3.&ut Maria virgo aperte jam in Dei Ecclesia templis arisque coleretur, & numen Deo par obtineret, de qua scribit Epiphanius, se non audere affirmare utrum mortua sit, an in ipso corpore immortalis facta.Extabat quidem jam Irenæi dictu de Mariæ laudibus,& patrocinio apud Deū pro nobis,si modo illius tantique viri germana sententia est, non autem insita, & translatitia:sed postea eæ Mariæ laudes in furorem euaserunt, & plane idololatricus cultus fieri cœpit, adeo ut ad illius simulachrum homines tanquam ad diuinum numen confugerent: Euagr. libro 5. cap.18. & illius etiam imaginem venerabundi ostentarent. Quod fecit illa Pulcheria soror Theodosij,ad quam Eudocia eiusdem Theodosij uxor, eam Hierosolymis & Iudæa Constatinopolin miserat,uti scribit Theodoret. Lector in Collecta.
units.tr: 1 Antidicomarianites.) This heresy takes its name from its doctrine, not from an author. They are called Antidikomarianitai [Ἀντιδικομαριανῖται] because they are antidikoi [ἀντίδικοι] of Mary, that is, adversaries of Mary, whose virginity they attack as far as they can. They are also called Antimarites and Helvidians, after a man named Helvidius, as Jerome says in the writing he published against him, a rustic man barely educated in letters but a disciple of Auxentius, the Arian bishop. Hence some think they are the offspring of the Arians. Others prefer to regard them as a most obscene offspring of the Apollinarists, as Epiphanius does, since the error of this sect was first conceived by the father Apollinaris and afterwards by his hearers, and no one doubts that Apollinaris lived before Helvidius. This heresy seems to have begun under its own name and separately from the Apollinarists, in the time of the emperor Theodosius the Great and of Siricius, bishop of Rome, in the year 355 after Christ's passion. It first became known and spread in Arabia, whence it crossed into Gaul and Italy; but it was at once suppressed and fell silent, both by Epiphanius, bishop of Cyprus, in the East, and by Ambrose in letter 79, and also by Jerome of Stridon, a Roman presbyter, in the West. For it seems to have had no defenders or patrons of great name or distinguished learning, except perhaps Bonosus the bishop, whom Ambrose mentions in the same letter 79. Moreover, by then praise of virginity and veneration of the blessed Mary, mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, had so greatly prevailed that whatever nonsense men babbled against Mary could easily be checked. Just as the refutation of this error confirms the true article of our faith, that he was born of the Virgin Mary, and takes away from the Jews an occasion of undermining the certainty of the Gospel on this point, which seems to be called into doubt if Mary is said to have been known by Joseph after the birth of our Lord Jesus Christ; so from the preposterous and immoderate defence and commendation of this virginity have grown occasions for the worship and adoration of Mary, and for disparaging marriage and extolling celibacy beyond measure. So much so that Siricius himself, under whose papacy this dispute was stirred, pronounced most openly, yet most impiously, that marriage is hateful to God and that those who are married cannot live in the flesh and please God; his opinion is found in the Decretum, dist. 82. Finally it came to this: only the celibate were considered blessed, happy, worthy of or partakers in the kingdom of heaven, against the plain voice of the Spirit of God (Heb. 13.4; 1 Tim. 4.3); and the Virgin Mary was openly worshipped in God's Church with temples and altars and was given a divine power equal to God's. Of her Epiphanius writes that he does not dare affirm whether she died or was made immortal in her very body. There was already a saying of Irenaeus about Mary's praises and her intercession with God for us, if indeed it is the genuine opinion of so great a man and not an interpolated and foreign addition; but afterwards those praises of Mary broke out into frenzy, and a plainly idolatrous worship began, so that men fled to her image as to a divine power (Evagrius, book 5, ch. 18), and they displayed her picture with reverence. This was done by that Pulcheria, sister of Theodosius, to whom Eudocia, wife of the same Theodosius, had sent her image from Jerusalem and Judaea to Constantinople, as Theodoret writes, Lector in Collecta.

units.la: 2 Clam post Christum.) Erroris huius sectæ summa, Mariam post editum Christū virginem non permansisse, Isidor. Nam errant qui hanc hæresin multiplicem constituunt. Quòd enim hæreticorum quidam Christum negant ex Mariæ substantia genitum, alij sine viri semine ex ea natum non concedūt:alij ex Maria Christum paruulum prodiisse non admittūt, sed jam plenæ staturæ hominem:alij deniq; virginem Θεοτό-κον. i. Dei matrem appellari non patiuntur, sed tantum Χριστοτόκον[?], ad alias hæres[]s pertinet, non autem ad Antidicomarianitas. Cur autem hoc isti senserint,ratio est,primùm quorundam veterum authoritas, qui Mariam post Christum à Josepho cognitam scripserunt. Alij autem malunt Josephum mortua Maria ex alia yxore liberos suscepisse. Epiphanius autem censet Josephum jam octogenariu fuisse, quum Mariam desponderet. Alia Antidicomarianitarum ratio sumitur ex Math.1. v.25. vbi Christus primogenitus appellatur. Sed vt Jurisconsulti respondent, Primus non ad sequentes, sed ad antecedentes tantum refertur. Tit.De reb.dubiis. D. Est primus quem nemo præcedit. Est vltimus, quem nemo sequitur. Quod autē ibidem addit Matthæus, Et non cognouit eam quousque peperisset: non arguit probatve Josephum cum ea post partu coijsse. Denique quod iidem afferūt quosdam in Scriptura nominari fratres Christi, vt Jacobum, Galat.1.versu 19. leue est. Fratris enim nomen ex more Hebræorum, omnes qui sunt eiusdem cognationis complectitur: quanquam ait Eusebius lib.2.cap.1. hunc Jacobum, qui iustus vel Oblia dictus est, à quibusdam putari esse filium Josephi viri Mariæ, sed falsò. Atque hæc sunt exigua huius hæreseos robora. Accedo igitur eorum sententiæ qui Mariam matrem Christi selectissimum Dei organum fuisse sentiunt, & eam ἀειπάρθενον [?]. i. ante & post partum virginem mansisse, & vixisse scribunt, non quòd tamen eam coniugem votū virginitatis vouisse, idque marito significasse assen tiar, vt est in Can.Beata. & Can. Sic quippe. 27. quæst.2. Et de hac quidem quæstione satis. Cui fuerunt contrarij Collyridiani, de quibus agemus in Arabicis hæreticis infrá.
units.tr: 2 Secretly after Christ.) The sum of this sect's error is that Mary did not remain a virgin after Christ was born (Isidore). For those err who make this heresy manifold. Some heretics deny that Christ was begotten of Mary's substance; others do not grant that he was born of her without a man's seed; others do not admit that the child came forth from Mary as a little child but as a man of full stature; others finally do not allow the virgin to be called Theotokos [Θεοτόκον], that is, Mother of God, but only Christotokos [Χριστοτόκον]. These belong to other heresies, not to the Antidicomarianites. The reason these men held this opinion is, first, the authority of certain ancients who wrote that Mary was known by Joseph after Christ was born; others prefer to hold that Joseph, after Mary died, had children by another wife. Epiphanius thinks Joseph was already an octogenarian when he betrothed Mary. Another argument of the Antidicomarianites is taken from Matt. 1.25, where Christ is called firstborn. But as the jurists reply, "first" refers not to those who follow but only to those who precede. Tit. De reb. dubiis, D: "He is first whom no one precedes; he is last whom no one follows." What Matthew adds, "and he did not know her until she had borne a son," does not prove or show that Joseph had intercourse with her after the birth. Finally, the same men argue that some are called brothers of Christ in Scripture, such as James (Gal. 1.19); this is a slight point. For by Hebrew usage the name brother embraces all who are of the same kinship. Although Eusebius (book 2, ch. 1) says that this James, who was called just or Oblias, is thought by some to be the son of Joseph, husband of Mary, this is false. These are the slight supports of this heresy. I therefore agree with those who hold that Mary, mother of Christ, was the most chosen instrument of God, and who write that she remained a virgin before and after childbirth and lived so; not that she, as a wife, had vowed virginity and signified this to her husband, as in Can.
