Beata and Can. Sic quippe, 27 q. 2. And enough on this question. Their opponents were the Collyridians, of whom we shall treat among the Arabian heretics below.

units.la: CAP. LVII. Messalianorum cur sic dicti. Erroris autem eorum capita tria commemorantur.
units.tr: CHAPTER LVII. Why the Messalians are so called. Three heads of their error are recorded.

units.la: MEssalianorum{1} postremam ponit Epiphanius haeresin, quod nomen ex lingua Syria est. Graece autem dicuntur{2} Εὐχῖται[?], ab o-rando sic appellati. Tantum{3} enim orant, ut eis, qui hoc de illis audiunt, incredibile videatur. Nam quum Dominus dixerit, Oportet semper orare, & non deficere: & Apostolus, Sine intermissione orate (quod sanissime sic accipitur, ut nullo die intermittantur certa tempora orandi) isti ita nimis hoc faciunt, ut hinc iudicentur inter haereticos nu-merandi. Quanvis nonnulli eos dicant de purga-tione animarum nescio quam phantasticam & ridiculam fabulam narrare, porcam scilicet cum porcellis suis videri exire de ore hominis quando purgatur: & in eum visibili similiter specie ignem, qui non comburat, intrare. His adiungit Epiphanius Euphemitas, Martyrianos, & Satanianos, & hos omnes cum illis tanquam unam haeresin ponit. Dicuntur Euchitae opinari Monachis non licere su-stentanda vita sua causa aliquid operari: atque ita seipsos Monachos profiteri, ut omnino operibus vacent. Usque ad istos ergo de haeresibus opus suum perduxit supradictus episcopus Cyprius, apud Graecos inter magnos habitus, & a multis in catholicae fidei sanitate laudatus. Cuius ego in commemorandis haereticis non modum, sed ordinem sum sequutus. Nam & aliqua ex aliis posui, quae ipse non pofuit: & aliqua non posui, quæ ipse posuit. Itaque alia latius quàm ipse, alia breuius explicaui, parémque in nonnullis exhibui breuitatem, omnia moderans, sicut intentionis meæ ratio postulabat. Proinde ille de octoginta hæresibus, separatis viginti, quas ante Domini aduentum extitisse, sicut ei visum est, computauit: reliquas post Domini ascensum natas sexaginta breuissimis libris quinque comprehendit, atque omnes in sex libros totius eiusdem sui operis fecit concludi. Ego autem qui secundum petitionem tuam eas hæreses memorare instituì, quæ post glorificationem Christi se aduersus doctrinam Christi, etiam sub velamine Christiani nominis extulerunt, quinquaginta septem ex Epiphanij ipsius opere in meum transtuli, duas in unum referens, ubi nullam differentiam potui inuenire: & rursus ubi ille ex duabus unam facere voluit, sub numeris suis singulas posui. Sed adhuc commemorare debeo siue quas apud alios reperi, siue quas ipse reminiscor. Nunc ergo addo quas Philaster posuit, nec posuit Epiphanius.
units.tr: The Messalians are the last heresy listed by Epiphanius. The name comes from the Syrian language, and in Greek they are called Euchitae [Εὐχῖται], from praying, which is what they are named for. They pray so much that it seems incredible to those who hear of it. For the Lord said, "Men ought always to pray and not to faint," and the Apostle said, "Pray without ceasing." (This is rightly understood to mean that there are never days without set times of prayer.) These people go to such an extreme that they are judged to be numbered among the heretics. Some report that they tell a strange and ridiculous fable about the purging of souls: that a sow with her piglets is seen coming out of the mouth of a man when he is being purged, and that a fire which does not burn enters him in visible form. Epiphanius joins to these the Euphemites, the Martyrians and the Satanians, and he lists all of them together as one heresy. The Euchitae are said to hold that monks may not work for the sake of sustaining their life, and so they profess to be monks in such a way that they are wholly given over to prayer. Up to these, then, the aforesaid bishop of Cyprus brought his work on the heresies. Among the Greeks he is held in high regard, and he has been praised by many for the soundness of his catholic faith. In recounting the heretics I have not followed his measure but his order. For I have included some things from other sources that he did not include, and I have left out some things that he included. So I have explained some matters at greater length than he did, others more briefly, and in some places I have kept to a similar brevity, moderating everything as the plan of my undertaking required. He counted eighty heresies, of which twenty, as it seemed to him, arose before the coming of the Lord. The remaining sixty, which arose after the Lord's ascension, he comprised in five very brief books, and he had all of them concluded within six books of his whole work. I, however, who according to your request have set out to recount those heresies which, after the glorification of Christ, have risen up against the teaching of Christ, even under the cover of the Christian name, have transferred fifty-seven from Epiphanius's own work into mine, combining two into one where I could find no difference, and conversely, where he wished to make one out of two, I have set down each under its own number. But I must still mention those which I have found among others, or which I recall myself. Now therefore I add those which Philaster listed and Epiphanius did not.

units.la: I In impressis omnibus quos mihi adhuc videre cōtigit, Psalliānorum. In quo error errori accumulatus est. Primus, quòd Psalliani pro Messaliani scriptum est corruptissimè. Secundus, quòd hanc ipsam Psalliānorum vocem Syriacam esse volunt, quæ plané Græca erat, & à verbo ψάλλω[?], quod fidibus canere significat, deducta. Quem tamen errorem plerique sunt secuti, præsertim F. Bernardus Lutzemburgus, ordinis, vt ipse loquitur, Prædicatorij, in quinque libris De hæreticis. Ego ve-rò sic[?] rò sic restituendum affirmo,Messalianorum.sed librariorum incuria maiusculæ hæ literæ Mef in P mutatæ sunt. Confirmant autem nostram sententiam infiniti pené authorum loci,sed imprimis Epiphanius, à quo Augustinus hæc sua sumpsit, Theodoretus,& Epiphanij abbreuiator , Ioannes Damascenus. Sed etiam ratio ipsa Augustini,qui Messalianorum vocabulum à Syriaca lingua deriuat. Et reɛté. Dicti sunt à verbo Chaldaico siue Aramæo ⁠tsalah, quod orare & precari Syris designat. Hebræis autem assare & vrere. Inde Methsalim in Benoni Piel, Precantes:sed Græci Tsade Hebræorum in duplex suum Sigma, propter ἀλφωνίω comutarunt. Hac voce vtitur Daniel capite 6.vers.10.
units.tr: 1 In all the printed editions that I have so far been able to see, the word is given as "Psalliani." Error has been piled upon error in this. First, "Psalliani" has been printed very corruptly for "Messaliani." Second, they want this very word "Psalliani" to be Syriac, when it was plainly Greek, derived from the verb ψάλλω, which means to sing to the lyre. Many have followed this error, especially Friar Bernardus Lutzemburgus, of the Order of Preachers, as he himself calls it, in his five books On Heretics. I, however, affirm that the word must be restored to "Messalianorum," and that through the carelessness of copyists the capital letters Mef have been changed into P. Our view is confirmed by almost endless passages from authors, but above all by Epiphanius, from whom Augustine took these matters of his, by Theodoret, and by Epiphanius's abridger, John of Damascus. Augustine's own reasoning confirms it too, for he derives the name Messalians from the Syriac language, and rightly so. The name comes from the Chaldee or Aramaic verb tsalah, which in Syriac signifies to pray and to beseech, while in Hebrew it means to roast and to burn. From this comes Methsalim in the Pael conjugation of Benoni, meaning "those who pray." But the Greeks changed the Hebrew tsade into their double sigma, on account of the alphabet's sound. Daniel uses this word in chapter 6, verse 10.

units.la: 2 Dicuntur Εὐχῖται. Variis appellationibus vna hæc & eadem hæresis nominata est propter authorum qui eam vel defenderunt vel propagarunt, vel interpolarunt, diuersa studia, quo maiore odio digna,& merito quidem, haberetur. Nam istos magis quàm Cainianos & Antitactas hæreticos impios , execrandósque esse testatur Theodoretus in Epitom. Diuinor. Ergo Messaliani dicuntur ob eam, quam exposuimus, causam:& Euchetæ Εὐχῖται, id est, Precatores, quæ vox plane Græca est, ἀπὸ τῆς εὐχῆς, quæ precationem significat. Martyriani, quòd quédam ex suis à duce militum Luppiciano necatum colunt, tanquam Dei Christianæque fidei martyrem. Satanici,vel Sataniani, quòd Satanam,quem vitæ nostrę prĕsidem,omniúmque actionum nostrarum moderatorem credunt, summisi venerantur,ne vt malus genius eos lçdat. Εὐφημῖται, vt ait Epiphanius, quòd [illegible, ~7 letters] & elogia quædam ex sacris Literis decerpta, in Dei laudem cantitent. Ἐνθουσιασταί, quòd insano furore abrepti, se quiduis esse somniant, & interrogati, An Prophetæ, an Abrahã, an Patriarchæ, an Christus, sint, omnia hæc se esse profitentur, & miseri persuadent. Itaque vt phanatici statim in medium hominum cœtum exiliunt, & saltant varie, ridiculéque gesticulantur, vel digitis crepant, tanquam his suis gestibus dæmonas impugnent, & à se eiiciant. Denique Spirituales vocantur, quòd se plane mundo renuntiasse, quanquam tamen salsissimè, iactitant: sed hoc illis cum Gnosticis commune nomen est. Hanc autem infelicem stirpem ex Montanistarum fémine natam quidam volunt: Epiphanius tamen ex Græcorum, id est, ethnicorum, & idololatrarum cœno haustam fæcem mauult. Ego vero etiam ex Anthropomorphitarū fonte scaturiisse dixerim, cum qua in multis conuenit. Certè monachismi, qui nunc sub Papatu stabilitus est, & viget, magnum dedit hoc erroris & hominum genus non tantum incrementum, sed etiam fundamentum. Quid enim aliud sunt nostri temporis Monachi, quàm Euchetæ restituti, nouoque nomine se celantes? Cœpit autem hæc hæresis initia quædam sua habere, iam inde sub Constantio imperatore, quemadmodum Epiphanius scripsit: pleno autem dogmate, & sua speciali que appellatione innotescere sub Valetiniano, & Valente Impp. & Damaso episcopo Romano, circa annū à Christo nato 341. cuius nō vnus quidam, sed plures statim authores extiterunt, in Mesopotamia praesertim, vnde primum censetur ad alias Ecclesias profecta. Dadoes enim, Sabbas, Hermes, Symeones, & Adelphius, qui Edessae eorum episcopus fuit (est autem Edessa ciuitas eius Arabiae quae & ad Euphratem pertinet, & Mesopotamiae vicina est) eodem exorti tempore, hoc venenum dis-seminarunt, & diffuderunt. Sensim autem pullulans haec arbor infausta, & ex ipsius fructu degustato, pessima percepta est a Latoio Melitenae episcopo (Melitene vero est Cappadociae ad Euphratem vergentis oppidum, vt ait Plinius libro 5. cap.24.) deinde abs Flauiano Antiochiae praesule damnata, vt est apud Theodoretum libro 4. histor. cap.11. tota Syria videbatur expulsa: sed in Pamphylia traducta est, vbi floruit, & tandem renouata in monasteriis, vniuersum pene terrarum orbe infecit. Diuisi vero fuerunt etiam ipsi inter se in varias sectas, magna successo-rum ambitione, omnes tamen dogmata haec retinuerunt: vt oratoria, quas ἀχαὶ[?] & ἀντίφεια[?] vocant, tanti facerent, vt ex iis solis tota hominum salus pendere censeretur, & diceretur. Synodo vero Ephesina damnata est, quia cum propter ipsum errorem displicuit: tum vero propter novum & insolitum tunc temporis inter Christianos & ecclesiasticos homines corporis habitum institutum. Vt enim hi quid melius quam vulgus Christianorum profiteri viderentur, contra Pauli praeceptum, 1. Corinth. comam alere suos iusserunt, & barbam radere, quod & naturae rerum repugnat, & formae virili. Est enim, vt ait Epiphanius, barba ipsa quodammodo dignitas & forma viri. Quare etiam Carthagi‐nẽsi Synodo eam radere clerici vetiti sunt, quod Synodi caput corruperunt perfidiosisimè postea Rom. pontifices in Decretal. epist. Tit. De vita & honestate clericorum, & Agathensi concilio cap. 20. iidem clerici comâ promittere, vel alere prohibentur: id quod etiam extat in Can. clerici distinct. 23. in Decret. Duo vero hæreticorum superiorum genera his nostris adueꝛsa‐bantur: Prodiciani à Prodico vetusto nebulo‐ne profecti, qui Deum omnino precandum esse negarunt, vt scribit Clemens Alexandrinus Strom. libro 7. & Audiani, qui Monachos otiosos & nihil operantes, quales isti suos esse volunt, vti ἀπρακτους homines, & excommunicandos prorsus reiiciunt & damnant. Ita diabolus sibi ipsi contrarius est, & serpens serpentem necat.
units.tr: 2 They are called Euchitae [Εὐχῖται]. This one and the same heresy has been given various names, on account of the different zeals of those who defended it, spread it, or corrupted it, by which it might be held in greater hatred, and rightly so. For Theodoret, in his Epitome of Divine Matters, testifies that these people are more impious and execrable than the Cainites and the Antitactae. So the Messalians are called by that name for the reason we have set out, and the Euchetae [Εὐχῖται], that is, the Prayers, a word which is plainly Greek, from ἡ εὐχή, meaning prayer. The Martyrians are so called because some of them worship as a god and a martyr of the Christian faith one whom they say was killed by the commander of the soldiers, Lupicianus. The Satanici, or Satanians, are so called because they humbly venerate Satan, whom they believe to be the guardian of our life and the governor of all our actions, so that he as an evil spirit may not harm them. The Euphemitae, as Epiphanius says, are so called because they sing praises to God, plucking from the sacred Scriptures certain words of praise. The Enthusiastae [Ἐνθουσιασταί] are so called because, carried away by insane frenzy, they dream that they are something, and when asked whether they are prophets, or Abraham, or the patriarchs, or Christ, they profess that they are all of these, and they miserably persuade others of it. And so, as if possessed, they leap at once into the midst of the assembly of people, and dance in various ways, and make ridiculous gestures, or snap their fingers, as though by these gestures they were attacking demons and driving them out from themselves. Finally they are called Spiritual, because they boast, though most foolishly, that they have wholly renounced the world. But this name is held in common with the Gnostics. Some want this unhappy stock to have sprung from a woman of the Montanists; Epiphanius, however, prefers to derive it from the dregs of the Greeks, that is, the pagans and idolaters. I, for my part, would say that it also welled up from the fountain of the Anthropomorphites, with whom it agrees in many respects. Certainly this kind of heresy and of men, which is now established and flourishing under the Papacy, has given to monasticism not only increase but even foundation. For what else are our monks of this age than the Euchetae restored, hiding themselves under a new name? This heresy began to have some beginnings of its own already under the emperor Constantius, as Epiphanius wrote, but it became known with its full doctrine and its own special name under the emperors Valentinian and Valens and Damasus, bishop of Rome, around the year 341 after the birth of Christ. Not one author only, but several at once, arose for it, especially in Mesopotamia, from which it is thought first to have gone out to other churches. For Dadoes, Sabbas, Hermes, Symeon and Adelphius, who was their bishop at Edessa (Edessa is a city of that part of Arabia which also belongs to the Euphrates and lies near Mesopotamia), arose at the same time and sowed and spread this poison. But this unhappy tree, gradually putting forth shoots, and once its fruit had been tasted, was condemned in the worst way by Letoius, bishop of Melitene (Melitene is a town of Cappadocia bordering on the Euphrates, as Pliny says in book 5, chapter 24), and then was condemned by Flavian, the prelate of Antioch, as is recorded in Theodoret, book 4 of his History, chapter 11. It seemed to have been driven out of all Syria, but it was carried into Pamphylia, where it flourished, and at last, renewed in the monasteries, it infected nearly the whole orb of the earth. They also were divided among themselves into various sects, through the great ambition of their successors, yet all of them retained these doctrines. So they valued prayers, which they call the akhai [ἀχαί] and the antiphonies [ἀντίφωνα], so highly that the whole salvation of men was thought and said to hang upon these alone. They were condemned by the Synod of Ephesus, partly because of the error itself, but partly also because of the new and unusual outward dress for men that was then introduced among Christians and churchmen. For these men, so that they might appear to profess something better than the common run of Christians, ordered their followers to grow long hair and shave the beard, contrary to the precept of Paul in 1 Corinthians. This is contrary both to the nature of things and to the manly form. For, as Epiphanius says, the beard is in a way the dignity and form of a man. Hence clerics were forbidden by the Council of Carthage to shave it, a canon which the Roman pontiffs afterwards most treacherously corrupted, in the Decretal epistles, title "On the life and honesty of clerics." And by the Council of Agde, canon 20, the same clerics are forbidden to grow or keep long hair, which is also found in the canon "Clerici," distinction 23, in the Decretum. Two kinds of the earlier heretics were opposed to our people: the Prodicians, who came from the ancient rogue Prodicus, and who denied that God was to be prayed to at all, as Clement of Alexandria writes in Stromata, book 7; and the Audians, who reject and wholly condemn as idle monks, doing nothing, such as these men want their own to be, men who are "inactive" (ἀπράκτους), and deserving of excommunication. So the devil is contrary to himself, and the serpent kills the serpent.

units.la: 3 Tantum enim orant. Fuerunt multiplicia istius erroris capita. 1 Deum vnum quidem colunt, velut numen quoddam singulare, & monarchicum, nō autem quale nobis à diuina Scriptura proponitur in tres distinctum personas, & τρισσὰ reipsa existentes. Id quod ex Sabellianorum putido & exoleto iam errore sumptū est. Epiphanius. Inde Deitæ nostri seculi nati, & qui olim Monarchici dicti sunt, hoc caput amplectuntur. 2 Deum corporeis oculis cerni & videri posse contendunt. Nam eius naturam sub sensus nostros cadere volunt, quod ex Anthropomorphitarum errore ab iis sumptum & interpolatum est, contra manifestissima Christi vocem, Ioann. 1. vers. 16. Nam quod ait Christus ipse Matth.5.v.8. mundos corde visuros Deum, ad oculos corporis proprie non pertinet, ut explicat Augustinus libr.i.De Trinitate, cap. 6.
units.tr: 3 For they only pray. This heresy had many heads. 1 They worship one God, as a certain single and monarchical deity, but not as Holy Scripture sets him forth, distinguished into three persons and actually existing as a triune God [τρισσὰ]. This comes from the stinking and long-stale error of the Sabellians (Epiphanius). From this sprang the Deists of our own age, who were once called Monarchians, and they embrace this head. 2 They contend that God can be seen and beheld with bodily eyes. For they want his nature to fall under our senses. This they took from the error of the Anthropomorphites and corrupted, against the most manifest voice of Christ, John 1:16. For when Christ himself says in Matthew 5:8 that the pure in heart will see God, this does not properly refer to the eyes of the body, as Augustine explains in De Trinitate 1, chapter 6.

units.la: 3 Satanam vitæ actionumque nostrarum præsidem non modo fingunt, a quo tota vita etiam inviti regamur, & agamur: sed etiam colunt, placant & ut malum genium, venerantur, ut averruncet mala. Itaque ut Antitactæ vitiis turpissimis indulgent. Theodoretus lib.4.hæret. fabul. & in Epitom. Decret. divin.
units.tr: 3 They not only imagine Satan to be the governor of our life and actions, by whom our whole life is ruled and driven even against our will, but they also worship, placate and venerate him as an evil genius, so that he may avert evils. Thus, like the Antitactae, they indulge in the most shameful vices (Theodoret, Haereticarum fabularum compendium 4; and in the Epitome of the Divine Decrees).

units.la: 4 Caput erroris & huius sectæ maxime proprium, Orationi & precationi totam animarum nostrarum salutis vim attribuunt, & Christi sanguini adimunt. Itaque & fidem & Evangelij prædicationem inutilem constituunt, quod idem postea fecerunt Gnosimachi hæretici, de quibus Joannes Damascenus. Contemnunt etiam divina Sacramenta, quod in unam certarum precum & verborum demurmurationem transferunt causam nostræ peccatorum remissionis, redemptionis, & liberationis. Unde & stolidos ignarosque prorsus homines istos esse oportuit, qui verbum Dei contemnerent: & superbos, qui operibus suis, id est, precationi, suam aliorumque salutem devincirent. Quod tamen utrunque nostræ ætatis Monachi sentiunt, & faciunt. Extant quidem passim in Scriptura precationis eximiæ laudes, ut ad eam homines incitentur, & docet Christus semper orandum, Luc.18. versu 1: & Paulus quoque 1.Thessal.5.versu.17. Denique Moses per preces hostes vicit, Exodi 17. versu ii. & David hoc sibi præsentissimum & tutissimum fuisse semper in omnibus malis remedium testatur, Pfalm.109.versu 4.quę etiam appellatur facrifi-cium,& incensum Domino gratissimum, Pfal. 141. versu 1. & Hofeæ 14. versu 3. & Christiani hominis exercitatio,Hebr.13.verf.15.tamen hæc elogia non ad ipsum orationis nostræ actum & dignitatem pertinent, neque ipsis nostris verbis vim & causam tatorum Dei bonorum tribuút, (est enim eorum verissima causa sola Dei beni-gnitas & gratia per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum pro nobis passum & crucifixum) sed modum ad Deum adeundi,& colloquendi tan-tum ostendunt. Est autem precatio vera & sin-cera ex fide ἀνυπόκριτῳ[?] profecta, quia est oratio fidei fructus,Iacob.1.versu 5. Rom. 10. verf. 14. Hi vero spoliantes Christum suo beneficio,ipsi labiorum suorum motui, & verborum a fe effusorum sono illa dona vindicant, cum magna Dei ipsius blasphemia. Habent igitur instar Iudæorum,vt vult Epiphan.magna extra vrbes septa in quibus precantur confusi & inconditi.
units.tr: 4 The chief head of this error, and the most peculiar to this sect, is that they attribute the whole power of our salvation to prayer and supplication, and take it away from the blood of Christ. Thus they also render faith and the preaching of the gospel useless. The Gnosimachi, heretics about whom John of Damascus writes, later did the same. They also despise the divine sacraments, since they transfer the cause of the remission of our sins, of our redemption and of our deliverance to a mere mumbling of certain prayers and words. Hence those men must have been utterly stupid and ignorant, who despised the Word of God, and proud, who by their works, that is, by prayer, bound their own salvation and that of others. Yet the monks of our own age hold and practise both of these things. Certainly, the Scriptures everywhere contain excellent praises of prayer, to stir men towards it. Christ teaches that one must always pray (Luke 18:1), and so does Paul (1 Thessalonians 5:17). Moses, too, conquered enemies by prayer (Exodus 17:11). David testifies that this has always been for him the most present and surest remedy in all evils (Psalm 109:4), and prayer is also called a sacrifice and incense most pleasing to the Lord (Psalm 141:1; Hosea 14:3), and a exercise of the Christian man (Hebrews 13:15). Yet these commendations do not pertain to the very act and dignity of our prayer, nor do they attribute to our own words the power and cause of the good things of God. For the true cause of these is solely the goodness and grace of God, through our Lord Jesus Christ, who suffered and was crucified for us. These passages show only the manner of approaching and conversing with God. Prayer is true and sincere when it proceeds from unfeigned faith [ἀνυπόκριτῳ], because prayer is the fruit of faith (James 1:5; Romans 10:14). But these men, robbing Christ of his benefit, claim those gifts for the movement of their lips and the sound of words poured out by themselves, with great blasphemy against God himself. They therefore resemble the Jews, as Epiphanius says, who pray in great enclosures outside the cities, confused and disorderly.

units.la: 5 Peccata & Satana orado fenfibiliter eiici,qui tam exiguus fiat, quàm fumus est, aut paruum animalculum.Sic itaque extenuatus exit visibiliter ex ore nostro, vti porca & scrofa cum porcellis: cuius loco visibiliter quoque succedit & ingreditur Spiritus sanctus. Plus dicunt etiam per mucum, sputum & execrationes Satanam abs nobis exspui. Hæc autem non tantum inepta sententia est, sed etiam falsa: quæ & Spiritum sanctum & diabolum corporeum statuit.
units.tr: 5 They hold that sins and Satan are expelled by prayer in a perceptible way, and that Satan becomes as small as smoke or a tiny little creature. Thus, shrunken, he goes out visibly from our mouth, like a sow with her piglets, and in his place the Holy Spirit visibly enters and takes his place. They also say that Satan is spat out of us through mucus, spittle and curses. This opinion is not only silly but also false, for it posits both the Holy Spirit and the devil as corporeal.

units.la: 6 Eleemosynas quæ non suæ fidei hominibus fiunt, quanquam egentibus, damnant:Ioannes Damascenus.
units.tr: 6 They condemn alms given to men who are not of their own faith, even though those men are needy (John of Damascus).

units.la: 7 Otiosi viuunt,& fi quis opus aliquod manuum agere aggrediatur, cum ex coe tu suo excommunicant. Opera enim manuum auersantur tanquam impia, contra Dei verbum tamen. Nam ait Dominus, In sudore vultus tui comedes panem tuum. Gen. 3. versu 19. Theff. 3. & Pfalm. 128. verf. 2. Itaque post cantillationes suas absolutas (eas enim certas numero, certisque horis tanquam pensum persoluunt) toto reliquo die otiosi stertunt. Theodoretus libro 4. Histor. cap. 11. Atque hoc ipsum vitae genus postea Monachi lubenter arripuerunt, & hodie etiamnum sequuntur, ut ex Cassian. libro 2. De canonico. noctur. colligi potest. Quod tamen vitae genus insectatur grauissime & damnat apertissime Augustinus in libro De opere Monachorum.
units.tr: 7 They live idly, and if anyone sets about some manual work, they excommunicate him from their assembly. For they shun manual labour as impious, yet this is against the Word of God. For the Lord says, "In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread" (Genesis 3:19; 2 Thessalonians 3; Psalm 128:2). Therefore, after their chantings are finished (for they perform these at fixed numbers and fixed hours, as a set task), they spend the rest of the day in idleness and snoring. (Theodoret, Historia ecclesiastica 4, chapter 11.) This very way of life the monks afterwards eagerly adopted and still follow today, as can be gathered from Cassian, De institutis coenobiorum 2, on the canonical night office. Yet Augustine, in his book De opere monachorum, most severely attacks and most openly condemns this way of life.

units.la: 8 Neque mendacium neque periurium execrantur, vel damnant, quod latitandi & celandae religionis gratia fit. Itaque impune sibi fidem suam negare permittunt, sed & iurare & peierare docent, ne detegantur. Id quod ab iis Prifcillianiftę postea didicere. In quo dupliciter peccant, quod & interrogatos homines fidem abnegare sine scelere posse putant, contra illud Apocal. 21. verf. 8. & Matth. 10. versu 33. & quòd mentiri permittunt Christianis, contra Pfalm. 5. versu. 7. Hinc quoque nata est illa Scholastico-rum sententia & defensio, de officioso mendacio minime damnando.
units.tr: 8 They neither execrate nor condemn lying or perjury, when it is done for the sake of hiding and concealing their religion. Thus they allow men to deny their faith with impunity, and they even teach them to swear and to perjure themselves so that they may not be discovered. The Priscillianists later learned this from them. In this they sin in two ways: first, because they think that men can deny the faith when questioned without sin, contrary to Revelation 21:8 and Matthew 10:33; second, because they permit Christians to lie, contrary to Psalm 5:7. From this, too, arose that opinion and defence of the Schoolmen, that the officious lie is by no means to be condemned.

units.la: 9 Baptismi vim ad precedentia tantum peccata delenda, non etiam ad futura abolenda & remittenda valere docent. Nouaculae enim comparant, qua pili tantum enati secantur & raduntur, latentes autem adhuc in carne non item. Theodor. in Epitom.
units.tr: 9 They teach that the power of baptism extends only to blotting out past sins, not to abolishing and remitting future ones. For they compare it to a razor, which cuts and shaves only the hairs that have grown, but not those still lying hidden in the flesh (Theodore, in the Epitome).

units.la: V Diuin. decret. 10 Sacramenta denique nihil nos Christianos iuuare. Itaque impunè & sine piaculo contemni. Quod & de Baptismo, & de sacra Domini Cœna ab iis dici manifestè scribit Theodoret.libr.4.hist. cap.ii.Si quis autem alia eorundem dogma nosse volet, legat Ioannis Damasceni opusculum De hæresibus. Atq; hæc fuit mali surculi monachismi scilicet mala stirps quæ serpentis diaboli veneno infecta, etiam nunc pestifer os profert fructus.
units.tr: V Divin. decret. 10 Finally, they say that the sacraments do nothing to help us Christians, and therefore they may be despised with impunity and without guilt. Theodoret clearly writes that they said this of both baptism and the Lord's Supper (Historia ecclesiastica 4, chapter 11). If anyone wishes to know other doctrines of these men, let him read the little work of John of Damascus De haeresibus. And this was the evil root of monasticism, that is, the evil stock of that shoot, which, infected with the poison of the serpent the devil, even now bears its pestilent fruit.

units.la: HAERESES EX Philastro ab Augustino collecta & transcripta. CAP. LVIII.
units.tr: Heresies collected and transcribed from Philastrius by Augustine. CHAPTER 58.

units.la: Metangismonitæ cur sic appellati. Erroris au-tem caput duplex.
units.tr: Why the Metangismonites are so called. The head of their error is twofold.

units.la: Metangismonitæ{1} dici possunt, qui Metangismon afferunt, dicentes sic esse in Patre{2} Filium, quomodo vas in vase, quasi duo corpora carnaliter opinantes, ita ut Filius intret in Patrem tanquam vas minus in vas maius. Unde & tale nomen hic error accepit, ut Μεταγγισμὸς Græce diceretur. Ἀγγεῖον quippe illa lingua vas dicitur, sed introitus unius vasis in alterum, Latinè uno nomine non potest dici, sicut Græce potuit Μεταγγισμός.
units.tr: The Metangismonites may be called those who teach metangismon, saying that the Son is in the Father in the way that one vessel is in another, supposing, as if they were two bodies in a carnal sense, that the Son enters into the Father as a smaller vessel into a larger. Hence this heresy also received its name, so that in Greek it is called Μεταγγισμός. For ἀγγεῖον in that language means vessel, but the entry of one vessel into another cannot be expressed in Latin by a single word, as the Greek Μεταγγισμός can.

units.la: Græca est appellatio huius hæreseos, à dogmate, non autem ab authore sic denominata. Dicti sunt autem & Metangæi & Metangismonitæ ἀπὸ τῆς Μεταγγισμῶς[?], vt etiam ex hoc Augustini loco docet Isidorus. Quòd autem μεταγγισμὸν[?] vna voce dici, reddiue Latinè non putat posse Augustinus, fallitur. Nam & transuasatio dicitur, vti conuasatio, & elutriatio, vt annotant Grammatici. Quo vero tempore cœperit hæc hæresis, non est obseruatum, quum tamen partim ex Sabellianorum, qui personas in diuinis confundunt, partim ex Anthropomorphitarum, qui Deum corporeum faciunt, erroribus conflata fuerit, proximè Anthropomorphitas sequuta videri potest. Sed neque vbi plurimum vigucrit, neque quandiu, commemoratur, & statim extincta esse verisimile mihi fit, quia pauci omnino de hoc hæreticorum grege scripserunt. Dogma tamen istorum tempore Ioannis Damasceni quodammodo notum vel renouatum videtur, quum lib. 1. De orthodoxa fide, De Trinitate scribens, diserte sæpius repetit, Personas neque confundi, neque comprehendi alias ab aliis: sed inter se ὑπόστασις[?], & haberi, vt vnitas sit motionis & operationis earum, quia, vt rectè sæpius dixit Augustinus, sunt indiuidua Trinitatis opera. Ἀδιάστατοι δὲ καὶ ἀγένητοι ἀλλήλων ὑποστάσεις[?], vt cap. 19. loquitur idem Damascenus. Inde natum est monstrosum illud Scholasticorum Theologorum dogma, de Circuminsessione Personarum, quam vocât, qui Ioan. 14. v. 11. sic ait Christus, Credite mihi, me in Patre, & Patrem in me esse, quem illi locũ nunquā intellexere. Quod autem Epiphanius in Marcionitis vocat Valentinianos, & Colarbasios, Metangismonitas,& Metempsychochitas, alio spectat, nimirum quod hominum animas in alia corpora tanquam liquores in alia vasa post mortem transfundi, inepte & falso contenderent. Sed hi nostri clutriatores nō de hominum animis: sed de ipsis diuinis Personis commenta sua finxerunt,inuexei untque.Atque eo ipso peior est & grauior hic error.
units.tr: The name of this heresy is Greek, taken from its doctrine, not from its author. They were called both Metangaei and Metangismonites, from Μεταγγισμός, as Isidore also shows from this passage of Augustine. But Augustine is mistaken in thinking that μεταγγισμός cannot be rendered in Latin by one word. For it is called transuasatio, as conuasatio and elutriatio are, as the grammarians note. The time when this heresy began has not been recorded; yet since it was compounded partly from the errors of the Sabellians, who confuse the persons in the divine being, and partly from those of the Anthropomorphites, who make God corporeal, it may seem to have followed closely after the Anthropomorphites. But neither where nor how long it flourished is recorded, and it seems to me likely that it was quickly extinguished, since very few of this company of heretics have written about it at all. Yet the doctrine of these men seems to have been in some measure known or revived in the time of John of Damascus, who, writing in the first book of De orthodoxa fide, On the Trinity, repeatedly and expressly says that the persons are neither confused nor comprehended one within another, but that they are distinct hypostases among themselves, and are so regarded that there is unity in their motion and operation, because, as Augustine rightly said more than once, the works of the Trinity are inseparable. Damascene says the same thing in chapter 19: the hypostases of one another are ἀδιάστατοι καὶ ἀγένητοι [undivided and uncreated]. From this arose that monstrous doctrine of the Scholastic theologians concerning the so-called circumincession of the persons, which Christ expresses in John 14:11, when he says: "Believe me that I am in the Father and the Father in me." They never understood this place. As for Epiphanius calling the Valentinians, Colarbasians, Metangismonites and Metempsychosists among the Marcionites, that refers to something else, namely the absurd and false contention that the souls of men are poured after death into other bodies, as liquids are poured into other vessels. But these our tipplers of the Trinity did not devise their fancies concerning the souls of men, but concerning the divine Persons themselves, and brought them in. And for this very reason this error is worse and more grievous.

units.la: 2 In Patre Filium.) Triplex erroris caput.
units.tr: 2 "The Son in the Father." Threefold head of the error.

units.la: 1 Filium in Patre tanquam vas minus in maiore esse & contineri, vt Christi sententia, Ego sum in Patre, locum habeat. Atqui hoc propter vnā eandémque Patris & Filij essentiam dictum est, non quòd corporali quodam situ vel complexu vna persona alteram ambiat, constringat, tangat & amplectatur. Quod de Deo sentire ridiculum est. 2 Deum esse corporeum, & corporali situ modóque ἀἯἃς[?] & habere suum vbi, in quo est. Hoc ex Anthropomorphitis tralatitium est. 3 Caput, quod ex duobus his superioribus necessario consequitur, nimirum in diuina essentia aliquid esse seipsa maius, aliquid etiam minus, quod est prorsus absurdum & ἀσώ-[?] Maius quidem, vt Pater: minus autem, vt Filius: contra quem errorem acerrimè verisimèque disputauit iampridem vir Dei Athanasius Alexandrinus Episcopus. Et hæc quidem de vipera ista minimóque serpente, sed tamen nocentissimo. Tanti est nimirum cùm de Deo cogitamus, à rebus corporeis ad coelestes animū mutatémque traducere.
units.tr: 1. That the Son is in the Father and contained in him as a smaller vessel in a larger, so that the saying of Christ, "I am in the Father," would have this sense. Yet this was said on account of the one and the same essence of the Father and the Son, and not because one person encircles, binds, touches and embraces the other in some bodily position or embrace. To think this of God is ridiculous. (2) That God is corporeal, and has his place by a bodily position and mode, and is somewhere, in which he is. This has been handed down from the Anthropomorphites. (3) The conclusion which follows necessarily from these two former points, namely that in the divine essence one thing is greater than itself and another thing is smaller, which is utterly absurd and ... The greater is the Father, the lesser is the Son. Against this error the man of God, Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, disputed long ago most fiercely and with truth. And these things concerning this viper, that very small but nonetheless most harmful serpent. So much is at stake when, in thinking of God, we turn the mind from bodily things to heavenly ones.

units.la: CAP. LIX. Seleuciani vel Hermiani cur sic dicti. Erroris autem eorum capita septem.
units.tr: CHAPTER 59. Why the Seleucians or Hermians are so called. Their errors are seven in number.

units.la: Seleuciani vel Hermiani ab authoribus Seleuco & Hermia, qui elementorum materiam{1}, de qua fictus est mundus, non a Deo factam dicunt, sed Deo coaeternam. Nec animam Deo tribuunt creatori, sed creatores esse animarum Angelos volunt, de igne & spiritu. Malum autem asserunt aliquando esse a Deo, aliquando a materia. Negant Salvatorem in carne sedere ad dextram Patris, sed ea se exuisse perhibent, eamque in sole posuisse, accipientes occasionem{3} de Psalmo, ubi legitur, In sole posuit tabernaculum suum. Negant etiam visibilem paradisum. Baptismum in aqua non accipiunt. Resurrectionem non putant futuram, sed quotidie fieri in generatione filiorum.
units.tr: The Seleucians or Hermians take their names from the authors Seleucus and Hermias. They say that the matter of the elements, out of which the world was fashioned, was not made by God but is coeternal with God. Nor do they attribute the soul to God the creator; they hold that the creators of souls are angels, made of fire and spirit. They assert that evil sometimes comes from God and sometimes from matter. They deny that the Saviour sits in the flesh at the right hand of the Father; they claim that he laid the flesh aside and placed it in the sun, taking their occasion from the Psalm where it is written, "In the sun he has placed his tabernacle." They also deny a visible paradise. They do not receive baptism in water. They do not think there will be a resurrection, but say that it happens every day in the begetting of children.

units.la: 1 Seleuciani vel Hermiani.) Antestari libet in plurimarum, quae sequuntur, haerefcon explicatione nos bonis probatisque authoribus destitui. Nam nec Philastrum, nec Alphonsum de Castro, nec alios aliles scriptores moramur, in quibus & diligen[?]. m & iudicium requirimus. Itaque quanquam inuestigandi studium in sequentibus haeresibus nobis non defuerit, unde tamen adiuuaremur ut in superioribus, non habuimus: contenti ergo erunt aequi nostri huius laboris iudices & lectores qualicunque opera nostra & diligentia. Sed ad Seleucianos & Hermianos, vel potius Hermogenistas accedamus. Videtur Philaster, & post cum Augustinus, duas eásque diuersas hæreses, quæ etiam diuerso tempore fuerunt, confudisse potiùs, quàm coniun-xisse. Harum prior ab Hermia vel Hermoge-ne (idem enim & unus utroque nomine dictus est) Hermogenianorum nominata est, extitit-que sub Severo Imperatore & Zepherino Episcopo Roman. circa annum à Christo passo 177. & tempore Tertulliani, & postea Samosa-teni. Fuit autem Hermogenes iste Afer natio-ne, cuius delirium de æterna huius mundi ma-teria, pulcherrimo opere refutauit Tertullian. deditque Manichæorum hæreseos, quæ postea producta est, jaciendæ magna fundamenta. Multi quidem Hermiæ & Hermii hæretici fuisse le-guntur (veluti Hermias vel Hermas Anthropo-morphitarum defensor, de quo Theodor. in hi-storiis: & alius Manichæorum discipulus, de quo idem Theodoretus lib. 1. Hæret. fabularū: item alius Sabbatii Episcopi fautor, de quo Nice-phor. lib. 14. cap. 13. & ipse hæreticus) cui tamen potius quàm Afro Hermogenianos istos erro-res tribuam, non habeo. Primùm, quòd eos in Hermogenem agens refutat Tertullian, deinde quòd notissima & perniciosissima fuit istius hæresis, adeò vt illius etiam in compendio suo me-minerit Isidorus: nec verisimile est eam ab Au-gustino Afro vel Philastro illius ætatis vicino scriptore præterrmitti potuisse. Nec verò nos varietas nominis perturbare debet. Idè enim & Hermias, & Hermas & Hermogenes dici solet. Denique Hermianorum hæreticorum nulli alii probati authores meminerunt, nisi pro Hermogenianis accipiantur. Seleuciani vero alij fuerūt ex ipsis Manichæorum fontibus, meo quidem iudicio, orti, tempore tamen Hermogenianis posteriores, eandem tamen de æterna mundi materia falsam sententiam secuti, qui post Manichæorum ortum innotuerunt circa annum à Christo passo 247. Eadem vero quæ Manichæi professi sunt, de mali origine, creatione mundi, resurrectione carnis: quædam tantum, quo laterent tutius & securius, in iam exosa & damnata hæresi interpolarunt & mutarunt, vt diuersi ab aliis esse censerentur. Huius sectæ nec Theodoretus qui Epiphanio posterior fuit: nec Damascenus, qui iunior Theodoreto vixit: nec etiam Nicephorus vel quarumlibet ineptiarum magnus coacervator, fecit mentionem vllam. Itaque pauca omnino à nobis de ea dici possunt. Et verisimile est à variis Manetis discipulis variis in locis & mundi plagis eundem errorem diuerso nomine sparsum propagatumq; viguisse, ne nos nominum diuersitas abducat.
units.tr: 1 The Seleucians or Hermians. I would like to say beforehand that in explaining most of the heresies that follow I am without good and approved authors. For I do not dwell on Philastrius, Alfonso de Castro, or other writers of various kinds, in whom we look for both diligence and judgment. So although I have not lacked zeal for investigation in the following heresies, I have not had the help that I had in the earlier ones. My fair judges and readers will therefore be content with my labour and diligence, whatever their quality. But let us come to the Seleucians and Hermians, or rather the Hermogenians. Philastrius, and after him Augustine, seem to have confused two distinct heresies, which also arose at different times, rather than joined them. The earlier of these was named the Hermogenians after Hermias or Hermogenes (for the same man is called by both names). It arose under the emperor Severus and Bishop Zephyrinus of Rome, about the year 177 after Christ's passion, and in the time of Tertullian, and afterwards of Samosatenus. This Hermogenes was an African by birth, whose madness concerning the eternity of this world's matter Tertullian refuted in a splendid work, and he laid great foundations for the later Manichaean heresy. Many heretics named Hermias or Hermius are read of (for example Hermias or Hermas, a defender of the Anthropomorphites, of whom Theodoret speaks in his histories; another, a disciple of the Manichaeans, of whom the same Theodoret speaks in book 1 of his Heretical Fables; and another, a supporter of Bishop Sabbatius, of whom Nicephorus speaks in book 14, chapter 13, and who was himself a heretic). I do not, however, have any reason to ascribe these Hermogenian errors to any of them rather than to the African. First, because Tertullian, when refuting them, is arguing against Hermogenes; second, because this heresy was very notorious and very pernicious, so much so that Isidore mentions it even in his summary; and it is not likely that Augustine, an African, or Philastrius, a writer near that age, could have passed it over. Nor should the variety of names disturb us, for he is commonly called Hermias, Hermas and Hermogenes alike. Finally, no other approved authors mention the Hermian heretics except as Hermogenians. The Seleucians, however, were some others, arising, in my judgment, from the very sources of the Manichaeans; yet they came later than the Hermogenians, following the same false opinion about the eternity of the world's matter, and became known after the rise of the Manichaeans, about the year 247 after Christ's passion. Indeed they professed what the Manichaeans professed about the origin of evil, the creation of the world, and the resurrection of the flesh; but certain points they altered and changed in an already hated and condemned heresy, so that, to lie hidden more safely and securely, they might be thought different from the others. Neither Theodoret, who was later than Epiphanius, nor Damascene, who lived younger than Theodoret, nor even Nicephorus, the great heaper-up of all kinds of trifles, makes any mention of this sect. So very little can be said of it by us. And it is likely that this same error, spread under various names by various disciples of Manes in various places and regions of the world, flourished, so that the diversity of names may not mislead us.

units.la: 2 Elementorum materiam. ) Septem hic recensentur duarum superiorum hæresèon capita, quorum alia ab Hermogene, alia à Manichæis defensa introductàque legimus. Ex his autem hoc est. 1 Materiam mundi huius esse Deo coæternam, non autem à Deo, vt cætera, factam & creatam. Hæc fuit proculdubio antiqua in Ecclesia controuersia, vt docet Eusēb.lib.5.cap.27. quæ tamen vulgò censetur Hermogenis commentum & delirium, quod postea interpolauit Manes. Nam idipsum à Philosophis Stoicis, vt pene omnia sua sumpserat Hermogenes, vt docet Tertull. 2 Ab Angelis de igne & spiritu, quae sunt tenuissimae es-sentiae, creatas esse hominum animas, & creari quotidie, non autem a Deo, contra manifestam Scripturae vocem, 1. Petr. 4. verf. 19. Deuteron. 31. verf. 16. Hebr. 12. verf. 9. Sed hoc ipsum omnium ex Platonis Timaeo in scholam Christianorum traductum est ineptissime. Est enim salsissimum. 3 Malum esse a Deo partim, partim a Materia, Manichaeorum dogma & delirium illi cum Marcionitis commune, & cum Philosophis plerisque, qui causam mali & confusionum, quae in his rebus cernuntur, tribuunt materiae, quam & caecam dicunt, & semper impetu quodam ad novas formas induendas ruere fingunt & contendunt. Collutiani vero haeretici, de quibus postea, huic dogmati profusus adversantur, vt Isidorus scribit, qui adeo malum a Dei natura putant alienum, vt ne mala quidem poenae, quae dicuntur (quales sunt afflictiones) a Deo proficisci & immitti velint, contra dictum Prophetae Amos 3. verf. 6. ita mutuis se vulneribus confodiunt haeretici. 4 Negant Christum ascendisse & sedere in carne ad dexteram Patris. Eum enim carnem suam, cum in coelum ascenderet, in sole deposuisse [?], quod perperam ex Psalm. 19. verf. 5. confirmare nituntur. Hoc Manicheanum est, vt superius docuimus, & Augustinus lib. 2. contra Faustum cap. 5. annotauit. Carpocrates quidem antea dixerat solam animam Christi in coelum ascendisse, quod perae-que impium & falsum quoque est. 5 Negant vllum visibilem paradisum primùm à Deo conditum, in quo Adamus & Eva à Deo colloca-ti fuerint, & ita hominem à Deo ipso malum peccatoremque creatum non subobscurè indi-cant. Præterea manifestissimè Scripturæ repu-gnant, Genes.2. vers.8. sed in eam sententiam propter allegorias Origenis & aliorum indu-ctos deceptosq; fuisse verisimile est, qui omnia illa ad suas speculationes revocant. 6 Baptismum in aqua fieri non probant propter clementi [?] vilitatem, quod est tamen signum à Christo ipso institutum, Actor.8. versu 36. & vox ipsa βαπτισμὸς [?] aqua fieri debere satis ostendit. Inde factum & receptum est, ut à Papistis multa adderentur tanquam Baptismi ornamenta, & signa potiora ipsa aqua, quale chrisma, sputum, cereus, & huiusmodi quædam nugæ, ut est in cano.Prima igitur. De consecrat.distin.4. 7 Negant resurrectionem carnis, quod illis est cum multis commune.
units.tr: 2 The matter of the elements. Seven points of the two earlier heresies are listed here, some of which we read were defended and introduced by Hermogenes, others by the Manichaeans. Of these the following are the points. (1) That the matter of this world is coeternal with God, and not made and created by God like the rest. This was without doubt an ancient controversy in the Church, as Eusebius teaches in book 5, chapter 27; yet it is commonly held to be an invention and madness of Hermogenes, which Manes afterwards elaborated; for Hermogenes had taken this very thing from the Stoic philosophers, as he had taken almost all his notions, as Tertullian teaches. (2) That human souls were created by angels out of fire and spirit, which are the most subtle essences, and are created daily, not by God, against the plain word of Scripture, 1 Peter 4:19; Deuteronomy 31:16; Hebrews 12:9. But this very thing was carried over most foolishly into the school of Christians from Plato's Timaeus, for it is extremely insipid. (3) That evil comes partly from God and partly from matter: a dogma and madness of the Manichaeans, held in common with the Marcionites, and with most philosophers, who attribute the cause of evil and of the confusions seen in these things to matter, which they call blind and imagine and assert always rushes with some impulse to put on new forms. The Collutians, however, heretics of whom we shall speak later, strongly oppose this dogma, as Isidore writes; they think evil so alien to the nature of God that they will not allow even the evils that are called punishments (such as afflictions) to proceed from God and be sent by him, contrary to the saying of the prophet Amos 3:6; thus the heretics pierce themselves with mutual wounds. (4) They deny that Christ ascended and sits in the flesh at the right hand of the Father. For, as they try to prove from Psalm 19:5, when he ascended into heaven he laid his flesh aside in the sun. This is Manichaean, as we taught above, and Augustine noted it in book 2 against Faustus, chapter 5. Carpocrates had earlier said that only the soul of Christ ascended into heaven, which is equally impious and false. (5) They deny that there was any visible paradise first founded by God, in which God placed Adam and Eve; and thus they not obscurely indicate that man was created evil and a sinner by God himself. Moreover, they plainly contradict Scripture, Genesis 2:8; but it is likely that they were led into this opinion, and deceived, by the allegories of Origen and others, who refer all those things to their own speculations. (6) They do not allow baptism in water to be performed, on account of its supposed meanness, though it is a sign instituted by Christ himself, Acts 8:36; and the very word baptismos [βαπτισμός] shows sufficiently that it must be done in water. From this it came about and was received that the Papists added many things as ornaments of baptism, and signs more important than the water itself, such as chrism, spittle, the candle, and similar trifles, as is found in the canon Prima igitur, De consecratione, distinctio 4. (7) They deny the resurrection of the flesh, which they hold in common with many.

units.la: 3 Occasionem de Psalmo.) Locus est Psal.19. versu 5. qui ad solem, cui Dominus in cœlo domicilium posuit, non ad Christum pertinet. Id quod omnes linguæ Hebraicæ docti sciunt. Itaque legendum est, Soli in illis tabernaculum posuit. Sed imperitia Hebraicæ linguæ sæpe à veteribus erratum est.
units.tr: 3 The occasion taken from the Psalm. The passage is Psalm 19:5, which refers to the sun, in which the Lord has placed a dwelling in heaven, not to Christ. All who are learned in the Hebrew language know this. Therefore it should be read, "In them he has placed a tabernacle for the sun." But through ignorance of the Hebrew language the ancients have often erred.

units.la: CAP. LX.
units.tr: CHAPTER 60.

units.la: Proclianitæ quibus successerint, & quid senserint.
units.tr: The Proclianites, who succeeded them, and what they held.

units.la: Proclianitæ secuti sunt istos, & addiderunt Christum non in carne venisse.
units.tr: The Proclianites followed these men, and added that Christ did not come in the flesh.

units.la: Vtrum Procliani vel Proclianitæ dicantur, nihil interest. Ratio enim Grammatica patitur vtrunque. A Proclo enim vel Proculo (quod idem est: quem enim Græci Πρόκλον[?], Romani Proculum dicunt) deriuantur, qui superioris hæreseos defensor: huius autem autor & parens fuit. Quis autem hic fuerit (nisi si fortasse is censeatur, qui Cataphrygarum erroris suspectus ab Eusebio commemoratur, libro 2. cap.25. Histor. deinde à Nicephoro lib.4.) explicari non potest. Sed is ante Manetem & Manichæos vixit: hic noster post-ca[?], vt alius mihi videatur. Obscuri enim nominis tota hæc hominum facta fuit, vt nec Isidorus, nec Platina ex recentioribus: nec Græci posteriores, qualis Damascenus vel Nicephorus vel Zonaras illius meminerint. Ex collocatione tamen suspicamur eos fuisse Seleucianis ætate proximos. Fuit autem Proclus quidam Constantinopol. Episcopus, post Maximum, Theodosij iunioris tempore, Ioan. Chrysostomi discipulus & amanuensis, vt Nicephorus scribit lib.14. cap.37. sed is nullius vnquam hæreseos damnatus est, sed ne accusatus quidem vel insimulatus. Hic autem noster hæreticus fuit. Huius autem sectæ vna hæc hypothesis propria (in reliquis enim senserunt cum Seleucianis) censetur, Christum in carne non venisse. Id quod aperte Antichristianum dogma vocat Ioannes 1. epi-stola, cap.4.vers.3. & totum salutis nostrae fun-damentum subruit, denique Deum mendacem constituit, & efficit falsam Euangelij praedica-tionem. Itaque plane blasphema sententia dicenda est. His autem simillimę fuerunt aliquę duę haereticorum familiae, quorum Ioan. Damascenus meminit. Ex iis autę alij Christolytæ (quod Christum dissoluerent, & Christum cum carne in coelum ascendisse negent) alij Aphtartodoci-tæ nominantur, quod Christum verum hom-inem fuisse negent, & vere passum, nostrisque infirmitatibus, excepto tamen peccato, corpus obnoxium assumpsisse. Quæ omnes sententiæ plane nostram salutem evertunt, & sunt repeti-ta Marcionitarum crambe.
units.tr: It makes no difference whether they are called Proclians or Proclianites, since grammar allows either. They take their name from Proclus or Proculus (for the Greeks call him Πρόκλος, the Romans Proculus, and it is the same man), who defended the earlier heresy, though he was its author and parent. Who he was cannot be explained, unless perhaps he is taken to be the man who, suspected of the error of the Cataphrygians, is mentioned by Eusebius (Hist. book 2, chapter 25) and then by Nicephorus (book 4). But he lived before Manes and the Manichaeans, whereas our man comes later, so he seems to me to be a different person. The whole history of these men has been lost in obscurity, so that neither Isidore nor Platina among the more recent writers, nor the later Greeks such as Damascene, Nicephorus or Zonaras, mention him. From his place in the sequence, however, we suspect they were close in time to the Seleucians. There was a certain Proclus, bishop of Constantinople after Maximus, in the time of Theodosius the Younger, a disciple and secretary of John Chrysostom, as Nicephorus writes (book 14, chapter 37). But he was never condemned for any heresy, not even accused or charged with one. Our heretic, however, was of another sort. The one distinctive doctrine of this sect (for in other matters they agreed with the Seleucians) is held to be that Christ did not come in the flesh. John in his first epistle, chapter 4, verse 3, plainly calls this an antichristian dogma, and it overthrows the whole foundation of our salvation; it also makes God a liar and renders the preaching of the Gospel false. It must therefore be called a plainly blasphemous opinion. Very similar to these were two other families of heretics, which John Damascene mentions. Of these, some are called Christolytes (because they dissolve Christ, and deny that Christ ascended into heaven with his flesh), others Aphthartodocetes, because they deny that Christ was a true man and truly suffered, and say that he took on a body liable to our infirmities, sin excepted. All these opinions plainly overturn our salvation, and they are the rehashed cabbage of the Marcionites.

units.la: CAP. LXI.
units.tr: CHAPTER LXI.

units.la: Patriciani cur sic appellati. Erroris eorum capita duo recensentur.
units.tr: Why the Patricians were so called. Two heads of their error are set out.

units.la: Patriciani{1} a Patricio nuncupati, substantiam carnis humanæ non a Deo, sed a diabolo conditam dicunt, eamque sic fingendam & detestandam putant, ut quidam eorum perhibeantur etiam morte sibi illata carere carne voluisse.
units.tr: The Patricians{1}, named after Patricius, say that the substance of human flesh was created not by God but by the devil. They think it is so monstrous and detestable that some of them are said to have wished to be rid of the flesh even by inflicting death on themselves.

units.la: {1} Patriciani.) Minutæ iam aliquot hæreses sequuntur, non quidem dogmatis, sed famæ & celebritatis ratione, qualis hæc. Pauci enim omnino huius meminerunt, & quod reliqui de ea scribunt, veluti Isidorus, Gratianus, & Bernardus Lutzemburgus, ex hoc Augustini loco transcriptum est ad verbum. Ac mihi quidem fit verisimile, cum hæc effet cœnosus Marcionitarum & Manichæorum fontis riuulus, ab vno aliquo dogmatum istorum discipulo & propagatore nouo Patricianorum nomine vocatam & donatam, quo lateret securius, lubentius-que reciperetur: quæ tamen statim extincta neque latius peruagata est. Nec vero nouum est, vt vnus & idem error variis a professorum nomine appellationibus, tanquam variæ essent hæreses, proponatur & damnetur. Ergo quis fuerit hic Patricius non est traditum. Neque enim is fuit qui a Socrate lib.3.Histor.cap.25.di-citur Episcopus Palti. (Paltos autem erat Syriæ ad Libanum sitæ oppidum) quia fidem orthodoxam ille tenuit. Hic autem noster Patri-cius fuit plane ἀλλόδοξος[?] & hæreticus, & quidem teterrimi dogmatis propugnator. Sed nec is Patricius est, cuius meminit Suidas & sub Iouiniano vixit. Extitit enim hæc hæresis, non tantum post Cerdonianorum, Marcionitarum & Manichæorum tempora: sed etiam, vt videtur, post Epiphanij ætatem, qui sub Arcadio Imperatore vixit, fortasse circa annum a Christo passo 387. Pauco vero tempore viguit ista secta permansitve, quę alia fuit quam Paternia-norum siue Venustianorum hæreticorum, de quibus postea hic ipse Augustinus. De his autem nostris idem Augustinus lib.2. contra aduersar. Legis & Prophetar. cap.12. sic ait, Fuerunt à quodam Patricio nonnulli Patriciani, qui sunt similiter aduersantes diuinis veteribus libris. Ioànes autem Damascenus Parermeneutas ap-pellasse videtur, quanquam quæ fuerit eorum hæresis & dogma non explicat accuratè. Venu-stianos tamen & Paternianos huius stirpis furculum fuisse sane crediderim.
units.tr: {1} The Patricians.) Now follow several minor heresies, important not for their doctrine but for their notoriety and fame, and this is one of them. Hardly anyone mentions it at all, and what the others write about it, such as Isidore, Gratian and Bernard of Luxembourg, is copied word for word from this passage of Augustine. It seems likely to me that, since this was a muddy little stream flowing from the spring of the Marcionites and Manichaeans, some disciple and promoter of those doctrines gave it the new name of Patricians, so that it might lie hidden more safely and be received more readily. Yet it was quickly snuffed out and did not spread widely. Nor is it new for one and the same error to be set forth and condemned under various names taken from its professors, as though they were different heresies. Who this Patricius was has not been recorded. He was not the man whom Socrates (Hist. 3.25) calls bishop of Paltus (Paltos was a town of Syria near Lebanon), for that man held the orthodox faith. Our Patricius was entirely of another opinion [allodoxos] and a heretic, indeed a champion of a most abominable doctrine. Nor is he the Patricius mentioned by Suidas, who lived under Jovian. For this heresy arose not only after the times of the Cerdonians, Marcionites and Manichaeans, but also, it seems, after the age of Epiphanius, who lived under the emperor Arcadius, perhaps around the year 387 after the passion of Christ. This sect flourished, or persisted, only for a short time. It was different from the Paternians or Venustians, the heretics of whom Augustine himself speaks later. Concerning these our Patricians, Augustine says in book 2 of his work Against the Adversaries of the Law and the Prophets, chapter 12: "Some Patricians came from a certain Patricius, who likewise oppose the divine old books." John Damascene seems to have called them Parermeneutae, though he does not explain accurately what their heresy and doctrine were. Yet I would certainly believe that the Venustians and Paternians were an offshoot of this stock.

units.la: 1 Substantiam carnis.) Tres videntur colligi posse[?] huius sectæ hypothescs[?]. 1 Substantiam carnis, id est, corporis à Deo conditam non esse, sed à diabolo. Isidorus. Caro enim apud eos corpus significat, non totam humanam naturam, id est, animam & corpus, quibus duabus partibus constamus singuli. Cur autem fallerentur, ratio est, quòd passim in Scriptura & opera carnis & concupiscentiæ damnantur, veluti Ga-lat.5.vers.19: Rom.8.vers.13: 1.Corinth.16.v.50: 1.Ioan.2. vers.16. Sed homonymia vocis hallu-cinantur turpissimè. Tunc enim caro non sub-stantiam ipsam corporis, sed vitiositatem illam quæ per peccatum Adami humanæ naturæ su-peruenit, tanquam vulnus & sauciatio quædam integro & valenti membro, designat. Quatenus enim caro pro ipsa corporis substantia sumitur, à Deo creata est, non autem à Diabolo. Quate-nus humanam etiam naturam denotat, Dei plane opus est, & carnem assumpsit Christus ipse filius Dei dilectissimus & qui sanctissimus sem per mansit. Ioan.1.vers.14. Hebr.2.vers.14. adeò vt Christum ipsum verum hominem fuisse, car-nemque assumpsisse negét, qui carnis substantiam execratur, & detestandum diaboli opus esse defendit. Id quod cum Marcionitarum & Manichæorum errore coniunctū est. 2 Chri-stianum hominem mortem sibi consciscere posse putant, vt se hac carnis mole, i. corpore nostro exuat. Hos intelligit Chryfoftomus in 1.cap. epistolæ Pauli ad Galatas. Ratio videri potest ducta ex Rom.7.v.24. his verbis, Miser homo ego, quis me eripiet ex isto corpore mortis? Sed de vitiis & peccatis, quæ in nobis hic viuentibus habitant & sæpe regnant, loquitur illic Paulus, quemadmodum alibi doctissime Augustin. interpretatur, lib. De natura & gratia cap.55. non autem ipsam corporis φύσιν detestatur, quam idem affirmat resurrecturam, 1.Corinthians.15.verf.53.
units.tr: 1 The substance of the flesh.) Three tenets of this sect seem to be deducible. 1. The substance of the flesh, that is, of the body, was created not by God but by the devil. (Isidore.) For among them "flesh" means the body, not the whole human nature, that is, soul and body, of which we each consist. The reason they went astray is that throughout Scripture the works of the flesh and the lusts are condemned, as in Gal. 5:19; Rom. 8:13; 1 Cor. 15:50; 1 John 2:16. But they are shamefully deceived by the ambiguity of the word. For "flesh" there designates not the substance of the body itself but that corruption which came upon human nature through the sin of Adam, like a wound or some kind of injury to a whole and healthy limb. Insofar as flesh is taken for the very substance of the body, it was created by God, not by the devil. Insofar as it also denotes human nature, it is plainly God's work, and Christ himself, the most beloved Son of God, who always remained most holy, took on flesh (John 1:14; Heb. 2:14). So they deny that Christ himself was a true man and had assumed flesh, since they execrate the substance of the flesh and maintain that it is a detestable work of the devil. This is joined with the error of the Marcionites and Manichaeans. 2. They think a Christian man can bring death upon himself so as to strip off this mass of flesh, that is, our body. Chrysostom has these people in view in his commentary on the first chapter of Paul's Epistle to the Galatians. The reasoning can be seen from Rom. 7:24, in these words: "Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?" But Paul there speaks of the vices and sins which dwell in us while we live here and often reign, as Augustine most learnedly explains elsewhere, in On Nature and Grace, chapter 55. He does not reject the nature of the body itself, which the same Paul affirms will rise again (1 Cor. 15:53).

units.la: 3 Error, Vetus testamentum mutilant & truncant, nec libros omnes qui sunt ἁγιόγραφοι ἢ ἐνδιάθηκοι [?] recipiunt. Augustin. lib.2. contra aduerf.Legis & Prophetas cap.12. Ita nimirum semper accidit, vt error errori cumulētur, & qui paruus primum videbatur, si antecedentia consequentiaque ex eo colligamus, magnus omninoque periculosus tandem appareat. Itaque vel leuissimos quosque haereticorum afflatus, quia sunt Satanæ flabella, diligentissime cauere, & tanquam omina infausta procurare debemus.
units.tr: 3. Error: they mutilate and truncate the Old Testament, and do not accept all the books that are hagiographa or endiathēka [?]. (Augustine, book 2 against the Adversaries of the Law and the Prophets, chapter 12.) Thus it always happens that error is piled upon error, and what at first seemed small, if we gather from it what goes before and what follows, finally appears great and altogether dangerous. Therefore we must most diligently guard against even the slightest breath of heretics, since they are Satan's fans, and avert them as unlucky omens.

units.la: CAP. LXII.
units.tr: CHAPTER 62.

units.la: Ascitæ cur sic dicti. Erroris autem eorum caput ecquod fuerit.
units.tr: Why the Ascitae were so called. And what was the chief of their error.

units.la: Scitæ[?] ab utre{1} sic appellati sunt. Ἀσκὸς[?] enim Græce, Latinè uter dicitur, quem gestare perhibentur inflatum & opertum circumire bacchantes, tanquam ipsi sint Evangelici utres novi vino novo repleti.
units.tr: The Scitae[?] were so called from the wineskin (uter). For in Greek ἀσκός is what in Latin is called uter, and they are said to carry it about inflated and covered, running about in frenzy, as if they themselves were the new wineskins of the Gospel, filled with new wine.

units.la: 1 Ascita ab utre.) Hi vero etiam Utrarij vel Utriculari dici possunt, quod ut à Græco ἀσκὸς Ἀσκίτης[?], ita à Latino Uter, Utrarius certè formatur. Quæ fuerit autem hæc hominum secta, ubi grassata, quandiu perstiterit, & quo primum authore cœperit, legisse me non memini. At ne apud Isidorum quidem huius facta mentio est, tam leuiter deiecta & explosa nimirum fuit. Fortasse ad pompæ eius, quæ in sacris Dionysij Bacchi Athenis fiebat, & in qua σκαφοφόροι & ἀσκοφόροι erant, quemadmodum Suidas scribit, similitudinem istos excitauit Satan, qui nova & prodigiosa plane ratione se Dei ministros & Evangelij præcones profiterentur, qui digni erant, ad Probi imperatoris Romani exemplum, nomine utris in aere pendere potius, quam viuere re. Hi vero sunt dissimillimi ab iis, quos Ascodrupetas Theodoretus appellat, de quibus diximus antea. Enthousiastæ tamen & prorsus fa-natici homines etiam isti fuisse mihi videntur, & in loci illius qui est apud Matthæum explicatione falluntur & hallucinantur.
units.tr: 1 Ascita from the wineskin.) These men may also be called Utrarii or Utriculari, for from the Latin uter the form Utrarius is certainly derived, just as from the Greek ἀσκός comes Ἀσκίτης[?]. I do not remember having read what this sect of men was, where it spread, how long it lasted, or under whose leadership it began. Indeed, not even Isidore mentions it; it was no doubt so lightly cast down and driven out. Perhaps Satan stirred them up by resemblance to the procession of Dionysus Bacchus at Athens in his sacred rites, in which there were σκαφοφόροι and ἀσκοφόροι, as Suidas writes. They professed to be ministers of God and heralds of the Gospel by a new and plainly monstrous method, and they deserved, after the example of the Roman emperor Probus, to hang in the air by the name of a wineskin rather than to live in reality. Yet these men are wholly unlike those whom Theodoret calls Ascodrupetae, of whom we spoke earlier. Still, these also seem to me to have been enthusiasts and utterly fanatical men, and they go wrong and wander in their explanation of that passage in Matthew.

units.la: 2 Quem gestare.) In impressis sic legitur, Quem perhibentur, hiulca prorsus oratione. Itaque vocabulum quod incuria librariorum excidit, reposuimus. Huius autem hæresis dogma recefet[?] Augustinus, quod utre inflatum & opertum circumferendum putant iis, qui ex Christi praecepto legitimè sanctum Euangelium praedicare velint, abusi sacro Dei verbo quod est apud Matthaeum 9. verf.17. & fortassis illo militum Gedeonis exemplo, quod extat in libro Iudicum cap.7. verf.16. Sed ineptissimè. Quid enim fiet, si ea quae [illegible, ~7 letters] Christi continent, omnia vsurpemus? Oportebit nos habere lampades ardentes in manibus nostris, eas circumgestare, lumbos etiam in suggestu praecinctos, & alia pene infinita, quae nos simias potius & ridiculos histriones, quàm graues verbi Dei concionatores demonstrabunt. Itaque insulsa, absurda, & nulla vel probabili ratione fulta fuit haec haeresis. Sed tanti est, verum & genuinum Scripturae sensum diligenter obseruasse.
units.tr: 2 Who carry.) In the printed editions it reads Quem perhibentur, a wholly halting construction. Therefore I have restored the word that fell out through the carelessness of the copyists. Augustine records the doctrine of this heresy: they think that those who wish to preach the holy Gospel lawfully, according to Christ's precept, must carry about a wineskin inflated and covered. They abuse the sacred word of God which is in Matthew 9, verse 17, and perhaps also the example of Gideon's soldiers, which is found in the book of Judges, chapter 7, verse 16. But this is most foolish. For what would happen if we took over everything that the words of Christ contain? We would have to hold burning lamps in our hands and carry them about, and have our loins girded even in the pulpit, and many other almost endless things, which would show us to be apes and ridiculous actors rather than grave preachers of God's word. Therefore this heresy was silly, absurd, and supported by no even plausible reason. But it is worth the trouble to have carefully observed the true and genuine sense of Scripture.

units.la: CAP. LXIII.
units.tr: CAP. LXIII.

units.la: Pattalorinchitae cur sic dicti. Error eorum ecquis fuerit.
units.tr: The Pattalorinchitae: why they are so called, and what their error was.

units.la: P[?]Attalorinchitae {1}intantum silentio studeant, ut naribus, & labiis suis digitum opponant, ne vel ipsam {2}taciturnitatem voce praripiant, quando tacendum sibi esse arbitrantur. Vnde etiam illis nomen est inditum. Πάτταλος enim Græcè dicitur palus, & ῥύγχος[?] nasus. Cur autem per palum digitum significare maluerint, à quibus nomen hoc compositum est, nescio, cùm Græcè dicatur digitus δάκτυλος[?], & possint utique Dactylorinchitae multò evidentius nuncupari.
units.tr: The Attalorinchitae keep such silence that they press a finger to their nostrils and lips, so as not to let even silence itself escape by voice, whenever they think they ought to be silent. That is where their name came from. For palus [Πάτταλος] is the Greek word for a stake, and nose [ῥύγχος]. But why those who gave them this compound name preferred to signify a finger by a stake, I do not know, since the Greek for finger is [δάκτυλος], and they could certainly have been called Dactylorinchitae much more clearly.

units.tr: {1} Patta-

units.la: I Pattalorinchitæ intantum.) Hæc hæresis Monachismi & operistarum fruticatio est, & solitudinis eius, quam ista hominum natio secuta est, atque amplexa, de qua meminit etiam Hierony.in Procæmio lib.2.ad Galat. Nam uti se à communi hominū cœtu, tàquam ferę bestiæ, monachi,subduxerūt,humanam mentem & naturam exuentes: ita varios errores genuerunt, multaque non tantum paradoxa instituerūt,sed ab humanitate ipsa &benecuolentia, quæ inter omnes homines esse debet, aliena probarunt, quod à Deo in sensum reprobum sunt traditi. Nec affirmari potest, vtrum Monachi hæreticorum variorum patriarchæ fuerint: an potius illi hæretici Monachorū patriarchæ & parætes. Pattalorinchitæ ex huiusmodi lustris & cauer-nis prodiere: qui & Silentiarii à silentio quod profitentur dici possunt, & à Cassiano libro 4. De instituţ. renuntiant. cap.17. Tabennesiotæ Monachi videntur appellati, quòd in regione Tabennæa (est autem Tabenne oppidum in extremis Ægypti & Cyrenaicæ regionis finibus situm, quod Plinius videtur Tabidium appellasse, & Garamantis[?] attribuisse lib.5. cap.5. non multum deceptus: quia, vt est in Æthici Cosmographia nuper D.Iofiæ Simleri[?] diligetia luce donata, & ab inferis reuocata, Cyrenaica regio etiam Garamātas habet) primùm hoc vitæ genus fuerit institutum & receptum. Id quod etiam Sozomeni autoritate confirmatur lib.6. Histor.Ecclesiast. cap.28. Ex quo eodem loco apparet hanc hæresin primùm in Ægyptiacis monasteriis natam (nam illius præcipuè regionis monachos laudat Cassianus, quod um-brarum more fuerint silentes, & ἀλαλοί[?]) circa ea ipsa tempora, quibus Eunomianorum error pullulauit, id est, anno a Christo passo 333. Fuit enim eo posterior. Cuius author Theonas quidam monachus Tabennesiota (qui cum Beno defertis illis post Ammonem praefuit) fuisse videtur, cuius cum magna feratur doctrinae & cognitionis trium linguarum laus, imprimis autem illius se-culi hominibus stupedus erat, quod per totos triginta annos siluit. Miror aute[?] ego, quomodo doctum eum intellexerint illius se-culi homines, cum tandiu ipsorum testimonio siluerit, neque quicquam scripsisse dicatur. Solum enim ex scriptis vel ex oratione homines eruditos agnoscimus: ex vultu autem, gestu, habitu peregrino, genibus flexis & lachrymis non intelligimus, ut ementita ea Theonae laus mihi videri soleat, cuius tamen tanta laus per totam Aegyptum fuisse videtur, tantaque celebritas, ut in media Alexandria templum eum habuisse scribat Epiphan.in Ariomanit. Ergo hic istius erroris parens & author a nobis & historicis Ecclesiasticis & a Cassiano imprimis statuitur, nisi quis adhuc antiquiorem eum esse malit, & a Pambone (qui & ipse Aegyptius monachus fuit) profectum censeat, qui ut est apud Socrat[?]libro 4. cap.23. cum ex Psal.34. vers.14. Serva ab iniuria linguam tuam, audiisset, in eo uno implendo edificendoque totum vitae tempus sibi collocandum duxit, silentiumque sibi ex eo perpetuum indixit. Certe tota haec rigida silentij obseruatio, Pythagoricorum inuentum est, qui discipulos suos per quinquennium continuum silere (quam ἡσυχίαν A. Gellius dixit) iubebat. Quanquam autem isti Silentiarij aperte hic ab Augustin. inter hæreticos recen-sentur, tamen peruicit Satan, vt hic error & mos (qui plane est inhumanus & agrestis) non tantum in plerisque monasteriis toleraretur & retineretur: sed nouo Carthusianorum mona-chorum nomine laudaretur, & vt sanctitas quæ-dam commendaretur. Sunt enim Carthusiani istius fœcis limus & sordes, & ipsi vere Pattalo-rinchitæ & Silentiarij damnati. Etsi Bernard. superstitione monachica iam plane fascinatus huiusmodi filetij affectati regulas probat epist. 341. sed vaniffimo argumento. Cum his autem no-stris sunt coniungedi alij hæretici, quorum memi-nit Epiphanius in Cataphrygibus, appellatque Ταγκοσφουγγίται. Porro hæc hæresis statim isto Pattalorinchitarum nomine periit, alieno autem & interpolato, id est, Monachorum retenta, & ad nostra vsque tempora propagata est.
units.tr: I. The Pattalorinchitae keep such silence. This heresy is an offshoot of monasticism and of the Operistae, and of that solitude which this race of men followed and embraced, of which Jerome also speaks in the preface to book 2 of his commentary on Galatians. For just as the monks withdrew from the common company of men like wild beasts, stripping off human mind and nature, so they produced various errors, and they set up many paradoxes, and approved of things alien to humanity itself and to the goodwill that ought to exist among all men. This was because God gave them over to a reprobate mind. Nor can it be affirmed with certainty whether the monks were the patriarchs of various heretics, or rather those heretics were the patriarchs and parents of the monks. The Pattalorinchitae came out of such brothels and caves. They may also be called Silentiaries from the silence they profess, and Cassian in book 4 of his De institutis, chapter 17, calls them the Tabennesiote monks. They seem to have been so named because in the region of Tabenna (Tabenna is a town on the far edge of the regions of Egypt and Cyrenaica, which Pliny seems to have called Tabidium, and assigned to the Garamantes in book 5, chapter 5, not far wrong, since, as the Cosmography of Aethicus, lately brought to light and recalled from the dead by the diligence of Josias Simler, shows, the region of Cyrenaica also has Garamantes), this way of life was first instituted and received. Sozomen's authority confirms this too, in book 6 of his Ecclesiastical History, chapter 28. From the same place it is clear that this heresy was first born in the Egyptian monasteries (for Cassian praises the monks of that region especially, because they were silent in the manner of shadows, and [ἀλαλοί]). It arose around the same time that the error of the Eunomians sprouted, that is, in the year 333 after Christ's passion, for it came somewhat later. Its author seems to have been a certain monk of Tabenna, Theonas, who, with Beno, presided over those deserts after Ammon. He is said to have had great praise for his learning and his knowledge of three languages, and he was especially a marvel to the men of that age, because he kept silence for thirty whole years. I wonder how the men of that age could have judged him learned, when by their own testimony he was silent for so long and is said to have written nothing. We recognise learned men only from their writings or their speech; from a face, a gesture, a strange dress, bent knees and tears we do not understand learning. So that praise of Theonas seems to me to be made up. Yet his praise seems to have spread through all of Egypt, and his fame was so great that Epiphanius, in his work against Arius, writes that he had a temple in the middle of Alexandria. So this man is set down as the parent and author of this error, both by us, by the ecclesiastical historians, and above all by Cassian. Unless someone prefers to make him older still, and holds that it came from Pambo (who was himself a monk of Egypt). According to Socrates, book 4, chapter 23, Pambo heard from Psalm 34:14, "Keep your tongue from evil," and thought that the whole span of his life should be devoted to fulfilling and building up this one thing alone, and so he imposed perpetual silence on himself.
