Certainly this whole rigid observance of silence was an invention of the Pythagoreans, who ordered their disciples to keep silence for five continuous years (which Aulus Gellius called [ἡσυχίαν]). Although Augustine openly counts these Silentiaries among the heretics, Satan nevertheless prevailed, so that this error and custom (which is plainly inhuman and boorish) was not only tolerated and retained in most monasteries, but was also praised under the new name of the Carthusian monks and commended as a kind of holiness. For the Carthusians are the dregs and filth of that sect, and they are truly Pattalorinchitae and condemned Silentiaries. Bernard, already entirely bewitched by monastic superstition, approves the rules of this affected silence in letter 341, though with a most empty argument. With these men of ours should also be joined other heretics, whom Epiphanius mentions among the Cataphrygians, and whom he calls [Ταγκοσφουγγίται]. Moreover, this heresy soon perished under the name Pattalorinchitae, but under another, altered name, that is, of the Monks, it was kept and has been propagated down to our own times.

units.la: 1 Vel ipsam taciturnitatem.) Istorum erro-ris caput fuit, quod futilibus quibusdam nugis, & operibus a rerum natura alienis, vim salutis tribuerent, id quod solent omnes hypocritæ. Itaque isti diuturno suo silentio laudes sanctæ vitæ vindicant, quod si rumpant, putant se dam-natos, credúntque se crimen inexpiabile per-petraffe. Vnde illud Ægyptij Harpocratis fa-ciunt, St, quemadmodum Varro lib.4. De lin-gua Latina scribit, & digito tanquā palo fortis-sime copescunt labia, ne vox vlla erumpat. Nec vana est coniectura tantam silentij obseruationem, támque rigidam non tantùm superiorum Monachorum,à quibus cœtus hi collecti erant, exemplo: sed etiam expresso voto,& iureiurando interposito fancitam, quò res augustior sanctiórque videretur. Ita nimirum hypocritæ illudere Deo volùt. Hæc Nouatianorum & Meletianorum.i.Operiftarum fruticatio est. Nec nouum est, vt huiusmodi quædam blasphema, & non tantùm inepta deliria imperiti & idolo-latræ homines Monachi introduxerint, quando & Iudæorum,& Samaritanorum ritus ab v-niuerfa Ecclesia damnatos,non tantùm inter fe fuifq; in lustris vfurparùt: sed etiâ in Ecclesiam inuexerunt, & reuocarunt, quemadmodum non tantùm Theodoretus libro 1. hiftor.cap.9. testatur: sed etiâ vniuersa Synodus Gangrenfis. Habuerunt autem hæc fere erroris fui funda-menta Silentiarij, quæ pro fe afferrent, Pfal.4. v.14.Iacob.3.v.2.Siquis in sermone non labitur, is perfectus est vir. Denique quod est scriptum Psalmo 39.versu 2.Quasi fiscella os meum,dum coràm fuerit improbus,capistrabo.Quæ omnia primùm non quid præstemus, ostendunt: sed quid præstare debeamus. Deinde non filetiùm importunum & ἀχαριστίαν[?] inducunt, sed tantùm linguæ moderationem suadent. Denique nullam salutis vim istis rebus tribuunt, sed tantùm metus Dei quædam effecta demonstrant. Atque adeo in Deù ipsum grauiter peccat, qui, quum opus est, non loquitur. Oratione enim quemadmodù & ratione homines à brutis maximè differimus, cuius qui vsum inter homines tollit, noñ modò magnas vitæ humanæ cõmo-ditates ditates tollit: sed etiam ex homine pecudem vel potius truncum & lapidem facit. Quamobrem recte, mea quidem sententia, habet proverbiū vetus, [?]σιωπᾶν, ἀλλὰ λαλεῖν, ὅπου χρεών. Atque hi sunt ingenij Satanici fœtus, detestabiles illi quidem, & blasphemi, sed tamen a multis excepti, nimirum ut discamus salutem nostram in veris suis causis quærere, non autem in nostris deliriis collocare. Hi sunt Carthusiani nostri temporis.
units.tr: 1. Even silence itself. The chief error of these men was that they attributed the power of salvation to certain trifling trivialities and works foreign to the nature of things, as all hypocrites are wont to do. So these men, by their long silence, claim the praise of a holy life; if they break it, they think themselves damned, and believe they have committed an inexpiable crime. Hence the Egyptians make that gesture of Harpocrates, as Varro writes in book 4 of his De lingua Latina, and with a finger, as with a stake, they most strongly restrain their lips, so that no voice may escape. Nor is it a vain conjecture that so strict and rigid an observance of silence was established not only by the example of the superior monks, from whom these groups were gathered, but also by an express vow and a sworn oath, so that the thing might seem more august and more holy. Thus, no doubt, hypocrites wish to mock God. This is the offshoot of the Novatians and Meletians, that is, of the Operistae. Nor is it new for ignorant and idolatrous monks to have introduced such blasphemous things, and not merely foolish delusions. They not only used among themselves and in their own dens the rites of Jews and Samaritans, which the whole Church had condemned, but they even brought them into the Church and recalled them, as not only Theodoret attests in book 1 of his History, chapter 9, but also the whole Synod of Gangra. The Silentiaries had as the chief foundations of their error the passages they cited in its support: Psalm 4:14 (in the Vulgate numbering, or Psalm 39), James 3:2, "If anyone does not stumble in speech, he is a perfect man"; and finally what is written in Psalm 39:2, "I will muzzle my mouth like a bridle while the wicked is before me." But all these passages show not what we actually do, but what we ought to do. Further, they do not introduce a troublesome silence or [ἀχαριστίαν], but only recommend moderation of the tongue. Finally, they attribute no power of salvation to these things, but only show certain effects of the fear of God. And so he sins gravely against God himself who does not speak when there is need. For it is by speech, as by reason, that we men differ most from the brutes, and whoever takes away the use of speech among men not only removes great conveniences of human life, but also makes a man into a beast, or rather into a log and a stone. Therefore the old proverb rightly holds, in my opinion, [σιωπᾶν, ἀλλὰ λαλεῖν, ὅπου χρεών] (to keep silent, but to speak where it is needed). And these are the offspring of a Satanic mind: detestable indeed, and blasphemous, yet received by many, no doubt so that we may learn to seek our salvation in its true causes, and not to place it in our own delusions. These are the Carthusians of our time.

units.la: CAP. LXIIII. Aquarii cur sic appellati. Eorum error quis fuerit.
units.tr: CHAPTER 64. Why the Aquarians were so called. What their error was.

units.la: Quary ex hoc appellati sunt, quod aquam offerunt in poculo sacramenti, non illud, quod omnis Ecclesia.
units.tr: They were called Aquarians because they offer water in the cup of the sacrament, not the wine that the whole Church uses.

units.la: 1 Aquarij ex hoc.) Hanc Aquariorum hæresin non tantum partim a Seuerianis, qui vini usum in Ecclesia damnarunt, profectam crediderim: partim etiam ab Helcesaitis, qui aquam pro Deo coluerunt, Thalctisque[?] Ephesij philosophi dogma, vel errore revocarunt: verum etiam cum Encratitis eandem fuisse affirmarim: sed propter nominis varietate, alia & diuersam censeri. Nec novum est, ut vnus & idem error, quia interpolatus, aut a diuersis sparsus est diuersis in locis, diuersarum quoque hæreseon[?] appellatione repetatur, & damnetur. Sic qui inter Græcos Encratitæ, apud Latinos Aquarij a.dogmacis parte sunt nominati. Itaque ad idem tempus utroque refero, & eandem illis infelicem stirpem assigno. Facit autem in hanc sententiam quodammodo Isidorus, qui Seuerianos istis Aquariis in recensendo proximos collocat. Malim tamen ipse Encratitarum schismaticos, & propaginem inauspicatam constituere. Et certe digni erat qui non in Christianorum numero censerentur, sed ad sacra prophanorum Athenien-sium quae vocatur Νηφάλια [?] & Ὑδροπαραστάται [?], quod in his pro vino aqua idolis libaretur, relegarentur. Erroris igitur caput est, Aquam in sancta Domini nostri Iesu Christi Coena pro vino substituendam & porrigendam esse. Quod isti sentire nec poterat, nec auderent, nisi & vinum damnarent ex deliriis Seuerianorum: & aquam magnificarent, quemadmodum Helcesaitae: & certa ciborum genera tanquam detestanda abominarentur, veluti Encratitae. Huius autem erroris prima fundamenta tunc iacta fuisse videntur, quum homines sancta & simplici Coenae institutione, quae a Christo ipso facta est, non contenti, sua commenta illi addiderunt. Quare duobus signis a Christo datis, nempe pani & vino, tertium adiecerunt, aquam, quam vino miscendam esse tradiderunt: non autem seorsim & separatim a vino bibendam. Atque hae vini & aquae mixtione, Christi cum Ecclesia vnionem significari docuerunt. Ita saepe Cyprianus in epistolis, ita Ambrosius in libris De sacramentis, si modo Ambrosij Mediolanensis episcopi illa germana scripta sunt, & non notha & falso inscripta. Ita in fecrat. Distinct.2. Sed & damnati Armenij, vt haeretici, quòd in Coena Domini aquam non adhiberent. His autem nihilo vel meliores, vel faniores alij haeretici, qui à Damasceno Barsaniani, siue Semidalitae nominantur, qui non tantum in caeteris cum Cainianis consentiunt, sed etiam hoc habent à se, sibíque peculiarem errorem etiam praeter Eutychiani Dioscori delirium, quòd in sacrosancta Domini nostri Iesu Christi Coena (in qua nihil immutandum docet Paulus, 1.Corinth.11.versu 23.) pro pane tantum similae & farinae quantum summis digitis comprehendere possunt, capiunt, eámq; summis labris degustát tantum, & pro vsu esúque panis & symboli Coenae substituunt, ita nihil usquam à Satana intactum in religione Christiana relictum est, sed omnia etiam augustissima quaeque foedè conspurcata. Deinde ascititia illa in Coenae sacramentum aqua variis laudibus commendata est, quia & Baptismus solam aquam habet, & in vino intemperantia esse dicitur, eóque iubentur reges abstinere. Ephes.5. versu 18 : Pro-verb.31.versu 4. Praeterea, miracula in aqua facta erant à Narcisso, vt ait Nicephorus libro 5.c.9. Postremò iam exorti Encratitae & Taciani ciborum aliquot, quemadmodum diximus, genera damnarant, ita paulatim confirmata Aquariorum sententia recepta est & probata, quae in Missa Papistica ex parte etiamnum hodie retenta est. tanti nimirum est à Dei institutione & ordinatione non requisisse.
units.tr: 1 The Aquarians are so called for this reason. I would believe that this heresy of the Aquarians came partly from the Severians, who condemned the use of wine in the Church, and partly from the Elkesaites, who worshipped water as God and drew their doctrine or error from Thales the Ephesian philosopher. I would also affirm that it was the same as the Encratites, but because of the difference in name it is counted as another and different sect. Nor is it new for one and the same error, once altered or spread by different people in different places, to be given the names of different heresies and condemned under them. Thus those among the Greeks who were called Encratites were named Aquarians among the Latins, from one part of their doctrine. So I refer both to the same time and assign to both the same unhappy stock. Isidore, who in his list places the Severians next to these Aquarians, supports this view to some extent. I would rather, however, regard them as schismatics of the Encratites and an ill-omened offshoot. And they certainly deserved not to be counted among Christians, but to be relegated to the sacred rites of the profane Athenians, which were called Nephalia [Νηφάλια] and Hydroparastatai [Ὑδροπαραστάται], because in those rites water was poured out to the idols in place of wine. So the chief point of this error is that water must be substituted for wine and offered in the holy Supper of our Lord Jesus Christ. They could not have held this view, nor would they have dared to, unless they also condemned wine, following the delusions of the Severians, and exalted water, as the Elkesaites did, and abhorred certain kinds of food as things to be detested, as the Encratites did. The first foundations of this error seem to have been laid when men, not content with the holy and simple institution of the Supper made by Christ himself, added their own inventions to it. So, besides the two signs given by Christ, bread and wine, they added a third, water, which they taught was to be mixed with the wine, and not drunk separately and apart from it. And by this mixing of wine and water they taught that the union of Christ with the Church is signified. So Cyprian often teaches in his epistles, and so Ambrose in the books On the Sacraments, if indeed those writings are genuinely Ambrose's, the bishop of Milan, and not spurious and falsely ascribed to him. So also in the Decretum, Distinction 2. The Armenians too were condemned as heretics because they did not add water in the Lord's Supper. But other heretics, called by Damascene the Barsanians or Semidalites, were no better or worse than these. They not only agree with the Cainites in other respects, but also have this peculiar error of their own, apart from the madness of Dioscorus the Eutychian. In the most holy Supper of our Lord Jesus Christ, in which Paul teaches that nothing is to be changed (1 Cor. 11:23), they take as much meal and flour as they can grasp with the tips of their fingers, taste it only with the edges of their lips, and use this in place of the bread and the sign of the Supper for eating and use. Thus nothing in the Christian religion has been left untouched by Satan, but even the most venerable things have been foully defiled. Then that spurious water added to the sacrament of the Supper was commended with various praises: because Baptism has only water, and because wine is said to lead to intemperance, and for this reason kings are ordered to abstain (Eph. 5:18; Prov. 31:4). Moreover, Nicephorus, book 5, chapter 9, says that miracles were performed in water by Narcissus. Finally, when the Encratites and Tatian had arisen and condemned certain kinds of food, as we have said, the opinion of the Aquarians was gradually confirmed, accepted and approved, and it is still partly retained today in the Papist Mass. Such is the price of not seeking what God instituted and ordained.

units.la: CAP. LXV. Coluthiani cur sic dicti. Erroris eorum caput.
units.tr: CHAPTER LXV. Why the Coluthians were so called. The chief point of their error.

units.la: Coluthiani à quodam Colutho, qui dicebant Deum non facere mala, contra illud quod scriptum est, Ego Deus creans mala.
units.tr: The Coluthians, from a certain Coluthus, who taught that God does not make evil things, against what is written: "I, God, create evil."

units.la: I {Coluthiani à quodam.) Coluthiani dicti sunt hi haeretici vel Collouthiani, quos tamen Collitianos à quodam Collitio, vocat Isidorus: sed, meo quidem iudicio, mendosè & corruptè, apud quem nomen illorum ex hoc Augustini loco (quem totum Isidorus transcripsit) restituendum puto. Platina verò pessimè in Eleutherio Quolitianos appellat. Quod etiam est ex hoc loco castigandum. Coluthiani verò cur dicti sint, ambigitur. Quidam enim à Coluthione nominatos putant. Est autem Coluthion, sicut & Cephron, oppidulum squallidæ & interne Lybiæ, quæ à Plinio libro 5. cap. 6. dicitur Mareotis, estque contermina Ægypto, à qua etiā Mareotis lacus apud Vibium Sequestrum D. Simleri nominatus est, in quæ deserta loca plures Christiani persequutionum tempore à præfectis Ægypti relegati scribuntur ab Eusebio libro septimo capite 11. Augustinus autem ex Epiphanio, vt opinor, à Colutho mauult dictos, qui fuit huius erroris princeps & author. Fuit autem Coluthus iste Alexandrinæ Ecclesiæ presbyter, Ario coæuus, quem etiam quanquam maleuolo quidem animo, detexit, & est persequutus. De quo & Theodoretus libro 1. historiae capite 4. & Nicephorus libro 8. capite 7. meminit, sed maxime Epiphanius haeresi 69. Ariomanitae, his verbis, Καὶ οἱ μὲν πρὶν ἐπληθύσθησαν Ἀρείῳ, ἐπὶ δὲ Κολλούθῳ, ἄλλοι δὲ Καρπωκράτη, ἐπὶ δὲ Σαρμάτᾳ. ὡς οὖν ἕκαστος ἐν τῇ ἰδίᾳ ἐκκλησίᾳ ἄλλος ἀλλὰ ... ἄλλος ἄλλο ἐν τῆς ... καὶ ἐπαινοῦ τῶν παρ᾽ αὐτῷ, οἱ μὲν Κολλουθιανοὺς ἑαυτοὺς ὠνόμασαν· ἄλλοι δὲ Ἀρειανοί. καὶ γὰρ ὁ Κολλοῦθος τινὰ βλασφημίαν ἐδίδαξεν, ἀλλ᾽ οὐκ ἐνέμεινεν ἡ ζῶντα αἵρεσις, ἀλλ᾽ ἐδὲς διεσκορπίσθη. Non commemorat igitur Epiphanius quid Coluthus senserit: sed ex hoc Augustini scripto intelligimus. Fuit autem alius Coluthus, de quo Suidas, Lycopolites & ἐπισκοπος sub Anastasio imperatore, qui ad hunc locum non pertinet. Coepit igitur haec haeresis sub Constantino Magno, quo tempore Arianus furor, circa annum a Christo passo 290. maxime in Ægypto, quae huiusmodi corruptelarum, quemadmodum & serpentum, feracissima regio semper fuit, videtur viguisse, nec diu tamen perstitisse: quia a tetriore & immaniori blasphemia, scilicet Ariani absorpta, & statim deleta est. Dum enim maioribus vitiis student homines, minora negligunt, & non consectantur. Quia tamen huius Philaster tam diserte meminit, etiam in Occidente grassata videri potest, uti in Ægypto, & Oriente.
units.tr: I. (The Coluthians from a certain man.) These heretics are called Coluthians, or Collouthians; Isidore, however, calls them Collitians, after a certain Collitius. In my judgment this is a mistake and a corruption, and in Isidore the name of these people ought, I think, to be restored from this passage of Augustine (which Isidore copied out entire). Platina, indeed, in the life of Eleutherius, calls them Quolitians, which should also be corrected from this passage. Why they were so called is uncertain. Some think they were named from Coluthion, since Coluthion, like Cephron, is a small town in the squalid and inland part of Libya, which Pliny (book 5, chapter 6) calls Mareotis, and which borders on Egypt; from it also the Lake Mareotis takes its name in Vibius Sequester, as D. Simler notes. Eusebius (book 7, chapter 11) writes that many Christians were banished to those desert places by the governors of Egypt in time of persecution. Augustine, however, following Epiphanius, as I think, prefers that they were named from Coluthus, who was the leader and author of this error. This Coluthus was an elder of the Alexandrian Church, a contemporary of Arius, whom he also exposed, though with an ill-will, and pursued. Theodoret (book 1 of his History, chapter 4) and Nicephorus (book 8, chapter 7) mention him, but above all Epiphanius in heresy 69, the Arian section, in these words: "And some were first multiplied under Arius, then under Coluthus, others under Carpocrates, then under Sarmatas. So each one, in his own church, different from the others... and some named themselves Coluthians, others Arians. For Coluthus taught a certain blasphemy, but that heresy did not persist while he lived; it was soon scattered." [Καὶ οἱ μὲν πρὶν ἐπληθύσθησαν Ἀρείῳ, ἐπὶ δὲ Κολλούθῳ, ἄλλοι δὲ Καρπωκράτη, ἐπὶ δὲ Σαρμάτᾳ. ὡς οὖν ἕκαστος ἐν τῇ ἰδίᾳ ἐκκλησίᾳ ἄλλος ἀλλὰ ... ἄλλος ἄλλο ἐν τῆς ... καὶ ἐπαινοῦ τῶν παρ᾽ αὐτῷ, οἱ μὲν Κολλουθιανοὺς ἑαυτοὺς ὠνόμασαν· ἄλλοι δὲ Ἀρειανοί. καὶ γὰρ ὁ Κολλοῦθος τινὰ βλασφημίαν ἐδίδαξεν, ἀλλ᾽ οὐκ ἐνέμεινεν ἡ ζῶντα αἵρεσις, ἀλλ᾽ ἐδὲς διεσκορπίσθη.] Epiphanius therefore does not record what Coluthus held, but we learn it from this writing of Augustine. There was also another Coluthus, of whom Suidas speaks, a Lycopolitan and bishop under the emperor Anastasius, who does not belong to this place. This heresy therefore began under Constantine the Great, at the time when the Arian frenzy arose, about the year 290 after Christ's passion. It seems to have flourished chiefly in Egypt, which has always been a region as fertile in such corruptions as in serpents, but it did not last long, because it was swallowed up and at once destroyed by the more foul and monstrous blasphemy of Arius. For while men pursue greater vices, they neglect and do not pursue the lesser. Yet since Philaster mentions it so clearly, it may appear to have spread also in the West, as in Egypt and the East.

units.la: 2. Deum non facere mala: Huius haereseos caput unum commemoratur (dogma enim Colouthianorum praetermisit Epiphanius) nimirum quod Deum poenas & supplicia sceleratis ho-minibus immittere & irrogare negarent, quia illa in Scriptura vocantur mala. Deus autē nul-lius mali author est. Quod vero isti dicunt, per-inde est, atque si Deum iustum esse negarent, sed scelerum otiosum spectatorem, non autem vltorē. Itaque Patres obiiciebant iam tum hunc Isaiæ locum, quem refert Augustinus. Est autem cap.45. versu 7. Ego Iehouah, &c. formans lu-cem, & creans tenebras, faciens pacem, & creans malum: ego Iehouah faciens omnia hæc. Item afferebant locum ex Amos cap. 3. versu 6. An erit malum in ciuitate, & Iehouah non faciet? Et quod negatur, & contenditur Deum nō esse authorem mali, distinguendum est. Nā est ma-lum duplex, quemadmodum Tertullianus do-cet, & sequenti capite hic ipse Augustinus, aliud nempe culpæ malum: aliud poenæ. Eius mali, quod est culpæ, non potest esse author Deus: eius autem, quod est poenæ, non potest non esse Deus author, si modo & iustus est, & Omnipo-tens. quod nemo sanus diffitetur. Huius autem erroris initia ex Marcionitarum dogmate (non-dum enim orti erant Manichæi) quod Collu-thianorum antecessit tempora, profecta viden-tur, dum homines imperite illud euitare conan-tur & studeant. Illi igitur Marcionitæ Deum ve-teris Testamenti authorem mali, omnisque re-rum perturbationis constituebant: isti Colluthiani vocis ambiguam significationem non at-tendentes, nullius mali causam esse contende-bant, dumque contentiose nimium inter se v-trique altercantur, veritatem, vt est in prouer-bio. bio, amiserunt. Itaque illis accidit quod ait Horatius Flaccus,
units.tr: 2. That God does not make evil things. One chief point of this heresy is recorded (for Epiphanius omitted the doctrine of the Coluthians): namely, that they denied that God inflicts and imposes punishments and torments on wicked men, because these are called evils in Scripture. But God is the author of no evil. What they say is just the same as if they denied that God is just, and made him an idle spectator of wickedness rather than an avenger. Accordingly the Fathers already objected to them this passage of Isaiah, which Augustine cites: Isaiah 45:7, "I am Jehovah, who form the light and create darkness, who make peace and create evil; I, Jehovah, do all these things." Likewise they cited a passage from Amos 3:6, "Shall there be evil in a city, and Jehovah not do it?" But the claim that God is not the author of evil must be distinguished. For evil is twofold, as Tertullian teaches, and as Augustine himself teaches in the following chapter: one is the evil of fault, the other the evil of punishment. God cannot be the author of the evil of fault; but of the evil of punishment God cannot fail to be the author, provided he is both just and almighty, which no sane person denies. The beginnings of this error seem to have come from the doctrine of the Marcionites (for the Manichaeans had not yet arisen), which preceded the times of the Coluthians, while men unskilfully tried to avoid it and strove to do so. The Marcionites therefore held that the God of the Old Testament was the author of evil and of all disturbance of things; the Coluthians, not attending to the ambiguous meaning of the word, contended that he was the cause of no evil; and while the two sides contend too contentiously among themselves, they lost the truth, as the proverb says. So it happened to them as Horace Flaccus says:

units.la: Dum vitant stulti vitia, in contraria currunt.
units.tr: While fools avoid their vices, they run into the contrary ones.

units.la: Tati est veram verborum significationem percepisse & obseruasse.
units.tr: It is a point of wisdom to have grasped and observed the true meaning of the words.

units.la: CAP. LXVI. Floriani cur sic dicti. Quis eorum error, & quàm Coluthianis contrarius.
units.tr: CAP. LXVI. Why the Florinians were so called. What their error was, and how it is contrary to that of the Colouthians.

units.la: Floriani à Florino,{1} qui è contrario dicebant, Deum {2} creasse mala, contra id quod scriptum est, Fecit Deus omnia, & ecce bona valde. Ac per hoc quamuis contraria inter se dicentes, tamen ambo diuinis eloquijs resistebant. Creat enim Deus mala, poenas iustissimas irrogando, quod Coluthus non videbat: non autem malas creando naturas, atque substantias, in quantum sunt natura, atque substantia, vbi Florinus errabat.
units.tr: The Florinians were named after Florinus, who said on the contrary that God created evils, against what is written: "God made all things, and behold, they were very good." So although these two contradicted each other, both were resisting the divine oracles. God does create evils, by inflicting most just punishments, which Colouthus did not see; but he does not create evil natures and substances, insofar as they are nature and substance, and here Florinus was wrong.

units.la: {1} Floriani à Florino.) Omnino vetus est haec haeresis: non autem potest Colouthianos, aut circa eorum tempora nata, etsi sibi mutuò illi repugnant. Florianos vel Florinianos (vtrunque enim dici potest) à Florino denominatos esse omnes authores consentiunt) praeter vnum Isidorum, qui huius sectae parentem Florianum appellat. Quidam etiam à Flora muliere vocatos putant, ad quam Ptolemaeus Valentiniani dogmatis assertor luculentissimè de fui erroris defensione scripsit, extatque apud Epiphanium ipsius epistola hæresi 33. Sed quando & Euseb. & Theodoretus,& alij authores classici ad Florianum eam referunt, de primo huius nominis authore mihi non videtur ambigendum. Fuit autem Florianus Romanæ ecclesiæ presbyter, una cum Blasto ( sic enim etiam apud Platinam legendum est, non autem Blasco ) huius ipsius dogmatis propugnatore ( cui etiam sæpe tanquam authori tribuitur,ut à Tertulliano,&Eusebio)sub Commodo imperatore, & Eleutherio Romano pontifice. Itaque circa annum à Christo passo 153. coepisse videtur hæc hæresis, Irenæo Lugdunensi episcopo adhuc in vivis agente,qui sæpe Florianum ipsum literis de errore abiurando commonefecit, ut est apud Eusebium libro 5. capite 20. sed obstinatus ille & peruicax perstitit. Ex quo factum est, ut ab Ecclesia palàm excommunicaretur: quemadmodum etiam &Blastus,sicut Theodor.lib.1.hære-tic.fabul.scribit.Blasti vero meminit in libr.De præscript. adversus hæreticos etiam Tertullian. Fuit autem hæc hæresis Valentiniani seminis seges & propago teterrima (etsi Montanistis ea attribuit Eusebius,sed falsò)que sic in Occidente,& Romæ præsertim omnia labefecit, Æonū deliriis, uti Valentinus in Ægypto & Syria virus venenoq; suo cuncta corruperat,latissimè peruagatam scribit Eusebius libro 5.Hist.cap.14,& 15.diu tamè retentam, defensámque isto nomine non legimus: sive quòd Occidens ab hæresi-bus magis immunis fuit: sive quòd non fuerint magni inter homines nominis authores istius se &c.[?] Coluthianis prorsus contraria fuit,& repugnans, ita nimirum infinita sunt mendaciorum diuerticula, sibíque aduersantia: veritatis autem via, vna & simplex.
units.tr: {1} The Florinians after Florinus. This heresy is altogether ancient, but it cannot have arisen among the Colouthians or around their time, though the two are opposed to each other. All authors agree that the Florians or Florinians (for both forms can be used) were named after Florinus, except Isidore alone, who calls Florianus the parent of this sect. Some also think they were named after a woman, Flora, for whom Ptolemy, the champion of Valentinus' doctrine, wrote a very clear defence of his error; his letter is extant in Epiphanius, heresy 33. But since Eusebius, Theodoret and other classical authors refer the sect to Florianus, there seems to me no room for doubt about the first author of this name. Florianus was a presbyter of the Roman church, together with Blastus (for so it must also be read in Platina, not Blasco), a champion of this very doctrine, to whom it is also often attributed as its author, as by Tertullian and Eusebius. This was under the emperor Commodus and Eleutherius, bishop of Rome. So this heresy seems to have begun about the year 153 after Christ's passion, while Irenaeus, bishop of Lyons, was still alive. He often admonished Florianus by letter to renounce his error, as is found in Eusebius, book 5, chapter 20, but that obstinate and stubborn man persisted. As a result he was openly excommunicated by the Church, just as Blastus was, as Theodoret writes in book 1 of his Heretical Fables. Tertullian also mentions Blastus in his book De praescriptione adversus haereticos. This heresy was a most foul seed and offshoot of the Valentinian stock (though Eusebius attributes it to the Montanists, but wrongly), and it so overthrew everything in the West, especially at Rome, with the follies of the aeons, as Valentinus had corrupted everything with his poison in Egypt and Syria. Eusebius writes that it spread very widely, Church History, book 5, chapters 14 and 15. Yet we do not read that it was long retained and defended under this name, either because the West was freer from heresies, or because there were no great authors of this name among men. It was entirely contrary to, and opposed to, the Colouthians. Thus, of course, the by-ways of falsehood are endless and contradict one another, but the way of truth is one and simple.

units.la: 2 Deum creasse mala. ) Variæ fuerunt huius hæreseos hypothecs[?], quanquam vnam tantum recenset Augustinus, nimirum quæ superiori errori repugnat, vt ex mutua collatione maior inter hæreticos ipsos discordia, atque fidei, rerumque credendarum incertitudo esse appareat. Superiores igitur hæretici Deum iniustum sceleratorum hominum vindicem negabant: isti peccati ipsius carumque rerum, quæ merito malæ & damnabiles sunt, authorem faciunt. Itaque Florianus incidit in Scyllam cupiens vitare Charybdin. Primum igitur huius erroris caput fuit, Deum creasse mala, quo nomine peccata complectuntur, & naturas rerum etiam prima sua origine, qualesque à Deo conditæ sunt, malas, prauas, & detortas, vitiosque obnoxias affirmant. Fortasse ita sentiunt ne nō Deum omnipotentem confiteri, aut ne deos plures ex dogmate Marcionitarum, quod iam notum erat, inducere viderentur, vnum boni, alterum mali conditorem. In quem errorem aperte postea Manichæi inciderunt. Itaque fuit hoc velut Manichianismi semen, & fundamentum, quod postea exædificatum est. Recte vero Patres ex Genes. 1. demonstrant. quæcunque à Deo facta sunt, bona condita fuisse: omnia vero sunt ab eo creata. Itaque diabolum & hominem ipsum se suamque naturam, quæ prius bona erat, corrupisse: & eius actus, quod malum & peccatum vel vitium rei dici debet, reique[?] iam conditæ superuenit, authorem esse. 1 De quo argumento aduersus Manichæos infinita pro pe scripsit Augustinus, isque legendus est. 2 error. Æonas Valentinianorum, eorumque propagines & productiones, vt alij ex aliis nascantur, renouarunt, suntque amplexi. Qua sententia non modò ridicula fit tota de Filij ex Patre generatione fides: sed etiam blasphemia de Deo opinio hominum animis inseritur; dum Deum hominum more fluxu feminis atq; ita partitione quadam separationeque substantiæ generasse fingunt. Theodoretus. 3 Iudæorum morem in celebrando Pascha retinent, præfractéq; obseruandum, aliásque Iudæorum ceremonias docent, atque ita latenter, vt ait Tertull. Iudaif-mum in Ecclesiam Dei reuocant, & reponunt. Cætera sunt Valentiniani, atque ita ex mala stir-pe malus surculus.
units.tr: 2 God created evils. There were various foundations for this heresy, although Augustine recounts only one, namely the one which opposes the earlier error. From mutual comparison it appears that there was greater discord among the heretics themselves, and uncertainty about the faith and the things to be believed. The earlier heretics denied that God was the unjust avenger of wicked men; these make God the author of sin itself and of those things which are rightly evil and blameworthy. So Florianus fell into Scylla while wishing to avoid Charybdis. The first point of this error, then, was that God created evils, under which name they include sins, and they affirm that natures of things, even from their first origin and as they were created by God, are evil, depraved, twisted and liable to vice. They perhaps held this view lest they seem either not to confess God omnipotent, or to introduce, from the doctrine of the Marcionites, which was already well known, several gods, one the creator of good and another of evil. Later the Manichaeans clearly fell into this error. So this was, as it were, the seed and foundation of Manichaeism, which was afterwards built up upon it. The Fathers rightly show from Genesis 1 that whatever was made by God was created good, and all things were created by him. Thus the devil and man himself corrupted themselves and their nature, which was previously good, and the act which ought to be called evil, sin or vice of a thing, comes upon a thing already created, and its author is not God. 1 Augustine wrote countless works against the Manichaeans on this argument, and they are worth reading. 2 Error. They renewed the Aeons of the Valentinians, and their offshoots and productions, so that some are born from others, and they embraced them. This opinion not only makes the whole faith about the generation of the Son from the Father ridiculous, but also inserts into men's minds a blasphemous opinion of God, while they pretend that God begot in the manner of men, by a flow of seed and a kind of division and separation of substance. Theodoret. 3 They keep the Jewish custom in celebrating the Passover, insist that it be observed, and teach other Jewish ceremonies, and so, as Tertullian says, they secretly call back and reinstate Judaism into the Church of God. The rest belongs to the Valentinians; thus from a bad stock comes a bad shoot.

units.la: CAP. LXVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER 67.

units.la: Æternales, & eorum error quis fuerit.
units.tr: The Eternalists, and what their error was.

units.la: H[?]æresin{1} quandam sine authore, & sine nomine Philaster commemorat, qua dicit hunc mundum etiam post resurrectionem mortuorum in eodem statu in quo nunc est, esse mansurum, neque ita esse mutandum, ut sit calum nouum, & terra noua, sicut sancta Scriptura promittit.
units.tr: Philaster records a certain heresy, without author and without name, which says that this world, even after the resurrection of the dead, will remain in the same state in which it now is, and will not be changed so that there is a new heaven and a new earth, as holy Scripture promises.

units.la: {1} Hæresin quandam.) Anonymam hanc hæ-resin refin commodioris disputationis causa, nos Æ-ternales nominauimus, quia mundi huius statu contra Dei verbum coftituunt, qualis nunc est, fore æternum. Id unde sumpserint ; præter-quàm ex philosophorum ( sunt enim patriar-chæ hærcticorum , quemadmodum scite dixit Tertullianus, philosophi) imprimis autem Pla-tonicorum,& Peripateticorum deliriis,non vi-deo , quorum utrique æternum quidem fore hunc mundum volunt, sed illi quidem Platoni-ci ortum initiumque habuisse concedunt : hi autem Peripatetici,fine initio & ortu fuisse sin-gunt , facratisimo Dei verbo & historiæ de creatione mundi apertisime repugnantes. Sic Ariftoteles Peripateticorum princeps scribit, & sentit libro 1. De cælo: & quod de Platonicis diximus, extat in Platonis Timaeo. Utriusque autem philosophorum familiæ magna laus in-ter Ægyptios Christianos, sed præsertim Ale-xandrinos, fuit, adeo ut ii plurimum sapere vi-derentur in fide Christi, qui plurimum in do-gmatis istorum philosophorum profecissent,& Ariftotelica schola Alexandriæ viguit, à Chri-ftianis sustentata, ut Eusebius libro 7. historiæ, cap. 32. tradit. Denique aliquando disputatum est inter Christianos, Utrum Platonis an Ari-ftotelis dogmata potius retinenda ediscendá-que effent, & præualuit sententia propter Ori-genistarum errores & allegorias à Platonicis acceptas, ut repudiata Platonicorum schola, A-riftotelicorum,fiue, qui iidem sunt, Peripateti-corum philosophia præferretur,atque tanquam verior, fimpliciorque in scholis Christianorum doceretur.Ex his tamen fructibus orta hæc hæ-resis latissime derivata est, & in scholas etiam medicorum perrupit. Nisi forte quis etiam ex illo Genesis loco perperam intellecto, ductam existimet, qui est cap.8. versu 22. vbi post dilu-vium sic ait Dominus, Adhuc omnes dies terrę,sementis & messis,frigusque & æstas[?],necnon æstas & hyems, dies quoque & nox non cessa-bunt: quasi perpetuus huius mundi status fore promittatur. Quanquam vero nec nomen nec locum, nec tempus, nec authorem huius erro-ris designent, neque Philaster, neque Augusti-nus: ex Petro tamen intelligimus pervetustam esse hæresin,quæ ab ipsis Apostolorum tempo-ribus cœperit,quando contra eos,qui mundum hunc immortalem statuebant, futurúmque vn-quam illum Dei extremum iudicium negabant, acerrime disputat cap. 3. posterioris suæ epistolæ.In Ægypto etiam viguisse crediderim,sed citissimè inter Christianos extinctam, tum propter manifestam Mosis historiam de mundi origine,&prima creatione:tum etiam propter apertam de mundi huius non tantùm mutatione quadam & absterione fœditatum , quibus iam propter hominis peccatum scatet, sed consum-ptione,& transitione sententiam,Apocalyps.21. versu 1:Psalmo 102.versu 26: Hebr.1. versu 12:2. Petri 3.ver.7.quo nihil dici potest apertius.Ad-datur etiam quæ dicit Paulus,1. Corinth.7.vers. 31, & Rom.8.versu 26. Et aperte Isaias 65.versu 17:66.versu 22. vaticinatur. Ex quibus omnibus locis facillime verisimeque iugulatur hic er-ror. Mihi autem ad Nepotianos vel Chiliastas hærehaereticos referendus esse videtur, quorum fructicatio, & rivus, & quidem foetidus proculdubio fuit, ita nimirum errore errorem pariente, & superfoetura quadam progignente. Hunc tamen praetermisit Isidorus.
units.tr: {1} A certain heresy.) For the sake of a more convenient discussion, we have named this anonymous heresy the Eternalists, because they hold, against the word of God, that the world will remain eternal in the state it is now. Where they took this from, I do not see, apart from the ravings of the philosophers (for they are the patriarchs of the heretics, as Tertullian aptly said, the philosophers), and above all of the Platonists and Peripatetics. Both of these want this world to be eternal, but the Platonists concede that it had a beginning and origin, whereas the Peripatetics imagine that it existed without beginning or origin, which plainly contradicts the most sacred word of God and the history of the creation of the world. So Aristotle, prince of the Peripatetics, writes and thinks in book 1 of On the Heavens; and what we have said of the Platonists is found in Plato's Timaeus. Both schools of philosophers enjoyed great esteem among the Christians of Egypt, and especially the Alexandrians, so that those who had advanced furthest in the doctrines of these philosophers seemed to be the wisest in the faith of Christ; and the Aristotelian school flourished at Alexandria, supported by Christians, as Eusebius records in book 7 of his History, chapter 32. Finally, it was once disputed among Christians whether the doctrines of Plato or of Aristotle were rather to be retained and learned, and the view prevailed, on account of the errors of the Origenists and the allegories taken from the Platonists, that the Platonic school should be rejected and the philosophy of the Aristotelians, or Peripatetics, which are the same, preferred, and taught in the schools of Christians as truer and simpler. Yet this heresy, born from these fruits, spread very widely and even broke into the schools of physicians. Unless perhaps someone thinks it was drawn from that passage of Genesis, wrongly understood, chapter 8, verse 22, where after the flood the Lord says: "While the earth remains, seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night shall not cease," as if a perpetual state of this world were promised. Although neither Philaster nor Augustine names the author, the name, the place or the time of this error, yet from Peter we understand that the heresy is very ancient, arising from the very times of the Apostles, when in chapter 3 of his second epistle he disputes most sharply against those who held that this world was immortal and denied that God's final judgment would ever come upon it. I would believe it also flourished in Egypt, but it was very quickly extinguished among Christians, both on account of the plain history of Moses about the origin of the world and the first creation, and also on account of the clear teaching that this world is not merely to be changed and cleansed of the filthiness with which it already abounds because of human sin, but to be consumed and passed away: Revelation 21:1; Psalm 102:26; Hebrews 1:12; 2 Peter 3:7, than which nothing can be said more plainly. To these is added what Paul says, 1 Corinthians 7:31, and Romans 8:26 (sic), and Isaiah plainly prophesies at 65:17 and 66:22. From all these passages this error is most easily and credibly refuted. But to me it seems that it should be referred to the Nepotians or Chiliasts, whose offshoot and stream, and indeed a foul one, it undoubtedly was, error thus begetting error and bringing forth a kind of offspring upon offspring. Isidore, however, passed over this.

units.la: CAP. LXVIII.
units.tr: CHAP. LXVIII.

units.la: Nudipedales, & eorum haeresis.
units.tr: The Nudipedalians, and their heresy.

units.la: ST alia haeresis, nudis pedibus semper ambulantium, eo quod Dominus dixerit ad Mosem, vel ad Iosue, Solve calceamentum de pedibus tuis. Et quod Propheta Isaias nudis pedibus iussus fuerit ambulare. Inde ergo haeresis est, quia non propter corporis afflictionem sic ambulant, sed quia testimonia taliter intelligunt.
units.tr: There is also another heresy of those who always walk barefoot, because the Lord said to Moses, or to Joshua, "Take off your shoes from your feet." And because the prophet Isaiah was commanded to walk barefoot. Their heresy lies in this: they do not walk so for the sake of afflicting the body, but because they understand these testimonies in that way.

units.la: 1 Nudis pedibus.) Est & hic error, qui vana superstitio potius, quam haeresis dicendus est, Monachismi fructicatio, & λόγιον[?], quemadmodum plures alij vel iam à nobis observati, vel qui postea notabuntur. Fuit enim hoc hominum genus, Monachorum dico, tam novis, & à communi aliorum Christianorum consuetudine remotis vivendi ritibus addictum, & gaudens, ut in dies iam receptos mutaret, probatos interpolaret, peregrinos induceret, denique nec finem nec modum in variando habitu, colore, gestu, ciborum genere statueret ullum. Inde enim orta sunt tot Monachorum genera, & in quoque genere tot sectæ, & diuortia, qui colore quidē, externisque rebus inter se differunt superstitione autem & falsa, atque adeo impia de operum suorum meritis, opinione sunt omnes inter se iidem, & æquales. Hunc autem errorem, de quo nunc agimus, peperit κακοζηλία[?], dum illi se sanctos Dei seruos imitari putant, quia externum eorum habitum repræsentarent, & simiarum more, fingerent. Sed infinita pene sunt in eo peccata, quæ Monachi admisere, quæque apud Euagrium libro primo capite 21. recensentur magnæ quidem animi vanitatis & arrogantiæ plena argumenta, quanquam a plerisque eius ætatis hominibus insulse probantur. Censent igitur hi nostri hæretici Christianos omnes, qui sancte, pie, & religiose viuere, versarique velint, pedibus nudis incedere debere. ob quam rationem a nobis Nudipedales sunt appellati. Vnde vero tam inepti dogmatis origo? Nimirum quod externis istis viuendi ritibus & operibus nostris vera sanctitas pietasque tribueretur, atque a fide, metu Dei, & interno homine ad hæc elementa, opera mortua, & externum hominem pessime transferrentur, Coloff.2.verf.20. Quod Novatiani iam docuerant. Afferebant tamen pro se tres imprimis Scripturæ locos. Primum ex Exodo cap.3.verf.5. Secundum Iosuæ cap.5.verf.15. Tertium autem ex Isa.20.verf.2. qui omnes specialia præcepta continent, fuerintque ea signa & symbola certarum rerum quæ non sunt ad imitationem & exemplum a nobis trahenda. Itaque errarunt graviter & alij monachi qui ad eiusdem Isaiæ imitatiorem nudi vixerunt, vt Euagrius scribit. Id quod abhorret ipsa honestas & humanus aspectus. Quando vero primùm coeperit haec haeresis, & quo authore instituta, vbi plurimum grassata, quandiu, & quàm latè propagata, non explicat Auguft. Circa Theodosij tamen iunioris tempora ( quando Imperatrix etiam ipsa Eudocia propter monachorum varios ritus Hierosolymis stupefacta, eos admirari & venerari visa est) extitisse in Syria & Iudaea praesertim crediderim, veluti circa annum à Christo passo 400. quae fuit aetas monachorum foecundissima, vt scribit Socrat.libr.6.cap.7. Tunc enim certatim quisque in pretio haberi studuit, & monachi nouas in dies profesionis regulas excogitare coeperunt. Vnde <bl>ΣΜΑΪ</bl>, & Armentarij monachi exorti. Meminerunt vero ante haec tempora Hieronymus & Egesippus festi Nudipedalium, sed illud inter Iudaeos obseruabatur mense septimo. Meminit etiam Tertullian.in Apologet.cap.40. sed ab ethnicis fiebat. Vt hi haeretici nihil aliud quàm veterem Iudaismum & Paganismum coniunxisse inuexisseque dici possint, & in iis ipsis rebus Christianam pietatem collocasse, quod plane blasphemum est. Hanc tamen haeresin hodie profitentur Cordigeri & Francisccani, qui dicuntur superbè Maioris obseruantiae. Sed superstitio nihil pensi habet, modo se suaque tueatur & commendet hominibus. Verba vero Tertulliani sunt haec, Denique cum ab imbribus aestiua, hyberna suspendunt, & annus in cura est, vos quidem quotidie pasti, statimque pransuri balneis & cauponis & lupanaribꝰ operati,Aquilicia Ioui immolatitio, Nudipedia populo denuntiatis,&c. Quæ omnia pulchrè cum monachorum moribus conueniunt. Sed ad alios notioresque hæreticos transfeamus.
units.tr: 1 Barefoot.) This is also an error, which should be called an empty superstition rather than a heresy, an offshoot of monasticism and a logion [λόγιον], like several others that we have already noted or will note below. For this class of people, I mean the monks, was devoted to new and strange ways of living, remote from the common custom of other Christians, and delighted to change the rites already received day by day, to alter those approved, and to introduce foreign ones. In short, they set no end or limit in varying their dress, colour, gestures and kinds of food. From this arose so many kinds of monks, and within each kind so many sects and divisions, which differ among themselves in colour and external matters, but are all alike in their superstitious and false, and indeed impious, opinion about the merits of their works. This error that we are now discussing was born of kakozelia [κακοζηλία], since they think they imitate the holy servants of God by copying their outward habit, and they make themselves like apes. Yet there are almost endless sins that the monks committed in this matter, which are listed by Evagrius in the first book, chapter 21. These are indeed strong evidence of great vanity and arrogance of mind, although most men of that age foolishly approved them. So these heretics of ours hold that all Christians who wish to live holily, piously and religiously must walk with bare feet, and for this reason they have been called Nudipedalians by us. But where does such a foolish doctrine come from? Surely from this: that true holiness and piety were ascribed to these external rites of living and to our works, and that men were turned away, from faith, the fear of God and the inner man, to these elements, dead works and the outward man, Colossians 2:20. The Novatians had already taught this. Yet they relied chiefly on three passages of Scripture: first, Exodus 3:5; second, Joshua 5:15; third, Isaiah 20:2. All of these contain special precepts, and they were signs and symbols of certain things, which are not to be drawn from them as a model or example for our imitation. So other monks too went seriously astray, who lived naked in imitation of this same Isaiah, as Evagrius writes. Decency and humane appearance itself shrink from this. When this heresy first began, and by whose authority it was founded, where it spread most, how long it lasted and how widely it was propagated, Augustine does not explain. Yet I would believe it existed, especially in Syria and Judaea, around the time of Theodosius the Younger (when the Empress Eudocia herself, astonished at the various rites of the monks at Jerusalem, seemed to admire and venerate them), about the year 400 after Christ's passion, which was the most fruitful age of monks, as Socrates writes in book 6, chapter 7. For then each eagerly sought to be held in high esteem, and the monks began to devise new rules of profession day by day. From this arose the Esmai [ΣΜΑΪ] and the Armentarian monks. Before these times, Jerome and Egesippus do mention the festival of the Nudipedalians, but among the Jews it was observed in the seventh month. Tertullian also mentions it in his Apology, chapter 40, but it was done by the heathen. So these heretics can be said to have merely combined and introduced the old Judaism and paganism, and to have placed Christian piety in these very things, which is plainly blasphemous. Yet the Cordeliers and the Franciscans, who proudly call themselves of the stricter observance, still profess this heresy today. But superstition has no scruples, provided it protects and commends itself and its own to men. Tertullian's words are these: "Finally, when they suspend the summer and winter fasts because of the rains, and the year is taken up with care, you indeed feed every day, and at once, about to dine, you are busy with baths, taverns and brothels, you announce to the people the Aquilicia as a sacrifice to Jupiter, the Nudipedia, and so on." All of which agree well with the morals of monks. But let us pass on to other, better-known heretics.

units.la: CAP. LXIX.
units.tr: CAP. LXIX.

units.la: Donatistæ siue Montenses vnde primum orti. Quos suæ sectæ vel defensores vel schismaticos habuerint. Circumcelliones qui fuerint. Denique Donatistarum erroris capita tria.
units.tr: The Donatists, or Montenses: where they first arose; who their defenders or schismatics were; what the Circumcellions were; and finally, the three heads of the Donatists' error.

units.la: DOnatiani vel Donatistæ{1} sunt, qui primum propter Cæcilianum contra suam voluntatem ordinatum Ecclesiæ Carthaginensis Episcopum schisma fecerunt, obi-cientes ei crimina non probata: & maxime quod à traditoribus diuinarum scripturarum fuerit ordinatus. Sed postea causam cum eo dictam atque finitam falsitatis rei deprehensi pertinaci dissensione firmata in hæresin schisma verterunt, tanquam Ecclesia Christi propter crimina Cæciliani, seu vera, seu, quod magis iudicibus apparuit, falsa, de toto terrarum orbe perierit, vbi futura promissa est, atque in{2} Africa & Donati parte remanserit: in aliis terrarum partibus quasi contagione communionis extincta. Audent rebaptizare Catholicos, vbi se amplius hæreticos esse firmarunt, cum Ecclesia catholica vniuersa placuerit, nec in ipsis hæreticis baptisma commune rescindere. Huius hæresis principem accipimus fuisse Donatum, qui de Numidia veniens, & contra Cæcilianum Christianam diuidens plebem adiunEiis[?] sibi eiusdem factionis Episcopis, Maiorinum a-pud Carthaginem ordinauit Episcopum. Cui[?] Ma-iorino Donatus Episcopus alius in eadem divisione successit, qui eloquentia sua sic confirmauit hanc haeresin, ut multi existimentur propter ipsum potius eos Donatistas vocari. Extant[?] scripta eius, vbi apparet eum etiam non catholicam de Trinitate habuisse sententiam: sed quanuis eiusdem substantiae, minorem tamen Patre Filium, & minorem Filio putasse Spiritum sanctum. Verum in hunc, quem de Trinitate habuit, errorem Donatistarum[?] multitudo intenta non fuit, nec facile in eis quisquam, qui hoc illum sensisse nouerit, inuenitur. Isti haeretici in vrbe Roma Montenses vocantur, quibus hinc ex Africa solent Episcopum mittere: aut hinc illuc Afri[?] Episcopi eorum pergere, si forte ibi eum ordinare placuisset. Ad hanc haeresin in Africa ut illi pertinent[?], qui appel-lantur Circumcelliones, genus hominum agreste, & famosissimae audaciae, non solum in alios immania facinora perpetrando: sed nec sibi insana feritate parcendo. Nam per mortes varias maxime pracipitiorum[?] & aquarum, & ignium seipsos necare consueuerunt, & in istum furore alios, quos potuerint utriusque sexus seducere, aliquando ut occidantur ab aliis, mortem, nisi fecerint, comminantes. Veruntamen plerisque Donatistarum displicent tales, nec eorum communione contaminari se putant, qui Christiano orbi terrarum dementes obiiciunt ignotorum crimen Afrorum. Multa & inter ipsos facta sunt schismata, & ab iis se diversi coetibus aliy atque aliy separarunt, quorum separationem cetera grandis multitudo non sensit. Sed apud Carthaginem Maximianus {4} contra Primianum ab eiusdem erroris centum ferme Episcopis ordinatus, & à reliquis trecentis decem· cum eis duodecim, qui ordinationi eius etiam præsentia corporali interfuerunt, atrocissima criminatione damnatus compulit eos nosse, etiam extra Ecclesiam dari posse baptismum Christi. Nam quosdam ex eis cum eis, quos extra eorum Ecclesiam baptizauerant, in suis honoribus sine vlla in quoquam repetitione baptismatis receperunt, nec eos, vt corrigerent, per publicas potestates agere desiterunt, nec eorum criminibus per sui concilij sententiam vehementer exaggeratis communionem suam contaminare timuerunt.
units.tr: The Donatians, or Donatists, are those who first made a schism, opposing Caecilian, who was ordained bishop of the Church of Carthage against their will. They charged him with crimes that were not proved, chiefly that he had been ordained by traditors of the divine Scriptures. Later, however, when the case had been heard and decided against them, and they were caught in the falsity of their accusation, they hardened their stubborn dissent and turned the schism into a heresy. They claimed that the Church of Christ had perished throughout the whole world on account of Caecilian's crimes, whether true or (as the judges more readily held) false, and that it remained only in Africa and in the part of Donatus; in other parts of the world it had been extinguished, as it were, by contagion of communion. They dare to rebaptize Catholics, once they have declared themselves more fully heretics, although the universal Catholic Church has decided otherwise, and they do not cancel the baptism common to heretics themselves. We understand that the author of this heresy was Donatus, who came from Numidia and, dividing the Christian people against Caecilian, gathered to himself bishops of the same faction and ordained Majorinus bishop at Carthage. After Majorinus another bishop, also named Donatus, succeeded him in the same division. By his eloquence he so confirmed this heresy that many think those men were called Donatists chiefly because of him. His writings survive, and in them it appears that he also held an unorthodox opinion about the Trinity: although the Son was of the same substance, he thought the Son less than the Father and the Holy Spirit less than the Son. Yet the multitude of Donatists did not pay close attention to this error that he held concerning the Trinity, and hardly anyone among them is found who knew him to have held it. These heretics in the city of Rome are called Montenses, and from Africa they are accustomed to send them a bishop from here, or African bishops of theirs go there, if perhaps it had pleased them to ordain one there. Those who are called Circumcellions belong to this heresy in Africa: a rustic race of men of notorious audacity, who not only commit monstrous crimes against others but also spare themselves in their mad savagery. For they were accustomed to kill themselves by various deaths, chiefly by precipices, waters and fires, and to drive others of either sex whom they could seduce into the same frenzy, sometimes threatening them with death, unless they did it, so that they would be killed by others. Nevertheless, most Donatists dislike such men, and think they are not defiled by communion with those who, madly, cast in the face of the whole Christian world the crime of the Africans that is unknown to them. Many schisms also arose among the Donatists themselves, and various groups separated from one another, whose separation the rest of the great multitude did not notice. But at Carthage Maximian, ordained against Primian by almost one hundred bishops of this error, together with the remaining three hundred and ten, and with the twelve who were present in person at his ordination, was condemned for the most atrocious accusation. He compelled them to acknowledge that the baptism of Christ can be given even outside the Church. For some of those whom they had baptized outside their Church they received into their own offices without any repetition of baptism, nor did they cease to bring them to correction through the public powers, nor, though their crimes were vehemently magnified by the sentence of their council, did they fear to defile their communion.

units.la: I Donatiani vel Donatistæ.) Non est hoc loco religiose ratio temporis obseruata, vt coæui & contemporanei hæretici commemorarentur, sed Philastrum secutus Augustinus, prout quæque hæresis occurrebat, descripsit. Parum autem Græcis hominibus nota fuisse videtur, qui eam omnes, paucis modo exceptis, veluti Theodoreto libr.4. Hæreticar. Fabul. & Ioanne Damasceno, prætermittunt. Huius enim nec historia ecclesiastica, nisi admodum subobscure & in aliena, id est, Nouatianorum hæresi meminit: nec Nicephorus magnus alioquin alienorum scriptorum compilator & [illegible, ~8 letters], nec Epiphanius ipse, quanquam ante illius secula iam celeberrimi Donatistæ erant, qui paulo post Nouatianos in eadem orbis plaga, id est, Africa sunt exorti. Causam vero ignorationis fuisse censuerim magnum locorum & regionum interuallum, cum Donatistæ in extremis pene Africæ Occidentalis finibus, & Numidia fuerint, quæ longissime distat ab Oriente, Syria & Ægypto, vbi plurimum receptæ & grassatæ sunt hæreses omnes.
units.tr: I Donatiani vel Donatistae.) Here the order of time has not been carefully observed, so that heretics who were contemporaries and of the same age might be recorded together; rather, Augustine, following Philastrius, described each heresy as it came to hand. Yet the Greeks seem to have known little of them, since almost all of them, with only a few exceptions, pass them over, as Theodoret in book 4 of his Heretical Fables does, and John of Damascus. Indeed, the Ecclesiastical History does not mention them, except very obscurely and in connection with another's heresy, namely that of the Novatians. Nor does Nicephorus, otherwise a great compiler of other writers' works, nor Epiphanius himself, though the Donatists were already very famous in their age and had arisen in the same region of the world, that is in Africa, shortly after the Novatians. I would judge that the cause of this ignorance was the great distance of places and regions, since the Donatists were almost at the far edges of Western Africa and in Numidia, which lies very far from the East, Syria and Egypt, where all heresies were most widely received and flourished.

units.la: Deinde quòd Donatistæ primùm repressi sese pcnè in sola Africa continebant: in Italiam autem aut alias nationes, quòd postea fecere, nondum diffundebant. Caput tamen & ipsi postea exeruerunt, & venena sua latissimè sparserunt. Ortum verò est hoc malum sub Constantino Magno (id quod vel ex sola historia & accusatione Cæciliani satis intelligi potest, qui ab ipso Constantino Magno auditus & absolutus est) & Syluestro Episcopo Roman. circa annum à Christo passo 298. etiam ante Sardicense Concilium, vt Augustinus ipse libro 3. contra Cre-scon.docet. Non autem sub Iulio Pontifice, vt putat tamen Platina: nec sub Liberio Roman. præsule, vt scribunt alij. Nam temporis ealcu-lus & ratio eos apertisimè refutat. In Africa verò regione primùm inualuit hæc pestis, & Carthagine præsertim, quæ in ea ipsius Africæ parte sita est, quæ proprie Africa dicta est, & à Græcis Lybia, estque ad Orientem pergentibus posterior & vicinior Ægypto, quàm ipsa Numidia. Ex Numidia verò Donatus iste dictus à Casis Nigris (ad distinctionem eius Donati, qui Carthagine hanc ipsam hærefin fortis-sime postea desedit) primus huius sectæ author fuit oriundus. Nam cùm ad Carthaginefem Episcopatũ Donatus iste aspiraret, eàque spe (ele & to sibíque prælato Cæciliano) excidisset, eum perfidiæ atq; abiurati nominis fideiq; Christianæ apud Ecclesiam accusauit, quòd in persecutione, quæ sub Maximiano & Diocletia. Impp. acciderat, sacros codices hostibus fidei & ido-lolatris Christianos persequentibus comburendos tradidisset. De quo ipso ab eodem Donato omnes alij Episcopi, qui Cæcilianum Episcopū ordinarant, accusati sunt, sed omnes falso, vt causæ euentus ter apud diuersos iudices actæ docuit. Itaque nec Cæcilianum pro Episcopo, nec eius cœtum pro vera Dei Ecclesia se agnoscere posse prædicabat, quæ perfidis & traditoribus sacrorum codicum hominibus constaret, neque satis pura & immaculata ipsius iudicio esset. Atqui ipse & Donatistarum cœtus totus scatebat vulneribus, & sanie non tantum erroris impurissimi, sed etiam improborum morum, vt docet sæpissimè Augustin. Collegit igitur sibi priuatim Ecclesiæ homo ambitiosus & arrogans, & schisma Carthagine fecit cœtumque suum solū esse sanctā illam Ecclesiā, quam crederemus contendit. Quod etsi primum irrisum est, & facillimè à plerisq; refutatum, Concilióque Carthagine collecto damnatū, peruicacia tamen indomitáque istorum audacia defensum est, ex quo cœpit esse manifesta hæresis, corruptis iam plerisque Sacræ scripturæ locis. Tamq; valida & potes euasit breui tempore, vt multos fautores haberet, tum viros tum mulieres, imprimis autem ditissimam illam mulierem Carthaginensem nomine Lucillam, vt Augustin. scribit, quæ suis opibus eorum Episcopos & cœtus laute sustentauit. Erupit igitur longius hoc venenū, nec se solius Carthaginis mœnibus coercuit, sed ita totam Africam peruasit, & infecit, vt multæ ciuitates eaequé totæ hac peste tabe-scerent. fcerent & corriperentur. Vnde facti insolentes illi vim in Africa orthodoxis inferebant, donec aduersus eos missus ab Honorio Imperatore Dulcitius Tribunus militum eorum vim & iniuriam in Christianos compescuit. Nec totius Africae regno contenti homines periuri & contumaces, in alias & transmarinas regiones traiecerunt, quas labefactarunt. Ex quo factum est, vt imperatorum legibus coercerentur, illisque poena, nisi conuerterentur ad fidem orthodoxam, imponeretur grauissima, quae extat libro 1. Codic. Iustinia. cuius meminit saepe Augustin. & eam defendit libro 2.Contra liter.
units.tr: Next, because the Donatists were at first restrained, they kept themselves almost wholly within Africa alone; they did not yet spread into Italy or other nations, as they later did. Nevertheless they themselves afterwards raised their head and scattered their poisons very widely. This evil arose under Constantine the Great (which can be understood sufficiently from the history alone and from the accusation of Caecilian, who was heard and acquitted by Constantine the Great himself), and under Silvester, bishop of Rome, about the year 298 after Christ's passion, even before the Council of Sardica, as Augustine himself teaches in book 3 against Cresconius. It did not arise under Pope Julius, as Platina nonetheless thinks, nor under Liberius, bishop of Rome, as others write. For the calculation and reckoning of time clearly refutes them. This plague first took hold in the region of Africa, and especially at Carthage, which lies in that part of Africa that was properly called Africa, and which the Greeks call Libya; to those travelling eastward it is the farther and nearer to Egypt than Numidia itself. Now this Donatus, who was called "of the Black Houses" from Numidia (to distinguish him from that other Donatus who later most strongly held this same heresy at Carthage), was the first originator of this sect, being a native of that region. For when this Donatus aspired to the bishopric of Carthage, and had fallen from that hope (Caecilian having been preferred to him), he accused him before the Church of perfidy, of abjuring the name and the Christian faith, because in the persecution that had happened under the emperors Maximian and Diocletian he had handed over the sacred codices to be burned by the enemies of the faith and the idolaters persecuting Christians. All the other bishops who had ordained Caecilian as bishop were accused by this same Donatus concerning this matter, but all falsely, as the outcome of the case, tried three times before different judges, showed. Therefore he proclaimed that he could acknowledge neither Caecilian as bishop nor his assembly as the true Church of God, since it consisted of perfidious men and traditors of the sacred codices, and was not sufficiently pure and spotless by his judgment. And yet he himself and the whole Donatist assembly were festering with wounds and with the pus not only of the most impure error but also of wicked morals, as Augustine very often teaches. Therefore this ambitious and arrogant man gathered a church for himself privately and made a schism at Carthage, and he contended that his own assembly alone was that holy Church which we believe in. Although this was at first laughed at and very easily refuted by most people, and although it was condemned by a council gathered at Carthage, it was nevertheless defended by the obstinacy and unbroken audacity of these men; from that time the heresy began to be manifest, the passages of Holy Scripture having by then been corrupted in many places. And it soon became so strong and powerful that it had many supporters, both men and women, above all that very wealthy woman of Carthage named Lucilla, as Augustine writes, who with her riches lavishly supported their bishops and assemblies. So this poison broke out further and was not confined within the walls of Carthage alone, but so invaded and infected the whole of Africa that many cities were wholly rotting and being corrupted by this plague. From this, those arrogant men began to inflict violence on the orthodox in Africa, until Dulcitius, a tribune of soldiers sent against them by the emperor Honorius, restrained their violence and injustice against Christians. Nor were these perjured and obstinate men content with the kingdom of all Africa; they crossed into other regions beyond the sea, and there they undermined the faith. As a result, they were restrained by the laws of the emperors, and the most severe penalty was imposed on them unless they were converted to the orthodox faith; it is found in book 1 of the Codex of Justinian, which Augustine often mentions, and which he defends in book 2 against the letters of Petilian.

units.la: Petilian. Diu vero perstitit hæc hæresis, quando etiam Tiberij fecundi imperatoris Conftantinopolitani ætate vixit, & Gregorius Magnus de fui seculi Episcopis & Magistratibus coqueritur, quod magna eorum culpa & negligentia fieret, vt hic tam grauis error & pestilens, tamen in Ecclesia latius serperet, & diutius obtineret.
units.tr: Petilian. This heresy persisted for a long time, and it even lived on in the age of Tiberius II, the Emperor of Constantinople. Gregory the Great complains about the bishops and magistrates of his own age, that through their great fault and negligence so grave and pestilential an error spread more widely through the Church and held its ground for longer.

units.la: Postea tamen iugulata est hæc hæresis, atque conquieuerat, nisi miseri & insani Anabaptistæ eam ab inferis hoc nostro seculo reuocassent.
units.tr: Yet this heresy was afterwards strangled and had quietened down, had not the wretched and insane Anabaptists revived it from the dead in our own age.

units.la: Dicuntur autem Donatiani & Donatistæ, de cuius vocis declinatione & analogia incidit Augustino cum Cresconio Grammatico quæstio, vt ipse lib.2.contra eum cap.2. scribit a Donato a Casis Nigris, Numida, qui primus huius dogmatis propinator fuit, & altare contra altare, vt ait August. erexit. Sed primum Carthagine pars Maiorini (quod aduersus Cæcilianum Catholicæ Ecclesiæ Episcopum constitutus, illic erat Donatistarum præsul Maiorinus, id est, altare contra altare in Dei Ecclesia erat erectum, ut Augustinus loquitur) vocabantur. quemad-modum ipsi Catholicos à Comitis Macarij nomine, qui Carthagini Cæciliani tempore præfuit, Macarianos appellabant: tamen postea obtinuit, ut hi hæretici Donatistæ passim diceretur. Romæ vero Campates, ut ait Hieronymus in Epist. contra Luciferia. à campo: & Montenses, à monte, ut opinor, in quem latèter & clam conueniebant, quo nomine eos appellat Augustinus lib. 2. contra Petilian. cap. 108. Quòd autem Parmenianistæ etiam nominati sunt, ut ait Augustinus à Parmeniano Donati ipsius discipulo, quem egregium existimabant, hoc non men acceperunt, ut Manichæi ab Adamantio acerrimo Manichæi dogmatis propugnatore Adamantij sunt vocati, ut idem August. scribit. Breuius vero ista persequor, quòd scripta Augustini tum in epistolis, tum in disputationibus & libris aduersus eos editis certè quidem vtilissima & doctissima nota omnibus esse existime, ex quibus huius pestis & hæreseos tota vis & ratio luculenter intelligetur. Scripsit etiam aduersus eos Optatus Episcopus Mileuitanus libros 4. Donatus autem habitus est doctus sua ætate, cuius etiam libros vidit Hieronymus. Alius autem fuit Donatus Euraæ Epiricæ Episcopus orthodoxus, de quo Nicephorus libro duodecimo capite 45. qui nihil ad hanc sectam & tempus pertinet.
units.tr: The Donatists are so called after Donatus. A question arose between Augustine and the grammarian Cresconius about the declension and analogy of this word, as Augustine himself writes in his second book against him, chapter 2. Donatus was a Numidian from Casae Nigrae, who was the first promoter of this doctrine, and who, as Augustine says, "set up altar against altar." At first, at Carthage, the party of Maiorinus was called by that name, because Maiorinus had been set up as their bishop against Caecilian, bishop of the Catholic Church; there, as Augustine puts it, altar had been set up against altar in the Church of God. In the same way they called the Catholics Macarians, after the name of the count Macarius, who had governed at Carthage in Caecilian's time. Nevertheless, in the end it prevailed that these heretics were everywhere called Donatists. At Rome they were called Campatians, as Jerome says in his letter against the Luciferians, from the field (campus); and Montenses, from the mountain, I suppose, on which they gathered secretly and furtively, a name by which Augustine calls them in his second book against Petilian, chapter 108. That they were also called Parmenianists, as Augustine says, after Parmenianus, a disciple of Donatus himself, whom they regarded as outstanding, they took this name just as the Manichaeans were called Adamantians after Adamantius, a most fierce defender of the Manichaean doctrine, as Augustine likewise writes. I pursue these matters only briefly, because I think the writings of Augustine, both in letters and in disputations and books published against them, are certainly most useful and learned and should be known to all, and from them the whole force and reasoning of this plague and heresy will be clearly understood. Optatus, bishop of Milevis, also wrote against them in four books. Donatus himself was considered learned in his own time, and Jerome saw his books. But there was another Donatus, the orthodox bishop of Eura in Epirus, of whom Nicephorus writes in book 12, chapter 45; he has nothing to do with this sect or period.

units.la: 2 Atque in Africa & Donati parte.) Copulam, &, addidimus, quæ deest in impressis, & ex cuius præterminsione fit tota hæc oratio hiulca, male sonans & obscura. Sed etiam in quibusdam recentioribus qui hunc Augustini locum citant, ita transcriptum inueni. Sequuntur iam huius sectae variae hypotheses, & eae quidem blasphemae & tetrae, e quibus 1 est: Ecclesiam Dei eam demum esse in his terris agnoscendam & sequendam, quae omni ruga, macula & peccato quantumuis levi careat, & pura sit, quia sanctus esse debet ille coetus, qui Ecclesia vocatur. Sanctus autem non est, cui adhuc peccatum inhaeret, Ephes.1.verf.4: 5.verf.26. Itaque perfectionem iustitiae & angelicam sanctitatem hic ab hominibus requirunt, quam etiam se suosque illos impuros coetus habere iactant & profitentur, tam sunt arrogantes, caeci & a vero suae infirmitatis & rebellionis sensu alieni. Unde se ab eorum coetu separant, quos peccatores & non satis puros indicant, ut seorsim coetus colligant & schisma faciant. Hoc dogma nostro seculo Anabaptistae renovarunt: fuitque Pelagianismi, qui secutus est, magnum certe fundamentum. At si quis se sine peccato esse glorietur, medax est: nec coram Deo quisquam mortalium hic degentium iustus, excepto modo uno Christo, reperietur, 1.Ioan.1.verf.8. Ia-cob.3.verf.2. Psal.143.verf.2. Et si operibus nostris iustificamur, frustra Christus mortuus est, Galat.2.verf.21. Ex quo satis apparet unde hic error natus sit, quaeque eius concipiendi prima femina primíque afflatus fuerint, infernalis nimirum & diabolica de suorum operum merito, iustitia & perfectione opinio semel iam animis hominum a Satana infusa contra meritum. & gratiam Christi, quam prorsus tollit & reii-cit. Unde isti haeretici vere ad operistas perti-nent, sunt que ex eorum numero & grege. Itaque suos tantum coetus veram Dei Ecclesiam esse & dici. 2 Neminem ad bene viuendum esse compelledum urgendumque censen t, non tantum quidem ne sit coacta & inuita pietas & obedientia Dei: sed ut libera & effrenis sit vi-tiorum erroru mque omnium licentia & grassatio. Augustinus. Hoc quidem superiori sen-tentiae, per quam tam exactam & puram pu-tam sanctimoniam vitae a piis efflagitant,plane contrarium est: sed nec mirum,nec nouum est, ut haeretici seipsos repugnantibus inter se dog-matis tanquam proprio gladio iugulent & ne-cent. 3 Haereticos negant ullo modo magi-stratus quanquam pij & fidelis autoritate coer-cendos, castigandos vel comprimendos, ne eo-rum venenum latius serpat, vel ut ipsi haeretici resipiscant. Vetus tamen Ecclesia contra Sa-mosatenum grassantem & turbantem Eccle-sias, Adriani imperatoris authoritatem implo-rauit, & cum de hoc argumento luculenter dis-putarit, epist.48.50.204. aliisque pene infinitis locis Augustinus, non puto mihi necesse fusius istos refutare. Fuit quidem istius primum sen-tentiae ipse, ut coercendos a magistratu haereti-cos negaret, sed ratione ipsaque rerum expe-rientia convictus & sapientior factus priorem sententiam commutauit. Itaque adversus Do-natistas lex lata est ab Impp. Arcadio & Theo-dosio, quae multa eos comprimeret, vel in er-rore perseuerantes: vel latius grassantes. Nam utriusque Dei tabulæ custos est verus piusque Magistratus, & de hoc argumento extant doctis. nostræ ætatis virorum uberrimi aduersus Anabaptistas, qui hoc venenum nobis reflarut, tractatus. Ita vero in hoc argumento excandue-runt Donatistæ, ut multa contra Magistratum, & sanctam illam Dei ordinationem, ut vocat Paulus Rom.13. euomerent, & impie blatte-rarent, tanquam semper Ecclesiæ lupi & pe-stes Magistratus essent. Quod ipsum, sed aliis verbis, Anabaptistæ nobis hodie reponunt.
units.tr: 2 And in Africa and in the part of Donatus.) I have added the conjunction "and", which is missing from the printed editions, and whose omission makes this whole sentence halting, harsh and obscure. But I have found it so transcribed also in some more recent writers who cite this passage of Augustine. There now follow the various tenets of this sect, and they are blasphemous and foul. The first is that the Church of God is to be recognised and followed on this earth only where there is no wrinkle, stain or sin, however slight, and where it is pure, because the assembly called the Church must be holy; but he is not holy in whom sin still dwells (Ephesians 1 and 5, vv. 4, 26). Hence they demand here from men a perfection of righteousness and an angelic holiness, and they boast and profess that they themselves and their own impure assemblies have it, so arrogant, blind and alien are they to the true sense of their own weakness and rebellion. Hence they separate themselves from the assembly of those whom they declare sinful and not pure enough, so that they may gather separate assemblies and make a schism. The Anabaptists have renewed this doctrine in our own age; it was certainly the great foundation of the Pelagianism that followed. But if anyone glories that he is without sin, he is a liar; nor will any mortal living here be found righteous before God, except the one Christ (1 John 1:8; James 3:2; Psalm 143:2). And if we are justified by our works, Christ died in vain (Galatians 2:21). From this it is clear enough whence this error arose, and what were the first seed and first breath of its conception: namely, the infernal and diabolical opinion, once poured by Satan into men's minds, that righteousness and perfection are owed to the merit of their own works, against the merit and grace of Christ, which it utterly removes and rejects. Hence these heretics truly belong to the Works-men, and are of their number and flock. Accordingly they hold and say that only their own assemblies are the true Church of God. 2 They judge that no one is to be compelled or urged to live well, not only lest godliness and obedience to God be forced and unwilling, but so that there may be a free and unbridled licence and rampage of all vices and errors. Augustine. This is plainly contrary to the former opinion, by which they demand such an exact and pure holiness of life; but it is neither surprising nor new that heretics slay and kill themselves with their own sword, by doctrines that contradict one another. 3 They deny that heretics may in any way be restrained, chastised or suppressed by the authority of the magistrate, however godly and faithful, lest their poison spread more widely, or so that the heretics themselves may repent. Yet the ancient Church appealed to the authority of the emperor Hadrian against Samosatenus, who was raging and troubling the Churches; and since Augustine has argued this question at length in letters 48, 50 and 204, and in almost countless other places, I do not think I need to refute them at greater length. He himself at first held the opinion that heretics should not be restrained by the magistrate, but, convinced by reason and by the very experience of things, he became wiser and changed his earlier view. Accordingly a law was passed against the Donatists by the emperors Arcadius and Theodosius, which curbed them greatly, whether they persisted in their error or spread more widely. For the true and godly magistrate is the guardian of both tables of God's law, and on this subject there are very rich treatises by learned men of our own age against the Anabaptists, who have revived this poison among us. Yet the Donatists so raged over this question that they vomited forth many things against the magistrate and that holy ordinance of God, as Paul calls it (Romans 13), and impiously babbled that the magistrates were always the wolves and plagues of the Church. This same thing, though in other words, the Anabaptists hurl back at us today.

units.la: 4 Sacramentorum vim & effectum ex Mini-stri illa præbentis dignitate, sanctitate, & manu metiuntur, non ex ipsius Dei authoris, cuius illa sunt, promissione, & spiritus Dei ἐνέργεια[?]. Itaque baptismum infamem & pollutum censent & appellant, qui ab infami & polluto ministro datus est etiam credenti, & pio homini, nedum adhuc infanti & parvulo. Hæc sane Hieronymi sententia in Pauli epist. ad Galat.cap.3.
