Si igitur qui in Christo baptizati sunt, Christū induerunt, manifestum est eos qui non sunt induti Christum, nō fuisse baptizatos in Christo, dat aliquod huic Donatistarum errori fulci-mentum, nisi dextre explicetur.
units.tr: 4 They measure the force and effect of the sacraments by the dignity, holiness and hand of the minister who dispenses them, not by the promise of God the author himself, to whom they belong, and by the operation [ἐνέργεια] of the Spirit of God. Hence they judge and call baptism infamous and polluted when it has been given, even to a believer and a godly man, let alone to an infant and little child, by an infamous and polluted minister. Indeed this is the opinion of Jerome in his commentary on Paul's epistle to the Galatians, chapter 3: "If therefore those who have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ, it is clear that those who have not put on Christ were not baptized into Christ." This gives some support to this error of the Donatists, unless it is rightly explained.

units.la: 5 Rebapti-zant à Catholicis & orthodoxis iam baptiza-tos, quod erat consequens, quia putant eos à traditoribus & malis ministris tinctos: itaque non esse baptizatos. Afferunt pro sese Cypriani martyris & Episcopi Carthaginensis sententiam, cui sex libris De unico baptis. respondit Augu-stin. Nec enim Christi baptismate semel tincti sunt rebaptizandi, ut recte ex Dei verbo definiuit Ecclesia, nec hoc ipsum à Donatistis fieri instituit primus eorum author Donatus,vt Au-gust.scripsit:sed illius successores hunc errorem aliis iam ab eo acceptis addiderunt. 6 Vio-lentas sibi manus afferunt,ne à Magistratu capti propter errorem puniantur, idque fieri licere salua conscientia docent,& appellant martyriu. Plurimi enim se propterea occiderut,&quos-dam ab hoc consilio Augustinus ipse,quaquam ab iis insidiis petitus, revocauit. 7 Obuios sibi quosque in plateis & agris homines à suis erroribus alienos cædunt & iugulant furiose, maximè ij qui inter eos Circumcelliones ap-pellantur. Nam rectè se id posse contendunt. Donatistis autem istis similes fuerunt alij hære-tici quos Damascenus Thymoleontas nominat, homines plane sanguinarij, truculenti,& qui religionem ipsam in occasionem sæuitiæ & ho-micidij impiè arriperent, Theodoret. August. Isidorus. 8 Arianis consentiunt,dum Filium Patre minorem faciunt: & Filio Spiritum san-ctum subiiciunt,Augustinus & Isidorus.Itaque Theodoret.lib.4. Hæreticar.fabular. eos Aria-nis annumerat,& libro 3.contra Cresco.Gram-mat. cap.34. scribit Augustin. ipsum Donatum Carthaginensem Episcopum Sardicensi syno-do, quæ, vt ait Augustinus, fuit Ariana, inter-fuisse illiqué subscripsisse. 9 Purgationes quasdam magicas ostentant & inuehunt, ia-ctántque reuelationes & enthousiasmos vt sua dogmata plausibilius confirment, & se sanctos perfectósque fumosius glorientur.Ista vero purgatio fit ab iis osse, quod manu complectentes &c & occultantes, mysteria quædam peragunt per quæ sanctificari se, Platonicorum & Ethnico-rum more, somniant, non autem solo sanguine Christi, & vi Spiritus sancti. i.Petr.i. Ioan.Da-mascen. Atque huius fontis hæc tot sunt sordes & fœtidi riui.
units.tr: 5 They rebaptize those who have already been baptized by the Catholics and the orthodox; this followed, because they think those people were washed by traditors and evil ministers, and so were not baptized at all. They cite in their favour the opinion of Cyprian, the martyr and bishop of Carthage, to which Augustine replied in six books On the One Baptism. For those who have been once washed in the baptism of Christ are not to be rebaptized, as the Church rightly defined from the word of God; nor did their first author Donatus institute this practice of rebaptizing among the Donatists, as Augustine wrote, but his successors added this error to others that they had already received from him. 6 They lay violent hands on themselves, so that they may not be captured by the magistrate and punished for their error; and they teach that this may be done lawfully and with a clear conscience, and they call it martyrdom. For many killed themselves on this account, and Augustine himself recalled some from this purpose, although he was himself sought out by such plots. 7 They furiously strike down and slaughter men who are alien to their errors and whom they meet in the streets and fields, especially those who among them are called Circumcellions; for they contend that they may rightly do so. Other heretics, like the Donatists, whom Damascene calls Thymoleontes, were also of this kind: men altogether bloodthirsty and savage, who impiously seized upon religion itself as an occasion for cruelty and murder (Theodoret, Augustine, Isidore). 8 They agree with the Arians in making the Son less than the Father, and in subjecting the Holy Spirit to the Son (Augustine and Isidore). Hence Theodoret, in book 4 of his Heretical Fables, counts them among the Arians; and in book 3 against Cresconius the grammarian, chapter 34, Augustine writes that Donatus himself, bishop of Carthage, was present at the Synod of Sardica, which, as Augustine says, was Arian, and subscribed to it. 9 They display and introduce certain magical purifications, and they boast of revelations and enthusiasms in order to confirm their doctrines more plausibly, and to glory more vaingloriously that they are holy and perfect. This purification is effected by the mouth, which they perform by taking hold of and concealing certain mysteries with the hand, by which, in the manner of the Platonists and Gentiles, they dream that they are sanctified, and not by the blood of Christ alone and the power of the Holy Spirit (1 Peter 1; John; Damascene). From this fountain come all these many filths and foul streams.

units.la: 3 Appellantur Circumcelliones.) Multa fuerunt in secta & coetu Donatistarum schismata. Alij enim Rogatistæ dicti sunt: alij Maximiani-stæ: illi à Rogato & Rogatiano, hi verò à Maximiano: alij Circumcelliones, quòd in agris cellas quasdam & tuguriola veluti austeram Eremitarum vitam imitantes, haberent, in quibus habitabant primum soli: postea verò cum quibusdam mulieribus. Sed illinc in homines suæ doctrinæ aduersarios impunè irruebant, quos iugulabant & trucidabant obuios, adeò vt minora leuioràque fuisse quorumuis latronum & prædonum facta, quàm Circumcellionum istorum scribat August.lib.3.contra Cresco[?].Gram-mat. cap.42. & seq. Alij Parmenianistæ: alij verò Cirtenses, non autem, vt quidam volunt, & perperam legunt, Circenses, & ita in epistolis Augustini est emendandum. Dicti sunt autem Cirtenses, quòd Donatistarum primi & maiores Secundo Tigisitano Episcopo procurante apud Cirtam oppidum Numidiæ (est autem in Numidia Cirta duplex, vna metropolis, vt Pomponius Mela docet: altera colonia, vt Antonini itinerarium habet) concilium suum habuerint, à quo postea Cirtenses sunt appellati, quasi qui fidem Cirtæ conscriptam sequerentur. Augustinus ipse nostram sententiam confirmat, lib.3. contra Cresco. Grammat. cap. 26. & 27. Ergo Circumcelliones fuerunt inter eos immanissimi.
units.tr: 3 Appellantur Circumcelliones.) There were many schisms within the sect and assembly of the Donatists. Some were called Rogatists, others Maximianists: the former from Rogatus and Rogatianus, the latter from Maximianus. Others were called Circumcelliones, because in the countryside they had certain cells and little huts, imitating the austere life of the hermits, in which they lived at first alone, but afterwards with certain women. From there they rushed with impunity upon the opponents of their teaching, and slaughtered and butchered whomever they met, so that, as Augustine writes in book 3 against Cresconius the grammarian, chapter 42 and following, the deeds of any robbers and plunderers were lighter and milder than those of these Circumcellions. Others were called Parmenianists, and others Cirtenses, not Circenses as some wish and wrongly read; and so it should be corrected in the letters of Augustine. They were called Cirtenses because the first and leading Donatists, under the leadership of Secundus, bishop of Tigisis, held their council at Cirta, a town of Numidia (there are two Cirtas in Numidia: one a metropolis, as Pomponius Mela teaches, the other a colony, as the Itinerary of Antoninus has it), and afterwards they were named from it, as if they were those who followed the creed drawn up at Cirta. Augustine himself confirms our opinion in book 3 against Cresconius the grammarian, chapters 26 and 27. Therefore the Circumcellions were among them the most savage.

units.la: 4 Hanc Historiam & schisma Donatistarum saepe repetit Augustinus, & extat in libris adversus Petilian. literas: sed maxime lib.3. contra Cresco. cap.27. & 28.
units.tr: 4 Augustine often repeats this history and schism of the Donatists, and it is found in his books against Petilian's letters, but especially in book 3 against Cresconius, chapters 27 and 28.

units.la: CAP. LXX. Priscillianistæ cur sic dicti. Ex quibus erroribus conflati & nati. Erroris autem eorum capita septem enumerantur.
units.tr: CHAPTER 70. Why the Priscillianists are so called. The errors from which they were compounded and born. Seven heads of their error are listed.

units.la: PRiscillianistæ[?] quos in Hispania Priscillianus instituit, maxime Gnosticorum & Manichæorum dogmata permixta sectantur. Quanuis & ex aliis hæresibus in eas sordes tanquam in sententiam quandam horribili confusione confluxerint. Propter occultandas autem contaminationes, & turpitudines suas habent in suis {2}dogmatibus & hæc verba,
units.tr: The Priscillianists, whom Priscillian founded in Spain, follow chiefly the doctrines of the Gnostics and Manichaeans mixed together. Yet from other heresies too they have flowed together into that filth, in a horrible confusion, as into a single system. To conceal their defilements and their shameful practices, they have in their teachings also these words:

units.la: Iura, periura, secretum prodere noli.
units.tr: Swear falsely, perjure yourself, but do not betray the secret.

units.la: Hi animas dicunt eiusdem naturæ atque substantiæ, cuius est Deus, ad agonem quendam spontaneum in terris exercendum per septem calos, & per quosdam gradatim descendere principatus, & in malignum principem incurrere, à quo mundum hunc factum volunt, atque ab hoc principe per diversa carnis opera seminari. Astruunt etiam fatalibus astris homines colligatos, ipsumque corpus nostrum secundum duodecim signa cæli esse compositum, sicut hi qui Mathematici vulgò appellantur, constituentes in capite Arietem, Taurum in cervice, Geminos in humeris, Cancrum in pectore, & inde catera nomina- tim signa percurrentes ad plantas usque perveniunt, quas Piscibus tribunt, quod ultimum signum ab Astrologis nuncupatur. Hæc & alia fabulosa, vana, sacrilega, quæ persequi longum est, hæresis ista contexit. Carnes tanquam immundas escas etiam ipsa denvitat[?]. Coniuges, quibus hoc malum potuerit persuadere, disiungens, & viros a nolentibus fœminis, & fœminas a nolentibus viris. Opificium quippe omnis carnis non Deo bono & vero, sed maligni angelis tribunt, hoc versutiores etiam Manichæis, quod nihil Scripturarum canonicarum repudiant, simul cum Apocryphis legentes omnia, & in authoritate sumentes, sed in suos sensus allegorizando vertentes, quicquid in sanctis Libris est, quod eorum evertat errorem. De Christo Sabellianam sectam tenent, eundem ipsum esse dicentes, non solum Filium, sed etiam Patrem, & Spiritum sanctum.
units.tr: They say that souls are of the same nature and substance as God, and that they must wrestle a voluntary contest on earth, passing through seven heavens and gradually descending through certain principalities, and falling into the malignant prince, by whom they hold this world was made, and by whom they are sown through the various works of the flesh. They also maintain that men are bound by the fated stars, and that our very body is composed according to the twelve signs of the heavens, just as those whom the common people call Mathematicians teach: they place the Ram in the head, the Bull in the neck, the Twins on the shoulders, the Crab on the breast, and then run through the remaining signs by name, down to the feet, which they assign to the Fishes, since that is the last sign, called by the Astrologers the ultimate. This heresy has woven together these and other fabulous, empty, sacrilegious notions, too many to pursue. It even rejects flesh as unclean food. It separates spouses whom it has been able to persuade of this evil, keeping husbands from unwilling wives and wives from unwilling husbands. They ascribe the making of all flesh not to the good and true God but to the angels of the evil one, and in this they are more crafty even than the Manichaeans, because they reject none of the canonical Scriptures, reading all the apocryphal books together with them and taking them as authoritative, while twisting into their own senses by allegory whatever is in the holy Books that would overthrow their error. Concerning Christ they hold the Sabellian sect, saying that he is the same being as the Son, the Father, and the Holy Spirit.

units.la: I Priscillianistæ, quos.) Quo tempore Satan varijs erroribus sparsis in Orientali Ecclesia grassabatur, exorta est in Occidente hæc infernalis Priscillianistarum Erynnis, quæ teterrimarum hæresεon[?] omnium, quæ præcesserant, farrago & colluvies fuit. Nec enim diabolus, qui salutis nostræ hostis est, à turbandis Dei Ecclesiis, in hac mundi plaga, quamquam hæresibus minus obnoxia, & patente, cessare potuit. Itaq; Occidentales Christianos aggressus est, apud quos in unum tanquam fasciculum coniecit singula, quæ in Oriente per varios & diversos hæreticos iam iacti, disseminarique curaverat. Vocata vero est hæc Priscillianistarum hæresis, non à Priscilla quidem, quæ fuit Montani scortum, & longè ante huius erroris principia vixit, etsi è Galatia, vbi plurimum Montaniste viguerunt, ortum protectumque hoc malum sentit Hieronymus: sed à Priscilliano homine, vt omnes authores scribunt, imprimisque Isidorus, & ipse Hispanus, & Hispalensis Episcopus, Hispano. Hic ab Helpidio rhetore in fide institutus & edoctus est: Helpidius autem ipse à Marco quodam Monacho, qui Ægyptia Memphi profugus, propter Valentis edictum de revocandis ad suas curias & ad publica munera subunda, Monachis (vt apparet ex L. Quidam ignauię sectatores. C. De Decurionibus lib.10.) venit in Hispaniam: sed iam Gnosticorum, & Manichæorum labe & veneno plane tabidus & infectus, quemadmodum inter Monachos errores omne genus aluntur. Ita igitur fascinatus Priscillianus, errorem suum in Hispania sparsit, sub Gratiano imperatore, & Damaso episcopo Romano, circa annum à Christo passo 348. etsi Sigeberto tardius hoc malum propagatum videtur: sed propagationem non autem originem ipsam spectauit Sigebertus. Gratanter autem & auidè exceptus à plurimis in Hispania, imprimis ab Instantio, & Saluiano episcopis, à quibus Priscillianus ipse episcopus constitutus est in Laletanis populis (qui sunt citerioris Hispaniæ, vt Plinius lib. 3. cap. 3. scribit) Adygino tamen Cordubensi episcopo reclamante, & eum errorem grauiter oppugnante. Peruicit tamen hæc lues & obtinuit, ita vt non tantum Hispanias, sed etiam Gallias, & in Italia plurimos corrumperet. Sed & in Africanas ecclesias, traiecto mari, peruenit, vbi a nonnullis excepta, retentaque est. Itaque quod Priscillianistae docebant de mendacio & periurio, illud nimirum religionis causa esse concessum, multis etiam in Africa placuit, aduersus quos libros De mendacio scripsit Augustinus. Latissime igitur vagata est, & furiose pene in toto Occidente grassata, adeo vt coercenda etiam publicis Synodis, & imperatorum edictis fuerit, ne noceret pluribus. Itaque Synodo Romana, quae a Damaso[?] & Ambrosio collecta est: & Gallicana, quae Burdegalam conuenit, cuique Martinus ipse Turonensis episcopus interfuit: & Toletana, error Priscillianistarum damnatus est, & Priscillianus ipse excommunicatus, atque anathemate percussus, fugere Gratiani imperatoris iussu coactus est: Quanquam id sub Innocentio primo, qui longe tempora Damasci sequutus est, contigisse mauult Platina, errore calculi & temporis manifesto deceptus. Sed homo pertinax Priscillianus, caelum non animum mutauit. Nam ad Maximum, qui in Galliis imperium aduersus Gratianum inuadere coeperat: idcoque tyrannus vulgo nominatur, confugit (vel vt alij volunt, ad eum ex synodo Burdegalensi prouocauit) vbi sua venena euulgare Treuiris conatus, Indatij (alij vero Vrsatium appellant, alij Paulinum fuisse malunt:) & Itatij episcoporum diligentia comuictus, refutatus, damnatusque haereseos ab Euodio Maximi praefecto, Treuiris, quae est vrbs celeberrima Germaniae, morte multatus est, quum etiam illud prius confessus esset, se saepius in suis conventiculis mulieres suae sectae addictas, foede costuprasse & violasse: (inter quas fuit Euchrotia Delphidij Rhetoris uxor, ut ex Ausonio a Iosepho Scaligero est annotatum) cuius tamen ossa in Hispaniam relata esse dicuntur. Vide librum 4. Seueri, De vita S. Martini, & Sigeberti Chronicon. Ad Orientem tamen huius erroris & sectae ne fama quidem videtur peruenisse. Illius enim nec Epiphanius, qui Gratiani tempora sequutus est, nec Theodoretus, nec authores historiae Ecclesiasticae, nec Nicephorus, nec denique Damascenus meminit, nisi fortasse hi sint, quos ipse Ethnophronas appellat (quidda enim isti cum Priscillianistis, in lyderum & astrorum obseruatione commune habuerunt.) Priscillianistarum tamen nomen non extat. Perstitit autem in Occidente diutissime haec haeresis, quado sub Leone primo, ut apparet ex ipsius epistola 93. cap. 12. & sub Gregorio Magno adhuc viguit, & aliquot postea seculis. Tempore Orosij & Augustini adhuc in Hispania repullulasse, facile ex Orosij ipsius scripto ad Augustinum colligitur, quod extat Tomo 6. Sed & tempore quoque Bernardi Clareuall. adhuc restasse quasdam illius fruticationes apparet ex ipsius Serm.63. in Cant. Cantico.
units.tr: The Priscillianists, whom.) At the time when Satan was raging in the Eastern Church with various scattered errors, this infernal Fury of the Priscillianists arose in the West, which became the hodgepodge and sink of all the most foul heresies that had gone before. For the devil, who is the enemy of our salvation, could not cease from disturbing God's Churches in this corner of the world, though it is less exposed to heresies and more open. And so he attacked the Western Christians, among whom he gathered into one bundle, as it were, the individual things that he had already thrown and had caused to be spread abroad in the East through various and diverse heretics. This Priscillianist heresy takes its name not from Priscilla, the harlot of Montanus, who lived long before the beginnings of this error, though Jerome thinks this plague arose and grew up from Galatia, where Montanism flourished most; rather it takes its name from Priscillian, a man, as all the authors write, and above all Isidore, who was himself a Spaniard and Bishop of Seville. Priscillian was instructed and taught in the faith by Helpidius the rhetorician. Helpidius himself came to Spain from a certain monk, Marcus, who had fled from Memphis in Egypt, on account of the edict of Valens about summoning monks back to their councils and to the bearing of public burdens (as appears from the law Quidam ignaviae sectatores, C. De Decurionibus, book 10). But by then Marcus was thoroughly rotten and infected with the stain and poison of the Gnostics and Manichaeans, just as every kind of error is nurtured among monks. Thus bewitched, Priscillian spread his error in Spain under the emperor Gratian and Pope Damasus, about the year 348 after Christ's passion, although Sigebert seems to have thought this plague spread later. But Sigebert looked at the spread of it, not at its origin. Eagerly and greedily received by many in Spain, above all by the bishops Instantius and Salvianus, by whom Priscillian himself was made bishop over the people of Lalletania (who belong to Hither Spain, as Pliny writes in book 3, chapter 3), although Hyginus, Bishop of Cordoba, protested and vigorously opposed that error. Nevertheless this pestilence persisted and took hold, so that it corrupted not only the Spains but also the Gauls, and very many in Italy. It crossed the sea and reached the African churches as well, where it was received by some and held fast. Hence what the Priscillianists taught about lying and perjury, namely that it is permitted for the sake of religion, pleased many in Africa too, against whom Augustine wrote his books On Lying. So it spread very widely and raged almost madly through the whole West, so that it had to be restrained even by public synods and imperial edicts, lest it harm many more. Accordingly, the error of the Priscillianists was condemned by the Roman Synod, which was gathered by Damasus and Ambrose, by the Gallican Synod, which met at Bordeaux and in which Martin himself, bishop of Tours, took part, and by the Synod of Toledo; Priscillian himself was excommunicated and struck with anathema, and was compelled by the order of the emperor Gratian to flee. Although Platina prefers to say this happened under Innocent I, who followed long after the time of Damasus, he was deceived by a plain error of calculation and of chronology. But Priscillian, a stubborn man, changed his sky but not his mind. For he fled to Maximus, who had begun to seize the empire in the Gauls against Gratian, and for that reason is commonly called a tyrant (or, as others hold, he appealed to him from the Synod of Bordeaux). There he tried to spread his poisons at Trier, but was refuted and condemned for heresy through the diligence of the bishops Instantius (others call him Ursacius, others prefer Paulinus) and Itacius, and was put to death at Trier, a very famous city of Germany, by Evodius, the prefect of Maximus. Before that, he had confessed that he had often in his conventicles foully defiled and violated women devoted to his sect (among whom was Euchrotia, the wife of the rhetorician Delphidius, as Joseph Scaliger has noted from Ausonius). Yet his bones are said to have been carried back to Spain. See book 4 of Severus, On the Life of St. Martin, and Sigebert's Chronicle. Yet the rumour of this error and sect seems never to have reached the East. For neither Epiphanius, who followed the time of Gratian, nor Theodoret, nor the writers of Church history, nor Nicephorus, nor finally Damascene mention it, unless perhaps these are the ones whom Epiphanius himself calls the Ethnophronas (for they had something in common with the Priscillianists in the observation of planets and stars). Still, the name of the Priscillianists does not occur. This heresy persisted in the West for a very long time: under Leo I, as appears from his letter 93, chapter 12, it still flourished, and under Gregory the Great, and for some centuries afterward. That it had sprung up again in Spain in the time of Orosius and Augustine is easily gathered from Orosius's own writing to Augustine, which is found in volume 6. And that some of its offshoots still remained even in the time of Bernard of Clairvaux is clear from his Sermon 63 on the Song of Songs.

units.la: Variae fuerunt huius sectae sordes, omnes tamen ex alieno coeno hauste, & imprimis Gnosticorum & Manichaeorum lacunis derivatae: quarum aliquot capita recensset hoc loco Augustinus. Nos autem ex variis & & diuersis authoribus hæc tot congessimus.
units.tr: The filth of this sect was various, yet all of it was drawn from another's mud and derived chiefly from the pools of the Gnostics and Manichaeans. Augustine recounts some of its heads in this place, but we have gathered these many from various and diverse authors.

units.la: 1 Mundum huc a maligno deo & angelo conditum esse, non a bono Deo. Hoc Simoniano-rum, & Manichæorum delirium fuit, nec in eo quicquam illi noui aut inauditi dixere, qui tamen refutantur, Genef.1. Psalmo 33. & infinitis aliis Scripturæ locis.
units.tr: 1. That the world was created here by an evil god and angel, not by the good God. This was the delirium of the Simonians and Manichaeans, and in it they said nothing new or unheard of; yet it is refuted in Genesis 1, Psalm 33, and in countless other passages of Scripture.

units.la: 2 Confundunt perso-nas in Trinitate, & eundem esse Patrem, Filium, & Spiritum sanctum contendunt, qui pro diuersis officiis & operibus, diuersa nomina for-tiatur. Hoc Sabellianum est. Augustinus etiam contra Origenistas c.4. meminit.
units.tr: 2 They confuse the persons in the Trinity, and contend that the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are one and the same, and that they take different names according to their different offices and works. This is Sabellian. Augustine also mentions it in his work against the Origenists, chapter 4.

units.la: 3 Animam humanam eiusdem esse, atque Deum ipsum, ef-fentiç[?]. Itaque Deus sit[?] oportet, & tot propterea dij, quot sunt hominum animæ. Quamobrem Deus peccare potest, & subiici diabolo, & inferni pœna torqueri, quia his omnibus malis obnoxia est humana anima. Hoc certè Mani-chæanum est.
units.tr: 3 That the human soul is of the same substance as God himself. Therefore, they say, the soul must be God, and there are as many gods as there are human souls. For this reason God can sin, be subject to the devil, and be tormented with the punishment of hell, since the human soul is liable to all these evils. This is certainly Manichaean.

units.la: 4 Animas hominum quum sunt in hæc corpora mittendæ, ex quodam prom-ptuario sumi, vbi conditæ sunt, seruanturque. Hoc Origenianum est. Quum autem demittuntur in has terras per varia principum cælestium regna, qui sunt orbes, & sphæræ cælestes, mea-re, à quibus singulis domum[?] aliquot anima nostra accipit, quemadmodum illa Hesiodi Pando-ra. Hoc & poeticum, & prorsus ethnicum est, & profanum.
units.tr: 4 That souls of men, when they are about to be sent into these bodies, are taken from a certain storehouse where they were created and kept. This is Origenian. But when they are sent down into these lands through the various kingdoms of the heavenly rulers, which are the orbs and celestial spheres, and pass through each of these, our soul receives some [gift] from each, just as in Hesiod's story of Pandora. This is both poetic and utterly heathen and profane.

units.la: 5 Astris & syderibus, eorumq; constellationi, signis item duodecim Zodiaci, & Planetis, more Astrologorum, vitæ humanæ cursum attribuunt, à quibus nos regi, vitæque nostræ actiones gubernari, & administrari censent, ut felices sint, vel infelices, bonæ item, vel prauæ.Quod autem Zodiaci signum cuique humani corporis membro asignent, explicat hic Augustin.& nos ex Irenæo diximus alibi: Hoc magicum est,& damnatæ,iudiciariæque Astrologiæ plane delirium, quod ne sequamur, aut probemus, sæpius verbo Dei interdictum fuit, Hier.10.Deuteron.18. Isaiæ 44. versu 25: & aliis.
units.tr: 5 That the course of human life is assigned to the stars and constellations, to the twelve signs of the Zodiac and to the planets, after the manner of the astrologers, and that we are ruled by them, and that the actions of our life are governed and directed by them, so that people are happy or unhappy, good or wicked. As for which sign of the Zodiac they assign to each member of the human body, Augustine explains this here, and we have spoken of it elsewhere following Irenaeus. This is magic, and the delirium of condemned judicial astrology, which we are often forbidden by the Word of God to follow or approve: Jeremiah 10, Deuteronomy 18, Isaiah 44:25, and elsewhere.

units.la: 6 Inuitos hos malos fieri,& peccare, vt syderum coactosinon sponte, neque animi electione. Hoc a Stoicis sumptum, qui peccata homino minum fato suo tribuunt: sed plane falsum. Nã perditio nostra a nobis ipsis est, non a stellis, & earum vi & impulsu. de quo vide Ioannem Da-mascenum libro 2. de orthodoxa fide. capite 7.
units.tr: 6 That these wicked men are made and sin against their will, as if compelled by the stars, not of their own accord and not by free choice of mind. This was taken from the Stoics, who ascribe the sins of men to their fate; but it is plainly false. For our ruin is from ourselves, not from the stars and their power and impulse. On this see John of Damascus, book 2 of On the Orthodox Faith, chapter 7.

units.la: 7 Mendacia & periuria religionis fuę[?] celan-dæ gratia, fieri bona conscientia, & Dei numi-ne saluo & illæso, docent blasphemi homines. Hoc videtur quidem proprium eorum fuisse, sed tamen habent etiam hoc ipsum cum Audia-nis commune. Vnde istud est eorum, Iura, per-jurà, secretum prodere noli. Vide Augustinum tum in Enchiridio, tum in libro De mendacio, ad Consent. Item Bernard. Clareuallenf. ser-mo 65.in Cantic.canticor. & refutatur apertis-sime, Iob.13.verf.7.
units.tr: 7 Lies and perjuries, for the sake of concealing their religion, can be committed with a good conscience and with God's divinity safe and unharmed, the blasphemous men teach. This indeed seems to have been peculiar to them, but they nevertheless share this very thing with the Audians. Hence that saying of theirs: "Swear falsely, forswear yourselves, but do not betray the secret." See Augustine both in the Enchiridion and in his book On Lying, to Consentius. Also Bernard of Clairvaux, sermon 65 on the Song of Songs; and it is most clearly refuted at Job 13:7.

units.la: 8 Carnes vt pollutas omnino creaturas damnant, & earum esum improbant, adeoque quicquid ex carne vel carnis opus esse videtur.
units.tr: 8 They condemn flesh as wholly polluted creatures, and disapprove of eating it, and so whatever seems to be flesh or to come from flesh.

units.la: 9 Coniugia propterea damnant, & quos possunt ad diuortia cum proprijs vxoribus facienda inducunt. quanquam ex ijs quidam cum virginibus connubia contracta probant & concedunt, vt scribit Bernard. Clareuallenf. ferm. 66. Cantic. Hoc ut & superius dogma est & Manichaeorum, & Gnosticorum, contra illud Christi, Quos Deus coiunxit, homo non separet, Matth. 19. v. 6. Papistae tamen praetextu religionis profitendae, & ingressus Monasterij, ut loquuntur, idem pene etiam coiugibus permittut. Can. Notificasti. & Can. Qui vxorem. Vide etiam Augustinum epist. 199. Prophetas Dei tanquam abreptitios, & fanaticos homines non tantum reiiciunt, sed etiam vt ignaros Dei voluntatis accusant, & condemnant. Quod est Gnosticorum, contra illud Act. 20. v. 27. Atque hae sunt tot & tam noxiae vnius haereticorum sectae, sententiae, & pestes, quas illi a Satana afflati, in orbem terrarum euomuerunt.
units.tr: 9 For this reason they condemn marriage, and they induce those whom they can to divorce their own wives. Yet some of them approve and allow marriages contracted with virgins, as Bernard of Clairvaux writes in sermon 66 on the Song of Songs. This is both the doctrine mentioned above and that of the Manichaeans and Gnostics, against the saying of Christ, "What God has joined together, let not man put asunder," Matthew 19:6. The Papists, however, under the pretext of professing religion and of entering a monastery, as they put it, permit almost the same thing to married persons: canon "Notificasti" and canon "Qui uxorem." See also Augustine, letter 199. They not only reject the prophets of God as men carried off and fanatical, but also accuse and condemn them as ignorant of God's will, which is the Gnostics' view, against Acts 20:27. And these are the many and so pernicious opinions and plagues of this one sect of heretics, which, inspired by Satan, they spewed out over the whole world.

units.la: CAP. LXXI.
units.tr: CAP. LXXI.

units.la: Feri & inhumani haeretici cur sic dicti. Erroris eorum caput duplex hic enumeratum.
units.tr: Fierce and inhuman heretics, and why they are so called. The twofold head of their error is listed here.

units.la: Dicit Philaster esse alios haereticos, qui cum hominibus non sumunt{1} escas, sed verum cum aliis, qui eiusdem sectae non sunt, an etiam inter seipsos faciant, non exprimit. Dicit etiam eos de Patre & Filio recte, de Spiritu autem sancto, non catholice sapere, sed quod eum opinentur esse creaturam.
units.tr: Philaster says there are other heretics who do not take food with men, but only with those who are not of their sect. He does not say whether they also refuse to eat among themselves. He also says that they hold rightly about the Father and the Son, but about the Holy Spirit they do not think catholically; they consider him a creature.{1}

units.la: {1} Non sumunt escas.) Fuit & hic quoque agrestis viuendi mos, & ritus, Monachismi fru-ticatio, & infelix affectatae solitudinis, & no ne-cessariae fructus, per quem videntur isti contra naturam ipsam humanam pugnasse, illíque bellum indixisse, ut in reprobum sensum traditi, plane censeri debeant. Praeclare enim Aristoteles hominem ζῷον πολιτικόν. i. animal gregabile, & ad societatem natum esse definiuit, & Augustinus libro De bono coniugali, capite 1. adeo ut si omnia nobis tanquam virgula divina suppeditarentur, solitudinem tamen, ut recte & vere sentit M. Tullius Cicero libro 1. De officiis, fugeremus. Nam etiā magnitudo ipsa animi remota a communitate, coniunctioneque humana feritas quaedam & immanitas est nominanda. Sed & cognitionis studium vincit consociatio hominum, atque communitas. Quamobrem inter reliqua Dei erga genus humanum beneficia hoc quoque recensetur. Psalm.107. versu 40. quod in locis frequentibus, non in desertis & solitudine habitamus. Hi tamen pro summa laude & sanctitatis commendatione duxerunt, si more ferarum aspectus hominum, & commercia fugerent, incidentes in illam poenam, quae a Domino pro summa Nebucadnezari fuit inflicta, ut est apud Danielem 4. His autem similes sunt, qui iura naturae temerantes, & constitutum a Deo rerum ordinem peruertentes, noctem ad preces destinarunt, quae quieti concessa esse debet. sed hi etiam fuerunt Monachi. Quanquam non dubito Isidorum inter haereticos referre, qui hoc nocturnarum matutinarum institutum damnant, eosque Nyctages appellare: sed iam sui seculi naevis & superstitione infectus Isidorus id sentit. Nec vero tam ab omni humanitatis sensu alienę viuendi rationes quoquam instituì, vel institutæ probari potuissent, nisi iam sanctitatem vitæ ex suis operibus, meritis, & ritibus humano ingenio excogitatis homines metirentur, contra manifestam Pauli sententiam, Coloss.2. Neque etiam solitariis, & lucifugis hominibus Monachis, qui sunt natura [illegible, ~8 letters], huiusmodi opinionum portenta obrepere potuisse mirum videtur, quum absurdiora quædam & immaniora iis in mentem venire legamus apud Euagrium libro 1. capite 21. quæ tamen omnia Monachismi nomine & velo recepta & commendata sunt. Ait igitur ille, Rursus alii diversa ratione viventes, ipsi se solos domiciliis includunt, quæ tantum habent latitudinis, tantumq; altitudinis, ut neque corpora sua erigere, neque liberè iacere queant. Alii cum bestiis agentes, latebris quibusdam incognitis abditi, precationes ad Deü faciunt. Quin est aliud quoddam genus conversationis, viri & mulieres, ardenti solitudini sei-psos committentes ac sola naturæ pudenda contegentes, cætera nudi, terram depascuntur (un-de & armenta vocantur, Græce [illegible, ~7 letters], &c, ut ait Nicephorus libro 14. cap.58. [illegible, ~8 letters]) ita ut sui-bus & bestiis similes reddantur, aspectusque ipsorum, & mens quoque ab humana forma & mente dissideat, & homines visos fugiant. Sed & quidam Circulatores se vocant, quod omni pudore abiecto inter homines ad risum aliis movendum nudi versantur, ut idem Euagrius scribit. tot nimirum fuerunt monstrorum genera, quæ Monachismus tantopere tamen laudatus peperit. Istis vero longè festiviores alii
units.tr: {1} Do not take food.) This too was a rustic manner and rule of living, the bramble-growth of monasticism and the unhappy fruit of affected solitude and unnecessary abstinence. By it these men seem to have fought against human nature itself and declared war upon it, so that they must plainly be considered as given over to a reprobate mind. For Aristotle admirably defined man as a zōon politikon, that is, a gregarious animal born for society. Augustine, in the book On the Good of Marriage, chapter 1, says that even if everything were supplied to us as if by a divine wand, we would still flee solitude, as Cicero rightly and truly thinks in book 1 of On Duties. Even greatness of mind, when cut off from community and human fellowship, must be called a kind of savagery and brutality. Moreover, the desire for knowledge is won by the association and fellowship of men. Therefore among God's other benefits toward the human race this too is counted: that we dwell in populous places and not in deserts and solitude (Psalm 107:40). Yet these men, for the highest praise and commendation of holiness, thought it good to shun the sight and company of men like wild beasts, thereby falling into the punishment that the Lord inflicted on Nebuchadnezzar, as is told in Daniel 4. Similar to them are those who, violating the laws of nature and overturning the order of things established by God, assigned the night to prayers, when it ought to be given to rest. But these too were monks. Although I do not doubt that Isidore counts among the heretics those who condemn this institution of nocturnal and morning services and call them Nyctages, Isidore, already infected with the blemishes and superstition of his own age, holds this view. Nor could such ways of living, so alien to all human feeling, have been introduced by anyone, or once introduced, been approved, unless men had already measured the holiness of life by works, merits, and rites devised by human ingenuity, against the plain sentence of Paul (Colossians 2). Nor does it seem strange that such monstrous opinions crept in upon solitary, light-shunning monks, who are by nature [illegible], since we read of even more absurd and monstrous things coming into their minds in Evagrius, book 1, chapter 21. Yet all of these were received and commended under the name and veil of monasticism. He says: "Again, others living in a different way shut themselves alone in dwellings which have so much breadth and height that they can neither stand upright nor lie down freely. Others, living with the beasts and hidden in certain unknown lairs, make their prayers to God. Indeed there is another kind of life: men and women, committing themselves to a burning solitude and covering only their private parts, otherwise naked, graze on the earth (whence they are also called 'herds', in Greek [illegible], etc., as Nicephorus says in book 14, chapter 58), so that they become like swine and beasts, and their appearance and mind also differ from human form and reason, and they flee from the sight of men." But some also call themselves Circulators, because, with all shame cast aside, they go about naked among men to make others laugh, as the same Evagrius writes. So many were the kinds of monsters that monasticism, so greatly praised, brought forth.

units.la: Greek words aster "Græce" and in the Nicephorus citation are only partly legible on the scan; marked as illegible. The Greek in the "natura" phrase is also not clear enough to read. Monachi,& ipsi quoque inter hæreticos recen- siti à Ioanne Damasceno,& Heicetæ dicti, qui cum Monacharum mulierum cœtu in mona- sterijs saltant,& tripudiant, & id putant Chri- stianum,neque lasciuum,quos Damascenus da- mnat.Hi vero nostri feri & agrestes homines, inter hæreticos recensentur ab antiquis Chri- stianis,& merito, licet eos Eremitarum natio sequatur adhuc hodie, qui Eremitæ à Papistis non damnantur. Vocantur autem à nobis isti, feri,& inhumani, siue agrestes:ab alijs vero vi- dentur Girouagi nominari,quorum vitæ & in- stituto plane repugnat vita Christi, qui cum hominibus,vt cæteri, comedit, & versatus est, Matth.ii.versu 19.& illud quod est in Ecclesia- stico, Væ homini soli. Huius hæreseos meminit Isidorus, apud quem medum est.Sic enim apud eum, Aliæ(hæreses)cum hominibus manducat. Legendum tamen ex hoc Augustini loco, non manducant. Videtur extitisse temporibus Theo- dosij iunioris,post Christum passum,anno 420. in Syria & Palæstina præsertim,vbi tetriora quæ in ipsis Ægypti solitudinibus & defertis Mona- chorum portenta vixerunt,vt ille Euagrij locus docet. Horum duplex fuit dogma. 1 Homi- num commercium & consortium ad vitæ æter- næ facilem assequutionem esse fugiendum. 2 Spiritum sanctum esse creaturam. Ita qui homi- num societatem refugerunt, fuerunt in Deum ip- sum blasphemi.
units.tr: Far more festive than these were other monks, also counted among the heretics by John of Damascus, called Heicetae, who dance and leap in the monasteries together with companies of nuns and think this is Christian and not wanton. Damascene condemns them. But these fierce and rustic men of ours are counted among the heretics by the ancient Christians, and rightly so, although the race of Hermits still follows them today, and the Hermits are not condemned by the Papists. We call these men fierce, inhuman, or rustic, but others seem to call them Girovagi (wanderers). Their life and institute plainly contradict the life of Christ, who ate and dwelt with men as others do (Matth. 11:19), and that saying in Ecclesiasticus, "Woe to the man who is alone." Isidore mentions this heresy, and in him it reads thus: "Other heresies eat with men." But it should be read, from this passage of Augustine, "do not eat." It seems to have arisen in the times of Theodosius the Younger, after the passion of Christ, in the year 420, especially in Syria and Palestine, where the more hideous monstrosities that lived in the very deserts and solitudes of Egypt among the monks flourished, as that passage of Evagrius shows. Its doctrine was twofold: (1) that the company and fellowship of men must be avoided if eternal life is to be easily attained; (2) that the Holy Spirit is a creature. Thus those who shrank from the fellowship of men were blasphemers against God himself.

units.la: CAP. LXXII. Rhetoriani cur sic dicti. Error eorum quis fuerit.
units.tr: Chapter 72. Why the Rhetorians are so called. What their error was.

units.la: Rhetorio' quodam exortam hæresin dicit nimium mirabilis vanitatis, qua omnes hæreticos rectè ambulare, & vera dicere affirmat, quod ità est absurdum, ut mihi incredibile videatur.
units.tr: Someone called Rhetorius says that a heresy of extraordinary folly arose, according to which all heretics walk rightly and speak the truth. This is so absurd that I find it hard to believe.

units.la: Quis fuerit hic Rhetorius, nusquam alibi inuenio explicatum. Est tamen hæc hæresis Apellitarum surculus, ut ex Euseb. lib.5. cap.13. videtur colligi posse. Atque hi ipsi ab alijs, veluti à Damasceno, Lampetiani, à Lampetio quodam dicuntur, qui liberam cuique esse debere religionis, quam velit, & quam veram putat, professionem docent, quia nihil coactum aut inuitum Deo placet. Est quidem illud Epi-phanij in Apostolicis hæreticis dictum certissimum, ἐχ ἐπαναγκὲς ἢ διδαχῆς, ἀλλ' ἐκ προαιρέσεως ἡ δικαιοσύνη[?]. quod etiam Socrates libro 3. capite 25. probat, propterea tamen non debet quodlibet humani ingenij commentum admitti, &, ut Ἰουδαῖος[?] & probus numus recipi: sed ea tantum doctrina, quæ cælestis est, & verbo Dei consentiens, audienda. Immane verò est istud, quen-que hæreticum vera dicere in eo in quo censetur hæreticus, quæ dicendi ratio etiam in ipsis verbis contradictionem, ut aiunt, implicat, sic-que ipsa tollit & refutat. Cuius erroris nullum certè potest esse fundamentum, nisi quis fortasse[?] illud Pauli afferat, Rom.14.verf.5. Quisque abundat in suo sensu. quod plane alio pertinet, neque ad hunc errorem confirmandū facit. Sed & quod hæretici, ut docet Hilarius in libro ad Constantium, iam ad suos errores defendendos autoritate scripturæ passim niti videbantur, magnum huius Rhetorianorū erroris fundamentū vel fulcimentū fuit. Jovinianus imperator perpe-rā[?] laudatur à Themistio, quòd libera esse cuiusque hæretici religione siverit[?]. Istud tamen Rhetorianorū cogitari, nedum dici non potuit, nisi propter allegorias in Scripturæ interpretatione iam inductas, homines exististimassent in scripto Dei verbo nihil certū, nihilque definitū inesse, sed velut nasum cereum à quoque, pro animi sui sensu in varias & contrarias partes & sententias torqueri posse. Hanc igitur de sacræ Scripturæ dubia & ancipiti intelligentia opinionem non modò hæreticam esse pronuntiat hoc loco Augustinus: sed etiam stupedam & [illegible, ~6 letters], quam tamen Papistæ tuentur, & in primis literis Clementis Romani pontificis, de Synodo Tridentina colligenda datis, diserte totidemque pene literis retulerunt, & descripserunt. Quo autem tempore collocanda sit hæc hæreticorum familia, ignoro, nisi post Apellitas, & post annum à Christo passo 150. Quo vero in loco, nisi in quibusdam Occidentis partibus viguerit, dici non potest, quia de ea silent omnino homines Græci, & certe est minuta hæresis, cuius ne Jsidorus quidem meminit, eam tamen amplexi sunt & retinet hodie Mahumetani, qui quenque in sua religione saluum fore docent, & credunt.
units.tr: I cannot find anywhere else an explanation of who this Rhetorius was. Still, this heresy seems to be an offshoot of the Apellites, as can be gathered from Eusebius, book 5, chapter 13. Others, such as Damascenus, call these same people Lampetians, after a certain Lampetius, who taught that everyone should be free to profess whatever religion he wishes and thinks true, since nothing forced or unwilling pleases God. Epiphanius, among the Apostolic heretics, certainly says something true: οὐκ ἐξ ἀνάγκης ἢ διδαχῆς, ἀλλ' ἐκ προαιρέσεως ἡ δικαιοσύνη, and Socrates proves the same in book 3, chapter 25. Yet for that reason we must not admit every invention of the human mind, nor accept it like a Jewish coin, or a sound one. Only the teaching that is heavenly and agrees with the Word of God should be heard. It is monstrous, however, that a heretic should speak the truth in the very thing for which he is judged a heretic. This manner of speaking, as they say, even contradicts itself in its own words, and so destroys and refutes itself. There can certainly be no foundation for this error, unless someone perhaps cites that saying of Paul, Rom. 14:5, "Let every man abound in his own sense." That clearly refers to something else and does nothing to confirm this error. But also, as Hilary teaches in his book to Constantius, the heretics were already everywhere seeking to defend their errors by the authority of Scripture, and this was the great foundation, or prop, of the error of these Rhetorians. The emperor Jovian is constantly praised by Themistius because he allowed each person freedom of heretical religion. Yet the Rhetorians could not have conceived, let alone expressed, this opinion, unless people, because of the allegories already introduced into the interpretation of Scripture, had thought that nothing certain or defined is contained in the written Word of God, but that it can be twisted by anyone, like a nose of wax, into various and contrary parts and opinions according to his own mind. Augustine therefore pronounces this opinion about the doubtful and ambiguous understanding of Holy Scripture to be not only heretical in this passage, but also foolish and [illegible, ~6 letters]. Yet the Papists defend it, and especially in the letters of Clement, Roman pontiff, given concerning the gathering of the Council of Trent, they have reported and copied it clearly, and in nearly the same words. At what time this family of heretics should be placed, I do not know, except that it was after the Apellites and after the year 150 after Christ's passion. In what place it flourished, unless in certain parts of the West, cannot be said, because the Greek writers are entirely silent about it. It is certainly a minor heresy, which not even Isidore mentions. Yet the Mahometans have embraced it and still hold it today, teaching and believing that everyone will be saved in his own religion.

units.la: CAP. LXXIII. Theopaschitæ, vel Theopasiani, quid senserint.
units.tr: The Theopaschites, or Theopasians: what they held.

units.la: Lia est hæresis, quæ dicit in Christo diuinitatem doluisse, quum figeretur caro eius in cruce.
units.tr: That heresy is the one which says that the divinity suffered in Christ when his flesh was nailed to the cross.

units.la: 1 Diuinitatem doluisse.) Minuta hæc hæresis, si author spectetur: ceterum perniciosissima, si dogma perpendatur, quæ videtur teterrimorum postea errorum occasio & causa fuisse, vt ex tribus Theodoreti dialogis apparet, Eutychianorum nempe, dum in Christo diuinam naturam passam esse contendunt: & Nestorianorum, dum vt hic error euitaretur, stulti homines duas in Christo naturas, tanquam duas personas fingunt, & separant. Anonymos est hic error apud Augustinum & Isidorū, sed nos ex Nicephoro libro 15. cap. 28. Θεοπασχίτας, id est, Deipasianos appellauimus, ad veterum imitationem, qui Sabellianos Patripasianos vulgò nominabant. Ergo naturas in Christo confuderunt, & quod humanæ proprium est, tribuerunt diuinæ, quia vna est persona, & vnum est ὑποστάσις, Dominus noster Iesus Christus. Quanquam vero sanguine suo dicitur Deus redemisse, & acquisiuisse sibi Ecclesiam, Act. 20. verf. 28. quanquam item Deus gloriæ dicitur crucifixus, 1. Corinth. 2. versu 8. passio tamen crucifixióque proprie ad humanam tantùm Christi naturam pertinet. Diuinæ vero tribuitur Dialectica tatum & verbali, vt aiunt, praedicatione, non autem Physica[?] & reali, per ἰδιωμάτων κοινωνίαν[?], & propter hypostaticam diuinae cum humana natura vnionem. Nā in Christo deitas habitat personaliter, id est, vt loquitur Paulus, σωματικῶς[?]. De qua re luculentissima est apud Patres orthodoxos disputatio, imprimis in tribus illis Theodoreti dialogis aduersus Eutychen, qui Eranistes dicitur, apud Vigilantium, & Leonem primum Romanum episcopum, in epistola ad Chalcedonense concilium. Augustinus libro 3. contra Maximin. Arianum cap.26[?].Si ergo attendas distinctionem substantiarum, Filius Dei de coelo descendit: Filius hominis crucifixus est. Si vnitatem personae, & Filius hominis descendit de coelo, & Filius Dei est crucifixus. Videtur vero ex Arianismo tanquam fonte deductus foetidus iste riuulus. Sublata enim Christi diuinitate, & imminuta, quod Arius fecit, facile postea fuit blasphemis hominibus, & Satanae ipsi, quidlibet absurdum de Christo comminisci, eius facta dictaque plurima reprehendere, & damnare, quod fecerunt hi haeretici, quos Damascenus Theocatagnostas nominauit. A dextris enim & sinistris, ex tā impuro fonte riui innumerabiles extiterunt, & scaturiuerunt, & illi quidem omnes impuri, & saepe sua origine foedliores, & sordidiores. Fuerunt autem isti Marcionitis, & Docetis plane dogmate contrarij. Nam Christum vllo modo vere passum negant: isti etiam in diuina natura laborasse, & cruciatus vere tolerasse contendunt, ita nimirum sibi ipsi non constat mendacium, & seipsum repugnantibus erroribus euertit. Quo vero tempore, quóve primùm authore cœperit, non reperit Augustinus, sed nec Philaster ipse comme morauit. Quidam à Seucritis & Armeniis hæreticis profectum hunc errorem putant. Alij ex Nicephoro à Petro Gnapheo, libro 15. cap.28. sed falluntur magna temporum ignorantia. Vixerunt enim hi omnes aliquot post Eutychen hæreticum seculis, à quo sua deliria sumpserunt illi. Eutyches autem ipse post defunctum Augustinum, qui hunc errorem iam pullulantem viderat, natus est, ut manifestissime ratio temporis istorum sententiæ repugnet. Quantum vero coniicere potui, præsertim ex tertio Theodoreti dialogo, qui dicitur Impatibilis, temporibus Apollinaris & Eusebij Emiceni fabricari & spargi cœpit, sub Constantio, Constantini Magni filio, & Iulio Romano episcopo ut docet Socrates libro 2. circa annum à Christo passo 311. Durauit autem diutissime. Sustentata enim est hæc hæresis ab Eutychianis, & ab iis pertinaciter defensa, maximè vero à Petro Gnapheo sub Zenone imperatore, & nunc quoque inter Armenios, qui se Christianos appellant, permansif[?] se fertur. Grassata vero est in Asia, & Syria Orientali præcipuè, ut quanvis initio paruus error videretur, successu temporis, atque obstinationis accessione, grauissimus postea factus est, tanti est nimirum, vel latum quidem vnguem à vera de Christi duabus naturis fide discedere, sèque tetris istis erroribus mancipare.
units.tr: 1 The divinity suffered.) This heresy is minor if one looks at its author, but very pernicious if one weighs its doctrine. It seems to have been the occasion and cause of the most hideous errors that followed, as appears from the three dialogues of Theodoret: namely, those of the Eutychians, who contend that the divine nature suffered in Christ; and those of the Nestorians, who, in order to avoid this error, foolishly imagine and separate two natures in Christ as though they were two persons. This error is anonymous in Augustine and Isidore, but from Nicephorus, book 15, chapter 28, we have named them Theopaschites [Θεοπασχίται], that is, Deipasians, in imitation of the ancients, who commonly called the Sabellians Patripassians. They therefore confused the natures in Christ, and attributed to the divine nature what is proper to the human, since there is one person and one hypostasis, our Lord Jesus Christ. Although it is said that God redeemed the Church with his own blood and acquired it for himself (Acts 20:28), and although likewise the Lord of glory is said to have been crucified (1 Corinthians 2:8), yet suffering and crucifixion pertain properly to the human nature of Christ alone. The divine nature is ascribed only a dialectical and, as they say, verbal predication, not a physical and real one, by the communication of properties [ἰδιωμάτων κοινωνία], and on account of the hypostatic union of the divine with the human nature. For in Christ the deity dwells personally, that is, as Paul puts it, bodily [σωματικῶς]. Concerning this matter there is a most lucid discussion among the orthodox Fathers, above all in those three dialogues of Theodoret against Eutyches, which is called Eranistes; in Vigilius; and in Leo the First, bishop of Rome, in his letter to the Council of Chalcedon. Augustine, book 3 against Maximinus the Arian, chapter 26. If, then, you attend to the distinction of substances, the Son of God came down from heaven, the Son of man was crucified; if to the unity of person, the Son of man came down from heaven, and the Son of God was crucified. This foul rivulet seems to have been drawn from Arianism as from its source. For once the divinity of Christ was removed and diminished, as Arius did, it was easy afterwards for blasphemous men, and Satan himself, to invent anything absurd about Christ and to find fault with and condemn many of his deeds and words, as those heretics did whom Damascene named Theocatagnostae. For on the right and on the left, from so impure a source, innumerable streams arose and gushed forth, and all of them were impure, and often more foul and filthy in their origin. These heresies were indeed wholly contrary in doctrine to those of Marcion and the Docetists. For those deny that Christ truly suffered in any way; these, on the other hand, contend that he labored in the divine nature and truly endured torments. Thus, of course, a lie is not consistent with itself, and by its contradictory errors it overthrows itself. At what time, and by whose authorship it first began, Augustine did not discover, nor did Philastrius himself mention it. Some think this error came from the heretics Severians and Armenians. Others, following Nicephorus, attribute it to Peter the Fuller (Gnapheus), book 15, chapter 28, but they are mistaken through great ignorance of the chronology. For all these men lived some centuries after the heretic Eutyches, from whom those madmen took their delusions. Eutyches himself was born after Augustine had died, who had seen this error already sprouting; so the chronology of those men's opinions manifestly contradicts it. As far as I could conjecture, especially from the third dialogue of Theodoret, which is called Impassible, this heresy began to be fabricated and spread in the time of Apollinaris and Eusebius of Emesa, under Constantius, son of Constantine the Great, and Julius, bishop of Rome, as Socrates teaches in book 2, around the year 311 after the passion of Christ. It has lasted a very long time. For this heresy was sustained by the Eutychians, and was stubbornly defended by them, above all by Peter the Fuller under the emperor Zeno; and it is said to remain even now among the Armenians, who call themselves Christians. It raged especially in Asia and Eastern Syria, so that although at first it seemed a small error, with the passage of time and the addition of obstinacy it later became very grave indeed. So much does it matter that one should depart even a little from the true faith concerning the two natures of Christ, and surrender oneself to those foul errors.

units.la: CAP. LXXIIII. Triformii & Tritheitæ quid senserint.
units.tr: CAP. LXXIIII. What the Triformites and Tritheites held.

units.la: ST[?] alia, quæ triformem sic asserit Deum vt quadam pars eius sit Pater, quaedam Filius, quaedam Spiritus sanctus, hoc est quod Dei vnius partes sint, quæ istam faciunt Trinitatem, velut ex iis tribus partibus compleatur Deus, nec fit perfectus in seipso vel Pater vel Filius vel Spiritus sanctus.
units.tr: Some others assert a triform God, so that one part of him is the Father, another the Son, and another the Holy Spirit. That is, the parts of the one God are what make up this Trinity, as if God were completed out of those three parts, and neither the Father nor the Son nor the Holy Spirit is perfect in himself.

units.la: 1 Triformem sic asserit. ) Innominata est hæc hæresis, à nobis tamen commodioris disputationis gratia Triformij vel Triformiani nominentur, qui quauis cum Tritheis, & Tetratheis hæreticis, de quibus Nicephorus lib. 8. cap.49. & 50. conuenire videantur, habent tamen aliquid ab vtrisque diuersum. Ac à Tritheis quidem, quòd hi nostri sunt priores, Trithei verò posteriores, quorū autor fuisse scribitur Ioannes Grammaticus cognomento Philoponus patria Alexandrinus & Ægyptius, qui sub Phoca Imperatore, & Bonifacio tertio Romano Pontifice, vixit circa annum à Christo passo 574. Triformiani verò vel cum Metangismonitis, vel paulò post circa annum à Christo passo 370. cum de Dei essentia & trium in ea personarum distinctione propter Sabellianos, Anthropomorphitas, & postea natos Arianos variè disputari & sentiri coepisset, & in eo argumento errarent multi in Ecclesia. Vt enim Sa-bellianorum bellianorum errorem vitarent homines, hunc nouum nec minus periculosum temerarij excuderunt, quia ex suo sensu potius quàm ex ipsissimo Dei verbo sapere voluerunt, & dum vitant stulti vitia, in contraria currunt. Præterea Tritheitæ Dei naturam & essentiam triplicem faciunt, non autem vnam & eandem, vt docet Isidorus: & personas non tantùm reipsa inter se distinguunt, sed loco & situ separant & diuellunt, quemadmodum tres homines inter se totis subiectis & locis differunt, veluti Paulus, Petrus, Ioannes.
units.tr: 1 They assert a triform God.) This heresy has no name, but for the sake of a more convenient discussion let us call its adherents Triformites or Triformians. Although they seem to agree with the Tritheite and Tetratheite heretics, of whom Nicephorus writes in book 8, chapters 49 and 50, they hold something different from both. They differ from the Tritheites, who are our earlier group, while the Tritheites came later; their author is said to have been John the Grammarian, surnamed Philoponus, a native of Alexandria in Egypt, who lived under the emperor Phocas and Boniface III, bishop of Rome, about the year 574 after Christ's passion. The Triformites, or those who came with the Metangismonites or a little after them, arose about the year 370 after Christ's passion, when the distinction of the divine essence and of the three persons within it began to be disputed and understood in various ways, on account of the Sabellians, the Anthropomorphites and the Arians who had arisen later, and many in the Church went astray on this question. For in order to avoid the error of the Sabellians, men devised this new and no less dangerous novelty, rashly, since they preferred to be wise according to their own sense rather than according to the very word of God; and while foolish men avoid one vice, they run into its opposite. Moreover, the Tritheites make the nature and essence of God threefold, not one and the same, as Isidore teaches; and they separate and divide the persons not only in reality from one another but also in place and position, just as three men differ from one another in their whole substance and places, for example Paul, Peter and John.

units.la: Sunt enim Tritheitæ, qui tres deos constituunt seorsim & reapse separatos à sese, non autem in vna & eadem diuina essentia tres hypostases diuersas & distinctas credunt.
units.tr: For there are Tritheites who set up three gods, separate from one another in reality, and do not believe that there are three distinct hypostases in one and the same divine essence.

units.la: Triformiani verò diuinam naturam vnam quidem & eandem in tribus personis constituunt, sed non totam. Cogitant enim diuinam essentiâ velut quiddam compositum vel aggregatum, quæ in tribus illis hypostasibus coalescentibus vel coniunctis inter se tota & perfecta fit: in singulis verò personis fit imperfecta. Itaque faciunt Trinitatem velut monstrum quoddam & corpus quod tribus diuersis formis tanquam capitibus constet, qualem suum Geryona finxerunt profani poetæ. Quo deliramento quid in tanta & tam sancta re, qualis est Sacrosancta Trinitas, fœdius & absurdius vel dici, vel etiam cogitari potest? Tetratheitæ etiâ à Triformianis differunt, & tempore & dogmate. Nam Tetratheitæ ante Anastasium primum Imperatorem extitêre, quando traditum legimus eum edicto suo proposuisse, vt, ex iam inter multos recepta sententia, Quaternitas pro Trinitate ado-raretur, circa annum a Christo passo 485. propter quod impium edictum a Deo ictus fulmine misere periit, Hormisda sedem Romaní moderante. Itaque nostris Triformianis ætate sunt recentiores isti, quorum tamen mansit viguitque sententia etiam sub Phoca Imperatore, sub quo Theodosiani, Damianistae, & Angelitae vocati sunt, quemadmodum Nicephor. tradit, lib. 18. cap. 49. ex eadem quidem occasione, ex qua superiores orti, nimirum, ut Sabellianorum errori obviam iretur, sed malo nodo peior cuneus quęsitus est ab imperitis hominibus & iam multis hæreseon sordibus inquinatis & imbutis. Ad verbum autem Dei non recurrebant. Dogma vero Tetratheitarum hoc fuit, præter tres illas diuinas hypostases & personas existere quartam quandam essentiam, quæ trium communis esset, & se tribus illis communicaret, propter quam communicationem dii fierent. Atqui nec tres illæ personæ aliud sunt, quam ipsa diuina natura: nec illa aliud est nec alibi, nec alio modo subsistit, quam in tribus illis personis, tota in omnibus, tota in singulis, cuius non participatione tantum aliqua, sed tota possessione, quæque persona Deus est, Pater, Filius & Spiritus sanctus tres personæ, sed unus & idem Deus. Triformiani vero quatuor essentias, ut Tetratheitę,non constituunt. Quare ab iis dogmate diffe-runt. Huius hæreseos meminit Isidorus, quam sicut & superiores ut euitaret S.Bernardi seculo Gilbertus Porretanus docuit, sed salsissime, diuinas personas non realitate quadam, sed tan-
units.tr: The Triformites, however, set up one and the same divine nature in three persons, but not the whole of it in each. For they think of the divine essence as something composite or aggregated, which becomes whole and perfect when those three hypostases coalesce or are joined together, but in each single person it is imperfect. Thus they make the Trinity like a sort of monster, a body that consists of three different forms as if of heads, like the Geryon that the profane poets invented. What could be said or even thought in such a great and holy matter, as the most sacred Trinity is, that is more foul and absurd than this delirium? The Tetratheites also differ from the Triformites both in time and in doctrine. For the Tetratheites arose before the emperor Anastasius the First, when we read that he, by his edict, proposed that, since the opinion was already widely accepted, a Quaternity should be worshipped instead of the Trinity, about the year 485 after Christ's passion; on account of this impious edict he was struck by a thunderbolt from God and perished miserably, while Hormisdas governed the see of Rome. Therefore these men are more recent in age than our Triformites, whose opinion nevertheless persisted and flourished even under the emperor Phocas, under whom they were called Theodosians, Damianists and Angelites, as Nicephorus relates in book 18, chapter 49. They arose from the same occasion as the earlier ones, namely to oppose the error of the Sabellians, but, as the saying goes, a wedge worse than the knot was sought out by unskilled men who were already soiled and steeped in many filthy heresies. Yet they did not have recourse to the word of God. The doctrine of the Tetratheites was this: besides those three divine hypostases and persons there exists a certain fourth essence, which is common to the three and communicates itself to those three, and by that communication they become gods. But those three persons are nothing other than the divine nature itself, nor does that nature exist as anything else, or elsewhere, or in another way, than in those three persons, whole in all, whole in each; and each person is God by a possession not merely partial but whole. Father, Son and Holy Spirit are three persons, but one and the same God. The Triformites, however, do not set up four essences as the Tetratheites do, and so they differ from them in doctrine. Isidore mentions this heresy, which Gilbert of Poitiers also taught, as Bernard's age did (as did the earlier ones, to avoid it), though very foolishly, saying that the divine persons are not in some reality but merely...

units.la: CAP. LXXV. Aquei quid senserint.
units.tr: CAP. LXXV. What the Aqueans held.

units.la: [?]Lia est, quæ dicit aquam{1} non à Deo creatam, sed ei semper fuisse coæternam.
units.tr: It is a heresy which says that water was not created by God, but has always been coeternal with him.

units.la: I Aquam non à Deo.) Hæc superiorum hæresèon particula est, partim ex Materiarijs sive Hermogenianis, partim ex Audianis decerpta. Illi enim materiam mundi huius Deo coæternam constituebant: hi vero tria mundi huius principia faciebant, ex quibus unum esset aqua. Nostri igitur hoc postremum Audianorum dictum temerè sunt amplexi, quia de Aquæ creatione non videtur meminisse Moses Genef.1. sed tantum de illius congregatione in unum locum, & aquarum cœlestium sive superiorum ab inferioribus separatione. Sed facilis solutio est. Cum enim dicitur Deus creasse cœlum & terram, & in huius creatæ terræ globo & corpore aqua illi superfusa continetur, necesse est aquam quoque à Deo creatam confiteri, & intelligere. Isti tamen propter varias a-quæ laudes tum à profanis hominibus, tum à su-perioribus hæreticis, quales Seueriani, Encratitæ, Aquarij decantatas, aquæ elementum increatum esse & Deo coæternum impiissimè sen-serunt, atque docuerunt. Itaque à nobis Aquei dicti sunt, ut ab Aquariis, de quibus antea, discernerentur. Laudauit aquam Pindarus in Pythiis, [ὕδωρ μὲν ἄριστον?] dixit. Thales Milesius philosophus Pindaro vetustior eam rerum omnium primum principium esse voluit, ut omnes scribunt, imprimis autem Diogenes Laertius, & Clemens Alexandr. Sromat. lib. i. à quo procul-dubio hæ fæces sunt desumptæ, & in scholas Christianorum translatæ. Plures enim deos inuehunt, Deum scilicet & aquam, dum utrumque faciunt æternum, quæ tamen sunt dissimi-lis naturæ, non eiusdem. Hæc sententia plane profana est. Nec diu perstitit hæc hæresis, nec certum authorem habet, nec nomen, quanquam eius obiter meminit Isidorus. Quo vero tempore cœperit incertum est, nisi ad Aquario-rum tempora referamus, circa annum à Chri-sto passo 145. Vbi grassata sit, à quibus defensa & propagata, non explicatur, & statim interci-disse verisimile est, cum pauci illius meminerint, & facile tam inepta deliria verbo Dei de-iiciuntur ex meris Philosophorum nugis ficta & traducta.
units.tr: Water not from God. This is a part of the earlier heresies, drawn partly from the Materiarians or Hermogenians and partly from the Audians. The former held that the matter of this world was coeternal with God, while the latter made three principles of this world, one of which was water. Our people therefore rashly embraced this last opinion of the Audians, because Moses does not seem to mention the creation of water in Genesis 1, but only its gathering into one place and the separation of the heavenly or upper waters from the lower. The solution is easy, however. When it is said that God created heaven and earth, and water is contained over the globe and body of the created earth, we must confess and understand that water too was created by God. Yet these men, moved by the various praises of water sung both by profane people and by earlier heretics such as the Severians, Encratites and Aquarians, most impiously held and taught that the element of water is uncreated and coeternal with God. For this reason they were called Aqueans by us, to distinguish them from the Aquarians mentioned above. Pindar praised water in his Pythian odes, saying [ὕδωρ μὲν ἄριστον] "water is best." Thales of Miletus, a philosopher older than Pindar, held that it was the first principle of all things, as all writers relate, above all Diogenes Laertius and Clement of Alexandria in the first book of the Stromata; and from these dregs, without doubt, this error was taken over and transferred into the schools of the Christians. For they introduce several gods, namely God and water, while they make both eternal, though they are of unlike nature and not of the same. This opinion is plainly profane. Nor did this heresy last long; it has no certain author and no name, although Isidore mentions it in passing. The time when it began is uncertain, unless we refer it to the times of the Aquarians, about the year 145 after the passion of Christ. Where it spread, by whom it was defended and propagated, is not explained, and it is likely that it soon died out, since few have mentioned it; and such absurd fancies, invented and drawn from the mere trifles of the philosophers, are easily cast down by the Word of God.

units.la: CAP. LXXVI. Melitonij quid senserint.
units.tr: CHAPTER LXXVI. What Melito's followers held.

units.la: Lia dicit corpus hominis, no animam esse imaginem Dei.
units.tr: Another says that the body of man, not the soul, is the image of God.

units.la: I Alia dicit. ) Hanc non nominat hïc Augustin.in indice tamen huic operi præfixo siue ex glossematc, siue ex veteri codice Melitonij appellantur, quam nos appellationem retinuimus. Quis tamen fuerit hic Melito, nondum legisse me memini. Nec enim is est, de quo Euseb. libr. 4. cap. 21. & Nicephor. libr. 4. cap. 10, qui & Sardicensis Episcopus & orthodoxus fuit Antonini Pij temporibus. Hæc enim hæresis omnino recentior videtur fuisse, & Anthropomorphitarum siue Audæorum surculus quidam, vt indicat Theodoret.in Epitom.diuinor. decretor.cap. De homine, qui cum Deum corporeum fingerent, imaginem Dei in homine non in anima, quæ spiritualis est: sed in corporę, quod lineamentis, membris, & dimensionibus aspectabilibus constat, collocabant. In quo ex cœlesti & spirituali fit terrena, mortalis, & corporea diuina natura, non sine insigni in Deū ipsum blasphemia. Itaq; repudianda est tam pra ua & aliena à veritate Scripturæ interpretatio, quæ fit de cap. 1. Genef. vers. 27. Veterem tamen fuisse de ea re quæstionem & inter Patres vexatam apparet ex Irenæi libro 5. cap. 1. Augustin. libr. 3. de Genef. ad liter. cap. 19. & aliis authoribus, veluti Ambrosio, Chrysostomo & Basilio in Exameris, sed tamen in hominis anima, non in corpore semper ab iis posita est imago Dei in homine. Quid sit autem illa, & qualis, explicat Paulus Coloss. 4. verf. 10. Ephes. 4. verf. 24. nec melior interpres quærendus erat. Ergo ad Anthropomorphitas istos refero, & ad eorum tempora. Huius hæresis meminit Isidor. lib. 8. etymologiar.
units.tr: Another says: this is not named here by Augustine, but in the index prefixed to this work, whether by a gloss or from an old manuscript of Melito, it is called so, and we have retained that name. Yet I do not recall having read who this Melito was. For he is not the one of whom Eusebius (book 4, chapter 21) and Nicephorus (book 4, chapter 10) speak, who was bishop of Sardis and orthodox in the times of Antoninus Pius. This heresy seems to have been altogether more recent, and to be a certain offshoot of the Anthropomorphites or Audaeans, as Theodoret indicates in the Epitome of Divine Decrees, chapter "On Man": since they imagined God to be corporeal, they located the image of God in man not in the soul, which is spiritual, but in the body, which consists of lineaments, members and visible dimensions. In this, the heavenly and spiritual divine nature becomes earthly, mortal and corporeal, not without a notable blasphemy against God himself. Therefore that interpretation of Genesis 1:27, so perverse and alien to the truth of Scripture, must be rejected. Yet that this was an old question, and one disputed among the Fathers, appears from Irenaeus, book 5, chapter 1; Augustine, On the Literal Meaning of Genesis, book 3, chapter 19; and other authors, such as Ambrose, Chrysostom and Basil in the Hexaemeron; but the Fathers always placed the image of God in man in the soul of man, not in the body. What that image is, and of what kind, Paul explains in Colossians 3:10 and Ephesians 4:24, and no better interpreter was to be sought. Therefore I refer this to those Anthropomorphites and to their times. Isidore mentions this heresy in book 8 of the Etymologies.

units.la: CAP. LXXVII. Opheorum error quis fuerit.
units.tr: CAP. LXXVII. What the error of the Ophei was.

units.la: Alia dicit innumerabiles mundos, sicut opinati sunt quidam philosophi gentium.
units.tr: They say there are innumerable worlds, as some philosophers of the Gentiles have thought.

units.la: I Innumerabiles mundos.)In indice præposito huic operi vocantur Ophei qui hoc delirium amplexi sunt, siue quòd ab Ophitis hæreticis orti sunt, siue quòd Opheus quidam eorū author fuerit, quos tamen à Valentinianis & Basilidianis potius ortos esse iudico, qui 365. cœlos constituunt. Quid enim facilius fuit, quàm post cœlorum globos inductos facere mundos innumerabiles? Quod autea[?] ab ethnicis philosophis traditum erat, quemadmodum à Democrito Abderita, & Epicuro Atheniensi. Id quod in eorum vita refert Diogenes Laertius, libr. 9. & 10. Lactant. De ira Dei. cap. 10. Origenes quidem libr. 3. περὶ ἀρχῶν[?], cap. 5. opinatur præter hunc visibilem & conspicuum mundum, alium quoque que esse, qui etiam ante hunc cōditus sit à Deo. Quæ sententia huic, quem nunc exponimus, errori, magnum firmamentum videtur attulisse, & tamen falsa est. In principio enim creauit Deus cœlum & terram, nec antea vllus mundus erat vel visibilis vel inuisibilis. Nec tunc Deus mundos plures condidit, sed hunc tantum conspicuum, quem incolimus, cuiúsque nobis Genef.cap.1. origo explicatur. Et rectè Patres argumentantur vnum esse mundum, quia vnus est Deus. Est enim opus Dei mundus. Neque verò prætermissura erat Scriptura, si plures essent mundi, ne alium præter vnum & verum Deum, eorum conditorem existimaremus: aut ne Deũ ipsum tanti opificij laude priuaremus. De quo in prima Physicæ nostræ Christianæ parte, quæ tamen nondum edita est, abūdè diximus. Quod autem ad hanc hæresin attinet, neque illius originem, neque durationem, neque sedem vsquam legimus. Huius tamen breuissimè quidem meminit Isidorus, & fuit minuta hæresis, quę magnos authores aut patronos diuturnámque ætatem habuisse minimè mihi videtur, eám que ad Basilidianos refero.
units.tr: I Innumerable worlds.) In the index prefixed to this work the Ophei are named, those who embraced this madness, whether because they arose from the heretical Ophites, or because a certain Opheus was their author; yet I judge they arose rather from the Valentinians and Basilidians, who posit 365 heavens. For what was easier than, after introducing the globes of the heavens, to make innumerable worlds? This had been handed down by the pagan philosophers, as by Democritus of Abdera and Epicurus of Athens. Diogenes Laertius reports this in their lives, books 9 and 10. Lactantius, On the Anger of God, chapter 10. Origen, in book 3 of On First Principles, chapter 5, thinks that besides this visible and conspicuous world there is another also, created by God before this one. This opinion seems to have given great support to the error we are now expounding, and yet it is false. For in the beginning God created heaven and earth, and before that there was no world, either visible or invisible. Nor did God then make several worlds, but only this visible one which we inhabit, whose origin is explained in Genesis chapter 1. And the Fathers rightly argue that there is one world, because there is one God. For the world is the work of God. Nor would Scripture have passed over in silence if there were several worlds, lest we should think there was another maker of them besides the one true God, or lest we should deprive God himself of the praise of so great a work. On this I have spoken fully in the first part of our Christian Physics, which has not yet been published. As for this heresy, we read nowhere of its origin, its duration or its seat. Isidore mentions it very briefly, and it was a minor heresy, which I do not think had great authors or patrons or a long life; and I refer it to the Basilidians.

units.la: CAP. LXXVIII. Tertullii & eorum error quis fuerit.
units.tr: CHAP. LXXVIII. Who the Tertullians were and what their error was.

units.la: Lia[?] sceleratorum animas{1} conuerti in dæmonas dicit, & in qnaque animalia suis meritis congrua.
units.tr: They say that the souls of the wicked are changed into demons, and into animals fitting to their deserts.

units.la: Neque hic, neque apud Ifidorum nominatur hæc hæresis, tamen in indice huic operi præfixo vocantur hi Tertullij, quam nos appellationem retinuimus. Tamen quis fuerit hic Tertullus,neque quado primum coeperit, vbi recepta vel propagata sit,quandiu perstiterit hæc hæreticorum secta non reperio apud probatos vllos authores,quibus à me fides habeatur, aut quorum authoritatem aliis ipse commendare vel possim, vel audeam. Dogma igitur istorum hoc fuit, Sceleratorum hominū animas conuerti in dæmonas ipsos siue diabolos:vel in animantia iis vitiis & ei turpitudini similia, cui ipsi viuentes addicti fuerint. Atque hanc sententiam & μετεμψύχωσιν potius, quàm μετενσωμάτωσιν ex Pythagoreorum primùm, post autem Manichæorum & Priscillianistarum (qui Pythagoreorum errores secuti sunt) deliriis sumptam esse docet cùm Diogenes Laert.in vita Pythagoræ,tum Augustin. ipse libro septimo de Genesi ad liter.cap.9.& 11. Quam Claudian. poeta pulcherrimè libr.2.in Ruffin.his versibus expressit,
units.tr: Neither here nor in Isidore is this heresy named. Yet in the index prefixed to this work these people are called the Tertullians, and I have kept that name. But who this Tertullus was, when he first began, where the sect was received or spread, and how long it lasted, I cannot find in any approved authors whose testimony I can vouch for or recommend to others.
