The doctrine of these people was this: the souls of wicked men are turned into demons or devils themselves, or into animals similar to the vices and baseness to which they were given over while alive. He teaches that this opinion was taken from the delusions of the Pythagoreans first, and afterwards of the Manichaeans and Priscillianists, who followed the errors of the Pythagoreans, and that it is transmigration of souls [μετεμψύχωσιν] rather than transmigration into bodies [μετενσωμάτωσιν]. Diogenes Laertius in the life of Pythagoras says so, and Augustine himself in the seventh book of his work On the Literal Meaning of Genesis, chapters 9 and 11. The poet Claudian expressed it very finely in the second book Against Rufinus, in these verses:

units.la: Nam iuxtà Rhadamantus agit, cùm gesta su-perni Curriculi,totósque diu prospexerit actus, Exæquat damnum meritis,& multa ferarum Cogit vincla pati:truculentos ingerit vrsis: Prædonésque lupis:fallaces vulpibus addit. At qui desidia semper,vinóque grauatus Indulgens Veneri voluit torpescere luxu, Hūc suis immūdæ pingues detrudit in artus. Qui iusto plus esse loquax arcanáque suit[?] Prodere, piscosas fertur victurus in undas, Ut nimiam pensent aeterna silentia vocem.
units.tr: For Rhadamanthus, when he has surveyed the deeds of the upper course and long examined every act, matches the punishment to the merits, and forces the wild beasts' chains upon many: he sets the savage ones among bears, makes robbers into wolves, and deceivers into foxes. But the man who was always weighed down by idleness and wine, and who wished to grow numb indulging in Venus' luxury, he thrusts into the filthy bodies of pigs. And the one who talked more than was right and betrayed secrets is said to be going to live in the fishy waves, so that eternal silence may make up for his excessive voice.

units.la: Nec tamen mirum est ista ab haereticis recipi & recoqui ex impiis philosophorum insomniis, cùm Eusteb. lib.5. de vita Constantini figmenta Platonis, de animabus hominum post mortem circa Stygem fluuium oberrantibus laudet & admittat. Denique hoc Tertulliorum delirium confirmauit fabula potiùs, quàm historia iacta-ta tunc, & à Nicephoro libro 8. cap.35. narrata, nempe à Georgio quodam Episcopo conver-sos in humanam formam porcos, qui antea ex hominibus porci metamorphosi quadam facti erant. Certè ἀπωτωτίτη[?] merito iudicanda est haec sententia, quae praeter omnium Physicorum philosophorum regulas, formas εἰδωλικῆς[?] & essentias rerum confundi posse censet. Quid enim aliud docet, cùm humanas animas in diabolos vel pecudes mutari contendit, quàm hominem, diabolum, & pecudem non esse diversas rerum species & genera: aut si esse confitetur, ea tamen non sua propriaque forma & essentiali consta-re, propter quam inter se tota natura distin-guantur, & tale quidda sint, quae forma illis adi-mi non possit? Sed tanti est nimirum in philo-sophicis nugamentis immorari, & praeter Dei verbum sapere. Nos igitur istos ad Manichaeos blasphemos homines reuocamus, & ad Priscil-lianistarum aetatem & tempora reducimus.
units.tr: Yet it is no wonder that heretics receive these things and warm them up again from the impious dreams of the philosophers, since Eusebius in the fifth book of the Life of Constantine praises and accepts Plato's fictions about the souls of men wandering after death around the river Styx. Finally, this delirium of the Tertullians was confirmed by a fable rather than a history, a story told at that time and recounted by Nicephorus in book 8, chapter 35: that certain pigs, which had earlier been turned from men into pigs by some metamorphosis, were converted back into human form by a certain bishop George. Certainly this opinion deserves to be judged utterly absurd [ἀπωτωτίτη], since, against all the rules of the natural philosophers, it holds that forms [εἰδωλικῆς] and essences of things can be confused. For what else does it teach, when it contends that human souls are changed into devils or beasts, than that man, devil and beast are not different kinds and genera of things? Or, if it admits that they are different, it nevertheless holds that they do not consist of their own proper and essential form, by which entire natures are distinguished from one another, and that they are such things that the form cannot be taken from them? But it is surely a waste of time to dwell on these philosophical trifles and to be wise beyond the word of God. We therefore refer these men back to the blasphemous Manichaeans, and trace them to the age and times of the Priscillianists.

units.la: CAP. LXXIX. Liberatorum error quis fuerit.
units.tr: CHAPTER 79. What the error of the Liberationists was.

units.la: Alia, descendente ad inferos{1} Christo, credidisse incredulos, & omnes inde existimant liberatos.
units.tr: Another holds that, when Christ descended into hell, the unbelievers believed, and they all suppose that they were set free from there.

units.la: I )Nos Liberatores appellauimus, qui nomine carebant. Videntur autem isti primum à Marcionitis, post autem ab Origenistis & Chiliastis profecti, qui damnatos homines, imò vero diabolos ipsos aliquando saluos futuros, nempe post millesimum à die resurrectionis annum contendebant. Isti vero nostri iam salutem consecutos esse quosdam incredulos docent, eos nimirum, qui tempore descensionis Christi in inferis erant & detinebantur. Christum enim apud eos, cum ad inferos venisset, concionatum esse volunt, eosque credidisse, atque ita è grauissimis inferni poenis ereptos ad coelum cum Christo euolasse, & traductos fuisse. Alterius, autem & huic plane contrariae haereseos meminit Isidorus his verbis, Aliae liberationem hominum apud inferos factam Christi descensione non credunt. Huius autem erroris duplex occasio statui posse videtur. Ac prima quidem, locus Petri in priore epistola cap.3.verf.19. perperam & conuersus, & à Patribus intellectus. Sic autem habet, Nam & Christus semel pro peccatis passus fuit iustus pro iniustis, vt nos ad Deum adduceret, mortificatus quidem carne, viuificatus autem spiritu, per quem spiritibus, qui erant in carcere, pro-sectus prædicauit. Ex quo loco Christum ad in-feros. i. locum damnatis destinatum, postmor-tem descendisse veteres crediderunt, & scripse-runt. In quo ab iis tamen peccatum est gravis-simè. Secunda huius erroris occasio fuit, quòd iam ex communi omnium sententia receptum erat, Christum idcirco ad inferos venisse, vt fideles & dignos, qui viui constanter in fide perseverassent, in vitam æternam, & in ipsum adeò paradisum tanquā author & princeps vitæ traduceret. Eo enim ipso die, quo descedcrat [?], cum iis ereptis Christum exiisse ex inferis credebat.
units.tr: We have called them Liberationists, since they lack a proper name. These men seem to have proceeded first from the Marcionites, and afterwards from the Origenists and Chiliasts, who maintained that condemned men, and indeed the devils themselves, would at some time be saved, namely after a thousand years from the day of the resurrection. But these, our men, teach that certain unbelievers have already obtained salvation, namely those who were in hell and held there at the time of Christ's descent. For they hold that Christ, when he came to the dead, preached there, and that they believed, and so were snatched from the most grievous punishments of hell and flew up to heaven with Christ and were carried across. Isidore mentions another heresy, quite contrary to this one, in these words: "Others do not believe that the liberation of men was accomplished among the dead by the descent of Christ." Now the double occasion of this error seems to be such as can be identified. The first is the passage of Peter in his first epistle, chapter 3, verse 19, which was wrongly turned and understood by the Fathers. It reads thus: "For Christ also once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God, being put to death in the flesh but made alive in the Spirit, by whom he also went and preached to the spirits that were in prison." From this passage the ancients believed and wrote that Christ, after his death, descended into hell, that is, to the place appointed for the damned. In this, however, they sinned most gravely. The second occasion of this error was that it was already received by the common opinion of all that Christ came to hell for this reason: that he might lead the faithful, and those worthy who had lived and persevered constantly in faith, into eternal life, and indeed into paradise itself, as the author and prince of life. For they believed that on the very day on which he had descended, he went out of hell with those so rescued.

units.la: Hæc tradit ex Patrum dogmate Nicephorus lib.1.cap.27.& 31. & Irenæus lib.4.cap.45. Nam varia fuit huius de descensu Christi ad inferos articuli interpretatio, qui à nonnullis Ecclesiis retentus, à nonnullis verò omnino prætermis-sus est. Quo primùm autem author cœperit, vbi item (nisi fortasse in Ægypto, & Arabia vi-cinisque regionibus, vbi Chiliastæ & Origeni-stæ viguerunt) innotuerit, & perstiterit hæc hæ-resis, difficile est definire, cùm fuerit à paucis cognita. Gregorius Magnus libro 5. epist.17.in-dict.15. tradit Georgium & Theodorum presbyteros Constantinopolit. Ecclesiæ hoc ipsum docuisse & defendisse, qui, si Nicephoro credi-mus lib.14. cap.13. sub Theodosio Iuniore Imperatore, & Innocentio Romano Episcopo, circa annum à Christo passo 385. extiterunt, quan-quam apud eundem Nicephorum, Timotheus pro Theodoro legitur. Sed quia hanc hæresin Augustinus à Philastro sumpsit, qui ante Theodosij Iunioris imperium obierat, ad hoc tem-pus referri nō potest. Potius in Origenistarum tempora colloco, quando tunc quoque Theodorum & Georgium Origenis fautores fuisse idem Nicephor. lib.5. cap.21. scribit, qui ipsius dogmata acutissimè acerriméque defenderunt. Statim tamen concidisse crediderim, neque illius venenum latius propagatum multis nocuis-se. Sed ad alias hæreses transcamus.
units.tr: Nicephorus records this from the doctrine of the Fathers in book 1, chapters 27 and 31, and Irenaeus in book 4, chapter 45. For the interpretation of this article of the descent of Christ into hell varied: it was retained by some Churches, but altogether passed over by others. When this author began, and where (unless perhaps in Egypt, Arabia and the neighbouring regions, where the Chiliasts and Origenists flourished) this heresy became known and persisted, is hard to determine, since it was known to few. Gregory the Great, in book 5, letter 17, indiction 15, relates that the presbyters George and Theodore of the Church of Constantinople taught and defended this very thing. If we believe Nicephorus, book 14, chapter 13, they arose under the emperor Theodosius the Younger and Innocent, bishop of Rome, around the year 385 after Christ's passion, although in the same Nicephorus the name Timothy is read instead of Theodore. But since Augustine took this heresy from Philastrius, who had died before the reign of Theodosius the Younger, it cannot be referred to this time. I rather place it in the times of the Origenists, since Nicephorus, book 5, chapter 21, likewise writes that Theodore and George were then supporters of Origen, who defended his doctrines most acutely and vigorously. Yet I believe they soon collapsed, and that their poison was not spread widely enough to do much harm to many. But let us pass on to other heresies.

units.la: CAP. LXXX. Natiuitariorum error quis fuerit.
units.tr: CAP. LXXX. What the error of the Natiuitarii was.

units.la: Alia sempiterne{1} natum non intelligens Filium, putat illam natiuitatem sumpsisse a tempore initium, & tamen volens coæternum Patri Filium confiteri, apud illum fuisse, antequam de illo nasceretur, existimat, hoc est, semper eum fuisse, verumtamen eum semper per Filium non fuisse: sed ex quo de illo natus est, Filium esse cœpisse. Has hæreses, quæ absque authorum nominibus sunt, putaui in hoc opus meum[?] de Philastri opere transferendas: & alias quidem[?] ipse commemorat, sed mihi appellanda hæreses non videntur. Quascunque autem[?] sine nominibus posui, nec ipse earum nomina commemorauit.
units.tr: Another heresy, not understanding the Son as eternally begotten, holds that that birth took its beginning from a point in time. Yet, wishing to confess the Son coeternal with the Father, it holds that he was with him before he was born of him; that is, that the Father always existed, but was not always Father through a Son. Rather, from the time he was born of him, he began to be Son. I have thought these heresies, which are without the names of their authors, should be carried over into this work of mine from the work of Philastrius. Some of them he indeed mentions by name, but they do not seem to me to be heresies that should be called by a name. As for those I have set down without names, he himself did not mention their names either.

units.la: {1} Alia sempiterne natum.) Mirum est Augustinum, qui postrema ætate sua ista scribebat, non agnouisse a quo fit ortus hic Natiuitariorum vel Initiariorum error (sic enim eos docendi distinguendíque ab aliis hæreticis gratia,nomi-no) cum ipse lib.15. de Trinitate cap.20. eum Eunomio tribuat, qui ab Arianis profectus est. Ridenda est,ait,Eunomij dialectica, a quo Eunomiani hæretici orti sunt,qui cum non potuis-set intelligere, nec credere voluisset vnigenitum Dei Verbum Filium Dei esse natura, id est de substantia Patris genitum, non naturæ vel substantiæ dixit esse Filium, sed Filium voluntatis Dei, volens afferere accedentem Deo voluntatem, qua gigneret Filium: sicut nos aliquando aliquid volumus,quod antea non volebamus,propter quod mutabilis intelligitur nostra voluntas, quod absit, vt in Deo esse credamus. Non enim ante voluit Pater gignere vel potuit, quam genuit: sicut nec ante fuit, quam genuit, quia ab æterno fuit, & ab æterno genuit. Idem Augustus libro 65.quæst.7. De qua re sunt subtiles Scholasticorum disputationes in lib.1.Mag. Sententiarum dist.6.cap.1. Quærunt enim vtrum necessitate an quadam noua & superveniente voluntate Pater Filium genuerit, quasi Deus esset mutabilis, vel nouum aliquod consilium illi superueniisset. Itaque fuerunt isti Eunomianorum surculus vel ramunculus infelix quidem, sed tamen qui duobus Scripturæ locis niti videbantur. Primus est Ioan.1. versu 1. In principio erat Sermo,& Sermo erat apud Deum, & Sermo ille erat Deus. Alter locus est Psalm.2.vers.7.Ego hodie genui te. ex quibus coniunctis argumentabantur,Ab æterno quidem fuisse Sermonem, sed non ab æterno fuisse Filium, sed ex certo tantum tempore,quod initium habuiffet[?], quia dictum est, Hodie, quæ vox est fi-gnificans tempus. Sed respondet ex epistola ad Hebræos 12. verf.8. Augustinus, vocem Hodie in Christo æternum statum denotare, quia qui hodie est & heri, idem est in perpetuum. Id quod & Prouerb.8. & Ioann.17. verf.5. aperte confirmatur. Hic tamen ipse error nostro secu-lo videtur à Serueto impio renouatus, qui Patrem fingit genituriẽtem[?] quidem ab initio: demùm autem Filium reipsa genuisse, cùm Chri-stus ex Maria virgine natus est. In quo tamen apparent isti, qui certè ab orthodoxis patri-bus statim extincti sunt, & communi primitiuæ Ecclesiæ voce damnati, Seruetanis nostri tem-poris tolerabiliores, minúsque blasphemi, qui tamen à quibusdam non tantùm priuatis ho-minibus, sed regnis & proceribus probantur, vt in iis suum venenum spargere sinantur, ma-gno totius Reip. Christianæ detrimento. Vide-tur igitur cœpisse hæc hæresis post Eunomia-nos iam natos & notos, post annum à Domino passo 331. Nec diu tamen floruisse, vel propa-gata perdurafse. Verum enim est illud quod o-mnes Ecclesiæ retinebant, Deum Patrem, non ante Deum quàm Patrem fuisse, sed ab æterno & Patrem & Deum fuisse, Filiúmque sibi ὁμοούσιον[?] genuisse. Sed tanti est vel vno Satanæ halitu licet leuissimo afflatum fuisse, illúmque semel hausisse. Huius hæreseos etiam Isidorus memi-nit, sed breuiter.
units.tr: {1} Another heresy, not understanding the Son as eternally begotten.) It is remarkable that Augustine, who was writing these things late in his life, did not recognise from whom this error of the Natiuitarii, or Initiarii (for so I name them, for the sake of teaching and distinguishing them from other heretics), arose, since he himself, in book 15 of On the Trinity, chapter 20, attributes it to Eunomius, who came from the Arians. "The dialectic of Eunomius is to be laughed at," he says, "from whom the Eunomians, heretics, arose. Since he could not understand, nor was willing to believe, that the only-begotten Word of God is the Son of God by nature, that is, begotten of the substance of the Father, he said that he was the Son not of nature or substance, but of the will of God, wishing to assert that a will came to God by which he would beget a Son. Just as we sometimes will something which we did not will before, so that our will is understood to be changeable, which God forbid we should believe of God. For the Father did not will to beget before he begat, nor was he able to; just as he was not before he begat, since he existed from eternity and begat from eternity." The same Augustine, in book 83 of the Questions, question 7. There are subtle disputations of the Scholastics on this matter, in book 1 of the Master of the Sentences, distinction 6, chapter 1. For they ask whether the Father begat the Son by necessity, or by some new will coming upon him, as if God were changeable, or as if some new purpose had come upon him. So these were the unhappy offshoot or little twig of the Eunomians, yet they seemed to rely on two passages of Scripture. The first is John 1:1: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." The other is Psalm 2:7: "I have begotten you today." From these two they argued that the Word existed from eternity, but that the Son did not exist from eternity, only from a certain time, which had a beginning, because it is said "today," a word which signifies time. But Augustine answers from the Epistle to the Hebrews 12:8 (sic) that the word "today" in Christ denotes an eternal state, because he who is "today and yesterday" is the same for ever. This is clearly confirmed also by Proverbs 8 and John 17:5. Yet this very error seems in our own age to have been revived by the impious Servetus, who imagines the Father as begetting indeed from the beginning, but only really begetting the Son when Christ was born of the virgin Mary. In this, however, those people appear, who were certainly quickly extinguished by the orthodox Fathers and condemned by the common voice of the primitive Church, to be more tolerable than the Servetans of our time and less blasphemous. Yet these are approved not only by private individuals but by kingdoms and nobles, so that they are allowed to spread their poison among them, to the great detriment of the whole Christian commonwealth. It seems, therefore, that this heresy began after the Eunomians were already born and known, in the 331st year after the Lord's passion. Nor did it flourish for long, nor did it last when spread abroad. True is that which all the Churches held: that God the Father was not God before he was Father, but was both Father and God from eternity, and begat a Son consubstantial [ὁμοούσιον] with himself. But however little it is, it is a great thing to have been touched by even one breath of Satan, however slight, and to have once drawn it in. Isidore also mentions this heresy, but briefly.

units.la: CAP. LXXXI.
units.tr: CHAPTER LXXXI.

units.la: Luciferiani cur sic dicti. Erroris autem eorum caput vnum relatum.
units.tr: Why the Luciferians were so called. One head of their error is related.

units.la: Vciferianos[?] à Lucifero Caralitano Episcopo exortos, & celebriter nominatos, nec Epiphanius, nec Philaster inter haereticos posuit, credo tantummodo schisma, non haeresin eos condidisse credentes. Apud quendam tamen, cuius nomen in eodem eius opusculo non inueni, in haereticis Lucifer-ianos positos legi, per hac verba, Lucifer ni, inquit, quum teneant in omnibus catholicam veritatem, in hunc errorem sultissimum[?] prolabuntur, vt animam{1} dicant ex transfusione generari, eandemque dicunt & de carne, & carnis esse substantiam. Vtrum ergo ipse propter hoc quod de anima ista sentiunt, si tamen vere ita sentiunt, eos inter haereticos ponendos esse crediderit, an etiam si id non sentirent, sive non sentiant, ideo tamen sint haeretici, quia dissensionem suam pertinaci animositate firmarunt, alia quaestio est, neque hoc loco mihi videtur esse tractanda.
units.tr: The Luciferians, who arose from Lucifer, bishop of Caralis, and became famous, were not counted among the heretics by Epiphanius or by Philaster. I believe they thought he had founded a schism, not a heresy. Yet in a certain writer, whose name I did not find in that same little work of his, I have read the Luciferians listed among the heretics, in these words: "Although Lucifer's followers hold the Catholic truth in all things, they slip into this most grave error, that they say the soul is generated by transfusion, and that it is of the same substance as the flesh." Whether he counted them heretics because of this opinion about the soul (if indeed they really hold it), or whether, even if they did not hold it, or do not hold it, they are heretics because they confirmed their dissent with stubborn obstinacy, is another question, and it does not seem to me that it should be treated in this place.

units.la: I Luciferiani primum, postea vero Homonymiani dicti sunt, vt Nicephorus libro 9. cap. 16. & ante eum Socrat. libro 3. cap. 15. tradunt. Luciferiani à Lucifero episcopo, qui huius sectae primus autor fuit. Homonymiani vero cur sint appellati, nemo explicat, fortasse quod in errore suo tuendo homonymia vocis, Caro, fallerent, quemadmodum in huius sectae hypothesibus apparebit. Fuit
units.tr: The Luciferians were first so called, and afterwards Homonymians, as Nicephorus relates in book 9, chapter 16, and Socrates before him in book 3, chapter 15. They were called Luciferians after Lucifer the bishop, who was the first author of this sect. Why they were called Homonymians no one explains. Perhaps it was because in defending their error they deceived people by the ambiguity of the word "flesh" (caro), as will appear from the tenets of this sect.

units.la: {1} A Lucifero Caralitano.) autem hæc secta primum schisma, non ita valde quidem periculosum, ut hic Augustinus docet, & Ambrosius in Orat. funebri, de obitu fratris, estque in Canone Aduocauit.24.quaest.1. itém-que Ruffin. lib.1. cap.30. sed ex schismate facta est hæresis, ut aliæ multæ, dum ad sui facti, & sessionis defensionem animosius quàm prudentius verbo Dei abutitur, illúdque falsa interpretatione corrumpit. Huius enim erroris & discessionis à communi Ecclesiæ cœtu faciendæ causa fuit Luciferi episcopi tum ambitio, tum etiam ira, quemadmodum in historiæ Ecclesiasticæ libello, qui Indicatio hæresi. dicitur, traditum est, adeò ut ex paruis initiis lugubres exitus habuerit, fuerítque magnarum occasio in Ecclesia dissensionum, & ὅπλον φιλονεικῶν, ut Gregor. Nazianzenus scripsit. Quum enim Paulinum creatum à se Antiochiæ episcopum præter communem totiùs plebis consensum, sed tantùm ad unius, quanquam sanioris populi partis votum, intellexisset sperni, neque acceptari ab Eusebio Vercellensi episcopo (qui ab Alexandrina Synodo illuc missus erat perturbationis Ecclesiæ tollendæ gratia) excandescens Lucifer, se, sibíque consentientes alios, ab Eusebio separavit, & Alexandrinam illam Synodum, quanquam orthodoxam, & cui etiam Athanasius ipse interfuerat, damnauit. Fuit autem Lucifer Caralitanus episcopus, uti Ruffinus libro 1. cap.20. Socrates lib.3. ca.9, & 15. Sozomen. lib.5. cap.12, & 13. unanimiter tradunt. Est autem Caralitanum Sardiniæ oppidū, à Caralitano promontorio (quod Africam spectat) denominatum, tum, & colonia populi Rom. quemadmodum Plinius libro 3.hiftor.Natural.cap.7.tradit. Vn-de etiam Caralitani populi dicti. Quò magis miror quid venerit in mentem Isidoro, & aliis cum sequutis, ut Luciférum Smyrnæ episcopum (est autem Smyrna Æoliæ in minori Asia ciuitas) facerēt, quum tanto locorum interuallo distet Smyrna à Sardinia insula, quæ est in mari Ligustico, vel Africo potius: sed fortasse mirum non videbitur, qui apud eundem Isidorum in eadem hæresi, obseruabit aliud quoque mendum esse, & pro his verbis, Instanti persequutione, legendum ex Theodoreto libro 3. histor.cap.4. Constantij persequutione. Nam à Constantio Constantini filio excitata est in orthodoxos episcopos illa persequutio, de qua meminit Isidorus, & in qua hic Lucifer & Eusebius Vercellensis episcopus, vnà cum Hilario Pictauiensi episcopo, in exilium acti sunt: illi quidem duo priores in Thebęorum(quæ est Ægypti pars deserta)regionem: hic verò partim in Illyricum, partim in Asiam, quòd damnationi Athanasij Alexandrini episcopi, à Constantio factæ, id est, orthodoxæ fidei condemnationi ab isto imperatore Ariano scriptæ, assentiri & subscribere noluissent, ut Ruffinus lib.1. Socrat. libro 3. Sozomen. lib.5. Theodor. lib.3. luculenter tradunt. In hoc autem exilio toto reliquo imperij Constantij tempore vixerunt, quo mortuo, sunt subdolè ad perturbationem Ecclesiæ, & mouendas iterum orthodoxorum cum Arianis contentiones, à Iuliano Apostata re-vocati, & suis sedibus restituti. Et certè Lucifer iste, tempore demum Iuliani Apostatæ imperatoris, & Liberij episcopi Romani, circa annum à Christo passo 333. iam reuocatus secessit à fide Ecclesiæ, in qua semper antea permanserat. In Oriente autem, & Antiochiæ maximè hoc hæreticorum genus viguit, vt Nicephorus libro 8. capite 17. & Socrates libro 5. cap. 5. tradunt. Diu tamen permansisse & perstitisse non videtur, (quanquam aduersus Lucifierianos & Hieronymus scripsit, & Augustinus) quia sua iam ætate paucos huius sectæ homines superfuisse scribit libro 1. capite 30. Ruffin. Theodoretus autem suo seculo prorsus esse desiisse, lib. 3. Historiæ cap. 4. Ipse vero Lucifer in Sardiniam rediit, vbi tamen pauca, aut nulla sui erroris vestigia reliquit, nimirum in longinquis regionibus placuit, qui in propria fede displicuit, & damnatus est.
units.tr: {1} From Lucifer of Caralis.) This sect was at first a schism, not indeed very dangerous, as Augustine teaches here, and Ambrose in his funeral oration on the death of his brother. It is also in the canon Advocauit, 24 q. 1, and likewise in Rufinus, book 1, chapter 30. But from a schism it became a heresy, as many others have, while it abuses the word of God more zealously than wisely in defending its deed and its separation, and corrupts it by false interpretation. For the cause of this error and of the separation from the common assembly of the Church was the ambition, and also the anger, of Bishop Lucifer, as is recorded in the little book of ecclesiastical history called Indicatio haereseos. So from small beginnings he came to a mournful end, and he was the occasion of great dissensions in the Church, and an "instrument of contention" (hoplon philoneikon), as Gregory Nazianzen wrote. For when Lucifer perceived that Paulinus, whom he had himself created bishop of Antioch, was being despised, not with the common consent of the whole people but only with the vote of one part of the people, though the saner part, and was not accepted by Eusebius of Vercelli (who had been sent there by the Alexandrian synod to remove the disturbance of the Church), he flared up. He separated himself and others who agreed with him from Eusebius, and condemned that Alexandrian synod, orthodox though it was, and one in which Athanasius himself had taken part. Lucifer was bishop of Caralis, as Rufinus, book 1, chapter 20, Socrates, book 3, chapters 9 and 15, and Sozomen, book 5, chapters 12 and 13, unanimously relate. Caralis is a town of Sardinia, named after the Caralitan promontory, which faces Africa, and it was also a colony of the Roman people, as Pliny relates in book 3 of the Natural History, chapter 7. Hence the people are also called Caralitani. So I wonder all the more what came into the mind of Isidore, and of others who followed him, to make Lucifer bishop of Smyrna (Smyrna is a city of Aeolia in Asia Minor), since Smyrna is so far distant from the island of Sardinia, which lies in the Ligurian sea, or rather the African sea. Perhaps it will not seem surprising, however, that anyone who examines the same Isidore in the same heresy will notice another error too: instead of the words "by the persecution of the moment" (instanti persequutione), one should read, from Theodoret, book 3 of the History, chapter 4, "by the persecution of Constantius" (Constantij). For it was by Constantius, son of Constantine, that the persecution which Isidore mentions was stirred up against the orthodox bishops, and in which this Lucifer and Eusebius of Vercelli, together with Hilary of Poitiers, were driven into exile. The first two went into the region of the Thebaid, a desert part of Egypt; Hilary went partly into Illyricum and partly into Asia. This was because they refused to assent to and subscribe the condemnation of Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, made by Constantius, that is, the condemnation of the orthodox faith written by that Arian emperor, as Rufinus, book 1, Socrates, book 3, Sozomen, book 5, and Theodoret, book 3, clearly relate. They lived in this exile for the whole remaining time of Constantius's reign. When he died, they were recalled by Julian the Apostate and restored to their sees, so that the disturbance of the Church and the renewed contentions between the orthodox and the Arians might be stirred up secretly. And indeed this Lucifer, at last, in the time of the emperor Julian the Apostate and of Liberius, bishop of Rome, about the year 333 after the passion of Christ, having been recalled, withdrew from the faith of the Church, in which he had always remained before. This kind of heretic flourished especially in the East and at Antioch, as Nicephorus, book 8, chapter 17, and Socrates, book 5, chapter 5, relate. Yet it does not seem to have lasted long or to have persisted, although both Jerome and Augustine wrote against the Luciferians. Augustine writes, in book 1, chapter 30 (Rufinus), that in his own time few men of this sect survived. Theodoret, however, says that in his century it had altogether ceased, book 3 of the History, chapter 4. Lucifer himself returned to Sardinia, where he left few or no traces of his error. No doubt he found favour in distant regions, though he had given offence in his own see and been condemned.

units.la: 2 Vt animam dicant.) Quanquam ambigere videtur hoc loco Augustinus, vtrum schismatica an hæresis fuerint Luciferiani, propter paucas huius hominum sectæ hypotheses sibi notas, tamen si quæ fuerint, & quàm erroneæ spectentur, ἀναμφισβήτως inter hæreticos censebuntur. Fuerunt igitur hæc Luciferianorum dogmata: 1 Mundum hunc vniuersum diaboli opus esse, (Hieronymus aduersus eos scribes,) quia in maligno positus sit, 1. Ioannis 5. Hic est paralogismus à qualitate ad rei subflatiam & sumptus error à Cerinthianis & Marcionitis. 2 Animas humanas ex carne sumi, & transfusione siue ex traduce alterius animæ generari. Quæ sententia animas nostras facit corporeas, non autem spiritus. Nam vt recte Damascenus lib. 2, capite 12. de orthodoxa fide, definit, fluxus, tradux, & propagatio propria sunt corporum πα- Ѻ, non autem spirituum. Spiritus autem, qualis est anima hominis, nec carnem nec ossa habet, Luc. 24. vers. 39. Et quod totus homo caro esse dicitur, Genesis 6. versu 3. est de vitiositate, non de natura corporea intelligendū. Nec enim omnes hominis partes sunt corporeae, quaquam omnes sunt corruptae. Itaque homonymia vocis, Caro, fefellerunt imperitos, & nō satis attetos. Hic error a Tertulliano sumptus, est sane vetus. Quomodo autem fiant animae, & in nobis nascantur, varię sunt hominum sententiae, etiā Patrum, de quibus est epistola Augustini ad Hieronymum legenda, quemadmodum & illa quae est ad Optatum. 3 Poenitentiam clericis post ordinem in Ecclesia & gradu acceptum, lapsis denegant: laicis autem lapsis, nullo tempore spem veniae & reconciliationis adimunt, quod grauiori poena clericos castigados esse censerent. Atque illud quidem verum est, si de ea poena agimus quae ab Ecclesia often diculi tollendi gratia infligitur: non est tamen cuiquam spes remissionis peccatorum eripienda, quum Christus pro omnibus sit mortuus: & Petrum, post Apostolatum lapsum, poenitente ipse receperit, & Paulum persequutorē in suum gregem, & ad Apostolatum etiam admiserit, 1 Timoth. 1. vers. 13. Haec vero Luciferianorum sententia ex Nouatianorum, & Meletianorum lacunis & faecibus hausta est, ad quas hanc haeresin refero. 4 Inde natus est error sequens, Episcopos, vel qui minorem in Ecclesia dignitatem habuerūt, si semel in hæresin inciderint, quanuis postea resipuerint, erroremque ex animo abiurarint, nunquam tamè in pristinum, vel alium minorem gradum admittèdos, quòd spes apud Deum ipsum prioris loci & adoptionis obtinendæ sit illis adempta.Isidorus. Hæc ratio falsa est, quàquam vtrum qui in errorem & hæresin lapsi sunt episcopi, vel alij clerici, sint, errore damnato, vel in priorem sedem, vel in parem, vel in inferiorem gradum reponendi, dubia & perplexa fuit apud Patres orthodoxos quæstio, quum eos alij recipi posse concederent, alij negarent. Id quod anxiè in Alexandrina Synodo disputatum esse tradit Ruffinus lib. i.Histor.cap.28.& in scriptis aduersus Donatistas Augustinus, itémque epist.50. modò fieri posse concedit, modò negat. Denique de ea re diuersa responsa Gratianus collegit tota dist. 50. in Decret. Tandem verò tota hæc controuersia concilio Agathensi ita definita est, vt clerici qui prius hæretici erant, errore deposito, ídque ex animo, & seria publicáque pœnitentia, & exomologesi accedente, si è re Ecclesiæ videatur ita fieri oportere, in suis gradibus & ordinibus retineri possint: ad maiores tamen & superiores vocari neque possint, neque debeát. Idé Hilerdensi concilio, cap.5.In quo ipso noua electione & ordinatione vsa est Ecclesia, quemadmodum dixit Christus ipse Petro lapso, Pasce oues meas, iterata quadam ad Apostolatum vocatione vtens, Ioannis 21. Hanc fuisse veterem Ecclesiæ disciplinam, post Luciferianorū tempora pora, apparet ex Leonis epist.3, & 83. & Synodo Martini, cap.36. estque relatum in Canone Saluberrimum. & Can. Daibertum 1. quaest.7. itemque variis exemplis & argumentis docetur Can. Ioannis Chryfoftom. diftinct. 50. Itaque Luciferiani Athanafium, & Alexandrinam Synodum damnarunt, quę episcopos poeniten-tes, in priorem gradum reponeret. Atque hi nimirum fuerunt αὐθαδείας [?], & ambitionis Luciferianæ peftilentiffimi fructus, dum Paulinum episcopum a fe creatum defendere quo iure, quaeve iniuria contendit, nec Eusebij modestum iudicium ferre potest.
units.tr: 2 That they say the soul.) Although Augustine seems here to hesitate whether the Luciferians were a schismatic body or a heresy, on account of the few tenets of this sect known to him, yet if there were any, and one considers how erroneous they are, they will without doubt be counted among the heretics. These, then, were the doctrines of the Luciferians: (1) that this whole world is the work of the devil (Jerome writing against them), because it lies in the power of the evil one, 1 John 5. This is a paralogism from quality to the substance of the thing, and an error taken from the Cerinthians and the Marcionites. (2) That human souls are drawn from the flesh and generated by transfusion, or by traduction, from another soul. This opinion makes our souls corporeal, not spiritual. For, as Damascene rightly defines in book 2, chapter 12, of On the Orthodox Faith, flow, traduction and propagation are properties of bodies, not of spirits. A spirit, such as the soul of man, has neither flesh nor bones, Luke 24 v. 39. And that the whole man is called flesh, Genesis 6 v. 3, must be understood of corruption, not of bodily nature. For not all parts of man are corporeal, although all are corrupted. So the ambiguity of the word "flesh" deceived the unskilled and those not sufficiently attentive. This error was taken from Tertullian and is indeed old. How souls come to be and are born in us, there are various opinions of men, even of the Fathers. On this, Augustine's letter to Jerome should be read, as also the one to Optatus. (3) They deny repentance to clerics who, after their ordination and having received rank in the Church, have lapsed; but to lay people who lapse they take away all hope of pardon and reconciliation at any time, because they judged that clerics should be punished with a heavier penalty. This is true if we are speaking of that penalty which the Church imposes in order to remove public scandal. Yet no one should be deprived of hope of forgiveness of sins, since Christ died for all. Peter, after his lapse following his apostolate, received him back when he repented, and Paul, the persecutor, he also admitted into his flock and into the apostolate, 1 Tim. 1 v. 13. This opinion of the Luciferians was drawn from the dregs and filth of the Novatians and the Meletians, to whom I refer this heresy. (4) From this there arose the following error: that bishops, or those who held a lesser dignity in the Church, if once they fell into heresy, must never be admitted to their former or any other lower rank, even though they afterwards repented and renounced the error from their heart, because the hope of obtaining from God himself their former place and adoption is taken from them. Isidore. This reasoning is false. Yet whether bishops or other clerics who have fallen into error and heresy are, once the error is condemned, to be restored to their former see, or to an equal or lower rank, was a doubtful and perplexing question among the orthodox Fathers, since some conceded they could be received and others denied it. Rufinus relates that this was disputed anxiously in the Alexandrian synod, book 1 of the History, chapter 28. Augustine, in his writings against the Donatists, and likewise in letter 50, now concedes that it can be done and now denies it. Finally, Gratian gathered diverse responses on this matter throughout distinction 50 of the Decretum. At last this whole controversy was settled by the council of Agde, so that clerics who had previously been heretics, having renounced the error (and that from the heart, with serious and public repentance and exomologesis), may, if it seems to the advantage of the Church that this be done, be retained in their own grades and orders; yet they can and ought not be called to higher and superior ones. The same is laid down in the council of Ilerda, chapter 5. In that very case the Church used a new election and ordination, just as Christ himself said to the fallen Peter, "Feed my sheep," employing a kind of repeated calling to the apostolate, John 21. That this was the ancient discipline of the Church, after the time of the Luciferians, appears from Leo's letters 3 and 83, and from the Synod of Martin, chapter 36. It is related in the canon Saluberrimum and in the canon Daibertum, 1 q. 7, and it is likewise taught by various examples and arguments in the canon of John Chrysostom, distinction 50. Thus the Luciferians condemned Athanasius and the Alexandrian synod, which would restore penitent bishops to their former rank. And these, no doubt, were the most pestilential fruits of Luciferian arrogance (authadeias) and ambition, when he contends, by what right or what injustice, that he defends Paulinus, whom he himself created bishop, and cannot bear to accept the modest judgement of Eusebius.

units.la: CAP. LXXXII.
units.tr: CAP. LXXXII.

units.la: Iouinianistæ cur sic dicti, quando primùm nati. Erroris autem eorum capita quatuor recensentur.
units.tr: Why the Jovinianists were so called, and when they first arose. Four heads of their error are listed.

units.la: Ouinianistas{1} quoque apud ipsum reperi, quos iam noveram. A Iouiniano quodam monacho ista hæresis orta est ætate nostra, quum adhuc iuvenes essemus. Hic omnia peccata, sicut Stoici philosophi, paria esse{2} dicebat, nec posse peccare hominem lavacro regenerationis accepto, nec aliquid prodesse ieiunia, vel à cibis aliquibus abstinentiam. Virginitatem Mariæ destruebat, dicens eam pariendo fuisse corruptam. Virginitatem etiam sanctimonialium, & continentiam sexus virilis in sanctis eligentibus cœlibem vitam coniugiorum castorum atque fidelium meritis adæquabat, ita vt quadam virgines prouecta iam ætatis in vrbe Romana, vbi hæc docebat, eo audito, nupsisse dicantur. Non sane ipse vel habebat, vel habere volebat vxorem, quod non propter aliquod apud Deum maius meritum in regno vitæ perpetuæ profuturum: sed propter præsentem prodesse necessitatem, ne homo coniugales patiatur molestias, disputabat. Cito vero ista hæresis oppressa, & extincta est, nec vsque ad deceptionem aliquorum sacerdotum potuit peruenire.
units.tr: I also found the Jovinianists in him, whom I already knew. This heresy arose in our own age from a certain monk named Jovinian, when we were still young men. He taught that all sins are equal, as the Stoic philosophers held, that a man who has received the washing of regeneration cannot sin, and that fasting or abstaining from certain foods profits nothing. He denied the virginity of Mary, saying she had been corrupted by giving birth. He also made the virginity of nuns and the continence of men who choose the celibate life in holiness equal to the merit of chaste and faithful marriages, so that some women of advanced age in the city of Rome, where he taught this, are said to have married after hearing him. He himself neither had nor wished to have a wife. He argued that this was not because marriage would bring some greater merit before God in the kingdom of eternal life, but because celibacy served the present necessity, so that a man need not suffer the troubles of marriage. The heresy was soon suppressed and extinguished, and it never spread so far as to deceive some priests.

units.la: Iouiniani quoque nominantur, quemadmodum & Iouinianistæ, a Iouiniano, cuius etiam meminit Augustinus alibi, sed maxime libro 2. Retractation.cap.22. Hieronymus duobus libris aduersus hunc ipsum editis. Ambrosius epist. 82. ad Vercellenses. Cœpisse vero mihi videtur hæc hæresis sub Iouiniano imperatore, & extremis temporibus pontificatus Liberij episcopi Romani, circa annum a Christo passo 335. Quod vt credam, hac præsertim ratione sum inductus, quod quemadmodum & Sozomen. lib. 6. capite 3. & Nicephor. libro 10. capite 39. tradunt, ab imperatore Iouiniano lex aduersus eos seuerissima condita est, qui sacras & Deo dicatas virgines vel rapere, vel etiam attentare essent ausi, adeo vt capite punirentur. Quod ideo necessarium fuisse putant, vt ediceretur, quia homines quidam, vt illi scribunt, improbi & impudici scelestas cum istis virginibus sacris, & Vestalibus nuptias contraherent, vel vi illis illata, vel persuasione adhibita: quorum alterum, nempe vim, ad tempora Iuliani Apostatæ refero, quibus in eas virgines sæuire & illudere licuit: alterū autem, nempe perfuasionem, ad dogma istius Iouiniani. scribit enim Augustinus Iouinianum disputando coniugium Monialibus persuasisse. Extat lex in Cod. Iustinian. lib.i. Tit. De episcop.Audient.L.Si quis non dicam rapere. Fuit autem huius hæresfeos author & nomen prope Græcis hominibus ignotū, quādoquidē neque Niceph. neque eo posterior Ioan.Damasce. inter hæreticos meminere: quum tamen alterius cuiusdam Iouiniani Pergensis episcopi (qui fuit Arianus, hoc nostro posterior) mentionem faciat Nicephorus libro ii. capite 21: Latini vero scriptores hanc non prætermittunt, vt infestum sibi venenū, veluti Philaster, Hieronymus, Augustinus, Isidorus, quam tamen statim extinctam, neque latius peruagatam, scribit hoc loco Augustinus, cuius neque episcoporum, vel presbyterorum vnus patrocinium suscepit, nimirum ita omnes iam illo seculo virginitatis laudibus, & immodica abstinentiæ commendatione, & encomiis præoccupati, contrarias sententias facilè repudiabant. Clàm tamen a plerisque probabatur, etsi non prodiret palàm, vt Augustinus libro De bono coniugali, capite 10. docet, quòd Iouiniani & scripta & rationes non tantùm plausibiles, sed multis in rebus verbo Dei consentaneæ videretur. Itaque aduersus has ipsas scribere coactum se tandem fuisse, ne palàm reuiuisceret hæc sententia, testatur Augustinus libro 2. Retractat. Liber Augustini aduersus Iouinianum, est De bono coniugali. gali, extátque operum eius Tomo 6. Romæ hæc hæresis & secta primùm cœpit, vbi monachus, & postea clericus fuisse videtur Iouinia-nus, cuius raro Patres meminerunt, nisi vt damnarent. Itaque quis fuerit, praeterquam quod Romanus dicitur, nihil pene certi habemus.
units.tr: Jovinian's followers are also called Jovinians, as are the Jovinianists, after Jovinian, whom Augustine also mentions elsewhere, chiefly in book 2 of the Retractations, chapter 22. Jerome mentions him in two books written against him, and Ambrose in letter 82 to the Vercellenses. This heresy seems to me to have begun under the emperor Jovian, near the end of the pontificate of Liberius, bishop of Rome, around the year 335 after the passion of Christ. I am led to this view chiefly by the following reason: as Sozomen (book 6, chapter 3) and Nicephorus (book 10, chapter 39) report, the emperor Jovian issued a very severe law against those who dared to abduct, or even to attempt to abduct, sacred virgins dedicated to God, and it made the offence punishable by death. They think this law was needed because, as those writers relate, wicked and shameless men were marrying these sacred virgins and Vestals, either by force or by persuasion. I refer the first, the use of force, to the time of Julian the Apostate, when it was permitted to rage against those virgins and mock them. The second, persuasion, I refer to the doctrine of this Jovinian, for Augustine writes that Jovinian persuaded nuns in debate to marry. The law exists in the Code of Justinian, book 1, title On Episcopal Audience, law "Si quis non dicam rapere." The author of this heresy and his name were almost unknown to the Greeks, since neither Nicephorus nor John of Damascus, who came later, mention him among the heretics. Nicephorus does mention another Jovinian, bishop of Perga, who was an Arian and later than our man (book 2, chapter 21). The Latin writers, however, do not pass over this poison, which they treated as a hostile thing: Philaster, Jerome, Augustine and Isidore. Yet Augustine writes in this passage that it was soon extinguished and did not spread widely. None of the bishops or presbyters took up its defence. Clearly by that age all were already filled with praise of virginity, with immoderate commendation of abstinence and with eulogies, and so they readily rejected opposing views. Nevertheless, as Augustine shows in his book On the Good of Marriage (chapter 10), it was secretly approved by many, though it did not come into the open, since the writings and arguments of Jovinian seemed not only plausible but in many matters consistent with the word of God. Augustine testifies in book 2 of the Retractations that he was at last compelled to write against these very views, so that this opinion would not openly revive. Augustine's book against Jovinian is On the Good of Marriage, and his works are in volume 6. This heresy and sect first began at Rome, where Jovinian seems to have been a monk and later a cleric. The Fathers rarely mention him except to condemn him. So, apart from being called a Roman, we have almost no certain knowledge of who he was.

units.la: Damnata & reiecta tandem est hæc hæresis, & sententia Vclensi Synodo, sub Honorio imperatore, anno salutis & à Christo nato 419. cui coetui præfuit Ponatianus episcopus Telensis.
units.tr: This heresy and opinion were finally condemned and rejected by a synod at Vela under the emperor Honorius, in the year of salvation 419 after the birth of Christ. Ponatianus, bishop of Telensis, presided over that assembly.

units.la: Quæ vero huius impugnationis & sententiæ, quæ Virginitatis & Ciborum abstinentiæ tantam commendationem iam receptam damnaret occasio fuerit, quæri potest. Ac mihi quidé alia nō videtur, quàm quod viris bonis iam tum displicebant immensæ illæ rerum, quæ per se sunt ἀδιάφορα, laudes, per quas in iis salutis nostræ prora & puppis, pene neglecto Christi sanguine constituebatur, nuptiæ spernebantur, & damnabatur, denique operum nostrorum merita non sine aperta in Dei gratia blasphemia, inducebantur. Itaque, quæ quantaque essent earum rerum & φιλοθρησκειῶν [?] ad salutem nostram vis, cœptum est disputari: & ex huiusmodi disputationibus intelligi per se nullius eas esse ad remissionem peccatorum nostrorum momenti: sed catenus vtiles censendas, quatenus meliori cuidam fini subseruiunt, qui est animorum ad Deum colendum nostrorum præparationi, quia in iis nulla legitimi Dei cultus pars ponen-da est. Nam quum sint mediæ, & per se ἀδιάφορα, & bonæ & malæ esse possunt, prout illius animus & finis est, qui iis vtitur, sed neque à Deo ipso huiusmodi res præceptæ,& obseruari iussæ sunt, vt frustra in iis pietatem collocent homines. Quare de coniugio & cœlibatu, sic Paulus 1.Corinth.7.verf.27.Alligatus es vxori? ne quę-[?]re dissolutionem:Solutus es ab vxore ? ne quæore vxorem. Et quicquid illic idê disputat, propter instantem,vt ipse versu 26.diserte ait,necessitatem consulit, non autem vt laqueum hominum conscientiis, vel præceptum non nubendi cuiquam iniiciat.Bernard. Homil.1.Missus est.Laudabilis virtus virginitas:sed magis neccessaria humilitas.Illa consulitur,ista præcipitur.Potes denique sine virginitate saluari:sine humilitate nō potes. Sine humilitate, audeo dicere, virginitas Mariæ non placuisset. Quod ad ciborum abstinentiam, vel discrimen, ita idem Paulus Rom. 14.versu 3.Qui edit, non edentem ne pro nihilo habeto:& qui non edit,edentem ne condemnato.Esca enim nos non commendat Deo: neque est regnum Dei esca & potus ver.17.& 1.Corin. 8. versu 8. Quantæ tamen fuerint virginitatis & ieiunij laudes à Patribus scriptæ apparet, cum Basilius, Chrysostomus, Gregorius, tum Nazianzenus,tum Nysssenus,Ambrosius,Hieronymus, Augustinus etiam ipse in tertium vsq; cælum homines virgines & cœlibes, vel abstinentes quibusdam cibis extulerint.
units.tr: One may ask what occasion gave rise to the opposition to this opinion, which condemned the great praise already accepted for virginity and abstinence from food. For my part I see no other cause than that good men were already displeased by those immense praises of things that are in themselves indifferent [ἀδιάφορα], by which the prow and stern of our salvation were set, almost ignoring the blood of Christ. Marriage was despised and condemned, and finally the merits of our works were introduced, not without open blasphemy against the grace of God. Therefore people began to debate how great these things were, and what power they had for our salvation. From such debates it became clear that in themselves they have no weight for the forgiveness of our sins. They may be counted useful only so far as they serve a better end, which is the preparation of our minds to worship God, since no part of the lawful worship of God lies in them. For they are intermediate and in themselves indifferent, and may be good or bad according to the mind and purpose of the one who uses them. Nor has God himself prescribed or commanded such things to be observed, so that men should not place their piety in them in vain. Concerning marriage and celibacy, Paul says in 1 Corinthians 7:27: "Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek a dissolution. Are you loosed from a wife? Do not seek a wife." Whatever else he discusses there, he gives this advice, as he plainly says in verse 26, because of the present necessity, not to cast a snare on men's consciences or to lay down a rule that no one may marry. Bernard, Homily 1 on "Missus est": "Virginity is a praiseworthy virtue, but humility is more necessary. The former is counselled, the latter is commanded. In the end you may be saved without virginity, but not without humility. Without humility, I dare to say, the virginity of Mary would not have pleased God." As to abstinence from food, or the distinction of foods, Paul says the same in Romans 14:3: "Let him who eats not despise him who eats, and let him who eats not judge him who eats. For food does not commend us to God." And in verse 17: "The kingdom of God is not food and drink." Also 1 Corinthians 8:8. Yet how great the praises of virginity and fasting were in the writings of the Fathers appears from the fact that Basil, Chrysostom, Gregory, Gregory of Nazianzus, Gregory of Nyssa, Ambrose, Jerome, and even Augustine himself, raised virgins and celibates, or those abstaining from certain foods, up to the third heaven.

units.la: Cur Iouinianum hæreticum esse censeant Patres, nisi fortasse propter hoc vnum caput, quæri potest.Quod vt facilius intelligatur,illius hypotheses recensêo.
units.tr: One may ask why the Fathers judged Jovinian a heretic, unless perhaps because of this one head. To make this easier to understand, I will set out his hypotheses.

units.la: Peccata omnia inter se paria esse. Hoc quidem Stoicorum dogma, vel potius deliriũ fuit, quemadmodum Cicero, Plutarchus, & Diogenes Laertius tradunt. Quod cum verbi diuini veritate non consentit. Quamquam enim omnis peccati authoramentum est mors, eaque æterna, vt docet Paulus Rom. 6. versu 23. fitque peccatum quodlibet ἀνομία[?], 1. Ioannis 3. versu 4. & qui in vno peccat, omnium reus fit censendus, Iacobi 2. versu 10. certum est peccata alia aliis grauiora etiam à Deo quoque definiri, quod in Achami peccato apparet, vbi circumstantiæ à Deo ipso enumerantur, quæ augent delictum, Iosue 7. versu 11. & Ezechiel. 16, aliud exemplum exstat. Nam ab eadem meta longius recedi ab vno quàm ab alio potest. Sed fortasse hoc nō sen sit Iouinianus: sed quum, vt tradit Thomas Aquinas in libro Contra detrahent. Regul. cap. 6, Nullum viduarum vel virginum maius esse, propter cœlibatum, meritum, quàm coniugum, doceret & defenderet, ex hoc ipsius dicto aduersarij colligebant, ergo paria esse omnium merita: & si paria merita, ergo peccata paria & æqualia. Itaque hæc fuit tantum ἀκουλιστωεις[?], quæ à virginitatis præconibus ficbat: non autem ipsius Iouiniani sententia. Sic enim multa aduersus quosdam absurda collecta sunt artificiosè, vt eorum & nomen & doctrina inuidia apud Ecclesiam premeretur, & grauaretur.
units.tr: First hypothesis: all sins are equal to one another. This was indeed a dogma of the Stoics, or rather a delirium, as Cicero, Plutarch and Diogenes Laertius report. It does not agree with the truth of the divine word. For although death, and eternal death, is the wages of every sin, as Paul teaches in Romans 6:23, and any sin is lawlessness (1 John 3:4), and whoever offends in one point is guilty of all (James 2:10), it is certain that some sins are heavier than others, and God himself defines them so. This appears in the sin of Achan, where God himself enumerates the circumstances that aggravate the offence (Joshua 7:11). Another example is in Ezekiel 16. For one may depart farther from the same goal by one sin than by another. But perhaps Jovinian did not hold this view. When, as Thomas Aquinas reports in his book Against the Detractors, chapter 6, he taught and defended that no widows or virgins had greater merit on account of celibacy than married people, his opponents drew this inference from his words: therefore the merits of all are equal, and if the merits are equal, then the sins are equal too. So this was only an inference, drawn artificially by the advocates of virginity, and not the opinion of Jovinian himself. Many absurdities were thus cleverly gathered against certain men, so that both their name and their teaching would be pressed down and burdened by the hatred of the Church.

units.la: 2 Hypothesis, Homines post Baptismum non peccare. Hoc si ita simpliciter dixit Iouinianus, plane errauit. Sin vero vt operum & cœlibatus merita (per quæ peccata deleri docent Monachi) tolleret, voluit quæ à Christianis peccata committuntur, ea à Christo deleri, neque iam pec-cata cata propter ipsius sanguinem censeri, non video cur damnari debuerit. Peccare vero homines Christianos etiam post Baptismum, docet cum Ioannes priore epistola, capite 1. versu 8. tum haec a Christo instituta precatio, Matthaei 6. Dimitte nobis debita nostra.
units.tr: 2 Hypothesis: that men do not sin after baptism. If Jovinian said this simply, as stated, he plainly erred. But if he meant to remove the merits of works and of celibacy (through which the monks teach that sins are blotted out), and meant that the sins Christians commit are blotted out by Christ, and are no longer counted as sins on account of his blood, I do not see why he should have been condemned. That Christians sin even after baptism, John teaches in his first epistle, chapter 1, verse 8, and so does the prayer instituted by Christ himself, Matthew 6: "Forgive us our debts."

units.la: ʒ Coniugium caelibatui, & nuptias virginitati adaequabat, tum quod utrumque per se est ἀδιάφορον[?], nullaque veri cultus Dei pars: tum etiam quod ex nimiis istis virginitatis praeconiis, coniugium non tantum in contemptum, sed in odium Christianorum adductum erat, adeo ut qui coniuges essent, in carne viuere dicerentur, & Deo placere non posse censerentur, atque etiam ab impio Syricio Romano episcopo, iam tum tales pronuntiati essent. Praecessit enim Syricius aetatem Iouiniani. Ambrosius quidem libr. 9. epist. 80, & 81. iam sui seculi falsae opinioni tanquam tyranico imperio cedens, Iouinianum damnat, & Syricium laudat: sed plus posse apud nos debet veritas verbi Dei; quam vllius hominis authoritas.
units.tr: 3 Jovinian made marriage equal to celibacy and wedlock equal to virginity, both because each in itself is indifferent [ἀδιάφορον] and neither is any part of the true worship of God, and also because, from those excessive praises of virginity, marriage had been brought into contempt among Christians, indeed into hatred, so that those who were married were said to live in the flesh and were judged unable to please God. Indeed, the impious Siricius, bishop of Rome, had already pronounced such people so before Jovinian's time, for Siricius preceded Jovinian's age. Ambrose, in book 9, letters 80 and 81, yielding to the false opinion of his own age as if to a tyrant's rule, does indeed condemn Jovinian and praise Siricius. But the truth of God's word ought to carry more weight among us than the authority of any man.

units.la: Hoc cur erroneum sit, neque Hieronymus infestissimus coniugij osor & hostis, & pene Manichaeanus, vel Tatianus docet, neque alius quisquam veterum probauit. Quod enim ait Paulus, melius esse nubere, quam uri, non euincit malas esse nuptias, quod tamen affirmat, & colligit Hieronymus, aduersus quem lucu-lenter Theodorus Beza in libr. De polygamia, & diuortio, in contrariam partem vere dispu-tauit. Vera certe est haec Augustini sententia, lib. De bono coniugali, cap. 8. Coniugium non sic dicimus bonum, ut in fornicationis comparationem fit bonum, alioquin duo mala erunt, quorum alterum peius. Sicut autem iciuniis sacrilegorum meliora sunt prandia iustorum: ita nuptiæ fidelium, virginitati anteponuntur impiorum. Veruntamen neque prandium ieiunio, sed iustitia sacrilegio: neque nuptiæ virginitati, sed fides impietati præfertur. Denique idem Augustin. lib. Quæst. Veteris & Noui testamenti. quæst. 127. versutos & hypocritas appellat qui istas virginitatis laudes inuehunt, quas aperte Satanæ præstigias esse vult. Mariam Domini no stri matrem non negauit esse, & permansisse vir ginem Iouinianus, & sine viri coitu vixisse, quod Heluidius fecit: sed negauit tantum non abrupta ea pelle, quæ virginitatis indicium esse dicitur, peperisse Christum: quin Hieronymus ipse Christum cruentatum ex virginis aluo exiisse fatetur. Sed ad prægrauandam Iouiniani sententiam hæc addita sunt. Et vulgo ita dicebant Patres, Virgo peperit, quia virgo concepit, & nō seruato rerum ordine ex integro matris corpore, integrum corpus Christus assumpsit. Augustinus contra Felician. Arianum, capite 8.
units.tr: Neither Jerome, the most hostile enemy and detractor of marriage, almost a Manichaean, nor Tatian teaches why this is erroneous, nor has any other of the ancients approved it. For what Paul says, that it is better to marry than to burn, does not prove that marriage is evil, although Jerome affirms this and draws that conclusion. Theodore Beza, in his book On Polygamy and Divorce, has argued brilliantly and truly against Jerome on the opposite side. Certainly the true opinion is that of Augustine, in the book On the Good of Marriage, chapter 8: "We do not call marriage good in such a way that it is good only in comparison with fornication; otherwise there would be two evils, one worse than the other. But just as the feasts of the righteous are better than the fasts of the sacrilegious, so the marriages of the faithful are preferred to the virginity of the impious. Yet neither is a feast preferred to fasting, but righteousness to sacrilege; nor marriage to virginity, but faith to impiety." Finally, the same Augustine, in the Questions on the Old and New Testament, question 127, calls those who promote these praises of virginity crafty hypocrites, and wishes plainly that they are the deceits of Satan. Jovinian did not deny that Mary was the mother of our Lord and remained a virgin, and lived without intercourse with a man, as Helvidius did. He denied only that she bore Christ without that membrane being torn away which is said to be the sign of virginity. Indeed Jerome himself confesses that Christ came out of the virgin's womb bloodied. But these things were added to weigh down Jovinian's opinion. And the Fathers commonly spoke thus: "The virgin bore because the virgin conceived"; and, the order of things not being kept, Christ took a whole body from the whole body of his mother. Augustine, against Felician the Arian, chapter 8.

units.la: Ieiunia, & huiusmodi corporales exercitationes, quas Paulus vocat, 1. Timoth. 4. versu 8. spernebat: imo res medias pro ἀδιαφορεῖς habebat. Ieiunia non spernebat necessaria, & quæ essent animorum ad Deum precandum præparationes, & non superstitiosa, qualia sunt in Papatu hodie omnia. Virginitas autem primum res fuit & ad tempus suscepta, & libera etiam in fœminis, vt docet Cyprianus: pòst autem tanta illius admiratio homines cœpit, vt res in votum perperpetuum abierit. Primus autem Basilius virgines instituit consecrare, ut ait Ruffinus libro 2.capite 13.
units.tr: He despised fasts and similar bodily exercises, which Paul calls "of little profit," 1 Timothy 4, verse 8; indeed he held them to be things indifferent. He did not despise fasts that were necessary and were preparations of the soul for prayer to God, and that were not superstitious, such as nearly all of them are in Papacy today. Virginity, however, was at first something undertaken for a time, and was free even for women, as Cyprian teaches. But afterwards such great admiration for it seized men that the thing turned into a perpetual vow. Basil was the first to institute the consecration of virgins, as Rufinus says in book 2, chapter 13.

units.la: CAP. LXXXIII.
units.tr: CAP. LXXXIII.

units.la: Arabici qui fuerint. Erroris eorum caput unum enumeratum.
units.tr: The Arabians: who they were. One article of their error is set out.

units.la: CVM Eusebij historiam perscrutatum essem, cui Ruffinus a se in Latinam linguā translata subsequentium etiam temporum duos libros addidit, non inveni aliquam haeresin, quam non legerim apud istos, nisi quam in sexto libro ponit Eusebius; narrans eam extitisse in Arabia. Itaque hos haereticos, quoniam nullum eorum ponit authorem, {1} Arabicos possumus nuncupare, qui dixerunt {2} animas cum corporibus mori, atque dissolui, & in fine seculi utrumque resurgere. Sed hos disputatione Origenis praesentis, & eos alloquentis, celerrime dicit fuisse correctos.
units.tr: When I had carefully examined the history of Eusebius, to which Rufinus added in his Latin translation two books covering later times, I found no heresy that I had not read of among these writers, except the one Eusebius records in his sixth book, reporting that it arose in Arabia. Since he names no author for these heretics, we may call them {1} Arabians, who said {2} that souls die together with the bodies and are dissolved, and that both rise again at the end of the age. But he says that these were very quickly corrected by the disputation of Origen, who was then present and addressed them.

units.la: {1} Arabicos possumus.) Ferax haereseon Arabia, quemadmodum & illi vicina Aegyptus. Uti enim serpentes utraque regio alit, humano generi nocentissimos: sic utraque protulit dogmata saluti animorum nostrorum prorsus pestifera: quale fuit hoc Arabicorum sive Arabiorum haereticorum. Utroq; enim modo dici possunt, etiam Suida teste. sed & Arabes quoque. A loco vero, ubi primum nati sunt, sic denominantur, qui est Arabia illa infelix, atque vasta illa deferta, in quibus mons Sina (qui nunc S. Catharinæ à monasterio illic condito vocatur) situs est. Eâ denique ipsa est quæ Ægypto vicina, & Petræa ab oppido Petra denominata est. A dogmate vero dicuntur à Damasceno in libro De hæresibus Ὑπνοψυχῖται, id est, ad verbum, Animimortales, Tnetopsychitæ, vt est in vulgari versione. Cœpit autem hæc hæresis sub Philippo Imperatore & Antherò Episcopo Romani circa annum à Christo passo 217. Origene iam voto & celebri, qui ad hos hæ:eticos confutandos à synodo illic collecta euocatus est, vt tradunt Eusebius libro sexto capite 37. & Nicephor. libro 5. capite 23. tantumque disputando effecit, vt non modò conquiescerent, sed etiam mutarent sententiam, errorémque suum reuocarent. Itaque statim siluit & extincta est hæc hæreticorum secta, & penè in sola Arabia grassata est, quanquam illius Isidorus meminit, sed tantùm ex hoc Augustini loco illi nota fuit. Quidam tamen sentiunt hos ipsos diutissimè permansisse, nimirum vsque ad Constantis, qui fuit Heraclij nepos, imperium, quod incidit in annum à passo Christo 710. quos se latissimè in Syriam & Persidem ipsam postea diffudisse aiunt, & suo de animorum mortalitate errori Monophysitarum delirium addidisse. Denique hos ipsos esse, qui à Paulo Diacono lib.19.Historiar. Charurgitæ nominantur, mutata iam nota & odiosa illa Arabicorum appellatione. Sed repugnat tum ratio temporis, tum meliorum auctorum, nempe Eusebij & Nicephori authoritas, qui hos statim eradicatos scribunt. Denique variæ ex eadem Arabia hæresis natæ sunt, non tantùm hæc vna, quemadmodum postea Mahumetana, cuius iam tum femina iaciebantur, & sterñebantur in ea regione fundamenta, quando gentem Saracenorum quæ illic habitat, scs per infestissimè solitam esse persequi eos qui Christi nomen profitebantur, scribit Eufeb. libro 6. cap. 42. Sed & hæresis Collyridianorum illic quoque post hos Arabicos nata est, quemadmodum scribit Epiphanius, vel ex Scythia & superiore Thracia, in eas regiones delata illic ita pullulauit, vt totam gentem impia idololatria & superstitione imbuerct. Hi vero Collyridiani ἀπὸ τῆς κολλυρίδος [?], id est, torta panis & tortilis placentæ genere, quam Mariæ virgini super stitiose offerunt, sunt dicti, & primum sub Theodosio maiore Imperatore, & Syricio Episcopo Roman. circa annum à Christo passo 357 noti, sed tamen etiam à Ioanne Damasceno, in lib. De hærefib. commemorati. Dogmate sunt prorsus hæreticis Antidicomarianis contrarij. Hi enim B. Mariam prorsus de suo gradu deijciunt. Isti vero Collyridiani, dum eam colunt, in Dei numen & locum euehunt, suntque, vt ait Epiphanius apertissimè, idololatræ, & hæc eorum hæresis εἰδωλολατρίας [?]. Vnus enim Deus Pater, Filius & Spiritus sanctus colendus est: Μαριὰμ ἡ μήτηρ [?], ait ille, θεοτοκείτω [?]. Nec enim minus peccant qui τὴν Μαριὰμ ἀξιάζουσιν [?], ait idem, quàm qui infamant & vituperant. Illa quidem Christi mater est, nō suo tamen merito, sed mera Dei gratia: & ad cæterorum hominū morem ex viri & mulieris semine & coitu nata, ne bcnis quidem Angelis par aut æqualis, nedum Deo ipsi. Quæ omnia sunt Epiphanij. Quo magis miror quid venerit Papistis in mentem, ut eam etiam ὑπερδουλείᾳ[?] quadam colendam esse tanquam ex Patrum sententia dicerent. Fuit autem Collyridianorum cultus qui Mariæ exhibebatur huiusmodi, & leuis præ hodierno, nempe quòd stata anni die tortas & placentas quas Græci κολλυρίδας[?] vocât, in honorem Mariæ virginis cuidam puellæ in sella curuli vel thensa velo tecta sedenti offerrent. Quod imprimis fiebat à mulieribus, quia hic sexus est mirum in modum, ait Epiphanius, hebes & superstitiosus. Quod cùm damnet idem ille Epiphan. quid faceret si immanem idololatriam & cultum, qui nunc ei defertur, vel videret, vel solùm audiret?
units.tr: {1} Arabians we may call them.) Arabia was as fertile in heresies as neighbouring Egypt. Just as both regions breed serpents most harmful to the human race, so both have put forth doctrines utterly deadly to the salvation of our souls, and of this kind was the heresy of the Arabic, or Arabian, heretics. Both forms may be used, as Suidas attests, and also Arabes. They take their name from the place where they first arose, that unhappy and vast Arabian desert in which Mount Sinai lies (now called St Catherine's, from the monastery founded there). This is the Arabia next to Egypt, which is called Petraea from the town of Petra. Damascene, in his book On Heresies, calls them from their doctrine Hypnopsychitae [Ὑπνοψυχῖται], that is, word for word, "soul-sleepers", or Tnetopsychitae [Θνητοψυχῖται], "mortal-souled", as in the common version. The heresy began under the Emperor Philip and Bishop Anterus of Rome, about the year 217 after Christ's passion, when Origen was already old and famous. He was summoned there by a synod gathered to refute these heretics, as Eusebius (book 6, chapter 37) and Nicephorus (book 5, chapter 23) relate, and by his disputation he achieved so much that they not only ceased but also changed their opinion and retracted their error. At once this sect fell silent and was extinguished, and it raged almost only in Arabia. Isidore does mention it, but he knew of it only from this passage of Augustine. Some think, however, that these same people lasted a very long time, indeed until the reign of Constans, grandson of Heraclius, which falls in the year 710 after Christ's passion. They say that afterwards they spread widely into Syria and Persia itself, and added to their error about the mortality of souls the madness of the Monophysites. Finally, these are the ones whom Paul the Deacon, in book 19 of his Histories, calls Charurgitae, the hated name Arabian having now been changed. But both the chronology and the authority of the better writers, Eusebius and Nicephorus, who write that they were at once uprooted, contradict this. Various heresies arose from the same Arabia, not only this one. Later the Mohammedan heresy arose, whose seeds were already being sown and whose foundations were being laid in that region, when Eusebius (book 6, chapter 42) writes that the Saracen people who live there were accustomed to persecute most savagely those who professed the name of Christ. The heresy of the Collyridians also arose there after these Arabians, as Epiphanius writes, either brought into those regions from Scythia and upper Thrace; it sprouted there so that it imbued the whole people with impious idolatry and superstition. These Collyridians are named from κολλυρίς [κολλυρίδος], that is, a kind of twisted bread and curled cake, which they superstitiously offer to the Virgin Mary. They were first known under the Emperor Theodosius the Elder and Siricius, Bishop of Rome, about the year 357 after Christ's passion, but John Damascene also mentions them in his book On Heresies. In doctrine they are utterly opposed to the Antidicomarianites, for those cast the Blessed Mary entirely down from her rank. The Collyridians, while worshipping her, raise her into the divinity and place of God. As Epiphanius says most plainly, they are idolaters, and their heresy is one of idolatry [εἰδωλολατρία]. "God alone is to be worshipped: the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Let Mary the mother," he says, "be called God-bearer [θεοτόκος]." For, says the same author, those who honour Mary [τὴν Μαριὰμ ἀξιάζουσιν] sin no less than those who slander and disparage her. She is indeed the mother of Christ, but not by her own merit, rather by the sheer grace of God; and she was born, like other men, from the seed and coition of man and woman, not equal or even comparable to the good angels, much less to God himself. These are all words of Epiphanius. So I wonder all the more what came into the minds of the Papists, that they should say she is to be worshipped with a certain hyperdulia [ὑπερδουλεία], as if from the judgment of the Fathers. The worship of Mary that the Collyridians offered was of this kind, and milder than today's: on a fixed day of the year they offered twisted cakes and flat cakes, which the Greeks call κολλυρίδες [κολλυρίδας], to a certain girl seated on a curule chair or litter covered with a veil, in honour of the Virgin Mary. This was done chiefly by women, because this sex is, as Epiphanius says, remarkably weak-minded and superstitious. Since this same Epiphanius condemns it, what would he have done had he seen, or only heard of, the monstrous idolatry and worship that is now paid to her?

units.la: 2 Dixerunt animas.) Nazareorum surculus fuit hæc hęresis, qui hominum & pecudum animas eiusdem esse naturæ & essentiæ dixerunt. Itaque etiam humanas animas mortales esse voluerút manifesto errore. Nam quoad bestiarum animas, illæ quidem sunt mortales, vt est Psalm. 49. vers. 21. Humanæ verò non item, sed Dei gratia & sustentatione manent immortales, & post hanc mortem redeunt ad Deum qui dedit illas. Ecclesiast. 12. vers. 7. Matth. 10. versu 28. Unde Deus dicitur Deus spirituum & animorum nostrorum, quos ad se recipit, non dissoluit autem per corporis nostri mortem, Hebr. 12. vers. 9, 1. Petr. 4. versu 19. Quòd si animæ non moriuntur, nec resurgunt. Neque nos etiam credimus animorum, sed carnis, id est, corporum tantùm, vt Paulus ipse explicat 1. Corinth. 15. resurrectio-nem. nem.Duplex vero locus videtur ab istis ad impim-pij sui dogmatis defensionem prolatus. Primus ex Genes.6.vers.3:2.v. 7. hominem esse carnem, & sumptum de pulvere terrae. Respondeo vero utrumque locum de corpore tantum hominis, non de anima sumendum & intelligendum esse, argumento vers.19. cap.3: Eccles.12.versu 7. Alter locus est ex 1. Timoth. 6. versu 16, Solus Deus habet immortalitatem. Respondet Theodoret. Dialog.3. qui dicitur Impatibilis, Substā-tia quidem solus, non autem communicatione solus immortalis est, id est, per se suaque vi & propria solus Deus est immortalis, non autem omnino solus immortalis. Nam Angeli & humanae animae Dei beneficio & gratia sunt immortales, Auguft. lib. contra Felicia. Arian. cap. 7. & 15. & libr. 6. cap. 6. de Trinit. & lib. 7. cap. 6. de Genesi ad literam. Cur autem hunc errorem facile arriperent Arabes, ratio est, quod moribus dissolutissimis fuere & homines praedę & latrociniis assueti, magnique totius numinis contemptores. Unde vetus proverbium apud Suidam, Αἰγύπτιος αὐλητής, Arabicus tibicen. Huic autem errori affines sunt Psychopannychitę nostri temporis, qui etsi animas cum corporibus dissolui vel mori non putant: eas tamen cum corporibus in sepulchris suis dormire & stertere ad diem usque extremi iudicij, & novissimae resurrectionis impie afferunt & docent, contra illud Christi, Hodie mecum eris in paradiso, Luc.23.versu 43. & illud Pauli, Cupio dissolui & esse cum Christo, Philipp.1.vers. 23. Quae certe sententia prope est, ut animorum humanorum mortalitatem inducat. Tanti est nimirum vanis animi sui speculationibus indulgere, aut sese vitiis, lasciuiaque dedere, quod vtrique & Arabici, & Psychopannychitæ (aduersus quos eruditissimè piæ memoriæ D. Caluinus scripsit) fecerunt.
units.tr: 2 They said souls.) This heresy was an offshoot of the Nazarenes, who said that the souls of men and of beasts are of the same nature and essence. So they also held, with manifest error, that human souls are mortal. As to the souls of beasts, they are indeed mortal, as Psalm 49:21 says. Human souls, however, are not so; by God's grace and sustaining power they remain immortal, and after death return to God who gave them (Ecclesiastes 12:7; Matthew 10:28). Hence God is called the God of our spirits and souls, whom he receives to himself and does not dissolve at the death of our body (Hebrews 12:9; 1 Peter 4:19). If souls do not die, neither do they rise; nor do we believe in a resurrection of souls, but of the flesh, that is, of bodies only, as Paul himself explains in 1 Corinthians 15. Two passages seem to have been brought forward by them in defence of their impious doctrine. The first is Genesis 6:3 and 2:7, that man is flesh and taken from the dust of the earth. I reply that both passages must be taken and understood of the body of man only, not of the soul, as the argument of Ecclesiastes 3:19 shows. The other passage is 1 Timothy 6:16, "God alone has immortality." Theodoret answers in his Dialogue 3, which is called Impassible: God alone is immortal in substance, but not alone immortal by communication; that is, God alone is immortal through himself, by his own power and nature, but not absolutely alone immortal. For angels and human souls are immortal by God's benefit and grace (Augustine, against Felix the Arian, chapters 7 and 15; On the Trinity, book 6, chapter 6; On Genesis according to the Letter, book 7, chapter 6). The reason the Arabians readily seized upon this error is that they were most dissolute in their morals, accustomed to plunder and robbery, and great despisers of the whole deity. Hence the old proverb in Suidas: "an Egyptian flute-player, an Arabian piper." Akin to this error are our contemporary Psychopannychists, who, though they do not think that souls are dissolved or die with the bodies, nevertheless impiously assert and teach that souls sleep and snore with their bodies in the tombs until the day of the last judgment and the final resurrection. This is against Christ's words, "Today you will be with me in paradise" (Luke 23:43), and Paul's, "I desire to depart and be with Christ" (Philippians 1:23). This opinion certainly comes close to introducing the mortality of human souls. So great is the harm of indulging in vain speculations of one's own mind, or of giving oneself over to vice and wantonness, as both the Arabians and the Psychopannychists did; against the latter the most learned Calvin, of pious memory, wrote.

units.la: HAERESES AB IPSO Augustino additæ.
units.tr: Heresies added by Augustine himself.

units.la: CAP. LXXXIIII.
units.tr: CHAP. LXXXIV.

units.la: Aliæ hæreses, è quibus prima est Heluidianorum, & quod illius dogma fuerit.
units.tr: Other heresies, of which the first is that of the Helvidians, and what that sect's doctrine was.

units.la: IAM nunc illæ commemorandæ sunt hæreses, quæ à nobis non apud istos reperta sunt, sed in recordationem nostram quomodocunque venerunt. Heluidiani exorti ab Heluidio ita virginitati Mariæ contradicunt, vt eam post Christum alios etiam filios de viro suo Ioseph peperisse contendant: sed mirum ni istos, prætermisso Heluidij nomine, Antidicomaritas Epiphanius appellat.
units.tr: Now let me recall those heresies which were not found by us among them, but which have come to mind in some way.
