The Helvidians, who arose from Helvidius, so contradict the virginity of Mary that they maintain she bore other sons after Christ by her husband Joseph; but it is remarkable that Epiphanius, passing over the name of Helvidius, calls these men Antidicomarites.

units.la: 1 Heluidiani exorti.) Transitio est. Iam enim præter eas hæreses, quas tum ex Eusebij & Epiphanij libris, tum etiam Philastri commentario decerpsit, descripsitque Augustinus, alias affert ab illis omnibus praetermissas, à se autem collectas. E quibus prima est haec Heluidianorum, aduersus quam animosus Virginitatis defensor Hieron. scripsit, etsi verè improbanda est Heluidij sententia. De qua nunc nihil est necesse pluribus agere, cùm supra cap.56.in Antidicomarianis de ea sit abundè disputatum. Ad quem etiam locum nos remittit Augustinus.vbi praetermisimus illud quod nunc videtur addendum, Epiphanium in Antidicomar.scribere Iosephum ex alia vxore & priore quàm Maria sex liberos sustulisse. Itaque venio ad alias.
units.tr: 1 The Helvidians arose.) This is a transition. For apart from those heresies which he gathered and described from the books of Eusebius and Epiphanius, and also from the commentary of Philaster, Augustine brings forward others omitted by all of them, which he himself collected. Of these the first is this heresy of the Helvidians, against which the zealous defender of virginity, Jerome, wrote, although Helvidius's opinion is truly to be rejected. There is no need to say more about it now, since it was fully discussed above in chapter 56, among the Antidicomarianites. Augustine also refers us to that place, where we passed over what now seems worth adding: that Epiphanius, in the Antidicomarianites, writes that Joseph had fathered six children by another wife, prior to Mary. So I come to the others.

units.la: CAP. LXXXV.
units.tr: CHAPTER 85.

units.la: Paterniani siue Venustiani haeretici quid senserint.
units.tr: What the heretics called Paternians or Venustians held.

units.la: Paterniani{1} inferiores partes humani corporis non a Deo, sed a diabolo factas opinantur, & omnium ex illis partibus flagitiorum licentiam tribuentes impurissimè viuunt. Hos etiam Venustianos quidam vocant.
units.tr: The Paternians hold that the lower parts of the human body were made not by God but by the devil, and, granting themselves licence for every kind of shameful act with those parts, they live in the most impure way. Some also call them Venustians.

units.la: 1 Paterniani inferiores. ) Ignota pene haeresis & minuta: quae tamen ex pessimis fontibus Eunomianorum, & Patricianorum haereticorum profluxit, quemadmodum apparet ex dogmatis cōsensione.{1} Appellatur vero his nominibus, Paterniani à Paterno quodam ignobili authore, & hoc nomine meminit eorum Isidorus. Venustiani, vt hic scribit Augustin. à scelere & la-
units.tr: 1 Paternians, the lower parts. An almost unknown and insignificant heresy, yet one that flowed from the worst sources, the Eunomians and the Patricians, as is clear from the agreement of their doctrines. They are called Paternians after a certain obscure author, Paternus, and Isidore mentions them under this name. Venustians, as Augustine writes here, from crime and lasciviousness, to which they are wholly given.

units.la: {1} Paterniani: the reference mark stands aster the first word of the italic paragraph and beside the numbered section. sciuia,cui sunt addictissimi.A Venere enim(quā impudicissimarum voluptatum & actionum deam & patronam Christiani homines semper oderunt & merito infamarunt,vt apparet ex Nicephoro libr.14. cap. 49. & ex eo quòd Veneris templum ad Libanum & Heliopolin Christiani funditus ante reliquorum deorum fana euerte-runt,vt idem tradit lib.8.cap.33.&Sozomen.lib.5.cap.10.)à Venere,inquam,dicti sunt Venustia ni ab illius seculi hominibus Latinè loqui stu-dentibus,qui aptius Veneriani vel Venerij dicerentur. Quanquam enim,vt tradit M.Tull.à Venere venustas deducta est:aliud tamen est venu-stas (quae est corporis pulchritudo & apta quaedam inter se membrorum conformatio) aliud autem Venus & libido,à qua istos appellare,nō autem à venustate veteres illi voluerunt. Dicitur quidem Venus hortis praesse, & Venus pro o-leribus apud Varronem accipitur. Denique Venus, vt in suis in Festum Pompeium commentariis annotat vndecunque doctissimus, Iosephus Scaliger, à veniendo nominata est, quasi dea peregrina, non autem à turpi aliqua actione: tamen vsus ratioque etiam profanae Mytho-logię,vt docet lib.2.Mythol.Fulgentius, ita obtinuit,vt pro spurcissimarum libidinum dea Venus haberetur,à qua salaces isti homines Vene-rij,& Veneriani siue Venustiani sunt appella-ti. Videntur autem hi ipsi à Ioanne Damasceno ἠθικοπροσκόπται[?]. i. morum & honestatis irrisores dicti,Ethicoprofcoptae:quòd omnem vitae sanctae instituendae rationem irriderent & spernerent, & Cynicorum more lasciua & obscœna quæque agere non erubescerent. Nec vero mirum est unam & eandem hæresin alio a Græcis, & Latinis nomine vocari, quemadmodum in Helvidianis docuit Augustinus, quos Antidicoma-ritas appellant Græci. Cœpisse vero videtur hoc hominum genus & sœcta post Eunomianos & Patricianos hæreticos, ex quibus utrisque, uti dixi, conflata est sub Arcadio Imperatore, post annum a Christo passo 387. quæ quandiu inter illius ætatis homines fuerit, non est annotatum. Certe nostro sæculo & memoria impurissimus quidam nebulo G. Postellus Sorbonista-rum Parisiensium delicia, hunc blasphemum error em rorem impudenter quidè, sed tamen liberè Lutetiæ renouauit, dixitque nos a Christo ab umbilico tantum ad caput salvos esse factos: reliquas autem nostri partes & inferiores umbilico non a Dei Filio, sed a Ioanna quadam scorto ipsius (quam etiam incestuosus homo matrem suam appellabat) redemptas liberatasque esse. Quale opinionum portentum canem illum etiam publicè in media Academia euomuisse, sciunt omnes, qui eum profitentem Cl. Ptolemæi 100. canonas mecum Lutetiæ audierunt. Paternianis autem adiungunt quidam Symmachianos tanquam eiusdem dogmatis & erroris socios, qui mihi verius & commodius videntur ad Ebionitas vel Photinianos, quorum venena aliis propinarunt, ipsiqúe biberunt, posse referri. Christum enim negarunt Deum esse Deique Filium: sed tantum hominem ex Iosephi mariti & Mariæ coniugis coitu ad cæterorum hominum morem natum, ut scribit Eufeb. lib. 6. cap. 17. Præterea sunt istis nostris Paternianis ætate longè priores. Coeperunt enim non, vt quidam volunt,sub Theodosio maiore, sed antea,quando Symmachus eorum author etiam ante Origenis tempora vixit & floruit, vt omnes fatentur, & sciunt. Paternianorum verò hypothesis hæc fuit, Inferiores humani corporis partes, qualis anus,penis,pedes,&c. (quòd tegerentur tanquâ obscœnæ,vt docet Paulus 1.Corinth.12.verf.23. nisi fortasse Cynici & inuerecùdi esse volumus) non à Deo creatas esse, sed à diabolo. Hi sanè Adamiftis hæreticis plane fuerunt contrarij & disimiles. Nam Adamiftæ quòd nullum inter humani corporis membra aspectu & contrectatione turpe & obscœnum ducerent, nudi agebant: hi verò quòd nimiam in quibusdam membris nostris fœditatem agnoscant, negant illa esse Dei opera:quia quæcunque fecit Deus, illa sunt & bona & aspectu iucunda. Vtrique falluntur.Nam ab initio quidem & ante peccatum fuerunt honesta omnia humani corporis membra: post peccatum autem fœditas quædã & inhonestus aspectus in iis membris remansit, quibus ad libidinem explendam vtimur, vt docet Augusti[?]lib.4.contra Iulian.Pelagian.cap. 16.Sed longius progressi sunt Paterniani. Cum enim inferiores hominis partes diabolo tanquam opifici tribuissent, in omne se fœdæ libidinis genus,quæ istis membris perageretur, veluti, fcortationis & ventris ingluuiei profuderunt, vnde sunt Venustiani appellati. Quare & isti, vti plerique alij hæretici, vitiis voluptatibúsque corporis habenas laxarunt,qui propter-ca
units.tr: {1} Paternians: the reference mark stands after the first word of the italic paragraph and beside the numbered section. They were called Venustians by the men of that age who studied to speak Latin, from Venus, whom Christians have always hated and rightly branded as the goddess and patroness of the most shameless pleasures and deeds, as appears from Nicephorus, book 14, chapter 49, and from the fact that Christians utterly overthrew the temple of Venus at Lebanon and Heliopolis before the shrines of the other gods, as the same author relates in book 8, chapter 33, and Sozomen, book 5, chapter 10. Yet, as Cicero tells us, venustas is derived from Venus; but venustas (which is the beauty of the body and a certain fitting arrangement of the limbs one with another) is one thing, and Venus and lust are another, and it was from the latter, not from venustas, that the ancients meant to name these men. Venus is indeed said to preside over gardens, and in Varro Venus is taken to mean vegetables. Finally, as the most learned Joseph Scaliger notes in his commentaries on Festus Pompeius, Venus was named from venire, "to come", as a foreign goddess, and not from any shameful action; but usage and reason, even of profane mythology, as Fulgentius teaches in book 2 of his Mythologies, so prevailed that Venus was regarded as the goddess of the most filthy lusts, and from her these lewd men were called Venerians or Veneriani, that is, Venustians. Now these same men are, I think, called by John of Damascus ethicoproscoptae [ἠθικοπροσκόπται], that is, scorners of morals and of decency, because they mocked and despised every rule of holy living and were not ashamed to do lascivious and obscene things after the manner of the Cynics. Nor is it any wonder that one and the same heresy is called by one name by the Greeks and by another by the Latins, as Augustine taught concerning the Helvidians, whom the Greeks call Antidicomarites. This kind of men and sect seems to have begun after the heretics Eunomians and Patricians, out of which two, as I have said, it was compounded under the emperor Arcadius, after the year 387 from the passion of Christ; how long it lasted among the men of that age is not recorded. Certainly in our own century and memory, that most impure scoundrel G. Postellus, the darling of the Sorbonnists of Paris, shamelessly yet openly revived this blasphemous error at Lutetia, and said that we had been saved by Christ only from the navel upward, but that our other and lower parts had been redeemed and freed from the navel down not by the Son of God but by a certain prostitute, Joanna, whom that incestuous man even called his mother. All who heard him profess the hundred canons of the famous Ptolemy with me at Lutetia know what a monstrous opinion that dog once vomited publicly in the middle of the Academy. Some also join with the Paternians the Symmachians as companions of the same doctrine and error, but they seem to me more truly and suitably to be referred to the Ebionites or Photinians, whose poisons they administered to others and drank themselves. For they denied that Christ was God or the Son of God, but said He was only a man, born from the union of Joseph, his husband, and Mary, his wife, as ordinary men are born, as Eusebius writes in book 6, chapter 17. Moreover, they are far earlier in time than our Paternians. For they began not, as some wish, under Theodosius the Great, but earlier, when Symmachus, their author, lived and flourished even before the time of Origen, as all admit and know. The hypothesis of the Paternians was this: that the lower parts of the human body, such as the anus, the penis, the feet, and so on (which are covered as obscene, as Paul teaches in 1 Corinthians 12:23, unless perhaps we wish to be Cynics and shameless), were not created by God but by the devil. These men were plainly contrary and unlike the Adamite heretics. For the Adamites, because they did not think any member of the human body shameful or obscene to see or touch, went about naked; but these, because they recognised a great foulness in certain of our members, deny that they are the works of God, because whatever God made is both good and pleasing to the eye. Both are mistaken. For from the beginning, and before sin, all the members of the human body were honourable; but after sin a certain foulness and unseemly appearance remained in those members which we use to satisfy lust, as Augustine teaches in book 4 against Julian the Pelagian, chapter 16. But the Paternians went further. For when they had assigned the lower parts of man to the devil as their maker, they poured themselves into every kind of foul lust that is carried out with those members, such as fornication and gluttony of the belly; and from this they were called Venustians. Therefore these men, like many other heretics, let loose the reins of vices and bodily pleasures; and for this reason

units.la: [end] ea sunt non tantum ex aris Christianorum, sed ex universo hominum coetu & choro depellendi, & in porcorum haras & stabula detrudendi, ex Epicureorum potius hortis & schola, quàm ex sanctis Christianorum præceptis & disciplina profecti & nati, qui, ne nobis suis illis turpibus voluptatibus nauseam moveant, sunt plane dimittendi.
units.tr: [end] they must be expelled not only from the altars of Christians but from the whole assembly and choir of men, and thrust into the pig-pens and stables of swine; they arose and were born from the gardens and school of the Epicureans rather than from the holy precepts and discipline of the Christians; and, lest their shameful pleasures cause us nausea, they must simply be dismissed.

units.la: CAP. LXXXVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER LXXXVI.

units.la: Tertullianistæ cur sic dicti. Erroris autem eorum capita quatuor descripta.
units.tr: Why the Tertullianists were so called. Four heads of their error are set out.

units.la: E[?]rtullianistæ à Tertulliano{1}, cuius multa leguntur opuscula eloquentissimè scripta, usque ad nostrum tempus paulatim deficientes in extremis reliquiis durare potuerunt, in urbe Carthaginensi. Me autem ibi posito ante aliquot annos, quod etiam te meminisse arbitror, omni ex parte consumpti sunt. Paucissimi etiam, qui remanserunt, in Catholicam transierunt, suamque Basilicam, quæ nunc etiam notissima est, Catholicæ tradiderunt. Tertullianus ergo, sicut scripta eius indicant, animam dicit{2} immortalem quidem, sed eam effigiatum corpus esse contendit. Neque hanc tantum, sed ipsum etiam Deum corporeum esse dicit, licet non effigiatum. Nec tamen hinc hæreticus creditur factus. Posset enim quoquo modo putari ipsam naturam substantiamque diuinam corpus vocare:non tale corpus, cuius partes alia maiores,alia minores valeant vel debeant cogitari, qualia sunt omnia quae proprie dicimus corpora: quamuis[?] de anima tale aliquid sentiat:sed potuit, vt dixi, putari corpus Deum dicere,quia non est nihil, non est inanitas,non est corporis vel animae qualitas,sed vbique totus, & per locorum spatia nulla partitus, in sua tamen natura atque subsistentia immutabiliter permanet. Non ergo ideo est Tertullianus factus haereticus, sed quia transiens ad Cataphrygas, quos ante destruxerat, coepit etiam secundas nuptias contra Apostolicam doctrinam, tanquam stupra damnare: & postmodum etiam ab ipsis diuisus, sua conuenticula propagauit. Dicit sane ipse animas hominum peccatrices post mortem in daemones verti. Statum autem anima credit per traducem propagari.
units.tr: The Tertullianists, from Tertullian{1}, whose many very eloquently written little works are still read, managed to survive in the city of Carthage, slowly dwindling until our own time, and lingered in their last remnants. When I was stationed there some years ago, as I think you also remember, they had been wholly wiped out. The very few who remained passed over to the Catholic Church and handed over their meeting-house, which is still very well known today, to the Catholics. Tertullian, then, as his writings show, says that the soul is indeed immortal, but he maintains that it is a shaped body. He says not only this of the soul but also that God himself is corporeal, though not shaped. Yet he was not thought a heretic for this. For it could be supposed that by "body" he meant the divine nature and substance itself, not a body of the kind whose parts can be thought of as larger or smaller, as all things we properly call bodies are; although he did hold something of that sort about the soul. But, as I said, he could be thought to call God a body because God is not nothing, not emptiness, not a quality of a body or soul, but is wholly everywhere, divided into no parts across spaces of place, and yet remains unchangeably in his own nature and subsistence. So Tertullian did not become a heretic for this reason, but because, passing over to the Cataphrygians, whom he had earlier refuted, he began to condemn second marriages as fornication, contrary to apostolic doctrine; and afterwards, separated from them too, he spread his own little conventicles. He certainly also says that the souls of men, sinners after death, are turned into demons. He believes that the soul is propagated by traducianism.

units.la: Tertullianus quis fuerit, notius est ex Hieronymo, Augustino, Historia ecclesiastica, & ipsius adeo Tertulliani scriptis, doctisque in ea Beati Rhenani commentarijs, quàm vt explicari debeat. Carthaginensis fuit, Patre proconsulari & centurione natus, iuris ciuilis studijs primum addictus, in iisque clarus habitus, quemadmodum etiam Eusebius lib.2.Histor.cap.2.tradit, quando etiam hodie in corpore Pandectarum a Triboniano ex diuersis Iurisconsultis collectarum extant quaedam scriptorum & responsorum Tertulliani fragmenta docta & erudita. Sed experpetuo ipsius stylo & dicendi genere summum fuisse Iurisconsultum apparet. A studijs vero Iuris ciuilis & Romani.i.humani, ad diuini iuris cognitionem.i. Theologiam traduɛtus,in ea plurimum profecit, adeò quidem vt post Victorem & Apollonium Latinorum Patrum & scriptorum primus celebretur,quemadmodum Hieronymus scribit, cuius lectione tantopere Cyprianus ipse Episcopus postea Carthaginensis delectatus est, vt magistrum suum appellaret. Lactantius lib.5. cap.1,Tertulliani eruditionem laudat:eloquentiam vero,quasi duriorem non probat.Et certè habet quædam dura & aspera: quædam obscura & inuoluta:quædam etiam fassa, quanquam vbique (qualis fuit illius seculi felicitas, & hominum illius ætatis ingenium)mirum magnúmque animi in Deum zelum spirat, & præ se fert. Acutus scriptor & grauis, & qui totum hominem desyderet, imò etiam sæpe ingenij communem captum superat. Presbyter Carthaginensis creatus est, postquam fidem Christianâ ampleƈti cœpit, quam variis opusculis contra hęreticorum errores tutatus est. Sed ad Cataphrygum seu Montanistarum deliria & dogmata tandem delapsus & ipse hæreticus fuit, contráque Ecclesiam volumina cõtexit,& sex libros prô furiosa illa Montanistarum ecstasi, quæ Anabaptistarum reuelationibus non erat absimilis, edidit. Denique contra Apollonium, qui Cataphrygum errores confutauerat, & ipse scripsit. Cur verò hæretico-rum blasphemias vir tam disertus & tali, quemadmodum loquitur libro ii. de Genesi ad literam, cap.25. Augustinus, corde sequerétur, occasio illis à clericis Romanis, (Romæ enim aliquandiu versatus est, quemadmodum & in Africa ipsa,vt ex ipsius scriptis apparet) præ-bita est, qui eum nimis externa illa ieiunij, ci-borum abstinentiæ, virginitatis exercitia ex-tollentem & admirantem seuerius primum tra-ctarunt, & velut plane Montanistam excom-municarunt,cùm hæc ille ex immoderato quo-dam sanctitatis zelo, & regnantis inter multos lasciuiæ odio potius, quàm ex concepta Cata-phrygum hæresi tantopere commendaret suis scriptis. Itaque Ecclesia expulsus & in segre-gum numerum relatus, cœpit in orthodoxos tanquam Psychicos & animales debacchari, at-que sensim in Gnosticorum,id est,Spiritualium quos ipse vocat, & Cataphrygum præcepta de-labi, quæ postea aperte defendit, ut apparet ex ipsius libro de Monogamia. Vixit autem Ter-tullianus sub Seuero Imperatore, cuius sæpe ipse meminit, uti in oratione ad Scapulam, in Apologet.c.4.lib.1.aduersus Marcion.vt omni-no mirer, cur huius ætatem quidam docti viri ad Alexandri Mammeæ filij, vel Origenis tem-pora potius quàm ad Seueri referendà conten-dant. Ipse anni 160. à Christo nato meminit in libro de Monogamia. Nicephorus quoque lib, 4.cap.12.& 34. sub Seuero collocat. Cœpit de-nique hæc hæresis sub eodem Seuero Impera-tore & Zephyrino Episcopo Romano. (quan-quam Platina sub Callixto, nescio tamen quo argumento motus, mauult reponere) circa an-num à Christo passo 170. In Africa viguit, & Carthagine potissimum, unde oriundus erat. In Asiam penetrasse non videtur. Nec enim il-lius meminit Epiphanius,qui Tertulliano longè posterior fuit,& ignota primis Græcis videtur hæc hæresis. Quanquam enim Anthropo-morphitæ aliquod caput cum Tertulliano consentiens secuti sunt, veluti de Deo corporali, neutri tamen ab aliis sua dogmata videntur mutati, sed potius fuisse eiusdem erroris quidè patroni, alij tamen aliis dissimiles, quàdo Anthropomorphitarum hæresin, qui Deo membra assignant, ipse in libro De Trinitate refutat & arguit. Nec etiam præcipuè propter hoc caput damnatus est Tertullianus, sed propter alia, vti docet hoc loco Augustinus. Itaque potius ad Montanistas, vel Cataphrygas hanc hæresin tanquam furculum ad suam germanámque stir-pem refero.
units.tr: Who Tertullian was is better known from Jerome, Augustine, the ecclesiastical histories, and his own writings, and from the learned commentaries of Beatus Rhenanus on them, than it needs to be explained here. He was a Carthaginian, born of a proconsular father and a centurion, first devoted to the study of civil law and famous in it, as Eusebius also records (Book 2 of his History, chapter 2). Even today, in the body of the Pandects gathered by Tribonian from various jurists, some learned and erudite fragments of Tertullian's writings and opinions survive. Yet from his style and manner of speaking throughout it is clear that he was a supreme jurist. Then he turned from the study of civil and Roman, that is, human, law to the knowledge of divine law, that is, theology, and made great progress in it, so that after Victor and Apollonius he is reckoned the first of the Latin Fathers and writers, as Jerome writes. Cyprian himself, later bishop of Carthage, was so delighted by reading him that he called him his master. Lactantius, in Book 5, chapter 1, praises Tertullian's learning, but does not approve of his eloquence, as being somewhat harsh. And indeed he has certain harsh and rough passages, certain obscure and tangled ones, and some that are indeed careless; yet everywhere he breathes and displays a remarkable and great zeal for God (such was the good fortune of that age and the talent of the men of that time). He was a sharp and serious writer, who demands the whole man, and often rises even above the ordinary grasp of mind. He was made presbyter of Carthage after he began to embrace the Christian faith, and he defended it in various little works against the errors of heretics. But at last he fell into the frenzies and doctrines of the Cataphrygians or Montanists, and himself became a heretic, wrote volumes against the Church, and published six books in defence of that wild ecstasy of the Montanists, which was not unlike the revelations of the Anabaptists. Finally he also wrote against Apollonius, who had refuted the errors of the Cataphrygians. But why such an eloquent man should have followed the blasphemies of the heretics with his heart, as Augustine says in Book 2 of On Genesis according to the Letter, chapter 25, the occasion was given them by the Roman clergy (for he lived for some time at Rome, as also in Africa itself, as his writings show). These men, first treating him more severely as he extolled and admired those outward exercises of fasting, abstinence from foods and virginity, and as if he were plainly a Montanist, excommunicated him. Yet he commended these things in his writings out of an immoderate zeal for holiness, and rather out of hatred of the wantonness that reigned among many, than from any conceived heresy of the Cataphrygians. So, expelled from the Church and listed among the separatists, he began to rage against the orthodox as Psychics and animals, and gradually slipped into the precepts of the Gnostics, that is, of the Spiritual ones, as he himself calls them, and of the Cataphrygians, which he afterwards openly defended, as appears from his book On Monogamy. Tertullian lived under the emperor Severus, whom he often mentions, as in his speech to Scapula, in the Apologeticus, chapter 4, and in Book 1 Against Marcion. So I am quite surprised that some learned men insist on placing his age in the times of Alexander Mamaea's son, or of Origen, rather than under Severus. He himself mentions the year 160 after the birth of Christ in his book On Monogamy. Nicephorus also places him under Severus, in Book 4, chapters 12 and 34. Finally this heresy began under the same emperor Severus and Zephyrinus, bishop of Rome (although Platina, for some reason I do not know, prefers to place it under Callixtus), about the year 170 after Christ's passion. It flourished in Africa, and especially at Carthage, whence he came. It does not seem to have penetrated into Asia. Epiphanius, who was far later than Tertullian, does not mention him, and this heresy seems unknown to the earliest Greeks. For although the Anthropomorphites followed some point agreeing with Tertullian, such as a corporeal God, neither of them seems to have changed his teachings from the others; rather they were indeed defenders of the same error, yet each differed from the others. Epiphanius in his book On the Trinity refutes and convicts the heresy of the Anthropomorphites, who attribute members to God. Nor was Tertullian condemned especially for this point, but for other things, as Augustine teaches in this place. So I refer this heresy rather to the Montanists or Cataphrygians, as a shoot to its own true stock.

units.la: 2 Animam dicit.) Variæ fuerunt erroris qui Tertulliano tribuitur, hypotheses, è quibus est hæc. 1 Deum esse corporeum quidem, non tamen effigiatum, aut in membra distributum. Tertulliani hæc verba sunt aduerf. Pra-xeam, Quis enim negabit Deü corpus, etsi Deus spiritus est? Spiritus enim corpus sui generis in sua effigie. Idem confirmat, vel potius conten-dit in libro De anima, qui proculdubio est Tertulliani (illius enim meminit in commentario De resurrectione carnis:) sed tamen in lib. De Trinitate, negat Deum membra habere. Hoc itaque, quod dicimus, eum sensisse testatur idé Augustinus libro 10. De Genef.capite 25,& 26: quem illius errorem hic excusat Augustinus, quòd generaliter corpus accipiat pro οὐσία[?], quasi nihil subsistat, quod non propter humanæ aciei imbecillitatem sit corpus appellandum. Itaque ne videretur Deum constituere, aut pro-ponere velut inane quiddam, & φάνταςμα, sed ut omnes intelligerent esse veram per seque subsistentem ὑπόστασιν[?], Deum corpus esse dixit, abutens nomine corporis, ut vult Augustinus. Quemadmodum de Eccles. dogma. capite 12, dicitur o-mnis creatura etiam Angelica, esse corporea, id est, ἀσωμάτως[?] quiddam habere. Et Hilarius etiā Pictauiensis, eodem modo alicubi loquitur.
units.tr: 2 He says the soul.) There were various hypotheses of the error attributed to Tertullian, of which this is one. 1 That God is indeed corporeal, but not shaped or divided into members. These are Tertullian's words against Praxeas: "For who will deny that God is a body, even though God is a spirit? For the spirit is a body of its own kind, in its own shape." He confirms the same, or rather maintains it, in his book On the Soul, which is undoubtedly Tertullian's (for he mentions it in his commentary On the Resurrection of the Flesh); yet in his book On the Trinity he denies that God has members. Therefore Augustine too bears witness, in Book 10 of On Genesis, chapters 25 and 26, that he held what we are saying. Augustine excuses this error here, because Tertullian takes "body" in a general sense for substance (οὐσία [ousia]), as if nothing subsisted which should not be called a body because of the weakness of human sight. So, lest he should seem to make God something empty and to set him forth as a phantasm (φάνταςμα [phantasma]), but so that everyone might understand that God is a true and self-subsisting hypostasis (ὑπόστασιν [hypostasis]), he said God is a body, abusing the name of body, as Augustine puts it. In the same way, in On the Ecclesiastical Dogmas, chapter 12, it is said that every creature, even the angelic, is corporeal, that is, has something incorporeal (ἀσωμάτως [asōmatōs]). Hilary of Poitiers also speaks in the same way somewhere.

units.la: 2 Animam humanam uti & Angelos ipsos cs-se corpora: tenuia quidem, sed quæ tamen effi-giem delineationemque membrorum habeat, ut à Dei natura distinguantur, quam fecit cor-poream. Unde animam crescere, adolescere, ci-bos desiderare, & in cæteris una cum corpore συμπαθῆν[?], & conuenire. Ista omnia non ex Sorani medici, sed ex suo ipsius sensu & iudicio a-criter defendit Tertullianus in libr. De anima. Definimus, ait, animam dei flatu natam, im-mortalem, corporalem, effigiatam, substantia simplicem: & alio capite tribuit animæ longitu-dinem, latitudinem, sublimitatem, effigiem, se-xum, habitum, terminum, uti corpori, quia non est ubique diffusa, ut Deus: sed certo ubi com-prehensa. Respondeo vero hoc verum esse, cir-cumscriptam & definitam esse animam proprie tate naturæ, non autem loco & dimensionibus comprehensam, ut corpus.
units.tr: 2 That the human soul, like the angels themselves, is a body: thin indeed, yet one that has the image and outline of members, so that it is distinguished from God's nature, which he made corporeal. Hence the soul grows, matures, desires food, and in the other respects suffers along with (συμπαθῆν [sympathēin]) and agrees with the body. Tertullian vigorously defends all these things in his book On the Soul, not from the physician Soranus but from his own feeling and judgment. "We define," he says, "that the soul, born of God's breath, is immortal, corporeal, shaped, and simple in substance." And in another chapter he ascribes to the soul length, breadth, height, form, sex, condition and limit, as to a body, because it is not diffused everywhere, as God is, but is contained in a definite place. I reply that this is true: the soul is circumscribed and defined by the property of its nature, but it is not contained by place and dimensions as a body is.

units.la: 3 Animam humanam ex traduce esse: & ut ipse in lib. De anima loquitur, ex una redundare, & cum carne in utero seminari, quia ex uno Adamo omnes peccatum originale hausimus. Hoc postremum quidem verum est, antecedens tamen falsum.
units.tr: 3 That the human soul comes by traducianism, and, as he himself says in the book On the Soul, flows out from one source and is sown together with the flesh in the womb, because we all drew original sin from the one Adam. The latter claim is indeed true, but the premise is false.

units.la: Potest enim ad nos ex primo parente peccatum deriuari, etsi neque est peccatum substantia, vt Manichæi volunt: neque anima ex traduce, vt censent Pelagiani. 4 Animas sceleratorum hominum in dæmonas esse tandem conuerten- das. Augustinus hic,& Isidorus. Ipse quidem in libro De anima, contendit nullam esse animam sine dæmone comite, tamen non asserit verten- dam in dæmonem, imò contra <bl>μετεμψύχωσιν</bl> & <bl>μετενσωμάτωσιν</bl> tum Platonicam, tum Pythagori- cam inuehitur,quam impugnat. Hùc tamen er- rorem Tertulliano Augustinum affinxisse, non facile crediderim, quum in eum fit æquior: & propter ipsius peccata tremedum potius quàm ridendũ esse, idem dicat. 5 Secundas nuptias aperte dãnat ex disciplina Montanistarũ, in lib. De monogamia. Sic enim esse debere vnũ tan- tum coniugium,vt vnus est Deus. Papistarum sententia de bigamis hinc orta.Ambros.libro 1. De officiis,cap.vltimo, Vna tantùm,nec repe- tita nobis copula permittitur, & in ipso coniu- gio lex est,non iterare coniugium.Quod quan- tum ab hoc errore Tertull.dissideat,non video: vti nec illud, quomodo fere Montanistæ non sint,qui eos,qui ad secundas conuolant nuptias, Bigamos probrose vocant, & ab omni dignita- te Ecclesiastica arcent. 6 Mariam post Chri- stum editum semel nupsisse, quod eius di&tum afferebat pro se Hel′ idius, refutat Hieronym. & eleuat,quòd Tertullianum hominem Eccle- siæ esse neget. 7 Paracletum & Spiritum no- uæ Prophetiæ, quem falsò Cataphryges iacta- bant se accepisse, & vberiorem quidem, quàm ipsi Domini nostri Iesu Christi discipuli, ubiq; commendat & approbat Tertullianus, maxime in lib. aduersus Praxeam, in fine. & libro De monogamia. 8 Hominem Christianam bona conscientia sub principe suo, si sit ethnicus, militare posse negat, & usum armorum omnino Christianis interdicit, imo vero etiam eos iudices quos vocant, capitales & criminales esse vetat, in libro De idololatria, quia usum gladij Christianis adimit. Hoc Anabaptistas peperit, in hoc errore pertinacissimos[?]. Itaque iampridem Tertulliani opuscula damnata sunt, communi quodam consensu Ecclesiae, vt appareret ex Can.Sancta.distinct.15. Quaedam autem tribuuntur Tertulliano, quae non sunt erronea, veluti quòd panem & vinum in Coena Domini figuram & σύμβολα[?] corporis & sanguinis ipsius esse dixerit in libro 4. aduersus Marcionem. Sed sic Papae etiam ipsi sunt loquuti, vti Hilarius 2. in Canone Corpus Christi. De Consecr. distinct.2. vt intelligant Papistae quantum à capitis sui doctrina discesserint. Quaedam etiam dure de Trinitate & distinctione Personarum diuinarum dixit. Itaque cum magno iudicio legendus est Tertullianus: quemadmodum etiam veteres Patres scriptores Ecclesiastici pene omnes.
units.tr: For sin can be derived to us from our first parent, although sin is not a substance, as the Manichaeans hold, nor is the soul derived by traduction, as the Pelagians think. 4 That the souls of wicked men are at last to be turned into demons: Augustine here, and Isidore. In his book On the Soul, Tertullian indeed argues that no soul exists without a demon as companion, yet he does not assert that it is to be turned into a demon. On the contrary, he attacks and refutes both the Platonic and the Pythagorean doctrines of metempsychosis [μετεμψύχωσις] and metensomatosis [μετενσωμάτωσις]. I would not readily believe, however, that Augustine attributed this error to Tertullian, since he is fairer to him, and he says that because of Tertullian's own sins the man is to be trembled at rather than laughed at. 5 He plainly condemns second marriages, following the discipline of the Montanists, in the book On Monogamy. For, he says, there ought to be only one marriage, just as there is only one God. The Papists' opinion about bigamists arose from this. Ambrose, in the first book of De officiis, last chapter: "Only one union is permitted to us, and it is not to be repeated; and the law within marriage itself is not to marry again." How far Tertullian differs from this error I do not see, nor how it is that the Montanists are almost not Montanists, since they reproachfully call those who rush into second marriages bigamists and bar them from all ecclesiastical dignity. 6 That Mary bore no children after Christ was born, only once married, which the words of Helvidius were advancing in his support, Jerome refutes; and he rebukes him for denying that Tertullian was a man of the Church. 7 The Paraclete and the Spirit of new prophecy, which the Cataphrygians falsely boasted they had received, and which Tertullian everywhere commends and approves, and more fully than the very disciples of our Lord Jesus Christ, especially in the book Against Praxeas, at the end, and in the book On Monogamy. 8 He denies that a Christian can with a good conscience serve in the army under his prince if the prince is a pagan, and he forbids Christians the use of arms altogether; indeed, in the book On Idolatry he also forbids them to be judges, as they are called, in capital and criminal cases, because he takes from Christians the use of the sword. This gave birth to the Anabaptists, who are most obstinate in this error. Accordingly, the little works of Tertullian were condemned long ago by a common consensus of the Church, as appears from the canon Sancta, distinction 15. Certain things, however, are attributed to Tertullian which are not erroneous, such as that in the Lord's Supper the bread and wine are a figure and symbols of the body and blood of Christ, as he says in the fourth book Against Marcion. But the Popes themselves have spoken in this way too, as Hilary, in the canon Corpus Christi, De consecratione, distinction 2, so that the Papists may understand how far they have departed from the doctrine of their own head. He also spoke harshly about the Trinity and the distinction of the divine Persons. Therefore Tertullian must be read with great judgement, as indeed almost all the ancient Fathers and ecclesiastical writers must be.

units.la: CAP. LXXXVII. Abelonitæ cur sic dicti. Erroris autem eorum caput vnum.
units.tr: CHAPTER LXXXVII. Why the Abelonites are so called. Their error, in one point.

units.la: STquadam hæresis rusticana in campo nostro ad est, Hipponensi: vel potius fuit. Paulatim enim diminuta, in una exigua villa remanserat, in qua quidem paucissi-mi, sed omnes hic fuerunt, qui omnes modo correcti, & catholici facti sunt, nec aliquid illius supersedit erro-ris. Abelonij vocantur Punica declinatione nominis. Hoc nonnulli dicunt ex filio Adae nominatos, qui est vocatus Abel, unde Abelianos, vel Abeloitas eos possumus dicere. Non miscebantur uxoribus, & eis tamen sine uxoribus viuere sectā[?] ipsius dogmate non licebat. Mares ergo & femina sub continentiae professione simul habitantes, puerum & puellam sibi adoptabant in eiusdem coniunctionis pacto successores suos futuros. Morte praeuentis quibusque singulis alii subrogabantur, dum tamen duo duobus disparis sexus in illius domus societate succederent. Utrolibet quippe parente defuncto, uno remanenti, usque ad eius quoque obitum filii seruiebant, post cuius mortem etiam ipsi puerum & puellam similiter adoptabant. Nec unquam eis defuit, unde adoptarent, generantibus circumquaque vicinis, & filios suos inopes ad spem hereditatis aliena dantibus libenter.
units.tr: There is a certain rustic heresy in our territory of Hippo, or rather there was one. For it had gradually dwindled and remained in one small village, where indeed there were very few people, but all of them lived there, and all of them have now been corrected and made Catholics, and nothing of that error survives. They are called Abelonians, from the Punic inflection of the name. Some say they were named after the son of Adam called Abel, whence we may call them Abelians or Abeloites. They did not mix with wives, yet it was not permitted by their doctrine to live in that sect without wives. Men and women therefore lived together under a profession of continence, and they adopted for themselves a boy and a girl, who in the agreement of this fellowship would be their successors in future. When any one of them died first, another was substituted in his place, provided that two of opposite sex always succeeded in the society of that household. Indeed, when either parent died and one remained, the adopted children served the survivor until that person's death too, and after that death they likewise adopted a boy and a girl. Nor did they ever lack anyone to adopt, since neighbouring people on every side bred children and willingly gave their needy sons to others in hope of inheritance.

units.la: 1 Abelonij vocantur.) Mirum plane futurum erat, si cum Adamus, Cain, Seth, suos imitatores habuissent, Abel nullos sui admiratores & cultores nancisceretur. Itaque & hunc quoque in occasionem haereseos fanatici homines arripuerunt: qui propterea Abelonij, Abeliani, Abeloitae vel Abelitae dici possunt, quorum tamen nec certus autor, nec tempus traditur.
units.tr: 1 The Abelonites are so called. It would certainly have been strange if, when Adam, Cain and Seth had their imitators, Abel should have had no admirers and worshippers. So these fanatical men also seized upon him as an occasion for heresy; for which reason they may be called Abelonites, Abelians, Abeloites or Abelites. Yet no certain author of them is recorded, nor any time.

units.la: Nec enim, hoc pene capite & loco Augustini excepto, quicquam de iis à Latinis scriptoribus commemoratum est: sed nec à Græcis, quibus fuerunt ignoti. Si quis tamen coniecturis locus est, videntur ante postremam Augustini ætatem & nati & extincti. Ac nati quidem sub Arcadio Imperatore, & Anastasio Roman. Episcopo post annum à Christo passo 370. Extincti vero postea sub Theodosio Iuniore. Scripsit enim senex Augustinus hoc opusculum de Hæresibus. Fuerunt autem hi propago non Cataphrygarum & Montanistarum, ut quidam existimant: sed potius Encratitarum & Tatianorum, quorum dogma perspicue interpolarunt. Cum enim illi nuptias & coniugium prorsus damnarent: hi nomen quidem coniugij & nuptiarum retinuerunt, vim autem & effectum earum prorsus sustulerunt. Vetuerunt enim coniuges sese ipsis uti, tanquam coitus in coniugio esset Christianis hominibus fugiendus, & diaboli potius quàm Dei opus, propterea que opus carnis appellabant, & peccatum originale ex eo nasci, & in homines propagari dicebant, quod quidem disphiceret Deo. Deinde Abelis (qui humanæ iustitiæ primarius dicitur ab antiquis, & ab Augustino eius societatis, quæ est Dei ciui-tas & Ecclesia, princeps, & primus) exemplum proferebat, quem etsi non negabant fuisse coniugem, usum tamen unquam uxore sua nō con-cedebant, quia nullos filios suscepisse legitur, quemadmodum Cain & Seth, quorum soboles refertur & commemoratur à Mose. Ad sub-sidium autem & coniseruationem suæ sectæ, synagogæ, quam esse Dei Ecclesiam censebant, adoptionis beneficio vtebantur, vt quia natura filios propter suæ sectæ dogma suscipere non poterant, haberent adoptiuos. Et certè videtur hoc Augustini ipsius dictum libro 2. De consensu Euangelistarum, cap. 1. magnum quoddam huius sectæ firmamentum dedisse. Exemplo Ioseph & Mariæ, inquit, magnificè insinuatur fidelibus coniugatis, etiam seruata pari consensu continentia, posse permanere, vocarique coniugium non permixto corporis sexu, sed custodito mentis affectu. Idem in libro De bono coniugali, capite 1. Poterat esse in utroque sexu, etiam sine tali commixtione, alterius regentis, alterius obsequetis amicabilis quædam & germana coniunctio. Cuiusmodi sententiæ plerunque apud veteres occurrunt, ex nimia continentiæ & cœlibatus admiratione profectæ. Quod ad Abelem, Moses neque cum uxorem habuis-se scribit, neque filios suscepisse, vt temerè ad huius erroris defensionem hoc exemplum affer-ratur. Coepit autem in agro Hipponensi, eóque Regio, quemadmodum diserte annotat hic Augustinus. Fuit enim in Numidia, quæ Africæ pars est, duplex Hippo. Hippo Regius in ea Numidia quæ proprie ita appellata est, Romanorum colonia, cuius fuit episcopus Augustinus. Alter Hippo Zarithos dictus, maritimum oppidum, vt est in Itinerario Antonini, pulcherrimè nobis opera D. Iosiæ Simleri felicitérque restituto, in ea Numidiæ regione, quæ Zeugitana cognominatur. Longius autem aut latius non videtur hic error Abelonitarum peruagatus,
units.tr: For, apart from this chapter and a passage of Augustine, nothing about them has been mentioned by Latin writers, nor indeed by Greek writers, to whom they were unknown. If, however, there is room for conjecture, they seem to have both arisen and died out before Augustine's last age: they arose under the Emperor Arcadius and Anastasius, Bishop of Rome, about 370 years after the passion of Christ, and died out afterwards under Theodosius the Younger. For the aged Augustine wrote this little work On Heresies. They were not, as some think, an offshoot of the Cataphrygians and Montanists, but rather of the Encratites and the followers of Tatian, whose doctrine they plainly corrupted. For while those men utterly condemned marriage and wedlock, these retained the name of wedlock and marriage but utterly abolished its force and effect. For they forbade spouses to use one another, as though intercourse in marriage were something Christian men must shun, a work of the devil rather than of God; therefore they called it the work of the flesh, and said that original sin was born from it and propagated into human beings, which indeed would be displeasing to God. Then they put forward the example of Abel, who is called by the ancients the first of human righteousness and by Augustine the chief and first of that fellowship which is the City of God and the Church. Though they did not deny that he had been a husband, they did not allow that he ever used his wife, because it is read that he begot no children, unlike Cain and Seth, whose offspring is recounted and recorded by Moses. And to support and preserve their sect, which they judged to be the Church of God, they used the benefit of adoption, so that, since by nature they could not have sons consistent with the doctrine of their sect, they might have adopted ones. And indeed it seems that a saying of Augustine himself, in the second book On the Harmony of the Evangelists, chapter 1, gave this sect a great support: "By the example of Joseph and Mary," he says, "it is magnificently shown that married believers, even while preserving continence by mutual consent, can remain, and that the union is called marriage not through a mixing of the bodily sexes but through the preservation of an inward disposition of mind." The same in the book On the Good of Marriage, chapter 1: "There could be in both sexes, even without such mingling, a certain friendly and genuine partnership, the one ruling and the other obeying." Sayings of this kind occur frequently among the ancients, arising from an excessive admiration of continence and celibacy. As for Abel, Moses neither writes that he had a wife nor that he begot sons; this example should not be rashly brought forward in defence of this error. It began in the territory of Hippo, and in that region, as Augustine here expressly notes. For in Numidia, which is part of Africa, there were two Hippos: Hippo Regius in that Numidia which is properly so called, a Roman colony, of which Augustine was bishop; and another Hippo called Zarithos, a maritime town, as is found in the Itinerary of Antoninus, most beautifully and fortunately restored to us by the work of Josias Simler, in that region of Numidia which is named Zeugitana. But this error of the Abelonites does not seem to have spread further or wider,

units.la: neque etiam diutius permansisse, sed in ipsis cunis extinctus, & verbo Dei confossus, siluisse, quem neque nos revocare, neque nimia perquisitione illustrare debemus.
units.tr: nor to have persisted longer, but to have been extinguished in its very cradle and pierced through by the Word of God, and to have fallen silent. We ought neither to revive it nor to illuminate it by excessive inquiry.

units.la: CAP. LXXXVIII.
units.tr: CAP. LXXXVIII.

units.la: Pelagiani cur sic dicti. Erroris autem eorum capita quinque recensentur.
units.tr: Why the Pelagians are so called. Five heads of their error are listed.

units.la: PElagianorum est haeresis hoc tempore omnium recentissima, a Pelagio{1} Monacho exorta, quem magistrum Caelestius sic sequutus est, ut sectatores eorum Caelestiani etiam nuncupentur. Hi Dei{2} gratia (qua praedestinati sumus in adoptionem filiorum per Jesum Christum in ipsum, & qua eruimur de potestate tenebrarum, ut in eum credamus, atque in regnum ipsius transferamur, propter quod ait, Nemo venit ad me, nisi fuerit ei datum a Patre meo: & qua diffunditur charitas in cordibus nostris, ut fides per dilectionem operetur) in tantum inimici sunt, ut sine hac posse hominem credant, facere omnia divina mandata: quum, si hoc verum esset, frustra Dominus dixisse videretur, Sine me nihil potestis facere.
units.tr: The heresy of the Pelagians is the most recent of all at this time. It arose from the monk Pelagius, whom Caelestius followed as his master so closely that his followers are even called Caelestians. These men are so hostile to the grace of God (by which we are predestined to the adoption of sons through Jesus Christ, by which we are rescued from the power of darkness so that we believe in him and are transferred into his kingdom, on account of which he says, No one comes to me unless it has been given him by my Father; and by which the love of God is poured into our hearts, so that faith works through love) that they believe a man can, without this grace, do all the divine commands. Yet if this were true, the Lord would seem to have spoken in vain when he said, Without me you can do nothing.

units.la: Denique Pelagius a fratribus increpatus, quod nihil tribueret adiutorio gratiae Dei ad eius mandata facienda, correctioni eorum hactenus cessit, ut non eam libero arbitrio praponeret, sed infideli callidita-te supponeret, dicens ad hoc eam dari hominibus, ut quae facere per liberum iubentur arbitrium, facilius possint impleri per gratiam. Dicendo utique, ut fa-cilius cilius possint, voluit credi, etiamsi difficilius, tamen posse homines sine gratia divina facere iussa. Illam vero gratiam Dei, sine qua nihil possumus facere, non esse dicunt, nisi in libero arbitrio, quod nullis suis praecedentibus meritis ab illo accepit nostra natura, ad hoc tantum ipso adiuuante per suam Legem & doctrinam, ut discamus quae facere, & quae sperare debeamus: nos autem, ad hoc per donum Spiritus sancti, ut quae didicerimus esse facienda, faciamus. Ac per hoc diuinitus nobis dari scientiam confitentur, qua ignorantia pellitur: charitatem autem dari negant, qua pie viuitur: ut scilicet, quum sit Dei donum scientia, quae sine charitate inflat: non sit Dei donum ipsa charitas, quae ut scientia non inflet, aedificat. Destruunt etiam orationes, quas facit Ecclesia, sive pro infidelibus, & doctrina Dei resistentibus ut convertantur ad Deum: sive pro fidelibus, ut augeatur eis fides, & perseuerent in ea. Haec quippe non ab ipso accipere, sed a seipsis homines habere contendunt, gratiam Dei, qua liberamur, dicentes secundum merita nostra dari. Quod quidem Pelagius in episcopali iudicio Palastino damnari metuens, damnare compulsus est: sed in posterioribus suis scriptis hoc inuenitur docere. In id etiam pro-grediuntur, ut dicant vitam iustorum in hoc seculo nullum omnino habere peccatum, & ex his Ecclesiam Christi in hac mortalitate perfici, ut sit omnino sine macula & ruga, quasi non sit Christi Ecclesia, quae in toto terrarum orbe clamat ad Deum, Dimitte nobis debita nostra. Parvulos etiam negant secundum Adam carnaliter natos, contagium mortis antiquae prima natiuitate contrahere. Sic enim eos sine ullo peccati originalis vinculo afferunt nasci, ut prorsus non sit quod eis oporteat secunda natiuitate dimittti: sed eos propterea baptizari, ut regeneratione adoptati admittantur ad regnum Dei, de bono in melius translati, non ista renouatione ab aliquo malo obligationis veteris absoluti. Nam etiamsi non baptizentur, promittunt eis extra regnum quidem Dei, sed tamen aeternam & beatam quandam vitam suam. Ipsum quoque Adam dicunt, si non peccasset, fuisse corpore moriturum, neque mortuum merito culpa, sed conditione naturae. Objiciuntur illis & alia nonnulla, sed ista sunt maxima, ex quibus intelliguntur etiam illa vel cuncta, vel pene cuncta pendere.
units.tr: Then Pelagius, rebuked by the brothers because he gave no place to the help of God's grace in doing his commands, yielded to their correction so far that he did not set grace above free will, but subordinated it with crafty unfaithfulness, saying that it is given to men so that what they are commanded to do by free will may more easily be accomplished through grace. By saying that they may more easily do it, he wished it to be believed that men can still do what is commanded without divine grace, even if with more difficulty. They say that the grace of God, without which we can do nothing, is nothing other than free will, which our nature received from him by no merit of its own, and which God helps only by his Law and teaching, so that we may learn what we ought to do and hope for; and we, by the gift of the Holy Spirit, so that we may do what we have learned ought to be done. In this way they confess that knowledge is given us by God, by which ignorance is driven away, but deny that love is given, by which we live godly; so that, while knowledge, which puffs up without love, is God's gift, love itself, which builds up and does not puff up like knowledge, is not God's gift. They also destroy the prayers which the Church makes, whether for unbelievers who resist the teaching of God, that they may be converted to God, or for believers, that their faith may be increased and they may persevere in it. For they contend that men do not receive these things from him, but have them from themselves, saying that the grace of God by which we are freed is given according to our merits. Pelagius, fearing to be condemned at the episcopal court of Palestine, indeed condemned this, under compulsion; but in his later writings it is found that he teaches it. They go so far as to say that the lives of the righteous in this world have no sin at all, and that from this the Church of Christ is perfected in this mortality, so that it is altogether without spot or wrinkle; as if that were not the Church of Christ which throughout the whole world cries to God, Forgive us our debts. They also deny that infants, born carnally according to Adam, contract the contagion of the old death by their first birth. For they assert that they are born so free from any bond of original sin that there is no need for them to be forgiven by a second birth; rather, they are baptized so that, adopted by regeneration, they may be admitted to the kingdom of God, being translated from good to better, and not absolved by this renewal from some evil of the old obligation. For even if they are not baptized, they promise them, outside indeed the kingdom of God, but nonetheless some eternal and blessed life of their own. They also say that Adam himself, if he had not sinned, would have died in the body, and would not have died as a consequence of guilt but by the condition of nature. Several other things are objected to them, but these are the greatest, from which it is understood that all or nearly all of those other things depend upon them.

units.la: I A Pelagio Monacho.) Recens omnino haeresis, Augustino iam sene. Pelagiani autem & Caelestiani communi nomine vulgo sunt appellati isti haeretici, non etiam Iulianistae: quanquam iisdem etiam temporibus Iulianum patronum haberent, hominem notum, aduersus quem scripsit iam gradaeuus Augustinus, quemadmodum aduersus duos illos superiores. Sed hi parentes & primi authores huius sectae fuisse videntur: Iulianus autem horum tantum discipulus & cliens, quanquam Caelestium Pelagii ipsius discipulum & μαθητὴν[?] appellat Augustinus libro 2. capite 7, & 41. De nupt. & concupisc. Pelagiani vero, vel Pelagianistae (utraque enim terminatione vocatos inuenio) a Pelagio dicti sunt, qui hoc nomine & speciali haereseos distinctione primum innotuerunt sub Theodosio iuniore imperatore, & Innocentio primo episcopo Romano, circa annum a Christo passo quamquam tamen qui hæc tempora sequuti sunt authores Græci, nec hominis, nec nominis, errorisve huius meminerit,siue quod illis ignota fuerit hæc hæresis, siue quod statim propter Synodum Palæstinam, in qua damna-ta fuerat, extincta inter eos perierit: siue deni-que, quod Græci scriptores liberi arbitrij vim ex philosophorum prophanorum doctrina ni-mium iam extollentes,& prædicantes hunc Pe-lagianorum errorem vel leuem vel nullum existi-mauerunt,qui tamen est teterrimus,&omnium Iustitiariorum,siue Operistarum hæreticorum, qui sequuti sunt,sons & scaturigo vere dici po-test. Itaque neque Theodoretus in libro De fa-bul.hæretic.neque Ioannes Damascenus,neque cuiuslibet rei compilator & rhapsodus Nice-phorus Callistus hos hereticos commemorant.
units.tr: Pelagius the Monk.) A heresy quite recent, when Augustine was already old. These heretics were commonly called by the common name of Pelagians and Caelestians, not Julianists, although in those same times they had Julian as their patron, a man well known, against whom Augustine had already written in his old age, as against those two earlier ones. But these seem to have been the parents and first authors of this sect; Julian was only their disciple and client, although Augustine calls Caelestius a disciple of Pelagius himself, [μαθητήν], in book 2, chapters 7 and 41 of On Marriage and Concupiscence. The Pelagians, or Pelagianists (for I find them called by either ending), took their name from Pelagius. They first became known under this name and as a special distinction of the heresy under the younger emperor Theodosius and Innocent I, bishop of Rome, about the year after the Passion of Christ. Yet the Greek authors who followed these times mention neither the man, the name, nor this error. Whether this heresy was unknown to them, or whether it perished among them at once because of the Palestinian Synod in which it had been condemned, or finally because the Greek writers, already extolling the power of free will too much from the teaching of profane philosophers, thought this error of the Pelagians slight or no error at all, although it is most foul and can truly be called the source and fountain of all the Justiciaries or Operists, the heretics who followed them. Thus neither Theodoret in his book On Heretical Fables, nor John of Damascus, nor Nicephorus Callistus, a compiler and rhapsodist of any subject, mention these heretics.

units.la: Latinis vero episcopis fuerunt notissimi, quos varie multumque vexarunt, vt ex scriptis Am-brosij De vocatione Gentium, Hieronymi ad-uersus Pelagianos, Augustini ipsius toto 7.To-mo facile apparebit. Isidorus vero etiam huius meminit.Fuit autem Pelagius huius tam impiæ blasphemiæ author, Monachus primum Ro-mæ,postea vero ad presbyterij dignitatem euec-tus,vt Augustinus in epistolis scribit,alij etiam ad episcopale culmen putant peruenisse. A pa-tria vero Britannia, quæ maritima Galliæ regio est (vbi olim Armoricæ ciuitates vocabantur) Brito cognominatus, vt a Pelagio Samosatensi episcopo, qui pius&orthodoxus fuit, & ante hunc sub Valente vixit, distinguereτur. de quo meminit Theodoretus libro 4. hist. capite 13. itémque ab alio Pelagio, qui Tarentus dictus est, nostro huic æqualis, sed orthodoxus. Illo vero seculo cœperat iam Britania in Gallia vocari ea Galliæ postrema plaga, in quam Britâni (qui nunc Angli dicuntur) ex Albione infula,& è patriis sedibus partim à Maximo tyranno traducti fuerant, vt Martinus Polonus in suo Chronico tradit, vt eorum imperium propagaretur: partim à Scotis populis, & Anglis (qui sunt Saxonici populi) rege Vertunegaro duce, vt ait Pomponius Lætus, pulsi fuerant, quod sub Valentiniano fecundo accidit, ante hanc hærefin enatam. Nec mirum est tam pestilentem errorem ab homine Britone excogitari sparsíque potuisse. Illo enim seculo, vt docet Aufonius lepidissimo epigrammate, mixti Gallis, profugi Britones isti non nisi mali habebantur. Aufonij vero epigramma sic habet,
units.tr: But among the Latin bishops they were very well known, and they troubled them in various ways and at length, as will readily appear from the writings of Ambrose On the Calling of the Gentiles, Jerome against the Pelagians, and from Augustine himself in the seventh volume of his works. Isidore also mentions them. Pelagius was the author of this impious blasphemy. He was first a monk at Rome, and afterwards was raised to the dignity of presbyter, as Augustine writes in his letters; others think he even reached the episcopal summit. He was surnamed Briton from his native Britain, which is a maritime region of Gaul (where the cities of Armorica were once called). He was so distinguished from Pelagius of Samosata, a bishop who was pious and orthodox and who lived before him under Valens, of whom Theodoret writes in book 4 of his History, chapter 13; and likewise from another Pelagius, called of Tarentum, a contemporary of ours but orthodox. In that age Britain had already begun to be called in Gaul that furthest region of Gaul, into which the Britons (who are now called Angles) had been transferred partly from the island of Albion and their ancestral seats by the tyrant Maximus, as Martin of Poland relates in his Chronicle, so that their empire might be extended; and partly, as Pomponius Laetus says, they had been driven out by the Scots and the Angles (who are Saxon peoples) under the leader Vertunegarus, which happened under Valentinian II, before this heresy arose. Nor is it strange that so pestilent an error could be devised and spread by a man of Britain. For in that age, as Ausonius teaches in a most witty epigram, those Britons who fled and were mixed with the Gauls were regarded as nothing but bad. The epigram of Ausonius runs thus:

units.la: Siluius hic bonus est: Quis Siluius iste Britannus? Aut Brito hic non est Siluius, aut malus est.
units.tr: Silvius here is good. What Silvius is that? A Briton? Either Silvius here is not a Briton, or he is bad.

units.la: Quum autem egressus Roma, peregrè ageret in Syria, Nouatianorum & Meletianorum, id est, Operiftarum[?], qui plurimi in illis regionibus erant, veneno semel hausto, longius progressus est Pelagius, & operum merita, liberúmque hominis arbitrium Dei gratiæ repugnans, aperte induxit. Ex Nouatianorum enim fontibus ortum esse hûc errorem non dubito, potiùs quàm ex Manichæorum deliriis, quanquam Augustinus libro 4. ad Bonifacium, magnam esse Manichæorum & Pelagianorum in dogmatibus plerisque consensionem docet. Habitus autem Pelagius pro fui seculi ratione non indoctus, &c libros complures scripsit, quorum sparsim meminit Augustinus Tomo 7.velut libro 4.De li-bero arbitrio: De fide sua,lib.unum: Ad virgi-nem sacram: Ad virginem Demetriadem: item epistolas ad Innocentium,ad Paulinum episco-pum:ad Constantinum episcopum.Pelagio pa-raspistes [?] fuit Celestius, qui ita cum Pelagio ter-rarum orbem videtur partitus, ut Pelagius in Oriente,Italia,Gallia,& Anglia hoc virus spar-geret, quod fecit. Celestius autem in Africa, ubi degebat.Successit vero Celestio Ammianus quidam diaconus Celedensis, & alibi Iulianus, is de quo diximus, qui tempore Prosperi poe-nitentiam simulavit, ut in Ecclesiam admissus plures corrumperet: sed a Sixto Romano epi-scopo recipi prohibitus est. Coepit autem pri-mum in Palaestina regione, Syriae hæc hæresis ipso Pelagio spargente & tutante, sed ibi concilio propterea congregato damnatus, & quaedam revocare se simulans,ut infra dicetur, Romam venit, ubi epistola apud Innocentium se suamque doctrinam purgare conatus est. Inde in Angliam profectus, ubique veneni sui affla-tum & femina maxima & nocentissima reliquit, quae brevi tempore ita pullulaverunt, ut totum Christianum orbem occuparent, & infecerent misere. Denique tam alte huius erroris radices hæserunt, ut ne nunc quidem extirpari possint. Manent enim in Papatu ubi Semipelagianismus apertissime docetur. Duravit vero etiam ipso Pelagianorum nomine libere sub Iustino imperatore, qui etiam illis favit, sub Gregorio Magno, ut apparet ex epist.14. lib.5. Atq; etiam sub Heraclio imperatore, maximè in Anglia. Postremo Bernardi tempore recruduit epistol. 240. etsi quatuor Synodis, Palæstina, Carthagi-nensi secunda, Mileuitana, & Araufiaca iam erat damnatus hic error. Denique à Bernardo epist. 190. cum ab Abailardo quodam suo seculo esset renouatus. Nam cum pulcherrimè refutat idem Bernardus.
units.tr: When Pelagius left Rome and was living abroad in Syria, where there were very many Novatianists and Meletians (that is, Operists), he drank of their poison once and for all and went further, openly introducing the merits of works and man's free will in opposition to the grace of God. I do not doubt that this error arose from the springs of the Novatianists rather than from the ravings of the Manichaeans, although Augustine in book 4 to Boniface teaches that there is a great agreement between the Manichaeans and the Pelagians in most of their doctrines. Pelagius, judged by the standard of his age, was not unlearned, and wrote several books, which Augustine mentions here and there in the seventh volume: for example, book 4 of On Free Will; On His Own Faith, one book; To a Holy Virgin; To the Virgin Demetrias; likewise letters to Innocent, to Paulinus the bishop, and to Constantine the bishop. Caelestius was Pelagius' assistant, and he seems to have divided the world with Pelagius in such a way that Pelagius scattered this poison in the East, in Italy, in Gaul and in England, which he did; while Caelestius did so in Africa, where he lived. Caelestius was succeeded by a certain Ammianus, a deacon of Celeda, and elsewhere by Julian, whom we have mentioned, who in the time of Prosper feigned repentance so that, once admitted into the Church, he might corrupt many; but he was forbidden to be received by Sixtus, bishop of Rome. This heresy first began in the region of Palestine in Syria, Pelagius himself spreading and defending it; but there he was condemned by a council convened for that purpose, and, pretending to retract certain things, as will be said below, he came to Rome, where he tried to clear himself and his doctrine in a letter to Innocent. From there he went to England and everywhere left behind the breath of his poison, both among women of the highest rank and the most harmful, and this in a short time sprouted so that it occupied the whole Christian world and miserably infected it. Finally the roots of this error have so deeply taken hold that they cannot be uprooted even now; for they remain in Papacy, where Semipelagianism is most openly taught. Indeed the name of the Pelagians itself lasted freely under the emperor Justin, who even favoured them, under Gregory the Great, as appears from letter 14 of book 5, and also under the emperor Heraclius, especially in England. Lastly, in the time of Bernard it revived, letter 240; although this error had already been condemned by four synods: Palestinian, the second Carthaginian, Milevitan, and Arausican. Finally, Bernard condemned it in letter 190, when it had been renewed in his century by a certain Abelard; for Bernard himself refutes it most excellently.

units.la: 2. Hi Dei gratia. Quàm sæuum & immane fuerit pus & venenum quod postremis temporibus Satan per os impurũ Pelagij euomuit, dici non potest. Inde enim totius Christianæ fidei pestis enata est: inde gratuita illa Dei gratia, per quam salui simus, abolita: inde Christi Domini nostri mors euacuata: inde promissiones Dei gratuitæ esse desierunt: inde merita operum nostrorum inducta: inde denique homines sese suasque vires colere & mirari cœperunt, Dei autem Spiritum contemnere, & ipsius in illis opus & efficaciam non tantum obliuisci, sed etiam negare & prorsus extinguere. Cur autem tam tetri errores nascerentur, tamque facile admitterentur, nō hæc tantum ratio est, quòd generalem illam à fide Euangelij (per quam ad Dei gratiam tanquam ad solum & vnicum salutis nostræ fundamentum reuocamur) Apostasiā de qua Paulus 2. Thessal. 2. euenire oportuit, ut mundus iustas laceratas & deprauatas Dei veritatis poenas lueret, suasque tandem audaciæ miserrimum fructum sentiret: sed præterea duplex occasio videtur fuisse. Ac prima quidem recepta iam inter Græcos episcopos, sed ex profanorum tamen Philosophorum scriptis hausta, hæc sententia,nos αὐτεξούσιον[?] (quod liberum arbitrium & ęque ad bonum & malum per se propensam voluntatem interpretantur) bonos vel malos esse. Itaque quae bene agcremus[?], non tantum sponte & volentes nos, sed ea ipsa eligentes, & proprio motu impulsos facere. Altera, quod Praedestinatorum exorta iam haeresis, mirum in modum absurda videretur, qua tamen refelli posse non censebant, nisi homini liberum arbitrium, per quod sua ipsius sponte & impulsu aeque ad bona atque mala eligenda, perpetrandaque ferretur, tribuerent. Fuit enim hoc Praedestinatorum, qui dicti sunt, haereticorum dogma, neque mala opera hominibus a Deo electis, & praedestinatis fugienda, vel obesse: neque reprobis esse bonis operibus studendum: quia nullo modo iis confirmari iuvarique possent.
units.tr: 2. On the grace of God. It cannot be said how cruel and monstrous the poison and pus were that Satan vomited through the impure mouth of Pelagius in these last times. From it came the whole plague of the Christian faith. By it that free grace of God, through which we are saved, was abolished. By it the death of our Lord Jesus Christ was emptied of its effect. By it God's promises ceased to be free. By it the merits of our works were introduced. And finally, by it men began to cherish and admire themselves and their own powers, to despise the Spirit of God, and not only to forget his work and efficacy in them but even to deny them and utterly extinguish them. The reasons why such foul errors arose and were so readily admitted are not only this: the general apostasy from the gospel of faith (by which we are called back to the grace of God as the only foundation of our salvation), the apostasy of which Paul speaks in 2 Thessalonians 2, had to come, so that the world might pay the just penalty for its torn and corrupted hold on God's truth, and at last feel the most wretched fruit of its own audacity. Yet there seem to have been two further occasions. The first was the opinion, already accepted among the Greek bishops but drawn from the writings of the profane philosophers, that we are autexousion [αὐτεξούσιον] (which they interpret as free choice, a will inclined by itself equally to good and to evil), and so good or evil. Hence they thought that whatever good we do, we do not merely willingly and voluntarily but by choosing it and being moved by our own impulse. The second was that the heresy of the Predestinarians, which had already arisen, seemed wonderfully absurd, yet they did not think it could be refuted unless man were granted free will, by which he is carried by his own accord and impulse to choose and to perform good and evil alike. For this was the doctrine of the heretics called Predestinarians: that evil works are neither to be shunned by men elected and predestined by God, nor do they harm them; and that the reprobate are not to strive after good works, because in no way can they be strengthened or helped by them.

units.la: Dum enim doctrinam de praedestinatione Dei pessime intelligunt, & explicant, hominū ad bona opera studia extinxerunt: malorum autem, ad quaelibet scelera committenda, audaciam non tantum ir-ritarunt, sed etiam inflammarunt. Ortus vero erat hic error pauco ante Pelagium tempore, mirum sub Honorio imperatore, quemadmo-dum Sigebertus ait. Ex quo factum est, ut pul-cherrimum De praedestinatione Sanctorum tractatum ederet Augustinus, docerétque quo-modo ea doctrina quae salubcrrima[?] est, omninoque Ecclesiae scitu necessaria, praedicari & populo explicari posset. Huic Praedestinatorum sectaeque successerunt nostro hoc seculo Libertini homines spurci & foedi, digni qui canes potius & porci quam homines appellentur. His igitur tot erroribus impulsi & fatigati iam hominum animi facile lubenterque Pelagianorum errorem tanquam salutare quoddam pharmacum amplexi sunt. Sed dum vitant stulti vitia, in contraria currunt, quia ad verbum Dei in controuersiis & negotio de fide non recurrunt, maluntque suis definitionibus, quàm diuina veritate niti. Pelagianorum autem hypotheses fuerunt multæ, ut tradit variis in locis Augustinus. Quarum tamen omnium fundamenta hæc fuerunt, ut idem scribit libro 4. ad Bonifacium cap. 2. Quod hominem imprimis laudare conarentur, Quod nuptias commendare vellent, Quod Legem diuinam extollere se hoc modo pulcherrimè iudicarent, Quod liberum arbitrium iam ab aliis inductum pulchrè sic explicari ducerent, Quod sanctos homines dignis laudibus prosequi hac ratione putarent. Prima vero hypothesis hæc fuit, ut in libro Hypognosticῶν[?] copiosè traditur. Adam moriturum fuisse, etsi non peccasset, lege & conditione naturæ. Hac præmunitione subdolè suam sententiam confirmare conabantur, ne mors poena peccati diceretur censeretúrque, quæ sic in omnes homines transit, quemadmodum & peccatum ipsum. sic Paulus Romanorum quinto, versu duodecimo.
units.tr: For while they understand and explain the doctrine of God's predestination very badly, they have quenched men's zeal for good works, and they have not only provoked but even inflamed the boldness of the wicked to commit any crime whatever. This error had arisen a little before the time of Pelagius, in the reign of the emperor Honorius, as Sigebert says. Because of it Augustine published his excellent treatise On the Predestination of the Saints, and taught how that doctrine, which is most wholesome and altogether necessary for the Church to know, might be preached and explained to the people. After the Predestinarians and their sect there followed in our own age the Libertines, vile and filthy men, worthy to be called dogs and pigs rather than men. Therefore men's minds, impelled and worn out by so many errors, readily and gladly embraced the error of the Pelagians as a kind of wholesome remedy. But while foolish men shun vices, they run into the opposite ones, because in controversies and matters of faith they do not return to the Word of God, and prefer to rest on their own definitions rather than on divine truth. Now the Pelagian positions were many, as Augustine relates in various places. Yet the foundations of all of them, as he writes in book 4 to Boniface, chapter 2, were these: that they tried above all to praise man; that they wished to commend marriage; that they judged they were excellently exalting the divine law in this way; that they held it to be well explained that free choice had been introduced by others; and that they thought in this way they honoured holy men with fitting praises. The first position was this, as is fully set out in the book Hypognosticon [Ὑπογνωστικῶν]: Adam would have died even if he had not sinned, by the law and condition of nature. By this preamble they craftily tried to confirm their opinion, so that death would not be called or considered the punishment of sin, though it passes into all men in the same way as sin itself; so Paul says in Romans 5:12.

units.la: 2. Peccatum Adami ipsi soli nocuisse, non etiam aliis hominibus ipsius posteris, nisi solo exemplo peccandi. Ergo & hoc erit tantum Christi beneficium, ait Bernard. ut suo exeplo nobis profuerit, beneque viuere docuerit. Siquidem pro qualitate vulneris allata est medicina & remedium doloris. Perspicuè contrà Paulus Hoc inducunt ut peccatum originale negent,& à parentibus in liberos generatione traduci. 3 Libido concupiscentiaque quæ nobis natura inest, bonum est, nec in ea est quicquam, cuius nos pudere debeat. Hoc aiunt,ut originale peccatum ostendant nullum in liberos transfire, qui ex ea libidine nascuntur, suntque fructus coniugij, id est, honestæ Dei institutionis & sanctissimi vinculi.
units.tr: 2. Adam's sin harmed only himself, and not other men, his posterity, except by the example of sinning. Therefore, says Bernard, this too will be the only benefit of Christ: that by his example he has profited us and taught us to live well. For medicine and a remedy for the pain have been brought in proportion to the kind of wound. Paul speaks plainly against this. They put this forward in order to deny original sin, and that it is passed on from parents to children by generation. 3. Lust and concupiscence, which are natural to us, are good, and there is nothing in them of which we ought to be ashamed. They say this to show that original sin does not pass into the children who are born from that lust, and that they are the fruits of marriage, that is, of the honourable institution of God and of its most holy bond.

units.la: Coniugium quidem per fe sancta quædam res est & à Deo instituta : propter peccatum tamen hominis quædam sunt in coniugij usu pudenda. Nam nec ipsa coniugum libido in ipso etiam coniugij usu hodie propter idem peccatum pura puta est coram Deo , ut doceatur Pfalm. 51. versu septimo. 4 Paruulos non trahere neque habere à parentibus peccatum originale. Contrà Paulus Roman. 5.versu 12. & Ephef.2. versu 2. natura filij iræ omnes nascimur. 5 Paruulos fidelium, etsi non baptizentur, salvos tamen fore, vitaque æterna fruituros,sed extra regnum Dei tamen futuros.
units.tr: Marriage indeed is in itself a holy thing and instituted by God; yet because of man's sin there are some things in the use of marriage that are shameful. For even now the lust of the spouses, even in the very use of marriage, on account of the same sin, is not pure before God, as is taught in Psalm 51:7. 4. Infants do not inherit from their parents, nor do they have, original sin. Against this, Paul in Romans 5:12 and Ephesians 2:2 says that by nature we are all children of wrath. 5. The infants of believers, even if they are not baptized, will nevertheless be saved and will enjoy eternal life, but they will be outside the kingdom of God.

units.la: Duo ineptifsima. Primum quòd omnes paruulos etiam fidelium salvos esse definiunt. Secundum, quòd vitam æternam extra Dei regnum impiissime constituunt. Huic autem dogmati (per quod dignitas Baptismi contemptusque omnino inducebatur) Patres orthodoxi ut occurrerent, primùm quidem Baptismum commendarunt, sed dum nimio vindicandi à contemptu Baptismi studio præcipites feruntur, & ipsi in alium errorem incurrerunt, incideruntque in Scyllam dum cupiunt vitare Charybdin. Affirmarunt enim omnes paruulos qui sine baptismo moriuntur, omnino damnatos est & infelices. Vnde natus est error de praecisa necessitate baptismatis, & de vi operis operati, per quod in Baptismo salutem coferri Scholastici etiam nunc docent blasphemè ad terrenum aquae elementum transferentes, quod est soli Dei gratiae insolidum accepto ferendum & vindicandum, nimirum salus hominum, remissioque peccatorum. 6 Homines habere e-tiam nunc post peccatum liberum arbitrium, quod sit sibi ipsi ad bene agendum sufficiens, & sine Dei gratia [?]. Contrà vero Paulus nos in peccatis mortuos esse docet, nisi Dei Spiritu viuificemur, Ephes.2.v.1. Hic autem cùm premeretur in synodo Palaestina Pelagius, quid igitur Dei gratiae in nobis nostrisque operibus bonis relinqueret, respondit hoc nimirum, Quod Dei gratia naturam ipsam nobis dedisset, per quam homines sumus. Iam verò homines facti ipsi per nos nullo accedente diuinae gratiae adiutorio bene agim[?]us & viuimus. Hoc dogma Scholastici interpolarunt, & adhuc ex parte retinet, quae est summa Christianae doctrinae inter eos labes, & vera gratiae Dei Christique beneficij abolitio. 7 Meritis operum nostrorum dari gratiam Dei. Hinc monstrosa illa vocabula nata, gratia de Congruo, & de Condigno quae apud Papistas censentur aurea. 8 Doctrinam de Praedestinatione sanctorum non modo irrident & subsannant, sed prorsus ex Dei Ecclesia explodunt contra D. Pauli sententiam Romanos.
units.tr: These are two most foolish claims. First, that all infants, even those of believers, are saved. Second, that they impiously establish eternal life outside the kingdom of God. But the orthodox Fathers, who opposed this doctrine (through which the dignity of Baptism was altogether disparaged and contempt for it was introduced), first indeed commended Baptism; but while in their eager zeal to vindicate Baptism from contempt they were carried headlong, they themselves fell into another error, and while they wished to avoid Charybdis they fell into Scylla. For they affirmed that all infants who die without baptism are utterly damned and wretched.
