From this arose the error about the absolute necessity of baptism, and about the power of the ex opere operato [operis operati], by which the Scholastics even now teach blasphemously that salvation is conferred in Baptism, transferring to the earthly element of water what must be ascribed and vindicated wholly to the grace of God alone: namely, the salvation of men and the remission of sins. 6. Men still have free will after sin, which is sufficient for itself to do good, and without the grace of God. On the contrary, Paul teaches that we are dead in sins unless we are made alive by the Spirit of God (Ephesians 2:1). When Pelagius was pressed on this at the Synod of Palestine, as to what then was left of the grace of God in us and in our good works, he answered, of course, that God's grace had given us nature itself, by which we are men; and that men, once made, do good and live well by themselves, with no help of divine grace added. The Scholastics have corrupted this doctrine, and still partly retain it, and this is the chief stain on Christian doctrine among them, and a true abolition of the grace of God and the benefit of Christ. 7. The grace of God is given on account of the merits of our works. Hence those monstrous terms arose, "grace of congruity" and "grace of condignity," which among the Papists are considered golden. 8. They not only mock and scoff at the doctrine of the predestination of the saints, but also cast it utterly out of the Church of God, against the opinion of St Paul in Romans 9, 10, and Ephesians 1.

units.la: 9.10. 9.10. & Ephes.1. Atque hæc fuerunt Pelagianæ hæreseos venena nocentissima notissimaque, de quibus vide Augustin.epist.89.90.92.94.
units.tr: 9. 10. 9. 10. and Ephesians 1. These were the most harmful and most notorious poisons of the Pelagian heresy; on them see Augustine, Letters 89, 90, 92, 94.

units.la: CAP. LXXXIX.
units.tr: CAP. LXXXIX.

units.la: Peroratio operis in qua docet varia esse hæreticorum genera, quorum errores nosse sit perutile.
units.tr: The concluding remarks of the work, in which he teaches that heretics come in many kinds, and that it is very useful to know their errors.

units.la: Cæ[?] quàm multas commemorauimus hæreses, nec tamen modum tuæ postulationis impleuimus. Ex quo enim Christiana religio, ut verbis tuis utar, hereditatis promissa nomen accepit, quæ hæreses orta sint, quomodo commemorare omnes potui, qui omnes nosse non potui? Quod ideo existimo, quia nullus eorum quorum de hac re scripta legi omnes posuit. Quandoquidem inueni apud alium, quas apud alium non inueni, & rursum apud illum quas ille non posuit. Ego autem propterea plures quàm ipsi posui, quia collegi ex omnibus quas omnes apud singulos non inueni, additis etiam his quas ipse recolens apud vllum illorum inuenire nō potui. Vnde merito credo nec me posuisse omnes, quia nec omnes qui de hac re scripserunt legere potui, neque hoc quenquam eorum videose[?]-cisse quos legi. Postremo etiamsi omnes scripserint, posuisse quod non puto, utrum omnes sint utique nescio. Et ideo quod vis me loquente finiri, non saltem potest me cognoscente comprehendi. Audiui scripsisse de hæresibus sanctum Hieronymum, sed ipsum eius opusculum nec in nostra bibliotheca inuenire potuimus, nec unde possit accipi scimus. Quod si tu scieris peruenias ad illud, & forsitan habebis melius aliquid quàm hoc nostrum: quamuis nec ipsum, licet hominem doctissimum, omnes hæreses arbitrer indagare potuisse. Et certè Abeloitas nostra regionis hæreticos quàtum existimo, ille nesciuit. Si fortè & alibi alios in obscurissimis locis reconditos, eiusque notitiam ipsa locorum obscuritate fugientes. Iam verò illud quod habent tuæ literæ, vt omnia omnino dicamus quibus hæretici à veritate dissentiunt, etiamsi omnia scirem, facere non possum, quanto minus possim qui omnia scire non possum. Sunt enim hæretici, quod fatendum est, qui singulis, vel nō multò amplius dogmatibus oppugnant regulam veritatis, sicut Macedoniani vel Photiniani atque aliì quicunque ita sese habent. Illi autē, vt ita dixerim, fabulones, id est, qui fabulas vanas easdémque longas, perplexásque contexuerunt, tam multis falsis dogmatibus pleni sunt, vt ipsi quoque illa numerare non possint, aut difficillimè possint. Nec vlli alieno vlla hæresis facilè sic innotescit vt suis: vnde nec earum quas commemoraui omnia dogmata mè dixisse profiteor. Quis enim non videat quantam res ista operam, & quàm multas literas flagitet? Nec ideò tamen parum prodest errores istos, quos huic operi intexui, lectos cognitosque vitare. Quid enim contra ista sentiat catholica Ecclesia, quod à me dicendum putasti, superfluo quaritur, cum propter hoc scire sufficiat eam contra ista sentire, nec aliquid horum in fidem quenquam debere recipere. Quomodo autem quà contra hàc veritas habet, asse renda ac defendenda sint, modulum operis huius excedit. Sed multum adiuuat cor fidele, nosse, quid credendum non sit, etiamsi disputandi facultate id refutare non possit. Omnis itaque Christianus catholicus
units.tr: Though I have recounted so many heresies, I have not fully met the demands of your request. For how could I recount all the heresies that have arisen since the Christian religion received the name of the promised inheritance, to use your words, when I could not know them all? I think this is so because none of those whose writings on this subject I have read has listed them all. For I have found in one author what I did not find in another, and again in another what that one did not list. I have listed more than they did, because I gathered from all of them the heresies that I did not find in any single one, and I added those which, on reflection, I could not find in any of them. So I rightly believe that I have not listed them all, since I could not read all who have written on this subject, and I do not see that any of those I have read has done so. Finally, even if all of them had written, I still do not know whether they have listed them all, which I do not think they have. So what you want to be finished in my telling cannot be grasped even in my knowing. I have heard that Saint Jerome wrote a work on heresies, but we could not find that little book in our library, nor do we know where it might be obtained. If you know where it is, you may go to it, and perhaps you will find something better than this work of ours, although I do not think that even he, a most learned man, could have tracked down all the heresies. And certainly, as I believe, he did not know our own heretics of this region, the Abelonites. Perhaps there are others somewhere in very obscure places, hidden away and escaping knowledge through the very obscurity of their locations. As for what your letter asks, that I should say absolutely everything by which heretics dissent from the truth, I cannot do that even if I knew everything, much less when I cannot know everything. For there are heretics, and this must be admitted, who attack the rule of truth with a single dogma, or not many more, as the Macedonians or the Photinians and whoever else are of that sort. But those others, if I may so put it, are fabulists, that is, men who have woven vain and long and complicated fables, and they are so full of many false dogmas that they themselves cannot count them, or can do so only with the greatest difficulty. Nor is any heresy as easily known to outsiders as to its own adherents; hence I confess that I have not stated all the doctrines even of those heresies I have recounted. For who does not see how much labour this matter demands, and how many books? Yet it is no small benefit to read and learn the errors which I have woven into this work, so that they may be avoided. For what the catholic Church thinks against these errors, which you thought I should state, is sought in vain, since for this purpose it is enough to know that she thinks against them and that no one should accept any of them as faith. How the truth, as opposed to these, is to be asserted and defended exceeds the scope of this work. But a faithful heart is greatly helped by knowing what is not to be believed, even if it cannot refute these errors by the skill of disputation. Therefore every Christian catholic

units.la: ista non debet credere, sed non omnis qui ista non credit, consequenter debet se Christianum Catholicum iam putare vel dicere. Possunt enim & hæreses alia quæ in hoc opere nostro commemorata non sunt, vel esse vel fieri, quarum aliquam quisquis tenuerit, Christianus catholicus non erit. Quid ergo faciat hæreti cum deinceps requirendum est, ut cum hoc Domino adiuvante vitamus, non solum ea quæ scimus, verum etiam quæ nescimus sive quæ iam orta sunt, sive quæ adhuc oriri poterunt, hæretica venena vitemus. Hu-ius autem sit iam voluminis finis, quem propterea vobis antequam totum hoc opus perficerem credidi esse mittendum, ut eum quicunque legeritis, ad id quod restat implendum, quod tam magnum esse cernitis, me orationibus adiuvetis.
units.tr: ought not to believe these things; but not everyone who does not believe these things ought therefore to consider or call himself a Christian catholic at once. For there may be, or may arise, other heresies not mentioned in this work of ours, and whoever holds any one of them will not be a Christian catholic. What, then, should be done about heretics? This must be sought henceforth, so that, with the Lord helping us, we may avoid not only the poisons of heresy that we know, but also those that we do not know, whether they have already arisen or may yet arise. Here, then, let this volume end. I thought I should send it to you before I finished the whole work, so that whoever of you reads it may help me with your prayers to complete what remains, which you see is so great a task.

units.la: Hactenus Augustinus.
units.tr: Thus far Augustine.

units.la: Videtur autem polliceri secundam quandam disputationem de eo quod facit hæreticum hominem. Nec tamen eam promissionem repræ-sentauit, sive aliis negotiis distractus, sive quòd necessariam non iudicauit, sive quòd temporis iniuria perierit.
units.tr: He seems to promise a second discussion about what makes a man a heretic. However, he did not make good on that promise, whether because he was distracted by other business, or because he did not judge it necessary, or because it was lost through the ravages of time.

units.la: ALIAE HAERESES ex veteri exemplari Gemblensi transcriptae, & huic Augustini catalogo additae. CAP. XC.
units.tr: OTHER HERESIES, transcribed from the old Gembloux manuscript and added to this catalogue of Augustine. CHAP. XC.

units.la: Timotheanorum error quis fuerit?
units.tr: What was the error of the Timotheans?

units.la: Timotheani{1} dicunt{2} Filium Dei verum quidem hominem ex virgine Maria natum, sed non ita unam reddidisse personam, ut non in unam sit redactus naturam, conflatorium quoddam volentes fuisse interiora virginis, per quod duae naturae, id est, Deus & homo, in unam resolutae & compactae massam, unam Dei & hominis exhibuerint formam, immutatam videlicet naturarum proprietatem, efficientiarum{3} coitione. Et ad confirmandam huiusmodi impietatem, qua Deum asserit a sua versum natura, cogunt Evangelista testimonium dicentis, & verbum caro factum est, quod ita interpretantur, Divina natura in humanam versa est. O abolitionem illi inuiolabili impingentem substantia! Huius impietatis initium Timotheus, apud Byzam Bithyniae modo exulans civitatem, continentis & religiosae vitae imagine multis illudit.
units.tr: The Timotheans{1} say{2} that the Son of God, a true man born of the Virgin Mary, did not so unite himself to the person that he was not also brought into one nature. They hold that the womb of the Virgin was a kind of crucible, in which the two natures, that is God and man, were melted and fused into one mass, and displayed one form of God and man, the natures' properties being changed, by the coming together of their operations. To confirm this impiety, by which they assert that God was turned from his own nature, they press the testimony of the Evangelist, who says, "And the Word was made flesh", which they interpret to mean that the divine nature was turned into the human. O what an overthrow of substance, which strikes against that inviolable substance! The beginning of this impiety was Timothy, who, while living in exile at Byza, a city of Bithynia, mocked many with the appearance of a continent and religious life.

units.la: Quæ sequuntur hæreses non sunt ab Augustino collectæ, sed à quodam additæ, qui unde quædam sumpserit, quæ primo hoc capite traduntur, non video, neque etiam quomodo cum aliis scriptoribus huic nostro conveniat. Timotheum igitur huius hæreseos authorem facit, quem & Byzæ in Bithynia exulasse ait, & monachicam vitam professum fuisse, cuius fuco & prætextu multos deceperit. At primum dubium non est, hunc esse Timotheum qui à Græcis historiæ Ecclesiasticæ scriptoribus Αἴλουρος [?], id est, Felis vel à cæsiis oculis vel à malignitate nominatur, ex monacho primum Presbyter: post autem Alexandriæ factus Episcopus seditione populari, in qua Proterium Alexandriæ Episcopum (ut ipsius sedem & locum invaderet) crudelissimè etiam in medio baptisterio & ipso die Paschæ trucidauit, quemadmodum cum Euagr.libr.2.cap.8.tum vero Nicephorus lib.15.cap.17 [?], luculentissimè tradunt. Propter quod facinus horrendum & excommunicatus & de throno deiectus est, & in exilium actus non Byzam quidem aut in Bithyniam: sed Gangrem (quæ, ut ait Plinius lib.6.cap.2.civitas est Cappadocum) in qua iam præceptor eius Dioscurus, & ipse Alexandrinus Episcopus, sed propter nefariam Flauiani Episcopi Antiocheni cædem, & Eutychianam hæresin depositus & relegatus exulabat, quemadmodum idem Nicephorus eodem lib.15.cap.16.scribit: ut procul dubio mendum esse hoc loco appareat, & pro Byza Gangre sit reponenda, quando etiam nusquam Byza Bithyniæ civitas esse dicitur: sed Thraciæ, vt & Plinius docet,& Socrat.libro 4. cap.15.& Sozomen.libr.6.cap.13.In eo verò exilio per annos octodecim vixit, cui interim successerat in Alexandrino Episcopatu populo petente Timotheus 15. qui & Basilicus & Salophaciałus ab Euagrio,lib.2.cap.11. cognominatur,quòd eiusdem cum Proterio Episcopo sententiæ fuisset, illíque familiaris. Sed mortui Salophaciali offa postea Petrus Mongus vel Moggus(utroque enim modo vocatur,id est admissa rius &publicus asinus)in eius locum substitutus in gratiam Timothei Æluri,& odiū Chalcedonensis synodi effodit, vt Theodorus lector & Euagr.lib.3.cap.11.itémque Nicephor.lib.16.cap. 13. tradunt, adeò variis hominum odiis iactata fuit Dei Ecclesia,& acerbè oppugnata orthodoxa de duabus in vna Christi persona naturis fides & sententia ab iis qui contra sentiebant, & Eutychen probabat.Hic tamen Timotheus Ælurus ex longo exilio postea à Basilisco Imperatore reuocatus est,& Alexandrinis,qui iam Eutychiano fascino dementati erant,petentibus restitutus,quo maximè tempore videtur hæc hæresis cœpisse,& tum ab eo ipso fidenter introductum etiam ab aliis Episcopis & monachis ipsius fautoribus fortiustutiusque defensa fuisse, authore ipso triumphate & præclarissimam Episcopatus sedem obtinente.Itaque huius erroris initiū colloco sub Basilisco(qui Zenoni succesit.) Impe atore,vel potius sub Zenone ipso, (tempora enim istius Basilisci Zenoni tribuuntur, quòd imperium sibi ademptū recuperauit Zeno)& sub Simplicio Roman.Episcopo, circa ca annū à Christo passo 447. vt valdè mihi hallucinari videantur, qui hanc hærefin vel ad tempora Honorij Imperatoris vel Marciani tefe- runt, cūm & Eutyche & Diofcuro iam mortuis excitatam, & ex impiis eorum blasphemiis interpolatam conflatámque esse constet: Huius ipsius hæreseos meminit author libelli qui appellatur De Ecclesiast. dogmatib. cap.2. & Petrus Lombardus lib.3. distinct.1.cap. Diligeter, ex quo eam disseminatam, propagatam & hoxiam fuisse colligi potest. In Ægypto vero maxime viguit, vbi tanquam in suo regno debacchatus est furiose in Chalcedonensem synodum Timotheus. Mansit vero vel ipso suo nomine vel Monothelitarum & Monophysitarum appellatione diutissime, & certissima, quemadmodum Eutychiana hæresis, Christianæ fidei corruptela fuit. Successores habuit Theodosianos hæreticos, & Caianitas vel Caianos (vtroque enim nomine dicuntur) à Caiano Alexandrino, vt docet Damascenus, Episcopo distos, nō autem à Gaina qui fuit dux militaris & barbarus sub Arcadio, vt docet Socrat.libr.6.cap.5. Hi idem, quod nostri, dogma professi sunt, & vixerunt, cœperúntque sub Iustiniano secundo Imperatore, & Constantino Roman. Episcopo, circa annum à Christo passo 675. Dioscuriani delirij innouatores, vt Isidorus tradit libro 8. Etymologia. & est in cano. Quidam 24. quæst. 3. Fuit enim Iustinianus iste Eutychiana labe infestus, quam etiam defendit, sub quo Theodosiani & Eutychiani in Ægypto etiam reflorue- rút. Nec vero hic est Theodosius, à quo Theodosiani,de quibus nunc, vocantur,de quo Eua-grius libro 2.cap.5.meminit. Nam etsi ille fuit Chalcedonensi synodo contrarius, aetate tamen hoc nostro prior est:sed is est potius de quo Ioannes Damascen.libr.De haeresib.scribit, fuitque Alexandrinus Episcopus.Theodosiani vero isti & Iacobitae postea dicti sunt, & Monophysitae, quibus etiam coniungit idem Damascenus & Aphthartodocitas, & Barsanianos, tanquam in eodem de utraque in Christo natura dogmate consentientes & concordes.
units.tr: The heresies that follow were not gathered by Augustine but were added by someone else. I cannot see where he took some of the things handed down in this first chapter, nor how they agree with other writers. He makes Timothy the author of this heresy, and says that he was in exile at Byza in Bithynia and had professed the monastic life, by whose mask and pretext he deceived many. But first, there is no doubt that this is the Timothy whom the Greek writers of Church history call Ailouros [Αἴλουρος], that is, Cat, either from his grey eyes or from his malice. First he was a monk, then an elder, and afterwards he was made bishop of Alexandria by a popular uprising, in which he most cruelly slew Proterius, bishop of Alexandria, in the middle of the baptistery and on the very day of Easter, in order to seize his see and place. Euagrius (book 2, chapter 8) and Nicephorus (book 15, chapter 17 [?]) relate this most clearly. On account of this horrible crime he was excommunicated and deposed from his throne, and sent into exile, not indeed to Byza or to Bithynia, but to Gangra, which, as Pliny says (book 6, chapter 2), is a city of the Cappadocians. There his teacher Dioscurus, himself also bishop of Alexandria, was already living in exile after being deposed and relegated, on account of the impious murder of Flavian, bishop of Antioch, and his Eutychian heresy, as the same Nicephorus writes in the same book 15, chapter 16. So it clearly appears that there is an error in this place, and that Gangra should be put in place of Byza, since Byza is nowhere said to be a city of Bithynia, but of Thrace, as Pliny also teaches, and Socrates (book 4, chapter 15) and Sozomen (book 6, chapter 13). In that exile he lived for eighteen years. Meanwhile, at the request of the people, Timothy, also called Basilicus and Salophaciolus by Euagrius (book 2, chapter 11), had succeeded him in the see of Alexandria. He was so named because he held the same opinion as the bishop Proterius and was close to him. But after the death of Salophaciolus, Peter Mongus, or Moggus (for he is called by both names, that is, the one admitted and the public donkey), was put in his place. To please Timothy Aelurus and out of hatred for the Council of Chalcedon, he dug up the dead man's bones, as Theodore the reader and Euagrius (book 3, chapter 11), and likewise Nicephorus (book 16, chapter 13), relate. So greatly was the Church of God tossed about by the various hatreds of men, and so fiercely was the orthodox faith and doctrine assailed by those who thought otherwise and approved Eutyches, concerning the two natures in the one person of Christ. Yet this Timothy Aelurus was afterwards recalled from his long exile by the emperor Basiliscus, and was restored at the request of the Alexandrians, who were by then out of their minds with the Eutychian spell. It was at this very time, as it seems, that this heresy began, and then, having been boldly introduced by him, it was also defended more strongly and more firmly by other bishops and monks, his supporters, while the author himself triumphed and held the most famous episcopal see. Therefore I place the beginning of this error under Basiliscus, who succeeded Zeno as emperor, or rather under Zeno himself (for the times of this Basiliscus are assigned to Zeno, since Zeno recovered the empire that had been taken from him), and under Simplicius, bishop of Rome, about the year 447 after Christ's passion. Those seem to me to be greatly mistaken who bring this heresy down to the times of the emperor Honorius or Marcian, since it is agreed that it was stirred up after Eutyches and Dioscurus were already dead, and was compounded and enlarged from their impious blasphemies. The author of the book called On the Dogmas of the Church (chapter 2) mentions this very heresy, and Peter Lombard (book 3, distinction 1, chapter "Diligenter"), from which it can be gathered that it was spread, propagated and nourished. It flourished most of all in Egypt, where Timothy raged furiously against the Council of Chalcedon as though in his own kingdom. It remained, both under its own name and under the name of the Monothelites and Monophysites, for a very long time, and, like the Eutychian heresy, it was most certainly a corruption of the Christian faith. It had as successors the Theodosian heretics and the Caianites, or Caianians (for they are called by both names), who took their name from Caianus, bishop of Alexandria, as Damascene teaches, and not from Gaianus, who was a military commander and barbarian under Arcadius, as Socrates teaches (book 6, chapter 5). These held the same doctrine as ours, and they lived and began under the emperor Justinian II and Constantine, bishop of Rome, about the year 675 after Christ's passion. They were the revivers of the mad doctrine of Dioscurus, as Isidore relates (book 8, Etymologies), and it is in the canon "Quidam", 24, quaestio 3. For this Justinian was infected with the Eutychian stain, which he also defended, and under him the Theodosians and Eutychians revived in Egypt. Nor is this the Theodosius from whom the Theodosians, of whom we now speak, are named; Euagrius mentions him in book 2, chapter 5. For although that Theodosius opposed the Council of Chalcedon, he is earlier in time than this one. Rather, he is the one of whom John Damascene writes in his book On Heresies; and he was bishop of Alexandria. But these Theodosians were afterwards called Jacobites and Monophysites, and Damascene also joins to them the Aphthartodocites and the Barsanians, as agreeing and holding in harmony the same doctrine about the two natures in Christ.

units.la: 2 Dicunt filium Dei.)Obscura sententia nisi explicetur & illustretur. Itaque etsi sumus de Eutychianae haereseos riuulis foetidis illis quidem fusius postea dicturi, hoc tamen loco breuiter annotabimus, Erratu a Timotheanis fuisse in hypostatica duarum, quae sunt in una & eadem Christi persona, naturarum unione & coniunctione. Alij quidem ipsas naturas, diuinam dico & humanam, ita coaluisse in Christo voluerunt, ut diuina (quae potentior est) humanam, quae infirmior erat, ipsa assumptione absorbuerit. Itaque totum quicquid est in Christo iam Deum esse contendunt. Timotheani vero aliud dixerunt, Ipsas nimirum Christi naturas in Mariae utero conflatas in unam quandam tertiam naturam velut massam, quae iam nec diuina sit nec humana proprie, quia istiusmodi unione & conflatura proprietates utriusque naturae coierunt & perierunt: sed inde tertium quiddam volut productum, quod vocetur Christus. Nimirum quemadmodum ex aqua & melle commixtis fit hydromel: item ex melle & aceto fit oxymel, quod iā neque acetum est ne-que mel,& tamen quiddam tertium ex vtroque compositum,quod vtriusque proprietates confusas habeat, non autem in ipso malagmate di-ftinctas. Boethius in lib.De duabus Naturis & Vna persona Christi.Idem igitur in Christo accidisse impiissimè docent, quasi Dominus noster Iesus Christus post affumptum hominem amplius neque verus Deus, neque verus homo fit,sed velut chimæra quædam & monftrū horrendum ex Deo & homine confusis inter fe & tribulatis compactum & coflatum. Hoc postea renouauit impurus Seruetus, veluti fi duæ ceræ colliquescant,aut duo humores inter fe velut vi num & aqua, confundantur. Iam vero Theo-dofiani hæretici hanc tertiam naturam quam à Timotheanis acceperunt totam mortalem esse afferunt, vt ait Ifidorus.At Caianitæ vel Caiani qui secuti sunt, contrà malunt tertiam eam naturam totam esse immortalem & impatibilem, adeò vt totum Christi ex Theodofianorū sententia fuerit mortale & patibile.Ex Caianorum vero,qui & ipsi propago Eutychianorū fuerūt, dogmate totum Christi fuit impatibile. Atque vtraque hac sententia vere suo specialique [illegible, ~3 letters] honore spoliatur Christus. Nec enim noster apud Deum mediator est, fi totus & tantum est Deus: neque etiā est nobis vitæ æternæ author, princeps & largitor,fi totus & tatum est homo.
units.tr: 2 Dicunt filium Dei.) This statement is obscure unless it is explained and clarified. Therefore, although we shall later speak more fully of the foul streams of the Eutychian heresy, we shall note briefly here that the Timotheans erred concerning the hypostatic union and conjunction of the two natures, which are in one and the same person of Christ. Some wished that the natures themselves, I mean the divine and the human, should so coalesce in Christ that the divine (which is the stronger) absorbed the human, which was weaker, by the very act of assumption. Hence they contend that whatever is in Christ is now altogether God. The Timotheans, however, said something different: that the natures of Christ, melted together in the womb of Mary, became one third nature, as it were a single mass, which is now neither properly divine nor human, because by such a union and fusion the properties of both natures came together and perished. Instead, something third, as it were produced from them, is called Christ. Just as from water and honey mixed together comes hydromel, and from honey and vinegar comes oxymel, which is neither vinegar nor honey, yet is a third thing compounded of both, having the properties of both confused, not distinct within the mixture itself (Boethius, in his book On the Two Natures and One Person of Christ). They impiously teach that the same thing happened in Christ, as if our Lord Jesus Christ, after assuming man, were no longer true God or true man, but were like a chimera, or some dreadful monster, compounded and fused from God and man confused and mingled with each other. Afterwards the impure Servetus revived this, as if two waxes were melted together, or two liquids, such as wine and water, were mixed. Now the Theodosian heretics affirm that this third nature, which they received from the Timotheans, is wholly mortal, as Isidore says. But the Caianites or Caianians, who followed, on the contrary prefer to say that this third nature is wholly immortal and impassible, so that, according to the Theodosians' opinion, all of Christ was mortal and passible; while from the doctrine of the Caianians, who were themselves offshoots of the Eutychians, all of Christ was impassible. And by both of these opinions Christ is stripped of his true and proper honour. For our mediator with God is not truly a mediator if he is wholly and only God; nor is he the author, prince and giver of eternal life to us if he is wholly and only man.

units.la: Ex utraque vero Christi natura tertium quiddam fuisse conflatum, quod nec homo post incarnationem manserit, nec Deus, salsissimum certè quidem est,quiꝫ & naturas in Christo cõfundit, quas distinguit Scriptura, Roman.1.verf.3: 1.Pet.3.verf.13:2.Corinth.13.verf.4: & ei dicto aduersatur, quod pronuntiat verissimus Dei Propheta Isaias cap.7.verf.14. & confirmat Paulus, 1.Timoth.3.v.16. atque etiam explicat Matthæus 1.verf.23. Est autè, Christum post assumptum hominem manere & esse Emmanuelem, id est, Deum verum in nostra carne & natura, quam verè assumpsit, atque retinet. Est enim Deus, ut loquitur Ioan.1.verf.14.nobiscum habitans. Ergo & Deus manet, & homo: non autem est quiddam ex utroque mistum, conflatum & tertium. Quæ omnia ab aliis & doctis quidem viris præclare contra Eutychianos & eorum patriarchas Apollinaristas iampridem velut à Cyrillo, Theodoreto, Vigilio, Leone & aliis sunt disputata. Itaque non tradam fusius.
units.tr: That a third thing, compounded out of both natures of Christ, came into being, which after the assumption of the human nature was neither man nor God, is most certainly absurd, since it confounds the natures in Christ, which Scripture distinguishes (Rom. 1.3; 1 Pet. 3.13; 2 Cor. 13.4). It also contradicts the saying of the most truthful prophet Isaiah, Isa. 7.14, which Paul confirms (1 Tim. 3.16) and Matthew explains (Matt. 1.23). Christ, after taking on man, remains and is Emmanuel, that is, true God in our flesh and nature, which he truly assumed and still retains. For he is God, as John says, "dwelling among us" (John 1.14). Therefore he remains both God and man, and is not something mixed and compounded out of both and a third thing. All these points have already been argued clearly by other learned men against the Eutychians and their patriarchs, the Apollinarists, by Cyril, Theodoret, Vigilius, Leo and others. Therefore I will not treat them at greater length.

units.la: Vulgò in impres-sis corruptus locus & obscurus, ubi sic legitur, Immutatam videlicet naturarum proprietate efficientiarum coitionem.Sic reponendum est, ut fecimus. Naturarum enim immutatam volebant proprietatem, propterea quòd earum effecta confusa esse dicerent & putarent. Cur autem putarent, ratio est, quòd in Scriptura quæ humanæ naturæ propria sunt, divinæ tribuuntur: & quæ divinæ verè competunt, tribuuntur etiam humanæ, ut cūm Deus gloriæ dicitur Christus, 1.Corinth.2.verf.8. Deus sanguine suo redemisse Ecclesiam, Actor.20. versu 28. Filius hominis fuisse in cœlo antequam in illud ascenderet, Ioann.3. versu 13. Quæ phrases per idioma-tum communionem propter naturarum vnionem in vna Christi persona recte intelliguntur, sunt que à nobis accipiendæ, nō quasi Deus ipse passus sit: aut humanitas Christi in cœlo iamtum ante ascensionem fuerit. Itaque huiusmodi prædicationes extra eam naturam, cui proprie competunt, sunt tantum dialecticæ: non autem Physicæ enuntiationes. Physicas tamen esse Timotheani volebant, & idcirco pro hæreticis merito sunt habiti. Quem errorem iustissimè quidem damnatum à patribus hodie Vbiquitarij, imprimis autè Iacobus Smidelinus, Οʹ[?] Βεά-[illegible, ~40 letters] cum ni-hil aliud haberet, unde homo ambitiosus vanæ gloriolæ laureolam aucuparetur, impiè funestèque renouauit[?].
units.tr: In the printed editions this passage is corrupt and obscure, where it reads thus: immutatam videlicet naturarum proprietate efficientiarum coitionem. It must be restored as we have done. For they wanted the property of the natures to be changed, because they said and thought that the effects of the natures were confused. The reason they thought so is that what belongs to human nature is ascribed in Scripture to the divine, and what truly belongs to the divine is also ascribed to the human: as when Christ is called "the Lord of glory" (1 Cor. 2.8), God is said to have redeemed the Church with his own blood (Acts 20.28), and the Son of man is said to have been in heaven before he ascended into it (John 3.13). These phrases, rightly understood through the communication of properties on account of the union of the natures in the one person of Christ, are to be received by us, not as if God himself suffered, or as if the humanity of Christ was already in heaven before the ascension. Thus such predications, outside that nature to which they properly belong, are merely dialectical, and not physical statements. Yet the Timotheans wanted them to be physical, and for this reason they were rightly counted among the heretics. This error, most justly condemned by the Fathers, the Ubiquitarians today, and above all Jacob Schmidlin, have renewed in an impious and deadly way, [illegible, ~40 letters], since he had nothing else by which an ambitious man might win for himself the laurel of empty glory.

units.la: Nestoriani cur sic dicti. Erroris autem eorum caput vnum.
units.tr: Why the Nestorians are so called. The first point of their error.

units.la: Nestoriani à Nestorio{1} Episcopo Patriarcha Constantinopolitano, qui contra fidem Catholicam dogmatizare ausus est, Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum hominem tantum: nec id quod mediator Dei & hominum factus est, in utero virginis de Spiritu sancto fuisse conceptum: sed postea Deum homini fuisse permixtum, nec Deum hominem passum sepultumque dicebat, euacuare contendens omne nostrum remedium, quo verbum Dei sic hominem suscipere di-gnatum est in utero Virginis, ut una persona fieret Dei & hominis, propterea sic singulariter & mira-biliter natus, mortuus etiam pro peccatis nostris, cum ea, quæ non rapuerat, soluerét, Deus homo a mor-tuis resurgens ascendit in cœlum.
units.tr: The Nestorians are named after Nestorius, bishop and patriarch of Constantinople, who dared to teach against the Catholic faith. They held that our Lord Jesus Christ was merely a man, and that what was made the Mediator of God and men was not conceived in the virgin's womb by the Holy Spirit. Rather, they said, God was afterwards joined to the man, and God did not suffer or get buried as man. Their aim was to destroy our entire remedy, by which the Word of God deigned to take on man in the Virgin's womb, so that God and man became one person, and so that he, born in this singular and wonderful way, also died for our sins, paying with what he had not taken, and God-man rose from the dead and ascended into heaven.

units.la: I Nestoriani à Nestorio. ) Cùm iampridem fidem Christianam variis modis labefactare te-tasset Satan, variisque ad eam rem machinis & instrumentis usus multum tum in Oriente tum in Occidente eam de sua veritate propulisset, tandem maioribus viribus conixus prorsus extinguere & semel eruertere voluit, ne toties sibi laborandum colluctandumque[?] esset. Itaq; cùm per Arianos magna iam istius totius fidei Christianæ ruinæ initia fecisset, quicquid veræ lucis & cognitionis restabat per Nestorianos & Eutychianos vel omnino tollere, vel prorsus involuere ut incertum & obscurum cœpit. Fue-runt enim istæ hæreses duæ ut tempore ad Ma-humetismum & Papismum constituendum po-stremæ: ita totius Christianæ fidei internecio, quæ ipsas pietatis reliquias erroris teterrimi veneno iugularunt, & funestissimis[?] exéquiis sepe-lierunt. Nam ut de hoc argumento agens Theo-doretus, & pie quidem scribit, prius per exter-nos & manifestos hostes Satan adversus Eccle-siam arma sumpserat: sed per Nestorium fidem oppugnans, domesticum & latentem hostem, ipsumque adeò Ecclesiæ pastorem in ipsius Ec-clesiæ viscera armavit, qui omnem divinitatis & humanitatis unigeniti inficiationem & abnegationem, ipso tamen orthodoxæ fidei illustran-dæ & defendendæ prætextu, inducereṫ. Itaque fuit Nestorius totius diabolicæ nequitiæ ca-pax instrumentum, vereque totius Ecclesiæ in-cendium, ut scribit Socrates libro 7. cap.29. & officina blasphemiæ, ut loquitur Euagrius lib.1. cap.2. Quid enim nobis in fide salvum manere potest, si ipsum illius fundamentum subruitur, quod ille fecit? Est autem hoc fundamentum & fidei & salutis nostræ, ut Paulus docet 1. Timoth.3. vers.16, Deum in carne manifestatum fuisse, & Filium Dei ex muliere hominem factum esse, Galat.4. vers.4. utraque natura in unam eandemque personam assumpta, non in duas pluresque personas diuisa & separata, ut sit vere noster Emmanuel, Redemptor, Mediator, & Deus & homo idem & unus Jesus Christus, utrunque in unam personam concilians, & inter utrunque medians, seque interponens, Matth.1.vers.23:1.Timoth.2.vers.6. Quare neque tetriorem neque fœdiorem errorem, neque pestilentius illum venenum Nestoriana peste Satan in Ecclesiam unquam induxit, ex qua post-ea Eutychiana secuta est, deinde Mahumetana, quando Mahumetum ipsum in sua illa nova blasphemia cudenda Sergio quodam monacho Nestoriano adiutum fuisse constat. Cœpit vero hæc hæresis sub Theodosio Juniore & Cœlestino primo Pontifice Romano circa annum à Christo passo 400. vel, ut alij putant, 399. Primum autem Constantinopoli exorta & nata est, Nestorio iam illic Episcopatum obtinente, sed inde progressa totius Orientis regiones & Ecclesias celerrime peruasit atque miserè corrupit, maximè verò vtranque Armeniam: vbi etiamnum hodie regnat, quanquam Arme-niaca synodo iampridem damnata & anathe-matizata fuit. Habuit autem Nestorius tum A-nastasium, & Photium, presbyteros Constan-tinopolitanos, tum etiam Phriulcum Heracleæ episcopum, & alios plures Orientales epis-copos sibi statim assentientes, fauentésque, quem-admodum docet Socrat.lib.7.c.34. etiam quum Ephesina Synodus, cui primum interfuit, & à qua damnatus hæreseos depositusque est, ageretur, adeò vt ab iis Nestorius vir sanctissimus passim appellaretur. Perstitit verò hæc tanta tamque atrox in Christum blasphemia diutissi-mè, & successores habuit, defensoresque obsti-natissimos. Mortuo enim Nestorio, non tatum Xeneas quidam Ægyptius, & Hierapolis in Ægypto episcopus, de quo Euagr.li.3.c.31. sed etiā Theodorus Mopsuestiæ (quæ, vt Sozomenus ait, Ciliciæ ciuitas est) episcopus, hunc errorem renouauit, acerrimeque propugnauit scriptis aduersus duodecim Cyrilli capita, & Synodum Ephesinam editis: qui sub Iustiniano etiam mortuus, publicè Synodo damnatus est, quemadmodum idem Euagr. libro 4. capite 38. refert, quanquam tamen Theodoretus libro 5. capite 40. histor. videtur hunc ipsum Theodorum laudare, sed durante adhuc infelici illa Theodoreti cum Cyrillo propter duodecim illa capita dissensione. Hunc Theodorum Nestorianum esse, primum Acatius Melitensis episcopus, & Rabula Edessenus deprehenderunt. Ergo & sub Anastasio imperatore, & postea sub Heraclio viguit, imprimisque a Syris Monachis defensa est, & saepe sub disputationis de duabus in Christo naturis praetextu interpolata, & velut crambe bis.cocta iterum appositā. Denique novo Christolytarum nomine, quorum meminit Dam-mascenus, repetita. Ephesina Synodo prima, cui praefuit Cyrillus Alexandriae episcopus, sub Theodosio iuniore, confutatus est hic error: deinde a Zenone imperatore, tota Edessae civi-tatis schola, quod Nestorianum dogma probaret, euersa est, vt Theodoretus libro 2. scribit. Denique legibus etiam publicis & Romanis, punita & coercita, vt apparet ex l. Damnato. C. De haeretic. & Manich. & meminit etiam illius legis Euagr. libro 1. capite 12. & post eum Nicephorus libro 14. vt nihil isto dogmate tetrius, putidius, & odiosius vniuersis Ecclesiis, totiqué terrarum orbi vnquam fuerit. Quis autem huius sectae & haereseos primus author fuerit, vel censendus sit, quaesitum iampridem legimus. Quidam enim a Photinianis haereticis velut propaginem quandam deducunt: alij a Samosatenianis, vel Paulianis potius ortam malunt, quemadmodum Suidas in voce Nestorius. quorum omnium sententiam refutat Socrates libro 7. cap. 32. Verisimilius diceretur a Manichaeis professa, qui, vt scribit Augustinus libro 23. contra Faustum, docent alium esse in Christo Filium Dei, alium autem Filium Mariae (non tantum autem aliud) & Filium Dei in Baptismo Christi descendisse in Filium Mariae. Itaque duas in Christo personas constituunt, quod & Helcesaitæ ab iisdem Manichæis profecti & edocti faciunt, & ante vtrosque Cerinthiani, Gnostici, & Colarbasij. Sane Hieronymus, qui ante tepora Theodosij huius vixit, meminit eorum, qui duos in Christo Filios faciunt, vnum Filium Dei, alterum Filium Mariæ, quos insanos vocat, vt hunc errorem iampridem quaedam initia habuisse facile constet. Verius tamen mihi cum Arianis videntur coniungendi. Nam hi primum in tolleda destruendaque vera de Mediatoris nostri persona, fide impetum fecerunt, magnaque in ea ruinas ediderunt, quos tantum sunt sequuti & imitati alij, qui in eodem fidei orthodoxæ capite fœdissimè impegerunt, velut hi Nestoriani & postea Eutychiani, quos vtros-que idcirco ad Arianos velut ad propria stirpem & patriarchas suos refero. Huius autem dogmatis quanquam apertus defensor, & disse-minator fuit Nestorius, repertor tamen dicitur fuisse Anastasius illius presbyter & cum eo Antiochia Constantinopolim traductus, Nestorioque familiaris, vt docet Socrates lib.7. & Nicephorus libro 14. Obtinuit tamen, vt Nestoriani, non autem Anastasiani dicerentur. Fuit autem Nestorius Germanicia (quod erat Comagenæ prouinciæ oppidulum) oriundus, homo disertus, sed ambitiosus, qui per varias ciuitates obambulans, sedesque subinde mutans, fama sanctæ cuiusdam & austerae vitæ, ad episcopatum Antiochenum tandem peruenit. Inde post Sisinnij mortem Constantinopolitanus episcopus factus, sæuum se & crudelem in omnes hæreticos mirum in modum statim præbuit, adeo vt in iura magistratus inuaderet, dum ipse præpi-[?]piti ira raptus, manu propria eorum templa incendit, de quo est ab ipso imperatore Theodo-fio iuniore reprehensus. Tandem virus illud suum de duabus in Christo personis per Anastasium presbyterum euomuit. Quod quam esset noxium, primus Eusebius quidam, cognomine Dorylæus rhetor deprehendit, & demonstrauit, quemadmodum refert Euagr.lib.i.cap.9. Vocatus igitur ad Synodum Ephesinam, quæ propterea à Theodosio iuniore collecta erat, primum adfuit: postea quum doctissimis Cyrilli velitationibus & disputationibus imparem se sentiret, secessit, neque postea euocatus, etiã post trinam denuntiationem adesse voluit. Itaque ob errorem anathematizatus, & ob contumaciam quoque depositus est, quum ad eum antea Cyrillus literas priuatim dedisset, & ad refipiscentiam inuitasset, quibus Nestorius ipse in errore tamen persistens, vicissim respondit.
units.tr: I The Nestorians, from Nestorius. Satan had long been trying to undermine the Christian faith in various ways. Using many devices and instruments, he had driven it from its truth in both East and West. At last, exerting greater forces, he wanted to extinguish it completely and overthrow it once and for all, so that he would not have to labour and struggle against it so often. So, having already made great inroads into the whole Christian faith through the Arians, he began either to remove altogether whatever remained of true light and knowledge, or to bury it so that it became uncertain and obscure, through the Nestorians and Eutychians. For these two heresies came last, in time, to establish Mohammedanism and Papism. Thus the ruin of the whole Christian faith, which strangled the last remnants of piety with the poison of a most foul error and buried them with most deadly funeral rites, was complete. For Theodoret, writing on this subject, rightly says that Satan had earlier taken up arms against the Church through external and open enemies. But attacking the faith through Nestorius, a domestic and hidden enemy, he armed the very minister of the Church against the very bowels of the Church. Nestorius introduced a denial and repudiation of the divinity and humanity of the only-begotten, yet under the pretext of illustrating and defending the orthodox faith. So Nestorius was an instrument capable of all diabolical wickedness, truly a fire consuming the whole Church, as Socrates writes in book 7, chapter 29, and a workshop of blasphemy, as Evagrius puts it in book 1, chapter 2. For what can remain safe for us in the faith if its very foundation, which he undermined, is overthrown? This is the foundation both of faith and of our salvation, as Paul teaches in 1 Timothy 3:16: that God was manifested in the flesh, and, as in Galatians 4:4, that the Son of God was made man of a woman. Both natures were assumed into one and the same person, not divided and separated into two or more persons, so that Jesus Christ is truly our Immanuel, Redeemer and Mediator, both God and man, the same and one Jesus Christ, uniting both in one person, standing between both and interposing himself (Matthew 1:23; 1 Timothy 2:6). Therefore Satan never introduced into the Church a more foul or hideous error, or a more pestilent poison, than the Nestorian plague. From it the Eutychian heresy followed afterwards, and then the Mohammedan, since it is established that Mohammed himself, in coining that new blasphemy of his, was aided by a certain Nestorian monk named Sergius. This heresy began under Theodosius the Younger and Celestine the first Roman Pontiff, around the year 400 after Christ's passion, or, as others think, 399. It first arose and was born at Constantinople, where Nestorius already held the episcopate. From there it spread very quickly through all the regions and churches of the East and corrupted them miserably, and especially both Armenias, where it still reigns today, although it was condemned and anathematized long ago by an Armenian synod. Nestorius had as supporters at once Anastasius and Photius, elders of Constantinople, as well as Phriulcus, bishop of Heraclea, and many other Eastern bishops, as Socrates teaches in book 7, chapter 34. This support continued even while the Synod of Ephesus, at which he first appeared and by which he was condemned as a heretic and deposed, was in session. So much so that Nestorius was everywhere called a most holy man by them. This so great and so atrocious blasphemy against Christ persisted for a very long time, and it had successors and most stubborn defenders. For after Nestorius died, not only Xenaias, an Egyptian and bishop of Hierapolis in Egypt, about whom Evagrius writes in book 3, chapter 31, but also Theodore, bishop of Mopsuestia (a city of Cilicia, as Sozomen says), renewed this error. He defended it most fiercely in writings against the twelve chapters of Cyril and the Synod of Ephesus. Theodore died under Justinian and was condemned publicly by a synod, as Evagrius again reports in book 4, chapter 38. Yet Theodoret, in book 5, chapter 40 of his history, seems to praise this same Theodore. But that was while the unhappy quarrel between Theodoret and Cyril over the twelve chapters was still going on. Acacius, bishop of Melitene, and Rabbula of Edessa were the first to detect that Theodore was a Nestorian. So this heresy flourished under the emperor Anastasius and later under Heraclius. It was defended especially by the Syrian monks, and often slipped back in under the pretext of disputing about the two natures in Christ, like cabbage reheated after being boiled twice. Finally it was revived under the new name of Christolytes, which Damascene mentions. This heresy was refuted first at the first Synod of Ephesus, presided over by Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, under Theodosius the Younger. Later, under the emperor Zeno, the whole school of the city of Edessa was overthrown because it upheld the Nestorian doctrine, as Theodoret writes in book 2. Finally it was also punished and restrained by public laws, Roman ones too, as appears from the law "Damnato" in the Code, On Heretics and Manichaeans. Evagrius also mentions that law in book 1, chapter 12, and after him Nicephorus in book 14. Nothing more foul, more putrid or more hateful has ever existed among all the Churches and throughout the whole world than this doctrine. Who was the first author of this sect and heresy, or who should be considered so, has long been a matter of inquiry. Some trace it, as a kind of offshoot, from the heretics called Photinians. Others prefer that it arose from the Samosatenes, or rather from the Paulians, as Suidas says under the word Nestorius. Socrates refutes the opinions of all of them in book 7, chapter 32. It might more plausibly be said that it was professed by the Manichaeans, who, as Augustine writes in book 23 against Faustus, teach that the Son of God is one thing in Christ and the Son of Mary another (not merely another thing), and that the Son of God descended at Christ's baptism upon the Son of Mary. So they set up two persons in Christ. The Elchasaites, who came from the same Manichaeans and were taught by them, do the same, as did the Cerinthians, Gnostics and Colarbasians, who came before both. Indeed Jerome, who lived before the time of Theodosius, mentions those who make two sons in Christ, one the Son of God and the other the Son of Mary, and calls them mad. So it is easily clear that this error had some beginnings long ago. Yet it seems to me more truly to be linked with the Arians. For they first attacked and destroyed the true doctrine of the person of our Mediator, and caused great ruin in it. Others merely followed and imitated them, and fell most foully on that same article of the orthodox faith, as did these Nestorians and afterwards the Eutychians. For this reason I trace both to the Arians, as to their own stock and patriarchs. Although Nestorius was the open defender and disseminator of this doctrine, it is said that its inventor was Anastasius, his elder, who was brought from Antioch to Constantinople with him and was close to Nestorius, as Socrates teaches in book 7, and Nicephorus in book 14. Nevertheless it prevailed that they should be called Nestorians, not Anastasians. Nestorius was born at Germanicia, a small town of the province of Commagene. He was an eloquent man but ambitious, who wandered through various cities, changing his seat from time to time. Relying on the reputation of a certain holiness and austere life, he at last attained the episcopate of Antioch. After the death of Sisinnius he was made bishop of Constantinople. There he at once showed himself wonderfully fierce and cruel towards all heretics, so much so that he invaded the rights of the civil magistrate, when, carried away by headlong anger, he burned their temples with his own hand. For this the emperor Theodosius the Younger himself reproved him. At last he vomited out his poison about two persons in Christ through the elder Anastasius. How harmful this was was first detected and shown by a certain Eusebius, surnamed Dorylaeus, a rhetorician, as Evagrius reports in book 1, chapter 9. Summoned to the Synod of Ephesus, which Theodosius the Younger had therefore convened, Nestorius at first attended. Later, feeling himself no match for the most learned arguments and disputations of Cyril, he withdrew, and when summoned again afterwards he would not appear, even after three summonses. So he was anathematized for his error and deposed for his obstinacy. Cyril had earlier written to him privately and invited him to repentance. Nestorius, still persisting in his error, replied to him in turn.

units.la: Constantinopoli igitur in Nestorij locum sufsectus est Maximianus. Nestorius autem in monasterium quoddam, quod duobus stadiis Antiochia abest, & Euprepium dicitur, abiit, ubi per annos quatuor latitauit. Postea Ioannis Antiocheni episcopi literis admonitus imperator Theodosius iubet Nestorium deportari Oasin oppidum (quæ & Ibis, vel Ibin, ut est in itinerario Antonini, dicitur) ad extremos Ægypti & Africæ fines, quæ Romano imperio parebat, Thebaeisque vicina erat, etsi septem dierū[?] terrestris itineris spatio remotam scribit Herodotus libro 2. Sed aliter Ptolemaeus, cui potius est assentiendum. Vicinam enim facit, quem vi-de, libro 4. capite 5. Hoc exilium fuit Nesto-rio valde durum, tum propter incultam & inso-litam regionem, tum ob Blemmyarum & No-madum, barbararum gentium, excursiones, à quibus captivus abductus est, posteaque Ro-manis redditus. Neque tamen propterea resi-puit haereticus obstinatus. Tandem vero in eo-dem exilio senio misere confectus periit, lingua prius, ut omnes tradunt, à vermibus corrosa, & excisa[?]: & terra ipsa sub eo dehiscente, eúmque cooperiente & deglutiente, ut memorabile aliquod tantae tamque impiê in Christum blasphe-miae in Nestorio illius authore, quemadmo-dum in Dathan, Core, & Abiron, exemplum posteris extaret. Has igitur pœnas luit canis impurissimus, & impiissimus Nestorius. Quae nos brevissimè ex pluribus Socrat. lib.7. Euagrij lib.1. Nicephori lib.14. capitibus collegi-mus, ut nota esset eorum temporum historia, sequunturisque Nestorianis, si qui forte erunt, ad resipiscentiam prodessent.
units.tr: Maximianus was therefore appointed at Constantinople in Nestorius' place. Nestorius withdrew to a monastery called Euprepius, two stadia from Antioch, where he lay hidden for four years. Afterwards, prompted by a letter from John, bishop of Antioch, the emperor Theodosius ordered Nestorius to be deported to the town of Oasis (also called Ibis, or Ibin, as it is in the Itinerary of Antoninus), at the far borders of Egypt and Africa, which was subject to the Roman empire and lay near Thebais. Herodotus, in book 2, writes that it was seven days' land journey away, but Ptolemy, whom we should rather follow, says otherwise; he makes it near, as you may see in book 4, chapter 5. This exile was very hard for Nestorius, both because of the wild and unfamiliar country and because of the raids of the Blemmyes and the Nomads, barbarous peoples, by whom he was taken captive and afterwards restored to the Romans. Yet the obstinate heretic did not for that reason repent. At last, in that same exile, he died wretchedly worn out by old age, his tongue first, as all report, eaten away and cut off by worms, and the earth itself gaping open beneath him and swallowing him up, so that there might stand for posterity a memorable example of so great and impious a blasphemy against Christ in Nestorius its author, just as in Dathan, Korah and Abiram. So this is the punishment paid by that most filthy and most impious dog, Nestorius. I have gathered these things very briefly from several chapters: Socrates, book 7; Evagrius, book 1; Nicephorus, book 14, so that the history of those times might be known, and in case any Nestorians, should there be any, might be helped to repent.

units.la: 2 Christum hominem tantum.) Quisquis ille fuit, qui ad Augustini catalogum has tres haereses addidit, parum & disertus & doctus mihi fuisse videtur. Nec enim commode quae fuerit Nestorianae haereseos summa explicat. Igitur ex aliis, imprimis autem Isidoro lib.8. Etymologia. colligemus, 1 Christum duabus personis iisque separatis, & seorsim consistentibus constare, non tantum duabus naturis. Itaque seorsim & separatim in Christo esse Dei Fi-lium, & Mariae Filium, & alium esse Dei Fi-lium, lium, alium autem Filium Mariæ, non tantum autem aliud. Quæ igitur, vt ait Damascenus, infirmitatis opera sunt in Christo, veluti dormis-se, edisse, bibisse, lachrymasse, ea omnia Filium Mariæ operatu esse sine Dei Filio. Quæ autem egregia & miraculosa sunt Christi opera, illa Filium Dei in eodem Christo operatum esse sine Filio Mariæ. Quare nec eum Filium qui ex Maria natus esset, Dei Filium esse, neque etiam Deum. Per contumeliam enim eum trimestrem Deum appellabat, vt refert Socrates lib.7.c.34. Quæ sententia quàm sit absurda, facile ex his apparebit. Primum, quòd ita distrahit naturas in Christo, vt non distinguat, sed prorsus separet & loco seiungat. Itaque naturæ Christi diuinæ humana natura iam non erit vnita, & [?]ἀσυγχύτως[?], vel, vt loquitur Paulus, [?]σωματικῶς[?] coniuncta, & inhabitans, Coloss.2. versu 9. Ex quo sequitur, non vnum nobis datum esse Christum, sed duos. Deinde ex eo efficitur, Filium Dei neque assumpsisse humanam naturam, neque semen Abrahæ, neque etiam carnis & sanguinis nobiscum participem fuisse, contra apertissimū Scripturæ testimonium, quod est Hebr.2. versu 14, & 16. Secundum, Christus iste qui ex Maria natus est, non erit mediator noster, si ab eo in aliam personam separetur Filius Dei, id est, diuina ipsius natura. Solum enim erit homo Filius Mariæ. Itaque nec fons vitæ erit, nec lux mundi, nec naturam habuerit quæ pœnæ peccatorum nostrorum perferendæ satis esse potuerit, sed ab ea pœna fuerit illa natura absorpta. Quod enim in vero & nō Nestoriano Christo humana natura pœnas illas peccati immensas tolerare potuit, factum est, quoniam à divina natura, cui hypostaticè unita erat, sustentabatur. Extra unionem igitur, non erit sustentata: vel plures eodem modo eademque sustentatione nostri mediatores, præter unum Christum esse potuerunt. Quod est impiissimum, & summè blasphemum. Denique nō alio modo Deus in Christo fuerit, & habitaverit, quàm est in nobis, & in reliquis sanctis, Petro, Paulo, Ioanne, gubernatione nimirum & ἐνεργείᾳ[?] Spiritus sui: nō autem ἑνώσει[?], & naturæ unione, ut loquitur Ioannes. Quare non magis in Christo Deus in carne manifestatus erit quàm in Petro, & in me: quod est plane horrendum, impium, & blasphemum.
units.tr: 2 Christ merely a man.) Whoever it was who added these three heresies to Augustine's catalogue seems to me to have been neither very eloquent nor very learned, for he does not explain conveniently what the substance of the Nestorian heresy was. So from other writers, above all Isidore, book 8 of the Etymologies, I will gather the following: first, that Christ consists of two persons, and those separated and standing apart, not merely of two natures. Accordingly, the Son of God and the Son of Mary are separately and distinctly in Christ, one being the Son of God, another the Son of Mary, and not merely a different aspect of one person. Therefore, as Damascene says, the works of weakness in Christ, such as sleeping, eating, drinking, weeping, all these were performed by the Son of Mary without the Son of God; while the excellent and miraculous works of Christ were performed by the Son of God in the same Christ without the Son of Mary. Hence he who was born of Mary was not the Son of God, nor even God. By way of insult he called him "God of three months," as Socrates reports, book 7, chapter 34. How absurd this opinion is will easily appear from what follows. First, because it so divides the natures in Christ that it does not distinguish them but utterly separates them and sets them apart in place. Thus the human nature will no longer be united with the divine nature of Christ, nor joined [ἀσυγχύτως, without confusion] or, as Paul puts it, [σωματικῶς, bodily] and dwelling in him, Colossians 2:9. From this it follows that Christ has not been given to us as one, but as two. Next, from this it follows that the Son of God neither took upon himself human nature nor the seed of Abraham, nor was he a partaker with us of flesh and blood, against the very plain testimony of Scripture, Hebrews 2:14 and 16. Second, that Christ who was born of Mary will not be our mediator, if the Son of God, that is, his divine nature, is separated from him into another person. For he will be only a man, the Son of Mary. Thus he will be neither the fountain of life nor the light of the world, nor will he have a nature which could have been sufficient to bear the punishment of our sins, but that nature will have been swallowed up by that punishment. For the fact that in the true Christ, and not the Nestorian one, the human nature could bear those immense penalties of sin, is because it was sustained by the divine nature to which it was hypostatically united. Outside that union, then, it will not be sustained; or else several mediators in the same way and with the same sustaining could exist besides the one Christ. This is most impious and most blasphemous. Finally, God is not in Christ and dwells in him in any other way than he is in us and in the other saints, Peter, Paul, John, namely by the governance and [ἐνεργείᾳ, operation] of his Spirit, and not by [ἑνώσει, union] and the union of nature, as John puts it. Hence God will not be manifested in the flesh in Christ any more than in Peter or in me, which is plainly horrible, impious and blasphemous.

units.la: 2 Filium Dei in Christo esse Mariæ Filio assessorem[?] tantum: vel, ut in singulis nostrum, habitatorem, uti in templo quodam, & in eo solum esse discrimen, quod maiori efficacia, energia, & effusione operationis & virtutis in Christo, quàm in sanctorum ullo habitaverit, & agat.
units.tr: 2 That the Son of God in Christ is merely an assistant to the Son of Mary, or, as in each of us, an inhabitant, as in some temple, and that the only difference is that he has dwelt and acts in Christ with greater efficacy, energy and outpouring of operation and power than in any of the saints.

units.la: Itaque non aliter Deum in homine Christo esse dicebat, quàm adoptione & merito, fuitque hęc impia illius vox, ut refert Gregorius Maximus, Non invideo Christo Deo facto, quia, si volo, & ipse possum fieri. Falsissimum verò istud est. Neque enim Deus in Christo vel ut hospes, vel ut sustentator, vel ut sanctificator diuitaxat[?] habitavit, sed humanam naturam assumpsit, efficiens eam suam sibique propriam unione personæ, non cofusione tamen naturæ.
units.tr: Thus he used to say that God was in the man Christ in no other way than by adoption and merit. This was that impious utterance of his which Gregory Maximus reports: "I do not envy Christ, made God, for if I wish, I too can be made so." But that is most false. For God was not in Christ merely as a guest, or as a sustainer, or as a sanctifier, but he took upon himself human nature, making it his own and proper to himself by the union of person, yet without confusion of nature.

units.la: 3 Hominem sive humanitatem in Christo adæquabat Filio Dei, id est, divinæ naturæ Nestorius. Itaque appellationem Dei in homine Christo restringebat ad dignitatis exæquationem, quæ in humana natura facta erat. Cyrillus in lib. De incarnatione vnigenit. cap. 27. Blasphemum & hoc ipsum est. Nam primum naturas confundit, earumque proprietates, quæ tamen in vna & eadem Christi persona distinctæ manent. Passus enim & mortificatus est χρ̄ σαρκί, ait Scriptura: viuificatus autem χρ̄ πνεύματι, Roman. i. v. 3: i. Petr. 3. versu 18. Deinde inducit Deum factitium, & non æternū. Si enim homo in Christo Deus est factus adæquatione, ergo ille homo est Deus factiti, & mutuatitia diuinitas, nō naturalis, & propria. Quod est plane ridiculum.
units.tr: 3 Nestorius made the man or humanity in Christ equal to the Son of God, that is, to the divine nature. Accordingly, he restricted the title of God in the man Christ to an equality of dignity, which had been conferred upon the human nature. Cyril, in his book On the Incarnation of the Only-begotten, chapter 27, calls this blasphemous too. For first, it confuses the natures and their properties, which nevertheless remain distinct in the one and the same person of Christ. For Scripture says that he suffered and was put to death in the flesh [σαρκί], but was made alive in the Spirit [πνεύματι], Romans 1:3; 1 Peter 3:18. Next, it makes God something made and not eternal. For if the man in Christ became God by equality, then that man is a made God, and a borrowed divinity, not natural and proper. This is plainly ridiculous.

units.la: 4 Mariam virginem, quæ peperit Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, non Θεοτόκον dicendam, sed Χριστοτόκον. Quum enim esset orta quæstio, vtrum illa ἀνθρωποτόκος an Θεοτόκος esset appellanda, ad vtrunque scopulum euitandum, Χριστοτόκον nominandam dixit Nestorius, negauit autem vel esse Θεοτόκον vel vocandam. Euagrius lib. i. cap. 7. Qui tamen refutatur à Socrate lib. 7 cap. 32. Nam sic veteres etiā, velut Origenes & Eusebius, loquuti sunt: & res ipsa indicat, quum idem Christus sit Deus & homo, Θεοτόκον dici & posse & debere. Quod quemadmodum sit intelligendum, Augustus libro contra Felic. cap. 12. explicat his verbis, Sic post partum virginis nō alius Dei Filius, & alius hominis: sed idē Christus Dei & hominis Filius. Et sicut in vno homine aliud est corpus, & aliud animus: sic in vno Mediatore aliud Dei, & aliud hominis Filius, sed idem tamen, & non alius Dei quàm homo minis Filius,quanuis pro-pter aliud,Dei:& pro-pter aliud hominis filius.Genuit ergo Maria,& non genuit Filium Dei.Genuit,quando ex ipsa secundum carnem natus est Christus: non ge-nuit,quando de Patre sine initio extitit Filius. Hactenus August. Papistæ quidam addiderunt insulsum quiddam. Putant enim in eo quoque hæreticos fuisse Nestorianos,quòd sub vtraque specie omnes ipsi Cœnę Domini communicaret, & omnibus communicandum esse tam laicis quàm clericis contenderent ex Dei verbo. Id quod Papistarum inscitiam arguit.Nec enim in eo à Nestorianis erratum est, quicquid à Stani-slao Hosio Varmiensi episcopo in Dialog. de Vtriusque speciei communione contrà dispu-tetur.Nec enim prætermissus fuisset hic error à Synodo, sed damnatus, vt alij eiusdem Nestorij errores fuisset.Imo hæc Nestorij sententia oste-dit iam tunc à quibusdam corrumpi & immuta-ri cœptam Cœnæ institutionem quæ à Christo facta fuerat. Atque hæc sunt tot vnius erroris ca-pita, & vnius spiritus pestes, tantique est veram hypostaticæ naturarum in Christo vnionis vim & definitionem nosse.
units.tr: 4 The virgin Mary, who bore our Lord Jesus Christ, is not to be called Mother of God [Θεοτόκον], but Mother of Christ [Χριστοτόκον]. For when the question arose whether she should be called Mother of man [ἀνθρωποτόκος] or Mother of God [Θεοτόκος], Nestorius, to avoid both rocks, said she should be named Mother of Christ [Χριστοτόκον], but he denied that she was to be called Mother of God [Θεοτόκον] or be so called. Evagrius, book 1, chapter 7. Yet he is refuted by Socrates, book 7, chapter 32. For the ancients too, such as Origen and Eusebius, spoke in this way, and the thing itself shows that, since the same Christ is God and man, he both can and ought to be called Mother of God [Θεοτόκον]. How this is to be understood Augustine explains in his book against Felix, chapter 12, in these words: "So after the virgin's child-bearing there is not one Son of God and another of man, but the same Christ is Son of God and of man. And just as in one man the body is one thing and the soul another, so in the one Mediator there is one thing that is Son of God and another that is Son of man, yet the same, and not one Son of God and another Son of man, though for one thing he is called Son of God and for another Son of man. Mary therefore bore, and did not bear, the Son of God. She bore him when, according to the flesh, Christ was born of her; she did not bear him when the Son existed from the Father without beginning." Thus far Augustine. Certain Papists have added something foolish here. For they think the Nestorians were heretics also in this, that they gave communion to everyone in the Lord's Supper under both kinds, and contended from God's Word that it must be given to all, laymen as well as clergy. This shows the ignorance of the Papists. For in this the Nestorians did not err, whatever is disputed against it by Stanislaus Hosius, bishop of Warmia, in his Dialogue on the Communion of Both Kinds. Nor would this error have been passed over by the Synod, but condemned, as the other errors of the same Nestorius were. Indeed, this opinion of Nestorius shows that even then the institution of the Lord's Supper, as Christ had made it, was already being corrupted and altered by some. And these are so many heads of one error and plagues of one spirit, and so great is the importance of knowing the true meaning and definition of the hypostatic union of the natures in Christ.

units.la: CAP. XCII. Eutychiani cur sic dicti. Erroris autem eorum caput unum.
units.tr: CAP. XCII. Why the Eutychians are so called. Their error, one head.

units.la: Eutychiani ab {1}Eutyche quodam Constan-tinopolitana Ecclesia presbytero Monacho exorti sunt, qui quum viderentur restare[?] Nestorium, in Apollinarem Ma-nichaeumque nich&umque[?] transiuit,& humanitatis in Christo denegas veritatem, quicquid a Verbo nostrae proprietatis receptum est, diuina tantummodo ascribit essentiae, vt sacramentum salutis humanae (quod non nisi in utraque subsistentia est) nostram in Christo naturam negando dissoluéret, stulta impietate non insufficiens vniuerso corpori auferri, quod capiti defuisset.
units.tr: The Eutychians arose from one Eutyches, a monk and presbyter of the church of Constantinople. When he seemed to have been left behind by Nestorius, he passed over to Apollinaris and the Manichaeans, and denied the truth of humanity in Christ. Whatever was received from the Word into our nature, he ascribed to the divine essence alone, so that by denying our nature in Christ he would dissolve the sacrament of human salvation, which can exist only in both subsistences. In his foolish impiety, he took away from the whole body what was lacking in the head, and so was not sufficient for the whole.

units.la: 1 Eutychiani ab Eutyche.) Verè hic illud Horatianum vsurpari potest, Dum vitant stulti vitia, in contraria currunt. Nam quum Nestorij errore effugere conatur Eutyches, in alium ipse incidit, & longè quidem tetriorem, & superiore fœdiorem, quem qui postea sequuti sunt, Eutychiani sunt denominati: sed & Eutychitae, & Eutychianistae, vt apparet ex l.Quaecunque.& l.Ariani, C.de hæret.& Manich. Quanquam Theodoretus lib.1. hæretic. fabul. Eutychitas alios ab istis fuisse docet, & alius fuit Eutychianus (qui & ipse hæreticus, licet etiam fuerit alius Eutychianus orthodoxus) alius verò Eutyches iste, a quo cœpit hæc hæresis. Fuit autem Eutyches Constantinopolitanus Archimandrita, quem Abbatem postea vocarunt, superbiæ superstitionisque monachicæ plenus, homo arrogans, & αὐθάδης[?], qui totam hæretici cœni fœcem & excrementa impurissima colliges, tandem hanc hæresin condidit, quæ velut immanis hydra innumeras postea alias peperit, & ecclesiæ pestem, fideique Christianæ internecionem in Oriente tandem prorsus attulit. Hic igitur Satanæ malitia & Monachus (sunt enim Monachifmi fructus blasphemiæ in doctrina hor-rendæ, & hæreses pene irradicabiles, tā est pertinax & rationi [illegible, ~7 letters] hoc hominum genus.) Hic igitur iā senex sub Theodosio iuniore jam sene, quum Nestorium refutare vellet, & dogma de duabus in Christo personis revellere, dixit post unionem naturarum in Christo, non jam duas, sed unam tantum, nempe divinam naturam mansisse. Hoc quum publice profitere-tur, & inter suos monachos effutiret, deprehendit esse erroneū Eusebius Dorylæus episcopus (est autem Dorylum civitas Phrygiæ, ut ait Plinius lib.5.cap.29.) qui & Nestorii primus detexerat. Itaque res tota ad Flavianum tunc urbis Constantinopolitanæ episcopum delata est: sed quum non resipiscceret vetulus monachus, & senex obstinatus, Synodus provincialis a Flaviano Constantinopolin collecta est, in qua præsens, auditūsque Eutyches damnatur, & deponitur. De quo conquestus apud Theodosiū imperatorem, habuit Chrysaphium quendam inter cubicularios principis primarium sibi suoque errori fauentem, tum in odium Flaviani (oderat enim hypocrita & impius Chrysaphius pium hominem, & Dei servuum Flavianum) tum ruente jam Dei Ecclesia, & Satana (Domino Deo juste verbi sui contemptum, & tot jam in Oriente enatas hæreses vlciscente) libere grassante etiā in media principis aula. Itaq; ut iterū Eutychis causa disceptaretur, convocata est Synodus Ephesum, quæ fuit secunda Ephesina Synodus, cui Flavianus interfuit: præfuit Diofcurus homo, si vllus alius, nequam, & ad omne scelus audaaudacissimus, Alexandrinus episcopus, qui Cyrillo pio episcopo successerat, Chrysaphiique aulici merus satellcs, vt eius fauore ad maiorem dignitatem eucheretur. Diofcurus igitur Eutychem absoluit, tumultuose omnia agit, & Flauianum in ipso Synodi coetu de fede vi deturbatum calcibus ita, spectantibus alijs episcopis, & non obstantibus, proculcat & proterit, vt inde saucius elatus, triduo post moreretur. Vnde hæc Synodus Ephefina fecunda, Ληστρικὴ & prædonum conuentus dicta est, & postea Chalcedon. Syno do prorsus abolita, depositus Diofcurus, & in exilium actus, rescissa omnia illius acta, & pia Flauiani memoria in integrum etiam promulgatis legibus restituta.l.Quoniam. C. De epifc. Sed post absolutionem suam Eutyches liberius dogma suum tueri coepit. Itaque serpsit venenū latius & validius, vt iam multæ de eo dogmate controuersiæ in Ecclesia orerentur, cui plane or thodoxi contradicebant, imprimisque Leo primus Rom. tunc episcopus & omnes Occidentales Ecclesiæ. Quare mortuo iam Theodosio, à Martiano imperatore collecta Chalcedone (quæ Bithyniæ ciuitas est, ex aduerso obiecta Byzantio) Synodus est, quæ Eutychem & audiuit, & damnauit, nec propterea tamen error postea pullulare desijt, tã alte nimirū mali radices hærent, & homines hæresibus iam assueti, eas diligunt. Hæc tū ex Euagr.lib.1.cap.2:2.cap.4.&16.Theodor.lib.4.hær.fab. Niceph. lib.14.cap.47.& feq.collegimus. In exilium autem pul sus est ab imperatore Eutyches, in quo miserè & in hæresi perseuerans, periit. Ergo cœpit hæc hæresis proprie sub Martiano imperatore, & Leone primo Rom. pontifice, circa annum à Christo passo 422. Viguit in toto Oriente latissimè, citissimèque propagata, in Ægypto maximè, & Constantinopoli diu & seruata, & variis nominibus Monothelitarum, Monophysitarum, Acephalorum, Agnoetarum, & Iacobitarum interpolata, donec aliquod Constantinopolitani imperij vestigiū inter Christianos mansit. Nam ea pessimè etiā imperatores ipsi, imprimis Heraclius, & eius posteri tanquam tabe & veneno infecti sunt, adeò ut propterea grauissimas aduersus Occidentales ecclesias inimicitias exercuerit; Romámque ipsam, quæ nondum huic errori assentiebatur, ut docet Carolus Sigon. lib. 2. De regno Italico.
units.tr: 1 The Eutychians, from Eutyches. Here one may truly apply the saying of Horace: "While fools avoid their vices, they run into the opposite ones." For when Eutyches tried to escape the error of Nestorius, he fell into another, and a much fouler one, worse than the former. Those who afterwards followed it were called Eutychians, but also Eutychites and Eutychianists, as appears from the law Quaecunque and the law Ariani, Code, On Heretics and Manichaeans. Yet Theodoret, in book 1 of the Heretical Fables, teaches that the Eutychites were different from these, and that there was another Eutychian (who was himself a heretic, although there was also another, orthodox Eutychian). The Eutyches in question, from whom this heresy began, was a Constantinopolitan archimandrite, whom they later called abbot, full of monastic pride and superstition, an arrogant man and self-willed [αὐθάδης], who gathered together all the dregs and most impure excrement of heretical filth. At last he devised this heresy, which, like a monstrous hydra, afterwards bore countless others, and at last brought in the East a plague to the Church and the complete ruin of the Christian faith. So this was the malice of Satan and of a monk (for the fruits of monasticism are blasphemy in horrible doctrine, and heresies that can scarcely be uprooted; this kind of men is so stubborn and so [illegible, about seven letters] to reason). Here, then, this now aged man, under Theodosius the Younger, who was also old, wished to refute Nestorius and to tear up the doctrine of two persons in Christ. He said that after the union of the natures in Christ, there remained not two but only one nature, namely the divine. When he professed this publicly and babbled it among his fellow monks, Eusebius, bishop of Dorylaeum, detected that it was erroneous. (Dorylaeum is a city of Phrygia, as Pliny says in book 5, chapter 29.) This same Eusebius had been the first to expose Nestorius. So the whole matter was referred to Flavian, then bishop of the city of Constantinople. But since the old monk would not repent, and the old man was obstinate, Flavian gathered a provincial synod at Constantinople, in which Eutyches, present and heard, was condemned and deposed. Complaining of this to the Emperor Theodosius, he had as his supporter a certain Chrysaphius, the chief among the emperor's chamberlains, who favoured him and his error. Chrysaphius did this partly out of hatred of Flavian (for the hypocritical and impious Chrysaphius hated the pious man, the servant of God, Flavian), and partly because the Church of God was already collapsing, while Satan, as the Lord God justly avenged the contempt of his Word and the many heresies already sprung up in the East, ran freely even in the middle of the emperor's court. Therefore, so that the cause of Eutyches might be debated again, a synod was convened at Ephesus. This was the second Synod of Ephesus, in which Flavian took part. It was presided over by Dioscorus, a man, if any was, wicked and most bold in every crime, bishop of Alexandria, who had succeeded the pious Cyril and was a mere satellite of the courtier Chrysaphius, so that by his favour he might be raised to greater dignity. So Dioscorus absolved Eutyches, carried everything out tumultuously, and trampled and crushed Flavian, who had been thrown from his see in the very assembly of the synod, with his feet, while the other bishops looked on and did nothing to prevent it. Flavian was carried out wounded and died three days later. For this reason the second Synod of Ephesus was called the Robber Synod [Ληστρικὴ], a gathering of plunderers, and afterwards the Synod of Chalcedon utterly abolished it. Dioscorus was deposed and sent into exile, all his acts were annulled, and the pious memory of Flavian was restored in full, with laws promulgated to that effect. See law Quoniam, Code, On Bishops. But after his absolution, Eutyches began to defend his doctrine more freely. So the poison spread more widely and more strongly, so that many controversies over that doctrine arose in the Church, and orthodox men openly opposed it, above all Leo the First, then bishop of Rome, and all the Western churches. Therefore, after Theodosius had died, a synod was gathered at Chalcedon (a city of Bithynia, facing Byzantium across the strait) by the Emperor Marcian. It heard Eutyches, condemned him, and yet the error did not cease to sprout afterwards, for of course the roots of evil run so deep, and men accustomed to heresies love them. I have gathered these things from Evagrius, book 1, chapters 2 and 22, chapters 4 and 16; from Theodore, book 4 of the Heretical Fables; and from Nicephorus, book 14, chapter 47 and following. Eutyches was driven into exile by the emperor, and there he persisted miserably in his heresy and perished. So this heresy properly began under the Emperor Marcian and Leo the First, bishop of Rome, about the year 422 after Christ's passion. It flourished very widely throughout the whole East, spread very quickly, and was kept alive for a long time in Egypt most of all and at Constantinople. It was variously disguised under the names of Monothelites, Monophysites, Acephali, Agnoetae and Jacobites, until some trace of the Constantinopolitan empire remained among Christians. For the emperors themselves were most badly infected by it, above all Heraclius and his successors, as if by a plague and poison. So for this reason they carried on very grave enmities against the Western churches, and even against Rome itself, which had not yet assented to this error, as Carolus Sigonius teaches in book 2 of De regno Italico.

units.la: Postea vero propter transubstantiationem inuectam in Cœna Domini, & eam quoque hærefin velut cæteras tandem Papistus suscepit, ne quid illi ad mysterium iniquitatis plane peragendum deesset. Denique nulla tenacior, diuturniorque unquam hæresis fuit, quæ nunc etiam prætextu corporalis carnis & hominis Christi in sacra Cœna præsentiæ acerrimè defenditur & revocatur. Qui autem illius rami & propagines fuerint, postea docebimus.
units.tr: Afterwards, however, on account of transubstantiation introduced into the Lord's Supper, the Papists at last adopted this heresy like the others, so that nothing might be lacking to them for completing the mystery of iniquity.
