In short, no heresy was ever more stubborn and long-lasting, and even now it is most fiercely defended and revived under the pretext of the bodily flesh and the presence of Christ's human nature in the Lord's Supper. What its branches and offshoots were, I will teach later.

units.la: 2 Diuina tantummodo ascribit.) Suidas Eutychem Maneti & Apollinario successisse scribit. Theodoret. in dialogis tribus aduersus eum editis, ex Valentini & Apollinarij cœno & lacunis haustam fuisse Eutychis fæcem verius tradit. Quæ autem fuerit illius sententia, apparet ex ipsius verbis & responso quod in Chalcedonensi Synodo interrogatus fecit, quemadmodū refert Euagr.lib.2.c.16. Sunt autem hæc verba, Ex duabus quidem naturis scio Christum ante vnionem constituisse: post vnionem vero vnam duntaxat in illo fuisse scio, & agnosco. Boethius in libro De duabus naturis, & Vn. Ex duabus Naturis Christum esse confiteor, in duabus co-sistere nego. Itaque ipsa assumptionis vel conceptionis conditione, humanam naturam à diuina absorptam fuisse dixit, quia ea præualebat, vt & Leo, & Theodor. & Vigilius, & Damascenus, & Isidorus scribunt. 2 Proprietates naturarum quoque confusas esse post assumptionem docuit, quod erat consequens. Itaque vt dilucidè & perspicuè vtrumque errore Chalcedonense concilium damnaret, dixit Christum vnum & eundem non tantùm duabus [?]ιοιαις, id est, essentijs: sed duabus [?]φυσεσι, id est, naturis inconfusè, inconuertibiliter, indiuulsè, & inseparabiliter constare. Vocem enim [?]φυσιν vsurparunt Patres vt non tantùm essentias ipsas, diuinam nimirum & humanam post vnionem: sed etiam earum proprietates saluas esse demonstrarent; Boethius, Nestorius rectè tenens duplicem in Christo esse naturam, sacrilegè confitetur duas esse personas: Eutyches verò rectè tenens vnam esse personam, impiè credit vnam quoque esse naturam. 3 Verbum Deum negauit quicquam humanum ex virgine Maria assumpsisse, vel nobis [?]ὁμοουσιον & [?]ὁμοιοσιον fuisse, Theodor. lib.4. hær.fab.& Suidas. Quidam tamē ex Eutychian. vt Vigil. lib.1. docet, mitigare tam absurdam sententiam voluerunt, dixerúntque non ab initio & momento quidem conceptionis in Christo humanam naturam absorptam, sed demum post ipsius resurrectionem, & corporis glorificationem. Idem tradit Boethius. 4 Diuinam naturam passibilem constituit, quæ in Christo crucifixa & mortua fuerit. 5 Deum factitium & nouum inducit, & Christum deificatum potius quàm Deum agnoscit. Hæc sententia quatæ[?] blasphemiæ plena fit, vel ex eo fatis ostendi-tur, quòd si huiusmodi est Christus, qualem Eutychiani fingunt, nec pro nobis passus est, quia similem nobis naturam non habuit: nec resurrexit, quia quum Deus solùm fuerit, mori non potuit. Itaque nec redemptor noster, nec Iesus est, & omnis historia Euangelica falsissi-ma est: spesque Christianorum, quæ Christo Dei verbo innititur, vanissima. Atque hoc errore nihil immanius, nihil tetrius, nihil fœdius ne cogitari quidè potest, & in eo omnium errorum cumulus est. Itaque fuit hæc palmaris Satanæ aduersus fidem victoria, & totius fundamenti Christianæ doctrinæ subuersio, propter quam libere postea triumphauit Satan. Quædam etiam perperam de resurrectione eum docuisse tradunt.
units.tr: 2 He ascribes [it] only to the divine. Suidas writes that Eutyches succeeded Manes and Apollinaris. Theodoret, in three dialogues published against him, more truly relates that Eutyches' dregs were drawn from the mire and pools of Valentinus and Apollinaris. What his opinion was appears from his own words and from the answer he gave when questioned at the Synod of Chalcedon, as Evagrius reports in book 2, chapter 16. These are his words: "I know that Christ consisted of two natures before the union; but after the union I know and acknowledge that in him there was only one." Boethius, in his book On the Two Natures, and Vigilius: "I confess that Christ is from two natures; I deny that he consists in two." Thus, by the very condition of the assumption or conception, he said that the human nature was absorbed by the divine, because the divine prevailed, as Leo, Theodore, Vigilius, Damascene and Isidore write. He also taught that the properties of the natures were confused after the assumption, which followed from the rest. So, in order to condemn both errors clearly and plainly, the Council of Chalcedon declared that Christ, one and the same, consists not only in two ousiai [οὐσίαι], that is, essences, but in two physeis [φύσεις], that is, natures, unconfusedly, unchangeably, indivisibly and inseparably. For the Fathers used the word physis [φύσις] to show that not only the essences themselves, the divine and the human after the union, but also their properties, remain intact. Nestorius, rightly holding that there is a double nature in Christ, sacrilegiously confesses that there are two persons; Eutyches, rightly holding that there is one person, impiously believes that there is also one nature. 3 He denied that the Word of God had taken anything human from the virgin Mary, or that it was homoousion [ὁμοούσιον] or homoiousion [ὁμοιούσιον] with us, as Theodoret, book 4 of the Heretical Fables, and Suidas relate. Yet some of the Eutychians, as Vigilius teaches in book 1, wished to soften so absurd an opinion, and said that the human nature was absorbed in Christ not from the beginning, at the moment of conception, but only after his resurrection and the glorification of his body. Boethius also hands down the same. 4 He made the divine nature passible, so that it was crucified and died in Christ. 5 He introduces a made-up and new God, and recognises Christ as deified rather than as God. That this opinion is full of blasphemy is sufficiently shown by this: if Christ is such as the Eutychians imagine, he did not suffer for us, because he did not have a nature like ours; nor did he rise again, because, being God alone, he could not die. So neither is he our Redeemer nor Jesus, the whole Gospel history is most false, and the hope of Christians, which rests on Christ the Word of God, is most vain. Nothing is more monstrous, nothing more foul, nothing more shameful than this error, and in it is the sum of all errors. So this was Satan's signal victory against the faith, and the subversion of the whole foundation of Christian doctrine, after which Satan triumphed freely. They also report that he taught some things wrongly about the resurrection.

units.la: HÆRESES A NO-vis[?] additæ. CAP. XCIII.
units.tr: HERESIES ADDED AT NO-vis[?] CHAP. XCIII.

units.la: Quæ fuerunt Eutychianæ hæreseos infelices propagines & fruticationes.
units.tr: Which were the unhappy offshoots and branches of the Eutychian heresy.

units.la: Vandiu synodi Chalcedonensis valuit in Ecclesia, imprimis autem Orientali, autoritas, fuit aliqua Ecclesiarum tranquillitas & quies, etsi Eutychianorum reliquiæ per suos aliquem in dies nouum errorem moliri & insusurrare, sed tamen clam propter imperatorum edicta, & ob metum exilij, non cessarent. Nam qui Synodo Chalcedonensi non subscribebant, interim se Διακρινόμενοι[?], quasi medios & Ambigentes, vocarunt. Itaque ex una illa Eutychis hæresi, tanquam ex immani fonte & hydra, multa hæreseōn millia, quemadmodum Nicephorus lib.18.cap.45. scribit, extiterunt, quæ non eruperunt statim, sed tum demū, postquam imperatorum (qui secuti sunt huiusmodique vesania imbui se fuerunt) fauore subnixi venena sua euomere hominès[?] sunt liberè ausi. Qui tot pene nomina diuersarum hæreseōn sortiti sunt, quot fuerunt homines de iis rebus loquentes: nos tamen prætermissis diuersis eiusdem erroris appellationibus, quæ pene sunt infinitæ, capita ipsa hæreseon diuersa referemus. Ac primi quidem ex Eutychianis pullularunt ij, qui dicti sunt Monophysitæ, & alio nomine Ægyptij, Schematici, vt ait Damascenus, & Theopaschitæ, cuius primus author fuisse videtur Dioscurus Alexandrinus Episcopus sub Martiano & Valentiniano imperatoribus, & Leone primo Roman. Episcopo, circa annum à Christo passo 425. Dixit enim Dioscurus, præceptorem impium Eutychen imitatus, Ex duabus naturis suscipio, Duas naturas non suscipio. Vnam igitur duntaxat in Christo agnoscunt naturam Monophysitæ, diuinam nempe, quam etiam passam fuisse aperte profitentur. Concilium Chalcedonense omnino damnant. Hi in Ægypto plurimum regnarunt, & postea per totam Syriam. Itaque statim tota Ægyptus in eam sententiam abiit, & prima ex omnibus Romani imperij prouinciis, & quidem vniuersa, ab orthodoxa & vera fide defecit, illos episcoporum suorum errores infelix secuta. Hanc hærefin postea sub Phoca Imperatore pertinacissimè defendit, latèque propagauit Joannes Grammaticus cognomento Philoponus genere Alexandrinus, vt docet Nicephor. lib. 18. cap. 47. Acephali qui & Seueritæ & Iulianistæ à Iuliano Halicarnasseo, & à loco Contobabditæ & Angelitæ dicti sunt, vt ait Damascenus, deinde ex eodem impietatis fonte fluxerunt, qui sic appellati sunt quòd nullos Episcopos, haberent, neque Presbyteros, adeò vt conuentus etiam publicos sacramentorumque administrationem passim negligerent, vt ait Nicephor. lib. 18. cap. 45. 45.& 49.& lib.17.cap.7.8. non quòd primus eo rum autor ignoretur, vt vult Ifidorus. Hi natu-rarum proprietates inconfusas in Christo post vnionem manere negant. cofusas[?] enim esse dicent, etsi de duabus in eo naturis non magno-pere contendunt, quas etiam agnoscunt, modo earum proprietates confusae concedantur. Ita-que ex ea parte concilium Chalcedonense, & i-psi oppugnat, quod non modo naturas in Christo esse post vnionem dixit inconfusas, sed etiam earum proprietates. Vsi sunt ad suæ sententiæ confirmationem similitudine aceti sumpta ex Gregor. Nysseno, cuius vt gutta in mari effusa perdit suas vires, ita humanitas cum diuinitate vnita suas proprietates. Horum autor primus fuit Seuerus Antiochenus Episcopus sub Anastasio Imperatore, & Gelasio Rōmān. Episcopo, circa annum à Christo passo 462. Euagr. lib. 3. cap. 33. & lib. 4. cap. 4. Hanc haeresin postea tutatus est Theodosius Alexandrinus Episcopus acerrimè. Vnde etiam Theodosiani sunt dicti:
units.tr: For as long as the authority of the Council of Chalcedon held sway in the Church, especially in the East, there was some calm and quiet among the churches. Even so, the remnants of the Eutychians did not cease to devise and whisper some new error through their followers, though secretly, because of the emperors' edicts and for fear of exile. Those who would not subscribe to the Council of Chalcedon meanwhile called themselves Diakrinomenoi [Διακρινόμενοι], as if they were middling and doubtful. So from that one Eutychian heresy, as from a monstrous spring or hydra, many thousands of heresies arose, as Nicephorus writes in book 18, chapter 45. They did not break out at once, but only later, when they had the support of emperors who had been steeped in this same madness, and then men dared to spew out their poisons openly. Those heresies received almost as many names as there were men who spoke about these matters. We, however, will pass over the various names of the same error, which are nearly endless, and report only the main heads of the different heresies. The first of the Eutychians to sprout were those called Monophysites, also known as Egyptians, Schematici (as Damascene says), and Theopaschites. Their first author seems to have been Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, under the emperors Martian and Valentinian and Leo I, bishop of Rome, about the year 425 after Christ's passion. For Dioscorus, imitating his impious teacher Eutyches, said: "I receive two natures from them; I do not receive two natures." The Monophysites therefore acknowledge only one nature in Christ, namely the divine, which they openly profess was also made to suffer. They utterly condemn the Council of Chalcedon. They held great power in Egypt, and afterwards throughout all Syria. Thus at once the whole of Egypt went over to this opinion, and it was the first of all the provinces of the Roman empire, and indeed the whole of it, to fall away from the orthodox and true faith, following the errors of its unhappy bishops. This heresy was afterwards defended most stubbornly under the emperor Phocas, and widely spread by John the Grammarian, surnamed Philoponus, an Alexandrian by birth, as Nicephorus teaches in book 18, chapter 47. Then from the same fountain of impiety flowed the Acephali, also called Severians and Julianists after Julian of Halicarnassus, and Contobabdites and Angelites after a place name, as Damascene says. They were so called because they had no bishops or elders, and so they widely neglected even public assemblies and the administration of the sacraments, as Nicephorus says in book 18, chapters 45 and 49, and book 17, chapters 7 and 8. Not that their first author is unknown, as Isidore claims. These men deny that the properties of the natures remain unmixed in Christ after the union. For they say that they are mixed, though they do not greatly contend about there being two natures in him, which they also acknowledge, provided that their properties are allowed to be mixed. Thus in this respect the Council of Chalcedon attacks them too, because it declared that the natures in Christ remain unmixed after the union, and also their properties. To confirm their opinion they used the likeness of vinegar, taken from Gregory of Nyssa: just as a drop poured into the sea loses its strength, so the humanity united with the divinity loses its properties. The first author of this was Severus, bishop of Antioch, under the emperor Anastasius and Gelasius, bishop of Rome, about the year 462 after Christ's passion (Evagrius, book 3, chapter 33, and book 4, chapter 4). This heresy was afterwards defended most fiercely by Theodosius, bishop of Alexandria, and hence they were also called Theodosians.

units.la: Agnoetæ à dogmate sic nominati, non ab authore. Nam à primo ipsorum parente The-miftio philosopho, qui Valentis imperatoris ætate vixit, post annum à Christo passo 321, Themistiani dicti sunt, quanquam corrupte a-pud Isidorum Gnoitæ pro Agnoetæ nominantur. Hanc haeresin felicissimè quidem multis sepultam, postea sub Mauricio Imperatore & Gregorio Magno Episcopo Rom. circa annum à Christo passo 572. Theodosius Alexandriæ miserè renouauit & sub Phoca propagauit, vt & Damascenus tradit & Gregorius Magnus libr.8.epist.42.ne non ante Antichristi exortum, à quo mysteriū iniquitatis peractum est, omnes hæreses regnasse & sese effudisse videréntur. Hæc docet diuinam Christi naturam (quam illi solam post vnionem ex Eutychis & Diofcuri dogmate relinquit) quædam ignorāsse veluti horam extremi iudicij, & vbi Lazarus post mortem conditus esset, transferens impiis-sime ad diuinam Christi naturam, quæ humanæ propria fuerunt. Nicephor. lib. 12. cap. 30. & lib. 18. cap. 15. Hi vero ἀγνοῶν [?] non definiebant, vt Suidas, ἐξὼν μοχθηρίας [?]: sed σεμνὴν γνῶσιν [?], qui postea in tres sectas sese diuiserunt, Damianos, Pauliános & Petritas. Nicephor. lib. 18. cap. 49.
units.tr: The Agnoetae were so named from their doctrine, not from their author. Their first ancestor was the philosopher Themistius, who lived in the time of the emperor Valens, after the year 321 after Christ's passion, and so they were called Themistians. Yet Isidore corruptly names them Gnoitae instead of Agnoetae. This heresy, though it had been most happily buried by many, was afterwards wretchedly revived at Alexandria by Theodosius under the emperor Maurice and Gregory the Great, bishop of Rome, about the year 572 after Christ's passion, and was spread under Phocas, as Damascene relates and Gregory the Great in book 8, epistle 42. So that all heresies might seem to have reigned, and poured themselves out, before the rise of Antichrist, by whom the mystery of iniquity was carried out. This sect teaches that the divine nature of Christ (which they alone leave after the union, following the doctrine of Eutyches and Dioscorus) was ignorant of certain things, such as the hour of the last judgment and where Lazarus was buried. Most impiously they transfer to the divine nature of Christ what belonged to his human nature (Nicephorus, book 12, chapter 30, and book 18, chapter 15). Yet they did not define their ignorance, as Suidas says, [ἐξὼν μοχθηρίας] from which wickedness, but [σεμνὴν γνῶσιν] a solemn knowledge. Later they divided themselves into three sects: the Damians, the Paulians, and the Petrites (Nicephorus, book 18, chapter 49).

units.la: Iacobitæ qui à Iacobo quodam homine gen-te Syro, & ob paupertatem Zanzalo denomina-to vocantur. In Syria sub Phoca Imperatore & Bonifacio tertio nati, circa annum à Christo passo 575. totam Syriam à fide Christi auerte-runt, quæ Ægyptum secuta de Christo mediatore rectè sentire desijt. Hi eandem prorsus, quam primi Eutychiani sententiam amplec-tuntur & defendunt, atque ita impune orthodoxos irrisere, vt eos Melchitas vocarent, quòd imperatorum fidem sequerentur. Hi postea Anastasium, vel, vt alij, Athanasium Patriarcham habuerunt, qui Antiochiæ Episcopus factus Heraclium imperatorem illum quidem optimum sua tabe miserè & subdolè infecit. Nicephorus lib. 18. cap. 52. Itaque hi vti superiores, concilium Chalcedonense damnant & anathematizant.
units.tr: The Jacobites are so called from a certain man named Jacob, of Syrian race, and because of his poverty surnamed Zanzalus. Born in Syria under the emperor Phocas and Boniface III, about the year 575 after Christ's passion, they turned all Syria away from the faith of Christ. Egypt followed them, and ceased to think rightly about Christ the mediator. These men embrace and defend exactly the same opinion as the first Eutychians, and they mocked the orthodox so freely that they called them Melchites, because they followed the emperors' faith. Afterwards they had Anastasius as their patriarch, or, as others say, Athanasius. He was made bishop of Antioch and wretchedly and deceitfully infected the emperor Heraclius, who was otherwise a very good man, with his poison (Nicephorus, book 18, chapter 52). So these men, like those above, condemn and anathematize the Council of Chalcedon.

units.la: Armenij à prouincia dicti, quòd eodem Eu-tychis errore paulò post etiam duæ Armeniæ maior & minor non modò labefactatæ fuerunt, sed prorsus à vera fide de utraque in Christo natura abductæ, opera infelicis cuiusdam Euchanij vel Ethami, qui cognominatur Mantacunes, vt scribit Nicephorus lib.18.cap.53. Hi negant Christum corpus humanum ex virgine Maria assumpsisse, sed illud ab ipso conceptionis momento incorruptibile habuisse contendunt, quod ipsum per se adorant. Unde φαντασ- ιαστὰς, & ἐκλυκολητὰς dicti sunt ab orthodoxis, quos ipsi vicissim remordentes Manichæos & Phantasiastas contumeliose vocabant. Nicephorus lib.18.cap.45. Pascha more Iudaico celebrant. Quaternitatem, non Trinitatem in diuinis personis inducunt. Diuinitatem passam dicunt, & Chalcedonense concilium repudiant. Hi etiam ab Episcopo, de quo maxime gloriantur, Gregoriani sunt appellati, quos tamen alij corrupte Georgianos nominant. Dicti sunt etiam Staurolatræ, sive ipsorum lingua Chazinzarij, quia crucem Domini colunt & venerantur. Sed & hi in varias se sectas postea diduxerunt, quorum una est Arziburorum, qui ita à ieiunio dicuntur. Nicephorus libr.18.cap.54. Videntur autem exorti primum sub Phoca Imperatore & Bonifacio quarto, circa annum à Christo passo 577. è Petri illius Gnaphei Episcopi Antiocheni & Iacobitarum hæreticorum coeno profluentes.
units.tr: The Armenians are named from their province. Shortly afterwards, through the same error of Eutyches, both Armenias, Greater and Lesser, were not only shaken but wholly drawn away from the true faith concerning both natures in Christ, through the work of a certain unhappy man named Euchanius or Ethamas, who was surnamed Mantacunes, as Nicephorus writes in book 18, chapter 53. These men deny that Christ took a human body from the Virgin Mary, but contend that he had that body incorruptible from the very moment of conception, and they worship it in itself. Hence the orthodox called them [φανταστιασταί] Phantasiasts and [ἐκλυκολητάι], and in turn they, biting back, insultingly called the orthodox Manichaeans and Phantasiasts (Nicephorus, book 18, chapter 45). They celebrate Passover in the Jewish manner. They introduce a quaternity, not a Trinity, in the divine persons. They say that the divinity suffered, and they reject the Council of Chalcedon. These men were also called Gregorians after their bishop, of whom they especially boast, though others corruptly call them Georgians. They were also called Staurolatrae, or in their own language Chazinzarii, because they worship and venerate the cross of the Lord. But they too afterwards split into various sects, one of which is that of the Arziburi, so named from their fasting. (Nicephorus, book 18, chapter 54.) They seem to have first arisen under the emperor Phocas and Boniface IV, about the year 577 after Christ's passion, flowing out of the mire of Peter Gnaphaeus, bishop of Antioch, and the heretical Jacobites.

units.la: Monothelitæ à dogmate sic vocati ex iisdem Apollinaristarum & Eutychianorum facibus deriuantur, & statim post Armenios in Ægypto nascuntur, vbi emergunt, pullulant, & confirmantur. Eorum author primus Cyrus Alexandrinùs Episcopus, patroni autem Sergius Cois-tantinopolitanus Patriarcha, & Macarius, sub Heraclio Imperatore, & Bonifacio quarto & quinto, circa annum à Christo passo 579. innotescunt. Cùm enim propter asiduas de vna tantùm in Christo physi & natura controuersias Eutychiani se exosos viderent, huc eundem errorem retinuerunt quidem, sed nomine Voluntatis interpolarunt & fucarunt. Itaque negarunt in Christo duas esse voluntates, quia sibi contrarias, & quia duas in Christo post vnionem fuisse naturas reipsa non concedebat, etsi tamen verbis profiterētur se de eo nolle contendere. Itaque humanam voluntatem, quæ in Christo fuit, [?] appellabat, quòd ipsa per se nulla esset, neque à se moueretur, quicquam-ve vellet, & eam se vocem à Gregorio Nysseno accepisse iactabant. Refutantur autem apertissimè loco Scripturæ, qui est Luc. 22. versu 42. Sed huius erroris occasio hæc fuit. Cùm Heraclius Imperator tot litium & contentionum seminā, quæ durabant propter Chalcedonense concilium & duas in Christo naturas repudiatas, tollere vellet, Anastasium quem alij Athanasium vocare malunt, Antiochiæ Episcopum, vbi tum ipse Imperator diuersabatur, interrogauit, An non duas in Christo naturas vnitas ipse admitteret? Anastasius vir subdolus cùm in Chalcedonensis concilij defensionem propensum Heraclium cerneret, hoc quidem cócessit, sed deprecatus ne tamen duas in Christo voluntates (quas iam Cyrus Episcopus in Ægypto sustulerat) fateri cogeretur. Quo responso atto-
units.tr: The Monothelites are so called from their doctrine, and derive from the same torches of the Apollinarians and Eutychians. Immediately after the Armenians they were born in Egypt, where they emerged, sprouted and were confirmed. Their first author was Cyrus, bishop of Alexandria, and their patrons were Sergius, patriarch of Constantinople, and Macarius, under the emperor Heraclius and Boniface IV and V, and they became known about the year 579 after Christ's passion. For when the Eutychians saw themselves hated because of their constant disputes about the one physis and nature in Christ, they kept the same error, but disguised and falsified it under the name of will. So they denied that there were two wills in Christ, because they were contrary to each other, and because they did not in fact concede that there were two natures in Christ after the union, though they professed in words that they did not want to contend about it. Thus they called the human will, which was in Christ, [?], because in itself it was nothing, did not move itself, and wanted nothing, and they boasted that they had received this term from Gregory of Nyssa. But they are most plainly refuted by a passage of Scripture, Luke 22:42. The occasion of this error was as follows. When the emperor Heraclius wanted to end the many lawsuits and quarrels that continued because of the Council of Chalcedon and the rejection of two natures in Christ, he questioned Anastasius, whom others prefer to call Athanasius, bishop of Antioch, where the emperor himself was then staying, asking whether he himself did not admit the two natures united in Christ. Anastasius, a crafty man, seeing that Heraclius was inclined to defend the Council of Chalcedon, did concede this, but he begged that he should not be forced to confess two wills in Christ (which Cyrus, bishop in Egypt, had already abolished). The emperor, astonished at this answer as absurd, and self-refuting (for if there are two distinct natures in Christ, there must be two wills too), questioned Sergius, bishop of Constantinople, about this whole matter. Sergius, since he had long favoured the opinion of Eutyches and Cyrus, and Anastasius popular…

units.la: attonitus Imperator tanquam absurdo, seque ipsum refutante, (Nam si duæ sunt in Christo naturæ distinctæ, sint & duæ voluntates oportet) de hac tota re Sergium Constantinopolitanum episcopum interrogavit. Sergius utpote qui Eutychis & Cyri sententiam iampridem probaret, & Anastasio populari suo gratificari cuperet, veram esse illius sententiam respodit.
units.tr: The emperor, astonished at this as an absurdity that refutes itself (for if there are two distinct natures in Christ, there must also be two wills), asked Sergius, bishop of Constantinople, about the whole matter. Sergius, who had long approved the opinion of Eutyches and Cyrus and wished to please his fellow countryman Anastasius, replied that Anastasius's view was true.

units.la: Itaque in Monothelitarum errorem incidit his Episcoporum insidiis deceptus imprudens Heraclius, quem & Honorius episcopus Roma. & Pyrrhus Constantinopolit. & imperatores alii Heraclii successores sunt amplexi, regnavitque aliquot deinde seculis furiosissime & latissime.
units.tr: And so the emperor Heraclius, deceived by these snares of the bishops, fell unwittingly into the error of the Monothelites. Honorius, bishop of Rome, Pyrrhus of Constantinople, and the other emperors who succeeded Heraclius embraced it, and it held sway for several centuries, most furiously and most widely.

units.la: Tandem omnes istæ superiores sectæ & contentiones a Constantino Pogonato Imperatore Heraclii pronepote profligatæ videbantur magno pietatis zelo, collecta ab eo Constanti-nopolin Synodo, quæ Sexta universalis & oecu-menica dicta est, ubi Sergius etiam mortuus excommunicatus est, & ante eam etiam explosæ fuerant ab Agathone Romano Episcopo sub Heraclio, congregata Romæ synodo ex Occidentalibus pene Ecclesiis omnibus: & post u-tranque, Hispalensi synodo multisque aliis anathematizatæ. Sed tamen propterea nunquam illi obmutuerunt aut conquieverunt: tanta est nimirum hæreticorum pervicacia, & in fide oppugnanda immanitas & impunitas. Nam etiam post illam Constantinopolitanam synodum re-vocata, repetitaque est imprimis Monothelitarum hæresis a Gregorio Constantinopolit. & Macario Antiocheno Episcopis, adeo ut etiam Iustinianum fecundum Imperatorem exulem[?] monachus quidam ea tabe polluerit & infecerit. Vnde in imperium ope Terbellini Bulgarorum regis restitutus Rom. Episcopos adhuc in hoc fidei capite recte sentientes persecutus est. Nam Sergium Episcopum Romae per Zachariam praefectum militum, etiam in media vrbe propterea vinciri iusserat: & antea Constans Heraclij filius per Olympium ducem suum propter eandem causamMartinum Episcopum Roman.adduci Constantinopolim voluerat, vbi in tetterrimo carcere periit Martinus, vt etiā tradit Carolus Sigonius libr.2.de regno Italico.
units.tr: At last all these earlier sects and controversies seemed to be overthrown by Constantine Pogonatus, great-grandson of Heraclius, with a great zeal for piety. He gathered at Constantinople the synod called the Sixth, universal and ecumenical, where Sergius, though already dead, was excommunicated. Before that council the same errors had been driven out by Agatho, bishop of Rome, under Heraclius, when a synod was assembled at Rome from almost all the churches of the West; and afterwards they were anathematized by the synod of Toledo and by many others. Yet for all that, these heresies never fell silent or came to rest. So great, no doubt, is the obstinacy of heretics, and the savagery and impunity with which they assail the faith. For even after that council of Constantinople, the Monothelite heresy was revived and renewed above all by Gregory, bishop of Constantinople, and Macarius, bishop of Antioch. So much so that a certain monk polluted and infected the emperor Justinian the Second, then in exile, with this poison. Hence, restored to the empire with the help of Terbellis, king of the Bulgarians, he persecuted the bishops of Rome, who still held sound opinions on this article of faith. For he had ordered Sergius, bishop of Rome, to be arrested for this reason, even in the middle of the city, through Zacharias, prefect of the soldiers. And earlier, Constans, son of Heraclius, had wished to have Martin, bishop of Rome, brought to Constantinople for the same cause, through his commander Olympius; there Martin perished in a most foul prison, as Carolus Sigonius also relates, book 2 of De regno Italico.

units.la: Antea quidem & statim post concilium Chalcedonense,non modo a Dioscuro &Xenęa pugnacissime defensa fuerat Eutychis haeresis: sed etiam post vtriusque mortem a Theodoro quodam, & Petro Gnapheo Antiocheno Episcopo sub Leone Imperatore, & Simplicio Ro-man.Episcopo repetita & sustetata.Quinetiam post Gnapheum damnatum fuit nihilominus ab Acatio Constantinopolitano Episcopo sub Zenone Imperatore & Felice Episcopo Rom. circa annum a Christo passo 454.acerrime propugnata, adeo ministris & alastoribus suis nunquam caruit Satan in pestem Ecclesiae. Inde Acatiani haeretici dicti sunt, de quibus est in can. Acatius 1.& 2.24. quaest. 1. & cano. Secundum. Distinct.19.& apud Euagr.libr.2.cap.16. Sozomen.libr.7.cap.11.denique Nicephorum Callistum lib.16.cap.16.Sed vt omnes tandem Eutychianae haeresis reliquias tolleret Iustinianus primus, Constantinopolim vniuersalem synodum conuocauit, quæ quinta generalis & œcumenica dicta est, à qua omnes iste pestes & fæces damnatæ prorsusque iugulatę & extersæ videbantur, nisi postea Satanę astu & interpolatis Monophysitarum, &c. nominibus miserè reuixissent. Nam & Iustinianus ipse earū oppugnator Theodorę vxoris blanditiis illectus tandem Aphthartodocitarum veneno imbutus & infectus est.
units.tr: Earlier, indeed, and immediately after the Council of Chalcedon, the heresy of Eutyches had been defended most vigorously not only by Dioscorus and Xenaias, but also after the death of both, it was revived and sustained by a certain Theodore, and by Peter Gnapheus, bishop of Antioch, under the emperor Leo, and by Simplicius, bishop of Rome. Moreover, even after Gnapheus was condemned, it was nonetheless stoutly championed by Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, under the emperor Zeno, and by Felix, bishop of Rome, about the year 454 after Christ's passion. So Satan never lacked ministers and supporters to be a plague to the Church. Hence the Acacians were so called, concerning whom see the canon Acatius 1 and 2, causa 24, question 1, and the canon Secundum, distinction 19; and in Evagrius, book 2, chapter 16; Sozomen, book 7, chapter 11; and finally Nicephorus Callistus, book 16, chapter 16. But in order finally to remove all the remnants of the Eutychian heresy, Justinian the First summoned a universal synod to Constantinople, which is called the fifth general and ecumenical council. By it all these plagues and dregs seemed condemned and utterly throttled and wiped out, except that afterwards, by Satan's cunning and under the interpolated names of the Monophysites, they miserably revived. For Justinian himself, who had opposed them, was at last enticed by the flatteries of his wife Theodora, and was imbued and infected with the poison of the Aphthartodocetae.

units.la: CAP. XCIIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XCIIII.

units.la: Mirabiliarij & Enthousiastæ quid docuerint & quàm latè stragem in Ecclesia ediderint.
units.tr: What the Mirabilarians and Enthusiasts taught, and how widely they spread ruin in the Church.

units.la: Mirabiliarij, Miracularij & Miratores licti[?] sunt ij omnes, qui miraculorum se vel ab aliis editorum prætextu vel nouum in Ecclesia Dei errorem induxerunt, vel veterem renouarunt. Cùm enim propter tot nouas hæreses in dies enascentes nihil iam ex scripto Dei verbo in negotio fidei certò constitui posse videretur, quod singuli hæretici Sacras scripturas ad se traherent, & ex iis sui erroris confirmationem petere se iactarent, visa est tandem hæc expeditissima & optima veritatis dignoscendæ ratio, si ad miracula recurreretur, ut eorum vera doctrina esse censeretur, qui fecissent miracula: Vel si uterq; eorum, qui contraria docebant, ederet miracula (quod sæpe astu Satanę & iusto Dei iudicio contingebat) illius tantum vera sententia haberetur, qui vel plura vel maiora, id est, magis stupeda & inaudita operaretur. Itaque postremis maxime temporibus, quæ has tot hæreses proxime secuta sunt, & ante vicinam Antichristi parturitionem hæc hæresis inualuit, vt apparet ex Nicephoro lib.8.cap.35.lib.14.cap.45.& tota Nicena synodo secunda, vbi potissimum propter iactata miracula cultus idolorum siue imaginum in Ecclesiam inuectus & approbatus est. Hoc eodem fundamento nituntur pene omnes errores, qui præter atque etiam contra manifestum Dei verbum siue in Papismo, siue in Mahumetismo defenduntur. Hoc eodem nouæ in dies hæreses & superstitiones finguntur & commendantur, vti ex Gregorij Turonensis & similium scriptorum historia facile colligi potest. Itaque omnium hæreseon magnum isti Mirabiliarij fundamentum iaciunt, sed tamen salsissimum & imbecillimum. Neque enim nos primum reuocat Christus ad miracula, sed ad Scripturas diuinas, Ioan.5. vers.39. vti etiam Petrus in 2. Epist.1.vers.19. Deinde cum Satanæ ipsi data sit a Deo efficacia & vis, per quam signa & miracula operatur, vt qui soli Dei verbo acquiescere noluerunt, decipiantur, vt ait Paulus 2. Thess.2.vers.9.& 10, quam inualidum est hoc vnicum miraculorum fundamentum ad veritatem doctrinæ dignoscendam? Mirabiliariis sese adiunxerunt. Enthousiastæ, qui & ἐνθουσιασταὶ [?] dicti sunt. Hi ecstasi se rapi fingunt, vt cum Deo vel Spiritu ipsius colloquantur. Vnde postea varios errores cudunt & ingerunt. Hac arte vsus Mahumetes terrarum orbem decepit. Hac Anabaptistæ grassantur. Hoc etiam fundamentum [?]eiiertunt Ioan. & Paulus. Ac Ioannes quidem qui diiudicandos & probandos esse spiritus doc-cet. Paulus autem qui verum eorum examen esse Dei verbum scriptum affirmat, 1. Ioann. 4. verf. 1; 1. Corinth. 14. verf. 32. Itaque quicunque harum visionum prætextu aliquid à Dei verbo scripto dissentiens nobis annuntiant, etiamsi Angeli essent, sunt vt pseudoprophetæ reiicendi, atque anathematizandi, Galat. 1. verf. 8. Hæc igitur duo, Miracula nimirum & Enthousiasmi sunt firmissima tum superiorum hæresèon, tum etiam Papismi & Mahumetismi (quæ duæ sunt omnium fecium sentinæ, & tota omnium hæresèon colluuies) fundamenta: sed salsissima & infirmissima.
units.tr: The Mirabilarians, Miracularians and Admirers were called all those who introduced a new error into the Church of God, or revived an old one, under the pretext of miracles either performed by themselves or reported by others. For since, on account of so many new heresies springing up daily, nothing seemed any longer certain in matters of faith from the written Word of God, because each heretic drew the holy Scriptures to himself and boasted that he sought confirmation of his error from them, this seemed at last the most expedient and best way of discerning the truth: to have recourse to miracles, so that the doctrine of those who had worked miracles would be held to be true; or, if each of two men teaching opposite things worked miracles (which often happened through the cunning of Satan and by the just judgment of God), the view of the one who worked more or greater miracles, that is, more astonishing and unheard of ones, would be held true. Accordingly, especially in the latest times, which closely followed these many heresies and preceded the approaching birth pangs of Antichrist, this heresy gained strength, as is clear from Nicephorus, book 8, chapter 35, book 14, chapter 45, and the whole Second Council of Nicaea, where the worship of idols or images was introduced and approved into the Church chiefly on account of the miracles boasted of. Almost all the errors that are defended, beyond and even against the manifest Word of God, whether in Papism or in Mahumetism, rest on this same foundation. On this same foundation new heresies and superstitions are invented and commended day by day, as can easily be gathered from the history of Gregory of Tours and similar writers. Thus these Mirabilarians lay a great foundation for all heresies, but a most false and feeble one. For Christ does not recall us to miracles but to the divine Scriptures, John 5, verse 39, as Peter also does in 2 Peter 1, verse 19. Moreover, since power and efficacy, by which he works signs and miracles, has been given to Satan himself by God, so that those who were unwilling to acquiesce in the Word of God alone should be deceived, as Paul says in 2 Thessalonians 2, verses 9 and 10, how weak is this single foundation of miracles for discerning the truth of doctrine? The Enthusiasts (who are also called ἐνθουσιασταί [enthousiastai]) joined themselves to the Mirabilarians. They pretend that they are carried away in ecstasy so that they may converse with God or his Spirit, and from this they then devise and impose various errors. Mahumet deceived the whole world by this art. The Anabaptists rage by this same method. John and Paul also reject this foundation: John, who teaches that spirits are to be judged and tested, and Paul, who affirms that the written Word of God is the true test of them, 1 John 4, verse 1; 1 Corinthians 14, verse 32. Therefore whoever under the pretext of such visions announces to us anything that dissents from the written Word of God, even if they were angels, are to be rejected as false prophets and anathematized, Galatians 1, verse 8. These two things, namely miracles and enthusiasms, are therefore the firmest foundations both of the aforementioned heresies and of Papism and Mahumetism (which are the two sewers of all filth and the whole sink of all heresies), but they are most false and most weak.

units.la: CAP. XCV. De Papismo, qui est alter omnium superiorum hæresèon alueus & mare, quod eas in Occidente & Septen-trione recipit & absorbet.
units.tr: CAP. XCV. On Popery, which is the other channel and sea of all the foregoing heresies, receiving and absorbing them in the West and North.

units.la: [?]Papismus[?] tandem exortus est. Qui su-periores omnes hæreses partim vt alueus recepit: partim vt mare absorbuit, alieno quidem nomine, sed tamen earum dogmate retento & confirmato. Est autem Papismus vniuersa Antichristi proprie dicti doctrina, & regnum in Ecclesia Christo contrarium, mysteriumque illud iampridem à Paulo 2. Thess. 2. prænuntiatum, quod ex istis erroribus omnibus velut corpus quoddam conflatum & productum, magno Satanæ enixu magnisque Iivaus[?] tandem in Occidente & Septentrione editum est. Cuius seminandi initia sub ipsis adeo Apostolis iacta iam fuerunt: pariendi autem tempus demum fuit Phocae imperatoris in Mauritium perfidisimi imperium, & Bonifacij tertij Episcopatus. Hoc propter ambitiosam & infelicem illam de primo Episcoporum Episcopo in Ecclesia designando, constituendoque contentionem inter Constantinopolitanam & Romanam sedem accidit. Obtinuit autem in ea lite Romanus Pontifex Phocæ imperatoris beneficio, cui gratificatus erat. Nam propter cædem Mauritij omnibus odiosus erat Phocas. Sed illi, faciente suadenteque Bonifacio, à S.P.Q.R. tanquam legitimo Imperatori acclamatum est. Circa annum autem à Christo passo 574. nata est hæc Ecclesiæ uniuersæ internecio, pestis & tyrannis, quæ Christi regnum postea funditus deleuit, ex omnium hæreseon erroribus, velut deforme monstrum, composita. De qua pluribus ageremus, nisi luculenter de toto hoc argumento in libello nostro, qui est de Antichristo, iam dixissemus.
units.tr: Popery finally arose. It took up all the foregoing heresies, some as a channel does and some as the sea swallows, under another name indeed, but still keeping and confirming their doctrine. Popery is the whole doctrine of Antichrist properly so called, and a kingdom opposed to Christ in the Church. It is that mystery foretold long ago by Paul in 2 Thess. 2, a body compounded and produced from all these errors, and at last brought forth in the West and North by Satan's great effort and great labour. The beginnings of this seed were sown under the Apostles themselves, but the time of its birth came only with the rule of the Emperor Phocas over the most treacherous Maurice, and with the episcopate of Boniface III. This came about through the ambitious and unhappy contest between the Constantinopolitan and Roman sees over designating and establishing a first bishop of bishops in the Church. In that dispute the Roman Pontiff prevailed, by the favour of the Emperor Phocas, whom he had flattered. For Phocas was hated by all because of the murder of Maurice. But at the urging and persuasion of Boniface, he was acclaimed by the S.P.Q.R. as lawful Emperor. Around the year 574 after Christ's passion this destruction, plague and tyranny of the whole Church was born. It was put together, like a monstrous deformed thing, from the errors of all heresies, and it afterwards utterly destroyed the kingdom of Christ. We would treat this at greater length, did we not already have set out this whole subject clearly in our book on Antichrist.

units.la: CAP. XCVI. De Mahumetismo, qui est alter omnium superiorum hæreseon alueus & mare, quod eas in Oriente & Meridie ebibit & absorpsit.
units.tr: CHAPTER 96. On Mahumetism, the other sink and sea of all the foregoing heresies, which drank up and swallowed them in the East and the South.

units.la: Ahumetifmus Papifmum secutus est proxime. Nam anno 12. Heraclij imperatoris, sub extremo pontificatu Bonifacij quinti, circa annū a Christo passo 589. nata est primum haec mundi lues, & haeresis plusquam blasphema, vel potius haeresēon lacuna, vt docet Damascenus: adeo vt inter vtriusque blasphemiae exortum siue initia, x v tantum annorum spatium fere intercesserit. Totum autem Orientem & Meridiem celerrime occupauit Mahumetifmus, quemadmodum Papifmus totum Occidentem & Septentrionem: atque ita duplex & bipartitum factum est Satanae regnum: e quibus Mahumetifmus quidem naturas in Christo abolet & negat: Papifmus autem officia & verum munus Mediatoris, & titulum Christi tollit & abrogat. Mahumetifmus autem a Mahumete (quem alij Mahumede, alij Machometem, Damascenus Magmedum vocat, nos autem receptam iam & tritam pronuntiationem sequimur) dictus est. Fuit autem ille Mahumet ex Arabum Ismaelitarum (qui Agarenorum nomen ab Agar ancilla Sarae retinuerunt) gente, Abdalae principis Arabum filius, Munichialensis, quae est prouin-cia ad mare Elamiticum in Arabia Petraea, lit-cet postea se Saracenos tanquam a Sara dici voluerint Agareni, vt Sozomen. lib.6. cap.38. scribit. Sub Philippo imperatore persecuti sunt Christianos, vt tradit Euscb.libr.6.cap.42. Sub Valente vero primum Mosis cuiusdam Monachi monitu & admiratione Christiani facti sunt, vt Ruffin.libr.2.Histor.cap.6.commemorat. Atque in fide Christi a monachis qui phrő-tisteria & asceteria sua in Arabicis desertis habebant, instituti, permanserunt in ea, donec variis & pene infinitis novarum subinde haere-sèon tempestatibus & fluctibus agitata & submersa vera fidei doctrina, tandem in Ægypto, Arabia, & Syria extincta est: imprimis autem, ut diximus, erroribus Eutychianorum, qui omne Orientem & Meridiem, praesertim vero Ægyptum & Arabiam, mire vexarunt & tandem prorsus subuerterunt. Mahumet igitur Arabs & Ismaelita, homo ambitiosus, astutus, ἀλλαξω[?], & ad mundi totius perniciem natus, religionis Christianae dissidia pertæsus, Sergio monacho Nestoriano (qui tum exul in Arabia versabatur) adiutore, & Ioanne Antiocheno Ariano, itemq; Iudæo quodam Selan astrologo, & Bar-ra Persa Iacobita suggestore, nouum prorsus dogma & inauditae antea blasphemiae plenum commentus est, quod Eubolara[?], Aomar, Odmen, & Hali Saracenis & Arabibus patrocinatibus & commendantibus a Saracenis ipsius Mahumeti popularibus primum solis: post autem ab Arabibus universis qui Mahumetum etiam expulerant, receptum est. Hinc magna huic doctrinae laus accessit, quæ statim ab Ægyptiis vicinis populis recepta, & propter iam tadiu incertam apud se fidei Christianae doctrinam probata est. Deinde vi armorum ab ipso Mahumeto, qui exercitum collegerat suaque dogmata armis tuebatur, late propagata est. Nā ab Heraclio (cui primum militauerat) vnà cum tota Saracenorum gente defecit, quia su-perperbo [?] quæstoris Romani conuitio, per quod eos stipendia flagitantes canes vocauerat, offensus fuerat. Itaque Syriam inuasit. Deinde Africa Vandalorum & Arianorum erroribus plane in vera fide fluctuantem. Demum ita exercuit, vt totum Orientem iam propter Turcarum potentiam occupet, estque in eo horrendum Dei in homines verbum ipsius contemnentes & lacerantes iudicium. Gratulatur autem sibi impostor ille Azoa.20. quòd ab opinionibus Christianorum inter se diffidentium liberatus fit. Hæc autem docet, per quæ ipse reuincitur. Primum in cap.Martij, omnes Saracenos in infernum ituros pronuntiat. deinde, Euangelium esse ait lucem veteris Testamenti, Azoa.21. Dauidis Psalterium probat, Azoa.7. Christum verè Prophetam fuisse & Dei verbū: Christum item in cœlū cum carne cuolasse: Antichristi aduentum, Resurrectionem carnis concedunt Mahumetani, & iudicium extremum. Azoa.16, & 17. Idololatriam, id est, cultum & templa imaginū damnant: item Magiam, aleas lusum, & scacorum. Præterea vsuras & fœnus, & litium vim illam & multitudinem, quæ est inter Christianos infinita. Azoa. 11.13.23. Cum infidelibus familiaria commercia non probant. Nimiam item episcoporum & Monachorum veneratio-nem detestantur, & mortuorum sanctorum cultum & inuocationem, qua vnà re maximè tanquam vera idololatria semper sunt offensi Saraceni. Atque hæc quidem illi damnant, ex quibus intelligitur, quanta tunc fuerit tum in doctrina ipsa, tum in moribus Ecclesiæ corruptio. Hæc enim omnia damnauit Mahumetus, qui-bus à Christianis offendiculum præberi tunc videbat. Et certè hæc omnia vitia in Ecclesia passim regnabant. Illa autem quæ sequuntur, docent, quæ, vt verè Saracenica, & blasphemia, & impia, & ex omnium hæresεon cloacis & sordibus collecta, à nobis merito damnantur: quæ eadem ostendunt quàm varia errorum genera iam populariter recepta, & in mediis ipsius Ec-clesiæ visceribus grassantia fuerint. 1 Ne-gant esse tres in vna eadémque diuina essentia personas. Sabellianum, & Arianum est. 2 De creatione mundi, & dæmonum natura, & pro-pagatione, tum Manichæorum, tum Valenti-nianorum absurda & nugatoria dogmata re-tinent. 3 De septem cælis & eorum intelli-gentiis eodé modo quo Valentiniani & ethnici fabulantur, in quo & Dei generalem tantum prouidentiam constituunt: & Angelorum cul-tum inducunt. Azoa.23,& 25. 4 Diuinam es-sentiam negant esse simplicissimam, sed & eam cum Anthropomorphitis corporalem fingunt, & Deo præter essentiam tribuunt animam. Ita-que semper de Deo tanquam de pluribus qui-busdam rebus vnitis plurali numero loquun-tur. 5 Christum negant esse Deum, ex Ario, sed creaturam tantùm appellant, etsi magnum quidem & sanctum Prophetam eum fuisse a-gnoscunt, cum Carpocrate. 6 Christum ne-gant esse verum Dei Filium, quia Deum sine v-xore Filium genuisse putant, cum Cerdone, ab-surdum & ἀπάτωρ[?], etsi ex sancto Spiritu con-ceptum concedunt. Azoa.9,& 11. 7 Christũ neque passum, neque crucifixum volunt: sed phantasma pro eo Iudæis esse oblatū, quod illi delusi pro Christo in cruce fixerūt. Manichæa-num & Marcioniticum istud. Azoa.ii. 8 Diabolos tandem salutem consequuturos, cum O-rigenistis docent. 9 Vitam æternam, Epicu-reorum more, in voluptatibus corporis, etiam in cælo collocant, cum Cerinthianis. Azoa. 23. 10 Infernum & pœnas inferni fabulosè expli-cant, ad modum inferni Vergiliani, Purgatorii-que Papistici. Azoa.21, & 25. 11 Legis cere-monias, imprimis circuncisionem, delectum ci-borū, & corporis, imprimis autem ani, lotio-nes vti necessarias ad salutem retinent & ob-seruant, cum Ebionitis. Azoa.12, & 16. 12 Iu-rant per creaturas veluti per ficum, & ficctum, item per oliuetū, cum Priscillianistis. 13 Bel-la pro sola religionis causa, & vt inuiti homines cogantur suscipere ipsorum dogma, geri opor-tere docent. Azoa.6.7.18, & 19. 14 Matrimonij sanctam institutionem tollunt, profanant, & polluunt: pluresque cuique vxores habere con-cedunt. Diuortia extra causas verbo Dei ex-pressas fieri concedunt, Azoa.8, & 9. 15 Operum merita inducunt, per quæ se saluos fore sperant, cum Pelagianis. Azoa.18, & 41. Itaque varias ceremonias habent, & diuersas vitæ ra-tiones, velut monachismos quosdam instituit, & obseruat. 16 Deficientibus à fide ipsorum veniam cum Nouatianis in perpetuum dene-gant. 17 Peccata alia mortalia, alia venialia constituunt. Azoa.10. 18 Orandum omnino versus Orientem docent, vt sit Deo accepta oratio, & certum precationum numerum quo-que die uti necessarium præscribunt. Azoa. 10. & 17. & 19. Neque pro incredulis orandum esse volunt. 19. Omnia Sacramenta à Christo instituta tollunt. Deniq; infinitum esset reliquos errores persequi, contra quos & Ioannes Cantacuzenus Græcè nomine Achæmenidis Persæ, ad fidem conuersi, scripsit, conuertit autem Gualterus D. eximius, & Pius secundus, & Richardus quidam tempore Bernardi, & D. Philippus Melanchthon.
units.tr: Mahumetism followed Papism closely. In the twelfth year of the emperor Heraclius, toward the end of the papacy of Boniface V, in about the year 589 after Christ's passion, this plague of the world and heresy beyond all blasphemy first arose, or rather the pit of heresies, as Damascene teaches. So little time, barely fifteen years, passed between the rise, or beginnings, of these two blasphemies. Mahumetism very swiftly occupied the whole East and South, just as Papism occupied the whole West and North. Thus Satan's kingdom became double and divided in two. Of these, Mahumetism denies and abolishes the natures in Christ, while Papism takes away and abrogates the offices and true work of the Mediator and the title of Christ. Mahumetism takes its name from Mahumet, whom others call Mahumed, others Machometes, and Damascene calls Magmedus; but we follow the pronunciation now received and familiar. This Mahumet was of the race of the Arab Ishmaelites, who kept the name Agarenes from Hagar, Sarah's maidservant, and was the son of Abdalas, a prince of the Arabs, a native of Munichialis, a province on the Elamitic sea in Arabia Petraea, although afterwards the Saracens wished to be called Agarenes as though descended from Sarah, as Sozomen writes in book 6, chapter 38. Under the emperor Philip they persecuted the Christians, as Eusebius relates in book 6, chapter 42. Under Valens, however, they were first made Christians through the advice and wonder inspired by a certain monk named Moses, as Rufinus records in book 2 of his History, chapter 6. And they remained in the faith of Christ, having been instructed by monks who had their phrontisteria and asceteria in the Arabian deserts; they persisted in it until, the true doctrine of the faith having been tossed and submerged by the various and almost countless storms and waves of new heresies, it was at last extinguished in Egypt, Arabia and Syria. Above all, as we have said, it was by the errors of the Eutychians, who sorely troubled the whole East and South, especially Egypt and Arabia, and at last utterly overthrew them. Mahumet, therefore, an Arab and an Ishmaelite, an ambitious and crafty man, [ἀλλαξω], born for the ruin of the whole world, weary of the dissensions of the Christian religion, devised, with the help of Sergius, a Nestorian monk who was then living in exile in Arabia, and of John of Antioch, an Arian, and also of a certain Jew named Selan, an astrologer, and of Bahira, a Persian Jacobite as his prompter, an entirely new dogma full of a blasphemy never heard before. It was first received by the Saracens, his own countrymen, with Eubolara, Aomar, Odmen and Hali supporting and commending it; afterwards it was received by all the Arabs, who had also driven Mahumet out. From this, great praise came to this doctrine: it was at once received by the neighbouring Egyptian peoples, and approved because the Christian doctrine of the faith had long been uncertain among them. Then, by force of arms, it was widely spread by Mahumet himself, who had gathered an army and defended his doctrines with weapons. For he defected from Heraclius, under whom he had first served, together with the whole Saracen nation, being offended because a Roman quaestor had insulted them, calling them dogs for demanding their pay. And so he invaded Syria; then Africa, which was wholly unsettled in the true faith by the errors of the Vandals and Arians; and at last he so prevailed that he now occupies the whole East, on account of the power of the Turks, and in it is the dreadful judgment of God against men who despise and tear apart his word. That impostor rejoices, however, in the Azoar 20 that he has been freed from the opinions of Christians who distrust one another. He teaches these things by which he himself is refuted. First, in the chapter on Marty, he declares that all Saracens will go to hell. Then he says that the Gospel is the light of the Old Testament, Azoar 21; he approves David's Psalter, Azoar 7; he holds that Christ was truly a Prophet and the Word of God, and that Christ ascended into heaven with his flesh; the Mahumetans also concede the coming of Antichrist, the resurrection of the flesh and the last judgment, Azoar 16 and 17. They condemn idolatry, that is, the worship and temples of images; likewise magic, dice-play, and chess. Moreover, they condemn usury and interest, and that force and multitude of lawsuits which is endless among Christians, Azoar 11, 13, 23. They do not approve of familiar dealings with unbelievers. They likewise detest excessive veneration of bishops and monks, and the cult and invocation of dead saints, a point on which the Saracens have always been most offended, as though it were true idolatry. Now these things they condemn, and from them it can be understood how great was the corruption then both in the doctrine itself and in the morals of the Church. For Mahumet condemned all these things, which he saw were then a stumbling block to Christians; and certainly all these vices reigned everywhere in the Church. But the things that follow show what is truly Saracenic, blasphemous and impious, gathered from the sewers and filth of all heresies, and rightly condemned by us; they also show how many kinds of error had by then been widely received and were raging in the very bowels of the Church. 1. They deny that there are three persons in one and the same divine essence; this is Sabellian and Arian. 2. Concerning the creation of the world, the nature of demons and their propagation, they retain the absurd and trifling doctrines both of the Manichaeans and of the Valentinians. 3. Concerning seven heavens and their intelligences, they fable in the same way as the Valentinians and the heathen, and in this they posit only a general providence of God, and introduce the worship of angels, Azoar 23 and 25. 4. They deny that the divine essence is most simple, but also imagine it corporeal, with the Anthropomorphites, and attribute to God a soul besides his essence. Hence they always speak of God as of several united things in the plural number. 5. They deny that Christ is God, with Arius, and call him only a creature, although they acknowledge that he was a great and holy Prophet, with Carpocrates. 6. They deny that Christ is the true Son of God, because they think God begot a Son without a wife, with Cerdo, an absurdity, and [ἀπάτωρ], fatherless; yet they concede that he was conceived of the Holy Spirit, Azoar 9 and 11. 7. They will have Christ neither suffered nor crucified; but that a phantasm was offered in his place to the Jews, whom they, deceived, fixed to the cross instead of Christ. This is Manichaean and Marcionite, Azoar 11. 8. They teach that at last the devils will attain salvation, with the Origenists. 9. They place eternal life, after the manner of the Epicureans, in pleasures of the body, even in heaven, with the Cerinthians, Azoar 23. 10. They explain hell and its punishments fabulously, after the manner of the Virgilian hell and the Papistical Purgatory, Azoar 21 and 25. 11. They retain and observe the ceremonies of the law, above all circumcision, the distinction of foods, and washings of the body, and especially of the anus, as necessary for salvation, with the Ebionites, Azoar 12 and 16. 12. They swear by creatures, as by a fig tree, and a fig, likewise by the olive, with the Priscillianists. 13. They teach that wars must be waged for the sole cause of religion, and that unwilling men must be compelled to accept their dogma, Azoar 6, 7, 18 and 19. 14. They abolish, profane and pollute the holy institution of marriage, and they allow each man to have several wives. They permit divorces to be made for causes not expressed in the Word of God, Azoar 8 and 9. 15. They introduce the merits of works, through which they hope to be saved, with the Pelagians, Azoar 18 and 41. Hence they have various ceremonies and diverse rules of life, and they have instituted and observe certain monastic orders. 16. They deny forgiveness in perpetuity to those who fall away from their faith, with the Novatians. 17. They establish some sins as mortal and others as venial, Azoar 10. 18. They teach that one must pray always toward the East, so that the prayer may be acceptable to God, and they prescribe the use of a certain fixed number of prayers each day, Azoar 10, 17 and 19. They will not have prayer made for unbelievers. 19. They abolish all the sacraments instituted by Christ. In short, it would be endless to pursue the remaining errors, against which John Cantacuzenus, a Persian by the Greek name Achaemenides, who was converted to the faith, wrote; and Walter D., a distinguished man, and Pius II, and a certain Richard in the time of Bernard, and Dr Philip Melanchthon, translated it.

units.la: CAP. XCVII. Quanta sit hodie in Oriente Ecclesiæ vastitas, & quantis erroribus labefactentur, atque laborent ij qui in ea mundi plaga Christianum nomen profitentur.
units.tr: CHAPTER XCVII. How great the desolation of the Church is today in the East, and by what errors those who profess the Christian name in that region of the world are shaken and troubled.

units.la: [?]isum est autem his omnibus addere quædam ex volumine Alcorani & ipsius refutatione trascripta, ex quibus quanta sit hodie in Oriente vastitas Eccle-siæ: quantique errores, & quam sæui pro vera fide regnent etiam inter eos, qui Christianum nomen illic sibi assumunt, luculenter apparebit. Sic igitur illa se ad verbum habent.
units.tr: It seemed good, moreover, to add to all of this some passages copied from the volume of the Koran and its refutation, from which it will clearly appear how great the desolation of the Church is today in the East, and how great the errors and how cruel the contests for the true faith reign even among those who there claim the Christian name for themselves. Thus those passages stand, word for word.

units.la: Denique gens Christianum nomen profitentium, universa diuisa est in decem nationes, & velut diuersas eiusdem tamen religionis professiones præcipuas.
units.tr: Finally, the whole nation of those who profess the Christian name is divided into ten nations, which are, as it were, the principal and distinct professions of the same religion.

units.la: I Latinorum, qui parent imperatori Germaniæ, & Romanæ ecclesiæ: uti Germania ipsa, Gallia, Hispania, Italia, Anglia, Scotia, Po-lonia.
units.tr: 1. Of the Latins, who obey the emperor of Germany and the Roman Church: namely Germany itself, France, Spain, Italy, England, Scotland, and Poland.

units.la: 2 Græcorum, qui imperatori Græcopa-rebant olim, & nunc Constantinopolitano Patriarchæ, qui non obediunt Romanæ ecclesiæ.
units.tr: 2. Of the Greeks, who once obeyed the Greek emperor and now obey the Patriarch of Constantinople, and who do not obey the Roman Church.

units.la: 3 Indorum, siue Æthiopum, quorum princeps est Presbyter Ioannes, in cuius terra est corpus sancti Thomæ. Hic habet sub se reges septuaginta duos, & quādo progreditur aliquò crucem ligneam ante se portari iubet: quum in bellum it, duodecim cruces aureas.
units.tr: 3. Of the Indians, or Ethiopians, whose prince is Presbyter John, in whose land is the body of St Thomas. He has seventy-two kings under him, and whenever he goes anywhere he orders a wooden cross to be carried before him; when he goes to war, twelve golden crosses.

units.la: 4 Iacobitarum, à Iacobo hæretico discipulo Alexandrini Patriarchæ. Sunt in Oriente, Chaldæa & Arabia multi. Circumciduntur & ferro candente sibi suisque crucem imprimunt. Aiunt in Christo tantum esse diuinam naturam. Soli Deo confitentur. Damnati concilio Cedensi.
units.tr: 4. Of the Jacobites, named after Jacob, the heretic and disciple of the Patriarch of Alexandria. There are many of them in the East, in Chaldaea and Arabia. They circumcise themselves and imprint a cross on themselves and their people with a red-hot iron. They say that in Christ there is only a divine nature. They confess God alone. They were condemned by the Council of Chalcedon.

units.la: 5 Nestorianorum, à Nestorio hæretico Constantinopolitano episcopo, qui duas in Christo personas posuit. Tartariam habitant latissimam, & in India maiore. Conficiunt corpus Christi in fermento.
units.tr: 5. Of the Nestorians, named after Nestorius the heretic, bishop of Constantinople, who posited two persons in Christ. They inhabit the very broad Tartary, and Greater India. They make the body of Christ with leaven.

units.la: 6 Moronitarum, à quodam Moronite hæretico, qui vnam tantum in Christo voluntatem ponunt. Hi sunt militares viri. Campanis, vt nos vtuntur. Libyam incolunt, & Phœniciam. Lingua vtuntur Arabica.
units.tr: 6. Of the Maronites, named after a certain heretic Maro, who hold that there is only one will in Christ. These are military men. They use bells as we do. They live in Libya and Phoenicia, and use the Arabic language.

units.la: 7 Armeniorum, à loco, vbi habitant scili-cet prope Antiochiam, & in vtraque Armenia. Habent suum Catholicum, cui parent omnes vulgari sermone in Ecclesia & officio faciendo vtuntur, vt omnes intelligant quæ geruntur[?], Ie[?]iunant quadragesimam: die tamen veneris car-nes edunt. Sacerdotes eorum habent coronas in capite rotundas, alij quadratas. Hierosolyma quotannis votiva peregrinatione veniunt, magni exercitus instar erectis vexillis.
units.tr: 7. Of the Armenians, named from the place where they live, namely near Antioch and in both Armenias. They have their own Catholicos, whom all obey. In the Church and in performing the office they use the vernacular, so that everyone understands what is being done. They keep the Lenten fast, but on Friday they eat meat. Their priests wear round crowns on their heads, and others square ones. Every year they come to Jerusalem on votive pilgrimage, like a great army with banners raised.

units.la: 8 Georgianorum, à beato Georgio, cuius imaginem in præliis & vexillis ferunt. Mediam & Persiam, & Caspium mare incolunt. Lingua Græca utuntur, & eorum more administrant sacramenta. Fœminæ barbam habent, vt viri. Sacerdotes coronas in capite rotundas, alij quadratas. Magni exercitus instar Hierosolymam quotannis votiva peregrinatione veniunt erectis vexillis.
units.tr: 8. Of the Georgians, named after St George, whose image they carry in battles and on their banners. They inhabit Media, Persia, and the Caspian Sea. They use the Greek language and administer the sacraments in their manner. The women have beards, like men. Priests wear round crowns on their heads, and others square ones. Like a great army, they come to Jerusalem every year on votive pilgrimage with banners raised.

units.la: 9 Suranorum, à Sur ciuitate in Assyria. Lin-gua vulgari utuntur Saracenica in officiis Mis-sæ. Græco more conficiunt in fermento. Horum ritus sequuntur quidam in terra sancta, qui dicuntur Samaritani. Obediunt Græcis, quorum doctrinam in multis amplectuntur.
units.tr: 9. Of the Surani, named from the city of Sur in Assyria. They use the vernacular Saracen language in the offices of the Mass. They celebrate in the Greek manner with leavened bread. Some who are called Samaritans in the Holy Land follow their rites. They obey the Greeks, whose doctrine they embrace in many points.

units.la: 10 Mozarabum. Hi partim sunt in Africa, partim in Hispania, ex Arabia profecti. Utuntur in officiis lingua Latina, & Romanæ ecclesiæ parent. Conficiunt in azymis, in multis tamen à Latinis dissentiunt. Inter suæ tantum gentis homines coniugia ineunt. Singulis horis singulos Psalmos dicunt. Natio deuota. Nunc pauci omnino restant.
units.tr: 10. Of the Mozarabs. Some of these are in Africa and some in Spain, having come from Arabia. They use the Latin language in their offices and obey the Roman Church. They celebrate with unleavened bread, yet differ from the Latins in many points. They marry only among men of their own race. They say single psalms at each hour. A devout nation. Now only a very few remain.

units.la: Hactenus ista, ex quibus intelligitur quàm nunc miser sit & prorsus infelix orbis terrarum status, qui Christiana fidem olim per Apostolo-rorum & aliorum prædicationem semel ample-xus, eam deseruit, nouisque doctrinis delectatus, ita discerptus iam distractusq; est, vt purae religionis illic, vbi olim florentissimae fuerunt Ecclesiae, vestigia vel nulla omnino, vel admo- dum exigua nunc restent. Ac mihi tot haereses & tantas, tum in Deum, tum in Christum ipsum tamque horrendas blasphemias a Gentibus, & praeputiatis (quibus magna sua misericordia Dominus tam liberaliter salutem Euangelium- que suum communicauerat) excogitatas, per- tinaciterque defensas intuenti horret animus, venitque saepe in mentem fore, vt propter tam grauem verbi nominisq; sui contemptum, Dominus Deus a Gentibus suum Euangelium, iu- sto suo iudicio auferens, transferat iterum tra- ducatque ad Iudaeos a quibus primum ortum est. Nam si Deus illis naturalibus ramis non per- cit, vt ait Paulus, vide ne tibi, qui oleaster[?] es, & in eorum locum tantum insitus, non parcat.
units.tr: Thus far these things, from which it is understood how wretched and utterly unhappy the state of the world is now, which once embraced the Christian faith through the preaching of the Apostles and others, but then abandoned it and, delighting in new doctrines, has been so torn apart and divided that now there remain there either no traces at all of pure religion, where the Churches once flourished most, or only very slight ones. And when I look upon so many and such great heresies, against God as well as against Christ himself, and such horrible blasphemies devised and stubbornly defended by Gentiles and the uncircumcised, to whom the Lord, in his great mercy, had so generously communicated salvation and his Gospel, my mind shudders, and it often comes to mind that, because of such grave contempt for his Word and his name, the Lord God, by his just judgment, will take his Gospel away from the Gentiles, and transfer and lead it back again to the Jews, from whom it first arose. For if God did not spare the natural branches, as Paul says, take heed lest he not spare you either, who are a wild olive and have been grafted in only in their place.

units.la: Ac certe notada[?] est illa maxime necessaria Pauli admonitio & sententia ad nos Gentes, Rom.ii. versu 22. Vide igitur benignitatem & seueritatem Dei: in eos quidem, qui ceciderunt, seueritatem: in te vero benignitatem, si permanseris in benignitate: alioquin & tu excideris. Quod tam horrendum suum iudicium. Deus, Pater misericordiarum, per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum a nobis auertat. cui laus & gloria in secula seculorum, & vltra.
units.tr: And certainly that most necessary admonition and sentence of Paul to us Gentiles is worth noting, Rom. ii. vers. 22: Behold therefore the goodness and the severity of God: toward those who fell, severity; but toward you, goodness, if you continue in his goodness; otherwise you also will be cut off. May God, the Father of mercies, turn this so dreadful judgment of his away from us through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be praise and glory for ever and ever, and beyond.

units.la: Amen.
units.tr: Amen.

units.la: Vt autem melius intelligeretur qui-bus sensim gradibus in tantam tum doctrina, tum morum sanctorum calamitatem Ecclesia Dei Apostolorum praedi-catione tam feliciter & diligenter plantata incideris, adiunximus pro colophone & coro-nide totius huius argumenti appositum pij cuiusdam viri scriptum. quod ille nobis vo-bisque liberaliter communicauit, ex quo tan-ti Ecclesiae lapsus ratio, & ruina gradus, fa-cillime colligentur. Sic autem habet.
units.tr: But so that it may be better understood by what gradual steps the Church of God, so happily and diligently planted by the preaching of the Apostles, fell into such a calamity both of doctrine and of holy morals, we have added, as a colophon and crown of this whole argument, a writing of a certain pious man, which he generously communicated to us and to you, from which the cause of so great a fall of the Church and the stages of its ruin will be very easily gathered. It reads as follows.

units.la: Isaiae 63.
units.tr: Isaiah 63.

units.la: Miserationum Domini recordabor.
units.tr: I will remember the mercies of the Lord.

units.la: TRACTATUS de Ecclesia.
units.tr: A Treatise on the Church.

units.la: CUM[?] agitur de vera Ecclesiæ notitia, non potest illa certius tradi, quam si ad Caput suum, id est ad Christum, Ecclesia semper revocetur. Quum enim Ecclesia nihil aliud sit quàm Christi corpus & complementum, omnis etiam Ecclesiæ vita & habitus ex ipsius cum Christo coalitione & connexione pendeat necesse est. Hoc autem uno illo modo efficitur, dum vera ac certa Christi agnitio Ecclesiæ traditur verbi Ministerio ad eum finem ab ipso Christo ordinato, ut accedente ex eiusdem Christi promissione Spiritus sancti efficacia & virtute, fides in animis audientium quodammodo concipiat & pariat. Christum Redemptorem & Pastorem Ecclesiæ perpetuum. Hæc enim illa Christi agnitio efficit, ut Christi cum Ecclesia coniunctio & communicatio foveatur & augescat in dies, sub spe beatæ tandem ab illo obtinendæ immortalitatis. Quæritur igitur an cum Apostoli hoc unum fundamentum in vera Ecclesia instituenda semel posuerint, an inquam, ab eo discessum fuerit interiecto ab illis ad nos usque intermedio tempore. Quod si de eo iudicium fieri ex parte potest ex ipsa quâ vocant apparetia[?], omnino statuendum erit rem vel suo loco stetisse hactenus, vel nihil tanti momenti accidisse, quod Ecclesiæ Fidem defecisse testari possit. Manent enim voces & verba dogmatum fidei: Manet etiam forma quædam Ministerij Ecclesiastici in ordinaria successione pastorum. Hę sunt igitur Regni cœlorum claues pastoribus ordinariis in Apostolorum persona traditæ, quæ quidem ab eodem quem illi primum acceperunt Spiritu directæ, omnia deinde in Ecclesia ita disposuerunt, ut quomodo Christi agnitio tradenda per illas esset, penes illarum administros fuerit statuere. Quod si aliter de Ecclesiæ statu & administratione quis sentit, videat imprimis quid agat, quum nulla difficultas cum pace Ecclesiæ non fit commutanda potius, quam ut convulso semel tantę molis fundamento, ubi tandem consistat pedemve quis figat, statui vix possit. Quicquid fit, possessio quamdiuturna bonę fidei plurimum momenti habere merito semper iudicabitur. Et quum unius Christi res hic agatur tanquam veri Ecclesiæ suæ Domini, si quid de ipsius iure interversum esse poterit, nemo ipso certius novum opus nuntiare potuit: quod tamen ab ipso factum esse non constat. Hæc sunt nempe ordinaria Ecclesiæ visibilis & militantis, ut loquuntur, insignia ac documenta: Hæ adversus omnem innovatio-nem iuris exceptiones: de quibus in alteram partem pronuntiare, res est in speciem omnium fortasse difficillima. Meretrix sum (inquit apud HieroHieronymum adu. Luciferianos Ecclesia.) sed tamen mater tua sum. Non seruo unius thori castitatem: Talis eram quando conceptus es. cum Ario adulterium committo: Feci & antea cum Hebione. Nescio quid te unus adulter offendit.& in eodem supra, Rarissima esse fidem illam agnoscit secundum quam fiat nobis, quae simplicitas est mentis & deuota Deo anima. Nolim, inquit, secundum illam mihi fieri. Alia vero est fides dogmatum, quam ego profiteor. Haec sunt illius verba ad conciliandam Ecclesiae unionem, cui omnia condonari vult. Aliud deniq; esse Haereticum sensu, aliud quasi societate quadam. Equidem istiusmodi multa tum quidem usurpari potuerunt, quae tamen vix perinde alio quouis tepore admitti possent sine dextra quadam interpretatione. Et quum omnia satis superq; subducta fuerint, ex duobus in speciem inconuenientibus, vnum alteri omnibus modis ita praeponderat, ut omnis aduersus illud disceptatio absurdissima sit. Sit Deus verax, inquit Apostolus, omnis autem homo mendax. Haec est, inqua, solida omnium difficultatum conciliatio, haec verę religionis summa, haec coscien-tiae quies, ut omne os obstruatur, & omnes dent gloriam Deo. Quemadmodum igitur non ita veritas Christi in sublime attollenda est, ut nullus ipsius sensus & usus in mundo superfuisse aliquando existimetur, (quod absit) ita sane ac multo minus Christi nomen Ecclesiae alligan-dum affigendumve est, ut veritatis ipsius prae-iudicio, fides & honor quidam Ecclesiae assera-tur. Immo vero singulare illud & nunquam fatis prædicandum incomparabilis Domini miserationis in Ecclesia tot sæculis sustinenda argumentum eo vnicè referatur, vt arcana ipsius dispensatio adoretur in omnibus, iudicium verò & misericordia tum erga patres, tum erga filios agnoscatur atq; prædicetur. Neque enim Christus est per Ecclesiam, etsi non sit sine Ecclesia. Ecclesia autem à Christo est, per Christum, & propter Christum. Proinde sic nomen sponsæ Ecclesiæ tribuitur, vt maneat & ancilla Domini sui. Sic illi depositum veritatis & Talenta heri sui creduntur, vt non sua sed illius fide administrentur. sic illi Spiritus veritatis vt arrabo coniugij destinatur, vt in digito veritatis eluceat, non ad illius arbitrium recò datur vel gestetur.
units.tr: When the true knowledge of the Church is under discussion, it cannot be handed down more certainly than if the Church is always called back to its Head, that is, to Christ. For since the Church is nothing other than the body and fulfilment of Christ, the whole life and condition of the Church must necessarily depend on its union and connection with Christ. This, however, is brought about in one way only: when the true and certain knowledge of Christ is handed down to the Church through the ministry of the Word, the end for which Christ himself ordained it, so that, with the efficacy and power of the Holy Spirit added according to the promise of the same Christ, faith is in some measure conceived and brought forth in the minds of the hearers. Christ is the Redeemer and perpetual Pastor of the Church. For this knowledge of Christ is what brings it about that the union and communion of Christ with the Church is nourished and grows day by day, under the hope of the blessed immortality to be obtained from him at last. The question, therefore, is whether, when the apostles laid this one foundation for establishing the true Church once for all, the matter has since then departed from it through the intermediate time that stretches from them down to us. If judgment on this can be made in part from the very appearance they point to, it must be concluded altogether either that the matter has remained in its place until now, or that nothing of such moment has happened as could show that the faith of the Church has failed. For the words and phrases of the doctrines of faith remain; there also remains a certain form of ecclesiastical ministry in the ordinary succession of pastors. These, then, are the keys of the kingdom of heaven, handed to the ordinary pastors in the person of the apostles, who, directed by the same Spirit they first received, afterwards so arranged everything in the Church that it rests with their ministers to determine how the knowledge of Christ is to be handed down through them. But if anyone thinks otherwise about the state and administration of the Church, let him first consider what he is doing, since no difficulty ought to be changed at the cost of the peace of the Church, rather than, once the foundation of so great a structure has been shaken, one can scarcely establish where he may finally stand or set his foot. Whatever the case, long possession held in good faith will always rightly be judged to carry very great weight. And since the matter here concerns Christ alone, as the true Lord of his Church, if anything about his right could have been overturned, no one could have announced a new work more certainly than he himself; yet it is not established that he has done so. These, indeed, are the ordinary marks and proofs of the visible and militant Church, as they say; against every innovation of right these are the exceptions; and to pronounce on the other side concerning them is perhaps, in appearance, the most difficult of all things. "I am a harlot," says the Church in Jerome, against the Luciferians, "but I am still your mother. I do not keep the chastity of one bed. I was such when you were conceived. I commit adultery with Arius; I did so before with Ebion. I know not what one adulterer offends you." And in the same place: she acknowledges that that faith is very rare by which we are made simple of mind and a soul devoted to God. "I would not," she says, "have it done to me according to that. But the faith of doctrines, which I profess, is another thing." These are his words, aimed at reconciling the union of the Church, to which he wants everything forgiven. Finally, it is one thing to be a heretic in sense, another to be as it were in a certain fellowship. Indeed, many such things may have been used at that time which yet could scarcely be admitted at any other time without some twisted interpretation. And when everything has been reckoned sufficiently and more than sufficiently, of two things which seem inconsistent, one so far outweighs the other in every respect that any dispute against it is most absurd. "Let God be true," says the Apostle, "but every man a liar." This, I say, is the solid reconciliation of all difficulties, this is the sum of true religion, this is the rest of conscience, that every mouth may be stopped and all may give glory to God. Therefore, just as the truth of Christ is not to be exalted so high that it is thought that no sense or use of it has remained at any time in the world (which God forbid), so, and much less, is the name of Christ to be bound to or fastened upon the Church, so that by prejudice of that truth itself some faith and honour of the Church may be asserted.
