Indeed, that singular and never sufficiently proclaimed argument of the incomparable mercy of the Lord, sustained in the Church through so many centuries, should be referred to this alone: that his secret dispensation is adored in all things, and that his judgment and mercy, both toward the fathers and toward the sons, are acknowledged and proclaimed. For Christ is not through the Church, although he is not without the Church. The Church, however, is from Christ, through Christ, and on account of Christ. Accordingly, the name of bride is given to the Church so that she may remain also the handmaid of her Lord. Thus the deposit of truth and the talents of her master are entrusted to her, so that they may be administered not by her own but by his faith. Thus the Spirit of truth is given to her as the pledge of marriage, so that he may shine forth on the finger of truth, and is not handed over or carried at her own discretion.

units.la: Denique sic in Christo & Ecclesia Deus cum hominibus coiungitur, vt vnius Dei in Christo opus extet ad Ecclesiæ salutem: Ecclesia verò in sese mere passiue sese habeat, vniúsque Christi opus censeatur. Neque enim (quod est totius istius cötrouersiæ expediendæ summum caput) ita cum Ecclesia transfegit Christus, vt dum ab illa abest corpore illo suo quod in cœlum euectum est, sua illi omnia absolutè resignaret: sed potius se illi interfuturum pollicetur, ac nunquam defuturum confirmat (præsenti nimirum spiritus efficacia in verbi sui luce propaganda:) dummodo quæ ab ipso mandata accepit, ipsius non suo nomine tradat, ipsi non sibi acquirat quod acquiret, rem denique Domini non suo sed illius Spiritu gerat. Quod si quid secus incidat, (vti manifeste euenturum prædicit Dominus) adeò non esse accipiendam ipsius indi-gnationem gnationem silentio male tectam pro certa adprobatione malæ administrationis, ut potius inopinato rediturum se & summo iure tantam improbitatem vindicaturum adfirmet. Hoc illud est igitur Mysteriū quod nos omnes exercet neque immerito: sed ita tamen, ut quicumque in Christum unum apud Apostolos suos veritatem omnem pro Ecclesiæ notitia tradentem intenti erunt, illorum pedes à laqueo euellendi sint: qui secus, iustas dent pœnas prævaricatricis erga heram ex ancilla factam obseruantiæ, in-superhabito Domino ac perpetuo redemptore, qui est Deus benedictus in sæcula. Amen.
units.tr: Finally, God is so joined with men in Christ and the Church that the work of the one God in Christ stands for the salvation of the Church, while the Church itself is regarded as purely passive in itself, and the work is counted as that of Christ alone. For (and this is the chief point for settling this whole controversy) Christ did not so depart from the Church that, while he was absent from her in that body of his which was carried up into heaven, he simply handed over all his things to her. Rather, he promises that he will be present with her, and confirms that he will never fail her, namely by the efficacy of his Spirit present in the spreading of the light of his Word, provided that she hands on, not in her own name but in his, what she has received as commands from him, and does not acquire for herself what she acquires, and in short carries on the Lord's business not by her own spirit but by his. But if anything goes otherwise (as the Lord has plainly foretold it will happen), he affirms that his indignation is not to be taken as a certain approval of bad administration, which is ill concealed by silence, but that he will rather return unexpectedly and with full right avenge such wickedness. This, then, is that mystery which troubles us all, and not undeservedly; yet in such a way that whoever are intent on Christ alone, who through his apostles hands down all truth as the knowledge of the Church, must have their feet plucked from the snare; while those who do otherwise will rightly pay the penalty of a faithless servant, who, from being a maidservant, has become unfaithful to her mistress, having disregarded the Lord and perpetual Redeemer, who is God blessed for ever. Amen.

units.la: Primum igitur duo ista ponenda sunt necessario, secundum quæ tota de Ecclesiæ statu disquisitio peragatur. Unum, Quod Ecclesia mu-tationibus non uniusmodi obnoxia esse possit, ac proinde non esse idem semper de illius ha-bitu faciedum iudicium. Alterum, neque ullam huiusmodi mutatione adde & perturbationem in Ecclesiam incidere posse, quin semper Domino ius suum[?] in illam maneat, quo etiam ad suo-rum consolationem arcana dispesatione[?] utatur: neque tamen ex eo effici (quod quidam velint ac mercentur magno) ut illa etiam species administrationis Ecclesiæ quæ non iam spirituale illud caput refert, sed humanum pro spirituali præ se fert, legitima habenda sit. Sed ut in damni incendij, naufragij, casu plæraque sine certo ordine admittuntur, quæ non per se probentur, vel optentur, sed ut res ferunt, magis tolerantur: ita etiam in statu Ecclesiæ visibilis, quæ & Catholica audire vult, factum esse Domini prouidentia & factum iri quandiu ipsi ita videbitur, ut quum ex istorū mente & actis ipsis ius omne ipsius ad illos devolutum credi velint, liberum tamen sit ipsi Domino quod per istos sit ratum habere eatenus, ut neque personas illorum probet, neque acta ut in personis considerata.
units.tr: First, therefore, these two things must necessarily be laid down, according to which the whole inquiry into the state of the Church is to be carried out. One: that the Church can be liable to changes of more than one kind, and therefore that the judgment to be made about her condition is not always the same. The other: that no change or disturbance of this kind can fall upon the Church without the Lord's right remaining over her, by which he also uses a secret dispensation for the comfort of his own; yet it does not follow from this (as some wish and greatly desire) that that form of administration of the Church which no longer carries that spiritual head but presents the human in place of the spiritual is to be regarded as lawful. Rather, just as in a fire, a shipwreck, or some accident many things are allowed without a fixed order, which are not approved or chosen in themselves, but are rather tolerated as circumstances bear them, so also in the state of the visible Church, which also wishes to be heard as Catholic, it has happened by the providence of the Lord, and will happen for as long as it seems right to him, that, although they want all his right to be believed to have passed to them from their own mind and deeds, it is nevertheless free for the Lord himself to ratify what is done through them only so far as he neither approves their persons nor their acts as considered in their persons.

units.la: Hoc tantum valet usurpatio nominis Ecclesiæ quod ad istos, ut tanquam serui subductitij ab hero tandem pro merito accipiantur, ac non ut extranei leuiori iudicio obnoxij sint. Quod autem non unō interea loco reliquiæ quędam Ecclesiarum ex veteri stirpe veritatis tandiu defossa excitantur vi illa spiritus Christi opus suum per medias abyssos fouentis, illud etiam ita accipi non potest, quasi igitur emortua fuerit Ecclesia.
units.tr: This much only is achieved by the usurpation of the name of the Church: that those people, like runaway slaves, are at last rightly taken back by their master, rather than being regarded as outsiders subject to a lighter judgment. But that in the meantime, in not a few places, remnants of Churches from the old stock of truth, long buried, are raised up by that power of the Spirit of Christ which cherishes his work through the midst of the abysses, cannot be taken to mean that the Church has therefore died out.

units.la: Etenim unam eandemque dogmatum fidem cum Ecclesia ipsa Romana habemus, quæ quidem fides perpetuum fuit iam inde ab Apostolis totius Ecclesiæ vexillum. Sed quia res ipsa loquitur sub illo Symboli fidei titulo, & veritatem omnem supprimi iam olim, & pleraque omnia quæ cum illo directe pugnent tradi & inculcari, illud dicimus, neque integram cordis fidem ad iustitiam, neque oris confessionem ad salutem profiteri nos posse cum illis, qui Deum quidem reuera nosse fatentur, dictis autem ipsis nedum operibus, plane abnegant. Quod igitur nobis cum illis est iustissimo nostro animi do-lore dissidiū, quo magis leue videri possit, quatenus & fidem, & Sacramenta, & Scripturas eas-dem tractamus, & quæ tantum ab illis accepi-mus, illa nos ab iis seiungere cogunt, & Doctores ipsos Ecclesiasticos ac synodos purioris antiantiquitatis eadem cum illis veneratione quan-uis certiore fide prosequimur, eo magis spiritus ille aduersarij Christi deprehendedus est, cuius os impudens omnia ita permisceat, ut quū sine Christi & Ecclesiae nomine stare se non posse intelligat, sub illis tamen tantorum nominum praestigiis, vim omnem pietatis quatum in ipso est, convellat. Videat Dominus & requirat. Nos vero nostra omnia faciamus quae Domini sunt, ut Psalmos, lectiones pias, & reliqua illa venaranda in se pietatis auitae etiam sub Papatu vestigia: sed ita simul ut Domini unus simus, neque oleū peccatoris interea caput nostrum demulceat.
units.tr: For we hold one and the same faith in doctrines as the Roman Church itself; and this faith has been from the Apostles onward the perpetual banner of the whole Church. But since the matter itself speaks under that title of the Creed, and since all truth was long ago suppressed, and almost everything that directly conflicts with it is handed down and inculcated, we say this: we cannot profess with them a sincere faith of heart unto righteousness, nor a confession of mouth unto salvation, with those who indeed confess that they know God, but by their words, not to speak of their works, plainly deny him. Therefore, the dissension we have with them, which causes us the most just grief of mind, may seem the lighter for this reason: we handle the same faith, the same sacraments and the same Scriptures, and what we have received only from them, those things compel us to separate ourselves from them; and we pursue the ecclesiastical teachers and the synods of the purer antiquity with the same reverence as they do, though with a surer faith. The more, then, is that spirit, the adversary of Christ, to be detected, whose impudent mouth so mixes up everything that, understanding it cannot stand without the name of Christ and the Church, it nevertheless, under the disguises of such great names, overturns as far as it can all the force of piety. Let the Lord see and require it. As for us, let us do all the things that are the Lord's, such as the Psalms, pious readings, and those other traces of ancestral piety, worth seeking out, even under the Papacy; but so that at the same time we be the Lord's alone, and the oil of the sinner does not in the meantime soothe our head.

units.la: His igitur obiter ita dispunctis, quod praeci-pui momenti est, agamus. Quaeritur igitur qui fieri potuerit, si factum detur, ut Ecclesia tatum[?] a se mutata fuerit (quum ita fideliter atque feliciter instituta & confirmata fuisset primum) ut quod ad visibilem illam attinet, nihil minus habenda sit, quam quod audire vult, ut vera sit Ecclesia. Quaeritur etiam quibus ex notis hoc totum certo deprehendi possit, quum videlicet res illa in se plus quam dici possit & annorum serie & rerum varietate inuoluta videatur.
units.tr: Having thus briefly set these things in order, let us now deal with what is of chief importance. The question, then, is how it could have come about, if it be granted that it happened, that the Church, having been at first so faithfully and happily founded and established, should have so changed itself that, as far as its visible form is concerned, it is by no means what it wishes to be heard as being, namely the true Church. The question is also by what marks all this can be surely recognised, since that matter in itself seems wrapped up in more than can be said, both in the sequence of years and in the variety of events.

units.la: Primum igitur statuendum illud nobis est, agi hic de eo[?] tu[?] illo hominum variis locis & temporibus hic agente, qui Dei veri cultum sub spe & fide salutis aeternae ab ipso per unius Christi nomen accipiendae profiteatur. quanuis autem istiusmodi coetus neque haberi neque regi possit sine hominum ministerio, uti ex ipsa Domini ordi-natione constat, non tamen ex eo consequitur
units.tr: First, then, we must establish this: we are speaking here of that gathering of men, in various places and times, which professes the worship of the true God in hope and faith of eternal salvation to be received from him through the name of Christ alone. Although such an assembly can be neither had nor governed without the ministry of men, as is clear from the Lord's own ordinance, it does not follow from this

units.la: Ecclesiam ab hominum ministerio pedere absolute, sed quatenus illorum opera uti Domino visum fuerit. Horum autem hic sensus est, neque quum pastores sincere munere suo funguntur, aliud tamen quam ut testes & praecones veritatis habendos esse, neque quum illi ab officio cessant, Dominum ipsis alligatum esse, quin in Ecclesiae omnem regendae curam recipiat. Ratio est, quia quocunque modo regatur Ecclesia, Ecclesia est, generatio Christi sit & quasi partus Spiritus S. semper agnosci debeat. Iam vero ut primaria illa nota Spiritus Domini cuius veluti vtero Ecclesia gestatur, extra quoque percipiatur, ac non in cogitatione aliqua volitare existimetur, instituit Dominus ipse Verbum suum per Apostolos consignandum Ecclesiae, ex quo & fidem & cultum omnem ipsi gratum perpetuo hauriret, atque in se exhiberet. Sunt autem Verbi scripti summae quaedam partes duae, quibus Ecclesiae administratio legitima & irrefixa continetur. Una est in verbi ipsius auditione & interpretatione recta, posita, quae in Christi beneficio & veritate ampletenda omnes a summo ad infimum contineat. Altera in rituum paucissimorum eodem verbo praescriptorum religiosa observatione, quae spiritualem Ecclesiae conditionem per eundem Christum testificetur, ut in illius fide & cultu omnes tanto magis confirmentur. Sunt istae (inquam) substantiales verae Ecclesiae notae. Quod autem ad ritus sive modos agendi pro variis circumstantiis rerum, locorum, temporum, personarum, quibus vix etiam carere potest omnis conuentus Ecclesiasticus clefiafticus, quoniam in eiusmodi rebus usur-pandis aedificatio una pro legitimo scopo fem-per habenda est,quicquid, inquam, ijs in rebus positum est, proprie ordinem externum spe-ctat, nō autem ad conscientiam per sese pertin-git. Istiusmodi fuerunt fortasse iam olim quae prout Ecclesiae decentius visum erat, in locis, horis, vasis, oblationibus, & reliquis eiuf-modi rebus externis,fimplicisime fine ulla cul-tus adstrictione obseruabantur. Quum igitur nihil ex illis ritibus ad Dei cultum proprie per-tineat,nimis absurdum fuit summam Religio-nis Christianae in illis repositam tradcre,etiam-fi nihil illic verae Christi institutioni repugnans notari posset.Neque enim dubito hoc affirma-re, quod fi quid ab Apostolis ipsis fine ulla ex-ceptione traditu ordinatumve quod ad externa ista attinet liquido obtenderetur, quod tamen in abusum deinde tractum fit quacunque occa-fione, illud inquam etiamsi (quod cum venia dictum fit) de ipfiffimamet Missa ostendi pof-set, deque ipso Romani Antistitis Primatu, totum illud tamen illis ipsis auctoribus, & au-ctore qui in illis egit Spiritu resecandum abro-gandumque esse, nequid unquam Ecclesiae lu-minibus, Christi Domini nempe beneficio & veritati singulari ac perpetuae,vel tantillum of-ficiat.Dicamus igitur,Si Ecclesia regimen illud certum quo Christi agnitio continetur, uti o-mnino debuit, integrum retinuit, quanuis non una ex causa intus vel extra conflictata fit, Ec-clefiam quoque recte sibi tum coftitiffe. Quod fi eadem illa Ecclesia a natiua illa puritate per humanam infirmitatem ita degenerauit sensim, ut tamen ipsam lucem veritatis, aliquo modo retineret, & sibi applicaret, ita tum quidem laborare illa coepisse, ut tamen pax illius studiose adhuc retinenda fuerit. At vero si tanquam remoto pudore & metu, suo tantum ingenio uti praesumpsisse hominum ille coetus sub humano capite, Christo & verbo ipsius insuperhabito, deprehendatur & convincatur, tum demum sub illo visibilis Ecclesiae nomine Filium illum perditum caput extulisse certo statuamus, quicum nihil esse sibi commune pij omnes testari debeant, quantum dederit Dominus.
units.tr: that the Church depends absolutely on the ministry of men, but only insofar as the Lord sees fit to use their work. The meaning of this is as follows: when the ministers faithfully discharge their office, they are to be regarded as nothing other than witnesses and heralds of the truth; and when they cease from their office, the Lord is not bound to them, so that he does not take over the whole care of governing the Church. The reason is that however the Church is governed, it is the Church, and it must always be recognised as the offspring of Christ and, as it were, the birth of the Holy Spirit. Now, so that this primary mark of the Spirit of the Lord, in whose womb the Church is carried as it were, may also be perceived from outside, and not be thought to float about in some mere notion, the Lord himself appointed that his Word be sealed to the Church through the Apostles, from which it might continually draw in and exhibit within itself both faith and every worship pleasing to him. There are, however, two main parts of the written Word, by which the lawful and unbroken administration of the Church is contained. One lies in the hearing and right interpretation of the Word itself, placed in the embrace of the benefit and truth of Christ, which contains all things from the highest to the lowest. The other lies in the religious observance of a very few rites prescribed in the same Word, which testifies through the same Christ to the spiritual condition of the Church, so that all may be the more confirmed in its faith and worship. These, I say, are the substantial and true marks of the Church. As for the rites or modes of acting, adapted to the varying circumstances of things, places, times and persons, of which almost no ecclesiastical assembly can be without, since in using things of this kind edification is always to be held as the one lawful aim, whatever, I say, has been laid down in these matters properly concerns external order, and does not in itself pertain to conscience. Of this kind were perhaps, long ago, those things which were observed, as seemed more fitting to the Church, in places, hours, vessels, offerings and other such external things, most simply and without any binding to worship. Since, then, none of those rites properly pertains to the worship of God, it was far too absurd to place the sum of the Christian religion in them, even though nothing contrary to the true institution of Christ could be noted there. For I do not doubt affirming this: that if anything that was handed down or ordained by the Apostles themselves, without any exception, were clearly shown to concern those external matters, but which was afterwards turned to abuse on whatever occasion, even if (to speak with pardon) it could be shown of the Mass itself, and of the very Primacy of the Roman Bishop, all that must nevertheless be cut away and abrogated by those very authors, and by the Spirit who acted in them, lest it ever in the slightest degree obstruct the lights of the Church, namely the singular and perpetual benefit and truth of Christ the Lord. Let us say, then: if the Church retained entire that certain rule by which the recognition of Christ is contained, as it ought to have done, then, although it was troubled from within and without for more than one reason, we may rightly say that the Church too had constituted itself. But if that same Church, through human weakness, so gradually degenerated from its native purity that it nevertheless retained in some way and applied to itself the light of truth itself, then we should say it had begun to suffer in such a way that its peace was still to be zealously retained. But if, as though shame and fear were laid aside, that assembly of men is found and convicted of having presumed to use only its own wit, under a human head, with Christ and his Word set aside, then we may certainly conclude that under the name of the visible Church that lost Son has raised up a head, with whom all the godly ought to testify they have nothing in common, as far as the Lord has granted.

units.la: Ut autem omnium istorum verior & expref-sior demonstratio velut oculis ipsis subiiciatur, ex qua nempe & occasiones & inclinationes rerum in Ecclesia denotentur, hominibus ad res tantas nunquam satis ut par erat attentis post Apostolorum excessum: constituentur a nobis quinque veluti ætates Ecclesiæ, quibus ætatibus totum illius cursum & peregrinationem ab Ascensione Domini ad hæc tempora perstringemus.
units.tr: But so that a truer and clearer demonstration of all these things may be set before the eyes, by which both the occasions and the tendencies of events in the Church may be marked out, since men were never sufficiently attentive to such great matters as they should have been after the departure of the Apostles, we shall establish five, as it were, ages of the Church, and through these ages we shall outline its whole course and pilgrimage from the Ascension of the Lord to the present times.

units.la: Sit igitur prima Ecclesiæ ætas sub Apostolis ipsis ac primariis ipsorum discipulis, per annos fere septuaginta, post Domini ascensionem, ad Traianum.
units.tr: Let the first age of the Church, then, be under the Apostles themselves and their chief disciples, for about seventy years after the Lord's ascension, down to Trajan.

units.la: Secunda ætas a Traiano ad Constantinum sub Martyribus illis numerosissimis, per annos ducentos & amplius.
units.tr: The second age, from Trajan to Constantine, under those very numerous martyrs, lasting two hundred years and more.

units.la: Tertia ætas a Constantino ad Phocam sub eximiis & doctissimis Episcopis quos Doctores Ecclesiæ vocarunt, per annos circiter trecentos.
units.tr: The third age, from Constantine to Phocas, under the outstanding and most learned bishops whom they called the Doctors of the Church, lasting about three hundred years.

units.la: Quarta à Phoca ad Carolū Magnū sub initia insignium mutationum tam in Ecclesia quàm in Republica, per annos ducentos plus minus.
units.tr: The fourth, from Phocas to Charlemagne, at the beginning of remarkable changes both in the Church and in the commonwealth, lasting roughly two hundred years.

units.la: Quinta demùm à Carolo illo Magno ad Carolum Austriacum, & quod ab illo hactenus ex-currit, per annos fere octingentos: quo quidem tempore maximè coepit Dominus aliquot in lo-cis Ecclesiæ suæ reliquias colligere, & suis na-talibus restituere. Et sanè nostra fraus omnis est, & indignissima ingratitudo, quod tam in-comparabile Domini beneficium quandoque interuerti videtur ac retroferri. Sed ille nobis sit spes à turbine, & umbraculum ab æstu, qui refugium fuit suis semper à generatione in ge-nerationem.
units.tr: Finally, the fifth, from that Charlemagne to Charles of Austria, and what has run on from then until now, lasting almost eight hundred years. In this period, in particular, the Lord began to gather together in several places the remnants of his Church and to restore them to their native condition. Indeed, the whole fault is ours, and a most shameful ingratitude, that so incomparable a benefit of the Lord should at times seem to be overturned and turned back. But may that be our hope against the whirlwind and our shade against the heat, he who has always been a refuge for his own from generation to generation.

units.la: Quod igitur ad primam illam ætatem quam Apostolis præcipuè tribuimus, attinet, agnosci-mus ex ipsius veritatis testimonio, nihil non il-lic sincerissimum fuisse ac vegetissimum. Nam & verbi prædicatio qua Christi agnitio tradi-tur, tanquàm ex ipsius Christi ore in egregiis illis ipsius organis personuit, & tota Ecclesiæ admi-nistratio spirituale suam innovationem & quasi à Legis iugo liberationem appositissimè testata est. Quanquam autem vix colligere potuerim quis ordo quaeve ratio docendi vel agendi in ministerio Apostolorum tencretur[?], quia videlicet in tan-tis rerum initiis occasiones & circunstantiæ non eadem idem ferunt, adeoque plerique initia quæ-dam fidei, uti in cap. 6. ad Hebr. citantur, tantùm primò caperent, in genere tamen non dubito, quin duplex forma docendi observata fuerit jam inde. Una, quæ ad initiandos spectaret: altera deinde ad adultos in fide pascedos, magisque ac magis confirmados, quod notat Apostolus 1. ad Thes. 3. dum ait, ut copleamus quæ desunt fidei vestræ. Atque horum omnium summam ex scripturis peti solitam, ad Christi beneficium ut ad scopum relatam, ad fidei analogiam & fidei appendices Baptismum & Coenam, & reliqua eiusmodi exactam fuisse, persuasum habeo. quæ vero peculiariter agenda, urgenda, toleranda publice vel privatim, illa inquam ita prudentiæ Ecclesiæ reliqua, ut semper libertas illa spiritualis a Christi beneficio inseparabilis ad omnium ædificationem cum charitatis usu retinenda assereretur. Sed tamen hic quoque dissimulari non debet, quod ab Ecclesia vix unquam separatum iri sperari potest, nempe, non una ex occasione fœlicissimam illam Ecclesiæ sub Apostolorum Ministerio educationem non ita passim processisse, quin eodem fere momento initia quoque malorum a Satana immissa sint, quæ deinde optimis quibusque non satis ad opus Domini attentis, ipsius Christi Agnitionis fundamenta ia[?] inde perturbarent. Vidit enim Satan quod res erat: non posse certius aut gravius noceri operi Domini, quam si ipsiusmet occasione ad illud tentandum ab ipsis initijs abuteretur. Neque tamen hoc quodcunq; extiterit adeo de Apostolo-[?]lorum integerrima fide & opera detrahit quidquam, ut potius insignia illa Spiritus sancti[?] luminaria tanto purius enitescant, ubi lucem illam ab illis oblatam, non ea qua decuit ratione perceptam, & ad suum usum relatam fuisse contendimus. Hinc igitur iudicium de reliquis Ecclesiæ ætatibus ducendum est. Neque enim vn-quam se melius habere potuit quàm sub Apostolis ipsis Ecclesia, cum incomparabili illo Spiritus dono perfusa, & lucem veritatis certissimā undique circumferret, & purissimum adhuc succum ac sanguinem generationis illius spiritualis retineret. Quid igitur ætas illa prima pati iam tu potuerit expendendum nobis est. Hoc autem non potest commodius exquiri, quàm si in vna illa Christi agnitione hæreamus, in qua vere proram & puppim status Ecclesiæ posita esse initio constituimus. Christi igitur agnitio duo præcipuè complectitur. Vnum est, vt quis in seipso Christus sit, Alterum, vt quid in nobis, intelligatur. Primum, diuinæ & humanæ naturæ vnionem personalem, alterum, officium siue beneficium personæ illius quæ Christus est, erga Ecclesiam complectitur: ac in summa, vt qui fer[?]-uator & dicitur & creditur, & tantum potuisse & reuera præstitisse ostendatur. Debitum enim Humanæ naturæ in Adamo reæ coram Deo nō potuit solui, nisi per æquiualens aliàs indebitū. Vnúsque extitit secundum Dei promissionem Iesus Christus Filius ille Dei Deus Homo qui vt ad eam rem exactè præstandam idoneus à Deo Patre missus in mundum, totum illud salutis nostræ negotium in seipso suorum omniū nomine perageret. Vnum est etiam illud Mysterium Christi, in quo vno infinuādo totus est Apostolus nominatim, vtpote in quo vno Ecclesiæ vita plane continetur, si dextrè accipiatur vt par est: vt & contra, sanitas Ecclesiæ stare nō possit, illo eodem arcano quoquis modo obscurato, nedum indigne sepulto, vti tādem accidit. Ergo quod ad illam de Christi persona & in illa existentibus naturis veritatem attinet, quan-tis nihil non molitus sit Satan ab initio, quo illam quacunque posset vel per ementitos ex Iu-daeis Christianos, vel per alios quosuis subuer-teret, quia tamen res erat apertior in sese, quàm vt vere piū quenquam per illa tempora lateret, nihil effecit Satan, quod Ecclesiæ tandem magis in bonum non cederet. Nam & monstrosa illorum ingenia qui de Christi naturis vel persona, vel etiam de tribus in vno Deo subsistentibus personis, extra Dei verbum quasi cum ratione insaniendo impie loquebantur, non in-commode retecta sunt, eorumq; damnatæ bla-sphemiæ: & piorum tanto magis confirmata in rebus sacris tractandis fides atque reverentia. Sic igitur illa hostilis impressio Ciuitatem Dei perfidis ciuibus repurgauit, vt veros atque probos tanto magis ea occasione commendaret. Hoc autem toto de Hæresibus, Augustini libro, & commentario illi adiuncto appositè comprehenditur. Atqui non in eo constitit Satan, vt per apertos tantum illos hæresiarchas bellum veritati inferret, quod ipsum tam strenuè repelli sentiret. Sed potius quasi nihil aliud valde Ecclesiæ aliunde timendum esset, dum in illa dogmatum in sese longe præcipuorum assertione bona ex parte ipsam distinet, interea non vna ex occasione ipsa illius præcordia ita tentauit, vt quasi aliud agens, ab illa liquida & exacta Mysterij Christi perceptione & seria professione pios adeo i-psos nihil minus cogitantes sensum auerteret. Neque vero res illa nunc quidem longa demo-stratione indiget, quando ipsæ Scripturæ Apo-stolicæ hoc omnes quasi uno ore clamitant. Si quidem Ecclesia in synagoga primum educata & ad Gentes traduci coepta, rarissima adeo fuit illa spiritualis prudentia & moderatio in plerisque, quæ quid & quorsum & à quibus & quamdiu tolerandum condonandumve esset, satis apposite videret, ut vel optimis quibusque oculi in illis rebus caligarent. Sic igitur illa Gentiū cum Iudæis sub Christi nomine in Ecclesiam coalitio suas difficultates experiebatur à subdolis o-perariis, ut vix satis Apostoli ipsi apud hos vel illos exaudirentur, dum appositam inter omnes unionem ita procurant, ut semper ad Christum agnoscendū revocent, & in eo retineant. Quod autem ad Gentes peculiariter attinet, vel ex ali-quot prioris ad Cor.locis constat, itemque ex 2. & 3. Apocalyp. nominatim, non defuisse & illic initia infelicia scandalorum, quæ quidem cum securitate & inflatione multa radices agerent passim, quantumcunque spiritus etiam Domi-ni per Apostolos intercederet, vel in herba nata femina necaret. Eius autem quam notavimus præcipuæ occasionis longe maximi in Ecclesia irrepentis mali per illegitima & minime nati-vam Christi Domini agnitionem, argumenta certissima colligi possunt (uti diximus) ex perpe-tuis Apostolorum testimoniis. Etenim vnum illud fere habent propositum, ut veritate de Christi beneficio traditam afferant aduersus impor-tunos homines & improbissimos seductores, qui quidem omnia Christi nomini tribuendo, reipsa homines vel in seipsis vel in euancscenti-bus pædogogiæ l[?]egalis ritibus adsigebant. Te-stis perpetua ad Galatas epistola. Testis & bo-na pars secundi ad Colossenses epistolę capitis. Imprimis autem hoc totum quamscitissime ab omnibus simul Apostolis quasi ad ipsum Spiri-tus Christi tribunal his paucis verbis traductu notari potest, notissimo illo loco Actorum Apostolorum, Quidam ex nobis egressi turbarunt vos labefactantes animas vestras, iubentes circuncidi & seruare Legem, QVIBVS NON MAN-DAVERAMVS. Sic igitur illi falsomandatarij iam tum sese ingerebant, & quantum erat in ipsis Christi lucem ac beneficium per Ecclesias suffocabant: unde, ut etiam diximus, ventura ætas post Apostolos eam infirmitatem contraheret, quæ tădem Ecclesiam per sese vel sine ulla externa impressione subrueret. Quæ enim Christi agnitio illa est, ubi quid ab illo ad Ecclesiam proveniat, fere ignoratur? Hoc autem subiectis aliquot exemplis illustrare operæpretium erit, ut quanti fuerit momenti ista sub initia ipsa Ecclesiæ gliscens lactis vivifici indigestio, certius connotetur, & ad reliquas ætates porrigatur. Quū igitur articuli fidei quos vocat in omnibꝰ Ecclesiis rectè intelligeretur & personarent, multum aberat tamen ut quis esset usus illius incomparabilis Symboli satis apposite quemadmodum Apostoli docuerant, apud quaplurimos constaret. Baptismus nempe quo homines in Ecclesiæ cœtum sub Christi nomine aggregabantur, eo iam referebatur, ut per illud lauacrum ab omnibus peccatis ante admissis ablui homines statuendo, plenam & exactam (pro inchoata tātum) Spiritus sanctificationem atque ab illa manantem innouationem adeptos esse existimarent. ita videlicet Sacramentū beneficij Christi interpretabantur, vt ipsummet Christi beneficium vel ignorarent vel confunderent. Ablutio enim in Baptismo accepta perpetuam sordium omnium expurgationem non eo sensu habet, quasi nihil superesset in baptizatis non innouatum & sanctificatum: sed quatenus perfusio sanguinis Christi omnes omnino baptizatorum in fide maculas quod ad reatum abstergit: ac simul arcanū sanctificationis germen immittit, quod suo tempore & modo Spiritu Christi in suis membris testetur atque exerat. Coniuncta erat & altera quaedam ignorantiae nebula, quae ad istam fouendam valeret. Plerumque enim quaenam esset illa peccati originalis labes, & quam profundi illius recessus vel maxime ante, vel etiam post Baptismum pauci attendebat. Inde illa utriusque hominis status nempe & sine & in Christo consideratio descriptio sub verbis carnis & spiritus ad sensum humanum detorta: quasi caro non homine totum vt Adami prolem, sed tantum affectus pravos, Spiritus autem non etiam hominem totum internum a Spiritu Christi quasi in incem editū, sed rationem & intellectum vt nobilissimā hominis partem designaret. Haec autem & Iudaeis etiam noua, & Graecis absurda videbantur, ex communi omnium sensu ac iudicio. Inde etiam illa operum ita anxia apud plerosque inculcatio, & cum ea statim coalescens exquisitior vitæ ratio, à coniugio & cæteris vitę vsibus remotior, tàquam per se acceptior Deo: Inde etiam vitæ cuiusdã socialis in Ægypto maxime, quasi sub Marci illius Petri discipuli nomine, ab Apostolorum exemplo ducta quædam informatio. Inde illa Legis & Euangelij indiscreta acceptio: quasi aut Euangelium lex quædam, sed magis spiritualis effet, aut noua quæda salutis obtinendæ ratio, quasi Lex vnos Iudæos spectaret. Denique vel vnum istud caput de recto intellectu & vsus & differentiæ Legis & Euangelij minus dextre perceptum iam ab initio, totam rem Ecclesię ita permiscuit, vt vix vnquam deinde quid omnino sibi vellet Christi Domini nomen, & quousque illud porrigeretur, neq; in doctrina neq; in ritibus Ecclesię satis attéderetur. Quoniā enim Euangelij luce vetus hominum [?] primùm impetebatur, in eo fere capite non pauci acquiescebant, vt Christianum nomen [?] profligaret, ac proinde Christus Dominus vnus verus Deus auctor melioris vitę per suam resurrectionem & adito propter illam Martyrio prædicaretur. Alij paulo vlterius progressi, non tantum imitandum sibi in cruce subeunda pro veritatis testimonio Christi exemplum statuebant, sed etiam vt auctorem omnis gratię in sua per Baptismum innouatione & sanctificatione agnoscebant.
units.tr: As for that first age, which we mainly attribute to the Apostles, we acknowledge from the testimony of truth itself that nothing there was not most pure and most vigorous. The preaching of the Word, by which the knowledge of Christ is handed down, sounded forth as if from Christ's own mouth through those outstanding instruments of his, and the whole administration of the Church bore fitting witness to its spiritual renewal and, as it were, its liberation from the yoke of the Law. Yet, although I can hardly determine what order or method of teaching and acting was observed in the Apostles' ministry, since in such beginnings occasions and circumstances do not always bring the same results, and although many suppose that certain first principles of faith, as cited in Hebrews 6, were only taken up at first, I do not doubt that from the very beginning a twofold form of teaching was observed. One was directed to those being initiated; the other was for feeding adults in the faith and confirming them more and more, which the Apostle notes in 1 Thessalonians 3, when he says: "that we might supply what is lacking in your faith." I am persuaded that the substance of all this was customarily drawn from the Scriptures and referred to the benefit of Christ as its goal, and that it was set out in accordance with the analogy of faith, with Baptism and the Supper as appendages of the faith, and with other such things. But as for what was to be done, urged, or tolerated, publicly or privately, the Church left these matters to its prudence, so that that spiritual liberty, inseparable from the benefit of Christ, was always maintained and asserted, with the exercise of charity for the building up of all. Yet here too it must not be passed over that one can hardly hope the Church will ever be entirely free of this: on more than one occasion that most happy education of the Church under the ministry of the Apostles did not proceed so smoothly that, at almost the same moment, the beginnings of evils introduced by Satan did not also appear, which afterwards disturbed the very foundations of the knowledge of Christ, since the best men were not sufficiently attentive to the work of the Lord. For Satan saw how things stood: that the work of the Lord could not be harmed more surely or more seriously than if he misused the very occasion of that work from its very beginnings to attempt it. Yet whatever arose in this way does not detract in any degree from the most upright faith and labour of the Apostles; rather, those remarkable lights of the Holy Spirit shine all the more purely, when we maintain that the light offered by them was not received in the way it ought to have been and was not turned to its proper use. From this, then, we must form our judgement of the remaining ages of the Church. For the Church could never have been in a better state than under the Apostles themselves, bathed in that incomparable gift of the Spirit, bearing on all sides the light of most certain truth, and retaining the purest juice and blood of that spiritual generation. We must therefore consider what that first age could already suffer. This cannot be inquired into more conveniently than if we cling to that one knowledge of Christ, in which we have laid down that the prow and stern of the Church's state truly rest from the beginning. The knowledge of Christ comprehends chiefly two things. One is who Christ is in himself; the other is what he is for us. The first embraces the personal union of the divine and human natures; the second embraces the office or benefit of the person who is Christ towards the Church; and, in sum, that he is shown to be the Saviour who is both named and believed to be such, and to have been able to do so much and to have truly accomplished it. For the debt of human nature, guilty in Adam before God, could not be paid except by an equivalent that was otherwise not owed. And according to God's promise there came forth Jesus Christ, that Son of God, God and Man, who, sent by God the Father into the world as one fit to perform this task fully, carried through in himself the whole business of our salvation in the name of all his own. There is also that one mystery of Christ, in which, when it is set forth, the whole Apostolic teaching is contained by name, since in this one thing the life of the Church is entirely comprehended, if it is rightly understood as it should be; and conversely, the health of the Church cannot stand if that same mystery is in any way obscured, let alone shamefully buried, as in the end has happened. Therefore, as regards the truth concerning the person of Christ and the natures existing in him, Satan from the beginning set in motion every device he could, so as to overturn it, whether through false Christians from among the Jews or through any others whatever. Yet because the matter was too plain in itself for any truly pious person to be ignorant of it in those times, Satan accomplished nothing that did not in the end turn to the greater good of the Church. For those monstrous minds who impiously talked about the natures or the person of Christ, or even about the three persons subsisting in the one God, raving beyond the Word of God as if with reason, were exposed without difficulty, and their damnable blasphemies were condemned; and the faith and reverence of the godly in handling sacred things were all the more confirmed. Thus that hostile assault purged the City of God of its faithless citizens, and by that occasion commended the true and upright all the more. All this is aptly comprehended in Augustine's book On Heresies and the commentary added to it. Yet Satan did not rest content with waging war on the truth through those open heresiarchs alone, since he perceived that they were resisted so vigorously. Rather, as if nothing else were to be feared from elsewhere by the Church, while it was distracted for the most part by the assertion of doctrines that were by far the chief in themselves, meanwhile on more than one occasion he so attacked its very heart that, as if doing something else, he turned away from the clear and exact perception and sincere profession of the mystery of Christ even those godly who were thinking of nothing less. Indeed, this matter does not now need a long demonstration, since the Apostolic Scriptures themselves cry this out, as with one voice. For the Church, first educated in the synagogue and then beginning to be brought over to the Gentiles, was so rarely possessed of that spiritual prudence and moderation in most people, which saw well enough what should be tolerated or pardoned, and what, and to what end, and by whom, and for how long, that even the best men's eyes grew dim in these matters. Thus the union of Gentiles with Jews in the Church under the name of Christ experienced its difficulties from crafty workers, so that the Apostles themselves were scarcely heard by this party or that, while they laboured to bring about a unity among all, always recalling them to acknowledge Christ and holding them fast in him. As for the Gentiles in particular, it is clear from several passages in the first Epistle to the Corinthians, and from Revelation 2 and 3 by name, that there were also unhappy beginnings of scandals there, which in many places took root with carelessness and conceit, and which, however much the Spirit of the Lord interceded through the Apostles, were choking the plant as it sprang up. Now, the most certain proofs of this chief occasion we have noted, of that by far greatest evil creeping into the Church through an illegitimate and not native knowledge of Christ the Lord, can be gathered (as we have said) from the constant testimonies of the Apostles. For nearly all of them have this one purpose: to set forth the truth about the benefit of Christ against importunate men and most wicked seducers, who, while attributing everything to the name of Christ, in fact fastened men either to themselves or to the rites of the fading pedagogy of the Law. The Epistle to the Galatians is a constant witness, and so is a good part of the second chapter of the Epistle to the Colossians. Above all, this whole matter can be most aptly noted, as if brought before the tribunal of the Spirit of Christ by all the Apostles together, in those few words of that most well-known passage of the Acts of the Apostles: "Certain men who went out from us troubled you, unsettling your souls, bidding you be circumcised and keep the Law, TO WHOM WE HAD NOT GIVEN SUCH COMMAND" (Acts 15). Thus those false messengers were already then pressing in, and as far as they could they smothered the light and benefit of Christ throughout the churches. Hence, as we have also said, the age to come after the Apostles would contract that weakness which at last overthrew the Church, even without any external assault, from within itself. For what knowledge of Christ is that, where what comes from him to the Church is for the most part unknown? It will be worthwhile to illustrate this by a few examples, so that the weight of that indigestion of the living milk, which swelled up at the very beginnings of the Church, may be more clearly marked and carried on to the later ages. Now, although the articles of faith, as they are called, were rightly understood and proclaimed in all the churches, it was far from being the case that the use of that incomparable Creed, as the Apostles had taught it, was fittingly known to very many. Baptism, by which men were incorporated into the assembly of the Church under the name of Christ, was already being referred to this end: men judged that by that washing, when they were cleansed of all sins committed before, they had attained a full and exact sanctification by the Spirit (which was only begun), and the renewal flowing from it. They so interpreted the sacrament of the benefit of Christ that they either did not know or confused the very benefit of Christ itself. For the washing received in Baptism does not have the sense of a perpetual cleansing of all defilements, as if nothing remained in the baptized that was unrenewed and unsanctified; rather, it does so insofar as the sprinkling of Christ's blood wipes away, as far as guilt is concerned, all the stains of the baptized in faith, and at the same time implants the hidden seed of sanctification, which in its own time and manner attests and puts forth its strength in his members by the Spirit of Christ. There was also joined to this another mist of ignorance, which would help to foster it. For few paid attention to what that stain of original sin was, and how deep its hidden recesses were, either before or even after Baptism. Hence came that consideration and description of the two states of each man, namely without Christ and in Christ, twisted by the words flesh and spirit into a human sense: as if "flesh" designated not the whole man as the offspring of Adam, but only the depraved affections; and "spirit" not the whole inward man, quickened as it were into a new life by the Spirit of Christ, but reason and understanding, as the noblest part of man. These notions seemed new even to the Jews, and absurd to the Greeks, by the common sense and judgement of all. From this too came that anxious insistence on works in the minds of many, and along with it at once a more exacting rule of life, more withdrawn from marriage and the other uses of life, as if it were in itself more acceptable to God. From this too came a certain social form of life, especially in Egypt, as if under the name of that disciple of Peter, Mark, drawn from the example of the Apostles. From this came that indiscriminate reception of Law and Gospel: as if the Gospel were a kind of law, only more spiritual, or a new way of obtaining salvation, as if the Law concerned only the Jews. Finally, that one head, the right understanding and use and difference of Law and Gospel, grasped too poorly from the beginning, so confused the whole matter of the Church that afterwards it was hardly ever sufficiently considered, either in doctrine or in the rites of the Church, what the name of Christ the Lord truly meant and how far it extended. For since men of the old kind were first assailed by the light of the Gospel, not a few in that chief point rested content to overthrow the Christian name, and so Christ the Lord was proclaimed as the one true God, the author of a better life through his resurrection and, on account of it, through martyrdom. Others, going a little further, not only set up Christ's example of undergoing the cross for the witness of truth as one to be imitated, but also acknowledged him as the author of all grace in their own renewal and sanctification through Baptism.

units.la: Paucissimi verò ad summum ipsum Christi agnitionis punctum attendebant, vt perpetua beneficij ipsius & perfectæ erga Patrem obedientiæ imputatio sitientissimo conscientię ore sincera fide semper hauriretur, ad obtinendam apud Deum solidam & gratuitam iustificatio-nem. Denique quid in fide quid in operibus po-situm esset,quæ fidei vis,quæ origo,quis operū vsus & scopus promiscuè plurimum, non autē enucleatè,plerique expendebant. Quōd autem ad ritus etiam attinet, quànuis ea tum simplici-tas & sobrietas usurparetur quæ Apostolicam ingenuitatem satis referret, neque tamen ea in parte satis commodè etiam exemplum Apo-stolorum à Domini ipsius institutione ductum obseruabatur. Quia enim in Cœna Domini mentio fiebat sacrificij corporis, Ipsius pro nobis omnibus oblati semel, ut illius deindè communicatio atque perceptio pios omnes in tanti beneficij prædicatione exerceret, videri iam tum etiam potuit inesse actioni illi Cœnæ Domini species quædam augustæ oblationis. quia item communicatio ipsa corporis Christi in panis illius fractione arcani aliquid habe-bat quod sola fide caperetur, affixa est etiam impensa quædam reuerentia tum ipsis Symbo-lis in scse, tum illi etiam actioni quæ etiam my-steriorum nomine donata fuit, parum fortasse oportune.quia deniq; in ipsa illa actione Chri-stus Dominus panem manibus tenens ita gra-tias Patri egerat, creditum est fere iam tum e-tiam in illa agendi ratione subesse & confecta-tionis alicuius realis argumentum, & oblatio-nis quoque exemplum. Contulit & ad illam o-pinionem non parum consuetudo illorum tem-porum, quum ad mensam Ecclesiæ quisque mu-nera illa offerret, quę gratiarum actionem erga Deum, charitatem & communionem erga proximos testarentur. ex quibus etiam panis & vinum secernebantur in vsum Cœnæ Domini. quæ ergo propter illa munera concipiebantur benedictiones ad Deum, iam aliquē ad Cœnæ Domini pro sacrificio peculiari habendæ gradum faciebant.quanuis omnia istiusmodi initio vix in sese periculosa haberetur.Tanti momenti est non tantùm quid & à quibus, sed quæ etiam mente & consilio fiat factúmve sit scriò expendere.Hinc enim illa deinde Traditionum indigesta moles sub Apostolorum nomine bona quam vocant fide sensim irrepsit, cuius cùm certa fundamenta neque ex Apostolorum scriptis neque ex vllo vsu qui illorum prouidentissimam mentem referat colligi possint, tamen antiquitatis nomine sacrosanctæ habentur. Notari potest & vnum vel alterum exemplum simile superiori in eo, quòd quæ fiebant ab Apostolis, non vti par erat ex illorum intentione deinde ab alijs vsurpata sint.Vnctionis vsum ergà ægrotos Apostolicum fuisse satis constat:quorsum illud?Nempe vt testimonium esset virtutis & gratiæ Christi etiam erga ipsa corpora, ex quo præcipua illa Christi vnctio spiritualis erga animas commendaretur (& tamen plerosque simplici tactu ab Apostolis sanatos esse constat.) Factum est & inde præpostere vt vnctio quoque ad omnia illa applicaretur,in quibus gratia & virtus spiritus Christi requireretur, vt verbi gratia, in baptismo vel post baptismum catechumenorum, in ordinationibus etiam ministrorum Ecclesiæ.& tandem nullus vnctionum finis. In Baptismo quidem adultorum nominatim, vti tunc plurimum fiebat, aliquot interrogationes fieri solebant & abrenunciationes requirebantur; non illæ quidem fine suo vsu & fructu: sed quod ad nouas cerimonias attinet, humano affectu vt & iudicio inuectas fuisse probabilius multo est. Fit quidè oleo curatorum mentio etiam à Tertulliano: sed vt neque rei promiscuæ & iam tum recscentis.
units.tr: Very few, however, attended to the chief point of the knowledge of Christ: that his benefit and his perfect obedience toward the Father are perpetually imputed to us, and that the thirsty mouth of the conscience should always drink this in with sincere faith, so as to obtain a solid and free justification before God. Finally, most people considered in a confused way, rather than clearly unfolding, what lay in faith and what in works, what the power of faith was, its origin, and what the use and aim of works were. As for rites, although at that time a simplicity and sobriety were practised which fairly reflected apostolic plainness, in this respect the example of the Apostles, drawn from the Lord's own institution, was not observed well enough. For because mention was made in the Lord's Supper of the sacrifice of his body, offered once for all for us all, so that the communion and reception of it might then exercise all the godly in proclaiming so great a benefit, it could already seem that a certain appearance of solemn oblation attached to that action of the Lord's Supper. Also, because the communion of Christ's body in the breaking of that bread had something secret which is grasped by faith alone, a certain reverence was attached, perhaps not very fittingly, both to the symbols themselves and to that action, which was even given the name of mysteries. Finally, because Christ the Lord, holding the bread in his hands, gave thanks to the Father in that very action, it was then believed, almost, that such a manner of acting contained a hint of some real consecration and also an example of offering. The custom of those times contributed no little to that opinion: when each person brought to the table of the Church those gifts which bore witness to thanksgiving to God, to love and to fellowship with neighbours, and from which bread and wine were set apart for use in the Lord's Supper. So the blessings pronounced to God over those gifts already brought someone a step toward regarding the Lord's Supper as having a peculiar sacrificial character, although at the beginning all such things were hardly thought dangerous in themselves. It is of great importance to weigh seriously not only what is done and by whom, but also with what mind and purpose it is done. For from this there then crept in gradually, under the name of the Apostles and in what they call good faith, that shapeless mass of traditions. Although no sure foundations for these can be gathered either from the writings of the Apostles or from any practice that reflects their most provident mind, they are nevertheless held sacrosanct in the name of antiquity. It may also be noted that one or two examples similar to the above show that what the Apostles did was afterwards taken up by others, but not as was fitting according to their intention. The Apostolic use of anointing the sick is quite certain. To what end was it? Namely, that it might be a testimony to the power and grace of Christ even toward the bodies themselves, by which that chief spiritual anointing of Christ toward souls was commended (and yet it is certain that the Apostles healed most people by a simple touch). From this it also came about, absurdly, that anointing was applied to all those things in which the grace and power of Christ's Spirit were thought to be required: for example, in baptism, or after the baptism of catechumens, and even in the ordination of ministers of the Church. In the end there was no limit to anointings. In the baptism of adults, indeed, as was then very commonly done, some questions were usually asked and renunciations required. These were not without their own use and fruit, but as for the new ceremonies, it is much more probable that they were introduced by human feeling and judgement. Mention is indeed made of the oil of the healed by Tertullian, but it is not clear that this was already then a settled and common practice.

units.la: Alterum etiam notari potest quod ad ordinem Ecclesiæ spectat, nempe quod ab exemplo quoque Apostolorum non à sensu ductum sit.
units.tr: Another point may also be noted concerning the order of the Church: namely, that it was not derived from the example of the Apostles but from human feeling.

units.la: Solebant omnino sancti illi viri in cœtu Ecclesiæ honorem aliquem vel seniori habere, vel alicui alteri, qui idonea occasione inter fratres quasi primarius sederet: quod Petro etiam deferri potuisse nolim in dubium reuocare.
units.tr: Those holy men were accustomed, in the assembly of the Church, to give some honour either to an elder or to some other person who, on a suitable occasion, sat as it were foremost among the brothers. I would not wish to call into doubt that such deference might have been paid even to Peter.

units.la: Nam & ratio omnino postulat, vt in communi cœtu aliquis vel sua vice vel alio quouis ordine præsidcat, dūmodo ordo istiusmodi nullam gradum inter æquales & plane collegas, differentiam inuehat. Factum hinc igitur vt nomen Episcopi eo sensu irrepserit per multas Ecclesias, quasi Episcopus perpetuus aliquis ordinandus esset, qui reliquis compresbyteris excelleret & superior haberetur. Hoc vero Apostolicum nõ esse,tum eorum exemplo, tum doctrina constat.
units.tr: For reason itself requires that in a common assembly someone preside, either in turn or by some other arrangement, provided such an arrangement introduces no distinction of rank among equals who are plainly colleagues. Hence it came about that the name of bishop crept in, in that sense, through many churches, as if a perpetual bishop were to be ordained who would excel the other elders and be regarded as superior. That this is not apostolic is clear both from their example and from their teaching.

units.la: Primatus vero Romanæ sedis Petri nomini & apostolatui accensus, nescio qua credulitate quasi in cœlum sublatus est iam olim, quanuis non illa tum quidem impotentia & ambitione, quæ paulo post in plerisque retecta est. Et fortasse occasionem illi opinioni dedit, quòd pro illo tempore Hierosolyma cuersa prorsus, Ecclesia[?] Christi alteram sedem in urbe imperij pri-maria & quasi altera Hierosolyma, scilicet, inuenisset. Sunto igitur pauca de multis exempla interuersę Ecclesię educationis siue in doctrina siue in ritibus: ex quibus iterum hoc statuatur, sementem videlicet ab ipsis initiis submissam inde esse, quæ zizania cum vero frumento ede-ret.ac proinde quanuis ad ultimum usque diem ista rerum confusio iam diu producta duratura videtur ex Domini ipsius admonitione, non esse tamen ad illam stertendum[?] quasi ad caligi-nem ex spissitudine tot sæculorum Ecclesiæ ob ductam. Manent igitur ista ex totius istius ætatis disquisitione firmata: Apostolorum nempe studium, fidem & sapientiam verè cœlestem omnino in Ecclesia instituenda & quodammodo parturienda certissimè constitisse: extitisse item illius hunc fructum singularem, quod veri Dei agnitio & Christi Domini melioris vitæ autoris prædicatio orbem terrarum quodammodo innouarit. Reliqua vero quæ verè tum Christi beneficium, tum illius percipiendi rationem spectarunt, nō eadem attentione percepta iam tum qua decebat: incidisse item eiusmodi tempora, quę bonos viros in parte veritatis afferenda occupatos, humanis iam morbis implicaret, unde tandem Ecclesia tanto plus detrimenti caperet, quanto res eæ temporis tractu profundius radices egerunt. In genere enim veritas illa Dei quæ nouissimis sæculis ab ipso Christo palam est tradita, ita omnibus hominum mentibus superior est, si intus non autem in cute tantum inquiratur, ut vixullo sęculo liquidò in suis partibus praecipuis ferio agnita fuerit. Semper enim quod Dei est humano more accipitur.
units.tr: The primacy of the Roman see, attached to the name and apostleship of Peter, was lifted up to heaven long ago by I know not what credulity, although not then with that impotence and ambition which were uncovered in many a little later. Perhaps what gave occasion to that opinion was that, Jerusalem having by then been wholly overthrown, the Church of Christ had found another seat in the chief city of the empire, as it were a second Jerusalem. Let a few examples out of many be set down here of the corrupted education of the Church, whether in doctrine or in rites. From these it is again established that the seed which would produce tares along with the true wheat was sown from the very beginnings. Therefore, although this confusion of things, long since produced, seems likely to last until the last day, according to the Lord's own warning, we should not drowse over it as if in a darkness caused by the thickness of so many centuries. These things therefore remain established by the whole investigation of that age: that the zeal, faith and truly heavenly wisdom of the Apostles were certainly employed in founding the Church and in a way bringing it to birth; and that this was its singular fruit, that the knowledge of the true God and the proclamation of Christ the Lord, author of a better life, in some sense renewed the world. But the rest, which truly concerned both Christ's benefit and the manner of receiving it, was not then perceived with the attention it deserved. Such times also befell as occupied good men in setting forth part of the truth while entangling them in human diseases, whence the Church at last suffered all the more harm, the more deeply those things took root over the course of time. For in general that truth of God which in the last ages was openly delivered by Christ himself so far surpasses all human minds, if it is sought within and not merely on the surface, that in no age has it been clearly and seriously recognised in its chief parts. For what belongs to God is always received in a human manner.

units.la: Quumque doctrina de Christo homini suam perpetuo nuditatem improperet, ut unâ sibi in Christo iustitiâ, sapietiam, sanctificationem, re-demptionem oblatam amplestatur, quid hoc valeat & quousque pervadat non modo rarissime cogitatum est semper, sed qui ab eo longissime discessit, modo ne contra ferri videretur, maxime à sapientia ac iustitia humana apud homines est comedatus. Atque hoc ita se habuisse subsequuta deinde quae nos ad se vocant facula ostenderunt:quę quidè non ita degenerassent à pietatis notitia solida & simplici ad tot extra-neas novitates, nisi exsucceum illud primae aetatis lac habuissent. Sic igitur Domino visum est apud gentes & populos solem illũ Christi Do-mini retegere, ut simul etiam suos non uno mo-do humiliaret, & ut Mysterio iniquitatis quod iam tũ interi incipiebat, ianua panderetur, quod nostra hæc, nouissimorum nouissima sæcula in cœlũ ysque os ponentia testatur. Et de illa qui-dem prima ætate hactenus. Quæ enim extra A-postolorum scripta apud hos vel illos auctores de temporibus Apostolorum leguntur, illa ita partim fabulosa sunt, partim etiam implicita, ut fere iam tum cum executu Apostolorum tene-brae rediisse videantur, & quiduis credi coepisse in multis Ecclesiae rebus.
units.tr: Since the doctrine of Christ constantly reproaches man with his own nakedness, so that he embraces in Christ alone the righteousness, wisdom, sanctification and redemption offered to him, what this means and how far it reaches has not only been very rarely considered, but whoever has departed furthest from it has been most readily embraced among men by human wisdom and righteousness, provided only that he did not seem to be carried against it. That this was so, the later events which call us to themselves show. These would not have degenerated so far from the solid and simple knowledge of piety into so many strange novelties, unless they had had that sour milk of the first age. Thus it seemed good to the Lord to uncover that sun of Christ the Lord among the nations and peoples, so that at the same time he might humble his own in more than one way, and so that the door might be opened to the mystery of iniquity, which was already then beginning to work within. This our own age, the last of the last ages, reaching up to heaven, bears witness. Concerning that first age, so far. For what is read about the times of the Apostles in the writings of this or that author outside the Apostolic writings is partly fabulous and partly so obscure that, almost as soon as the Apostles had departed, darkness seems to have returned, and people began to believe almost anything in many matters of the Church.

units.la: Ætas secunda primae equidem ita respondit, ut quae ab illa integra acceperat, optima fide & incoparabili zelo adversus cruentissimas mul-torum annorum perfequutiones constanter afferucrit ; quæ secus, in illis bonam fidem nimis simpliciter agnouerit, ac nihil in melius in usu doctrinæ vel Sacramentorum reformarit. Sic & veram de Deo uno doctrinam adversus totius orbis tum πολυθεΐαν τῆ εἰδωλολατρίαν [?] latissime propagauit: & tum Hæreticos, tum eorum patriarchas Philosophos de Deo & de Christo impie sentientes præsentissimo veritatis clypeo excepit: & denique quod potuit, & plusquam potuit adulta ista Ecclesiæ ætas laudatissime præstitit. Unum illud maxime isti ætati nocuit, quod dum non satis attendit quid vere Apostolicum a suis patribus haberet, humanos potius sensus & di-uerticula humanæ sapientiæ sensim captare cœpit. Atque ea occasione abusus est Satan nomi-natim, ut quum istorum fidem atq; zelum frustra contentis persecutionibus tentaret, eorundem infirmitatem & simplicitatem quandam in beneficij Christi doctrina non ita exacte perscrutanda aleret ac foueret. Ritus autem & ceremonias quasdam hæc quoque ætas nimis cupide amplexa est. Accidit vero hoc totum isto sæculo tanto incommodius, quanto & a summa integritate, & a cognatione quadam cum Apostolico isto superiore commendatius fuit. Quæ-cunque enim tum vel primum enata, vel latius propagata sunt illius generis, quæ ad simplicitatem & ingenuitatem illam Christianissimi obscurandam faciebant, illa omnia ab ætate infecu-ta deinde pro summa qua istam prosequebatur reuerentia, tanquam mere Apostolica, ac nihil minus quam quod erant humanæ metis fœtus, habita sunt, & pro talibus ad posteros omnes sine ulla exceptione transmissa. Quod igitur ad illam partem doctrinæ attinet quæ ista ætate aperte adhuc oppugnabatur tum ab Hæreticis, tum ab aliis plane extraneis hostibus, eluxit omnino singulare tum etiam Christi donum in afferendis ab Ecclesia ex Scriptura dogmatis fidei & disciplinæ quoque vigore sincere & enucleate. Et qui à sanctis viris tū impensus est labor, toti Ecclesiæ magno usui fuit, erítque semper vel ad illa ipsa quæ indignè deinde scriptis illorum adsuta sunt, conuincenda. Sed tamen si quis attente consideret, plane reperiet duo quædam in illis etiam merito desiderari. Magna enim linguarum ignorantia tum ita bonos viros torquebat, vt in plena luce plerumque palparét: quod malum etiam deinceps creuit in dies ad nostra usque tempora. Interea vero ista etiam [?]ætas suis spiritualibus donis non prorsus destitu-ta, illis etiam plus quàm par esset acquierit, dum verae Scripturæ tractationi minus serio incumbit: unde perpetuum Ecclesiæ detrimentum.
units.tr: The second age indeed answered the first in such a way that what it had received whole from it, it preserved with the best faith and incomparable zeal through the most bloody persecutions of many years. In other matters, however, it accepted good faith too simply and reformed nothing for the better in the use of doctrine or the sacraments. So too it widely spread the true doctrine of the one God against the polytheism and idolatry of the whole world [πολυθεΐαν καὶ εἰδωλολατρίαν]. It met the heretics, and their patriarchs the philosophers, who thought impiously about God and Christ, with the most ready shield of truth. Finally, it accomplished, most praiseworthily, whatever it could, and more than it could, as the mature age of the Church. One thing above all harmed that age: while it did not sufficiently attend to what was truly apostolic in what it had from its fathers, it gradually began to seek out human sentiments and the byways of human wisdom. Satan took advantage of this opportunity by name. When he tried in vain to wear down their faith and zeal with persecutions, he nurtured and fostered their weakness and a certain simplicity in not examining the doctrine of Christ's benefit too exactly. This age also embraced certain rites and ceremonies too eagerly. This happened the more harmfully in that century, because it was the more commendable for its great integrity and its kinship with the earlier apostolic age. For whatever of that kind arose or spread more widely then, which tended to obscure that most Christian simplicity and sincerity, all of it was held by the following ages, out of the great reverence with which they pursued that one, as purely apostolic and by no means what it was, the offspring of human minds. So it was handed down to all posterity without exception. As for that part of doctrine which at that time was still openly attacked, both by heretics and by other entirely foreign enemies, there shone forth a singular gift of Christ: the Church drew from Scripture, sincerely and clearly, the dogmas of faith and also the vigour of discipline. The labour which those holy men then undertook was of great use to the whole Church, and will always be useful for refuting even those things which were later unworthily stitched onto their writings. Yet if anyone considers carefully, he will plainly find that two things are rightly to be missed in them as well. For great ignorance of languages so troubled those good men that they mostly groped about in full light, and this evil grew day by day down to our own times. Meanwhile that age, not altogether lacking in spiritual gifts, also acquired more of them than was fitting, while it applied itself less seriously to the true handling of Scripture. Hence came perpetual loss to the Church.

units.la: Nam & melius plerunque dicunt quàm probet, dum scripturas minus dextrè accipiunt: & quod ab illis optimè dicitur, ita quidem traditur, vt ferè quid tenendum sit vel secus tractasse contenti, cur hoc ita tenendum sit omittant, id est artè magis quàm vsum artis persequantur. Atqui in Ecclesia omnia ad vsum referenda sunt. Videamus igitur quid ista ætas humani passa sit, & quibus occasionibus, & quo etiam euentu. Quū [?]igitur non voce scripturæ tantum, sed ipso corporis muro obiecto, id est vita vero impensa, Christianis passim desertandum esset aducersus recrudescentes subinde persequutiones, fa-ctum est inde vt laudatissima Martyrij aditio pro summo & fere singularis Euangelij scopo iudicaretur, & tantumnon ambiretur. Quum etiam aduersus Philosophos consistendum esset, qui simplicitati veritatis contumeliosè pro suo ingenio insultarent, non raro optimi Dei servi ita se contorserunt, vt illorum artes euaderet, vt magis ex ipsorum scriptis, quam ex scripturae sensu decertarent. Hoc autem non inconsulte catenus, vt suo ipsos gladio iugularent. Sed quoniam ipsa intus Ecclesia toto veritatis Christi pabulo reficienda erat, vt & micae ipsae ad extraneos peruenirent, vix vere de Christi beneficio perpetua vita sibi cuique in Ecclesia appli-cando reliquiae tum appositè apponebantur.
units.tr: For they often say better than they prove, since they take up the Scriptures less skilfully. What is said well by them is handed down in such a way that they are content, for the most part, to have treated what must be held, or otherwise, and they omit why it must be held thus; that is, they pursue the art more than the practical use of the art. Yet in the Church everything must be referred to use. Let us see, therefore, what this age suffered at human hands, on what occasions, and with what outcome. Since Christians had to defend themselves everywhere, not only with the voice of Scripture but with the very wall of the body set before them, that is, by devoting their lives, against persecutions that broke out again from time to time, it came about that the most praiseworthy eagerness for martyrdom was judged the highest and nearly the only aim of the Gospel, and was almost courted. Since they also had to stand against the philosophers, who insulted the simplicity of the truth contemptuously according to their own cleverness, the best servants of God often twisted themselves so as to escape those arts, and contended more from the philosophers' own writings than from the sense of Scripture. This was not unwise, so far as it went, since it struck them down with their own sword. But since the Church itself within had to be fed with the whole food of Christ's truth, so that even the crumbs might reach outsiders, scarcely any remnants were then fittingly set before each person within the Church, to apply the benefit of Christ to his own perpetual life.

units.la: Denique Ecclesia tota externis hostibus vexata, internam inediam minus agnouit, aut my-steriis, vti iam instituta esse poterant, suas angustias sustinuit ex parte, aut sub Christianismi titulo palpitantem adhuc Iudaismum in quibus-dam retinuit, neque a Paganismo ad Christia-nismum inflexo in omnibus abhorruit. Scripturae porro sensum & usum per allegorias euagando mirum in modum ornari a se plerique post Origenē & ante illum, tum sibi, tum aliis, persuaserunt.
units.tr: Finally, the whole Church, harassed by external enemies, paid less heed to its inner hunger. It endured its own straits partly by mysteries, as they could already be arranged, and under the title of Christianity it retained in some respects a Judaism still fluttering, and it did not shrink from what had been turned from Paganism to Christianity in all respects. Moreover, many after Origen, and before him, persuaded both themselves and others that the sense and use of Scripture were wonderfully adorned by wandering into allegories.

units.la: Glisccebat & illis temporibus speciosa illa [?]τῆς ἀ-ναγωγῆς opinio, maxime propter incubentes Ecclesiae tepestates, coiugali interea castitate quasi inferiori à continentia loco habenda. fit.n.metio istiusmodi exemplorum apud mulieres & virgines Christianas multis locis extantiu[?]: quod ad monachos autem attinet tum re tum nomine, praeter anaanachoretas & solitarios quosdam Ægypti, vix scio an vlla tum virorū examina eiusmodi coe-perint: & magis sub aetatis frequentis initiū istos nidificasse probarim: tantum pastores plerique quos Episcopos & Presbyteros vocabant,iam a vita coniugali pede ita referebat, vt fere in mo-res hoc abiret. Sed nec mulieres ipsæ vel vir-gines ita continentiam affectabant, vt nodum plane stringerent vti deinde accidit:nec domos parentum ea occasione relinquebant: adeo vt minus mali illic fuisse, immo & non parum sæpe virtutis & pietatis videri posit. Attamen in genere omnis illa vitæ informatio, quæ quanuis Dei cultus speciem extra Dei vocationem & Christi gratiæ fidem quærit aut constituit, non potest diu cum beneficij Christi agnitione con-sistere. Sed quemadmodū Similæ amant suos ca-tulos, ita etiam quæ minimi verè in pietatis pro sessione facienda sunt, quia tamen ab humani sensus fundo prodeunt, omnes passim in sui ad-mirationem, plerosque ad æmulationē rapiunt. Quasi vero satis Christianus non esset, qui & in in Christi beneficio salutis omne ratione ponē-ret, atque ita cum sua infirmitate seriō ac per-petuo ex Domini virtute & vocatione lucta-retur. Doctrina denique verae fidei & verorum operum non certo aliquo examine ab Euange-lio petito, sed vt res ferebant recto studio tra-ctabatur. Abstetio item a promiscuis cibis, ob-seruatio quoque memoriae præcipuorū Domi-ni ad salutem nostram operum statis præter die Dominicum diebus huic aetati placere coepit, quum tamen istiusmodi ἐθελοθρησκείας [?] in herba iam anté Apostolus enecasset. Signaculum porro Crucis Christi in mysteriis quæ vocabant, & nominis Christi promiscua vsurpatio ad ipsius vim erga infideles afferendam ita passim in vsu fuit, vt summa quædam Christianæ professionis illic sita crederetur. Atqui prædicatio crucis & beneficii tanti in illa à Christo Domino hominibus consignati, illa sunt verè quibus & crucis & Christi mentio applicanda est: neque sine periculo vnum absque altero proponitur. Adeo enim similis sui manet semper Satan, vt modò ne ita illum vrgeat viua illa Christi prædicati expressio in ministerio verbi, omnia vel ipse primus signis & verbis inanibus quasi ad illa cohorrescens tribuere se fingat: quod sane nō pau cis iam olim imposuit, quorum exempla nullo iudicio nunc ab aduersariis repetuntur. Mortuorum item pro Christi nomine commemoratio in coetu Ecclesiæ hoc sæculo eam venerationē adiunctam habuit, quæ non ita multum iam ab inuocatione, quam & deinde peperit, distaret.
units.tr: In those times also the attractive notion of the mystical [τῆς ἀναγωγῆς] grew strong, chiefly because of the storms that beset the Church, while conjugal chastity was meanwhile to be regarded as of lower rank than continence. There are many examples of this kind extant among Christian women and virgins. As for monks, in fact and in name, apart from some anchorites and solitaries of Egypt, I scarcely know whether any such assemblies of men had begun to form at that time; and I would prove that they nested rather at the beginning of the more frequent age. Only the many pastors whom they called bishops and presbyters were already drawing back from married life, so that this practice almost passed into custom. Yet the women themselves, or the virgins, did not so aspire to continence as to tie a knot wholly, as happened later, nor did they leave their parents' homes on that account; so that it may seem there was less evil there, and indeed often not a little virtue and piety. Nevertheless, in general, that whole way of life which, although it seeks or establishes a semblance of the worship of God outside God's calling and faith in Christ's grace, cannot long remain consistent with the acknowledgment of Christ's benefit. But just as monkeys love their young, so also those things which are truly of least importance in performing piety, since they nonetheless come from the bottom of human feeling, carry everyone off in admiration of themselves and most into emulation. As if a man were not Christian enough, who places all reason of salvation in Christ's benefit, and so struggles earnestly and continually with his own weakness by the power and calling of the Lord! Finally, the doctrine of true faith and of true works was handled not by some fixed test drawn from the Gospel, but as circumstances carried it, with a zeal that was merely correct. Likewise, abstinence from promiscuous foods, and the observance of certain days, besides the Lord's Day, for the memory of the Lord's chief works for our salvation, began to please this age, although the Apostle had already, long before, smothered such self-chosen worship [ἐθελοθρησκείας] while it was still in the blade. Moreover, the sign of the Cross of Christ in the rites they called mysteries, and the indiscriminate use of Christ's name to bring its power to bear upon unbelievers, were so widespread in practice that a kind of summary of Christian profession was believed to lie there. Yet the preaching of the cross and of so great a benefit, sealed to men by Christ the Lord, are truly those by which mention of the cross and of Christ ought to be applied; and one is not set forth without danger apart from the other. Satan always remains so like himself that, lest the living expression of Christ's preaching in the ministry of the word press him too hard, he pretends that he himself first ascribes everything to empty signs and words, as though shrinking from those things. This indeed he imposed long ago on not a few, and examples of it are now repeated by our adversaries without any judgment. Likewise the commemoration of the dead in the name of Christ, in the assembly of the Church in this century, had attached to it such veneration as was not far, by then, from the invocation which it afterwards also brought forth.

units.la: Et quasi satis hoc non esset ad pietatem erga illos testandam, ad ipsorum quoque sepulchra quæ μνημεῖα[?] vocabantur, cœtus Ecclesiæ constituebant: vnde deinde Stationum nomina, & altarium initia. Prima enim in Ecclesiis altaria illa fuisse probabile est, quæ eadem sepulchrorum Martyrum summa erant fastigia: quibus etiam sepulchris tectoria ampliora superducta sunt, quæ & templa Christianorum, & memoriæ Martyrum appellarentur.
