Iam vero quasi de salute ante Baptismum morientium minus constaret, quàmque[?] etiam de illorum qui extra Ecclesiæ commucommunionem positi decesserant, statu labora-retur, inofficiosa quadam pietate & pro his &c pro illis commendationes inuectae sunt, quasi nempe ita nominis Christi veneratio amplifi-caretur, quum ad mortuos vsque non extra spe aliquam salutis, porrigeretur. Opinio vero oblationis cuiusdam, atque eiusdem oblationis effi-cacitatis perinde etiam vires collegit, vnde tan-dem aliquando Sacrificium praesens ex opere operato pro viuis & defunctis obtinuit. In Bap-tismo perinde etiam ceremoniae superadditae sunt, quae etiam totam rei per se sanctissimae commendationem atque pondus deinde sibi vendicarunt. Vnum etiam notari potest ex Tertull. maxime autem ex Cypriano, quod per Ecclesias tum vsitabatur: vt qui quouis scandalo offenderentur Ecclesiam, illi adirent confessores in carcere martyrio devotos, & ab illis pace apud Ecclesiam cum remissione ordinariae ceu surae impetraret. Vnde magnae turbae in Ecclesia iam tum, & sanctorum post mortem interpel-latio insinuata. Vltimo quod ad ordinem pastorum in Ecclesia attinet, & sibi quisque tu Episcopus, quasi altera Christi figura, supra populum & clerum quem vocant, thronum erexit: & Romanus ille Pontifex sibi minime omnium hac in parte defuit. Tum enim imprimis quasi solo egressus caput ad nubila vsque extollere ausus est, maxime in Occidentis partibus: ac nisi a suis collegis vt Irenaeo, Cypriano & aliis in suo ordine retineretur, ne sub persequutionum quidem mole ambitiosam illam cernitem cri-gere difficilet [?]. Nec temere illum ita libro De Pudicitia vellicasse stylo suo censorio Tertulianum credibile est: Pontifex (inquit) Maximus quod Episcopus Episcoporum dixit, Ego Mœchia & Fornicationis funes dimitto, O Edictum cui adscribi non poterit, Bonum Factum. Denique ubi semel hoc receptum est, ut saluo Christianæ veritatis iure quod ad conscientiam & pium animi propositum attinet, quidlibet audere ius fasque sit, non potest tractu temporis non multu damni sanitas Ecclesiæ pati, dum vera agnitio i la[?] Christi tot illis modis internum vigorem & gustum amittit.
units.tr: And as if this were not enough to show their devotion, they also set up assemblies of the Church at the tombs of the saints, which were called memorials [μνημεῖα]. From these came the names of the Stations and the beginnings of altars. It is probable that the first altars in the churches were the highest tops of the martyrs' tombs. Larger roofs were also built over these tombs, and these were called Christian temples and memorials of the martyrs. Then, as if it were uncertain whether those who died before baptism were saved, and as if there were doubt about the state of those who died outside the communion of the Church, commendations for both were introduced out of a misguided piety, as though the veneration of Christ's name would be increased by extending some hope of salvation even to the dead outside the Church. The notion of a certain offering, and of the efficacy of that offering, then gathered strength, until at last the present sacrifice was obtained for the living and the dead by the work worked. Ceremonies were also added to baptism, which in time claimed for themselves the authority and weight that belonged to the thing itself, which is most holy in itself. One thing can also be noted from Tertullian, and especially from Cyprian, as it was then practised throughout the churches: those who had been offended by any scandal would approach the confessors who were devoted to martyrdom in prison, and obtain from them peace with the Church, with the remission of the ordinary satisfaction, as it were. From this, great disturbances in the Church and the intercession of the saints after death were already being introduced. Lastly, as regards the order of ministers in the Church, each man made himself a bishop, as it were another figure of Christ, and set up a throne above the people and the clergy, as they call them. The Roman Pontiff was by no means lacking in this respect. For at first, as if coming out of the ground, he dared to raise his head to the clouds, especially in the parts of the West. And unless his colleagues, such as Irenaeus, Cyprian and others, had held him in his place within his own order, he would hardly have raised that ambitious crest even under the weight of persecutions. Nor is it credible that Tertullian, in his book On Modesty, lightly nipped him with his censorious pen: The Pontiff Maximus, that is, the Bishop of bishops, says: I dismiss the sins of adultery and fornication. O edict to which the words "Well done" cannot be added. Finally, once this had been accepted, namely that, with the right of Christian truth safe as far as conscience and the pious purpose of the mind are concerned, it is lawful and right to dare anything, the health of the Church cannot, over the course of time, avoid suffering much harm, while the true knowledge of Christ loses its inner vigour and savour through so many such means.

units.la: Hæc sunt igitur infirmitatis etiā ætatis istius secundæ testimonia, quæ satis admonebant quam non modò constanter, sed etiam prudenter in cælesti illa Euangelij luce percipienda versari omnes decerent, nisi malum malo cumulatum vellent. Atqui non in eo stetit illa iam Ecclesiæ inclinatio, sed non sine Domini iusto iudicio res eæ ulterius progressæ sunt, ex quibus deinde Catholicismi illa turris pro Euangelica exstrueretur.
units.tr: These, then, are the testimonies of the weakness of that second age, which sufficiently warned that all ought to live not only steadfastly but also wisely in receiving the heavenly light of the Gospel, unless they wished to heap evil upon evil. But that decline of the Church did not stop there. By the just judgment of the Lord, those things went further, and from them the tower of Catholicism was then built in place of the Gospel.

units.la: Tertia igitur ætas ita sese habuit primum, ut quę vel à præcedente acceperat aduersus hæreticos bella pro veritate profligāda, vel etiā recens illata sustinenda, illa eadem insigni pietate & eruditione freta, confecerit. Quum enim undique velut agmine facto portentosa utique ingenia Ecclesiam lacesserent, ut quæ ab externis persecutionibus recreari incipiebat, tato graui* a suis nomine tenus domesticis impeteretur, non defuit tamen operi suo Dominus. Euicit enim Spiritus ipsius in afferenda & Dei gloria, & personæ Christi ac naturarum certissima illa veritate: quum & Ariani funestissimi, & Manichæi nefandi, & Donatistæ plusquam amentes, & alij fere innumeri hinc inde ordines aduersus Ecclesiam ducerent. Quod autem ad illam beneficij Christi agnitionem attinet, ita iam olim res ea à recto intellectu deflexerat, ut vix ipse Pelagius beneficij Christi & omnis ipsius veritatis reipsa aduersarius, pro hęretico haberetur: quasi nimirum philosophia & Christiana doctrina in gratia iam plane rediissent. Siquidem mutato nomine, & mitigatis quibusdam Pelagij asperitatibus, non pauca tum in Ecclesia audiebantur, quæ cum illo facere videretur. Unus tamen extitit Augustinus singulari Domini prouidentia, qui hoc ipsum bellum imprimis tentaret & perageret: quanquam à sui seculi hominibus fortasse ne satis quidem exauditus. An vero & ipse Augustinus Pelagium legitimè oppugnans, nihil pluris etiam sanctificationi per Baptismum oblatæ tribuerit quàm Scriptura doceat, subsisto. Video enim morbum illum ita occupasse Ecclesiam per illa tempora, ut innovationem naturæ hominis in Baptismo, ferè unam, eamque quasi plenam omnino prædicarent. Unde etiam alterum tum malum plurimum obtinuit, nimirum sacramentis ipsis inesse vim illam spiritualem quasi inhærentem, adeò ut qui nō baptizatus excederet, à gloria Dei alienus futurus censeretur: & baptismi valde anxia administratio homines, imprimis recepto illo dogmate torqueret. Græci autem Scriptores & Doctores Ecclesiastici per ista tempora insignes, mirum in modu humanas quas somniabant vi-res extollebat. Haec est enim illa Ecclesię veluti Helena, cuius occasione omnia coflagrare coeperùt. Nempe vbi homo sibi addicitur, & posse per se aliquid iactatur, ne otium intendatur & segnitia, scilicet: quasi vero gratia Christi dex-tre tradita, non omnes hominis partes vna sa-tis ad bonum excitet, in eoque confirmet.
units.tr: The third age, therefore, first conducted itself in such a way that it carried out, relying on the same remarkable piety and learning, the wars against heretics that it had inherited from the previous age, or that had recently been waged and had to be sustained. For when the monstrous minds, as it were in battle array, attacked the Church from every side, the Church, which was beginning to be refreshed after external persecutions, was assailed by its own people, in name at least, with such heavy blows. Yet the Lord did not fail in his work. For his Spirit prevailed in asserting both the glory of God and the most certain truth concerning the person of Christ and his natures, when the most deadly Arians, the wicked Manichaeans, the Donatists, more than mad, and almost countless other orders here and there, led their forces against the Church. As for the recognition of Christ's benefit, the matter had long since so far departed from right understanding that Pelagius himself, who was in fact an opponent of Christ's benefit and of all his truth, was scarcely regarded as a heretic. It was as if philosophy and Christian doctrine had by then altogether returned to grace. Indeed, under a changed name, and with some of Pelagius's harshness softened, not a few things were then heard in the Church that seemed to agree with him. Yet Augustine stood alone, by a singular providence of the Lord, to undertake and carry through this very battle, although he was perhaps not even adequately heard by the men of his own age. I will leave it open whether Augustine himself, in legitimately opposing Pelagius, attributed to the sanctification offered through baptism nothing more than Scripture teaches. For I see that the disease had so seized the Church in those times that they preached almost only one renewal of human nature in baptism, and that a complete one. From this there also arose another great evil of that time, namely that a certain spiritual power was inherent in the sacraments themselves, so that whoever died unbaptized would be judged alien to the glory of God, and the very anxious administration of baptism tormented men, especially given that dogma. The Greek writers and the Church's teachers who were notable in those times extolled, in a remarkable manner, the human powers which they dreamed of. For this is that Helen of the Church, on whose account everything began to burn. Indeed, where man is credited to himself and boasts that he can do something by himself, the idea is that he will not be idle or slothful. As if, forsooth, the grace of Christ, delivered to the right hand, did not stir up all parts of man at once for good and confirm him in it!

units.la: Reliqua porrò illa, quae vt superioris aetatis nguos ante notauimus, ista demum plane Eccle siam ita affecerunt, vt quasi apostolica passim obtinerent. Etenim vix ipsa Coenae Domini institutio simpliciter retinebatur, quum vt sacri ficium corporis Domini passim actio illa com-mendaretur. Scio quidem emolliri hoc ita posse, quia veteres illi plurimum in Coenae Domini celebratione & adnexis illi precibus tribuebat, ideo quasi propitiatorium quiddam illam actionem sępe in omnibus coetibus Ecclesię & mane & vesperi vsurpasse. Sed vtvt se res habuerit, vix quidem video quomodo non crassius multo tum senserint de sacrosancto illo ritu, quam quod vnum Apostolus a Domino accepisse se testatus olim fuerat. Et quod ad elementorum quae & Sacramenta dicta sunt, vsum attineret, sic etiam illorum veneratio aucta est iis temporibus, vt quamuis non aperte diceretur, illa in Mysteriis desinere esse quod erat natura, habentur tamen vt vasa quaedam quibus res ipsae significatae & promissae continerentur. Ex quibus duobus capitibus, ita iam tum inter se im-plicitis operatorium Missae sacrificium, quod Ecclesiam tandem inebriauit, ortum duxisse constat.Et extat in vita Gregorij Romani Papę primi historia quędam iltius infcitię index. Venerat in Ecclesiam ex usu illorum temporum Romę Matrona quędam ad horam cœtus solennis, quę & panem ad mensam Gregorio ut cæterę obtulerat. (hoc autē MISSARVM nomine id est MISSIŌNVM siue muneru, intelligebatur.)
units.tr: The remaining matters, which we noticed earlier as the faults of the former age, at last afflicted the Church so thoroughly that they prevailed everywhere as if they were apostolic. For the very institution of the Lord's Supper was scarcely retained in its simplicity, since that action was everywhere commended as a sacrifice of the body of the Lord. I know that this can be softened by the argument that the ancients attributed great weight to the celebration of the Lord's Supper and to the prayers joined with it, and so often used that action in all the assemblies of the Church, morning and evening, as if it were a kind of propitiatory. But however the matter stood, I can scarcely see how they did not think far more crudely at that time about that most sacred rite than the Apostle, who once testified that he had received only one thing from the Lord. And as regards the use of the elements, which are also called sacraments, their veneration in those times increased to such an extent that, although it was not openly said that those things in the mysteries ceased to be what they were by nature, they were nonetheless regarded as vessels in which the things signified and promised were contained. From these two points, so closely intertwined at that time, it is clear that the operative sacrifice of the Mass arose, which at last intoxicated the Church. And there is extant in the life of Gregory, the first Roman Pope, a certain story that shows that ignorance. In accordance with the custom of those times, a certain Roman matron had come to the Church for a solemn assembly, and she had offered bread at the table to Gregory, as others did. (Here, by the name MISSARUM, that is, of the MISSIONS or offerings, this was understood.)

units.la: Gregorius quum ad Sacramentorum celebrationem ventum eflet, Matronę illi Mysteria traditurus dixerat, Corpus Domini confervet animam tuam: illa subrisit. quod animadvertens Gregorius partem illam Domini corporis super altare deposuit, & actione tandem finita, mulierem coram populo cur risisset interrogauit. Respondit illa tandem, Quia panem quem propriis manibus fecisse me cognoueram, tu corpus Dominicum perhibebas. Hæc erat illorum temporum eruditio, ut quæ sacramentaliter dici accipive commode possent, illa crude prolata aut scandalum parerent, aut horrorem incuterent. Sed tamen illis adhuc sæculis communicatio publica & ordinaria & integra omnium fidelium, non manca & quasi ad terrorem instituta retinebatur: nisi quod res eo sensim vergebat. Et quum quo plus ritibus etiam non pessimo consilio tribuitur, eo magis & prædicationi doctrinæ, & attentioni illius detrahitur, sic omnino ab auribus ad oculos fere omnis Ecclesiæ administratio transferri cœpit: ut iam plusquam Iudaico iugo opprimi Ecclesiam suo tempore queratur Augustinus ille, si quisquam alius, pacis Ecclesiæ supra modū etiā studiosus. In summa autem quod ad numerosos illos ritus attinet quibus Liturgia Ecclesiæ non tam exor-nata est ut creditur (quanquam in eo nouissima ætate statum non fit) quàm plane conspurcata, vnum audiamus apud Caslandrum Rupertum ita quod res est, appositè scilicet, scribentem.
units.tr: When Gregory had come to the celebration of the sacraments, he said to the matron, who was about to receive the mysteries: "May the body of the Lord preserve your soul." She smiled. Gregory noticed this and placed that part of the Lord's body upon the altar. When the action was at last finished, he asked the woman in front of the people why she had laughed. She answered at last: "Because I knew that I had made the bread with my own hands, and you were calling it the body of the Lord." Such was the learning of those times: things that could fittingly be spoken or received in a sacramental sense, when stated crudely, either caused scandal or inspired horror. Yet even in those centuries the public, ordinary and whole communion of all the faithful was still retained, not maimed and instituted as if to terrify, except that the matter was gradually tending that way. And as more and more is attributed to rites, even not wholly bad ones, so much more is taken away from the preaching of doctrine and from attention to it. Thus, in this way, almost the whole administration of the Church began to be transferred from the ears to the eyes. So that Augustine, if anyone, who was excessively eager for the peace of the Church, complains that in his time the Church was oppressed by a yoke more than Jewish. In sum, as regards those numerous rites by which the liturgy of the Church is not so much adorned, as is believed (although in our most recent age there is no change in this), but rather plainly defiled, let us hear one thing from Cassander, and Rupertus, who writes aptly as the matter actually stands.

units.la: Olim, inquit, non tanto exterioris apparatu de-coris Missarū solennia celebrabatur, nec ab vno quolibet hæc omnis religiosi obsequij gloria consummata & perpolita. Et sicut traditum à Domino per Moysem veteris sacrificij ordinem præcipuè Dauid & Solomon Sacerdotū & Leuitarum ministerio, cantorum multiplici numero, Psalmorum diuinorum tripudio, templi vel altaris illustri gloria, sacrorumque multitudine vasorum splendidius amplificauerunt: sic traditum à Domino mirabilem sacrificij ritum per primos Apostolos sancta Romana Ecclesia suscipiens religiosa fide amplexata fideli cura conseruauit, diligenti apparatu exornauit. Non quidem sanctius hinc est, quàm erat prius, quam ad sola Domini verba, solámque orationem Dominicam consecrabatur: sed maximè decuit, ut fides quæ adhuc erat illo tempore rudis, & ut ait quidam tam doctus quàm fidelis,
units.tr: Formerly, he says, the solemn Masses were celebrated without such outward splendour, and this whole glory of religious service was not completed and polished by any one person. Just as the Lord handed down the order of the old sacrifice through Moses, and David and Solomon especially enlarged it more splendidly, with the ministry of priests and Levites, a great number of singers, the dancing of the divine Psalms, the illustrious glory of the temple or altar, and a multitude of sacred vessels, so the holy Roman Church received the marvellous rite of sacrifice handed down by the Lord through the first Apostles, embraced it with religious faith, kept it with faithful care, and adorned it with diligent preparation. Certainly it was not holier then than it had been before, when it was consecrated only with the Lord's words and the Lord's Prayer alone. But it was most fitting that faith, which was still rude at that time, should be adorned, and especially in this part should be gilded as in its head, as a certain writer, as learned as he was faithful, says:

units.la: -agresti turbida cultu, Nuda humeros, intonsa comas, exerta lacertos,
units.tr: rough with rustic dress, bare shoulders, unkempt hair, arms bared,

units.la: Vbi ornari potuit, maximè in hac parte tanquam in capite suo deauraretur. Ita nimirum iustificatur superstitio à filiis suis, quum legitimus Dei & Christi cultus in ritibus & cerimoniis quasi honorificè sepultus, exhibetur. Et tamen ex hac veritatis agnitione illud boni colligi potest, quod etiam reipsa constat, nempe illam quam vocant, consecrationem, non esse unius sæculi, ac proinde parum sibi in plerisque constare. quæ enim illic ita leguntur, Pro REDEMPTIONE ANIMARUM SVARUM, ex Græco petita sunt, vbi vox isti respondens eo sensu vsurpatur, non vt aliquid obtinendum indicetur, sed vt pro obtento gratiæ agantur, unde & nomen ἀξίωσις[?]. Vt autem integritatis & modestiæ illius etiamnum sæculi ac Romæ præsertim testimonium insigne extet, audiamus quid pro ambitu Damasi & Vrsicini ad obtinendam illam sedem Episcopalem accidterit. sic enim de Viuentio urbis tum Præfecto loquitur Ammianus lib.27. Et hunc, inquit, seditiones discordantes populi terruere cruentæ, quæ tale negotium excitauere. Damasus & Vrsicinus supra humanum modum ad rapiendam Episcopalem sedem ardentes, scissis studiis asperrimè conflictabantur, adusque mortis vulnerumque discrimina adiumentis utriusque progressis: quos nec corrigere sufficiens Viuentius, nec mollire vi magna coactus secessit in suburbanum: & in concertatione superauerat Damasus, parte quæ ei faucebat instante. Constatque in Basilica Sicinini (vbi ritus Christiani est cōventiculum) uno die centum triginta septem reperta cadauera peremptorum: efferatámque plebem ægre postea delinitam. Neque ego abnuerim, ostentationem rerum considerans urbanarum, huius rei cupidos, ob impetrandum quod appetunt, omni contentione laterum iurgari debere: quum id adepti, futuri sint ita securi, ut ditentur oblationibus matronarum, procedántque vehiculis incedēntes,circunspectè vestiti, epulas curantes profu-fas, adeo vt eorum conuiuia regales superent mensas: qui esse poterant beati reuera, si magnitudine vrbis despecta quâ vitiis opponunt, ad imitationem quorundam Antistitum prouincialium viuerent: quos tenuitas edendi potandíque parcissimè, vilitas etiam indumentorû & supercilia humum spectantia, perpetuo numini verisque eius cultoribus, vt puros commendant & verecundos. Hæc ille, Valentiniani primi temporibus, (vt Ethnicus, Christianis tamen nunquam iniquus) quum Ecclesia post centesimum fere annum à cruce respirans, fauore Cæsarum innixa non modicè luxuriaret.
units.tr: Thus superstition is indeed justified by its sons, when the lawful worship of God and Christ is displayed in rites and ceremonies, as if honourably buried. Yet from this recognition of the truth something good can be gathered, which is also clear in fact: namely, that what they call consecration is not of a single age, and therefore agrees with itself very little in most respects. For the words read there, "For the REDEMPTION OF THEIR SOULS", are taken from the Greek, where the corresponding word is used in a sense that does not indicate something to be obtained, but thanks given for something already obtained, whence also the name [ἀξίωσις?]. To show the notable witness of that integrity and modesty, still present in that age and especially at Rome, let us hear what happened in the ambition of Damasus and Ursinus to obtain that episcopal see. For Ammianus, book 27, speaks thus of Viventius, then prefect of the city: "And bloody seditions of a divided people terrified him, which such a business stirred up. Damasus and Ursinus, burning beyond human measure to seize the episcopal see, fought bitterly with divided factions, their supporters pressing matters even to the peril of death and wounds. Viventius, being unable to correct them and, forced by great violence, withdrew to the suburbs. In the contest Damasus prevailed, his party pressing hard. And it is recorded that in the Basilica of Sicininus, where the Christian rite has its assembly, one hundred and thirty-seven bodies of the slain were found on a single day; and the enraged people were afterwards with difficulty soothed." I would not deny, considering the display of city life, that those who desire this office ought, to obtain what they seek, to contend with every exertion of strength, since once they have obtained it they will be so secure that they grow rich from the offerings of matrons, ride about in carriages, dress splendidly, and provide lavish feasts, so that their banquets surpass royal tables. They could truly have been blessed, if, despising the greatness of the city, which they set against vices, they had lived in imitation of certain provincial bishops, whom the scantiness of food and drink, the cheapness of clothing, and eyes fixed on the ground commend to the eternal divinity and its true worshippers as pure and modest. So he speaks, in the times of Valentinian I (as a pagan, yet never unfair to Christians), when the Church, recovering almost a hundred years after the cross and leaning on the favour of the emperors, was living in no small luxury.

units.la: Quinam autem mores promiscuè Christianorum fuerint tum Romæ tum alibi, testantur Hieronymus, Sidonius, Saluianus.
units.tr: What the morals of Christians were in general, both at Rome and elsewhere, is attested by Jerome, Sidonius and Salvian.

units.la: Reliquas ve-rò Ecclesiæ per hoc sæculum corruptelas, quæ tamen nihil minus quàm quod erant, haberentur, paucis etiam perstringemus, vt cumulum ipsum non attingamus. Inucnio igitur in genere bonos illius ætatis viros & bene eruditos hoc fere sibi proposuisse, vt homines sui sæculi in eo statu quem tolerabilem iudicabant, retinerent: quum reuera, si de Ecclesia ad Doctrinam Apostolorum redigenda omnino quæsitum fuisset, vix vllus fortasse de eo quod sequendum esset, statuere potuisset. quum enim aliquid controuersiæ tum in Ecclesia incidebat, recurrebatur continuò ad vsum receptum, vel ad expositio-nes quas Patrum traditiones vocabant: quasi nempe extra illum veluti canalem apostolicæ doctrinæ certitudo percipi satis non posset. In quibufquibusdâ itêm particularibus quicquid positum inuenerant in Ecclesia, magis commendabant, quàm vt de eo inquirerent, nedû vt distinctè ex Dei verbo iudicarent. Vnus Mediolani per illa tempora Ambrosius improbabat illam ad sepulcra mortuorum oblationem alimentorum, quanuis pauperibus deinde restituendam: vti Augustini matri hoc agere satagenti ac non ita ita ingredi coemiterium permissæ, ab ipso Ambrosio per Augustinum filium responsum legitur. Et tamen idem Ambrosius quàm reuereter reliquias Martyrum quorundam eruit & prosequitur? quàm impensè etiam idem continen-tiam & virginitatem commendat, quasi ôinne punctum pietatis in eo sit positum, vt quis à coniugio quàmalienissimus [?] sit: cui deinde omnes perinde adstipulati sunt, atque ille à Basilio & aliis superioribus istâ percepta totâ animi intentione inculcarat. Inde igitur latens illud eóque perniciosius schisma, idémque omnium malorum in Ecclesia fomentum, nempe perse-ctionis sub Monachatus instituto professio, cuius sumptus auctor isto vergente seculo notadus est Benedictus ille, sub cuius nomine tot deinde monachorum examina Ecclesiam repleuerunt. Inde inquam factum est, vt quicunque istis sese non addiceret, ille semiChristianus habere-tur, vt in carne viuens, Deo minus placens, Baptismi polluti reus: qui contrà istis adiungeretur, tantùmnon Angelicam integritatem in terra profiteri diceretur. Pastorū autem coniugatorum rarissima iam tum exempla superērat: quum quod moribus semel ita inualuerat, prō lege quadā apostolica vanissima credulitate pas-sim haberetur. Imo hoc fere singulare argu-mentum declamatorium de continetia, seu vir-ginitate, omnium & ora & stylos occupabat. Quale enim illud est Hieronymi ita Paulę matri de Eustochij virginitate gratulantis! Noluit, in-quit, militis esse vxor, sed Regis: grande tibi beneficium praestitit: Socrus Dei esse coepisti. & quae reliqua ita apud illos detrita sunt, non sine aperta quicquid praetexant, coniugalis vitae fug-gilatione. Sic igitur omnia tu in Ecclesia ad illa quaedam vitae genera referebantur, quasi ad sin-gulare & certissimum Christianae professionis & agnitionis Christi compendium. Coepit quo-que his iisdem temporibus & de statu mortuo-rum ante omnem quam volebant impletam iu-stitiam, tanquam in Purgatorio sequestram Do-mini fœueritatem pro aeternis poenis experien-tium, disceptari: Cuius rei tandem Gregorius suis illis dialogis praesertim maximam fidem fe-cit, tanquam re tot visionibus scilicet explorata. Itidem & illorum qui ex hac vita cum Martyrij corona, vel altera quauis integritatis peculiaris nota decesserant commemoratio tum quoque & imploratio quaedam inuecta est ad illorum memorias. Inde pedetentim etiam ipsorum & merita quae dicuntur, & inuocatio, quasi magnū pietatis Christianę adminiculū, mundo ita sponte iam caecutienti obtrusa sunt. Et quod veluti corollarium istis omnibus accessit, cessante in dies ordinaria verbi administratione, (cessante etiam illius causa, nempe sincero scripturae intellectu & tractatione) imagines illa occasione templis tèmplis Christianorum irrepserunt, quas etiam commendat ex suo sensu bonus ille Gregorius. Paulinus autem Nolensis Episcopus Augustini [illegible, ~8 letters] ita se egregie eleuasse gloriatur scan[?] [?]alu ex cōuentu ad Felicis Martyris ædem cum ēpulis profusis fieri solito, dum totam ædem historia martyrij Felicis depicta circumuestit. Neque enim aliunde quàm ex ista imaginum positione, idola deinde sine vllo pudore, contra omne Ecclesiæ purioris vsum passim in templis Christianorum intumuerunt. Postremo etiam tituli illi munerum Ecclesiasticorum, Episco- patus nempe, ita sub ordinis aliquius prætextu in metropoles & dioeceses ad Imperij Notitiæ formam redacti fuerunt, vt fere saluo tantum nomine, administratio Ecclesiæ in humanę po- sitiæ formam & dignitatem degeneraret. ac Romę nominatim hoc obtinebat ferè ante Gre- gorii, nisi riualis tum Constantinopolitanus Patriarcha, vti vocabant, plurimum inuidisset. Et tamen vel vnum exemplum cognitionis Ec- clesiasticæ à Romano Concilio ad Arelatense sub Constantino demandatæ satis etiamtum osten- debat, præsidentiam illam Romanam non esse iuris ordinarij, sed positui, vt loquuntur. Non quòd insicias eam Ecclesiæ Romanæ homen magni tam olim ponderis, adde & vsus, in Ec- clesia Christiana fuisse. Hoc enim vel vnius A- postolici[?] historia testatur. Sed hoc dico primum humano consilio & studio, atque vt se res da- bant, sedem illa occasione vrbis imprimis ita in sublime euecta fuisse. Ingenia etiam Occiden- talium non ita mobilia, vti Orientalium efficiebant, ut quicunque motus alias per orbem Ecclesias agitarent, statim pars quæ læsa videri volebat, Romam accurreret, ubi etiā quasi obuiis ulnis accipiebatur[?]: tanquam in altero Asylo Ecclesiastico. Unde etiam interdictæ sunt tandem nominatim in Carthaginensi Synodo traiectiæ appellationes sub pœna excomunicationis.
units.tr: We will also briefly touch on the remaining corruptions of the Church during this century, which were nonetheless held to be anything but what they were, so as not to reach the full heap of them. I find, then, that the good and well-learned men of that age generally set themselves this aim: to keep the people of their time in the state which they judged tolerable. In reality, if a complete reform of the Church according to the teaching of the Apostles had been sought, hardly any one of them could perhaps have decided what ought to be followed. For when some controversy arose in the Church, people immediately had recourse to the accepted usage, or to the explanations which they called the traditions of the Fathers, as if certainty could not be sufficiently grasped outside that channel, as it were, of apostolic doctrine. In certain particular matters, they commended whatever they had found established in the Church more than they inquired into it, let alone judged it clearly from the Word of God. At Milan in those times Ambrose disapproved of the offering of food at the graves of the dead, although it was to be given afterwards to the poor; and it is read that, when Augustine's mother was eager to do this and was not allowed to enter the cemetery in the usual way, Ambrose gave his answer through Augustine, her son. Yet the same Ambrose, how reverently he digs up and honours the relics of certain martyrs! How earnestly he also commends continence and virginity, as if every point of piety lay in being as far as possible from marriage! All the others then agreed with him, just as he had inculcated, with his whole mind, what he had received from Basil and other earlier writers. From this there arose that hidden and all the more pernicious schism, and the source of all evils in the Church, namely the profession of perfection under the monastic institute, whose chief author, at the turn of this century, is noted to have been that Benedict under whose name so many swarms of monks then filled the Church. Hence, I say, it came about that whoever did not devote himself to these things was regarded as a half-Christian, living in the flesh, less pleasing to God, guilty of a polluted Baptism; while whoever joined them was said to profess almost angelic integrity on earth. Examples of married ministers were already very rare by then, while what had once thus prevailed by custom was everywhere held, through a most vain credulity, as a kind of apostolic law. Indeed, this one commonplace argument about continence or virginity almost occupied every mouth and pen. What else is Jerome's saying, when he congratulates Paula, his mother, on the virginity of Eustochium? "She did not want to be the wife of a soldier, but of a King; she has conferred a great benefit on you: you have begun to be the mother-in-law of God." And the rest is worn out among them, not without an open flight from married life, however they may disguise it. So everything in the Church was referred to certain kinds of life, as to a unique and most certain summary of Christian profession and of the acknowledgement of Christ. At the same time, in these very times, there also began to be debate about the state of the dead before the full satisfaction which they wished for had been made, as if in Purgatory souls were undergoing, in place of eternal punishments, the severity of the Lord's chastisement; of this matter Gregory, especially in his Dialogues, made the greatest impression, as if it had been established by so many visions. Likewise, the commemoration and a certain invocation of those who had departed this life with the crown of martyrdom, or with some other distinctive mark of integrity, was then introduced, together with their memorials. Gradually, then, both their so-called merits and invocation, as a great aid to Christian piety, were thrust upon a world already spontaneously growing blind. And, as a kind of corollary to all these things, there came the cessation day by day of the ordinary administration of the Word, and the cessation of its cause, namely the sincere understanding and handling of Scripture; on that occasion images crept into the temples of the Christians, which even the good Gregory commends in his own sense. Paulinus, bishop of Nola, boasts that he had so splendidly removed from Augustine's congregation the banquets, lavishly provided, which were customarily held at the church of the martyr Felix, by surrounding the whole church with a depiction of the history of Felix's martyrdom. Indeed, from no other source than this placing of images, idols afterwards swelled up everywhere in the temples of Christians without any shame, against the whole practice of the purer Church. Finally, those titles of ecclesiastical offices, namely the episcopates, were also so reduced, under the pretext of some order, to the metropolitan cities and dioceses, in the form of the imperial register, that the administration of the Church, with the name almost alone kept, degenerated into the form and dignity of a human position. And at Rome this state of things obtained almost until Gregory's time, had not the rival Patriarch of Constantinople, as they called him, greatly envied it. And yet the single example of the ecclesiastical cognisance entrusted under Constantine by the Roman Council to Arles showed clearly enough even then that that Roman presidency was not of ordinary right but, as they say, of positive appointment. Not that I deny that the Roman Church had great authority and weight in the Christian Church of old, and custom as well; for even the history of the Apostles alone bears witness to this. But I say this first: by human counsel and zeal, and as circumstances then allowed, that see was above all raised so high on account of the city. Moreover, the minds of Westerners were not as changeable as those of Easterners made them, so that whatever movements stirred the Churches throughout the world, immediately the party which wished to appear injured ran to Rome, where it was also received, as if with open arms, as in another ecclesiastical asylum. Whence, at last, appeals carried across the sea were expressly forbidden at the Council of Carthage, under penalty of excommunication.

units.la: Illa igitur Romanæ sedis Maiestas per ista tempora non extabat, quæ insequentibus demum agnosci voluit: tantum eousque ventum erat, ut pro Ecclesiæ totius bono, quantum expediret, honoratissimè inter reliquas Ecclesiæ Rom. deferretur. En igitur quo tandem infœlix humana sapientia rem Ecclesiæ deduxerit, cuius Apostoli legitimi architecti à Domino institu-ti erant, ut illorum gnomon & exemplum perpetuò obseruaretur, si quidem non malis hominibus non iam olim mens læua fuisset. Hucusque igitur Ecclesiam quantumuis debilitatam & minimè in plærisque natiuam illam Christi agnitionis vitam exhibentem, substitisse tamen, & illius pacem retinendam fuisse agnoscimus.
units.tr: Therefore the majesty of the Roman see did not yet exist in these times; it was a dignity that later generations chose to acknowledge. Matters had only reached the point where, for the good of the whole Church, the Roman Church was honoured above the other churches as far as was fitting. Here, then, is where unhappy human wisdom finally led the affairs of the Church, whose legitimate architects the Apostles had been appointed by the Lord, so that their rule and example should always be observed, if only men had not, long before, been evil-minded. Up to this point, then, we acknowledge that the Church, though weakened and in many respects no longer showing that native life of knowing Christ, nevertheless survived, and that its peace was to be kept.

units.la: Neque verò hanc Ecclesiæ instante inuersione [illegible, ~8 letters] reliquit Dominus: quemadmodum illa doctrinæ corruptio glisceb at in dies, quum minimè propter alluuionem illam superstitionum deprehenderetur, ita etiam mores Ecclesiæ plané prophani erant & plusquam degeneres. Quid enim aliud accidere potuisset, ipsis Ecclesiæ oculis, auribus, lingua, sensibus deniq; omnibus in ministerij interuersione plané obturatis, ut neque cursus neque habenæ satis certæ deinceps superesset. Obnitebantur quidem & obtona-bant. bant per aliquot sæcula pij quidam Episcopi, & Gregorius ipse in eo quoque saltem fidelem Ecclesiæ operam impendebat. Sed ne sic quidē illa revocari serió potuit ad aliquam frugem, maximè quum unicus tum salutis portus in Monachatus aditione reponeretur. Exundarut [?] igitur per Europā maximè & Asiā quæ est ad Orientē horrenda illa Barbarorum etiam nomine terribilium examina numerosa, quæ Mahemedis imposturis & regno exedificando via tandem sternerent. Sic, inquam, Dominus ipse vindicare cœpit suo iusto iudicio illorum ingratitudinem qui Evangelij ipsius contemptu quasi professo, patrum quoque suorum in piis olim excarnificandis, scelera apud ipsius tribunal in memoriam revocabant.
units.tr: Yet the Lord did not abandon the Church in this approaching upheaval [illegible, ~8 letters]. Just as that corruption of doctrine grew day by day, and was not noticed because of that flood of superstitions, so too the morals of the Church were utterly profane and more than degenerate. For what else could have happened, when the eyes, ears, tongue and, in short, all the senses of the Church were completely stopped up by the overturning of the ministry, so that neither a course nor a sufficiently sure rein remained for it thereafter? Certainly some pious bishops struggled and thundered against this for several centuries, and Gregory himself at least devoted his faithful effort to this end. But even so, the Church could not seriously be recalled to any sound condition, especially since the only harbour of salvation was placed in entry into the monastic life. Therefore those vast, terrible swarms of barbarians, dreadful even by name, poured out over Europe especially and over Asia towards the East, and these were to pave the way for Mahomet's impostures and the building up of his kingdom. Thus, I say, the Lord himself began to avenge, by his just judgment, the ingratitude of those who, in open contempt of his Gospel, recalled before his tribunal the crimes they had committed in slaughtering their own fathers, who had once been pious men.

units.la: Quarta porro Ætas quam à sexcentesimo a Christo anno recensuimus, neque valde remorari nos potest, neque tamen simpliciter disputandi. Plane enim illi convenit quod de sui sæculi Ecclesia Jeremias querebatur appositissimè. Quis det mihi in solitudine diversorium viatorum, ut derelinquam populum meum, & recedam ab eis? Universi enim sunt adulteri, & cœtus prævaricatorum. Quæ igitur per istam ætatem substitutæ Ecclesia visibilis, illa quasi extremum veritatis spiritum sensim emisisse dici potest, ac proinde una subsequentis & ultimi comparatione nomen illud Ecclesiæ retinuisse potuit: quum reipsa vix iam pro Christi Ecclesia agnosci mereretur. Quid enim ad illā Christus pertinuit, quæ & verbum ipsius & Sacramenta, ut exsuccum cortièm complectèdo, veritatem. ipsam in solida agnitione beneficij Christi, cum omne genus superstitionibus quasi magno cum quæstu pietatis commutasset. Inde igitur inter cætera istius Ætatis probra illud vnū summum plane rebus ita in deterius labentibus momen-tum attulit: quod de imaginibus & picturis in templis Christianorū erigendis serio tandem cautum est, vnde manifesta scisio tandem ex-titit inter Ecclesias Orientis & Occidentis. Quanquam in aliis plerisque ineptiis & hæ & illæ Ecclesiæ, eodem Spiritu vanitatis & igno-rantiæ in præceps ferrentur. Neque ad hanc rem magis idonei testes citari possunt Nice-phoro Callisto & Gregorio Turonensi isto-rum sæculorum magnis fautoribus.
units.tr: Moreover, the fourth age, which we have counted from the six hundredth year after Christ, cannot detain us long, nor yet can it be discussed in a merely simple way. For what Jeremiah complained of in the Church of his own age fits this one very aptly: "Oh, that I had in the wilderness a lodging place for travellers, that I might leave my people and go from them! For they are all adulterers, an assembly of traitors." Whatever visible Church then subsisted through that age may be said to have gradually breathed out its last breath of truth, and therefore, when compared with the later and final age, it could keep the name of Church, although in truth it hardly deserved to be acknowledged as the Church of Christ any longer. For what had Christ to do with a Church which, embracing his word and sacraments like a dry husk, had exchanged the truth itself, the solid knowledge of Christ's benefit, for every kind of superstition, as though for a great profit of piety? Hence, among the other disgraces of this age, this one thing brought the greatest weight to affairs that were thus sinking into worse ruin: that it was at length seriously decided that images and pictures should be set up in the temples of Christians, whence a clear split at last arose between the Churches of the East and the West. Yet in many other follies both these and those Churches were carried headlong by the same spirit of vanity and ignorance. Nor can witnesses more suitable for this matter be cited than Nicephorus Callistus and Gregory of Tours, great partisans of these centuries.

units.la: Ac ne in singulis istius ætatis corruptelis hæ-reamus, sic habendum est semel, non posse co-pendiosius illius formam & statum tradi, quàm si remanente Christianismi verbotenus feré nomine, reipsa humanam administrationem & spiritum ac caput humanum in illa extitisse at-que obtinuisse dicamus. Quum enim Respubli-ca ipsa mutationem prima pateretur, & vix am-plius Imperij sedes Romæ propter motus in Oriente continuos staret, omnino sibi quantū-uis dissimulanter consilium illud cœperunt Oc-cidentis prouinciæ, vt in fidem quandam Epis-coporum hoc ipsum omnino captantium ex-emplo Romani ipsius Episcopi sese dederent. Sic enim boni Ecclesiarum sub Romanensi Pa-stores sese rebus omnibus immiscebant, vt & cum Cæsaribus & cum Barbaris quasi pacis se-questri pleraque omnia tractarent. Atque istam imprimis occasionem Romana sedes arripuit, qua tantum sibi apud Occidentis Ecclesias fastigium adrogaret, cuius iam olim fundamenta ex innata superioris sæculi credulitate iacta habebat. Vacabat igitur fere tum sedes impe-rij in Italia, quum etiam Roma repetitis vasta-tionibus plurimum deformata esset: ac proinde Cæsares ipsi Rauennæ potius Exarchatus nomi-ne Vicarium Occidentis instituissent. Quanquam etiam suum ad illam loci translationem mo-mentum habuit imprimis Episcopi Romæ do-minatio iam plane si nomē excipias, Regia, & Religioso nomine Ecclesiæ ita subnixa, ut vix iam Cæsaris nomen præ fulgore pontificio Ro-mæ diu cū aliqua dignitate agnoscceretur. Qua-obrem illa dominatione externa Ecclesię semel ita constituta, ipsissima omnino Imago Be-stiæ illic etiam extitisse credenda est: quum (vt iam in ipso Pontifice notauimus) omnia iam sui iuris Ecclesia esse vellet, id est illius nomine e-mentito omnes mundi dignitates ad se superba illa Romani Imperij prædatrix synagóga(Chri-sto quasi in cœlum cum verbi doctrina rele-gato) vindicaret. Hinc igitur ultimus etiam cu-mulus abominationis invectæ{*} est. istius enim sæ-culi egregij Episcopi ac veluti flos præcipuus nihil aliud fuisse comperiuntur quā Unctores, Mirabiliarij, Benedictionarij, Processionarij, Rituarij denique & Mystagogæ, ut qui ad idola tum pasim emergentia commendanda ipsimet tanquam altera idola accederent. Atque ex istis fere etiam delecti fuerunt tot illi nomine San-ctuli vel peculiares patroni, quibus aliquanto post eorū obitū noua passim tepla & altaria se-ques ętas instituit, quum vel ipsi superstites tantum non adorarentur: quasi nempe in ipsis etiā mortuis potiora omni doctrina miracula & apparitiones ad omnem vsum & occasionem editæ perpetuò repullularent. Imprimis autem pro omni & doctrinę auditione & Ministerij di-sciplina duo ista quędā Ecclesiam tum ita occuparunt, vt in illis etiam defixæ omnium mentes hærerent: vnum, Pontificis Romani atque sub illo reliquorum Ecclesiæ procerum Maiestas supra omnes creaturas veneranda & implorāda. Nil oriturum aliās, nil ortum tale fatentes. (Sic enim Christi Domini virtus omnis & gratia in illud novū caput translata credebatur, vt omni alia re infuperhabita, illud vnum & audiretur & prædicaretur.) Alterū accessit etiā, operosa nē-pe cæremoniarum moles in Mysterijs peragendis: quæ quidem Mysteria tum plane Missarum nomine iam recepto commendarentur. Atque in istis quidē Mysterijs illud minus corruptum superat, quod etiam vtraque species quā vocant tradebatur populo, & satis frequens in Ecclesia comunio retinebatur. Quorum vtrunque sequenti ætate interpolatum est tandē, quasi sub specie quadam indulgentię erga vulgus promiscuum, minus ad tantas res percipiendas ordinario comparatum. Sed tamen vt veneratio elementorum hac ætate ferè ad adorationis speciē accessit, ita imprimis opinio illa sacrificij operatorij increuit. Atque illud nominatim Purgatorij illius ignis isto iā post Gregorium sæculo plurimū exæstuantis argumento. Miseri enim homines omnem sibi in pace tum viuis tū mor-tuis procuranda rationem in Missarum celebra-tione repositam credebant. Unde magnum rei Pontificiæ incrementum. Siue igitur statu politi cum, siue Ecclesiasticum per istam ætatem expedamus, tunc omnino accidisse comperiemus quod Dominus exprobrat suis per Prophetam: illis nempe rerum omnium perturbationibus testari ipsum apud suos, ut scirent, inquam, quantum inter Dei cultum & veritatem, & hominum tyrannide atque imposturas interesset. Qui igitur extrema hac ætate pietatem aliquâ retinue-runt, non potuerunt nō ex tantis angustiis apud Dominum ingemiscere, & tamen vix summam malorum partem senserunt propter illius iam secuti sæculi tenebras densissimas.
units.tr: But lest we linger over each corruption of this age, it must be held once and for all that its form and state cannot be described more briefly than by saying that, while the name of Christianity remained almost in words, in reality a human administration, a human spirit and a human head were present and prevailed in it. For when the commonwealth itself was undergoing its first change, and the seat of the empire at Rome could hardly remain any longer because of the continual disturbances in the East, the provinces of the West, though dissembling as much as they could, began to take up that plan of placing themselves under a kind of trust in the bishops, all of whom were aiming at exactly this, following the example of the Roman bishop himself. For the good pastors of the Churches under the Roman pontiff thus mixed themselves into all affairs, so that they transacted most things with the emperors and with the barbarians alike, as mediators of peace. And it was above all this opportunity that the Roman see seized, so that it might claim for itself such a height of eminence among the Churches of the West, the foundations of which it had long ago laid from the innate credulity of the previous century. The imperial seat in Italy was then almost vacant, and Rome itself, repeatedly ravaged, had been much disfigured; hence the emperors themselves had rather set up a vicar of the West at Ravenna, under the title of exarch. Yet the domination of the Roman bishop, now already, except for the name, royal, and so supported by the religious name of the Church that the name of Caesar could scarcely be recognised for long at Rome with any dignity, had also a great influence on that transfer of place, owing to the splendour of the papacy. Therefore, once that external domination of the Church had been established in this way, we must believe that the very image of the Beast existed there as well: since (as we have already noted in the Pontiff himself) that proud robber-synagogue of the Roman empire, wanting all things to be under its own right, that is, claiming in that counterfeit name all the dignities of the world for itself, had relegated Christ, as it were, to heaven together with the doctrine of the word. Hence also the final heap of abomination was introduced. For the eminent bishops of this age, and its chief flower, are found to have been nothing other than anointers, wonder-workers, blessers, processionists, ritualists and, finally, mystagogues, who, to commend the idols then emerging everywhere, approached as though they were other idols themselves. And from these almost were chosen all those many so-called saints or peculiar patrons, to whom, some time after their deaths, the following age everywhere set up new temples and altars, when even the living ones were almost adored; as if, indeed, in the dead themselves, miracles and apparitions, produced for every use and occasion, more powerful than all doctrine, kept sprouting up continually. Above all, for all hearing of doctrine and the discipline of the ministry, two things so occupied the Church at that time that the minds of all were fixed and stuck in them: one, the majesty of the Roman pontiff and, under him, of the other leaders of the Church, to be venerated and implored above all creatures, the people confessing that nothing would arise otherwise, and that nothing such had arisen. (For thus all the power and grace of the Lord Christ was believed to have been transferred to that new head, so that, all else being disregarded, that one thing alone was both heard and preached.) The other was added as well: namely, the laborious mass of ceremonies in performing the mysteries, which were then recommended under the now established name of Masses. And in these mysteries, indeed, the less corrupted feature remained, that both kinds, as they are called, were still given to the people, and a fairly frequent communion was kept in the Church. Each of these was at length interpolated in the following age, as if under some appearance of indulgence towards the common crowd, less fitted to perceive such great matters. Yet, just as the veneration of the elements in this age came close to a kind of adoration, so above all that opinion of a work-performing sacrifice grew. And this is especially shown by the fire of that purgatory, which after Gregory in that century blazed up greatly. For wretched men believed that every means of securing peace for themselves, both living and dead, was placed in the celebration of Masses. Hence came the great increase of the Papal affair. Therefore, whether we consider the political state or the ecclesiastical one through this age, we shall find that there happened exactly what the Lord reproaches his people for through the Prophet: that by all those upheavals he bore witness to himself among his own people, so that they might know, I say, how great the difference is between the worship of God and the truth, and the tyranny and impostures of men. Those, therefore, who in this last age kept some piety could not help groaning before the Lord under such great distress, and yet they scarcely felt the sum of the evils, on account of the very dense darkness of the age that had by then followed.

units.la: Quinta igitur ætas hoc vnum habuit commune cum tribus superioribus, quòd ea quæ ab hominibus invecta acceperat, magis ac magis excoluit atq; in sublime extulit. Eiusmodi sunt autem duo illa capita de Pontificia Maiestate, & de Sacrificii Missæ efficacitate, quasi totus in illis duobus Dei cultus, totum Christi beneficium, plena omnium rerum sacrorum scatu-rigo agnosceretur. Ad hanc autem rem ita promouendā magnā occasionem attulit noua quaedam facies statuum atque ordinum tum in Ecclesia tum etiam in Republica. Qui enim nouissi-mo sæculo Episcopi dicti sunt, illi vt plurimum rebus huius vitæ addicti: nihil minus quâ quod dicebantur, curare coeperunt: sic igitur quum idem & Ecclesiæ & Reipublicæ capita ac principes haberi vellent, omnia semel susque deque vel [?]sunt. Ac ne quid interea deesset, quod mūdo iam ad nova illa numina stupenti reliquam mentem adimeret, tota Ecclesiæ forma in ceri-monias, ædificia operosa, superstitiones ac pompas, vestes, ornamentaque theatrica, tanquam nova totidem sacramenta immutata est. Pauci ii aliquot monachi rythmos & prosas concipie-bant, quibus deinde cultus Ecclesiæ quem vocant, persoluaret[?]. Iide aliquando etiā concionabatur. Parochi enim vel plebani quos vocabant iam plane alieni erant à verbi Dei tractatione. Conciones autem quæuis (si Bernardi fortasse vnius sinceritatem excipias) nihil aliud erant, quàm fabellæ de igne purgatorij, de visionibus monachis & monialibus oblatis, de sanctulorū reliquiis, & reliquis eiusmodi nugis. Disciplina Ecclesiæ si quę retineri videbatur, ad Officiales sedium, episcopali relegabatur, qui videlicet pro sua spirituali prudentia, ex foro conscientiæ rabulariam scholam instituerunt. Imprimis autem Ecclesiastici hoc sæculo sui omnia fori esse, se vero nullius præterquâ sui, credi volue-runt. Imò Dominus ille Apostolicus sedis Im-perij vsurpator ita callidè egit cum Carolo Ma-gno, vt bonam partem Italiæ ab ipso armis Lango-bardorum liberatam, sibi quocunq; illius mu-nere delatam quasi manu iniecta arriperet. Sic enim sedem Petri plurimum scilicet exornati mundo persuadebatur. Atque ista etiam occasione factum est, vt quum iam nominis Christiani Ecclesiæ minus inter se communionis re-tinerent, propter Romani Pontificis vsurpationem Græcis Ecclesiis & Asiaticis quæ superarat[?] hunquam[?] probatam, quæ deinde per reliquam Europam in Papæ dominationem consenserat, sub illo quoque Catholicæ Ecclesiæ nomen sibi vendicaret. Sic inquam factum est, vt de scisa Ecclesia, Romana vna triumphum ageret, dum à se sub iugum missas eo tamen nomine liberas & Catholicas Ecclesias pronuntiauit, quod ad se vnum vt nouum ac indubitatū Caput omniū omnia etiam deferrent. Quod ne etiam vlla ex parte aliter quispiam interpretaretur, idioma i-psum Latinum Romanense in Catechismis & aliis quibusdam actibus Ecclesiasticis inuectū est, vbi aliqua superioris sæculi puritas & sim-plicitas in vernaculo sermone in Ecclesiis su-perfuerat. Quanuis enim Romana lingua per Imperij Romani ambitum propagata esset, non omnis tamen Ecclesiæ administratio illi linguæ ad hoc vsq; Caroli tempus cesserat. Exorti sunt etiam media ista ætate noui post tot alios monasticos Mendicantium ordines, vel vni præcipuè ad istam Babelis turrim exaedificandam apposi-tissimi. Sic enim Satanam ludificari mundum oportuit, vt illos vermes & scarabeos ex fæce Pontificiæ Ecclesiæ enatos tanquam nouos A-postolos & noui illius cœli Angelos passim propagaret. Atque isti vicissim vt Pontificij numinis creaturæ nihil non ad illius Maiestatem amplificandam commeti sunt, vt dignos se illo suo Ioue heroas ostenderent. In vno autem optimè inter istos & Pontificem conuenit, quod ad illa superiora adiectum prorsus deploratam istius sæculi cæcitatem detegit. Quicquid enim Scriptura de Christi agnitione & veritate passim prodidit, illud totum diserte transcriptum est in Virgine Matrem plane in omnibus. Cultus denique diuinus in Concilio Claromontano Virgini Matri institutus est, Anno Dom: M.X C V I. quasi iam illa una perinde Christum in coelis, atque Papa in terris repraesentaret. Quamobrem ita cessit nouis istis Ecclesię transformatoribus opus suum, ut vel ipsimet adora-rentur a populis & gentibus. Adeoque Reges summi passim hoc vno summam pietatem sibi testari coram Deo viderentur, si omnia Pontifici & Pontificiis accepta ferrent. Neque enim vllus[?] pudor in istis residuus fuit, ut spiritualia a temporalibus quæ vocant distinguerentur, quatenus dominationem suam & vsurpationem ad tempus dissimulatam plenis buccis profiteri præsumpserunt. Qua de re ne qua disceptatio su-peresset deinde, Lothari j Tertij Caesaris submissio coram illa Bestia Romæ sedente, pro ædè Laterani inscripta extat ad perpetuā rei memo-riam hoc distichō comprehensa (vt innumera exempla satis nota non attingam)
units.tr: The fifth age, then, had this one thing in common with the three before it: it cultivated more and more, and raised to great heights, the things it had received that had been introduced by men. Of this kind are those two chapters on the Pontifical Majesty and on the efficacy of the Mass, as if the whole worship of God, the whole benefit of Christ, were recognised as lying in those two, and as if every sacred thing were overflowing in them. A great occasion for promoting this came from a new arrangement of offices and orders, both in the Church and in the commonwealth. For those who in the most recent age were called bishops, for the most part given over to the affairs of this life, began to care for nothing less than what they were called, and so, since they wished to be regarded at once as the heads and princes of both the Church and the commonwealth, everything was turned upside down together. And lest anything be lacking that might deprive a world already stunned by these new deities of its remaining wits, the whole form of the Church was changed into ceremonies, elaborate buildings, superstitions and pomp, vestments and theatrical ornaments, as if they were so many new sacraments. A few monks composed rhythms and prose hymns, by which the worship of the Church, as they call it, might then be paid. Sometimes these men even preached. For the parish priests, or plebani as they were called, were now quite estranged from the handling of the Word of God. Moreover, all the sermons (unless you except the sincerity of Bernard alone, perhaps) were nothing but fables about the fire of purgatory, visions granted to monks and nuns, relics of little saints, and other trifles of that sort. Whatever discipline of the Church seemed still to be retained was referred to the officials of the episcopal seats, who, by their own spiritual prudence, set up a school of wrangling from the forum of conscience. Above all, the churchmen of this age wished it to be believed that all things were under their own jurisdiction, and that they were answerable to no one but themselves. Indeed, that lord of the Apostolic See, the usurper of the Empire, dealt so cunningly with Charles the Great that he seized, as if by a laid hand, a good part of Italy, freed from the Lombards by Charles's arms, and offered to him by his favour. For in this way it was persuaded to the world, very much to its own adornment, that this was the See of Peter. And on this same occasion it came about that, while the churches of the Christian name now kept less communion with one another, on account of the usurpation of the Roman Pontiff, the Roman Church claimed for itself the name of the Catholic Church, as also the Greek churches and those of Asia (which had once hardly approved it) and which afterwards had consented to the domination of the Pope throughout the rest of Europe. So it came about, I say, that, the Church being split, the Roman church alone celebrated a triumph: while pronouncing free and Catholic those churches that it had brought under the yoke, it claimed that they must, for that very reason, bring all things to it alone as the new and undoubted head of all. And lest anyone interpret this in any other way, the Latin language itself, the Roman tongue, was introduced into the Catechisms and certain other ecclesiastical acts, where some of the purity and simplicity of the earlier age had survived in the vernacular in the churches. For although the Roman tongue had been spread throughout the compass of the Roman Empire, not all the administration of the Church had yielded to that language until the time of Charles. There also arose in this middle age, after so many other monastic orders, the new orders of the Mendicants, most suited, above all others, to build that tower of Babel. For Satan had to mock the world in this way, so that he might spread those worms and beetles, born from the dregs of the Pontifical Church, everywhere as new apostles and angels of that new heaven. And these men in turn, as creatures of the Pontifical deity, have left nothing undone to enlarge his majesty, so that they might show themselves heroes worthy of their Jupiter. But in one thing these men and the Pontiff agreed admirably, and this, added to the aforementioned matters, reveals the utterly deplorable blindness of this age. For whatever Scripture has everywhere taught about the knowledge and truth of Christ, all that has been expressly transferred to the Virgin, in every respect the Mother. Finally, divine worship was instituted for the Virgin Mother at the Council of Clermont, in the year of the Lord 1095, as if she alone now represented Christ in heaven just as the Pope represents him on earth. Hence the work of these new transformers of the Church so prospered that they themselves were worshipped by peoples and nations. And so the greatest kings everywhere seemed to show their own great piety before God by this one thing alone, if they attributed everything to the Pope and the Papists. For no shame remained in these men, so that spiritual matters might be distinguished from those called temporal, since they dared openly to profess, with full cheeks, their domination and usurpation, which had been hidden for a time. Therefore, lest any dispute remain afterwards, the submission of the Emperor Lothar III before that Beast sitting at Rome survives, inscribed for the Lateran church and recorded for perpetual memory in this couplet (I shall not touch on the countless well-known examples):

units.la: Rex venit ante fores, iurans prius urbis honores, Post homo fit Papa, sumit quo dante coro-nam.
units.tr: The king comes before the doors, swearing first the honours of the city; afterwards he becomes the man of the Pope, and receives the crown from his giving.

units.la: Accidit etiam occasio alia valde opportuna ad istius regni Pontificij molem plurimum erigen-dam, quia enim Saraceni per ista tempora Asia valde perturbabant, & Syriam ac Iudaeam cum reliquis illis prouinciis: factum est vt Pontificiorum arte omnia Occidetis regna aduersus illos concitarentur, quasi sub titulo asserendae vel propugnandae aduersus illos terrae illius sanctae, ac nominatim Sepulchri illius ipsius Domini. sic enim oportuit mortuos tū obseruare mortuos & quem viuentem in cœlis vix ac ne vix quidem cogitabant, illius a monumento iam olim egressi venerationem in rebus mortuis fa-teri. Inde igitur Domini Ecclesiastici dum sua Capitolia Romae, atque alibi palatia seruant, fabula illa de sepulchro Domini violatoper orbem sparsa commodissime etiam abuti perrexerunt, vt ipsi soli rerum Domini atque arbitri rerum omnium sederent. Neque eos expectatio fefellit. Sparsis enim ista peregrinationum Orientalium infaustissima occasione per omnes ordines reipublicae aemulationibus ac rixis, inde etiam sui iuris plaeraque omnia reddiderunt. Neque tamen defuerunt subinde etiam hac nouissima aetate qui nouum istud Ecclesiae opus pro suo captu nuntiarent. Certum est enim de Be-rengario, illum hoc ipsum aduersus Missae correctionem asseruisse, quod etiam ex Bertrami Presbyteri doctrina accipere potuerat. In coena Domini figuram tantum sacrificij Christi ex hiberi: item, ipsa elementa panis & vini manere id quod essent natura in sua substantia. Et quantuis ad Palinodiam adactus tandem fuerit, sen-tentiam tamen in animo retinuisse magis con-stat. Bernardus autem Clareuallensis Abbas vnus post Augustinum, vt Augustinus post Apostolos vnus de Dei iustitia aduersus peccatum, eiusdemque misericordia aduersus peccatores perpetua etiam post Baptismum ita sensit & scripsit, vt Apostolicum in illo sensum agnosce-re possis, liberum item hominis arbitrium siue gratiæ antidoto turgens appositissimè traduxit. Dominationem externam Papatus heroicè imprimis oppugnauit. Spirituale enim illam bonus vir modò rite exerceretur, & probauit & commendauit plurimum. uti omnino ab uno extremo in alterum fere optimi delabuntur. Nullum gladium, nullum venenum tibi ita formido (inquit ad Eugenium) ut libidine dominandi. Rivus qua fluit cauat terram, sic discursus temporalium conscientiam rodit. Sarculo Prophetæ opus est tibi, non sceptro: ille ad operandum non ad imperandum permittitur. Alio iure argentum habeas, Apostolico non habes. Cadit Asina, & est qui sublevat. Perit anima, & nemo qui reputat. Et in epistolis: Romani valdè diligunt munera; sequuntur retributiones. Nudè nuda loquor: nec retego verenda, sed inverecunda confuto. Utinam tantùm in cameris ista fierent, utinam soli ista viderimus & audierimus. Utinam nobis reliquerint[?] moderni Noæ, unde à nobis possent aliquatenus operiri. Nunc vero cernente orbe, mundi fabulam soli tacebimus? caput meum undique coquassatum est; & ego sanguine undique ebulliente putaverim esse tegendum. quicquid apposuero, cruentabitur. & maior erit confusio, voluisse celare cum celari nequiverit. Item, Et olim quidem eratis contra Apostolum Petrum dominantes in clerum, imo & contra coapostolum eius Paulum dominabamini fidei totius orbis. At nunc novum aliquid adiecistis, usurpantes amplius & in ipsam religionem. quid restat nisi ut adiiciatis & Angelis sanctis dominari? Item: de Concilio: Illud concilium probo, & ei me affectu interesse textor, in quo non hominum traditiones obstinatè defensantur, aut superstitiones obseruantur, sed diligenter humiliterque inquiritur quæ sit voluntas Dei bona, & beneplacens, & perfecta. Hæc ille ex mediis tenebris ad lucem adspirans, quū alioqui in plerisque aliis sui teporis næuos retineat. Nec verò dubitandum alios quoque ius illud Dei aliquatenus agnouisse in defissimis etiam illis tenebris: sed quoniam Dominus habet sua momenta quibus solem ipsum veritatis reducat, multum tempus elapsum est in Ecclesia sine vero Ephod, & sine vero propheta. quod si qui non plane inter cæcos cæcutierunt, vix tamen ita oculos aperire audebant, quin & luce reperta ingemiscerent, ac simul lumina demitterent & os clauderent. Eiusmodi extitere per Italiam etiam, Galliam ac Germaniam & aliis in locis, qui tyrannidis Papisticæ mysteria vtcunq; traduxerunt. Sed vel neglecti passim diu fuere, vel ita terrore immanis bestiæ perculsi, vt vel metu ipso obruerentur. Qui vero ampliore Spiritus Christi virtute freti, & Ecclesiam Romanam cum suo capite se non agnoscere, & vnum Dei verbum pro vita Ecclesiæ requirendum esse profiteri ausi sunt aliquot Europæ locis, illi vt veræ Ecclesiæ reliquiæ dissectæ[?], inauditis criminum notis cooperti, tanquam immane ausi nefas, omnibus diris deuoti, omnibus viribus obsessi[?] & tantum non excarnificati fuerunt. Nam & ipsa Bohemorum & Valdensium nomina nonnisi cū horrore aliquo proferebantur.
units.tr: Another very opportune occasion also arose for greatly raising the mass of this Pontifical kingdom. For because the Saracens in those times were sorely troubling Asia, and Syria and Judaea with the other provinces, it came about, by the cunning of the Papists, that all the kingdoms of the West were stirred up against them, as if under the pretext of defending and protecting that holy land, and especially the very Sepulchre of the Lord. For in this way it was necessary that the dead should, by observing the dead, and should confess with the veneration of things dead the one who, living in heaven, they scarcely or not even at all thought about, he who had long since come forth from the tomb. Thence, while the churchmen kept their own capitols at Rome and palaces elsewhere, they went on most conveniently abusing that fable, spread throughout the world, about the violated sepulchre of the Lord, so that they alone might sit as lords and arbiters of all things. Nor did expectation disappoint them. For, the most unhappy occasion of those Eastern pilgrimages being scattered abroad, through rivalries and quarrels among all the orders of the commonwealth, they also made most things subject to their own right. Nor did there lack, even in this most recent age, men who proclaimed this new work of the Church according to their own capacity. For it is certain that Berengar, in opposition to the correction of the Mass, maintained this very thing, which he could also have drawn from the teaching of the priest Bertram: that in the Lord's Supper only a figure of the sacrifice of Christ is offered, and likewise that the elements of bread and wine remain in their own substance what they are by nature. And although he was at last driven to recant, it is nevertheless more certain that he kept this opinion in his mind. Bernard of Clairvaux, however, alone after Augustine (as Augustine alone after the Apostles) thought and wrote about the justice of God against sin, and about his constant mercy towards sinners, even after baptism, in such a way that you may recognise in him the Apostolic sense; and he skilfully brought in the free will of man, swelling with the antidote of grace. He vigorously attacked the external domination of the Papacy. For he greatly approved and commended the spiritual rule of the Pope, provided it were rightly exercised; and so, almost always, the best men slide from one extreme to the other. "I dread no sword, no poison, so much as the lust for ruling" (he says to Eugenius). "As a stream cuts the earth where it flows, so the rush of temporal affairs gnaws at the conscience. You need the prophet's mattock, not the sceptre: he is permitted to work, not to command. You may have silver by another right, but not by the Apostolic. The ass falls, and there is someone to raise it up. The soul perishes, and no one considers it." And in his letters: "The Romans very much love gifts; they follow rewards. I speak naked things naked: I do not uncover what should be veiled, but I confute the shameless. Would that these things were done only in chambers, would that we alone had seen and heard them. Would that the modern Noahs had left us something by which they could in some measure be covered by us. But now, with the whole world looking on, shall we alone keep silent about the fable of the world? My head is shaken on every side, and with blood boiling up on every side I would think it should be covered. Whatever I put on will be stained, and the confusion will be greater, if I wished to hide what cannot be hidden." Again: "And formerly, indeed, you lorded it over the clergy against the Apostle Peter; nay, you lorded it against his fellow-apostle Paul over the faith of the whole world. But now you have added something new, usurping even over religion itself. What remains but that you should add lordship over the holy Angels also?" Again, concerning a Council: "I approve that council, and I weaver of it am present with affection, in which the traditions of men are not stubbornly defended, nor superstitions observed, but diligently and humbly it is inquired what is the good, and pleasing, and perfect will of God." Thus he, striving upward from the midst of darkness towards the light, while otherwise retaining in many things the blemishes of his own time. Nor must we doubt that others also in those most dense shadows acknowledged in some measure that right of God; but since the Lord has his moments by which he brings back the sun of truth itself, much time has passed in the Church without the true Ephod and without a true prophet. And if some did not wholly stumble blindly among the blind, yet they hardly dared to open their eyes in such a way that, even when light was found, they would not groan, and at the same time lower their lights and close their mouths. Such men arose in Italy, France and Germany, and in other places too, who in some way exposed the mysteries of Papistical tyranny. But they were either neglected in many places for a long time, or were so struck with terror of the monstrous beast that they were overwhelmed by fear itself. Those, however, who, relying on a greater power of the Spirit of Christ, dared to profess that they did not acknowledge the Roman Church with its head, and that the one Word of God must be sought for the life of the Church, in some places of Europe, these, as remnants of the true Church, were torn apart, covered with unheard-of charges of crimes, and, as if they had dared an immense wickedness, were devoted to every curse, beset with all forces, and were all but butchered. For even the very names of the Bohemians and the Waldensians were uttered only with some horror.

units.la: Quis igitur fieri potuisse credat, vt Ecclesia illa Domini qua nihil olim sanctius sol vidit, nec terra tulit, imo quam Spiritus ipse Domini Iesu Christi coelitus verbi praedicatione concepit atque edidit primum per Apostolos, qua deinde per eosdem tam longe lateque propagauit, quam tandiu tamque mirabiliter fouit & asseruit[?] aduersus continuas domi forisque tempestates, ut in illa Misericordia & Veritas obumbrarent sibi, Iustitia & pax oscularentur se: Quis inquam fieri potuisse credat ut ab illo lacte Evangelij, educatione Spiritus, cultu charitatis atque simplicitatis incomparabilis, ita sensim in humanam primum infirmitatem relaberetur, ut purum fidei usum in plerisque non satis attendendo, tandem etiam in plerisque omnibus & in superstitiosam planeque idololatri-cam cultus Dei speciem, & in prophanam do-gmatum ipsorum fidei interpolationem, & in superbam adeo absolutae dominationis usurpationem erumperet, omnis & Dei iuris & iudi-cij ipsius secura, uti novissimi isti dies testantur, & tamen Ecclesiae nomen illis moribus, illis ritibus, illis imposturis suo loco manentibus, quacunque fide vindicari posse? Sedeo (inquit) Regina, nec vidua sum, nec luctum videbo. Ergo sua hic omnis uni Domino gloria cedat & defraudatur[?], qui quidem iusto suo iudicio errare fe-cit nos a viis suis, & induravit cor nostrum ne ipsum timeremus, ut loquitur Ecclesia apud Prophetam Isa.63.Sic ille, inquam, videre fecit populum suum dura, propinauit nobis vinum soporiferum, ut tamen metuentibus se dederit vexillum, ad eleuandum propter veritatem, ut eadem agnoscit Ecclesia Psal. 60. Quidquid enim accciderit ab illa Ecclesiae interuerfione ad nostrum vsque saeculum, illud tamen constare oportuit & credi, Christum Dominum semel in altum euectum apud omnes populos praedicari debuisse, vt omnium Dei electorum obedientia impleretur, ac reliqui omnes tanto magis Dei iudicio obnoxij redderetur. Huius Dei operis quantum exactum sit hactenus, quantumve exigendum superfit, & qua ratione totū illud constiterit constaturumque sit, ille vnus nouit qui vnus facit magna nobiscum, & Sanctum nomen eius. Quanuis enim cessante iam olim sincera Ecclesiae administratione, fides quoque non periclitata fit tantum quod ad sensum & verum vsum maxime, sed etiam nomen ipsum Christianismi quod ad homines attinet, professionis externae vim quandam potius quam vel scientiae lucem vel morum integritatem exhibuerit, non temere tamen etiam sub illa plane nouercali Ecclesiae gubernatione, notae illae foederis Dei haeserunt, & verbi Dei lectio quaedam vel aspersio potius miseras piorum animas intus anhelates sustinere potuit, vt & ipso rum gemitus ac desideria nunquam Dominum latuerunt. Asylum enim Ecclesiae est remissio peccatorum, vt eleganter scribit Augustinus. Et quod nostri misertus Dominus tatam[?] verbi sui lucem restituit Ecclesiae suae, vt Christum ipsum quasi facie ad faciem contueri possit, si in ipsius verbum tam serio cor intendat, quam sincere & limpide nunc illuxit, quis poterit adeo incom-parabile beneficium ipsius vel animo concipere, nedum voce complecti, ac multò minus rei-psa agnoscere! Sed tamen singulari ipsius miseratione neque frustra cessit hactenus, neque porrò cessura est tanta ipsius liberalitas, quæcunque sit nostra omnium ingratitudo. Nostrū modò erat videre ne ab illo ergastulo & plus quàm agnoscamus plerunque horribili mortis umbra liberati pereffluueremus passim, & fere aliis simi les, nisi etiam deteriores, euadaremus. Qui sunt enim mores nostri, ut & coram Deo proficiamus in ipsius veritatis obedientia, & in nobis ipsis ad seriam mortificationem à luxu communi & affectibus carnis reuocandis, & aduersus proximos quosuis ad illos & Domino lucrifaciendos, & nobis demerendos? Quando igitur extabit illud Domini oraculum ad suos, Dicite fratribus vestris, Populus mi & sororibus vestris, Misericordiam consequutæ? Expostulate cū matre vestra, quoniam ipsa non est vxor meā & ego non sum vir eius: ut auferat fornicationes suas à facie sua, & adulteria de medio uberū suorum. Hoc audimus in Ecclesia aliquando, sed parū afficimur: quia alio metes auertimus. Hinc nixus ille Ecclesiæ subsistit. Dies angustiæ. Dies increpationis, Dies Blasphemiæ dies hæc: vene-runt Filij usque ad matricem, & virtus non est ad pariendum. Videat Dominus desolationes nostras, & brachio illo suo spem suorum sustineat, electos undique colligat, omnium nostrum misereatur, ut tandem os unum & caro una in Christo Domino censeamur, quia nomen eius invocatum est super nos. Iustant enim magis ac magis extrema omnia, & totus in eo est Satan ut nomen Ecclesiæ cum veritate committát, atque intus & extra bella seuiant, & scandala exundet. Et qui in aliis cæcitatem merito improbamus, in nobis nō deprehendimus oculorū apertionē tanto indigniorem, dum nobis fere viuimus plerique, & nostra tantum quærimus, non quę Iesu Christi.
